specificity.statement: It’s pretty simple: the dwelling must be simple in design, it can be up to 70 square metres, it must meet the building code, the building work must be done by authorised professionals, and councils have to be notified before and after construction.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the bill's operative conditions with a size threshold, a compliance standard, a workforce requirement and a notification mechanism — concrete enough for a listener to check against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s why I think we need a much broader improvement to our building and construction sector that could actually address productivity, that could actually increase housing supply in a substantial way, and that could lift the quality of what we’re building and bring down the cost of the materials and the techniques that are needed to build energy efficient, healthy buildings that have proper ventilation, so we don’t get this problem with black mould, so we don’t get the problems that we see so often in Aotearoa.
specificity.explanation: A stacked list of desirable outcomes — productivity, supply, quality, lower material costs, ventilation — with no mechanism, no figure, no timeframe and no named measure. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’re dreaming if we think this is addressing the housing crisis.
rigor.explanation: The inference runs from the regulatory impact statement's estimate of roughly 7,800 additional dwellings — a small number relative to the housing shortfall — to the conclusion that the bill will not resolve the housing crisis. The step from the estimate to the conclusion holds; the supporting claim that many of these will be spare rooms or short-term rentals is asserted without evidence, which is the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: As the previous speaker Arena Williams said, I think all parties in this Parliament want to see better-quality housing and a better supply of housing, delivered at a better price for people, so that they can afford to live—but we don’t want that to be done in an “election slogan” way of what sounds good on the hustings but has no data or work done behind it to say that this is actually the problem we’re facing and this is the best way to solve it.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism of how the policy was developed — that it was driven by an election slogan rather than analysis — while explicitly crediting all parties, including opponents, with wanting the same outcome. No person is attacked and no bad faith is imputed to an individual.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That’s why I think we need a much broader improvement to our building and construction sector that could actually address productivity, that could actually increase housing supply in a substantial way, and that could lift the quality of what we’re building and bring down the cost of the materials and the techniques that are needed to build energy efficient, healthy buildings that have proper ventilation, so we don’t get this problem with black mould, so we don’t get the problems that we see so often in Aotearoa.
focus.explanation: Squarely directed at the building and construction regulatory system rather than at any opposing party; the alternative she wants is about the sector's performance, not about the Government's character. Vague, but wholly on-policy — the vagueness is Specificity's problem, not this one's.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The shortcomings or the limitations of planning is that it enables something, but it doesn’t necessarily make that thing a reality.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House: planning reform is a necessary but not sufficient condition for houses being built. The necessary/sufficient distinction is drawn correctly and is backed by the following sentence about the further steps that come after enabling. Marked down slightly because the intervening steps are asserted rather than evidenced.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The shortcomings or the limitations of planning is that it enables something, but it doesn’t necessarily make that thing a reality.
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism of the bill itself — what an enabling planning change does and does not achieve. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That’s not to criticise this bill—it’s to say it’s a good first step, but there are probably other elements that we have to consider as well as to why it is that the construction sector has been the hardest hit by job losses.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that construction is the industry that has suffered the largest job losses in the current downturn.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ employment/filled-jobs by industry (HLFS and Business Employment Data) over 2024–2025: true if construction recorded the largest absolute or proportional fall in employment of any industry over that period, false if another industry fell further.

veracity.statement: This is also important in the context of councils’ consenting systems because, at the moment, council consents are at the lowest they have been over the last seven years, and I think there’s a lot of different reasons for that, but this takes some of that out.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the current volume of building consents issued by councils is the lowest in seven years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ building consents issued series (annual/rolling-year new dwellings consented) to the quarter ending nearest October 2025: true if the current level is lower than in each of the preceding six years, false if any of those years was lower.

veracity.statement: They do not even have aerial trucks—lots of them don’t have trucks in general, and won’t be able to come out and service the fires if they happen in these granny flats.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as present fact that firefighting brigades lack aerial appliances and that many lack fire appliances altogether, such that they could not respond to fires in these dwellings.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: FENZ fleet and appliance-allocation records plus the NZPFU/FENZ appliance availability reporting: true if a substantial share of brigades have no operational appliance and aerial appliances are unavailable across most of the network, false if brigades are generally appliance-equipped and aerial appliances are stationed per the standard urban coverage model.

specificity.statement: We’re really happy that there are still some good safeguards within this bill that will require the dwelling to still meet the building code, for the work to be notified to council, and for those people that are building or constructing those granny flats to have the right authorisations, which is really important.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete safeguards in the bill — building code compliance, notification to council, and authorisation requirements for the builder. Checkable against the bill text. Short of 1.0 because no thresholds, clauses or timeframes are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s time we started saying yes to easing planning restrictions and unshackling ourselves from the bureaucracy of local planning laws.
specificity.explanation: Points at a direction — loosening local planning rules — but names no rule, threshold, cost or timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Those changes have been outlined and my colleagues have mentioned those changes around the project memorandum, the design plans and liability protections, and also the building requirements that will be required.
specificity.explanation: Lists the four areas the select committee amended by name, which is more than a slogan, but says nothing about what any of the changes actually do.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is a common-sense change. It's something that's talking about trusting tradespeople, trusting people to design houses that fit their needs on their land, providing homes that provide something that's designed for their family, whether it's a granny, a grandpa, a koro, an uncle, a parent, a kid, anybody—someone who you might want to rent a building out to.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the measure before the House and who it is meant to serve; no party framing, no characterisation of opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is a common-sense change. It's something that's talking about trusting tradespeople, trusting people to design houses that fit their needs on their land, providing homes that provide something that's designed for their family, whether it's a granny, a grandpa, a koro, an uncle, a parent, a kid, anybody—someone who you might want to rent a building out to.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues and an open-ended list of family members. No figure, threshold, mechanism or timeframe — nothing a listener could check or act on. This is the deliberate contrast with the same speaker's PIM passage.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The reason we've gone with a PIM instead of a certificate of acceptance or other such accreditation is because a PIM is just a way of letting a council know.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument chosen (project information memorandum), the alternative rejected (certificate of acceptance) and the function it serves. Missing only the operative detail of how the notification works.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So this bill simply puts the councils in the position of being a provider of information and then a keeper of that information once the building is constructed. It also gives them the ability to be able to collect development contributions.
specificity.explanation: States the concrete change to the council's statutory role — from consenting authority to information provider and record keeper — and names a retained power (development contributions). No figures or commencement date.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Section 72 allows councils to grant consent for building. Section 67 allows councils to take a liberalised view of a project and allow something to happen.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that two existing provisions of the Building Act 2004 already give territorial authorities the discretion he says they should use: s 72 to grant consent, and s 67 to take a more permissive view of a project.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of ss 67 and 72 of the Building Act 2004 on the NZ Legislation website. True if s 72 empowers a territorial authority to grant a building consent in the circumstances it covers and s 67 confers a discretion to relax the ordinary requirements; false if either section does something materially different from the power described (e.g. if it imposes a duty on a party other than the council, or confers no consenting discretion at all).

veracity.statement: This bill delivers on a part of the coalition agreement. It was something that New Zealand First specifically campaigned on, so we are delighted that we're now actually able to deliver this campaign promise.
veracity.explanation: Two factual claims about the past: that this measure appears in the current coalition agreement, and that New Zealand First campaigned specifically on it in 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National–New Zealand First coalition agreement (published December 2023) and NZ First's 2023 election policy material. True if the agreement contains a commitment matching this bill's subject (consent-free small stand-alone dwellings / granny flats) and NZ First's published 2023 policy includes it; false if the commitment appears only in the National–ACT agreement, only in a post-election work programme, or has no NZ First campaign counterpart.

veracity.statement: This started off talking about 60 square-metre buildings. After consultation—there was consultation before the legislation was introduced—it was raised to 70 square metres.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific change in the size threshold for the exempt building class between the pre-introduction consultation proposal (60 m²) and the bill (70 m²).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's pre-introduction discussion document on consent-free granny flats and the bill as introduced. True if the discussion document proposes a 60 m² limit and the bill as introduced sets 70 m²; false if either figure differs, or if the increase happened at a different stage (e.g. at select committee rather than before introduction).

rigor.statement: These are the sort of things that have got in the way of people trying to build in New Zealand. It's meant that there's been a loss of trust between the industry, the people operating in it, and the councils.
rigor.explanation: Engages the policy (s 71 and RFI practice under the Building Act) but the causal conclusion — a sector-wide loss of trust — rests on assumed shared recognition rather than anything offered. An appeal to the audience's own experience standing in for evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And what's more, that building certainly would not be a building which will fall under this regime regardless, because this regime is quite clearly about simple stand-alone single-story—no mezzanines—buildings complying with the Building Act and also delivered by licensed building professionals and other licensed practitioners—electricians, gas fitters and so on.
rigor.explanation: A valid rebuttal by scope: if the regime's stated eligibility criteria are as described, the counter-example offered falls outside it and cannot bear on the regime. The conclusion follows from the premises given.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, I would invite anybody, particularly if you go to field days, to go and talk to a lot of the building providers there—go and see what it is that they're doing. And I think you'll find a lot of reassurance about the quality of the buildings that they're producing.
rigor.explanation: Answers a raised concern about build quality with an appeal to anecdote and personal impression — go and look, and you will be reassured. No inspection data, defect rate or standard is offered, and 'you'll find reassurance' assumes the conclusion it is meant to support.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If we want to get the cost of housing down, we actually have to get the cost of building down. We could crash the market, but all you do by crashing the market is put people off actually building new houses because the cost of building a new house then becomes less than the value you can get for selling that house because existing houses are worth more than the new houses.
rigor.explanation: The opening step is a false dichotomy — build costs and a market correction are presented as the only two routes to lower housing costs. The supporting chain is then incoherent: build cost falling below sale value is an incentive to build, not a deterrent, so the stated reason contradicts the conclusion it is offered for.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There are three or four pages in Schedule 1 of all the component parts of what makes a complying building for this piece of legislation, so I think we've answered that particular issue.
rigor.explanation: Offers the length of the schedule as proof that the definitional concern was addressed. Volume of drafting is not responsiveness — a real gap between what was shown (three or four pages exist) and what was concluded (the issue is answered).
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And what's more, that building certainly would not be a building which will fall under this regime regardless, because this regime is quite clearly about simple stand-alone single-story—no mezzanines—buildings complying with the Building Act and also delivered by licensed building professionals and other licensed practitioners—electricians, gas fitters and so on.
civility.explanation: Directly contests another member's argument in a genuinely disputed exchange and stays entirely on the example and the regime's scope; nothing is directed at her.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Of course, the size of the building is defined and, as we’ve heard, initially the policy position was going to be that it’s 60 square metres and now it’s 70 as the bill was introduced, and that hasn’t changed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a two-part factual claim about the policy history: that the original proposed floor-area limit for exempt small stand-alone dwellings was 60 square metres, and that the bill as introduced set it at 70 square metres, unchanged since introduction.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The MBIE granny-flat discussion document / Cabinet paper and the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill as introduced, plus the Transport and Infrastructure Committee's report-back version. True if the consultation proposal specified a 60 m² maximum floor area and the bill as introduced and reported back specifies 70 m²; false if either figure differs or the reported-back bill altered the 70 m² limit.

specificity.statement: At 70 square metres, it could be a small three-bedroomed home with one bathroom.
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete figure and translates it into a checkable, picturable outcome (a three-bedroom, one-bathroom dwelling), rather than asserting the buildings are 'not small' as a generality. Short of full precision — no layout, no cost, no source for the comparison.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: By simplifying the consenting process for small stand-alone dwellings, we are cutting red tape, supporting innovation, and enabling faster delivery of quality homes. It is a smart, balanced move to meet growing demand while maintaining safety and standards.
specificity.explanation: Trying to convey substance about the bill, but supplies only a string of generic virtues — 'cutting red tape', 'supporting innovation', 'smart, balanced' — with no figure, threshold, timeframe or named mechanism beyond the bill's own title. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Councils, as was described by an ex-mayor of a council, are held liable for substandard building work. So you can’t just say to councils, “Oh, it’s the vibe of the thing. We just want you to permit these things and we don’t want any paperwork or anything.” But then, “Council, if something goes wrong, you’re going to get sued and the ratepayers are going to have to pay for it.” That is not how the world works.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure: the premise (councils carry liability for defective building work, borne by ratepayers) supports the conclusion (you cannot ask councils to consent loosely while leaving that liability in place). The conclusion tracks the premise. Marked down slightly because the opposing position is put in an exaggerated form ('it's the vibe of the thing') that no one actually advanced — a mild strawman of the ACT contribution.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Councils, as was described by an ex-mayor of a council, are held liable for substandard building work. So you can’t just say to councils, “Oh, it’s the vibe of the thing. We just want you to permit these things and we don’t want any paperwork or anything.” But then, “Council, if something goes wrong, you’re going to get sued and the ratepayers are going to have to pay for it.” That is not how the world works.
civility.explanation: A contested rebuttal of an opponent's argument where she had a clear opportunity to turn on the ACT member she is answering. The disagreement stays entirely on the substance — liability, incentives, statute — and the sharpest line ('That is not how the world works') is aimed at the proposition, not the person.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It is interesting that the commentary to the bill notes that the Resource Management Act component of allowing these small, stand-alone dwellings to not have to go through a consenting process is going to be done through a proposed National Environment Standards for Granny Flats that is expected to take effect by the end of 2025.
divination.explanation: Relays a forecast, sourced to the bill commentary, that the National Environmental Standard covering the Resource Management Act side of granny flats will be in force by the end of 2025. She is reporting the expectation rather than committing to it herself.
divination.subject: other
divination.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Gazette / legislation.govt.nz record for the National Environmental Standards for Granny Flats (or equivalently named NES made under the Resource Management Act). True if the standard was made and in force on or before 31 December 2025; false if it had not commenced by that date.

veracity.statement: The uncertainty in the construction sector has meant that a lot of construction companies haven’t received the same levels of work that they would expect or that they had been used to expecting.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that construction firms have experienced a material drop in the volume of work available to them relative to previous norms. Present/past claim about sector conditions, not a forecast.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ building consents issued for new dwellings and construction industry activity/GDP series for 2023–2025, plus construction-sector liquidation and employment data; true if construction work volumes fell materially below the preceding years' levels, false if activity was flat or rising.

veracity.statement: As I said in my first reading speaking, I’m really looking forward to how this is going to help the over 50 percent of migrants in my community now that we’ve got the parent visa up and running.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that migrants make up over 50 percent of her electorate's community, and that the parent visa category is operational as at October 2025. The former is stated loosely in live speech; the intended reading is that her community is more than half migrant.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: 2023 Census overseas-born share of usual residents for the speaker's electorate (Takanini) — true if above 50%, false if materially below; and Immigration NZ records on whether the Parent Boost Visa was open for and accepting applications on 7 October 2025.

veracity.statement: The National Government, as we’ve heard tonight, have made decisions that absolutely have caused a dramatic slowdown in new builds, and we’ve seen that manifest in various ways right across New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that new-build activity has slowed dramatically and that government decisions caused it. Note this is scored as the speaker's own assertion, not relayed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ building consents issued for new dwellings, comparing the period from October 2023 onward with the preceding years; true if new-dwelling consents/starts fell materially over that period AND the fall can be traced to identifiable government decisions rather than pre-existing drivers, false if the decline predates the government's decisions or is attributable to interest rates and the construction cycle.

specificity.statement: Taking up the recommendation from Mr Wallace of Master Plumbers to ensure that digital tools are used to record the work and, therefore, be able to, at a national level, monitor what’s been built—it’s estimated 13,000 dwellings could be constructed over a 10-year period—I think it would be really good for any potential issues to be able to be identified and addressed as quickly as possible.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific submitter and recommendation (digital record-keeping by trade professionals), a specific mechanism (national-level monitoring of completed work) and a quantified estimate with a timeframe (13,000 dwellings over 10 years). Falls short of 1.0 because the desired action is a general endorsement rather than a stated requirement or amendment.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the speed to see this construction and this legislation take place, we cannot lose the focus on making sure that all New Zealanders have a warm home that is safe and that is dry.
specificity.explanation: A general exhortation to maintain housing quality. No figure, mechanism, threshold or named standard; nothing here could be checked or acted on. Note this is not a Focus failure — it is squarely about the policy, just carrying no detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Principally, this bill shouldn’t become, essentially, a Trojan horse for lowering building standards, leading to what is quite patently riskier construction practices if not done right.
civility.explanation: Hard, loaded criticism of the legislation itself — 'Trojan horse' is a strong charge against the measure, not against any member. No person is impugned and no bad faith is imputed to an individual.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Principally, this bill shouldn’t become, essentially, a Trojan horse for lowering building standards, leading to what is quite patently riskier construction practices if not done right.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that riskier construction follows is asserted as 'quite patently' true, and the support offered nearby is that severe weather has devastated homes — which establishes that building failures are costly, not that this bill lowers the standards. A gap between what is shown and what is concluded, plus an appeal to the vividness of past disasters.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It means that local government could be left managing not just stormwater but stormwater drainage and road capacity as things develop, with less information and fewer resources.
rigor.explanation: The 'less information' half follows directly from the stated premise that consent records are the counting mechanism. The 'fewer resources' half does not — nothing offered connects removing consents to reduced council funding, and development contributions are a separate regime. Partly supported inference with an unbacked extension.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: As Professor John Turkey pointed out, without building consents, authorities almost certainly will lose that robust oversight of how many new dwellings are being added and the pressure on local infrastructure.
divination.explanation: Relays an expert forecast that removing the building-consent requirement for these dwellings will leave consenting authorities without a reliable count of new dwellings and of the infrastructure load they create. The speaker is reporting the prediction, not making it in her own right.
divination.subject: other
divination.falsification_criterion: After the exemption comes into force, whether councils can report a count of exempt small stand-alone dwellings built in their district and use it for infrastructure planning — false if the Act's completion-notification requirement yields a usable national/local dataset comparable to consent records, true if councils report they cannot account for the dwellings built.

focus.statement: The National Government, as we’ve heard tonight, have made decisions that absolutely have caused a dramatic slowdown in new builds, and we’ve seen that manifest in various ways right across New Zealand.
focus.explanation: Names a real policy outcome (a slowdown in new builds) and holds the government to account for it, which is legitimate scrutiny. But no specific decision, programme or figure is identified — 'made decisions' and 'manifest in various ways' leave the weight on the party rather than the measure. Mid-range: a real policy point in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: If we look at the statistics that are readily available for anybody to check in to, specific statistics that were released in April this year show that 33,595 new homes consented in the year to February this year—February 2025—and that was down 7.4 percent from the year before.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific figures from an official release: 33,595 new dwellings consented in the year ended February 2025, and a 7.4 percent fall on the prior year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 'Building consents issued' release for February 2025 (published April 2025): true if the number of new dwellings consented in the year ended February 2025 is 33,595 (± rounding to the nearest hundred) and the annual change is -7.4%; false if either figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: It’s the worst February for home consents since 2012.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the February 2025 monthly new-dwelling consent count is the lowest of any February in the thirteen years since February 2012.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ monthly new dwellings consented series, February values 2012–2025: true if February 2025 is lower than every February from 2013 onward, false if any intervening February is lower.

veracity.statement: The previous Labour Government had built more houses, more social houses, for instance, since the 1970s, and to sit on this side of the House and watch all of that momentum disappear through what I believe to be poor decisions from the current Government—you can’t turn that ship around lightly.
veracity.explanation: The intended claim (the sentence is a live-speech compression) is that the 2017–2023 Labour Government added more social/public houses than any government since the 1970s. Extracted on the intended reading, not the literal word order.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: HUD Public Housing Quarterly Report / Kāinga Ora stock series: true if net additional public housing places delivered 2017–2023 exceed those of every other parliamentary term since 1970, false if any earlier term delivered more.

veracity.statement: This drop came straight after the Government stopped Kāinga Ora building houses and cut $1.5 billion from the public housing build and that maintenance fund as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two government actions: that Kāinga Ora was stopped from building houses, and that $1.5 billion was cut from the public housing build and maintenance funding.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024/2025 Vote Housing and Urban Development appropriations and the Kāinga Ora build programme decisions announced following the 2024 Kāinga Ora review: true if the reduction to public housing build and maintenance funding totals approximately $1.5 billion and new Kāinga Ora builds were halted or wound back, false if the appropriations show no cut of that scale.

veracity.statement: When we think of the 20,000 construction jobs that have already been lost—which is 20,000 workers—we can only look at this particular bill, whilst we support it, being such a trivial, small step in the overall situation that we’re facing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 20,000 construction jobs have already been lost.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey / filled jobs by industry for construction: true if employment in the construction sector fell by approximately 20,000 over the period from its recent peak to the September 2025 quarter, false if the fall is materially smaller.

specificity.statement: If we look at the statistics that are readily available for anybody to check in to, specific statistics that were released in April this year show that 33,595 new homes consented in the year to February this year—February 2025—and that was down 7.4 percent from the year before.
specificity.explanation: Carries an exact count, an exact percentage change, a named period and the month of the source release — someone could go and check it directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Where I come from, there’s a single Kāinga Ora house in Lyttelton, for instance—one house, and they’re selling that, and the woman who’s lived there for 42 years has been unceremoniously told that, in her 70s, she has to leave.
specificity.explanation: Names a location, a count, a tenure length and the tenant's approximate age — a concrete, checkable instance rather than a general complaint about divestment.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This drop came straight after the Government stopped Kāinga Ora building houses and cut $1.5 billion from the public housing build and that maintenance fund as well.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: the consent drop is attributed to the funding decisions purely by temporal sequence ('came straight after'). A causal mechanism is plausible but none is offered, and consents cover the whole market rather than the public build programme, so the inference outruns what is shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think if this Government is hell-bent on divesting from the public good, public housing, it would have been much more preferable for them to get their own house in order before considering selling this single house that is actually quite life-destroying for the individual involved.
civility.explanation: Pointed and edging toward motive — 'hell-bent on divesting from the public good' imputes a disposition rather than arguing the policy — but it is aimed at the Government collectively, insults no individual member, and the substance of the objection is about the sale itself.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When we think of the 20,000 construction jobs that have already been lost—which is 20,000 workers—we can only look at this particular bill, whilst we support it, being such a trivial, small step in the overall situation that we’re facing.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — assesses the bill's scale against a named sector outcome rather than characterising the opposing party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Whilst the contributions from the other side tonight haven’t been very substantive and we haven’t gleaned much more information from that tonight, we now found ourselves at the end of this process.
focus.explanation: A general characterisation of the other side's debating performance. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named; strip out the part about the opposing benches and nothing about the bill remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Has the Prime Minister made statements in support of the America and Arab - led peace process, and how many letters has he received in support of that from members of the Opposition or their leaders?
focus.explanation: Names a real foreign-policy matter (the peace process) but the weight of the question is a party point about letters from the Opposition, which carries no policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I actually think we should be very proud of the efforts of President Trump and the Arab nations that actually are creating a pathway to peace, to stop the killing, and to create the ceasefire, but I have received zero letters that I am aware of.
focus.explanation: Half the answer engages the substance of the ceasefire process; the other half takes up the invitation to score a point about the Opposition rather than policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The economy is where it is now because harmful and painful inflation in 2021, in 2022, in 2023—fuelled by reckless Government spending—had to be brought down over time with high interest rates. As I said in my previous question, interest rates affect economic activity. New Zealand experienced a deep protracted downturn.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the economic mechanism — inflation, interest rates, the downturn — rather than on the character of the party opposite.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If she is taking credit for the latest interest rate cut, will she also take responsibility that this cut is because of a stagnating economy caused by her Government’s inaction?
focus.explanation: Engages a named economic event (the interest rate cut) and its cause; 'inaction' is party framing rather than a named measure, which keeps it short of full policy engagement.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is her economic plan to talk about growth, hope interest rates come down, and house prices grow?
focus.explanation: A genuine point about the content of the Government's economic plan, but delivered as a characterisation of the other side with no measure, figure or mechanism named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How many customary marine titles have been granted under this Act that will now be subject to challenge on the passing of his amendment bill?
focus.explanation: Names the Act, the specific instrument (customary marine titles) and the specific consequence of the amendment bill, and asks for a countable answer. Textbook scrutiny of a measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does teachers, principals, support staff, and Ministry of Education specialist staff all going on strike show that she is “growing and strengthening the education workforce”; if so, how?
focus.explanation: Sets a specific stated commitment against a specific observable outcome (a strike across four named workforce groups). Accountability for a named claim, not party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The economy is where it is now because harmful and painful inflation in 2021, in 2022, in 2023—fuelled by reckless Government spending—had to be brought down over time with high interest rates. As I said in my previous question, interest rates affect economic activity. New Zealand experienced a deep protracted downturn.
rigor.explanation: A real causal chain is laid out (spending → inflation → high rates → downturn) and each link is stated rather than assumed, but the step from 'Government spending' to the whole of the inflation is asserted, not shown — a gap between what is offered and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does she agree with another business leader from the Mood of the Boardroom, who said, “The Government is ineffective. There is no compelling leadership and strategic plan evident that will turn New Zealand around.”?
rigor.explanation: The support offered for the conclusion is entirely the standing of an unnamed business leader — an appeal to authority. No evidence about outcomes is offered that would hold up if the authority were removed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It has often been a reflection I have had that if some of the reforms that we are making had been made six years ago, how much better off our economy would be now. If only fast-track legislation had been in place such that we didn’t still have major infrastructure projects in this country being held back by red tape.
rigor.explanation: The counterfactual is the whole argument: the present reforms are defended by asserting an unobservable alternative history. Nothing is offered — no modelling, no comparator jurisdiction — to connect the reforms to the claimed better outcome, so the conclusion rests on the assumption it is meant to establish.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, anybody in a boat can access the foreshore and seabed, from any particular angle.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur. The premise concerns access by sea; the claim it is offered against concerns land parcels blocking access from the shore. Establishing that boats can reach the foreshore does nothing to establish that people on foot can.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our approach, as a Government, is to address the underlying foundations for growth which includes low and stable inflation to create a lower interest rate environment; having responsibly managed books; driving reforms across the areas that have held New Zealand’s economy back for too long, including low rates of educational achievement, byzantine consenting processes, excessive regulatory burdens, and a dire approach to overseas investment.
specificity.explanation: Names four concrete reform areas rather than gesturing at 'growth', but supplies no figure, no mechanism and no timeframe for any of them — a direction with some detail, missing the how and the by when.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In our emergency departments, 73.9 percent of patients were admitted, treated, or discharged within six hours during that quarter, up from 71.2 percent during the same period last year, despite increased attendances. For faster cancer treatment, 86.3 percent of patients started their treatment within 31 days following diagnosis, up from 83.5 percent at the same time last year.
specificity.explanation: Four figures, the named targets they belong to, the quarter covered and the comparison period. Anyone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If his goal is to guarantee the rights of all New Zealanders, when will his Government be introducing legislation to address the 13,000 privately owned parcels of land that actually prevent people from accessing the foreshore and seabed?
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete figure and a concrete object of legislation — 13,000 privately owned parcels blocking coastal access — so the question could be answered or checked directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In our emergency departments, 73.9 percent of patients were admitted, treated, or discharged within six hours during that quarter, up from 71.2 percent during the same period last year, despite increased attendances. For faster cancer treatment, 86.3 percent of patients started their treatment within 31 days following diagnosis, up from 83.5 percent at the same time last year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the April–June quarterly results for two health targets — ED six-hour presentations at 73.9% (from 71.2%) and 31-day cancer treatment at 86.3% (from 83.5%) — together with the claim that ED attendances rose.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand's published quarterly health target results for the April–June 2025 quarter and the same quarter of 2024: true if the shorter-stays-in-ED and faster-cancer-treatment figures match those stated to within rounding, false if either figure or either baseline is materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, 82 percent of children are now fully immunised by age two, up from 76.5 percent last year, representing the largest annual gain across all health targets.
veracity.explanation: Two claims: the childhood immunisation rate at 24 months is 82%, up from 76.5% a year earlier; and that this 5.5-point gain is the largest year-on-year movement of any of the Government's health targets.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand's quarterly health target reporting for April–June 2025 versus the same quarter 2024: true if the immunisation figures are 82% and 76.5% and no other health target moved more than 5.5 points year on year; false if the figures differ materially or another target posted a larger annual gain.

veracity.statement: This is thanks to our Government’s Elective Boost, which has delivered more than 16,000 additional procedures, including hips, knees, and cataracts, between February and June by partnering with the private hospital sector.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Elective Boost programme delivered more than 16,000 additional elective procedures between February and June, via outsourcing to private hospitals.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand / Ministry of Health reporting on Elective Boost delivery volumes for February–June 2025: true if the count of additional procedures attributed to the programme exceeds 16,000, false if the reported figure is materially lower or is not an additional-procedure count.

veracity.statement: The Opposition member wants talk about the wait-lists; I would just remind her that the number of people waiting more than four months for a first specialist assessment (FSA), under her watch, increased by over 6,000 percent while they were in Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the number of patients waiting over four months for a first specialist assessment rose by more than 6,000 percent across the 2017–2023 Labour Government's term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand / DHB first-specialist-assessment wait-list series for late 2017 and late 2023: true if the count of patients waiting over four months rose more than 61-fold between those points, false if the increase is materially smaller or the series does not support a comparable start and end point.

veracity.statement: If his goal is to guarantee the rights of all New Zealanders, when will his Government be introducing legislation to address the 13,000 privately owned parcels of land that actually prevent people from accessing the foreshore and seabed?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 13,000 privately owned land parcels exist which prevent public access to the foreshore and seabed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: LINZ cadastral records and published analyses of private freehold titles adjoining the coastal marine area: true if approximately 13,000 privately owned parcels abut the foreshore in a way that blocks public land access, false if the count of such access-blocking parcels is materially different.

veracity.statement: I point to the fact that the previous Minister the member quoted at the start offered a 10 percent figure at one point.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Christopher Finlayson, the Minister who introduced the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011, publicly offered a figure of about 10 percent of the coastline in connection with customary marine title.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard, select committee evidence and contemporaneous media reporting of Christopher Finlayson's statements on the 2011 Act: true if he is recorded proposing or estimating a figure of around 10 percent of the coastline, false if no such statement by him can be found.

divination.statement: There are several cases that have been heard that will have to be re-heard in light of this legislation if it passes.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that already-heard customary marine title cases will have to be re-litigated as a consequence of the amendment bill, conditional on its passage. The forecast is about the courts' response, not about an action the speaker himself undertakes.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Court records and Ministry of Justice / Te Arawhiti reporting on customary marine title applications after the amendment bill's enactment: true if one or more applications already determined under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 are re-heard or remitted for fresh determination under the amended threshold; false if no previously-determined application is re-heard, or if the bill does not pass.

focus.statement: We are going through a difficult recovery. As I’ve said, it’s two speed at the moment. In our provincial industries, in the South Island, and our rural communities, they are experiencing growth but certainly in our cities it’s been very difficult.
focus.explanation: Engages the state of the economy directly — sectors and regions — rather than turning on the opposition. On-policy answer to an on-policy question.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When he’s been out and about, why hasn’t he been talking to the businesses who say that hiring staff is not their primary constraint for growth—given that only 4 percent are saying that—whilst 63 percent of businesses, according to the NZ Institute of Economic Research, are saying their real problem is not enough customers?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a specific government claim about the labour market against named survey evidence. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can I ask the Prime Minister: does he remember, with respect to the policies that he inherited, that the then former Prime Minister had had a huge sort of Guy Fawkes burn-up one night, and got rid of all those policies—how much more quickly could we have recovered if he had done that much earlier in his career?
focus.explanation: No policy, measure or figure is named — "all those policies" is left entirely unspecified. The whole content is a characterisation of an opponent's past conduct.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, I agree with the member that there must be tremendous regret from the Labour Government that had an absolute majority in the last three years and did very little with it, delivered nothing, increasing debt, spending, and borrowing.
focus.explanation: Entirely a general characterisation of the other party's term — "did very little", "delivered nothing". No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named, so nothing here is accountability.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Our policy is designed for 18- and 19-year-olds that are on jobseeker benefit. When you go on a jobseeker benefit, you’re deemed able and capable of working.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure itself — who the policy applies to and the benefit category it uses. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are five immutable laws of economics. The first is about spending; that drives into creating inflation. When you have high inflation because spending went up 84 percent, you end up with 12 to 13 interest rate rises. That then, because of high interest rates and high inflation, means that, actually, businesses get squeezed because the economy’s in a recession, and, as a result, people, unfortunately, lose their jobs.
focus.explanation: Genuinely about fiscal and monetary policy and its effect on employment, though it substitutes a general account of the past term for the specific youth employment figures put to him.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How many jobs did his $3 billion tax cut for landlords create?
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy, its cost, and the outcome it is being held to. Scrutiny of a named commitment, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are going through a difficult recovery. As I’ve said, it’s two speed at the moment. In our provincial industries, in the South Island, and our rural communities, they are experiencing growth but certainly in our cities it’s been very difficult.
specificity.explanation: Names sectors and regions but offers no figures, no timeframe and no mechanism; a direction with only partial detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When he’s been out and about, why hasn’t he been talking to the businesses who say that hiring staff is not their primary constraint for growth—given that only 4 percent are saying that—whilst 63 percent of businesses, according to the NZ Institute of Economic Research, are saying their real problem is not enough customers?
specificity.explanation: Two precise percentages and a named source; anyone could go and check the survey.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Assuming today's reduction is passed on in full, a family with a 25-year $500,000 mortgage would have minimum repayments of $400 less a fortnight than they were in the middle of last year.
specificity.explanation: A stated loan size, term, comparison date and dollar amount — the arithmetic can be reproduced by anyone.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government is helping. We have introduced discipline to Government spending and we remain focused on responsible economic management that supports recovery, delivers the public services New Zealanders expect, and drives reforms for growth.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — discipline, responsible management, reforms for growth — with no figure, mechanism, named programme or date. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that his cuts to jobseeker will impact over 2,000 18- and 19-year-olds who may be disabled, sick, or experiencing severe mental ill health, and, if so, how does he justify this?
specificity.explanation: Names the policy, the affected age band and a headcount; short of a source or a dollar figure, but concrete enough to check.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But, again, we are sending a message very clearly to young people in New Zealand, unapologetically: we want you connected to work, we want you connected to training, we want you connected to education.
specificity.explanation: A restated aspiration in triplicate — no mechanism, no number, no timeframe, nothing that could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why are there 10,000 more unemployed young people and 36,000 fewer jobs in this country since he took office, if not because of his Government’s billions of dollars of cuts to investment?
specificity.explanation: Two precise counts against a defined baseline (since the Prime Minister took office); directly checkable against official series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the last administration, with 3.2 to 3.5 percent unemployment, the Labour-Greens Government drove a 50 percent increase and put 60,000 more people on jobseeker benefit.
specificity.explanation: An unemployment range, a percentage increase and a headcount, all tied to a defined period — checkable as stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How many jobs did his $3 billion tax cut for landlords create?
specificity.explanation: Carries a dollar figure and a named measure, though the outcome asked about is left unquantified and undated.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: You cannot increase spending by 84 percent, drive up inflation, drive up interest rates, put the economy into recession, and raise unemployment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous government increased government spending by 84 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenses series: compare total core Crown expenditure in 2017/18 with 2023/24 (or the last Labour-set Budget). True if the increase is approximately 84%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: I’d just say for the 66 billion dollar man, who increased debt threefold, that we now write out a $10 billion interest bill each and every year, thanks to your mismanagement.
veracity.explanation: Two checkable claims: that the previous government tripled government debt, and that debt servicing now costs $10 billion a year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury net core Crown debt series 2017–2023 (true if it roughly tripled) and the Crown financial statements / Budget 2025 forecast line for core Crown finance costs (true if approximately $10 billion per annum).

veracity.statement: You put the country into the biggest recession in 35 years, you created the longest COVID hangover of any in the Western world, you actually made sure that you tripled the debt, for goodness’ sake, and we now have a $10 billion interest bill.
veracity.explanation: Two comparative claims: that New Zealand's recession under the previous government was the deepest in 35 years, and that New Zealand's post-COVID downturn was the longest of any Western country.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly real GDP since 1990 for the largest peak-to-trough contraction; and OECD quarterly GDP data for the duration of post-2020 output gaps across OECD members. True only if New Zealand ranks first on both, false if either fails.

veracity.statement: When he’s been out and about, why hasn’t he been talking to the businesses who say that hiring staff is not their primary constraint for growth—given that only 4 percent are saying that—whilst 63 percent of businesses, according to the NZ Institute of Economic Research, are saying their real problem is not enough customers?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in NZIER's survey only 4 percent of businesses name finding staff as their main constraint on growth while 63 percent name insufficient sales/demand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZIER Quarterly Survey of Business Opinion for the quarter preceding 8 October 2025: the reported share naming labour as the primary constraint and the share naming sales/demand. True if approximately 4% and 63%.

veracity.statement: Yeah, it’s difficult, unemployment has ticked up a bit, but it’s the same as what it has been over a 30-year average, it’s significantly below what it has been over the last 15 years, and—unlike that member—we’re just not happy to actually be the party of people who don’t work.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the current unemployment rate is level with the 30-year average and significantly below the average of the last 15 years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate for the September 2025 quarter compared with the mean of the series over the preceding 30 years and over the preceding 15 years. True only if it matches the 30-year mean and sits materially below the 15-year mean.

veracity.statement: If the dire current state of the New Zealand economy is all someone else’s fault, why is it that the New Zealand economy shrunk by almost 1 percent at a time when other economies around the world that have been hit harder by Donald Trump’s tariffs—many of whom had a higher rate of inflation at the peak of the global pandemic—have been growing faster than New Zealand?
veracity.explanation: Asserts New Zealand's economy contracted by almost 1 percent, and that comparable economies facing higher tariff exposure and higher peak inflation have grown over the same period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly real GDP for the June 2025 quarter (true if a contraction of approximately 0.9–1.0%), and OECD quarterly GDP growth for the same quarter across members with higher US tariff exposure and higher 2022 peak CPI. False if the contraction is materially smaller or if those comparators did not grow.

veracity.statement: The committee has decided to reduce the OCR by 50 basis points. This is the 8th OCR reduction since August last year. At that time, the OCR was 5.5 percent. It is now at 2.5 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the RBNZ Monetary Policy Committee cut the OCR by 50 basis points on this date, that this is the eighth cut since August 2024, and that the OCR has moved from 5.5 percent to 2.5 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ Monetary Policy Review of 8 October 2025 and the published OCR decision history: true if the 8 October decision was −50bp, the OCR is 2.5%, and there have been eight reductions since August 2024.

veracity.statement: Assuming today's reduction is passed on in full, a family with a 25-year $500,000 mortgage would have minimum repayments of $400 less a fortnight than they were in the middle of last year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a $500,000 25-year mortgage at today's floating rate costs $400 a fortnight less in minimum repayments than in mid-2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ floating first-mortgage rate series for June 2024 and October 2025 (adjusted for a full pass-through of the 50bp cut); compute the standard amortising repayment on $500,000 over 25 years at each rate. True if the fortnightly difference is approximately $400.

veracity.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that his cuts to jobseeker will impact over 2,000 18- and 19-year-olds who may be disabled, sick, or experiencing severe mental ill health, and, if so, how does he justify this?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than 2,000 18- and 19-year-olds with disability, illness or serious mental health conditions will be affected by the jobseeker changes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit statistics and the regulatory impact statement for the 18/19-year-old jobseeker parental assistance test: the estimated number of affected 18- and 19-year-old recipients recorded with a health condition or disability. True if above 2,000.

veracity.statement: Why are there 10,000 more unemployed young people and 36,000 fewer jobs in this country since he took office, if not because of his Government’s billions of dollars of cuts to investment?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that youth unemployment has risen by 10,000 and total filled jobs have fallen by 36,000 since November 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ HLFS unemployed count for the 15–24 age group, and the Monthly Employment Indicators filled-jobs series, comparing November 2023 with the latest release before October 2025. True if the changes are approximately +10,000 and −36,000.

veracity.statement: Does the Prime Minister understand, then, the basic maths that if there are four job seekers to every job that is available in this country, all of his cuts to jobseeker support couldn’t hope to possibly punish people into ghost jobs but will only deepen poverty and homelessness?
veracity.explanation: Asserts there are four job seekers for every available job in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ratio of MSD jobseeker support recipients (or HLFS unemployed) to online job vacancies (MBIE Jobs Online / Seek listings) at September 2025. True if approximately 4:1.

veracity.statement: In the last administration, with 3.2 to 3.5 percent unemployment, the Labour-Greens Government drove a 50 percent increase and put 60,000 more people on jobseeker benefit.
veracity.explanation: Asserts jobseeker benefit numbers rose by 50 percent, or 60,000 people, during the previous government's term while unemployment was 3.2–3.5 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets: jobseeker support recipient counts at the start and end of the 2017–2023 period, and the Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate over that period. True if the rise is approximately 60,000 and approximately 50%.

veracity.statement: This is a Government that is—I’ll tell you what the landlord cut did create: rents have gone down $5 a week, instead of up $180 a week.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that rents have fallen by $5 a week rather than rising by $180 a week, and attributes this to the restoration of interest deductibility for landlords.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE tenancy bond data / Stats NZ rental price index: change in median weekly rent over the year to September 2025. True if the median fell by approximately $5 a week; false if rents rose. The $180 counterfactual should be checked against whatever projection it is drawn from.

rigor.statement: You cannot increase spending by 84 percent, drive up inflation, drive up interest rates, put the economy into recession, and raise unemployment.
rigor.explanation: A single-cause chain — spending to inflation to rates to recession to unemployment — asserted as though it were automatic, with nothing offered to rule out the global inflation shock or to size any link in the chain.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If the dire current state of the New Zealand economy is all someone else’s fault, why is it that the New Zealand economy shrunk by almost 1 percent at a time when other economies around the world that have been hit harder by Donald Trump’s tariffs—many of whom had a higher rate of inflation at the peak of the global pandemic—have been growing faster than New Zealand?
rigor.explanation: A genuine comparative inference: it holds the tariff shock and the inflation peak roughly constant across countries to test the claim that the downturn is externally caused. The gap is that it treats cross-country growth differences as attributable to the current government without controlling for anything else.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I could give numerous examples of a previous Government hindering that task through excessive spending, keeping inflation higher for longer and preventing reductions in interest rates.
rigor.explanation: Claims numerous supporting examples and produces none — the causal conclusion about spending, inflation and the rate track rests on an offer of evidence rather than on evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Our policy is designed for 18- and 19-year-olds that are on jobseeker benefit. When you go on a jobseeker benefit, you’re deemed able and capable of working.
rigor.explanation: Answers an objection about people who are actually sick or disabled by pointing to how the category classifies them — the conclusion follows from a definition rather than from any evidence about the individuals, so the inference is circular relative to the objection raised.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There are five immutable laws of economics. The first is about spending; that drives into creating inflation. When you have high inflation because spending went up 84 percent, you end up with 12 to 13 interest rate rises. That then, because of high interest rates and high inflation, means that, actually, businesses get squeezed because the economy’s in a recession, and, as a result, people, unfortunately, lose their jobs.
rigor.explanation: Presents a contested causal chain as "immutable laws" — an appeal to law-like inevitability that does the work no evidence is offered for. It also concludes about job losses today from a mechanism that ended two years earlier, leaving the question's figures untouched.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does the Prime Minister understand, then, the basic maths that if there are four job seekers to every job that is available in this country, all of his cuts to jobseeker support couldn’t hope to possibly punish people into ghost jobs but will only deepen poverty and homelessness?
rigor.explanation: The core inference is sound: if vacancies are outnumbered four to one, sanctions cannot conjure the missing jobs. It overreaches at the end, treating "only deepen poverty and homelessness" as following necessarily when nothing was offered on the size or distribution of that effect.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’d just say for the 66 billion dollar man, who increased debt threefold, that we now write out a $10 billion interest bill each and every year, thanks to your mismanagement.
civility.explanation: "The 66 billion dollar man" is a mocking sobriquet fixed to an individual member rather than a criticism of a decision, and "your mismanagement" makes the failure personal. A clear step past robust criticism of the record.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Yeah, it’s difficult, unemployment has ticked up a bit, but it’s the same as what it has been over a 30-year average, it’s significantly below what it has been over the last 15 years, and—unlike that member—we’re just not happy to actually be the party of people who don’t work.
civility.explanation: "Unlike that member" attaches to an individual the imputation of being content with people not working — bad faith imputed to a person, not a criticism of a policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Can I ask the Prime Minister: does he remember, with respect to the policies that he inherited, that the then former Prime Minister had had a huge sort of Guy Fawkes burn-up one night, and got rid of all those policies—how much more quickly could we have recovered if he had done that much earlier in his career?
civility.explanation: Mockery directed at a named individual — the "Guy Fawkes burn-up" jibe and the closing swipe at his career are aimed at the member, not at any decision's merits.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I agree with the member that there must be tremendous regret from the Labour Government that had an absolute majority in the last three years and did very little with it, delivered nothing, increasing debt, spending, and borrowing.
civility.explanation: Dismissive of a party's record but lands on no individual. Attacking a party is Focus's problem, not Civility's, and it passes here cleanly.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does the Prime Minister understand, then, the basic maths that if there are four job seekers to every job that is available in this country, all of his cuts to jobseeker support couldn’t hope to possibly punish people into ghost jobs but will only deepen poverty and homelessness?
civility.explanation: "Does the Prime Minister understand the basic maths" edges toward the person's competence, but the substance stays on the policy and no insult lands.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It’s now growing again in quarter 3; the growth in quarter 4 will step up.
divination.explanation: Forecasts positive real GDP growth in the September 2025 quarter and a higher growth rate again in the December 2025 quarter.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly real production GDP releases: true if the September 2025 quarter records positive growth AND the December 2025 quarter records growth greater than the September quarter; false if either quarter contracts or if December growth does not exceed September.

veracity.statement: Growing and strengthening the education workforce is exactly what this Government is doing, and, as I’ve already told the member on numerous occasions, the schooling teacher workforce grew by 2.5 percent in 2024, delivering 864 new teachers—the largest year-on-year increase since records began in 2009.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three checkable facts: 2.5% growth in the schooling teacher workforce in 2024, 864 additional teachers, and that this is the largest annual increase in the series since 2009.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education Teacher Workforce / Education Counts staffing series for calendar 2024: true if the year-on-year change is ~2.5% and ~864 FTE/headcount teachers, and no year from 2009 onward shows a larger increase; false if the growth figure differs materially or an earlier year in the series exceeds it.

veracity.statement: On provisional figures for 2025, there’s been a 30 percent increase in domestic students enrolling in initial teacher education for the first time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 30% year-on-year rise in first-time domestic enrolments in initial teacher education on provisional 2025 figures.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education / Tertiary Education Commission provisional 2025 enrolment data for first-time domestic initial teacher education students: true if the increase on 2024 is ~30%, false if materially different or if the comparison base is not first-time domestic enrolments.

veracity.statement: Why were teachers offered a pay rise of less than inflation when Crown board members are getting up to an 80 percent increase?
veracity.explanation: Two embedded factual assertions: that the teachers' pay offer was below the inflation rate, and that Crown entity board member fees are rising by up to 80 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: (a) The NZEI/PPTA collective offer on the table in October 2025 compared against the Stats NZ CPI annual rate for the September 2025 quarter — true if the offered annual increase is below that rate; (b) the Cabinet Fees Framework / Public Service Commission 2025 fee determinations for Crown entity boards — true if any published increase reaches ~80%.

veracity.statement: The 4.7 percent that is on the table at the moment is a fair and reasonable offer that we hope the New Zealand Educational Institute and Post Primary Teachers’ Association members will take seriously.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the offer currently before NZEI and PPTA members is 4.7 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The pay offer documents / union and Ministry of Education bargaining updates current at 8 October 2025: true if the headline offer to NZEI and PPTA members is 4.7%, false if the figure differs or applies only to part of the term.

veracity.statement: Does the Minister for the Public Service’s comments that people are striking just to have a long weekend increase or decrease the likelihood of strike action?
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim about what another Minister said — that strikers were motivated by wanting a long weekend. Collins disputes making the remark, so the attribution itself is what is at issue.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public record of Judith Collins' statements as Minister for the Public Service in the weeks before 8 October 2025 (media transcripts, press conference recordings, Hansard): true if she is recorded characterising strike action as being for a long weekend, false if no such remark exists in the record.

veracity.statement: Our Government has turned around the delivery of school property, we’ve halved the cost of building new classrooms, and children deserve to live in safe, warm, dry classrooms and we’re delivering just that.
veracity.explanation: Central factual assertion is that the cost of building a new classroom has been halved under this Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education per-classroom capital cost figures for standard classroom builds, comparing the pre-2023 average with the 2025 average: true if the average unit cost has fallen by ~50%, false if the reduction is materially smaller or the comparison relies on a different classroom specification.

veracity.statement: We are determined to reverse the trend we inherited, which saw people under the age of 25 on jobseeker spend an average of 18 more years on benefit. This has been 49 percent longer than in 2017.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under-25 jobseeker recipients are projected to spend an average of 18 further years on benefit, and that this is 49 percent longer than the equivalent 2017 figure. Note the Minister gives the figure as 47 percent later in the same session.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit system actuarial valuation / future years on benefit projections for jobseeker recipients aged under 25, comparing the latest valuation with the 2017 valuation: true if the average is ~18 years and the increase on 2017 is ~49%, false if either figure differs materially or the 2017 comparison uses a different cohort definition.

veracity.statement: Why has she made it so that two parents who are both working 27 hours each on the minimum wage can now work 11 hours less a week and yet be financially better off?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a two-parent household on the minimum wage at 27 hours each would be financially better off working 11 hours less per week under the parental income test.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Modelling of the parental income test threshold combined with Working for Families abatement and the jobseeker entitlement for an 18–19-year-old, at the April 2025 minimum wage: true if net household income at 2×16 hours exceeds that at 2×27 hours, false if it does not.

veracity.statement: How can she claim that this change will incentivise young people when her Government has increased university fees, increased youth unemployment, cut the Apprenticeship Boost, and made life even harder for working Kiwi families struggling with the cost of living crisis?
veracity.explanation: Asserts three checkable government-record claims: tertiary fees have risen, youth unemployment has risen, and the Apprenticeship Boost has been cut.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: (a) TEC annual maximum fee movement settings for 2024 and 2025; (b) Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate for 15–24-year-olds, September 2023 quarter versus the most recent quarter before October 2025; (c) Budget 2024/2025 appropriations and eligibility settings for Apprenticeship Boost. True if all three moved in the stated direction, false if any did not.

veracity.statement: This survey follows an identical survey in 2022, and most critically, it shows that in nearly every single measure for nearly every type of person, attitudes to attendance are improving.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2025 ERO survey repeats a 2022 instrument and shows improvement on nearly every measure across nearly every respondent group.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The ERO report 'Back to class: How are attitudes to attendance changing?' and its 2022 predecessor: true if the questions are materially the same and the large majority of measures moved favourably across respondent groups, false if the instruments differ materially or a substantial share of measures were flat or worse.

specificity.statement: Growing and strengthening the education workforce is exactly what this Government is doing, and, as I’ve already told the member on numerous occasions, the schooling teacher workforce grew by 2.5 percent in 2024, delivering 864 new teachers—the largest year-on-year increase since records began in 2009.
specificity.explanation: Gives a percentage, an absolute headcount, a year, and a records baseline — fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why were teachers offered a pay rise of less than inflation when Crown board members are getting up to an 80 percent increase?
specificity.explanation: Names a quantified comparison (an 80 percent increase, a below-inflation offer) that could be checked directly, though the pay figure itself is left relative.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The 4.7 percent that is on the table at the moment is a fair and reasonable offer that we hope the New Zealand Educational Institute and Post Primary Teachers’ Association members will take seriously.
specificity.explanation: Carries a precise figure and names the two unions, though 'fair and reasonable' is evaluative and the term of the offer is not stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’ll tell you what I will do: I will be at four around-the-country, full-day curriculum roadshows where I will be presenting to teachers, principals, and school leaders, where we will be providing information on resourcing for new curriculum and professional learning and development, and unpacking some of the strategic leadership things that teachers and principals should be doing.
specificity.explanation: Names a count (four), a format (full-day roadshows) and an audience, but the content described — 'information on resourcing', 'strategic leadership things' — carries no dates, locations or substance.
specificity.subject: speaker
