specificity.statement: This Government has been backing teachers since the day that we took office with more professional learning and development, more resourcing, more moving of back-end resources to deliver to the front line, three-quarters of a billion dollars into learning support, and more intervention teachers in mathematics and literacy.
specificity.explanation: One real figure (three-quarters of a billion into learning support) embedded in a list of unquantified 'more X' claims with no timeframes or baselines.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The investment package includes $58 million for maintenance work for all schools, which is a 50 percent uplift in their school maintenance grant; $255 million for improvements for small, rural, and isolated schools; $100 million over five years to fund urgent and essential infrastructure work.
specificity.explanation: Itemised amounts, a percentage uplift, a named beneficiary group and a period — anyone could check this against the announcement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m advised that around 4,300 fewer 18- and 19-year-olds will be eligible for the jobseeker support as a result of the parental assistance test, which has two parts: the parental income test and the parental support gap test.
specificity.explanation: A quantified estimate of the policy's effect plus the named two-part mechanism producing it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why has she made it so that two parents who are both working 27 hours each on the minimum wage can now work 11 hours less a week and yet be financially better off?
specificity.explanation: A fully worked example with hours, wage rate and the resulting change — precise enough for the Minister or anyone else to recompute.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On this side of the House, we believe that all parents want the best for their children and to ensure that their 18- and 19-year-olds are set up for a great life, which means they’re in employment, education, or training.
specificity.explanation: A statement of belief with no figures, mechanism or timeframe — nothing here could be checked or acted on. The question concerned the Working for Families interaction; the answer commits to nothing.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Education Review Office, and in particular Ruth Shinoda, have done a superb job surveying 15,000 students, teachers, and parents about how they view the importance of school attendance and what ensures that children are more likely to attend.
specificity.explanation: Names the agency, the responsible official, the sample size and the subject matter of the survey — locatable and checkable, though no findings or figures are given here.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, the member might like to go and chat with the unions, because the offer on the table at the moment is a fair and reasonable offer that meets the unions’ calls for meeting inflation.
civility.explanation: Deflects the questioner toward the unions — dismissive in tone and edging toward the member, but it imputes no bad faith and attacks no one's character; the substance of the offer is addressed.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Will she accept responsibility for the anger that teachers, principals, and support staff are feeling, or will she continue to stick her head in the sand?
civility.explanation: 'Stick her head in the sand' is a jibe at the Minister personally, imputing wilful refusal to face the sector rather than engaging her position. Short of a direct insult but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Could the Minister explain what giant leap in comprehension it takes for people to realise that the first responsibility for a family member lies with the family and not the taxpayer?
civility.explanation: 'What giant leap in comprehension it takes' sneers at the understanding of those who disagree. No individual is named or directly insulted, but the condescension is the point of the question.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I’m advised that around 4,300 fewer 18- and 19-year-olds will be eligible for the jobseeker support as a result of the parental assistance test, which has two parts: the parental income test and the parental support gap test.
divination.explanation: Forecasts the future effect of the parental assistance test on the number of 18- and 19-year-olds eligible for jobseeker support.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit statistics for 18- and 19-year-olds receiving Jobseeker Support, comparing the twelve months after the parental assistance test takes effect with the pre-implementation baseline: true if the reduction attributable to the test is approximately 4,300 (within about 20%), false if it is materially larger or smaller.

focus.statement: Why has she incentivised parents on the threshold of the income requirement to reduce their hours just so 18- and 19-year-olds can access jobseeker?
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism of the measure itself — the abatement threshold in the parental income test and the work incentive it creates. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can she claim that this change will incentivise young people when her Government has increased university fees, increased youth unemployment, cut the Apprenticeship Boost, and made life even harder for working Kiwi families struggling with the cost of living crisis?
focus.explanation: Names four specific policy levers and ties them to the measure before the House; the closing 'cost of living crisis' clause is broad framing but the weight of the question is on named policies. This is scrutiny, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I believe the most important number in New Zealand today is the number of children who go to school, because the amount of education that we pass from one generation to another more powerfully defines our future than anything else we can do on this day.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference — the conclusion (attendance is the most important number) rests on the premise that intergenerational education transfer dominates all other levers. But that premise is a bare superlative offered with no support and no comparison to any alternative, so the conclusion is only as strong as an unargued assertion.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Critically, 82 percent of students from poorer families said that going to school is important for their future. That compares with 84 percent of students from wealthier families.
specificity.explanation: Two precise percentages drawn from a named survey population, directly comparable and checkable against the source report.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: An analysis of 22 scientific articles that are relevant shows that piglet mortality risk is 14 percent higher in systems that do not confine sows after farrowing.
specificity.explanation: Names the evidence base, the outcome measured and the effect size; someone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The 10-year transition time I have proposed is significant but this is a very big shift in farming systems for most of the pig industry. With the other changes I’m proposing, an independent economic analysis estimated the cost of transition at more than $675,000 for the average indoor pig farm. It’s only reasonable that those farming families have an opportunity to make this change.
specificity.explanation: Names the transition length, the source of the costing and a dollar figure per farm.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Over the next four years, we have budgeted to invest a record $61.8 billion in public infrastructure, and this number is only set to grow with new capital earmarked for allocation and is a huge step up from the $50.6 billion the previous Government invested between 2019 and 2023.
specificity.explanation: Two dollar figures, a period for each, and a stated basis of comparison.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In fact, we built more classrooms in the last year than the last Government did. We built more social housing in our last 23 months than that Government did in its last three years.
specificity.explanation: Names the outputs and the comparison periods, but gives no counts for either, so the size of the claimed difference cannot be checked from the statement alone.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Between now and Christmas, more than $7 billion worth of infrastructure projects will commence, including upgrades to Auckland City Hospital, Middlemore Hospital, Hawke’s Bay Hospital, the construction of a new acute mental health unit at Hutt Valley Hospital; over $5 billion worth of roading projects—the Ōtaki to north of Levin highway, Melling interchange, Waihoehoe Road, the Ōmanawa bridge; and more than $800 million in school property projects, which we’re building better and faster than ever before.
specificity.explanation: Dollar totals, a timeframe and named individual projects across three sectors; entirely checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he know that, to build his infrastructure pipeline, he will need the 761 private sector construction employers who have shut their doors and laid off their people in the last year, and how does he plan to stop the liquidations of two construction firms every day on his watch?
specificity.explanation: A firm count, a rate and a period, tied to a named sector — precise enough to check or to answer directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Critically, 82 percent of students from poorer families said that going to school is important for their future. That compares with 84 percent of students from wealthier families.
veracity.explanation: Asserts near-parity between poorer and wealthier students on a specific survey item.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education Review Office 2025 attendance survey report: true if it records approximately 82% of students from lower-decile/poorer households and 84% from wealthier households agreeing that school attendance matters for their future; false if the figures or the gap are materially different.

veracity.statement: Three years ago, it was four out of 10 parents who thought it was OK for their children to miss a week of school.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific historical baseline figure for parental attitudes to a week's absence.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2022 Education Review Office attendance survey of parents: true if roughly 40% of parents reported being comfortable with their child missing a week or more of school; false if the reported proportion is materially different.

veracity.statement: An analysis of 22 scientific articles that are relevant shows that piglet mortality risk is 14 percent higher in systems that do not confine sows after farrowing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific quantified finding from a specific body of literature relied on for the policy.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The review of 22 studies underlying MPI's advice on the draft pig welfare code: true if it reports piglet mortality risk approximately 14% higher in non-confinement farrowing systems; false if the cited review reports no such difference or a materially different effect size.

veracity.statement: Most of the rest of the world is at 33 days; we are reducing down to seven.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a 33-day post-farrowing confinement period is the international norm against which New Zealand's proposed seven days should be judged.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Comparative regulation of post-farrowing sow confinement in major pig-producing jurisdictions (EU Council Directive 2008/120/EC, plus Sweden, Norway, Switzerland, Australia, the United States): true if the modal permitted confinement period across those jurisdictions is about 33 days; false if most permit indefinite confinement or prohibit crates outright, either of which would make '33 days' unrepresentative.

veracity.statement: Is he aware that it is a profound behavioural need of mother pigs to build a nest 24 hours before giving birth, and if they are caged it is deeply distressing for them, they will literally paw the ground, often bloodying their snouts, trying to build a nest?
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific ethological findings about sow nest-building motivation and the physical signs of thwarting it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Peer-reviewed animal-behaviour literature on pre-partum nest-building in domestic sows (e.g. Applied Animal Behaviour Science reviews, NAWAC's code review evidence): true if nest-building is documented as a strongly motivated behaviour occurring roughly 24 hours before parturition and if thwarting it in crates is associated with stress indicators including snout abrasion from bar-directed rooting; false if the literature does not support the timing or the distress response.

veracity.statement: How does he justify extending the use of cruel farrowing crates indefinitely when every animal welfare organisation in New Zealand, including the National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee [NAWAC], and 73 percent of New Zealanders oppose the use of farrowing crates because of worse welfare outcomes for mother pigs and piglets?
veracity.explanation: A compound claim: that NAWAC and all animal welfare organisations oppose farrowing crates, and that 73% of New Zealanders do.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Two checks: (a) NAWAC's published advice and its reconsideration on the draft pig code — true if NAWAC's standing position opposes farrowing crates, false if it accepted limited post-farrowing crating; (b) the published polling behind the 73% figure (SPCA/Horizon or similar) — true if a national poll found approximately 73% opposition, false if no such poll exists or found materially different support.

veracity.statement: Over the next four years, we have budgeted to invest a record $61.8 billion in public infrastructure, and this number is only set to grow with new capital earmarked for allocation and is a huge step up from the $50.6 billion the previous Government invested between 2019 and 2023.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a four-year budgeted capital total and a specific comparison with the previous Government's 2019–2023 investment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 capital allowance and the National Infrastructure Pipeline / Treasury capital investment figures: true if the four-year budgeted public infrastructure capital total is approximately $61.8b and the comparable 2019–2023 figure is approximately $50.6b on a like-for-like basis; false if the two figures are drawn from different bases or are materially different.

veracity.statement: The private sector builds a significant amount of New Zealand’s infrastructure, and when private sector projects like Auckland port and major housing developments can’t even get a consent, that holds it back, which is why fast track is so important, and which is why today’s 50-basis-point Official Cash Rate reduction is also pretty important.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Official Cash Rate was reduced by 50 basis points on the day of the statement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand Monetary Policy Review of 8 October 2025: true if the OCR was cut by 50 basis points on that date; false if the cut was a different size or no cut was made.

veracity.statement: In fact, we built more classrooms in the last year than the last Government did. We built more social housing in our last 23 months than that Government did in its last three years.
veracity.explanation: Two comparative delivery claims: classrooms in the last year, and social housing over 23 months versus the previous Government's final three years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education school property delivery figures for new teaching spaces by year, and HUD/Kāinga Ora public housing supply reports: true if classrooms delivered in the year to mid-2025 exceed the highest comparable year under the 2017–2023 Government, and if net public housing places added over the 23 months to October 2025 exceed those added in the three years to October 2023; false on either count if the comparison reverses, and false if the housing figure counts gross builds against the predecessor's net additions.

veracity.statement: Isn’t the point that the damage is done, with 20,000 jobs gone after he decided to stop and pause infrastructure builds?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 20,000 jobs were lost following the Government's decision to stop and pause infrastructure builds.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ construction sector employment (HLFS or filled jobs) change between the December 2023 quarter and the June 2025 quarter: true if the fall is approximately 20,000; false if materially smaller or if the figure covers a different industry base.

veracity.statement: Does he know that, to build his infrastructure pipeline, he will need the 761 private sector construction employers who have shut their doors and laid off their people in the last year, and how does he plan to stop the liquidations of two construction firms every day on his watch?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a count of construction employers that closed in the past year and a daily rate of construction liquidations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Companies Office liquidation records and Centrix credit reporting for construction-sector insolvencies in the 12 months to September 2025: true if approximately 761 construction employers ceased trading and the liquidation rate averages about two firms per day; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: If the economy is recovering, then why are 200 New Zealanders leaving every day, including thousands of builders, heading to Australia instead of staying here to build in New Zealand?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a daily rate of New Zealanders departing for Australia, including a substantial number of construction workers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration estimates for New Zealand citizen departures to Australia in the year to mid-2025: true if departures average approximately 200 per day (about 73,000 a year); false if materially lower, or if the figure conflates all citizen departures with departures to Australia.

civility.statement: While education may not have done well for Duncan Webb, this Government thinks it's important.
civility.explanation: A jibe at a named member's education and by implication his intelligence; it engages nothing of substance and lands squarely on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Why was targeted consultation only undertaken with the pork industry across 2024 and 2025, while animal welfare organisations were blindsided on Friday with his plans to cancel the phase out of farrowing crates, and does he regard protecting animal welfare as his primary responsibility, or enacting the wishes of the pork industry?
civility.explanation: The consultation point is legitimate, but the closing clause imputes regulatory capture — that the Minister is serving the industry rather than his statutory duty — which goes to motive rather than to the decision.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The member seems to be labouring under the same misunderstanding her colleague Ginny Andersen had yesterday, in the last round of “Who’s got talent?”, in which she said that all changes in the construction sector are due to what public investment is happening in infrastructure.
civility.explanation: Mocks two named members personally — the '"Who's got talent?"' jibe frames a colleague's questioning as an audition rather than engaging what she said.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We just heard the Minister of Finance waxing and waning lyrical about some basic facts and basic maths, so let’s provide some of those basic facts and basic maths.
civility.explanation: Mildly condescending toward a named Minister — 'waxing and waning lyrical' dismisses her answers as empty rhetoric rather than engaging them — though it stops well short of a personal attack and immediately turns toward substance.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The 10-year transition time I have proposed is significant but this is a very big shift in farming systems for most of the pig industry. With the other changes I’m proposing, an independent economic analysis estimated the cost of transition at more than $675,000 for the average indoor pig farm. It’s only reasonable that those farming families have an opportunity to make this change.
rigor.explanation: Costed premise offered (independent analysis, per-farm figure) and the conclusion drawn — a long transition — follows from it. The gap is that cost alone does not settle the length of the transition, but no fallacy is committed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is why we are introducing a requirement that nesting materials must be provided prior to farrowing. So we are covering this. I have visited pig farms, where I have been there after piglets have been farrowed, and I saw absolutely no sign of any of that.
rigor.explanation: Answers a claim about documented ethological distress with a personal anecdote from farm visits — an appeal to anecdote, and one made after farrowing about behaviour said to occur before it, so it could not bear on the point even if representative.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I will make zero apologies for talking to the people that regulations in this House will affect the most. These are going to be massive changes for your average pig-farming operation. They needed to be consulted. We needed to ensure that we had a system that was practical and affordable for them, otherwise we would not have a pig-farming industry in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: A genuine reason for consulting farmers is offered, but the closing step — that without practicality and affordability there would be no pig industry at all — is asserted rather than shown, and the conclusion does not address why other affected parties were not consulted.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Let me explain: the statement of commitments does not indicate a drop in planned spending, it records, instead, at a particular point in time, where contracts have been signed that would involve the Crown spending money but the money hasn’t yet been paid or even owed. It doesn’t include forecast infrastructure spending where there is not yet a contract.
rigor.explanation: Identifies what the cited figure actually measures and shows why the inference drawn from it does not hold; the conclusion follows directly from the definition given.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, as has previously been traversed in this House, it is the case throughout New Zealand’s history that, as economies recover, fewer New Zealanders leave, and we expect that to be the case.
rigor.explanation: Rests entirely on an unsupported historical generalisation — no data or mechanism is offered linking recovery to departure rates — and the conclusion is simply the generalisation restated as a forecast.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Isn’t the point that the damage is done, with 20,000 jobs gone after he decided to stop and pause infrastructure builds?
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: the job losses are attributed to the pause on the strength of sequence alone, with nothing offered to connect the two or to exclude the private-sector downturn.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I will make zero apologies for talking to the people that regulations in this House will affect the most. These are going to be massive changes for your average pig-farming operation. They needed to be consulted. We needed to ensure that we had a system that was practical and affordable for them, otherwise we would not have a pig-farming industry in New Zealand.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the regulatory change, who it affects and the consultation process; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How does he justify extending the use of cruel farrowing crates indefinitely when every animal welfare organisation in New Zealand, including the National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee [NAWAC], and 73 percent of New Zealanders oppose the use of farrowing crates because of worse welfare outcomes for mother pigs and piglets?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named regulatory decision, citing named bodies and a named figure. This is the opposition's job and carries no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he know that, to build his infrastructure pipeline, he will need the 761 private sector construction employers who have shut their doors and laid off their people in the last year, and how does he plan to stop the liquidations of two construction firms every day on his watch?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named policy area against named outcomes; no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Yes, it is the case that, as the economy recovers, we expect that more jobs will be created in the construction sector.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that employment in the construction sector will grow as the wider economy recovers.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ construction sector employment (HLFS industry series or filled jobs, construction): true if construction employment by the December 2026 quarter is above the September 2025 quarter level; false if it is at or below that level.

divination.statement: Well, as has previously been traversed in this House, it is the case throughout New Zealand’s history that, as economies recover, fewer New Zealanders leave, and we expect that to be the case.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the number of New Zealanders leaving will fall as the economy recovers.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration estimates for New Zealand citizen departures, and departures to Australia: true if annual citizen departures for the year to December 2026 are lower than for the year to September 2025; false if they are the same or higher.

veracity.statement: But, again, some of those basic facts: there are 36,000 fewer jobs and there are 10,000 more unemployed young people in the two years since this Government came to office and implemented their economic policies of firing up the shredder and cutting billions of dollars of investment in our economy and in our people.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two employment figures for the two years since the change of government: a fall of 36,000 jobs and a rise of 10,000 in unemployed young people.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey / Business Employment Data comparing the December 2023 quarter with the September 2025 quarter: true if total filled jobs fell by approximately 36,000 and the number of unemployed 15–24 year-olds rose by approximately 10,000 over that period; false if either figure is materially different or moves in the opposite direction.

veracity.statement: That probably explains why New Zealanders are, unfortunately, leaving in boatloads to the tune of approximately 200 every single day to Australia, because that is this Government’s policy on where the jobs are.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a rate of departure of New Zealanders to Australia of roughly 200 people per day at the time of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration statistics for departures of New Zealand citizens to Australia in the 12 months to October 2025: true if the rate averages approximately 200 per day (about 73,000 a year) to Australia specifically; false if the Australia-bound figure is materially lower (e.g. if 200/day is only reached by counting all destinations).

veracity.statement: They have scaled back infrastructure in hospitals, resulting in 15,000 fewer construction sector jobs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fall of 15,000 construction sector jobs and attributes it to scaled-back hospital infrastructure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ filled jobs for the construction industry over the period since the change of government: true if construction employment fell by approximately 15,000; false if materially different. The attribution to hospital projects would additionally require Health NZ/Treasury records of deferred or cancelled hospital builds.

veracity.statement: In his own words, he is “wealthy and sorted”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Christopher Luxon used the words 'wealthy and sorted' about himself.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The recorded interview or media transcript being referred to: true if Luxon described himself as 'wealthy and sorted' (or in materially equivalent words) on the record; false if no such quotation exists or the words are materially misreported.

veracity.statement: It’s quite interesting to see, today, the Minister of Finance saying, “I didn’t take any credit for it”, despite, in the first question before that, saying the Government takes credit for it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister of Finance disclaimed credit for falling interest rates in one answer that day having claimed Government credit in an earlier question the same day.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of oral questions for 8 October 2025: true if the Minister of Finance both claimed Government credit for the fall in interest rates in an earlier question and said she took no credit for it in a later one; false if the record does not show both, or if the earlier answer claimed credit for something other than the interest rate fall.

specificity.statement: But, again, some of those basic facts: there are 36,000 fewer jobs and there are 10,000 more unemployed young people in the two years since this Government came to office and implemented their economic policies of firing up the shredder and cutting billions of dollars of investment in our economy and in our people.
specificity.explanation: Two named magnitudes over a defined period, attached to a named policy programme — checkable as stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Greens have spent the last 18 months outlining our solutions and our clear policies, which would see free early childhood education, free dentistry, and free GPs. We would create 40,000 good, green jobs because we used to make things in this country and we can do it again.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete policies and a job-creation figure, but supplies no cost, no mechanism and no timeframe for any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The next Labour Government won’t just be a Labour Government; it will be a Government for everybody in New Zealand, because when everybody thrives in New Zealand, our country thrives.
specificity.explanation: A closing slogan — no policy, figure, mechanism or timeframe. Commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That probably explains why New Zealanders are, unfortunately, leaving in boatloads to the tune of approximately 200 every single day to Australia, because that is this Government’s policy on where the jobs are.
rigor.explanation: A causal inference — job losses therefore emigration therefore government policy — offered on correlation alone, with nothing connecting the migration figure to the policies named. Hedged with 'probably', but the conclusion still outruns what was shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Cuts are not how you build a country. Evidentially, it’s how you break one, and it is abundantly clear that this Government’s economic policy is to kill the golden goose: to whittle down our infrastructure to such an anaemic state and then to pass it off at bargain-bin prices to the private sector, and also then to exploit the very environment that we trade on on the international stage.
rigor.explanation: Bare assertion dressed as evidence: 'evidentially' and 'abundantly clear' are offered in place of any premise, and the conclusion imputes an intended plan (deliberate run-down then privatisation) from the fact of spending cuts alone. Non sequitur.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They have lost control of this economy, and we all know that.
rigor.explanation: The only support offered for the conclusion is that everyone already agrees with it — a bare appeal to popularity, with no evidence advanced.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I really hope that New Zealanders understand just how much this Government laughs at the state of affairs which this Government is handing down to future generations, because this Government is choosing to intentionally make life harder for New Zealanders.
focus.explanation: About the other side's demeanour in the Chamber and their supposed motives, not about any measure, figure or outcome. No policy is named once the characterisation of the Government is removed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Greens have spent the last 18 months outlining our solutions and our clear policies, which would see free early childhood education, free dentistry, and free GPs. We would create 40,000 good, green jobs because we used to make things in this country and we can do it again.
focus.explanation: Squarely on policy — her own party's programme, set against the measure under debate.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The jeering from the other side of the House during the last speaker’s speech is exactly why that side of the House and the Government is so disconnected from everyday New Zealanders, because you can jeer and laugh at the teenagers who need jobs, you can jeer and laugh at the fact that we are doing nothing for climate change in this House because of that Government, and you can jeer and laugh at the fact that this economy is tanking because of their inaction, but they won’t think that’s funny, because they are so disconnected from everyday New Zealanders.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side's conduct and character in the Chamber. Climate and the economy are gestured at, but no measure, figure or outcome is named — strip out the jeering and there is nothing on the policy left.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government isn’t on the side of ordinary New Zealanders; they’re on the side of tobacco companies, of property speculators, of the oil and gas industry.
focus.explanation: Names sectors rather than measures — it gestures at policy areas (tobacco, property, oil and gas) but the weight of the statement is a claim about whose side the other party is really on, not about any specific decision or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Do you think Christopher Luxon has any idea what life is really like for everyday New Zealanders?
civility.explanation: Turns from the policy to the named individual, questioning his personal understanding and lived experience rather than his decisions. A personal attack, though a restrained one framed as a question.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Prime Minister is so out of touch that I bet you—and I’m willing to take a wager from anyone here in Parliament—that he hasn’t got a clue at all, because, in his own words, he is “wealthy and sorted”.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the Prime Minister personally — 'hasn't got a clue at all' — targeting the man rather than any decision or policy of his.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: After a period of consistent clarity about building, focusing on growth, focusing on investment, and giving confidence to the broader community, in our second and third terms the economy was growing well, and we managed to reverse the flow across the Tasman, and that’s going to happen again this time.
rigor.explanation: False analogy: the conclusion that the turnaround 'is going to happen again' rests entirely on one historical parallel (2008-2017), with no mechanism offered linking the earlier recovery's causes to present conditions.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This only further highlights that Māori will always be guilty by whakapapa, and that we will always be tried, convicted, and executed before the truth is revealed, whilst the wealthy get to hide behind name suppression and privilege.
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation: an unrestricted 'always' about all future coverage of Māori is drawn from the listed set of inquiries, and the contrast with name suppression for 'the wealthy' is asserted without any case or figure connecting the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: After a period of consistent clarity about building, focusing on growth, focusing on investment, and giving confidence to the broader community, in our second and third terms the economy was growing well, and we managed to reverse the flow across the Tasman, and that’s going to happen again this time.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the net migration flow from New Zealand to Australia will reverse again under the current government, as he says it did in National's second and third terms.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration series for NZ-citizen migration to/from Australia: true if the annual net loss to Australia falls to zero or becomes a net gain at any point before the resolve-by date; false if a net annual loss to Australia persists throughout.

specificity.statement: We’ve got every confidence that New Zealand will be zinging in the future and providing the opportunities for New Zealanders to get ahead and for their families to do well.
specificity.explanation: Closing a passage on economic management with no figure, mechanism, policy or timeframe — 'zinging', 'get ahead', 'do well' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There have been 14 inquiries in the last 18 months into Māori organisations and Te Pāti Māori, and not a single allegation was upheld.
specificity.explanation: A precise count over a stated window with a definite claim about outcomes, and the following sentences name the specific inquiries — checkable as stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s the Greens—it’s the sanctimonious “tofu wouldn’t melt in your mouth” Greens—who are the ones who are driving the division and acrimony within our body politic, aided and abetted by Labour.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the opposing parties are like, with a mocking party caricature and no named policy, measure or figure. No individual is insulted, so this is a Focus failure rather than a Civility one.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s interesting that we’ve seen Duncan Webb saying, “Well, no, actually, we’re going to stick to our guns. We think people should protest outside MPs’ houses.” and Mr Hipkins has said that they shouldn’t, but they both voted against the bill that we’ve got in the House that deals with it.
focus.explanation: Names a specific bill before the House and a specific recorded vote against it, alongside quoted positions — scrutiny of opponents' stance on a named measure, not content-free party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In addition to accusations and inquiries, the Government still attacks our people by continuing to keep te iwi Māori struggling: the cost of living crisis; the disestablishment of the Māori Health Authority; section 7AA, Oranga Tamariki; the Regulatory Standards Bill; Treaty principles bill; Marine and Coastal Area; removing tikanga Māori from justice systems; removing $30 million from Māori education.
focus.explanation: Names eight specific measures — a repealed statutory provision, two named bills, an abolished agency and a dollar figure — rather than characterising the governing parties in general. Opposition scrutiny of named policies is on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Chlöe Swarbrick and the Greens have been behind a lot of this, and the hypocrisy is, quite frankly, outrageous.
civility.explanation: Moves from the conduct to a named individual's character, imputing bad faith ('the hypocrisy is, quite frankly, outrageous') to Chlöe Swarbrick personally rather than criticising a position or a policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We are not afraid of scrutiny, we welcome truth, but what we reject completely is the colonial gaze that turns Māori excellence into suspicion and Māori success into scandal.
civility.explanation: Fierce criticism of media framing and of an institutional pattern, on a genuinely contested matter where he had ample opportunity to attack individuals, and does not — no person's character, competence or motives is impugned.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: You look at a quote from Benjamin Doyle saying that “No person should have to avoid going to the supermarket or the letterbox because they’ve been advised that doing so would expose them to violence.”, and yet, at the same time, you’ve got Ricardo Menéndez March writing letters in support of people who vandalise MPs’ offices and, at the same time, you’ve got the leader of the Greens in press conferences with a peace-loving actor who hands out the private addresses of MPs for people to go and hassle them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three matters of record: that Benjamin Doyle made the quoted statement, that Ricardo Menéndez March wrote letters supporting people who vandalised MPs' offices, and that the Green leader appeared at press conferences with a person who published MPs' private addresses.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous reporting and primary documents: the Doyle quote as published; any letter of support written by Ricardo Menéndez March for a person charged with or convicted of vandalising an MP's office; and footage or reporting of a Green Party press conference featuring an activist who had circulated MPs' home addresses. True if all three are documented; false if the Menéndez March letters or the press-conference appearance cannot be evidenced.

veracity.statement: It’s interesting that we’ve seen Duncan Webb saying, “Well, no, actually, we’re going to stick to our guns. We think people should protest outside MPs’ houses.” and Mr Hipkins has said that they shouldn’t, but they both voted against the bill that we’ve got in the House that deals with it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Duncan Webb said Labour supports protests outside MPs' homes, that Chris Hipkins said the opposite, and that both nonetheless voted against the bill currently before the House dealing with intimidation at MPs' homes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard division record for the relevant reading of the bill on intimidation at MPs' residences, plus the reported statements of Duncan Webb and Chris Hipkins. True if both MPs are recorded voting against and the two quoted positions are as described; false if the division record shows otherwise or either statement was not made.

veracity.statement: There have been 14 inquiries in the last 18 months into Māori organisations and Te Pāti Māori, and not a single allegation was upheld.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both a count (14 inquiries into Māori organisations and Te Pāti Māori since roughly April 2024) and that no allegation in any of them was upheld.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published findings of the inquiries he lists (Public Service Commission into Manurewa Marae and Te Whānau o Waipareira, Stats NZ census data, Te Whatu Ora data handling, Electoral Commission, Te Puni Kōkiri, SFO/Police). True if 14 such inquiries occurred in the window and none made an adverse finding; false if the number is materially different or any inquiry made an adverse finding — note his own account concedes Health New Zealand 'did not sufficiently protect public data'.

veracity.statement: Over a billion people saw the haka led by Hana in Parliament.
veracity.explanation: A viewership claim about the November 2024 haka led by Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke during the Treaty Principles Bill first reading.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Aggregate verified view counts for the haka footage across major platforms (TikTok, X, YouTube, Instagram) plus published media-reach estimates. True if credible aggregate reach reaches one billion viewers; false if the documented figure is an order of magnitude lower or if only view counts (not unique viewers) support it.

veracity.statement: When faced with the Treaty principles bill, over 100,000 people hikoi-ed and over 300,000 submissions were made—over 90 percent in opposition.
veracity.explanation: Three assertions: over 100,000 participants in the November 2024 hīkoi, over 300,000 submissions on the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill, and over 90 percent of those submissions opposed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's report on the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill for submission totals and the opposed/supportive breakdown, and police or organiser crowd estimates for the hīkoi reported at the time. True if submissions exceed 300,000 with over 90 percent opposed and hīkoi participation exceeded 100,000; false if the committee's figures or the crowd estimates are materially lower.

veracity.statement: The latest Electoral Commission figures show that, since April 2023, almost 31,000 voters have switched to the Māori roll, and more than 25,000 first-time voters have gone for the Māori electoral option.
veracity.explanation: Cites Electoral Commission roll-transfer data for two figures: net switches to the Māori roll since April 2023, and first-time enrolments choosing the Māori electoral option.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission published Māori electoral option / roll-transfer statistics for the period April 2023 to October 2025. True if the figures are approximately 31,000 switches and 25,000-plus first-time enrolments on the Māori roll; false if the published figures differ materially or measure something else (e.g. gross rather than net transfers).

veracity.statement: That COVID hangover was caused by the previous Labour Government spending $66 billion of taxpayer money and raking up debt, over twice, to 44 percent of gross domestic product.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two figures about the 2017–2023 Labour government: $66 billion of COVID-era spending, and net debt roughly doubling to 44 percent of GDP.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury fiscal data and the COVID-19 Response and Recovery Fund appropriations: true if total CRRF/COVID spending is approximately $66bn and net core Crown debt rose to roughly 44% of GDP (from roughly half that) over the term; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: That was the largest debt-fuelled spending binge in the developed world, according to the IMF.
veracity.explanation: A superlative comparative claim, attributed to the IMF, that New Zealand's COVID-era fiscal expansion was the largest of any developed economy.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IMF Fiscal Monitor database of discretionary COVID-19 fiscal support as a share of GDP across advanced economies: true if New Zealand ranks first; false if any advanced economy (e.g. the United States, United Kingdom, Japan, Canada) exceeds it on the IMF's own measure.

veracity.statement: Light rail to nowhere; the Skypath, $50 million of money spent and nothing delivered.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly $50 million was spent on the SkyPath / Auckland harbour crossing project with nothing built.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA Waka Kotahi published expenditure figures for the SkyPath / Northern Pathway project up to its cancellation: true if approximately $50m was spent and no crossing was constructed; false if the spend is materially different or a structure was delivered.

veracity.statement: The National Party has dipped into the 20s, that psychological number that has every backbencher shaking in their boots, watching their majority disappear.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Taxpayers' Union–Curia poll released that day put National's party vote below 30 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published Taxpayers' Union–Curia poll of early October 2025: true if National's party vote is recorded below 30.0%; false if it is 30% or above.

veracity.statement: What happened to the gentailer’s share prices on the day that the Government announced that set of significant but surgical reforms? The gentailer’s share prices soared. That's how significant they were in reforming a broken market.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that listed gentailer share prices rose sharply on the day the energy reform package was announced.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZX closing prices for the listed gentailers (Meridian, Mercury, Contact, Genesis) on the announcement date versus the prior close: true if they rose materially above normal daily variation; false if flat or down.

veracity.statement: Simon Bridges, a former leader of the National Party, made it clear that the National Party had let the country down, that it had missed its opportunity and was not delivering what should be there.
veracity.explanation: Relays a criticism attributed to Simon Bridges — the speaker is reporting what he said, not asserting it herself.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Simon Bridges' public statements and media commentary on the government's October 2025 energy reform package: true if he publicly criticised it as a missed opportunity that let the country down; false if no such comments exist or his commentary was supportive.

specificity.statement: We’ve got Fulton Hogan Land Development, and they’re delivering around 1,100 housing units to the total of $595 million—again, under this Government’s fast-track approvals regime, which never would have happened under the previous Government.
specificity.explanation: Names the developer, the location, a unit count and a dollar total, and identifies the consenting pathway. Someone could go and check the approval. Short of full marks only because no delivery timeframe is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In a few months, this Government—and it's set out in the Government's quarter four plan—will introduce a new resource management system with two focused laws: a natural environment Act which sets clear environmental rules suited to each region, so we stop arguing over trivia and focus on the real environmental risks that we need to manage.
specificity.explanation: Names the legislative vehicle, the number and type of Acts, and points to a published government plan with a rough timeframe. Held back from the top by 'in a few months' and by giving no thresholds or content for the environmental rules themselves.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We'll cap council fishing expeditions for more information, that drag out consents for months and years.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a real mechanism (limiting further-information requests) but supplies no cap, no statutory time limit and no enforcement route. A direction with some detail and no how-much.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Light rail to nowhere; the Skypath, $50 million of money spent and nothing delivered.
focus.explanation: Names two specific infrastructure projects and a specific spend-versus-delivery outcome. This is scrutiny of a named record, not content-free party-bashing, so it scores high; 'light rail to nowhere' is the only part carrying party framing rather than substance.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The National Party has dipped into the 20s, that psychological number that has every backbencher shaking in their boots, watching their majority disappear.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's poll standing and the internal state of its caucus. No policy, measure or outcome is named at all — this is the case Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Those four pretenders to the crown aren't even counting the cosplaying Prime Ministers of Winston Peters and David Seymour; they’re four job seekers from in his own ranks.
focus.explanation: Wholly about the other parties' internal leadership ambitions. No policy, figure or outcome is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We'll cap council fishing expeditions for more information, that drag out consents for months and years.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the consenting mechanism before the House. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think the only person in Auckland that doesn’t want that to go ahead is Helen Clark, but that is going to provide real economic opportunity for this country.
civility.explanation: Singles out a named individual for mockery, casting her as the lone obstructionist in a city of 1.7 million. Pointed and a little sneering, but it stops short of attacking her character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That is from the Government's own pollster, Curia, and I think this speaks very much to how weak and out of touch Christopher Luxon is showing New Zealanders he is.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on a named individual's personal qualities as a leader — 'weak' and 'out of touch' target the person, not a decision or a policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Those four pretenders to the crown aren't even counting the cosplaying Prime Ministers of Winston Peters and David Seymour; they’re four job seekers from in his own ranks.
civility.explanation: Mocks two named individuals as 'cosplaying Prime Ministers' — ridicule aimed at the people rather than at anything they have done or proposed.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: At best, Simon Watts stumbled to the cupboard and grabbed a Disprin—that's how far from a surgical set of reforms.
civility.explanation: An extended metaphor casting a named minister as bumbling. It does serve a point about the weakness of the reform package, but the mockery lands on the person, not just the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, unless trout grow legs and buy hiking boots, they’re not getting there. That’s not environmental protection; it’s performance art.
civility.explanation: Withering ridicule aimed entirely at a consent condition. No council officer or member is named or impugned — the target is the decision, which is exactly what the standard permits.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: There are at least four job seekers sitting on that front bench queuing up for that job, and Christopher Luxon’s days are numbered.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Christopher Luxon will lose the National Party leadership. Not a promise about the speaker's own action, and the outcome is publicly observable.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: National Party leadership records and public reporting: true if Christopher Luxon ceases to be leader of the National Party before the 2026 general election; false if he leads the party into that election.

divination.statement: What we have is a set of reforms that are not going to make energy cheaper for New Zealand households and businesses.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the announced energy reforms will not reduce electricity costs for households and businesses.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI electricity subindex and MBIE retail electricity price series: true if average residential and commercial electricity prices have not fallen in real terms by the end of 2027; false if they have fallen in real terms over that period.

rigor.statement: What happened to the gentailer’s share prices on the day that the Government announced that set of significant but surgical reforms? The gentailer’s share prices soared. That's how significant they were in reforming a broken market.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the policy: the market reaction is offered as evidence the reforms do not threaten gentailer margins. Real evidence and a real conclusion, but there is a gap — a share price rise on announcement day can reflect resolved uncertainty rather than a weak package, and nothing rules that out.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: These aren’t isolated tales; this is the Resource Management Act. The result is higher power bills, dearer groceries, slower housing investors who simply walk away.
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation: four anecdotes are asserted, without any frequency data, to be representative of an entire statute's operation, and then a further causal leap attributes power bills and grocery prices to it with nothing offered to connect them.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So the news today of the official cash rate dropping another 50 basis points and decreasing mortgage rates is welcome news for families struggling with mortgage repayments, but it is also welcome news for our growers, farmers, and businesses across Hawke’s Bay because it gives confidence and certainty and more money to invest in growing our economy and creating jobs, and this lifts wages for everyone.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on the day of the speech the Reserve Bank cut the Official Cash Rate by 50 basis points, and that mortgage rates are falling.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ Monetary Policy Review / OCR decision published 8 October 2025: true if the OCR was reduced by 50 basis points on that date, false if it was held, cut by a different margin, or no decision was released. Mortgage-rate direction checkable against RBNZ published new-lending mortgage rate series for the surrounding months.

veracity.statement: For years, I sat on the board of New Zealand Apples and Pears, and under the Labour Government the apple industry could never meet the $1 billion export mark.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that annual apple export earnings never reached $1 billion in any year of the 2017–2023 Labour government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / MPI apple (or apple and pear) export earnings by year: true if the annual export value stayed below $1 billion in every year from 2017 to 2023, false if it reached or exceeded $1 billion in any of those years. Note the measure must be held constant between the two halves of the comparison (apples alone vs apples and pears).

veracity.statement: In fact, our horticulture exports have hit record highs: $8.5 billion this year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure — $8.5 billion of horticultural exports in the current year — and that this is an all-time record.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries / Stats NZ horticultural export revenue for the year to June 2025: true if the figure is approximately $8.5 billion and exceeds every prior year, false if materially different or if an earlier year was higher.

veracity.statement: Around 360,000 Kiwis are employed in our food and fibre sector, about 15 percent of the total workforce.
veracity.explanation: Two linked factual claims: an employment headcount for the food and fibre sector, and that headcount as a share of total employment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries food and fibre sector employment estimate, against Stats NZ HLFS total employment: true if the headcount is around 360,000 and that is roughly 15 percent of total employment, false if either number is materially different.

specificity.statement: Growth and more growth means jobs and more jobs, it means higher wages, and it means a better future for New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: A slogan-level opening: no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named policy — nothing here that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Around 360,000 Kiwis are employed in our food and fibre sector, about 15 percent of the total workforce.
specificity.explanation: Gives a headcount and a workforce share for a named sector — precise enough that a reader could look both up.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They have used the Investment Boost package of this Government, which enabled a 20 percent tax deduction along with depreciation.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy, the mechanism and the rate, tied to an identified business that used it — checkable detail rather than a general claim about supporting business.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: A highlight in the last few weeks was visiting the Hastings Stortford Lodge saleyards, and it was amazing to see the farmer confidence back again, with record highs in farmer confidence because finally they have a Government that is backing them and allowing our farmers to do what they do best, and that is farm.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning resting on a single saleyard visit: record farmer confidence is attributed wholly to the change of government, with no evidence offered connecting the two and no consideration of commodity prices or interest rates, which the speaker herself credits elsewhere in the same speech.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: In Hawke’s Bay alone, our region is set to add another thousand new jobs in agriculture and horticulture.
divination.explanation: Forecasts net growth of about 1,000 jobs in agriculture and horticulture in the Hawke's Bay region. Not a promise about the speaker's own action — it is a projection about regional employment.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ regional filled-jobs / employment data for the Hawke's Bay region in the agriculture and horticulture industries: true if the count rises by approximately 1,000 or more above its October 2025 level, false if growth is materially smaller or negative.

veracity.statement: In fact, there are 20,000 fewer construction jobs in New Zealander under his watch.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific fall of 20,000 in construction employment over the two years since the change of government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey / Infoshare employment by industry, construction sector, comparing the September 2023 quarter with the most recent 2025 quarter; true if the fall is approximately 20,000 or more, false if materially smaller.

veracity.statement: There are 36,000 fewer people employed in New Zealand right now, over the past two years, under the watch of Christopher Luxon.
veracity.explanation: Asserts total employment in New Zealand has fallen by 36,000 over the two years to October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ HLFS total employed persons, September 2023 quarter versus the June/September 2025 quarter; true if the net fall is approximately 36,000, false if the level rose or fell by a materially different amount.

veracity.statement: Every single day, 200 New Zealanders leave our country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a rate of 200 New Zealanders departing per day. Ambiguous between gross departures and net loss of NZ citizens; the net-migration reading is the one commonly cited.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration estimates for the 12 months to the statement date; true if net departures of New Zealand citizens average about 200 per day (~73,000 a year), false if the annual figure is materially below that.

veracity.statement: Believe it or not, Apprenticeship Boost for civil engineering has been removed at a time when talking about infrastructure, when those people opposite are talking about wanting to drive growth, they have cut the Apprenticeship Boost for civil engineering.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that civil engineering apprenticeships have been removed from Apprenticeship Boost eligibility.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The MSD Apprenticeship Boost eligible-occupation/eligibility criteria published before and after the 2024–25 scheme changes; true if civil engineering apprenticeships were removed from eligibility, false if they remain covered.

veracity.statement: A 2016 report confirmed the scheme contributes more than $100 million annually to the regional GDP and supports over 1,300 full-time job equivalents.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 2016 report found the Kerikeri irrigation scheme contributes >$100m a year to regional GDP and supports >1,300 FTEs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2016 economic assessment of the Kerikeri irrigation scheme (Northland Regional Council / Te Tai Tokerau Water Trust commissioned work); true if it reports an annual regional GDP contribution above $100 million and more than 1,300 FTEs, false if the figures are materially lower or no such report exists.

veracity.statement: Our economy hasn’t grown; it’s gone backwards.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the New Zealand economy has contracted rather than grown over the period since the government took office.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ real GDP (production measure), September 2023 quarter versus the most recent published quarter; true if the level is lower than at the change of government, false if it is higher. Note the headline and per-capita series can differ — the headline series is the fair test of the unqualified claim.

specificity.statement: Let’s look at the 230 jobs in Karioi Pulp Mill and Tangiwai Sawmill in Ruapehu—230 jobs there. At the Penrose mill in Auckland, 75 jobs gone.
specificity.explanation: Named sites, named regions and exact job counts — directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We believe in an economy that serves everybody, not the other way around. We believe that every person deserves a fair pay that pays a decent wage; good jobs that grow local economies and grow local communities.
specificity.explanation: A statement of values with no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named policy — nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A 2016 report confirmed the scheme contributes more than $100 million annually to the regional GDP and supports over 1,300 full-time job equivalents.
specificity.explanation: A named source, a dollar figure and an FTE count attached to a named scheme.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Te Waihekeora reservoir: this reservoir near Dargaville—which I was privileged to attend the opening of recently, along with the Prime Minister—enables the development of nearly 1,000 hectares and provides crucial water supply to the largest employer in Dargaville, Silver Fern Farms, and also to the Dargaville township.
specificity.explanation: Named project, named location, hectares served and named beneficiaries.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I say to 18- and 19-year-olds in Northland that there are opportunities out there, opportunities that are better than being on welfare.
specificity.explanation: "Opportunities out there" names no job, employer, number or pathway, in a speech that elsewhere supplies plenty of detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Let’s look at the 230 jobs in Karioi Pulp Mill and Tangiwai Sawmill in Ruapehu—230 jobs there. At the Penrose mill in Auckland, 75 jobs gone.
focus.explanation: Names specific employers and specific outcomes rather than characterising the other party; legitimate scrutiny of the government's economic record.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: New Zealanders cannot go to the regions and look for a job, because there aren’t any jobs there.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the Prime Minister's stated suggestion that jobseekers move to the regions — on-policy, even though the inference is weak.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The truth is that New Zealanders are not fooled by the spin of Christopher Luxon.
focus.explanation: No policy, measure or figure is named — it is a claim about what the public thinks of the Prime Minister's character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When people are trying to find some sort of vision, some sort of hope in New Zealand, they’re being driven overseas, because the only green shoots going on here is for those members’ mates in those circles that they operate in.
focus.explanation: Once the insinuation about the other side's circles is removed there is no policy content left; nothing specific is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Te Waihekeora reservoir: this reservoir near Dargaville—which I was privileged to attend the opening of recently, along with the Prime Minister—enables the development of nearly 1,000 hectares and provides crucial water supply to the largest employer in Dargaville, Silver Fern Farms, and also to the Dargaville township.
focus.explanation: Entirely about a named piece of infrastructure, the area it irrigates and who it supplies — mechanism and effect, no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Government’s mismanagement and waste comes from cancelling new ferries and stopping and cancelling projects, contributing to 20,000 jobs—20,000 jobs—gone in construction; manufacturing closures in several regions across the country, costing vital, local jobs; and handing over hundreds of millions of dollars to tobacco companies, and billions of dollars to property speculators, to name just a few.
focus.explanation: Names specific decisions (ferry cancellation, tobacco excise, tax changes) and specific outcomes rather than characterising the other party in general.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: He’s out of touch and he’s refusing to take responsibility.
focus.explanation: No policy, figure or measure is named; it is entirely a characterisation of the person leading the other side.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: New Zealanders cannot go to the regions and look for a job, because there aren’t any jobs there.
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation: a list of specific plant closures is offered to support the universal conclusion that there are no jobs in the regions at all. The premises, even if true, do not reach the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The evidence is also visible in land values, which can be three to four times higher for irrigated land within the scheme area, reflecting the substantial, proven economic benefit of a secure water supply.
rigor.explanation: Treats a land-value differential as proof of economic benefit caused by irrigation. The correlation is real evidence, but the leap to "proven" skips confounders (land already better suited to horticulture, proximity, capitalised subsidy) — a gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Government’s mismanagement and waste comes from cancelling new ferries and stopping and cancelling projects, contributing to 20,000 jobs—20,000 jobs—gone in construction; manufacturing closures in several regions across the country, costing vital, local jobs; and handing over hundreds of millions of dollars to tobacco companies, and billions of dollars to property speculators, to name just a few.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: a list of decisions is asserted to have caused 20,000 construction job losses and nationwide manufacturing closures, with nothing offered to connect the decisions to the outcomes.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is no wonder that 200 people a day are packing up and leaving, every single day, and what that looks like in New Brighton is three children standing in the rain outside a food bank—and all that member can say is “Where are the parents?” That’s all that member can say.
rigor.explanation: Bare appeal to emotion and a single anecdote: net migration figures and three children outside one food bank are joined as if one explained the other, with no connecting reasoning.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The truth is that New Zealanders are not fooled by the spin of Christopher Luxon.
civility.explanation: Imputes deliberate deception ("spin") to a named person rather than engaging the substance of what he said. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: When people are trying to find some sort of vision, some sort of hope in New Zealand, they’re being driven overseas, because the only green shoots going on here is for those members’ mates in those circles that they operate in.
civility.explanation: Imputes cronyism — that members opposite govern for the benefit of their friends. That is an attack on the members' integrity, not on their policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is no wonder that 200 people a day are packing up and leaving, every single day, and what that looks like in New Brighton is three children standing in the rain outside a food bank—and all that member can say is “Where are the parents?” That’s all that member can say.
civility.explanation: "All that member can say", repeated, is mockery of a member personally rather than a response to the interjection's substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: He’s out of touch and he’s refusing to take responsibility.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the Prime Minister's personal character and judgement — out of touch, unwilling to accept responsibility — rather than on a decision or policy.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In the last quarter alone, GDP fell 0.9 percent, and whilst Christopher Luxon, like that member, likes to talk about rights and responsibilities, you’ll never hear him—or her—take responsibility for the damage they are doing to our economy.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that GDP fell 0.9 percent in the most recent quarter reported before 8 October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP (production measure), the June 2025 quarter release: true if real GDP fell approximately 0.9 percent quarter-on-quarter, false if it fell materially less or rose.

veracity.statement: Australia is up 0.6 percent, the United Kingdom is up 0.3 percent, the United States is up 0.8 percent, Japan is up 0.5 percent, and China is up 1.1 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts quarter-on-quarter GDP growth figures for five comparator economies over the same period as the New Zealand quarter just cited.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD quarterly national accounts / each country's national statistical agency, quarter-on-quarter real GDP growth for the reference quarter (June 2025): true if all five figures match within about 0.1 percentage point, false if any is materially different or drawn from a different period.

veracity.statement: Our first Māori MP was elected in 1867—James Carroll.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both a date for the election of the first Māori MP and the identity of that person.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Parliament / Te Ara records of Māori representation: true if James Carroll was elected in 1867 and was the first Māori MP; false if the first Māori MPs were elected in a different year or were different people, or if Carroll entered Parliament later.

veracity.statement: There was also Peter Buck; Āpirana Ngata; Māui Pōmare; Iriaka Matiu Rātana, the first female Māori MP who served for 20 years; and Whetu Tirikatene-Sullivan, the first female Minister, who, at the time she left Parliament, was the longest-serving female MP.
veracity.explanation: Two distinct claims: that Iriaka Rātana was the first Māori woman MP and served 20 years, and that Whetu Tirikatene-Sullivan was the first female Minister and the longest-serving female MP on leaving Parliament.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary service and ministerial appointment records: true only if (a) Rātana was the first Māori woman MP with about 20 years' service and (b) no woman was appointed a Minister before Tirikatene-Sullivan; false if an earlier woman held ministerial office, or if either service span is wrong.

veracity.statement: What an insult to our proud legacy, to the country that was the first to give women the vote in the world—the cowardice and ignorance of that passing shot by a member who did nothing to use the privilege afforded by being an MP in this Parliament and who threw passing shots and ran out the door, believing there would be no right of reply.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand was the first country in the world to grant women the vote.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Comparative suffrage histories and the Electoral Act 1893: true if New Zealand was the first self-governing country to grant women the parliamentary franchise; false if another sovereign country did so earlier.

civility.statement: In the last quarter alone, GDP fell 0.9 percent, and whilst Christopher Luxon, like that member, likes to talk about rights and responsibilities, you’ll never hear him—or her—take responsibility for the damage they are doing to our economy.
civility.explanation: Names an individual and imputes an unwillingness to take responsibility — pointed and moving from the record onto the person's disposition, without landing as a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They’re pushed there and, right now, those members are pushing.
civility.explanation: Imputes to members opposite the deliberate pushing of people into poverty — an attribution of bad faith rather than a criticism of a decision or policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In the last moments of the House sitting before the recent two-week recess, we were forced to endure insult and indignity in this House by the dishonourable speech given by an MP for whom we had accommodated his desire to give a departing speech, an MP who had spent, in terms of the life of this Parliament, a matter of moments here.
civility.explanation: Labels a colleague's speech 'dishonourable' and belittles the length of their service — the target is the member rather than anything they argued.
civility.subject: speaker
