veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable things: that Paul Goldsmith stated in a speech on this bill that the legislation creates and confers property rights, and that this characterisation is wrong because the Act recognises pre-existing rights rather than creating them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of Paul Goldsmith's speeches on the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill, plus the text of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011. True if Goldsmith said the legislation creates or confers property rights and the Act's own wording frames customary marine title as recognised rather than created; false if his speeches describe it only as recognising existing rights, or if the Act frames the title as conferred by statute.

veracity.statement: Along comes a guy named John Key with the National Party—and the Māori Party; we worked together in 2011 to pass the Marine and Coastal Area Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Marine and Coastal Area Act was passed in 2011 by a John Key-led National Government working together with the Māori Party.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The enactment record of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 and the third-reading division list. True if the Act was passed in 2011 under a National Government led by John Key with Māori Party votes in support; false if the year, the government of the day, or the Māori Party's support differs from that.

divination.statement: But they did it, and yet this Government is going to strip away conferred rights, rights that the court has actually already recognised.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the bill, once passed, will operate on customary marine titles that the courts have already recognised — that is, that its effect will reach backwards to recognitions already granted rather than applying only to undetermined applications.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill as enacted, read against the register of customary marine title orders and agreements already made. True if the amended test is applied so as to remove, reopen or override recognitions granted before enactment; false if orders already made by the courts are expressly preserved and only pending or future applications are affected.

specificity.statement: We announced a $5 million investment in a new centre court roof for Auckland’s Manuka Doctor Arena. This is the first infrastructure project from our $70 million major events and tourism package.
specificity.explanation: Two dollar figures, a named venue, a named funding package and the project's place within it. Fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This investment will help New Zealand stay match fit on the international stage. If we want to continue to attract world-class events to New Zealand, we need to have world-class facilities to go along with it.
specificity.explanation: Answering why the investment is needed, but supplies no figure, mechanism or timeframe — 'match fit', 'world-class facilities' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: No. what our economic plan is directly responsible for is more than half a billion dollars having been committed to rebuilding Nelson Hospital and the fast tracking of a major housing development that on her watch would have been tied up in red tape for years.
specificity.explanation: One firm figure attached to a named project (Nelson Hospital), but the housing development is unnamed and there is no timeframe or amount attached to it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why then are there 36,000 people who are not in work and liquidations are up 26 percent?
specificity.explanation: Two precise, checkable figures — a headcount not in work and a percentage rise in liquidations — put to the Minister as the basis of the question.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In what way is two plants closing and 249 jobs being lost in Tokoroa a sign that her plan is working?
specificity.explanation: A precise job-loss figure tied to a named town and a stated number of plant closures — checkable, even though it carries no proposal of its own.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill introduces 19 new, expanded marine protection areas, and is the largest increase in marine protection in Aotearoa New Zealand in over a decade. The amount of area that is to be protected here is twice the size of Singapore.
specificity.explanation: A count of protection areas, a comparative claim about the past decade and a concrete area comparison — enough detail that someone could check every element.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What is his message to the 32,000 Kiwis who signed the World Wide Fund for Nature’s petition urging his Government to remove the carve-out that allows commercial fishing in the Gulf’s high protection areas due to the risk that it sets a dangerous precedent where industry lobbyists could weaken future marine protections?
specificity.explanation: Names the petition, its organiser, the number of signatories and the exact statutory provision at issue. Every element could be checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In 2024, just this one event alone brought significant economic benefit to Auckland, resulting in 16,600 visitor nights to the region and injecting $3.4 million into the economy.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific measured outcomes of the 2024 ASB Classic: 16,600 visitor nights to Auckland and $3.4 million injected into the economy.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The economic impact assessment for the 2024 ASB Classic (Tennis Auckland / Auckland Unlimited or MBIE major-events reporting): true if it records approximately 16,600 visitor nights and approximately $3.4 million of economic impact for that event in 2024; false if the published figures are materially different or if no such assessment exists.

veracity.statement: It is also the case, though—I would point out to members—that the number of unemployed New Zealanders at this point still remains lower than Grant Robertson was forecasting it would be at this point.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the current level of unemployment is below what the 2023 pre-election forecasts projected for this point in time.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update 2023 unemployment forecast for the September 2025 quarter, compared with the Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey actual for that quarter: true if the actual number of unemployed is lower than the PREFU-forecast number; false if it equals or exceeds it.

veracity.statement: Because as the Treasury has previously acknowledged extensively on the record, they vastly overestimated their growth assumptions in the pre-election fiscal update, which may have been convenient for the Minister at the time but was inaccurate none the less.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Treasury itself has repeatedly conceded on the record that the PREFU 2023 GDP growth forecasts were far too optimistic.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's published forecast-performance reviews and evidence to select committee on the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update 2023: true if Treasury has on the record accepted that its PREFU 2023 growth assumptions were substantially too high; false if no such acknowledgement exists or if Treasury's stated forecast error was small.

veracity.statement: But I would also point out that the assertion that rents have gone up under our Government is not correct. In fact, what we have seen is downward pressure on rents since being elected after a period of extreme rent rises under the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Two claims: that rents have not risen since the Government took office in late 2023, and that rents rose sharply under the previous Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ rental price index and MBIE tenancy bond mean-rent data from November 2023 to September 2025: true if the rental price index is flat or lower over that period; false if rents rose materially over the period taken as a whole.

veracity.statement: Why then are there 36,000 people who are not in work and liquidations are up 26 percent?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific increase of 36,000 people not in work and a 26 percent rise in company liquidations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey change in the number of unemployed since the December 2023 quarter, and Companies Office / Centrix liquidation counts for the year to September 2025: true if the additional number not in work is about 36,000 and liquidations are about 26 percent higher year-on-year; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: On Tuesday, with the backing of all the parties that were present that day in this fine Parliament, the tautoko and support of iwi around Tīkapa Maona, and thousands of New Zealanders, we passed this bill that will triple marine protection in the Hauraki Gulf.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that the bill passed with the support of all parties present, and that it triples the area of marine protection in the Hauraki Gulf.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard division record for the third reading of the Hauraki Gulf marine protection bill, and DOC figures on protected area in the Gulf before and after the Act: true if every party present voted in favour and the protected area roughly triples; false if any party present voted against or the increase falls well short of threefold.

veracity.statement: A 2023 NZ Institute of Economic Research report stated that the economic value of the Hauraki Gulf is $100 billion and produces over $5 billion of value each and every year, to this country.
veracity.explanation: Relays figures attributed to a named 2023 NZIER report — a $100 billion asset value for the Gulf and over $5 billion of value generated annually.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2023 NZIER report on the Hauraki Gulf: true if it puts the Gulf's asset value at about $100 billion and annual value generated at over $5 billion; false if the report gives materially different figures or contains no such valuation.

divination.statement: With a covered centre court, we’ll be able to serve up more events year-round, and welcome even more fans, players, and international media.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that roofing the centre court will increase the number of events held there and the number of visitors attending. Not a promise of the Government's own action — the outcome depends on event organisers choosing the venue.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The event schedule for the Manuka Doctor Arena centre court in the twelve months following completion of the roof, compared with a comparable pre-roof year: true if the number of ticketed events hosted on centre court rises; false if it is the same or lower.

civility.statement: No. Is it just me or have I answered this question half a dozen times already?
civility.explanation: Mockery of the questioner for repetition rather than engagement with the question. Short of a direct insult, but dismissive of the person asking rather than the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Because as the Treasury has previously acknowledged extensively on the record, they vastly overestimated their growth assumptions in the pre-election fiscal update, which may have been convenient for the Minister at the time but was inaccurate none the less.
civility.explanation: 'which may have been convenient for the Minister at the time' imputes a self-serving motive to the then-Minister rather than confining the criticism to the forecast itself — insinuation of bad faith aimed at a person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: No. As my mother once said to me, if you can’t say anything nice, which I can’t right now, don’t say anything at all.
civility.explanation: A pointed riposte to a jibe about her numeracy. It implies there is nothing good to say about the questioner, but stops short of landing an insult on her.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Has she considered asking for help with her numeracy, considering that she considers negative growth to be a sign of recovery?
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the Minister's personal competence — suggesting she needs remedial help with numbers — rather than on the economic argument being made.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Higher unemployment is a result of an economic downturn driven by high interest rates—high interest rates needed to bring down inflation, fuelled by reckless and undisciplined Government spending.
rigor.explanation: A genuine causal chain — unemployment from downturn, downturn from rates, rates from inflation — but the final and most contested link (that the previous Government's spending caused the inflation) is simply asserted with nothing offered to support it. Reasonable shape, real gap at the end.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, if that member’s version of economics is that every Government should take responsibility for every firm that ever fails, then I invite her to have a chat with Barbara Edmonds.
rigor.explanation: Strawman. The question was whether specific policy settings contributed to one firm's collapse; the answer recasts it as the absurd position that governments are responsible for every business failure, and refutes that instead.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, as I pointed out to her colleague Ginny Andersen in the previous answer, a number of factors contribute to firms no longer being profitable. One of those factors is very high interest rates, which is why our Government has worked so hard to take pressure off inflation and ensure the Reserve Bank has had space to reduce those interest rates.
rigor.explanation: A real inference — multiple causes of firm failure, interest rates among them, hence the policy of easing inflation pressure. Valid as far as it goes, but the step from 'rates matter' to 'our actions created the space for cuts' is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: How can she justify her plan when it has led to rising power and rent costs and a failing construction industry that has forced Auckland-based business Pipe Vision to go under and to cut 100 jobs?
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: the failure of one named firm is attributed to the Government's plan without anything offered to connect the two, and a single business closure would not establish a policy-wide effect even if the link held.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But isn’t it ironic that the very member who asked that question today also, along with her party, voted for it yesterday.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque. Whether the questioner's party voted for the bill has no bearing on whether the commercial-fishing carve-out damages the Gulf, which is what was asked. The inconsistency, if real, does not answer the question.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, no. How could they possibly be left out when they are represented by Dana Kirkpatrick and Katie Nimon, two of the extraordinary members of Parliament in the National Party caucus?
focus.explanation: Asked about 837 job losses in Hawke's Bay and 40 roles at EIT, the answer names no policy, figure or outcome at all — it is entirely about the quality of her own party's MPs. Nothing on-policy remains once the party content is removed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can she justify her plan when it has led to rising power and rent costs and a failing construction industry that has forced Auckland-based business Pipe Vision to go under and to cut 100 jobs?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named government economic plan against named outcomes — power and rent costs, a named firm, a job figure. This is accountability, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why did he allow eleventh-hour lobbying to influence changes that now enable commercial fishing in high protection areas, when reports show that it will further damage the health of the Gulf?
focus.explanation: Squarely on a specific provision of the measure just passed — the commercial fishing carve-out in high protection areas — and the process by which it was changed. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What I can say is that we have aspirations for all young New Zealanders and it was fantastic, just last week, to meet with an organisation employing young disabled people.
specificity.explanation: Asked about a concrete access barrier to the Supported Living Payment, the reply offers a general aspiration and a single visit with no figures, mechanism or timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In August 2025, there were 135 more businesses in accommodation and food services than the previous month and that is trending up.
specificity.explanation: Named month, named industry classification, an exact figure and a stated comparison base — anyone could go to the series and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does she consider the more than 2,500 hospitality closures and almost 300 liquidations in the past 12 months evidence that her Government is driving economic growth for the hospitality industry?
specificity.explanation: Two exact counts, a defined sector and a defined 12-month window. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That's why I was pleased to see reports from the District Court's civil jurisdiction showing active cases down 20 percent in the year to July 2025 and the average age of active cases dropping by a remarkable 36 percent over the same period.
specificity.explanation: Named jurisdiction, named period, two percentage figures and the measure each applies to.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Budget 2025 contained funding of $18.3 million over four years to fund two additional High Court judges and associated staff, as well as expand the number of community magistrates by three and appointing the Chief Community Magistrate.
specificity.explanation: Dollar figure, funding term, headcounts and named roles. Fully checkable against the Budget documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That includes the Pacific Business Trust and Pacific Business Village, which placed hundreds of people in the last financial year; the partnership with Pacific Media Network, through the Moana Reo Media Fund, which, again, has placed hundreds of jobs; and Pacific Building Affordable Homes and Our Whare Our Fale, which are stimulating Pacific-led construction and employment, as just a few examples.
specificity.explanation: Five programmes are named, which is real detail, but the outcomes attached to them are 'hundreds' twice over and 'stimulating' once — no counts, no baseline, no timeframe beyond 'the last financial year'. A direction with detail, missing the how much.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he regret repeatedly cutting funding to the Ministry for Pacific Peoples, including cutting $22 million out of the Tupu Aotearoa work-ready programme at a time when Pacifica unemployment is 12.1 percent, more than double the national average?
specificity.explanation: Named ministry, named programme, exact dollar figure, exact rate and an explicit comparison to the national average.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Let me be clear that the jobseeker (health condition and disability) is, as I said in my primary answer, for temporary conditions. We have other systems like ACC to support people who have had severe accidents and the Supported Living Payment for those with permanent incapacity.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: the benefit targets temporary conditions, other instruments cover the severe cases raised, therefore the test is not unfair to them. It holds only if ACC and SLP in fact cover the three cases put to her (cancer treatment in particular fits neither cleanly), so there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded, but the structure is sound.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because we want to see them engaged in education, engaged in training, and preparing for work, and if they can't, then to be supported by their parents. It's a very simple policy.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered for the restriction, but the inference skips the premise the question rested on — that these recipients cannot work or train — and substitutes parental support without showing it is available. The conclusion rests on an assumption the question had already contested.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That's exactly why there are programmes to support them. We don't think that it is acceptable in a country like ours to leave a whole generation of New Zealanders to rot on welfare.
rigor.explanation: False dilemma: the alternatives are presented as restricting access on one hand or leaving a generation 'to rot on welfare' on the other, with nothing offered to rule out the middle case the question described — people who cannot train or work and still need income support.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I disagree. If you look at another quote from Hospitality New Zealand, you can see that they are incredibly supportive of the Government’s major tourism and events boost and they know the enormous difference that that will make.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority: a survey finding that 77 percent of CBD business owners feel unheard is answered with an industry body's endorsement of a different policy. The endorsement does not bear on the survey result, so the conclusion does not follow from what was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What does it say about the state of the economy when popular Wellington venue Fortune Favours is forced to close, saying, the “cost of living crisis has proven too difficult”, after business dropped nearly 45 percent in two years?
rigor.explanation: Argument from anecdote: the state of the national economy is inferred from one venue's closure. The example is real and specific, but a single case cannot carry the general conclusion invited.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: How can he say that the MSD programmes was actually for efficiencies when he previously claimed that it, and I quote, “was particularly to look at those who are not in employment, education, and training, different to MSD in that it wasn’t limited or capped by the age bracket, like MSD”?
rigor.explanation: A clean inference from a quoted prior statement: if the Minister earlier described the programme as distinct from MSD's in scope and age coverage, the claim that merging it generates efficiencies through duplication is inconsistent with his own account. The premise is supplied verbatim and the conclusion tracks it; it stops short of ruling out that both could be partly true.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That's exactly why there are programmes to support them. We don't think that it is acceptable in a country like ours to leave a whole generation of New Zealanders to rot on welfare.
civility.explanation: The policy point is fair game, but 'rot on welfare' is contemptuous language about the people receiving the benefit rather than about the policy. No individual is attacked, so this is a mild failure rather than an insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That member should have listened to the answer I gave to my first question, which was to say exactly that economic challenges from high inflation and high interest rates, which have led to an economic recession, have made it difficult for businesses to operate.
civility.explanation: The substantive content is fine, but it is prefaced with a jab at the questioner's attentiveness rather than simply restating the point. Pointed and a little condescending toward the person, short of an insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Thank you for that patsy question from the member across.
civility.explanation: Dismisses an opposition question about the Chief Justice's stated concerns as a 'patsy question' — a sneer at the questioner's motive rather than an engagement with what was asked. She goes on to answer substantively, which limits the damage, but the opening imputes bad faith.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Our investments into tourism and hospitality will mean more international visitors, more full tables in our restaurants, more jobs being created across the country, and a stronger economy overall.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Government's tourism and hospitality investment will produce higher international visitor numbers and higher hospitality employment. The investment is her own action, but the visitor and jobs outcomes are forecasts about the world.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international visitor arrivals and Stats NZ accommodation and food services filled jobs / employment indicator, comparing the 12 months to October 2026 against the 12 months to October 2025. True if both international arrivals and hospitality employment are higher; false if either is flat or lower.

veracity.statement: In August 2025, there were 135 more businesses in accommodation and food services than the previous month and that is trending up.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a net gain of 135 businesses in the accommodation and food services industry from July 2025 to August 2025, and an upward trend.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ monthly business/employment indicators for the accommodation and food services industry: true if the August 2025 business count exceeds July 2025 by approximately 135 and the recent months trend upward; false if the month-on-month change is materially different or negative.

veracity.statement: Hospitality job advertisements are up 3.8 percent in July compared to last July.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 3.8 percent year-on-year rise in hospitality job advertisements for July 2025 against July 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE Jobs Online / SEEK NZ Employment Report series for the hospitality (accommodation and food services) category: true if July 2025 advertisements are about 3.8 percent above July 2024, false if the change is materially different or negative.

veracity.statement: Does she consider the more than 2,500 hospitality closures and almost 300 liquidations in the past 12 months evidence that her Government is driving economic growth for the hospitality industry?
veracity.explanation: Asserts more than 2,500 hospitality business closures and close to 300 liquidations in the 12 months to about October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Restaurant Association of New Zealand closure tracking and Companies Office / NZ Herald liquidation records for hospitality businesses over the 12 months to October 2025: true if closures exceed 2,500 and liquidations approach 300, false if either figure is materially lower.

veracity.statement: How can hospitality in Auckland’s CBD thrive when the Heart of the City survey showed that 77 percent of business owners say that the Government does not listen to their needs?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a named survey by Heart of the City found 77 percent of business owners saying the Government does not listen to their needs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Heart of the City member/business survey report published in 2025: true if it reports approximately 77 percent of respondents saying the Government does not listen to their needs, false if the figure or the question asked is materially different.

veracity.statement: That's why I was pleased to see reports from the District Court's civil jurisdiction showing active cases down 20 percent in the year to July 2025 and the average age of active cases dropping by a remarkable 36 percent over the same period.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two figures for the District Court civil jurisdiction in the year to July 2025: active cases down 20 percent and average age of active cases down 36 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice court statistics (civil jurisdiction, District Court) for the year to July 2025: true if active case volume fell about 20 percent and the mean age of active cases fell about 36 percent year on year, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Budget 2025 contained funding of $18.3 million over four years to fund two additional High Court judges and associated staff, as well as expand the number of community magistrates by three and appointing the Chief Community Magistrate.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific Budget 2025 appropriation of $18.3 million over four years and what it funds: two High Court judges plus staff, three additional community magistrates and a Chief Community Magistrate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 Estimates for Vote Courts / Vote Justice: true if an $18.3 million four-year appropriation exists with those components, false if the amount, term or the positions funded differ materially.

veracity.statement: Does he regret repeatedly cutting funding to the Ministry for Pacific Peoples, including cutting $22 million out of the Tupu Aotearoa work-ready programme at a time when Pacifica unemployment is 12.1 percent, more than double the national average?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $22 million cut to the Tupu Aotearoa programme and a current Pacific unemployment rate of 12.1 percent, more than double the national rate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024/2025 Estimates for Vote Pacific Peoples for the Tupu Aotearoa appropriation, and the Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey for the September 2025 quarter: true if the appropriation was reduced by about $22 million and the Pacific unemployment rate is about 12.1 percent against a national rate below 6.05 percent; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: When will he accept responsibility and take action to help Pasifika into employment or training, when, in the last year alone, 6,100 more Pasifika people are now unemployed and 1,900 more Pasifika young people are not in education, employment, or training?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that over the past year Pacific unemployment rose by 6,100 people and the number of Pacific young people not in employment, education or training rose by 1,900.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey, Pacific ethnic group, September 2024 quarter against September 2025 quarter: true if the unemployed count rose by about 6,100 and the Pacific youth NEET count rose by about 1,900; false if either change is materially different.

focus.statement: Does she agree with the Disabled Persons Assembly who told 1News last night that disabled people face barriers to access the Supported Living Payment due to a lack of access to diagnoses, and, if so, does she accept there are several people with long term conditions who are on jobseeker support (health and disabilities)?
focus.explanation: Names a specific payment, a specific access barrier (diagnosis availability) and a named source. Squarely on the policy mechanism, with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is it fair to subject 18- and 19-year-olds who are receiving jobseeker support (health condition or disability) to the new parental assistance test when they're suffering from severe ill mental health, recovering from a car accident, or undergoing cancer treatment as reported by 1News?
focus.explanation: Names the measure (the new parental assistance test), the affected cohort and the specific circumstances at issue. Scrutiny of a named policy, not a swipe at the party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What I regret is the actions the previous Government took that put us in this position.
focus.explanation: Asked about a specific $22 million cut to a named programme, the answer names no policy, no figure and no outcome — only the previous Government in general. Content-free party attribution rather than scrutiny of any particular decision.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It all survived because we fought for it, Māori and non-Māori alike.
rigor.explanation: A causal conclusion — that te reo, tikanga, kura kaupapa, kapa haka and Matariki survived through deliberate effort rather than accident — supported by the sequence of campaigns she then enumerates (the 1972 petition, the land march, kōhanga reo, kura kaupapa, Wai 11). The inference tracks the evidence offered; the small gap is that collective effort is asserted as the whole cause before any of it is laid out, with no alternative explanation considered.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In 1970, Ngā Tamatoa and Ngā Kaiwhakapūmau i te Reo lobbied for the introduction of te reo Māori into all schools.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that two named organisations, Ngā Tamatoa and Ngā Kaiwhakapūmau i te Reo, were both active in 1970 and that both lobbied for te reo Māori to be taught in all schools.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Founding dates and campaign records for both groups (Te Ara / NZHistory entries, Ngā Kaiwhakapūmau i te Reo's own organisational history, contemporary press). True if both existed in 1970 and both campaigned for te reo in all schools that year; false if either was founded after 1970 or did not run that campaign then.

veracity.statement: Two years later, the Māori language petition, signed by over 30,000 New Zealanders, was carried to the very steps of this Parliament; ordinary people, extraordinary in their vision, stood up to say that the language of our tīpuna and of this whenua will not die.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the te reo Māori petition was presented to Parliament in 1972 (two years after 1970) carrying more than 30,000 signatures.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The parliamentary petition record and NZHistory/Te Ara accounts of the 1972 Māori language petition. True if the petition was presented to Parliament in 1972 with a signature count above 30,000; false if the date differs or the signature count was materially below 30,000.

veracity.statement: May I remind everyone in this House and out there that in 1975, just 5 percent of all Māori schoolchildren could speak and even understand their own mother tongue; 5 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure: that as at 1975, 5 percent of Māori schoolchildren could speak and understand te reo Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Richard Benton's NZCER national survey of Māori language use (1973–1979) and Te Taura Whiri / Te Ara summaries of it. True if the surveyed proportion of Māori schoolchildren who spoke te reo was approximately 5 percent around 1975; false if the figure was materially different or measured a different population.

veracity.statement: Ruātoki stepped up first. They became the first bilingual school in the entire country in 1978.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Ruātoki was New Zealand's first bilingual school and that it became so in 1978.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education / NZHistory / Te Ara records of the designation of Ruatoki School as New Zealand's first bilingual school. True if the designation was in 1978 and Ruatoki was first; false if the year was different or another school preceded it.

veracity.statement: In 1982, the first kōhanga reo, Pukeatua, was opened in Wainuiomata.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Pukeatua in Wainuiomata was the first kōhanga reo and that it opened in 1982.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Kōhanga Reo National Trust records and NZHistory accounts of the first kōhanga reo. True if Pukeatua Kōhanga Reo, Wainuiomata, opened in 1982 as the first; false if another kōhanga reo opened first or the year differs.

veracity.statement: That same year, the Waitangi Tribunal heard the te reo Māori claim Wai 11.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Waitangi Tribunal heard the te reo Māori claim (Wai 11) in 1985 — the year referred to in the preceding sentence, in which Te Kura Kaupapa Māori o Hoani Waititi opened.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal's Report on the Te Reo Maori Claim (Wai 11) and the Tribunal's record of hearing dates for that claim. True if hearings on Wai 11 took place in 1985; false if the hearings fell wholly in another year.

specificity.statement: May I remind everyone in this House and out there that in 1975, just 5 percent of all Māori schoolchildren could speak and even understand their own mother tongue; 5 percent.
specificity.explanation: Carries a precise, checkable figure tied to a named year and a defined population — someone could go to the survey data and verify it. It stops short of 1.0 only because the source of the figure is not named.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I would highlight Alo Vaka, which, amongst other things, developed 14 micro-credentialing courses in the last financial year and more than 6,000 micro-credentials delivered to Pasifika, particularly Pasifika youth.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific programme, a count of courses, a delivery volume and a time period — someone could check the Ministry for Pacific Peoples' annual report against it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the South Island, access to primary mental health support has improved from 75 percent in quarter one to 84.7 percent in quarter four—well above the target. The Southern district went from being one of the worst-performing districts, at 66.4 percent, to one of the best, at 91 percent of Southern residents accessing services within one week.
specificity.explanation: Region, district, four separate percentages and the quarters they refer to; fully checkable against the published target data.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When we came in, there were 185,000 New Zealanders suffering violent offences; we've reduced that down to 156,000 in the latest stats.
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures against a stated baseline and a stated end point; directly checkable against the victimisation survey.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I would highlight Alo Vaka, which, amongst other things, developed 14 micro-credentialing courses in the last financial year and more than 6,000 micro-credentials delivered to Pasifika, particularly Pasifika youth.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two countable programme outputs for the last financial year: 14 courses developed, 6,000+ micro-credentials delivered.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry for Pacific Peoples annual report / Alo Vaka programme reporting for the 2024/25 financial year; true if 14 micro-credentialing courses were developed and more than 6,000 micro-credentials were delivered, false if the figures are materially lower.

veracity.statement: In the South Island, access to primary mental health support has improved from 75 percent in quarter one to 84.7 percent in quarter four—well above the target. The Southern district went from being one of the worst-performing districts, at 66.4 percent, to one of the best, at 91 percent of Southern residents accessing services within one week.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific quarter-one and quarter-four figures for South Island and Southern district access within one week.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand quarterly mental health target data for the faster-access-to-primary-mental-health measure, Q1 vs Q4 2024/25; true if South Island moved 75% → 84.7% and Southern district 66.4% → 91%, false if the published figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: We’re also increasing the front-line mental health workforce, which has grown by 10 percent since coming into office, with the child and adolescent workforce growing by 19 percent and peer support lived experience by almost 100 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three workforce growth percentages measured since the Government took office in late 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand mental health workforce headcount/FTE data for late 2023 vs 2025; true if the total front-line mental health workforce grew ~10%, child and adolescent ~19% and peer support lived experience near 100%, false if the published series show materially different growth or a decline.

veracity.statement: It is also a fact that Māori are disproportionately overrepresented as victims of crime in New Zealand, which is why this Government is focused on restoring real consequences for crime and reducing the number of victims of crime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori are victimised by crime at a disproportionately high rate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey victimisation rates by ethnicity; true if the Māori victimisation rate is materially above the national rate, false if it is at or below it.

veracity.statement: No, I don't think that would be helpful to Māori victims of crime, and that certainly appears to be the Greens’ policy.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that defunding the police and letting offenders go without prosecution is Green Party policy.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Green Party published justice and police policy for the 2023 term; true if it commits to defunding police and to not prosecuting offenders, false if it proposes redirecting some funding or reducing reliance on police without either commitment.

veracity.statement: I certainly can confirm that Corrections and the broader justice sector are very focused primarily on reducing the number of victims of crime, regardless of their ethnicity; unlike the previous Government, which had a focus on reducing the number of people in prison irrespective of what was going on in the community.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government's justice focus was on reducing the prison muster.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2017–2023 Labour-led Government's stated justice targets, in particular the commitment to reduce the prison population by 30 percent; true if such a target was adopted, false if no prison-population reduction objective is on record.

veracity.statement: When we came in, there were 185,000 New Zealanders suffering violent offences; we've reduced that down to 156,000 in the latest stats.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fall from 185,000 to 156,000 New Zealanders victimised by violent offending since late 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey estimates of the number of people experiencing violent interpersonal offences, 2023 cycle vs the most recent cycle; true if the figures are approximately 185,000 and 156,000, false if they differ materially.

veracity.statement: They do feel safer than they did a couple of years ago, but we can do so much better as a country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealanders' subjective sense of safety has improved over roughly the past two years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey (or the Government's public safety perception measures) on feelings of safety, comparing the 2023 cycle with the most recent; true if reported perceptions of safety have improved, false if they are flat or worse.

veracity.statement: Was Moana Jackson wrong when he said, “the majority of those behind bars are Māori, and the system itself reflects a punishing and very real racism.”, or does he accept that the overrepresentation of Māori in prisons is a reflection of structural racism?
veracity.explanation: Relays Moana Jackson's assertion that Māori make up the majority of the prison population; the accompanying 'punishing and very real racism' characterisation is an interpretation and is not the checkable part.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections prison population statistics by ethnicity for the period referred to; the relayed claim that the majority of prisoners are Māori is true if more than 50 percent of the prison population identifies as Māori, false if it is 50 percent or less.

rigor.statement: It is also a fact that Māori are disproportionately overrepresented as victims of crime in New Zealand, which is why this Government is focused on restoring real consequences for crime and reducing the number of victims of crime.
rigor.explanation: The 'which is why' does not follow from the premise: that Māori are disproportionately victimised establishes a need to reduce victimisation, not that stiffer consequences are the mechanism that will do it. The causal link between the premise and the chosen policy is asserted, not shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In regards to structural racism, I would say that that’s a very easy phrase for an academic to use, but I would say to the thousands of New Zealanders—Māori, Pākehā, and from a wide variety of ethnicities—who get up early every morning to work at Corrections or the courts or in many parts of the justice sector, the suggestion that they are just mere cogs in the wheel of a structurally racist regime is an insult to those people who work hard every day to do the right thing for this country and to keep New Zealanders safe.
rigor.explanation: Strawman plus appeal to emotion: a claim about systemic outcomes is answered as though it were an accusation that individual Corrections and court staff are racist, and the conclusion rests on the offence that reframing would cause rather than on any evidence about outcomes.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, if you're wanting to reduce the number of victims of crime, a very good place to start is with that very, very small section of New Zealand society that creates multiple victims over and over again. The primary focus is effective rehabilitation of people who have been involved in violent crime, but there are some people that need to be kept out of society for a while so that the rest of society can be kept safe.
rigor.explanation: An incapacitation argument that is coherent in outline but leaves the asked-for step unsupported: nothing offered connects a higher prison population to fewer Māori victims, and the premise that a small group produces most victimisation is asserted without evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No, I don't think that would be helpful to Māori victims of crime, and that certainly appears to be the Greens’ policy.
focus.explanation: Adopts a loaded characterisation of another party's position rather than engaging any named measure; no policy document, mechanism or figure is identified — the content is what the Greens are supposedly like on crime.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does the Minister think that defunding the police and letting offenders go without prosecution has any chance of helping innocent Māori victims?
focus.explanation: The question exists to attach a caricatured position to opponents rather than to test a measure before the House; no specific policy, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I certainly can confirm that Corrections and the broader justice sector are very focused primarily on reducing the number of victims of crime, regardless of their ethnicity; unlike the previous Government, which had a focus on reducing the number of people in prison irrespective of what was going on in the community.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy contrast — it names a real prior objective (reducing the prison population) against a current one — but the second half is carried by party framing about what the previous Government was like rather than by any figure or mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What evidence does he have that a higher prison population makes Māori safer?
focus.explanation: Directs the Minister squarely at the evidence base for a specific policy direction and its claimed outcome; it is scrutiny of a named policy proposition, not commentary on the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can the Minister also confirm that Māori are disproportionately represented among the victims of crime, and would it help to go soft on the perpetrators for reasons of political correctness?
focus.explanation: The first half raises a real policy fact, but the second half swaps policy for a caricature of opponents' motives ('political correctness') with no measure, mechanism or figure attached.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Could the Minister tell us exactly how many Māori accused did Moana Jackson ever defend at court?
civility.explanation: A personal attack on a named individual's standing and credentials rather than on the argument attributed to him — it invites the House to dismiss the person, not the claim about structural racism.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In regards to structural racism, I would say that that’s a very easy phrase for an academic to use, but I would say to the thousands of New Zealanders—Māori, Pākehā, and from a wide variety of ethnicities—who get up early every morning to work at Corrections or the courts or in many parts of the justice sector, the suggestion that they are just mere cogs in the wheel of a structurally racist regime is an insult to those people who work hard every day to do the right thing for this country and to keep New Zealanders safe.
civility.explanation: 'A very easy phrase for an academic to use' dismisses the source rather than the claim — condescension toward the person who made the argument, short of a direct insult but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This sessional order has come from a submission from the Petitions Committee that they made to the Standing Orders Committee regarding petitions with highly discriminatory content, which currently must be uploaded to the Parliament website, even without the requisite number of signatures needed to be presented to the House.
specificity.explanation: Names the originating committee, the receiving committee, and the precise defect being remedied (automatic hosting regardless of signature threshold). Mechanism is identifiable and checkable, but carries no figures, dates or thresholds.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There was unanimous agreement on the Standing Orders Committee that this was a matter which should be addressed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Standing Orders Committee reached unanimity that petitions with highly discriminatory content required a rule change. A claim about a past committee proceeding, not an opinion about the merits.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Standing Orders Committee's report/minutes on the Petitions Committee submission regarding highly discriminatory electronic petitions; true if the committee's recommendation was recorded without dissent or minority view from any party member, false if any member or party recorded opposition or a differing view.

rigor.statement: This sessional order now gives the Clerk the ability to not post those petitions on the website. In fact, those petitions could still occur on a paper form by doing the rounds in the kind of old-fashioned way. But that doesn't give it the appearance of this Parliament approving, as in any way legitimate, petitions which are outright offensive.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference with premises and conclusion: the harm identified is the appearance of parliamentary endorsement, the paper route remains open, therefore the remedy removes the endorsement without removing the petition. The conclusion tracks the premises; the only gap is an unargued assumption that hosting is read as endorsement, which he states rather than establishes. No fallacy present.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This will not prevent paper petitions of that nature from going out in the community; I don’t think, therefore, that anyone could argue that this is about restricting people’s ability to canvass petitions in their communities.
rigor.explanation: The premise (an alternative paper channel survives) supports a narrow conclusion, but he draws a much wider one — that nobody could argue restriction is at issue. The availability of a lesser-reach channel does not establish the absence of any restriction, so the conclusion overreaches the premise; the 'no one could argue' framing also forecloses the objection rather than answering it.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: There is a reference in there to the prohibited grounds of discrimination under the Human Rights Act as a guiding light, but not the sole basis for refusing a petition, and this will be in place for six months, I suspect, that it will be seen as a useful innovation, and I hope will become a permanent feature of our Standing Orders, but that's not for today.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the six-month trial will be judged a useful innovation and carried into the permanent Standing Orders. The outcome rests with the Standing Orders Committee and the House at the next review, not with the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Standing Orders of the House of Representatives as adopted at the next full Standing Orders review following the trial; true if a permanent Standing Order empowering the Clerk to refuse to host electronic petitions with highly discriminatory content is adopted, false if the sessional order lapses or is not carried into the Standing Orders.

focus.statement: This will not prevent paper petitions of that nature from going out in the community; I don’t think, therefore, that anyone could argue that this is about restricting people’s ability to canvass petitions in their communities.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — what the sessional order does and does not do to petitioning. No party framing, no reference to opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It combines the four separate Acts that currently set out these arrangements.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Parliament Bill consolidates exactly four existing statutes governing Parliament's operation, privileges, remuneration and support agencies.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliament Bill as reported back and its explanatory note / general policy statement: true if the bill repeals and consolidates exactly four Acts (expected: Parliamentary Service Act 2000, Clerk of the House of Representatives Act 1988, Members of Parliament (Remuneration and Services) Act 2013, Parliamentary Privilege Act 2014); false if the number of Acts consolidated is other than four.

veracity.statement: The committee received 62 submissions, and several of them dealt with constitutional matters, as you would expect for a bill of this nature.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific submission count for the Parliament Bill Committee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliament Bill Committee's report to the House on the Parliament Bill, submissions section: true if the report records 62 submissions received, false if it records a materially different number.

veracity.statement: All the committee’s recommendations are unanimous, and I thank the committee’s members for their approach and diligent work on the bill under the guidance of the chairperson, the Rt Hon Adrian Rurawhe.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that every recommendation in the committee's report was unanimous and that Adrian Rurawhe chaired the Parliament Bill Committee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliament Bill Committee's report: true if it contains no minority or differing views on any recommendation and names Adrian Rurawhe as chairperson; false if any recommendation carries a dissenting/minority view or the chair was someone else.

specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Those powers, for example, of a security guard to detain someone or take them out of the gallery if they’re being disruptive or to exclude them from the premises if they’re causing undue harm are entirely appropriate, but we absolutely want to know how and why those powers are exercised.

focus.statement: Those additional mechanisms include the requirement to report the uses of detention, force, and handcuffs to the Chief Executive of the Parliamentary Service within three days; the requirement for Parliamentary Service to report on the number of uses of detention, force, handcuffs, seizures, and removal of persons in Parliamentary Service’s annual report; the requirement for an approved training course for security officers, to be consulted on with Police and the Ministry of Justice; the requirement for identity cards held and presented by parliamentary security officers to include name, role, photograph, and unique ID number; and other measures.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the content of the measure before the House — the specific oversight safeguards added at committee. No party content whatsoever.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But we have seen over the few years that risks to MPs have increased, and it is necessary to give powers to security staff, employees of Parliamentary Service and, in some cases, others to address those risks.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that security risks to Members of Parliament have risen over the past several years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary Service / Diplomatic Protection Service and NZ Police records of reported threats and security incidents involving MPs across roughly 2019–2025, together with any figures given in Parliamentary Service annual reports. True if reported threat and incident counts rose materially over the period; false if they were flat or declined.

veracity.statement: Some of us in the House will know that the number of submissions being made on bills has increased and the work associated with it has increased as well and the amount of work that Governments are pushing through has increased.
veracity.explanation: Three linked factual claims about trends: that select committee submission volumes have risen, that the associated committee workload has risen, and that the volume of legislation Governments are putting through has risen.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Office of the Clerk and Parliamentary Service annual reports for submission counts received by select committees per year, and the Parliament website's record of bills introduced and passed per year, comparing the current Parliament with the preceding two. rigor.statement: But we have seen over the few years that risks to MPs have increased, and it is necessary to give powers to security staff, employees of Parliamentary Service and, in some cases, others to address those risks.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House: increased risk is offered as the premise and the grant of powers as the conclusion. The premise supports doing something, but the step to 'it is necessary' to confer these particular powers on these particular people is asserted rather than shown — a gap between what is offered and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reason why was actually well articulated by advisers—that is that it is the executive who is bound by the Treaty, not Parliament. rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: given the premise that Treaty obligations run between the Crown (the executive) and Māori rather than between the legislature and Māori, the conclusion that recognising the Treaty in the Parliament Act was not constitutionally appropriate does follow. It leans partly on an appeal to the committee's advisers, but he supplies the substantive reason himself rather than resting on their say-so, which is what keeps it well above the middle.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In my personal opinion, what I have observed is that with a growing population, with growing complex issues in our communities, the current mechanisms that are in place to ensure that parliamentary services and the Office of the Clerk are adequately resourced to, for example, ensure that we meet the needs of our communities at the select committee, are just insufficient.
rigor.explanation: An argument about the policy is offered — population growth and increasing complexity are given as premises for the conclusion that the current resourcing mechanisms are insufficient. specificity.statement: Those powers, for example, of a security guard to detain someone or take them out of the gallery if they’re being disruptive or to exclude them from the premises if they’re causing undue harm are entirely appropriate, but we absolutely want to know how and why those powers are exercised.

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Those additional mechanisms include the requirement to report the uses of detention, force, and handcuffs to the Chief Executive of the Parliamentary Service within three days; the requirement for Parliamentary Service to report on the number of uses of detention, force, handcuffs, seizures, and removal of persons in Parliamentary Service’s annual report; the requirement for an approved training course for security officers, to be consulted on with Police and the Ministry of Justice; the requirement for identity cards held and presented by parliamentary security officers to include name, role, photograph, and unique ID number; and other measures.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates named mechanisms with a timeframe (three days), a named reporting vehicle (the annual report), named consultation partners (Police and the Ministry of Justice) and the exact contents of an ID card. Every element is checkable against the bill as reported back.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The committee made some amendments because we want to be very, very clear that there is additional training for those staff—because that was something that came through the submissions—and also, if there's an exercise of any of those powers, particularly issues where force is used or detention is used, the officer involved reports those within three days, and also—second tier—that the Chief Executive of the Parliamentary Service reports those in their annual report.
specificity.explanation: Names the actual mechanisms added by the select committee: a training requirement, an officer report within a stated three-day window whenever force or detention is used, and a second-tier reporting duty on a named office in a named document. Someone could check each against the bill. Short of 1.0 only because the scope of the training is not described.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There have been a number of amendments that have soothed some of those issues, but I also reflect that the good outcomes and the improvements have come from being able to take the time. specificity.explanation: Names no bill, no amendment, and no process change. specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I don't think they actually realised that they are published every quarter anyway, and, by crikey, I think we all know that the finance team are assiduous in pursuing every single receipt that we've got or haven't got.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliamentary Service members' expense disclosure releases on parliament.nz as at October 2025: true if members' expense and allowance information is routinely published on a quarterly cycle; false if publication is annual, ad hoc, on request only, or not made at all.

veracity.statement: However, at the moment, the budget for the agencies of Parliament—the Office of the Clerk and Parliamentary Services—is set by the executive, not by Parliament.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that, as the law stood in October 2025, the appropriations for the Office of the Clerk and the Parliamentary Service were determined through the executive's Budget process rather than by Parliament itself.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The appropriations process for Vote Office of the Clerk and Vote Parliamentary Service prior to the Parliament Bill, per the Clerk of the House of Representatives Act 1988, the Parliamentary Service Act 2000 and Treasury Budget documents: true if those appropriations were determined by Ministers through the ordinary Budget process; false if Parliament (or the Speaker/Parliamentary Service Commission) already fixed them independently of Ministers.

rigor.statement: There have been a number of amendments that have soothed some of those issues, but I also reflect that the good outcomes and the improvements have come from being able to take the time. I think there’s a number of pieces of legislation that would hugely benefit from a more considered approach.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: this bill improved, the improvement is attributed to time taken, therefore other legislation would benefit from the same. rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Our committee services at the moment are under huge pressure, and again, this is one of the issues of ramming through legislation too fast.

focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I will support this bill on behalf of the Green Party, but unless there is some budget allocated for improvements to parliamentary services and the support of the staff, we will not, as a country, be as well served as we should be.
specificity.explanation: Names the thing sought (budget for parliamentary services and staff support) but supplies no amount, no mechanism and no timeframe; the consequence clause is unquantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It is a very transparent process, what is being proposed—very similar to how Officers of Parliament operate as well—and so it would mean that all parties would be represented on a select committee to decide and to consider budget applications from the Office of the Clerk and from the Parliamentary Service, and would be scrutinised by, basically, all parties in Parliament.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the mechanism (a select committee with all-party representation), the bodies whose applications it considers (Office of the Clerk, Parliamentary Service) and the comparator regime, but gives no figures or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I'll summarise the changes that we made in increasing reporting and increasing monitoring, because there were concerns that were raised around whether there was enough reporting and monitoring of what those officers will be doing: if they use their new powers, that must be reported to the CEO within three days, and the CEO must report those at least annually.

specificity.statement: Just a really short call from me this afternoon, to say this is a really collaborative and proactive approach to the legislation around how this place actually operates and how it works, bringing together four different Acts to enable a modern framework for Parliament to work as best as it possibly can, and the agencies that support this incredible place.
specificity.explanation: One checkable detail (the bill consolidates four Acts) carried on a string of generic descriptors — 'collaborative', 'proactive', 'modern framework' — with no Acts named, no provisions and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The special select committee received 62 submissions from some notable New Zealanders who had given some of the constitutional, weighty matters great thought and great consideration.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count: that the Parliament Bill Committee received 62 submissions on the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliament Bill Committee's report to the House and the committee's published submissions list on parliament.nz; true if the number of submissions received is 62, false if the record shows a materially different number.

veracity.statement: Ultimately, the recommendations that the committee has made were unanimously agreed by members of Parliament representing every party in this current Parliament.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliament Bill Committee's report: true if it records unanimous agreement with no minority or differing views appended, and the membership list covers every party in the House; false if the report carries a minority view, a dissent, or omits a party.

veracity.statement: Just a really short call from me this afternoon, to say this is a really collaborative and proactive approach to the legislation around how this place actually operates and how it works, bringing together four different Acts to enable a modern framework for Parliament to work as best as it possibly can, and the agencies that support this incredible place.

rigor.statement: Over the years, of the 150 or so years of unbroken, stable political democracy, participatory democracy, in New Zealand, society has changed, attitudes have changed, and so too must this institution of Parliament evolve, change, modify, and reform itself.
rigor.explanation: A real inference — society and attitudes have changed, therefore Parliament must reform — but the conclusion is asserted rather than supported: nothing is offered connecting social change to any particular need for institutional reform. A gap between what is shown and what is concluded, leaning on the general appeal to modernisation.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is a very transparent process, what is being proposed—very similar to how Officers of Parliament operate as well—and so it would mean that all parties would be represented on a select committee to decide and to consider budget applications from the Office of the Clerk and from the Parliamentary Service, and would be scrutinised by, basically, all parties in Parliament.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (the proposed budget process is transparent) is supported by a stated mechanism — all-party representation on the deciding committee and all-party scrutiny of applications — plus an analogy to Officers of Parliament. The analogy carries some weight it does not earn, but the mechanism does most of the work and the inference largely holds.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In terms of security, I encourage MPs to actually go and speak to some of our security officers around Parliament, and especially some of the ones that have been around for a little while, and they'll happily tell you why these changes are necessary.
rigor.explanation: The case for the new security powers rests entirely on an appeal to anecdote and to the authority of the officers who would receive them — no evidence or reasoning is offered for why the changes are necessary, only an invitation to be told so by interested parties.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In April 2019, there was a decision taken to stretch those rules into a whole host of new tribunals, including the lawyers disciplinary tribunal and other tribunals as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in April 2019 the Courts Security Act regime was extended by decision to a range of tribunals, the Lawyers and Conveyancers Disciplinary Tribunal among them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ legislation website: whether an amendment or Order in Council commencing in April 2019 (e.g. the Tribunals Powers and Procedures Legislation Act 2018 amendments) applied the Courts Security Act 1999 to additional tribunals, and whether the New Zealand Lawyers and Conveyancers Disciplinary Tribunal was among them. True if such an instrument took effect in April 2019 covering that tribunal; false if no such extension occurred, or if it took effect in a materially different period or did not cover that tribunal.

veracity.statement: If you look at Australia, the UK, and Canada, there aren’t specific statutory powers or immunities as we’re writing them in.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the comparable Westminster-system Parliaments of Australia, the UK and Canada have no statutes conferring security powers or immunities on parliamentary security staff of the kind in this bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Statute books of the three jurisdictions: Australia's Parliamentary Precincts Act 1988 and Parliamentary Service Act 1999, the UK's Parliamentary Corporate Bodies Act 1992 and any security-officer powers provisions, and Canada's Parliament of Canada Act provisions establishing the Parliamentary Protective Service. True if none of the three confers statutory search/removal powers or immunities on parliamentary security staff; false if any of them does.

veracity.statement: I think, with 25 percent of our population identifying as having some sort of disability, there’s certainly a need for Parliament to consider whether it’s time for us to have that kind of review in place.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 25 percent of the New Zealand population identify as having some form of disability.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Disability Survey (most recent release before October 2025, plus the 2013 Disability Survey). True if the disabled-population share is approximately 25% on the official measure; false if the official figure is materially different (e.g. below ~20%).

rigor.statement: I did look to see if there had been complaints made or anything that was very obvious in the media space in this area, and I really couldn’t find anything, which says to me that the rules are set in a reasonable way.
rigor.explanation: Argument from absence of evidence: an informal, unsystematic search for media coverage or complaints is treated as showing the rules are reasonable. Absence of visible complaint is weak support for that conclusion — complaints about court security may simply not be reported, and the search method is not described. It is nonetheless a genuine inference about the measure, not a swipe at opponents.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I'm not suggesting that, but I think we're living in a world where things now happen that mean that the people who are at the front line—those are our security guards—need to be given appropriate powers.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that security staff need new powers rests on a single personal anecdote (a banner drop that frightened her) plus an unspecified claim that 'things now happen'. Argument from anecdote with a gap between the evidence offered and the conclusion drawn — no link is shown between the incident and the particular powers, and nothing is offered on why existing arrangements were inadequate.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There’s language, for example, in the drafting that says, “involves no physical contact” when they’re using electronic screening devices, or only the “external examination of the person’s clothes”.

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Speaking to a few legal colleagues about this, some raised issues about the institution that is the Independent Police Conduct Authority and whether it would be useful to expand the powers of an institution like that so that it also covered not only security staff on precinct here but all the other security officers who are using similar powers in the courts and in the tribunals.
specificity.explanation: Names the institution and the class of officers the proposed oversight would cover, but offers no mechanism, timeframe or drafting for how the extension would work — a direction with partial detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I think that perhaps we should look at some other iterations of this later, things like perhaps a buddy system.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete idea — a buddy system — but supplies no mechanism, eligibility, cost or timeframe, and defers it to an unspecified 'later'. There is a direction here but almost nothing anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Speaking to a few legal colleagues about this, some raised issues about the institution that is the Independent Police Conduct Authority and whether it would be useful to expand the powers of an institution like that so that it also covered not only security staff on precinct here but all the other security officers who are using similar powers in the courts and in the tribunals.

focus.subject: speaker

focus.explanation: Names the specific change the bill makes (the Parliamentary Library becoming a standard business unit) and its practical effect, which is real policy content — but closes with a party-framed aside implying that hard-working constituent MPs sit on one side of the House, which carries no policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I remember in 2004, I was working for Tariana Turia at the time and she crossed the floor on the foreshore and seabed Act—well, bill then.

veracity.statement: It started before that at the Privy Council, when Ngāti Apa ki te Rā Tō took a case to the Privy Council over its rights being breached.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZME's November 2024 announcement and media reporting of it; true if 14 regional community newspapers were announced for closure on/around 14 November 2024 with about 30 roles lost, false if the count of titles or roles differs materially. The bill claim resolves against news reporting of its status in mid-November 2024.

veracity.statement: The other thing I’ve got here—I like lists; this is a list of dates, and on this list there are 49 dates during which Cabinet met and the Minister, in response to a question about what he took to that Cabinet meeting to help, what he took to those Cabinet meetings for immediate action for our broadcasting and media sector, the answer, for all of these 49 dates, is nothing—nothing taken; nothing offered; no immediate action.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that across 49 identified Cabinet meeting dates the Minister's own answers record that he took nothing on broadcasting and media to Cabinet.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The written parliamentary question answers from the Minister of Media and Communications covering Cabinet meetings over the period; true if the answers for 49 such dates disclose no paper or item on the broadcasting/media sector, false if papers were disclosed for some of those dates or the count of dates is materially wrong.
