civility.explanation: Leaves the substance to comment on the questioner's memory — a mild personal jibe rather than engagement with the strike question.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does she stand by her statement “I am not aware of any of those conversations or any of the details that may or may not have been talked about” in relation to the strikes; if so, does she think it’s acceptable for the Minister of Education to not be across the detail?
civility.explanation: Pointed and edging toward the Minister personally, but the criticism is tied to a quoted statement and to a duty of the office rather than to her character.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: New Zealand commends the leadership of the United States, Donald Trump, Egypt, Qatar, Turkey, Indonesia, and other countries in bringing this deal together, and we view the events of the last 24 hours as providing momentum for peace and constituting a significant first step towards ending this devastating conflict—and not making stupid statements, like the people on my right.
civility.explanation: Ends an otherwise substantive statement by calling the members opposite makers of 'stupid statements' — a personal swipe at identifiable members present, not at their policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: First of all, that they recognise that it was the US President and others from Muslim countries who brought this about and that anti-Americanism or any other sentiment is of no value when you’re concerned about peace, and particularly if you’re some arrogant twit that arrived here five minutes ago and doesn’t give a concern about this country’s initiative and its peace over the years.
civility.explanation: Direct abuse of another member — 'arrogant twit that arrived here five minutes ago' attacks the person and their origins, not any argument they made.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, the silence over the past week from some of the so-called pro-Palestinian protesters around this country has been absolutely deafening.
focus.explanation: Asked how developments were received in New Zealand, the answer is entirely about what opponents and protesters have not said. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: To say, as I think it does, that the decision departed from the original intention of Parliament—it was probably untrue at the start, but it’s certainly untrue now.
civility.explanation: Blunt criticism of the bill's preamble as untrue, directed entirely at the document and the Government's rationale; no person is impugned and no bad faith is alleged.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because if a hapū and iwi have a customary right to exercise control in respect of a particular activity over a coastal area, these are rights which are familiar to jurisdictions around the world. We have fishing rights to rivers for trout in the UK that have been recognised since medieval times, and you can't dam the river with the resource consent or their equivalent there.
rigor.explanation: An argument from analogy: long-recognised UK riparian fishing rights that constrain development are offered to support the conclusion that customary marine rights are ordinary property rights. The analogy is apt and evidence is actually offered, but the inference has a real gap — nothing is supplied to show the two regimes are legally comparable, and the disanalogy (a statutory recognition threshold versus an existing title) is left unaddressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, obviously enabling one group of New Zealanders who had received customary marine title to grant resource consents is a very significant deviation from normal expectations of New Zealanders living in this country in a democratic, modern democracy to have an equal say in decisions affecting their lives and their environment and what goes on around them.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion is carried by 'obviously' rather than by anything offered. It treats an undefined 'equal say' as the democratic baseline while eliding the fact that property rights generally — riparian, private land, existing consents — routinely give particular holders differential say over what happens on their land, which is the premise that would have to be argued away. Assertion of a norm in place of an inference.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is still the view of the Government that it still deviates from Parliament’s intention, because we’ve seen a couple of decisions that have been made since the Supreme Court decision and the Supreme Court test which have seen very large proportions of coastlines in the Wairarapa and Kāpiti that have been given customary marine title.
rigor.explanation: Infers that the Supreme Court's test departs from Parliament's intention from the size of the areas subsequently awarded. That is reasoning backwards from outcome to intent: nothing is offered about what the two decisions actually found, whether the applicants met the statutory limbs, or why a large award is itself evidence of a wrong test rather than of coastline where the threshold was in fact met. The conclusion outruns the evidence supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Then the next one is whether he can give an example of where, in previous cases, a marine and coastal area, or a customary title, has been recognised, and what makes this particular one different to others that have been recognised in the past.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee — asks the Minister for precedent on customary title recognition and what distinguishes this case. Nothing about the other party; this is scrutiny of the bill's substance.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’ll be bringing in Amendment Paper 380, which has an amended preamble, and it’s required because the Supreme Court and the High Court have issued relevant judgments since the original bill was introduced, and so they’ve been added into Part 1, clause 4 and the preamble, and different parts of the legislation, and also to give effect to Cabinet’s decision that the bill won’t apply to Ngā Rohe Moana o Ngā Hapū o Ngāti Porou.
specificity.explanation: Names the amendment paper by number, the specific clause and preamble amended, the reason (intervening Supreme Court and High Court judgments), and a named carve-out. Someone could go and check each element. Short of 1.0 only because no dates or quantities are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Supreme Court agreed with the Government that the Court of Appeal had got that wrong, and indicated their own expression of what section 58 meant.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Supreme Court, in the appeal from the Court of Appeal's Edwards/Whakatōhea decision, upheld the Government's position that the Court of Appeal had misconstrued the second limb of section 58 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011, and substituted its own interpretation of that section.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Supreme Court's judgment on appeal from Re Edwards (Te Whakatōhea) — reported as [2024] NZSC 164 — read alongside the Crown's grounds of appeal. True if the Court allowed the Crown's appeal on the section 58(1)(b) 'exclusive use and occupation without substantial interruption' test, held the Court of Appeal's approach to be in error, and set out its own interpretation of section 58. False if the Court dismissed the Crown's appeal, endorsed the Court of Appeal's interpretation, or declined to state its own test.

veracity.statement: It is still the view of the Government that it still deviates from Parliament’s intention, because we’ve seen a couple of decisions that have been made since the Supreme Court decision and the Supreme Court test which have seen very large proportions of coastlines in the Wairarapa and Kāpiti that have been given customary marine title.
veracity.explanation: The factual component: that since the Supreme Court's decision, courts applying its section 58 test have granted customary marine title over very large proportions of the Wairarapa and Kāpiti coastlines.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: High Court customary marine title determinations under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 issued after the Supreme Court's Edwards judgment (late 2024) covering the Wairarapa and Kāpiti coasts, with the awarded coastal extent compared against the total coastline of each area. True if such decisions exist for both areas and award CMT over a majority or near-majority of each coastline. False if no post-Supreme Court determination covers one of those coasts, or if the areas awarded are a small fraction of the coastline.

specificity.statement: That was the goal and that’s how it was always explained: that you had to achieve two legs, the first being to recognise it through tikanga, and the second requiring applicants to have held a specified area and “exclusively used and occupied the area from 1840 to the present day without substantial interruption”.
specificity.explanation: Names the two-limb statutory test and quotes the operative threshold wording, including the 1840 date. Someone could go to the Act and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I would also like to point out the advice that the Minister received in this regard—again in the supplementary analysis paper—was that Te Arawhiti’s—what was then called Te Arawhiti—initial preference was in retaining the status quo and waiting for the Supreme Court judgment; page 14 of the supplementary report.
specificity.explanation: Names the advising agency, the document, the position taken, and the page number. Fully checkable against a named source.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Canadian case law that the Minister was talking about there were cases like Calder v Attorney-General of British Columbia that was decided in 1973, which sets out a framework that is used all around the world in common law jurisdictions to determine both the extinguishment of title by radical title of the Crown and customary rights and interests that exist in land after that has occurred, and also Guerin v the Queen in 1984.
specificity.explanation: Names two authorities with their years and states what doctrinal work each does. Precise enough to be looked up and argued with.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That was the goal and that’s how it was always explained: that you had to achieve two legs, the first being to recognise it through tikanga, and the second requiring applicants to have held a specified area and “exclusively used and occupied the area from 1840 to the present day without substantial interruption”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the test Parliament enacted in 2011 has two limbs — recognition through tikanga, plus exclusive use and occupation from 1840 to the present without substantial interruption.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Section 58 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 as enacted; true if it contains both a tikanga limb and an 'exclusively used and occupied ... from 1840 to the present day without substantial interruption' limb in substantially those words, false if the wording or structure differs materially.

veracity.statement: I would also like to point out the advice that the Minister received in this regard—again in the supplementary analysis paper—was that Te Arawhiti’s—what was then called Te Arawhiti—initial preference was in retaining the status quo and waiting for the Supreme Court judgment; page 14 of the supplementary report.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the supplementary regulatory impact analysis records Te Arawhiti's initial preference as retaining the status quo and awaiting the Supreme Court judgment, at page 14.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Page 14 of the supplementary regulatory impact analysis / departmental report accompanying the Takutai Moana amendment bill; true if it records that preference for Te Arawhiti, false if the page records a different preference or no such advice appears in the document.

veracity.statement: On page 15 of that analysis, point 44: “If the Supreme Court ruled in favour of the Crown, it could mean the additional time and resource on progressing amendments would not be required”, and the Supreme Court did rule in favour of the Crown.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that point 44 on page 15 of the analysis says what is quoted, and that the Supreme Court in fact ruled in the Crown's favour.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Page 15, paragraph 44 of the supplementary regulatory impact analysis for the quoted wording; and the Supreme Court's judgment of 2 December 2024 in the Re Edwards (Whakatōhea) appeals — true if the Crown's appeal was allowed and the Court of Appeal's test displaced in the Crown's favour, false if the Crown's appeal was dismissed or the outcome was materially against the Crown's position.

veracity.statement: The Canadian case law that the Minister was talking about there were cases like Calder v Attorney-General of British Columbia that was decided in 1973, which sets out a framework that is used all around the world in common law jurisdictions to determine both the extinguishment of title by radical title of the Crown and customary rights and interests that exist in land after that has occurred, and also Guerin v the Queen in 1984.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Calder v Attorney-General of British Columbia was decided in 1973 and Guerin v The Queen in 1984, and that Calder sets out the framework for extinguishment of title and surviving customary interests used across common law jurisdictions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Supreme Court of Canada reports for both cases; true if Calder is reported in 1973 and Guerin in 1984 and Calder is the leading authority on extinguishment/aboriginal title as described, false if the years are wrong or the doctrinal characterisation does not match the judgments.

civility.statement: Now, the member is quite within his rights to say that “That’s not the right threshold”, “It should be a different threshold”, “There should be no threshold”—that’s fine.
civility.explanation: Directly concedes the legitimacy of the opposing member's position and confines the disagreement to the threshold itself. No imputation of bad faith or attack on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They clarified what the intention was from 2011, and through this amendment, the Minister is coming along with a sledgehammer and smashing that nail into the wall, destroying the actual intention of 2011, which was clarified by the Supreme Court finding.
civility.explanation: Vivid and damning about the amendment itself — 'sledgehammer', 'destroying' — but the target throughout is the legislative act, not the Minister's character or competence. Hard criticism of a policy is the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Given that fact, further to my core question, how is it that, where the Court has clarified—in a magisterial decision of some substance and intelligence, in December 2024—very eloquently the intention of Parliament and found, in many interpretations, a middle-ground between the finding of the Appeal Court and the desire of the appellant, in a magisterial decision that clarifies the intention of Parliament 2011, the Minister still comes back to this House with these intense amendments to supposedly restore that intention?
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: the Supreme Court has settled the 2011 intention, so amendments to restore it are redundant. But the weight rests on an appeal to the authority and eloquence of the decision ('magisterial', 'of some substance and intelligence') rather than on its content, and there is a gap between a court clarifying the law and the Crown accepting the resulting threshold as the one it wants.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What’s important there is if we are to pass as a Parliament a pronouncement about how this law was meant to be taking into account, then that Canadian case law is relevant.
rigor.explanation: A clean conditional inference: the 2010 Minister grounded the tests in Canadian common law, so if Parliament now legislates about what those tests were meant to mean, the Canadian authorities bear on it. Premise and conclusion connect without a gap; the argument is offered on the merits, not on the Minister.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Given that fact, further to my core question, how is it that, where the Court has clarified—in a magisterial decision of some substance and intelligence, in December 2024—very eloquently the intention of Parliament and found, in many interpretations, a middle-ground between the finding of the Appeal Court and the desire of the appellant, in a magisterial decision that clarifies the intention of Parliament 2011, the Minister still comes back to this House with these intense amendments to supposedly restore that intention?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — names the December 2024 decision, the Court of Appeal finding, and what the amendments purport to do. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s fine for him to have a new policy direction, but why would we pass in legislation that the courts have made the wrong call, when, in 2011, that certainly seems to have been the intent.
focus.explanation: Engages the specific legislative mechanism at issue — enacting a statutory pronouncement that the courts misread the 2011 intent — and expressly allows the Minister his policy direction. No party-record content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I think, if we’re accurate about reflecting on the historical record and reflecting on what has occurred, in the preamble that is currently laid out in the bill, I would like the Minister to consider whether he would like to include the Tribunal’s finding that the Crown has breached the principle of tino rangatiratanga by exercising kāwanatanga over Māori rights and interests in takutai moana without providing any evidence for one of its key justifications, namely that the public’s rights and interests require further protection beyond what is already provided in the Act and that the Crown also failed to inform itself of Māori interests.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact instrument (the preamble of the bill before the Committee), the specific Tribunal finding to be inserted, and the particular principle said to be breached. A drafter could act on it. Falls short of 1.0 only because no clause number or proposed wording is offered.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Considering the deep impact that the decisions of this legislation will ripple out to te iwi Māori, I’m keen to understand from the Minister, in developing this amendment, did the Minister speak to Whakatōhea? Did the Minister speak to the tribes of Wairarapa? Did the Minister speak to the tribes of Aotea Harbour?
specificity.explanation: Names three specific groups and regions the Minister is asked to confirm he consulted, turning a general consultation complaint into a question with a checkable answer. Not 1.0 because no dates or documents are put to him.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My question to the Minister is: does that include all courts? Could that extend itself to other judiciary arms such as the Waitangi Tribunal, who are well-acknowledged in the House as storekeepers of a heck of a lot of evidence with respect to these matters that we’re debating here in the Chamber.
specificity.explanation: Anchored to a named provision he has just read out (the requirement that inferences by a decision maker be based on evidence of physical use and occupation) and asks a precisely bounded question about which bodies 'decision maker' captures, naming the Waitangi Tribunal. Concrete enough to demand a yes/no, though it stops short of citing the defined term in the Act.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: However, what smarts even more and rubs salt in the wound is the fact that there was consultation with commercial fishing interests, which have already got statutory protections.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the Crown consulted commercial fishing interests before finalising the proposed amendments, while (per her surrounding sentences) not consulting Māori, and that those fishing interests already hold statutory protections.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal's urgent inquiry report into the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill and the Ministry of Justice / Te Arawhiti consultation records disclosed to it: true if those records show engagement with commercial fishing industry bodies prior to the amendments being finalised; false if no such engagement is recorded. The statutory-protection limb is settled by whether the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 and the Fisheries Act 1996 preserve existing fishing rights.

veracity.statement: I think it’s also important to note that they found that the Crown breached its principles of active protection, as well as good government, by proposing those amendments.
veracity.explanation: Relays a finding attributed to the Waitangi Tribunal: that in proposing these amendments the Crown breached the Treaty principles of active protection and of good government. The claim is about what the Tribunal found, not the speaker's own assertion about the Crown.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Waitangi Tribunal's report on the takutai moana amendments: true if the report's findings expressly include breaches of the principles of active protection and good government; false if it finds no such breaches or grounds them in different principles.

veracity.statement: What we've seen in recent cases, based on the Supreme Court test, is entire coastlines being granted CMT.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that recent customary marine title determinations, applying the test set by the Supreme Court, have granted CMT over entire coastlines rather than discrete areas. The checkable content is the geographic extent of the orders actually made.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The customary marine title orders and judgments issued after the Supreme Court's decision in Whakatōhea (Re Edwards): true if any determination grants CMT over the whole of a coastline; false if the orders cover defined discrete areas, however large. Ambiguity turns on whether 'entire coastlines' is treated literally or as shorthand for contiguous multi-area grants.

divination.statement: As a result, applicants will be forced to have their cases reheard, burdening them further, financially and emotionally as well.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that, if the amendments proceed, existing customary marine title applicants will have to have their cases heard again under the new test. This is a forecast about an outcome for third parties, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The enacted Act's transitional provisions and subsequent High Court customary marine title proceedings: true if applicants whose cases were already heard or decided under the previous test are required to have them reheard or redetermined; false if the amendments apply only prospectively to undetermined applications and no rehearing is required.

focus.statement: It’s well and good that we have National Ministers turning up to celebrate 50 years of the Waitangi Tribunal, but, surely, if their research and their findings are valued enough, they should be reflected in the preamble of this bill.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy request inside it — put the Tribunal's findings in the preamble of this bill — but the weight of the sentence is a jab at National Ministers' ceremonial attendance rather than at the measure. A real policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: With respect to its application to other pieces of legislation, my question to the Minister on this part is: in recognising customary take of seafood and the issuing of permits as such, does that come under the customary title and occupation piece that the Minister is proposing here?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the amendment before the Committee: whether the redefined use-and-occupation test bears on existing customary fishing take and permitting. Names a specific downstream effect; no party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Whose specific rights are there mischief being caused to by the current, most recent interpretation of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, i.e., that of the Supreme Court?
focus.explanation: Directly interrogates the Minister's stated justification for the bill — that the current interpretation interferes with rights — by demanding whose rights those are. Names the Act and the court whose interpretation is at issue; no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s well and good that we have National Ministers turning up to celebrate 50 years of the Waitangi Tribunal, but, surely, if their research and their findings are valued enough, they should be reflected in the preamble of this bill.
civility.explanation: Sardonic about the government's conduct and edging toward imputing insincerity, but it lands on 'National Ministers' collectively and on the inconsistency, not on any individual's character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What we've seen in recent cases, based on the Supreme Court test, is entire coastlines being granted CMT. So that is why we believe this legislation is required: to restore the parliamentary intent, which was a high threshold, and specific parts of the coastline, not entire coastline.
civility.explanation: Answers a hostile line of questioning by engaging the substance — the test, the intended scope, the case outcomes — and attacks no one, despite a genuinely contested exchange in which he could have.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: To an earlier point the Minister made about the problem of customary marine title interfering with other users’ rights—and acknowledging the well-made point of my colleague Hūhana Lyndon that it seems that, frequently, it is the rights of non-Māori that are preferenced time and again over the rights of iwi Māori: for a Minister that purports to believe in property rights, I wonder that he can’t recognise the first property rights of this country, customary marine title, with a greater confidence and certainty.
civility.explanation: 'Purports to believe in property rights' imputes insincerity to the Minister personally — his stated principle is cast as a pretence rather than a position held inconsistently. Short of a direct insult, but it goes at the man's good faith rather than at the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What we've seen in recent cases, based on the Supreme Court test, is entire coastlines being granted CMT. So that is why we believe this legislation is required: to restore the parliamentary intent, which was a high threshold, and specific parts of the coastline, not entire coastline.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: original ministerial statements of intended scope + observed judicial outcomes exceeding that scope, therefore legislation to restore the intended threshold. The premises support the conclusion, but there is a gap — he has just conceded that quotes can be found on both sides, which weakens the appeal to ministerial statements as evidence of parliamentary intent, and intent expressed in speeches does not settle what the enacted words mean.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I would like to know from the Minister: are there other factors, such as he didn’t want to have to pay for the funding for legal representation through the courts for claimants, because that was causing the Crown’s books some concern, and he had quite a bit of pressure to bring things into line and there was no other foreseeable way to stop those costs?
civility.explanation: Framed as a question, but it imputes a motive to the Minister personally — that he legislated to avoid paying claimants' legal costs rather than on the merits. Short of a personal insult, but it edges past robust scrutiny of the decision into suggesting bad faith, so it sits between the 0.75 'pointed' band and the 0.5 'imputing bad faith' band.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So where and how is the constitutional right of Māori being recognised by the current actions of the Crown?
civility.explanation: A hard challenge to the Crown's conduct that attacks no individual — no imputation of motive, no mockery, no personal remark, in a debate that gave ample opportunity for all three.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I would like to know from the Minister: are there other factors, such as he didn’t want to have to pay for the funding for legal representation through the courts for claimants, because that was causing the Crown’s books some concern, and he had quite a bit of pressure to bring things into line and there was no other foreseeable way to stop those costs?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: it names the amendment paper's preamble, the claimant funding mechanism, and Crown court costs. Probing the rationale for a named piece of legislation is scrutiny, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In terms of whose rights we are talking about who would be potentially interfered with by the resource consent right, we’re talking about somebody who wanted to start new aquaculture, for example, somebody wanting to put in a jetty on their property, or somebody wanting to renew a consent for a jetty that they’ve had for generations.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of the provision under debate — which resource consent applicants the right would affect and how. Under pointed questioning about his motives he engages the substance rather than turning on the questioners.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So where and how is the constitutional right of Māori being recognised by the current actions of the Crown?
focus.explanation: Directed at the constitutional effect of the amendment he has been analysing rather than at the other party's character or record. Slightly below the top because it addresses 'the current actions of the Crown' in general rather than naming the specific recital or clause at that point.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ve already been told there’s cuts everywhere—cut, cut, cut—and yet we see this Government bringing legislation in, just in the preamble itself, changing the nature by which we have to prove our connection and provide evidence of physical use and occupation, which is inconsistent with the test based on tikanga.
focus.explanation: Names the preamble, the evidential standard it introduces and its inconsistency with the tikanga-based test — real policy content. Marked down from the top because the 'cut, cut, cut' framing carries some of the weight as a general characterisation of the Government rather than of the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In particular, I would like to know whether the cost pressures of claimant funding proceeding through the court process, which, in the year prior to this legislation being brought to the House and enacted, there was a substantial blowout—according to the scrutiny week that I sat on, as part of that—in terms of the court costs that the Crown was required to pay for.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Crown-funded claimant legal costs in the takutai moana court process overran substantially in the year before this legislation, sourced to select committee scrutiny week evidence. The claim is about the past and is checkable against appropriations; the criterion above was fixed before considering the likely answer.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Crown expenditure on claimant funding and Crown legal costs for Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act applications, as reported in Vote Justice / Te Arawhiti–Te Tari Whakatau estimates, annual reports and the 2024–25 scrutiny week evidence. TRUE if actual spend in the financial year preceding the amendment bill materially exceeded the appropriation or the prior year's spend; FALSE if spend was at or below appropriation and broadly flat on the prior year.

veracity.statement: I have met with a number, including Ngāti Raukawa ki te Tonga, Te Whānau-a-Apanui, Ngāti Kauwhata, and Ngāti Porou.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that he personally met with four named iwi/hapū groups during development of the amendment. A past-fact claim about his own conduct, checkable against published ministerial diaries; criterion stated before forming any view.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial diary disclosures for the Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations over the period the amendment was developed, plus any Official Information Act release of meeting records. TRUE if meetings with each of the four named groups appear in that record; FALSE if one or more of the named groups has no recorded meeting with the Minister in that period.

veracity.statement: There hadn’t been an Act of Parliament passed between 1854 and 2004 that actively extinguished the Māori right to the takutai moana, so it stands that it was still there in 2004.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of legislative history that no statute in that 150-year window extinguished Māori customary rights to the takutai moana. A past-fact claim resolvable against the statute book and the Court of Appeal's analysis; criterion fixed before considering the answer.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The statutory-history analysis in Ngati Apa v Attorney-General (CA, 2003) and the accompanying legal-historical record of foreshore and seabed legislation. TRUE if no Act passed between 1854 and 2004 is identified as clearly extinguishing Māori customary rights in the foreshore and seabed; FALSE if such an extinguishing statute is identified.

specificity.statement: I have met with a number, including Ngāti Raukawa ki te Tonga, Te Whānau-a-Apanui, Ngāti Kauwhata, and Ngāti Porou.
specificity.explanation: Answers 'which applicants have you met with' by naming four specific groups rather than asserting consultation in general terms — someone could go and check it. Falls short of 1.0 because no dates, number of meetings or what was discussed is supplied.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of whose rights we are talking about who would be potentially interfered with by the resource consent right, we’re talking about somebody who wanted to start new aquaculture, for example, somebody wanting to put in a jetty on their property, or somebody wanting to renew a consent for a jetty that they’ve had for generations.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (the resource consent right) and gives three concrete affected cases — new aquaculture, a new jetty, a jetty consent renewal — but supplies no figures, no scale of how many are affected, and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Thinking about the implications for decision makers, including the courts, to be based on evidence of physical use and occupation now and into the future, who is going to be financing the implementation of this?
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete mechanism — the physical use and occupation evidential test — and the actors it binds, but asks an open funding question without a figure, an appropriation, or a timeframe. A direction with some detail, missing the how much.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There hadn’t been an Act of Parliament passed between 1854 and 2004 that actively extinguished the Māori right to the takutai moana, so it stands that it was still there in 2004.
rigor.explanation: A clean inference: given the common-law principle that customary rights survive until clearly extinguished by statute, the absence of any extinguishing Act over the stated period does support the conclusion that the right persisted. The conclusion tracks the premise offered; whether the premise is factually correct is Veracity's question, not this one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’ve already been told there’s cuts everywhere—cut, cut, cut—and yet we see this Government bringing legislation in, just in the preamble itself, changing the nature by which we have to prove our connection and provide evidence of physical use and occupation, which is inconsistent with the test based on tikanga.
rigor.explanation: There is a genuine inference — a heavier evidential burden requires resourcing, and resourcing is being cut — and the tikanga-inconsistency point is a real argument about the measure. But the funding premise rests on an unquantified appeal to cuts 'everywhere' rather than to any appropriation for this process, leaving a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It leaves the courts in the position—or any decision maker, in fact, when they’re considering customary marine title—where, at some point, they need to hear evidence about physical use, but there’s no indication of whether that should be the only evidence, whether that should be the most heavily weighted evidence, or whether it must be one of a hundred things that they heard evidence on.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the drafting: because the clause directs decision makers to hear evidence of physical use without assigning it any weight, the test is indeterminate. The premises (no weighting stated) genuinely support the conclusion (courts cannot know how to apply it). No fallacy; a small gap only in that courts routinely weigh unweighted evidentiary factors.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: My question to the Minister is: were the words that are in this preamble now and that have some really serious concerns, including the word “physical” and how you are determining occupation, predetermined because the Minister simply directed officials to choose which option best suited the Government’s desire for an outcome and best suited the minimisation of costs to the Crown?
rigor.explanation: The premise (the RIS records that officials worked within the Minister's direction that the status quo was not feasible) is real and relevant, but it does not carry the conclusion drawn — that the specific preamble wording was predetermined to minimise Crown costs. A genuine gap between what the cited paragraph shows and what is inferred from it; the question form softens but does not close it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now we're all debating about where that threshold should be, and three different courts have had three different interpretations of that threshold. That’s why this Parliament is considering this Amendment Paper, which sets for Parliament to assert what it believes the threshold should be.
rigor.explanation: A valid inference given its premise: if successive courts have read the statutory threshold differently, Parliament restating its intended threshold responds to that. The gap is that judicial disagreement alone does not establish that the courts were wrong rather than the drafting unclear, so the conclusion is supported but not compelled.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, in terms of the references to the Court of Appeal case, it’s entirely unnecessary because they’re gone, they’ve been overruled, and the Supreme Court case itself is the one which prevails.
rigor.explanation: A stated premise (the Court of Appeal's reasoning was superseded by the Supreme Court) supporting a conclusion (reciting it in the preamble is unnecessary). The inference tracks, though it passes over the possibility that a preamble may recite superseded decisions for narrative or historical purpose — which he himself concedes elsewhere.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It leaves the courts in the position—or any decision maker, in fact, when they’re considering customary marine title—where, at some point, they need to hear evidence about physical use, but there’s no indication of whether that should be the only evidence, whether that should be the most heavily weighted evidence, or whether it must be one of a hundred things that they heard evidence on.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the amendment before the committee — what a decision maker must do with evidence of physical use. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is unfair. It is gobbledygook. It is getting around a problem the Government has with a populist commitment that doesn’t make sense in law.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine legal point inside it (the drafting 'doesn't make sense in law'), but the weight of the sentence is the political characterisation of the Government's motive rather than the mechanism, cost or effect of the amendment.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My question to the Minister is: does colonisation come into interruption? Does he consider that the change of the law and the removal of people from their land constitutes interruption as per subclause (7)(c)(ii) of the preamble.
focus.explanation: Directly engages the substance of the provision before the committee — what counts as 'substantial interruption' under the exclusive use and occupation limb. Names the subclause and puts a concrete interpretive question to the Minister.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My question to the Minister is: were the words that are in this preamble now and that have some really serious concerns, including the word “physical” and how you are determining occupation, predetermined because the Minister simply directed officials to choose which option best suited the Government’s desire for an outcome and best suited the minimisation of costs to the Crown?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny anchored in a named document (the regulatory impact statement) and a named drafting choice (the word 'physical'). Naming the policy artefact and the specific wording is accountability, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now we're all debating about where that threshold should be, and three different courts have had three different interpretations of that threshold. That’s why this Parliament is considering this Amendment Paper, which sets for Parliament to assert what it believes the threshold should be.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the measure before the House and the legal question it addresses — the section 58 threshold and why Parliament is legislating on it. No characterisation of opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If we’re going to give a genuine historical account of why we’ve got here, we should probably recognise that it’s really part of the Government’s approach to Māori and Māori interests, which is, basically, to roll back the progress that we’ve made over the past, I don’t know, 150 years or so.
focus.explanation: Leaves the preamble drafting behind for a general characterisation of the Government's overall posture toward Māori. No policy, measure, figure or named outcome — the '150 years' is rhetorical scale, not a specific commitment being held to account.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Having to prove physical use for somewhere like Ruapuke Island, where customary marine title has been granted to the whānau of Ruapuke, but where the sea between it and Rakiura or Invercargill might be used infrequently, is difficult and nonsensical, especially when you haven’t set out how that is intended to work for a court.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete place (Ruapuke Island), the relevant sea area (between Ruapuke and Rakiura/Invercargill), and the specific legal test being applied. Falls short of 1.0 because no figures, timeframe or clause reference are supplied.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My question to the Minister is: does colonisation come into interruption? Does he consider that the change of the law and the removal of people from their land constitutes interruption as per subclause (7)(c)(ii) of the preamble.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact provision and a concrete scenario (legislative change and removal of people from land), but leaves the test itself undefined and offers no figures, cases or thresholds.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Having to prove physical use for somewhere like Ruapuke Island, where customary marine title has been granted to the whānau of Ruapuke, but where the sea between it and Rakiura or Invercargill might be used infrequently, is difficult and nonsensical, especially when you haven’t set out how that is intended to work for a court.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that a customary marine title recognition order has been granted to the whānau of Ruapuke over the relevant area.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Recognition orders made under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 (High Court judgments and the Ministry of Justice / Te Arawhiti register of recognition orders) for the Ruapuke Island area; true if a customary marine title order covering Ruapuke has been granted to Ruapuke whānau, false if only an application or a protected customary rights order exists.

veracity.statement: Now we're all debating about where that threshold should be, and three different courts have had three different interpretations of that threshold. That’s why this Parliament is considering this Amendment Paper, which sets for Parliament to assert what it believes the threshold should be.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that three different courts have reached three different interpretations of the customary marine title threshold.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The High Court, Court of Appeal and Supreme Court judgments in Re Edwards (Whakatōhea) on the section 58 test in the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011; true if each articulated a materially different test for 'exclusive use and occupation without substantial interruption', false if two or more applied the same test.

veracity.statement: That's why the legislation was passed with the support of the National Party and the Māori Party at the time, and was set to strike a balance there with what was described, at the time, as a high threshold.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the original Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act was enacted with the votes of both the National Party and the Māori Party, and that the test it set was described at the time as a high threshold.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The division record for the third reading of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill in 2011, plus the Hansard and explanatory material from that debate; true if both National and the Māori Party voted in favour and the threshold was contemporaneously described as high, false if either party opposed it.

veracity.statement: So, in terms of the references to the Court of Appeal case, it’s entirely unnecessary because they’re gone, they’ve been overruled, and the Supreme Court case itself is the one which prevails.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Court of Appeal's decision on the customary marine title test was overruled and that the Supreme Court's decision is the governing authority.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Supreme Court judgment in Re Edwards (Whakatōhea) and its treatment of the Court of Appeal's interpretation of section 58; true if the Supreme Court set aside or displaced the Court of Appeal's test, false if it upheld the Court of Appeal's interpretation.

civility.statement: This is unfair. It is gobbledygook. It is getting around a problem the Government has with a populist commitment that doesn’t make sense in law.
civility.explanation: Blunt and dismissive, and it imputes a political motive — but the target is the Government's drafting and its commitment, not any individual member. Pointed and robust, edging toward bad faith without landing on a person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: My question to the Minister is: were the words that are in this preamble now and that have some really serious concerns, including the word “physical” and how you are determining occupation, predetermined because the Minister simply directed officials to choose which option best suited the Government’s desire for an outcome and best suited the minimisation of costs to the Crown?
civility.explanation: Imputes to the Minister personally that he steered officials toward a predetermined answer to suit the Government and save the Crown money. It is grounded in the quoted RIS wording rather than invented, which keeps it above a bare personal attack, but it is an imputation of bad faith aimed at an individual.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If we’re going to give a genuine historical account of why we’ve got here, we should probably recognise that it’s really part of the Government’s approach to Māori and Māori interests, which is, basically, to roll back the progress that we’ve made over the past, I don’t know, 150 years or so.
civility.explanation: Sharp about the Government's programme but insults no individual member; the criticism lands on an approach, not a person. Focus is what catches the party framing here, not Civility.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: When we were doing this, the opponents said that this was terrible and appalling; then, lo and behold, the Supreme Court agreed that it was a misreading.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Supreme Court held the Court of Appeal had misread the second limb of the section 58 test (the 'exclusive use and occupation' requirement).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Supreme Court judgment in the Whakatohea/Edwards takutai moana appeal (2024) on s58 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011; true if the Court held the Court of Appeal's interpretation of the exclusive use and occupation limb was wrong, false if it upheld the Court of Appeal's reading of that limb.

veracity.statement: For instance, the rights of Ngāi Tahu and Rakiura Māori in the Tītī Islands was recognised through a pathway of negotiation with the ground to recognise those special rights and have nothing to do with these concepts around physical use or adverse position.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Rakiura Māori and Ngāi Tahu rights in the Tītī Islands were recognised via negotiated settlement with the Crown, not via a physical-use or adverse-possession test. ('with the ground' is a transcription slip for 'with the Crown'.)
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act 1998 and the Titi (Muttonbird) Islands regime; true if those rights were vested/recognised through Crown negotiation and settlement legislation, false if they were established by a court applying a physical-use or adverse-possession test.

focus.statement: When we were doing this, the opponents said that this was terrible and appalling; then, lo and behold, the Supreme Court agreed that it was a misreading.
focus.explanation: A genuine point about a named court's reading of a statutory test, but framed around what 'the opponents' said and a vindication narrative rather than the provision itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is it the Minister’s opinion that the original intent of the legislation was to place the burden of proof not on iwi Māori but on those who wished to disprove that iwi Māori had exclusive use and therefore a right of customary title?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the bill — where the burden of proof sits under the customary title test. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I want to ask him whether there should be a definition of “physical use” in this section, because that is a concept which he has been talking about as an important part of this bill, and yet I have some questions around how that meaning should be interpreted.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific drafting question in the bill — whether a defined term is needed for a key operative concept.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The approach of the bill is to say that applicants must prove all the elements of the section 58 test now.
specificity.explanation: Names the provision and states the precise legal effect (onus on applicants for every element of the s58 test); a reader could check it against the clause.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For instance, the rights of Ngāi Tahu and Rakiura Māori in the Tītī Islands was recognised through a pathway of negotiation with the ground to recognise those special rights and have nothing to do with these concepts around physical use or adverse position.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific groups, the specific islands and the specific mechanism of recognition, though without dates or instrument names.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If I am physically using my lawn, do I have any physical use rights in the property that is 200 metres from my boundary? No. And so physical use is a very limited sort of a right.
rigor.explanation: An argument by analogy from private land law to customary marine title. The inference has some force — physical use does not generate rights beyond the area used — but the analogy is asserted rather than defended, and customary title is not claimed to work like fee simple neighbouring rights.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think it’s quite separate from the question of establishing the coastal and marine title kind of prima facie, because it’s essentially a defence to say that, yes, all that’s true but there’s been an extinguishment through these series of events, because if the onus lies the other way, and the hapū or iwi have to prove on the balance of probabilities—and I’m assuming that that didn’t occur—that would seem entirely unfair.
rigor.explanation: Sound structure: extinguishment is characterised as an affirmative defence, from which the conclusion that its onus sits with the party raising it follows. The final step leans partly on a bare appeal to fairness rather than the pleading principle already established, and an assumption is inserted mid-argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The point was around onus, and I’m loath to say that the member as elegant as Steve Abel didn’t quite capture, I think, what he perhaps intended, because there are two concepts: one is establishing marine title, and then another is to say that it’s been extinguished.
civility.explanation: Corrects another member's framing on a contested point while attacking nobody — the disagreement is placed entirely on the conceptual distinction, with the correction softened rather than used to belittle.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That key date that is missing from those series of events is the Cabinet decision on 28 November 2023, and that is clearly before the decisions of Whakatōhea Kotahitanga Waka (Edwards) v Te Kāhui Takutai Moana o Ngā Whānau me Ngā Hāpū o Te Whakatōhea.
specificity.explanation: Names an exact date, an identified Cabinet decision, and the named court proceeding it is said to predate. Someone could go and check the preamble against that record.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m wanting to speak to my tabled amendment to clause 8(1), to be found on page 8 of the Minister’s Amendment Paper 380. My proposed amendment is to seek to delete clause 8(1).
specificity.explanation: Names the exact clause, the Amendment Paper number and page, and the precise change sought. Fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Again, my point is a relatively short one, I think, and it’s about new section 9B, in particular, subclause (3)(b), which says that “This section prevails over—(b) section 7”—of the principle Act—“(Treaty of Waitangi (te Tiriti o Waitangi));”.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the exact new provision and subclause and quotes its operative words, against the named section of the principal Act. Precisely checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: What occurs on 28 November 2023 is that Cabinet endorses the coalition agreement between the parties as the basis on which the coalition Government will operate.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Cabinet formally endorsed the National–NZ First coalition agreement as the Government's operating basis on 28 November 2023, and (in the surrounding sentences) that a Cabinet circular instructed chief executives to implement it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cabinet Office records for late November 2023 — the Cabinet minute and the Cabinet Office circular issued to chief executives on the new Government's programme. True if a Cabinet decision dated 28 November 2023 endorsed the coalition agreements and was circulated as an instruction to departments; false if no such decision exists or it carries a materially different date.

veracity.statement: I raise that as an issue in my kāinga, Whangārei-terenga-parāoa, where the claimants stood in hearings and are waiting for a judgment right now, knowing that very few parcels of land around Whangārei-terenga-parāoa remain within Māori hands.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two present facts: that Whangārei takutai moana claimants have been heard and are awaiting judgment, and that very little land abutting Whangārei Harbour remains in Māori ownership.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: High Court Takutai Moana application register for Whangārei Harbour applications (hearing completed, decision reserved as at October 2025); and Māori Land Court / LINZ records on the proportion of land parcels adjoining Whangārei Harbour held as Māori freehold land. True if hearings are concluded with judgment reserved and Māori-held parcels abutting the harbour are a small minority; false if no hearing has been held or a substantial share of the abutting land remains in Māori title.

veracity.statement: The only thing I'd say in relation to that member's speech, of course, is that nothing in this legislation impacts on the ability of Māori or non-Māori to go and collect shellfish and have a connection with a piece of coastline that continues, and there's all sorts of arrangements in place in relation to customary fishing rights and shellfish-gathering rights and tītī gathering rights. All these things are not affected by this legislation, and they carry on.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Bill leaves fishing, shellfish-gathering and customary food-gathering rights entirely untouched.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill as reported back, checked against the fishing and access provisions of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 and the Fisheries (Kaimoana Customary Fishing) Regulations. True if no provision of the Bill amends or is capable of restricting fishing, shellfish or tītī gathering rights; false if any clause alters those rights directly or through the customary marine title bundle.

rigor.statement: So the proposal in this amendment is to delete this section, because it’s unfair. It is unfair on tangata whenua to have to show that somehow we’ve got a physical manifestation of connection to that space, when we may not own by Western law the whenua abutting that part of the takutai moana.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: the clause conditions recognition on physical activity or resource use, and historic alienation of abutting land makes that evidence harder to produce, so the test is argued to be unfair. The premises support the conclusion, though the link between land ownership and inability to evidence physical use is asserted rather than shown — the clause does not on its face require title.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So that is why. With those valuable rights, part of the balancing act that was achieved by this legislation was a high threshold, which is what we're trying to establish through this legislation.
rigor.explanation: The inference — customary marine title carries consequential rights such as resource consent approval, therefore the test to obtain it should be demanding — is a coherent proportionality argument. But it is a gap-to-conclusion: nothing offered connects the weight of those rights to this particular threshold rather than any other, so the premise supports 'a high threshold' only in the abstract.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, you can scoff, Minister, but that’s what the words of the Treaty of Waitangi say. Yet you’re saying here that this piece of legislation will override the Treaty of Waitangi. That’s exactly what this says.
rigor.explanation: Equivocation: the clause states that new section 9B prevails over section 7 of the 2011 Act — a statutory interpretive direction — and the conclusion drawn is that the Bill overrides the Treaty itself. Overriding a statute's Treaty clause and overriding the Crown's Treaty obligations are treated as the same thing without argument, and 'that's exactly what this says' asserts the identity rather than establishing it.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So the proposal in this amendment is to delete this section, because it’s unfair. It is unfair on tangata whenua to have to show that somehow we’ve got a physical manifestation of connection to that space, when we may not own by Western law the whenua abutting that part of the takutai moana.
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism of a named clause and its evidential threshold. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So that is why. With those valuable rights, part of the balancing act that was achieved by this legislation was a high threshold, which is what we're trying to establish through this legislation.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the mechanism at issue — what rights customary marine title confers and why the test is set where it is. No reference to the other party's record or character.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, you can scoff, Minister, but that’s what the words of the Treaty of Waitangi say. Yet you’re saying here that this piece of legislation will override the Treaty of Waitangi. That’s exactly what this says.
civility.explanation: Pointed and confrontational, and 'you can scoff' characterises the Minister's reaction as dismissive, but it lands on the argument and the text rather than on the Minister's character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: These are rights which existed before that, so to suggest that a decision maker then needs to interpret those rights—which are part of the common law of New Zealand—in a way which is, in effect, promoting their purposes and application, which are set out in what is a political narrative plonked on the top of something which purports to be legislation is a bizarre way to make law.
civility.explanation: Scathing about the drafting technique — 'plonked on the top', 'a bizarre way to make law' — but the target is the instrument, not any member. Slight edge for characterising the Government's preamble as a 'political narrative', which imputes motive to the drafters, so short of a clean 1.0.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, the last part of that member’s comments were irrelevant to this discussion.
civility.explanation: Dismissive of the member's contribution rather than of the member. Pointed and a little belittling, but it makes no claim about her character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Can we expect a National Government to now insert a preamble into every other piece of legislation for which they don't like decisions from the courts, like setting out perhaps their political campaign documents in the Crimes Act and asking judges to comply with that, or else!
rigor.explanation: Slippery slope: nothing is offered to connect one interpretive preamble in this bill to campaign documents being written into the Crimes Act. The reductio is asserted rather than argued, and the 'or else!' is an appeal to alarm. There is still a real inference about a real legislative mechanism, so it is assessable — it is just a weak one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Narrowing the things that the court can consider is particularly unhelpful for that court, because that very particular story that a member of this House was able to tell, that showed the relationship of her father’s iwi to the marine coastal environment would be exceedingly useful and informative for a court.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: if the clause bars evidence of spiritual or cultural association, evidence a court would find probative is excluded, so the court is worse placed to decide. The conclusion tracks the premise, but the support is a single anecdote offered in the House rather than any account of how often such evidence is decisive, which leaves a gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can we expect a National Government to now insert a preamble into every other piece of legislation for which they don't like decisions from the courts, like setting out perhaps their political campaign documents in the Crimes Act and asking judges to comply with that, or else!
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point (the use of interpretive preambles to direct courts) but carried in party framing about what 'a National Government' would do generally, rather than about the clause itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Narrowing the things that the court can consider is particularly unhelpful for that court, because that very particular story that a member of this House was able to tell, that showed the relationship of her father’s iwi to the marine coastal environment would be exceedingly useful and informative for a court.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of the clause and its effect on judicial fact-finding; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Inserting a preamble into a document is usually used in the context of Treaty settlements.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in current New Zealand legislative practice, preambles are predominantly a feature of Treaty settlement legislation rather than general statutes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Search legislation.govt.nz for Acts containing a preamble enacted in the modern era (say, since 1990) and classify them. True if Treaty settlement Acts make up the clear majority of statutes carrying a preamble; false if preambles are routinely used across general (non-settlement) legislation.

veracity.statement: As he well knows, what the section refers to is that it prevails over section 7 of the legislation, which has the title “Treaty of Waitangi”; it’s not the Treaty of Waitangi itself.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the overriding provision in the bill operates on section 7 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 — a section headed 'Treaty of Waitangi' — and not on the Treaty itself.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Read the text of the amendment/clause under debate together with section 7 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011. True if the clause is expressed to prevail over section 7 of that Act and section 7 is headed 'Treaty of Waitangi (Te Tiriti o Waitangi)'; false if the clause is expressed to override the Treaty or Treaty principles generally rather than that named section.

veracity.statement: Just in terms of the burden of proof question that’s been raised by a number of people, the 2011 Act says, in section 106, “Burden of proof”, in subsection (3), that “In the case of every application for a recognition order, it is presumed, in the absence of proof to the contrary, that a customary interest has not been extinguished”, and the bill does not change that.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that section 106(3) of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 contains the quoted presumption against extinguishment, and that the bill before the committee leaves that provision untouched.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare section 106(3) of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 with the quoted words, and check the bill and Amendment Papers before the committee for any amendment to section 106. True if the quotation matches and no amendment touches section 106; false if the wording differs materially or the bill amends section 106.

specificity.statement: Just in terms of the burden of proof question that’s been raised by a number of people, the 2011 Act says, in section 106, “Burden of proof”, in subsection (3), that “In the case of every application for a recognition order, it is presumed, in the absence of proof to the contrary, that a customary interest has not been extinguished”, and the bill does not change that.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act, the section, the section heading and the subsection, and quotes the provision. Fully checkable as given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s new section 58(1A)(a) in clause 8, but new section 58(1A)(b) is that it “is not based on a spiritual or cultural association”—it explicitly articulates that it must not be based on that.
specificity.explanation: Pins the objection to a named clause and new subsection and quotes the words at issue, so the point can be checked against the amendment paper directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: They’ve done that recently and they won’t be doing it for a long time to come, I imagine, but you never know, they might, and that is the system that we have, and we’re accountable for that.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that New Zealand voters will not turn out the current Government at the coming election — i.e. that the 2023-elected Government will be returned. Hedged ('I imagine', 'you never know'), but it is a forecast of a political outcome with a fixed date at which it can be tested.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The official Electoral Commission result of the next New Zealand general election (due by late 2026). True if the National-led Government is returned to office after that election; false if a change of government follows it.

specificity.statement: This is a prohibition on decision makers to not make an inference which is “based on a spiritual or cultural association with all or part of the area”.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision under discussion and quotes its operative words, so a listener can go to the clause and check the characterisation.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My question is really about whether the Minister is happy to stand up and do what he will be expected to do under the Regulatory Standards Bill when it’s passed and explain why he is not compensating, under this legislation, owners of property rights whose property rights are being significantly impaired by this.
specificity.explanation: Names the legislation, the mechanism and the affected group, but does not quantify the impairment or say what compensation would be owed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government has set aside $15 million towards the extra cost.
specificity.explanation: A single figure attached to a named purpose (the extra cost of rehearing the affected customary marine title cases); checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The change is that cultural or spiritual evidence needs supporting evidence of physical use, but tikanga and oral evidence remain important.
specificity.explanation: States the operative mechanism of the amendment in one line — a supporting-evidence requirement rather than an exclusion — which is checkable against the clause, though it gives no threshold for what counts as sufficient supporting evidence.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I raise this point again because it is important that we understand exactly what we are agreeing to here, and I don’t think it is something which many members in this House quite appreciate just how far-reaching that is.
civility.explanation: Pointed — it suggests colleagues have not grasped the clause — but it imputes no bad faith and lands on the substance of what the House is voting for rather than on any person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That can really add up, so my question is: why is there no compensation for the significant lost value where people have spent years both in cash and time in pursuing these claims?
civility.explanation: A direct challenge to the Government's choice, put entirely as a question about the policy; nobody's character, motive or competence is touched.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think the member knows the answer to that question, which is, no, it doesn’t.
civility.explanation: Implies the member asked a question he already knew the answer to — a mild imputation of insincerity aimed at the person rather than the point, though well short of an insult and immediately followed by a substantive answer.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Those are useful stories that tell us the existing history, and so to take out the ability of someone to make an inference about that use changes the system entirely.
rigor.explanation: The inference tracks the premises she laid out: written records of pre-1840 use largely do not exist, oral forms carry that record, so barring inferences from them removes the available evidence. The one gap is the leap to 'entirely', which is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Even if you discontinue, the court has a discretion to say, “In all of the circumstances, the litigation was properly brought, and the behaviour of the other side led to it being discontinued.”, and in those cases, the court can award costs, in my example, against the Government.
rigor.explanation: Valid conditional reasoning from a stated premise (the court's general costs discretion) to the conclusion that costs could fall on the Government even on discontinuance, which is what makes his question about clause 6 bite. It stops short of showing that the discretion survives the new clause, which is precisely what he then asks.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is not something that we wanted to do at all, but we felt that it was required, given the significant change to the threshold that first came through the Court of Appeal decision, and it has continued, in elements, through the Supreme Court decisions.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered for the action (the courts moved the threshold) and the conclusion that legislative correction is needed follows only if Parliament's original threshold was the one the courts departed from — a premise he asserts rather than argues here.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This whole House relies on testimony—oral testimonies—that we may question or test, but why would you deny something as powerful as the likes of the articulation of the relationship in a physical sense that an iwi produces on a regular basis in interaction, in telling their history with the land and the water?
rigor.explanation: An argument from consistency: the House accepts unsupported oral testimony as evidence, so a rule excluding iwi oral testimony is inconsistent. The analogy is real but loose — parliamentary debate and a statutory evidential threshold serve different purposes, and that disanalogy is not addressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That was not a service that existed in the decades leading up to the 1990s, because the Waitangi Tribunal did not operate.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Waitangi Tribunal was not operating in the decades before the 1990s, and so was not gathering and recording oral evidence of land use in that period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal establishment and jurisdiction record (Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975 and the 1985 amendment extending jurisdiction back to 1840) plus the list of Tribunal inquiries and reports issued before 1990. True if the Tribunal was not constituted or conducted no inquiries in the 1970s and 1980s; false if it was constituted and reported on claims during those decades.

veracity.statement: The Government has set aside $15 million towards the extra cost.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a $15 million provision has been made by the Government towards the additional costs arising from cases that must be reheard under this bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget/Estimates documentation for Vote Justice or Vote Treaty Negotiations, or the Cabinet paper and regulatory impact statement accompanying the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill. True if a provision of about $15 million for rehearing/associated costs appears; false if no such provision exists or the amount is materially different.

veracity.statement: I don’t have the exact figure, but more than $65 million has been spent by the people of New Zealand in support of claims that have been taken so far over the—what is it?—nearly 14 years since the legislation has passed, in support of claimants.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Crown funding of applicants under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 has exceeded $65 million cumulatively since 2011.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice Takutai Moana financial assistance scheme reporting, or answers to written parliamentary questions on total applicant funding since 2011. True if cumulative Crown funding to applicants exceeds $65 million; false if the total is materially below that.

focus.statement: My question is really about whether the Minister is happy to stand up and do what he will be expected to do under the Regulatory Standards Bill when it’s passed and explain why he is not compensating, under this legislation, owners of property rights whose property rights are being significantly impaired by this.
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure (the Regulatory Standards Bill), a specific standard within it (justifying impairment of property rights) and applies it to the clause before the committee. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Watch out, New Zealand, you’re getting the Greens, Te Pāti Māori, and Labour.
