focus.explanation: General characterisation of the Government's attitude to a region — no measure, figure, commitment or outcome is named, so nothing here can be held to account.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It does dilute Māori representation and therefore will directly impact on achieving Māori outcomes.
rigor.explanation: The 'therefore' does the work of an argument without one: no mechanism or evidence is offered linking reduced representation to worse outcomes, so the conclusion is asserted rather than supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because in the recapitalisation exercise, we’re having to ensure that we take away that debt from those that have got debt so that they have every chance of being successful in the future.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference that tracks its premise: if recapitalisation is funded by pooling, then institutions entering with reserves will not retain them all. The reasoning follows, though the funding link is stated rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would also say, for context, it does seem personal when this is the same Minister who, at the eleventh hour, in a different capacity, overturned a local government decision where local ratepayers had paid $18 million to get a decision made locally, in local democracy, around freshwater—it was this Minister who led the charge against that.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: an unrelated decision in a different portfolio is offered as evidence that this tertiary education decision is 'personal'. Nothing connects the two beyond the identity of the decision-maker.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: If I come back to the departmental report, clearly, submissions related to the Te Tiriti o Waitangi obligations were common amongst many submissions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the select committee's departmental report records Te Tiriti obligations as a frequently raised submission theme.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The departmental report on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill; true if the report records Te Tiriti o Waitangi obligations as a common theme across submissions, false if such submissions were few or not identified as a common theme.

veracity.statement: We had the wonderful example that Eastern Institute of Technology is in a community with 56 percent of the population Māori, and that is exactly what we expect to see reflected in the council of that entity.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a community served by the Eastern Institute of Technology has a 56 percent Māori population.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census ethnicity data for the territorial authorities/regions EIT serves (Hawke's Bay and Tairāwhiti); true if a community EIT serves has approximately 56% Māori population, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: Otago Polytechnic sadly have a debt of $16 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific debt figure for Otago Polytechnic.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Otago Polytechnic / Te Pūkenga annual financial statements and TEC financial reporting for the most recent reported year; true if reported debt or accumulated deficit is about $16 million, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: This is an opportunity for her to explain to the between 30 and 60 percent of people—of the whole workforce in Dunedin, between 30 and 60 percent, 30 percent at minimum—who work in health and education.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that between 30 and 60 percent of Dunedin's whole workforce — at minimum 30 percent — works in health and education.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ census employment-by-industry data for Dunedin city: combined share of the employed workforce in 'health care and social assistance' plus 'education and training'; true if that share is at least 30%, false if materially below 30%.

veracity.statement: What can she say to claims locally that there is a privatisation agenda in tertiary education, because we have seen a mental health programme cut from Otago Polytechnic that is now suddenly appearing via a private provider in Dunedin.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific factual sequence: a mental health programme cut at Otago Polytechnic and subsequently offered by a private provider in the same city.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Otago Polytechnic programme discontinuation records for 2024-25 and NZQA's register of approved providers/programmes in Dunedin; true if a mental health programme was discontinued at Otago Polytechnic and an equivalent programme is now offered by a private training establishment in Dunedin, false if no such closure or no such private offering exists.

veracity.statement: I would also say, for context, it does seem personal when this is the same Minister who, at the eleventh hour, in a different capacity, overturned a local government decision where local ratepayers had paid $18 million to get a decision made locally, in local democracy, around freshwater—it was this Minister who led the charge against that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the same Minister, in another portfolio, overturned a local freshwater planning decision that had cost ratepayers $18 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial decisions/announcements and Otago Regional Council records on the Otago Land and Water Regional Plan; true if this Minister, in an environment portfolio, blocked or halted notification of a regional freshwater plan on which the council had spent about $18 million, false if she took no such action or the sum is materially different.

specificity.statement: They were mostly themed around the removal of explicit Te Tiriti obligations for the vocational education sector, such as the obligations under section 9(1)(g) of the principal Act, the absence of effective engagement with Māori throughout the drafting process, and the potential lack of ongoing accountability to Māori and Māori representation through governance settings.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact statutory provision (section 9(1)(g) of the principal Act) and enumerates three distinct submission themes — checkable against the report.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, let me give her the opposite situation in SIT, who went into Te Pūkenga with $40 million in reserves. Only $15 million of that will be ring-fenced, so they will not come out with the full amount that they went in with.
specificity.explanation: Two named figures attached to a named institution and a named mechanism (ring-fencing of reserves on exit from Te Pūkenga); someone could check both amounts.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I would just point to the regulatory impact statement (RIS), page 3, which talks about the lack of consultation and the lack of being able to assess the risks, so one of my questions is: who bears those risks, particularly when there is active competition between polytechs in the way this has been set up?
specificity.explanation: Cites a named document and page and identifies the two deficiencies at issue; falls short of 1.0 because the risk-bearing question itself is left open rather than quantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m going to spell this out very clearly because I know that financial matters can be quite challenging for some members of the Labour Party, but let me make it very clear to you: there was no conflict of interest there.
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed at opposing members' competence — the suggestion that they cannot follow financial matters is about the people, not the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: A wonderful polytechnic, Otago Polytechnic, that has been so damaged by Te Pūkenga and all she wants to do is put out misinformation.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the member personally — that her sole purpose is to spread misinformation — rather than contesting what she said.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why would you take out from the charter a vital piece of the machinery, like the industry skills boards, the obligation that a Treaty clause conveys to engage fully with Māori leadership and with mana whenua to ensure that the right services are being delivered?
focus.explanation: Engages the measure before the House directly — a named provision (the industry skills boards charter and its Treaty clause) and the specific consequence he says removal has for service delivery. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I want to go to the pastoral support code that the Minister did speak to and that the Green Party did support, because that code is the anchor and maybe we need to review it—maybe we need to review it—because I’ve heard from Student Voice in particular that they want to strengthen it.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named instrument — the pastoral care code — and what should happen to it. No content about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They have been thrown under the bus by their leader, because remember, this mess was set up by the Rt Hon Chris Hipkins and followed on from the mess in the police and in health and in COVID.
focus.explanation: Answering a question about the disestablishment decision, the weight of this is the other party's general record and internal loyalties — police, health, COVID — rather than any provision, cost or outcome in the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And underlying that which I covered off in my opening statements is the real question: she hasn’t shown us the money—she hasn’t shown us how this is a more financially viable model than what was in place.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny on a specific dimension of the bill — whether the replacement model has been shown to be more financially viable than Te Pūkenga. No party framing; it names what is missing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Why would you take out from the charter a vital piece of the machinery, like the industry skills boards, the obligation that a Treaty clause conveys to engage fully with Māori leadership and with mana whenua to ensure that the right services are being delivered?
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested question on which he had ample opportunity to attack the Minister personally; instead the challenge is entirely to the decision and its effect. Standard civil conduct.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Look, I feel quite sorry for the members who are here today having to try to defend this.
civility.explanation: Pity offered to opposing members is condescension rather than engagement with their argument — short of a direct insult, but it belittles the people opposite instead of the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Submissions noted in the Ministry of Education departmental report that there were alternative options—these were not adequately considered because of the ideological agenda of this Government and the Minister.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the Minister personally (deciding by ideology rather than on the advice), which goes past criticising the decision itself, though it stops short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Now, if I think about the Māori community, in the communities that I represent in West Auckland, probably one in five of our people in the communities I serve are Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 20% of the population of the West Auckland communities he represents identify as Māori. Hedged with 'probably', but a stated proportion for a nameable area.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census usual resident population, Māori ethnicity share for the Te Atatū electorate / Henderson-Massey and Waitākere local board areas; true if the Māori share is approximately 20% (say 17-23%), false if materially below or above that band.

veracity.statement: Of course, this has nothing to do with the bill that we are currently looking at, but I can give the member assurance that total funding of approximately $18.5 million has been allocated to Māori and Pasifika trades training, and the funding was fully allocated in 2024-25.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that approximately $18.5 million was allocated to Māori and Pasifika Trades Training and that the allocation was fully taken up in the 2024-25 year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission funding allocations / Vote Tertiary Education appropriations for Māori and Pasifika Trades Training in 2024/25; true if the total allocation is around $18.5m and the TEC records it as fully allocated, false if the figure or the full-allocation claim differs materially.

veracity.statement: Perhaps the issue that it was going to take nearly a billion dollars over the next 10 years to have the IT systems operational is a good place to start.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that getting Te Pūkenga's IT systems operational was projected to cost close to $1 billion over ten years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga digital/IT business case and any TEC or Ministry of Education advice on its ten-year technology cost; true if the projected ten-year cost is close to $1 billion, false if the documented projection is materially lower.

veracity.statement: Perhaps it’s the fact that the polytech sector, under Te Pūkenga, did not get back to pre-COVID numbers, with internationals sitting at only a third, when the universities and the schools and the private training establishments were getting back.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that ITP enrolments did not recover to pre-COVID levels under Te Pūkenga, that international enrolments in the sector were about a third of pre-COVID levels, and that universities, schools and PTEs did recover.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Education Counts / Ministry of Education international and domestic enrolment series by provider type, comparing the latest Te Pūkenga-era year against 2019; true if ITP international enrolments are around one third of the 2019 level while university, school and PTE international enrolments are substantially closer to 2019, false if the sector comparison does not hold.

veracity.statement: She’s only got $20 million in that—she can’t afford it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister's strategic fund for the vocational education transition holds $20 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 / Vote Tertiary Education appropriations for the vocational education strategic (transition) fund; true if the appropriation is around $20 million, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: There are 106 pages in this legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a page count for the vocational education bill before the committee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The printed version of the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill as reported back from select committee; true if it runs to 106 pages, false if the page count differs.

rigor.statement: I want to go to the pastoral support code that the Minister did speak to and that the Green Party did support, because that code is the anchor and maybe we need to review it—maybe we need to review it—because I’ve heard from Student Voice in particular that they want to strengthen it.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (the code may need reviewing) rests only on a stakeholder group's stated preference — an appeal to an interested party's wish rather than evidence that the code is failing. A real inference about a real policy, but a thin one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Submissions noted in the Ministry of Education departmental report that there were alternative options—these were not adequately considered because of the ideological agenda of this Government and the Minister.
rigor.explanation: The causal step — that the alternatives went unconsidered because of an ideological agenda — is asserted, not shown. Nothing offered connects the departmental report's contents to a motive; it is motive attribution standing in for evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: She’s only got $20 million in that—she can’t afford it.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that she cannot afford it is drawn from the fund's size alone; no cost figure for what the fund has to cover is offered, so the gap between the premise and the conclusion is left unbridged.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Of course, this has nothing to do with the bill that we are currently looking at, but I can give the member assurance that total funding of approximately $18.5 million has been allocated to Māori and Pasifika trades training, and the funding was fully allocated in 2024-25.
specificity.explanation: A named programme, a dollar figure and a funding year — someone could look up the appropriation and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, if you look at the parent Act’s section 276, members of councils for the university sector, it has institutions which can be between eight to 12 council members. But for the polytech sector, which is governed by section 317, polytechs can have between six to eight members.
specificity.explanation: Names two specific statutory sections and gives the exact membership ranges each provides for. Fully checkable against the Act.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of the members other than those appointed by the Minister—of course, if it’s seven or eight, four will be appointed by the Minister; if it’s six, three will be, and the other members are to come from the community—the council will make a decision as to how that will occur.
specificity.explanation: Gives the exact split of ministerial appointments against council size and identifies the mechanism for the remaining seats. Concrete enough to check against the bill, though it leaves the community-selection process undefined.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the Education and Training Act as it is currently, with the provisions in relation to Te Pūkenga which this bill removes, there is a change from including a specific clause relating to polytechnics—which in the current Act is, I understand, section 318—to, in this, with the Minister’s bill, in Part 1 on page 9, amended section 267—it essentially puts academic freedom back into the primary academic freedom clause that applies to wānanga and universities as well.
specificity.explanation: Names the existing section, the amended section, the page of the bill, and the precise structural change being made. Someone could go to the bill and check the point exactly.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Now, if you look at the parent Act’s section 276, members of councils for the university sector, it has institutions which can be between eight to 12 council members. But for the polytech sector, which is governed by section 317, polytechs can have between six to eight members.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that s276 of the Education and Training Act 2020 sets university council membership at 8–12, and that s317 sets ITP council membership at 6–8.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Read ss 276 and 317 of the Education and Training Act 2020 as they stand at 14 October 2025 (and as amended by the bill for s317): true if s276 specifies a council of 8–12 members and s317 specifies 6–8; false if either range differs.

veracity.statement: Twenty-odd years ago there were 20 on a council.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that polytechnic councils had around 20 members roughly two decades before 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Council composition provisions of the Education Act 1989 as they stood around 2005, plus published polytechnic council membership lists from that period: true if ITP councils were commonly around 20 members before the Education Amendment Act 2010 reduced them, false if the typical membership was materially smaller.

veracity.statement: I also note that we are only on clause 7 of 39 of Part 1, about 41 pages, so there’s a number of very specific provisions which have not been discussed at all in this committee stage, that cover the substantive part of this bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Part 1 of the bill contains 39 clauses over roughly 41 pages and that the committee had at that point reached only clause 7.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill as reported back from the Education and Workforce Committee, plus the Hansard record of this committee stage: true if Part 1 runs to 39 clauses over approximately 41 pages and debate had reached clause 7; false if the clause count, page count or the point reached differs materially.

veracity.statement: They said to the Education and Workforce Committee in their submission that at no point was anyone able to articulate the problem that the reforms solved.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of Civil Contractors New Zealand's written submission to the select committee on this bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Civil Contractors New Zealand's written submission to the Education and Workforce Committee on the bill, published on the Parliament website: true if it states that no one was able to articulate the problem the reforms are trying to solve, false if it contains no such statement or says something materially different.

rigor.statement: We know that some universities will be smaller than some polytechnics, so I don’t think it’s necessarily to do in size.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: if institution size overlaps across the two sectors, size alone cannot explain a categorical difference in council-size rules. The conclusion largely follows, but it treats overlap at the margins as ruling out a size rationale based on typical scale, so there is a small gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Anywhere between six and eight is generally accepted as a good working board or council that will be able to represent the community but also be agile and nimble.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to unattributed common acceptance — 'generally accepted' — with no source, evidence or governance research offered to connect the 6–8 range to the claimed benefits. The conclusion rests on the assertion of consensus rather than on anything shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Look, the polytech sector has been collaborative for many years. It’s something of a myth that they haven’t been. The first nursing degrees were brought about through collaboration.
rigor.explanation: A general conclusion about the whole sector's behaviour over decades supported by a handful of illustrative cases — argument from anecdote. The examples are consistent with the claim but far too few to establish it.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If that’s good enough for the polytech sector, why not require it also for the university sector to work in a collaborative manner?
focus.explanation: Engages the measure directly — a named duty in the clause under debate — and asks why it is not extended to the other part of the sector. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m keen to know, in relation to section 314, why there is nothing in there, in the description of the characteristics, about the role that polytechs play in alleviating skills and workforce shortages.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named provision and a specific alleged omission from it. Entirely about the measure before the House, with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: In the past they have formed statutes and they have been different for each institution, and I would expect that, again, they will be different, so they won’t exclude any of the representation from staff or from students or from iwi.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the statutes adopted by the new individual polytechnic councils will not exclude staff, student or iwi representation. Not a promise about her own action — the statutes are made by each council.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The council statutes/constitutions adopted by the new ITP councils after establishment: true if none of them excludes staff, student or iwi representation from the non-ministerial seats; false if one or more adopted statutes makes no provision for one of those groups.

veracity.statement: Centralisation, where all of the decisions had to be made by a central entity that was supposed to be in Hamilton but was actually in Auckland—allowing those sorts of decisions to be made locally is incredibly important.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Te Pūkenga's central decision-making entity was nominally headquartered in Hamilton but in practice operated out of Auckland.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga's registered/head office location as recorded in its annual reports and Companies/Crown entity records, plus the location of its executive leadership team. True if the stated head office was Hamilton while the senior decision-making functions were in fact based in Auckland; false if executive functions were located in Hamilton as stated.

veracity.statement: That is exactly why NorthTec will be receiving the largest amount of any of the polytechnics—$3.648 million a year over the next two years, to ensure that they can keep that important provision going, because I know how much we must ensure access in those regions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both a specific strategic-funding figure for NorthTec and that it is the largest such allocation of any polytechnic.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission strategic/geographically-important funding allocations for the ITP sector for the 2026 and 2027 years. True if NorthTec's allocation is $3.648m per annum and no other polytechnic receives more; false if the figure differs materially or another ITP receives a larger amount.

veracity.statement: Nowhere is more important than in the Far North, where we’ve got the highest number of NEETs anywhere in the country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Far North has the highest level of young people not in employment, education or training in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey / MSD regional NEET statistics for 15-24 year olds. Read fairly as a rate rather than a raw count (by raw count Auckland would necessarily lead): true if Northland/Far North has the highest regional NEET rate in the most recent published data, false if another region is higher.

veracity.statement: You’ll see, in the earlier section, 317, that she will be appointing up to half of the current polytech council.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the bill's inserted section 317 provides — that the Minister may appoint up to half of a polytechnic council's members.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of new section 317 as inserted by clause 22 of the bill before the committee. True if it empowers the Minister to appoint up to half of the council's members; false if the proportion or the appointing power differs.

specificity.statement: That is exactly why NorthTec will be receiving the largest amount of any of the polytechnics—$3.648 million a year over the next two years, to ensure that they can keep that important provision going, because I know how much we must ensure access in those regions.
specificity.explanation: Names the institution, an exact dollar figure ($3.648 million), the period (per year for two years) and the comparative claim that it is the largest allocation — fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Online learning is not the only vehicle by which people engage in learning opportunities, and you haven’t offered the specificity that we need to assure us and give us confidence that this legislation is going to retain access for regional learners, actually going to have pūtea, money, available to invest in those learners, because you are committed to a 1:18 student ratio.
specificity.explanation: Names one concrete, checkable policy parameter (the 1:18 ratio), but the rest is a general demand for detail — no figures, mechanism or timeframe of his own is supplied.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I have had to make some changes because the unified funding system that had been put in was so disastrous.
civility.explanation: Blunt condemnation of an inherited funding policy — 'so disastrous' is harsh about the measure, but no person is attacked, no bad faith is imputed, and no one is mocked. Contested ground where an uncivil option was available.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Look, it is described as “may”, but it is, effectively, mandatory because the chair will be appointed.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur. The fact that a chairperson will in practice be appointed does not convert a discretionary 'may' into a mandatory duty, and it does not touch the question actually asked — whether the Minister could appoint someone from outside the council's membership. The conclusion outruns the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: My theory is that, if the chairperson and deputy chairperson are the ones who are supposed to be leading the council, it makes perfect sense for the Minister to consult the members of the ITP concerned on who their chairperson and deputy chairperson might be, because the members might know something about the person that the Minister might want to appoint as chairperson and deputy chairperson that she doesn’t necessarily know.
rigor.explanation: A clean premise-to-conclusion argument: the chair leads the council, council members hold information about candidates the Minister lacks, therefore consultation improves the appointment. No fallacy or appeal; the small gap is that it asserts rather than evidences the information asymmetry.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Look, it is described as “may”, but it is, effectively, mandatory because the chair will be appointed.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the drafting of the clause before the committee — responds to the specific 'may' versus 'must' point with no party framing at all. High focus despite the weak inference.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Online learning is not the only vehicle by which people engage in learning opportunities, and you haven’t offered the specificity that we need to assure us and give us confidence that this legislation is going to retain access for regional learners, actually going to have pūtea, money, available to invest in those learners, because you are committed to a 1:18 student ratio.
focus.explanation: Entirely directed at the measure before the House — mode of delivery, regional access, funding, and the named 1:18 student-to-tutor ratio. No party-record framing at all; this is scrutiny of a specific policy parameter.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My theory is that, if the chairperson and deputy chairperson are the ones who are supposed to be leading the council, it makes perfect sense for the Minister to consult the members of the ITP concerned on who their chairperson and deputy chairperson might be, because the members might know something about the person that the Minister might want to appoint as chairperson and deputy chairperson that she doesn’t necessarily know.
focus.explanation: Addresses the appointment mechanism in the inserted section and proposes a specific amendment to it. No characterisation of the other party anywhere in the argument.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It will see courses cancelled in the further-out parts of Northland: Kaikohe, Kaitāia, marae-based programmes.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that NorthTec will discontinue course delivery at its outlying Northland sites and its marae-based provision as a consequence of the restructure. Not a promise about his own action, and tied to named locations.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NorthTec's published programme and campus offerings for Kaikohe, Kaitāia and its marae-based programmes, compared against its 2025 offerings, plus any TEC/NorthTec announcements of course discontinuation. True if courses at those sites or the marae-based programmes are cancelled; false if delivery at those sites continues at comparable breadth.

focus.statement: Why is there not, for example in paragraph (b), the requirement to consult, for example, local institutions, regional industry groups, local community organisations, iwi and hapū?
focus.explanation: Engages the measure before the House directly — a named subsection of new section 315 and the specific consultation duty he says is missing. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Essentially in the main Education and Training Act, the main section 289(7) doesn’t apply but new section 341J does apply.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of the measure before the committee — which section applies to which institution — with no reference to the other party at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What advice are you receiving around the actual costs and funding that you need to establish this particular model for the 10-plus other polytechnics?
focus.explanation: Textbook scrutiny: a named model, a named cohort of institutions, and a demand for the cost advice behind it. Holding a minister to account for the finances of a specific measure is on-policy, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why is there not, for example in paragraph (b), the requirement to consult, for example, local institutions, regional industry groups, local community organisations, iwi and hapū?
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision (paragraph (b)) and enumerates the specific bodies he says should be consulted. A precise question, checkable against the drafting; short of 1.0 only because no wording or threshold is proposed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I just want to really assure the member, because I know he’s genuine in asking these questions, that we have no intention of setting polytechnics up that are not in the best possible financial state they can be in to give them an absolute chance to be successful going forward.
specificity.explanation: Answers a direct request for costings and advice with a statement of intention. No figure, no source of advice, no timeframe and no threshold for what 'best possible financial state' means. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Essentially in the main Education and Training Act, the main section 289(7) doesn’t apply but new section 341J does apply.
specificity.explanation: Names both provisions exactly and states the precise drafting asymmetry she is asking about. Anyone can go to the Act and the Bill and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It opens the door to consult with all of those entities that the member brought forward.
rigor.explanation: Equivocates between a permissive and a mandatory power. The question was why consultation with regional bodies is not *required*; the answer that a discretionary 'consult other persons or bodies that the Minister thinks fit' opens the door establishes only that it is permitted. The conclusion that the concern is covered does not follow from the premise offered.

rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In terms of the consent rather than just consulting, can I just say, it’s really, really difficult when a polytechnic gets into that downward spiral either academically or financially. But the conclusion rests on the current intent of the regime, which does not answer the objection raised, which was about what a later government could do with the same power. The gap between what is shown (present purpose) and what is concluded (no consent needed) is left open.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In the cluster that you’ve established is the anchor polytechnic of the Open Polytechnic, who are the educational delivery partner—that is their core business. rigor.explanation: A clean inference: the stated problem at Otago is financial, the assigned anchor's competence is educational delivery, therefore the model leaves the financial support role unassigned. The premises are stated, the hedge is marked, and the conclusion follows from them.

veracity.statement: Although I do note that Opposition members, including the Leader of the Opposition, has already committed to not re-establishing it again, but it does create a legislative safeguard to prevent that.

veracity.statement: The greatest financial relief that the federation can provide, of course, is the fact that the Open Polytechnic has 160-odd programmes online that can be available to the other institutions and that they won’t have to do the development of.

civility.statement: I think, probably, the member is underestimating the level of engagement that would go on, before you might get to that stage, to ensure that the polytechnic understands the areas that they have a deficit in—whether it’s academic or financial—and to ensure that they understand what can be done to help support them.

focus.statement: There was lots of opportunity there, but this Minister, under this legislation, has chosen to disestablish that successful model and re-establish a model with half the funding and more entities to manage, which just doesn’t make sense in any respect.

The premises are offered and do support the conclusion, but the step from 'the old model was expensive' to 'this bill reproduces it' is asserted rather than shown, which is the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When I meet with any institution at the moment, they say that they feel uncertain and that they are experiencing the instability. Any meaningful engagement with the sector will show the impact of consecutive years of change.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from his own meetings to the whole sector, then makes the generalisation self-sealing: 'any meaningful engagement will show' defines disagreement as not meaningful. Appeal to anecdote plus a no-true-Scotsman move.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I don’t understand removing these specific categories but then including a clause that says the council of a polytechnic should as far as is reasonably practicable reflect the communities in the region that the polytechnic serves.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference — she argues the bill is internally inconsistent in requiring councils to reflect their communities while deleting the enumerated characteristics that describe those communities. The inconsistency is real but not established: a general reflectiveness duty can subsume the specifics, and she does not close that gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In terms of the title, I support Shanan Halbert’s amendment, because I believe the Minister has created more instability in the sector, and I ask and plead that we can do something to ensure the staff, the students, and the community can feel affirmed and stable in the future, going forward, of vocational education.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on a bare statement of belief plus one institution's staffroom impressions, and closes with an appeal to emotion (mortgages, children, communities) in place of evidence that the bill increases instability.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That’s simply because we’re going back to a model that was so expensive. We ended up with millions of dollars of debt. Consecutive Governments had to continue to bail institutions out, and that, in fact, is one of the primary reasons why we established Te Pūkenga.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that governments repeatedly provided bailout funding to institutes of technology and polytechnics before Te Pūkenga, and that this financial position was a primary reason for creating Te Pūkenga.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: TEC and Ministry of Education records of Crown financial support to ITPs in the years before 2020, plus the Reform of Vocational Education Cabinet papers and regulatory impact statement. True if multiple ITPs received Crown bailout/recapitalisation funding across more than one government and financial viability is stated as a driver of the Te Pūkenga merger; false if such support was isolated to a single institution or a single government, or if the official rationale does not cite financial viability.

veracity.statement: I would have thought that at a time when we’re seeing significant issues—I mean, if I were to just look at disability unemployment rates, it’s gone up from 8.2 percent in 2022 to 14 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the unemployment rate for disabled people in New Zealand rose from 8.2 percent in 2022 to 14 percent as at the time of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey disability statistics: the unemployment rate for disabled people, 2022 reference period versus the most recent published quarter before October 2025. True if the 2022 figure is 8.2% (± rounding) and the latest figure is about 14%; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: The Government has had to bail them out several times over the years in terms of financial viability.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Western Institute of Technology at Taranaki (WITT), which he has just named, has required Crown bailout funding on multiple occasions over past years because of financial viability problems.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: WITT annual reports and TEC records of Crown financial support to WITT prior to the Te Pūkenga merger. True if WITT received Crown bailout, recapitalisation or exceptional support funding on two or more separate occasions; false if it received such support once or not at all.

civility.statement: Again, the reform that the Minister puts before the Chamber today doesn’t aid in offering any certainty or stability for the sector. It, in fact, offers more instability and more questions that remain unresolved.
civility.explanation: A blunt verdict on the reform itself, in a genuinely contested debate where he had every opportunity to turn on the Minister and does not. The criticism lands on the policy, so it is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: That is going to make a huge difference to those polytechnics and industry skills boards.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the pending recapitalisation of the polytechnic network will substantially improve the financial position of the polytechnics and the new industry skills boards. Not a promise of her own action — the recapitalisation is already committed; the forecast is about its effect.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Annual reports of the recapitalised polytechnics and TEC monitoring reports for the first full financial year after the recapitalisation is paid. True if a majority of recipient polytechnics report a materially improved operating result (deficit substantially reduced or surplus restored) relative to the year before payment; false if their operating results are broadly flat or worse, or if further Crown support is required in that period.

rigor.statement: It took on a responsibility for coping with inflation driven to stratospheric levels of danger as a consequence of a failed fiscal policy prior to our arrival.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a causal chain from the previous government's fiscal policy to the inflation peak with no mechanism, data or intermediate step offered — the conclusion is asserted rather than supported (bare assertion of causation).
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, given that the size of our economy is $440-odd billion, it takes a while to turn the super-tanker around.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on a metaphor: the size of GDP is offered as though it establishes the required lag, with nothing connecting the figure to any timeframe. Argument by analogy with no supporting step.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We had a plan, we’re delivering on that plan that places student achievement at the centre, and we are seeing results. This is what delivery looks like.
rigor.explanation: Concludes that achievement results are being delivered from evidence that is entirely self-reported perception (teachers, parents and students saying things feel better). Perception survey data does not establish measured achievement gains — a real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does she think it is reasonable to cut jobseeker for young people when over 218 applications for one role at a Tank Juice bar show that there are simply no jobs available?
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single vacancy at one juice bar to the conclusion that 'there are simply no jobs available' — a hasty generalisation from anecdote to a labour-market-wide claim.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How can she stand by her statement that “We have invested more in public infrastructure.”, when there are 20,000 fewer people working in construction?
specificity.explanation: Cites a specific quantity (20,000 fewer construction workers) against a named claim about infrastructure investment; someone could go and check both halves.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But as my colleague Mr Bishop has said, over $60 billion has been put aside for infrastructure, including the construction sector, over the next four years.
specificity.explanation: A dollar figure and a timeframe, but no breakdown of what the $60 billion covers or when it is spent.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Nearly 80 percent of primary teachers have accessed professional learning and development in delivering structured literacy, and ERO found that teachers who used the 1.1 million maths books, textbooks, workbooks, and teacher guides that we have delivered were four times more likely to change their teaching practice.
specificity.explanation: Percentages, a resource count and a named effect size, all attributed to a named report — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: These include Altum in Wellington, a school focused on classical education; Aotearoa Infinite Academy, a school focused on remote education; and Te Aratika High School, a school in Hawke’s Bay focused on giving vocational pathways to Māori and Pacific students who have been disengaged from education.
specificity.explanation: Three named schools with locations and stated focuses — concrete and directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are focused on easing the cost of living pressures and helping families to keep more of what they earn.
specificity.explanation: A statement of direction with no mechanism, amount, timeframe or named measure; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What I announced today is that we now have 70,000 people in case management with independent, individual employment plans.
specificity.explanation: A named count, a named mechanism (case management with individual employment plans) and a stated announcement date.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: How can she stand by her statement that “We have invested more in public infrastructure.”, when there are 20,000 fewer people working in construction?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that construction employment has fallen by about 20,000 people.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey / filled jobs series for the construction industry: true if employment in construction has fallen by approximately 20,000 between the change of government and the latest quarter available on 2025-10-15; false if the fall is materially smaller or employment has risen.

veracity.statement: But as my colleague Mr Bishop has said, over $60 billion has been put aside for infrastructure, including the construction sector, over the next four years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than $60 billion of government funding is allocated to infrastructure over the coming four years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Budget 2025 capital allowances and the National Infrastructure Pipeline / four-year capital intentions: true if the published four-year infrastructure investment figure exceeds $60 billion, false if the published figure is materially below that.

veracity.statement: Well, given that the size of our economy is $440-odd billion, it takes a while to turn the super-tanker around.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's economy is about $440 billion in size.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ nominal GDP (annual, expenditure measure) for the year to mid-2025: true if nominal GDP is approximately $440 billion, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Half of teachers reported that students’ English and maths have improved compared to last year. Parents agree, with over three-quarters reporting better progress for their children in both English and maths, and so do our young people.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific proportions reported in the Education Review Office report released that day: about half of teachers and over three-quarters of parents reporting improvement in English and maths.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The ERO report on implementation of the English and maths curriculum reforms released on or about 2025-10-15: true if the survey results give approximately 50% of teachers and over 75% of parents reporting improvement, false if the published proportions are materially lower or measure something else.

veracity.statement: Nearly 80 percent of primary teachers have accessed professional learning and development in delivering structured literacy, and ERO found that teachers who used the 1.1 million maths books, textbooks, workbooks, and teacher guides that we have delivered were four times more likely to change their teaching practice.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that nearly 80% of primary teachers have accessed structured-literacy PLD, that 1.1 million maths resources were delivered, and that ERO found users of them four times more likely to change practice.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The ERO report released on or about 2025-10-15 and Ministry of Education PLD/resource distribution figures: true if the report and ministry data give approximately 80% teacher PLD uptake, ~1.1 million resources delivered, and a roughly fourfold difference in practice change; false if any of the three figures is materially different or not found in those sources.

veracity.statement: These include Altum in Wellington, a school focused on classical education; Aotearoa Infinite Academy, a school focused on remote education; and Te Aratika High School, a school in Hawke’s Bay focused on giving vocational pathways to Māori and Pacific students who have been disengaged from education.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that three named charter schools with those locations and focuses were announced that week, taking the total to 14.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education / Associate Minister charter school announcements for the week of 2025-10-13: true if Altum, Aotearoa Infinite Academy and Te Aratika High School were announced as charter schools with those locations, and the approved total reaches 14; false if the names, locations or running total differ.

veracity.statement: That’s why we had 58 different applications for people to run new schools in this round, and I’m very much looking forward to announcing even more of these new schools as well as a growing number of State schools converting to charter status as the year completes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 58 applications to run new charter schools were received in the current application round.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Charter School Agency / Ministry of Education published application counts for the 2025 charter school funding round: true if the round received approximately 58 applications, false if the published count is materially different.

veracity.statement: Who is correct: the Prime Minister, who said that young people need to get off the couch, stop playing PlayStation, and go and find a job, or Student Job Search chief executive Louise Saviker, who said applications are outpacing job listings?
veracity.explanation: Relays two attributed statements: that the Prime Minister told young people to get off the couch, stop playing PlayStation and find a job, and that the Student Job Search chief executive said applications are outpacing job listings.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous media reports or transcripts of the Prime Minister's remarks, and reported comments by Student Job Search chief executive Louise Saviker, in the weeks before 2025-10-15: true if both quotes are substantively as characterised, false if either was not said or is materially misrepresented.

veracity.statement: Because under their watch, the number of young people that went on to benefit under the age of 25—the duration increased to 18 future years on welfare, a 49 percent increase since 2017.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the average future years on welfare for people going onto benefit under 25 reached 18 years, a 49 percent increase since 2017.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit system performance / valuation reports on average future years on main benefit for beneficiaries aged under 25: true if the figure is approximately 18 years and approximately 49% higher than the 2017 figure, false if either the level or the change is materially different.

veracity.statement: What I announced today is that we now have 70,000 people in case management with independent, individual employment plans.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 70,000 people are currently in MSD case management with individual employment plans.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD case management figures published or announced on 2025-10-15: true if approximately 70,000 clients are recorded as in case management with individual employment plans, false if the figure is materially different.

focus.statement: Who else is there to blame for her economic mismanagement, given that since she was asked this question last week, her Government has added teachers, firefighters, doctors, nurses, and the unions to that list?
focus.explanation: The weight of the question is about the Minister's blame-shifting behaviour rather than any named policy, measure or figure; 'economic mismanagement' is asserted in general terms.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We are not only very focused on the right navigational bearings but we’re leaving the storm and hurricane of destruction that was left to us by the last regime.
focus.explanation: No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — the content is entirely a characterisation of the previous government's record in general terms.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That was an education secretary under a Labour Minister, Peter Fraser, and I would love to see the Labour Party fulfil that kind of aspiration for the students of New Zealand rather than cuddle up to the unions.
focus.explanation: Turns from the charter school policy to characterising the Labour Party's relationship with unions; no policy, mechanism or outcome is named in the pivot.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They’re both correct, because what we do know is that we have a higher aspiration for young people, clearly, than the Opposition do.
focus.explanation: Answers a question about job availability by comparing the parties' aspirations; no policy, figure or mechanism is engaged in this sentence.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will she admit that instead of doing her job, she’s kicking 18- and 19-year-olds off jobseeker because she’s failing to get to her 50,000 jobseeker reduction target?
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy (removing 18- and 19-year-olds from jobseeker support) and a specific government target (50,000 reduction) — legitimate scrutiny of a named commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Who else is there to blame for her economic mismanagement, given that since she was asked this question last week, her Government has added teachers, firefighters, doctors, nurses, and the unions to that list?
civility.explanation: Pointed and attributes failure to the Minister personally ('her economic mismanagement'), but stops at her record and conduct rather than landing on her character or competence as a person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Will she admit that instead of doing her job, she’s kicking 18- and 19-year-olds off jobseeker because she’s failing to get to her 50,000 jobseeker reduction target?
civility.explanation: Goes past the policy to impute dereliction and bad motive to the Minister personally — 'instead of doing her job' and the suggestion she is acting to cover a missed target.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Does he stand by his statement on becoming Prime Minister two years ago, “We’re desperate to get to work to try and make things better for New Zealanders.”; if so, why do twice as many New Zealanders think things will be the same or worse in the next 12 months compared to those who think things will get better?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in current public opinion polling, respondents expecting the next 12 months to be the same or worse outnumber those expecting improvement by roughly two to one.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published New Zealand public-opinion polling from around October 2025 asking whether respondents expect things to get better/stay the same/get worse over the next 12 months (e.g. Ipsos NZ Issues Monitor, Talbot Mills, or a bank consumer-confidence series): true if the combined same-or-worse share is approximately double the 'better' share, false if the ratio is materially below 2:1.

veracity.statement: We had violent crime up 33 percent, gang membership up 51 percent; we had a four-fold increase in ram raids, and a doubling of retail crime.
veracity.explanation: Four numeric claims about changes under the previous government: violent crime +33%, gang membership +51%, ram raids up fourfold, retail crime doubled.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Crime and Victims Survey victimisation figures and NZ Police National Gang List / retail-crime and ram-raid statistics for 2017–2023: true if each of the four figures matches the published series within rounding, false if any is materially different or measured over a different period than implied.

veracity.statement: I’m proud to say there are 29,000 fewer victims of serious violent crime; there’s a 16 percent reduction in serious youth offending.
veracity.explanation: Claims a reduction of 29,000 in the number of victims of serious violent crime and a 16 percent fall in serious youth offending under the current government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Crime and Victims Survey (victims of serious violent crime, cycle-on-cycle change) and Police/Oranga Tamariki youth offending statistics: true if the 29,000 reduction and the 16 percent fall appear in those series for the stated period, false if the published changes differ materially.

veracity.statement: I consider that the member who was the education Minister for 5½ years did a pretty bad job, actually, making sure that over half our kids weren't at school regularly and that half of them couldn't read at the standard they needed to be going into high school, and 80 percent weren’t at the standard they needed in maths.
veracity.explanation: Three statistical claims about the period of Hipkins' education ministry: regular attendance below 50%, half of school leavers below the reading standard for high school, 80% below the maths standard.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education regular-attendance data for 2017–2022 and NMSSA / NCEA literacy-numeracy co-requisite pilot results: true if regular attendance was under 50%, the reading shortfall around 50%, and the maths shortfall around 80% in the years referenced; false if any figure is materially overstated.

veracity.statement: We didn't increase it 84 percent. We didn't triple the debt to $180 billion, writing out a $9 billion interest rate bill.
veracity.explanation: Claims the previous government increased government spending by 84 percent, tripled debt to $180 billion, and left an annual interest bill of $9 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenses, core Crown borrowings and finance-cost series in the Financial Statements of the Government for 2017–2023: true if core Crown expenses rose ~84%, debt roughly tripled to about $180 billion, and finance costs reached about $9 billion; false if the figures require a different baseline or period to hold.

veracity.statement: Just yesterday, you would have seen 86 percent confidence in our tourism operators—our second biggest industry, at 7.5 percent of our total GDP.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a recently published tourism-operator confidence reading of 86 percent, and that tourism is New Zealand's second biggest industry at 7.5 percent of GDP.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The tourism industry confidence survey released on 14 October 2025 (e.g. Tourism Industry Aotearoa) and the Stats NZ Tourism Satellite Account: true if the survey reports ~86% confidence and tourism's share of GDP is ~7.5% on the measure used, false if the confidence figure differs or tourism's GDP share on the cited basis is materially lower.

veracity.statement: We supported the initial pay equity legislation that came through the House, but that member took a paper to Cabinet and blew the cost from $3.5 billion up to $12 to $13 billion.
veracity.explanation: Claims National supported the original pay equity legislation, and that a Cabinet paper taken by Hipkins raised the projected cost from $3.5 billion to $12–13 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The division record for the Equal Pay Amendment Bill 2020 and the released Cabinet paper plus Treasury costings for the pay equity regime: true if National voted for the original bill and the costing moved from ~$3.5b to ~$12–13b following the paper identified, false if the cost change is attributable elsewhere or the figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: So why is he willing to accept a pay rise in line with inflation, claim a $50,000 housing allowance, and spend $44,000 on a helicopter ride so he could take a photograph for his Facebook, while his Government makes pay offers to workers like firefighters, nurses, and teachers that amount to pay cuts in real terms?
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Prime Minister accepted an inflation-linked pay rise, claimed a $50,000 housing allowance, and spent $44,000 on a helicopter trip.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Remuneration Authority determinations for the Prime Minister's salary, Parliamentary Service accommodation-entitlement disclosures, and DIA/ministerial travel expense releases covering the helicopter flight: true if a ~$50,000 accommodation entitlement was claimed and a ~$44,000 helicopter charter appears in the released expenses, false if the amounts or the claiming differ materially.

veracity.statement: How can she stand by her statement that she is, “making changes that will set our country up for a better future”, when 200 Kiwis a day do not see a better future and are choosing to leave the country?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that around 200 New Zealanders per day are currently emigrating.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration estimates for the year to around August 2025: true if departures of New Zealand citizens average roughly 200 per day (about 73,000 a year) on either the gross-departure or net-loss basis being invoked, false if the relevant figure is materially lower.

veracity.statement: How can she stand by her statement in April this year that “We’ve been seeing green shoots across the economy.”, when at that time the economy was shrinking by almost 1 percent?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that at the time of the Minister's April 2025 statement the economy was contracting by almost 1 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP series and the vintage of data available in April 2025: true if the most recently published quarterly or annual GDP change at that date was a contraction approaching 1 percent, false if the contemporaneous prints showed growth and the -0.9% quarter fell outside that window.

veracity.statement: As is the case with statistics, they’re so backward looking. The actual truth of the matter is that with the reduction and the improvement in terms of monetary policy, more liquidity is coming into the economy, banks are more confident, and the market is talking about yet another further reduction in monetary policy standards from 2.5 percent to some other figure.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the policy rate currently stands at 2.5 percent and that market expectation is for a further reduction from that level.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ Official Cash Rate decisions to 15 October 2025 and contemporaneous market pricing / bank economist forecasts: true if the OCR was 2.5% at that date and consensus pricing implied a further cut, false if the rate differed or markets priced no further easing.

specificity.statement: I’m proud to say there are 29,000 fewer victims of serious violent crime; there’s a 16 percent reduction in serious youth offending.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete, checkable figures attached to named measures; someone could look both up.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But what we're doing is lowering inflation, lowering interest rates, getting the economy moving, and actually getting people back to work.
specificity.explanation: A string of directions of travel with no figures, mechanisms, targets or timeframes — nothing here could be acted on or checked as stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Once fully rolled out, around 130,000 additional women will be eligible for free screening every two years.
specificity.explanation: A concrete population figure with a stated screening interval, tied to a named programme — checkable against the programme's own documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re delivering practical, life-changing results for New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: A summary boast with no measure, figure, mechanism or timeframe; nothing in the sentence itself could be checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The changes that we are making, both of a fiscal and a regulatory character, are both short term and medium term.
specificity.explanation: Names no change, no instrument, no amount and no date — the sentence classifies unnamed measures rather than describing any.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I consider that the member who was the education Minister for 5½ years did a pretty bad job, actually, making sure that over half our kids weren't at school regularly and that half of them couldn't read at the standard they needed to be going into high school, and 80 percent weren’t at the standard they needed in maths.
civility.explanation: A direct verdict on an individual member's competence in office ("did a pretty bad job"), rather than on the policy alone — but it is tied to his record and stops well short of abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And just look at the front bench across the road. Do you think there are any economically literate people in that front bench? It's unbelievable.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the intelligence and competence of the members opposite rather than on any argument they have made.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I know you might be worried about your union mates, but actually we're not worried about your unions.
civility.explanation: Imputes a personal motive to the member — that his concern is loyalty to "mates" rather than the issue — which is a sneer at the person rather than a response to the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Not surprising—can't do math, so not a surprise, but we're actually making it workable given the complexities around that regime, and it's still available for people today, and we encourage unions and members to make claims under the pay equity legislation that's there.
civility.explanation: "Can't do math" is a direct jibe at the member's personal competence, unconnected to the substantive point that follows it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So why is he willing to accept a pay rise in line with inflation, claim a $50,000 housing allowance, and spend $44,000 on a helicopter ride so he could take a photograph for his Facebook, while his Government makes pay offers to workers like firefighters, nurses, and teachers that amount to pay cuts in real terms?
civility.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny of ministerial expenses, but the framing ("so he could take a photograph for his Facebook") imputes vanity and self-interest to the person rather than testing the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And just look at the front bench across the road. Do you think there are any economically literate people in that front bench? It's unbelievable.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the other side are like; no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I know you might be worried about your union mates, but actually we're not worried about your unions.
focus.explanation: Drops the pay negotiations entirely to characterise the questioner's affiliations; no named policy, offer or figure survives once the jibe is removed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How has refusing to meaningfully negotiate with firefighters, doctors, nurses, and teachers, contributing to what may well be the largest strike action New Zealand's seen in a generation, made things better for New Zealanders?
focus.explanation: Names specific workforces, a specific government conduct (pay negotiations) and a specific consequence (strike action) — accountability for a named outcome, not party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How has scrapping pay equity agreements, therefore cutting the future pay for thousands of New Zealand workers, mostly women, made things better off for New Zealanders?
focus.explanation: Names a specific legislative change and the group it is said to affect; squarely on the measure rather than on the government's character.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We're now growing now; we're expected to grow even further in quarter four.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that quarterly GDP growth in the December 2025 quarter will exceed the growth currently being recorded.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP (production measure, seasonally adjusted) for the December 2025 quarter, released March 2026: true if December-quarter growth is positive and larger than the September 2025 quarter; false if the December quarter is negative or lower than the preceding quarter.

rigor.statement: The brakes were hit on the second day of April due to uncertainty around the Trump tariff.
rigor.explanation: A causal conclusion resting on coincidence of timing alone (post hoc): the date of the tariff announcement is offered as the sole basis for attributing the slowdown to it, with no other mechanism or evidence given.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But what Kiwis are sick of is unions prioritising their interests ahead of kids who haven't been in school, the kids that are about to go into exams over the next wee while, the tens of thousands of patients that have been waiting because they ran up the wait-list like 20 times since they were in power.
rigor.explanation: A false dichotomy — union pay claims are treated as necessarily coming at the expense of students and patients, with nothing offered to establish the trade-off — resting on an appeal to popular sentiment ("what Kiwis are sick of").
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It has long been a rite of passage for Kiwis to venture overseas.
rigor.explanation: Offered as the answer to a question about the current emigration rate: an appeal to tradition, which cannot address whether the present level is unusual or policy-driven.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As is the case with statistics, they’re so backward looking. The actual truth of the matter is that with the reduction and the improvement in terms of monetary policy, more liquidity is coming into the economy, banks are more confident, and the market is talking about yet another further reduction in monetary policy standards from 2.5 percent to some other figure.
rigor.explanation: Dismisses the contradicting evidence categorically (all statistics are backward-looking) and substitutes unattributed market sentiment as "the actual truth" — the conclusion rests on discarding measurement rather than on anything offered in its place.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Treasury forecast in Budget Economic and Fiscal Update indicated that we would continue, unfortunately, to see jobseeker numbers rise until December.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Budget Economic and Fiscal Update contained a forecast of rising jobseeker numbers through to December.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Treasury Budget Economic and Fiscal Update 2025 benefit-recipient forecasts; true if it projects Jobseeker Support numbers continuing to rise until December 2025, false if it projects a flat or falling track.

veracity.statement: But we’re not sitting around waiting and watching for that to happen, which is why we’ve got 70,000 people in case management, the most effective intervention that is possible.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 70,000 people are currently in MSD case management.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit and employment-service statistics for the quarter ending September 2025; true if roughly 70,000 clients are recorded in case management, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: We’re also branching out into new areas of research, with $70 million committed to AI technology, $71 million for future materials and magnet technologies, and $42 million to establish a biodiscovery platform, and we’ve more than doubled investment into our fast-growing gaming sector.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific funding commitments of $70m for AI, $71m for future materials and magnet technologies, and $42m for a biodiscovery platform, plus a more than doubled gaming-sector investment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 appropriations and MBIE science funding announcements; true if the three named amounts match the published commitments, false if the figures or the areas differ materially.

veracity.statement: How many of the 200 New Zealanders who leave our shores each day are qualified construction workers?
veracity.explanation: Embeds the claim that around 200 New Zealanders are departing the country each day.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration statistics for the year to mid-2025; true if departures of New Zealand citizens average approximately 200 per day (roughly 73,000 a year) on the measure implied, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: Why is construction activity the lowest it has been since 2019, when he promised more people wearing high-vis and hard hats?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that construction activity is currently at its lowest level since 2019.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ value of building work put in place / construction activity series to the September 2025 quarter; true if the latest reading is the lowest since 2019, false if any intervening quarter was lower.

veracity.statement: Why did the Government promise more people wearing high-vis and hard hats when there has been $2.9 billion less spent on roads, housing, and hospitals over the past year?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $2.9 billion year-on-year reduction in spending on roads, housing and hospitals.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury and agency capital expenditure figures for roads, housing and hospitals for the 2024/25 year against the prior year; true if the combined reduction is approximately $2.9 billion, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: On the matter of the hospital, it’s this Government that's actually accelerated the delivery of the Dunedin Hospital project.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the current Government has brought forward, rather than delayed, delivery of the new Dunedin Hospital.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published Health New Zealand / Ministerial timelines for the new Dunedin Hospital before and after the 2024 rescoping decision; true if the completion date moved earlier, false if it moved later or was unchanged.

specificity.statement: But we’re not sitting around waiting and watching for that to happen, which is why we’ve got 70,000 people in case management, the most effective intervention that is possible.
specificity.explanation: Names a mechanism (case management) and a caseload figure, but the trailing superlative commits to nothing measurable and no timeframe or outcome is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Can the Prime Minister guarantee that Aotearoa will protect 30 percent of our exclusive economic zone by 2030 as committed to under the 2022 global biodiversity framework; if not, why not?
specificity.explanation: Names a precise target (30 percent of the EEZ), a date (2030) and the instrument it derives from; a precise question is as checkable as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But, again, you know, this is a Government that is very focused on economic growth, right? We want to get things done and we want to get things built.
