veracity.statement: Even today, when debating my co-leader Marama Davidson, the Associate Minister of Education, David Seymour, in a New Zealand Herald interview, acknowledged that child poverty plays a huge role in attendance.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that David Seymour, in a New Zealand Herald interview on or about 15 October 2025 debating Marama Davidson, conceded that child poverty is a major driver of school non-attendance.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Herald interview/debate between David Seymour and Marama Davidson published on or around 15 October 2025; true if Seymour is recorded there acknowledging child poverty as a significant factor in school attendance, false if no such interview exists or he makes no such acknowledgement.

veracity.statement: You don’t need to believe me; you can just look at the Government’s own statistics of child poverty to see that more children are projected to not have their basic needs being met as a result of Government decisions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official government child poverty projections show an increasing number of children failing to have basic needs met, attributed to government decisions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/MSD child poverty projections published with Budget 2025 and the Stats NZ child poverty statistics release (material hardship measure); true if the official projections show the material hardship rate or number of children in material hardship rising, false if they show it flat or falling.

veracity.statement: The Hon David Seymour has been working really hard to improve attendance of students at schools and we have seen some really good results because of that hard work.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that school attendance has measurably improved under the current Associate Minister of Education's attendance programme.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education termly attendance data (regular attendance rate, defined as attending more than 90% of half-days); true if the regular attendance rate for 2024–2025 terms is materially higher than the equivalent terms in 2023, false if it is flat or lower.

rigor.statement: Because, on the one hand, they’re creating all these additional layers of bureaucracy around attendance management plans and then, on the other hand, quite happily allow material hardship for children to go up on their watch. That, to me, is contradictory.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House: requiring schools to address the underlying causes of absence while (he claims) government policy worsens those causes is internally inconsistent. The conclusion largely follows, but it leans on an unstated premise that the two policy areas are within the same decision-maker's control in the same way, and 'contradictory' overstates what is really a tension in priorities.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The member, the Green Party member who spoke before me, instead of supporting that, he was actually providing excuses for students to not attend school.
rigor.explanation: Strawman. The preceding speaker argued that attendance plans will not work unless the material causes of absence are addressed; that is recast as making excuses for non-attendance, and the rebuttal is then aimed at the recast position rather than the one actually advanced.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is due to the changes in clause 9 and clause 23, which subsequently were recommended to be changed to be a bit more workable.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact clauses at issue and refers to the select committee's recommended amendments, so the claim can be checked against the bill; but 'a bit more workable' carries no detail about what the changes actually do.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s really important to note that the ACT Party has been advocating for one of the subclauses to be removed. This is in section 127, inserted by clause 8, subclause (2)(e) and this is “to ensure that the school gives effective Te Tiriti o Waitangi,” and there are other subclauses to that.
specificity.explanation: Cites the precise legislative location — section 127, clause 8, subclause (2)(e) — and quotes the wording at issue, so anyone can look it up and check exactly what is being sought.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ve also seen how the ACT Party has had a free ride in their importing of culture wars in the provisions around freedom of expression.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy referent — the freedom of expression provisions in the bill — but the weight of the sentence is a characterisation of another party's motives ('free ride', 'importing culture wars') rather than engagement with what the provisions do.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: At the moment, what is happening because of those members sitting on the other side, our universities have been hijacked by the ideology, and we want to rescue universities from that, and that is why I am really pleased with this provision in this legislation.
focus.explanation: Gestures at 'this provision' but supplies no policy content — no mechanism, no example, no named course, rule or institution. The substance of the sentence is an accusation about what the other side has done to universities in general.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Again, all that we will see is our universities continuing to drop in some of those international rankings when it comes to how they’re perceived internationally.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that New Zealand universities will keep falling in international university rankings.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The QS World University Rankings and Times Higher Education World University Rankings editions released after this statement, compared with the preceding edition; true if the majority of the eight New Zealand universities fall in position, false if the majority hold or improve.

veracity.statement: In many areas, turnout was below 40 percent, and in some communities, it dropped into the 30s, which is a reflection of a voting system that is confusing, outdated, and disconnected from the lives of everyday New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 2025 local election turnout was below 40% in many areas and in the 30s in some communities.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official turnout figures for the October 2025 local authority elections as published by individual councils / DIA / LGNZ; true if a substantial number of councils recorded turnout below 40% and some below 40% into the 30s, false if typical turnout was materially higher.

veracity.statement: This directly contradicts the Prime Minister in Monday’s post-Cabinet press conference saying he’s discussing the Electoral Commission running the local elections with Minister Watts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Prime Minister said at the post-Cabinet press conference of Monday 13 October 2025 that he is discussing Electoral Commission administration of local elections with Minister Watts, and that this contradicts the Minister of Local Government's September answer.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The transcript or video of the post-Cabinet press conference of Monday 13 October 2025, plus the Minister of Local Government's September 2025 answer in the written/oral question record; true if the PM described such discussions with Minister Watts while the Minister had declined the same proposal, false if either half is not so recorded.

veracity.statement: In Mt Albert Library, people were waiting two hours to cast their special votes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a roughly two-hour queue for special voting at the Mt Albert Library station during the 2025 local elections.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council / electoral officer records or contemporaneous media reports of queue times at the Mt Albert Library special-voting station in October 2025; true if waits of about two hours are documented, false if reported waits were materially shorter.

veracity.statement: Under-resourcing voting systems is a form of voter suppression, though less blatant than this Government’s Electoral Amendment Bill, which would roll back voter enrolment for general elections by 13 days.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Electoral Amendment Bill would close enrolment 13 days before a general election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Electoral Amendment Bill as introduced in 2025 and its explanatory note; true if it closes the roll 13 days before election day (removing enrolment in the final 13 days), false if the period stated in the Bill differs materially.

veracity.statement: Private companies are not—however well meaning, however good the staff—subject to the Official Information Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the private companies contracted to administer local elections fall outside the Official Information Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Official Information Act 1982 and LGOIMA 1987 schedules of subject agencies, plus Ombudsman guidance on contractors holding information on a council's behalf; true if private election-services companies are not themselves subject agencies, false if they are listed or otherwise directly bound.

veracity.statement: Despite the attacks on te reo, Te Tiriti, and Māori customary rights by the coalition partners, a strong majority across the country—as of today, 520,113 voters—voted to keep Māori wards.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a national aggregate of 520,113 votes cast to retain Māori wards across the 2025 polls, and that this was a majority of votes cast on the question nationwide.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Aggregated preliminary results of every 2025 Māori ward poll, summed across all councils that held one; true if the pro-retention total is approximately 520,113 and exceeds the total voting to remove, false if the national aggregate favoured removal or the figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: That’s a huge step up from the first couple of decades of this century, when only Wairoa got through.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Wairoa was the only council to establish and keep a Māori ward through a poll between 2000 and roughly 2020.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The record of Māori ward establishment polls held under the Local Electoral Act between 2000 and 2020; true if Wairoa District Council was the only council whose Māori ward survived such a poll in that period, false if another council also succeeded.

veracity.statement: Anyone that’s visited a school—and I know many MPs in this House visit schools—knows that every single school has attendance management systems online, that they look at their data, that they use that, and here we have a bill that enforces this to happen.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that every school already operates an online attendance management system and uses the data.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education / ERO data on the proportion of schools with attendance management plans and electronic attendance systems; true if effectively all schools have them, false if a material share of schools do not.

veracity.statement: Only 13 percent supported this bill in its totality—13 percent out of hundreds of submissions that were received.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 13 percent of the several hundred submitters on the bill supported it in full.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The departmental report to the Education and Workforce Committee on the Education and Training Amendment Bill (No 2), which tabulates submitter positions; true if it records approximately 13% supporting the bill in its entirety out of several hundred submissions, false if the tabulated figure differs materially.

rigor.statement: In many areas, turnout was below 40 percent, and in some communities, it dropped into the 30s, which is a reflection of a voting system that is confusing, outdated, and disconnected from the lives of everyday New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Treats a turnout figure as establishing a single cause — that the voting system is confusing and outdated. Nothing is offered to connect the two; the causal attribution is asserted, not shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Postal voting is no longer fit for purpose in a digital age. Many young people don’t check their mailboxes, let alone know how to post something. Some don’t even have a mailbox.
rigor.explanation: A conclusion about the voting method supported by relevant but wholly unquantified assertions about young people's habits. The reasons bear on the conclusion, so this is not a non sequitur, but it leans on generalisation from impression rather than evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Anyone that’s visited a school—and I know many MPs in this House visit schools—knows that every single school has attendance management systems online, that they look at their data, that they use that, and here we have a bill that enforces this to happen.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the provision is redundant rests on a universal empirical premise established only by an appeal to common knowledge and to members' own school visits — anecdote standing in for evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This was something that was important to them, but I’m still yet to meet a university that says that this is one of their priorities.
rigor.explanation: An argument from the speaker's own absence of evidence — his not having encountered a university that prioritises the change is offered as showing none does. The inference reaches well past what a personal sample can support.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So that’s probably the influence on this Government—Don Brash pushing through legislation in this House that isn’t asked for and isn’t necessary.
rigor.explanation: From the single example the Minister happened to cite, concludes that a private individual is the driving influence behind the legislation. A non sequitur: one illustration offered in answer to a question does not establish authorship or motive.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I know that between Otago, between Canterbury that I visited, between Massey, Auckland, and the Auckland University of Technology, every university encourages academic freedom of speech, but there’s also got to be safety in place to ensure that that academic freedom of speech doesn’t translate into free hate speech—into free hate speech—in this country that we know impacts those that are most vulnerable.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from five universities he has visited to all universities, then moves from the freedom-of-expression provision to hate speech and harm to vulnerable people without establishing the step between them. The premise is anecdotal and the second link is asserted rather than argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My key concern is how this central government “Coalition of Chaos” is undermining local government at every opportunity.
focus.explanation: A derisive party label plus a sweeping charge against the coalition. No specific policy, measure, figure or outcome is named in it — the weight is on who the other side is rather than what they have done.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The bill removes some of the key parts of the Act that aim to promote and protect the rights of our tamariki and young people, such as those rights under Te Tiriti o Waitangi and under the National Education and Learning Priorities.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure before the House directly, naming the provisions said to be removed and who they affect. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Here we are, with the Government focused on big ideas and slogans, but this is a mish-mash of a bunch of small things that really speak to influences, I think, of the minor parties set up in this Government.
focus.explanation: Carries a real claim about the bill's content — that it is a collection of small unrelated changes — but the weight of the sentence is on coalition dynamics and the other side's sloganeering rather than on any named provision.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In September, I asked the Minister of Local Government this question: will he consider amendments to the Local Electoral Act to bring the administration of local body elections away from private companies and under the Electoral Commission?
specificity.explanation: Names the statute to be amended, the mechanism (moving administration out of private hands) and the agency that would take it over. Someone could act on this.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If we want to rebuild trust in local democracy, we need reform backed by the Greens, Labour, and National—and if any of the other smaller parties want to join us, that would be good.
specificity.explanation: Calls for "reform" while naming no change, mechanism, cost or timeframe — only which parties should support it. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Out of the 136 submitters that opposed this, they mainly focused on the unnecessary nature of the changes, the risks to academic freedom and erosion of university autonomy, concerns about safety and impacts on marginalised communities, and views that the changes were contrary to Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise count of opposing submitters and an itemised breakdown of their grounds, sourced to the select committee's departmental report. Fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Under-resourcing voting systems is a form of voter suppression, though less blatant than this Government’s Electoral Amendment Bill, which would roll back voter enrolment for general elections by 13 days.
civility.explanation: Goes beyond criticising the policy to imputing a motive — that under-resourcing and the Bill are means of suppressing votes. The charge of bad faith is directed at the Government rather than any named member, so it stops short of a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This bill, in my view—and I lean heavily into the university tertiary education component—is an absolute Government overreach, no matter which way you look at it.
civility.explanation: A blunt, unqualified condemnation of the bill in a contested second-reading debate. It is aimed squarely at the measure and attacks no person — the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: All of those things are good, but all of those things are still in the bill.
rigor.explanation: Engages the Opposition's written differing view on its own terms: if the safety, rights-based, anti-discrimination and Te Tiriti obligations all remain in the bill, then the charge that the bill 'narrows' the focus does not follow, since only the ranking changes. Valid rebuttal given its premise about the bill's contents.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What I heard, effectively, from the Opposition was “Everything’s fine.” No, it’s not fine.
rigor.explanation: Strawman. He had just read out the Opposition's stated position — that the bill's focus is 'narrow' and 'antiquated' and that other statutory duties should sit alongside achievement — which is not a claim that current outcomes are satisfactory. He then rebuts the substituted position with the achievement data. The data does not touch the argument actually made.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: All of those things are good, but all of those things are still in the bill.
focus.explanation: Directed squarely at the measure before the House — what the bill retains and what it reorders — rather than at the Opposition's character or record.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What I heard, effectively, from the Opposition was “Everything’s fine.” No, it’s not fine.
civility.explanation: Dismissive and pointed toward the Opposition's position, but it lands on no individual: no imputation of bad faith, no mockery of a person, no attack on competence. The misrepresentation is a reasoning failure, not an incivility.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For all students, only 23 percent were at the level that they were supposed to be—23 percent; 62 percent were at least a year behind where they should be.
specificity.explanation: Two precise proportions attached to a named cohort and assessment (year 8 maths achievement data from earlier in 2025). Anyone could look up the release and check both figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Education should not be indoctrination, and I think there are times when we stray into that space, and that can’t be the case.
specificity.explanation: A substantive criticism of what schools teach, but it names no subject, curriculum document, programme or instance, gives no measure of how often it happens, and proposes no remedy. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: For all students, only 23 percent were at the level that they were supposed to be—23 percent; 62 percent were at least a year behind where they should be.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in the 2025 Ministry of Education year 8 mathematics achievement results, 23% of all students were at the expected curriculum level and 62% were at least one year behind it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education year 8 mathematics achievement results published in 2025 (Curriculum Insights and Progress Study): true if the proportion at the expected curriculum level is ~23% and the proportion at least a year behind is ~62%; false if either figure is materially different or refers to a different cohort or year.

veracity.statement: For writing, pretty much the same for all students: 24 percent at level, 61 percent more than a year behind.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in the same 2025 year 8 achievement data, 24% of students were at the expected curriculum level for writing and 61% were more than a year behind.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education year 8 writing achievement results published in 2025 (Curriculum Insights and Progress Study): true if ~24% were at the expected curriculum level and ~61% more than a year behind; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: In the last assessment—in 2022-2023, before this Government took office—reading has dropped in that time, from 2000 to 2023, by a full year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's PISA reading performance fell between the 2000 cycle and the most recent cycle by an amount equivalent to one year of schooling.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD PISA New Zealand mean reading scores for 2000 and 2022, converted using the OECD's published score-points-per-year-of-schooling equivalence: true if the decline is approximately one year of schooling's worth of score points; false if the decline is materially smaller (or if scores did not decline).

veracity.statement: The term 2 attendance levels, where young people are at school for more than 90 percent of the time, in 2022, that was 40 percent—40 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in term 2 of 2022, 40% of students attended school more than 90% of the time (the Ministry's 'regular attendance' measure).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education term 2 2022 regular attendance statistics (attendance >90% of half-days): true if the published rate is ~40%; false if materially different.

focus.statement: It’s a distracted and out-of-touch Government that is obsessed with imported culture wars.
focus.explanation: Characterises the Government's general disposition — distracted, out-of-touch, obsessed with culture wars — without naming a policy, mechanism, figure or outcome. Party framing with no policy content; no individual is insulted, so this is a Focus failure rather than a Civility one.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is most evident in new section 281A(2)(d), inserted by clause 12, where it says, “universities, as institutions, should not take public positions on matters that do not directly concern their role or functions:”.
focus.explanation: Engages a named clause of the measure before the House and what it would require. Entirely on the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s really unacceptable that the Government has overreached to this extent, and it really speaks to the fundamental nature of how this Government has been wagged by the two dogs that are driving this coalition—ACT and New Zealand First.
focus.explanation: There is a policy point (overreach), but the weight of the sentence is a claim about coalition internal dynamics — which parties are said to be driving the Government. No measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That’s what the schools should be focusing on to ensure that every child learns, progresses, and succeeds, and this bill is about lifting student achievement, improving attendance, and making sure that every young New Zealander gets the best possible start in life.
focus.explanation: Directed at the bill and what it is meant to do in schools; says nothing about the other parties. On-policy despite carrying no detail — the vagueness is Specificity's problem, not Focus's.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It must be difficult being on the Opposition benches today, as we put this piece of legislation through the House this afternoon.
focus.explanation: Entirely about how the other side is supposed to be feeling. No policy, provision, figure or outcome is named — the content is the Opposition's discomfort. Aimed at a bloc rather than a person, so it is Focus rather than Civility that catches it.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In the select committee stage, I asked questions of the Minister about how many universities in 2024 had actually restricted speakers from their campuses. The Minister’s answer was zero. This bill is trying to fix a problem that’s not even a problem in the first place, and, in doing so, it’s a serious case of Government overreach into the freedom of expression of universities and a serious overreach on the ability of universities to be self-managing institutes.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House: evidence is offered (a nil answer from the Minister on 2024 campus speaker restrictions) and the conclusion — the bill addresses a non-problem — tracks it. Marked down because one year of one narrow indicator is thin support for 'not a problem in the first place', and the leap from 'unnecessary' to 'serious overreach' is asserted rather than argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s going to be the Government; it’s going to be a bunch of political people that will be judging universities, which should be independent of Government control, on how free they’re going to actually be in terms of freedom of expression. This is a very dangerous pathway that actually sets universities on a path to being Government-controlled institutions and to Government dictating what universities can and can’t teach, and what universities can and can’t proscribe.
rigor.explanation: Slippery slope. The premise is a requirement that universities publish statements of freedom of expression; the conclusion is Government control of what universities may teach. No mechanism is offered connecting the reporting requirement to curriculum control, and the intermediate steps are simply asserted. Squarely on the policy, so this is a reasoning defect, not a Focus one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Initiatives like the provisions in this bill are an attempt to break down the gates of academia and use the power of the State to force independent academic institutions to give platforms to the pedlars of hate speech—white supremacists, Islamophobes, racists, anti-trans activists, and Holocaust deniers—in order to give their views respectability by giving them access to independent academic institutions.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the bill's free-expression provisions are restated as an intent to compel platforms for white supremacists and Holocaust deniers, a purpose no proponent advanced, and nothing in the provisions is cited to show they would have that effect. The conclusion about motive rests entirely on the substituted version. This engages the bill's provisions, so it is a reasoning failure rather than a Focus one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As colleagues have already pointed out, the only example—the only example—that the Minister could come up with, when asked at select committee, was of the notorious incident of Don Brash, I think, being denied the opportunity to give a Hobson’s Pledge speech at Massey University. That is not a crisis that justifies this kind of heavy-handed intervention in the cherished, autonomous academic institutions that we should be taking care to look after.
rigor.explanation: An argument with a stated premise (a single cited instance) and a conclusion that tracks it (the scale of the problem does not warrant the scale of the remedy). A proportionality inference of this kind is sound as far as it goes; it is marked down because it rests on what one Minister recalled at one hearing standing in for the whole evidence base.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In the select committee stage, I asked questions of the Minister about how many universities in 2024 had actually restricted speakers from their campuses. The Minister’s answer was zero. This bill is trying to fix a problem that’s not even a problem in the first place, and, in doing so, it’s a serious case of Government overreach into the freedom of expression of universities and a serious overreach on the ability of universities to be self-managing institutes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that at select committee the Minister answered 'zero' to a question about how many universities restricted campus speakers in 2024. A claim about a past exchange on the committee record, not an opinion about the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee record (transcript and written questions/answers) for the education amendment bill considered in 2025: true if the Minister, asked how many universities restricted speakers from campuses in 2024, answered zero or none; false if the Minister gave a non-zero figure or no such exchange occurred.

veracity.statement: As colleagues have already pointed out, the only example—the only example—that the Minister could come up with, when asked at select committee, was of the notorious incident of Don Brash, I think, being denied the opportunity to give a Hobson’s Pledge speech at Massey University. That is not a crisis that justifies this kind of heavy-handed intervention in the cherished, autonomous academic institutions that we should be taking care to look after.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that the Massey University refusal of a Don Brash Hobson's Pledge speech occurred, and that it was the sole example the Minister could offer at select committee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee record for this bill, plus 2018 reporting and Massey University statements on the cancelled Hobson's Pledge event: true if the Minister, asked at select committee for examples, cited only the Massey/Don Brash cancellation, and that cancellation occurred; false if the Minister cited further examples or the Massey incident is misdescribed.

specificity.statement: This is most evident in new section 281A(2)(d), inserted by clause 12, where it says, “universities, as institutions, should not take public positions on matters that do not directly concern their role or functions:”.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision (new section 281A(2)(d), inserted by clause 12) and quotes its text. Anyone could open the bill and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s what the schools should be focusing on to ensure that every child learns, progresses, and succeeds, and this bill is about lifting student achievement, improving attendance, and making sure that every young New Zealander gets the best possible start in life.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic goals — learns, progresses, succeeds, lifting achievement, improving attendance, best possible start. No figure, target, timeframe or mechanism from the bill that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Look at the results this Government is achieving by focusing on the simple things in education and getting them done.
specificity.explanation: Invites the House to look at results without naming a single one — no attendance or achievement figure, no programme, no timeframe. 'The simple things' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It's not actually about protecting free speech, it’s about crushing dissent from universities and setting them up to be Government-controlled commissariats, controlled by David Seymour, who will be prescribing his vision of ideology on what free speech actually should be.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith: the stated purpose is called a pretext for 'crushing dissent', and a named member is cast as imposing his own ideology through 'commissariats'. Short of a direct insult, but it attacks motive rather than the provision, so it falls below the civil standard. The judgement is about the speaker's own conduct even though the target is someone else.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Who’s correct: the National Party leader’s office’s speaking notes, which have been read to us so dutifully, that this bill is about educational achievement; or the ACT Party members in this debate, and in their heckles, who are gleefully celebrating the demise of academic freedom and welcoming in an era where institutions will have sign up to a free speech statement that is, in fact, in line with the Government’s priorities for their free speech?
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to members opposite — National members are reading their leader's notes 'so dutifully' (condescension) and ACT members are 'gleefully celebrating the demise of academic freedom' (a motive attributed, not an argument answered). Short of a direct insult, but past the line.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Just to acknowledge, at the top of my contribution, that the member Cameron Brewer took only 25 seconds to claim to be more trusted in education but was unable to make an argument longer than 30 seconds to convince, which would suggest to me it’s not an argument he’s confident in and neither is it an argument he’s prepared to make on the record in the House.
civility.explanation: Turns from the argument to the named member, imputing lack of confidence and unwillingness to stand behind his position. Mocking rather than abusive, but it targets Brewer rather than anything he said.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is a bill that makes a number of pernicious changes mixed in with all the little, sort of smaller amendments. One—just to give you a flavour of what they’re focusing on—is an amendment to make it harder for unions to give notice of school strikes and require longer days.
focus.explanation: Names a specific provision of the bill before the House and what it does. Squarely on the measure, not on the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I mean, what has this Government got? One trick: bust the unions; bust the teachers’ unions; bust the universities.
focus.explanation: A characterisation of the Government's general motives rather than the measure. It gestures at the union and university provisions, so it is not content-free, but the weight is party framing rather than any named policy or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is another piece of legislation that proves and shows why National is more trusted in education compared to that lot these days, and so I commend this bill.
focus.explanation: A bill is before the House, so there was substance available to engage. Nothing in the statement names a provision, a mechanism, a cost or an outcome — it is a comparative claim about which party is trusted.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, making the three objectives of safety and rights, inclusion, and giving effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi subsidiary to one primary objective is contrary to the purpose of the Education and Training Act, which is to establish and regulate an education system that does four things.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual mechanism of the bill — the reordering of the statutory objectives — and measures it against the Act's stated purpose.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And whilst “needless” might be a word that we use to describe the ACT Party from time to time, “needless complexity” is not a term that we should see in our bills.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine drafting point here — that the bill adds complexity it does not need — but it is delivered wrapped around a jibe at the ACT Party, and the party framing carries about half the sentence.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is a bill that makes a number of pernicious changes mixed in with all the little, sort of smaller amendments. One—just to give you a flavour of what they’re focusing on—is an amendment to make it harder for unions to give notice of school strikes and require longer days.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a named mechanism (strike-notice requirements for unions) but gives no clause reference, no notice period and no figures — a direction with some detail, missing the how much.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, the Act as it is currently written requires school boards to ensure that schools are places where children and young people can achieve educationally, where they are safe, with their rights upheld, where they feel included, and that Te Tiriti o Waitangi is given effect to.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates the four statutory board objectives individually — concrete enough that a listener could go to the Act and check each one.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It has Te Hiwa Shirley Primary School, where a special welcome party is held every Monday, or has been previously held every Monday, at the school gate, to encourage attendance and to welcome children into that school environment and into that school community.
specificity.explanation: A named school, a named practice, a stated frequency and a stated purpose — concrete and checkable, though it carries no figures on the effect it claims for attendance.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: They want the Government to be focused on the real issues, like rising cost of living, like the economy that is shrinking, and like the 73,000 New Zealanders who have left under their watch.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure — 73,000 New Zealanders having left the country under the current Government — alongside a claim that the economy is contracting.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international travel and migration statistics for departures / net migration loss of New Zealand citizens over the period from the current Government taking office (late 2023) to October 2025; true if the net loss of NZ citizens is approximately 73,000, false if materially different (e.g. under 50,000 or over 100,000). The secondary claim resolves against Stats NZ quarterly GDP: true if real GDP contracted in the most recent published quarter.

veracity.statement: Now, the Act as it is currently written requires school boards to ensure that schools are places where children and young people can achieve educationally, where they are safe, with their rights upheld, where they feel included, and that Te Tiriti o Waitangi is given effect to.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the Education and Training Act currently requires of school boards, listing four objectives: educational achievement, safety and rights, inclusion, and giving effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Section 127 of the Education and Training Act 2020 as in force on 15 October 2025; true if it sets out board objectives covering educational achievement, physical and emotional safety with rights upheld, inclusiveness, and giving effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi, false if the section omits or materially differs from any of these.

rigor.statement: It means that no one other than you should be able to decide what New Zealanders think, believe, and talk about—and isn’t that straight from the quiet part out loud?
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur bordering on strawman: the premise (Court said academics who want public positions should stand for election) does not support the conclusion that Court alone should decide what New Zealanders think and believe. The inference skips from a claim about who holds a mandate to a claim about monopoly control of opinion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, making the three objectives of safety and rights, inclusion, and giving effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi subsidiary to one primary objective is contrary to the purpose of the Education and Training Act, which is to establish and regulate an education system that does four things.
rigor.explanation: A real inference with the premises supplied: he enumerates the Act's four purposes and argues that demoting three of four objectives conflicts with them. The gap is that a purpose clause does not strictly require equal weighting of the objectives, so the conclusion is stronger than what was shown, but the reasoning tracks the evidence offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, on the one hand, you have an organisation who claim to have authored large parts of the bill, saying that they think it’s a great idea—surprise, surprise—and then you have the Law Society and the Tertiary Education Union spelling out exactly the issues with this bungled bill.
rigor.explanation: Genetic fallacy: the supporting organisation's view is dismissed by pointing at who authored the bill rather than by answering what they said. The countervailing evidence (Rishworth KC, the TEU) is real, but the contrast is drawn on source rather than substance.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But instead, today, at a time when New Zealanders are facing a cost of living crisis, when we are seeing, day after day, people leaving New Zealand, people losing their jobs, this Government is choosing to waste their time with overreach into this area, where the experts are telling us it is not required.
rigor.explanation: Two inferences, both weak: an opportunity-cost argument (Parliament attending to this means it is neglecting the cost of living) that assumes legislative time is zero-sum, and an appeal to authority — though the authorities were named and quoted, which lifts it above a bare appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What we heard from Labour and the Greens is their contention that hearing different opinions is akin to some kind of violence.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the opposing position on the free-expression provisions is restated in an extreme form ('akin to violence') that is far easier to reject than what was argued. The misrepresentation, not the rudeness, is the defect.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So, on the one hand, you have an organisation who claim to have authored large parts of the bill, saying that they think it’s a great idea—surprise, surprise—and then you have the Law Society and the Tertiary Education Union spelling out exactly the issues with this bungled bill.
civility.explanation: 'Surprise, surprise' is sneering and imputes self-interest, but the target is an organisation and the bill, not any individual member. Pointed and robust without landing on a person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The most frightening thing I’ve ever seen Don Brash try and do is get into a speedway car or try to walk down a gangplank and get on a boat.
civility.explanation: Mockery of a named individual's physical clumsiness. It engages nothing about the bill's free-expression provisions; the humour is entirely at a person's expense.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I don’t know if anyone else in this room today thought that that sounded somewhat like a valedictory speech, Minister, when you go around thanking every single person in this House.
civility.explanation: Mockery directed at the Minister personally — needling her manner and implying she is on her way out — rather than at anything in the bill. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s a grab bag of a bill. It addresses issues that do not need a new Act; they are already covered in existing regulation or law.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the measure before the House — what the bill does and whether it duplicates existing law. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But instead, today, at a time when New Zealanders are facing a cost of living crisis, when we are seeing, day after day, people leaving New Zealand, people losing their jobs, this Government is choosing to waste their time with overreach into this area, where the experts are telling us it is not required.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy claim (the bill is unnecessary on expert evidence) wrapped in general framing about the Government's priorities and record rather than the bill's provisions.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I have sat here and listened to about seven speeches from the other sides, and do you know what? I have not heard—I have not heard—about lifting the educational achievements of our children, and that is absolutely shameful.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the other side did and did not say. No provision, figure or outcome of the bill is named. Strip out the characterisation of opponents and nothing about the policy remains — which is also why no Rigor score is emitted.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: New Zealand’s children cannot learn if they are not in school, and this bill delivers a much-improved approach to attendance management.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure directly — attendance management plans as a named part of the bill. Ordinary, on-topic support for a provision.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I know why that is: it’s because the promise that the National Government sold last election—to reintroduce regional autonomy for polytechnics—this bill does not achieve that.
focus.explanation: Names a specific election commitment and measures the bill against it. This is scrutiny of a named policy against a named promise — the opposition's job, and squarely on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s a grab bag of a bill. It addresses issues that do not need a new Act; they are already covered in existing regulation or law.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the matters the bill addresses (notably academic freedom and freedom of expression at universities) are already covered by existing statute or regulation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education and Training Act 2020 (academic freedom provisions) and the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990 s 14, plus the bill's departmental disclosure statement and regulatory impact statement; true if those instruments already impose the substantive protections the bill creates, false if the bill's provisions have no existing statutory equivalent.

veracity.statement: What we heard from Labour and the Greens is their contention that hearing different opinions is akin to some kind of violence.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Labour and Green members in this debate contended that hearing different opinions amounts to violence.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of the Labour and Green speeches in the second reading debate on the Education and Training Amendment Bill (No 2); true if any of those members asserted that exposure to differing opinions is or is akin to violence, false if none did and the position advanced was narrower.

veracity.statement: I am so pleased to get to this stage today as the bill fulfils the Government’s commitment to disestablish Te Pūkenga.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that disestablishing Te Pūkenga was a Government commitment and that this bill delivers it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 tertiary education policy and the National–ACT and National–NZ First coalition agreements for the commitment; the Act as passed for whether it in fact disestablishes Te Pūkenga. True if the commitment is documented and the Act disestablishes the entity, false if either limb fails.

veracity.statement: The cost is jobs—hundreds of jobs in the vocational sector: gone.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's vocational education reforms have cost hundreds of jobs across the sector.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga and successor polytechnic annual reports and TEC staffing data for 2023–2025, plus reported redundancy rounds; true if net staff reductions across the vocational sector since the reform programme began number in the hundreds or more, false if the net figure is materially smaller.

specificity.statement: This bill is about lifting school and student achievement, improving attendance, and ensuring every young New Zealander gets the best possible start at life.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic goals. No mechanism, no figure, no timeframe, no named provision of the bill — nothing a listener could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: New Zealand’s children cannot learn if they are not in school, and this bill delivers a much-improved approach to attendance management.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy area but 'a much-improved approach' carries no mechanism, threshold or figure. A direction with a little detail attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill will re-establish regional polytechnics, and Cabinet has taken decisions on the 10 polytechnics that will initially be established as stand-alone polytechnics. These 10 will stand alone on 1 January 2026, with two of them expected to be in the federation.
specificity.explanation: A count, a commencement date and a structural distinction (stand-alone versus federation). Someone could check on 1 January 2026 whether ten polytechnics stood alone.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The cost is jobs—hundreds of jobs in the vocational sector: gone.
specificity.explanation: An order of magnitude ('hundreds') and a named sector, but no figure, no institution and no period — half a checkable claim.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I am confident they will complete this work and that decisions will be able to be made about their establishment in the new year.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the polytechnics remaining inside Te Pūkenga will complete the financial-sustainability work required of them, and that establishment decisions for them will be made during 2026. The outcome turns on those institutions' finances, not solely on the Minister's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education / Tertiary Education Commission announcements and Cabinet decisions on the establishment of the polytechnics not among the initial ten; true if establishment decisions for all remaining polytechnics are announced during 2026, false if any remain undecided or are wound up rather than established.

veracity.statement: The Minister knows that the reports and the advice that she has had is that she needs at least $200 million to stand up 16 polytechnics.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official advice received by the Minister put the cost of standing up 16 stand-alone polytechnics at a minimum of $200 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education / Tertiary Education Commission advice to the Minister on the establishment cost of the new stand-alone polytechnics (released papers or OIA); true if that advice states a figure of at least $200 million, false if the advice contains no such figure or a materially lower one.

veracity.statement: When Christopher Luxon tells young people to get off the couch, stop playing PlayStation, and go and find a job, not only are there no jobs, but even if they’re trying to get into foundation learning, they can’t get in.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that Luxon publicly told young people to get off the couch, stop playing PlayStation and find work; and that young people seeking foundation learning places are being turned away.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: For the first limb, the media/transcript record of Christopher Luxon's public remarks — true if he made a statement in those terms, false if no such remarks exist. For the second, TEC/provider enrolment and unmet-demand data for foundation-level (Levels 1–3) provision — true if applicants are being declined places for want of capacity, false if provision is not oversubscribed.

veracity.statement: Twenty thousand construction workers have gone off to other parts of the world, and thousands of apprentices aren’t graduating or enrolling under their watch.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a net departure of 20,000 construction workers overseas, and a fall of thousands in apprenticeship graduations and enrolments during this Government's term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration data by occupation for construction workers over the term, and TEC industry-training statistics on apprenticeship enrolments and completions 2023–2025; true if departures are of the order of 20,000 and apprentice numbers have fallen by thousands, false if either series is materially different.

veracity.statement: This bill does not have industry backing—it does not have industry backing—and it came through clearly in the submissions that were made and that the Education and Workforce Committee heard.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that industry submitters to the Education and Workforce Committee on this bill were predominantly opposed to it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published submissions and the Education and Workforce Committee's report on the bill; true if industry-body submissions predominantly opposed the bill or the industry skills board model, false if industry submissions were predominantly supportive or mixed.

specificity.statement: The Minister knows that the reports and the advice that she has had is that she needs at least $200 million to stand up 16 polytechnics.
specificity.explanation: Carries a dollar figure, a named number of institutions and an identified source (advice to the Minister) — someone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Twenty thousand construction workers have gone off to other parts of the world, and thousands of apprentices aren’t graduating or enrolling under their watch.
specificity.explanation: One hard figure (20,000) attached to a named group, but the apprenticeship half is left at "thousands" with no period or baseline.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The National Government simply cannot afford this legislation. It takes us back to a model where we’ve already been and that we simply couldn’t afford.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: the reform recreates a prior structure, and that structure was unaffordable, so this one will be too. The step is a historical analogy that assumes the new model is materially the same as the old one, which is asserted rather than shown — a gap between premise and conclusion, but not a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It doesn’t make sense to disestablish workforce development councils and re-establish a whole new entity while giving them only half the funding that they used to have under the old model.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: names the bodies being disestablished, the replacement entity and the funding change. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I genuinely believe, with the 30 years of experience that the Minister has had in tertiary education, she knows today what she is doing. She knows that this doesn’t create better outcomes for learners, it’s not financially viable, and that, most of all, she has let industry down in the promise that she made back in the last election.
civility.explanation: Moves from the policy to the Minister's state of mind: says she knows the reform is bad for learners and unviable and is proceeding anyway. That is an imputation of bad faith rather than error — a real civility failure, though short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We haven’t seen the finances on our polytechs; we still have no details on the federations, and that is a good example of the emperor with no clothing, Minister.
civility.explanation: The mockery lands on the plan's missing detail rather than the Minister herself, but the "emperor with no clothing" jibe is addressed directly to her — pointed and edging toward the person without landing on them.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: With nearly one-in-seven jobs lost, with campuses closed across the board, and with programmes disestablished, it’s hard to see that this is what success looks like for this National Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that close to one in seven jobs in the polytechnic sector have been lost, alongside campus closures and programme disestablishments.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission / ITP sector staffing data (or Tertiary Education Union figures) for FTE roles across the polytechnic sector from 2019-20 to 2025; true if net losses are around 14% (one in seven) of the sector workforce, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: Again, I keep coming back to the words of the Treasury advice about how the ITP sector would, essentially, be the same, if not worse, than they would be coming out of Te Pūkenga as they did before Te Pūkenga was established.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Treasury's advice concluded the viability of the ITP sector after the reform would be the same or worse than under Te Pūkenga.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury advice and the regulatory impact statement on the vocational education and training reforms; true if that advice states the new institutions' financial viability would be the same or worse than the Te Pūkenga counterfactual, false if it does not say this.

veracity.statement: When I asked the Tertiary Institutes Allied Staff Association and the Tertiary Education Union, at the select committee stage for this bill, whether the level of disruption that they were encountering was worse or better or about the same as they did when Te Pūkenga was established, they both said that it was much worse now.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that two named unions told the select committee the current disruption was much worse than at Te Pūkenga's establishment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee's oral evidence transcript for the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill; true if TIASA and TEU representatives both answered that disruption was worse than during Te Pūkenga's establishment, false if either said the same or better.

veracity.statement: The original legislation said that they must act in a manner that contributes to an education system that honours Te Tiriti o Waitangi and supports Māori-Crown relations.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the wording of the industry skills boards' duties in the bill as introduced, before the select committee amendment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill as introduced, clause setting out industry skills board functions and duties; true if it required them to act in a manner contributing to an education system that honours Te Tiriti o Waitangi and supports Māori-Crown relations, false if the wording differs materially.

focus.statement: With nearly one-in-seven jobs lost, with campuses closed across the board, and with programmes disestablished, it’s hard to see that this is what success looks like for this National Government.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: names concrete outcomes of the named reform programme (job losses, campus closures, disestablished programmes) rather than characterising the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But now, all of a sudden, they have all those questions that they are trying to ask of this Government, and this Government is trying to fix that issue, that big disaster that was created by the previous Labour-led Government.
focus.explanation: Almost entirely about the opposition's inconsistency and the previous government's record; the only policy anchor is a general gesture at 'that big disaster', with no measure, figure or mechanism named.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If the federation model was going to be so successful, then, logically, polytechs would want to be a part of it, and they wouldn’t need to be forced to be part of it.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure, but with a gap: it assumes any genuinely beneficial arrangement would be adopted voluntarily, ignoring collective-action problems and the Minister's own stated reason (institutions not recognising their position) for compulsion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Minister said that it was not necessary to include provisions to require exit clauses for anchor polytechnics, because they’re being established by Order in Council, but ISBs are also being established by Order in Council. New section 380 also makes provisions to disestablish the industry skills boards via Order in Councils, so there is some inconsistency in the legislation.
rigor.explanation: Valid parallel-case reasoning: if establishment by Order in Council made exit provisions unnecessary, the bill would not need express disestablishment provisions for the identically-established ISBs; the inconsistency conclusion follows from the premises offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When you have a car that’s lost one-seventh of its functions, of its parts, or of its essence, how is that going to be a more viable car going forward?
rigor.explanation: False analogy: an institution's viability is not a linear function of headcount the way a car's is of its parts, and the analogy assumes the very proportionality it is offered to establish.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We all know that the polytechnic council’s job should be about ensuring that polytechs are able to run properly, they are able to maintain financial sustainability, and that they are able to deal with the operational challenges. So we wanted to focus on ensuring that people, those who are capable, those who are able to deliver in these jobs, are appointed.
rigor.explanation: Rests on a false dichotomy — that appointing for diversity and appointing capable people are alternatives — and opens with an appeal to shared assumption ('we all know') in place of a reason why the removed criteria would displace competence.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Minister said that it was not necessary to include provisions to require exit clauses for anchor polytechnics, because they’re being established by Order in Council, but ISBs are also being established by Order in Council. New section 380 also makes provisions to disestablish the industry skills boards via Order in Councils, so there is some inconsistency in the legislation.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact mechanism (Order in Council), the exact provision (new section 380) and the bodies concerned; someone could check the drafting directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The only people that the Minister had to consult when appointing or removing the chairperson or deputy chairperson is the chairperson or the deputy chairperson themselves. It doesn’t require the consent of the ITP council that she’s already appointing half of.
specificity.explanation: Precise account of the consultation mechanism, who must be consulted, and the proportion of council members the Minister appoints — checkable against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That is important because this is about local needs, this is about local jobs, and it’s about ensuring that local industries have a stronger voice.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic goods — local needs, local jobs, a stronger voice — with no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named provision that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The excuse of not requiring the consents of communities to be a part of the federation does not wash.
civility.explanation: Blunt rejection aimed at the Minister's justification rather than at her as a person; 'excuse' is pointed but stays on the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The decision of merging polytechnics was a disastrous decision, and just listening to the Labour member and the Green member there, it felt like they have finally woken up.
civility.explanation: The criticism of the merger decision itself is fair game, but 'finally woken up' is condescension directed at the two members who had just spoken rather than at their argument.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I do worry that the Government is opening itself up to potential legal challenges as a result of this inconsistency in drafting.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the drafting inconsistency around Order in Council establishment and disestablishment will attract legal challenge.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Court records and legal reporting on proceedings (e.g. judicial review) challenging decisions made under the Act's Order in Council provisions for anchor polytechnics, the federation, or industry skills boards; true if such a challenge is filed, false if none is by the resolve-by date.

focus.statement: Two things I wanted to say: first of all, to celebrate the re-establishment of community-based polytechs and the end of what we would regard as the failed centralisation model of Te Pūkenga, which was brought in by the last Government.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy (the Te Pūkenga centralisation model) and the specific change the bill makes. Criticism of the previous government's named programme is on-policy scrutiny, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I don’t think the Green Party’s actually been listening to the answers that the Minister gave on those particular questions.
focus.explanation: Once the characterisation of the Green Party is removed there is no policy content left — no measure, figure or outcome is named. It is a jibe about the other party's conduct in the debate. (Scored here only; there is no argument to assess for Rigor and no individual is attacked.)
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We can’t ignore the fact that there are staff on the line right now that don’t know whether they will have a job by Christmas, because that’s what these changes are bringing.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the consequence of the measure before the House — job security for staff at a named institution's sector on a stated timeframe. Scrutiny of a policy's effect, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One other thing I would say in that area is that if you are a long way away from your polytech, the drop-out rate and the inability to complete is much, much higher than it is if you live in the area very, very close, in the town that is there, so there is an extra need not only for extra resource or maybe hybrid models but also for extra pastoral care.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: premise (distance from campus correlates with non-completion) supports the conclusion (distant campuses need more resource, hybrid delivery and pastoral care). No fallacy; the gap is only that the premise is asserted rather than sourced.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But if we lose a programme, a tutor, if we lose a support staff member, if we lose a director and managers, then they don’t come back—and that’s a loss to the sector.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy — departures are irreversible, therefore capability is permanently lost — but the supporting premise is anecdote (the 'post-NorthTec glow', the forestry tutors) rather than any evidence on re-entry rates. A reasonable point resting on an appeal to anecdote.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They are our future, and this move doesn’t see them, because this move cuts, out of the purview of so many, the ability to be part of our creative economy.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to emotion built on an anecdote: a visit to one school of enthusiastic students is offered as grounds for the conclusion that the bill removes access to creative-economy careers. Nothing connects the school visit to the bill's provisions, so the conclusion does not follow.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: One other thing I would say in that area is that if you are a long way away from your polytech, the drop-out rate and the inability to complete is much, much higher than it is if you live in the area very, very close, in the town that is there, so there is an extra need not only for extra resource or maybe hybrid models but also for extra pastoral care.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that ITP students living far from their polytech drop out and fail to complete at a much higher rate than those living close to campus.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission / Ministry of Education course- and qualification-completion data for ITP learners, broken down by distance from campus or by satellite versus main-campus enrolment; true if completion rates are materially lower for learners far from their campus, false if the difference is negligible or reversed.

veracity.statement: The final thing I wanted to say is this also frees up industry training organisations, which had effectively been nationalised into Te Pūkenga by the last Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the previous government the ITOs were absorbed into Te Pūkenga — i.e. brought under a single Crown entity rather than remaining industry-owned bodies.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education (Vocational Education and Training Reform) Amendment Act 2020 and TEC transition records: true if the industry training organisations' arranging-training functions were transferred into Te Pūkenga (a Crown entity) and the ITOs disestablished, false if ITOs retained those functions independently.

veracity.statement: I am here to share the actual issues in the community, because maybe this House didn’t know that none of the iwi of Te Tai Tokerau actually knew that these changes were coming and that NorthTec was going to have to cut back so much.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a universal negative — that not one iwi of Te Tai Tokerau was told in advance of the changes or of the scale of NorthTec's cutbacks.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NorthTec / TEC / Ministry of Education consultation records and select committee submissions for the vocational education reform: true if no Te Tai Tokerau iwi was notified or consulted before the changes and NorthTec's retrenchment were announced, false if any documented pre-announcement engagement with an iwi of the rohe exists.

veracity.statement: Over 10 years of delivery of Māori-Pacific trade training; in December 2024, the door was shut on Te Matarau Education Trust and they were evicted from the building in NorthTec.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a dated, named event: the ending of Te Matarau Education Trust's decade-long trade-training delivery and its removal from NorthTec premises in December 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NorthTec and Te Matarau Education Trust records and contemporaneous reporting: true if Te Matarau's Māori-Pacific trade training arrangement with NorthTec ended and it vacated NorthTec premises in December 2024 after roughly a decade of delivery, false if the tenancy or delivery relationship continued past that date or ended in a materially different way.

veracity.statement: One of the reasons that business is booming so significantly for our gaming sector is because of a rebate scheme that Labour put in when we were last in Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that a game-development rebate scheme was introduced by the previous Labour government and that it is a cause of the sector's current growth.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget documents and MBIE/NZ Game Developers Association records: true if a game development sector rebate was introduced by the Labour-led government before the 2023 election and industry revenue data show growth attributable to it, false if no such Labour-introduced rebate exists or if the sector's growth predates and is independent of it.

specificity.statement: The final thing I wanted to say about those is the idea is to establish the ISBs by 1 January next year and then to transition them through to being their own stand-alone entities.
specificity.explanation: Names a mechanism (industry skills boards becoming stand-alone entities) and a dated milestone (1 January next year). Checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill is about strengthening regional responsiveness, improving industry alignment, and delivering the skills that our country needs.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — no figures, no mechanisms, no timeframes. Nothing here could be checked or acted on, in a summing-up where the speaker had just supplied concrete detail elsewhere.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Over 10 years of delivery of Māori-Pacific trade training; in December 2024, the door was shut on Te Matarau Education Trust and they were evicted from the building in NorthTec.
specificity.explanation: Names the organisation, the programme, the duration of delivery, the month and year, and the concrete outcome. Someone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re looking forward to having regional influence on the governance of UCOL in Whanganui, in the Manawatū, and I know that it is the same across New Zealand, so I commend the bill to the House.
specificity.explanation: Names one institution and one region, but supplies no mechanism, no figures and no timeframe — 'regional influence on the governance' is a direction with nothing attached to it, in a contribution where the governance changes were available to describe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Previously where they were obligated to, now, they are no longer required, under this bill, to take advice from our ISBs.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete legislative change — the removal of an obligation to give effect to industry skills board advice — which can be checked against the bill's text. Missing the clause reference and which bodies are affected.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I shared this recently in one of the many community huis that I’ve hosted on this issue—to my colleague, the Northland MP: he could have come; there’s been hundreds of people come to my meetings.
civility.explanation: Pointed at an individual member's absence rather than at any argument, but it stops at a reproach about attendance — no imputation of bad faith, no attack on character or competence. Robust and personal-adjacent rather than uncivil.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We still haven’t seen a cost-benefit analysis that would justify the policy design and the architecture of the system that the Minister has chosen.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no cost-benefit analysis supporting the design of the new vocational education system has been produced or released in the course of this bill's passage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published regulatory impact statement, departmental disclosure statement and Education and Workforce Committee papers for the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill; true if none contains a cost-benefit analysis of the chosen system architecture, false if a CBA was published or provided to the committee.

veracity.statement: The new system is much more complex than Te Pūkenga was and more complex than the old system, and the official said that in the regulatory impact statement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that the new structure is more complex than either Te Pūkenga or the pre-Te Pūkenga arrangement, and that Ministry of Education officials said so in the regulatory impact statement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Education regulatory impact statement for the bill; true if it states that the proposed system is more complex than Te Pūkenga and/or the pre-2020 ITP/ITO system, false if it makes no such statement or states the opposite.

veracity.statement: As we discussed during the earlier debate, this bill strips out references to Te Tiriti and it waters down commitments to engage with Māori institutions at the local level and the national level; commitments that were there to ensure that Māori are represented on the governance boards of the new polytechs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill removes Te Tiriti o Waitangi references and weakens statutory obligations to engage with Māori, including provisions securing Māori representation on polytechnic governance boards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the bill as passed against the Education and Training Act 2020 provisions it amends; true if Te Tiriti references are deleted and the Māori engagement/governance-representation duties are narrowed or removed, false if those provisions are retained or strengthened.

veracity.statement: And now at a time of very high youth unemployment, we have thousands fewer apprentices than we had a few years ago.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions about the present: that youth unemployment is very high, and that apprentice numbers are down by thousands relative to a few years earlier.
veracity.subject: speaker
