veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey youth (15–24) unemployment rate for 2025 quarters, and Tertiary Education Commission apprentice enrolment counts for 2025 versus 2021–22; true if the youth rate is elevated against its recent range and apprentice numbers have fallen by thousands, false if apprentice numbers are flat or higher.

veracity.statement: I got that round the wrong way deliberately because I believe “M” always comes before “N”, but that has had $23 million that went into Te Pūkenga and they’re going to come out with $11.7 million. So that’s about $12 million just gone down the toilet because of mismanagement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Nelson Marlborough Institute of Technology carried about $23 million in reserves into Te Pūkenga and will emerge with about $11.7 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NMIT and Te Pūkenga annual reports / TEC disestablishment balance sheets for the reserves attributed to NMIT at entry to Te Pūkenga and at re-establishment; true if the figures are approximately $23m and $11.7m, false if materially different.

focus.statement: As we discussed during the earlier debate, this bill strips out references to Te Tiriti and it waters down commitments to engage with Māori institutions at the local level and the national level; commitments that were there to ensure that Māori are represented on the governance boards of the new polytechs.
focus.explanation: Names a specific change in a specific bill (removal of Treaty clauses, weakening of Māori governance representation) and the group affected — legitimate scrutiny of the measure before the House, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In Part 1, we’ll see that there are a few particular conditions that enable the building of these so-called granny flats or small stand-alone dwellings—these being, first, that the dwelling has a simple design as defined and that authorised professionals, again as defined, will be those carrying out the work; that, second, they must provide records of the work to the relevant council or territorial authority, the keeper of the keys, the depository and repository of the records relating to the property, which is important, obviously, for ongoing ownership but also for other reasons that councils need to have such records; and that, third, the territorial authorities actually are informed in advance of the work taking place so they can provide what’s called a project information memorandum—or PIM—which contains key details relating to the property so that the authorised professionals can go ahead and conduct the work in a known, safe manner in accordance with the building code.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure before the committee: what the provisions do and how they operate. No reference to any other party.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Given the Government’s apparent unwillingness to invest in the new politics, the inevitable result will be fewer courses, fewer trainees, and fewer jobs in the system.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that under the new vocational education structure the number of courses offered, trainees enrolled and jobs in the system will all decline.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission and polytechnic annual reports for 2026 and 2027 versus 2025 baselines; true if course offerings, trainee/apprentice enrolments and staff numbers across the ITP network all fall, false if enrolments and provision hold steady or rise.

rigor.statement: Given the Government’s apparent unwillingness to invest in the new politics, the inevitable result will be fewer courses, fewer trainees, and fewer jobs in the system.
rigor.explanation: An inference about the policy, but a weak one: it moves from an assumed and unevidenced 'apparent unwillingness to invest' to an outcome asserted as 'inevitable', with no mechanism or figures connecting funding levels to the three predicted declines.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: At this point, I can’t help but think that the result is a victory for political hubris over evidence, stakeholder opinions clearly articulated, and common sense.
civility.explanation: Frames the outcome as the Minister's personal hubris rather than a policy disagreement — imputing vanity as the motive edges past robust criticism of the decision, though it stops short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m quite shocked, Phil Twyford usually gives a great speech—very good off the cuff, and he read that speech. I’m not sure whose it was, but I think the technical term is “projection”.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe at a named member — insinuating he did not write his own speech and labelling him with 'projection'. It targets the person rather than anything in the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I got that round the wrong way deliberately because I believe “M” always comes before “N”, but that has had $23 million that went into Te Pūkenga and they’re going to come out with $11.7 million. So that’s about $12 million just gone down the toilet because of mismanagement.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific institution and gives dollar figures on both sides of the transition ($23m in, $11.7m out, ~$12m lost) — concrete enough that someone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is a great day for New Zealand. It’s a great day for young and older learners, and it’s a great day for the New Zealand economy because it will enable people to get training and get jobs and have a great life.
specificity.explanation: Pure acclamation: no figures, no mechanism, no timeframe, no named provision — nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In Part 1, we’ll see that there are a few particular conditions that enable the building of these so-called granny flats or small stand-alone dwellings—these being, first, that the dwelling has a simple design as defined and that authorised professionals, again as defined, will be those carrying out the work; that, second, they must provide records of the work to the relevant council or territorial authority, the keeper of the keys, the depository and repository of the records relating to the property, which is important, obviously, for ongoing ownership but also for other reasons that councils need to have such records; and that, third, the territorial authorities actually are informed in advance of the work taking place so they can provide what’s called a project information memorandum—or PIM—which contains key details relating to the property so that the authorised professionals can go ahead and conduct the work in a known, safe manner in accordance with the building code.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the three statutory preconditions in Part 1 by mechanism — simple design, authorised professionals, records to the territorial authority, advance notification producing a PIM — all traceable to specific clauses. No figures or dates, which keeps it short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In that case, I’m very happy to let those members across the other side of the House who are hanging on every word know that whilst I can see from the looks on their faces they have struggled to keep up to this point, I will now speak a lot slower.
civility.explanation: Mockery of other members' ability to comprehend, with an offer to 'speak a lot slower' — condescension landing on the persons opposite rather than on any argument. Short of sustained abuse, so above 0.25.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I don’t know if you’ve been keeping up, but artificial intelligence is moving at great speed—at great speed—and ISBs are no longer required to consider emerging technologies.
civility.explanation: 'I don't know if you've been keeping up', repeated and addressed to a named member, is condescension toward the person — a real failure under the re-anchored scale, though it stops short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Questions about whether this additional transition and change is actually going to deliver for learners and why the Minister for Vocational Education is seeking so much high-level decision-making power over the sector when she’s claiming to give autonomy back to the regions.
civility.explanation: Pointed — it implies a gap between what the Minister claims and what she seeks — but the criticism attaches to the power the bill confers rather than to her character. Robust, edging toward the person without landing on them.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In that case, I’m very happy to let those members across the other side of the House who are hanging on every word know that whilst I can see from the looks on their faces they have struggled to keep up to this point, I will now speak a lot slower.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side of the House and how they look; names no policy, measure, figure or outcome. This is the tribalism case Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The first is that they are no longer required to consider specific consultation with Māori and underserved population groups.
focus.explanation: Engages a named provision of the measure before the House and what it removes — squarely on the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Questions about whether this additional transition and change is actually going to deliver for learners and why the Minister for Vocational Education is seeking so much high-level decision-making power over the sector when she’s claiming to give autonomy back to the regions.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: names the measure's mechanism (ministerial decision-making powers), the stated policy rationale (regional autonomy) and the affected group (learners). Holding a minister to a named commitment is on-policy, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Here we are correcting another failure of the former Labour Government, the centralisation of polytechnics—what a disaster.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy — the centralisation of polytechnics — which lifts it above party-bashing, but the framing ('another failure of the former Labour Government') carries much of the weight and no outcome or figure is given.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The first is that they are no longer required to consider specific consultation with Māori and underserved population groups.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill removes an existing statutory requirement for industry skills boards to consider specific consultation with Māori and underserved population groups.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the consideration/charter requirements in the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill as reported back against the corresponding provisions of the Education and Training Act 2020 governing workforce development councils; true if the Māori and underserved-population consultation consideration is absent from the new provisions, false if it is retained in equivalent form.

veracity.statement: It is something that submitters have very much opposed or opposed in part in their submissions—I believe only 11 percent were completely in support of the changes—and therefore we oppose this bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that only about 11 percent of submitters to the select committee were completely in support of the changes in the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee's report and the departmental report on submissions for the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill; true if the tally of submitters recorded as fully supporting the bill is approximately 11 percent of total submitters, false if materially different.

rigor.statement: I don’t know if you’ve been keeping up, but artificial intelligence is moving at great speed—at great speed—and ISBs are no longer required to consider emerging technologies.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: the pace of technological change is offered as the reason the removed consideration matters. The link is asserted rather than demonstrated (no evidence that the requirement was doing work), leaving a modest gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, we can disagree on a lot of things in this House, and we often do, but I think no one in this House could stand up and challenge the fact that work and how we work is changing radically and possibly more and faster than we have ever seen or are likely to see in our lifetimes.
rigor.explanation: The premise is established by an appeal to unanimity — 'no one in this House could stand up and challenge' — rather than by evidence about labour-market change. The underlying point is reasonable, but the support offered for it is consensus, not data.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The submission of E tū is also fairly robust in terms of speaking to the fact that the workforce development councils have been working well, and it’s very unusual for changes to be made in the face of a system and a structure that is already working well.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference — the system works, therefore change is unwarranted — but the sole support offered for the premise is a single stakeholder submission (appeal to authority), and 'unusual' does substitute for a reason why the change is wrong.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s about time sensibility returned to polytechs and vocational training that we all knew worked and delivered.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to tradition and to assumed common knowledge: 'we all knew' is offered in place of any evidence that the prior regional model worked or delivered, and the conclusion rests entirely on that assumption.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Well, the good news is that by the time that person leaves school, this Government will be history.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the current National-led coalition Government will have left office within the timeframe of an intermediate-school student finishing secondary school.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand general election results and subsequent government formation; true if the National-led coalition formed after the 2023 election is no longer the government of New Zealand at any point on or before 2030-12-31, false if it remains in office continuously through that date.

focus.statement: It’s an information process which doesn’t create a liability for council—deliberately and rightly—but the question is, then, how can insurers rely upon it? And, if they can’t rely upon it, how will banks?

specificity.statement: First of all, the question about a small stand-alone dwelling being a definition in the Building Act, could the Minister point us to that section in the Building Act? specificity.statement: I’d just like to know: if you already have, maybe, natural flow irrigation from the grey water, or if you seek to put in a composting toilet—again, with the correct plumbing people rather than doing it ourselves—how would that apply in a rural area, whether you do or don’t have another dwelling?

veracity.statement: However, I would say there are tens of thousands—probably hundreds of thousands—of dwellings in this country that do not have consents at the moment.

civility.statement: We checked with the council whether we needed anything. We did not need anything. Did they need to have the information that it even existed? They did not. rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of the combined foundation and building height, it’s 5 metres, 4 metres plus 1 metre—and that kind of way of enabling different structures on different ground conditions enables quite a variety of structures.

specificity.statement: I refer to Schedule 1A (2)(1)(c), and in that it describes the maximum height above the ground that a floor level can be.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The Building Act 2004 and the Building Code as at October 2025, plus the text of the granny flat bill's new Schedule 1A: true if neither imposes a maximum number of occupants on a stand-alone dwelling (building-density/occupancy-load provisions for crowd or communal buildings do not count); false if either the Act or the bill specifies an occupant limit for such dwellings.

focus.statement: I think it would be useful to just get a better understanding of that process, how that is triggered, and what options are available to the landowner after that point, because I actually agree with Mr Luxton that that could be counted to the intent of this, but I am not concerned, necessarily, because there might be some instances where that is warranted.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure before the House — the trigger for a council-required building consent and the landowner's options afterwards. No party framing at all; he even credits a member from an opposing party by name.

rigor.statement: So allowing for one of these to be built at marae doesn’t seem to create any problems that are foreseeable around the infrastructure that is at those marae. The plumbing is there.

rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s that fella, it’s Uncle Kelly who will get that kaumātua flat if you build it, if you just build one at Tapuihikitia Marae, because he is the caretaker of that place.
rigor.explanation: The case for the amendment is carried here by a single family anecdote: one man at one marae is offered as grounds for who would benefit nationally. Appeal to anecdote — it establishes that such a person exists, not that the allocation pattern generalises. It is not a bare emotional appeal, since it does point at a real mechanism (marae caretakers are unhoused near the marae they maintain), which keeps it off the floor.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In the building industry, we’re worried that the councils have got the ability to get in the way by using section 71 of the Building Act and putting in place something that is kind of like a resource consenting mechanism, where it’s saying that this is how you’ve got to comply. Now, I know of builders who have had buildings that have just been given a flat no, when there are processes and ways to mitigate that issue with the project which haven’t been accepted by the council.
rigor.explanation: A systemic conclusion about how councils will use section 71 rests on unnamed second-hand anecdotes ('I know of builders'). Appeal to anecdote: the examples are consistent with the conclusion but do not establish a pattern, and no count, region or decision is offered. It reasons about a named statutory power rather than about opponents, so it is a genuine if weak inference.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I would say that it’s a balance, and we attempt to strike the balance in this bill by saying that while a council cannot say no, or has not been invited to provide a consent or deny a consent, it’s nevertheless being asked to provide information about the land on which the granny flat is going to be built so that an informed decision can be made by a responsible professional.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the balance is struck follows only if disclosure to a responsible professional is enough to manage the risk. rigor.statement: I know the intent of the bill is to make this a seamless process, but in the new requirement of the memorandum to accompany the project information memorandum, if a council identifies that where the proposed granny flat is going to be built is an area where when there is severe weather it does flood and that there are flow issues, and the person is informed of that and they do it anyway, it makes the issue worse for those around them. Now, surely that is something that we do want to prevent, even though we want to see in the majority of cases that these things are seamless.
rigor.explanation: A valid externality argument: informed consent by the builder resolves risk to the builder, but the flow obstruction falls on neighbours who were never party to the decision, so disclosure alone does not close the gap. The conclusion follows from the premises offered, and the concession about the majority of cases is stated rather than dodged.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So allowing for one of these to be built at marae doesn’t seem to create any problems that are foreseeable around the infrastructure that is at those marae. The plumbing is there.

focus.explanation: Entirely about the operation of the bill and the Building Act provisions around it; no party framing.

focus.statement: I know the intent of the bill is to make this a seamless process, but in the new requirement of the memorandum to accompany the project information memorandum, if a council identifies that where the proposed granny flat is going to be built is an area where when there is severe weather it does flood and that there are flow issues, and the person is informed of that and they do it anyway, it makes the issue worse for those around them. veracity.statement: There are marae around the country who have adopted this because of Labour’s policy to fund some of this housing.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Housing and Urban Development / Te Puni Kōkiri reporting on the Whai Kāinga Whai Oranga (Māori housing) fund and predecessor programmes: true if funded marae-based papakāinga or kaumātua housing units were delivered at multiple marae under the 2017–2023 Labour government's programme, false if no such marae-sited dwellings were funded or built under it.

veracity.statement: When we consider areas that were hit with the Auckland floods and Cyclone Gabrielle, in intensive urban areas it was often the inability for the water to flow through residential dwellings that caused a problem, and I am keen to explore the advice that the Minister received about this.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in the 2023 Auckland Anniversary floods and Cyclone Gabrielle, obstructed water flow through densely built residential areas was frequently a cause of the damage.

specificity.statement: These matters can and will be addressed through resource management changes that essentially sit alongside the bill. specificity.explanation: Names a real workstream (resource management reform), the responsible Minister, and the mechanism sought (certainty without a resource consent). But there is no timeframe, no instrument named, and nothing said about whether marae sites specifically are covered — the how much and the by when are both missing.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What I’m looking for from you, Minister, is an indication as to how you see this interacting with councils, and whether councils are expected to be enabling, and taking the spirit of this bill as it is given, by using I think it’s section 67 to grant exemptions if they can, or section 72 to find mitigating abilities to make sure that things get built.
specificity.explanation: Names the precise statutory levers at issue — sections 67 (exemptions) and 72 (mitigation) of the Building Act — and states exactly what use of them he is asking the Minister to endorse. A precise question, checkable against the Act; short of 1.0 only because no figure or timeframe attaches.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I would say that it’s a balance, and we attempt to strike the balance in this bill by saying that while a council cannot say no, or has not been invited to provide a consent or deny a consent, it’s nevertheless being asked to provide information about the land on which the granny flat is going to be built so that an informed decision can be made by a responsible professional.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the actual mechanism: the council loses the consent decision but gains an information-provision duty, with the decision resting on a responsible professional. Concrete and checkable against the clause; no figures, thresholds or timing given.

rigor.statement: It's all well and good to have planning rules that enable things, but if we have had advice that the insurance companies have expressed concerns about this and indicated that in the future if the frequency is such that they then will no longer insure those areas and we knew that, or we could have put protections in for those people and didn't, then we're creating another problem.
rigor.explanation: A conditional argument that holds together: if insurers have warned they may withdraw cover and the bill enables building anyway, a future harm is created. The inference is valid given its antecedent; the weakness is that the antecedent is only hypothesised ("if we have had advice") rather than evidenced, so the conclusion is asserted a little further than what was shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If there's one lesson, after all the recent severe weather events, surely it is that there are certain areas of the country that shouldn't have residential dwellings on them, because of the tendency to have severe weather or natural hazard events.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered (the tendency of certain areas to flood or be hit by severe weather) and the conclusion tracks it, but the argument leans on "surely" and on the recent weather events as self-evident — an appeal to the obvious standing in for the evidence that would show which areas and at what risk threshold.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Forms are being developed, regulations are being drafted to give effect to all this, and in conjunction with guidance that the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment will promulgate, there will be every reason and no excuse that councils will be applying this in the same fashion, or be it of course in an individual case by case basis—results may vary, as they say in the advertising field.
rigor.explanation: Concludes that councils will apply the regime consistently from the existence of forms, regulations and MBIE guidance. There is a genuine gap: standardised paperwork is a precondition for consistency, not a demonstration of it, and the speaker's own closing concession ("results may vary") undercuts the conclusion he has just drawn.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, I’m coming at this particularly from a seniors perspective, because one of the things that we do see in terms of granny flats is that, if there isn’t proper insulation, that’s going to lead to damper granny flats, which would then lead on to additional health issues.
rigor.explanation: A causal chain — poor insulation to damp to health harm — where each link genuinely supports the next and the conclusion follows. Marked down because nothing is offered to support the links beyond "one of the things that we do see", and the seniors-specific step is asserted rather than argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It's all well and good to have planning rules that enable things, but if we have had advice that the insurance companies have expressed concerns about this and indicated that in the future if the frequency is such that they then will no longer insure those areas and we knew that, or we could have put protections in for those people and didn't, then we're creating another problem.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee — the interaction between the bill's enabling planning rules and insurability of dwellings in hazard-prone areas. No party framing at all.

focus.statement: Now, I’m coming at this particularly from a seniors perspective, because one of the things that we do see in terms of granny flats is that, if there isn’t proper insulation, that’s going to lead to damper granny flats, which would then lead on to additional health issues.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the substance of the bill: whether the standalone dwelling regime should carry an insulation requirement, and the consequences for occupants if it does not. No reference to another party.

specificity.statement: I think that’s a broader question that we need to address and we’re looking to do that as a Government—including with as much support as we can get across the aisle—whereby we’re allowing local councils to consolidate their functions, which will be helpful for them but also helpful for those looking to build, getting consistency within a region.

specificity.statement: That is where a council says, “Yep, look, the level that floods are expected to get to is X and therefore you can build there, but you must build at a level where the floor levels or the areas which you don’t want to get flooded are higher than the expected flood areas”.
specificity.explanation: Sets out an actual regulatory mechanism — a council-set expected flood level with a minimum floor height above it — which someone could act on. veracity.statement: As for the second category of question, I think we’ve covered insurance tolerably well except to say that the Insurance Council of New Zealand, I understand, did indicate their approval with the natural hazard provisions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Insurance Council of New Zealand indicated approval of the bill's natural hazard provisions. The claim is about a stated position of a named body on named provisions, not about whether those provisions are good policy.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The Insurance Council of New Zealand's written submission and any oral evidence on the granny flats / small standalone dwellings building bill, and any public ICNZ statement on its natural hazard provisions. True if ICNZ expressed support for or approval of those provisions; false if ICNZ opposed them, sought material change to them, or made no statement of approval.

rigor.statement: Also, in terms of insulation, there are certain requirements as to the way in which we must build in the building code as regards energy efficiency, which includes insulation. That’s already baked in by reason of the fact that building code compliance is still needed.
rigor.explanation: A valid conditional inference: if code compliance is still mandatory and the code sets energy-efficiency/insulation requirements, then insulation standards persist under the new certification route. The conclusion tracks the premises; no fallacy. Whether the code in fact contains those requirements is a veracity question, not scored here.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If we were in the business of failing to provide consents, or even to require them where they otherwise wouldn’t be required, on the basis that there might be hazards of which we’re unaware, then, simply, we’d be very hidebound and have an even greater issue of productivity and affordability, in terms of housing in this country, than we already do.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: regulating for unknown hazards would be unworkable, therefore the presumption against consent is justified. But the step from 'we can't know unknown hazards' to a material productivity and affordability cost is asserted rather than shown, and it treats the choice as binary — precaution or paralysis — when intermediate triggers exist (and he has just described one, council discretion). A genuine argument with a real gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Anyone who’s likely to be reading the legislation would be able to set aside their feelings of judgment or being judged and simply take that at its face value.
rigor.explanation: Offered as the reason the 'but otherwise legal' amendment is unnecessary, but the load-bearing premise — that readers will not draw an adverse inference from 'non-consented' — is a bare assertion about an empirical matter, with nothing offered in support. The conclusion rests on an unevidenced assumption about the audience.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Every time I’ve seen the word “non-consent”, it automatically makes me think that that’s a bad and naughty thing. I think that this amendment is quite sensible and to the point.
rigor.explanation: Premise and conclusion are both present, so there is an inference to assess, and it is a weak one: the sole support for amending the drafting is the speaker's own reported impression of the word. An appeal to personal anecdote generalised to how readers of the statute will construe it, with nothing else offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It makes sense to use that sort of “must” in the context where the council was after a development contribution, because there is an end point to that; the council are after money, so they’re incentivised to pursue that.
rigor.explanation: A coherent incentive argument: a statutory duty is self-enforcing where the duty-holder gains from performing it, so 'must' works for the development-contribution case and is weaker where the council merely owes an output and has no recourse attached. The premise-to-conclusion step holds; it leans slightly on the assumption that financial incentive is the operative driver of council timeliness.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I would say, however, that the Building Act doesn’t regulate horizontal infrastructure, but it’s a relevant question to the extent that we ask ourselves: how would infrastructure be funded if we’re adding to the housing supply?
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of law that the Building Act 2004 does not regulate horizontal infrastructure (three-waters networks, roading), so pressure on underground stormwater/wastewater from added dwellings falls outside the Act being amended.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Building Act 2004 definitions of 'building' and 'building work' and the treatment of network utility operators' infrastructure: true if reticulated water/wastewater/stormwater networks and roading sit outside the Act's consenting regime (governed instead by the LGA/RMA); false if the Act's definitions bring horizontal network infrastructure within building consenting.

veracity.statement: It could have several bathrooms, it could be large, it could be many floors, it could be a castle, it could be a swimming pool—it could be absolutely anything.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the clause 14 regulation-making power is unbounded as to what may be substituted into Schedule 1 — size, number of storeys, bathrooms, pools — so that 'absolutely anything' could be made a permitted small stand-alone dwelling. Extracted as hyperbole that is nonetheless checkable against the clause as drafted.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of clause 14 and Schedule 1 of the bill as reported back, plus any purpose or limiting provision governing the power: true if the power to amend Schedule 1 carries no stated bounds on floor area, height, storeys or building features; false if the clause is qualified by stated purposes, criteria or maxima that would exclude the examples given.

specificity.statement: The answer to that is that development contributions can and will be obtained. And the trigger for that in this legislation is the project information memorandum.
specificity.explanation: Names the funding mechanism (development contributions) and the specific statutory trigger in the bill (the project information memorandum), which is checkable against the clauses. Stops short of the top: no rate, no amount, no indication of when or in which cases contributions would actually be levied.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The addition of granny flats in large swathes of streets in that neighbourhood could, conceivably, put—it wouldn’t necessarily be a known natural hazard, as the trigger for the council to deny the consent, or to trigger the consent, but it would certainly put pressure on that infrastructure.
specificity.explanation: A concrete mechanism — cumulative granny-flat density loading remediated stormwater/wastewater infrastructure — but the suburb is not named, no number of dwellings or capacity figure is given, and the effect is hedged as 'could, conceivably'. Direction with some detail, no how much. Deliberately paired with high Focus: policy-directed but imprecise.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The addition of granny flats in large swathes of streets in that neighbourhood could, conceivably, put—it wouldn’t necessarily be a known natural hazard, as the trigger for the council to deny the consent, or to trigger the consent, but it would certainly put pressure on that infrastructure.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: identifies a gap between the bill's consent trigger (a known natural hazard) and a foreseeable consequence (cumulative load on remediated underground infrastructure). No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But this is a regulation-making power that allows the Minister a very, very wide range of powers to be able to change the sorts of homes that are built in the backyards of the people next door to you.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested point on an amendment the Minister has resisted, and the criticism lands entirely on the provision — the breadth of the clause 14 power — with no imputation about Penk's motives or competence. Pointed and wholly on the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As for the second point, it’s not the case that the “Henry VIII” power relates to the whole of Schedule 1A.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a checkable fact about the scope of the Order in Council (Henry VIII) power in the bill before the committee: that it does not extend to the whole of new Schedule 1A.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill as reported to the committee of the whole House: read the empowering provision for amendment by Order in Council against new Schedule 1A. True if that power is confined to part of Schedule 1A (e.g. clause 2) and cannot amend clause 1; false if it extends to the whole schedule.

specificity.statement: It will still be the case, whatever else happens, that it must be stand-alone, new, less than 70 square metres, and less than a single storey. That’s quite a tightly constrained envelope.
specificity.explanation: Names four concrete, checkable limits including a numeric floor-area threshold (70 square metres); someone could read the clause and verify each one.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The schedule that he refers to provides a period of three years in which development contributions can be charged in the way set out in this legislation, because it’s envisaged that, within that period of time, councils will have the ability to update their policies, practices, and procedures, and also in anticipation of resource management reform that will change the way development contributions are charged.
specificity.explanation: Gives a named timeframe (three years) and the mechanism it applies to (charging of development contributions under the schedule), but leaves the anticipated resource management reform and any replacement regime undefined.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s because, overall, we want a system that is as enabling as possible but that doesn’t enable building professionals who can’t or shouldn’t be trusted to continue to provide work that is substandard or delivered in an unethical fashion.
specificity.explanation: A statement of general intent — "as enabling as possible", work that is not "substandard" or "unethical" — with no threshold, mechanism or timeframe that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My questions relate to page 19 and, there, clauses 52, 53, and 54, which set out how the various pieces of information, the certificates that are given by professionals who are carrying out work in the building of small dwellings are meant to be handed on, and what happens with them in the scenario.
specificity.explanation: Pins the question to numbered clauses on a named page and to a specific documentary requirement (transfer of professionals' certificates), so the Minister and any reader can locate exactly what is being asked about. A precise question, not an announcement.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It will still be the case, whatever else happens, that it must be stand-alone, new, less than 70 square metres, and less than a single storey. That’s quite a tightly constrained envelope.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion ("quite a tightly constrained envelope") follows directly from the four enumerated constraints he has just listed. No fallacy; the inference tracks the premises offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In terms of the point around return of a development contribution or some land that had been set aside where that has taken place in consideration for providing or enabling the development to take place: if the development doesn't take place, then the development contribution which is used to support funding infrastructure isn't needed anymore for that purpose. So that would be why that would be returned.
rigor.explanation: A valid conditional inference: the contribution is levied to fund infrastructure for a development; if the development does not proceed, the purpose lapses, so the contribution is returned. The conclusion follows from the stated premise about what the contribution is for.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There will be instruments that councils use which you wouldn’t normally describe as policy, so is that what he means?
rigor.explanation: A sound inference: from the premise that councils act through instruments other than policy (plans, for instance), it follows that the drafting term "policy" may not cover the intended field. Premise supports the conclusion drawn.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I’m looking forward to hearing what will no doubt be a very passionate contribution from the Hon Julie Anne Genter, because, if nothing else, there’s always enthusiasm.
civility.explanation: Damning with faint praise aimed at a named member: "if nothing else" implies enthusiasm is all she brings. Condescending rather than a direct insult, and it is directed at the person rather than at any argument, so it falls short of the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So I was right; the recommendations were unanimous.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the select committee's recommended amendments to the bill were agreed unanimously by the committee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Transport and Infrastructure Committee's report on the Land Transport Management (Time of Use Charging) Amendment Bill; true if the report records the committee's recommendations as unanimous with no minority or differing views appended, false if any party recorded dissent from the recommendations.

veracity.statement: But anyway, I think I’m right in saying that there is cross-party support for this.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that support for the time of use charging bill extends across party lines rather than being confined to the governing parties.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The party vote records for the Land Transport Management (Time of Use Charging) Amendment Bill's readings in the 2025 sitting year; true if parties from both the Government and Opposition benches voted in support, false if the bill was supported only by Government parties.

veracity.statement: It will be a momentous day when that happens, because the first economic study into congestion charging, or time of use pricing, whatever you want to call it—I think I’m right in saying—was in 1994.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the first economic study of congestion charging in New Zealand was carried out in 1994, i.e. 31 years before this debate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport and NZ transport-economics literature on the earliest New Zealand study of road/congestion pricing (e.g. the Land Transport Pricing Study); true if the first such economic study dates to 1994, false if the earliest identified study is materially earlier or later.

veracity.statement: There were 218 submissions, a really diverse range of perspectives, and quite a lot of contributions from local government, because ultimately they’re the ones who are going to have to implement this alongside central government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific submission count for the select committee's consideration of the bill, and that a substantial share came from local government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Transport and Infrastructure Committee's report on the bill, which states the number of submissions received; true if the count is 218, false if the report records a materially different number.

rigor.statement: It’s a bit like Swiss cheese—you know, once you put one hole in place, you can’t stop.
rigor.explanation: Slippery slope by analogy: nothing is offered to show that granting one narrow exemption makes further exemptions unstoppable, and the analogy substitutes for the argument. The inference is undercut by the speaker's own position that narrow exemptions can be granted without broad ones.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The more people you exempt, the less effectiveness there is of the price signal. So by definition it’s not as effective and we do want to make the scheme effective.
rigor.explanation: A sound inference: if the scheme works by exposing drivers to a price signal, then exempting drivers necessarily narrows the signal's reach and so reduces effectiveness. The conclusion follows directly from the stated mechanism, with no fallacy or gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: NZTA and enforcement authorities must also consult the Privacy Commissioner and publish their privacy policies to ensure transparency and accountability.
specificity.explanation: Names the responsible bodies (NZTA, enforcement authorities), the office to be consulted (the Privacy Commissioner) and a concrete obligation (publishing privacy policies). Checkable against the reported-back bill; short of full marks only because no timing or standard for the consultation is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The committee has also recommended that any revenue left over after the scheme establishment and operational costs, should there be any, are prioritised on initiatives that improve the ability of people to move around the area affected by time of use charging scheme.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a real mechanism (surplus revenue hypothecated after costs) but the destination is left generic — "initiatives that improve the ability of people to move around" names no amounts, no categories of spending and no decision process, so the direction is clear while the substance is not.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Government is very proud of this change. It is the Government’s policy change that it announced to great fanfare that it would be making the size of these dwellings bigger. If that’s what it means, then it should say that.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee — what the bill actually does (enlarging permitted stand-alone dwellings) and whether the title states it. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Government is very proud of this change. It is the Government’s policy change that it announced to great fanfare that it would be making the size of these dwellings bigger. If that’s what it means, then it should say that.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: if the policy's announced substance is larger dwellings, the title should name it. Supported, though it moves from the Government's pride in the change to an obligation about drafting without closing that step.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I like that one in particular because, from my perspective, it lends itself a little bit more closely to the type of scenario that I’m envisioning, insofar as it is an extra house in the backyard and, by definition, therefore is one that’s drawing on the utility that’s already existing, it’s drawing on the infrastructure that’s already there.
rigor.explanation: The underlying point — a dwelling on an existing section draws on existing utilities — is sound, but 'by definition, therefore' asserts an entailment the proposed title does not carry; the naming conclusion rests on a definitional move that is not definitional.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Anyone can gain the benefit of a granny flat, of course; it’s multiple different scenarios in which that could be useful. So we don’t want to constrain it by being too definitive but, nevertheless, I think the title, technocratic as it is, describes well the intent and a certain amount of the content of the policy.
rigor.explanation: The premise (the dwellings serve many different household situations) genuinely supports the conclusion that the title should not be narrowed to one of them. The further claim that the current technocratic title describes the intent well is asserted rather than argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The key point is this: sitting in traffic is not just a nuisance, it is a drain on productivity, and our road taxes at the moment do not reflect when or where roads are used, meaning they fail to address actual demand and network performance.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that current road taxes cannot address demand or network performance follows from the stated premise that they are not time- or location-differentiated. The productivity-cost premise is asserted here rather than supported, but the inference itself holds.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: International experience shows that social licence matters, and this legislation puts the purpose at the front and centre of the reform.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to unspecified 'international experience' — no jurisdiction, evidence or mechanism is offered — and nothing connects the general claim about social licence to the conclusion that stating a purpose in the Act secures it.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That name change would be at least clearer with people about what is happening here and what the effect of this will be: 13,000 of these dwellings around the country.
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete national figure (13,000 dwellings) tied to the bill's effect, but gives no timeframe, no source and no distribution beyond 'around the country'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We think that there should be a monitoring component of this, especially around those broader regulation-making powers that can see these change without it returning back to the House, the nature of the buildings change.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the target precisely — the delegated regulation-making powers that can alter the dwellings without returning to the House — but supplies no mechanism, reporting requirement, threshold or timeframe for the monitoring proposed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A recent estimate—and there’s been a range—suggests Auckland could face an annual cost of $2.6 billion by 2026.
specificity.explanation: A named place, a dollar figure and a year — checkable as stated, though the estimate's source is not identified and 'a range' is left unquantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Traffic dropped by 7 percent—over 7 percent. Travel times improved by up to 40 percent in peak hours.
specificity.explanation: Two precise, checkable percentage outcomes attached to a named scheme and period; someone could go to the published New York data and test both.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: That name change would be at least clearer with people about what is happening here and what the effect of this will be: 13,000 of these dwellings around the country.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the legislation will result in about 13,000 additional stand-alone dwellings nationally.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE/Stats NZ building consent data for stand-alone dwellings consented under the new granny-flat exemption. True if roughly 13,000 (order-of-magnitude match) are consented nationally within ten years of the Act's commencement; false if the count is materially lower or higher over that period.

civility.statement: Let’s all just take a moment to enjoy the fact that there was serious criticism levelled at my colleague the Hon Chris Bishop and I when we were talking about granny flats from some who thought it was some combination of sexist and ageist or, maybe, that it discriminated on the basis of family status.
civility.explanation: Invites the House to enjoy the discomfort of critics and treats their objection as self-evidently silly rather than answering it — pointed and faintly derisive, but aimed at an unnamed group and landing on no individual.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: A recent estimate—and there’s been a range—suggests Auckland could face an annual cost of $2.6 billion by 2026.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a recent published estimate puts the annual cost of congestion to Auckland at $2.6 billion by 2026.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Locate the recent congestion-cost estimates for Auckland cited by the Ministry of Transport / NZTA (e.g. NZIER and Auckland Council work, and the Congestion Question programme). True if a credible recent estimate puts the annual cost at about $2.6 billion by 2026; false if no such estimate exists or the published figures are materially different.

veracity.statement: Traffic dropped by 7 percent—over 7 percent. Travel times improved by up to 40 percent in peak hours.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New York's congestion pricing scheme, introduced in early 2025, cut traffic by more than 7 percent and improved peak-hour travel times by up to 40 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MTA and NYC DOT reporting on the Congestion Relief Zone for 2025. True if vehicle entries into the zone fell by roughly 7 percent or more and published peak-hour travel-time improvements reach up to about 40 percent on affected routes; false if the official figures are materially lower on either measure.

veracity.statement: The committee’s recommendations on the changes to the bill were unanimous, which is not always the case, but it’s good when they can be unanimous, and that’s really good.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Transport and Infrastructure Committee's recommended amendments to the Land Transport Management (Time of Use Charging) Amendment Bill were agreed unanimously.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Transport and Infrastructure Committee's report on the Land Transport Management (Time of Use Charging) Amendment Bill. True if the report records the recommended amendments as agreed without dissent; false if any member or party is recorded as dissenting from the recommendations. A differing view or minority report on the bill as a whole does not by itself falsify the claim.

veracity.statement: It causes approximately $10 billion in social costs each year, including 3,000 cases of childhood asthma.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a quantified annual social cost of motor-vehicle air pollution in New Zealand and a specific childhood asthma case count attributable to it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Health and Air Pollution in New Zealand (HAPINZ 3.0) study's estimates of the social cost of motor-vehicle air pollution and of childhood asthma cases attributable to it; true if the motor-vehicle share is around $10 billion a year and attributable childhood asthma cases are around 3,000, false if either figure is materially different (e.g. the $10b figure covers all air pollution sources rather than vehicles, or asthma cases differ by more than a factor of two).

veracity.statement: We have higher fares, on average, than every city in Australia for public transport.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that average public transport fares in New Zealand exceed those of every Australian city.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: A comparison of average public transport fares (or standard adult single/zone fares) for New Zealand cities against every Australian capital and major city as at October 2025; true if no Australian city's average exceeds the New Zealand average, false if any Australian city is at or above it.

veracity.statement: In Brisbane, they set up a 50c fare to anywhere recently.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Brisbane recently introduced a flat 50-cent public transport fare covering any journey.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Queensland Government / Translink fare announcements; true if a flat 50-cent fare applying across the network was introduced in the period shortly before October 2025, false if no such fare existed or it was limited to particular services or trip lengths.

veracity.statement: Public transportation is very expensive; it’s got more expensive under this Government because of the policies of Simeon Brown, and I’m hoping that the current Minister will see fit to ensure that more of the budget can be used for transportation fares.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that public transport has become more expensive since the current Government took office, and attributes that to the transport policies of the then Minister.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public transport fare levels in Auckland and Wellington from late 2023 to October 2025, together with government decisions on fare subsidies (e.g. the ending of half-price fares and free/discounted child and youth fares, and NZTA farebox recovery direction); true if fares rose in real terms following those decisions, false if fares were flat or fell, or if the increases predate and are independent of those decisions.

veracity.statement: In the City of London, for example, I think it was 80 percent of the revenue initially was just going into additional bus operations.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 80 percent of the London congestion charge's revenue was initially spent on additional bus services.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Transport for London's published accounts of net congestion charge revenue and its application in the scheme's early years (2003 onwards); true if approximately 80 percent of the net proceeds went to bus network improvements, false if the share was materially different or the proceeds were spread across other transport programmes.

specificity.statement: It causes approximately $10 billion in social costs each year, including 3,000 cases of childhood asthma.
specificity.explanation: Carries a dollar figure, a time basis (each year) and a named health outcome with a case count — someone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Public transportation is very expensive; it’s got more expensive under this Government because of the policies of Simeon Brown, and I’m hoping that the current Minister will see fit to ensure that more of the budget can be used for transportation fares.
civility.explanation: Names a Minister but criticises his policies and their effect on fares rather than his character or competence, and ends by inviting the current Minister to act.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Public transportation is very expensive; it’s got more expensive under this Government because of the policies of Simeon Brown, and I’m hoping that the current Minister will see fit to ensure that more of the budget can be used for transportation fares.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy area (public transport fare subsidy and budget allocation) and a specific outcome (fares rising) rather than generalised party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It doesn’t make sense to use revenue from a congestion charging scheme to build additional capacity on a motorway. That completely defeats the purpose, because, when you put the congestion charge in place, that reduces the demand for the roads, and it increases the demand for the other forms of transportation.
rigor.explanation: A real inference with a stated mechanism: if the charge suppresses road demand and shifts it to other modes, then spending the proceeds on extra motorway capacity is self-defeating. The conclusion tracks the premises; the gap is that it assumes the demand shift is large and durable enough to make the added capacity redundant, which is asserted rather than evidenced.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: His Government sold the Bank of New Zealand and then he was the inaugural chair of the new Government-owned *Kiwibank.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two record facts about Jim Bolger: that the Bolger government sold the Bank of New Zealand, and that Bolger was the first chair of the state-owned Kiwibank.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/NZ Government records of the BNZ sale (date, purchaser, government in office) and Kiwibank's incorporation records and first board composition; true if BNZ was sold while Bolger was Prime Minister AND Bolger is recorded as Kiwibank's inaugural chair, false if either the sale occurred under a different government or someone else chaired Kiwibank first.

veracity.statement: His Government ushered in the *Employment Contracts Act and then subsequently he chaired a working group that led to the establishment of fair pay agreements.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Employment Contracts Act was passed under Bolger's government and that Bolger later chaired the working group whose recommendations produced fair pay agreements.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The enactment date of the Employment Contracts Act and the government in office at the time, plus MBIE records of the Fair Pay Agreements Working Group membership; true if the Act passed under Bolger's premiership AND Bolger chaired that working group, false if either does not hold.

veracity.statement: I do want to acknowledge Winston Peters today, the only remaining member of the House who served in Government with Jim Bolger during the time that he was Prime Minister.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Winston Peters is the sole current sitting MP who served in government during Bolger's premiership (1990-1997).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliamentary register of current MPs' first election dates cross-checked against ministerial and government caucus lists for 1990-1997; true if no other sitting MP served in a Bolger-era government, false if at least one other current MP did.

veracity.statement: He turned down a knighthood on leaving Parliament.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Bolger declined an offered knighthood at the point he left Parliament.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Honours records and contemporaneous reporting/biographical accounts of Bolger declining a knighthood around his 1998 departure from Parliament; true if a documented offer was declined at that time, false if no such offer/declination is recorded or if he accepted a knighthood.

veracity.statement: The Rt Hon Jim Bolger served as Aotearoa’s Prime Minister between 1990 and 1997.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the dates of Jim Bolger's tenure as Prime Minister of New Zealand: beginning in 1990 and ending in 1997.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The official record of New Zealand Prime Ministers (Department of Internal Affairs / Parliamentary Library list of Prime Ministers); true if Bolger took office in 1990 and left office in 1997, false if either the start or end year is materially different.

veracity.statement: He also wasn’t afraid to work across political lines during Kiwibank and working on fair pay agreements, both under Labour-led Governments.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Bolger, a former National Prime Minister, held roles connected with Kiwibank and with fair pay agreements, and that both of those roles occurred under Labour-led Governments.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kiwibank/NZ Post board appointment records and the membership of the Fair Pay Agreements Working Group, cross-checked against which party led the Government at the date of each appointment; true if Bolger held both roles and both appointments fell under Labour-led Governments, false if he held neither role or if the appointments fell under a National-led Government.

veracity.statement: He was, ironically, a republican serving his King Country electorate for 26 years, from 1972 until 1998.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Bolger was the member of Parliament for the King Country electorate for a continuous period of 26 years, entering Parliament in 1972 and leaving in 1998.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary Library records of members and electorates; true if Bolger was first elected in 1972, left Parliament in 1998, and represented the King Country electorate (including any renamed successor of it) throughout, false if the entry or exit year is different or the span is materially other than 26 years.

veracity.statement: It’s true to say that, 29 years ago, in 1996, we formed the first MMP Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the first Government formed under MMP was formed in 1996, by the speaker's party together with Bolger's, and that this was 29 years before the date of the statement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Election records for the 1996 general election and the date the resulting coalition Government took office; true if the first MMP election was held in 1996 and a National–New Zealand First coalition Government was formed that year, false if the first MMP Government was formed in a different year or by different parties. The '29 years ago' arithmetic checks against the statement date of 2025-10-16.

veracity.statement: He once remarked that his life was full of ironies, a reflection on his journey from privatising rail in the 1990s to later chairing its renationalised successor; and, as *Chris Hipkins had said, from selling the *Bank of New Zealand to later chairing *Kiwibank.
veracity.explanation: Asserts four checkable biographical/policy facts about Jim Bolger: that his government privatised rail in the 1990s, that he later chaired the renationalised rail operator, that his government sold the Bank of New Zealand, and that he later chaired Kiwibank.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Company and government records: (a) the 1993 sale of New Zealand Rail Ltd under the Bolger government and Bolger's later appointment as chair of KiwiRail (KiwiRail board records, c.2010); (b) the 1992 sale of the Bank of New Zealand to National Australia Bank under the Bolger government, and Bolger's chairmanship of Kiwibank / NZ Post. TRUE if all four are borne out by those records; FALSE if any of the sales occurred outside his government's term or he did not hold the chairmanships stated.

veracity.statement: Jim told me that he was nominated for the National Party candidacy in the King Country in 1972.
veracity.explanation: Relays Bolger's own account that he won the National Party candidate nomination for the King Country electorate in 1972.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand electoral records and contemporary reporting of the 1972 general election: TRUE if Bolger was the National Party candidate for King Country at the 1972 election (and so selected that year); FALSE if he was selected in a different year or for a different electorate.

veracity.statement: He presided over the recognition of Te Wānanga o Raukawa* and Te Wānanga o Aotearoa* as wānanga under the relevant education legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the formal recognition of Te Wānanga o Raukawa and Te Wānanga o Aotearoa as wānanga under New Zealand education legislation occurred while Bolger was Prime Minister (1990–1997).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Gazette notices and Ministry of Education records of establishment/recognition as wānanga under the Education Act 1989 (as amended 1990): TRUE if both institutions were recognised between November 1990 and December 1997; FALSE if either recognition falls outside Bolger's term as Prime Minister.

veracity.statement: Mr Bolger resisted pressure from what we understand was nicknamed the “Rat Pack”. I won’t name them, but names such as Bill English, Nick Smith, and others were included in it, and it was part of them pursuing neoliberal asset sales.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a faction within National in the 1990s was nicknamed the "Rat Pack", that Bill English and Nick Smith were among its members, and that the faction pushed asset sales against Bolger's resistance.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporary press reporting and political histories/biographies of the 1990s National Party (e.g. accounts of the 1990-96 caucus, Bolger and English biographies): true if a group nicknamed the "Rat Pack" is documented, if English and Smith are named as members, and if the group is recorded as pushing further privatisation/asset sales that Bolger resisted; false if the nickname or the membership is not attested, or if the group's documented agenda was not asset sales.

veracity.statement: Much has been covered of his career, but I would point out that his first election as Leader of the Opposition, in 1987, was a catastrophic loss, and yet he carried on.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 1987 general election was Bolger's first as National's Leader of the Opposition and that National lost it heavily.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary/electoral records: the date Bolger became Leader of the National Party, and the 1987 general election seat result. True if Bolger led National into the 1987 election as his first as leader and National lost decisively; false if he led National at an earlier general election, or if the 1987 margin was narrow.

veracity.statement: Then, he had to deal with, as Leader of the Opposition, the reforming Labour Government that turned the political landscape upside down, where they almost lost Remuera in 1987.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Remuera electorate was very nearly lost to Labour at the 1987 general election, as an illustration of the swing to the fourth Labour Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official 1987 general election electorate results for Remuera: true if the winning majority was narrow (of the order of a few hundred to ~1,500 votes on a normally safe National seat); false if the seat was retained comfortably.

veracity.statement: Progress was just sufficient for National to get re-elected in 1993, by a whisker.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that National was returned to government at the 1993 general election with only a very narrow majority.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official 1993 general election results: true if National won a bare majority of the 99 seats (i.e. a majority of one or two); false if it won a comfortable majority or failed to win a majority.

veracity.statement: But he led the country through strong period of growth in 1994 and 1995.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the New Zealand economy grew strongly in 1994 and 1995 under Bolger's premiership.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / RBNZ real GDP growth series for calendar years 1994 and 1995: true if annual real GDP growth in both years was well above the long-run average (roughly 4% or more); false if growth was at or below trend in either year.

veracity.statement: I’m going to miss “Sir Jim”, and I know he wasn’t a fan of knighthoods, but when we met, I told him he’d been Prime Minister for seven years and I was going to call him “Sir”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Jim Bolger served seven years as Prime Minister of New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official record of New Zealand Prime Ministers (NZ Parliament / DPMC list of ministries) for Jim Bolger's term dates; true if the elapsed span between his swearing-in and his resignation rounds to seven years, false if it is materially shorter or longer (e.g. five or nine years).

veracity.statement: Who would have believed that someone who left school at 15 years old, with no qualifications, goes on to become the Prime Minister and the Leader of the National Party?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Jim Bolger left school at 15 with no qualifications and later became both Leader of the National Party and Prime Minister.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published biographical record and parliamentary biography for James Brendan Bolger — true if he left secondary school at age 15 without qualifications and held both the National Party leadership and the office of Prime Minister; false if the school-leaving age/qualification detail or either office is contradicted by the record.

veracity.statement: Jim Bolger was elected to Parliament in 1972, as you have heard today—that was my last year in primary school.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Jim Bolger first entered Parliament at the 1972 general election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Parliament members' register / Electoral Commission results for the 1972 general election — true if Bolger was returned as an MP at that election, false if his first election was in a different year.

veracity.statement: There has been one member of Parliament between Jim Bolger and myself, and that was Shane Ardern.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that exactly one MP, Shane Ardern, held the Taranaki-King Country seat between Bolger's departure and Kuriger's election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The succession list of members for the Taranaki-King Country electorate on the Parliament website — true if Shane Ardern is the sole member listed between Bolger's final term and Kuriger's first, false if any other member intervened.

veracity.statement: Yes, I can, and what I can also confirm is that we’ve taken 21,000 people off welfare and into work.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 21,000 people have moved off a benefit and into employment since the Government took office.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit statistics / Jobseeker Support exit-to-work data for the period since November 2023; true if approximately 21,000 people have moved off a main benefit into work, false if the figure is materially lower or measures something other than exits into employment.

veracity.statement: Today, I am pleased to announce we have not only achieved but surpassed the Government target of a 15 percent reduction in serious and persistent youth offending.
veracity.explanation: Claims the Government's 15 percent reduction target for serious and persistent youth offending has been met and exceeded.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government Targets quarterly reporting for the serious and persistent youth offending target, measured against the stated baseline; true if the reported reduction is 15 percent or more as at October 2025, false if below.

veracity.statement: Multiple and unplanned care arrangements have been associated with negative outcomes for children, and that’s why it’s great to see that, in the last year, 86 percent of children in out-of-home placements have had stable living arrangements with two or fewer caregivers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 86 percent of children in out-of-home placements had two or fewer caregivers over the past year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki placement stability reporting for the year to mid-2025; true if approximately 86 percent of children in out-of-home care had two or fewer caregivers, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Oranga Tamariki has faced a sharp increase in reports of concern recently—up 44 percent overall.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 44 percent overall increase in reports of concern received by Oranga Tamariki.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki quarterly/annual reports-of-concern volumes; true if the year-on-year increase is approximately 44 percent, false if materially lower or if the comparison period differs.

veracity.statement: Why did she say last month that “We’ve got inflation under control” when inflation has increased over the last four quarters and is now at 3 percent?
veracity.explanation: The question asserts as fact that annual inflation has risen across four successive quarters and now stands at 3 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation prints for the four quarters to the September 2025 quarter; true if each successive annual rate is higher and the latest is 3.0 percent, false if the series did not rise or the latest print differs materially.

veracity.statement: Well, I said that last month because three years ago inflation was 7.3 percent and now it’s 3 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts annual inflation was 7.3 percent three years earlier and is 3 percent now.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual rate for the quarter around October 2022 and for the September 2025 quarter; true if the earlier figure is about 7.3 percent and the latest about 3.0 percent, false if either is materially different.

veracity.statement: Ultimately, the ultimate measure of affordability in the economy is whether wages are rising faster than inflation, which they are.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that wage growth is currently outpacing inflation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Labour Cost Index and average ordinary-time hourly earnings annual growth for the September 2025 quarter compared with annual CPI of 3.0 percent; true if the wage measure exceeds CPI, false if it is at or below it.

veracity.statement: Teachers are not getting a pay cut.
veracity.explanation: Denies that the Government's offer amounts to a pay cut for teachers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The terms of the Government's collective offer to teachers in October 2025: true if the offered base salary rates rise in nominal terms; false if any rate decreases. Resolver should also record the real-terms reading — offered annual increases against annual CPI of 3.0 percent — since that is what the claim was disputing.

veracity.statement: The Government agrees, which is why in Budget 2025, we made the single largest investment in learning support in a generation of over $700 million for a range of incredibly important initiatives to provide better support for kids who need it most.
