specificity.explanation: Names a specific negotiating partner, a specific status (negotiations started), and attaches a dollar figure to the projected gain. Someone could go and check each element.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Anybody who doesn't know that really just has to understand that 80 percent of all our goods exports that go overseas come from the primary sector.
specificity.explanation: A single precise, checkable proportion attached to a named sector and a named measure (goods exports).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have $629.4 billion fraud that goes on in this country, and this country does nothing about it.
specificity.explanation: A precise figure to one decimal place attached to a named phenomenon. Whether the number is right is Veracity's question; as a matter of checkable content it is highly specific.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: In fact, what we believe 2026 will be is the tightening of and the changing of the guard—thank goodness—and the reclaiming of a pen to reshape the laws that this country needs to have.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the 2026 general election will produce a change of government, putting the speaker's side in a position to legislate. Not a promise about the speaker's own action — the outcome turns on the electorate.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The official 2026 New Zealand general election result and the government formed after it. True if the National-led coalition is replaced and a government including Labour/Greens/Te Pāti Māori takes office; false if the incumbent coalition is returned to government.

focus.statement: We need to tax the wealthy. We need to tax those who are making all the biggest noises with the mass homeownership. We need to tax ghost houses. We need to tax and pursue tax evasion. We need to then be able to redistribute that money.
focus.explanation: Squarely on tax policy — names the bases she would tax (wealth, multiple-home ownership, vacant houses, evasion) and the purpose. No party-bashing content in this passage.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Obligating the Government to fund externally recommended levels while capping fees is fiscally risky.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual mechanism of the opposing policy — the combination of a binding funding obligation with a fee cap — and identifies the consequence she objects to. Entirely on the measure, not the party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They couldn’t organise a bun fight in a bakery.
focus.explanation: A content-free jibe about the other party's general competence. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named. No individual is insulted, so this is a Focus failure rather than a Civility one, and stripping out the swipe leaves no argument, so nothing is emitted for Rigor.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We can’t just go out there and say we’re going to ban the internet. It’s just not practical and it’s not the world we live in, particularly not for our young people.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the regulatory question before the House — what kind of online-harm intervention is workable — rather than on any party. The weakness is in the inference, not in what the statement is about.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I know that when I came to Parliament, I wanted to make a difference, and it really, really upsets me and it kind of annoys me that senior leadership of the other parties could do something about this.
focus.explanation: Criticism of other parties' leadership, but anchored to a specific measure — her deepfake member's bill and the option of debating it on the next member's day — rather than to their general character. A real policy point carried in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need to tax the wealthy. We need to tax those who are making all the biggest noises with the mass homeownership. We need to tax ghost houses. We need to tax and pursue tax evasion. We need to then be able to redistribute that money.
specificity.explanation: Names four tax targets, which is a direction with some content, but supplies no rate, threshold, revenue figure, timeframe or mechanism. 'Redistribute that money' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The report called for a significant uplift of up to 231 percent for very low-cost access practices.
specificity.explanation: Names the source, the practice category and an exact figure. Directly checkable against the report.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A new capitation model will be in place by July 2026.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific policy change and a delivery date. Not scored under Divination: this is a commitment about the speaker's own government's action, not a forecast of an external event.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our Government is also increasing the funding for GP trainees so that they’re on par with other specialist trainees and have their fees and exam costs funded for the duration of their training.
specificity.explanation: Names the group, the benchmark (parity with other specialist trainees) and the covered costs (fees and exams, for the full training duration), but gives no dollar figure, trainee numbers or start date.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Let us be bold. Let us be principled. Let us be relentless in our pursuit of a health system that works for everyone, because when we get primary care right, we build the foundation for a healthier, stronger New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: A peroration of generic virtues — bold, principled, relentless — with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named measure. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It was recycled, it was uninspired, it was lazy, and, worst of all, it merely reflected what is actually happening already.
civility.explanation: Harsh, but the target is the policy announcement, not a person. 'Lazy' edges toward the people who drafted it without landing on anyone by name or attribute, so this sits in the pointed-and-robust band rather than at the standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, they like it because you’re saying that you might hold yourselves to it, which is never going to happen.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith directly to the members opposite — that they have no intention of honouring what they are proposing. Short of a personal insult, but it attributes dishonesty rather than engaging the proposal.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In 2017, they pledged to reduce fees and review funding, but once in Government, that promise vanished.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Labour's 2017 election commitment on GP fees and primary care funding was made and then not delivered during its 2017-2023 term. She is asserting this herself, not relaying it, so the conduct on show is her own accuracy.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Labour's 2017 manifesto/health policy documents for a pledge to reduce GP fees and review capitation funding; then Budget 2018-2023 primary care decisions. True if the pledge exists and no fee-reduction or funding-review measure was implemented; false if a measure was implemented (e.g. the 2018 extension of very low cost access to Community Services Card holders, which cut fees for around 540,000 people).

veracity.statement: The report called for a significant uplift of up to 231 percent for very low-cost access practices.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2022 Sapere report on primary care/health funding commissioned by Minister Little recommended a funding uplift of up to 231 percent for very low cost access practices.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Sapere review of primary care capitation funding commissioned by the Ministry of Health in 2022; true if the report states an uplift of up to 231 percent for VLCA practices, false if the figure or the practice category differs materially.

veracity.statement: We’ve implemented the largest increase to baseline funding since capitation began.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the current government's uplift to primary care baseline (capitation) funding is the largest since capitation was introduced in 2002.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The annual capitation uplift percentages from 2002 to 2025 (Ministry of Health / Health NZ funding decisions and Budget documents); true if the 2024 or 2025 uplift exceeds every prior year's, false if any earlier year's uplift was larger.

veracity.statement: My colleague Dr Parmjeet Parmar has successfully called for the select committee inquiry to define the actual problems and hear from the experts that work in this field.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an ACT MP, Parmjeet Parmar, initiated a select committee inquiry into online harm to young people, and that it was granted.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Parliament select committee records for 2025 (Education and Workforce / Justice committee inquiry terms of reference and the initiating notice of motion); true if an inquiry into online harm to young people was established on Parmar's motion, false if no such inquiry exists or it was initiated by another member.

rigor.statement: We can’t just go out there and say we’re going to ban the internet. It’s just not practical and it’s not the world we live in, particularly not for our young people.
rigor.explanation: A strawman: nobody has proposed banning the internet, so rejecting that proposition does not support her conclusion against the age-verification and platform-regulation approaches actually on the table. The inference is about a real policy question, which is why it is scored here rather than skipped, but it defeats a position no one holds.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That industry has increased by 80 percent over the past two years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the New Zealand video game development industry has grown by 80 percent in the two years since the game development rebate was introduced.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Game Developers Association annual industry survey (or MBIE reporting on the Game Development Sector Rebate) for the two years to 2025; true if the sector's revenue or headcount grew by approximately 80 percent over that period, false if the reported growth is materially lower.

veracity.statement: For every dollar of taxpayers’ money invested in that sector, the return was nearly $5.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a return of close to five dollars for every dollar of public money put into the game development rebate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The cost-benefit or return-on-investment figure in MBIE's evaluation of the Game Development Sector Rebate, or the NZGDA survey; true if the reported ratio is approximately 5:1, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: We have 200 people a day on a plane heading overseas.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a current rate of roughly 200 people per day departing New Zealand to live overseas.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration statistics for the most recent 12 months before October 2025; true if departures of New Zealand residents (or net migration loss) average about 200 per day (~73,000 a year), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: We’ve had a massive summit which has resulted in $1 million being spent, and the only offers are that two of those have said that they might open an office in the future.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both the cost of the Government's infrastructure investment summit (about $1 million) and that its only concrete outcome was two parties saying they might open an office.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official cost figures for the 2025 Infrastructure Investment Summit released by MBIE/NZTE or via OIA, plus the Government's own list of announced outcomes; true if the spend was around $1 million and no commitments beyond two prospective office openings were announced, false if the cost differs materially or further commitments were announced.

veracity.statement: We’ve heard the Prime Minister himself say that this is a two-stage recovery.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Prime Minister has publicly characterised the economic recovery as occurring in two stages.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Transcripts of Christopher Luxon's press conferences, speeches and Hansard contributions in 2025; true if he described the recovery as two-stage or two-phase, false if no such statement exists on the record.

veracity.statement: Potholes on State highways across the country—95 percent of them have been repaired within 48 hours.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 95 percent of potholes on state highways nationally are repaired within 48 hours of being identified.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA Waka Kotahi pothole repair performance reporting for 2024–25; true if the reported share of state highway potholes repaired within 48 hours is about 95 percent, false if materially lower or if the measure is defined over a different period.

veracity.statement: That is directly off the back of the Hamilton section of the Waikato Expressway opening, which is a great thing, of course, but we saw a 50 percent increase in traffic on State Highway 21 and 1 at that Tamahere interchange, off the back of that great piece of road opening, because everyone wants to use it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 50 percent rise in traffic volumes at the Tamahere interchange on SH21/SH1 following the opening of the Hamilton section of the Waikato Expressway.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA traffic monitoring counts for SH1/SH21 at Tamahere before and after the Hamilton section opened in 2022; true if counts rose by approximately 50 percent, false if the increase is materially different.

veracity.statement: So it is absolutely fitting that we have seen $100 million committed towards the Southern Links project just this week, to explore, design, site investigations, and consenting to ensure that project can link up, because, unfortunately, we are already seeing massive congestion in the Tamahere region.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that $100 million was committed to the Southern Links project in the week before 22 October 2025, for investigation, design and consenting work.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government's roads of national significance announcement of October 2025 and NZTA project pages for Southern Links; true if $100 million was allocated in that week for pre-construction work, false if the figure or the timing differs materially.

veracity.statement: The last Government cancelled the extension of the expressway down to Piarere.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Labour government cancelled the planned Waikato Expressway extension from Cambridge to Piarere.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2023 NZ Upgrade Programme reprioritisation decisions and NZTA records for the Cambridge to Piarere project; true if the project was cancelled or deferred by the Labour-led government, false if it continued or was never funded to begin with.

specificity.statement: For every dollar of taxpayers’ money invested in that sector, the return was nearly $5.
specificity.explanation: A precise, quantified ratio tied to a named policy — someone could go and check it or use it to argue for the scheme's extension.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s what Labour offers that is different: making sure we build an economy from the ground up that works for everybody.
specificity.explanation: A slogan standing in for the policy contrast — no mechanism, no figure, no timeframe, and 'from the ground up' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Potholes on State highways across the country—95 percent of them have been repaired within 48 hours.
specificity.explanation: A named network, a percentage and a repair window — a performance claim someone could take to the agency's own reporting and check.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So it is absolutely fitting that we have seen $100 million committed towards the Southern Links project just this week, to explore, design, site investigations, and consenting to ensure that project can link up, because, unfortunately, we are already seeing massive congestion in the Tamahere region.
specificity.explanation: Names the project, the sum, the timing and precisely what the money buys (investigation, design, consenting) rather than construction — concrete enough to hold the Government to.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ve had a massive summit which has resulted in $1 million being spent, and the only offers are that two of those have said that they might open an office in the future.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named government initiative against a named cost and a named outcome, not general party-bashing — this is the accountability case that scores high.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s always comforting to have that after the dreariness of winter, and the last Government was an apt metaphor for winter—the dreariness; the dull, long, rainy days.
focus.explanation: Purely a characterisation of the other side, with no policy, measure, figure or outcome named. Nobody is personally insulted, so it passes Civility cleanly — this is exactly the tribal content Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The last Government cancelled the extension of the expressway down to Piarere.
focus.explanation: Names a specific project and a specific decision about it. Attacking the record of the other side on a named policy is on-policy, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: All we’ve heard are empty promises, and some vague pieces of paper this week on potential policy.
focus.explanation: A general dismissal of the other party's output with no policy, document or commitment identified — 'vague pieces of paper' names nothing that could be engaged with.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: One stage is for him and his mates, and the rest is for the rest of the country who are still waiting for the trickle-down to hit them.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the Prime Minister personally — that he is running the economy for the benefit of his friends. That is a jab at motive rather than at the policy, which is the failure this scale now marks.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That rebate introduced over two years ago kept jobs here, but not only did it keep jobs here; it grew them even more.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy, supported by figures she goes on to give, but it is post hoc: growth after the rebate is attributed wholly to the rebate, with nothing offered to rule out global demand or other drivers.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We know that if we own our future and we keep it here and we sustain those New Zealand companies to grow bigger and provide greater opportunities, not only does that grow our economy but that also makes our community stronger, it gives our people more money in their pockets, and it makes our country better.
rigor.explanation: A chain of asserted benefits with no connecting step: nothing is offered to show that domestic ownership produces larger firms, higher incomes or stronger communities. The conclusion is simply restated in progressively broader terms.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: All of these fantastic things that I’ve talked about—none of them would have happened under the last Government.
rigor.explanation: A counterfactual supported by real evidence — three named projects he says were cancelled or opposed. The support is genuine but narrower than the conclusion, which extends to 'all of these fantastic things' including ones no decision was ever taken on.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I’m standing proudly in solidarity with our workers, including 100,000-plus workers who will be striking tomorrow across the country to send a clear message that they are not being valued by this Government and directly impacted by the decisions of this Government.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that more than 100,000 workers will take strike action nationwide on the following day, 23 October 2025.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Union (NZNO, PSA, NZEI/PPTA) and media participation figures for the strike action on 23 October 2025; true if reported participation is at or above 100,000 workers, false if materially below.

veracity.statement: I want to remind us that—I think it was in 2023—a coroner rule that the preventable death, in 2023, of a woman at Waikato Hospital’s emergency department occurred while the ED was five nurses short.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a coroner found a woman's death at Waikato Hospital's emergency department in 2023 was preventable, and that the department was five nurses short at the time.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published coroner's finding for the named Waikato Hospital ED death; true if the coroner recorded the death as preventable and recorded a shortfall of five nursing staff on the shift, false if no such finding exists or the staffing shortfall differs materially.

veracity.statement: They want to deliver better care, but 90 percent of the shifts are understaffed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 90 percent of nursing shifts in the public health system are staffed below the required level.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Whatu Ora / NZNO care capacity demand management (CCDM) shift-staffing data for 2025; true if roughly 90% of shifts are recorded below target staffing, false if the recorded proportion is materially lower.

veracity.statement: That is a choice of this Government when, yes, they manage to find tax breaks and other ways of supporting wealthy landlords, tobacco companies, and fossil fuel barons—I hope that was OK, thank you very much.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government has provided tax breaks or comparable fiscal support to residential landlords, tobacco companies and fossil fuel interests.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024/2025 and tax legislation records: restoration of residential-landlord interest deductibility, the excise treatment of heated tobacco products, and any tax or subsidy changes benefiting oil and gas exploration; true if measures of that kind were enacted for each group, false if no such measures exist.

veracity.statement: I think I’m going to keep my gold medal quote of the week at where I was going to start, and that also goes to Mr Chris Hipkins, who yesterday said that he couldn’t “hand on heart” promise that Labour would build any roads.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on 21 October 2025 Chris Hipkins said he could not "hand on heart" promise that a Labour government would build any roads.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Media transcripts or recordings of Chris Hipkins' public remarks on 21 October 2025; true if he used that phrase in declining to guarantee road building, false if no such remark is on record or it is materially misquoted.

veracity.statement: No kidding that he can’t hand on heart promise that, because what happened last time they were in Government? They all got cancelled.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that all the roading projects in train were cancelled during the 2017–2023 Labour government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA state highway programme records 2017–2023; true if every major planned roading project was cancelled, false if any (e.g. Transmission Gully, Pūhoi to Warkworth) proceeded to completion or construction.

veracity.statement: People in Levin still remember 2018 when the expressway that National were going to build from Ōtaki to the north of Levin got cancelled—outright cancelled.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Ōtaki to north of Levin expressway, planned under the previous National government, was cancelled outright in 2018.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2018 Government Policy Statement on land transport and NZTA project records for Ōtaki to North of Levin; true if the project was removed from the funded programme in 2018, false if it remained funded or was only deferred/re-scoped.

veracity.statement: They are excited: $88.8 billion of new taxes, and tens of billions dollars more in debt.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Green Party's fiscal programme involves $88.8 billion of new taxation and tens of billions of dollars in additional debt.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Green Party's published 2025 alternative budget and its costings; true if the new revenue measures total approximately $88.8 billion over the stated forecast period and debt rises by tens of billions, false if the totals differ materially or rest on a different aggregation period.

veracity.statement: Their only plan to save money is to defund the police.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that defunding the police is the sole savings measure in the Green Party's fiscal plan.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Green Party's published fiscal plan and policing policy; true if police defunding is the only identified savings measure, false if the plan contains other savings or if its policing policy does not propose defunding.

civility.statement: The Prime Minister had the gall to completely dismiss what they are saying when the evidence is clear—sadly, very clear.
civility.explanation: "Had the gall" imputes bad faith to the Prime Minister personally rather than contesting the position — short of a direct insult, but no longer engaging only the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This is the person that Labour have got in charge of the education policy.
civility.explanation: A sneer at a named member's competence rather than at the education position she was arguing — the point lands on the person, not the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Stop siding with your union mates and actually come and support some people in uniform.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad-faith motive to a named member — that he opposes the bill out of union loyalty rather than on its merits — instead of contesting his stated reasons.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The other side of the House are far more outraged about my choice of words than they are about the actual situation that is happening in our healthcare system right now.
focus.explanation: A meta-complaint about the other party's reaction rather than about any health policy, measure or figure; only the passing gesture at "the situation in our healthcare system" keeps it off the floor.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: He could look to his left and see Megan Woods, he could look just behind him and look at Duncan Webb—all jumping ship because they can see what the future holds.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's internal state — which of its MPs are departing — with no policy, measure or outcome named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: “Ngā Pāti Māori” can’t agree on one word to say three times.
focus.explanation: Content-free mockery of another party's naming and internal disagreement; no policy, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Greens, instead, would choose to properly invest in public health systems, ensuring that our GP visits are free; that our nursing visits are free; that our dental care is free; that we provide vans in our rural areas and communities; diagnostic abilities; and also properly fund community and healthcare providers.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete measures (free GP, nursing and dental visits, rural vans) but supplies no cost, funding source or timeframe, so it gives a direction with only partial detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What we’re all about is affordability, decent healthcare and education, and safe communities.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named policy — nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: For shame—for shame from that member. No wonder he is on the list and didn’t win his electorate seat back.
civility.explanation: A clear personal attack: it drops the substance entirely and mocks another member for losing his electorate seat and entering on the list. It is not criticism of an argument or a policy but of the person's standing, so it sits at the personal-attack band rather than the 0.5 bad-faith band.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My question is around how clause 4(1) defines the “Auckland Future Fund” as including “any funds or assets (or both) that the Council adds to the AFF” in the future. Can the member indicate whether the Auckland Council has identified any other specific assets, beyond the Auckland Airport shareholding, that might be potentially transferred to the fund?
specificity.explanation: Names the exact clause, quotes its operative wording, and names the specific asset (the Auckland Airport shareholding) against which the question is framed. A precise question is as checkable as a precise answer; it falls short of 1.0 only because it asks for figures rather than supplying any.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Can the member confirm that this means that these decisions require proper governing body meetings with things like notice, agendas, and public access as per normal council procedures?
specificity.explanation: Names concrete procedural mechanisms — notice, agendas, public access — that could be checked against the Local Government Act requirements. It stops short of 1.0: no timeframes, thresholds or figures, and 'proper' and 'normal council procedures' are left to the answerer to pin down.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Auckland Future Fund Board actually recently appointed Vontobel Asset Management as its global investment manager, with the responsibility to manage that $1.3 billion in funds on behalf of Auckland Council.
specificity.explanation: Names the appointing body, the appointed firm, the role and the amount under management. Someone could go and verify every element of it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is why an Auckland Future Fund and trust will actually have an annual report coming out to give detail on what is going on, what is the investment, how is the return going; not only the annual report but also a six-months report, as well.
specificity.explanation: Gives named reporting mechanisms and a reporting cadence (annual plus six-monthly) with an indication of contents, which is a real answer rather than a platitude. It sits mid-scale because there is no statutory reference, no publication requirement and nothing said about where or by when the reports appear.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My question is around how clause 4(1) defines the “Auckland Future Fund” as including “any funds or assets (or both) that the Council adds to the AFF” in the future. Can the member indicate whether the Auckland Council has identified any other specific assets, beyond the Auckland Airport shareholding, that might be potentially transferred to the fund?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee — the scope of a definition in the bill and what it would let the council transfer. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can the member confirm that this means that these decisions require proper governing body meetings with things like notice, agendas, and public access as per normal council procedures?
focus.explanation: Engages clause 5 of the bill and the transparency consequences that flow from it. Legitimate scrutiny of a named provision, with no content about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I do worry that the other side is just eating up time in this debate for the sake of it.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's conduct in the Chamber. No clause, cost, mechanism or outcome is named — strip out the characterisation of the other side and nothing about the bill remains. Nobody is insulted personally, so Civility is untouched; this is precisely the tribalism Focus exists to catch. Not scored for Rigor: it is a characterisation of opponents, not an argument.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Also, I think there's some good news to tell other members as well, not only the airport shares—now, obviously we know that the airport shares, when they sell, they make extra profit from what they expected—but also recently Auckland Council have been willing to put another $45 million from the special dividends from Port of Auckland into the Auckland Future Fund as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Auckland Council has recently agreed to place a further $45 million, sourced from Port of Auckland special dividends, into the Auckland Future Fund. The checkable core is the existence of that decision and the $45 million figure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council governing body resolutions/minutes and Auckland Future Fund reporting for 2025: true if a council decision transfers approximately $45 million of Port of Auckland special dividends into the Auckland Future Fund; false if no such decision exists or the amount or source is materially different.

veracity.statement: The Auckland Future Fund Board actually recently appointed Vontobel Asset Management as its global investment manager, with the responsibility to manage that $1.3 billion in funds on behalf of Auckland Council.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions of present fact: that the Auckland Future Fund Board appointed Vontobel Asset Management as global investment manager, and that the mandate covers about $1.3 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council / Auckland Future Fund announcements and board papers from 2025: true if Vontobel Asset Management is named as the appointed global investment manager and the funds under management are around $1.3 billion; false if a different manager was appointed, no appointment had been made by 22 October 2025, or the sum is materially different.

focus.statement: I'm keen to understand from the member, if he can explain why the purpose in clause 3 refers to ensuring the Auckland Future Fund “continues” as a long-term financial investment, given that the fund has only just been established in statute.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: a named clause of the bill and the drafting question it raises. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There’s also another political party that proposed a very important future fund in recent days.
focus.explanation: Interrupts a clause-by-clause debate on the Auckland bill to claim credit for her own party's separate announcement. There is a policy referent but no content about it — the weight is party framing, not the measure before the committee.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Auckland Future Fund is not about storytelling; it’s not about writing an essay like what the other side do—they write essays and pretend they present a policy.
focus.explanation: Almost entirely about what the other party is "really like" — that their policy work is pretence. No individual is insulted so Civility passes it, and no mechanism, figure or provision of the bill is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think that, every time there’s a change of councillors, there is a chance that the direction of their priorities will change, and, for this, we want to make sure that this fund is set up in the long term and won’t be affected by other factors such as elections or a change of direction as well.
focus.explanation: Directly answers the question about the purpose of the legislation with the policy rationale — electoral cycles versus a ten-year investment horizon. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The question that I would actually like to hear from the member himself is around the purpose and the need for legislation, because there are many ways funds can be set up: you can get AI to write jargon for 12 pages and call it a future fund, apparently—that's OK.
focus.explanation: A real policy question — why does this need statute rather than a council resolution — but half the sentence is a swipe at another party's rival fund proposal rather than at the bill in front of the committee.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It's great to hear from the other side because we didn't hear from them during the select committee process—it would have been really nice—but we did hear from Carlos Cheung, and what a great advocate he is for Auckland.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's participation and about praising a colleague. No provision, figure or outcome of the bill is named.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I'm keen to understand from the member, if he can explain why the purpose in clause 3 refers to ensuring the Auckland Future Fund “continues” as a long-term financial investment, given that the fund has only just been established in statute.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, quotes the operative word, and states precisely what is being asked. Checkable against the bill text; short of 1.0 only because no figures or dates are involved.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: At the same time, in order to set up a supermajority of 75 percent, you do need to bring it to the House for legislation, and this is the main reason we bring this bill to the House as well.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism and the threshold and ties it to a concrete reason for legislating, but gives no statutory basis or detail for the claim that legislation is the only route.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: However, because there was no protection—there was no additional layer of protection for this fund—the fund was disestablished, and the money was actually being used for paying short-term debt and council spending.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as historical fact that the legacy Auckland diversified financial assets portfolio was disestablished and its money spent on short-term debt and council operating spending.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council and legacy Auckland City Council records on the diversified financial assets portfolio (the "rainy day fund"): true if the portfolio was wound up/disestablished and the proceeds applied to debt repayment and operating spending; false if it was retained, or if the proceeds were applied to some other purpose such as capital investment.

rigor.statement: However, because there was no protection—there was no additional layer of protection for this fund—the fund was disestablished, and the money was actually being used for paying short-term debt and council spending. This is why we are feeling it is important here today to set up an extra layer of protection to make sure this fund continue to benefit people in Auckland.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: a prior fund without statutory protection was spent down, therefore statutory protection is needed here. The precedent is directly analogous and the conclusion tracks it; the gap is that a single case is offered as the whole warrant.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think that, every time there’s a change of councillors, there is a chance that the direction of their priorities will change, and, for this, we want to make sure that this fund is set up in the long term and won’t be affected by other factors such as elections or a change of direction as well.
rigor.explanation: Premise (three-yearly elections change the composition and priorities of the council) supports the conclusion (a long-horizon fund needs insulation from that churn). Sound, though it does not establish why statutory rather than council-level protection follows.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Sadly, there seems to be an attempt here to filibuster on this bill, unnecessarily because actually the general public like it when we do support pieces of legislation.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the members opposite — that their questions are a deliberate time-wasting exercise rather than genuine scrutiny. Short of a personal insult, but it attacks motive rather than substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Mr Cheung has had the wonderful advantage and benefit of being gifted a bill from Auckland Council that is supported by everyone in this House.
civility.explanation: Pointed and faintly condescending toward the member in charge — "gifted" diminishes his effort — but it stops short of a direct attack on his character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Also, I think this member probably doesn’t work on those details, so she doesn’t understand that that’s a lot of hard work.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the named member's diligence and understanding rather than on anything she argued.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It's like white noise, but I'll start again.
civility.explanation: Dismisses a colleague's interjection as meaningless noise — mockery directed at the person interjecting rather than a response to what she said. Mild, but past the point of engaging the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Just this week, an announcement was made to invest in the East-West Link, an incredible piece of highway infrastructure that’s going to get tens of thousands of heavy trucks off local roads around Onehunga, Ōtāhuhu, and other suburbs in south-east Auckland—a project that is maybe five or six years overdue, which is about the term of the previous Labour Government that stopped it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable facts: that a government investment announcement on the East-West Link was made in the week of 22 October 2025, and that the previous Labour Government stopped the project.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA / Ministry of Transport and Beehive press releases for the week of 20-24 October 2025: true if an East-West Link investment announcement was made in that week, false if none was. Second limb: Cabinet/NZTA decisions on the East-West Link 2017-2018; true if the Labour-led Government cancelled, deferred or withdrew funding for the consented project, false if it proceeded or was stopped by another party.

veracity.statement: For example, I mentioned there used to be a fund called Diversified Financial Assets Portfolio, which was supposed to be a long-term fund, but due to mismanagement, the fund was disestablished and they've been used for short-term repayment, the short-term debt, and all that council spending as well. This is exactly the reason why we want to bring this bill to the House here right now, because we want to make sure the purpose of the fund will remain the same for the long term.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Auckland Council held a fund called the Diversified Financial Assets Portfolio, that it was intended as a long-term fund, and that it was disestablished and spent on short-term debt repayment and council spending.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council annual reports, long-term plan documents and treasury/investment policy: true if a Diversified Financial Asset Portfolio existed, was established with a long-term mandate, and was wound up with proceeds applied to debt repayment or operating spend; false if no such fund existed or if it was retained or realised for a different stated purpose.

veracity.statement: Then other sports could benefit. You could change the shape of the ground if you could invest in it and, maybe, then put a roof on it so that you don’t have to worry about whether it rains or not or whether the wind blows too hard. You can still have all your various sports, and you wouldn’t have—like we saw recently—a T20 game being cancelled down in Canterbury, because of the fact it rained for the second part of the match.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a T20 cricket match in Canterbury was recently cancelled because rain fell during the second part of the match.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Cricket / ESPNcricinfo scorecards for T20 fixtures played in Canterbury (Hagley Oval) in the weeks before 22 October 2025: true if a T20 was abandoned or called off with rain interrupting the second innings, false if no such match was rain-affected in that period.

focus.statement: Just this week, an announcement was made to invest in the East-West Link, an incredible piece of highway infrastructure that’s going to get tens of thousands of heavy trucks off local roads around Onehunga, Ōtāhuhu, and other suburbs in south-east Auckland—a project that is maybe five or six years overdue, which is about the term of the previous Labour Government that stopped it.
focus.explanation: Names a specific project, its beneficiaries and its cost bracket, and holds a named prior decision to account — that is on-policy scrutiny. Slightly short of 1.0 because the closing clause converts the delay into a general point about Labour's term rather than the decision itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Also, the Local Government (Auckland Council) Act 2009. It’s specifically relevant to the Auckland Council, and, therefore, a piece of legislation when it comes to the financial management, accountability, and use of funds of Auckland Council, of the Auckland Future Fund itself, it may be another relevant Act that needs to be taken into account.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the measure before the House — the completeness of clause 6's list of applicable legislation. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, Dr Cheung, this project could cost somewhere in the region of $3 billion to $4 billion, and I’m interested in your views on whether the Auckland Future Fund could be used to co-invest in projects where Auckland Council and its communities receive a benefit in order to make the overall dollar go further.
specificity.explanation: Carries a costed figure range and a named, concrete mechanism (the Fund co-investing alongside the Crown), though it does not put a quantum or timeframe on the council's share.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is why we are bringing the bill here, to make sure that, if they want to change the direction of the fund or want to change the initiative of the fund or how they invest the fund, they need to make sure they have 75 percent—which is called a supermajority of councillors—to agree.
specificity.explanation: States the actual mechanism and the threshold — a 75 percent supermajority of councillors to alter the fund's purpose. Checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Also, the Local Government (Auckland Council) Act 2009. It’s specifically relevant to the Auckland Council, and, therefore, a piece of legislation when it comes to the financial management, accountability, and use of funds of Auckland Council, of the Auckland Future Fund itself, it may be another relevant Act that needs to be taken into account.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific statute by title and year and ties it to a specific drafting question about the clause before the committee. Short of the top only because it does not identify the provisions that would need to be cross-referenced.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The advantages of having a future fund that can invest in that type of infrastructure, I think, would really benefit the wider population of not only Auckland but, actually, the country.
specificity.explanation: A generic benefit claim with no figure, no mechanism, no timeframe and no identified beneficiary group — nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: For example, I mentioned there used to be a fund called Diversified Financial Assets Portfolio, which was supposed to be a long-term fund, but due to mismanagement, the fund was disestablished and they've been used for short-term repayment, the short-term debt, and all that council spending as well. This is exactly the reason why we want to bring this bill to the House here right now, because we want to make sure the purpose of the fund will remain the same for the long term.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: an earlier long-term fund was liquidated for short-term purposes, therefore this fund needs a statutory lock on its purpose. The conclusion tracks the premise, but there is a gap — nothing offered to show a 75 percent threshold specifically would have prevented that outcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Then other sports could benefit. You could change the shape of the ground if you could invest in it and, maybe, then put a roof on it so that you don’t have to worry about whether it rains or not or whether the wind blows too hard. You can still have all your various sports, and you wouldn’t have—like we saw recently—a T20 game being cancelled down in Canterbury, because of the fact it rained for the second part of the match.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote: a single recent rained-off match is offered as the case for the Fund investing in a stadium roof. Nothing is put against it on cost, return or how often weather actually cancels events.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Auckland Council sold its Auckland Airport shares, a sale that went ahead without consultation with Māori—and not just any Māori: Ngāti Whātua and Waikato-Tainui.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Auckland Council's sale of its Auckland Airport shareholding proceeded without consulting mana whenua, specifically Ngāti Whātua and Waikato-Tainui.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council's consultation record for the airport shareholding divestment (2024 Long-term Plan consultation documents, council/committee minutes, and any mana whenua engagement records): true if no consultation with Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei or Waikato-Tainui on the share sale is documented; false if the council recorded engagement with either iwi on that decision.

veracity.statement: In fact, it lacks any statutory requirements for Māori representation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Auckland Council (Auckland Future Fund) Bill as before the committee contains no statutory requirement for Māori representation in the fund's governance.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Auckland Council (Auckland Future Fund) Bill as reported to the committee of the whole House: true if no clause requires Māori or mana whenua representation on the fund's governing or managing structures; false if any clause imposes such a requirement.

veracity.statement: And may I remind this House that in Tāmaki-makau-rau, we boast one-quarter of the entire Māori population—250,000 Māori call Tāmaki-makau-rau home.
veracity.explanation: Two linked demographic assertions: that Auckland holds a quarter of New Zealand's Māori population, and that the count is 250,000.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census Māori ethnic-group population for the Auckland region as a share of the national Māori population: true if the Auckland share is approximately 25% and the count is approximately 250,000; false if either figure is materially off (e.g. a count below ~225,000 or a share outside ~22–28%).

veracity.statement: Māori have never breached Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
veracity.explanation: An absolute historical claim that no Māori party has ever breached Te Tiriti o Waitangi, offered as fact rather than as a statement of the Crown's distinct obligations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal reports and the historical/legal literature on Treaty obligations: true if no recognised finding or accepted historical account records a breach of Te Tiriti by a Māori signatory or Māori party; false if such a documented instance exists. Note for the resolver: the Tribunal's jurisdiction extends only to Crown acts, so its silence is not by itself evidence for the claim.

veracity.statement: I want to remind the member, as well, the council actually have representatives from Houkura Independent Māori Statutory Board on the selection process for future fund directors.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Houkura (the Independent Māori Statutory Board) has representatives on the process that selects directors of the Auckland Future Fund.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council / Auckland Future Fund director appointment documentation (appointments policy, selection panel composition, council or Houkura minutes): true if Houkura members or nominees sit on the director selection panel or process; false if the selection process includes no Houkura representation.

veracity.statement: I also want to give you more good news, as well: recently, Auckland Council have increased their Achieving Māori Outcome Budget by 10 percent next year, to support projects like marae infrastructure, energy, and climate resilience.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific budget change: a 10 percent increase to Auckland Council's Māori Outcomes budget for the coming year, directed at marae infrastructure, energy and climate resilience projects.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council's adopted Annual Plan / Long-term Plan budget lines for Achieving Māori Outcomes across the relevant two years: true if the allocation rises by approximately 10 percent; false if the increase is materially different or the budget is flat or cut.

veracity.statement: Our one swimming pool, for example, built for the 1990 Commonwealth Games in Henderson, the West Wave pool, was for a population of around about 120,000 people. The population is now well over 200,000 heading towards 300,000 in West Auckland.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that the West Wave pool in Henderson was built for the 1990 Commonwealth Games serving a population of about 120,000, and that West Auckland's population is now well over 200,000.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: West Wave Aquatic Centre construction/opening records and Auckland Council facility history for the first claim; Stats NZ subnational population estimates for the Waitākere Ranges/Henderson-Massey/Whau local board areas for the second. True if the pool dates to the 1990 Commonwealth Games period and West Auckland's current population exceeds 200,000; false if the pool predates or postdates that period materially, or the population is at or below 200,000.

veracity.statement: Then we have around $2.6 billion dollars of vacant land and buildings that Auckland Council owns.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a valuation figure: approximately $2.6 billion of vacant land and buildings held by Auckland Council.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council's annual report / group property asset register valuation of non-service (vacant land and building) property: true if the carrying value is approximately $2.6 billion; false if materially different (e.g. below ~$2b or above ~$3.5b).

civility.statement: They were not afforded the respect that they deserve by being a prominent voice in consultation and decision making, but rather included as an afterthought.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism of how a consultation process treated iwi. It targets the process and the decision, not any individual member; no bad faith is imputed to a person.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My question: why does clause 3 not explicitly reference Māori communities or the Treaty of Waitangi, given the bill’s stated purpose to benefit current and future communities?
focus.explanation: Names a specific clause of the measure before the committee and puts a concrete drafting question about it. Opposition scrutiny of a named provision, with no party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My question: why does clause 3 not explicitly reference Māori communities or the Treaty of Waitangi, given the bill’s stated purpose to benefit current and future communities?
specificity.explanation: Identifies the exact clause, quotes its wording earlier in the passage, and specifies the omission being challenged. Someone could check the clause and act on the point; it stops short of proposing drafted wording.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: All it takes is to put the people and the planet before profit.
specificity.explanation: Offered as the prescription for what the Government should do, but it is a slogan: no mechanism, no amendment, no figure, nothing that could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I also want to give you more good news, as well: recently, Auckland Council have increased their Achieving Māori Outcome Budget by 10 percent next year, to support projects like marae infrastructure, energy, and climate resilience.
specificity.explanation: Names the budget line, gives a percentage and a timeframe, and lists the categories of spend. Missing only the dollar amount.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our one swimming pool, for example, built for the 1990 Commonwealth Games in Henderson, the West Wave pool, was for a population of around about 120,000 people. The population is now well over 200,000 heading towards 300,000 in West Auckland.
specificity.explanation: A named facility, a date, and three population figures anchoring the asset-adequacy argument. Checkable; no cost or proposal attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I love how he’s got all his answers written out for these questions from his colleagues!
civility.explanation: Sarcastic mockery of the member's conduct — imputes that the exchange is staged rather than engaging anything he said. Short of a direct insult, but it lands on the person, not the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We’ve already had you hold that up. Thank you for holding it up again.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic needling of the member for repeating a prop; engages nothing of substance. Mockery, so a real civility failure under the re-anchored scale, but not a personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I know that the member on the left-hand side doesn’t really care because they don’t really care about the future of Auckland, but I think most of the people involved with the TV would love to know what’s going on, what’s happened to my rates and my fund as well.
civility.explanation: Directed at a specific member and imputes bad faith — that they simply do not care about Auckland's future. That is an attack on the person's motives rather than on any argument they made.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We want to make sure and I think this is something that, on that side of the House, they’re not very good at it!
focus.explanation: A committee-stage debate on a specific bill, but this sentence names no clause, figure or measure — it is a generalised claim about what the other side is bad at. Nobody is personally insulted, so Civility passes; this is what Focus is for.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They just like to write essays or give us 11 pages of document or pictures, and I think this is not the way to actually do things.
focus.explanation: Characterises the other side's habits rather than the Auckland Future Fund provisions under debate. It gestures at their committee conduct, so not wholly content-free, but no policy, clause or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Clause 8(b) states, “with the intent of maintaining or increasing the real value of its capital over time.” I’m keen to understand from the member how “real value” will be defined and measured.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: quotes the clause and asks how its operative term will be applied. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Clause 8(b) states, “with the intent of maintaining or increasing the real value of its capital over time.” I’m keen to understand from the member how “real value” will be defined and measured.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact clause, quotes its wording, and asks a definite question about definition and measurement. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So as the proposal has been proposed, the expected return of the Auckland Future Fund is 7.42 percent, and within that, 2 percent will be used to retain the fund value to make sure the fund can keep growing as well.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete figures with a stated mechanism — the headline expected return and the portion retained for capital preservation. Checkable against the fund proposal.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I say that because it started on a high: a $38 million dividend was paid out from the June to December period in this year alone, making that period 13 percent higher than forecast.
specificity.explanation: A named amount, a named period, and a stated variance against forecast. Fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We set up a very high bar for the council, to make sure they can change the initiative or change the use of the fund only when they have a super majority, which means only 75 percent of the councillors have agreed to it.
specificity.explanation: Names the safeguard mechanism and the exact threshold (75 percent supermajority) required to change the fund's use. Concrete and checkable against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I ask because investment markets, as we know, can be volatile in the short term, and I want to ensure that the fund has appropriate flexibility to weather market downturns without being in a technical breach of the Act.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: short-term market volatility is offered as the premise, and the conclusion — that the measurement window must be long enough to avoid a technical breach — follows directly from it. No fallacy or appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This, to me, presents an issue, because what we're trying to do here is create a fund on behalf of Auckland's shareholders—citizens of Auckland—and if this is close to and controlled by council, I fear for the future of the fund.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the governance design — proximity to council is offered as the reason to doubt the fund's future — but the causal step from council control to poor fund outcomes is asserted rather than supported, and the conclusion rests partly on stated apprehension ('I fear') rather than evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think, as referred to before, without this legislation—like the one we talked about, the financial assessment portfolio, which was set up by a previous council before—because without the legislation, that fund wasn't performing well or they were being mismanaged or being misused, and they need to be disestablished.
rigor.explanation: A genuine argument about the measure — the absence of statutory protection is offered as the cause of an earlier fund's failure, and hence as the reason for this bill. But it rests on a single unexamined case and treats correlation as cause; no alternative explanation for that fund's performance is addressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Clause 8 also sets out principles but doesn’t specify consequences if the principles aren’t followed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that clause 8 of the bill establishing the Auckland Future Fund contains governing principles but no enforcement or consequence provision for non-compliance.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of clause 8 of the Auckland Future Fund bill as reported back to the House: true if clause 8 states principles with no attached consequence, remedy or enforcement mechanism for breach; false if clause 8 (or a cross-reference within it) specifies consequences.

veracity.statement: So as the proposal has been proposed, the expected return of the Auckland Future Fund is 7.42 percent, and within that, 2 percent will be used to retain the fund value to make sure the fund can keep growing as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Auckland Future Fund proposal carries an expected return of 7.42 percent, of which 2 percentage points are retained to preserve the fund's real value.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council's Auckland Future Fund establishment documents / statement of investment policy and objectives: true if the stated expected long-run return is 7.42% with a ~2% retention for capital maintenance, false if either figure differs materially. Note another member in the same debate cites 7.2 percent.

veracity.statement: Also, as I mentioned before, as a council-controlled organisation (CCO), they are actually subject to external auditing by the Auditor-General for its financial and service performance as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a council-controlled organisation is externally audited by the Auditor-General covering both financial statements and service performance.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Local Government Act 2002 and Public Audit Act 2001 provisions on audit of council-controlled organisations: true if the Auditor-General is the statutory auditor of CCOs and the audit covers service performance as well as financial statements, false if CCOs may appoint private auditors independently of the Auditor-General or if service performance is outside the audit scope.

veracity.statement: My question is around the words “council-controlled organisation” (CCO), which you’ve used—and although this is not decided completely as yet, we do note that the Auckland Council has had a predilection just recently of pulling all CCOs into council.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of recent record that Auckland Council has been bringing its council-controlled organisations back in-house.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council governing body resolutions and CCO reform decisions from 2024–2025: true if the council resolved to disestablish or absorb CCOs (e.g. moving Eke Panuku / Tātaki Auckland Unlimited functions into council, or transferring Auckland Transport functions), false if no such in-housing decisions were made in that period.

veracity.statement: I say that because it started on a high: a $38 million dividend was paid out from the June to December period in this year alone, making that period 13 percent higher than forecast.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that $38 million in dividends was paid out over the June–December period of 2025, and that this was 13 percent above forecast.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council / Auckland Future Fund quarterly and half-year financial reporting for the June–December 2025 period: true if dividends of approximately $38m were paid and reported as ~13% above forecast, false if the amount or the variance differs materially.

veracity.statement: We've got 1.3 million people living in Auckland, and I believe that the impact for this fund, for this legislation, goes way beyond Auckland.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the resident population of Auckland is 1.3 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates for the Auckland region at the nearest release to October 2025; true if the estimate is approximately 1.3 million, false if materially higher or lower.

rigor.statement: We know that for the member, the MP for Warkworth, there's a lot of transport logistics going on between Northland and the Port of Auckland as well. Imagine if all this funding, the return of this investment, can go back to improve our transport network in Auckland, that also benefits the people in Northland as well.
rigor.explanation: A real inference with a stated premise: freight moves between Northland and the Port of Auckland, therefore Auckland transport spending spills over to Northland. The link is genuine but nothing is offered on magnitude, so the leap from 'benefits Northland' to the earlier claim that the fund benefits all of New Zealand is only partly carried.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The suggestion there, to me, anyway—and I’m happy to be corrected by the member in the chair—is that it’s possible for Auckland Council to perceive a scenario where a fund is not an asset but they may still wish to include it in the Auckland Future Fund.
rigor.explanation: Standard statutory-interpretation inference: legislation is drafted concisely, so distinguishing 'funds' from 'assets' implies a case where the two come apart. The conclusion follows, though it rests on an assumption of non-redundant drafting that is not always safe.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: For example, during COVID, when we didn’t actually have tourists coming from overseas, and we got a lot of flights being cancelled because of the pandemic and, obviously, airport shares not doing well, that actually reduced the return of the fund. That affects the future planning for Auckland council as well, so I think it’s very important to diversify all investment to make sure we’ve got return from different areas, as well.
rigor.explanation: A worked concentration-risk argument: a single-sector holding was hit by a sector-wide shock, that shock flowed through to the council's income, therefore spread the holdings. The conclusion tracks the example offered; it stops short of 1.0 only because diversification is asserted rather than shown to have been the better outcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I appreciate the higher-level perspective from the member Grant McCallum, who talked of his aspiration for roofs, but I thought, in particular, I wanted to touch here on clause 4(1)(b)(i)—that’s on line 18—talking about the Auckland Future Fund (AFF) being the establishment of the fund in the Long-Term Plan.
specificity.explanation: Pinpoints the provision to the subparagraph and the line number, and names the instrument it operates through. Anyone could turn to the exact text being questioned.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’d be interested if the member Dr Carlos Cheung could just clarify what specific structures Auckland Council currently has potentially in mind. Could this potentially be a trust, a council-controlled organisation, or another entity?
specificity.explanation: Names concrete alternative vehicles the clause could produce, so the answer would be checkable — but the question itself carries no figures or timeframes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But at the same time, the fund itself is also subject to an external audit by the Auditor-General, of its financial and service performance as well.
specificity.explanation: Names the auditing body and the scope of the audit, which is a checkable accountability mechanism rather than a general assurance — though no frequency or reporting line is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I appreciate the higher-level perspective from the member Grant McCallum, who talked of his aspiration for roofs, but I thought, in particular, I wanted to touch here on clause 4(1)(b)(i)—that’s on line 18—talking about the Auckland Future Fund (AFF) being the establishment of the fund in the Long-Term Plan.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the drafting of the measure before the committee; no party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’d be interested if the member Dr Carlos Cheung could just clarify what specific structures Auckland Council currently has potentially in mind. Could this potentially be a trust, a council-controlled organisation, or another entity?
focus.explanation: Engages the governance mechanism in clause 7 and how it would operate in practice; no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Mr Chair, through you, if I could ask the member in charge: is there a chance, through this bill, for the Auckland Council to see the error of its ways and perhaps buy back into Auckland Airport, a gold-standard piece of monopoly infrastructure that’s expanding, pays a good dividend, and would be able to be leveraged to pay for Grant McCallum’s Taylor Swift concert?
civility.explanation: 'See the error of its ways' is a pointed jab at a decision and at an institution, not at any person, and the reference to a colleague is jocular rather than an attack. Robust and slightly condescending toward the council's judgement, but it lands on the decision.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I think in the future we're going to put more different assets into the fund as well.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that assets beyond the Auckland Airport share sale proceeds will be added to the Auckland Future Fund. Not a promise about the speaker's own action — the transfers would be Auckland Council's decision, not his.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Auckland Future Fund annual reports and Auckland Council Long-Term Plan documents; true if any fund or asset beyond the original Auckland Airport share sale proceeds has been transferred into the AFF by the resolve-by date, false if the fund still holds only the airport proceeds and their reinvested returns.

civility.statement: I was expecting the member in charge of the legislation from the Green Party to stand and take the first call on this bill, being it’s her piece of legislation, but she hasn’t turned up to the House.
civility.explanation: Not a direct insult, but it publicly imputes neglect of duty to a named-by-role member rather than engaging anything she has argued — a pointed personal jab at diligence.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I was expecting the member in charge of the legislation from the Green Party to stand and take the first call on this bill, being it’s her piece of legislation, but she hasn’t turned up to the House.
focus.explanation: Nothing about the measure before the House: it is entirely about another party's member and her absence. No policy, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This creates a significant administrative burden. More summonses must be sent out, more follow-ups are required, and more time is spent managing excusal requests. By raising the excusal age, we reduce that burden, making the system more efficient and more representative.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: the operational effect of the excusal threshold on court administration. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The supporting data came later, confirming that 47 percent of excusals are granted solely on the basis of age.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that age alone accounts for 47 percent of all granted jury-service excusals, as a matter of official data supplied to the bill's development.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice jury summons/excusal statistics for the period cited (as supplied to the Justice Committee on this bill): true if age-based automatic excusals were approximately 47% of all granted excusals, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Under current law, anyone aged 65 or over may request automatic excusal from jury duty, either permanently or for that particular occasion, and that request is granted without question.
veracity.explanation: Describes the pre-amendment statutory position: an as-of-right excusal available at 65, granted without any discretionary assessment, either permanently or for the occasion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The excusal provisions of the Juries Act 1981 as at October 2025: true if the Act gives persons aged 65+ excusal as of right on request (permanent or occasion-specific) with no discretion to refuse, false if the registrar retains discretion or the age differs.

veracity.statement: The threshold was originally 60, and it was then raised to 65 back in 1945.
veracity.explanation: A claim about the legislative history of the jury excusal age: that it began at 60 and was lifted to 65 by a 1945 enactment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative history of the jury-service age excusal provisions (Juries Act 1908 and its amendments, including any 1945 amending Act): true if the excusal age was 60 before 1945 and set to 65 by a 1945 amendment, false if either the earlier figure or the year is different.

veracity.statement: It considered the age of retirement of judges at 75 and the Ombudsman’s retirement age at 72, whereas international norms vary, with the excusal age of 70 in Australia, 76 in England and Wales, and even 80 in parts of the United States.
veracity.explanation: Four separate checkable benchmarks: the New Zealand judicial retirement age (stated as 75), the Ombudsman's retirement age (72), and jury excusal/upper age limits in Australia (70), England and Wales (76) and parts of the United States (80).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Senior Courts Act 2016 (judicial retirement age), Ombudsmen Act 1975 (Ombudsman's retirement age), and the jury statutes of the Australian states, the Criminal Justice and Courts Act 2015 for England and Wales, and the relevant US state jury statutes: true if each stated figure matches the governing provision as at October 2025, false if any is materially wrong.

specificity.statement: It considered the age of retirement of judges at 75 and the Ombudsman’s retirement age at 72, whereas international norms vary, with the excusal age of 70 in Australia, 76 in England and Wales, and even 80 in parts of the United States.
specificity.explanation: Five named comparators each attached to an exact age figure — every element is directly checkable against a statute.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The age of 72 strikes the right balance. It reflects capability, it respects contribution, and it aligns with other civic roles.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — 'reflects capability', 'respects contribution' — with no figure, mechanism or test by which the balance could be checked. The number 72 is the only concrete element and it is asserted, not derived.
specificity.subject: speaker
