veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki / CYF harm-in-care reporting and Safety of Children in Care annual reports; true if no prior year-on-year reduction in recorded harm is on record, false if any earlier reporting period shows a reduction.

veracity.statement: In relation to teachers, in the last three years, there has been a 14.5 percent increase in pay for teachers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a cumulative 14.5 percent pay increase for teachers over the three years to October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Successive primary and secondary teachers' collective agreements and Ministry of Education pay scale documents 2022-2025; true if the compounded base scale increase is approximately 14.5%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: It is simply a mischaracterisation for the Labour Party to say that tobacco companies have been given $300 million. That simply has not happened.
veracity.explanation: Denies that any $300 million benefit has been conferred on tobacco companies, in response to the excise treatment of heated tobacco products.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury and Customs costings of the heated tobacco products excise reduction, and Regulatory Impact Statements; true if no fiscal cost of that order accrued to tobacco manufacturers, false if the costed forgone revenue is around $300m (or the disclosed figure differs from $300m only in size, not in kind).

veracity.statement: Why do Government board members deserve an 80 percent pay rise while teachers get an effective pay cut?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Government board members have received an 80 percent pay rise, and that the teachers' offer is below inflation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cabinet Fees Framework revisions and Public Service Commission determinations for Crown entity board fees 2024-2025, against the CPI series and the current teachers' collective offer; true if the top of the revised fee ranges is around 80% above the previous ranges and the teachers' offer is below CPI, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Why do tobacco companies deserve $300 million while nurses are being offered an effective pay cut?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $300 million benefit to tobacco companies, disputed in the answer that follows.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury costing of the heated tobacco products excise reduction and the associated Regulatory Impact Statement; true if the forgone excise revenue attributable to tobacco manufacturers is approximately $300m, false if materially lower or if the incidence falls on consumers rather than companies.

veracity.statement: Why is he willing to spend $44,000 on a helicopter trip for his Instagram—the equivalent of nine months’ base salary for the firefighters he is offering an effective pay cut to?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $44,000 cost for a helicopter trip taken by the Prime Minister, and that this equals roughly nine months of a firefighter's base salary.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial expense disclosures / DPMC travel cost releases for the trip in question, against the FENZ collective agreement base rate for a qualified firefighter; true if the disclosed cost is around $44,000 and the ratio to nine months' base pay holds, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Are firefighters correct when they say they have to work with equipment that consistently breaks down, with no fleet replacement strategy, and are right now across the country putting their safety at risk protecting our communities from severe weather?
veracity.explanation: The speaker is expressly relaying firefighters' claim — that appliances consistently break down and that there is no fleet replacement strategy — and putting it to the Minister rather than asserting it himself.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: FENZ fleet documentation: existence of a published fleet/appliance replacement schedule as at October 2025, and the recorded rate of in-service appliance failures; true if no replacement strategy is documented and breakdown rates are elevated, false if a replacement schedule is published and failure rates are within normal range.

veracity.statement: Is it correct that in the past year the fire truck compliance servicing provider has done 446 emergency callouts, more than one a day, due to breakdowns of the ageing fleet?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count of 446 breakdown-related emergency callouts by the compliance servicing provider over the past year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: FENZ servicing contractor callout records for the 12 months to October 2025, obtainable by OIA; true if breakdown-related emergency callouts number approximately 446, false if materially different or if the callouts are not breakdown-related.

veracity.statement: Seasonally adjusted export values were up 0.9 percent in September, following increases of 7 percent in August and 2.2 percent in July.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three consecutive monthly seasonally adjusted goods export value movements from the Stats NZ overseas merchandise trade release.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ overseas merchandise trade, seasonally adjusted goods exports, monthly series for July, August and September 2025; true if the movements are +2.2%, +7% and +0.9% respectively, false if materially different.

rigor.statement: I’ve been advised that, for example, there has only been one recent breakdown that led to a two-minute delay in getting to a fire—that’s in the past several months, at least. So I think the characterisation of routine breakdowns and danger is simply not sustainable.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single cited incident to a conclusion about the whole fleet's reliability. A hasty generalisation: one non-serious breakdown does not establish that breakdowns are not routine, and no fleet-wide figure is offered against the 446-callout claim just put to him.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: All of this has led to a 14 percent reduction in young people being harmed.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: the listed interventions and the fall in recorded harm are asserted as cause and effect with nothing offered to connect them — no counterfactual, no attribution analysis, no control for changed reporting or resident numbers.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Actually, I was so effective at answering the question, praising these backbone firefighters, that they decided they did want to come back to the table 10 minutes after I answered the question.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc ergo propter hoc, in its purest form: the union making contact ten minutes after the answer is offered as proof the answer caused it. Nothing beyond the sequence is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There’s a real contradiction for the Labour Party here: they want the State to do more, they want more Government agencies to do more stuff—to invest in video games, to start sovereign wealth funds—and yet they don’t want to pay the people directing these proposed entities, or even the current ones, even nearly as much as directors get in the private sector.
rigor.explanation: A tu quoque. Even if the inconsistency is real, an opponent's inconsistency does not establish that the board pay rise is justified — the question asked why the rise was warranted, and the answer argues only that critics are not entitled to object.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yesterday, the Prime Minister was asked about this precise matter and said he was not aware that that’s what the Government is doing. So, again, this is misinformation from the Opposition.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur resting on an appeal to authority: a Minister's stated unawareness of a policy is not evidence the policy does not exist, so it cannot establish that the claim is misinformation.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, on the comment about the Prime Minister’s personal capacity and his personal residence, there’s no responsibility for that except to say that there is a tone that if someone’s worked hard all their life and done well, they should be dragged down and they should be embarrassed about their success and having a nice place on Waiheke.
rigor.explanation: Strawman. The question was about seeking a rates rebate while declining pay negotiations; it is answered as though the objection were to the Prime Minister being wealthy at all, which is not what was put.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I do note that due to current industrial negotiations, there appears to be a concerted campaign by some in the fire service, and particularly the New Zealand Professional Firefighters Union, to try and emphasise any incident and present it as being routine when, in fact, that characterisation is not true.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to named people in the fire service — that they are manufacturing a campaign for bargaining advantage — rather than contesting the evidence. Short of a direct insult, but it attacks motive rather than substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Why is he willing to spend $44,000 on a helicopter trip for his Instagram—the equivalent of nine months’ base salary for the firefighters he is offering an effective pay cut to?
civility.explanation: Scrutiny of spending is legitimate, but 'for his Instagram' imputes a vain personal motive to the Prime Minister rather than contesting the value of the trip. That is an attack on motive, not on the decision.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Why is he not willing to negotiate with teachers, firefighters, and nurses about fair pay but is willing to negotiate a rates rebate on his $10.5 million mansion?
civility.explanation: The pay comparison is fair scrutiny, but the sentence turns on the Prime Minister's personal wealth and residence rather than on any decision he made in office — a jibe at the person, sneering rather than substantive.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is very good news, and it has come because of a precise and deliberate set of actions by the Minister to improve the quality of staffing, to require staff to wear uniforms, to crack down on contraband—for example, by requiring staff to have clear bags so that they couldn’t smuggle contraband in—and by proactively managing behaviour in the sites.
specificity.explanation: Names four concrete operational mechanisms, including a specific one (clear bags for staff). Someone could check whether each was implemented.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have to balance all of these, and the offers that have been put on the table are designed to do that—to bring people together and connect the needs and the means of New Zealanders with the demands and the pressures from union organisers.
specificity.explanation: Asked what pay offer was on the table, the answer supplies no figure, no percentage, no timeframe and no mechanism — only the generic virtue of balance. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is it correct that in the past year the fire truck compliance servicing provider has done 446 emergency callouts, more than one a day, due to breakdowns of the ageing fleet?
specificity.explanation: A named figure, a named source of the figure, a defined period and a defined cause. Fully checkable — a precise question, and as specific as a precise answer would be.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Seasonally adjusted export values were up 0.9 percent in September, following increases of 7 percent in August and 2.2 percent in July.
specificity.explanation: Three figures, three named months, a named series and a named statistical agency. Directly checkable against the release.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There’s a real contradiction for the Labour Party here: they want the State to do more, they want more Government agencies to do more stuff—to invest in video games, to start sovereign wealth funds—and yet they don’t want to pay the people directing these proposed entities, or even the current ones, even nearly as much as directors get in the private sector.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point here (governance pay relative to the private sector, and the cost of agencies), but the weight of the sentence is a characterisation of what the other party wants.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, the Opposition know this because, when they were in Government, they said there should be zero tax on vapes, because they too subscribed to the principle—although the problem is that they don’t know it, because they wouldn’t know a principle if they tripped over one.
focus.explanation: Opens with a real policy precedent (the previous Government's treatment of vape excise) and closes on a content-free sneer about the other party's capacities. A policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is why they’re over there, and we adults are over here.
focus.explanation: Pure tribalism. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — the entire content is a contrast between the two sides of the House. Note that no individual is insulted, so this passes Civility; Focus is what catches it.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Dairy, meat, fruit, and wood together make up over half of New Zealand’s goods exports, and these figures are something to celebrate even though Willow-Jean Prime seems to disagree.
civility.explanation: Pointed aside implying a named member is against celebrating good export figures. It edges toward characterising her position unfairly but stops short of a personal attack, and the rest of the sentence is squarely on the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does she stand by her statement, “We have so many brilliant teachers, and when we back them we get results”, and, if so, does she think backing teachers means pitting them and unions against whānau and students?
civility.explanation: Robust and pointed: it puts the Minister's own words against a characterisation of her approach as deliberately divisive. That edges toward imputing motive, but it is framed as a question about the policy approach rather than an attack on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I would welcome that member joining Project Phoenix to help the efforts that we're doing on the ground on behalf of our community to support those who are in that very challenging position of either having lost or perhaps losing their jobs in the coming weeks.
civility.explanation: A courteously-worded invitation that carries an implication the questioner is scoring points rather than helping. Pointed, edging toward the member, but it never lands as an insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is it the case that she is now closer to adding 50,000 job seekers than she is to removing 50,000 job seekers, and, if so, will she resign if the target is not met?
civility.explanation: Robust — a resignation demand — but aimed at the Minister's performance against her own stated target, not at her as a person. Sharp without imputing bad faith.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Meat exports were up 18 percent, fruit up 33 percent, and wood up 8 percent.
specificity.explanation: Three named export categories with percentage changes over a stated period; directly checkable against the trade statistics release.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Since coming into Government, we have concluded a trade agreement with the Gulf Cooperation Council; concluded, signed, and entered into force a trade agreement with the United Arab Emirates; expedited early entry into force of the agreement with the European Union; launched formal negotiations with India; and we are pursuing new opportunities across South-east Asia.
specificity.explanation: Five named counterparties with the stage each agreement has reached; someone could check every item against the public treaty record. Loses a little for the closing 'pursuing new opportunities across South-east Asia', which names nothing.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: New Zealand makes things the world wants to buy, and the Government will keep backing hard-working Kiwi exporters.
specificity.explanation: A closing slogan: no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named policy. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is it backing teachers to have 55 percent—well over the OECD average of 33 percent—reporting that their stress is due to keeping up with curriculum or programme changes, especially when schools are already unable to properly staff existing subjects?
specificity.explanation: Carries a figure, a named comparator (the OECD average) and an identified cause of the reported stress. A precise question, checkable against the underlying survey.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The three-quarters of a billion dollars of learning support that they so desperately have been asking for.
specificity.explanation: A named funding stream with a dollar figure attached, though no timeframe or breakdown of what the money buys.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It's a very successful programme, well loved by communities across the country, and I'm advised that $3.5 million over the next couple of years will enable between 40 and 60 more schools to roll out bike tracks and bikes.
specificity.explanation: A dollar figure, a rough timeframe and a numeric range of schools. Loses a little for the vague 'next couple of years' and the unquantified 'well loved'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How many more job seekers are there now compared to when she came into office in November 2023?
specificity.explanation: A precise, answerable question with a defined measure and a defined baseline date. A precise question carries as much checkable content as a precise answer; it carries no figure of its own, which is what keeps it off the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How many of the 249 people who have lost their jobs recently in Tokoroa are now on jobseeker?
specificity.explanation: A concrete figure, a named location and a defined benefit category; the answer would be a single checkable number.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Meat exports were up 18 percent, fruit up 33 percent, and wood up 8 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts year-to-September 2025 growth rates for meat (18%), fruit (33%) and wood (8%) goods exports versus the same period a year earlier.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Overseas Merchandise Trade, annual figures for the year to September 2025 against the year to September 2024; true if each commodity group's export value growth matches the stated percentage within rounding, false if any is materially different.

veracity.statement: Stats NZ notes that a stand-out performer is kiwifruit, now a $4.5 billion a year industry, up from $2.6 billion just two years ago.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that kiwifruit export value is $4.5 billion a year as at the year to September 2025, up from $2.6 billion two years earlier, and attributes the observation to Stats NZ.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ overseas merchandise trade series for kiwifruit exports, year to September 2025 and year to September 2023; true if the values are approximately $4.5b and $2.6b respectively, false if either differs materially.

veracity.statement: In the year to September, goods exports to China increased 15 percent, those to Australia increased 10 percent compared to same period a year ago, and despite higher tariffs New Zealand’s goods exports to the United States continue to grow.
veracity.explanation: Asserts year-to-September 2025 goods export growth of 15% to China and 10% to Australia, and continued growth to the United States notwithstanding tariff increases.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Overseas Merchandise Trade by country of destination, year to September 2025 versus year to September 2024; true if China ≈+15%, Australia ≈+10% and the US figure is positive, false if any of the three is materially different or negative.

veracity.statement: This week’s data shows an annual trade deficit of only $2 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the annual goods trade deficit reported in the release of the week of 23 October 2025 was approximately $2 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Overseas Merchandise Trade release for September 2025, annual goods balance; true if the annual deficit is approximately $2 billion, false if materially larger or smaller.

veracity.statement: Why is she condemning basic requests for decent pay and working conditions when we lose 50 percent of high school teachers in the first five years?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 50 percent of secondary school teachers in New Zealand leave the profession within their first five years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education / Education Counts teacher attrition statistics, or a published PPTA or academic study of secondary teacher retention; true if roughly half of entrants have left teaching within five years, false if the five-year attrition rate is materially below that.

veracity.statement: Is it backing teachers to have 55 percent—well over the OECD average of 33 percent—reporting that their stress is due to keeping up with curriculum or programme changes, especially when schools are already unable to properly staff existing subjects?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 55 percent of New Zealand teachers report stress from keeping up with curriculum or programme changes, against an OECD average of 33 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD TALIS teacher survey results for New Zealand on the source-of-stress item covering changing curriculum/programme requirements; true if the New Zealand figure is approximately 55% and the OECD average approximately 33%, false if either differs materially.

veracity.statement: The three-quarters of a billion dollars of learning support that they so desperately have been asking for.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government has delivered approximately $750 million of learning support funding.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 and Budget 2025 learning support appropriations and the Minister's own announcements; true if the committed learning support package totals approximately $750 million, false if the figure is materially lower (e.g. the $646m Budget 2025 package with no further funding to make up the difference).

veracity.statement: But what I would say to the unions is the fact that they told principals and teachers to boycott the very thing that was going to provide them the supports that they needed to implement the curriculum is a real shame.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a teacher union or unions instructed principals and teachers to boycott the Ministry's curriculum roadshow events held in October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published PPTA/NZEI member communications or media reporting from October 2025; true if a union formally directed or advised members not to attend the curriculum roadshows, false if no such direction was issued.

veracity.statement: Despite global headwinds, more New Zealanders are moving off benefits and into jobs—over 20,000 last quarter alone.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than 20,000 people exited a main benefit into work in the quarter preceding October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD Benefit Fact Sheets / quarterly benefit statistics, work exits for the September 2025 quarter; true if work exits exceeded 20,000, false if materially fewer.

veracity.statement: But the good news is actually the unemployment rate has not gone up as high as the Treasury forecast when those guys left office.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the actual unemployment rate has stayed below the peak forecast by Treasury in its last set of forecasts prepared under the previous Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury PREFU/HYEFU 2023 forecast peak unemployment rate compared with the actual peak in the Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey to September 2025; true if the actual peak is below the forecast peak, false if it reached or exceeded it.

veracity.statement: We've seen it at 5.2 percent. It's higher than we would like, but it is the 30-year average.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the current unemployment rate is 5.2 percent and that this equals New Zealand's 30-year average unemployment rate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate for the most recent quarter as at October 2025, and the mean of the HLFS series over 1995-2025; true if the current rate is 5.2% and the 30-year mean is approximately 5.2%, false if either differs materially.

rigor.statement: That is a powerful example of innovation, productivity, and global demand delivering real value for New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: The premise offered is a rise in export revenue; the conclusion attributes it to innovation and productivity specifically. Revenue growth is consistent with price rises, volume, or exchange rates, so the inference to productivity and innovation is a gap between what was shown and what was concluded. Global demand is the one element the figure does support.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If they were at the bargaining table, like the Primary Principals’ Collective Bargaining Union, there would be a good outcome, but they’re not.
rigor.explanation: A counterfactual conclusion — that a good outcome would follow — rested entirely on an analogy with a single other bargaining unit. Nothing is offered to show the two negotiations are alike in the respects that matter, so this is a weak argument from analogy.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It is now down to 3.7 percent in the year to June 2025, and further improvement is expected in the September quarter, driven by continuing strong growth in exports.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the current account deficit as a percentage of GDP will narrow further when the September 2025 quarter balance of payments is published, on the back of export growth.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Balance of Payments and International Investment Position, September 2025 quarter release; true if the annual current account deficit is below 3.7% of GDP, false if it is 3.7% or wider.

focus.statement: Why is she condemning basic requests for decent pay and working conditions when we lose 50 percent of high school teachers in the first five years?
focus.explanation: Directed at a named policy problem — secondary teacher pay, conditions and retention — with a specific attrition figure attached. Legitimate scrutiny of the Minister's handling of a live issue, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, it's tempting to make comments around policy wobbles this week, but what I will say is the most important people who will benefit from the Bikes in Schools programme are our young kids who will learn how to ride a bike safely.
focus.explanation: Opens with a party-directed swipe about another party's 'policy wobbles', then explicitly sets it aside and answers on the named programme and who it benefits. Mostly on-policy, with the party framing left hanging on the front.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How many of the 249 people who have lost their jobs recently in Tokoroa are now on jobseeker?
focus.explanation: Names a specific number, a specific place and a specific policy measure, and asks the Minister to account for the effect of her portfolio on them. This is exactly the accountability an opposition MP is for.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What does she say to the South Waikato Mayor Gary Petley, who said the Government “doesn't give a toss” about regional New Zealand and, “All that Government [crap] they spin—it's all a smokescreen.”?
focus.explanation: Sits in a run of questions about the Tokoroa job losses, so there is a real policy context behind it, but the question itself carries no policy content — it relays a general charge about the Government's attitude and asks for a reaction to it. The weight is on characterising the Government rather than on any measure, figure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That was from a conversation that I’ve had with teachers and principals who have come out in the media with a different perspective on things and who have had enormous pressure put on them by the union. I would also say that that was backed up by a text message from a principal that I received after I made that comment, saying that my comments were so true—and the word “so” had about five “o”s on it.
rigor.explanation: A general claim that the sector is being silenced by union pressure is supported only by private, unnamed conversations and a single text message, with the number of letters in one word offered as corroboration — an appeal to anecdote, and the evidence offered cannot establish the general conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’m advised that patient safety measures, such as in-hospital deaths, surgical site infections, and in-hospital falls have been stable or improved over the last five years. Another indicator is hospital capacity. While bed numbers have increased by 175 over the past three years, the number of nurses employed has grown by more than 3,000 during that same time period, strengthening the level of care available to patients.
rigor.explanation: Genuine evidence is offered, but the inference is an aggregation gap: national headcount growth and system-wide outcome averages do not establish that staffing is safe on any particular ward, which is the question asked. The conclusion is broader than the premises support.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We inherited long waiting times, and unions which strike continue to extend those waiting times for patients.
rigor.explanation: Asked whether nurses raising safety concerns are wrong, the reasoning substitutes a different risk (waiting times) attested by cited officials — an appeal to authority plus an ignoratio elenchi: that waiting times are also a safety risk does not bear on whether ward staffing is unsafe.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Our mental health plan is working, with over 80 percent of people seen within three weeks for specialist services and the front-line mental health workforce growing around 10 percent since coming into office.
rigor.explanation: Two favourable metrics are offered as proof the plan is working, with no counterfactual or baseline trend — the attribution from metric to policy is asserted rather than shown, though the metrics are at least relevant to the claim.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Let me summarise my answer, which is this: under the last 21 months of the Government of which that member was in Cabinet, annual net departures of New Zealand citizens increased by 38,000. In the 21 months since this Government has been in office, that number was 5,800, so our record stacks up better than yours on that and many, many other things, including the fact we include numbers in our policies.
rigor.explanation: The comparison is of the *change* in annual net departures across two chosen 21-month windows, and the earlier window starts from a COVID-era base artificially suppressed by closed borders — so a large increase there and a small one now is largely an artefact of the baseline. The conclusion that the record "stacks up better" does not follow from the metric selected.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will she apologise to the education sector for promising pay rises when she was in Opposition and failing to deliver them now that she’s the Minister?
focus.explanation: Names a specific commitment (pay rises promised in Opposition) and a specific outcome (not delivered in government) — legitimate scrutiny of a named policy position, not content-free party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why is her Government handing Crown board directors pay rises of up to 80 percent while teachers and nurses are struggling to cope with the cost of living crisis?
focus.explanation: Names a specific government decision and a specific figure and holds the Government to account for it — scrutiny of a policy, not generalised party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, I find this an interesting question, because I understand that the member’s party is quite enamoured by Temasek, which, of course, is an interesting model for running Crown assets. Temasek is distinguished by a couple of things, members: one of them is that it often sells assets and purchases others, and another factor is that it pays its directors well because it wants the companies to be run well.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point (paying board directors more to get better-run Crown entities) is reached, but the answer to a question about director pay opens by characterising the questioner's party's enthusiasms — a real policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Unfortunately, one of the unions hasn’t even bothered to put the offer to its members before striking. If the unions were at the table in good faith, they would find that we are there, ready to negotiate.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that one of the education unions called a strike without first putting the Government's pay offer to its members.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Union (NZEI Te Riu Roa / PPTA) and Ministry of Education statements and contemporaneous media reporting on whether the union's members were balloted on, or had the Government's offer put to them before, the October 2025 strike; true if no offer was put to members before the strike was called, false if a member vote or offer consultation preceded it.

veracity.statement: Since coming into office, this Government has added around 2,000 more nurses to the public health system compared to 2023, alongside hundreds of additional doctors. That’s backed by a record additional $16.68 billion of investment in health over three Budgets.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a net increase of roughly 2,000 nurses and hundreds of doctors in the public health system since 2023, and $16.68 billion of additional health funding across three Budgets.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand employed-workforce headcount/FTE data for nurses and doctors, 2023 baseline versus the latest 2025 reporting, and Budget 2024–2026 health Vote appropriations; true if the nursing increase is around 2,000 and the cumulative additional health operating funding is around $16.68 billion, false if either is materially different.

veracity.statement: Our mental health plan is working, with over 80 percent of people seen within three weeks for specialist services and the front-line mental health workforce growing around 10 percent since coming into office.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that over 80 percent of people are seen within three weeks for specialist mental health services and that the front-line mental health workforce has grown by about 10 percent since November 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand mental health and addiction access/wait-time reporting (proportion seen within three weeks for specialist services) and mental health workforce headcount at November 2023 versus the latest 2025 figure; true if both are approximately as stated, false if either is materially lower.

veracity.statement: Of course, at that time, inflation was running at 5.6 percent. It’s now been back in band for more than five quarters. Food price inflation was running at 8.8 percent; it is now down to 4.6 percent. And the official cash rate had been rapidly rising, reaching a peak of 5.5 percent; it is now down to 2.5 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts CPI inflation of 5.6 percent in 2023 and within the 1–3 percent target band for more than five quarters since; food price inflation down from 8.8 percent to 4.6 percent; and the OCR down from a 5.5 percent peak to 2.5 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation series (2023 print and each quarter since), Stats NZ food price index annual change for the latest month, and the RBNZ official cash rate history; true if each figure matches the published series within rounding, false if any is materially different — including whether inflation has in fact been inside the band for five consecutive quarters.

veracity.statement: How can the estimated 100,000 Kiwis who have walked off the job today get ahead when they are overworked and undervalued by her Government?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an estimated 100,000 workers took strike action on 23 October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Union (NZNO, PPTA, NZEI, PSA) and media participation estimates for the 23 October 2025 public sector strike; true if credible estimates are around 100,000 participants, false if materially fewer.

veracity.statement: Why is her Government handing Crown board directors pay rises of up to 80 percent while teachers and nurses are struggling to cope with the cost of living crisis?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government has increased Crown entity board director fees by up to 80 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Cabinet Fees Framework and Public Service Commission determinations for Crown entity board member fees for 2024–2025 versus the previous framework; true if the maximum fee for any board category rose by around 80 percent, false if the largest increase is materially smaller.

veracity.statement: Is she surprised that 200 New Zealanders leave our shores each day—each day—when her Government refuses to pay hard-working front-line workers what they’re worth?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a current rate of about 200 New Zealanders departing the country each day, i.e. roughly 73,000 a year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration estimates for departures (and net departures) of New Zealand citizens over the most recent 12 months to October 2025; true if the figure implies about 200 a day, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: Let me summarise my answer, which is this: under the last 21 months of the Government of which that member was in Cabinet, annual net departures of New Zealand citizens increased by 38,000. In the 21 months since this Government has been in office, that number was 5,800, so our record stacks up better than yours on that and many, many other things, including the fact we include numbers in our policies.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that annual net departures of New Zealand citizens rose by 38,000 over the previous Government's final 21 months and by 5,800 over this Government's first 21 months.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration estimates for net migration of New Zealand citizens: the change in the annual figure over February 2022–October 2023 versus November 2023–August 2025; true if the two changes are approximately 38,000 and 5,800, false if materially different.

civility.statement: Unfortunately, one of the unions hasn’t even bothered to put the offer to its members before striking. If the unions were at the table in good faith, they would find that we are there, ready to negotiate.
civility.explanation: "Hasn’t even bothered" and the implication that the unions are not at the table "in good faith" impute idleness and bad faith rather than engaging their case — short of civil, though aimed at organisations rather than a named individual.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, our Government values greatly the work by nurses, teachers, firefighters, and others on the public payroll, and what we would say to them is that they would be able to get a pay rise much more rapidly if their union went back to the bargaining table instead of playing politics.
civility.explanation: "Playing politics" imputes bad faith motive to the unions instead of engaging their pay case — a real civility failure, though directed at organisations rather than a named individual, so it stops short of a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Since coming into office, this Government has added around 2,000 more nurses to the public health system compared to 2023, alongside hundreds of additional doctors. That’s backed by a record additional $16.68 billion of investment in health over three Budgets.
specificity.explanation: Two precise, checkable figures with a stated baseline year and a stated funding period — someone could go and verify both.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is it correct that the Care Capacity Demand Management (CCDM) system data, the tool to measure actual patient need presenting in our hospitals, shows that nurses are facing unsafe working conditions?
specificity.explanation: Names the particular measurement system and what it measures, so the question points at an identifiable dataset that could be checked — precise despite being a question rather than an announcement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Of course, at that time, inflation was running at 5.6 percent. It’s now been back in band for more than five quarters. Food price inflation was running at 8.8 percent; it is now down to 4.6 percent. And the official cash rate had been rapidly rising, reaching a peak of 5.5 percent; it is now down to 2.5 percent.
specificity.explanation: Four precise then-and-now figures against named indicators, each with an identifiable published source.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, I would just say that I've been working incredibly productively, not just with the mayor and the council but also the local union who values the work that I'm doing on the ground in the community.
specificity.explanation: Asked about redundancies at Kinleith, the answer conveys only that work is happening 'incredibly productively' — no programme, no figure, no timeframe, nothing anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We've seen a 60 percent increase in the proactive engagements that MSD is having on the ground, 83,000 people left benefits into jobs in the last year, despite it being challenging, so we are not shying away from the challenge.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete, checkable figures attached to a named agency and a stated period: a 60 percent rise in proactive engagements and 83,000 benefit exits into work in the last year.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There has been a 14 percent reduction in findings of harm since 2024.
specificity.explanation: A precise figure with a stated baseline year, drawn from a named report — directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Thirteen percent of children in return- or remain-home placements had a finding of harm.
specificity.explanation: A single precise rate attached to a defined placement category; checkable against the source report.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I acknowledge that the latest Safety of Children in Care report shows that, in the 12 months to 31 March 2025, there was an increase of 23 children and young people who had a finding of harm compared to the previous year.
specificity.explanation: Named report, exact reporting period, exact count of the year-on-year increase.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Earlier this week, I announced Government support of $34 million for the Bisset Road development in Kaikohe, within contractual arrangements, led by Ngāpuhi.
specificity.explanation: Named site, named delivery partner, exact sum and a stated timing for the announcement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Civil works are expected to start in November 2025, with the full development of a hundred homes to be expected to be completed by mid-2027.
specificity.explanation: A start month, a completion window and a unit count — the schedule is stated precisely enough to be held to.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Since December 2023, $426 million has been approved in three tranches for Māori-led delivery of around a thousand homes.
specificity.explanation: A total, a structure (three tranches), a start date and an output count.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We've seen a 60 percent increase in the proactive engagements that MSD is having on the ground, 83,000 people left benefits into jobs in the last year, despite it being challenging, so we are not shying away from the challenge.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (a) MSD proactive client engagements rose ~60 percent, and (b) 83,000 people moved off a benefit into work in the last year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD administrative data: the count of proactive client engagements for the year cited against the prior year (true if the increase is approximately 60 percent), and MSD's published 'exits from benefit into work' figure for the year cited (true if approximately 83,000, false if materially lower or if it counts all benefit cancellations rather than exits into work).

veracity.statement: There has been a 14 percent reduction in findings of harm since 2024.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that findings of harm within secure residential placements fell by 14 percent relative to 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki Safety of Children in Care report for the 12 months to 31 March 2025: the count of findings of harm in secure residences against the prior year's count. True if the fall is approximately 14 percent; false if the fall is materially different, or if the figure applies to a different population than secure residences.

veracity.statement: Thirteen percent of children in return- or remain-home placements had a finding of harm.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 13 percent of children in return- or remain-home placements had a finding of harm in the reporting period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki Safety of Children in Care report for the 12 months to 31 March 2025: the proportion of children in return- or remain-home placements with a recorded finding of harm. True if 13 percent within rounding; false if materially different.

veracity.statement: I acknowledge that the latest Safety of Children in Care report shows that, in the 12 months to 31 March 2025, there was an increase of 23 children and young people who had a finding of harm compared to the previous year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the number of children and young people in care with a finding of harm rose by 23 in the year to 31 March 2025 compared with the previous year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki Safety of Children in Care report, year to 31 March 2025: total children and young people with a finding of harm, against the same figure for the prior year. True if the difference is +23; false if the difference is materially different or in the opposite direction.

veracity.statement: Earlier this week, I announced Government support of $34 million for the Bisset Road development in Kaikohe, within contractual arrangements, led by Ngāpuhi.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a Government commitment of $34 million to the Ngāpuhi-led Bisset Road development in Kaikohe, announced in the week of 20 October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Associate Minister of Housing's announcement of 20–24 October 2025 and Ministry of Housing and Urban Development funding records for the Bisset Road, Kaikohe development. True if the committed Crown sum is $34 million; false if the figure differs materially or the support is conditional in a way not disclosed.

veracity.statement: Since December 2023, $426 million has been approved in three tranches for Māori-led delivery of around a thousand homes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts $426 million approved across three tranches since December 2023 for Māori-led housing delivery of roughly 1,000 homes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Housing and Urban Development / Te Puni Kōkiri Māori housing funding decisions from December 2023 onward. True if approvals total approximately $426 million across three tranches and the associated dwelling target is about 1,000; false if the total, the tranche count or the home count differs materially.

veracity.statement: Does she stand by her statement that Sir Brian Roche "is trying desperately to negotiate in good faith" when he's in charge of a Public Service Commission that ran anti-strike attack ads?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Public Service Commission, under Sir Brian Roche, ran advertising against the education strike. The contested element is the factual one — that the PSC placed such a campaign; 'attack ads' is the questioner's characterisation of it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public Service Commission advertising expenditure records and contemporaneous media reporting for October 2025. True if the PSC placed paid public advertising concerning the education strike or the bargaining; false if no such campaign was placed by the PSC (for example if the advertising was placed by another agency, or was purely procedural notice unrelated to the strike).

rigor.statement: We've seen a 60 percent increase in the proactive engagements that MSD is having on the ground, 83,000 people left benefits into jobs in the last year, despite it being challenging, so we are not shying away from the challenge.
rigor.explanation: The question was about a specific regional labour market where a mill and a plywood plant have both closed; national aggregates do not support the conclusion that the challenge there is being met. A real inference about a real policy, but with a gap between the evidence offered (nationwide totals) and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The introduction of standard operating practices, improved recruitment, training and programming, and a refreshed induction process—among many other things—is resulting in improved safety and wellbeing for those in secure residential care.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: a list of interventions is asserted to be the cause of a measured improvement, with nothing offered to connect any of them to the change, and 'among many other things' concedes the causes were not isolated.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would make the point, again, that their membership grows by the day because principals can see that their own unions are not acting in good faith, and they want to settle.
rigor.explanation: Circular: the disputed claim (that the other unions are not bargaining in good faith) is offered as the established cause of a membership shift, and the membership shift is then offered as evidence that principals see it. No independent evidence of either the growth or the motive is supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Those comments that I made this morning about unions who were bullying were in relation to conversations that I have had with teachers and principals who have spoken out in the media with a different view, and who have then had enormous pressure put on them by the union.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote: a general charge of bullying rests entirely on private conversations reported by the speaker, with no way for anyone else to weigh the evidence, and no account of how representative those cases are.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Civil works are expected to start in November 2025, with the full development of a hundred homes to be expected to be completed by mid-2027.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that civil works on the Bisset Road development begin in November 2025 and that all 100 homes are finished by the middle of 2027.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Far North District Council building consent and code-compliance certificate records for the Bisset Road, Kaikohe development, plus Ngāpuhi/MHUD project reporting. True if civil works commenced in November 2025 and all 100 homes were completed by 30 June 2027; false if completion slips past that date or fewer than 100 homes are delivered.

civility.statement: There are hundreds and hundreds of educators up and down the country who are coming to the Curriculum Roadshow and there are hundreds more watching online, and I would advise that member that she would have more friends if she answered her text messages.
civility.explanation: The closing clause leaves the substance entirely and turns on the questioner personally — a jibe about her being unpopular and unresponsive, aimed at the member rather than her argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does she stand by her statement that she has "hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of friends," and is that more than the 40,000 educators who are striking?
civility.explanation: Mockery aimed at the Minister personally — her claim about having friends is quoted back to belittle her rather than to test anything she has done. Short of a direct insult, but sneering.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does she stand by her statement that she has "hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of friends," and is that more than the 40,000 educators who are striking?
focus.explanation: A pay-and-conditions dispute involving 40,000 educators is the live policy question, and the figure appears here only as a peg for a personal gotcha. No policy, measure or outcome is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does she stand by her statement that Sir Brian Roche "is trying desperately to negotiate in good faith" when he's in charge of a Public Service Commission that ran anti-strike attack ads?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: names a specific official, a specific institution and a specific action (the advertising campaign) and tests it against the Minister's own characterisation of the bargaining. Accountability, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Parliamentary Service Act 2000 makes it clear that the Deputy Speaker can have the functions and powers of the Speaker, but it’s unclear in the Clerk of the House of Representatives Act 1988.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific contrast between the content of two named statutes: that the Parliamentary Service Act 2000 expressly allows the Deputy Speaker to exercise the Speaker's functions and powers, while the Clerk of the House of Representatives Act 1988 does not make this clear.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the current text of the Parliamentary Service Act 2000 and the Clerk of the House of Representatives Act 1988 on legislation.govt.nz. True if the 2000 Act contains an express provision conferring the Speaker's functions/powers on the Deputy Speaker and the 1988 Act contains no equivalent express provision; false if the 1988 Act contains such a provision, or if the 2000 Act does not.

veracity.statement: The ship has sailed, somewhat, to be honest, because the committee has reported the bill back unanimously, and, as I understand it, there’s no Amendment Paper from the member in relation to that—but I’m happy to look at it in the future.
veracity.explanation: Two checkable factual premises: that the select committee reported the bill back unanimously, and that the member has lodged no Amendment Paper on this point.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee report on the bill as presented to the House: true if the committee recommended the bill be passed with no differing or minority view recorded by any party; false if any party recorded opposition. Separately, the Order Paper / Amendment Papers lodged for the committee of the whole House on this bill: true if none stands in Ingrid Leary's name on clause 55, false if one does.

rigor.statement: Section 3 of the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act makes the legislature, the executive, and the judicial branches of Government subject to the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act, which means that powers in relation to Parliament have to be exercised in accordance with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act, and so that is an important check as well.
rigor.explanation: A valid inference: from the premise that s 3 binds the legislative branch, it follows that powers exercised in relation to Parliament must comply with the Act, and therefore that this operates as a constraint on the Speaker. No fallacy or gap — the conclusion is exactly what the premise supports.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The ship has sailed, somewhat, to be honest, because the committee has reported the bill back unanimously, and, as I understand it, there’s no Amendment Paper from the member in relation to that—but I’m happy to look at it in the future.
rigor.explanation: Reasons offered (unanimous report-back, no Amendment Paper lodged) genuinely support the procedural conclusion that a change cannot easily be made now, but they are deployed in answer to a question about whether the drafting is unclear, which they do not address — a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And so it’s really important that we recognise that the parliamentary security will be operating in a very professional way under clear rules, and, in fact, the regime for reporting such incidents, and carrying that out, is at arm’s length from the Speaker of the House.
rigor.explanation: The premise (reporting runs to the CEO of Parliamentary Service, not the Speaker) does support the arm's-length conclusion. But the further conclusion that security 'will be operating in a very professional way' is asserted rather than derived — a reporting structure is not evidence of professional conduct, so part of the conclusion outruns the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So, happy to have a look at it in the future, but I’m not convinced at the moment that there’s actually a problem worth solving.
civility.explanation: Declines a colleague's request squarely on the merits of the drafting question. Mildly dismissive of the concern itself, but imputes nothing to the member — no bad faith, no sneering, no attack on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: For example, is it the Minister’s view that the Speaker has authority and powers under this legislation to direct and control members of various workforces, such as security guards, the parliamentary colleagues or staff working with MPs, and the press gallery?
focus.explanation: Engages a named clause of the bill before the committee and the concrete scope of the power it confers, naming the specific workforces at issue. Entirely about the measure, with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So we’ve got this changed provision in clause 61, and there is a test in it and it talks about a disability that means they require ongoing daily care, and then there are a number of things that need to be fulfilled under paragraph (a)—with the member presumably being the one who provides the care—and paragraph (b) about financial dependence and the fact they’re not living with another person in a de facto relationship.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the paragraphs, and the individual limbs of the statutory test (ongoing daily care, care provided by the member, financial dependence, not in a de facto relationship). Concrete enough that anyone could check it against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What we need to remember is that under the new set of rules and under this new legislation, which we’ll talk about in Part 7, there’s a clear monitoring role and reporting role and the direct reporting is with the CEO of Parliamentary Service.
specificity.explanation: Names the Part of the bill and the specific office the reporting line runs to, but describes the monitoring and reporting roles only in general terms — a mechanism identified without its detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Why I say that is because several submitters made submissions on the Official Information Act to bring Parliament’s information under that as well. Those were deemed, by the committee, to be out of scope of this bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that submitters on the Parliament Bill sought to bring parliamentary information under the Official Information Act, and that the select committee ruled those submissions out of scope.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The special select committee's report on the Parliament Bill and the published submissions: true if one or more submissions proposed extending the Official Information Act to Parliament and the committee recorded them as outside the bill's scope; false if no such submissions exist or the committee addressed them on the merits.

veracity.statement: It’s worth noting that this power has never been exercised in New Zealand by the House of Representatives, so the committee has just voted to make it clear that imprisonment is not a punishment for contempt.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the New Zealand House of Representatives has never imprisoned anyone for contempt of Parliament.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary Practice in New Zealand (McGee) and the historical record of Privileges Committee punishments and House resolutions since 1854: true if no instance of the House committing a person to custody for contempt is recorded, false if any such committal is recorded.

veracity.statement: I’m advised that, in section 8 of the Parliamentary Privilege Act 2014, which will now become part of the Parliament Bill, the House has the powers exercisable by the UK House of Commons as at 1 January 1865.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of section 8 of the Parliamentary Privilege Act 2014 — that it confers on the House the powers of the UK House of Commons as at 1 January 1865.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of section 8 of the Parliamentary Privilege Act 2014 on legislation.govt.nz: true if it fixes the House's powers, privileges and immunities by reference to those of the UK House of Commons as at 1 January 1865, false if the section says something materially different or names a different reference date.

veracity.statement: So the Parliamentary Privilege Act was a response to court judgments and now it’s going to be a part of the Parliament Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Parliamentary Privilege Act 2014 was enacted in response to court judgments (he earlier names Attorney-General v Leigh).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliamentary Privilege Bill's explanatory note and the Privileges Committee report that preceded it: true if they state the legislation was a response to Attorney-General v Leigh and related judgments, false if the Act's stated origin is unrelated to court decisions.

specificity.statement: It brings together the Clerk of the House of Representatives Act 1988, the Parliamentary Service Act 2000, the Members of Parliament (Remuneration and Services) Act 2013, and the Parliamentary Privilege Act 2014.
specificity.explanation: Names four statutes with their years — the exact scope of the consolidation, checkable against the bill's repeal schedule. No hedging or generality.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So what this bill does is put in place a more independent process in which the House is in charge of its own budgets, there is some involvement of the executive but it’s a step forward from the status quo where I think most people would say it’s more biased towards the Government.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the mechanism in direction — the House controls its own budget with some executive involvement — but gives no figures, no description of what that involvement actually is, and no timeframe. A direction with the how left out.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We don’t want to labour the committee stage, but we do want to be seen to actually prosecute and to ask some questions to give confidence to the public so that they understand what this bill is about—and it’s not just for us as MPs finding a way, I guess, to feather our nest or to make it easy for us, but it’s to help make the system better.
specificity.explanation: Offers a rationale for questioning but no content: nothing named, no clause, no figure, no mechanism. 'Help make the system better' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m just wanting to seek clarification from the Minister that whenever we talk about adding land to the parliamentary precinct, this, obviously, will be in a way that fits in with current laws and isn’t about acquiring land, but is around doing right by modern laws.
specificity.explanation: Names the actual mechanism at issue (adding land to the precinct) and draws a distinction between adding and acquiring, but the standard he asks about — 'fits in with current laws', 'doing right by modern laws' — names no statute and no test, so the question is only half-formed.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It hasn’t really been a problem in practice, but there’s always the potential. Law is sometimes not about necessarily solving the problems of today; it’s about futureproofing to make sure we don’t endure problems in the future.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure before the committee: he concedes the counter-evidence (no observed problem with the current funding model) and supplies a stated principle — legislating against future risk — that supports the conclusion anyway. No fallacy; the gap is that the magnitude of the future risk is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I just want to recognise that in Part 3, the Speaker of the House will have the ability to delegate certain functions to the Deputy Speaker, which I think is wholly appropriate, in the same way that a Minister who also has responsibilities under the Public Finance Act, say, might delegate something to an Associate Minister or an under-secretary.
rigor.explanation: An argument by analogy: delegation by the Speaker to the Deputy is appropriate because Ministers already delegate statutory functions to Associates. The analogy is apt but carried alone — no reason is given why the parallel holds where the Speaker's role differs from a Minister's, so the conclusion rests on the comparison being accepted.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: This, if it becomes law and the House approves it, will become the Parliament Act 2025 and it will be the one place.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the bill will be enacted and will carry the short title 'Parliament Act 2025' — an outcome that depends on the House and on the timing of royal assent, not on the speaker alone.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The short title of the Act as enacted, on legislation.govt.nz: true if it is enacted as the Parliament Act 2025, false if it is enacted under a different year in its title or is not enacted at all.

focus.statement: I’m just wanting to seek clarification from the Minister that whenever we talk about adding land to the parliamentary precinct, this, obviously, will be in a way that fits in with current laws and isn’t about acquiring land, but is around doing right by modern laws.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee — the clause allowing land to be added to the parliamentary precinct, and what constraints govern how that land is obtained. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill gives parliamentary security officers statutory powers of consent, search, denial of entry, temporary seizure of specified items, and temporary detention.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates the exact statutory powers the bill confers — consent, search, denial of entry, temporary seizure, temporary detention — so the claim can be checked directly against the clauses. He could have said 'the bill modernises security powers' and did not.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So my question to the Minister is just to clarify that when we’re actually talking specifically—again, Subpart 1—about the actual definition of a security officer, that they are specifically employed by Parliamentary Services. Or does that go beyond it to contracted Armourguard-type of services?
specificity.explanation: Pins the question to a named part of the bill (Subpart 1), a defined term ('security officer'), a named employer (Parliamentary Services) and a named class of contractor (Armourguard). A precise question, answerable yes or no against the text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m looking at the bold part of clause 172A to about 175, and I think that’s to do with a definition of a “detected item”.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause range (172A–175) and the defined term at issue, which makes the query locatable, but the boundary is hedged ('to about 175') and no particular provision or effect is identified.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s quite interesting: security officers here currently lack those statutory powers and immunities. They rely on the common law and the rights of an occupier under the Trespass Act 1980.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that, prior to this bill, NZ parliamentary security officers had no statutory powers or immunities and operated only on common law and occupier's rights under the Trespass Act 1980.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ statute law in force before the Parliament Bill, plus the bill's departmental disclosure statement / regulatory impact statement and the review of parliamentary security. True if no enactment conferred search, seizure, detention or immunity powers on parliamentary security officers and their authority rested on common law and the Trespass Act 1980 occupier provisions; false if any such statutory power or immunity already existed.

veracity.statement: The review recommended that our parliamentary security officers be provided with legislative powers of detention as soon as practicable.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the review of parliamentary security contains a recommendation that parliamentary security officers be given statutory powers of detention, with an 'as soon as practicable' urgency.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published review of parliamentary security referred to in the debate. True if the review contains a recommendation to confer legislative powers of detention on parliamentary security officers, with wording to the effect of 'as soon as practicable'; false if it makes no such recommendation or recommends something materially different (e.g. powers other than detention, or no urgency qualifier).

rigor.statement: But part of making sure we never get to that point is making sure there’s appropriate security, so that’s what this section is about.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House — open access is preserved by granting security powers — but the causal link is asserted, not shown. Nothing is offered connecting statutory detention powers to continued public accessibility; the overseas parliaments cited are given as a contrast, not as evidence that security powers caused or preserved openness.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We know, from police experience, that just simply the act of arresting somebody can result in physical injuries for both the arresting officer and the person being arrested. Those things are never as straightforward as you might think they are.
rigor.explanation: Argues by analogy from a closely comparable case — police making arrests — to conclude that new detention powers create health-and-safety risk for parliamentary security officers, and therefore that training and support are needed. The analogy is apt and the conclusion tracks it; the support is experiential rather than data, which leaves a gap between 'can result in injuries' and the scale of risk actually created here.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The answer is that clause 136(1)(b) makes it clear that there can be contractors appointed if the chief executive considers it necessary and desirable, but they have to be qualified and trained to the equivalent standards.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact clause, the decision-maker, the statutory test and the qualification requirement — a listener could go to the bill and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, for example, clause 190B, the “Chief executive must report annually on the exercise of specified powers”—parliamentary security officers must report the exercise of certain powers; powers are not generally applicable if the police is involved.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, quotes its heading, and states the reporting duty and the police carve-out — a concrete, checkable safeguard rather than a general assurance.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My question is, without a clear process of the Speaker using his or her powers through the chief executive or others—the decisions that a security guard believes that they are making on reasonable grounds, which has a legal objectivity element to it—what is the interplay if the Speaker has given a direction that has not gone through a process that involves the chief executive or if there isn’t, kind of, a clear process?
specificity.explanation: Identifies the specific legal test and the specific actors involved, but the question is framed loosely and does not point to a clause or a concrete scenario the Minister could answer against.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In relation to the other point the member makes, parliamentary service officers can exercise powers only in the parliamentary precinct, a place where select committees are meeting, electorate offices where the chief executive has authorised it.
specificity.explanation: Answers the adjacency question with an exhaustive list of the three places the powers reach, and where they stop — concrete enough to act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There was, as the bill was originally drafted, a procedure in there that required that when an object was removed from someone, they had to be detained.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific mechanism in a specific draft of the bill and what it required; checkable against the bill as introduced, though no clause is cited.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have a clear plan and strong, concrete actions already under way to address energy supply risks and to unleash renewables in order to bring down prices, to give households and businesses more control over their power bills, and importantly, to keep our economy growing.
specificity.explanation: Claims a plan and 'concrete actions' while naming none — no measure, figure, mechanism or date. The adjectives carry the whole sentence.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It's slightly convoluted to get there, but, in a way that he's become known for, he's managed to find a tricky section of the tricky clause, and the references for the members notification are clauses 172A(2) and 173(1)(b) and 173(1)(c).
civility.explanation: Characterises an opposition member personally, but as a compliment on his forensic reading of the bill; engages the substance and attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The section is modelled on the Courts Security Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the parliamentary security officer powers in this part of the Parliament Bill were drafted on the model of the existing Courts Security Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliament Bill's explanatory note, regulatory impact statement and departmental report to the select committee; true if those documents state the security-officer powers are based on / modelled on the Courts Security Act 1999, false if they identify a different source or no such model.

veracity.statement: Because of our work to knock down the barriers to growth and investment, more electricity generation has been commissioned in the past 18 months than in the entirety of the last 15 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the volume of electricity generation commissioned in the roughly 18 months to October 2025 exceeds the total commissioned across the preceding 15 years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE Electricity Statistics / Electricity Authority generation commissioning records, measured in MW of new capacity commissioned; true if MW commissioned between roughly April 2024 and October 2025 exceeds MW commissioned between 2009 and 2024, false if the earlier 15-year total is larger.

veracity.statement: That is why this Government has commenced procurement for an importation terminal for liquefied natural gas (LNG).
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at 23 October 2025 the Government had already begun a procurement process for an LNG import terminal, not merely announced an intention to consider one.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE and ministerial records of procurement activity — a published RFP, EOI or equivalent process for LNG import terminal capability dated before 23 October 2025; true if such a process was open or under way, false if only a policy intention or feasibility study existed.

rigor.statement: I can't exactly remember when the Courts Security Act was passed, but no doubt the courts went through a similar exercise to what Parliament's gone through, which is realising that there needed to be a bit more statutory tramlines and, you know, rules around security at courts.
rigor.explanation: The support for the conclusion is an admitted supposition — 'no doubt' stands in for the history he says he cannot remember. Arguing that the precedent justifies this approach while conceding he does not know the precedent is a gap between what is offered and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Again, they’re not conceptual or imaginary because the very vexed questions that led to this legislation, in my view, were probably what we saw on the steps of Parliament and the lines that were crossed.
