focus.statement: Removing fair pay agreements that had the potential to lift salary and wages for some of the lowest-paid New Zealand workers isn’t going to take New Zealand forward.
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure being repealed, identifies who it affects, and states the expected consequence. Entirely on the policy, with no party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They want to abolish the Climate Emergency Response Fund, they want to abolish the Government investment in decarbonising industry, they want to abolish the clean car rebate—all examples of things that will take New Zealand backwards, that will turn back the clock on our effort to combat climate change.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete, checkable instruments — the Climate Emergency Response Fund, the industry decarbonisation investment, the clean car rebate. Loses ground only for carrying no figures, dates or magnitudes for the effect claimed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I want all of our young people in New Zealand to be free to be who they are; to not feel like they have to be someone who they are not when they walk through the school gate.
specificity.explanation: An aspiration with no mechanism, no measure, no timeframe and nothing checkable. Offered in a policy context (schools and gender diverse students) where a programme, funding line or guidance change could have been named, and none is.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: New Zealand First, of course, have also signed up to reintroduce charter schools, something they spent nine years in Opposition being vehemently opposed to.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable things: that the incoming coalition arrangements commit New Zealand First to reinstating charter schools, and that New Zealand First opposed charter schools throughout its nine years in Opposition (2008-2017).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National-NZ First coalition agreement (Nov 2023) and the Speech from the Throne on charter/partnership schools, plus NZ First's votes and public statements on the Education Amendment Act 2013 (partnership schools) and subsequent partnership-school legislation. True if NZ First is party to a commitment to reintroduce charter schools and voted/spoke against them while in Opposition; false if either limb fails (e.g. the commitment sits only in the ACT agreement, or NZ First supported partnership schools).

veracity.statement: We have the highest rate of Kiwis in jobs, with a 69.8 percent employment rate, having created 281,000 new jobs during our time in Government.
veracity.explanation: Claims a record employment rate of 69.8 percent and net creation of 281,000 jobs over the 2017-2023 term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey: the employment rate for the most recent quarter before Dec 2023 and the full series back to 1986. True if that rate is 69.8% (± rounding) and is the series maximum, and if the change in total employed persons between the Sept/Dec 2017 quarter and the Sept 2023 quarter is approximately 281,000; false if the rate is materially different, is not a series high, or the jobs change differs materially.

veracity.statement: We significantly increased health funding, including to Pharmac, and we abolished prescription charges, which resulted in 3 million free prescriptions for New Zealanders, something that I believe stopped New Zealanders ending up in our emergency departments with avoidable illnesses because they weren’t getting the medication that they needed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that removing the $5 co-payment resulted in 3 million free prescriptions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Whatu Ora / Pharmac dispensing data on prescriptions dispensed without a co-payment from 1 July 2023 to early December 2023. True if the count is approximately 3 million over that window; false if materially lower or if the figure counts something other than co-payment-free dispensings.

veracity.statement: When we became the Government in 2017, just 2 percent of the cars coming into the market were electric or hybrid vehicles. As we leave office, that is 37 percent—a huge improvement.
veracity.explanation: Compares the electric-or-hybrid share of vehicles entering the New Zealand fleet in 2017 with the share in 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA / Ministry of Transport light-vehicle registration statistics on the electrified (BEV, PHEV and hybrid) share of new and used-import light vehicle registrations for 2017 and for 2023. True if the shares are approximately 2% and 37% on a consistent basis; false if either figure is materially different or the two are drawn from incomparable bases.

veracity.statement: When we became the Government, less than half our exports were covered by free-trade agreements. Now, nearly three-quarters are.
veracity.explanation: Claims the share of New Zealand's exports covered by free-trade agreements rose from under 50 percent in 2017 to nearly 75 percent by late 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MFAT's published FTA coverage-of-exports figures for 2017 and 2023 (the series used in MFAT trade statements and the NZ-EU FTA impact analysis). True if coverage was below 50% in 2017 and in the 70-75% range in 2023; false if either endpoint is materially different.

veracity.statement: On that last note, I want to say that Pacific New Zealanders are a growing and significant part of the New Zealand economy, a growing and significant part of New Zealand society, and I think it’s telling that the incoming Government didn’t mention them once in the Speech from the Throne today—not one single time. That does not bode well for Pacific New Zealanders in the future.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Speech from the Throne delivered on 6 December 2023 contained no mention of Pacific New Zealanders.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Speech from the Throne read on 6 December 2023 (Hansard, 54th Parliament). True if no reference to Pacific peoples/Pasifika as a New Zealand population appears anywhere in it; false if any such reference appears. References to the Pacific region in a foreign-policy sense do not settle it either way.

focus.statement: New Zealand First, of course, have also signed up to reintroduce charter schools, something they spent nine years in Opposition being vehemently opposed to.
focus.explanation: Names three specific measures (90-day trials, no-cause evictions, charter schools) and a party's recorded position on each, which is accountability rather than tribalism; the weight of the point is nonetheless the opponent's inconsistency rather than the merits of the policies.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There have been record investments in transport, including fixing a record number of potholes over the last year; completing legacy infrastructure projects like Transmission Gully that were left in a heck of a mess by the outgoing National Government.
focus.explanation: Names a specific project (Transmission Gully), a specific delivery measure (pothole repairs) and a specific period; this is scrutiny of a policy record rather than content-free party framing, though the closing clause carries some partisan colouring.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So we leave Government proud of our track record, committed to holding the incoming Government to account, concerned about the direction that they are taking New Zealand in—which is backwards on all of the important measures that should be important to New Zealand’s future—and absolutely resolved that for the first time in New Zealand’s history, this will be a one-term National Government.
focus.explanation: The closing passage is almost entirely about the other side in general terms — 'backwards on all of the important measures' names no measure, no figure and no policy — with the substance replaced by an electoral prediction.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have the highest rate of Kiwis in jobs, with a 69.8 percent employment rate, having created 281,000 new jobs during our time in Government.
specificity.explanation: Carries a precise rate and a precise job count against a named period, both directly checkable against the official series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When we became the Government in 2017, just 2 percent of the cars coming into the market were electric or hybrid vehicles. As we leave office, that is 37 percent—a huge improvement.
specificity.explanation: Two dated percentages on a named measure; anyone can look up the registration series and check both endpoints.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One million free and healthy school lunches, 77,000 fewer children living in poverty, emissions in New Zealand falling for three years in a row, record levels of renewable electricity generation, 110,000 low-income Kiwi households getting cheaper power bills because of the Warmer Kiwi Homes scheme.
specificity.explanation: Named programmes attached to concrete counts (school lunches, 77,000 children, 110,000 households) and to named official series (emissions, renewable generation); each element identifies where it could be checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We significantly increased health funding, including to Pharmac, and we abolished prescription charges, which resulted in 3 million free prescriptions for New Zealanders, something that I believe stopped New Zealanders ending up in our emergency departments with avoidable illnesses because they weren’t getting the medication that they needed.
rigor.explanation: The count of free prescriptions supports only that prescriptions were dispensed without charge; the conclusion that emergency department presentations were averted is asserted rather than derived, with no ED data or counterfactual offered. A post hoc inference from a volume figure to a health outcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: On that last note, I want to say that Pacific New Zealanders are a growing and significant part of the New Zealand economy, a growing and significant part of New Zealand society, and I think it’s telling that the incoming Government didn’t mention them once in the Speech from the Throne today—not one single time. That does not bode well for Pacific New Zealanders in the future.
rigor.explanation: An argument from absence: the omission of a group from a single speech is offered as sufficient ground for a conclusion about how that group will fare under the new Government. No connecting premise links the speech's coverage to policy outcomes, and no alternative explanation for the omission is addressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There have been record investments in transport, including fixing a record number of potholes over the last year; completing legacy infrastructure projects like Transmission Gully that were left in a heck of a mess by the outgoing National Government.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested attack — blaming the previous National Government for the state of a major project — but it is aimed at a government's handling of a project, not at any person's character or competence. Robust criticism of a record is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: So we leave Government proud of our track record, committed to holding the incoming Government to account, concerned about the direction that they are taking New Zealand in—which is backwards on all of the important measures that should be important to New Zealand’s future—and absolutely resolved that for the first time in New Zealand’s history, this will be a one-term National Government.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the National-led Government formed in 2023 will not be returned to office at the next general election — an electoral outcome, not a promise about his own actions.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The result of the next New Zealand general election (due by late 2026) and the government formed after it. True if National does not lead the government formed following that election; false if National leads the government for a second consecutive term.

veracity.statement: This is important because smaller parties traditionally lose support after being linked up to a larger party in Government. This has happened every time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a historical regularity about New Zealand minor parties: that every small party that entered a governing arrangement with a larger party subsequently lost electoral support.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission official party-vote shares at successive general elections for each NZ minor party that entered a coalition, confidence-and-supply or cooperation arrangement (NZ First 1996-99, Alliance 1999-2002, United Future 2002-05, Māori Party 2008-17, ACT 2008-11, Greens 2017-20 and 2020-23). True if every such party's party vote fell at the following election; false if any counterexample exists.

veracity.statement: But the Greens have now not once but twice grown our support after being in a Government arrangement—unheard of.
veracity.explanation: Claims the Green Party increased its party vote at the elections following two separate governing arrangements with Labour.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission official Green Party party-vote percentages for 2017, 2020 and 2023. True if the 2020 share exceeds 2017 and the 2023 share exceeds 2020; false if either comparison shows a fall.

veracity.statement: This is an achievement that is unheard of anywhere in the world, and we did it with heart, with values, and with a vision that uplifted people instead of berating them, in a way that appealed to the best of our humanity rather than to the worst of it.
veracity.explanation: The checkable element is the comparative claim that no party anywhere in the world has increased its support at two successive elections following participation in government as a junior partner.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published national election results for junior governing partners in comparable parliamentary democracies (e.g. Germany, Ireland, Denmark, Norway, Sweden, the Netherlands). True if no junior coalition/support party is found to have raised its vote share at two consecutive post-government elections; false if at least one such case exists.

focus.statement: The leaders of our two biggest parties spent more time telling you who not to vote for, trying to scare people with how things will be under the other lot than they spent time talking about how we build the beautiful future our mokopuna deserve.
focus.explanation: Entirely about how the other parties' leaders campaigned — no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named. This is party-versus-party framing rather than engagement with any policy question.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The leaders of our two biggest parties spent more time telling you who not to vote for, trying to scare people with how things will be under the other lot than they spent time talking about how we build the beautiful future our mokopuna deserve.
civility.explanation: Aimed at the campaign conduct of the two major party leaders rather than at their character, but it imputes a motive — deliberately frightening voters — which edges past robust criticism toward attributing bad faith.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Because I’ve got to say, Chris Hipkins started the last term with 65 MPs, and he’s starting this one with 34.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Labour's seat count at the start of the 2020 term (65) and at the start of the 2023 term (34).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission official results: Labour's seat allocation after the 2020 general election and after the 2023 final count. True if 65 and 34 respectively; false if either number is materially different.

veracity.statement: But the Labour Government didn’t live up to that responsibility, and over the past six years violent crime went up 33 percent; serious assaults went up—I think it doubled; gang membership went up over 70 percent.
veracity.explanation: Three quantified claims about change between 2017 and 2023: violent crime +33%, serious assaults roughly doubled, gang membership +70%.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police victimisation statistics for violent offences and serious assaults 2017–2023, and the National Gang List membership count over the same period. True if violent crime rose about 33%, serious assaults roughly doubled, and gang list membership rose more than 70%; false if any figure is materially off.

veracity.statement: Around 40 percent of our kids are not attending school regularly.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the proportion of school students who fail the regular-attendance threshold.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education attendance statistics for 2023 (regular attendance = present for more than 90% of half-days). True if about 40% of students were not attending regularly; false if the share is materially higher or lower.

veracity.statement: Just last night we had the shocking and more sad news—not surprising—that actually in the Programme for International Student Assessment test, which is how countries are benchmarked against each other, in reading, maths, and science New Zealand has slid even further, and in all three of those subject areas, our results are the worst that they’ve ever been.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's PISA 2022 results, released the previous day, were the country's lowest ever in all three assessed domains.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD PISA 2022 results for New Zealand released 5 December 2023, compared against every prior NZ PISA cycle. True if the NZ mean scores in reading, mathematics and science are each the lowest recorded across the series; false if any one of the three is not a record low.

veracity.statement: That’s why Simeon Brown has already instructed officials to stop work on the ridiculous $16 billion Lake Onslow pumped hydro scheme.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that the responsible Minister had already directed officials to halt work on the Lake Onslow pumped hydro scheme, and that the scheme's cost was $16 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial announcements and MBIE/NZ Battery Project records for December 2023, plus the published cost estimates for the Lake Onslow option. True if work was directed to stop by that date and the estimate was around $16 billion; false if no such direction was given or the costing is materially different.

divination.statement: But inflation has become so entrenched and embedded from six years of reckless, wasteful Government spending that the Reserve Bank is already foreshadowing rates will have to stay higher for months to come.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that interest rates will remain elevated for months after December 2023, on the Reserve Bank's signalling.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Reserve Bank of New Zealand Official Cash Rate decisions following December 2023. True if the OCR was held at or above 5.50 percent with no cut before 30 June 2024; false if the OCR was reduced within that window.

rigor.statement: But inflation has become so entrenched and embedded from six years of reckless, wasteful Government spending that the Reserve Bank is already foreshadowing rates will have to stay higher for months to come.
rigor.explanation: Single-cause causal inference: attributes entrenched inflation solely to domestic government spending and treats the Reserve Bank's rate signalling as confirmation of that cause. No mechanism or evidence is offered ruling out the global inflation shock, so the conclusion outruns the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Just like there are laws of nature and there are laws of physics, there are laws of politics. Because if you want lower tax, you vote for us.
rigor.explanation: False analogy. Physical laws are invariant regularities; nothing is offered to show that voting behaviour and tax outcomes stand in any comparable relation, so the conclusion rests entirely on the metaphor.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Don’t tell me it wasn’t so because I spoke to those people on the election campaign, and I listened to them, and I literally held the hands of some of them—like that small-business owner who was trying so hard, but her business was going under and she hadn’t told her team yet because those families depended on those incomes.
rigor.explanation: Argument from anecdote, offered explicitly as grounds for rejecting any contrary account. Individual campaign encounters cannot establish the general economic claim they are advanced to prove.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Here’s what Labour has never understood: many of the tenants that they see as the perpetual victims of the so-called “evil capitalist” landlords have aspirations too.
rigor.explanation: Strawman. A caricatured position — that tenants are perpetual victims of evil capitalist landlords and have no aspirations — is attributed to opponents and then refuted, rather than any position they actually advanced on rental policy.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I just have to say, he is like—he is actually like an arsonist who, having thrown an accelerant all over the joint and lit the place up, he doesn’t just slink off, actually leaving the scene, realising he’s caused a huge amount of damage, he doesn’t actually fess up, put his hand up, apologise to the New Zealand people and actually say he got it wrong, he just simply loiters and hangs around at the scene of the crime, actually just waiting and watching everything.
civility.explanation: Extended likening of a named opponent to a criminal loitering at the scene of his own arson. The target is the person and his character, not any policy or decision.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: You got two new MPs and I say congratulations, but we heard from a bitter and a twisted and a negative Chris Hipkins, the one we saw during the campaign over there.
civility.explanation: Direct characterisation of a named member as bitter and twisted — an attack on personal character rather than on anything he argued.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Ginny Andersen probably isn’t asking herself why she survived because self-reflection may not actually be her thing.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe at a named member's capacity for self-reflection. Nothing about her portfolio decisions is engaged; the remark lands on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So I have to say, Labour is sitting over there wondering who to blame for them going from 65 MPs—the most ever in the history of MMP in this country—to the 32 uncomfortable people over there with survivors’ guilt that I see opposite me.
civility.explanation: Mockery of the opposition benches as 'uncomfortable people' with 'survivors' guilt'. Sneering rather than a direct insult to any individual, and no substance is engaged.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We will stop the wasteful Government spending and get the books back in order, because we know that every dollar the Government spends had to actually be earned by someone going to work and working hard.
civility.explanation: Blunt about the previous government's spending, but the criticism lands on the spending, not on any person. This is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I just have to say, he is like—he is actually like an arsonist who, having thrown an accelerant all over the joint and lit the place up, he doesn’t just slink off, actually leaving the scene, realising he’s caused a huge amount of damage, he doesn’t actually fess up, put his hand up, apologise to the New Zealand people and actually say he got it wrong, he just simply loiters and hangs around at the scene of the crime, actually just waiting and watching everything.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the Leader of the Opposition is 'really like'. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named anywhere in the passage.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: You got two new MPs and I say congratulations, but we heard from a bitter and a twisted and a negative Chris Hipkins, the one we saw during the campaign over there.
focus.explanation: The content is the opposition leader's temperament and the other party's seat count. No policy content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I have to say, Labour is sitting over there wondering who to blame for them going from 65 MPs—the most ever in the history of MMP in this country—to the 32 uncomfortable people over there with survivors’ guilt that I see opposite me.
focus.explanation: Wholly about the other party's electoral misfortune and internal blame-shifting. No measure, policy or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’re going to get going on infrastructure, including 13 new roads of national significance and public transport projects that actually get progressed, not just talked and talked and talked about by consultants.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy: names a specific programme and a specific count of projects. The dig at consultants is incidental to a real policy commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re going to get going on infrastructure, including 13 new roads of national significance and public transport projects that actually get progressed, not just talked and talked and talked about by consultants.
specificity.explanation: Names the programme and gives a count (13 roads), but supplies no costs, no timeframe and no list of which projects or which transport schemes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re going to restore the three strikes and we’re committed to training no fewer than 500 new front-line police officers in our first two years.
specificity.explanation: A named legislative change plus a hard figure and a deadline (500 officers, first two years) — checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are about attitudes on this side of the House, not platitudes.
specificity.explanation: A slogan built on wordplay. It commits to nothing and carries no figure, mechanism or named policy, despite sitting in a passage that is trying to convey the government's approach.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’ve got to say, if you’ve ever wondered why the Green Party needs to have two leaders, that speech by Marama Davidson was all the evidence you would ever need! It felt like it was written by an ad agency but, at the end of it, no one had a clue what they were actually selling—platitude after platitude—and that’s why they’re over there.
civility.explanation: Mockery aimed at a named member: the jibe is that Davidson personally is the reason her party needs two leaders, and that her speech was vacuous. It ridicules the member rather than engaging any substance, which under the re-anchored scale is well below the expected standard, though it stops short of sustained abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’ll just say that, if you’re going to go on camera and lie about your interactions with Brooke, you probably won’t be doing it again.
civility.explanation: A direct accusation of deliberate dishonesty against a named individual (Richard Wagstaff), delivered with an implied threat that he will not do it again. The target is the person's honesty rather than any argument or position he advanced.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Cameron Luxton, I think it’s probably true, has built more houses personally than the Government built in the six years that it had!
veracity.explanation: Asserts that one individual builder has personally built more houses than the 2017–2023 Labour-led government delivered over its six years in office. The comparison is between that MP's personal construction output and the government's total housing delivery.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora / HUD public housing delivery statistics and KiwiBuild completion figures for October 2017 – October 2023, compared with any public record of the number of dwellings Cameron Luxton personally built in that period. True if the government's delivered total is lower than his personal total; false if the government's total materially exceeds it.

veracity.statement: It is a team that includes, for the first time ever, three Green Party electorate MPs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Green Party won three electorate seats at the 2023 general election, and that this is the first time it has held three electorate MPs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official Electoral Commission 2023 general election electorate results plus the Parliamentary record of Green electorate MPs in earlier Parliaments; true if the Greens hold exactly three electorate seats in the 54th Parliament and never held three or more before, false if they hold fewer than three now or held three or more previously.

veracity.statement: Days after promising it, lifting the ban was nowhere to be seen on the Government’s 100-day plan.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that repealing the ban on new offshore oil and gas exploration, committed to in the coalition arrangements, was absent from the incoming Government's published 100-day plan.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National-led Government's 100-day plan as published in late November 2023; true if no item in that plan commits to lifting or repealing the offshore oil and gas exploration ban, false if such an item appears in it.

veracity.statement: Nearly 30,000 of you, so far, took an immediate stand and signed a petition telling the Prime Minister and his co-deputies that they had no mandate to tear up climate action.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a signature count of close to 30,000 on the Green Party's petition against reopening offshore oil and gas exploration, as at the date of the speech.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Green Party's published petition signature counter or its media releases for the oil and gas petition around 6 December 2023; true if the count was in the high 20,000s or above, false if materially lower (e.g. under 20,000).

veracity.statement: Like raising the price of electric cars by ending the Clean Car Discount—but only after the PM himself had benefited from it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Prime Minister personally received a Clean Car Discount rebate before his Government moved to end the scheme.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Reporting and any confirmation from the Prime Minister's office on whether Christopher Luxon claimed a Clean Car Discount rebate on an electric vehicle purchase before December 2023; true if he received the rebate, false if he did not.

focus.statement: I hope Ministers remember these electorates when their Crown limos get stuck in the inevitable traffic jams resulting from his decision to defund the Let’s Get Wellington Moving programme.
focus.explanation: Names a specific decision — defunding Let's Get Wellington Moving — and its claimed consequence, so there is real policy content; the weight is diluted by the 'Crown limos' framing aimed at Ministers as a class rather than at the transport policy itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Whatever they do and however they use their power, I can assure this House of one thing: the members opposite are not going to get away with their political violence lightly.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side's conduct in general terms. No measure, figure or named policy appears, so there is nothing on-policy for the listener to check or engage with.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If they think they have a problem with their own team leaking confidential papers to the media in the very first week, they best buckle up.
focus.explanation: Wholly about the other side's internal state — a leak within the governing parties. No policy, measure or outcome is engaged with at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Instead—instead—what we got is a random, visionless, and harmful grab bag of laws that are more about politicians’ pet projects and petty grievances than they are about addressing the challenges we face right now.
focus.explanation: There is a real object of criticism — the legislative programme in the Speech from the Throne — but it is engaged only through motive attribution ('pet projects and petty grievances') rather than through any named measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Like raiding the money raised from our biggest polluters through the emissions trading scheme to pay for their tax cuts for wealthy people, a decision that is about as far away from a climate dividend as you can possibly get.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named fiscal mechanism — emissions trading scheme revenue being used to fund tax reductions — and on who gains from it. This is scrutiny of a specific policy choice, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They’re here for people who make money from exploiting workers, renters, and our taiao.
focus.explanation: A claim about whose interests the Government really serves, with no measure, figure or named policy attached. Pure characterisation of the other side's motives.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Whatever they do and however they use their power, I can assure this House of one thing: the members opposite are not going to get away with their political violence lightly.
civility.explanation: Characterises the conduct of the members opposite as 'political violence' — an imputation of bad faith rather than a criticism of any policy, though it lands on a bench collectively rather than on a named individual.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Like raising the price of electric cars by ending the Clean Car Discount—but only after the PM himself had benefited from it.
civility.explanation: The second half turns from the Clean Car Discount decision to the Prime Minister personally, imputing self-interest — he took the rebate and then withdrew it from others. A sneer at the individual rather than at the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We refuse to spend all our time talking about the next outrageous thing Mr Seymour or Mr Peters said instead of focusing on what matters to people’s daily lives.
civility.explanation: Names two individuals and characterises their contributions as a running stream of 'outrageous' remarks. It is dismissive of the people rather than of any position they hold, though it stops short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Instead—instead—what we got is a random, visionless, and harmful grab bag of laws that are more about politicians’ pet projects and petty grievances than they are about addressing the challenges we face right now.
specificity.explanation: A verdict on the Government's whole legislative programme carried entirely by adjectives — 'random', 'visionless', 'harmful', 'grab bag'. Not one of the laws is named, so nothing here can be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Like raiding the money raised from our biggest polluters through the emissions trading scheme to pay for their tax cuts for wealthy people, a decision that is about as far away from a climate dividend as you can possibly get.
specificity.explanation: Names the revenue source (the ETS) and the use it is put to (tax cuts), which is a real mechanism, but supplies no amounts, no thresholds and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: People power won the oil and gas ban, and it is people power that is going to save it.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning about a real policy: the preceding sentence offers only the sequence — a petition ran, then the repeal did not appear in the 100-day plan — and the conclusion that public campaigning caused the ban and will preserve it is drawn straight from that sequence, with no other evidence of causation offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: A dividend would give the same amount to everyone, not higher tax cuts for the wealthy while people who need support the most completely miss out.
rigor.explanation: A clean definitional argument: it states what a dividend is (an equal per-person payment) and concludes that a distribution skewed toward higher earners is not one. The conclusion follows from the premise offered; whether the tax package is in fact skewed is a separate factual question.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: People power won the oil and gas ban, and it is people power that is going to save it.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the statutory ban on new offshore petroleum exploration permits will survive this Government rather than be repealed.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Crown Minerals Act 1991 as amended: true if the 2018 prohibition on granting new offshore petroleum exploration permits is still in force at the end of the 2023–2026 parliamentary term, false if Parliament has enacted a repeal or reversal of that prohibition before then.

civility.statement: But you wouldn't ask Rawiri Waititi if you wanted to know about hard work, would you?
civility.explanation: A direct personal jibe at a named member's work ethic, not at any argument or policy he advanced. The debate over volunteer labour versus money gave a real opportunity to answer on the substance, so the scale was live.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It's almost like he has the most wonderful form of selective amnesia.
civility.explanation: Sneering imputation of bad faith at a named member — a suggestion he is deliberately forgetting his own record, rather than a criticism of what he did as Minister.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So Grant Robertson and Chris Hipkins—thick as thieves; in fact, taxpayers might say that's exactly what they were—were conniving together to get fewer kids going to school, learning less for more money.
civility.explanation: Calls two named members thieves and attributes conspiratorial intent to them. The underlying point about spending and results could have been made about the record alone; this lands on the people.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Per person, after inflation, he increased expenditure by 30 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that real per-capita government expenditure rose 30 percent over Grant Robertson's tenure as Minister of Finance (2017 to 2023).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenses from the 2017 and 2023 fiscal years, deflated by Stats NZ CPI and divided by Stats NZ resident population: true if the real per-person increase is approximately 30 percent, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: The Programme for International Student Assessment examinations of 15-year-olds in science, literacy, and mathematics have been tested every three years since the turn of the century and we have just had the worst results ever for New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the PISA round reported in December 2023 produced New Zealand's lowest scores across science, reading and mathematics since PISA began.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD PISA mean scores for New Zealand in maths, reading and science across all cycles from 2000 to 2022: true if the 2022 results are the lowest recorded in each of those domains, false if any earlier cycle was lower.

veracity.statement: And yet we had not 2,500 bureaucrats in the Ministry of Education but 4,400.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Ministry of Education staffing grew from roughly 2,500 to roughly 4,400 over the period of the previous government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public Service Commission workforce data and Ministry of Education annual reports for FTE staff numbers in 2017 and 2023: true if the figures are close to 2,500 and 4,400 respectively, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: He was the Minister of Education for five years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Chris Hipkins held the Education portfolio for a five-year span.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official ministerial lists for Hipkins' appointment and departure dates as Minister of Education: true if the tenure is about five years, false if materially shorter or longer.

veracity.statement: We had people who argued with their colleagues and their family and persuaded, eventually, a quarter of a million New Zealanders to trust ACT with their party vote, beyond those in the Epsom electorate, who I am incredibly grateful to and thank for sending me to this place for a fourth time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts ACT received about 250,000 party votes at the 2023 general election, and that this is Seymour's fourth term as the member for Epsom.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission official 2023 general election results: true if ACT's party vote is close to 250,000 and Seymour has won Epsom in 2014, 2017, 2020 and 2023; false if either figure is materially different.

specificity.statement: Per person, after inflation, he increased expenditure by 30 percent.
specificity.explanation: A single figure with its two adjustments (per person, after inflation) named, so a reader knows exactly what quantity is claimed and where to look for it.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The truth is that if Labour MPs knew how to invest capital, they wouldn't be Labour MPs. They'd be rich.
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of the other party's members. No policy, programme, figure or outcome is named — strip the jibe about Labour MPs and nothing about productivity or investment remains. Nothing is scored for Rigor here, because there is no argument underneath the swipe.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I have to tell you that they returned today so rundown and clapped out that if this Labour Party was a used car it would be illegal to import them to New Zealand.
focus.explanation: A metaphor about the state of the opposing party with no policy content at all. It insults no individual, so Civility is untouched; this is the tribalism Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: You know, their Resource Management Act reforms managed to make the resource management law more complicated, but with novel terms such as te Oranga o te Taiao, which would need to be interpreted in new jurisprudence by the Environment Court, by which time we would probably be economically overtaken by Indonesia.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure: names the reform, a specific statutory concept introduced by it, and the court that would have to interpret it. Legitimate scrutiny of a named policy, whatever the quality of the reasoning.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In just about every area we found a Labour Party that spent more money and made more rules and got worse results.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy proposition here — spending up, regulation up, outcomes down — but it is stated as a general verdict on the other party across 'just about every area', with no measure, figure or programme named to anchor it.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You know, their Resource Management Act reforms managed to make the resource management law more complicated, but with novel terms such as te Oranga o te Taiao, which would need to be interpreted in new jurisprudence by the Environment Court, by which time we would probably be economically overtaken by Indonesia.
rigor.explanation: The inference from 'novel terms requiring new jurisprudence' to 'more complicated law' is offered with a reason and holds up, but the conclusion is carried past it by hyperbole — being economically overtaken by Indonesia is asserted with nothing connecting it to Environment Court delay.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The extraordinary thing is he didn’t seem to understand that the forward forecast for GDP for next year by the IMF has us at 159 in the world—just in front of Equatorial Guinea and doing less than 1 percent in terms of GDP—and he said that that was a success story.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the IMF's forward GDP forecast for the following year ranks New Zealand 159th in the world, immediately ahead of Equatorial Guinea, at under 1 percent growth.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The IMF World Economic Outlook (October 2023) projections for 2024 real GDP growth: true if New Zealand's projected growth is below 1 percent and its rank among listed economies is approximately 159th with Equatorial Guinea immediately below it; false if the rank or the growth figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: So $303,500 charity money to Te Pāti Māori, and what is going on when that can be allowed to survive in this country’s democracy?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a specific sum of charitable money, $303,500, reached Te Pāti Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Charities Services / Department of Internal Affairs findings and Electoral Commission donation returns for Te Pāti Māori: true if records show approximately $303,500 of charitable funds transferred to the party or its campaign, false if no such transfer is documented or the amount is materially different.

veracity.statement: It’s April in 2020, we’re on about 4.5, 5, almost 5.5 percent, and we were attacked by the SFO.
veracity.explanation: Asserts New Zealand First was polling roughly 4.5–5.5 percent in April 2020 at the time of the Serious Fraud Office action.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published April 2020 political polls (1 News Colmar Brunton, Newshub Reid Research) for New Zealand First's party vote: true if the party vote sits in the 4.5–5.5 percent band, false if materially lower; plus SFO/Electoral Commission records dating the referral or investigation to that period.

veracity.statement: Why, the Greens never had a meeting. They never had a meeting.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Green Party held no public meetings during the 2023 general election campaign.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Green Party 2023 campaign event listings, contemporaneous local media reports and candidate social media: true if no public campaign meetings can be documented, false if any public meeting is documented.

specificity.statement: The extraordinary thing is he didn’t seem to understand that the forward forecast for GDP for next year by the IMF has us at 159 in the world—just in front of Equatorial Guinea and doing less than 1 percent in terms of GDP—and he said that that was a success story.
specificity.explanation: Names the source (IMF), the metric (forward GDP forecast), a rank (159), a comparator country and a numeric threshold — fully checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So $303,500 charity money to Te Pāti Māori, and what is going on when that can be allowed to survive in this country’s democracy?
specificity.explanation: Gives an exact dollar figure and a named recipient party; the claim can be checked against donation and charity records.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But had we got a decent go, we’d be sitting here with far more than the members we’ve got now. And that’s a fact.
rigor.explanation: A counterfactual about vote share asserted as established fact. Nothing is offered to connect media coverage to seat numbers — bare assertion, with 'that's a fact' substituting for evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Any money you like—you’re going that way, because these people want their seats back, and they’re better organised, and they will be, when the time comes.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Greens, whom he is addressing, will lose ground at the next general election because better-organised opponents will reclaim seats.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Official Electoral Commission results for the next New Zealand general election: true if the Green Party's seat count falls below its 2023 total of 14, false if it holds or increases.

civility.statement: Uh-uh, no you’re not and never will be, and certainly not someone who is so decolonised he wears a cowboy hat—so decolonised he wears a cowboy hat.
civility.explanation: Mocks an identifiable individual member's dress and sincerity, repeating the jibe for effect. The target is the person, not any policy or argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Unlike that member—she couldn’t fill a telephone booth.
civility.explanation: A direct belittling jibe at a named member who had just interjected, aimed at her personal standing rather than any argument she made.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And the sooner you go, the better, so that somebody can step up and start to rebuild what was once a great party, but it’s forgotten the workers.
civility.explanation: Tells a named member to his face that his departure would be an improvement — pointed at the individual rather than at a policy, though short of sustained abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Te Pūkenga was a disaster under Chris Hipkins’ watch that does need to be unravelled.
civility.explanation: Harsh about an institution and the record of the minister responsible, but it attacks no one personally — under the re-anchored scale, holding a named person's watch to account for a policy failure is civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We’re going to stop putting significant natural areas (SNAs) where some pimply teenager out of planning school looks at your farm on Google Earth and says, “That looks like a bit of biodiversity. You can’t have that any more.”, because if you do that, people won’t want to do conservation because the pimply teenagers at the local council will take your property rights.
civility.explanation: Council planners are mocked twice by appearance and youth ('pimply teenager out of planning school'), which lands on the people doing the work rather than on the SNA policy itself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Government pushed hundreds of thousands of what they deemed the most dangerous firearms into the grey and black market in what may have been one of the stupidest, most irresponsible policies that any Government has rushed through this Parliament.
civility.explanation: About as brutal as criticism of a policy gets — 'stupidest, most irresponsible' — yet no individual is attacked. Under the re-anchored scale that is civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We are going to see a healthcare system that is not focused on the vision of reorganising the wiring diagram in Wellington, but, instead, on a Ministry of Health and a health system that treats all New Zealanders equally, based on need, using good data—not lazy and bigoted discrimination based on race—and that focuses on ensuring that the patients are getting the results, not that administrators are happy or that the health system is doing right by identity politics.
civility.explanation: Calling the existing arrangements 'lazy and bigoted' imputes bad faith and bigotry to those who designed and run them, which goes past criticising the policy — though it stops short of naming and insulting an individual.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Those people who aren’t so intellectual, they tend to be afraid of debate, and so they will call you racist and they’ll shout you down and they’ll try and block the motorway.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the intelligence and character of those who disagree — they are unintellectual, fearful, and reflexively abusive. This lands on people, not on any argument they have made.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: You see, as I mentioned, the Labour Party spent like drunken sailors and were about as effective at getting useful things done.
civility.explanation: Mocking, but aimed at a party rather than any individual; no person's character, competence or worth is attacked. The tribalism is Focus's problem, not Civility's.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The reason that we want to get rid of these damaging policies like the Natural and Built Environment Act and the Spatial Planning Act is that Labour’s vision was one of central control: centralised politics, centralised healthcare, centralised three waters—give the Minister for the Environment more power over what is built in your street.
focus.explanation: Names two specific Acts and a specific mechanism (ministerial power over local building consent), which is squarely on-policy; the 'Labour's vision' framing adds party colour but the policy content carries the sentence.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, you’re not going to get that from the Green Party, who have not elected an MP who has studied science past high school in 12 years.
focus.explanation: Having just raised a policy question (split-gas methane targets), the statement pivots entirely to the composition and qualifications of another party. No policy, measure or figure is named — this is about the other team, not the argument.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: You see, as I mentioned, the Labour Party spent like drunken sailors and were about as effective at getting useful things done.
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of the other party's general record. No programme, figure, appropriation or outcome is named — strip out the party-bashing and nothing remains.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s why this Government will be strongly committed—more committed than any Government in history—to dealing to the red tape and regulation that wastes people’s time going through compliance activities that add nothing to the public welfare but dramatically impoverish people and, eventually, all of us in their private welfare.
specificity.explanation: A commitment to 'dealing to red tape' with no named regulation, no target, no mechanism and no timeframe — nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government is going to make sure that if you attack someone in a sole-charge workplace or a workplace attached to their dwelling house, then that’s an aggravating factor, or if you’re a member of a gang, you’re going away for longer, because being kind to crims hasn’t worked.
specificity.explanation: Names two concrete sentencing mechanisms — an aggravating factor for attacks in sole-charge or dwelling-attached workplaces, and longer sentences for gang membership. Checkable and actionable; short of full marks only for the missing timeframe and penalty quantum.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, this Government says that if she’s prepared to pay the costs of the healthcare and if she’s prepared to guarantee there’ll be no costs on the State, her mum can have a five-year visitor visa to come in and out of New Zealand as much as she likes and be in this country.
specificity.explanation: A named visa instrument with a stated duration (five years), multi-entry conditions, and the two eligibility conditions attached to it. Someone could check whether the policy was delivered as described.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: And I’m proud to be the first Minister for Regulation, with a Ministry for Regulation and a Regulatory Standards Bill setting out the principles of how you make laws that do make sense and then go through the enormous stock of out-of-date rules and regulations that waste our time and money.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no New Zealand minister has previously held a Regulation portfolio and that a Ministry for Regulation is being established alongside a Regulatory Standards Bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The DPMC/Parliament list of ministerial portfolios and warrants: true if no minister before December 2023 held a portfolio titled Minister for Regulation, false if any earlier ministerial list records one.

veracity.statement: We’re going to have a split-gas approach to methane and other greenhouse gases because we actually do follow the science, and the science says that methane has different characteristics from carbon dioxide.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that methane has materially different atmospheric characteristics from carbon dioxide.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IPCC AR6 Working Group I on atmospheric lifetime and radiative forcing of CH4 versus CO2: true if methane is a short-lived gas with a lifetime and global warming potential materially different from CO2's, false if the two are equivalent in those respects.

veracity.statement: Now, you’re not going to get that from the Green Party, who have not elected an MP who has studied science past high school in 12 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no Green MP first elected in the twelve years to 2023 has studied a science subject beyond secondary school.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary member profiles and published biographies for every Green MP first elected between 2011 and 2023: false if any one of them holds tertiary study or a qualification in a science discipline, true if none does.

veracity.statement: The Government pushed hundreds of thousands of what they deemed the most dangerous firearms into the grey and black market in what may have been one of the stupidest, most irresponsible policies that any Government has rushed through this Parliament.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that hundreds of thousands of newly-prohibited firearms went unsurrendered under the 2019 buyback and passed into illicit circulation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police buyback collection figures (firearms handed in and compensated) set against published pre-ban estimates of prohibited firearms in circulation: true if the credible shortfall is in the hundreds of thousands, false if the best available estimate of unsurrendered prohibited firearms is materially lower.

veracity.statement: People pulled back from being landlords, and tenants were the ones that suffered, with record increases in rent over the six years that we’ve just seen with this Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that rent increases over the six years of the previous government were the largest on record.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ rental price index and MBIE tenancy bond data for 2017–2023: true if the cumulative rent increase over that six-year period exceeds every earlier six-year window in the series, false if any earlier period matched or exceeded it.

rigor.statement: I’m pleased to see that 2017 baselines for the number of public servants will be a starting point for getting costs under control. Because you don’t just have to pay these people; they then get bored and make you jump through extra hoops which further damages our productivity.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that additional public servants damage productivity rests on an unevidenced motive attribution — that they 'get bored' and invent compliance work. Nothing is offered to link headcount to compliance burden; it is a bare assertion dressed as a causal mechanism.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When it comes to crime, it is time to call time on the experiment of Labour. That is, if only we are kind to criminals, they’ll be kind back.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the previous government's justice approach is restated as the caricature 'be kind to criminals and they'll be kind back', and the conclusion that it should be abandoned is drawn against that caricature rather than the actual policy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’re going to stop putting significant natural areas (SNAs) where some pimply teenager out of planning school looks at your farm on Google Earth and says, “That looks like a bit of biodiversity. You can’t have that any more.”, because if you do that, people won’t want to do conservation because the pimply teenagers at the local council will take your property rights.
rigor.explanation: There is a genuine inference about the policy — that designating SNAs deters voluntary conservation because landowners fear losing property rights — but the causal step is asserted rather than evidenced, resting on the caricature instead of any account of landowner behaviour.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’re going to have a split-gas approach to methane and other greenhouse gases because we actually do follow the science, and the science says that methane has different characteristics from carbon dioxide.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — treat methane on a separate track — does follow from the stated premise that methane behaves differently from CO2. The step from 'different characteristics' to 'therefore a split target' is left implicit, which is the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: People pulled back from being landlords, and tenants were the ones that suffered, with record increases in rent over the six years that we’ve just seen with this Government.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc: rent increases are attributed to landlords exiting, and that exit to the previous government's tax and tenancy changes, with nothing offered to exclude the obvious alternatives (interest rates, construction costs, migration and population growth).
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Those people who aren’t so intellectual, they tend to be afraid of debate, and so they will call you racist and they’ll shout you down and they’ll try and block the motorway.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that opponents of the proposed debate on the Treaty principles will respond by publicly labelling it racist and by mounting disruptive protest action including blocking a motorway.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous news reporting and police records of protest action against the Treaty Principles Bill: true if opponents publicly characterised the proposal as racist AND protest action obstructed a motorway or equivalent major road; false if neither occurred by the resolve-by date.

civility.statement: Oh, but he’s too new and too unlearned to even make a defence of it.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on another member's knowledge and competence rather than on any argument he made.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And so no more of this darn humbug, and you can put the tā moko on and dance around and carry on in a way that we find very strange because where I come from, that’s conferred upon you; you don’t just paint yourself like some tattoo shop.
civility.explanation: Mockery aimed at another member personally — his moko, his bearing — likened to self-application at a tattoo shop. Nothing here engages an argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And I wish he was as bright as his mother, and paid more attention.
civility.explanation: Contemptuous jibe at a named member's intelligence, made by unfavourable comparison to his mother.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The coalition documents read like a manifesto of white supremacy and cultural genocide.
civility.explanation: Brutal criticism of policy documents, which the re-anchored scale permits, but it imputes racist intent rather than only bad policy. No individual is attacked, so it stays well above the personal-attack band.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: OK, so if they’re the Māori voice and they got only 3 percent of the vote most of the time, and yet they say the Māori people are 18 percent of the population, it means that one-sixth of the Māori people might support them and five-sixths don’t.
rigor.explanation: A real numerical inference, and an invalid one: it divides a party's share of the WHOLE electorate by the Māori share of the population, which only yields 'one-sixth of Māori support them' if every one of that party's votes came from Māori and every Māori voted. The conclusion does not follow from the two figures offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Removing the prison reduction target and cultural reports in the justice system proves that this Government is intent on locking up more brown people and throwing away the key.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: two named policy reversals are said to 'prove' an intention. Reversing a target and removing cultural reports is consistent with several motives; nothing is offered to bridge the policy change to the imputed intent.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: OK, so if they’re the Māori voice and they got only 3 percent of the vote most of the time, and yet they say the Māori people are 18 percent of the population, it means that one-sixth of the Māori people might support them and five-sixths don’t.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete, checkable figures (3 percent of the vote, 18 percent of the population) and an explicit arithmetic conclusion someone could test.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Repealing section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act will undo all the progress that has been made to try and fix a systemically racist organisation that, over generations, has stolen our kids.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision (section 7AA) and the Act, so the claim can be located and checked; what 'all the progress' consists of is left undefined, which is the only thing holding it below the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We’re not going to have a French Polynesian name that’s an insult to everybody in the South Island.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 'Aotearoa' is a French Polynesian name rather than a New Zealand Māori one. The 'insult to the South Island' half is opinion; the checkable assertion is the name's origin.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Standard etymological sources on the name Aotearoa (Williams' Dictionary of the Māori Language, Te Ara / Encyclopedia of New Zealand, Māori Dictionary): true if the name is shown to originate in French Polynesia (e.g. Tahitian or Marquesan usage for these islands), false if it is a New Zealand Māori coinage/usage for the country or its North Island.

veracity.statement: They’re there clapping at the back—that’s what they want: clearly with no idea that it was once the most successful economy in South America, and look at the cot case it is today.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Venezuela was at one time the most successful economy in South America and is economically ruined today.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Comparative GDP-per-capita series for South American countries (Maddison Project Database, World Bank, IMF): true if Venezuela ranked highest in the region on that measure at some point in the twentieth century and its current GDP per capita has collapsed to among the lowest; false if it never led the region on the standard series.

veracity.statement: You have elected the largest Te Pāti Māori caucus in the history of this Parliament, and may I remind Winston: you only won five seats; we won six.
veracity.explanation: Two seat-count claims about the 2023 general election: that Te Pāti Māori returned six MPs (its largest caucus ever) and that New Zealand First returned only five.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission official 2023 general election results and the resulting party caucus sizes: true if Te Pāti Māori returned six MPs and New Zealand First five, false if either figure differs (e.g. if New Zealand First's list entitlement returned a different number of members).

veracity.statement: We are rangatira who never ceded our sovereignty, never bowed down to a foreign power.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori rangatira did not cede sovereignty when signing te Tiriti o Waitangi.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal's Te Paparahi o Te Raki (He Whakaputanga me te Tiriti) stage 1 report and the Māori-text scholarship on kāwanatanga vs tino rangatiratanga: true if the authoritative finding is that the signatory rangatira did not cede sovereignty in February 1840, false if the finding is that sovereignty was ceded.

veracity.statement: The racist signals that the election of this Government has sent are so strong that Public Service departments are pre-emptively wiping te reo Māori from official documents and rolling back years of progress overnight.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a present fact that public service departments were removing te reo Māori from official documents in the weeks following the 2023 election, without being required to.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public Service Commission and departmental communications, plus contemporaneous reporting from November–December 2023: true if identifiable government agencies removed or demoted te reo Māori names/text in official documents in that period, false if no such agency changes are documented.

focus.statement: We want this country to be called New Zealand, and if we’re going to change the name, then we’re going to ask all New Zealanders first.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual question at issue — the country's official name — and names a mechanism for deciding it (putting it to all New Zealanders) rather than characterising opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Repealing section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act will undo all the progress that has been made to try and fix a systemically racist organisation that, over generations, has stolen our kids.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure: a named statutory provision, a named agency, and the specific consequence claimed for repealing it. Legitimate scrutiny of a stated government commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We will fight against the short-sightedness of a Government that would allow oil and gas exploration during a climate crisis—absolute foolishness.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy — permitting oil and gas exploration — and states an objection to it, so this is policy engagement rather than party-bashing; the weight is diluted somewhat by the generalised charge of 'short-sightedness' against the Government as a whole.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: First of all, I want to mihi and thank the Government made up of parties funded and supported by the hyper-rich, the 2 percenters who own more than 50 percent of the wealth, the hyper - anti-Māori, the hyper - Hobson Pledgers, the Julian Batchelors, the anti-environmentalists, and the anti-minorities.
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of who the governing parties are and who backs them — 'anti-Māori', 'anti-environmentalists', 'anti-minorities' — with no policy, measure or outcome named for the House to weigh.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They don’t take pride in being Māori; they take pride in being labelled as professional politicians, but they belong to parties that don’t have the best interests of Māori at heart—proposing to review, rewrite, and referend our Te Tiriti.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy referent at the end — proposals to review, rewrite and hold a referendum on Te Tiriti — but the bulk of the statement is about what the members opposite are really like and which parties they belong to.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We didn’t need billboards in pink sponsored all over the place—centrefold adverts in the New Zealand Herald.
focus.explanation: Purely about another party's campaign advertising. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is at issue; strip out the comparison with the other party's billboards and nothing remains.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As Moana Jackson laid out in the Matike Mai kaupapa, we must strive for self-determination, self-sufficiency to be implemented by 2040, on the 200th anniversary of the Treaty of Waitangi.
specificity.explanation: Cites a named framework (Matike Mai) and a hard target date (2040), which is checkable, but the substance — 'self-determination, self-sufficiency' — carries no mechanism, cost or intermediate milestone.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: An Aotearoa hou looks like taking climate change seriously. It means investing in clean energy and restoring our taiao, protecting and preparing communities for climate adaptation, transitioning to regenerative and organic culture, banning seabed mining.
specificity.explanation: One concrete and actionable item (banning seabed mining) inside a list of broad directions — 'investing in clean energy', 'climate adaptation' — with no figures, instruments or timeframes attached to any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government started with a policy platform made up of 15 policies which stand to disestablish, disband, disconnect our Tiriti, our reo; undo inequity solutions, prison their way to justice—oh, how unoriginal, how uninspiring.
specificity.explanation: Supplies a count (15 policies) and the broad areas they touch, which gives a reader something to go and look for, but none of the fifteen are named and the effects are described only in general verbs — 'disestablish, disband, disconnect'.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: A Government awarded Fossil of the Day award—how awesome are you guys!
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the new New Zealand Government was given the Climate Action Network's Fossil of the Day award, a real and documented award issued daily at UN climate conferences.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Climate Action Network International's published Fossil of the Day awards for COP28 (Dubai, Nov–Dec 2023); true if New Zealand was named a Fossil of the Day recipient at that conference during or shortly before December 2023, false if no such award to New Zealand appears in CAN International's daily announcements.

veracity.statement: First of all, I want to mihi and thank the Government made up of parties funded and supported by the hyper-rich, the 2 percenters who own more than 50 percent of the wealth, the hyper - anti-Māori, the hyper - Hobson Pledgers, the Julian Batchelors, the anti-environmentalists, and the anti-minorities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific distributional fact about New Zealand wealth — that the top 2 percent own more than half of it. Published NZ figures are usually reported for the top 1 percent, top 5 percent and top 10 percent, so the resolver will need to check whether the top-2-percent share exceeds 50 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Economic Survey (net worth) distribution of household wealth for 2021 or 2023, or Reserve Bank / Treasury wealth-distribution analysis; true if the wealthiest 2 percent of New Zealanders hold more than 50 percent of total net wealth, false if the share held by the top 2 percent is materially below 50 percent.

civility.statement: We are resilient and we are beautiful, huia feathers or not, and we will not be bullied or stood over by men on that side of the House who embarrass themselves, who ridicule our culture.
civility.explanation: Moves from the substance to the people opposite: the named group of members are said to 'embarrass themselves' and to ridicule her culture. That is a judgement about their conduct and character rather than about any argument they have made.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They don’t take pride in being Māori; they take pride in being labelled as professional politicians, but they belong to parties that don’t have the best interests of Māori at heart—proposing to review, rewrite, and referend our Te Tiriti.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the personal identity and motives of Māori MPs opposite — telling the House they take no pride in being Māori and are in it for the professional status. That goes past their arguments to who they are.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: You see, those whose hearts are full of hate and envy don’t understand that the more you attack us, the stronger we will grow.
civility.explanation: Attributes hate and envy to those she is arguing against — an imputation of bad character and bad faith rather than an engagement with anything they have said.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I look opposite me and I see tobacco lobbyists, I see gun lobbyists, I see Hobson’s Pledge lobbyists, I see absolute profiteers, landlords, conspirators, and climate change deniers.
civility.explanation: A sustained characterisation of the members opposite as lobbyists, profiteers and conspirators — an attack on the character and motives of people, not on any argument or policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I feel aroha that you represent voters who are not worldly, who do not embrace indigenous peoples, who are anti-Māori, and who are unable to embrace the reo anywhere, but I also get that you will now be comfortable calling yourselves flightless birds and hope that you can handle it when the Māori version comes off and the English signs are up for places like Urenui, English for Uretiti, Rahotu—but wait, Shane, I have one more—and the English sign for Kaitīeke.
civility.explanation: Condescension ("not worldly") and an imputation of anti-Māori motive directed at the members opposite through their voters, plus a named jibe at a specific member. Short of sustained abuse but well past pointed.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What is unfair to our new Prime Minister is that you have started your legacy as a Prime Minister by attacking Māori and attacking our environment, but, worse, attacking our mokopuna.
civility.explanation: Frames the Prime Minister's programme as deliberate attacks on Māori, the environment and children — an imputation of bad faith aimed at him, though it stops short of a personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Nicola Willis does not understand how important the language is.
civility.explanation: A judgement about a named member's personal understanding rather than about the merits of the policy she announced.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Because, as you can see, Winston has gone off track somewhat and Jonesy just can’t shut his mouth.
civility.explanation: "Jonesy just can't shut his mouth" is a personal jibe at a named member; "gone off track" is a judgement about another named member's conduct rather than his position.
civility.subject: speaker
