veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 transport policy documents and the subsequent Government Policy Statement on land transport / NZTA National Land Transport Programme allocations; true if an additional pothole-repair or road-maintenance fund of approximately $500 million is committed, false if no such allocation exists or the figure is materially different.

specificity.statement: New Zealand’s tax system has ranked 136 th out of 162 countries for promoting equity—that is the reality.
specificity.explanation: A precise, sourceable ranking with both position and denominator; someone could go and look it up. Whether it is accurate is a separate question.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Not even $500 million was spent in the entirety of Northland on roads over the 11-year period—nine years of that was under the National Government, and they are planning to spend over $2 billion for an extra kilometre lane in central Wellington because they believe that it will make it 30 seconds faster for them to drive from the airport to the Beehive.
specificity.explanation: Two named figures, a named region, a named period and a named project — precise enough that a reader could go and check both halves against spending records.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s wrong, and it’s an inequity that this Government could address, but they will choose not to because, ultimately, they represent the elite interests of the landed gentry—those who own property and want to continue to have the benefit of untaxed capital gains where that wealth becomes concentrated, and that means we can’t afford to invest in public services.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point here — the untaxed treatment of capital gains and its fiscal consequence — but most of the sentence's weight is carried by characterising who the Government represents rather than by the tax mechanism itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: However well-meaning many of those individuals might be, the reality is this is a Government that was bought and paid for by vested interest by the super-rich who want to continue to maintain a hierarchy, who want to roll back the protections for workers because it means that they can have cheaper labour to make bigger profits.
focus.explanation: No policy, measure or figure is named. The whole sentence is about who the other side really is and whose interests they serve — the general character of the opposing parties rather than anything before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What a hash they made of it—what an absolute hash of it.
focus.explanation: A blanket verdict on the previous Government's performance with no policy, programme, figure or outcome named. Nothing here is specific enough to be scrutiny; it is the other team in general.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It’s wrong, and it’s an inequity that this Government could address, but they will choose not to because, ultimately, they represent the elite interests of the landed gentry—those who own property and want to continue to have the benefit of untaxed capital gains where that wealth becomes concentrated, and that means we can’t afford to invest in public services.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the incoming National-led Government will not act on the taxation of income from capital assets during its term. This is a prediction about another party's future conduct, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Tax legislation and Budget/tax-policy announcements from December 2023 to the end of the parliamentary term: false if the Government enacts or formally announces a capital gains tax or an equivalent broad tax on income from capital assets; true if no such measure is enacted or announced by the end of the term.

civility.statement: They are ignorant fools, this Government, and I would love to be able to say that we could work with them to propose some economically rational projects that would actually improve the economic productivity of our cities, that would improve the health and wellbeing of our people and of our children.
civility.explanation: 'Ignorant fools' is a direct attack on the intelligence of the members opposite, not on their transport policy. The policy argument sits alongside it, but the insult lands on people.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: You don’t believe that because you’re a bunch of landlords who want to keep getting richer at the expense of everyone else.
civility.explanation: Directly addressed to the members opposite, imputing that their stated position is held out of personal financial self-interest. A personal attack on motive rather than an engagement with the tax argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I would suggest that they might say that you are delusional and that we do need good infrastructure.
civility.explanation: Calls the other member delusional, only lightly distanced by putting the word in the mouths of hypothetical constituents. The target is her state of mind, not her argument.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think it’s because those three parties can agree on very little, and that’s why their agenda is not one that is framed in the positive of common aspirations, but one framed in the negative; one that will take us backwards.
focus.explanation: The weight of the point is the coalition parties' internal disagreement and what they are 'really like', offered as an explanation for the tone of the Speech from the Throne. It gestures at the Government's agenda but names no measure, figure or outcome, so it sits close to party framing rather than policy scrutiny.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I don’t think the National Party caucus—the grown-ups in the room—wants to be the laughing stock of this country, but that’s what you’re going to hear this summer when you go to your barbecues back in your electorate.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's standing and internal composition — who the 'grown-ups' are and how the public regards them. No policy, figure or outcome is named; strip out the material about the other side and nothing remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We were interested to see that the very important commitment to primary care—which is the backbone of our health system—made by the ACT Party, didn’t make it into the coalition agreement, but they dangled a 13 percent funding increase for general practice in front of them during the campaign.
focus.explanation: Named party commitment, a named figure and a named document — an opposition MP holding a governing party to a specific campaign promise. This is scrutiny, not tribalism, and belongs at the top of the scale.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: And to the member opposite, I can also reassure him that 70 percent of smokers also want to quit.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 70 percent of current smokers in New Zealand want to stop smoking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Health Survey / ASH Year 10 and adult smoking survey data on the proportion of current smokers reporting they want to quit; true if published survey data puts it at or near 70%, false if materially lower (e.g. under 60%).

veracity.statement: These laws would have been tremendously beneficial, and I was shocked, like many New Zealanders, to hear that the Government proposed to repeal these laws in order to fund their tax cuts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the incoming Government's reason for repealing the smokefree legislation was to raise revenue for its tax package.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National–ACT and National–NZ First coalition agreements, National's 2023 fiscal plan, and Ministers' contemporaneous statements; true if the fiscal plan or Ministers book the tobacco excise revenue retained by repeal as a funding source for the tax package, false if the repeal is costed separately from and not relied on by the tax package.

veracity.statement: We were interested to see that the very important commitment to primary care—which is the backbone of our health system—made by the ACT Party, didn’t make it into the coalition agreement, but they dangled a 13 percent funding increase for general practice in front of them during the campaign.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that ACT campaigned on a 13 percent funding increase for general practice, and that no equivalent primary care commitment appears in the coalition agreement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: ACT's published 2023 health policy for the 13 percent general practice funding figure, and the text of the National–ACT coalition agreement (24 November 2023) for the primary care commitment; true if ACT's policy states a ~13% increase and the coalition agreement contains no corresponding primary care funding commitment, false if the figure differs materially or the agreement carries such a commitment.

veracity.statement: It was written by the Vice-Chancellor of Waikato University, not by the National Party.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that National's third medical school policy was authored by the Vice-Chancellor of the University of Waikato rather than developed by the National Party itself.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Documents and reporting on the origin of National's 2023 third medical school policy, including any Waikato University proposal and National's own policy development records; true if the policy document originated with the Waikato Vice-Chancellor, false if National developed it internally with Waikato input only as a stakeholder.

veracity.statement: We will hold the Government to account on its commitment to have modern medicines more available in our communities—yes, for cancer, but also available medicines being delivered by pharmacies, as we have done by removing the $5 co-payment across the country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Labour government removed the $5 prescription co-payment nationwide.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2023 documents and Pharmac/Ministry of Health records on the $5 prescription charge; true if the charge was removed for all patients from 1 July 2023, false if it remained in place or was removed only for some groups.

divination.statement: Those people who hold up our community—the Cancer Society people, the health workers, the principals of our schools—are opposed, and many of them have mobilised in a rally that will be held here in Parliament next week.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that a public rally against the smokefree repeal, organised by health and community groups, will take place at Parliament in the week following 7 December 2023.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: News reporting and Parliament grounds event records for 11–15 December 2023; true if a public rally opposing the smokefree repeal was held at Parliament in that week, false if no such rally took place.

civility.statement: To be honest, I almost feel sorry for him, because I’m not sure if the Minister of Health has ever had such a bad start to his job.
civility.explanation: Mock pity directed at the Minister personally rather than at the policy — condescension about how he is performing as a person, not criticism of the repeal itself. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Within 24 hours, the internet has named the Minister of Health “Dr Cigareti” and named the finance Minister “Nicotine Willis”.
civility.explanation: Relays and amplifies mocking nicknames attached to two named colleagues. The target is the individuals, not the policy — mockery of the person, which the re-anchored scale treats as a genuine failure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I thought that speech before was more self-reflection than anything else, but someone whom I greatly respect on the other side of the House is the Hon Peeni Henare, who spoke yesterday.
civility.explanation: A mild dismissal of a colleague's speech as self-regarding — pointed and slightly personal, but glancing, and immediately paired with genuine respect for another member. Edges toward the person without landing on them.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Hon Julie Anne Genter—you’ve got to admire her passion, but she sometimes lets that get away with her, and just controlling her emotions a bit more might make her points a lot more marked than they were.
civility.explanation: Wrapped in a compliment, but the substance is condescension about a named member's emotional self-control rather than about anything she argued. The target is the person's temperament, not her case.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And I am also going to call out the casting of doubt on these measures, because that is a typical tactic from the tobacco industry: to say that something won’t work, to say that there’s some minor objection that means it can’t be implemented when the policy benefit that comes from the implementation is just so great—this Government needs to take responsibility for this.
rigor.explanation: Genetic fallacy: objections to the measures are dismissed by attributing them to the source (tobacco industry tactics) rather than by answering them. That an argument resembles one the tobacco industry makes says nothing about whether the implementation objection holds.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Ordinary people up and down the country are laughing at you because of the ridiculousness of funding your tax cuts by making more people smoke.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to ridicule and popularity: the offered ground for the policy being wrong is that ordinary people are laughing at it. The statement does engage the actual mechanism (repeal revenue funding tax cuts), so there is an inference to assess — and it rests entirely on public mockery rather than on any consequence of the mechanism.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Calling people fools is not a way to win an argument. Just because they disagree with you does not mean they don’t have a valid point of view, and I think we should all just remember that when we’re making our speeches.
rigor.explanation: A valid inference: disagreement alone does not establish that a position is unsound, therefore an insult does not discharge the argument. The conclusion follows from the premise offered, with no fallacy — it is in fact a correct identification of ad hominem.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: On the property, they’re going to walk off the range and start shooting animals. This range doesn’t need this licence—it’s needless, it’s pointless, it’s wasteful spending, and it’s all those sorts of things that my colleague the Hon Andrew Bayly was talking about before—how businesses are being dragged down by those needless costs.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real regulation: because hunting happens off the range anyway, the range licence adds nothing. But the premise only shows the range is not the only place shooting occurs, not that range safety standards are pointless, and one constituent's case is then generalised to 'businesses' at large — a hasty generalisation on top of a gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yes, that’s right—$15.7 billion will be roughly $30 billion by the time it’s built.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows arithmetically from the premises he has just offered ($15.7b estimate, 98% average overrun). The remaining gap is applying a worldwide average to one specific project as though it were a point estimate, but given its assumptions the inference is sound.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s exactly like light rail, but it’s also had a perverse effect on the electricity prices today, and we’ve seen the forward prices in electricity much higher than the market would suggest otherwise they should be.
rigor.explanation: A causal claim — Onslow is why forward electricity prices are elevated — supported only by the two things coinciding. A deterred-investment mechanism is gestured at later ('sword of Damocles'), but nothing is offered to rule out the other drivers of forward prices, so the inference is largely post hoc.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If you want to go backwards, it’s virtually impossible to maintain things. So I put to you, let’s get moving forward, and we might make some progress.
rigor.explanation: False analogy. Facts about bicycle balance carry no weight at all on whether a legislative programme should repeal or add measures; the metaphor is doing the work an argument would have to do.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yes, it’s expensive. Yes, a lot of work is still to be done, but just tossing it out is handing to the existing electricity generators and gen-tailers, monopoly, monopsony rights to make super-profits—and we’ll wait and see.
rigor.explanation: Concedes the strongest point against his position and still offers a mechanism: Onslow functions as a competitive lever, so removing it restores pricing power to incumbent gentailers. The gap is that nothing is offered to show the lever would be effective enough to discipline prices, and 'monopoly, monopsony' overstates a concentrated market.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Are we going to ban people in rugby clubs who might have a patch on the back of their jersey?
rigor.explanation: A slippery slope resting on a false equivalence: it treats any patch as indistinguishable from gang insignia, when the definitional question of what counts as a gang patch is precisely what the legislation would answer. The definitional problem he raises is real, but this way of putting it does not follow.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s well intentioned, I get that, but all the shooting ranges—there’s quite a lot of perverse regulation in it whereby the owner of the gun has to be the licensed person transporting it in a vehicle, for example, so that those people in firearms clubs can’t transport firearms easily between clubs for shooting competitions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the post-2019 firearms rules require the gun's owner (not merely any licence holder) to be the person transporting it, preventing club members from carrying each other's firearms to competitions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Arms Act 1983 and the Arms Regulations/Arms Legislation Act 2020 provisions on possession and transport of firearms: true if the rules require the registered owner personally to be the licensed person transporting the firearm in a vehicle; false if any licence holder of the appropriate endorsement may lawfully transport another person's firearm.

veracity.statement: What’s been forgotten is it was going to cost $15.7 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Lake Onslow pumped-hydro scheme carried an official cost estimate of $15.7 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZ Battery Project / MBIE detailed business case costing for the Lake Onslow pumped-hydro option: true if the published capital cost estimate is approximately $15.7 billion, false if the estimate is materially different.

veracity.statement: The average cost overrun of a large hydro project is 98 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific average cost overrun figure for large hydro projects worldwide, and attributes the research to the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment's published work on the NZ Battery/Lake Onslow proposal and the international large-dam cost-overrun literature it draws on (e.g. Ansar et al., 'Should we build more large dams?'): true if the reported mean cost overrun for large hydro projects is approximately 98%, false if the figure is materially different or if no such PCE finding exists.

veracity.statement: Yes, we do appreciate the farmers—50 percent increase in export revenue in the primary sector when we were in office, through COVID and many other challenges.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that primary-sector export revenue rose by 50 percent over the 2017–2023 Labour government's term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries food and fibre export revenue for the years ending June 2017 and June 2023: true if the increase over that period is approximately 50%, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: In fact, the ACT Party and the Taxpayers’ Union brought out someone saying that the 29 percent—or might be about 30 percent now—is way below that in the UK under a Conservative Government of 49 percent.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim made by a visiting speaker: that New Zealand's public spending at ~29–30% of GDP is far below the UK's ~49% under a Conservative government.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.subject_name: ACT Party and Taxpayers’ Union guest speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: UK ONS/OBR total managed expenditure as a share of GDP for the 2022/23 or 2023/24 financial year, compared with NZ Treasury core Crown expenses as a share of GDP for the same period: true if the UK figure is approximately 49% and the NZ figure approximately 29–30%, false if either is materially different.

veracity.statement: We had suffered underfunding in road maintenance because the previous National Government had increased the weight of trucks and had a sweat-the-assets campaign that resulted in underfunding and a degradation of our roading network that continues today in spite of the huge amount of increasing money that we in Government put on.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two things about the 2008–2017 National government: that it raised permitted truck weights, and that it ran a deliberate 'sweat the assets' approach that left road maintenance underfunded.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2010 amendments to the Vehicle Dimensions and Mass Rule permitting High Productivity Motor Vehicles, plus NZTA/Waka Kotahi state highway and local road maintenance funding levels across the 2008–2017 National Land Transport Programmes: true if truck mass limits were raised and maintenance funding fell in real terms over that period, false if either did not occur.

civility.statement: One of the other things that I think is going to be really good is we are going to reverse the union-inspired, innovation-stifling, productivity-lowering pay agreements, also known as the fair pay agreements—that’s the new name for it, by the way.
civility.explanation: Loaded, dismissive language aimed entirely at a policy (the Fair Pay Agreements regime) and its supposed effects. No person is attacked or impugned. Under the re-anchored scale, brutal criticism of a policy is the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What’s been forgotten is it was going to cost $15.7 billion.
specificity.explanation: A single named project attached to a precise dollar figure that anyone can look up in the business case. Checkable and actionable; it lacks only the source and date of the estimate.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They have literally been ground down, and the relief from them—they were set up as public enemy number one, and it actually really hurt those people.
focus.explanation: A characterisation of how the previous government regarded farmers, with no measure, cost or outcome named. There is a real grievance underneath about regulatory cost, but as stated the weight is on the other side's attitude rather than on any policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is a backtrack Speech from the Throne from a backtrack Government.
focus.explanation: A wordplay label applied to the government as a whole. No measure, figure or outcome is named — the content is entirely a characterisation of the other side, which is what Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The National - ACT - New Zealand First coalition has offered no support and no idea how they’re going to support councils to put in place vital water infrastructure that each and every New Zealander needs.
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure (repeal of the Water Services Entities Act 2022) and a specific gap in its replacement — how councils will fund water infrastructure. This is scrutiny of a named policy, not party-bashing; it loses a little only because 'no idea' shades into characterising the coalition rather than the plan.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: A very good investment by Waikato University in Steven Joyce—$1 million paid to him over three years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Waikato University paid Steven Joyce $1 million over a three-year period for work on its medical school proposal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waikato University's disclosed payments (annual reports / OIA release) to Steven Joyce or his firm for medical school advisory and advocacy work; true if the total is around $1 million over roughly three years, false if materially lower or if no such engagement existed.

veracity.statement: We wrote out a cheque for $35 million just to keep them afloat, and in fact there were other polytechs up and down this country—up and down this country—that were going broke.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the previous government paid roughly $35 million to keep Tai Poutini Polytechnic solvent, and that other polytechnics were also insolvent at the time.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission funding records and Tai Poutini Polytechnic annual reports for the relevant years; true if a bailout of about $35 million was made, false if the sum is materially different or no such payment appears.

veracity.statement: Well, all I say is: let’s see you be honest, because last time, those waiting lists were manipulated so the figures looked great but the patients didn’t.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the previous National government elective surgery waiting lists were manipulated so that reported figures improved without patients being treated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health and Auditor-General reviews of elective surgery waiting list management between 2008 and 2017; true if official findings record patients being removed from or kept off lists in ways that improved reported wait times, false if reviews found no such practice.

veracity.statement: I hate to point this out, but the Labour Government didn’t do it for six years, and they did vote down my motion on Statehood, but it’s nice to see us all by consensus recognise that Palestine exists.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2017–2023 Labour government did not recognise Palestinian statehood and that the House voted down her earlier motion on Palestinian statehood.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard record of Ghahraman's notice of motion on Palestinian statehood and the vote taken on it, plus MFAT statements on New Zealand's recognition position 2017–2023; true if the motion was declined or defeated with Labour opposed and no recognition occurred, false if the motion was agreed to or no such motion exists.

veracity.statement: It’s not so nice that it took the deaths of 7,000 children—that we know of—to do it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that at least 7,000 children had been killed in Gaza by the date of the speech, 7 December 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Gaza Ministry of Health casualty figures as reported by UN OCHA for early December 2023, disaggregated by age; true if reported child fatalities were at or above roughly 7,000, false if materially below.

veracity.statement: It’s over because every 10 minutes in Gaza a child is murdered.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a rate of child deaths in Gaza of approximately one every ten minutes at the time of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: UN OCHA / WHO reported child fatality counts in Gaza divided by elapsed days for the period cited; true if the implied rate is about one child per ten minutes (roughly 144 per day), false if the rate is materially lower.

veracity.statement: In the first four weeks, we surpassed the death toll of children that we’d seen in Ukraine in almost a year.
veracity.explanation: Compares child fatalities in Gaza in the first four weeks after 7 October 2023 with child fatalities in Ukraine over roughly the first year of the full-scale invasion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: UN OHCHR verified child casualty figures for Ukraine from February 2022 to early 2023 against UN OCHA / Gaza Ministry of Health child fatality figures for 7 October to 7 November 2023; true if the Gaza four-week figure exceeds the Ukraine year figure, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: It was a National Government that stood up for Palestine in the General Assembly of the United Nations and gave Palestine official status in that forum.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand under a National-led government supported the UN General Assembly resolution granting Palestine official (non-member observer state) status.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: UN General Assembly voting record for resolution 67/19 of 29 November 2012 on Palestine's non-member observer state status, and the identity of the New Zealand government at that date; true if New Zealand voted in favour while National led the government, false if it abstained, opposed, or a different government was in office.

civility.statement: Well, isn’t that a great investment of taxpayers’ money to Steven Joyce to lobby for a medical school that has been investigated and in fact is just not viable because of the scale.
civility.explanation: Sarcasm aimed at a named individual, casting him as a paid lobbyist rather than engaging the merits of the medical school case. Imputes motive to the person, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, all I say is: let’s see you be honest, because last time, those waiting lists were manipulated so the figures looked great but the patients didn’t.
civility.explanation: Pre-emptively imputes dishonesty to the ministers opposite ('let’s see you be honest'). Not a direct insult, but it attributes bad faith rather than testing the target itself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And we have to hold that they have more in common with the kids that we know, the little ones that we hold close in our lives, than they have in common with the likes of Brian Tamaki, with the likes of the Biden administration, and little comms people writing up statements that fall short again and again—fall short to uphold our humanity.
civility.explanation: 'The likes of' and 'little comms people' are dismissive of named individuals and of staff as people rather than of any position they hold. Pointed and sneering without landing a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is outrageous, unethical, and it’s a measure of the backtrack Government that we now have in place.
focus.explanation: Follows a real policy point about the Smokefree Environments amendments, but this statement itself carries no mechanism, figure or outcome — the weight is the 'backtrack Government' framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Just do an analysis in a few months’ time of where the donations came from, who donated, and what resultant policies have come into this House.
focus.explanation: Invites an inference about the other side's donors and motives. No policy, measure or outcome is named — the content is entirely about what the other party is 'really like'.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I hate to point this out, but the Labour Government didn’t do it for six years, and they did vote down my motion on Statehood, but it’s nice to see us all by consensus recognise that Palestine exists.
focus.explanation: Names a specific motion and a specific recorded outcome — accountability for a concrete parliamentary act, not general party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We wrote out a cheque for $35 million just to keep them afloat, and in fact there were other polytechs up and down this country—up and down this country—that were going broke.
specificity.explanation: A named institution, a named amount and a stated purpose; someone could go and check the appropriation.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have to stand strong, as Aotearoa New Zealand has done in the past, on an independent, principled platform calling for immediate, permanent, unconditional ceasefire—calling on our friends, on our allies, on our trading partners, on our Five Eyes network, on the family of nations in the Commonwealth, and on our Pasifika neighbourhood to do the same.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete ask (an immediate, permanent, unconditional ceasefire) and the specific forums through which it should be pressed, but supplies no timeframe or instrument beyond advocacy.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The model had failed, and so what we attempted to do was bring some alignment and some economies of scale.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (the pre-merger model had failed) is supported by the evidence just offered — multiple polytechnics running out of money — and the remedy proposed follows from it. A real, if compressed, inference; the causal step from insolvency to 'the model' is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Let’s see what happens on the ground, because the big ideological approach that people should pay less tax is the one that leaves this country a huge hole and deficit in infrastructure, as we’re seeing, as we’ve seen in transport, as we’ve seen in water care.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy — tax reduction causes an infrastructure deficit — but the link is asserted and the supporting examples (transport, water) are named without any figures or mechanism connecting them to tax policy. A gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s only been with decades upon decades of dehumanisation that this current atrocity is able to happen with so much silence.
rigor.explanation: A single-cause historical claim offered as the explanation for present events, with nothing supplied to connect the asserted cause to the effect. Assertion in place of inference.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Let’s see us go back to the failed, dysfunctional, disjointed polytech model that we have. That’s what this Government will do.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the incoming government will disestablish Te Pūkenga and return vocational education to separate regional polytechnics. A prediction about another party's action, not a promise about the speaker's own.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Legislation and Cabinet decisions on the future of Te Pūkenga; true if Te Pūkenga is disestablished and standalone regional polytechnics are re-established, false if Te Pūkenga remains as a single national institution.

veracity.statement: Hamilton East is home to the world famous Hamilton Gardens, a 54-hectare public garden that was once a rubbish dump but now has 23 international gardens, 1.2 million visitors a year, and is in the top 1 percent of Tripadvisor’s international travel experiences in the world.
veracity.explanation: Asserts four checkable facts about Hamilton Gardens: its area (54 ha), its former use as a rubbish dump, the number of international gardens (23), annual visitors (1.2 million), and a Tripadvisor ranking claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hamilton City Council / Hamilton Gardens published figures for site area, garden count and annual visitor numbers, and Tripadvisor's own Travellers' Choice ranking data. True if the area is ~54 ha, the site was a former municipal refuse tip, the international garden count is 23, and annual visitation is ~1.2 million; false if any of these figures is materially different (e.g. visitors well under 1 million, or fewer than 23 international gardens).

veracity.statement: The University of Waikato’s Artificial Intelligence Institute has created some of the world’s most popular open-source tools for machine learning, and imagine, if we can, housing New Zealand’s long overdue and first graduate medical school.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the University of Waikato's AI Institute produced open-source machine learning tools that are among the world's most popular, and (implicitly) that New Zealand currently has no graduate-entry medical school.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: University of Waikato AI Institute publication and software records, plus download/citation counts for its open-source releases (notably the WEKA toolkit). True if a Waikato-originated open-source ML toolkit ranks among widely-used ML software by downloads or citations; false if no such tool exists or its usage is marginal. Second limb: Medical Council of NZ / university records on whether any NZ medical school offered graduate-entry-only training as at December 2023.

veracity.statement: Only last week, I had the privilege of attending the opening of New Zealand’s first accessible and inclusive playground in Claudelands, which removes all barriers for those with physical and neurological disabilities, by the Magical Bridge Trust.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Magical Bridge playground at Claudelands, opened in late November/early December 2023, was New Zealand's first accessible and inclusive playground, and that it removes all barriers for people with physical and neurological disabilities.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hamilton City Council and Magical Bridge Trust opening records for the Claudelands playground, plus records of earlier accessible/inclusive playgrounds in New Zealand (e.g. council-built accessible playgrounds predating December 2023). True if no comparable fully-inclusive playground opened in NZ before it; false if an earlier NZ playground was built and marketed to the same inclusive-design standard.

specificity.statement: Hamilton East is home to the world famous Hamilton Gardens, a 54-hectare public garden that was once a rubbish dump but now has 23 international gardens, 1.2 million visitors a year, and is in the top 1 percent of Tripadvisor’s international travel experiences in the world.
specificity.explanation: Carries an area figure, a garden count, an annual visitor number and a named ranking source — every element is concrete and checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are moving on from the binary rates and development contribution models that have stymied our ability to unlock growth faster, and we will now enable special purpose vehicles, infrastructure funding and financing tools, tolls, overseas investment where appropriate, and value-capture models, which can be appropriately deployed on a case by case basis.
specificity.explanation: Names five distinct funding mechanisms (SPVs, IFF tools, tolls, overseas investment, value capture) and the models being replaced, so the direction is checkable — but supplies no amounts, thresholds or timeframe for any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I believe in less government, personal choice, and responsibility—a Government that sets up the right macro policy settings that enables success, and then gets out of the way.
specificity.explanation: A statement of governing philosophy carrying no checkable content: "less government", "the right macro policy settings" and "gets out of the way" name no measure, figure, mechanism or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Long-term projections forecast this site to remove 65,000 long-haul truck journeys off the road—with an associated 66 percent reduction in carbon emissions for each container movement—for international companies like Maersk, and, of course, New Zealand’s distribution hub for Kmart—which moved out of Auckland, just to comment on that—and New Zealand’s own Waitomo Group.
divination.explanation: Relays a forecast that the Ruakura Inland Port will, once developed, displace 65,000 long-haul truck journeys and cut emissions per container movement by 66 percent. The source of the projections is not named in the speech.
divination.subject: unclear
divination.falsification_criterion: Tainui Group Holdings / Ruakura Superhub freight reporting and NZTA or Ministry of Transport road-freight data for the Waikato corridor. True if annual long-haul truck journeys displaced by rail-served movements through the inland port reach approximately 65,000 and a per-container emissions reduction of around 66 percent is documented; false if the displaced-journey figure is materially below that once the site is substantially built out.

civility.statement: More recently, as a Hamilton city councillor, I understand the challenges of local government and I have seen how central government has disrespected local government for the last six years with disingenuous engagement and how we must do it differently and work together to achieve good and sustainable outcomes.
civility.explanation: "Disingenuous engagement" imputes bad faith rather than merely criticising the previous government's process, which is a real civility cost. It is tempered by being aimed at an institution rather than any individual and by ending on a cooperative proposal, so it sits above a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If employers are doing well, then employees have the opportunity to thrive also. We can’t penalise one and not expect it to impact on the other.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about employment policy, but the conditional is asserted rather than supported — no evidence or mechanism connects employer prosperity to employee outcomes — and the second sentence sets up a false dichotomy in which any cost imposed on employers necessarily harms employees.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And I know some people don’t start at the start line, and I know some people aren’t born with the same opportunity. But if they have that desire, the coaches, the mentors, the community leaders, and the aunties and the uncles, the business community will emerge.
rigor.explanation: Concedes unequal starting positions and then concludes that support networks will materialise for anyone who wants them badly enough. Nothing is offered to bridge the gap — it is a bare assertion resting on an appeal to optimism, and it does not follow from the premise it just conceded.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Inflation has been out of the Reserve Bank’s target range now for 2½ long years, and New Zealanders are doing it tough in a cost of living crisis.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that annual CPI inflation has been continuously above the Reserve Bank's 1–3% target band for roughly two and a half years as at December 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly CPI annual inflation series and the RBNZ 1–3% target band: true if annual inflation first exceeded 3% around mid-2021 and remained above 3% through the December 2023 quarter; false if the band was re-entered at any point in that period or if the breach began materially later than mid-2021.

veracity.statement: Instead of just delivering income tax relief, they experimented with broken policies like the cost of living payment and, during their term in office, managed to increase Government spending by 80 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that government spending rose by 80 percent over the 2017–2023 Labour-led government's term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenditure figures for the 2017/18 and 2022/23 fiscal years: true if the increase is approximately 80% (say 70–90%), false if materially outside that range on the standard core Crown expenses measure.

veracity.statement: Is the Government not just wasting the House’s time removing the Reserve Bank’s dual mandate, as the governor said in response to my questioning in 2022 that it had not changed their approach to monetary policy and targeting inflation—virtue-signalling, if you will?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Governor of the Reserve Bank told her, in select committee questioning in 2022, that the dual mandate had not changed the bank's approach to monetary policy.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Finance and Expenditure Committee transcript / Hansard record of the Reserve Bank's 2022 appearance: true if the Governor stated the employment objective had not changed the bank's monetary policy approach, false if no such exchange occurred or the answer was materially different.

veracity.statement: I hear them scoffing over here—brought in all that Indonesian coal, trying to excuse themselves, and not even using New Zealand coal, which would have been a better, cleaner substitute.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the previous government New Zealand imported Indonesian coal rather than using domestic coal. The 'better, cleaner substitute' half is a judgement; the checkable part is the imports.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ coal import statistics and Genesis Energy/Huntly fuel disclosures for 2018–2023: true if substantial Indonesian coal imports occurred over that period alongside available domestic supply, false if imports were negligible or not sourced from Indonesia.

veracity.statement: It hardly got there, and when the handbrake went off, they ran amok and in the last year have brought in 118,000 immigrants—that’s a massive record for this country—with no infrastructure, no houses, no health, no nothing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 118,000 migrants arrived in the most recent year and that this is a record for New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration estimates for the year to about October 2023: true if annual net migration is approximately 118,000 and is the highest on record, false if the figure or the record claim is materially wrong on the measure a reasonable reader would take (net migration).

veracity.statement: Does he agree with Winston Peters in 2017 that “last year, 465,000 hectares of land was sold to foreigners. That’s up to four times on the year before. We in New Zealand First are going to stop land sales to foreigners and house sales to foreigners who don’t come and live here.”; if not, why not?
veracity.explanation: Relays a 2017 claim by Winston Peters that 465,000 hectares of land were sold to foreign buyers in the preceding year, up roughly fourfold on the year before. The checkable content is the relayed figure and the quotation's accuracy.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Overseas Investment Office annual decision statistics for 2016 and 2015, plus the Hansard or media record of the 2017 statement: true if approvals for the year covered were about 465,000 hectares and roughly four times the prior year and Peters said this, false if the land area or the multiple is materially different or the quotation is not his.

veracity.statement: Does he agree with the statement made by then Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters in 2018 that the oil and gas ban “makes sense” and that introducing the ban was the change that New Zealanders wanted?
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim about what Winston Peters said in 2018 — that the offshore oil and gas exploration ban 'makes sense' and reflected the change New Zealanders wanted. The checkable content is whether he said it.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2018 public record (Hansard, press conference transcripts or contemporaneous reporting) of Winston Peters' statements on the offshore oil and gas exploration ban: true if he used the quoted words in support of the ban, false if no such statement exists or his stated position was materially different.

specificity.statement: Instead of just delivering income tax relief, they experimented with broken policies like the cost of living payment and, during their term in office, managed to increase Government spending by 80 percent.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific policy (the cost of living payment) and gives a checkable magnitude (80 percent over a defined period), though no dollar figures or baseline are supplied.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re already taking actions through our 100-day plan, including ending the ute tax, abolishing the Government’s broken Resource Management Act reforms, restoring flexibility in the labour market, and cancelling Labour’s plans for fuel tax hikes next year.
specificity.explanation: Names four distinct, identifiable actions against a defined 100-day timeframe, but supplies no amounts, dates or mechanisms for any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Now, as the Reserve Bank wrestles with trying to bring inflation back under control, our Government will clarify the bank’s objectives and support public confidence that inflation can and will be returned below 3 percent.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that annual inflation will return below 3 percent. No timeframe is given, so the earliest fair judgement is over the Reserve Bank's stated medium term.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly CPI annual inflation: true if any quarterly print by the resolve-by date records annual inflation below 3.0%, false if annual inflation remains at or above 3.0% throughout.

divination.statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister: right now at COP 28, they are wrestling with that very issue, and they’ll be probably working days longer than that because they haven’t come to an agreement.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the COP28 negotiations will run past their scheduled close because no agreement has yet been reached.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The UNFCCC record of COP28's scheduled closing date (12 December 2023) against the date the final plenary actually concluded: true if the conference ran days beyond the scheduled close, false if it closed on or before schedule.

rigor.statement: Is the Government not just wasting the House’s time removing the Reserve Bank’s dual mandate, as the governor said in response to my questioning in 2022 that it had not changed their approach to monetary policy and targeting inflation—virtue-signalling, if you will?
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure itself: if the dual mandate did not change the bank's operating approach, removing it changes nothing. The step from 'no change in approach' to 'wasting the House's time' leans on a single authority's testimony and ignores the credibility/signalling rationale the Government offered, so there is a genuine gap — but it is an argument about the policy, not a swipe.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Unlike what the previous finance Minister said, it is not foreign grown; it’s home grown, and massively so, because of their squanderous expenditure.
rigor.explanation: A causal conclusion — inflation is domestically generated and caused by the previous government's spending — offered with nothing to support it beyond the assertion itself. No data on tradables versus non-tradables inflation, no mechanism, and the rival explanation the previous Minister gave is dismissed rather than answered. This is an argument about fiscal policy, so it is assessable, but the inference is bare.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But, of course, where new information or evidence emerges, we acknowledge that and don’t just carry on like a bigoted lefty shill.
civility.explanation: Answering a question from the Green co-leader, the speaker characterises the questioner's side as a 'bigoted lefty shill' — abuse aimed at character and motive rather than at any argument. The insult is the speaker's own conduct regardless of who it targets.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because like everything the Labour Party put its hands on, they didn’t interpret it properly.
focus.explanation: The question was about the Overseas Investment Act commitment; the answer names no measure, figure or outcome and consists entirely of a general characterisation of the other party's competence. No individual is insulted, so this is a Focus failure rather than a Civility one.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does the Acting Prime Minister agree with David Seymour that “you can’t trust Winston Peters, and a lot of things will be much, much harder than they otherwise would.”, and that Winston Peters is “just a muppet; the problem is he can’t work with anyone. The good news is he’s going down on flames; he’s yesterday’s man.”, and, if not, why not?
focus.explanation: The question names no policy, measure, figure or outcome. Its entire content is the coalition parties' opinions of each other — the internal-division case Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But they hardly got the job and they thought they got there by themselves. And when the handbrake left, what a mess they were.
focus.explanation: Wholly about the other party's character and its dependence on NZ First — no policy, measure or outcome is named. Nothing survives if the party-framing is removed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Given our coalition Government has begun work on a new rule, I wanted to ensure road-controlling authorities avoid wasting public money—something the Opposition doesn’t care about—on finalising speed management plans only to have to revisit these plans under a new rule.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point about sequencing regulatory work, but a content-free swipe at the Opposition's attitude to public money is inserted into the middle of it.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does the Acting Prime Minister agree with David Seymour that “you can’t trust Winston Peters, and a lot of things will be much, much harder than they otherwise would.”, and that Winston Peters is “just a muppet; the problem is he can’t work with anyone. The good news is he’s going down on flames; he’s yesterday’s man.”, and, if not, why not?
civility.explanation: Hipkins does not author the insults, but he chooses to put “muppet” and “yesterday's man” to the House as the vehicle of his question, deploying mockery of a named individual rather than contesting anything he has done.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And if I may say to the member, Opposition does appear to suit him.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe about the member's diminished standing rather than anything he has argued — mockery aimed at the individual, not at a position.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Has she sought advice from officials on their preferred option of minimum employment standards to ensure there is no race to the bottom for low-wage workers, and, if not, is that because she is more interested in disproven right-wing ideology than in lifting wages?
civility.explanation: The first half is a legitimate question about advice sought; the second imputes a motive to the Minister personally — that she is driven by ideology rather than an interest in wages — which is an attack on her good faith rather than on her policy.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: My evidence for that is in their first week of being a parliamentary Opposition, they asked 6,000 questions, which kind of suggests in 2020 to 2023, they had no answers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Labour lodged 6,000 parliamentary questions in its first week as Opposition (early December 2023).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliament written-questions register for the week beginning 5 December 2023: true if questions lodged by Labour members that week total approximately 6,000; false if the count is materially lower (e.g. in the hundreds).

veracity.statement: As the member well knows, the statement he is referring to was made before I was sworn in as the Minister of Finance.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the quoted remark about the smokefree legislation's ~$1 billion impact predates her swearing-in as Minister of Finance.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The date of the quoted Willis statement against the date of the Sixth National Government's swearing-in (27 November 2023): true if the remark was made before that date, false if made on or after it.

veracity.statement: I note that during his time as finance Minister, he collected hundreds of millions of dollars in tobacco tax revenue, which was used for a wide range of purposes, including health and education services and Working for Families payments.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that tobacco excise revenue in the hundreds of millions was collected during Grant Robertson's tenure as Minister of Finance and applied to general government spending.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/NZ Customs tobacco excise and excise-equivalent duty revenue for the 2017/18–2022/23 fiscal years: true if annual revenue was at least in the hundreds of millions and flowed to the Crown account rather than being hypothecated, false if materially lower or ring-fenced.

veracity.statement: I’ve been advised by officials that, for serious and violent offenders who pleaded guilty in 2021–22, their best estimate is that between 4,600 and 7,800 offenders were issued with a sentencing discount of greater than 40 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that officials advised a best estimate of 4,600–7,800 serious and violent offenders pleading guilty in 2021–22 received sentence discounts above 40 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice advice to the Minister of Justice (obtainable via proactive release or OIA) on sentencing discounts: true if it contains an estimate in the 4,600–7,800 range on that basis, false if the advice gives a materially different range or no such estimate.

veracity.statement: I’m pleased to inform the House that the coalition Government is prioritising its plan to restore law and order after six years of a Government being focused on reducing prison numbers without reducing crime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that over the previous government's six years the prison population was deliberately reduced while crime was not reduced.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections prison muster and Police recorded-victimisation statistics for 2017–2023, plus the previous government's stated prison-population target: true if the muster fell against an explicit reduction target while victimisations did not fall, false if the muster rose or victimisations fell over the period.

veracity.statement: But I want to acknowledge, when it comes to the fair pay agreements, nobody will be worse off with the removal of the fair pay agreements, because there have not been any fair pay agreements finalised.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at 12 December 2023 no fair pay agreement had been finalised under the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's register of fair pay agreement bargaining and finalised agreements as at December 2023: true if no agreement had been concluded or brought into force, false if one or more had been finalised.

veracity.statement: There have been six fair pay agreements that are currently in a bargaining process.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that exactly six fair pay agreement bargaining processes were under way in December 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's published list of approved FPA bargaining initiations as at December 2023: true if six processes were active, false if the count was materially different.

veracity.statement: Is she aware that bus drivers, cleaners, and early childhood education teachers earn at least 30 percent more pay in Australia, where sector-based bargaining is in place, and, if so, why should New Zealanders settle for less?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that bus drivers, cleaners and early childhood education teachers are paid at least 30 percent more in Australia than in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Comparable occupational earnings data — Stats NZ Linked Employer-Employee Data / occupational wage series against ABS Employee Earnings and Hours for the same occupations, on a like-for-like currency basis: true if the Australian median for all three exceeds the New Zealand median by 30 percent or more, false if any of the three falls materially short.

specificity.statement: Changes that I have announced today will remove deadlines for speed management plans and allow road-controlling authorities to stop blanket speed limit reductions on our roads while we write a new rule.
specificity.explanation: Names two concrete mechanisms — removing speed management plan deadlines and permitting road-controlling authorities to halt reductions — but gives no figures, no date and no detail on the replacement rule.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This new rule that I will develop next year will require road-controlling authorities to implement variable speed limits on roads approaching schools during pick-up and drop-off times.
specificity.explanation: A named mechanism (variable speed limits), a defined location (roads approaching schools), a defined trigger (pick-up and drop-off times) and a rough timeframe. Missing only the actual limits and a firm date.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’ve been advised by officials that, for serious and violent offenders who pleaded guilty in 2021–22, their best estimate is that between 4,600 and 7,800 offenders were issued with a sentencing discount of greater than 40 percent.
specificity.explanation: A named cohort, a named year, a numeric range and a stated threshold, with the source of the estimate identified. Directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As well as the measures listed in our 100-day plan, we have committed to limiting total sentence discounts to 40 percent.
specificity.explanation: A named commitment with a hard numeric cap, tied to a published plan. Missing only a date for implementation.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That is the focus of our Government—to have a thriving economy where businesses have more money to pay their staff more.
specificity.explanation: A statement of general aspiration — a thriving economy, businesses paying more — with no mechanism, figure, instrument or timeframe attached. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is she aware that bus drivers, cleaners, and early childhood education teachers earn at least 30 percent more pay in Australia, where sector-based bargaining is in place, and, if so, why should New Zealanders settle for less?
specificity.explanation: Three named occupations, a stated pay differential and a named institutional cause. A precise question, checkable in the same way a precise answer would be.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Given our coalition Government has begun work on a new rule, I wanted to ensure road-controlling authorities avoid wasting public money—something the Opposition doesn’t care about—on finalising speed management plans only to have to revisit these plans under a new rule.
rigor.explanation: A sound inference: if the governing rule is about to change, work finalising plans under the old rule would have to be redone, so pausing it avoids duplicated cost. The conclusion tracks the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I note that during his time as finance Minister, he collected hundreds of millions of dollars in tobacco tax revenue, which was used for a wide range of purposes, including health and education services and Working for Families payments.
rigor.explanation: A tu quoque: the fact that the questioner's own government also collected and spent tobacco revenue does not establish that funding tax cuts from reversed smokefree measures is defensible. The premise is about the critic, not the policy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: No, I haven’t seen that report, and I don’t agree with the sentiments there.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that the criticism is wrong — is reached in the same breath as an admission that the material was never read. Rejecting a proposition whose contents you have not examined is an inference with nothing behind it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But I want to acknowledge, when it comes to the fair pay agreements, nobody will be worse off with the removal of the fair pay agreements, because there have not been any fair pay agreements finalised.
rigor.explanation: A gap between premise and conclusion: that no agreement has been finalised establishes that no one loses a current entitlement, not that no one is worse off. Workers in live bargaining lose the prospective gain, which is what the claim needs to rule out and does not.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But it’s been my observation that the Greens—the economies that they admire are all in the Third World.
focus.explanation: A question about employment legislation and wages is before him; the reply names no policy, measure, figure or outcome and is entirely a characterisation of another party's supposed sympathies.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, you are going to hold us to that—you won’t have to hold us to that because unlike that member, we keep our promises. We don’t just make them and break them one after the other; we keep them.
focus.explanation: The question was about policies to raise incomes before Christmas. Once the comparison with 'that member' is removed there is no policy content left — no measure, figure, mechanism or named commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can he stand by his decision to use parliamentary urgency to push through legislation that will increase unemployment and insecure working conditions, while reducing wages, when people are trying to survive a cost of living crisis and put more kai on the table for Christmas?
focus.explanation: Names a specific procedural decision (use of urgency), the legislation it was used for, and the outcomes claimed to follow. This is scrutiny of a government action, not party-bashing; the Christmas framing is rhetorical but does not displace the policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Well, first of all, the integrity of the person answering this question on the subject of incomes and wages is that that threshold was set in the previous Government, not by Labour or the Greens but by New Zealand First.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the minimum wage level in force was set by New Zealand First within the 2017–2020 coalition Government, rather than by Labour or the Greens.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2017 Labour–New Zealand First coalition agreement and Labour's 2017 manifesto; true if the minimum-wage increase programme of that term originated as a New Zealand First-negotiated coalition commitment and not as Labour policy, false if Labour independently campaigned on and drove the same increase.

veracity.statement: That is the purpose and the focus of this Government—that with the reforms that are going to go ahead, running a far more successful economy, and ensuring that no one is left out in housing, education, and health, and in terms of infrastructure access, then people will be uplifted; not like the disaster we had, where there were all those tens and tens and tens of thousands utterly forgotten, and the homeless went up by 35 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure: that homelessness rose by 35 percent under the previous (2017–2023) Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ severe housing deprivation estimates and MHUD emergency/transitional housing register data for 2017–2023; true if a recognised homelessness measure rose by approximately 35% across that period, false if the change is materially different or no measure supports the figure.

veracity.statement: We could be closed down within three days because of their short-sightedness, and Megan Woods is the person who never acted in international interests—just allowed the refinery that is so critical to this country in an emergency to be not operating any longer.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that following the conversion of Marsden Point, New Zealand's fuel supply could be exhausted within about three days of a supply interruption.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE fuel security / onshore stockholding data for 2023 giving days of cover for petrol, diesel and jet fuel; true if cover is around three days, false if the reported cover is materially longer (e.g. two to three weeks).

veracity.statement: Why is this Government planning to bring back 90-day trials, which will disproportionately punish tangata whenua, particularly rangatahi trying to get their foot in the door of the job market, when the research commissioned by the Treasury in 2016 found no evidence that trial periods increased firms’ overall hiring but instead just make it easier for firms to sack people without cause and with fewer dismissal costs?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that research commissioned by the Treasury in 2016 found no evidence that trial periods increased firms' overall hiring, and instead lowered the cost of dismissal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2016 Treasury-commissioned Motu study of New Zealand's 90-day trial period (Chappell & Sin); true if it reports no statistically significant increase in overall hiring attributable to trial periods, false if it found a significant hiring increase or was not commissioned by Treasury in 2016.

veracity.statement: I’m advised that the 1:480 ratio was never finalised, nor was it funded adequately by the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two facts about the previous Government's handling of the police-to-population ratio: that the 1:480 ratio was never formally settled, and that it was not adequately funded.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police annual reports, Budget 2018–2023 police appropriations and Cabinet/Police advice on the officer-to-population ratio; true if no finalised 1:480 target was adopted and funding fell short of the number of officers it implied, false if the ratio was an adopted, funded target.

veracity.statement: They delivered 1,800 additional police officers, and they’re now committed to an additional 500.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand First delivered 1,800 additional police officers, a reference to the 2017–2020 coalition commitment.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police constabulary staffing figures for 2017 to 2020–21 and Police announcements on the 1,800 additional officers commitment; true if constabulary numbers rose by about 1,800 over that period, false if the increase was materially smaller.

rigor.statement: The fact is—if anyone understands economics—a willing business and a willing worker are critical to employment. So whether it’s one month, two months, or three months, the fact of the matter is that the sound connection of those two will work.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the 90-day trial policy, and a weak one: from the premise that employment needs willing parties it does not follow that the length of a trial period is immaterial. Non sequitur — the premise is about the existence of a match, the conclusion is about the terms governing its termination, and the cited Treasury evidence is not engaged at all.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: On the marae, Megan, you keep quiet. You do. Willie knows that; he keeps quiet too. You don’t shout out like some bunch of clowns at university.
civility.explanation: Named, personal and condescending — instructs a member by first name to be quiet, invokes marae protocol against her, and likens her conduct to 'clowns'. Nothing here engages the substance of the question.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, you are going to hold us to that—you won’t have to hold us to that because unlike that member, we keep our promises. We don’t just make them and break them one after the other; we keep them.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to a named individual member — that they make promises and break them 'one after the other'. Short of a direct insult, but it is an attack on the member's honesty rather than on any argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We could be closed down within three days because of their short-sightedness, and Megan Woods is the person who never acted in international interests—just allowed the refinery that is so critical to this country in an emergency to be not operating any longer.
civility.explanation: Moves from the Marsden Point decision to the person: names a member and asserts she 'never acted in international interests', an attack on her judgement and motives rather than on the decision itself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Just following on from the speaker who has resumed his seat, the reality is that there was a slight delay in the translation, reflective of the rudimentary nature of the Māori language and my ability to make it sound more sophisticated in English.
civility.explanation: Mockery delivered in the middle of a live dispute about whether te reo questions must be answered: it disparages the language the questioner used as 'rudimentary' while praising his own facility in English. Not procedural boilerplate — there was every opportunity to make the translation point without the sneer.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: So those pricings should go down.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that petrol prices will fall following the removal of the fuel charge imposed by the previous Government, which he has just described as unfair charging.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE weekly retail petrol price data for the region affected by the charge, compared before and after its removal; true if the pump price falls by approximately the amount of the removed charge, false if prices do not fall or rise once the charge is gone.

specificity.statement: Why is this Government planning to bring back 90-day trials, which will disproportionately punish tangata whenua, particularly rangatahi trying to get their foot in the door of the job market, when the research commissioned by the Treasury in 2016 found no evidence that trial periods increased firms’ overall hiring but instead just make it easier for firms to sack people without cause and with fewer dismissal costs?
specificity.explanation: Names the policy (90-day trials), the affected group, the commissioning agency and year of the research relied on, and the specific finding attributed to it. Someone could go and check every element.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How many Constabulary Full Time Equivalents does Police expect to need to train each year for the next two years in order to maintain the 1 to 480 ratio, and will the Government’s commitment for “no fewer than 500 new frontline police within the first two years” be in addition to that?
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable question: names the staffing measure, the exact ratio, the timeframe, and quotes the government commitment verbatim. A question this concrete is as specific as an announcement carrying the same figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: To be clear, the regulatory impact statement from MBIE from 2021 recommended against introducing a fair pay agreement system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that MBIE's 2021 regulatory impact statement on fair pay agreements recommended against introducing the FPA system.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's 2021 Regulatory Impact Statement on fair pay agreements; true if MBIE's stated recommendation/preferred option was against introducing an FPA system, false if it recommended for it or expressed no recommendation against.

veracity.statement: To be clear, there have not been any fair pay agreements finalised, so no one is worse off.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of record that no fair pay agreement had been finalised by 12 December 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's register of fair pay agreement bargaining and concluded FPAs as at December 2023; true if no FPA had been finalised/ratified, false if at least one had been.

veracity.statement: Does the Minister accept that on paragraph 13 of that RIS, it clearly states that depending on the sector and occupations where FPAs are concluded, they could disproportionately benefit some population groups covered, including women, young people, Māori, and Pacific peoples?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that paragraph 13 of the MBIE regulatory impact statement contains the quoted wording about disproportionate benefit to particular population groups.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of paragraph 13 of the MBIE regulatory impact statement referred to (the RIS cover sheet dated 28 November 2023 and the underlying RIS); true if the wording matches substantially as quoted, false if paragraph 13 says something materially different.

rigor.statement: To be clear, there have not been any fair pay agreements finalised, so no one is worse off.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy, but it equivocates: that no FPA has been concluded shows no realised loss, not that nobody is worse off from removing the bargaining process and its expected benefits.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: No, because this Government believes that the fair pay agreement system would have made vulnerable workers worse off. This is because of disemployment effects where businesses who could not stomach the added cost to their businesses lay off workers or close up entirely or don’t offer any more jobs.
rigor.explanation: A stated causal mechanism (added cost leading to disemployment) is offered, so the conclusion is not bare — but nothing is offered to show the effect outweighs the wage gains the system was meant to deliver, so it leans on an assumed magnitude.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does the Minister accept that on paragraph 13 of that RIS, it clearly states that depending on the sector and occupations where FPAs are concluded, they could disproportionately benefit some population groups covered, including women, young people, Māori, and Pacific peoples?
