rigor.explanation: A real inference about the process: select committee scrutiny is the mechanism by which affected parties are heard, urgency removes it, therefore this bill escapes that check. The premise supports the conclusion, and she notably includes businesses among those denied a hearing rather than only her own side. Docked because the leap from 'no select committee on this bill' to 'a breach of fundamental democratic rights' overstates what the premise delivers — urgency is a standing feature of the House's rules.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need to repeal this Act so that we can leave flexibility with the employer and the employee, and give them greater control over the relationship they have.
specificity.explanation: Names the action (repeal this Act) and a direction (flexibility, control), but supplies no provision, no cost, no timeframe and no account of what flexibility is currently lost. A listener could not check or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The National Party and the ACT Party opposed the development and introduction of the fair pay agreement legislation, and this repeal has been well signalled—very, very clearly signalled—through the entire campaign period, through the coalition agreements, and through the 100-day plan of this Government. We have a clear mandate from the voters to do this.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that both governing parties opposed the FPA legislation throughout its passage, and that the repeal was signalled in the election campaign, the coalition agreements and the 100-day plan.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard division records for the Fair Pay Agreements Bill (2021-22): true if National and ACT voted against at its readings; plus the published National–ACT coalition agreement and the Government's 100-day plan — true if repeal of the fair pay agreement legislation appears in both documents, false if it appears in neither.

veracity.statement: The most important thing to note about the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment’s regulatory impact statement that was produced in 2021 on the Fair Pay Agreements Act is that the ministry recommended against introducing fair pay agreements. They argued that the improvements for employees would be marginal at best and would achieve this at a significant cost to employer flexibility.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two things about a named document: that MBIE's 2021 regulatory impact statement recommended against introducing fair pay agreements, and that it characterised the gains for employees as marginal at best against a significant cost to employer flexibility.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of MBIE's 2021 Regulatory Impact Statement on fair pay agreements: true if its recommendation section advises against proceeding with the FPA system and describes employee benefits as marginal at significant cost to employer flexibility; false if it recommends the FPA option or reaches a materially different assessment.

veracity.statement: There have been six fair pay agreements that have been initiated since the fair pay agreement legislation came into force. However, all are in the very early stages of bargaining. No agreements have been finalised in any industry or any occupation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a count of six initiated fair pay agreements since the Act came into force on 1 December 2022, and that none had been concluded as at December 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's register of initiated fair pay agreements as at December 2023: true if exactly six initiation applications had been approved and none had been ratified or brought into force; false if the count differs materially or any agreement had been finalised.

veracity.statement: Two hundred thousand to 300,000 working people stood to benefit from fair pay agreements.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a coverage figure: that between 200,000 and 300,000 workers would have been covered by, and better off under, the fair pay agreements that had been initiated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE / NZCTU coverage estimates for the six initiated fair pay agreements (bus drivers, hospitality, security, commercial cleaning, early childhood education, supermarkets), cross-checked against Stats NZ industry employment counts: true if the combined covered workforce falls in the 200,000–300,000 range, false if it is materially outside it.

rigor.statement: The National Party and the ACT Party opposed the development and introduction of the fair pay agreement legislation, and this repeal has been well signalled—very, very clearly signalled—through the entire campaign period, through the coalition agreements, and through the 100-day plan of this Government. We have a clear mandate from the voters to do this.
rigor.explanation: The inference is from 'we signalled it' to 'we have a mandate from the voters to do this'. Appeal to electoral mandate: an election result is a single aggregate choice and does not establish voter endorsement of this specific measure, still less of passing it under urgency. A real but weak inference about a real policy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The fair pay agreements could lead to worse outcomes for workers by raising the costs of doing business. If bargained wage increases meant businesses cannot remain competitive, the fair pay agreements would have resulted in lower employment or reduced hours of work—which is not good for workers in our economy.
rigor.explanation: An explicitly conditional argument: given the stated antecedent (wage increases that cost competitiveness), the conclusion about employment and hours follows. The gap is that nothing is offered to show the antecedent would hold, and the hedged 'could' does most of the work — but the inference itself is valid.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: All of these people understand that fair pay agreements were a way forward for New Zealand to address the embarrassing low productivity that we have and that has gone on for a number of years, and also the low-wage economy that we have had for a number of years.
rigor.explanation: The support offered for the policy's merits is that the workers she met on the forecourt understand it to be a way forward — an appeal to popularity resting on an anecdotal, self-selected sample. Nothing is offered linking industry bargaining to the productivity or wage outcomes claimed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety has been questioned regularly about the advice that she’s received, and it’s quite obvious from the speech that she has just given that her answers, in the sense that she hasn’t had any advice, are correct, because none of her explanation as to why fair pay agreements need to be repealed is actually backed up by evidence.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the conclusion that the Minister received no advice is inferred solely from the speaker's own assessment that the speech lacked evidence. A speech is not the advice record, and the speech in fact cited MBIE's 2021 regulatory impact statement, so the premise is doing no work.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They say—well, yes, the Labour Government used urgency. Yes, we did. But there should always be a justification and reason, and a good reason, for urgency, and there isn’t one in this instance.
rigor.explanation: The concession is handled honestly rather than deflected, and the principle (urgency requires justification) is a sound premise. But the operative conclusion — that no good reason exists here — is bare assertion; the Government's stated reason (acting before agreements are finalised) is not engaged.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government has committed to repealing the fair pay agreement legislation by Christmas 2023 as part of the coalition agreement between the National Party and the ACT Party, and I am committed to acting quickly to remove this legislation before any fair pay agreements are finalised and the transition arrangements become more expensive and more complex.
specificity.explanation: Names the legislation, the source of the commitment (the coalition agreement), a deadline (Christmas 2023) and the operative reason for the timing (acting before agreements are finalised). Checkable and actionable; short of a full mechanism or costing.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The most important thing to note about the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment’s regulatory impact statement that was produced in 2021 on the Fair Pay Agreements Act is that the ministry recommended against introducing fair pay agreements. They argued that the improvements for employees would be marginal at best and would achieve this at a significant cost to employer flexibility.
specificity.explanation: Names the issuing agency, the document, its year, and the specific finding attributed to it. Someone could pull the document and check the characterisation.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There have been six fair pay agreements that have been initiated since the fair pay agreement legislation came into force. However, all are in the very early stages of bargaining. No agreements have been finalised in any industry or any occupation.
specificity.explanation: A checkable count and a clear statement of bargaining stage; no dates or industries named for the individual agreements.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are a Government that wants to see higher wages for workers; we want to see a thriving, competitive business sector; we want to see more and better jobs in our economy; and we want to ease the pain of the cost of living crisis.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic aspirations — higher wages, a thriving sector, more jobs, less cost-of-living pain. No figure, mechanism, timeframe or named step that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Two hundred thousand to 300,000 working people stood to benefit from fair pay agreements.
specificity.explanation: A checkable numeric range attached to a named policy, though stated as a bracket with no source and no breakdown by industry.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We are doing this bill to send a clear signal to businesses that this Government understands the pressures that businesses have faced in an environment of increasing inflation and a Labour-led Government that has piled on regulations on to businesses that are finding it a struggle to cope.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point — the compliance burden on business and the purpose of the bill — but half the sentence's weight is a general characterisation of the previous Labour-led Government's approach rather than a named regulation or measured cost. A policy claim wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government has shown its true colours in these last few days. The first thing they did was to attack jobs, with the repeal of the dual mandate. The next thing they did was to repeal the fair pay agreements—to attack wages and conditions that working people would like to see in their workplaces, that would have helped New Zealand.
focus.explanation: Two specific measures are named — the repeal of the Reserve Bank's dual mandate and this repeal bill — which is legitimate scrutiny. But they are marshalled as evidence of the Government's 'true colours' rather than argued on their effects, so the weight of the passage is party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The reason is because they are an anti-worker Government. They don’t stand with working people. They stand against working people, and that’s why they’re repealing this piece of legislation.
focus.explanation: Offered as the answer to why the Government is prioritising this bill, but it names no provision, cost, figure or outcome — it is a claim about what the other party is really like, restated three times. The bare mention of 'this piece of legislation' carries no policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Far from being fair or even being about pay, the fair pay agreements were about harming the very workers they were meant to help.
civility.explanation: About as harsh as a description of a policy gets, but the target is the policy alone — no member, no person's competence or motives. Under the re-anchored scale, brutal criticism of a measure is civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This bill is a disgrace, and I do not support it.
civility.explanation: A flat condemnation, but of the bill. No member is named, no motive imputed to a person, no attack on anyone's competence or character.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We do not believe that that bill would have improved workers’ outcomes or business outcomes in our economy in New Zealand.
civility.explanation: A repeal debate is genuinely contested and offered a real chance to attack the previous Government's members; instead the criticism lands wholly on the legislation and its expected effects, naming no one.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: These are clear examples of why this Government is repealing the Fair Pay Agreements Act. We do not believe that all employees and all employers within scope should be forced into an agreement where it doesn’t work for the worker and it doesn’t work for the business.
rigor.explanation: The case for repeal rests entirely on submissions quoted from one side of the argument — Federated Farmers, Horticulture NZ, a promotions company, a hospitality business, the Shipping Federation — all of them interested parties predicting harm. No data, no counter-submission, and no mechanism is offered; the inference is an appeal to selected authority and anecdote, treating a curated sample of forecasts as though it established the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need a flexible labour market that focuses on productivity growth, that focuses on reducing regulation, and focuses on reducing inflation so that everybody can have more food on their table for themselves and their families but where businesses have the confidence to flourish and employ more, and where business owners have more money to pay their staff more.
specificity.explanation: A chain of generic goods — productivity growth, less regulation, lower inflation, more confidence, higher pay — with no figure, no mechanism, no timeframe and no named measure beyond the repeal itself. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We need a flexible labour market that focuses on productivity growth, that focuses on reducing regulation, and focuses on reducing inflation so that everybody can have more food on their table for themselves and their families but where businesses have the confidence to flourish and employ more, and where business owners have more money to pay their staff more.
focus.explanation: Squarely about labour-market policy and what the speaker wants it to achieve; no party framing, no characterisation of opponents. Vague, but vague about the policy — the deduction belongs to Specificity, not here.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It was in the coalition agreement. It is part of our 100-day plan.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that repeal of the Fair Pay Agreements Act appears both in the coalition agreement(s) signed after the 2023 general election and in the incoming Government's published 100-day plan.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the National–ACT and National–NZ First coalition agreements (published 24 November 2023) and the Government's published 100-day plan; true if repeal of the Fair Pay Agreements Act is named in the coalition agreement and listed among the 100-day plan items, false if absent from either.

veracity.statement: FPAs are a blunt tool initiated by unions and a small number of employees, yet they apply to every employee and employer in an industry or occupation, regardless of whether or not they want it or want to be included.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two things about the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022 as it operated: that only unions (plus a small proportion of employees) could initiate an FPA, and that a concluded FPA bound every employer and employee in the covered industry or occupation irrespective of their consent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022, initiation and coverage provisions: true if initiation was restricted to unions meeting a representation threshold (10% or 1,000 covered employees, or a public-interest test) and a concluded agreement bound all employers and employees in the covered occupation/industry without their consent; false if coverage was opt-in, or if employers or non-union employees could initiate or exclude themselves.

veracity.statement: At the time, we had a huge membership in terms of unions. Sadly, I think that came down to about 20 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand union membership density fell to roughly 20 percent following the 1991 Employment Contracts Act and the end of compulsory unionism.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand union membership density series (MBIE/Department of Labour union membership returns and the Victoria University CLEW series): true if density fell to approximately 20% of wage and salary earners in the decade after the Employment Contracts Act 1991; false if it remained materially above ~25% or fell materially below ~15% over that period.

veracity.statement: So what I’d like to speak to is the words of Brooke van Velden that have been haunting this House and have made me recall back, actually, right back into the 1990s, and those words were that no workers will be any worse off without fair pay agreements.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister, Brooke van Velden, stated that no workers will be worse off following the repeal of fair pay agreements.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard record of Brooke van Velden's speeches on the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill and her contemporaneous public statements: true if she asserted that no worker would be worse off without fair pay agreements; false if no such statement is on the record or the statement attributed differs materially in its claim.

veracity.statement: Well, the OECD and a lot of those people who have done research—including the Rt Hon Jim Bolger—have been on the page of saying that this would be good for New Zealand’s productivity.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the OECD, other researchers, and Jim Bolger have taken the position that fair pay agreements (sector-level bargaining) would be good for New Zealand's productivity.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD publications on collective bargaining and productivity (notably 'Negotiating Our Way Up', 2019) and the OECD Economic Surveys of New Zealand, plus Jim Bolger's public statements as chair of the Fair Pay Agreement Working Group: true if the OECD published analysis supporting coordinated/sector-level bargaining as productivity-enhancing and Bolger publicly endorsed fair pay agreements; false if the OECD took no such position on New Zealand or Bolger did not endorse the policy.

focus.statement: FPAs are a blunt tool initiated by unions and a small number of employees, yet they apply to every employee and employer in an industry or occupation, regardless of whether or not they want it or want to be included.
focus.explanation: Describes the mechanism of the measure before the House — who can initiate an FPA and who it binds. No party framing at all; entirely about how the policy works.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s a sad thing, really, about Jim Bolger, but he came right in later years by supporting the Treaty of Waitangi, unlike the rest of this useless National Party and the hopeless ACT Party and the New Zealand First lot who’ve forgotten their roots, sadly.
focus.explanation: Three parties characterised in general terms — 'useless', 'hopeless', 'forgotten their roots' — with no policy, measure, figure or outcome named. This is the content-free party framing Focus exists to catch; no individual is insulted, so Civility passes it cleanly.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If you’ve worked on the factory floor, you know that you can’t negotiate because there’s a total imbalance in terms of bargaining power. So the whole notion that individuals have a right and have a chance to negotiate is just a load of nonsense.
focus.explanation: Engages the substantive question the repeal turns on: whether individual employees can bargain effectively without collective coverage. No party framing in the passage.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: These are the people who National and ACT don’t care about. They don’t give a damn about them.
focus.explanation: Entirely a claim about the other parties' motives and character. No policy, provision, figure or outcome is named, and nothing survives if the reference to the opposing parties is removed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, if anything’s going to take us back to the 1970s and 1980s, it’s this Act, because all it’s going to do—the long game here is very simple. It’s to create a situation whereby we end up with nationwide strikes and very little productivity because nothing gets done.
focus.explanation: Directed at the measure before the House and its claimed consequences rather than at the opposing party's character. The argument is weak, but it is an argument about the Act.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But those opposite want to take us back to 1991. They’re not interested in being cutting edge.
focus.explanation: A characterisation of the opposing side's motives and outlook with no measure, provision or outcome named. Whatever policy point sits behind it has dropped out; what remains is about what the other team is 'interested in'.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Businesses need flexibility to innovate, and FPAs restrict the flexibility both employers and employees want.
rigor.explanation: A premise-and-conclusion structure, but the linking step is asserted rather than shown: nothing is offered connecting FPA coverage to reduced innovation, and the claim that employees want the flexibility is a bare assertion about the preferences of the people the Act covers.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If you’ve worked on the factory floor, you know that you can’t negotiate because there’s a total imbalance in terms of bargaining power. So the whole notion that individuals have a right and have a chance to negotiate is just a load of nonsense.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the policy — asymmetric bargaining power means individual negotiation is illusory — but it rests on an appeal to personal and shared experience ('if you've worked on the factory floor, you know') rather than evidence, and it moves from an imbalance to a 'total' one and thence to the conclusion that individual bargaining is worthless, which is stronger than the premise supports.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, if anything’s going to take us back to the 1970s and 1980s, it’s this Act, because all it’s going to do—the long game here is very simple. It’s to create a situation whereby we end up with nationwide strikes and very little productivity because nothing gets done.
rigor.explanation: A slippery slope: nothing is offered to connect sector-level bargaining to nationwide strikes or to a collapse in output, and the intermediate steps are simply asserted as the Act's 'long game'. The conclusion outruns anything supplied to support it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: My electorate is driven by farming and multiple small and medium family-owned businesses that are often operating on very small margins. They’re much more vulnerable to ill-thought-through legislation than larger businesses.
rigor.explanation: A real inference with a plausible premise — thin margins leave less capacity to absorb compliance costs, so small firms are more exposed than large ones. The gap is that nothing connects this general point to the Fair Pay Agreements Act specifically; the conclusion about this bill is left to be assumed rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Businesses need flexibility to innovate, and FPAs restrict the flexibility both employers and employees want.
specificity.explanation: 'Flexibility to innovate' names no term of the agreement, no cost, no sector and no mechanism by which an FPA constrains anything. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In those days, my hourly rate was $4.20 an hour, which doesn’t sound like much, but when you’re 16 and you get paid penal rates at the weekend—double time—$8.40 is not a bad wage.
specificity.explanation: Carries actual figures and a named mechanism: a base rate, the penal-rate multiplier, and the resulting weekend rate. Concrete enough that the effect being described can be followed and checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Businesses across the districts of Central Hawke’s Bay, Tararua, Masterton, Carterton, and South Wairarapa are struggling under the weight of legislation that the last Government introduced.
specificity.explanation: Names five districts precisely but leaves the substance vague: no legislation is identified, no cost or compliance burden is quantified, and 'struggling under the weight' describes no measurable effect. Geographic precision is doing the work that policy detail should.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, it was great to hear about all the experience that the member Carl Bates had, which was absolutely nothing. So thank you for that nothing contribution.
civility.explanation: A sarcastic dismissal aimed squarely at the named member's competence and worth as a contributor, not at anything he argued. The target is the person, not the position.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But people know in the House, and if you’ve worked in the unions and if you’ve worked on the factory floor, which most of that lot haven’t—most of them wouldn’t even know what a factory was.
civility.explanation: Mockery of opposing members personally — not of their argument but of their supposed ignorance of working life. 'Wouldn't even know what a factory was' is a jibe at their competence and background rather than a point about the bill.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That was the biggest load of rubbish I’ve heard in a really long time, and there’s been quite a lot of rubbish spoken in this House.
civility.explanation: Wholesale contemptuous dismissal of the preceding speech without engaging any part of it. It stops short of a direct attack on the member himself, but sneering at a contribution as 'the biggest load of rubbish' is no longer civil engagement with the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m quite surprised, listening to the Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety’s speech—and I know she’s a new Minister, and maybe she doesn’t have her full staff on board yet, but I actually participated in the select committee process, and we received 1,700 submissions.
civility.explanation: Pointed jab at the Minister personally — the aside about being new and lacking staff implies she does not know her own portfolio. Short of an insult, but it lands on the person rather than the repeal.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Because the Minister, while she may have claimed that she has met with the with the union sector, she has not been able to substantiate the details of those conversations to back up her arguments on why this piece of legislation and repealing fair pay agreements is a good thing.
civility.explanation: "May have claimed" casts doubt on whether the Minister is telling the truth about her own consultation — an imputation of bad faith aimed at the person, not the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If the advice that the Minister received is not good enough, she may want to turn her face from the ivory tower to the streets to listen to the experiences of those workers.
civility.explanation: The "ivory tower" jibe is directed at the Minister personally, painting her as aloof and out of touch rather than engaging what the advice actually said.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I’m quite surprised, listening to the Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety’s speech—and I know she’s a new Minister, and maybe she doesn’t have her full staff on board yet, but I actually participated in the select committee process, and we received 1,700 submissions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the select committee process on the Fair Pay Agreements Bill received 1,700 submissions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee's report on the Fair Pay Agreements Bill (2022) and Parliament's submission record; true if roughly 1,700 submissions were received, false if the count is materially different.

veracity.statement: Fair pay agreements are a form of industry-level bargaining. They’re common across the world, in countries that we would like to compare ourselves to: in Germany, in France, in Italy, in Australia.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that sector- or industry-level bargaining of the kind FPAs create is a common arrangement in Germany, France, Italy and Australia.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD/ILO data on collective bargaining structures and coverage for those four countries; true if each operates sectoral/occupational bargaining (or, in Australia, the modern awards system) setting industry-wide minimum terms, false if any of the four lacks such a mechanism.

veracity.statement: He chaired the working group that set the groundwork up for the Fair Pay Agreements Bill that was passed by our Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Jim Bolger chaired the working group whose work preceded the Fair Pay Agreements Bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's record of the Fair Pay Agreements Working Group (2018), its terms of reference and membership; true if Jim Bolger was its chair, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: They are, as in the Minister’s own advice that she received in the regulatory impact statement, more likely to be Māori, they’re more likely to be Pasifika, they’re more likely to be women, and they’re more likely to be young people.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the regulatory impact statement for the repeal records that the workers affected are disproportionately Māori, Pasifika, women and young people.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Regulatory Impact Statement published with the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill; true if it identifies those groups as disproportionately represented among workers who would be covered, false if it does not.

veracity.statement: One of the conditions of that EU free-trade agreement is that countries don’t deregulate their labour laws in order to give themselves a competitive advantage, and I understand a complaint has been raised to that nature.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the EU–New Zealand FTA contains a condition against weakening labour law to gain competitive advantage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the EU–New Zealand Free Trade Agreement, Trade and Sustainable Development chapter; true if it contains a non-derogation/non-regression clause barring the weakening of labour law to gain a trade or investment advantage, false if no such provision exists.

veracity.statement: In a country that has a terrible record when it comes to health and safety standards for our workers, repealing a key piece of legislation that would have improved the safety of our workers is a stain in this Government’s track record and their commitment to keep our workers safe.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a premise that New Zealand has a poor workplace health and safety record.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: WorkSafe NZ work-related fatality and serious-injury rates benchmarked against comparable OECD countries (Safe Work Australia, UK HSE, ILO series); true if New Zealand's work-related fatality rate is materially higher than those comparators, false if at or below them.

veracity.statement: Finally, I want to commend, too, the many workers who—despite there not being a select committee submission process—have put their livelihoods, their stories on the line to make the case on why fair pay agreements are a thing to be protected.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that this repeal bill had no select committee submission process.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bill record for the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill; true if the bill was passed without referral to a select committee and without a call for public submissions, false if a submission process was held.

rigor.statement: These types of agreement create a floor and not a ceiling in relation to terms and conditions. If employers want to offer something above what is in the fair pay agreement, there is absolutely nothing preventing them from doing that.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the mechanism: the conclusion that FPAs are a floor rather than a ceiling is supported by the stated reason that nothing bars employers from offering above the agreed terms.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So someone who was in favour of what we introduced was the Rt Hon Jim Bolger, and I respect and thank Jim Bolger for his work.
rigor.explanation: The support offered for the policy is the endorsement of a former National Prime Minister — an appeal to authority. It bears on the policy rather than on opponents, but the endorsement does not itself establish that the scheme works.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If your premise of running a business relies on the exploitation of workers, then you’re not running a business.
rigor.explanation: Definitional fiat — a no-true-Scotsman move that settles the question by redefining "business" rather than by showing that low-wage firms could pay more.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They’ve spoken about the impact it will have on employers, but their trickle-down economics, their trickle-down beliefs that those gains for employers will be passed down to workers, is nothing but a myth.
rigor.explanation: Engages the policy argument but rebuts it by assertion: the transmission from employer gains to worker pay is declared "a myth" with no evidence or mechanism offered against it.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They are, as in the Minister’s own advice that she received in the regulatory impact statement, more likely to be Māori, they’re more likely to be Pasifika, they’re more likely to be women, and they’re more likely to be young people.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure: it identifies who the repeal affects and sources that to the bill's own regulatory impact statement. Named policy, named evidence, named outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ve seen, perhaps in their haste to put out a press release saying they’ve achieved their 100-day goals, the drafting of their legislation was amiss in some instances, and I’m foreshadowing that we’ll be putting some Amendment Papers—as they’re now called—into the committee of the whole House stage to seek to address those.
focus.explanation: A real point about the bill — drafting defects and the amendments proposed to fix them — though partly wrapped in a jab about the Government's 100-day press release.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s a sad day to stand up and take a call on the second reading of the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill, shepherded by a Government that seems to want to make our lowest-income workers have a terrible time ahead of Christmas; a Government that is full of platitudes, happy to celebrate our essential workers when it was convenient and turn their back on them and turn the clock back in time as soon as they take the reins of power.
focus.explanation: Names the bill, but the weight of the statement is a characterisation of the Government's motives and character rather than any provision, cost or effect. No individual is insulted, so this is a Focus point, not a Civility one.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They need to remember that they have turned their backs on those workers as soon as they entered the halls of power.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the other side is like — no policy, figure or outcome is named, only their alleged betrayal on taking office.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One of the conditions of that EU free-trade agreement is that countries don’t deregulate their labour laws in order to give themselves a competitive advantage, and I understand a complaint has been raised to that nature.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific instrument and the specific obligation relied on, which is enough for someone to go to the agreement text and check. Falls short of 1.0 because neither the chapter nor the complaint is identified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And I note in the departmental disclosure statement which was released with this bill that there was also an issue raised in relation to that under the Legislation Act 2021, which actually doesn’t allow existing rights to be repealed if they’re existing at the time of the repeal—so some interesting issues for the Government to have to address in this piece of legislation that they have moved through very, very quickly.
specificity.explanation: Names the document (the departmental disclosure statement), the statute (Legislation Act 2021) and the particular legal problem, so the objection can be looked up and tested.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In conclusion, I look forward to the committee stage, when we can look through the legislation in detail, but I just wanted to say that in the Labour Party we will always stand up for working people, and this is not the end of this fight.
specificity.explanation: A peroration: no figures, mechanisms, timeframes or named provisions. "Stand up for working people" commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Unlike members opposite, who operate in theories and ideals, I have successfully employed and retained over 100 staff, many of whom were bus drivers.
focus.explanation: A bill is before the House, but the weight of this is a characterisation of the other side ('theories and ideals') set against the speaker's own credentials. No provision, cost or mechanism of the repeal is named, so there is only faint policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: All I’m hearing from the other side of the House is catastrophising.
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of how the other side is arguing. No policy, figure or provision is named, so nothing here engages the repeal itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But it is typical of them and their one-size-fits-all approach to almost everything.
focus.explanation: Generalises from the bill to the other party's character across 'almost everything'. Once the party framing is removed nothing about the repeal remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Be honest about who your most wealthy and collective donors were and what their purposes are to get you into Government.
focus.explanation: Directed wholly at the other parties' funding and motives. No clause, cost or effect of the repeal is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As I mentioned earlier, I have successfully employed and retained hundreds of employees, none of which was done through an FPA.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal anecdote. That one employer retained staff without a fair pay agreement does not support the conclusion that the mechanism is unnecessary across the labour market — the sample is the speaker's own firm, selected for having succeeded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s not as though we’re tearing up a workers’ utopia. This is a bill that hasn’t even taken effect yet.
rigor.explanation: The inference is sound on its own terms: if the mechanism was never operative, then repealing it removes nothing workers currently hold. The premise is contestable, but that is a separate question from whether the conclusion follows from it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Camilla Belich actually made the actually obvious point that union members probably wouldn’t be affected by this because they collectively bargain anyway. So where is the problem?
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur by ignored counter-example. That union members are unaffected does not show there is no problem, since the stated purpose of the mechanism is to cover workers who are not union members and cannot collectively bargain — the very group the premise excludes.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There’s different cost structures in different regions of New Zealand. It’s a different cost of living in Auckland than it might be in Balclutha. So the complexity of bringing these things together is a lot more challenging than the members opposite would make out.
rigor.explanation: A real inference with an illustrative case supplied: regional variation in cost structures is offered as a reason that a nationally-bargained instrument is harder to design. The conclusion tracks the premise, though the size of the difficulty is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Confidence to the food market owner in Whanganui who said she would have to close if fair pay agreements went through.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to a single unnamed anecdote. One constituent's stated expectation about her own business is offered as grounds for a national repeal, with nothing connecting that case to the general effect claimed.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s not as though we’re tearing up a workers’ utopia. This is a bill that hasn’t even taken effect yet.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Fair Pay Agreements regime being repealed had not yet come into operation at the time of the December 2023 second reading.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The commencement date of the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022 and the MBIE record of fair pay agreement bargaining initiations approved before 12 December 2023; true if no part of the Act was in force and no bargaining process had begun, false if the Act was in force and applications to initiate bargaining had been approved.

veracity.statement: We have a track record in three consecutive coalitions that we’ve been involved in; having a rise to the minimum wage has been part of that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand First has been part of three consecutive coalition arrangements and that a minimum wage increase featured in each of them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 1996 National–NZ First coalition agreement, the 2017 Labour–NZ First coalition agreement and the 2023 National–NZ First coalition agreement, checked against the minimum wage orders made in each term; true if a minimum wage rise was a negotiated component of all three, false if it is absent from any of them or if the arrangements were not consecutive.

veracity.statement: Extraordinarily, in 2017, we had to bring them kicking and screaming to the table to do that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in the 2017 coalition negotiations the Labour Party had to be forced by New Zealand First into agreeing to raise the minimum wage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Labour's 2017 election manifesto and campaign statements on the minimum wage, plus the 2017 Labour–NZ First coalition agreement; true if raising the minimum wage was an NZ First demand that Labour resisted, false if Labour independently campaigned on raising it before negotiations began.

veracity.statement: We know, as Māori, how we’re always the last hired and the first fired. That’s an undeniable fact.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Māori are systematically the last to gain employment in an upturn and the first to lose it in a downturn.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey Māori unemployment and employment rates compared with the total population across at least two labour-market cycles; true if Māori unemployment is consistently higher and rises earlier and faster in downturns while recovering later, false if Māori rates track the national series without that lag.

civility.statement: Be honest about who your most wealthy and collective donors were and what their purposes are to get you into Government.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith rather than engaging the argument: the governing parties are said to be legislating to serve donors who bought them into office. It stops short of a direct personal insult, but attributing a corrupt motive is a genuine civility failure under the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I know, because none of the losers on the other side were anything apart from working in offices.
civility.explanation: A direct insult to the members opposite ('losers'), aimed at who they are rather than at any argument they made about the bill.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Yeah, well more of an achievement than a mug like yourself.
civility.explanation: A bare personal insult directed at an individual member, with no argument attached to it at all.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But there remain some deep, systemic issues that have impacted in the areas of employment and industry that most disproportionately are represented by Māori, by Pacific people, by women, by young people, and by people with a disability in those areas and trades specifically that have, for decades and far too long, exploited those workers who are at most risk and are most vulnerable to being exploited—not just with lower pay but also with hours that are mucky and that impact on their other responsibilities in the rest of their lives, with learning and development conditions and training so that they can actually build upon their work, no matter what that work is—that have been impacted on by a lack of decision making and input from workers, including their ability to be safe and well in their workplace.
specificity.explanation: Names the affected groups and the dimensions of harm (pay, hours, training, workplace voice), which is more than a slogan, but supplies no figure, no sector, no provision of the bill and no measurable claim anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Indeed, we are giving the present of confidence this Christmas—a confidence in a new 2024.
specificity.explanation: A seasonal metaphor carrying no mechanism, figure or timeframe. 'Confidence in a new 2024' commits to nothing that could be checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So, in 1991, when Jim Bolger brought in voluntary unionism, we were in shock because it smashed the union movement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a Bolger-led government introduced voluntary (non-compulsory) unionism in 1991 and that union membership collapsed as a result.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Employment Contracts Act 1991, passed under Jim Bolger's National government: true if it abolished compulsory union membership; and NZ union density statistics (Department of Labour / Stats NZ union membership returns) for 1991-1995: true if membership fell sharply over that period, false if it held steady or rose.

veracity.statement: The Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety, Brooke van Velden, has been told that young people, Māori, and Pasifika people will not benefit with the loss of these fair pay agreements (FPAs).
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the responsible Minister received official advice that young, Māori and Pasifika workers would be disadvantaged by repealing the Fair Pay Agreements Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE advice and the regulatory impact material prepared for the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill: true if that advice to the Minister identifies young, Māori and Pasifika workers as groups who lose from repeal, false if no such advice was given to her.

veracity.statement: We spend $2 billion a year in this country subsidising rents because people can’t earn enough to pay the rent—multiple billions of dollars every year because employers don’t pay high enough wages.
veracity.explanation: Asserts annual state spending of about $2 billion on rent subsidies.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD / Treasury reported annual expenditure on the Accommodation Supplement (and related housing subsidies) for the year in question: true if the figure is around $2 billion, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: Italy, France, Germany, Australia—they all have nationwide systems of minimum standards for pay and conditions to stop a race to the bottom.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that four named comparator countries each operate national sector-wide systems of minimum pay and conditions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD collective bargaining coverage data and each country's labour law (Australian modern awards; French, Italian and German sectoral agreements and their extension mechanisms): true if all four have nationwide sectoral or award-based minimum standards, false if any one lacks such a system.

veracity.statement: Well, can I remind them that 97 percent of businesses in New Zealand are small businesses—those that employ fewer than 20 people. There are 546,000 of them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a proportion (97%) and a count (546,000) of New Zealand businesses employing fewer than 20 people.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Business Demography Statistics for the year referenced: true if enterprises with fewer than 20 employees are about 97% of all enterprises and number about 546,000, false if either figure is materially different.

civility.statement: I’m not trying to be personal. But he is useless, I tell you.
civility.explanation: A bare personal insult directed at a named member (Simeon Brown), attacking his worth rather than any policy position. The disclaimer does not soften it.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It must be because of all the money men who are backing them. There is no other reason.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side's imputed motives and donors; names no policy, mechanism, figure or outcome from the bill under debate.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This shameful piece of legislation will make it more difficult for workers to join a union and have a direct impact on how unions can promote worker interests.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House and its claimed effect on union membership and union activity, not on the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They have got survivor’s guilt; they kept their jobs and their voters haven’t, and so they’re now coming back in Opposition and trying to do everything that they didn’t.
focus.explanation: Wholly about the other party's electoral fate and supposed psychology; no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: They are a disgrace to this nation, and we’re going to get them out in the next two years.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the National–NZ First–ACT coalition will be removed from office at the next general election.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The official result of the next New Zealand general election as declared by the Electoral Commission: true if the National/NZ First/ACT coalition does not form the subsequent government, false if it returns to office.

rigor.statement: My manager has been with me for 16 years. Do you think he’d be hanging around if I didn’t do a good job and he wasn’t on a fair pay arrangement—and he damn well is. He didn’t need to be part of a union to achieve it at all, and my other workers, including a number of Māori who have worked for me, still to this day also keep in touch.
rigor.explanation: Argument from personal anecdote: one employer's own staff retention is offered as grounds for a conclusion about whether workers nationally need collective bargaining. A single favourable case cannot establish the general claim.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When wages are as low as they are in New Zealand right now, employers inevitably chose to hire cheap labour instead of investing in the technology, the plant, the capital, that will really drive productivity up. That’s why our productivity is much lower than in Australia, because New Zealand firms don’t invest in technology to improve productivity.
rigor.explanation: A stated causal mechanism (low wages → substitute labour for capital → low productivity), but the trans-Tasman productivity gap is attributed to that single cause with nothing offered to rule out others, and 'inevitably' asserts a necessity the premises do not support.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We spend $2 billion a year in this country subsidising rents because people can’t earn enough to pay the rent—multiple billions of dollars every year because employers don’t pay high enough wages.
specificity.explanation: Gives a named quantity and an annual period for a specific category of government spending, which a listener could go and check.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, can I remind them that 97 percent of businesses in New Zealand are small businesses—those that employ fewer than 20 people. There are 546,000 of them.
specificity.explanation: Two exact figures with the defining threshold stated, immediately checkable against official business statistics.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The most important thing to know about the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment’s advice is that they recommended against introducing fair pay agreements, arguing that the improvements for employees would be marginal and would be achieved at a significant cost to employer flexibility, and a blunt tool like fair pay agreements would not have been successful at improving employment outcomes for disadvantaged workers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that MBIE's departmental advice on the Fair Pay Agreements Bill recommended against introducing the regime, on the stated grounds that employee gains would be marginal, that they would come at significant cost to employer flexibility, and that the mechanism was too blunt to help disadvantaged workers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's Regulatory Impact Statement and departmental advice on the Fair Pay Agreements Bill (2021-22), as published on mbie.govt.nz / the Bill's disclosure statement. True if that advice recommended against proceeding and contains the marginal-benefit, employer-flexibility-cost and blunt-tool reasoning described; false if the advice recommended the regime or contains no such reasoning.

specificity.statement: The most important thing to know about the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment’s advice is that they recommended against introducing fair pay agreements, arguing that the improvements for employees would be marginal and would be achieved at a significant cost to employer flexibility, and a blunt tool like fair pay agreements would not have been successful at improving employment outcomes for disadvantaged workers.
specificity.explanation: Names the source of the advice and reproduces its specific grounds (marginal employee improvement, cost to employer flexibility, blunt tool, disadvantaged workers) — someone could go to the document and check it. No figures, which keeps it short of 1.0.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: New Zealand’s small and medium businesses are bursting with entrepreneurship, creativity, and innovation, and deserve a Government that empowers them because that’s how we create opportunities.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues and an undefined commitment to 'empower' — no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named policy, and nothing here that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Disadvantaged workers would actually have been made worse off under fair pay agreements because businesses would have hired fewer people or reduced the hours of work offered to existing workers because of the costs imposed on them.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House: imposed costs -> reduced hiring and hours -> disadvantaged workers worse off. The chain is coherent and the premise-to-conclusion step follows, but the magnitude of the labour-demand response is simply asserted, and the support offered is an appeal to the cited departmental advice rather than evidence of the effect itself.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Disadvantaged workers would actually have been made worse off under fair pay agreements because businesses would have hired fewer people or reduced the hours of work offered to existing workers because of the costs imposed on them.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the mechanism of the policy being repealed and who it affects — no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The previous Government made hiring staff too difficult, too expensive, and disincentivised employers from taking risks.
focus.explanation: A policy-directed criticism, but pitched at the previous Government's general record rather than a named measure, figure or outcome; the deciding test (does it name a specific policy or outcome?) fails.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The previous Government made hiring staff too difficult, too expensive, and disincentivised employers from taking risks.
civility.explanation: Blunt criticism of a predecessor government's record in a contested repeal debate, where there was ample opportunity to turn on individuals. No person is attacked, no bad faith imputed.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There’s an amazing woman called Marjorie Corman Aaron, who actually found through research that a woman who went in and negotiated aggressively for higher pay was the least likely to get hired. But a man who went in and aggressively negotiated the pay was most likely to get hired. This is real research—this is the truth of the matter. So women, in particular, by negotiating together as a group, end up doing better for all of them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a named researcher, Marjorie Corman Aaron, produced research finding that women who negotiate aggressively for pay are the least likely to be hired while men who do so are the most likely.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published research by Marjorie Corman Aaron on gender and negotiation outcomes in hiring; true if she authored a study reporting that pattern, false if the finding belongs to other authors (e.g. Bowles/Babcock/Lai) or if no such study exists under her name.

veracity.statement: So one of the issues with the duopoly in the supermarket sector is that we have Countdown, which is an Australian-owned company. They do have a collective agreement in place and the workers in that supermarket normally earn around $2 an hour more than those in a Pak ’N Save or a New World, which are New Zealand - owned.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Countdown workers, covered by a collective agreement, are paid roughly $2 an hour more than workers at Pak 'N Save and New World.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Countdown/Woolworths NZ collective agreement rates versus Foodstuffs (Pak 'N Save / New World) store pay rates as at late 2023; true if the typical hourly gap is approximately $2, false if the gap is materially smaller or absent.

veracity.statement: If you look at section 3, “Object of this Act”, you will see that one of the things it states is “(a)(ii) by acknowledging and addressing the inherent inequality of power in employment relationships;”, and, furthermore, to promote collective bargaining.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that section 3 of the Employment Relations Act 2000 contains the quoted words at (a)(ii) and that the objects include promoting collective bargaining.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The current text of section 3 of the Employment Relations Act 2000 on legislation.govt.nz; true if s 3(a)(ii) reads as quoted and collective bargaining appears among the objects, false if the wording or the subsection reference differs.

veracity.statement: And we even saw some supermarkets temporarily increase pay by 10 percent and then at the end of the lockdown say, “Oh no, sorry, you’re not worth that anymore. We’re going to take that away from you.”, and there was community outrage about that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that some New Zealand supermarkets raised pay by 10 percent during COVID-19 lockdown and then withdrew the increase when lockdown ended, prompting public criticism.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Company announcements and contemporaneous news reporting on supermarket COVID-19 pay increases in 2020; true if a major chain announced an increase of about 10 percent and removed it at the end of lockdown, false if no such increase or no such withdrawal is documented.

veracity.statement: Both National and ACT campaigned strongly against the introduction of fair pay agreements.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that both National and ACT campaigned in opposition to fair pay agreements before the 2023 election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National and ACT policy documents, campaign material and public statements from the 2020 and 2023 election campaigns, plus their votes on the Fair Pay Agreements Bill; true if both parties publicly opposed the policy, false if either was neutral or supportive.

rigor.statement: There’s an amazing woman called Marjorie Corman Aaron, who actually found through research that a woman who went in and negotiated aggressively for higher pay was the least likely to get hired. But a man who went in and aggressively negotiated the pay was most likely to get hired. This is real research—this is the truth of the matter. So women, in particular, by negotiating together as a group, end up doing better for all of them.
rigor.explanation: The evidence offered concerns individual negotiation and gender bias in hiring decisions; the conclusion drawn is about collective bargaining producing better wages for women. The cited research does not bear on group negotiation, so the conclusion does not follow from the premise — a non sequitur.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Even in my patch—I had an email from someone working in this area who’d been trying to get a collective agreement for up to eight years. So for people to say “You can just work it out.”, eight years of just trying to work it out hasn’t worked.
rigor.explanation: A single case is a legitimate counterexample to the universal claim she is answering ("you can just work it out"), so the local inference holds. But it is one anecdote from one correspondent doing the work of a general conclusion about how bargaining functions across the sector — an appeal to anecdote for the broader point.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I have heard from small and medium business owners across the Wairarapa electorate that are suffering as a result of the last Government’s poor legislation. They don’t have the same capacity to absorb blanket, top-down costs that large businesses do, and they’re suffering right now from the cost of living crisis inherited from over there that is strangling our communities.
rigor.explanation: The support offered is unnamed anecdote ("I have heard from"), and the causal step — that the previous government's legislation and its inheritance produced the cost of living crisis now hurting these businesses — is asserted rather than shown. The premise that small firms absorb blanket costs less easily does not establish that this legislation caused the suffering described: post hoc reasoning resting on anecdote.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So one of the issues with the duopoly in the supermarket sector is that we have Countdown, which is an Australian-owned company. They do have a collective agreement in place and the workers in that supermarket normally earn around $2 an hour more than those in a Pak ’N Save or a New World, which are New Zealand - owned.
specificity.explanation: Names the companies, the mechanism (a collective agreement) and gives an hourly figure — someone could go and check the pay rates against it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Employers within our communities have a relationship with their employees that’s built on trust—trust that the employer and employees uphold; trust that they will behave fairly and reasonably to each other. There’s trust that rates of pay and working conditions reflect the market, the industry, and the location.
specificity.explanation: This is the substantive case for repeal, so it is trying to convey content, but it carries none that could be checked or acted on — no figures, no mechanism, no named condition. It rests entirely on the repeated assertion of "trust".
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So for people to think this is funny—you know, they laughed before when my colleague Camilla Belich was talking about security guards who die on the job. They die on the job—they get stabbed. People, again, are laughing when I talk about security guards.
focus.explanation: A bill is before the House, but this passage is entirely about how members opposite are behaving in the chamber. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — the content is the other side's reaction rather than the repeal itself.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Yeah, it’s interesting watching the people across on the other side laugh. It’s not funny, the story I’m about to tell here, Katie Nimon—it’s not funny.
civility.explanation: Singles out a named member and imputes to her the character failing of laughing at a distressing story about a low-paid worker. Short of a direct insult, but it targets the person's conduct and disposition rather than any argument she has made.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I also stand here as an uri of a man whose photo still shines in the corner of my tūpuna ’hare Waimirirangi (Haere-ki-te Rā), Matiu Rata, the very reason the Waitangi Tribunal exists, which also, only at the weekend gone, handed over a key report to my people of Ngāpuhi, further embedding the truth that we never ceded sovereignty, and our whenua as well as constitutional power must come back to us.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions about the past: that Matiu Rata was responsible for the creation of the Waitangi Tribunal, and that the Tribunal delivered a report to Ngāpuhi in the weekend before 12 December 2023 finding that sovereignty was never ceded.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: (a) The parliamentary record for the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975 — true if Matiu Rata, as Minister of Māori Affairs, introduced/sponsored the Act that established the Waitangi Tribunal; false if the Tribunal was established by another Minister or instrument. (b) Waitangi Tribunal publication records for December 2023 — true if a Te Paparahi o Te Raki (Ngāpuhi) inquiry report was handed over in the week ending 10 December 2023 and finds the rangatira did not cede sovereignty; false if no such report was released in that window or if it makes no such finding.

veracity.statement: He advocated for the rights of women, and here I am as the first wahine to take the Tai Tokerau seat.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no woman has previously held the Te Tai Tokerau electorate, and that her tūpuna Eparaima Kapa advocated for women's rights.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary record of every MP elected for Te Tai Tokerau since the seat's creation in 1996 (and, if the claim is read to include the predecessor Northern Maori seat, its members too) — true if all previous holders were men, false if any woman held the seat before 2023.

veracity.statement: Like many whānau living in their rohe in the 1960s, we were swept up in the Māori urban diaspora, forced by meticulous and deliberate Government policy of assimilation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 1960s Māori urban migration was driven by deliberate government assimilation policy, not merely by economic drift.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 1961 Hunn Report and Department of Māori Affairs records on relocation/resettlement schemes and 'pepper-potting' — true if official policy of the period explicitly promoted urban relocation and assimilation of Māori; false if the historical record shows no such policy and urban migration was unassisted by government programmes.

rigor.statement: In my opinion, the whole motu should have been there, because if Ngāpuhi never ceded sovereignty, no iwi or hapū in the motu ceded sovereignty.
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation: the conclusion that no iwi or hapū anywhere ceded sovereignty is drawn from a finding about one iwi's signing. Nothing is offered to bridge Ngāpuhi's circumstances to those of every other signatory, whose signings occurred at different places and times; the inference would need a premise that the Treaty's effect was uniform, which is not supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Today, from the removal of bilingual signage on our national roads to rearranging the names of Government agencies, the immediate actions of this coalition signals a strong reluctance to treasure our national language and taonga tuku iho.
focus.explanation: Names two specific government actions (bilingual road signage, renaming of government agencies) and draws a policy conclusion about them. This is scrutiny of named measures, not content-free party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Today, from the removal of bilingual signage on our national roads to rearranging the names of Government agencies, the immediate actions of this coalition signals a strong reluctance to treasure our national language and taonga tuku iho.
civility.explanation: Genuinely contested political ground, and the criticism lands entirely on the coalition's decisions rather than on any individual. No person is attacked.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Today, from the removal of bilingual signage on our national roads to rearranging the names of Government agencies, the immediate actions of this coalition signals a strong reluctance to treasure our national language and taonga tuku iho.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the incoming coalition government has removed bilingual road signage and rearranged the names of government agencies. The characterisation of 'reluctance to treasure our national language' is the speaker's interpretation; the checkable part is the two actions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2023 National-NZ First and National-ACT coalition agreements and the incoming Ministers' December 2023 directions: true if those documents/directions provide for halting or removing the bilingual road signage programme and for requiring public service departments to use their English primary names; false if no such commitment or direction exists.

veracity.statement: Incredibly, 74 percent, or 58,000 hectares, of our Māori-owned land are landlocked with no legal access, although the Government is the neighbour for much of this land.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 74 percent, or 58,000 hectares, of the Māori-owned land in her iwi's rohe is landlocked without legal access, and that the Crown owns much of the adjoining land.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Māori Land Court / Te Puni Kōkiri landlocked Māori land records for the Mōkai Pātea rohe referred to: true if approximately 74 percent (about 58,000 ha) of Māori-owned land there has no legal access, false if the proportion or area is materially different.

veracity.statement: We were one marae that delivered 65,000 vaccinations for all whānau across Tāmaki-makau-rau.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Manurewa Marae, of which she was CEO, administered 65,000 COVID-19 vaccinations across Auckland.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Whatu Ora / Ministry of Health COVID-19 vaccination delivery records and Manurewa Marae's own reported totals for 2021-22: true if the marae's vaccination count is approximately 65,000, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: Tāmaki-makau-rau is a vibrant city with 250,000 Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the size of the Māori population of Auckland as 250,000.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census Māori ethnic group count for the Auckland region: true if approximately 250,000, false if materially below that figure.

specificity.statement: Incredibly, 74 percent, or 58,000 hectares, of our Māori-owned land are landlocked with no legal access, although the Government is the neighbour for much of this land.
specificity.explanation: Gives a percentage, an absolute hectare figure and a named condition (no legal access) for a defined body of land — checkable against land records.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So, in this debate on Part 1, I’d like to ask the Minister why there are no transitional savings and related provisions in this bill.
focus.explanation: Directed entirely at a specific drafting feature of the measure before the committee (the absence of transitional savings provisions in Part 1). No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Australia has higher productivity—I looked at some statistics tonight, and I think there was 1.4 percentage growth in productivity here when there was over 2 percent in Australia, up to 2019.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that NZ productivity growth ran at about 1.4 percent against over 2 percent in Australia, on a series ending in 2019.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD / NZ Productivity Commission labour-productivity growth series for New Zealand and Australia over the period ending 2019; true if NZ averages around 1.4% and Australia above 2% on a comparable measure, false if the two are close or the ordering is reversed.

veracity.statement: Minister, I know that you’re aware that the Productivity Commission has said we have been working harder than almost any other country for less money.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the NZ Productivity Commission has published a finding that New Zealanders work longer hours than almost any other country while producing less output per hour.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Productivity Commission publications (e.g. the "Productivity by the numbers" series and its OECD comparisons); true if a Commission report states that New Zealanders work among the longest hours in the OECD for below-average output per hour worked, false if no such finding appears.

veracity.statement: When we look at the question from the member Camilla Belich about why there are no transitional clauses in the bill: this is because for the bargaining of all the initiated fair pay agreements, they are in very early stages, which means that there will be no fair pay agreements that have been finalised before the legislation is repealed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that every initiated fair pay agreement was at a very early stage of bargaining as at December 2023, and that none would be finalised before repeal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's record of fair pay agreement initiations and bargaining progress to December 2023; true if no initiated FPA had reached a ratified or finalised agreement and all were in early bargaining, false if any had concluded bargaining or reached ratification.

specificity.statement: Australia has higher productivity—I looked at some statistics tonight, and I think there was 1.4 percentage growth in productivity here when there was over 2 percent in Australia, up to 2019.
specificity.explanation: Carries two figures, a comparator country and an end date, though the source of the statistics is left unnamed and the measure is hedged with "I think".
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I know that I have some different views on productivity, but I also am concerned that we’re about to dismantle the Productivity Commission and these are the kinds of institutions that have, in the past, been relied upon to give us advice.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the incoming Government will disestablish the New Zealand Productivity Commission.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Official records of the Commission's status; true if the New Zealand Productivity Commission is formally disestablished or closed, false if it is still operating as a Crown entity at the resolve-by date.

rigor.statement: How are we going to stop the drain of young talent going to Melbourne to work as a barista if in fact in New Zealand we cannot offer the same kind of wages, because everybody is going to the bare minimum all the time and hoping that that will sometimes make a profit?
rigor.explanation: A real argument about the policy, but it assumes its own conclusion: the rhetorical question presupposes both that repeal means "everybody is going to the bare minimum" and that wage levels are the driver of trans-Tasman migration, neither of which is established. Complex question resting on an unsupported causal premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So that is why we are repealing the Act in totality: because we’re repealing the bargaining process that sits behind the Act.
rigor.explanation: Circular. Asked why initiated agreements cannot be allowed to conclude, the answer offers the repeal itself as the reason for the repeal — the conclusion restates the premise, and no independent ground for ending the initiated bargaining is supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When we look at the question from the member Camilla Belich about why there are no transitional clauses in the bill: this is because for the bargaining of all the initiated fair pay agreements, they are in very early stages, which means that there will be no fair pay agreements that have been finalised before the legislation is repealed.
