civility.explanation: Pointed: 'forgot to mention' hints at selective presentation by the questioner, edging toward the person without landing on them. The substance of the rebuttal is about the bargaining process, not about Sepuloni.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I want to note for the member that the Equal Pay Act already creates a framework for inequalities between gender if you are in an equivalent role, but I very much enjoyed her contribution.
civility.explanation: Substantively engages the gender pay gap point by naming the existing statutory framework, but the closing 'I very much enjoyed her contribution' is a mildly patronising sign-off that treats the member's concern as diverting rather than serious. Edges toward condescension without becoming a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: To date, there has been $481,250 in funding been provided to bargaining sides that have initiated fair pay agreements, and there has been $750,000 provided to the New Zealand Council of Trade Unions.
specificity.explanation: Exact dollar figures attached to named recipients, in direct answer to a question about expenditure. Anyone could go and check the appropriations. She could have answered with a general characterisation and did not.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I know that’s probably an occupation foreign to most of the other side, who probably haven’t even cleaned their offices.
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed at members opposite personally — imputing that they are too privileged to have done manual work — rather than at their position on the bill.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Being a bus driver is not the most glamorous job, Madam Chair—well, you wouldn’t know, of course, probably having everyone drive for you!
civility.explanation: A personal jibe at the Chair, imputing privilege and detachment from ordinary work; it lands on the individual, not on any argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So the Minister might argue that repealing fair pay is just tidying things up, but I’d argue that it’s far tidier and healthier to provide good conditions and support bus drivers in Aotearoa rather than encouraging them to head to Australia.
civility.explanation: Directly contests the Minister's likely position on a contested repeal while attacking no one; the disagreement stays on the substance of what the bill does.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I know that’s probably an occupation foreign to most of the other side, who probably haven’t even cleaned their offices.
focus.explanation: No policy content: the sentence is entirely a characterisation of what the other side are like, with no measure, figure or outcome named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Or will you just walk all over these workers, like National and National Governments always have done in the past?
focus.explanation: A live consultation question is wrapped in a general claim about what National governments are always like; the weight of the sentence is party characterisation rather than the bill's provisions.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: New clause 8 specifies that the Ministry for Business, Innovation and Employment must undertake a specific analysis and report to the Minister on the particular impact of market flexibility.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the amendment before the committee — what it would require, of whom, and why.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As I said earlier, and I’ll continue to say with regards to this kaupapa, here we are, a week or so away from Christmas, and we’re putting up this bill.
rigor.explanation: Bare appeal to emotion: the proximity of Christmas is the only thing offered against the bill, and nothing connects the timing to the merits of repealing fair pay agreements.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Axing fair pay agreements will shave up to $10,000 a year off a bus driver’s salary—that’s just according to the Council of Trade Unions, who are a very reliable source, as we all know.
rigor.explanation: The figure is supported only by the assertion that the source is 'a very reliable source, as we all know' — a bare appeal to authority, with no mechanism or workings offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s for that very reason—because if you have a bottom line in terms of employment pay and working conditions that operate in Gisborne or in in Southland or in Northland, and if you are a dairy worker, for example, in any of the different areas or a manufacturer in those areas, it means that you can uplift your family and go to a different part of New Zealand and you are guaranteed the same wages and conditions.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference — a national pay and conditions floor makes terms portable between regions, therefore workers can move more freely — and the conclusion tracks the premise. The remaining gap is that worker mobility is asserted, not shown, to be what 'market flexibility' means for employers.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: My good friend here Helen White has represented bus drivers in Auckland as a lawyer in former times, and they’ve had a real push in terms of their conditions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Helen White acted professionally as a lawyer for Auckland bus drivers before entering Parliament, and that those drivers ran a campaign over their conditions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Helen White's professional record as an Auckland employment lawyer (NZ Law Society records, her parliamentary biography and maiden speech, and contemporaneous reporting of Auckland bus driver employment disputes); true if she is documented as acting for Auckland bus drivers, false if her practice did not include them.

veracity.statement: It’s normal for four or five bus drivers to quit each week because the conditions are just too much for them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a rate of bus driver resignations — about four to five a week — as the normal state of affairs, and attributes it to working conditions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Turnover figures for the bus operators under discussion (Auckland and Wellington operators, and Tramways Union / regional council reporting) for 2022–23; true if reported resignations average roughly four to five drivers a week, false if the recorded rate is materially lower.

veracity.statement: It’s more like about 98 percent of our businesses are small businesses, and a lot of those ones are in fierce competition.
veracity.explanation: Corrects an earlier figure and asserts that about 98 percent of New Zealand businesses are small businesses.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Business Demography Statistics for 2023: the share of New Zealand enterprises falling under the standard small-business threshold (fewer than 20 employees); true if the share is about 98 percent, false if materially lower, and it would also settle whether the 80 percent figure she is correcting is the accurate one.

veracity.statement: Dunedin bus drivers have even had to pee behind bushes and limit their water intake—not like in the Chamber—so that they can keep at work because there are no toilets.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Dunedin bus drivers have lacked toilet facilities on route, to the point of urinating outdoors and restricting how much they drink.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Otago Regional Council and Tramways Union statements, driver submissions and media reporting on toilet access for Dunedin bus drivers in the years to 2023; true if documented accounts exist of drivers without route toilet facilities, false if the facilities were in place.

veracity.statement: So my question to the Minister is: does the Minister acknowledge that bus drivers in Australia, who have benefited from sector-based bargaining, are paid 40 percent more than here in New Zealand, and, if so, how will she bridge the gap without sector-based bargaining here?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Australian bus drivers, working under sector-based bargaining, are paid 40 percent more than their New Zealand counterparts.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Average bus and coach driver pay in Australia (ABS earnings data and the relevant Fair Work modern award / sector agreements) compared with New Zealand rates (Stats NZ earnings data and operator collective agreements) as at 2023, adjusted to a common currency; true if the Australian figure is around 40 percent higher, false if the gap is materially smaller.

divination.statement: Axing fair pay agreements will shave up to $10,000 a year off a bus driver’s salary—that’s just according to the Council of Trade Unions, who are a very reliable source, as we all know.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that repealing the fair pay agreements regime will reduce a bus driver's annual pay by as much as $10,000, relaying a Council of Trade Unions estimate.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Bus driver pay rates in collective agreements and Stats NZ earnings data after the repeal, compared with the rates in force in December 2023 and with the pay settings the pending bus driver fair pay agreement would have set; true if any substantial group of bus drivers ends up as much as $10,000 a year worse off, false if bus driver pay holds or rises over that period.

specificity.statement: Axing fair pay agreements will shave up to $10,000 a year off a bus driver’s salary—that’s just according to the Council of Trade Unions, who are a very reliable source, as we all know.
specificity.explanation: A named policy, a dollar figure, an affected occupation and an attributed source — someone could go and check the estimate.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: New clause 8 specifies that the Ministry for Business, Innovation and Employment must undertake a specific analysis and report to the Minister on the particular impact of market flexibility.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the agency and the reporting obligation; loses a little because 'impact of market flexibility' is not itself defined as a measurable quantity.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So my question to the Minister is: does the Minister acknowledge that bus drivers in Australia, who have benefited from sector-based bargaining, are paid 40 percent more than here in New Zealand, and, if so, how will she bridge the gap without sector-based bargaining here?
specificity.explanation: A named comparator jurisdiction, a percentage gap and a named bargaining mechanism — a question precise enough to be answered or checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Allowing the system to continue for one sector would go against the commitment that we brought to this House, but also our commitment to New Zealand voters, who are expecting us to deliver on our commitment from the campaign.
rigor.explanation: An argument is advanced — the sector carve-out should be rejected — but the only reason offered is an appeal to the Government's own electoral mandate. Nothing is said about whether a supermarket-sector exemption would be good or bad on its merits, so the conclusion rests on an appeal to authority (the campaign commitment) rather than on the effects of the amendment.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Nobody will be worse off this Christmas because there have not been any fair pay agreements finalised.
rigor.explanation: The inference is sound on its own terms: if no agreement was ever in force, repealing the Act removes no existing wage entitlement. The gap is that it answers a claim about foregone future gains with a fact about current entitlements, so the conclusion is narrower than the rebuttal it is offered as.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We do that by encouraging good wages and good working conditions right across a sector and we don’t do that by having a race to the bottom of who can pay their workers the least and have the most restrictive working conditions possible.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: the only two options offered are sector-wide bargaining or a race to the bottom, with nothing establishing that the alternatives are exhaustive or that the existing Employment Relations Act framework produces the second.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I’d refer the member to the tables on pages 42 to 50 of the 2021 regulatory impact statement.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific document and an exact page range for the cost figures asked about — the member could go and check it. Falls short of 1.0 only because the figures themselves are not stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So the new clause 6 that is proposed to amend this bill is that the Royal assent of the bill is contingent on a review by the International Labour Organization (ILO), ensuring that New Zealand is compliant with all international obligations including ILO conventions and free-trade agreements.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the mechanism (Royal assent made contingent on a review) and the reviewing body. No timeframe or process detail for how the review would be commissioned, which keeps it short of full precision.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What we’re simply saying to the Minister is that, look, let’s assume that it doesn’t go to plan and that we have a review undertaken in three years to investigate how the terms and conditions, particularly for those who are disproportionately affected—and we’ve all heard that; that’s not us making it up, those are facts.
specificity.explanation: Gives a mechanism (a statutory review) and a timeframe (three years) and identifies who it would examine, but leaves the review's terms, who conducts it and what would trigger action undefined.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We went into that election clearly indicating that we would repeal this law, and the voters responded in kind.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that repeal of the Fair Pay Agreements Act was a stated pre-election commitment of the parties now in government, and that they won the election on it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: ACT and National published policy/manifesto material for the 2023 general election, plus the National–ACT coalition agreement: true if both parties publicly committed before the October 2023 election to repealing the Fair Pay Agreements Act; false if repeal was not a stated pre-election position.

veracity.statement: Nobody will be worse off this Christmas because there have not been any fair pay agreements finalised.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of record that no fair pay agreement had been completed under the 2022 Act before the repeal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE / Employment New Zealand's record of fair pay agreements bargained and concluded under the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022 as at December 2023: true if no fair pay agreement had been finalised and brought into force; false if any had.

veracity.statement: I’d like to clarify that point right now that there is no ability with the proposed fair pay agreements that would result in strikes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the fair pay agreements regime as legislated contained no mechanism by which strike action could arise.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The industrial-action provisions of the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022: true if the Act prohibited strikes and lockouts in relation to fair pay agreement bargaining; false if it permitted or created any avenue for strike action arising from the FPA process.

veracity.statement: So there’s been a lot of discussion in this Chamber and allegations from those members opposite that the introduction of fair pay agreements would not only introduce the opportunity for more striking but it’s actually been alleged by, in fact, Nicola Willis, when I was on Newstalk ZB with her last week, that it would make all those who were part of a fair pay agreement required to be part of a union, and that’s just not true.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim attributed to another member — that fair pay agreements would compel union membership — and asserts it is false.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Two checks: (a) the Newstalk ZB interview recording or transcript from the week before 12 December 2023, for whether Willis said fair pay agreement coverage would require union membership; and (b) the coverage provisions of the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022, for whether employees covered by an agreement had to be union members. The relayed allegation is false if the Act extended coverage to all employees in scope regardless of union membership.

veracity.statement: They have told us that they were restrained or constrained because of time lines.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that officials from MBIE told the House their advice on the repeal was constrained by the timeframes imposed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The departmental disclosure statement and regulatory impact statement for the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill, and MBIE's evidence to the House: true if MBIE recorded that its analysis or consultation was limited by the time available; false if no such constraint was stated.

focus.statement: So the new clause 6 that is proposed to amend this bill is that the Royal assent of the bill is contingent on a review by the International Labour Organization (ILO), ensuring that New Zealand is compliant with all international obligations including ILO conventions and free-trade agreements.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure before the committee — a specific amendment and what it would require. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: But we should not forget that the ones that are most penalised in this are those people that clean our floors, that look after our children, that drive our buses, that will be earning less this Christmas, that will afford less on their table, fewer Christmas presents.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that low-paid workers in cleaning, childcare and bus driving will earn less over the coming Christmas period as a result of the repeal.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Quarterly Employment Survey average hourly earnings for the cleaning, childcare/education support and road passenger transport sectors: true if earnings in those sectors fall between the September 2023 and March 2024 quarters; false if they hold steady or rise.

civility.statement: They will have less money because of the selfishness and the self-interest that this bill inflicts upon New Zealanders.
civility.explanation: Imputes selfishness and self-interest as the motive behind the bill rather than arguing its effects. No individual member is named or insulted, which keeps it above a personal attack, but ascribing bad faith is a genuine civility failure under the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I don’t want to make this debate about whether we are opposed to employers, because sometimes the value is that we should be about promoting and encouraging good employers to be great employers.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested repeal debate in which she explicitly declines to frame the argument as a fight against a group, and engages the substance instead. Attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It just would not make sense in practice for that review because there have not been any fair pay agreements finalised. There is nothing to compare the impact of that review to. So the whole concept of the Amendment Paper does not work in practice.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the amendment before the committee: if no fair pay agreements were ever finalised, a review of the repeal's sector-by-sector impacts has no baseline, so the review clause is inoperable. The conclusion tracks the premise offered; no fallacy or appeal. Judged on validity only, not on whether the premise is true.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We have from multiple submissions, from evidence overseas—and I’m just noting that this Government has said it will be evidence based—and from the full impact statement that we saw when the first piece of legislation came through this House that workers will be better off with the protection of a fair pay agreement.
rigor.explanation: An argument about the measure, but the support is named only by category — 'multiple submissions', 'evidence overseas', 'the full impact statement' — with no finding, figure or mechanism drawn from any of them. It leans on an appeal to authority (the sources are cited rather than used), leaving a gap between what is shown and the conclusion that workers will be better off.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, it’s actually both of those things, because there’s a connection between higher wages and productivity. Again, having studied employment relations at university, I like to look at the evidence.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority — specifically the speaker's own credentials — offered in place of the evidence. The asserted 'connection between higher wages and productivity' is stated but never shown, and its direction is left unspecified, so the conclusion that both explanations hold is not supported by anything actually presented.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It just would not make sense in practice for that review because there have not been any fair pay agreements finalised. There is nothing to compare the impact of that review to. So the whole concept of the Amendment Paper does not work in practice.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at 12 December 2023 no fair pay agreement had been finalised (concluded/ratified) under the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's register of fair pay agreement bargaining as at December 2023: true if no FPA had been ratified or determined by the Employment Relations Authority at that date (initiated-but-unconcluded bargaining does not count as finalised); false if any FPA had been finalised.

veracity.statement: The fair pay agreement system does actually specify that the only entities who could represent employees in bargaining are entities, and not employees themselves, and so in effect, no, the person doesn’t have to join a union, but they can only be represented by a union in that bargaining process.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a two-part claim about the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022: that a worker was not required to join a union to be covered by a fair pay agreement, and that on the employee side only a union (not an individual worker) could act as bargaining representative. The garbled clause about 'entities' is live-speech repetition; the substantive claim is the one to check.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022, Parts on bargaining sides and employee bargaining parties: true if the Act restricts employee-side bargaining parties to eligible unions while extending coverage to all employees in scope regardless of union membership; false if the Act permitted non-union employee bargaining representatives, or conditioned coverage on union membership.

veracity.statement: It’s pretty plain and simple and we have a coalition commitment to repeal the fair pay agreements by Christmas, which is what we intend to do.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2023 coalition arrangements contained a commitment to repeal the fair pay agreements legislation, with a stated deadline of Christmas 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National–ACT and National–NZ First coalition agreements (24 November 2023) and the Government's published 100-day plan: true if repeal of the Fair Pay Agreements legislation appears as a coalition commitment with a before-Christmas 2023 timing; false if the commitment is absent or carries no such deadline.

veracity.statement: The reason for that is that they have sector-based bargaining. It’s called enterprise bargaining.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Australia's higher wages are the product of sector-based bargaining, and identifies the Australian system's name for that arrangement as 'enterprise bargaining'.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Australia's Fair Work Act 2009 and Fair Work Commission material on enterprise agreements: true if 'enterprise bargaining' denotes bargaining at sector/industry level; false if enterprise agreements are made at the level of an individual enterprise or employer rather than across a sector (the two being distinct bargaining levels, with multi-employer/supported bargaining a separate later stream).

focus.statement: Those on that side of the Chamber—and in fact many New Zealanders—love to make a lot of noise, a lot of statements, around the fact that if you go across the Ditch to Australia, people will earn more money.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point here — the trans-Tasman wage comparison, which she goes on to link to bargaining structure — but it is carried inside a characterisation of what the other side of the Chamber 'loves' to say. A real policy claim wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My amendment to clause 2 will replace “on the day after Royal assent” with “three years and one day after Royal assent”.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, quotes the exact wording being removed and the exact wording replacing it. Fully checkable against the Amendment Paper and actionable as drafted.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Will she admit that what this bill is doing is clawing back the rights and opportunities for working people in this country who are doing it tough.
civility.explanation: A hard challenge directed at the Minister, but entirely about the bill's effect on workers rather than about the Minister herself. The 'will she admit' framing is pointed and edges toward suggesting something is being concealed, which keeps it just below a clean 1.0; no attack on the person lands.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is a commitment to industry who wish to exploit, and we will oppose it.
civility.explanation: Attributes an exploitative motive to industry and, by implication, to the bill's backers, but no individual member is attacked and the target is the measure itself.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is a commitment to industry who wish to exploit, and we will oppose it.
focus.explanation: Directed at the bill under debate rather than at the other party generally, but it names no mechanism, figure or outcome — a characterisation of the measure rather than engagement with it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: By repealing that—what this bill proposes—we go back to what things were before the Fair Pay Agreements Act came in.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: names the Act being repealed and states the effect of the repeal, with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So the questions that I have for the Minister, which I will flag first up so she can consider them: when will the Royal assent be sought? How many proceedings are under way that the Royal assent will cut across? How have participants to the proceedings been notified that the Royal assent will extinguish their proceedings and any legal rights that ensue from those proceedings? What natural justice issues does the Minister anticipate, given the Royal assent will cut across those proceedings? And how will parties be compensated for costs of the proceedings under way?
focus.explanation: Entirely on clause 2 of the bill and the legal consequences of its commencement; no reference to the other party's record or character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My understanding is that Royal assent will happen as it does for all other bills that leave this House in the normal process, but I also want to make it very clear that my purpose in bringing this bill to the House is for all bargaining processes to stop and cease, and that the law itself ceases and the bargaining process thereunder ceases.
focus.explanation: Addresses the commencement mechanism and the bill's intended operation directly, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Now, if we consider where we were before fair pay agreements came in in comparison to Australia, who had the equivalent of fair pay agreements, their wages and their conditions, over a period of roughly 30 years, improved considerably; New Zealand’s did not.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Australia had an equivalent of fair pay agreements and that over roughly 30 years Australian wages and conditions improved considerably while New Zealand's did not.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Comparison of Australian and New Zealand real wage growth over c.1990-2020 using ABS Wage Price Index / OECD average annual wages against Stats NZ Labour Cost Index / OECD series; true if Australian real wages and conditions rose materially more than New Zealand's over that span, false if the two series track each other or New Zealand's rose comparably. Separately, whether Australia's modern awards system is a fair equivalent of the Fair Pay Agreements regime per an industrial-relations comparison (e.g. Fair Work Commission award coverage vs the FPA Act 2022 scheme).

veracity.statement: So what we see here is that the fair pay agreements were a new piece of law enacted in 2021 that allowed parties to come to the table to renegotiate longstanding issues which had been in court before or they were party to mediations that were already under way.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the fair pay agreements legislation was enacted in 2021.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand legislation record for the Fair Pay Agreements Act — the date it passed its third reading and received Royal assent; true if that occurred in 2021, false if in any other year.

veracity.statement: At the same time, we have a number of commercial firms who employ these 35,000 cleaners around New Zealand, who have also engaged their own representatives and have come to the table in good faith to bargain around a floor for conditions, be it pay or—in the case of cleaners—training.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the coverage of the cleaners' fair pay agreement bargaining is approximately 35,000 cleaners employed across New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's approved initiation application for the cleaning-sector fair pay agreement and its stated coverage estimate, or Stats NZ employment counts for ANZSIC building-cleaning services; true if the covered workforce is around 35,000, false if materially different (e.g. under 25,000 or over 50,000).

rigor.statement: Now, if we consider where we were before fair pay agreements came in in comparison to Australia, who had the equivalent of fair pay agreements, their wages and their conditions, over a period of roughly 30 years, improved considerably; New Zealand’s did not.
rigor.explanation: Offers a real comparison as evidence for the conclusion that repeal returns New Zealand to a worse-performing settlement, but the causal step from Australia's award system to its wage growth is asserted, not shown — the inference rests on a correlation between two national systems with many other differences.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What the issue is is that because we haven’t been through the ordinary public process, we haven’t had the benefit of the regulatory impact analysis, and we haven’t had the benefit of time that would usually be given to the sort of legislation where a Government might consider cutting across proceedings that are under way currently, parties to those proceedings haven’t had time to adjust and to change their approach.
rigor.explanation: A valid inference from a stated premise: if the bill skipped select committee and the usual timeline, then the regulatory impact analysis and the adjustment period that would ordinarily precede legislation extinguishing live proceedings are absent. The conclusion tracks the premise; the small gap is that no alternative route to that analysis is ruled out.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So the questions that I have for the Minister, which I will flag first up so she can consider them: when will the Royal assent be sought? How many proceedings are under way that the Royal assent will cut across? How have participants to the proceedings been notified that the Royal assent will extinguish their proceedings and any legal rights that ensue from those proceedings? What natural justice issues does the Minister anticipate, given the Royal assent will cut across those proceedings? And how will parties be compensated for costs of the proceedings under way?
specificity.explanation: Five separately answerable questions naming a specific mechanism (Royal assent), a specific class of affected parties (those in proceedings under way) and specific asks (timing, counts, notification, compensation). A precise question is as checkable as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My understanding is that Royal assent will happen as it does for all other bills that leave this House in the normal process, but I also want to make it very clear that my purpose in bringing this bill to the House is for all bargaining processes to stop and cease, and that the law itself ceases and the bargaining process thereunder ceases.
specificity.explanation: States the intended effect unambiguously — bargaining under the Act ceases — but supplies no timing, no count of affected proceedings and no mechanism for the transitional questions that were asked.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We can look at the wages that we have now and the productivity we have and we can see that the status quo is not working.
rigor.explanation: An inference is offered — current wage and productivity levels imply the status quo has failed — but the premises are only gestured at, with no figures and no link shown between those levels and the absence of fair pay agreements. A real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Throughout the debate there also has been a lack of ability to produce evidence as to why this must be repealed; yet there’s a sense of urgency around the commencement—basically, this Act coming into force on the day after the Royal assent.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure before the House: the absence of evidence offered sits oddly with commencement the day after Royal assent. It leans on absence of evidence, but the burden legitimately sits with the party proposing the change, so the gap is modest rather than fallacious.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In three years’ time, if it’s a failed experiment as you suspect it will be, you will see, and you’ll be able to prove that on the basis of evidence.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows from the premise: if the objection to fair pay agreements is that they will not work, letting the already-initiated bargaining run its course would produce exactly the evidence needed to settle that. A valid conditional, and it grants the opponent's assumption rather than caricaturing it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But to the point that was actually about this section, I heard a lot about delay, but this is not a Government that delays; this is a Government of action.
rigor.explanation: The reason offered for not delaying is that the Government does not delay — the conclusion restates the premise. Circular, with nothing offered about the commencement date itself.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s regretful in this situation that we haven’t had the opportunity to see a fair pay agreement in place.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no fair pay agreement was ever concluded and in force under the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022 before this repeal bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's register of fair pay agreement bargaining initiated under the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022, and the Gazette record of any agreement brought into force; true if no fair pay agreement had been finalised or come into force as at December 2023, false if at least one had.

veracity.statement: She has otherwise stated, predominantly, the words “I believe” over and over and over and over—not “I know” or “as the evidence points out” or “evidence shows”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a checkable fact about the Minister's own contributions to this debate: that her justifications were phrased as personal belief and did not cite evidence.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard transcript of Brooke van Velden's contributions to the committee of the whole House on the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill, 12 December 2023; true if her substantive justifications are predominantly 'I believe' formulations with no citation of data, reports or research, false if she cited identifiable evidence sources.

veracity.statement: The company locked out the bus drivers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an Auckland bus operator responded to a strike notice over drivers taking toilet breaks by locking the drivers out.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Employment Relations Authority records and contemporaneous reporting on Auckland bus operators; true if a lockout notice was issued against Auckland bus drivers in response to the strike action described, false if no such lockout is recorded.

veracity.statement: So we are reversing all other changes but retaining this one, so it’s not in the bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the repeal bill leaves the amendment expressing Employment Court fees in GST-exclusive form intact by being silent on it, while reversing the other changes made by the Fair Pay Agreements Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Act 2023 and the Employment Court Regulations 2000 as amended; true if the GST-exclusive fee amendment survives the repeal, false if the Act repeals or reverses it.

veracity.statement: One piece of evidence that was not presented in the case made for this repeal is how does the supposed flexible labour market, which I would say is a synonym for the flexibility of employers to exploit workers—how did you seek evidence on the impact on disabled workers, who currently have three times the unemployment rate of non-disabled workers and an average median income of $255 less per week than non-disabled workers?
veracity.explanation: Asserts two statistics about disabled New Zealanders: an unemployment rate three times that of non-disabled people, and a median weekly income $255 lower.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey disability statistics for the unemployment rate, and Stats NZ disability/income statistics for median weekly income; true if the disabled unemployment rate is approximately three times the non-disabled rate and the median weekly income gap is approximately $255 in the most recent release before December 2023, false if either figure is materially different.

civility.statement: They deserve a Minister who can back a piece of legislation with evidence, with solid arguments, and so this is why I’m testing whether she would be open to delaying the commencement of the bill to allow for her arguments to be backed up by actual solid figures and facts rather than just vibes.
civility.explanation: The substantive request (delay commencement to gather evidence) is legitimate, but characterising the Minister's case as 'just vibes' is a sneer at her rather than an engagement with what she argued. Short of a direct insult, but past pointed.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It seems to me that the most appropriate name would be the “Poor Pay Promise Bill”, because it is indeed the fulfilment of a commitment to industry that they will be allowed to continue to exploit workers, continue to not guarantee basic wages—livable wages—and fair pay.
civility.explanation: No individual is insulted, but the statement imputes bad faith — that the repeal exists to let employers exploit workers as a favour to industry — rather than engaging the case made for it. That is a real civility failure under the re-anchored scale, though a mild one.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So we have identified industries that have come forward and said that there’s appetite for this solution.
specificity.explanation: A substantive claim offered as evidence, but no industry is named, no number given and no stage of bargaining stated — nobody could check or act on it as put.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But to the point that was actually about this section, I heard a lot about delay, but this is not a Government that delays; this is a Government of action.
specificity.explanation: Answers a detailed request to delay commencement with a slogan: no timeframe, no mechanism, no reason relating to the commencement clause.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One piece of evidence that was not presented in the case made for this repeal is how does the supposed flexible labour market, which I would say is a synonym for the flexibility of employers to exploit workers—how did you seek evidence on the impact on disabled workers, who currently have three times the unemployment rate of non-disabled workers and an average median income of $255 less per week than non-disabled workers?
specificity.explanation: Carries two precise, checkable figures — a 3× unemployment ratio and a $255 weekly median income gap — attached to a named group and a named policy question. Precision here is independent of whether the figures are right.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think it is premature of the Minister to outline that expectation right here, right now, when in fact the bill has not been given Royal assent, and I think it is an important point and distinction to make.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House: the premise (the bill has not yet received Royal assent, so the Act remains in force) genuinely supports the conclusion that the Minister's stated expectation that bargaining cease is premature. Marked down slightly because the gap between 'not yet law' and 'the expectation is improper' is asserted rather than argued, given passage was effectively certain.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Once the Fair Pay Agreements Act is repealed, bargaining for initiated fair pay agreements will cease as there will be no legislative mechanism to bring any agreements into force.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows from the premise offered: if the statutory machinery that gives an agreement legal force is removed, bargaining under it has no terminus. A reason is supplied and it carries the conclusion; no fallacy or appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: They have not had an opportunity to think about what they think an appropriate commencement date might be for this bill, because it has not been subjected to the normal scrutiny process that all other bills generally are expected to go through.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill was not referred to a select committee and received no public submissions process, unlike the ordinary course for bills.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliament bill record for the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill (bills.parliament.nz) and the Hansard urgency motions of 12 December 2023: true if the bill passed all stages without referral to a select committee and with no call for public submissions; false if a select committee stage (even truncated) took submissions.

veracity.statement: The Fair Pay Agreements Act and associated regulations came into force on 1 December 2022.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific commencement date for the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022 and its associated regulations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The commencement provisions of the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022 on legislation.govt.nz and the associated regulations' commencement clause: true if both took effect on 1 December 2022, false if either commenced on a materially different date.

veracity.statement: Both the National Party and the ACT Party opposed the development and introduction of the fair pay agreements legislation at that time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that National and ACT both opposed the Fair Pay Agreements Bill through its passage in 2021-2022.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard division records for the Fair Pay Agreements Bill's readings in 2021-2022: true if National and ACT cast votes against at each reading, false if either party supported it at any stage.

civility.statement: Fair pay agreements were never about fairness. They forced a minority of union workers’ views on all affected workers and businesses, and this Government opposes the views that were put forward by the previous Government and that law.
civility.explanation: A blunt, contemptuous verdict on the policy and on the previous government's law, but it lands on the measure, not on any person. No individual's character, competence or motives are impugned. Under the re-anchored scale, brutal criticism of a policy is the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Under that system, unions and employer associations could bargain for employment terms and conditions that covered all employees in an industry or occupation.
specificity.explanation: Names the actual mechanism of the repealed regime — who bargains (unions and employer associations), over what (employment terms and conditions), and the coverage scope (all employees in an industry or occupation). Concrete enough to check against the Act; short of full marks only for carrying no thresholds or figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are a Government that wants to see higher wages for workers and a thriving economy, a thriving, competitive business sector.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic aspirations — higher wages, a thriving economy, a competitive business sector — with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named measure. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We are doing this to send a clear signal to businesses that this Government understands the pressures that businesses have faced in an environment of increasing inflation and a Labour-led Government that has piled on regulations.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy rationale (removing regulatory cost from businesses facing inflation), but roughly half the weight is a general characterisation of the previous Labour-led Government as having 'piled on regulations' — no specific regulation, figure or outcome is named alongside the repeal itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is not a dictatorship where Ministers get to decide what goes and what doesn’t. It will be decided under the legislative framework that we have.
focus.explanation: Engages the legal mechanism at issue — whether existing rights under the Legislation Act survive the repeal regardless of ministerial intent. Squarely on the measure, not on the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What do the countries that do have fair pay and conditions for these types of workforces have in common? And the answer is quite simple. They have industry awards very similar to the system that would have been initiated under the fair pay agreements.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the policy design being repealed and the international evidence for it; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When you are presented with an employment contract, are you given an option of not accepting that employment contract? Most of the time you are not. You are told, in most industries, when you get an employment agreement, that this is the agreement. Take it or leave it.
focus.explanation: Addresses the substantive objection raised about how fair pay agreements bind parties, rather than the interjector's party.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is not a dictatorship where Ministers get to decide what goes and what doesn’t. It will be decided under the legislative framework that we have.
civility.explanation: Pointed, and the word 'dictatorship' edges toward the Minister personally, but the target remains the claimed scope of ministerial power rather than the Minister's character.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s frankly unconscionable that these fair pay agreements are being taken away from these workers just before Christmas.
civility.explanation: Harsh moral language, but aimed at the decision and its timing rather than at any member. Fierce criticism of a policy choice sits near the top of the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, some of us have been here a little longer than others.
civility.explanation: A condescending dig at other members' inexperience rather than a point about the bill — short of a direct insult, but it is about the people opposite rather than the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What do the countries that do have fair pay and conditions for these types of workforces have in common? And the answer is quite simple. They have industry awards very similar to the system that would have been initiated under the fair pay agreements.
rigor.explanation: A genuine comparative argument, but it infers causation from a shared feature across selected countries with no control for other differences — a correlational/selection gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When you are presented with an employment contract, are you given an option of not accepting that employment contract? Most of the time you are not. You are told, in most industries, when you get an employment agreement, that this is the agreement. Take it or leave it.
rigor.explanation: Answers the compulsion objection by analogy with individual employment contracts, but the analogy is imperfect — that employees already lack choice does not establish that added statutory coverage involves no further compulsion. A real inference about the policy, and a weak one.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There was an Act to allow equal pay to occur, and it was passed I think in the 1990s and repealed very shortly thereafter by the National Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a statutory equal-pay mechanism was enacted in the 1990s and repealed soon afterwards by a National government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand statute record for the Employment Equity Act 1990 and its repealing Act: true if the Act was passed in 1990 and repealed by a National-led government within roughly a year; false if no such Act exists, if it was enacted outside the 1990s, or if the repeal was not by a National government or came years later.

divination.statement: I know that the time will come when fair pay agreements also are in force again under the next Labour Government.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that fair pay agreement legislation will be re-enacted and in force under a future Labour government — an outcome contingent on an election result, not solely on the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand statute record and government formation: true if a Labour-led government enacts legislation establishing sector-wide fair pay agreements (or an equivalent industry-award bargaining system) and it is in force by the resolve-by date; false if no such legislation is in force by then.

specificity.statement: The people that would have benefited from fair pay agreements, as I was saying, are the most vulnerable in our country: our bus drivers, our hospitality workers, our security guards, our commercial cleaners—some of the people that clean this very building that we’re in—early childhood education teachers, and our supermarket workers.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific occupational groups affected, which is checkable against the agreements initiated, but carries no numbers, wage figures, coverage counts or timeframes.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They have no relation, they have no connection, they have no empathy in terms of what we’re talking about.
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of the other side's background and feelings; no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named. This is the party-directed content Focus exists to catch — no individual is insulted, so Civility passes it cleanly.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The thing is, the Treasury already warned the far-right Government that repealing the legislation would hurt our most vulnerable workers: Māori, Pasifika, wāhine—our women, our women workers.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure before the House by citing official advice on who it affects — legitimate scrutiny with a named source and named affected groups — though the 'far-right Government' label carries some party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: ACT, National, and New Zealand First—they are bonded by their malice towards beneficiaries, renters, workers, and the environment.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the other parties are supposedly like — their shared motive — with no policy, figure or outcome named. Attributing malice to parties rather than a named person leaves Civility untouched; this is the tribalism Focus measures.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So there was a competitive process between different bus companies, and the one that could pay the lowest wages won.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism: how competitive tendering for bus contracts transmits into wage-setting, which is the case for the bargaining floor the bill removes.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We hear that sort of kōrero all the time from the right, this trickle-down economics, which is a myth: pretending that bosses will pay workers decent wages out of the goodness of their hearts.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the opposing position is restated as 'bosses will pay well out of the goodness of their hearts', a claim no one on that side advanced, and the conclusion that the position is a myth rests on that reformulation rather than on the actual argument about labour-market flexibility. There is a real policy inference here, so it is eligible, and it is a weak one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What it did was it sunk people, sunk people to the absolute bare minimum, and we have terrible child poverty as a result.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc: child poverty is attributed to low-wage settings as a single cause, with no evidence offered linking the two and no other contributing factor considered. The statement engages the actual policy, so it is eligible; the inference is the weak part.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But our people just want to do their job, and these idiots, sadly, do not understand the whole line of collective bargaining.
civility.explanation: A direct insult ('these idiots') aimed at the members opposite, attacking their intelligence rather than the case they make. The insult is the speaker's own conduct, so subject remains the speaker.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I need to give you fools a history lesson because you don’t know anything about equal pay for work of equal value.
civility.explanation: Addresses opposing members directly as 'fools' and asserts their ignorance; the attack lands on the people, not the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That is a problem, because you are sinking people, in the Government today.
civility.explanation: A blunt charge about the consequences of the Government's decision in a sharply contested debate — she had ample opportunity to turn on individuals and did not. The attack stays on the action, not the person.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The thing is, the Treasury already warned the far-right Government that repealing the legislation would hurt our most vulnerable workers: Māori, Pasifika, wāhine—our women, our women workers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Treasury, specifically, gave prior advice that repealing the fair pay agreement legislation would harm vulnerable workers, and names the affected groups.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's published advice and the departmental regulatory impact material on the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022 Repeal Bill (Treasury advice releases and the MBIE/Treasury RIS, December 2023): true if Treasury advice states that repeal would disproportionately harm low-paid workers, specifically Māori, Pacific and women workers; false if no such Treasury warning exists, or if the warning came only from another agency.

veracity.statement: But when you see Jim Bolger turning, maybe there’s a chance for him, and I mihi to Jim Bolger today for his work in shaping these fair bargaining agreements.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that former National Prime Minister Jim Bolger had a hand in designing the fair pay agreements system being repealed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's record of the Fair Pay Agreements Working Group (2018): true if Jim Bolger chaired or served on the group that designed the fair pay agreement framework, false if he had no such role.

veracity.statement: The response of their employer at the time was to lock them out, because that was enough—that was enough—for them to tip all those workers out on the street and not pay them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that after a strike notice limited to taking toilet breaks, the Auckland bus operator responded by locking the drivers out and withholding their pay.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Employment Relations Authority filings and contemporaneous news coverage of the Auckland bus drivers' dispute referred to: true if the operator issued a lockout notice in response to the toilet-break strike notice and drivers were stood down without pay, false if no lockout occurred or drivers continued to be paid.

veracity.statement: The 80 percent of people who aren’t in unions were going to have a minimum floor.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that about 80 percent of New Zealand workers are outside union membership and would have been the beneficiaries of the fair pay agreement floor.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE union membership returns / Stats NZ figures on union density among New Zealand employees around 2023: true if roughly 80% of employees were not union members (density near 20%), false if density was materially higher.

divination.statement: This new Government should be ashamed of the hollowness of this move, because if Labour regain the Government benches—which is going to happen in three years—our first hundred days will be about restoring mana and rights back to workers.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Labour will be back on the Government benches in about three years, i.e. after the election due in 2026. The accompanying first-hundred-days pledge is a promise about the speaker's own party's action, not a forecast, and is not scored here.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The official declared result of the next New Zealand general election (Electoral Commission): true if Labour is in government following that election, false if the incumbent National-led parties are returned to government.

specificity.statement: This new Government should be ashamed of the hollowness of this move, because if Labour regain the Government benches—which is going to happen in three years—our first hundred days will be about restoring mana and rights back to workers.
specificity.explanation: 'Restoring mana and rights back to workers' names no mechanism, no instrument to be reinstated, no amount and no measure beyond the hundred-day framing; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government could have centred the voices of those most impacted, by having taken submissions. They chose not to.
focus.explanation: Names a specific, concrete feature of the measure before the House — that no submissions were taken on this repeal bill. Legitimate process scrutiny, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is a Government that is here to take us backwards, turn the clock back to the failed neo-liberal ideology that has caused rising inequality in this country, and I look forward, in terms of this Government, to be proved right in three years.
focus.explanation: Characterises the other side's ideology and direction in general terms. No measure, figure or outcome is named; strip out the party framing and no policy content remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They should be the Opposition—they should be the Opposition after this disgraceful day.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side's standing in the House. No policy, provision, figure or outcome is named — remove the party framing and nothing remains.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This Government could have centred the voices of those most impacted, by having taken submissions. They chose not to.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no public submissions were called for on the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill and that this was a deliberate choice by the Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bill record for the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill (2023): true if the bill was passed without referral to a select committee and without public submissions being called for; false if a select committee process taking submissions occurred.

veracity.statement: Because the economic illiteracy that they have presented with this bill is, frankly, a disservice to the 200,000 to 300,000 workers who would have benefited from fair pay agreements.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that between 200,000 and 300,000 workers would have been covered by fair pay agreements had the Act survived.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE regulatory impact statements and the coverage estimates for the FPA bargaining processes initiated before repeal (bus drivers, hospitality, security guards, cleaners, supermarket workers): true if the covered workforce totals within the 200,000–300,000 range; false if materially outside it.

veracity.statement: New Zealand First supports the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill for the reason that the Fair Pay Agreements Act is bad legislation—it’s the reason why we put the handbrake on it when we were last in Government and didn’t let it see the light of day.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand First blocked fair pay agreements legislation during its previous term in government (2017–2020), so that no such law was enacted then.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative record of the 2017–2020 Parliament plus contemporaneous reporting: true if no fair pay agreements bill was introduced or passed during that term and NZ First is documented as having withheld support; false if FPA legislation advanced with NZ First's support in that term.

veracity.statement: Camilla Belich inadvertently let the truth slip out in her second reading speech, when she reflected that unionised workers were actually unlikely to benefit from this, because they could already collectively bargain—so mechanisms are already in place for workers in those industries.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Camilla Belich stated in her second reading speech that unionised workers were unlikely to benefit from fair pay agreements because they could already bargain collectively.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard record of the second reading debate on the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill: true if Camilla Belich's speech contains that statement about unionised workers; false if it does not or if the reported sense is materially different.

civility.statement: If they think that the flexibility of poverty wages is going to lead to any of those outcomes, I suggest that they go back to school and read up on basic economics.
civility.explanation: Telling members opposite to "go back to school" is condescension aimed at their competence rather than at the policy. Short of direct abuse, but well past pointed.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: To be really clear, the repeal of this legislation is an absolute assault on workers.
civility.explanation: About as harsh as criticism of a measure gets, and it lands entirely on the legislation. No person is impugned, so under the re-anchored scale this sits at the standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There are all sorts of guises and pretences based on belief—is what we keep hearing from the Minister: based on belief.
civility.explanation: "Guises and pretences" imputes insincerity to the Minister personally rather than contesting her reasons. Short of an insult, but it is a bad-faith imputation.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Because the economic illiteracy that they have presented with this bill is, frankly, a disservice to the 200,000 to 300,000 workers who would have benefited from fair pay agreements.
specificity.explanation: Carries a named policy and a numeric range of affected workers — someone could go and check the coverage figure. No mechanism or timeframe, so short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The FPA is simply a mandated union bargaining tool and we will not stand for it.
specificity.explanation: A characterisation of the Act with no mechanism, coverage figure or provision named. Nothing here that could be checked or acted on beyond the label.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This was a solution looking for a problem; it would stifle flexibility in our labour market, it would decrease the appetite for employers to take a risk and employ people.
specificity.explanation: Three asserted effects with no magnitude, mechanism or timeframe — a direction of travel only, nothing a reader could check.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We do have small businesses who do their work to guarantee good wages, and, actually, the research shows that those working environments do lead to higher productivity; they lead to higher satisfaction.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy, but it rests on a bare appeal to unnamed authority ("the research shows") and asserts a causal direction — good wages producing productivity — without offering anything to rule out the reverse.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Let me tell you, Mr Speaker, that those workers and New Zealanders of backgrounds across the range, overwhelmingly—overwhelmingly—wanted change, and in my electorate and across New Zealand, we delivered it.
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation from anecdote: a self-selected sample of door-knocked constituents is offered as evidence of a national mandate, and "wanted change" is equivocated into support for this particular repeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It was actually illuminating that Minister van Velden notified the House that very few of these agreements were actually started. That shows that either it is not a priority or they were just too hard to get off the ground.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: the two offered explanations are not exhaustive — low uptake is at least as consistent with the Act having been in force barely a year, which the inference simply excludes.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Camilla Belich inadvertently let the truth slip out in her second reading speech, when she reflected that unionised workers were actually unlikely to benefit from this, because they could already collectively bargain—so mechanisms are already in place for workers in those industries.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur by over-generalisation: from "unionised workers can already bargain collectively" the conclusion is drawn about all "workers in those industries", which silently assumes the non-unionised majority is covered too.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We have low unemployment and employers are screaming out for those good workers, and if not here, we have the competition from Australia. So market forces are actually fully in action.
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation: the premises concern demand for sought-after ("good") workers, while the conclusion is about the labour market as a whole, including the low-paid workers the Act targeted.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: The Greens will ensure that this is a one-term Government and that the workers take back the power in this Chamber.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the government formed after the 2023 election will not be returned at the following general election.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The result of the 2026 New Zealand general election and the government formed after it: true if the National–ACT–New Zealand First coalition does not return to government; false if it is returned.

specificity.statement: Through to 30 November 2023, $579 million was paid out in rebates, $13.5 million was spent in cost to establish and operate the scheme, while $290 million has been received from charges.
specificity.explanation: Three named dollar figures against a named cut-off date, each traceable to a published account of the Clean Car Discount scheme.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In fact, over $122 million was provided as subsidies to people purchasing electric vehicles worth over $70,000 in the last 18 months.
specificity.explanation: A dollar total, a vehicle price threshold and a time window — someone could go and check it against the rebate data.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On this side of the House, we are the party of infrastructure, we are the party which gets things done, and we will be rolling out policies to implement 10,000 electric vehicle chargers by 2030 to actually ensure that people purchasing electric vehicles have the confidence to be able to charge their vehicles and travel around New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Carries a hard number and a date (10,000 chargers by 2030), which is checkable and actionable, though it is prefaced with slogans and says nothing about cost or delivery mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That is not the direction that any country in this world needs to be heading when it comes to meeting the needs of tackling climate change.
specificity.explanation: Trying to convey a substantive objection but supplies no emissions figure, no target, no mechanism and no timeframe — a general statement of direction that nobody could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Through to 30 November 2023, $579 million was paid out in rebates, $13.5 million was spent in cost to establish and operate the scheme, while $290 million has been received from charges.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the scheme's rebates paid, administration cost and charges collected up to 30 November 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport / NZTA Clean Car Discount financial reporting to 30 November 2023; true if rebates paid are ~$579m, operating and establishment cost ~$13.5m and charges received ~$290m, false if any figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: In fact, over $122 million was provided as subsidies to people purchasing electric vehicles worth over $70,000 in the last 18 months.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than $122m of Clean Car Discount rebates went to buyers of electric vehicles priced above $70,000 in the 18 months to roughly November 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA Clean Car Discount rebate records broken down by vehicle purchase price for the 18 months to 30 November 2023; true if rebates on vehicles over $70,000 total more than $122m, false if materially less.

veracity.statement: In fact, those cars will be coming here—and I note even Ford announced yesterday that on 1 January, the day after this scheme ends, they are reducing the price of their vehicles by $5,000.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on 11 December 2023 Ford announced a $5,000 price reduction on its vehicles effective 1 January 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ford New Zealand's public pricing announcement of 11 December 2023 and contemporaneous motoring/news coverage; true if Ford announced a price cut of about $5,000 taking effect 1 January 2024, false if no such announcement was made or the amount or date differ materially.

veracity.statement: How fiscally responsible is it, then, for the Tesla-loving Prime Minister’s household to be able to access the very rebate that his Government seeks to remove?
veracity.explanation: Presupposes as fact that Christopher Luxon's household received a Clean Car Discount rebate on a Tesla.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA Clean Car Discount rebate records and contemporaneous reporting on the Luxon household's vehicle purchase; true if a rebate under the scheme was claimed for a vehicle owned by his household, false if no such rebate was received.

focus.statement: I think that’s the philosophy of the former Government—and that is one of the reasons why they are now in Opposition, because they had a view that money simply grew on trees.
focus.explanation: No policy, figure or measure is named — it is a characterisation of the other party's outlook and an explanation of their election defeat. Nothing here bears on the bill before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But actually, what they are the party of is—they want to subsidise people who can already afford to buy a very high-end electric vehicle and provide them more subsidies; that is actually who the party is, over on the other side.
focus.explanation: There is a policy point buried in it (who the EV subsidy accrues to), but the weight of the sentence is a claim about what the other party fundamentally is, not about the scheme's design or effects.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because it’s all about, actually, taking from others, but when it concerns themselves, it’s a different consideration, as far as they see that.
focus.explanation: Names no policy, figure or outcome — it is a claim about the other side's general disposition and double standards rather than about the repeal before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I hear the former Minister for a lot of things—emphasis on “former”—complaining about this bill.
civility.explanation: Mockery aimed at an individual member rather than at her argument — the jibe is about her having lost office and having held many portfolios, and carries no engagement with what she said.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I have to say that his pathetic attempt at addressing the House with this piece of legislation has meant that all of those aspirations, that he might still hold, no longer exist.
civility.explanation: Lands on the person: 'pathetic' is directed at the Minister's performance and personal prospects rather than at any claim he made about the bill.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: How fiscally responsible is it, then, for the Tesla-loving Prime Minister’s household to be able to access the very rebate that his Government seeks to remove?
civility.explanation: The mocking epithet 'Tesla-loving' and the framing of personal benefit impute self-interest to the Prime Minister rather than engaging the case for repeal. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But the point is, this policy was taking from those who didn’t have a choice and giving it to people who could afford to pay for those vehicles, and so by ending this scheme we are ending the reverse Robin Hood scheme.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: given the stated premise that the scheme transfers from constrained buyers to wealthier ones, the redistributive characterisation follows. The gap is that 'no choice' is asserted rather than shown, so it falls short of fully supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because what we know is that car manufacturers around the world are switching to electric in all of their production chains; we don’t need to be providing very expensive subsidies to make them do that.
rigor.explanation: A genuine argument about the policy, but with a real gap: the premise concerns global manufacturers' supply decisions while the conclusion is about New Zealand consumer demand subsidies. Supply-side conversion does not by itself establish that domestic purchase incentives are redundant.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They voted for change because, unlike the previous Labour Government, they knew what a mess our economy had been put into and they knew that we had to have change to get maximum flexibility in our businesses to get our country out of the mess that it had been put in by the previous Labour Government.
focus.explanation: A third-reading speech on a specific repeal bill, but the content is the previous government's record in general terms — no clause, figure, mechanism or named outcome. The bill is referenced only as 'a small part of making that change'.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: One of the things that we built into collective agreements with retail was that if you worked a Tuesday to Saturday roster, the Tuesday would be treated like a Monday.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance of the repealed regime: a concrete term of the kind a sector agreement would set. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They’re all wrong, apparently—even business leaders, according to Simon Court. He just said they’re all wrong.
focus.explanation: A response to an interjection: entirely about what a member opposite said, with no policy content once that is removed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If they’re forced to lay off staff, reduce production, or close their doors, everyone suffers, and the fair pay agreement will do nothing—nothing—to lift the productivity that New Zealand desperately needs.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure itself — its effect on employers and on productivity — though it opens by framing the opposing case as 'rhetoric' rather than answering it.
focus.subject: speaker
