veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporary news coverage and attendance/pōwhiri records for the 20 January 2024 national hui at Tūrangawaewae and the January 2024 Rātana celebrations — true if David Seymour is absent from both, false if he is recorded as attending either.

veracity.statement: From the beginning: who should New Zealanders believe, the Hon David Seymour, who rejects that there is a partnership with Māori; or the Prime Minister, who confirmed today that he views the Treaty of Waitangi as akin to a partnership between the Crown and Māori, which has been the position of every Prime Minister—National and Labour—since 1984, and will the Prime Minister reiterate that at Waitangi?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that treating the Treaty as akin to a Crown–Māori partnership has been the stated position of every New Zealand Prime Minister, National and Labour, since 1984.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements of each Prime Minister from 1984 onward (Lange, Palmer, Moore, Bolger, Shipley, Clark, Key, English, Ardern, Hipkins, Luxon) on Treaty partnership — true if each accepted a partnership characterisation while in office, false if any is on record rejecting it.

focus.statement: I’ve had many conversations with the Minister of Defence, who shares with me how ignored the Defence Force felt by the last Government.
focus.explanation: Asked what specifically would be cut from Defence, the answer names no policy, figure or programme and pivots to a general characterisation of how the previous government made the Defence Force feel. Party framing carries almost all the weight.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Has the Minister spoken to the Hon Judith Collins in wake of her comments that she is “going to need money for Defence”, and what specifically in the Defence Force is she aiming to cut?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy: a named minister, a quoted public statement, and a direct question about what the savings programme will cut. Legitimate scrutiny, no party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, if the Minister had listened in the House last year, you would have heard me talking to this issue.
civility.explanation: A condescending jab at the questioner's attentiveness rather than a response to the substance — short of a direct insult, but it lands on the member rather than the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I just acknowledge, also, it’s a very sad day for the Green Party, actually, having lost their last true environmentalist.
civility.explanation: No individual is insulted — the retiring member is being praised — but the sting is a sneer at the sincerity of a whole party, delivered under cover of a tribute. Short of a personal attack, past the standard.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The fact is that, as the incoming Government and with the advice that we got, it became immediately apparent that there were big issues around recruiting. They can’t fill current recruit wings, the Australians are here recruiting our police officers, and we’ve got senior police officers that are getting ready to retire.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (recruitment is a serious constraint) is supported by three concrete, distinct mechanisms — unfilled wings, external poaching, imminent retirements. The inference tracks what is offered; no fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: How can he justify the proposal by New Zealand to allow bottom trawling in the South Pacific to catch up to three years’ worth of total allowable catch in a single season, up to 200 percent above annual catch limits, when this is far more than the 10 percent annual carry-over allowed under New Zealand’s domestic law?
rigor.explanation: A real inference: the international position is inconsistent with the domestic standard, so it needs justification. The gap is that domestic ACE carry-over and a high-seas catch-limit regime are not necessarily like-for-like, which the argument assumes rather than establishes.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would like to ask that people be mindful and that when you are going around and out and about, you are able to see that the number of patched bikers on the roads has greatly reduced, and we are headed towards increased legislation that will ban—completely ban—patches and insignia in public places.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote plus a post hoc inference: casual roadside observation is offered as evidence of a policy effect, and the effect is attributed to a patch ban that on his own account has not yet been legislated. The conclusion cannot follow from a cause that has not occurred.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Reserve Bank’s dual mandate, which has not worked, will be amended to make sure that its focus is on price stability alone, and on helping the situation with everyone out there who is struggling with day-to-day living and the cost of living—of buying food, and getting around and continuing to live.
rigor.explanation: 'Which has not worked' is asserted with nothing offered to support it, and the conclusion that a single price-stability mandate will relieve household cost of living is a non sequitur — no link is drawn between the mandate change and grocery or transport costs.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The fact is that, as the incoming Government and with the advice that we got, it became immediately apparent that there were big issues around recruiting. They can’t fill current recruit wings, the Australians are here recruiting our police officers, and we’ve got senior police officers that are getting ready to retire.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three present-tense facts about police recruitment as at January 2024: that recruit wings are not being filled to capacity, that Australian forces are actively recruiting NZ police officers, and that a cohort of senior officers is nearing retirement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police recruitment data on wing intake versus capacity for 2023–24 (OIA / annual report), and contemporaneous reporting or Australian state police recruitment campaigns targeting NZ officers. True if wings were running under capacity and Australian forces were running NZ recruitment drives; false if wings were filled and no such campaigns existed.

veracity.statement: We’ve got a big job to do, and the Police have got a big job to do, in reducing what has been a massive increase in violent crime in this country over the last six years, and we’re committed to doing that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that violent crime in New Zealand rose by a large margin over the six years to January 2024. The checkable element is the direction and magnitude of the change over that window; 'massive' is the quantitative claim being made.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Crime and Victims Survey violent-offence victimisation rates and NZ Police recorded victimisations for violence, 2017/18 through 2023/24. True if the series shows a large increase over that period; false if flat, or if the rise is small relative to the sampling error or attributable to reporting-rate change alone.

veracity.statement: Is his Government reversing New Zealand’s commitment, which it pushed for and agreed to as last year’s conference of the South Pacific Regional Fisheries Management Organisation (SPRFMO) to protect 70 percent of high-biodiversity areas, including seamounts, in the South Pacific?
veracity.explanation: Asserts as background that at the 2023 SPRFMO Commission meeting New Zealand advocated for, and agreed to, a measure protecting 70 percent of high-biodiversity areas including seamounts in the South Pacific.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The SPRFMO Commission's 2023 meeting report and the associated NZ proposal papers. True if New Zealand proposed or co-sponsored, and joined consensus on, a bottom-fishing measure using a 70 percent high-biodiversity-area protection threshold; false if no such figure or NZ sponsorship appears in the record.

veracity.statement: Does he agree with the previous National Government’s Minister for fisheries, who said that when the SPRFMO convention was ratified under the John Key National Government that “We need to protect these important fisheries for future generations. Ratification shows our strong commitment to sustainable management and ensures [that] we have an important influence on the work of the SPRFMO.”, and, if so, is he concerned that New Zealand is the only country still bottom trawling in the Pacific?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand is the only country whose vessels still conduct bottom trawling in the Pacific — in context, the South Pacific high seas covered by the SPRFMO convention area.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: SPRFMO bottom-fishing activity records and vessel registers for the convention area covering 2023–24. True if New Zealand-flagged vessels were the only ones recorded bottom trawling in the SPRFMO high-seas area; false if vessels of any other member state also did so in that period.

veracity.statement: On top of that list of challenges is, really, that the gang numbers have exploded.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a large increase in gang membership in New Zealand in the period preceding January 2024. The checkable element is the size of the recorded gang population over recent years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police National Gang List membership counts, 2017 through 2023 (published via OIA and Police reporting). True if the recorded membership rose substantially over that period; false if it was flat or declining, with allowance made for changes in list-recording practice.

focus.statement: Is this yet another example of broken promises, and will the 6.5 percent cut to the Police budget affect front-line services like it did last time National was in Government and see front-line officers pulled off the street to do non-sworn duties?
focus.explanation: Names a specific figure (6.5 percent) and a specific operational consequence (sworn officers doing non-sworn duties) — legitimate scrutiny of a named budget decision. Discounted slightly because the weight is carried by the party comparison to 'last time National was in Government'.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No, I think that, as the incoming Government again, it became very apparent that the Police are under severe financial pressure because of the actions of the previous Government. We’ve been very clear that we’re going to deliver world-class front-line services, and the Police, like every other agency, is asked to look at their corporate services and their back-office services to see whether or not cuts can be achieved.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual budget question — where savings are being sought (corporate and back-office services) versus what is protected. Some weight goes to blaming the previous Government, which is why this is not a 1.0.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will he commit that any cost savings found in the Police budget will remain with Police as stated in National’s Back Pocket Boost policy documents?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy: a named policy document, a specific mechanism (savings retained by the agency), and a concrete commitment to be held to. Textbook scrutiny.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I just acknowledge, also, it’s a very sad day for the Green Party, actually, having lost their last true environmentalist.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's character — that its remaining members are not genuine environmentalists. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named. This is precisely the content-free party jibe Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is his Government reversing New Zealand’s commitment, which it pushed for and agreed to as last year’s conference of the South Pacific Regional Fisheries Management Organisation (SPRFMO) to protect 70 percent of high-biodiversity areas, including seamounts, in the South Pacific?
focus.explanation: Names a specific international measure, a specific threshold, and a specific class of protected feature, and asks whether a named commitment is being reversed. Accountability for a named commitment, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is he concerned about New Zealand’s international reputation, when organisations like the Deep Sea Conservation Coalition have said that “The New Zealand government may now be the main obstacle to a proposed conservation measure that its own scientists spent the past year developing”?
focus.explanation: On the policy — a named conservation measure and New Zealand's position on it, sourced to a named organisation. Marked down slightly because the question pivots to reputation rather than the mechanism or effect of the measure itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he agree with the previous National Government’s Minister for fisheries, who said that when the SPRFMO convention was ratified under the John Key National Government that “We need to protect these important fisheries for future generations. Ratification shows our strong commitment to sustainable management and ensures [that] we have an important influence on the work of the SPRFMO.”, and, if so, is he concerned that New Zealand is the only country still bottom trawling in the Pacific?
focus.explanation: A named convention, a named prior government position, and a specific present-day fishing practice. Testing a government against a bipartisan commitment on a named measure is scrutiny of the highest kind, not party attack.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is this yet another example of broken promises, and will the 6.5 percent cut to the Police budget affect front-line services like it did last time National was in Government and see front-line officers pulled off the street to do non-sworn duties?
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable question: a named percentage, a named budget, and a concrete outcome to look for. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: No, I think that, as the incoming Government again, it became very apparent that the Police are under severe financial pressure because of the actions of the previous Government. We’ve been very clear that we’re going to deliver world-class front-line services, and the Police, like every other agency, is asked to look at their corporate services and their back-office services to see whether or not cuts can be achieved.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (corporate and back-office review) but supplies no figure, no savings target and no timeframe, and does not say whether savings stay with Police.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will he commit that any cost savings found in the Police budget will remain with Police as stated in National’s Back Pocket Boost policy documents?
specificity.explanation: Names the policy document and the exact provision at issue; someone could go and check the document and the outcome. No figure or date, so short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, I can confirm for the member that we’re going to make sure that the front line are resourced properly and are actually delivering the service that this country deserves.
specificity.explanation: 'Resourced properly' and 'the service this country deserves' commit to no figure, mechanism or date. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is his Government reversing New Zealand’s commitment, which it pushed for and agreed to as last year’s conference of the South Pacific Regional Fisheries Management Organisation (SPRFMO) to protect 70 percent of high-biodiversity areas, including seamounts, in the South Pacific?
specificity.explanation: A named organisation, a named forum and year, a numeric threshold and a named feature type. Anyone could go to the SPRFMO record and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I disagree with that characterisation. This is a Government that’s going to be focused on lowering emissions and making sure we meet our climate change commitments.
specificity.explanation: A statement of general direction with no target, mechanism, figure or date, and no reference to the fisheries measure that was asked about. Nothing checkable is offered.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How can he justify the proposal by New Zealand to allow bottom trawling in the South Pacific to catch up to three years’ worth of total allowable catch in a single season, up to 200 percent above annual catch limits, when this is far more than the 10 percent annual carry-over allowed under New Zealand’s domestic law?
specificity.explanation: Two numeric limits (200 percent, 10 percent), a stated time unit (three years' catch in one season), and the two regimes being compared. Fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is going to be a Government that will balance sustainable fishing along with good economic opportunity.
specificity.explanation: A pairing of two generic virtues with no limit, mechanism, figure or timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Again, as I said before, this will be a Government that will balance environmental goals with making sure we maximise commercial opportunities.
specificity.explanation: A restatement of the same generic balancing formula; no threshold, mechanism or date is supplied in response to a question containing precise figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The police will be given powers to issue dispersal notices when gangs gather in public spaces.
specificity.explanation: A named legal instrument and the trigger for its use — concrete and checkable against the bill. Short of the top because no timeframe or threshold for issuing a notice is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Reserve Bank’s dual mandate, which has not worked, will be amended to make sure that its focus is on price stability alone, and on helping the situation with everyone out there who is struggling with day-to-day living and the cost of living—of buying food, and getting around and continuing to live.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific statutory change — removing the employment limb of the Reserve Bank's mandate — which is concrete and checkable. The second half, on relieving household costs, supplies no figure, mechanism or date.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: These things, they do take a little bit of time, and I ask people who are out there to be patient and give things time for change.
specificity.explanation: An open-ended request for patience: no timeframe, no measure, and no statement of what change should be visible by when. Nothing that could be checked against later.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My response to that reflection and question by the Deputy Prime Minister is: we reiterate that Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the Treaty of Waitangi, is an absolute sacrosanct document fundamental to this country’s past, present, and future, and it will help us get the country back on track after what we’ve ended up with in the last three years.
focus.explanation: A real constitutional position on Te Tiriti, but the closing clause redirects to a swipe at the previous three years rather than any named policy or outcome. A policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does the Minister’s iwi support the Treaty principles bill, and will he be discussing that with his iwi at Waitangi?
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure before the House (the Treaty principles bill) and asks about a specific occasion. Legitimate scrutiny of a Minister's position on a named bill, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: To the Minister for Māori Crown Relations: Te Arawhiti, can the Minister confirm, during the Waitangi period of time, the Government will be focused on concrete, measurable, key performance indicator - orientated results for our rangatahi, housing, and health rather than transcendental notions contained in the He Puapua United Nations report?
focus.explanation: Names policy domains and a named document, so there is genuine policy content, but the framing ('transcendental notions') carries more of the weight than any specific proposal in it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yes, we will be absolutely committed to ruthlessly focusing on the outcomes of education, housing, health, and many other things that have been left behind for our various Māori communities throughout the motu.
focus.explanation: Answers on the policy domains rather than turning the invitation into an attack on the previous Government, which the question offered him.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: On 26 January, I announced that this Government will not proceed with the previous Government’s plans to lower the voting age to allow 16- to 17-year-olds to vote in local elections. Changing the voting age for local government is not a priority for this Government. We want to see councils focused on efficient delivery of local infrastructure and services for their communities.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure itself and what the Government will do with it; no party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Who is correct: the Minister when he said it’d be a waste of Parliament’s time to be progressing a bill and hearing select committee submissions on a bill that we are not going to be supporting or the Prime Minister when he said, “we will pursue a Treaty principles bill to select committee, and that’s as far as it will go.”?
focus.explanation: Quotes two specific stated positions on named legislation and asks which governs. Accountability directed at a specific inconsistency, not general party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is it correct that she indicated she wanted advice from the Ministry of Health on a tobacco excise tax freeze in a document she annotated and signed on 20 December?
focus.explanation: Squarely on a specific ministerial decision on a named policy. Textbook scrutiny of a named action, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can the Minister be clear that he is walking back on the coalition agreement that is undertaken to New Zealanders that he will deliver 500 additional police within two years?
focus.explanation: Holds a Minister to a named commitment with a specific number and deadline, immediately after he restated it differently. Named policy, named outcome — scrutiny, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My response to that reflection and question by the Deputy Prime Minister is: we reiterate that Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the Treaty of Waitangi, is an absolute sacrosanct document fundamental to this country’s past, present, and future, and it will help us get the country back on track after what we’ve ended up with in the last three years.
specificity.explanation: Asserts the Treaty is 'sacrosanct' and 'fundamental' and that it will get the country 'back on track' — no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named measure. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yes, we will be absolutely committed to ruthlessly focusing on the outcomes of education, housing, health, and many other things that have been left behind for our various Māori communities throughout the motu.
specificity.explanation: Lists policy areas and an adverb ('ruthlessly'), but supplies no target, figure, mechanism or date despite the question asking specifically about measurable KPIs.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On 26 January, I announced that this Government will not proceed with the previous Government’s plans to lower the voting age to allow 16- to 17-year-olds to vote in local elections. Changing the voting age for local government is not a priority for this Government. We want to see councils focused on efficient delivery of local infrastructure and services for their communities.
specificity.explanation: Dated announcement, named policy, and the exact ages affected. Someone could check the decision and its scope.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I have written to the chairperson of the Justice Committee to inform him that the coalition Government does not intend to support the Electoral (Lowering Voting Age for Local Elections and Polls) Legislation Bill through further parliamentary stages and request that the committee ends consideration of this bill.
specificity.explanation: Names the bill in full, the committee, the action taken and the request made. Concrete and checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is it correct that she indicated she wanted advice from the Ministry of Health on a tobacco excise tax freeze in a document she annotated and signed on 20 December?
specificity.explanation: Names the agency, the subject of the advice, the form of the record (an annotated and signed document) and the exact date. A precise question, as checkable as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m pleased to announce that the latest New Zealand Health Survey figures released in December show that the daily smoking rates among adults have more than halved in the last decade, from 573,000 in 2011-12, to 284,000 last year.
specificity.explanation: Named source, named release, two absolute figures and the years they apply to. Directly checkable against the published survey.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government’s ambitious target of getting 80 percent of our tamariki to curriculum by the time they finish intermediate by 2030 is our North Star.
specificity.explanation: A numeric target, a defined cohort and a deadline. Checkable and actionable, though the measurement standard for 'to curriculum' is left open.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, around New Zealand, students are returning or starting school this week to find new timetables in place that mean that no matter where they go to school or who their teacher is, they have consistent delivery of at least an hour a day of reading, writing, and maths.
specificity.explanation: Names the requirement (an hour a day each of reading, writing and maths) and its start, but leaves the scope of 'no matter where they go to school' — which schools are actually bound — undefined.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he stand by his guarantee that there’ll be no cuts or reprioritisations to the Police budget in order to deliver 500 extra police; if so, what advice has he received, if any, on the impact the proposed 6.5 percent to 7.5 percent cut to the Police budget would have on public safety?
specificity.explanation: Names the guarantee, the headcount commitment, the exact percentage range of the proposed cut, and the specific advice sought. Precise enough to be answered or refuted directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government’s policy is to deliver 500 additional police officers over the term of this Government, which is three years, and we’ve been very clear that we understand the challenges around that, because, as the incoming Government, we discovered that it was difficult to fill existing recruit wings, that the Australians are here recruiting our police officers, and that we’ve got lots of senior police officers that are coming up to retirement.
specificity.explanation: Gives the headcount and the timeframe he is now working to, and names three concrete obstacles, but attaches no figures to any of them — how many wings are unfilled, how many officers lost, how many retiring.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: To the Minister for Māori Crown Relations: Te Arawhiti, can the Minister confirm, during the Waitangi period of time, the Government will be focused on concrete, measurable, key performance indicator - orientated results for our rangatahi, housing, and health rather than transcendental notions contained in the He Puapua United Nations report?
civility.explanation: Dismissive of a report and of an approach to policy, not of any person. Under the re-anchored scale, hard criticism aimed at a document rather than an individual sits near the top.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is she seriously saying that she requested advice on the tobacco excise tax freeze but because the document canvassed other matters, she was being truthful when she denied having sought the advice to the media?
civility.explanation: The substance — a documented inconsistency — is legitimate, but 'is she seriously saying' adds an incredulous edge that leans toward the Minister's honesty rather than the record. Pointed and robust, edging toward the person without landing on her.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: To the Minister for Māori Crown Relations: Te Arawhiti, can the Minister confirm, during the Waitangi period of time, the Government will be focused on concrete, measurable, key performance indicator - orientated results for our rangatahi, housing, and health rather than transcendental notions contained in the He Puapua United Nations report?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that He Puapua is a 'United Nations report'. The checkable claim is who authored and published it, not what it recommends.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The provenance of the He Puapua report: true if He Puapua was produced or published by a United Nations body; false if it was commissioned by the New Zealand Government (the Declaration Working Group convened by Te Puni Kōkiri in 2019) and is a domestic report on implementing UNDRIP.

veracity.statement: Furthermore, the last Government could not conjure up one single reason why lowering the voting age was a good idea.
veracity.explanation: An absolute claim ('not one single reason') about whether the previous Government ever articulated a rationale for the bill it introduced. Checkable against the bill's own accompanying documents.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The explanatory note and any regulatory impact statement for the Electoral (Lowering Voting Age for Local Elections and Polls) Legislation Bill, plus the previous Government's stated response to the Supreme Court's Make It 16 declaration of inconsistency: false if any reason for lowering the voting age was stated in those documents or in the bill's first reading debate; true if no reason was ever advanced.

veracity.statement: I did not state that I had not requested specific advice.
veracity.explanation: A claim about what she herself said in a specific broadcast interview — settled by the interview record, independent of what the annotated document shows.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The recording or transcript of the Radio New Zealand interview with Guyon Espiner referred to in the exchange: false if she stated there or elsewhere in that interview that she had not sought or requested advice on a tobacco excise freeze; true if she made no such statement.

veracity.statement: I’m pleased to announce that the latest New Zealand Health Survey figures released in December show that the daily smoking rates among adults have more than halved in the last decade, from 573,000 in 2011-12, to 284,000 last year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific adult daily-smoker counts a decade apart, and that the drop exceeds 50 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking counts for 2011/12 and 2022/23: true if the estimates are approximately 573,000 and 284,000 respectively (i.e. a fall of more than half); false if either figure is materially different or the fall is less than half.

veracity.statement: Recent release of provisional NCEA data showed, for the third year, rates of achievement have declined, and we are going to turn this around.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a three-year consecutive decline in NCEA achievement rates, sourced to the provisional data released before this statement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZQA provisional NCEA achievement rates for the 2023 school year and the two preceding years: true if the rate fell in each of three consecutive years; false if any of those three years showed a rise or flat result.

veracity.statement: Well, around New Zealand, students are returning or starting school this week to find new timetables in place that mean that no matter where they go to school or who their teacher is, they have consistent delivery of at least an hour a day of reading, writing, and maths.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the hour-a-day timetabling requirement was universally in place for students returning that week, not merely announced or phased.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education requirements in force at the start of Term 1 2024 and their coverage: true if the one-hour-a-day literacy and numeracy requirement applied to all schools from the first week of Term 1 2024; false if it applied only to some schools, or took effect later in 2024.

veracity.statement: Is it the Government’s policy to deliver 500 extra police within two years as per the coalition agreement with New Zealand First?
veracity.explanation: The question asserts a premise about what the coalition agreement contains — a specific headcount and a two-year deadline — which is settled by the text of that agreement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published National–New Zealand First coalition agreement (November 2023): true if it commits to 500 additional police officers within two years; false if it states a different number, a different timeframe, or no timeframe.

veracity.statement: The Government’s policy is to deliver 500 additional police officers over the term of this Government, which is three years, and we’ve been very clear that we understand the challenges around that, because, as the incoming Government, we discovered that it was difficult to fill existing recruit wings, that the Australians are here recruiting our police officers, and that we’ve got lots of senior police officers that are coming up to retirement.
veracity.explanation: Among the reasons offered, the checkable factual claim is that Australian forces were in New Zealand recruiting serving officers at the time.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Evidence of Australian police forces actively recruiting New Zealand Police officers in New Zealand during 2023–24 — recruitment campaigns, advertised roadshows, or NZ Police attrition-to-Australia figures: true if documented, false if no such recruitment activity occurred.

rigor.statement: Well, this would be a distraction for local government when they should be focused on making sure that they are efficiently delivering local infrastructure and services for their communities.
rigor.explanation: A claim with a reason — the age change should not proceed because it would distract councils — but the distraction is asserted rather than shown, and no link is offered between an electoral franchise change and councils' delivery capacity. A real gap between what is offered and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yes, it is important that there is a clear and constant age for voting in a democracy. A split age would create an imbalance in terms of the voting ages between central and local government.
rigor.explanation: Circular: the conclusion (there should be one constant voting age) is supported only by restating it as its own premise — a split age creates 'an imbalance between the voting ages', which is what a split age is. No independent harm from divergence is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This drop in daily smokers is reflected across all ethnic groups, but, significantly, drops have been seen in Māori and Pacific peoples, where we have seen drops from 37.7 percent to 17.1 percent and 22.6 percent to 16.4 percent respectively between 2011-12 and 2022-23. This supports the reasons for continuing on the trajectory that we’re on.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the decline measured to 2022/23 occurred under the previous settings, so it cannot by itself support continuing on the current Government's changed course. The conclusion swaps 'the trajectory that produced this data' for 'the trajectory we are now on' without connecting them.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I was being truthful at the time, in relation to that statement. Being offered something and asking for something are two separate matters.
rigor.explanation: The offered/asked distinction is sound in the abstract but does not bear on the case: she has just confirmed she asked for the advice, so the premise does not reach the conclusion that the earlier denial was truthful. A non sequitur.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’ve received lots of positive feedback about our plans, but, in particular, an Auckland high school principal wrote to me saying that he is excited about our plans; that the cellphone ban will “remove a major distraction to learning, reduce cyberbullying, and promote social interaction between students”; and that a timetable focused on the basic subjects will ultimately lift educational achievement for all students.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote and authority: one principal's enthusiasm is offered as support for the policy's effects. A single unnamed correspondent's expectation is not evidence that the ban will reduce cyberbullying or that the timetable will lift achievement.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It was nothing but a speech that was punitive to certain communities and people in New Zealand and it was all about repealing legislation, and I wonder if that is because they have no ideas of their own.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy handle here — the Government's programme being repeal-led — but the weight of the sentence is a characterisation of the other side as idea-less rather than engagement with any named measure. Rigor is deliberately omitted: strip out the part about the other party and no argument remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I am unsure how that will help improve the lives of everyday New Zealanders, but we do know that that legislation is being repealed in order to be able to afford the tax cuts that we do know will benefit the rich and the high-income earners.
focus.explanation: Names a specific piece of legislation, a specific fiscal decision and who is said to benefit. This is scrutiny of a named policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I just completely disagree with bringing in the 90-day trials, because that doesn’t help everyday Kiwis with the cost of living—not that I can see.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure — 90-day trials — and the criterion the Government set for itself. Arguing badly about a real policy is still on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government has no hopes, no dreams, and no aspirations for people with disabilities.
focus.explanation: A sweeping characterisation of the other side's intentions. Disability policy is the surrounding topic, but no measure, figure or commitment is named, so there is nothing here to hold the Government to.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: During the campaign period, Christopher Luxon said that they would have a laser-sharp focus on the cost of living crisis and on improving the lives of everyday New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Luxon made a specific campaign commitment, characterised as a 'laser-sharp focus' on the cost of living.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 campaign material and Luxon's recorded campaign speeches/interviews; true if he committed to a focus of that description on the cost of living, false if no such commitment is on record.

veracity.statement: I am unsure how that will help improve the lives of everyday New Zealanders, but we do know that that legislation is being repealed in order to be able to afford the tax cuts that we do know will benefit the rich and the high-income earners.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that the smokefree legislation was repealed to fund the tax package, and that the tax cuts favour high-income earners.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The coalition's published fiscal plan and Treasury costings for the tax package; true if revenue attributed to the smokefree repeal (tobacco excise) is booked as a funding source for the tax cuts and Treasury's distributional analysis shows higher-income households gaining most; false if the repeal contributes no revenue to the package or the gains are not skewed to high earners.

veracity.statement: They got rid of the fair pay agreement legislation—legislation that would simply set baselines and pay and conditions for Kiwis.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the incoming Government repealed the fair pay agreement legislation, and characterises what that legislation did.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The statute record for the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022 and its repeal Act; true if the repeal was enacted before 30 January 2024 and the Act's purpose provisions cover minimum terms and conditions, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: In fact, we learn that Whaikaha now has to look for 7.5 percent cuts.
veracity.explanation: A specific claim that Whaikaha — Ministry of Disabled People has been set a 7.5 percent baseline savings target.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/Ministerial baseline savings instructions to agencies for Budget 2024 and Whaikaha's own advice; true if Whaikaha's assigned savings target is 7.5 percent, false if it is a different figure or none.

veracity.statement: We increased the minimum wage every year, we brought in fair pay agreement legislation, and we abolished prescription fees.
veracity.explanation: Three checkable claims about the previous Labour Government's own record.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE minimum wage review records for each year 2018–2023, the passage of the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022, and the Budget 2022/2023 decision on the $5 prescription co-payment; true if the minimum wage rose in every year of the term, the Act passed, and the co-payment was removed; false if any of the three did not occur.

veracity.statement: We introduced the first Matariki public holiday, we increased funding for Whānau Ora by 145 percent, and we introduced New Zealand histories in schools—an opportunity that too many of our previous generations have missed out on, and with me being one of them.
veracity.explanation: Claims three specific achievements of the previous Government, the checkable core being the 145 percent increase in Whānau Ora funding.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Puni Kōkiri / Vote Māori Development appropriations for Whānau Ora across the 2017–2023 term, plus the Te Kāhui o Matariki Public Holiday Act 2022 and the Aotearoa New Zealand's histories curriculum rollout; true if the appropriation rose by approximately 145 percent over the term and the other two occurred, false if the funding increase is materially different.

rigor.statement: So I just completely disagree with bringing in the 90-day trials, because that doesn’t help everyday Kiwis with the cost of living—not that I can see.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy, and a weak one: the support offered is her own experience as an employer plus an argument from absence of evidence ('not that I can see'). The conclusion is broader than what was shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In fact, we learn that Whaikaha now has to look for 7.5 percent cuts.
specificity.explanation: Names the agency and gives a precise percentage — checkable against the savings instructions. Falls short of 1.0 only because no dollar figure or timeframe is attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It would have saved, on average, $133 per week for families in order to go back to work, however that might be—whether or not it was both parents—to be able to bring in additional income to support them.
specificity.explanation: Carries a precise dollar figure attached to a named policy (20 free ECE hours for two-year-olds) set out in the preceding sentence. Not 1.0 because the population the average covers is left loose.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We introduced the first Matariki public holiday, we increased funding for Whānau Ora by 145 percent, and we introduced New Zealand histories in schools—an opportunity that too many of our previous generations have missed out on, and with me being one of them.
specificity.explanation: Three named policies and one precise percentage — concrete enough for someone to look up. No dates or dollar amounts, which keeps it below the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Whaikaha wasn’t one of them, so how can we believe her when she says things like that?
civility.explanation: Questions the Minister of Finance's credibility rather than only her position, which edges onto the person — but it is anchored to a specific alleged inconsistency rather than being a bare sneer, so it sits above the 0.5 failure line and well short of a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They’ve crashed the economy, law and order is spiralling out of control, our kids are not even going to school, and that’s the legacy of that last Government.
focus.explanation: Sweeping characterisation of the other side's whole record across three domains; no policy, measure or figure is named, so there is nothing here to hold anyone to account against.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They’re a lion in Opposition, but a lamb in Government.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's character and posture. No policy, measure or outcome is named; nothing survives if you remove the reference to the other side.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s summed up by one Labour MP who got booted out, and when he got vox popped out the front of Parliament, his response was “Oh, my lifestyle’s gone from champagne socialism to lemonade.”, and that’s exactly what was happening: champagne socialism, while everyone out of the beltway of Wellington was hurting.
focus.explanation: An anecdote about one opponent's lifestyle stands in for the other party's whole record. No policy, programme or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They were a Government that was a failed socialist experiment, because there’s only one trick in Labour’s playbook, and that’s to centralise.
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation: a single asserted motive (centralisation) is offered as proof of a much larger conclusion (a 'failed socialist experiment'), with no evidence that centralising produced failure. The inference is about real reforms, so it is assessable — and it does not hold.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We warned them that they would die on the hill with things like three waters, and that’s why, when they look around here today, less of their colleagues are back, because they sat here like lemmings and didn’t represent their electorates.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc, single-cause reasoning: the election result is attributed to one named reform and to members' silence, with nothing offered to connect the two beyond the sequence of events.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s very clear when talking to officials that announcements were being made that even the officials knew could not be delivered.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to unnamed authority: private conversations with unidentified officials are offered as the sole warrant for a claim about undisclosed announcements. Nothing is presented that anyone could weigh.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because our Minister of Health is a GP, our Minister of Police was a bravery award - winning police officer, our tertiary education Minister, Penny Simmonds, ran a polytech, a tertiary education institution. The difference is that on this side of the House, we know what we’re doing.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to credentials: prior occupation is offered as proof of competence in ministerial office. The conclusion ('we know what we're doing') does not follow from the premises, which say nothing about performance in the portfolios.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We warned them that they would die on the hill with things like three waters, and that’s why, when they look around here today, less of their colleagues are back, because they sat here like lemmings and didn’t represent their electorates.
civility.explanation: 'Sat here like lemmings' is mockery imputing mindless conformity to other members rather than engaging what they did or did not do. It stops short of a direct insult to a named person, but it lands on the members rather than the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: When they promised local government that they could opt in, but Official Information Act documents revealed it was an all-in from the very start, they misled New Zealanders, and they should not be returned back to the Treasury benches for a very long time.
civility.explanation: Robust and edges toward imputing bad faith ('misled New Zealanders'), but the accusation is levelled at a party's handling of a named policy and is tied to documentary evidence rather than to any individual's character.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Their own Heather Simpson report said to go from 20 to about six to eight, but they went from 20 to zero in the middle of a pandemic, and Kiwis are paying the price now because they’re stuck on waiting lists because of that Government’s focus on growing the bureaucracy.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that the Simpson review recommended reducing DHBs to about six to eight, and that the previous Government instead abolished all 20.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Health and Disability System Review (Simpson) final report, June 2020: the number of DHBs it recommended the country move to. True if it recommended roughly six to eight; false if it recommended a materially different number (e.g. 8–12). Second limb: the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 and Health NZ establishment records on whether all 20 DHBs were disestablished in July 2022.

veracity.statement: When they promised local government that they could opt in, but Official Information Act documents revealed it was an all-in from the very start, they misled New Zealanders, and they should not be returned back to the Treasury benches for a very long time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an opt-in was offered to councils while official documents released under the OIA show the reform was always intended to be compulsory.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Internal Affairs Cabinet papers and OIA releases on the Three Waters reform programme. True if councils were publicly offered an opt-in/opt-out while contemporaneous internal documents already assumed all councils would be included; false if the opt-in was genuine at the time it was offered and the decision to make it mandatory came later.

veracity.statement: Remember the $1.9 billion, and the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission came out in its first report and said that despite the $1.9 billion, there was no material improvement?
veracity.explanation: Asserts both the size of the previous Government's mental health package and a specific adverse finding by the Commission's first monitoring report.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Hiringa Mahara / Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission's first monitoring report on the 2019 Wellbeing Budget mental health package. True if the report concluded there had been no material improvement in access or outcomes despite the $1.9 billion; false if it reported material improvement or did not make that finding.

specificity.statement: Their own Heather Simpson report said to go from 20 to about six to eight, but they went from 20 to zero in the middle of a pandemic, and Kiwis are paying the price now because they’re stuck on waiting lists because of that Government’s focus on growing the bureaucracy.
specificity.explanation: Names the review, gives the recommended range, the actual number and the timing, and identifies the claimed consequence. Someone could go and check every element.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Remember the $1.9 billion, and the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission came out in its first report and said that despite the $1.9 billion, there was no material improvement?
specificity.explanation: Names the figure, the body and the report, and states the finding attributed to it — all directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The biggest barrier to timely mental health and addiction support in New Zealand is the lack of mental health workforce, and, as we heard the Prime Minister announce in the Speech from the Throne, our commitment is to train more psychiatrists and more psychologists.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a named constraint and the two professions to be trained, but gives no numbers, no funding, no training places and no timeframe — a direction with only partial detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The time for big slogans is over. It’s about delivery, and that is the difference with this new coalition Government.
specificity.explanation: A slogan in its own right: no deliverable, target, date or mechanism is named, so there is nothing anyone could check or hold the Government to.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, that was a vibrant speech from the previous MP, who’s clearly had quite a lot of coffee today, given the subject material and the passion with which that that was delivered.
civility.explanation: A light but personal jibe: it characterises the previous speaker's manner (over-caffeinated) rather than engaging anything he said. Edging toward the person without landing hard on them, so pointed rather than a real failure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So I just want to encourage Mr Doocey to take a bit of time and maybe go back through some of the Cabinet papers that were around at the time the next time he’s got the temptation to stand up and expound in the House about the evils of socialism, because, actually, if you just spend all of your Government’s time checking out what the previous Government did because that sounds like a good slogan, then you’re not going to leave the country in a better place.
civility.explanation: Condescending toward a named member — advising him to go and do his reading, and framing his contribution as a temptation to sloganeering. Short of an insult, but the sneer lands on the person rather than on the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, the Government did not make that choice to go further than the Simpson report because of some kind of socialist centralising instinct; the Government went further than the Simpson report because the experience of trying to get information and to coordinate a pandemic response through the DHBs proved to be so hard, so challenging, and so nigh-on impossible, it became clear that we were only going to get a nationwide response with a nationwide health service.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: pandemic coordination through DHBs was unworkable, therefore a national health service was required. The premise supports the direction, but the jump to 'only' a nationwide service excludes the middle option actually on the table (Simpson's regional authorities) without argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If the first thing that you do is take six years’ worth of work—all of that work by public servants, all of the work that was done by professionals to get that system up and running—and you throw it out and you seem, as yet, to have no plan to replace that programme with anything else other than to say, “Well, we’re just going to return it to communities, but also we’re not going to provide any additional funding to it because this Government’s not about providing additional funding.”—OK; again, you can argue the toss on that—how on earth do you square the circle of saying that you’re going to fix the problem, but not by using balance sheet separation and not by using any kind of amalgamation to get scale for outside investment?
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the policy: if the two funding mechanisms (balance sheet separation, amalgamation for scale) are removed and no new money is offered, the investment gap cannot be closed. The step is largely sound but rests on an unstated false-dichotomy premise — that no third financing route could exist.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In fact, the one thing that I think we can discern from the media since the Government got elected is that the highest priority of this Government is revisiting the Treaty of Waitangi.
rigor.explanation: Infers the Government's highest priority from the volume of media coverage. That is an appeal to salience — coverage tracks controversy rather than a government's ranking of its own work programme — so the conclusion outruns the evidence offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Can you tell me what is more wasteful than supporting a Government bill to select committee, getting the Parliamentary Counsel Office to draft it, getting advice from officials—which, so far, appears to be pretty negative about it—taking it through Cabinet, spending the Minister’s time on it, pouring thousands if not hundreds of thousands of dollars’ worth of Government time and resource into developing a bill, and then killing it the moment it makes it out of select committee?
rigor.explanation: Turns the Government's own 'cutting waste' premise against a specific course of action, itemising the public resource consumed by advancing a bill its sponsors intend to defeat. The inference holds; it is weakened only by being put rhetorically rather than showing that the process cost exceeds other waste.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, the Government did not make that choice to go further than the Simpson report because of some kind of socialist centralising instinct; the Government went further than the Simpson report because the experience of trying to get information and to coordinate a pandemic response through the DHBs proved to be so hard, so challenging, and so nigh-on impossible, it became clear that we were only going to get a nationwide response with a nationwide health service.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance of the health restructure — the Simpson recommendations, the DHB system, and the stated mechanism behind the decision. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is one of the things that worries me: at the moment, as far as I can tell, the new Government’s agenda is basically a Government of revenge to get rid of everything that the previous Government did.
focus.explanation: A sweeping characterisation of the other side's motives. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — strip out the claim about what the Government is 'really' driven by and no policy content remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But let’s not pretend that a political campaign by a political party is the same thing, and I’ve yet to discern a clear plan from this Government for what the replacement for three waters is for the more than $100 billion worth of asset replacement that has to happen in this country when it comes to the three waters infrastructure.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: it names a specific policy (the three waters programme and its replacement) and a specific quantum of work the Government has not accounted for. Holding a government to account on a named programme is on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But let’s not pretend that a political campaign by a political party is the same thing, and I’ve yet to discern a clear plan from this Government for what the replacement for three waters is for the more than $100 billion worth of asset replacement that has to happen in this country when it comes to the three waters infrastructure.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the required three waters asset replacement in New Zealand exceeds $100 billion — a quantified claim about the scale of the infrastructure need, separable from the accompanying complaint that no replacement plan exists.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published estimates of New Zealand's three waters infrastructure investment requirement — the Water Industry Commission for Scotland modelling commissioned by DIA and the DIA three waters reform documentation. True if the national asset renewal/investment estimate over the reform horizon exceeds $100 billion; false if credible official estimates put it materially below $100 billion.

veracity.statement: Let’s not forget that the reason why that programme was such a high priority for the previous Government was that people died in Havelock North as a result of poor water infrastructure.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that people died in the Havelock North water contamination event and that the deaths were a consequence of poor water infrastructure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government Inquiry into Havelock North Drinking Water (2017) and Hawke's Bay DHB reporting on the August 2016 campylobacter outbreak. True if deaths were attributed to the contaminated water supply; false if no deaths were linked to the outbreak.

veracity.statement: Relentlessly focused—so relentlessly focused on the cost of living that I have yet to hear a cost of living initiative from this Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, in hyperbolic form, that the new Government had produced no cost-of-living initiative in its first two months despite campaigning on being relentlessly focused on the cost of living.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The record of policy announcements and legislation by the National-led coalition between taking office on 27 November 2023 and 30 January 2024, as listed in Beehive releases and the legislative programme. True if no measure announced or enacted in that period was directed at household cost of living; false if any such measure was (for example the repeal of the Auckland regional fuel tax or announced tax relief).

veracity.statement: I think that is critically important in terms of our overall climate change response, and I thank all parties who were in the House who supported it on third reading, which was everyone in the House at the time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that every party in the House at the time supported the zero-carbon legislation at its third reading — i.e. that the third reading was unanimous.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The division record for the third reading of the Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Bill (November 2019). True if the bill passed without any member or party voting against; false if any member or party recorded a vote against.

specificity.statement: Can you tell me what is more wasteful than supporting a Government bill to select committee, getting the Parliamentary Counsel Office to draft it, getting advice from officials—which, so far, appears to be pretty negative about it—taking it through Cabinet, spending the Minister’s time on it, pouring thousands if not hundreds of thousands of dollars’ worth of Government time and resource into developing a bill, and then killing it the moment it makes it out of select committee?
specificity.explanation: Names the actual mechanism step by step — select committee, Parliamentary Counsel Office drafting, official advice, Cabinet, ministerial time — and gives an order-of-magnitude cost. Someone could check the process cost, though the dollar range is loose.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Next time these guys get on to that side of the House, they’re just going to do exactly the same thing in response, and all of those grand plans that you’ve got that you’re going to spend the next three or six or nine years developing, they’re just going to get in and reverse them in the first three months, because that’s, apparently, what new Governments do because that’s the standard that’s been set by this Government.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that whichever bloc next takes office will reverse this Government's programme within its first three months, mirroring what he says has been done to the previous Government's work. Conditional on a change of government occurring at the next election.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The legislative and policy record of the first three months of the next change of government following the 2023 National-led coalition. True if the incoming administration repeals or reverses the flagship programmes of this Government within its first three months in office; false if those programmes are substantially left in place over that period.

focus.statement: We are looking now at a Government with no vision, and it is not speaking to those people like me, with a young baby in their arms, looking for something that we could be proud of in the New Zealand that will be our home for many decades to come.
focus.explanation: A general characterisation of the government as visionless and out of touch. No measure, figure, commitment or outcome is named, so there is nothing on-policy to engage with — this is party framing rather than scrutiny of a named policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: You have to wonder whether things that have made a huge difference in the lives of the South Aucklanders that I represent in Manurewa are going to stay—things like the school donations programme, which means that parents in Manurewa don’t have to pay the donations that were actually compulsory payments to our public schools.
focus.explanation: Names a specific programme (the school donations scheme), what it does, and who it affects, and asks whether the savings exercise puts it at risk. That is scrutiny of a named policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They’re the cuts to things like public services that people rely upon, and it makes you wonder, when looking at that list and the departments that are up to find a 6.5 or 7.5 percent cut, what kind of services we can expect to be able to rely upon in the future—things that make us pay more for the everyday lives that we already lead.
specificity.explanation: Carries the actual savings targets (6.5 and 7.5 percent) and points at a specific list of departments, which is checkable. But the consequence side — which services, which departments, what it would cost people — is left entirely open.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: You have to wonder whether things that have made a huge difference in the lives of the South Aucklanders that I represent in Manurewa are going to stay—things like the school donations programme, which means that parents in Manurewa don’t have to pay the donations that were actually compulsory payments to our public schools.
specificity.explanation: Names the programme and states its mechanism (parents no longer paying donations), which is checkable, but gives no figures, no funding amount and no evidence that the programme is in fact under threat.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What we need is a vision for the future from our elected representatives to move forward and define something that not only honours those principles of the Treaty but also realises the dream of the Treaty to protect our taonga, to protect our natural environment, and to have a climate where people can breathe and live in our country.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic aspirations — vision, honouring principles, protecting taonga and the environment. No mechanism, no measure, no timeframe and no figure; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: You’ve got to wonder whether those things are safe and sacrosanct, given that all Public Service departments are being asked to find these cuts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that every Public Service department has been asked to find the baseline savings, with no exceptions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government's Budget 2024 baseline savings instruction (Finance Minister's December 2023 letter to ministers / Treasury guidance on the 6.5%–7.5% targets): true if all Public Service departments were given a savings target, false if any department (e.g. Police, Health, Corrections, Defence) was exempted or given a nil target.

veracity.statement: I was watching the news, and it was the day that the Rt Hon Dame Jacinda Ardern had introduced in this House the legislation that she had talked so much about in her parliamentary career and that she had always wanted to bring to this House, about child poverty reduction, and for me, as a young mum, I saw that piece of legislation as a moment that articulated everything that Labour stood for, for me.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that child poverty reduction legislation was introduced to the House by Jacinda Ardern on this date (30 January) in 2018.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bills record for the Child Poverty Reduction Bill: true if it was introduced on 30 January 2018 and in the name of Jacinda Ardern, false if the introduction date or the member in charge differs.

veracity.statement: It’s important, then, to look at those broken promises in the context of what New Zealanders can expect as leadership from our politicians, and again here I speak to those 10,000 people who came and made the pilgrimage to Tūrangawaewae when asked by the Kīngitanga to come and have a kōrero about the principles of Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an attendance figure of 10,000 people at the Kīngitanga-called hui at Tūrangawaewae marae.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous attendance estimates for the 20 January 2024 national hui at Tūrangawaewae (organiser, police and news-media counts): true if estimates cluster around 10,000, false if they are materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: I am so proud of Rino Tirikatene and his grandfather and his aunt who have served in this Parliament too, but Kelvin also stands on the shoulders of his tupuna Karaitiana Takamoana, who was a representative of Eastern Māori in 1871.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that Karaitiana Takamoana held the Eastern Maori seat from 1871, and that he is a tupuna of Kelvin Davis.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's historical register of members for the Eastern Maori electorate (true if Takamoana was elected to that seat in 1871, false if the seat or year differs), plus Davis's publicly stated whakapapa for the descent claim.

rigor.statement: She was trying to do a set of reforms that we all know in our heart of hearts need to happen. Someone needs to pay for the pipes. The councils can’t pay for the pipes; we should probably pay for the pipes.
rigor.explanation: An argument about water reform, but a weak one. The first step is an appeal to assumed universal agreement ('we all know in our heart of hearts') rather than evidence, and the conclusion rests on an unsupported premise that councils simply cannot fund the pipes, with no alternative funding option considered — a false dichotomy between councils paying and central government paying.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We do not need to relitigate the principles of the Treaty, because we have been having that debate for many, many years.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion does not follow from the premise offered: that a debate has run for a long time does not establish that it is settled or should not be reopened. It is an appeal to the duration of the discussion in place of a reason, and it assumes what it sets out to show.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I want, as well, to speak about the contrast between being in a forum like that and having the vision of these young New Zealanders resting so weightily on my shoulders, and then hearing from what is a shambolic and divided approach to the Treaty of Waitangi from this coalition Government.
civility.explanation: 'Shambolic and divided' is harsh, but it is aimed at the Government's approach to the Treaty, not at any member's character, competence or motives. Hard criticism of a policy position is the expected standard, not a civility failure.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our police should always be given the powers and resources they need to do the job they do best: keeping us safe.
specificity.explanation: A policy position where powers, resources or funding could have been named, but neither the powers nor the resources are identified and no figure, mechanism or timeframe is attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Social investment in our youth to help build their mental resilience and protect them from the lure of gangs; social investment to combat youth crime, where positive mentors teach our troubled youth self-discipline.
specificity.explanation: Gestures at a mechanism (mentoring, resilience-building) but names no programme, no funding, no delivery agency and no timeframe; 'social investment' is left as a label rather than a described intervention.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Social investment in housing: when I worked at Te Mahia Community Village, a transitional housing facility in Takanini, I saw the significant drop in antisocial behaviour when social wraparound services are partnered with housing providers.
specificity.explanation: Names the facility, its location and the mechanism (wraparound services partnered with housing providers), but the key quantity — the 'significant drop' in antisocial behaviour — carries no figure, period or measure.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Social investment in housing: when I worked at Te Mahia Community Village, a transitional housing facility in Takanini, I saw the significant drop in antisocial behaviour when social wraparound services are partnered with housing providers.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal anecdote: a single first-hand observation at one facility is offered as support for a general policy of pairing wraparound services with housing. No data, comparison group or counterfactual is offered, and the inference from one site to a general claim is not bridged.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: While I strongly commend the traditional school systems, I also place merit in alternative school programmes and alternative education programmes and charter schools, because not every child learns the same way.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered and it points in the right direction, but there is a real gap between premise and conclusion: variation in how children learn supports pedagogical variety, not the charter-school governance model specifically. Nothing connects the stated premise to that particular institutional form.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: To me, it’s because if our people cannot read and write to begin with, they risk being shut out from society and the world.
rigor.explanation: A plausible mechanism — literacy as the gateway to participation — is offered to answer why education underlies poverty, unemployment and crime. The link to exclusion is reasonable, but the step from exclusion to the three specific outcomes she raised is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If I felt that the National Party was anti-Māori, I would not be part of the National Party.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal testimony. Her own continued membership is offered as evidence the party is not anti-Māori, but the conclusion rests entirely on her perception; a party's policies could have that effect without her feeling it, so the conclusion does not follow from the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Takanini is enriched, with over 50 percent of its residents born overseas.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a majority of residents of the Takanini electorate were born outside New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census usual-resident birthplace data for the Takanini general electorate (or the statistical areas covering it); true if the overseas-born share exceeds 50%, false if it is 50% or below.

veracity.statement: A fifth the size of New Zealand, Lebanon gave me my parents, John Hanna Fahd Rahme and Dalida Watfa Habib Rahme.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Lebanon's land area is approximately one fifth that of New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Standard land-area figures for both countries (e.g. CIA World Factbook / Stats NZ: Lebanon ~10,450 km², New Zealand ~268,000 km²); true if Lebanon's area is roughly 20% of New Zealand's, false if the ratio is materially different.

veracity.statement: You ran the campaign the way you wanted, and in Takanini, I’m proud that we achieved the highest swing of the country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Takanini electorate recorded the largest swing to National of any electorate at the 2023 general election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission 2023 general election results for Takanini compared with the notional 2020 results on the 2023 boundaries, against the equivalent swing in every other general electorate; true if Takanini's swing to National was the largest in the country, false if any other electorate's was larger.

veracity.statement: We are proudly 50 percent Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the East Coast general electorate's population is 50 percent Māori — a demographic claim about the electorate she represents.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census ethnicity/Māori-descent figures for the East Coast general electorate; true if the Māori share is approximately 50% (say 45-55%), false if materially outside that range.

specificity.statement: I am proud to be part of a Government that provides for all New Zealanders, that uses practical common sense, that looks after taxpayer dollars, a Government that understands the benefit of infrastructure over ideology, and one that will fix the roads.
