If you may recall, I pointed out that that was an interesting point because it’s a leap year and that the report that’s outstanding would be completed by 15 February.
specificity.explanation: Two firm dates for two distinct things — the commission's wind-up on 29 February and completion of the outstanding report by 15 February. Directly checkable against the record.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We know that since the 1960s, this country has had a lagging productivity growth rate compared to our international peers, which has led to the fact that any worker in New Zealand can go to Australia and earn, on average, 30 percent more income over there and that any worker can go to America and earn 35 percent more income in America.
specificity.explanation: Carries a start date, two named comparator countries and two percentage figures — precise enough that someone could go and check it or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: My reflection is that there is actually a huge amount of people out there and bodies of organisations that will take up the mantle, and this organisation, although they’ve done some important work, their kaupapa—which is around improving productivity and understanding the key policies that will help to improve productivity in this country—will actually be taken up and adopted and delivered by other important people and organisations in the country.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure, and a weak one: the premise is that other bodies researching productivity exist (Motu, the New Zealand Initiative, universities, Treasury, the OECD), and the conclusion is that the commission's function will be taken up and delivered. Nothing is offered to bridge existence to assumption of the role — no mandate, commissioning arrangement or resourcing. A non sequitur from capability to succession.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I do just have to note the incredible irony, but, in fact, it’s so fitting that it was a previous ACT Party coalition agreement that set up the Productivity Commission, back in the day when the ACT Party was more like a real libertarian party and cared about good governance instead of just representing billionaires.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Productivity Commission was established as a result of an earlier ACT Party coalition (confidence and supply) agreement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2008 National–ACT confidence and supply agreement text and the origins of the New Zealand Productivity Commission Act 2010; true if the agreement provided for establishing a productivity commission, false if the Commission originated independently of any ACT coalition agreement.

veracity.statement: I remember very well, between 2011 and 2017, there were fantastic reports coming out from the Productivity Commission, even though it was a John Key - led Government and Mr Seymour was involved in one of those Governments.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that David Seymour held a role in a John Key–led Government during the 2011–2017 period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary and ministerial records for David Seymour between 2011 and 2017 — date of election to Parliament and any executive appointment under a Key-led administration; true if he held such a role in that window, false if he held none.

focus.statement: I do just have to note the incredible irony, but, in fact, it’s so fitting that it was a previous ACT Party coalition agreement that set up the Productivity Commission, back in the day when the ACT Party was more like a real libertarian party and cared about good governance instead of just representing billionaires.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy hook (who created the body now being disestablished), but the weight of the sentence is a characterisation of what the ACT Party has become rather than any feature of the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Thank you very much, Mr Chair, for reminding me of that, because, as the Hon Duncan Webb was saying, it is quite possible that the more appropriate title would be a title that was making note of the fact that the current ACT Party is more interested in creating more direct Government bureaucracy that they can control in an autocratic way rather than having an independent commission that’s providing independent advice, because they don’t like that independent advice.
focus.explanation: Contains a real institutional point about the bill — replacing an arm's-length commission with ministerially controlled capacity — but it is delivered as a claim about the other party's motives rather than about the mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But the Minister really should answer the very serious question about what provisions are being made for the people who will be unemployed as a result of this bill and this part, at the end of the month that starts tomorrow. And we haven’t heard that answer from the Minister.
focus.explanation: Straightforward scrutiny of the measure before the committee — the employment consequences of this part of the bill and the date they bite. Naming the affected group and the timeframe makes it accountability, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, again, we could talk about how the title of the bill, Mr Chair, could be something like the “Expanding Government Bureaucracy for the Purposes of the ACT Party Bill”, so that they can act on behalf of their 1 percent donors rather than actually doing something that would genuinely improve the productivity of this country.
focus.explanation: Nominally about the bill's title, but the content is an imputation about who the ACT Party serves. No provision, cost, mechanism or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I just listened to that spewing of bile and all I thought is, “I hope they make her the next co-leader for the good of New Zealand.”!
focus.explanation: Carries no policy content at all — it is entirely a response to the opposing member and her party, with a live measure before the committee to engage instead.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But the Minister really should answer the very serious question about what provisions are being made for the people who will be unemployed as a result of this bill and this part, at the end of the month that starts tomorrow. And we haven’t heard that answer from the Minister.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a specific group (Commission staff who lose employment), a specific mechanism (this part of this bill) and a timeframe (end of the month starting tomorrow), but supplies no figures or detail of the provisions sought.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Those obligations, the member asked, will be passed over to the Treasury. Of course, if the Treasury indicates that it needs support in order to honour that commitment to those staff, then then we’ll ensure that we do that.
specificity.explanation: Names the receiving agency and the mechanism by which staff obligations transfer, but gives no numbers, no timeframe and no description of what 'support' would consist of.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: One is that the Minister has not risen to answer—and will not—the very relevant question put to him by two members now on this side of the Chamber.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Minister will decline to respond to the question about provisions for Productivity Commission staff before the debate on this part concludes.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record for the remainder of this committee stage; true if the Minister made no response addressing provisions for the affected staff, false if he rose and addressed that question.

civility.statement: And the second point is simply that we could come up with a much more relevant title for this bill—one that points out the absolute hypocrisy of this fake libertarian Minister.
civility.explanation: Turns from the bill to the Minister personally — calling him a fake and charging him with absolute hypocrisy is an attack on his sincerity rather than on his policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I just listened to that spewing of bile and all I thought is, “I hope they make her the next co-leader for the good of New Zealand.”!
civility.explanation: Characterises another member's speech as bile and follows with a sneer about her leadership prospects; the target is the member, not anything she argued.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: However, I also just make the point that if they’re very talented people—and I agree that they are—then I think they’re going to be just fine.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy consequence, but a weak one: talent is offered as sufficient for re-employment with nothing about labour market conditions or the number of roles available — a non sequitur that also assumes the conclusion he is asked to justify.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s a relatively simple question for the Minister for Regulation, and that’s “Why?”, because this is an organisation that was created at the behest of the ACT Party and that the Minister, in his first and his second reading speeches last night, told us had done good and excellent work, and yet he brings a bill to the House to disestablish it.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions about the past: that the Productivity Commission was created at the ACT Party's instigation, and that the Minister praised its work as good and excellent in his first and second reading speeches the previous night.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: (a) The 2008 National–ACT confidence and supply agreement and the New Zealand Productivity Commission Act 2010 establishment record — true if the Commission's creation was a term secured by ACT, false if it originated elsewhere; (b) Hansard for the first and second reading speeches on the New Zealand Productivity Commission Act Repeal Bill on 30 January 2024 — true if David Seymour describes the Commission's work in commendatory terms, false if he does not.

veracity.statement: It’s on the record that Mr Seymour has said that the Productivity Commission, he thinks, has been hijacked, and he said that on 5 September 2023.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that David Seymour publicly described the Productivity Commission as having been hijacked, and dates that statement to 5 September 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Media reports, ACT Party releases and any speech or interview transcript from 5 September 2023 — true if Seymour is recorded on that date saying the Productivity Commission had been hijacked or captured, false if no such statement exists on that date or the wording materially misrepresents what he said.

focus.statement: But if that is the Minister’s concern, why did he not reappoint people that he considered would bring the commission back to where he felt it should be?
focus.explanation: Names a concrete alternative to the measure before the House — using the appointment power rather than repeal — and puts it directly to the Minister. Squarely on the policy question, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So my questions for the Minister are: what arrangements are in place to support those people to stay within the Public Service? And what support has been given to the Treasury who will now take responsibility for all of the outstanding matters?
focus.explanation: Asks about the operation of a named provision — the transfer of employment liabilities to Treasury — and the fate of identified staff. Scrutiny of the measure's implementation, with no party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I want to just graft on to what was said there by the previous speaker, Grant Robertson, because I, years ago, worked for the Law Commission, which is an independent organisation, and those kinds of independent organisations are really rich in having a focus and a capacity for people to engage with them.
focus.explanation: Engages the substantive question the bill raises — what independent statutory bodies provide — rather than the other party's character or record.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In response to Grant Robertson, clause 9 is there to give effect to the policies that were agreed on in Part 2, and, as he says, it’s a very simple clause.
focus.explanation: Addresses the clause put to him and what it does. Entirely on the measure before the committee.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Perhaps the appropriate title for the Act—and we could always put an amendment on the Table—would be the “David Seymour Vanity Regulation Ministry Establishment Act”, because that’s what’s really going on here.
focus.explanation: Nothing about the bill's effect, cost or mechanism survives once the jibe about the Minister's motives is removed. The 'alternative title' device carries no policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But we know that that party—the ACT Party—doesn’t like to be challenged, and the National Party likes to go along with the ACT Party.
focus.explanation: A characterisation of two parties' general dispositions. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — this is what the statement is entirely about.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s really disappointing that what we’ve got here is a piece of legislation where the National Party has allowed the ACT Party to shuffle off to one side an independent voice for the very thing that the National Party claims it’s in favour of, which is productivity.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point — the bill removes the institution dedicated to the objective the government professes — but it is carried almost entirely in party framing about who allowed whom to do what, rather than in the measure's effects.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: No, no, no, this—this—is an absurd piece of legislation, and it does strike me that the only credible thing that we’ve heard is that the Minister wants his vanity project with the ministry of regulation and the only way he could get that through was to sacrifice the Productivity Commission.
civility.explanation: Calling the legislation absurd is criticism of the measure and costs nothing. But 'his vanity project' imputes a personal motive — self-aggrandisement — to the Minister, and 'sacrifice' frames him as trading away a public institution for it. That is bad faith attributed to the person, not the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, I can see the Minister for Regulation raising his eyebrows at one of the organisations which I have great respect for—from what I can see—so I would like to know how he intends to continue that tradition of independence if, in fact, when people say things he doesn’t like to hear and that don’t go along with his ideology, he is prepared to dismantle them.
civility.explanation: Framed as a question, but the premise built into it is that the Minister abolishes institutions that contradict his ideology — an imputation of bad faith aimed at the person rather than a criticism of the repeal itself. Short of an insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: As for a number of other comments that he made, I could engage with him on that, but it doesn’t really seem worth it.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the member rather than the argument — the stated reason for not replying is that engaging with him is not worth the effort. Condescension directed at a person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Perhaps the appropriate title for the Act—and we could always put an amendment on the Table—would be the “David Seymour Vanity Regulation Ministry Establishment Act”, because that’s what’s really going on here.
civility.explanation: Names the Minister and attaches 'vanity' to him personally, mocking his motive rather than contesting the repeal. A clear personal attack, delivered as a joke about the title.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So it strikes me, Minister, that the real reason you’re abolishing the commission is because you don’t like its independent views, and, what’s more, the chair of the commission—you were unkind enough to say that you would not have appointed him.
civility.explanation: Attributes a concealed motive to the Minister and reports him as 'unkind enough' to disparage the chair. The charge is against the person's good faith rather than the merits of repeal.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There is a group of highly specialised expert researchers who produce incredibly interesting and important work at the commission who go on 29 February under clause 2 and as a result of clause 11 that was within Part 2.
specificity.explanation: Names the date the terminations take effect, the commencement clause and the operative clause, tying a concrete consequence to identified provisions. Checkable against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In response to Grant Robertson, clause 9 is there to give effect to the policies that were agreed on in Part 2, and, as he says, it’s a very simple clause.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the clause and its relationship to Part 2, but supplies no mechanism, figure or reason beyond restating that the clause enacts what Part 2 already decided. A direction with little detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I want to just graft on to what was said there by the previous speaker, Grant Robertson, because I, years ago, worked for the Law Commission, which is an independent organisation, and those kinds of independent organisations are really rich in having a focus and a capacity for people to engage with them.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote: a general claim about the value of independent organisations rests entirely on the speaker's own past employment at one different body. No evidence is offered that the property generalises, and the Law Commission's engagement record says nothing about the Productivity Commission's.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So it strikes me, Minister, that the real reason you’re abolishing the commission is because you don’t like its independent views, and, what’s more, the chair of the commission—you were unkind enough to say that you would not have appointed him.
rigor.explanation: An inference with evidence behind it — a dated public statement about the Commission being hijacked, plus a stated view on the chair's appointment — but the conclusion, that this is 'the real reason' for the repeal, outruns what those two remarks establish about motive. A real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill currently seeks to amend the Social Workers Registration Legislation Act 2019 to delay the repeal of the experience pathway for social worker registration from 28 February 2024 to 28 February 2028.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute, the exact mechanism being changed, and both the original and the new commencement dates. Fully checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Social Workers Registration Board estimate that there are 700 unfilled social worker vacancies.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Social Workers Registration Board's own estimate of unfilled social worker vacancies is 700 at the time of the second reading (31 January 2024).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: SWRB workforce/vacancy reporting or the departmental regulatory impact statement for the Social Workers Registration Legislation Amendment Bill; true if a Board estimate of approximately 700 unfilled vacancies is on record for 2023-24, false if the Board's published estimate is materially different or if no such Board estimate exists.

veracity.statement: Initially, registration for social workers was voluntary; however, in February 2021, registration became mandatory.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two facts about the registration regime: that registration was voluntary under the original scheme, and that mandatory registration took effect in February 2021.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Social Workers Registration Act 2003 and the commencement provisions of the Social Workers Registration Legislation Act 2019; true if the 2003 scheme was voluntary and the mandatory-registration provisions commenced within February 2021, false if registration was mandatory from the outset or the commencement date falls in a different month or year.

veracity.statement: In 2017, Cabinet agreed to repeal the experience pathway with a delayed commencement date.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the decision to repeal the section 13 experience pathway, with commencement deferred, was taken by Cabinet in the calendar year 2017.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cabinet minutes and the regulatory impact statement / departmental disclosure statement for the Social Workers Registration Legislation Bill; true if a Cabinet decision to repeal the experience pathway with delayed commencement is dated in 2017, false if the decision was taken in a different year or did not include a delayed commencement.

rigor.statement: Delaying the repeal of the experience pathway will act as a short-term mechanism to help reduce workforce pressures in the social work sector by continuing to provide an alternative means of entering the profession.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House: if the pathway is a route into registration and the sector is short-staffed, keeping it open should ease that shortage. The conclusion tracks the premises, but nothing is offered on the size of the effect — how many registrations the pathway actually supplies against 700 vacancies — so there is a gap between what is shown and the claim that it will 'reduce workforce pressures'.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The background to this particular bill that we are working with and now looking to change is actually back to when we were in Opposition, when I introduced a member’s bill to this House to make registration for social workers mandatory.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that she personally introduced a member's bill to make social worker registration mandatory while Labour was in Opposition, and that this was the origin of the mandatory-registration regime the current bill amends.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's members' bill ballot register and the Hansard first-reading record: true if a member's bill in Carmel Sepuloni's name proposing mandatory registration of social workers was lodged/introduced during Labour's 2008-2017 period in Opposition; false if no such bill appears under her name.

veracity.statement: The pay equity extension will lift the pay of around 5,000 employees.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2022 extension of the social worker pay equity settlement to the Government-funded NGO sector covers approximately 5,000 employees.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Cabinet paper and MSD/Public Service Commission documentation on the November 2022 extension of the social worker pay equity settlement: true if the stated coverage is approximately 5,000 employees, false if the documented figure is materially different.

focus.statement: It wasn’t supported by the Government at the time, but then the Minister went on to introduce legislation and then, interestingly, we took office, and then I was the one that got to shepherd that legislation through.
focus.explanation: A named policy (mandatory social worker registration) is in view, so this is not pure tribalism, but the weight of the sentence is the political history of who blocked it, who introduced it and who got the credit rather than the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We have to acknowledge that there has been a decline of people taking up this opportunity to become social workers, going back, I think, to 2015, and so we are not meeting the current demand and trends are expected to continue.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: falling entry into the profession since 2015, therefore the extended experience pathway is needed. The step from falling supply to unmet demand is asserted rather than shown, and 'trends are expected to continue' is offered with no source — a reasonable argument with a genuine gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So if we don’t address poverty-level wages, high rents, and difficult-to-navigate institutions, the demand for social workers will only continue to be needed, and these experience pathways will continue to, unfortunately, be critical, because the systems we created are failing our communities.
rigor.explanation: Concludes that demand for social workers will persist because 'the systems we created are failing our communities' — but that causal premise is the conclusion restated, and nothing is offered to connect wages, rents or institutional complexity to social-work demand. Begging the question.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The pay equity extension will lift the pay of around 5,000 employees.
specificity.explanation: A named policy instrument with a quantified effect on a stated population — someone could go and check the coverage figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As has been canvassed by previous speakers, the experience pathways have been really, really important in diversifying our workforce and getting a broader range of experiences, as well as indigenous models of practices.
specificity.explanation: Asserts the pathway has been important for diversity and indigenous practice without any figure, mechanism or timeframe — no registration numbers, no demographic breakdown, nothing a listener could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: They will need to be registered to work in these roles, and this is likely to drive an increase in demand for the experience pathway over the coming years.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the pay equity extension will push unregistered social service workers toward registration, increasing uptake of the experience pathway in the years following the statement.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Social Workers Registration Board annual reports for 2024/25 and 2025/26: true if applications for registration via the experience pathway rise relative to the 2023/24 baseline; false if they are flat or fall.

veracity.statement: In February 2021, the requirement to be registered became mandatory, so everybody needed to be registered.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that mandatory registration for social workers commenced in February 2021 under the registration regime.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The commencement provisions of the Social Workers Registration Legislation Act 2019 and Social Workers Registration Board records of when mandatory registration took effect; true if mandatory registration commenced in February 2021, false if it commenced in a different month or year.

veracity.statement: It is important to point out that the Social Workers Registration Legislation Act 2019 provided for the repeal of section 13 of the Social Workers Registration Act, which allowed for experience in lieu of recognised qualifications as a pathway for registration.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2019 amending Act repealed section 13 of the Social Workers Registration Act 2003, the experience-in-lieu registration pathway.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Social Workers Registration Legislation Act 2019 on legislation.govt.nz; true if it provides for the repeal of section 13 of the Social Workers Registration Act 2003, false if section 13 was left in force or amended by some other instrument.

veracity.statement: It is worthy to note that from 2019, over 4,000 social workers who registered were registered under the recognised qualification pathway, and less than 100 registered under the experience in lieu pathway.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two registration counts since 2019 — more than 4,000 registrations via recognised qualifications and fewer than 100 via the section 13 experience-in-lieu pathway.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Social Workers Registration Board annual reports / registration statistics for 2019 onwards broken down by registration pathway; true if qualification-pathway registrations exceed 4,000 and section 13 registrations number under 100, false if either count falls materially outside those bounds.

specificity.statement: It is worthy to note that from 2019, over 4,000 social workers who registered were registered under the recognised qualification pathway, and less than 100 registered under the experience in lieu pathway.
specificity.explanation: Gives a start year, two counts and the two named registration pathways — someone could go to the Board's figures and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I can’t imagine why this hasn’t been taken up on a much larger scale, because I personally know so many social workers who are out there doing work and I know that some are still not registered.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that uptake should have been much larger rests entirely on the speaker's personal acquaintance with unregistered social workers — an appeal to anecdote, with nothing offered about eligibility for that pathway or the barriers he himself goes on to say are not understood.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There is the flip side of a delay of four years, casting the possibility of doubts on the service of social workers. Hence, I do support Minister Upston’s idea to shorten the extension from four years to two.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: a longer transition prolongs uncertainty about practitioners' status, therefore shorten it. The premise is asserted rather than evidenced — no indication of how much doubt four years versus two would cause — but the conclusion does track the reason given.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We don’t believe that this pathway is actually the answer to this shortage, mainly because only 3 percent of social worker registrations are actually using this pathway.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House, and a weak one: low uptake of a pathway shows its current scale, not whether it is the right remedy for the shortage. The premise supports 'this pathway is small', not 'this pathway is not the answer' — a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: However, it’s equally clear that we are short of social workers at the moment, and, if this legislation is not passed, we’re going to have a group of social workers—and I hear it is 3 percent of the social workers who are practising at the moment—who are no longer going to be able to practise as of four weeks from today, so I think there is some incumbency on us to get this job done fast.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the premises: given a workforce shortage and a cohort losing the right to practise on a fixed date four weeks away, urgency follows. No fallacy; the inference is straightforward and the deadline does the work.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If it’s a three-year process and they’re only just starting on that journey now and you cut them off for two years, how’s that going to work out? We will just lose some people and penalise some people, and I wonder whether we need to do that.
rigor.explanation: A sound inference from a stated arithmetic mismatch: if the qualification takes three years and the transition window is two, people mid-training are cut off. The conclusion follows from the premises offered; it stops short of the top only because 'lose some people' is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I put on to the record the very stories and the experiences that I have had the benefit of seeing and hearing from firsthand, which are that in many situations, men who have used violence have had the most positive experience for healing and restoration when they have been supported to work with other men who have had those same experiences.
rigor.explanation: Argument from anecdote: a general claim about what works 'in many situations' rests entirely on what the speaker personally saw and heard, with no evaluation, comparison or outcome data offered. The reasoning is on the policy rather than the other side, so it is a genuine Rigor item, but the support offered does not carry the generalisation.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We don’t believe that this pathway is actually the answer to this shortage, mainly because only 3 percent of social worker registrations are actually using this pathway.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the alternative (non-degree) registration pathway accounts for about 3 percent of social worker registrations. Not a verdict — the resolver checks the SWRB figure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Social Workers Registration Board registration statistics (or the bill's regulatory impact statement) on the proportion of registrations granted via the section 13 recognised-experience pathway rather than a recognised qualification; true if approximately 3 percent, false if materially different (e.g. under 1 percent or above 6 percent).

specificity.statement: An extension from two years instead of the four seems more practical to address some of the industry shortages that we do have currently, but we must focus on providing more social workers, and this is something the industry has to address.
specificity.explanation: The first half names a concrete parameter — a two-year rather than four-year extension — which is checkable and actionable. The second half is a direction with no mechanism, no figure and no timeframe: 'we must focus on providing more social workers' commits to nothing and hands the problem to 'the industry'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: However, it’s equally clear that we are short of social workers at the moment, and, if this legislation is not passed, we’re going to have a group of social workers—and I hear it is 3 percent of the social workers who are practising at the moment—who are no longer going to be able to practise as of four weeks from today, so I think there is some incumbency on us to get this job done fast.
specificity.explanation: Carries a proportion (3 percent), a timeframe (four weeks from today) and a named consequence (loss of the right to practise). Marked down from the top because the 3 percent is hedged as second-hand ('I hear') and no source or numbers of people are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I understand that what we are, essentially, trying to do here is find an intentional balance between making use of the incredible experience and heart that is across our communities, on many different levels, who want to do the essential work of social work while maintaining a pathway towards professionalising and, most importantly, ensuring that it is safe practice.
specificity.explanation: Describes the bill's purpose in wholly general terms — 'an intentional balance', 'experience and heart', 'a pathway towards professionalising'. No figure, no date, no clause, and nothing about the mechanism the bill actually uses to strike that balance. Substantive in intent, so eligible, but there is nothing here anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well done on being opportunistic there—thank you.
civility.explanation: A sarcastic retort to an interjection that imputes a motive — opportunism — rather than engaging anything said. It is mild and lands on no one's character, competence or worth, so it sits just above the 0.5 failure line rather than at a personal attack. Scored against the speaker: an aside aimed at another member is still her own conduct.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Could the Leader of the House let us know whether he’ll be introducing or progressing any legislation of the new Government that does anything other than repeal or disestablish anything?
focus.explanation: There is a real point underneath — that the announced programme is dominated by repeal bills — but it is put as a characterisation of the Government's agenda rather than an engagement with any named measure, cost or effect. Policy-adjacent, mostly party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yes. And that question was about as effective as a Marama Davidson etymology lesson.
focus.explanation: The question was about whether Ministers have declared conflicts of interest; after a one-word answer the rest of the statement is a jibe at another member. No policy, measure or figure is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, on behalf of the Prime Minister, I’m a great admirer of the wisdom that David Seymour brings to many matters. The other thing I would note is that, in spite of his prognostication, this coalition Government is far more united and effective than the Opposition’s worst nightmare—in fact, we’re your nightmare dressed up as a daydream.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the relative state of the two sides — coalition unity versus the Opposition's hopes. No policy, mechanism, figure or outcome is named at any point.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yes, we do, because, actually, it is fantastic to have an Associate Minister committed to reducing smoking rates. It’s fantastic to have a Minister who asked for a range of advice. I can’t imagine the psychology of someone who doesn’t want a Minister who is (a) committed to reducing smoking and (b) interested in listening to advice.
rigor.explanation: Strawman. The concern being raised is about who wrote the material the Associate Minister passed to officials; the answer recasts it as opposition to a Minister who wants to reduce smoking and takes advice, then argues against that instead. The conclusion is defended only against a position nobody advanced. This is a genuine inference about the policy question, not a bare jibe, so it is scorable here.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Yes, we do, because, actually, it is fantastic to have an Associate Minister committed to reducing smoking rates. It’s fantastic to have a Minister who asked for a range of advice. I can’t imagine the psychology of someone who doesn’t want a Minister who is (a) committed to reducing smoking and (b) interested in listening to advice.
civility.explanation: "I can’t imagine the psychology of someone who doesn’t want…" imputes irrationality or bad faith to the questioner rather than answering the substance. Short of a direct insult, but it is sneering at the person asking, not at the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Yes. And that question was about as effective as a Marama Davidson etymology lesson.
civility.explanation: A named member is used as a byword for ineffectiveness — a personal put-down aimed at Marama Davidson's competence, not at any argument she made. The insult is the speaker's own conduct regardless of who it targets.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, on behalf of the Prime Minister, I’m a great admirer of the wisdom that David Seymour brings to many matters. The other thing I would note is that, in spite of his prognostication, this coalition Government is far more united and effective than the Opposition’s worst nightmare—in fact, we’re your nightmare dressed up as a daydream.
civility.explanation: Teasing and self-referential, but no individual is attacked; the barb is aimed at the Opposition collectively. Robust party banter of this kind engages nobody's character.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, I’ve had assurances from all coalition partners in this Government that they have had no funding from the tobacco industry, and I am confident that there has been no undue influence on the policies of this Government by the tobacco industry.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, on the Prime Minister's behalf, that no coalition party (National, ACT, New Zealand First) has received funding from the tobacco industry. The checkable part is the funding claim, not the speaker's state of confidence.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission party donation and loan returns for National, ACT and New Zealand First covering the 2020–2023 period, plus any declared donations from tobacco companies, their subsidiaries or registered tobacco-industry lobbyists. True if no such donation appears on the record; false if any tobacco-industry donation to a coalition party is on the declared record as at 1 February 2024.

divination.statement: Well, you know, the member has been in Cabinet, so she’ll be aware that the Prime Minister is responsible for all Ministers. In respect of Casey Costello, I have full confidence in her, and I’m sure that, in time, that member will too.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Carmel Sepuloni will come to hold confidence in Casey Costello as a Minister. This is a prediction about another person's future position, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Public statements by Carmel Sepuloni (Hansard, press releases, media interviews) about Casey Costello's performance as a Minister. True if she publicly expresses confidence in, or withdraws her call for the dismissal of, Casey Costello before the end of the parliamentary term; false if she continues to criticise Costello's fitness for office or to call for her dismissal.

veracity.statement: I’ve seen a report showing that the median wage in 2010 was $40,000, and that now it has risen to $65,000.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific figures: the New Zealand median wage in 2010 ($40,000) and the current median wage ($65,000).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ median annual earnings from wages and salaries (Household Labour Force Survey / NZ Income Survey) for 2010 and for the most recent year before February 2024; true if both figures match to within rounding of the nearest $5,000, false if either is materially different.

veracity.statement: A person working 40 hours a week on the minimum wage in 2010 was earning $27,000.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the annual full-time earnings of a minimum-wage worker in 2010.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's published historical minimum wage rates for 2010 multiplied by 2,080 hours (40 hours × 52 weeks); true if the product rounds to about $27,000, false if it differs by more than roughly $1,500.

veracity.statement: Well, sadly, you have to go all the way back to 1 October 2010, when the National Government reduced personal income taxes after Budget 2010.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the most recent reduction in personal income tax took effect on 1 October 2010, following Budget 2010.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Taxation (Budget Measures) Act 2010 commencement date and the Inland Revenue history of personal income tax rates and thresholds; true if the 1 October 2010 changes lowered personal rates and no later change reduced them, false if any subsequent enacted change reduced personal rates or thresholds.

veracity.statement: However, the incoming Labour Government cancelled them, and then introduced a new top tax rate of 39 percent.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions about the record of the 2017 Labour-led Government: that it repealed the personal income tax reductions legislated in 2017, and that it later legislated a 39 percent top personal rate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Families Package (Income Tax and Benefits) Act 2017, which repealed the threshold changes legislated in the Taxation (Budget Measures: Family Incomes Package) Act 2017, and the Taxation (Income Tax Rate and Other Amendments) Act 2020; true if both a repeal and a new 39 percent top rate are on the statute book, false if either is absent.

veracity.statement: This came from Australia, where the Labor Government has just announced the third in a series of personal income tax reductions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Australian Labor Government had recently announced a personal income tax reduction and that it was the third in a sequence.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Australian Government announcements on personal income tax in the weeks before 1 February 2024, and the legislated staging of the Australian personal income tax plan; true if a reduction was announced in that period and it was the third stage of the series, false if no such announcement was made or it was not the third.

veracity.statement: I have to say that I am delighted to see the new-found interest from the Opposition member in the necessity to reduce taxation. If only he’d taken one of the six opportunities he had to do so.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Grant Robertson had six occasions on which he could have reduced personal income tax and took none of them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Budgets delivered by Grant Robertson as Minister of Finance (2018–2023) and the personal income tax measures in each; true if there were six and none reduced personal income tax rates or thresholds, false if the count differs or any Budget reduced them.

veracity.statement: That is why we increased the number of security staff in emergency departments (EDs) by an additional 200 staff across 32 EDs over the Christmas and new year period.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 200 additional security staff were placed across 32 emergency departments over the 2023–24 Christmas and New Year period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Whatu Ora / Ministry of Health announcements and staffing records for the ED security programme over December 2023 – January 2024; true if the additional headcount and site count match the figures stated, false if either is materially lower.

veracity.statement: Just last week, guards that were provided through our ED security boost helped to swiftly remedy a fight in Christchurch Hospital’s emergency department between gang members.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific incident: a fight between gang members in Christchurch Hospital's emergency department in the week before the statement, resolved by security staff from the programme.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Whatu Ora incident reporting and contemporaneous news coverage of Christchurch Hospital ED for the week before 1 February 2024; true if such an incident occurred and programme security staff intervened, false if no such incident is recorded in that period.

veracity.statement: Can the Minister of Finance confirm that wage growth comes from investments and entrepreneurship and productivity growth allowing employers to pay their workers more, and that legislating up the wage from Wellington is not the only or the best way for Kiwis to get ahead—in fact, for the 97.1 percent of workers who are not on the minimum wage, that’s the only way for them to get ahead?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 97.1 percent of New Zealand workers are not paid the minimum wage — that is, that 2.9 percent are.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's Minimum Wage Review estimate of the number of employees paid at or below the minimum wage, divided by total employees from the Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey for the same period; true if the share not on the minimum wage is 97.1 percent to within a percentage point, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: How does the Minister justify the decision to raise the minimum wage today by less than the rate of inflation—effectively, cutting the wages of thousands of low-paid workers in New Zealand?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the minimum wage increase announced was smaller than the prevailing rate of inflation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The percentage minimum wage increase announced by MBIE for the following April, compared with the Stats NZ CPI annual inflation rate most recently published at the date of the statement; true if the wage increase percentage is lower, false if it equals or exceeds it.

veracity.statement: How does cutting the budget of the Waitangi Tribunal, which has exclusive authority to determine the meaning and effect of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, contribute to “fixing the bad outcomes of colonisation”?
veracity.explanation: Asserts, as a premise, that the Waitangi Tribunal holds exclusive authority to determine the meaning and effect of Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Section 5(2) of the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975; true if it confers exclusive authority on the Tribunal to determine the meaning and effect of the Treaty as embodied in the two texts, false if that authority is not exclusive or not conferred.

specificity.statement: I’ve seen a report showing that the median wage in 2010 was $40,000, and that now it has risen to $65,000.
specificity.explanation: Two dated, named figures anyone could look up and check against the official series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yes, I am delighted to be in a coalition Government that is committed to growing this economy so that we can have higher incomes and higher living standards for all New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Answering a question about the sources of wage growth, this offers only generic aspirations — no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named policy. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Colonisation brought to New Zealand things like Westminster democracy, the rule of law, economic development.
specificity.explanation: Asked what specifically the 'good' outcomes were, he names three — concrete enough to be identifiable, but they are broad institutional categories with no detail attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, all Government agencies are being asked to make savings. The member will be aware of the coalition Government commitment around looking at the scope, purpose, and the nature of the inquiries of the Waitangi Tribunal. That work has yet to begin, but it will begin in due course.
specificity.explanation: Names the commitment and its three headings but attaches no amount, no terms of reference and no date beyond 'in due course'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That is why we increased the number of security staff in emergency departments (EDs) by an additional 200 staff across 32 EDs over the Christmas and new year period.
specificity.explanation: A count of staff, a count of sites and a defined period — checkable in full.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will the Minister rule out cutting the top income tax rate from 39c to 33c in this term of Government?
specificity.explanation: Names the exact rates and the exact period at issue. A question this precise admits only one kind of answer, and is as checkable as any announcement.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This means that someone earning the median wage back in 2010 was firmly in the 17.5 percent personal income tax bracket, and now they are firmly in the 30 percent tax bracket.
rigor.explanation: A valid inference given the stated premises: if thresholds are unchanged and the median wage moved from $40,000 to $65,000, the median earner does cross into the higher bracket. Whether the premises are accurate is Veracity's question, not this one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I thought this was highly relevant for New Zealand as it shows that such reductions are commonplace and can be adopted by Governments of all political stripes.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single foreign example to the conclusion that such reductions are 'commonplace' and cross-partisan — a hasty generalisation from one instance. The argument is squarely about the policy, so Focus is unaffected; the defect is in the inference.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I am told that there has been a noticeable reduction in the number of people who have been abusive towards staff. This has improved due to the increased presence of security in our EDs and has ensured people feel safer when they access care in their times of need.
rigor.explanation: Causation is asserted from second-hand impressions gathered on hospital visits — a post hoc inference resting on anecdote, with no comparison period or measure offered to rule out other causes. The statement is squarely on the policy; the weakness is in the inference alone.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Can the Minister of Finance confirm that wage growth comes from investments and entrepreneurship and productivity growth allowing employers to pay their workers more, and that legislating up the wage from Wellington is not the only or the best way for Kiwis to get ahead—in fact, for the 97.1 percent of workers who are not on the minimum wage, that’s the only way for them to get ahead?
rigor.explanation: A false dichotomy: from the premise that productivity growth raises wages, it concludes that for everyone off the minimum wage productivity is 'the only way' to get ahead. Nothing offered rules out the other routes (collective bargaining, tax changes, transfers), and 'not the only or the best way' is asserted rather than argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I have to say that I am delighted to see the new-found interest from the Opposition member in the necessity to reduce taxation. If only he’d taken one of the six opportunities he had to do so.
civility.explanation: Sarcasm directed at the member rather than his argument — 'new-found interest' imputes insincerity and the follow-up is a jibe at him personally. Short of an insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Unlike that member, I don’t view history in a binary way.
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed at the questioner rather than her question — it attributes simplistic thinking to her personally as the opening of the answer.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: How can it be mansplaining to answer a question from a woman in Parliament? Seriously, like—ridiculous.
civility.explanation: Exasperated dismissal of a member's interjection. 'Ridiculous' lands on the accusation rather than the person's character, but the sneering tone is directed across the House rather than at the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I have to say that I am delighted to see the new-found interest from the Opposition member in the necessity to reduce taxation. If only he’d taken one of the six opportunities he had to do so.
focus.explanation: A question about the coalition tax agreement is answered with the opponent's own record instead. The reference to six Budgets carries some policy anchoring, but the weight of the remark is party point-scoring.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can it be mansplaining to answer a question from a woman in Parliament? Seriously, like—ridiculous.
focus.explanation: Time on a substantive question about Treaty outcomes spent entirely on the spat with the other side. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, all Government agencies are being asked to make savings. The member will be aware of the coalition Government commitment around looking at the scope, purpose, and the nature of the inquiries of the Waitangi Tribunal. That work has yet to begin, but it will begin in due course.
focus.explanation: Engages the policy question put to him — the savings requirement and the coalition commitment on the Tribunal's scope — without diverting to the questioner's party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How, then, can the ACT Party system of taxation be being considered by the Minister when a core plank of it she has just ruled out?
focus.explanation: Holds the Minister to a named commitment in the coalition agreement against what she has just said. Named policy, specific inconsistency alleged — scrutiny, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How does the Minister justify the decision to raise the minimum wage today by less than the rate of inflation—effectively, cutting the wages of thousands of low-paid workers in New Zealand?
focus.explanation: Names the specific decision, the benchmark it is measured against and the group affected. Squarely on the policy before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How does cutting the budget of the Waitangi Tribunal, which has exclusive authority to determine the meaning and effect of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, contribute to “fixing the bad outcomes of colonisation”?
focus.explanation: Names a specific funding decision and a specific institution and tests them against the Minister's own stated objective. Legitimate scrutiny of a named measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What is she doing to ensure the safety of tamariki in State care in response to the report by Oranga Tamariki which has shown that more children than ever are being harmed under her watch?
focus.explanation: Names a specific agency, a specific published report and a specific outcome (harm in State care). This is scrutiny of a named policy area, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I am dedicated to making real change in this area, and some of that space is around making sure caregivers have the right support wrapped around them to take care of our most vulnerable and making sure that we are making sure that the best interests of our young people are the first and foremost in decision making when it comes to our young people.
focus.explanation: Squarely directed at the care policy — caregiver support and decision-making criteria — with no reference to the other party. High Focus despite carrying almost no detail.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can she justify removing section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act when rates of abuse for tamariki Māori in the Crown’s care have almost doubled in the last five years?
focus.explanation: Engages the measure itself — the repeal of section 7AA — and the outcome it is said to bear on. Textbook opposition scrutiny of a named policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why did she tell Radio New Zealand, “I haven’t looked at a freeze on the excise duty at all” when the notes she gave to officials said, “Freeze the excise rates on smoked tobacco for three years starting 31 December 2023”?
focus.explanation: Entirely about a named policy proposal (a tobacco excise freeze) and what the Minister said about it. Accountability for a specific measure, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Given the Minister’s renewed commitment to the National and New Zealand First coalition agreement of 500 new police within two years, when did he first become aware that Police’s current recruitment practices would not enable police to achieve any desired growth without other interventions?
focus.explanation: Holds the Government to a named commitment in a named agreement with a stated number and deadline. Scrutiny of a specific policy target, not commentary on the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: What is she doing to ensure the safety of tamariki in State care in response to the report by Oranga Tamariki which has shown that more children than ever are being harmed under her watch?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an Oranga Tamariki report shows harm to children in care at a record high.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki 'Safety of Children in Care' report for the quarter/year referenced; true if findings of harm for children in care are the highest recorded in the series, false if earlier periods were higher.

veracity.statement: How can she justify cutting 600 staff at Oranga Tamaki when understaffing is a major factor in the increased rates of harm we are seeing under her watch?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 600 staff are being cut at Oranga Tamariki.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki change proposals, Budget savings targets and staffing figures for 2024; true if a reduction of about 600 roles was decided or formally proposed, false if no such reduction existed at the date of the question.

veracity.statement: How can she justify removing section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act when rates of abuse for tamariki Māori in the Crown’s care have almost doubled in the last five years?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that rates of abuse of tamariki Māori in State care have almost doubled over the five years to early 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki 'Safety of Children in Care' annual reports, findings of harm for tamariki Māori in care, 2018/19 to 2022/23; true if the rate roughly doubled, false if the increase is materially smaller.

veracity.statement: Repealing section 7AA is something that I have campaigned on for the last three years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the speaker has publicly campaigned for the repeal of section 7AA for three years prior to February 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard speeches, ACT Party releases and media statements by Karen Chhour from 2021 onward; true if she publicly advocated repeal of section 7AA from about 2021, false if her advocacy began materially later.

veracity.statement: That health briefing refers to proposals and notes. I want to be clear they were not my proposals or notes. They were not things I had written.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the proposals and notes referred to in the health briefing were not written by the speaker.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The documents released under the OIA and Ministry of Health records of what was provided to officials, together with any authorship metadata; true if no part was authored by Costello, false if any of the notes are shown to be hers.

veracity.statement: Why did she tell Radio New Zealand, “I haven’t looked at a freeze on the excise duty at all” when the notes she gave to officials said, “Freeze the excise rates on smoked tobacco for three years starting 31 December 2023”?
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that Costello made the quoted statement to RNZ and that the notes she gave officials contained the quoted excise-freeze proposal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The RNZ interview transcript/recording and the notes released to the Ministry of Health; true if both quotations appear as stated, false if either is absent or materially misquoted.

veracity.statement: It is unfortunate the actions have been distorted by a media article. The fact is I was asked a question about whether I had sought specific advice. I had not sought specific advice, which is the question I answered, and I referred to a range of advice I had sought from officials.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the speaker had not sought specific advice on the matter she was asked about by RNZ.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The briefing and notes Costello provided to the Ministry of Health and the officials' record of what advice she requested; true if no request for advice on a tobacco excise freeze was made by her, false if the documents show she asked for such advice.

veracity.statement: How can the public trust her to take action on youth vaping when she is secretly sending notes to officials that nicotine isn’t harmful?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the notes Costello sent officials say nicotine is not harmful.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The released notes provided to the Ministry of Health; true if they assert nicotine is not harmful (or materially equivalent), false if they contain no such claim.

veracity.statement: I am pleased to share with the House that I’ve recently announced $26.8 million of funding for flood resilience projects across the country, of which $12.3 million has been for flood risk mitigation across 13 projects, and $14.5 million for Future of Severely Affected Land Category 2 support across four projects.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $26.8m flood resilience package split $12.3m across 13 mitigation projects and $14.5m across four Category 2 projects.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Minister for Emergency Management and Recovery's funding announcement of January/February 2024 and the associated project list; true if the totals and project counts match, false if they differ materially.

veracity.statement: Well, as I’ve said many times in this House, I became aware as the incoming Minister that Police faced major challenges around recruiting due to the fact that the Australians are here recruiting our police officers, they were finding it difficult to fill recruit wings, and we’ve got many police officers that are fast approaching retirement age.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Australian police forces were actively recruiting New Zealand police officers in New Zealand, that recruit wings were not being filled, and that a large cohort is near retirement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Police recruitment reporting and workforce age data for 2023-24, plus records of Australian state police recruitment campaigns run in New Zealand; true if Australian campaigns were operating here and recruit wings were undersubscribed, false if neither is borne out.

civility.statement: I acknowledge that the reports do not reflect well on Oranga Tamariki or the previous Minister for Children.
civility.explanation: A contested exchange where an attack on the predecessor was available; instead the criticism stays on the reports and the record, and lands on no one personally.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: How can the public trust her to take action on youth vaping when she is secretly sending notes to officials that nicotine isn’t harmful?
civility.explanation: 'Secretly' imputes concealment and bad faith to the Minister personally rather than contesting the substance of the notes. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Did she deny seeking advice on a tobacco excise tax freeze when asked by Radio New Zealand, despite having actually sought that advice, because she did not want to be questioned on her plans to give tax breaks to the tobacco industry?
civility.explanation: Goes beyond contesting the facts to assert a concealment motive — that she denied it to avoid scrutiny of favours to the tobacco industry. That is an allegation about the Minister's character, not about the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I am dedicated to making real change in this area, and some of that space is around making sure caregivers have the right support wrapped around them to take care of our most vulnerable and making sure that we are making sure that the best interests of our young people are the first and foremost in decision making when it comes to our young people.
specificity.explanation: An intention plus generic goods ('right support', 'best interests'); no mechanism, funding, timeframe or named programme that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How can she justify cutting 600 staff at Oranga Tamaki when understaffing is a major factor in the increased rates of harm we are seeing under her watch?
specificity.explanation: A named agency, a numbered staffing reduction and a stated causal concern — precise enough to be checked and answered directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: No commitments have been made on what’s going to happen in staffing levels. Those decisions are still ongoing and those discussions are still ongoing.
specificity.explanation: Conveys only that no decision exists — no numbers, no process, no date by which the decision will be made, where all three were available to give.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How can she justify removing section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act when rates of abuse for tamariki Māori in the Crown’s care have almost doubled in the last five years?
specificity.explanation: Names the exact statutory provision and the Act, and attaches a quantified trend over a stated period.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I take this role very seriously, and every report of harm of a child is disappointing. My focus is to make sure that every child—Māori or non-Māori—is safe, loved, and cared for.
specificity.explanation: A statement of seriousness and an unobjectionable aspiration; nothing checkable or actionable, in answer to a question about accepting responsibility.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why did she tell Radio New Zealand, “I haven’t looked at a freeze on the excise duty at all” when the notes she gave to officials said, “Freeze the excise rates on smoked tobacco for three years starting 31 December 2023”?
specificity.explanation: Two direct quotations, a named broadcaster, a named tax instrument, a duration and a start date — the contradiction alleged is fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I am pleased to share with the House that I’ve recently announced $26.8 million of funding for flood resilience projects across the country, of which $12.3 million has been for flood risk mitigation across 13 projects, and $14.5 million for Future of Severely Affected Land Category 2 support across four projects.
specificity.explanation: A total, two component figures, project counts and a named funding category — fully itemised and checkable against the announcement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government has funded the Flat Point Flood resilience project, early flood warning systems in the eastern Wairarapa, sewer resilience and flood relocation support in Masterton, and water protection in Riversdale.
specificity.explanation: Four named projects in named locations, but no amounts or delivery dates attached to any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yes; the Government will deliver 500 net more police on the beat in two years.
specificity.explanation: A precise number, the 'net' basis on which it will be measured, and a timeframe — the commitment can be audited on its face.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What specific interventions is he considering in order to meet his renewed commitment to the 500 new police in two years, and will he rule out lowering current recruitment standards as one of them?
specificity.explanation: Ties the question to a numbered commitment with a deadline and names the exact intervention to be ruled in or out — a precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is unfortunate the actions have been distorted by a media article. The fact is I was asked a question about whether I had sought specific advice. I had not sought specific advice, which is the question I answered, and I referred to a range of advice I had sought from officials.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy conduct at issue: her answer was accurate because the question was narrowly about seeking specific advice. The distinction between 'sought specific advice' and 'provided notes proposing the measure' is asserted rather than shown, so there is a genuine gap between the premise and the conclusion that the answer was not misleading.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The question cannot have been credibly answered, because how could a historical document contain a policy proposal for December 2023?
rigor.explanation: A valid inference from a stated premise: a document consisting only of historical positions could not contain a proposal keyed to a future date, so the 'historical positions' answer does not account for the dated proposal. The conclusion tracks the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In this particular case, we are going to stop giving around $6 million a year to the Productivity Commission to produce more reports.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Productivity Commission's annual funding was approximately $6 million a year, the sum being withdrawn by the repeal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Vote Finance / Estimates appropriations for the New Zealand Productivity Commission for the 2023/24 financial year; true if the annual appropriation is close to $6 million, false if materially different (e.g. under $3m or over $10m).

veracity.statement: He’s criticised the Government over the years for not picking up these reports and implementing them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Seymour has repeatedly criticised governments for failing to act on Productivity Commission reports.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard speeches and ACT/Seymour press releases 2011–2023 mentioning the Productivity Commission; true if he is on record criticising governments for not implementing its reports, false if no such statements exist.

veracity.statement: It says, quite shortly, quite bluntly that the employment contracts are terminated.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the New Zealand Productivity Commission Act Repeal Bill expressly terminates the employment agreements of Commission staff, with no accompanying protective provision.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the New Zealand Productivity Commission Act Repeal Bill as passed; true if a clause provides for the termination of employees' employment agreements, false if the bill instead transfers or preserves them.

veracity.statement: I’ve certainly seen the three different draft bills that failed in this House previously under the ACT Party’s watch, and I can only hope the same will happen for the next one.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that three ACT-sponsored regulatory-standards-type bills have previously been introduced to the House and failed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bills register for ACT-sponsored regulatory standards / regulatory responsibility bills (e.g. 2006, 2011, 2021); true if three such bills were introduced and none passed, false if the count or the outcome differs.

specificity.statement: We are going to take that money and we’re going to establish a ministry of regulation, whose job it will be to uphold and enforce the quality of lawmaking in New Zealand and to review the red tape and regulation that stifles so much productive activity up and down this country, so that New Zealanders can get on with building their homes, their families, their businesses, and their lives without undue restriction from badly made laws.
specificity.explanation: Names the replacement body and its two functions, and (in context, from the preceding sentence) the money being redirected, but gives no timeframe, staffing or scope detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That means that those people are being looked after, as best as can be hoped with a range of personal circumstances, as we go through this process.
specificity.explanation: On a contested point where detail was available (redundancy terms, redeployment, transfer provisions), commits to nothing checkable — 'looked after' and 'as best as can be hoped' carry no mechanism or figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s not just Regulations Review Committee, Legislation Design and Advisory Committee, the Attorney-General, other select committees, ministry officials, the Attorney-General report, regulatory impact statements, departmental reports and statements; no, we’re going to have another one of those.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates eight named existing regulatory-scrutiny mechanisms by name — checkable, concrete content.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We are going to take that money and we’re going to establish a ministry of regulation, whose job it will be to uphold and enforce the quality of lawmaking in New Zealand and to review the red tape and regulation that stifles so much productive activity up and down this country, so that New Zealanders can get on with building their homes, their families, their businesses, and their lives without undue restriction from badly made laws.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House and what replaces it — mechanism and purpose, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: One is for the Opposition to actually read some of the fabulous work that the Productivity Commission has done, so that they will have some policy ideas to take to New Zealanders and show how they can actually make New Zealand a better place than they did last time.
focus.explanation: Names no policy, figure or outcome; the content is a characterisation of the other party's general record and ideas. Insults no individual, so Civility is untouched — this is the tribalism case Focus exists for.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is not a Government that builds up; it’s a Government that tears down.
focus.explanation: A general characterisation of the governing parties with no policy, measure, figure or outcome named. No individual is attacked, so Civility passes it cleanly.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think a better analogy is that, when we’re doing a bad job, it’s time to stop asking for more large reports on what to do and start implementing the advice that we’ve already got.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy dressed as an analogy: continuing to commission advice and implementing existing advice are not mutually exclusive, and nothing is offered to show that abolishing the advisory body causes implementation of past reports.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s not just Regulations Review Committee, Legislation Design and Advisory Committee, the Attorney-General, other select committees, ministry officials, the Attorney-General report, regulatory impact statements, departmental reports and statements; no, we’re going to have another one of those.
rigor.explanation: The inference is that a new body must be redundant because many scrutiny mechanisms already exist; the enumeration is real but nothing is offered to show the existing mechanisms cover the proposed ministry's function, so there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So he’s got no care for those people whatsoever.
rigor.explanation: Argument from silence: from the Minister not stating compensation or transfer arrangements in his speech, concludes he has no care at all. Absence of a statement is not evidence of the underlying state, and the categorical 'whatsoever' outruns the premise.
