True if the central estimate is $200 billion or more; false if the accepted range is below that (e.g. the $120–185 billion figures).

divination.statement: I’d suggest you won’t be voted in next time.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that local government leaders who opposed the reform and are now proposing large rates rises will be voted out at the next local election. A prediction about others' electoral fate, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Results of the October 2025 New Zealand local body elections for the mayors and councillors the speaker is addressing — those who campaigned against the Three Waters reform and are consulting on the large rates increases he names (Far North, Hamilton, Buller, Porirua). True if a majority of those incumbents lost their seats or did not return; false if a majority were re-elected.

focus.statement: Lots of leaders, no leadership, and so too for this coalition Government.
focus.explanation: A content-free characterisation of the coalition Government. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — strip out the party framing and nothing is left. This is the tribalism case Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But we’re also trying to do this in a way that maintains local ownership, local control, and local delivery, and for that reason, I commend this bill to the House.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the measure before the House and the design principle it is meant to serve; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I would like to hear from the Minister of Local Government about his plans for engaging with Ngāi Tahu meaningfully on the significant repeal of Te Mana o te Wai.
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure (the repeal of Te Mana o te Wai) and a specific process question (Crown engagement with Ngāi Tahu). No party framing at all; this is scrutiny of a named policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’d like to ask the Minister of Local Government whether the purpose of the bill as described in clause 3 is to make small communities that belong to a body corporate pay for their own water infrastructure.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure before the House at clause level and asks about a specific consequence for a specific class of community. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Have you had that assurance from your officials—and I’d love your guarantee on this—that under whatever you plan to do here, you absolutely will have the kind of balance sheet separation that means that this infrastructure can actually be provided at lower cost by the entity?
focus.explanation: Goes straight to the financing mechanism at issue — whether the replacement arrangement achieves balance sheet separation and therefore cheaper borrowing. Nothing about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The question I therefore have is: what advice did he seek, and what advice did he receive that repealing was the best way to achieve this Government’s objectives? Did he explore the possibility of amending the existing legislation to achieve those objectives?
focus.explanation: Asks about the advice underpinning a named legislative choice and about the alternative of amendment — squarely on the bill's purpose, with no characterisation of the other side.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In the Manuherikia, old mining offtakes have now been used for intensive dairy—constant irrigation of what was dry land resulting in a trickle that’s hardly called a river—and it has seriously degraded biodiversity.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that historic gold-mining water races in the Manuherikia catchment are now used to irrigate dairy land, that this has reduced the river to a trickle, and that biodiversity has been seriously degraded.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Otago Regional Council water-allocation records and Manuherikia catchment flow/ecology monitoring (ORC minimum-flow work, NIWA/ORC macroinvertebrate and habitat reporting): true if consented abstraction originating in mining-era races supplies irrigation that has driven residual flows to near-minimum levels and monitoring records significant ecological decline; false if the abstraction has a different origin or monitoring shows no material flow or biodiversity decline.

veracity.statement: I understand that there was a letter sent on 31 January to stakeholders advising them that there would be repeal and change and that stakeholders had until today to respond.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific consultation letter dated 31 January 2024 went to water-reform stakeholders announcing repeal, with responses due by 13 February 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Department of Internal Affairs / Minister of Local Government stakeholder correspondence of 31 January 2024 and its stated response deadline: true if such a letter exists with a 13 February 2024 deadline, false if no such letter was sent or the deadline differs materially.

veracity.statement: They’ve had a lot of water woes, and I would point out to the Minister that only last week in the Otago Daily Times, one of the residents was complaining about vomiting blood, being taken to hospital, because of the bad water infrastructure.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Otago Daily Times reported, in the week before 13 February 2024, a Waipori Falls resident hospitalised after vomiting blood, attributed to the local water supply.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Otago Daily Times coverage from roughly 5–13 February 2024 on Waipori Falls water: true if an article reports a resident vomiting blood and being taken to hospital with the water supply given as the cause, false if no such report exists or the report does not make that attribution.

veracity.statement: Meanwhile, the residents of the 35 households have had 130 days straight of boil-water notices. On most days, they’ve had a maximum of around seven hours of water a day.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an unbroken boil-water notice of about 130 days affecting 35 households at Waipori Falls, with supply typically limited to around seven hours a day.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Taumata Arowai / Clutha District Council boil-water notice records and supply logs for Waipori Falls as at 13 February 2024: true if a continuous notice of roughly 130 days was in force over about 35 households with daily supply of the order stated, false if the notice was materially shorter, intermittent, or the supply figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: It could also include other councils that are completely different, like the Tararua District, which have a relatively small number of ratepayers, a massive area, a large number of towns, each with their own treatment systems, and the fourth-largest roading network in the country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Tararua District Council has the fourth-largest roading network of any territorial authority in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA / Road Assessment and Maintenance Management data on local road network length by territorial authority around 2023–24: true if Tararua District ranks fourth by total (sealed plus unsealed) local road kilometres, false if it ranks materially differently.

veracity.statement: It could also include other councils that are completely different, like the Tararua District, which have a relatively small number of ratepayers, a massive area, a large number of towns, each with their own treatment systems, and the fourth-largest roading network in the country.
veracity.explanation: Prior recorded for the Tararua roading-network ranking claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: As above: NZTA local road length by territorial authority; fourth place or not.

specificity.statement: I understand that there was a letter sent on 31 January to stakeholders advising them that there would be repeal and change and that stakeholders had until today to respond.
specificity.explanation: Carries a dated document and a named deadline — someone could go and check both — though it stops short of describing what the letter proposed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Meanwhile, the residents of the 35 households have had 130 days straight of boil-water notices. On most days, they’ve had a maximum of around seven hours of water a day.
specificity.explanation: Household count, duration in days and daily hours of supply — precise and directly checkable against council and regulator records.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It could also include other councils that are completely different, like the Tararua District, which have a relatively small number of ratepayers, a massive area, a large number of towns, each with their own treatment systems, and the fourth-largest roading network in the country.
specificity.explanation: Names a particular council and gives a concrete, rankable characteristic of it, though the rest — 'relatively small', 'massive area' — carries no figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Have you had that assurance from your officials—and I’d love your guarantee on this—that under whatever you plan to do here, you absolutely will have the kind of balance sheet separation that means that this infrastructure can actually be provided at lower cost by the entity?
civility.explanation: Insistent and sceptical, but aimed entirely at the proposal and the advice behind it; the Minister's person, competence and motives are left alone.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The question I therefore have is: what advice did he seek, and what advice did he receive that repealing was the best way to achieve this Government’s objectives? Did he explore the possibility of amending the existing legislation to achieve those objectives?
civility.explanation: A contested repeal he opposes, put entirely as a question about advice and options; no imputation of motive or attack on the Minister.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I know that Mayor Brown said he doesn’t want to, but it just seems to me, for the life of me, that’s the only thing you could do; you could only put up the rates and you’d have to put them up a lot. It wouldn’t be a little bit.
rigor.explanation: Argument from personal incredulity feeding a false dichotomy: because the speaker cannot see another route, rates rises are declared the only option. Debt, asset recycling, staging or central funding are not considered and ruled out, so the conclusion outruns what was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reason I raise this is because all the advice that I have seen from the department and from those agencies—including credit agencies but also agencies that have reviewed the Government’s proposals, the Government’s preliminary work, the alternative model that was put forward by Communities 4 Local Democracy, which is remarkably similar to what this Government has signalled they are going to do—says that unless balance sheet separation is maintained, none of the things that the Government is claiming they will prioritise will be able to be achieved.
rigor.explanation: An appeal to authority: the conclusion rests on unquoted advice the speaker alone has seen, from bodies described by category rather than named or cited. The sources are at least the right ones for the question and the reasoning tracks what they are said to conclude, but the absolute step — without separation, none of the objectives can be achieved — is asserted on that authority rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My second question is: what advice has he had regarding the impact on the Te Awa Tupua (Whanganui River Claims Settlement) Act that this legislation has?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: it names a specific Act and asks about a specific interaction between it and the repeal bill. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: May I draw the attention of the Minister to the fact that the way with which the Local Government Act is applied in terms of the relationship with hapū and iwi is inconsistent.
focus.explanation: Engages the substitute framework the bill restores — the Local Government Act's iwi/hapū obligations — rather than the other party's record.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, the Government’s objective is to repeal the legislation and replace it with Local Water Done Well. We campaigned on that, we were elected to do that, and we are now delivering that, as we promised.
focus.explanation: On-policy despite the weak inference: it names the replacement programme and answers about the bill's purpose rather than characterising the opposition. The reasoning defect is Rigor's, not Focus's.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’d like the Minister to tell the committee whether he’s had advice from Standard & Poor’s or any of the other rating agencies on the question of, post repeal of this legislation, whether or not the entities will be able to achieve balance sheet separation.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the bill's financial mechanism and what advice underpins it; no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My second question is: what advice has he had regarding the impact on the Te Awa Tupua (Whanganui River Claims Settlement) Act that this legislation has?
specificity.explanation: Names the Act in full and asks for an identifiable class of advice, so the Minister could answer it checkably; short of 1.0 because no clause, figure or timeframe is pinned down.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: May I draw the attention of the Minister to the fact that the way with which the Local Government Act is applied in terms of the relationship with hapū and iwi is inconsistent.
specificity.explanation: 'Inconsistent' is asserted without measure, though the surrounding sentences supply concrete instances (no input into asset management planning, chasing councils for information). Credited for that nearby detail; no figures or named councils.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As a young woman from the Pipiwai Valley—Te Orewai hapū Ngāti Hine Te Iwi—our families have had 10 months of no fresh drinking water from Te Awa o Hikurangi.
specificity.explanation: Names the valley, the hapū, the river and the duration — concrete enough that someone could go and check it or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of Auckland and the issue with Watercare, we’re working closely with Auckland Council around the options they have in front of them to achieve financial sustainability for Watercare, and that work is happening at pace.
specificity.explanation: Names Watercare and Auckland Council but identifies none of the 'options', no mechanism, no dollar figure and no date — 'at pace' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’d like the Minister to tell the committee whether he’s had advice from Standard & Poor’s or any of the other rating agencies on the question of, post repeal of this legislation, whether or not the entities will be able to achieve balance sheet separation.
specificity.explanation: Names the source of advice sought (Standard & Poor's and other rating agencies), the mechanism at issue (balance sheet separation) and the point in time (post repeal). A precise question, as checkable as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As a young woman from the Pipiwai Valley—Te Orewai hapū Ngāti Hine Te Iwi—our families have had 10 months of no fresh drinking water from Te Awa o Hikurangi.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific duration (ten months) of loss of fresh drinking water from a named river for a named community, dating from Cyclone Gabrielle a year earlier.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Whangārei District Council / Northland Regional Council drinking-water and Cyclone Gabrielle recovery records for the Pipiwai Valley supply, plus Te Orewai hapū and local news reporting: true if the community was without potable supply drawn from the Hikurangi awa for approximately ten months up to February 2024, false if the outage did not occur or was materially shorter.

veracity.statement: This bill doesn’t repeal Te Mana o te Wai.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the repeal bill leaves the Te Mana o te Wai framework untouched — a claim about the contents of the bill itself, not about future policy intentions toward the NPS-FM.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Water Services Acts Repeal Bill as introduced: true if no clause repeals or amends the provisions giving effect to Te Mana o te Wai (the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management hierarchy of obligations), false if any clause does.

rigor.statement: Well, the Government’s objective is to repeal the legislation and replace it with Local Water Done Well. We campaigned on that, we were elected to do that, and we are now delivering that, as we promised.
rigor.explanation: Asked whether repealing achieves the Government's objectives, he defines the objective as the repeal itself — circular, so the conclusion is true by construction and says nothing about effects. The supporting move is an appeal to electoral mandate rather than to anything the bill does.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You could argue that balance sheet separation is a means to financial sustainability, but there’s plenty of evidence and plenty of literature out there to show that, actually, balance sheet separation is a very powerful tool in significantly increasing the amount of borrowing against existing revenue or assets.
rigor.explanation: The distinction he draws — that separation is a borrowing-capacity tool, not the same thing as financial sustainability — genuinely supports his conclusion that the Minister answered a different question. But the load-bearing support is an unnamed 'plenty of evidence and plenty of literature': an appeal to unspecified authority in place of a cited source.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We have had some questions about balance sheet separation, but it’s my argument that they haven’t been directly or adequately addressed by the Minister in his response.
civility.explanation: A contested exchange where imputing evasion was readily available, but the criticism lands on the adequacy of the answer rather than on the Minister's honesty or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So my first question of five to the Minister is: under paragraph (b) of clause 3, if a purpose of the bill is “to disestablish the Northland and Auckland Water Services Entity and make related transitional arrangements;”, is it implied in that purpose that Aucklanders will be better off because of the disestablishment of that entity, Minister?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: it cites a named paragraph of a named clause and asks what outcome that stated purpose implies for a named population. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Secondly, given the plans to repeal the urban development legislation and move that to the Resource Management Act, does the Minister consider that mandating some kind of water sensitive urban design and helping nature clean up our water would be a cheaper and more effective way than always putting in more expensive infrastructure?
focus.explanation: Engages a policy mechanism directly — where urban development rules sit, and whether mandated water sensitive urban design substitutes for built infrastructure. Nothing about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I would also like you to look at your colleagues smearing local mayors—whether it’s Councillor Foster, myself, previous Mayor Prendergast, previous Mayor Wilde—when there were huge millions, whether it was moving from $11 million in 2009 just on the capital expenditure of the water network, through to more than $30 million in the current forecast; whether the attitude that we were not aware of underground damage for earthquakes—we were working on cross-contamination, we were working on a number of things—from some of the members of this House is helpful to a future partnership that will last longer than the next three years.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy thread here — water network capital expenditure rising from $11 million to over $30 million — but the weight of the statement is about how members opposite have characterised mayors, not about the repeal before the committee.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Because, as you’ll see, if you go to clause 5 and track through to Schedule 1, there are no savings provisions or transitional arrangements proposed under Schedule 1.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact clause and schedule and states precisely what she says is absent from them. A reader can open the bill and check it or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Secondly, given the plans to repeal the urban development legislation and move that to the Resource Management Act, does the Minister consider that mandating some kind of water sensitive urban design and helping nature clean up our water would be a cheaper and more effective way than always putting in more expensive infrastructure?
specificity.explanation: Names an approach (water sensitive urban design) and a legislative vehicle, but 'some kind of' and 'cheaper and more effective' carry no figures, threshold or timeframe — a direction with the how and how much missing.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our Local Water Done Well policy will ensure that councils are able to have financially sustainable models for water infrastructure in New Zealand, accessing long-term funding and financing so they can make the investments that they need in this important infrastructure.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy, but everything after that is a string of generic goods — 'financially sustainable models', 'long-term funding and financing', 'the investments that they need'. No mechanism, no figure, no date a listener could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For those who haven’t had the summer that Wellingtonians have, to update you on the situation that Wellington is in with respect to water, we have extensive damage to drinking-water pipes that has meant that perhaps 45 percent of our water supply leaks onto the roads and gutters around the city.
specificity.explanation: A quantified statement of the problem — a named city, a named cause (pipe damage) and a figure for the share of supply lost. Checkable against the network operator's own reporting.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Because, as you’ll see, if you go to clause 5 and track through to Schedule 1, there are no savings provisions or transitional arrangements proposed under Schedule 1.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Schedule 1 of the water services repeal bill before the committee contains no savings or transitional provisions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of Schedule 1 of the bill as it stood before the committee of the whole House on 2024-02-13 (the Water Services Acts Repeal Bill): true if Schedule 1 contains no savings or transitional provisions, false if it contains any such provision.

veracity.statement: Many people have spoken about people’s health and the water, and I would like to know if in any of this process of repeal he has considered any care for the other species that depend on the clean water of our awa, or the shellfish that depend on the lack of sedimentation—sedimentation from dealing with stormwater improperly, including that famous road of national significance Transmission Gully and the subsequent degradation of the Porirua Harbour.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, as the premise of the question, that improperly handled stormwater and sediment from the Transmission Gully road project degraded Porirua Harbour.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Greater Wellington Regional Council Porirua Harbour sediment monitoring and any enforcement action (abatement/infringement notices) against the Transmission Gully consent holders for sediment discharge: true if regulator records attribute measurable sediment degradation of the harbour to Transmission Gully construction discharges, false if monitoring or enforcement records show no such attribution.

veracity.statement: The Government has stated that we will be repealing Labour’s 10-entity model, which was a co-governed, 10 entity, mandated model. And the Northland and Auckland Water Services Entity, which was the only entity which was actually under way—we are repealing the model, and therefore we are repealing that entity as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Northland and Auckland Water Services Entity was the only one of the ten entities under the previous Government's model that was actually being stood up.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Internal Affairs and National Transition Unit establishment records as at February 2024: true if the Northland and Auckland entity was the only one of the ten with an establishment board appointed and transition work under way, false if any other entity had reached the same stage.

veracity.statement: The mayor has—including putting out a tweet yesterday, saying that it’s great to see the Government repealing this legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Mayor of Auckland posted publicly on 12 February 2024 welcoming the Government's repeal of the water services legislation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Wayne Brown's public X/Twitter account posts dated 12 February 2024: true if a post that day expresses support for the Government repealing the water services legislation, false if no such post exists or its content does not support the repeal.

veracity.statement: For those who haven’t had the summer that Wellingtonians have, to update you on the situation that Wellington is in with respect to water, we have extensive damage to drinking-water pipes that has meant that perhaps 45 percent of our water supply leaks onto the roads and gutters around the city.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 45 percent of Wellington's drinking-water supply was being lost to leaks in the network as at February 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Wellington Water's reported network water loss / non-revenue water figure for the 2023-24 summer: true if the reported loss is approximately 45 percent, false if materially lower (e.g. below 35 percent).

rigor.statement: The Government has stated that we will be repealing Labour’s 10-entity model, which was a co-governed, 10 entity, mandated model. And the Northland and Auckland Water Services Entity, which was the only entity which was actually under way—we are repealing the model, and therefore we are repealing that entity as well.
rigor.explanation: A valid, if modest, inference: the entity exists only as a creature of the model being repealed, so repealing the model entails repealing the entity. The conclusion tracks the premise offered; no fallacy or gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In addition, the future impact of further diminished water supply is not only that the restrictions become more harsh but that the diminished amount of water moves so slowly through the pipes that it increases the likelihood of bacterial contamination and us being unable to drink the water at all.
rigor.explanation: A real causal chain about the policy problem — lower throughput, longer water age in the mains, greater contamination risk — and the conclusion does follow from it. Marked down because no evidence, threshold or authority is offered for the link; it is asserted as a mechanism rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is absolutely essential that we get past some of the petty politics that were raised by other members in this Chamber earlier, and actually get on to the issue of how these reforms will support balance sheet separation and the ability for us to be able to get on and pay for the work that needs to be done.
civility.explanation: Dismisses other members' contributions as 'petty politics' — pointed and faintly condescending toward colleagues in a genuinely contested debate — but it lands on their contributions rather than on any person, and immediately redirects to the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I asked that question, the Hon Phil Twyford asked that question, and the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall asked that question—and the Minister of Local Government has not said the words “balance sheet separation” once.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that three named Labour members each raised balance sheet separation in this committee stage and that the Minister's replies never used the phrase.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard transcript of the committee stage of the Water Services Acts Repeal Bill on 12-13 February 2024: true if Twyford and Verrall each put a question on balance sheet separation and no reply by Simeon Brown up to this point contains the phrase 'balance sheet separation'; false if he used the phrase or if those questions were not asked.

veracity.statement: What we see in this bill is that Part 1 provides the transitional, savings, and related provisions, and if you look into Schedule 1 it says that there is none.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fact about the text of the bill before the House: that Part 1 carries the transitional, savings and related provisions and that Schedule 1 states there are none.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Water Services Acts Repeal Bill as introduced (2024): true if the Part 1 provision (clause 5) refers transitional, savings and related provisions to Schedule 1 and Schedule 1 records that there are none; false if Schedule 1 contains such provisions or the referral sits elsewhere.

veracity.statement: This is the normal part of any piece of legislation to have this in as default, that as the water entities legislation hadn’t actually come into force, there was no actual transitional provisions or savings, hence why the schedule is there.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the water services entities legislation had not come into force as at February 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The commencement provisions of the Water Services Entities Act 2022 and the Water Services Legislation Act 2023, and DIA records of whether the entities were legally established before 13 February 2024: true if no part of the entities regime had commenced, false if the Act had commenced and entities had been established.

veracity.statement: And can he guarantee that the purpose, which we are told is to reduce the cost—which, you know, apparently was going to be huge under the Labour proposal; we’d already spent over a billion dollars and it was going to carry on!
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than one billion dollars had already been spent on the previous government's three waters / affordable water reform programme.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DIA, Treasury and Auditor-General reporting on cumulative appropriated and actual expenditure on the Three Waters / Affordable Water Reform programme to February 2024: true if the total spent exceeds $1 billion, false if materially below.

veracity.statement: That Act is not very old; it was passed last year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Water Services Economic Efficiency and Consumer Protection Act was passed in 2023, the year before this February 2024 debate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The date of third reading and Royal assent of the Water Services Economic Efficiency and Consumer Protection Act 2023 on the NZ legislation register: true if assented during 2023, false if any other year.

focus.statement: I asked that question, the Hon Phil Twyford asked that question, and the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall asked that question—and the Minister of Local Government has not said the words “balance sheet separation” once.
focus.explanation: Names a specific mechanism central to the bill's rationale (balance sheet separation) and holds the Minister to account for not addressing it; this is scrutiny of a policy question, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why is it that the rights of those employees who will now be made redundant are under clause 17, not within the Part 1 transitional, savings, and related provisions?
specificity.explanation: Names the exact clause, the exact part of the bill and the exact class of rights at issue; the Minister could check and answer it directly. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Of course, our policy Local Water Done Well, which we’re developing, will ensure councils are able to have the revenue sufficiency and the ability to have long-term funding and financing for water services and infrastructure in their communities.
specificity.explanation: Names a policy but supplies no mechanism, figure, threshold or timeframe — 'revenue sufficiency' and 'long-term funding and financing' are generic goods that could not be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And I do want to mention, before I close, that the consumer aspect is also really important—that one of the problems we have is that ratepayers pay for their water one way or another, but they have almost no ability to take issue with the quality of the service they get, whether it be the brown water that comes into the bathtub in Geraldine or the water that doesn’t come at all in some parts of Gore, or the water that spills all over the street in Wellington.
specificity.explanation: Names three specific places and three specific service failures, which is concrete, but offers no figures, no mechanism and no description of the redress that is missing.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is the normal part of any piece of legislation to have this in as default, that as the water entities legislation hadn’t actually come into force, there was no actual transitional provisions or savings, hence why the schedule is there.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: if the regime being repealed never took effect, there is nothing to transition from, so an empty schedule follows. The conclusion tracks the premise, though it leaves the employee-rights placement question untouched.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: So, with the Water Services Economic Efficiency and Consumer Protection Act 2023, my question is: why is it that he’s getting rid of it when we know that it will need to be replaced and, essentially, there’ll be something very similar put in its place?
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Government will have to legislate a substantially similar economic regulation and consumer protection framework for water services to replace the Act it is repealing.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Legislation enacted by the current Government for water services economic regulation and consumer protection: true if a statute is passed conferring economic regulation of water suppliers (e.g. on the Commerce Commission) plus consumer protection/dispute resolution comparable to the repealed Act; false if no such replacement framework is enacted.

civility.statement: So it just strikes me as really disappointing and a little confusing that the Minister has chosen to repeal this piece of legislation, fundamentally a piece of legislation which increases effectiveness, increases innovation, and increases efficiency and increases quality—all things that I think both you and I, Minister, would agree are good things in respect of water.
civility.explanation: A contested repeal with ample opportunity for a personal attack; the criticism lands entirely on the decision and explicitly reaches for shared ground with the Minister rather than impugning him.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government is going to be developing an economic regulation regime that works for councils, and we’re progressing this later in the year.
specificity.explanation: Names a domain (economic regulation for councils) and a rough timeframe, but supplies no mechanism, no design, no figures and no date beyond 'later in the year'. A direction rather than checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s not just the Commerce Commission’s powers, though—the Water Services Commissioner—but there’s also an extended remit for the Consumer Advocacy Council and the independent consumers’ dispute resolution that that Act provides for.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific statutory machinery at stake — Commerce Commission powers, the Water Services Commissioner, the Consumer Advocacy Council's remit and the dispute-resolution provision. Someone could open the Act and check each. No figures or dates, which keeps it short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As I said earlier, that legislation was designed for the 10 entities, which were, of course, never set up, and so that legislation is no longer required.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House, but the conclusion overreaches the premise: that an Act was drafted alongside the 10-entity model does not establish that none of its provisions operate independently of it — the very separability Williams had just set out (Commerce Commission oversight, Consumer Advocacy Council remit) goes unaddressed. A hasty generalisation from origin to redundancy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It absolutely would not interfere with the Government’s work programme to design something that they say will be better for councils, because to protect consumers within the system, we need to have something that gives the Commerce Commission these extra powers and provides an independent voice for consumers within it.
rigor.explanation: The reason offered (consumers need a regulator and an advocate during the transition) supports keeping the provisions, but it does not support the separate and stronger claim that retention 'absolutely would not interfere' with the Government's design work — that assertion is stated rather than argued. A gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, for colleagues in the committee, the reason that this matters is that if there is not sufficient balance sheet separation, then it will be incumbent upon the councils—and, certainly, Standard & Poor’s will believe that the councils are responsible, and the councils, in the event of something going wrong, will have to bail the entities out.
rigor.explanation: A coherent chain: absent separation, a ratings agency attributes the entity's obligations to the council, which therefore carries the bail-out risk. The step from 'S&P will believe' to 'will have to bail the entities out' leans on the agency's judgement standing in for the legal position, but the inference is broadly tracked by what he offered about the earlier S&P conversations.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Standard & Poor’s were extremely clear that balance sheet separation was critical to enabling the reforms that we were proposing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the ratings agency Standard & Poor's, in conversations during the design of the repealed Water Services Acts, stated that balance-sheet separation of the water entities from councils was critical to the reforms proceeding.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: S&P Global Ratings published commentary or advice on the New Zealand three waters reform (2021–2023), and DIA/Treasury records of engagement with ratings agencies released under the OIA: true if S&P stated that separation of water entity debt from council balance sheets was necessary for the reform's debt-financing model; false if S&P made no such statement or expressed a materially weaker view.

veracity.statement: As most people in this House will know, most local authorities in New Zealand are up against their debt ceilings.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a majority of New Zealand's local authorities were, as at February 2024, at or close to their borrowing limits.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Local Government Funding Agency covenant reporting and councils' 2023/24 annual plans, measuring debt-to-revenue against each council's applicable LGFA limit: true if more than half of the 78 local authorities were at or within a few percentage points of their limit; false if only a minority were.

civility.statement: Now, what we heard from the Minister was a repetition of the information that was readily available in the policy document.
civility.explanation: Robust criticism of the content of the Minister's answer in a genuinely contested committee debate. It characterises what was said rather than the person saying it, though the dismissiveness edges toward the Minister without landing on him.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It was presented in a way that made it look like the majority of councils support this, and so I think it’s important for the committee’s understanding of the purpose of this, the rationale behind the proposal to repeal, to know what councils the Minister has been working with, as he claimed, in the development of this policy.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: it ties a specific claim the Minister made in justification of the repeal (that he worked with councils) to a specific request for which councils. Legitimate scrutiny of a named policy claim, with no party-directed content.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are, effectively, two options for local councils: they can delay setting their long-term plan until 30 June, or they can delay it by one year and just put in place a one-year annual plan instead.
specificity.explanation: Two named options with a concrete date and a concrete alternative instrument (a one-year annual plan); a council could act on this directly. Falls short of 1.0 only because the conditions attaching to each option are not given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My question to the Minister of Local Government goes back to Te Tiriti o Waitangi principles, and want to query the Minister in terms of his Government’s engagement with the 19 iwi of Tāmaki-makau-rau and the 12 iwi of Te Tai Tokerau and the many, many hapū of that region and the 219 marae of that region for the proposal to disestablish the Northland and Auckland water services entity.
specificity.explanation: Counts the exact bodies whose consultation is at issue (19 iwi, 12 iwi, 219 marae) and names the specific proposal. A precise question is as checkable as a precise answer; it stops short of 1.0 because no date or form of engagement is specified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The ones that I was able to quickly find, in my research into whether there are international obligations in relation to water, are the UN resolution on the human right to water and sanitation that was passed by the General Assembly on 3 August 2010, and also the human right to safe drinking water and sanitation that was passed on 22 February 2016.
specificity.explanation: Two named international instruments with adoption dates and the adopting body — enough for anyone to go and check, and enough for the Minister to answer against.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Going back to my question that I asked and that was not addressed: was the iwi of Wanganui consulted about the impact on Te Awa Tupua (Whanganui River Claims Settlement) Act or not?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific settlement Act and the specific iwi, and puts a closed yes/no question that can be checked against the consultation record.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The good news for the committee: there was only one employee, which was the CEO. The bad news was that he had a very high salary.
civility.explanation: The 'good news/bad news' framing turns an easily identifiable individual's pay into a joke at his expense rather than criticising the entity or the policy. Not a direct insult, but it lands on a person rather than on the substance, so below the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Minister made some comments before, which I wanted also to know if he thought they were appropriate, in terms of stating publicly the salary of an easily identifiable individual and making a joke about the number of employees at that entity.
civility.explanation: Directly challenges the Minister's conduct in the House, but describes what he did rather than what he is; no imputation of bad faith or attack on character. Pointed, and just short of the fully impersonal standard because it puts the Minister's own judgement in issue.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The last Government employed people on $700,000 salaries for those water entities, and that person was employed for that entity. But that is all part of the wasteful expenditure of the last Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government employed water services entity staff, including the Northland and Auckland entity chief executive, on salaries of $700,000.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Remuneration disclosures for the Water Services Entity (Northland and Auckland) / National Transition Unit establishment chief executive — the Department of Internal Affairs annual report or the OIA release the Minister refers to. True if the establishment CEO's salary was approximately $700,000, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: That number had actually already been released under an Official Information Act request, and it’s worth noting that three of the four establishment chief executives were made redundant by the previous Government when they shifted to 10 entities, so if they want to complain, they should look in the mirror.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (a) the CEO salary figure was already public via an OIA response and (b) three of the four establishment chief executives were made redundant by the previous Government when the water reform model moved from four entities to ten.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Internal Affairs / National Transition Unit records of the four water services entity establishment chief executives appointed under the four-entity model and their status after the April 2023 move to ten entities. True if three of the four were made redundant, false if fewer were.

veracity.statement: The ones that I was able to quickly find, in my research into whether there are international obligations in relation to water, are the UN resolution on the human right to water and sanitation that was passed by the General Assembly on 3 August 2010, and also the human right to safe drinking water and sanitation that was passed on 22 February 2016.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the UN General Assembly adopted a resolution on the human right to water and sanitation on 3 August 2010, and a resolution on the human right to safe drinking water and sanitation on 22 February 2016.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: UN General Assembly resolution records for the resolutions on the human right(s) to water and sanitation. True if the adoption dates match those given, false if the resolutions were adopted on materially different dates or by a different UN body.

focus.statement: The last Government employed people on $700,000 salaries for those water entities, and that person was employed for that entity. But that is all part of the wasteful expenditure of the last Government.
focus.explanation: A specific figure and a specific appointment are named, which is on-policy scrutiny, but the closing sentence generalises it into 'wasteful expenditure of the last Government' — a real policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That number had actually already been released under an Official Information Act request, and it’s worth noting that three of the four establishment chief executives were made redundant by the previous Government when they shifted to 10 entities, so if they want to complain, they should look in the mirror.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque. Whether the previous Government also made establishment chief executives redundant has no bearing on whether this disestablishment handles the CEO's employment properly, which was the question put. The conclusion ('they should look in the mirror') does not follow from the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The issue is in relation to the existing Treaty settlements, and the Act simply amends references to the Acts we’re repealing, and because those Acts and the entities hadn’t come into force, the actual impact is negligible, but we will continue to engage with iwi as we work through the policy development.
rigor.explanation: The inference is sound in form: if the amendments to settlement Acts only cross-reference legislation that never took effect, the practical impact on those settlements is small. Marked down because 'negligible' is asserted rather than shown, and no settlement Act is worked through to demonstrate it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think the Minister of Local Government, if he truly believes, as I’m told, that they’re upholding Te Tiriti o Waitangi, should actually answer that question. Failure to do so means that they’re not, in my opinion, and I’m going to listen very carefully now.
rigor.explanation: Argument from silence: a Minister's failure to answer a question in the committee stage is treated as establishing that the Government is not upholding Te Tiriti. Non-response has many causes and does not support the conclusion drawn, though the inference is at least about the substantive obligation rather than about the other side.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So we know that this Government wants to change the balance amongst that hierarchy—which can only mean more pollution, in my opinion.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy, and a weak one: rebalancing a statutory hierarchy of obligations does not entail more pollution. No mechanism, modelling or evidence connects the two; the leap is asserted ('can only mean'), a non sequitur softened only by 'in my opinion'.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is very significant, and I think needs an answer because it is generally considered unacceptable—or that you need a very good justification—to have a “Henry VIII” clause.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (this needs justification) follows from the mechanism she has just laid out, but the supporting premise leans on convention — what is 'generally considered unacceptable' — rather than an argument for why delegating amendment of a statutory definition is objectionable here. A legitimate appeal to a recognised legislative-scrutiny standard, but an appeal nonetheless.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You cannot hold one landowner responsible for a blockage that is allowed to happen by a landlord a kilometre upstream.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the premises he has laid out immediately before: a stream can run through hundreds of separate private properties, so a blockage's cause and the property where its effects land can be different holdings. Given that, individual landowner liability does not attach coherently. Valid inference; the only gap is that it is asserted rather than tied to what the bylaw actually requires.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But worse than that, it will have to be redone. Because we know that competition and efficiency work is necessary and consumer protection work is necessary.
rigor.explanation: The inference is valid in form — if the regulatory work is necessary, repealing it means doing it again — but the load-bearing premise is delivered as a bare 'we know', with nothing offered for why economic regulation and consumer protection of water services are necessary. A real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Now, that hierarchy at the moment is that first we care about the health of the water, and we’re doing regulation; secondly, the health of people; and third, consumptive or commercial uses.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the current ordering of the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy of obligations as it stands in the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management 2020: (1) water bodies and freshwater ecosystems, (2) health needs of people, (3) other social/economic/cultural well-being.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Clause 1.3(5) of the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management 2020 as in force in February 2024; true if the three priorities are ordered water body health, then people's health needs, then other consumptive/commercial uses, false if the ordering or membership differs.

veracity.statement: They chose not to spend, not to invest, and the anniversary weekend floods a year ago exposed the fact that, in our largest city, which is home to about a third of the country’s population, the council for decades has simply not been doing the job of investing adequately in stormwater networks.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that Auckland holds roughly a third of New Zealand's population, and that the January 2023 Auckland Anniversary floods demonstrated decades of inadequate council investment in stormwater networks.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates for June 2023 (true if Auckland's share is roughly 30-35% of the national total, false if materially outside that); and the independent review of the Auckland Anniversary weekend flooding response (Bush review) plus Auckland Council stormwater asset-management and renewals reporting — true if these find long-run underinvestment in the stormwater network, false if they attribute the flooding to causes other than investment levels.

veracity.statement: This is a problem because Auckland Council has a 2015 bylaw that says that any stream that abuts a private property or runs through it is the responsibility of the private landowner and not the council’s responsibility.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of a specific instrument: that Auckland Council's 2015 stormwater bylaw places responsibility for streams on or abutting private land on the landowner rather than the council.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Auckland Council Stormwater Bylaw 2015 and its associated guidance; true if it assigns responsibility for watercourses on or adjoining private property to the landowner, false if the council retains that responsibility under the bylaw.

veracity.statement: The Commerce Commission has already begun work on setting up the Water Services Commissioner, and I understand made an appointment of someone who’s expected to assume that role.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at February 2024 the Commerce Commission had started implementation work for the Water Services Commissioner role created by the Water Services Economic Efficiency and Consumer Protection Act 2023, and had appointed a person expected to take it up.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Commerce Commission media releases, board/appointment announcements and its 2023/24 annual report; true if they record preparatory work on the water services regulatory regime and an appointment to (or designated for) the Water Services Commissioner role before 13 February 2024, false if no such work or appointment is recorded.

specificity.statement: So that is anything that Ministers change—by regulation that doesn’t come through this House—will amend the definition of Te Mana o te Wai in a piece of legislation that we’re not even repealing today.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument (the national policy statement as secondary legislation), the mechanism (a ministerial amendment made by regulation, without passing through the House), and the precise legal effect (altering a defined term in the Water Services Act 2021, which survives the repeal). Someone could go to the clause and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is a problem because Auckland Council has a 2015 bylaw that says that any stream that abuts a private property or runs through it is the responsibility of the private landowner and not the council’s responsibility.
specificity.explanation: Names the body, the year, the instrument and the exact allocation of responsibility it creates. Precise enough that a reader could pull the bylaw and verify the mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Not a familiar technique, but rather than repealing it, just place it on hold, which is what my clause 10(1) would do: suspend it.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause and the precise legal mechanism — suspension in place of repeal — which he then spells out (no powers, no rights or obligations, no cause of action, revival by Order in Council). Concrete and checkable against the Amendment Paper; it stops short of full marks only because no dates or amounts attach.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So that is anything that Ministers change—by regulation that doesn’t come through this House—will amend the definition of Te Mana o te Wai in a piece of legislation that we’re not even repealing today.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee — the drafting effect of the Schedule 2 amendment on section 14(1). No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I’m really keen to know what advice the Minister has had on what will be the environment now for councils and what kind of accountability, what kind of responsibility, will they be held to in the discharge of their responsibilities.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny directed at the consequences of the repeal — what replaces the statutory stormwater duties and the two regulators. Asks about the mechanism and the accountability regime, not about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s a pity, because some of the work that the previous Government has done around economic efficiency and competition, the new Government has actually picked up and, I must say, done really well with.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested repeal debate in which he credits the governing party for continuing his side's work. Engages the substance and attacks no one; the opportunity to be uncivil was plainly there and was not taken.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, the ability to bring things back from the brink of death isn’t really something I’d want to confer on that particular Minister, but here we have it—giving it to you there.
civility.explanation: Turns from the legislation to the individual Minister, implying he cannot be trusted with the revival power. Light and jocular rather than abusive, but it is a slight on the Minister personally rather than on the policy — short of a direct insult, and no longer fully civil.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: You’ll have to come up with a whole new framing of it which does fundamentally the same thing.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that after repealing the Water Services Economic Efficiency and Consumer Protection Act 2023, the Government will have to legislate afresh for substantially the same functions — economic regulation and consumer protection for water services. A prediction about the Government's future conduct, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The legislative record for the 54th Parliament; true if a Government bill is enacted or introduced that establishes economic regulation and/or a consumer protection framework for water services performing substantially the functions of the repealed Act, false if the term ends with no such replacement regime legislated.

specificity.statement: We are repealing their three waters, co-governed, mega-entities reform, and we will be putting in place our own consumer regulation in terms of those issues that he mentions as part of our Local Water Done Well policy.
specificity.explanation: Names the reform being repealed and the named replacement policy, and identifies consumer regulation as the mechanism, but gives no design detail, timeframe or figures for what that regulation will be.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Whilst sitting in the chair during this committee stage, instead of answering basic, simple, relevant questions, he’s tweeted a picture of himself standing next to the Mayor of Waimakariri, the Mayor of Manawatū, and the Mayor of Whangārei, and I wonder if that was his consultation.
specificity.explanation: Names three identifiable mayors and a specific, timestamped act, offering a concrete and checkable alternative account of the consultation claimed. Falls short of 1.0 because it stops at an insinuation rather than a stated count of councils consulted.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The third aspect that I’m really interested in hearing more from the Minister on is about the provisions allowing local authorities to actually defer their entire long-term plan by a year and be replaced by what’s been called an “enhanced annual plan” for the next financial year.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a particular provision, the named instrument it substitutes, and the deferral period. Lacks figures or a clause reference, which keeps it short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I want to ask about clause 14 and the relationship it has to the rest of the provisions there, because I can see that you’ve talked about how there was only one employee, but I can see that there’s a board there.
specificity.explanation: Cites a numbered clause and a concrete factual distinction (one employee versus the board) that pins down exactly what is being asked about, though no figures or consequences are supplied.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But the legislation is not worth putting on ice because it relates to a fundamentally different approach to how we want to deal with water infrastructure, and that’s why we’ll be repealing it and replacing it.
rigor.explanation: A genuine reason is offered — the Act was built for a model the Government rejects — but the conclusion overreaches the premise: Webb's proposal was to suspend the Act so its useful parts could be salvaged, and a difference of overall approach does not by itself show that no provision is worth keeping. Real inference about the measure, with a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It was worked on while we were in Opposition, and then we took it to a thing called the election and New Zealanders voted for it. So not only did we work with local councils but New Zealanders voted for it, and now we’re delivering it.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to electoral mandate standing in for the evidence actually sought. The question was which councils were consulted; that a party won an election does not establish that any particular council was worked with, so the conclusion does not follow from the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is a Government that, I understand, talks a lot about property rights. These are contractual rights, and it just doesn’t seem at all necessary to go so far.
rigor.explanation: The premise is about the Government's professed commitment to property rights; the conclusion is that the provision is unnecessary. Inconsistency with a stated principle is not evidence about necessity, so the conclusion does not follow — an appeal to the other side's own rhetoric standing in for an argument on the merits.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It seemed really unfair and unreasonable to expect a private party who happened to back on to one of those areas to be responsible for the clearing of that when in fact they hadn’t even produced the debris.
rigor.explanation: A clean inference from a stated principle: liability for clearing should track responsibility for causing, the landowner did not cause the debris, therefore imposing the duty on them is unfair. The premise is offered explicitly and the conclusion tracks it.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It was worked on while we were in Opposition, and then we took it to a thing called the election and New Zealanders voted for it. So not only did we work with local councils but New Zealanders voted for it, and now we’re delivering it.
civility.explanation: "a thing called the election" is condescension aimed at the questioner rather than the substance — short of a direct insult, but a sneer rather than an engagement, which under the re-anchored scale is a real if minor failure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: He has time to send tweets, I note, whilst he’s in the chair.
civility.explanation: A sarcastic jibe imputing that the Minister is neglecting his duty rather than engaging the substance of the answer he is chasing. Not a direct insult, but it turns on the person's conduct rather than the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I thank the member for that question, and I would just like to note that our policy, Local Water Done Well, was announced about 12 months ago.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that National's Local Water Done Well policy was publicly announced approximately twelve months before 13 February 2024, i.e. around early 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National Party policy release and contemporaneous news coverage dating the launch of the policy branded "Local Water Done Well"; true if first announced between roughly November 2022 and April 2023, false if the launch date falls materially outside that window (e.g. mid-2023 or later).

veracity.statement: The Minister stood in the theatrette and said to the nation that he’d been working alongside councils in developing this policy.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Simeon Brown, at a press conference in the Beehive theatrette, publicly stated he had worked alongside councils in developing the Local Water Done Well policy.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Video, transcript or contemporaneous reporting of the Minister's post-Cabinet/announcement press conference on the water services repeal; true if he stated he worked alongside councils in developing the policy, false if no such statement was made.

veracity.statement: Whilst sitting in the chair during this committee stage, instead of answering basic, simple, relevant questions, he’s tweeted a picture of himself standing next to the Mayor of Waimakariri, the Mayor of Manawatū, and the Mayor of Whangārei, and I wonder if that was his consultation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that during this committee stage the Minister posted to Twitter/X a photograph of himself with the mayors of Waimakariri, Manawatū and Whangārei.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Simeon Brown's Twitter/X timeline for 13 February 2024; true if a post from that day shows him with those three named mayors, false if no such post exists or the people pictured are not those mayors.

focus.statement: I want to know what councils he’s worked alongside.
focus.explanation: Directly scrutinises a specific claim the Minister made about how the policy was developed. Naming the consultation claim and demanding the underlying detail is accountability on a named policy process, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I just want to hear from the Minister: what are the potential implications for those councils who expected that the assets and associated debt would be moving and may now be looking at funding those water services improvements themselves?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the transitional provisions — who carries the assets and debt, and who funds the improvements if the transfer does not occur. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’d also like an answer to the question that I have about the board members and the employees and why, when we do these things, we have to cut out rights, which I understood were sort of sacrosanct in the National Party faith, anyway, because Mr Seymour talks about property rights all the time.
focus.explanation: A real policy point — the extinguishment of board members' and employees' contractual rights under the bill — but half its weight is carried by party framing about what National and Mr Seymour profess rather than by the provision itself.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: All of the things that we’re putting in place are simply about providing flexibility and choices to councils around the consultation requirements, around the time frame in which they need to finalise their LTPs, and whether they wish to delay that by one year, but also some protections in terms of the annual plan to ensure that if they were to delay by 12 months, their next annual plan would have the right information that it would need to have in place around all of the issues, including water services, roading, and other services that councils provide.
specificity.explanation: Names real mechanisms — consultation requirements, the LTP finalisation timeframe, a one-year deferral option, and annual-plan information requirements — but gives no dates, thresholds or statutory clauses, so it is a direction with detail rather than something checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There was a facility to be able to actually get ownership back to private ownership if a number of conditions were met: if 75 percent of the shareholders of that mixed urban-rural supply—and they were sort of deemed shareholders—were able to agree on it.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism, the class of scheme, the shareholder threshold and the qualification that the shareholders were deemed — precise enough that someone could go to the Act and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, as it turns out, the Far North District Council—we estimate that without water services reforms, by 2051, every ratepayer there will end up paying another $8,690.
specificity.explanation: A named council, a dollar figure to the dollar, a counterfactual condition and a date. Precise and checkable against the modelling.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: All of the things that we’re putting in place are simply about providing flexibility and choices to councils around the consultation requirements, around the time frame in which they need to finalise their LTPs, and whether they wish to delay that by one year, but also some protections in terms of the annual plan to ensure that if they were to delay by 12 months, their next annual plan would have the right information that it would need to have in place around all of the issues, including water services, roading, and other services that councils provide.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the transitional provisions of the measure before the committee; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, under the repeal, I guess that leaves many of my constituents wondering: what does it mean for the investment that they’ve put into those mixed-use schemes?
focus.explanation: Directs the committee at a named consequence of the repeal for a named class of affected people. No party content whatever.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In terms of the question around the establishment boards, they are not employees, so they are not entitled to redundancy.
rigor.explanation: A clean inference: redundancy entitlements attach to employment, the board members are appointees rather than employees, therefore no entitlement arises. Granting the premise, the conclusion follows; whether the premise is accurate is Veracity's question.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One of the councils I have in mind is Rangitīkei—a rating base of 16,000 entities. How could they afford the water services reforms?
rigor.explanation: A relevant premise is offered — a small rating base — but the conclusion of unaffordability is carried by a rhetorical question rather than by any cost figure linking the base to the required investment. Argument from incredulity, on a real policy point.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That CEO had a redundancy clause in the contract, and that redundancy clause has been honoured.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the disestablished water services entity's chief executive had a contractual redundancy clause and that the payment under it was made.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The CEO's employment agreement and the entity's/DIA's disclosure of severance payments (annual report or OIA release): true if the contract contained a redundancy clause and a payment was made under it; false if no such clause existed or no payment was made under it.

veracity.statement: There was a facility to be able to actually get ownership back to private ownership if a number of conditions were met: if 75 percent of the shareholders of that mixed urban-rural supply—and they were sort of deemed shareholders—were able to agree on it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the water services legislation now being repealed contained a mechanism returning mixed urban-rural schemes to private ownership on the agreement of 75 percent of the deemed shareholders.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Water Services Legislation Act 2023 and the Water Services Entities Act 2022 as amended, on transfer of mixed-use rural supplies: true if a return-to-private-ownership mechanism conditioned on agreement by 75 percent of deemed shareholders appears; false if no such threshold or mechanism is in the Acts.

veracity.statement: There was an absolutely disastrous outcome, really, in the flooding, which my colleague Phil Twyford has referred to, particularly in West Auckland, where the fact that Watercare had neglected its stormwater system—the creeks, the small rivers—really did create a disaster.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that neglect by Watercare of its stormwater network — creeks and small streams — caused the West Auckland flooding disaster.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Which body held the Auckland stormwater function at the time of the January 2023 Auckland Anniversary floods, and the findings of the independent review of that response: true if Watercare held the stormwater network and a review found neglect of it caused or worsened the West Auckland flooding; false if stormwater sat with Auckland Council's Healthy Waters unit or no such finding of neglect was made.

divination.statement: Now, as it turns out, the Far North District Council—we estimate that without water services reforms, by 2051, every ratepayer there will end up paying another $8,690.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that in the absence of the reforms, the annual per-ratepayer water cost in the Far North will be $8,690 higher by 2051.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Far North District Council water charges in 2051 against the DIA water services reform modelling on which the figure rests: true if the average Far North ratepayer's annual water cost in 2051 is around $8,690 above the reform-scenario figure; false if the eventual cost is materially below that.

civility.statement: I note, however, that the MP for Northland has not argued in favour of his constituents, so I’ll do it on his behalf.
civility.explanation: Pointed and aimed at a particular member rather than at the policy — it charges him with failing his own constituents. Short of an insult or an imputation of bad faith, but it lands on the person, not the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In the end, they actually hadn’t talked to many councils at all in developing this policy, certainly not those that are most affected.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government consulted few councils, and not the most affected ones, when developing the water services repeal policy.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Regulatory Impact Statement and Department of Internal Affairs consultation record for the Water Services Acts Repeal Bill, plus the Minister's own answers in this committee stage; true if only a small number of councils were consulted and the small/high-cost councils named (Buller, Central Hawke's Bay, Chatham Islands, Tararua) were not among them, false if a broad council consultation took place.

veracity.statement: Costs of service without reform, in the Minister’s own advice—for James Meager’s constituents—is $8,690 per year, per ratepayer, just for water; and he’s about to vote for this repeal.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that departmental advice to the Minister puts the unreformed cost of water service for Ashburton district ratepayers at $8,690 per household per year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Department of Internal Affairs / Water Services Reform cost-of-service modelling for Ashburton District Council; true if the no-reform annual household cost for Ashburton is $8,690 (or rounds to it) in that advice, false if the published figure is materially different or no such figure exists.

veracity.statement: What this bill is proposing to repeal is a bespoke guarantee to the people of Chatham Islands that the Government will pay for their water services moving forward.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the legislation being repealed contained a specific Crown guarantee to fund Chatham Islands water services, so that the repeal removes it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Water Services Entities Act 2022 as amended by the Water Services Legislation Act 2023, and any accompanying Crown funding agreement covering the Chatham Islands; true if a Crown commitment to pay for Chatham Islands water services is in the repealed provisions, false if the legislation only excluded the Chathams from an entity without committing Crown funding.

veracity.statement: In fact, under the legislation we’re repealing, those entities weren’t going to be set up until mid-2026.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the water services entities created by the legislation being repealed were not scheduled to be established until mid-2026.
veracity.subject: speaker
