rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The empirical evidence that says the number on jobseeker benefit has gone up by 76,000 when there’s been a 50 percent reduction in the number of sanctions applied in the last six years.
rigor.explanation: Offered as empirical evidence that sanctions get people into work, but it is a bare correlation between two trends presented as causation — a post hoc inference, with nothing offered to rule out the labour market, policy changes or population growth.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, as I said to the House yesterday, it was the last Government which caused the congestion in Auckland—$228 million on consultancy reports for light rail and didn’t even deliver a business case.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: money spent on light rail consultancy, even if wasted, does not establish that it caused Auckland's congestion. The evidence offered addresses a different proposition from the conclusion drawn.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: If they doubt that matter about education, a former Labour Minister—none other than Richard Prebble—is pointing out how hopeless their performance was in the last three years, where 55 percent and more of Māori are not even at school.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than 55 percent of Māori students are not at school over the last three years, and that former Labour Minister Richard Prebble has said Labour's education performance was hopeless.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education attendance statistics for Māori students over 2021–2023: true if the share of Māori students not regularly attending school was 55 percent or higher; false if materially below that. Also checkable that Richard Prebble is a former Labour Minister and made this claim in the period referenced.

veracity.statement: Can I say that’s a superb question, and out there there’s about 895,000 people who need to know that—and a whole lot more coming up to 65 years of age.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 895,000 people currently receive, or depend on, New Zealand Superannuation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Social Development / Work and Income statistics on the number of New Zealand Superannuation recipients as at early 2024: true if approximately 895,000 (within rounding), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Could I ask the Minister, as to the so-called $1.2 billion shortfall, how does it compare with the $29 billion that was going to be assigned to light rail in Auckland?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that $29 billion was to be assigned to Auckland light rail. The headline published capital estimate was substantially lower, though larger whole-of-life or upper-bound figures have been cited.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Light Rail Ltd business case and Treasury/Ministry of Transport costings: true if a published estimate of about $29 billion for the Auckland light rail project exists; false if the published estimates top out materially below that.

veracity.statement: The empirical evidence that says the number on jobseeker benefit has gone up by 76,000 when there’s been a 50 percent reduction in the number of sanctions applied in the last six years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 76,000 increase in jobseeker benefit recipients alongside a 50 percent reduction in sanctions applied over the last six years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit statistics and sanctions data for the six years to early 2024: true if jobseeker support recipients rose by approximately 76,000 and the number of sanctions applied fell by approximately 50 percent over that period; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, as I said to the House yesterday, it was the last Government which caused the congestion in Auckland—$228 million on consultancy reports for light rail and didn’t even deliver a business case.
veracity.explanation: Asserts $228 million was spent on consultancy reports for Auckland light rail without a business case being delivered.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport / Auckland Light Rail Ltd spending records to the end of 2023: true if approximately $228 million was spent on consultancy and advisory work for Auckland light rail and no completed business case was delivered; false if the spend is materially different or a business case was in fact delivered.

veracity.statement: Why does he still stand by that Government decision to axe the regional fuel tax; a decision that has required Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown to stop work on multiple projects that are funded by that tax?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the repeal of the Auckland regional fuel tax caused Mayor Wayne Brown to stop work on multiple projects funded by that tax.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council and Auckland Transport statements, minutes or programme decisions in late 2023 / early 2024: true if work on more than one regional-fuel-tax-funded project was stopped as a result of the announced repeal; false if no such projects were halted.

focus.statement: Will he commit to preventing the gaming of targets, such as the practice of admitting emergency department patients to non-existent virtual wards so that the six-hour target can be met?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the health-target policy and how it could be circumvented. No party framing at all — legitimate scrutiny of a named measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why does he still stand by that Government decision to axe the regional fuel tax; a decision that has required Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown to stop work on multiple projects that are funded by that tax?
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy decision (repeal of the regional fuel tax) and a specific consequence (halted council projects). Scrutiny of a named measure, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: How can the Minister justify creating a $1.2 billion shortfall in the plan to decongest Auckland over the next four years, when congestion will cost us about $5 billion in productivity in the same period?
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Auckland congestion will cost about $5 billion in lost productivity over the next four years.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Published Auckland congestion-cost estimates (NZIER / Auckland Council / Ministry of Transport) covering 2024–2028: true if the cumulative estimated productivity cost of Auckland congestion over that four-year period is around $5 billion; false if the published estimates are materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: I’m advised by officials that since 2017, $26.3 million of taxpayer funding was spent on crafting section 27 reports designed to encourage lighter sentences.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a cumulative figure for legal aid spending on section 27 cultural reports from 2017 to early 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / legal aid expenditure records on section 27 report writing, summed from FY2016/17 to FY2022/23; true if the total is approximately $26.3 million, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, members might be interested to know that the cultural report provider Hard 2 Reach, headed by lifetime Mongrel Mob member Harry Tam, boasts on its website that offenders “have received sentence discounts of up to 35 percent because of factors raised in our reports”.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions of fact: that Harry Tam heads the provider Hard 2 Reach and is a lifetime Mongrel Mob member, and that the firm's website carried the quoted sentence-discount claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hard 2 Reach website as at February 2024 (live or Wayback Machine capture); true if it contains the quoted wording about discounts of up to 35 percent, false if no such wording appears. Company records / public reporting for whether Harry Tam heads the provider.

veracity.statement: A naive approach to justice exemplified by Labour’s only clearly articulated justice sector target to reduce the prison population by 30 percent irrespective of what’s happening in our community, on our streets, and in our houses has been followed by a rise in violent crime, an explosion in retail crime, ram raids, gang membership, and paying for the victims of crime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that Labour set a target of reducing the prison population by 30 percent and that violent crime, retail crime, ram raids and gang membership rose over that period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Labour government policy announcements 2018 for the existence and size of the prison-population reduction target; NZ Crime and Victims Survey and NZ Police recorded-crime/retail-crime and gang-list statistics for 2017/18 to 2023 for the trend claims. True if the 30 percent target was set and the named measures rose over the period, false if either fails.

veracity.statement: The section 27 reports that went from $40,000 a year in 2017 to $7.5 million will not be funded anymore.
veracity.explanation: Asserts annual expenditure on section 27 reports of about $40,000 in 2017 rising to about $7.5 million in the most recent year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice legal aid expenditure on section 27 cultural reports by financial year; true if the FY2016/17 figure is approximately $40,000 and the latest reported year approximately $7.5 million, false if either is materially different.

specificity.statement: I’m advised by officials that since 2017, $26.3 million of taxpayer funding was spent on crafting section 27 reports designed to encourage lighter sentences.
specificity.explanation: Carries a dollar figure, a start year and a named statutory provision — someone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will the Minister implement the promises set out in the National Party’s Real Consequences For Crime document, which states “Ending taxpayer funding for written cultural reports is expected to save around $20 million over four years. National will direct all of this funding towards victim support services, which represents an increase of 29 percent”; if not, what increases in funding for victims will the Minister commit to?
specificity.explanation: Names a document, a saving, a timeframe and a percentage increase; a precise question is as checkable as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are committed to providing more support to the victims of crime in the justice system, and we’re working with officials to assess the best options for supporting victims through the savings generated.
specificity.explanation: A direction with no amount, no mechanism and no date, offered in reply to a question that named a figure and a percentage.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government has committed to wider changes to sentencing laws to restore real consequences for crime. That includes capping sentence discounts at 40 percent, and my colleague Minister McKee is leading work to reinstate three strikes legislation.
specificity.explanation: A numeric cap, a named piece of legislation to be reinstated and the responsible Minister.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Last week, the Government announced ending the 30 percent target. Our focus is on reducing violent crime, lowering the number of serious repeat youth offenders, and then on the nuts and bolts of the justice system, which is the hard, gritty task of dealing with the chronic delays to justice—we can’t continue to have Kiwis waiting years to get an outcome for their changes.
specificity.explanation: Names three priority areas and a concrete policy change (ending the 30 percent target), but no figures, targets or timeframes attach to the new direction.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will the Minister implement the promises set out in the National Party’s Real Consequences For Crime document, which states “Ending taxpayer funding for written cultural reports is expected to save around $20 million over four years. National will direct all of this funding towards victim support services, which represents an increase of 29 percent”; if not, what increases in funding for victims will the Minister commit to?
focus.explanation: Holds the Government to a named, quantified commitment in its own policy document. Scrutiny of a specific promise, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will he increase grants for victims of crime to access support services such as mental health assistance, counselling, or help with travel costs to court cases or hearings, as set out in the National Party Real Consequences For Crime document, or is that just another broken promise by National?
focus.explanation: Names specific supports and a specific policy document, but the closing 'another broken promise by National' shifts part of the weight onto general party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Six years of loose spending, of hopeless, naive law and order policies, of waffle, and of almost comically poor delivery came to an end last year. Now our country has a coalition Government led by the Rt Hon Christopher Luxon that has the capability, the plan, and the determination to get our country back on track.
focus.explanation: A general characterisation of the previous Government — 'waffle', 'poor delivery' — followed by boosterism for his own. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, because there is a great deal of pressure on the legal aid budget and we need to spend our money wisely.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered for the policy — budget pressure — but the step from 'the legal aid budget is under pressure' to 'this particular line should be cut' is asserted rather than shown; nothing connects the saving to the pressure.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Unconstrained Government spending by Labour has added to the inflation that every family knows about and is struggling with. That inflation has forced higher interest rates for families and businesses. Those higher borrowing costs are squeezing the economy.
rigor.explanation: A coherent causal chain — spending to inflation to interest rates to a squeezed economy — each link following from the last. The weak point is the first step: fiscal spending is treated as the sole driver of inflation with nothing offered to rule out the other causes.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: A naive approach to justice exemplified by Labour’s only clearly articulated justice sector target to reduce the prison population by 30 percent irrespective of what’s happening in our community, on our streets, and in our houses has been followed by a rise in violent crime, an explosion in retail crime, ram raids, gang membership, and paying for the victims of crime.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: 'has been followed by' does the work of 'caused', with no mechanism linking a prison-population target to retail crime or ram raids, and no alternative explanation considered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: New Zealanders are sick and tired of reading about people convicted of serious violent offences that would attract significant prison sentences and finding that those sentences are whittled down by a series of discounts. So offenders end up on home detention playing PlayStation, which is not dealing real consequences for crime.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on an appeal to popular feeling ('sick and tired') plus a vivid image rather than evidence; the 'so' does not follow — nothing shows that discounts routinely convert serious violent sentences into home detention.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And the previous Government led by—including Willie Jackson, leaned too heavily away from those core human rights, most notably in the move away from equal voting rights in Canterbury and through some of the co-governance arrangements, and they never made a case.
rigor.explanation: Two concrete instances are offered in support of the general claim, which is more than assertion, but 'leaned too heavily away from core human rights' is not shown to follow from them — the step from a specific representation arrangement to a rights conclusion is skipped.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Six years of loose spending, of hopeless, naive law and order policies, of waffle, and of almost comically poor delivery came to an end last year. Now our country has a coalition Government led by the Rt Hon Christopher Luxon that has the capability, the plan, and the determination to get our country back on track.
civility.explanation: Scathing about a party and a government, but no individual is attacked; naming the Prime Minister is neutral. Harsh party criticism passes Civility cleanly.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And we’re going to deal with the boondoggles that were left unchecked by Andrew Little, by Kris Faafoi, by Kelvin Davis, by Kiri Allan, and by Ginny Andersen and all the long crew of justice people who made no progress.
civility.explanation: Names five individuals in a roll-call and dismisses them as having 'made no progress' — an attack on their personal competence rather than on any decision they made.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: First is a decent road—ridiculously described as a holiday highway by the Hon Phil Twyford and so many MPs on the other side. A decent road is the best thing you can do for Northland.
civility.explanation: Names an individual member and calls his characterisation 'ridiculous' — mockery aimed at the position rather than the man, so pointed and edging toward the person without landing on him.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is very appropriate that Paul Goldsmith began his contribution talking about comically poor delivery because he then gave us a five-minute demonstration of what that looks like.
civility.explanation: Mockery aimed squarely at another member's personal performance rather than at any policy or argument he made — a clear jibe at competence, though a light one rather than sustained abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Then we had the very, very strange situation with the Hon Casey Costello’s office and the mysterious document that appeared out of nowhere, as if by magic.
civility.explanation: Insinuation rather than substance: 'as if by magic' implies concealment on the Minister's part without stating the charge, which is sneering short of a direct insult. Scrutiny of the document's provenance could have been put without the innuendo.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is one of the most morally repugnant decisions any New Zealand Government has taken, and it’s one of the first decisions that this Government has taken.
civility.explanation: About as fierce as condemnation gets, but the target is a decision, not a person. No individual's character, competence or worth is attacked, so under the re-anchored scale this sits near the top.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Government got off to a shambolic start before Christmas, proving that they had no plan to take New Zealand forward, only a plan to cancel things, stop things, repeal things, and take us backwards.
focus.explanation: A general characterisation of the other side's competence and direction. No measure, figure, programme or outcome is named — 'cancel things, stop things, repeal things' is party framing rather than a policy point. Not scored for Rigor: strip out the part about the other team and no argument remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They said they were going to repeal and replace the water reforms that we put in place. Well, they’ve got a plan to repeal them, but there’s no plan to replace them.
focus.explanation: Names a specific commitment (repeal and replace the water reforms) and holds the Government to the second half of it. Textbook opposition scrutiny of a named policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: They made a big song and dance about the fact that they were going to get back to work faster and then brought us back to work on roughly the same timetable that Parliament would normally come back to work based on.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2024 sitting programme began at approximately the same time of year as Parliament's usual resumption, despite the Government having claimed it would return earlier.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's official sitting calendars: the first sitting day of 2024 compared with the first sitting days of the preceding several years. True if the 2024 date falls within roughly a week of the recent norm; false if it is materially earlier.

veracity.statement: We had Mark Mitchell saying, “Oh, actually, I couldn’t guarantee 500 police within two years.”. and then saying, “Oh, but actually I did.”, because he had been corrected by the Prime Minister.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in the first sitting week of 2024 Mark Mitchell first said he could not guarantee 500 additional police within two years and then reversed that position after the Prime Minister contradicted him.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard and contemporaneous media transcripts for the sitting week of late January / early February 2024: true if Mitchell is recorded declining to guarantee 500 police in two years and subsequently affirming the guarantee after the Prime Minister's comments; false if no such sequence appears.

veracity.statement: Then we’ve got minimum-wage workers who saw the whites of the Government’s eyes when it came to their real commitment to supporting low-income New Zealanders: an increase in the minimum wage that is well less than the cost of living.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the minimum wage increase announced for 2024 is smaller, in percentage terms, than the prevailing rate of inflation — so minimum-wage earners lose real income.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's announced adult minimum wage rate effective 1 April 2024 as a percentage increase on the previous rate, compared with Stats NZ CPI annual inflation at the time of the announcement. True if the wage increase is materially below annual CPI; false if it matches or exceeds it.

veracity.statement: We saw them scrapping universal free prescriptions, so people pay more every time they go to the pharmacy. We saw them scrapping free early childhood education for two-year-olds, adding extra costs onto Kiwi families.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific reversals by the incoming Government: removal of the universal $5 prescription co-payment exemption, and cancellation of the planned extension of the 20 hours free ECE entitlement to two-year-olds.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government's December 2023 mini-Budget documents and Pharmac/Ministry of Health and Ministry of Education announcements: true if both the universal free prescriptions policy and the free ECE extension for two-year-olds were reversed or cancelled; false if either remained in place.

veracity.statement: That’s one of the first decisions they took: 7,000 more children living in poverty.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official advice on the decision to change benefit indexation projects approximately 7,000 additional children living in poverty.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Treasury/MSD regulatory impact statement and Budget documents on indexing main benefits to CPI rather than average wages: true if the official estimate of additional children in poverty is around 7,000, false if the documented estimate is materially different or no such estimate exists.

veracity.statement: This Monday’s event is, however, the first time in the event’s 21 years of history in Parliament that it is officially celebrated as Lunar New Year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the February 2024 Parliament event was the first in the series' history to be officially named and celebrated as Lunar New Year rather than Chinese New Year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary event records, invitations and media coverage of the annual Chinese/Lunar New Year celebrations at Parliament since 2002: true if 2024 is the first officially titled 'Lunar New Year', false if an earlier event carried that title.

divination.statement: They’re simply pushing back onto councils the water crisis that we have in New Zealand and the result is going to be very simple: ratepayers, Kiwi families will pay more—and those rates increases will start very soon.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that returning water infrastructure responsibility to councils will produce higher rates bills for households, and that the increases will arrive shortly rather than in the medium term.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Territorial authority annual plans and long-term plans adopted for the 2024/25 rating year, and Stats NZ / LGNZ figures on average rates increases: true if average residential rates rise materially above the prior year's average increase in 2024/25, false if increases are flat or below trend.

specificity.statement: That’s one of the first decisions they took: 7,000 more children living in poverty.
specificity.explanation: A named decision (changing how main benefits are indexed) attached to a precise, checkable quantity — 7,000 additional children in poverty. Someone can go and test the figure against the official advice.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Under the National-led Government and the visionary leadership of our Minister of Finance, the Hon Nicola Willis, we are embarking on a path towards a stronger economy—one that uplifts every individual in a community.
specificity.explanation: Intended to convey a substantive economic direction, but supplies no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named measure — 'a path towards a stronger economy' that 'uplifts every individual' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The most shameful decision that they have taken is to encourage more New Zealanders to smoke so that they can fund tax cuts.
rigor.explanation: Engages a real policy (the smokefree repeal and the tobacco excise take), but the inference is a strawman plus imputed motive: nothing offered connects the repeal to a deliberate aim of increasing smoking, and the fiscal link to tax cuts is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So why is it, then—why is it, then—that even the National Government, who has done considerable work with the establishment of institutions and initiatives that seek to uphold the mana motuhake of mana whenua and tangata whenua—why is this House wasting money inciting racism and ignorance; a narrative that is leaning into the worst of us instead of the best of us, and targeting Māori whānau—Māori whānau—with the ignorance?
civility.explanation: Very hard on the House's action and imputes a racist motive to it, but the target is an institution and a measure, not any individual member. No person is insulted, so it stays well above the failure band; the imputation of motive keeps it short of a clean 1.0.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Today, this House repealed the disastrous, power hungry, Wellington-centric three waters reforms.
civility.explanation: Three hostile adjectives, all aimed at a piece of legislation. No member is touched, so under the re-anchored scale this brutal criticism of a policy sits near the top.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We heard a lot last night from the Labour shadow Leader of the House, Kieran McAnulty, who threw around a bunch of funny numbers about Ashburton council’s water infrastructure needs.
civility.explanation: 'Threw around a bunch of funny numbers' about a named member imputes carelessness or bad faith rather than disputing the figures. Sneering short of a direct insult — a genuine failure on the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Yep, pipes and drains may not be sexy, and it’s hard for attention-seeking politicians to cut a ribbon on something buried six feet under the ground, but it’s the stuff that well-functioning, exceptional councils should deliver on.
civility.explanation: Imputes vanity as a motive, but to an unnamed class of politicians rather than any individual, and the sentence carries a real point about unglamorous infrastructure. Edging into the failure band without landing on a person.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So why is it, then—why is it, then—that even the National Government, who has done considerable work with the establishment of institutions and initiatives that seek to uphold the mana motuhake of mana whenua and tangata whenua—why is this House wasting money inciting racism and ignorance; a narrative that is leaning into the worst of us instead of the best of us, and targeting Māori whānau—Māori whānau—with the ignorance?
focus.explanation: Directed at a specific measure — the proposed Treaty principles bill, named in the immediately following sentence — rather than at a party's general character. It engages the bill's effect rather than its mechanism or cost, which holds it below 1.0.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The residents of Tauranga want answers about what happened: what checks were happening, what monitoring procedures were in place, and what allowed for this leak to go undetected for so long?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance — asks about the inspection and monitoring regime for a named asset failure. Ordinary accountability questioning with no party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: While previous Governments have put forward fantasy projects for Auckland and Wellington, it is essential that we do not forget the regions and that we do not leave essential cities like Tauranga to put up with avoidable road closures on top of the worst congestion in the country.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point about regional infrastructure prioritisation, but a good share of the sentence's weight is a sweeping characterisation of previous governments' projects as 'fantasy' with no project named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: After six long years of non-delivery, we are here to get the job done.
focus.explanation: A blanket characterisation of the previous government's whole record. No policy, measure, figure or missed target is named, so there is nothing here to check — this is party framing rather than scrutiny.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That is not even up for debate—this has been affirmed time and time again with various reviews, evaluations, Treaty settlements, and research.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the claim immediately preceding it — that the signatories did not cede sovereignty — has been repeatedly affirmed by official reviews, evaluations, settlements and research, to the point of being settled. Not a verdict: the narrow Tribunal finding and the broader 'not even up for debate' framing may resolve differently.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal's Te Paparahi o Te Raki (Wai 1040) stage 1 report and subsequent Tribunal reports and Treaty settlement deeds. True if the body of official reviews consistently finds that the rangatira who signed Te Tiriti did not cede sovereignty; false if that finding is absent, isolated, or contradicted across those official records.

veracity.statement: On Friday of last week, a 4-metre cavity was discovered on State Highway 29A in Tauranga.
veracity.explanation: A dated, located and dimensioned claim about a specific roading failure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA, Tauranga City Council and local news records for the week beginning 5 February 2024. True if a cavity of about 4 metres was discovered on State Highway 29A in Tauranga on Friday 9 February 2024; false if no such event occurred, or the location, date or dimensions differ materially.

veracity.statement: While previous Governments have put forward fantasy projects for Auckland and Wellington, it is essential that we do not forget the regions and that we do not leave essential cities like Tauranga to put up with avoidable road closures on top of the worst congestion in the country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Tauranga has the worst congestion of any city in New Zealand. Which measure applies matters: headline travel-time indices and per-capita delay measures can rank differently.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Congestion rankings for New Zealand urban areas covering 2023 — the TomTom Traffic Index and NZTA/Ministry of Transport travel-time-delay data. True if Tauranga ranks worst among New Zealand cities on the standard delay measure; false if Auckland or another centre ranks worse.

veracity.statement: Today, this House repealed the disastrous, power hungry, Wellington-centric three waters reforms.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the repeal of the three waters legislation completed its passage through the House on the day of the speech.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard and legislation.govt.nz records for 14 February 2024. True if the Water Services Acts Repeal Bill passed its third reading in the House that day; false if it did not.

rigor.statement: Both local and central government have responsibility for the assets involved, which demonstrates the importance of clear communication between councils and the New Zealand Transport Agency.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: split ownership of the assets is offered as the reason coordination matters, and the conclusion tracks the premise. It stops short of showing that a communication failure was what actually occurred here, so the step from 'shared responsibility' to 'this is why it happened' is left unmade.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As a result, South Canterbury has been consistently rated and recognised as having the best drinking water in the country.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc: 'as a result' attributes the water-quality standing to local council control on the strength of the two co-occurring, without ruling out source water, geology or scale. Taste-test recognition is also treated as equivalent to water quality generally.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Western Bay of Plenty is one of the fastest growing regions of New Zealand and is expected to be the home of more than 250,000 people by 2050.
specificity.explanation: Carries a named region, a population figure and a date — checkable content rather than a direction of travel. Short of 1.0 only because no mechanism or action attaches to it.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: The Western Bay of Plenty is one of the fastest growing regions of New Zealand and is expected to be the home of more than 250,000 people by 2050.
divination.explanation: Forecasts the sub-region's population passing a stated threshold by a stated year. The resolve-by date is far in the future, so this is pending, not wrong.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates for the Western Bay of Plenty sub-region (Tauranga City plus Western Bay of Plenty District). True if the usually resident population exceeds 250,000 at or before the 2050 estimate; false if it remains at or below 250,000.

veracity.statement: So of the 49 steps that they are going to take, 24 broadly use a negative word in them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a countable fact about the coalition's published 100-day plan: that 24 of its 49 items are phrased with a 'negative' operative verb (repeal, stop, abolish, cancel, cease).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National-led coalition's published 100-day plan (49 items, released December 2023); count the items whose operative verb is one of repeal/stop/abolish/cancel/withdraw/disestablish/remove/cease. True if that count is approximately 24, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: In fact, so intent are they on doing this, they have rushed a number of bills through this House, under urgency, without full discussion, and with committee stages that have not been given their full rein.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the incoming government passed multiple bills under urgency without a full select committee process in its first months.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard's urgency motions and the Parliament bills database for December 2023 – February 2024; true if several Government bills were passed through all stages under urgency with no select committee referral, false if bills followed the ordinary select committee process.

veracity.statement: It turned out that the price of petrol in Auckland is roughly the same as everywhere else in the country anyway.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that while the Auckland regional fuel tax was in force, Auckland pump prices were broadly comparable to the rest of New Zealand, i.e. the 11.5c/litre levy did not show up as an Auckland premium.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE weekly retail petrol price monitoring and regional price comparisons for 2023–24; true if the Auckland average 91 price sits within a few cents of the national average, false if Auckland sits materially above it (on the order of the 11.5c levy).

veracity.statement: And that’s why our Government has returned main benefit indexing to the Consumers Price Index, which has been the case for over 30 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that CPI indexation of main benefits was the settled arrangement for more than three decades before the recent change to wage indexation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The indexation provisions of the Social Security Act and its amendments, plus the 2019 Budget decision to index main benefits to average wage growth; true if CPI indexation applied continuously for 30+ years up to 2019, false if the period was materially shorter or interrupted.

specificity.statement: So of the 49 steps that they are going to take, 24 broadly use a negative word in them.
specificity.explanation: A precise, countable claim — a named document, a total (49) and a subtotal (24) that anyone can check against the plan.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And that’s why National and our coalition partners are working to bond nurses to New Zealand. If they work for five years, then we will be paying them $4,500 a year towards their student loans.
specificity.explanation: A named mechanism (student loan bonding), a dollar figure ($4,500 a year) and a duration (five years). Someone could check the scheme against this description or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: These pragmatic and innovative programmes and policies that we are implementing will help to improve our economic development and also will lift our overall incomes and help to get our economy and our country back on track.
specificity.explanation: A closing summary built from generic virtues — 'pragmatic', 'innovative', 'back on track' — with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named policy, even though concrete measures were available in her own preceding sentences.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Of the 49 steps that that Government has chosen to take, more than half of them are negative. More than half of them say “reduce”, “repeal”, “replace”, “stop”. This is an incredibly negative Government.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy programme, but a weak one on two counts: the premise contradicts her own count moments earlier (24 of 49 is not more than half), and the conclusion treats the grammatical polarity of a verb as a proxy for the character of a government — a non sequitur, since repealing a law can be a positive programme.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Income is perhaps the most impactful social determinant of health outcomes. And that’s why for me it’s vitally important that for the health of our country we have sustainable economic development, which will help lift incomes for everyone.
rigor.explanation: A genuine premise-to-conclusion chain (income drives health, so pursue growth), and the first step is well supported. The gap is in the second: 'lift incomes for everyone' is asserted rather than shown — aggregate growth distributing to all is exactly the step that needs an argument, and none is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They’ve got no ideas. In fact, their only idea seems to be: not Labour.
focus.explanation: Names no policy, measure, figure or outcome. Strip out the characterisation of the other party and nothing remains — this is the content-free tribalism Focus exists to catch. No individual is insulted, so Civility is untouched.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: That might seem innocuous, but the appalling consequence of it is that 7,000 children will move into poverty.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that switching main benefit indexation from wages to CPI will push approximately 7,000 additional children into poverty. Not a promise about her own action, and the outcome is a measured social statistic.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Treasury/MSD regulatory impact and child poverty modelling for the CPI-indexation change, read against Stats NZ child poverty statistics; true if the official estimate of additional children in poverty attributable to the change is of the order of 7,000 by 2027/28, false if materially lower or if no such increase is estimated.

civility.statement: Now, those child poverty reduction goals are tough, and it has been hard to meet them, but to take actions that push children into poverty is absolutely appalling.
civility.explanation: Condemnation as fierce as it gets — 'absolutely appalling' — but aimed entirely at a decision, not at a person. She even concedes the targets are hard to meet. Under the re-anchored scale this is the standard, not a deduction.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It feels at times like we’re in a Third World country when you look at some of the terrible statistics that have been rolling out under the past Government.
focus.explanation: Gestures at 'terrible statistics' but names no policy, measure or figure; the weight of the sentence is a general characterisation of the previous Government's era rather than any specific outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Alongside the two existing medical schools we have in New Zealand, we’ll now have a third medical school with a different entry pathway, a graduate entry pathway, so that people can come in with another undergraduate degree, work through a four-year programme instead of six at the other medical schools, and indeed come out the end as a GP.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the design of the measure itself — the entry pathway and programme length — with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We hear members on the other side talking about a million dollars of consultancy, but what about that last Government and the hundreds of millions chucked at light rail alone?
focus.explanation: Names a real policy and an order of magnitude (light rail spending), so it is not content-free, but the sentence's work is deflecting a criticism onto the other side's record rather than answering it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It hasn’t been easy, though, sitting on the sidelines at home, watching this House over those mere four weeks give an assault on vulnerable workers in Aotearoa in this country, an assault on Māori—indigenous people of Aotearoa—and an assault and broken promises to our Aucklanders and ratepayers of Tāmaki-makau-rau.
focus.explanation: Points at three areas of government activity but names no bill, measure or figure in any of them, so the sentence rests on a characterisation of what the Government is doing rather than on identifiable policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Alongside that, we see the impact of transport projects being cut by the Minister for Auckland and the Minister of Transport, the Hon Simeon Brown—the $1.7 billion hole that is left in transport infrastructure in Tāmaki-makau-rau, Auckland.
focus.explanation: Names the decision, the responsible portfolios, the affected area and a figure for the shortfall. This is scrutiny of a specific policy outcome, which is the job of an opposition member, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We are seeing the numbers of GPs declining, unfortunately, in this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the count of general practitioners in New Zealand is falling as at February 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RNZCGP Workforce Survey and Medical Council of New Zealand workforce data for the years to 2023: true if the number of practising GPs, or GPs per 100,000 population, fell over that period; false if it rose.

veracity.statement: When you look at our closest partner, Australia, and the number of medical schools they have per capita, on a similar comparison we should indeed be looking at a fifth medical school now, not a third.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Australia's medical schools per head of population, applied to New Zealand, would justify a fifth school rather than a third.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Count of accredited medical schools listed by Medical Deans Australia and New Zealand divided by Australia's population: true if that per-capita rate, applied to New Zealand's ~5.3 million people, implies four or more schools; false if it implies three or fewer.

veracity.statement: We hear members on the other side talking about a million dollars of consultancy, but what about that last Government and the hundreds of millions chucked at light rail alone?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government spent hundreds of millions of dollars on light rail alone.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Light Rail Ltd and Ministry of Transport reporting of total expenditure on the Auckland light rail project up to its cancellation in 2023: true if the total is in the hundreds of millions, false if it is materially below $100 million.

veracity.statement: There have even been instances of police cars having to transport patients to the hospital because there’s no ambulance available.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that police cars have been used to transport patients because of ambulance unavailability.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police, Hato Hone St John records or contemporaneous news reporting of police vehicles conveying patients to hospital because no ambulance was available: true if one or more such instances are documented before February 2024; false if no such case can be found.

veracity.statement: And anyone who knows anything about infrastructure and transport in this country actually knows the investment under the previous Government: $77 billion pipeline planned for the next five years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure — a $77 billion five-year infrastructure pipeline planned under the previous Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Infrastructure Commission (Te Waihanga) infrastructure pipeline reporting as at 2023: true if the reported forward five-year pipeline value is approximately $77 billion; false if materially different.

rigor.statement: When you look at our closest partner, Australia, and the number of medical schools they have per capita, on a similar comparison we should indeed be looking at a fifth medical school now, not a third.
rigor.explanation: A per-capita scaling argument: given Australia's ratio of medical schools to population, New Zealand's population implies four or five schools. The arithmetic step is sound; the gap is the unstated assumption that Australian provision is the right benchmark for New Zealand, so it is a reasonable inference leaning on an analogy rather than a fully supported one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And for a member like Mr O’Connor to be opposing support for health into the rural sector is an absolute disgrace.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the criticism actually made from the other side was about consultancy spending, which is recast as opposition to rural healthcare so that it can be condemned. The conclusion is drawn against a position the member did not take.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yes, I will use the word “outrageous”, because as I stood on that side of the House last time, people on this side of the House said it was outrageous, that it was an assault on democracy that we were pushing things through urgency in this House.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque: the members now using urgency once condemned it. That establishes inconsistency on their part, which is a fair point, but it does not itself show that the current use of urgency is wrong — the conclusion runs slightly ahead of what the premise supports.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Alongside the two existing medical schools we have in New Zealand, we’ll now have a third medical school with a different entry pathway, a graduate entry pathway, so that people can come in with another undergraduate degree, work through a four-year programme instead of six at the other medical schools, and indeed come out the end as a GP.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (graduate entry), the entry requirement (a prior undergraduate degree), the duration (four years against six) and the intended output (GPs). Someone could check or act on this; it stops short of 1.0 only for lacking numbers of places or a start date.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It hasn’t been easy, though, sitting on the sidelines at home, watching this House over those mere four weeks give an assault on vulnerable workers in Aotearoa in this country, an assault on Māori—indigenous people of Aotearoa—and an assault and broken promises to our Aucklanders and ratepayers of Tāmaki-makau-rau.
specificity.explanation: Three 'assaults' asserted with no legislation named, no provision cited and no numbers; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Alongside that, we see the impact of transport projects being cut by the Minister for Auckland and the Minister of Transport, the Hon Simeon Brown—the $1.7 billion hole that is left in transport infrastructure in Tāmaki-makau-rau, Auckland.
specificity.explanation: Carries a dollar figure, a named domain (transport infrastructure) and a named location; missing the breakdown of which projects and over what period.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Mr O’Connor is walking out of the room because he’s scared about that.
civility.explanation: Turns from the argument to a named individual, imputing a motive — fear — to his physical movement in the Chamber. Nothing about the substance is at stake; it is a personal jab.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Without three waters, without water infrastructure legislation, we can see that rise up to 25 percent that Aucklanders will be paying in their water rates in the coming years.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that, following repeal of the water services legislation, Auckland water rates will rise by up to 25 percent in the coming years.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council and Watercare published water charge decisions for the years following February 2024: true if an annual water price increase approaching 25 percent is adopted within that period; false if increases stay near the roughly 9 percent of the preceding year.

veracity.statement: It was a historic election, where you had a single-party Government for the first time under MMP, and it managed to lose half of its members—half of its members—in one fell swoop. It was swept from power.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable facts about the 2020 and 2023 general elections: that the 2020 result produced the first single-party majority government under MMP, and that that party lost about half of its MPs at the following election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission official results for the 2020 and 2023 general elections; true if Labour won an outright single-party majority in 2020 (the first under MMP, 1996 onward) and its caucus fell by roughly half in 2023, false if either leg is materially wrong.

veracity.statement: High inflation, high interest rates brought on—oh, we know now that it’s not really driven by international inflation rates. It’s driven by domestic rates. It’s driven by too much spending, and what did that give us? Not a lot, apart from a lot of debt and a lot of pain.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's recent inflation was driven by domestic rather than imported price pressure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI decomposition into tradables and non-tradables inflation, and RBNZ Monetary Policy Statement analysis, for 2022–2023; true if non-tradables (domestic) inflation was the dominant contributor over that period, false if tradables (imported) inflation was.

veracity.statement: The polling said that we were more divided than ever before.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that published opinion polling recorded social division at a record high in the period before the 2023 election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published New Zealand polling on social cohesion or perceived division (e.g. Ipsos NZ Issues Monitor, Kantar/Curia social cohesion questions) for 2022–2023; true if a poll recorded perceived division at the highest level in its series, false if no such published result exists or the series shows no record high.

veracity.statement: Today, we’ve removed the divisive three waters—divisive for many reasons.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Three Waters legislation was repealed on the day of the speech, 14 February 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand legislation and Hansard record; true if the Water Services Acts Repeal Bill completed its third reading and repealed the Three Waters legislation on 14 February 2024, false if it was repealed on another date or had not yet passed.

veracity.statement: What we know is that our construction industry actually has not been improving in productivity, and we have to be laser-focused on making sure that we are more efficient and more effective because we want to increase living standards.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that productivity in the New Zealand construction industry has not improved.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ industry productivity statistics for the construction industry (labour productivity and multifactor productivity series); true if the series is flat or declining over the past decade, false if it shows material sustained growth.

veracity.statement: Since our first activation of toitū te Tiriti on 5 December around the motu, even reaching overseas, to the karanga of our King, Kīngi Tūheitia Pōtatau Te Wherowhero VII, at Tūrangawaewae to a gathering of 12,000 people, to the protection and guidance of Rātana, from the karanga of our two ariki, to the 64,000 who walked the bridge at Waitangi, we have seen Māori and non-Māori walk alongside each other as a direct response to this Government.
veracity.explanation: Two attendance figures are asserted: 12,000 at the Tūrangawaewae hui called by Kīngi Tūheitia, and 64,000 walking the bridge at Waitangi.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Organiser, police and contemporaneous media attendance estimates for the Hui-ā-Motu at Tūrangawaewae on 20 January 2024 and for the Waitangi Day 2024 bridge walk; true if the reported estimates are around 12,000 and 64,000 respectively, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: I put a post up a few days ago on my Facebook page: “If you could sum up the Hui-aa-motu, Ratana & Waitangi in 3 words what would it be?” Over 330 comments, with not one negative thing to say about our direct response.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a specific Facebook post drew over 330 comments and that none of them criticised Te Pāti Māori's response.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The speaker's public Facebook post asking people to sum up the Hui-ā-Motu, Rātana and Waitangi in three words, posted in early February 2024; true if it carries more than 330 comments and none are critical of the response, false if the comment count is materially lower or negative comments are present.

veracity.statement: My generation will not stand for people yelling at us to get an education when our grandparents gave their blood, sweat, and tears to establish kaupapa Māori like Kura ā Iwi, Te Aho Matua, kura kaupapa, wharekura, kōhanga reo. Government didn’t do that; we did that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the kaupapa Māori education institutions named — kōhanga reo, kura kaupapa Māori, wharekura, Kura ā Iwi — were established by Māori communities rather than by the Crown.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The founding history of kōhanga reo (from 1982) and kura kaupapa Māori (from 1985) in Ministry of Education and Waitangi Tribunal records; true if these were initiated and set up by Māori communities and only later given state funding and statutory recognition, false if they were Crown-initiated programmes.

focus.statement: Now, I guess you could say that in the wake of that, the Leader of the Opposition said that they needed to take a good, hard look at themselves in the mirror and say, “What went wrong?” Well, they don’t seem to have started that process at the moment, so maybe we will help them out.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the opposition party's internal soul-searching. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — the content is what the other side is 'really like' after losing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: High inflation, high interest rates brought on—oh, we know now that it’s not really driven by international inflation rates. It’s driven by domestic rates. It’s driven by too much spending, and what did that give us? Not a lot, apart from a lot of debt and a lot of pain.
rigor.explanation: A causal chain — domestic inflation, therefore government spending, therefore debt and pain — asserted without a mechanism or any figure connecting the links. Post hoc: the spending and the inflation coincided, and that coincidence is treated as the cause. It is a real argument about a real policy question, just a weakly supported one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because we’ve got to get rid of those things before they confuse the people—it doesn’t matter who it is—who have got to implement something that the previous Government has put in place that we don’t want to carry on.
rigor.explanation: A genuine reason is offered for front-loading repeals: agencies should not spend effort implementing measures the government intends to scrap. The inference from 'we will not keep this' to 'repeal it early' holds. The gap is that nothing is offered to show the confusion or wasted effort is actually occurring — the premise is asserted.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I put a post up a few days ago on my Facebook page: “If you could sum up the Hui-aa-motu, Ratana & Waitangi in 3 words what would it be?” Over 330 comments, with not one negative thing to say about our direct response.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote from a self-selected sample. Comments on the speaker's own Facebook page come from her own followers, so the absence of criticism there tells you about the audience, not about how the response was received generally — which is the conclusion being drawn.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I have been hearing a lot of kōrero around “We are not getting rid of Te Tiriti.” My answer is that if you even dare touch, you even dare change or alter a single word or letter, you are getting rid of Te Tiriti.
rigor.explanation: An all-or-nothing inference: any alteration, down to a single letter, is equated with abolition. Nothing is offered to bridge the gap between amending a text and removing it, and the premise does the work of the conclusion by definition. It does engage the actual question before the House, so this is a weak argument about a real measure rather than a jibe.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There’s a big, big mirror to be looked at, and that’s why we’re engaging on a proper COVID inquiry; not a butt-covering exercise.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith — that the existing inquiry was designed to protect those responsible rather than to find out what happened. The sneer lands on the previous government's motives collectively rather than on any named individual, so it stops short of a personal attack, but it is no longer purely a criticism of the inquiry's design.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s very, very clear that we have an infrastructure deficit. What is not clear is that it is not just about how much money we spent but how well we spend it, how efficiently we spend it, and how effective we are about what we choose to do.
specificity.explanation: Asserts a deficit with no size attached, then a string of generic virtues — spending well, efficiently, effectively. No project, figure, timeframe or mechanism is named, so there is nothing here anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I could talk about the many different policies, bills, and laws of this coalition Government and what it is bringing to our country, from the axing of a smoke-free country to the removal of reo in spaces, to the repeal of the three waters bill, section 27 in justice, section 7AA in Oranga Tamariki.
specificity.explanation: Names five distinct measures, two of them by statutory section (s 27 sentencing reports, s 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act). Someone could go and check each one. It falls short of the top because no figure, timeframe or effect is attached to any of them — it is a list of targets rather than an account of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Look, it’s pretty simple: Te Tiriti is every single person’s landlord agreement in our country. It is what keeps us all safe. It is what not only keeps Māori safe but every single soul that walks on this whenua.
specificity.explanation: A metaphor followed by a general assurance. No article, guarantee, mechanism or effect of Te Tiriti is named, so there is nothing in it that could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Now, this Government is in the midst of passing legislation to limit the increases in benefit rates, and that’s going to compound the problems of people who are on benefits and who struggle to repay their bills.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the government was, as at February 2024, passing legislation to restrict the size of main benefit increases (the change from wage-based to CPI-based indexation).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand legislation record for the Social Security (Benefits Adjustment) / benefit indexation amendment before the House in early 2024; true if a bill limiting the annual adjustment of main benefit rates was in progress on 14 February 2024, false if no such measure was before Parliament.

veracity.statement: In fact, we know as a fact, through the work we’ve done in child poverty reduction, that there are many people who are on benefits who are in poverty.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as established fact that a substantial number of people receiving main benefits live in poverty.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ child poverty statistics / Household Economic Survey breakdowns by main source of household income; true if material hardship and low-income rates among benefit-receiving households are substantially elevated (a large share of such households below the poverty measures), false if benefit-receiving households show poverty rates comparable to the general population.

veracity.statement: Bankruptcy has its own stigma and, of course, the no-asset procedure can only be used once, and, of course, people actually want to repay their debts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific legal restriction: that a debtor may enter the no asset procedure only once.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The eligibility provisions for the no asset procedure in the Insolvency Act 2006 (Part 5, subpart 4) and the Insolvency and Trustee Service's published criteria; true if prior entry into a no asset procedure disqualifies a debtor from entering another, false if repeat entry is permitted.

veracity.statement: There are no particular prohibitions in the current law as to the amount of the attachment orders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the existing law places no cap on the amount that may be deducted under a District Court attachment order, leaving it to the judge's assessment of ability to pay.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The attachment order provisions of the District Court Act 2016 and the District Court Rules; true if the statute prescribes no maximum deduction (only an ability-to-pay assessment), false if a statutory maximum or percentage limit on attachment order deductions exists.

civility.statement: Now, this Government is in the midst of passing legislation to limit the increases in benefit rates, and that’s going to compound the problems of people who are on benefits and who struggle to repay their bills.
civility.explanation: Direct criticism of the Government's benefit legislation and its consequences, aimed entirely at the policy; no member is impugned and no bad faith is imputed.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, this Government is in the midst of passing legislation to limit the increases in benefit rates, and that’s going to compound the problems of people who are on benefits and who struggle to repay their bills.
focus.explanation: Names a specific government measure (limiting benefit rate increases) and the specific group it affects, rather than characterising the governing parties in general. Legitimate scrutiny of a named policy.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But the member who drafted this bill, Anahila Kanongata’a, has indicated that she thinks it’s appropriate that that amount be capped at 5 percent. So 5 percent of the net amount of the benefit can be deducted, but no more.
specificity.explanation: States the exact mechanism the bill uses — a hard cap of 5 percent of the net benefit on compulsory court deductions. A precise, checkable figure applied to a named base.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So they find themselves with only a few tens of dollars a week to feed themselves and their family, and we know what then happens: poor nutrition, and poor nutrition leads to poor health outcomes.
rigor.explanation: A real causal chain about the policy — residual income after deductions leads to poor nutrition, which leads to poor health. The first link is supported by the preceding account of compulsory outgoings, but the nutrition-to-health step is asserted as self-evident ('we know what then happens') with nothing offered to connect the magnitudes. A reasonable inference leaning on an appeal to common knowledge.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Having worked in that field, I know that once that kind of thing happens, penalty interest accrues, legal costs accrue, and the debt becomes many times larger sometimes than it originally was.
rigor.explanation: A claim about how judgment debts escalate, offered on the strength of the speaker's own professional experience alone — an appeal to personal authority and anecdote rather than to the statutory interest and cost provisions he could have cited.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It has been troubling to note that by 2015, the Commerce Commission noted that the numbers of orders per month increased approximately 400 percent after that change—from approximately 200, to over a thousand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a Commerce Commission observation in 2015 recorded monthly attachment orders rising from roughly 200 to over a thousand — an approximately 400 percent increase — following the 2014 change to the civil debt enforcement law.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Commerce Commission (or MSD/Ministry of Justice) reporting from 2015 on monthly District Court attachment order volumes; true if the monthly figure rose from ~200 to >1,000 after the 2014 amendment, false if the reported volumes or the attributed source differ materially.

veracity.statement: Also, the District Court already has the power to limit an attachment order on beneficiaries. Currently, that limit is at 40 percent of their income.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that existing law already lets the District Court cap attachment orders against beneficiaries, and that the current cap is 40 percent of income.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The District Court Act/Rules provisions on attachment orders and the protected earnings rate; true if the court may already limit orders and the maximum deduction is 40 percent of the debtor's income (i.e. 60 percent protected), false if the statutory rate or the discretion differs.

veracity.statement: Unlike other jurisdictions—for example, in parts of Australia, there are mechanisms to wipe attachment orders when it becomes basically impossible for people to pay them—we have very little recourse to wipe those attachment orders and to adequately limit them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a comparative fact: some Australian jurisdictions provide a statutory mechanism to extinguish attachment/garnishee orders where repayment is impossible, and New Zealand law provides little equivalent recourse.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Australian state civil enforcement legislation (e.g. NSW/Victorian garnishee and instalment-order provisions allowing an order to be set aside or debt written off for hardship) compared with the NZ District Court Act enforcement provisions; true if at least one Australian state provides a wipe/discharge mechanism absent in NZ, false if no such mechanism exists or NZ has an equivalent.

specificity.statement: It has been troubling to note that by 2015, the Commerce Commission noted that the numbers of orders per month increased approximately 400 percent after that change—from approximately 200, to over a thousand.

veracity.statement: So, I understand, when we’re looking through this bill and we’re looking at 86 percent of attachments are to beneficiaries—that in itself speaks loudly.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / Ministry of Social Development data on District Court attachment orders by debtor income source (the figure cited in the bill's explanatory material): true if approximately 86 percent of attachment orders are made against recipients of a main benefit, false if the share is materially different.

veracity.statement: So they buy the debt and they get attachment orders on it, and they take these debts along to WINZ—the attachment orders—in bulk lots and get them bulk processed through the WINZ systems.

veracity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So they buy the debt and they get attachment orders on it, and they take these debts along to WINZ—the attachment orders—in bulk lots and get them bulk processed through the WINZ systems.
specificity.explanation: Describes a concrete mechanism end to end — debt purchase, attachment order, bulk lodgement, automated processing through MSD systems — which is checkable and actionable. Stops short of the top: no firms named, no volumes, no dates.

rigor.statement: In other words, it would make sure that people lending money did so responsibly. So that’s one of the first reasons to support this bill. It is because of the industrialised process—at the moment, the industrialised process encourages poor lending behaviour.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: if attachment orders can no longer be obtained cheaply and automatically, lenders bear the recovery risk and must credit-check. civility.statement: I just want to address the issue that was raised by the member from New Zealand First, worrying about the victims of crime. Actually, he’s got a point.

civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I just want to address the issue that was raised by the member from New Zealand First, worrying about the victims of crime. Actually, he’s got a point.

veracity.statement: If you look at the District Court Act, it already provides for a protected earnings rate (PER) below which a person’s net earnings from all sources, including benefits, cannot fall after any deductions, including any civil debt attachment orders, and if you look at the District Court Act, it already provides for a protected earnings rate and the PER is set at 60 percent, meaning that no more than 40 percent of a person’s net earnings can be deducted.

veracity.statement: We believe also that the fifth Labour Government introduced the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act, or the CCCFA legislation, in 2003 during the Clark years, and then it was heavily amended in the Jacinda Ardern years and, of course, it’s unworkable for a lot of people having to present their Netflix accounts to their bank manager at the ANZ.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand legislation record for the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act — its year of enactment and the government in office at the time, plus the dates of its major amendments; true if enacted in 2003 under the fifth Labour Government and materially amended between 2017 and 2023, false if either date or government is wrong.

veracity.statement: This is a bill about beneficiaries—a 25-year-old on a single person’s jobseeker benefit is given $337 a week net.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Social Development published main benefit rates in force in February 2024 for Jobseeker Support, single, 25 years or over, net of tax; true if the weekly net figure is $337 (± rounding), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: We heard today that that Government’s actions will see 7,000 more children in poverty, and here’s a tiny thing they could have got on board with—not even asking them to pass it today, just to send it to select committee.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an estimate presented that day puts the effect of the Government's actions (the change to benefit indexation) at 7,000 additional children in poverty.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Official child poverty impact analysis of the 2023-24 change from wage to CPI indexation of main benefits (Treasury/MSD regulatory impact or Budget child poverty analysis); true if a published official estimate puts the increase at approximately 7,000 children, false if no such estimate exists or the figure is materially different.

specificity.statement: If you look at the District Court Act, it already provides for a protected earnings rate (PER) below which a person’s net earnings from all sources, including benefits, cannot fall after any deductions, including any civil debt attachment orders, and if you look at the District Court Act, it already provides for a protected earnings rate and the PER is set at 60 percent, meaning that no more than 40 percent of a person’s net earnings can be deducted.
specificity.explanation: Names the governing Act, the mechanism (protected earnings rate applying to all net income after deductions) and the exact percentages, so the claim can be checked against the statute.
