rigor.statement: In that book, one thing he does talk about is that in societies, countries, jurisdictions that have tried to liberalise drugs, there’s one drug where all the rules they apply really go out the window—and that’s methamphetamine or P.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that methamphetamine is the standing exception to liberalisation rests entirely on a single popular-science book by a journalist — an appeal to authority, with no study, jurisdiction or outcome data offered to support the generalisation.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And that was where we had a bit of a policy failure by both parties, actually, because we were still looking at a problem we had with heroin that hadn’t been a problem for about 10 years.
rigor.explanation: A conclusion (a bipartisan policy failure) offered with a stated mechanism (drug policy still aimed at a heroin market that had ceased to exist while the meth market grew). The inference tracks the reason given; the gap is that no evidence is offered that the mis-targeting caused the outcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You cannot compare the need for vaccine access passed under urgency to something which is a treatment for a mild symptom.
rigor.explanation: A proportionality argument with the relevant difference stated: urgency was justified for COVID because of imminent mass mortality, and the harm averted here is far smaller. The inference holds, though it weighs only the benefit side and sets aside the diversion risk she raises elsewhere.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We could very well get back to the situation again where people who can’t afford P—and despite the fact we are awash with the stuff, it is actually relatively expensive still, and if it becomes a cheap option to go and get hold of your pseudoephedrine to make this product again locally, we will actually have the cycle starting again.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that restoring over-the-counter pseudoephedrine will revive domestic methamphetamine manufacture from pharmacy-sourced precursor — the 'cycle' of pill-shopping and local cooking seen in the 2000s.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NZ Police / ESR clandestine laboratory detection statistics and pharmacy pseudoephedrine diversion reporting for the period after pseudoephedrine returns to pharmacy sale; true if clandestine lab detections or seizures of pharmacy-sourced pseudoephedrine rise materially above the 2023 baseline, false if clan-lab detections remain flat or fall and the meth supply stays import-dominated.

specificity.statement: Of course, this is about choice for New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Offered as the rationale for the bill but carries no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named provision — a value slogan that could be attached to almost any measure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Four weeks only leaves people who are expert in this, who work in communities, who work in pharmacy—it only leaves them a week or two to put in their submission, if that.
specificity.explanation: Names the actual reporting period (four weeks), converts it into the working time left to submitters (a week or two) and identifies who is affected. Checkable against the committee's timetable, though no dates are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As I outlined intentionally in my first reading speech with regard to the mechanism that requires us to have an amendment bill here and not just an Order in Council, as is the case for an introduction of a new classification, there is the opportunity for the Minister to bring in a bill that, for example, amended that inconsistency, which would require that an Order in Council is all that would be required for that down-classification or that declassification.
specificity.explanation: Names the actual legislative mechanism at issue and the concrete remedy — amend the primary Act so declassification can proceed by Order in Council rather than by an amendment bill. Actionable, though no clause or timeframe is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Look, I hear the Minister’s desire, being really, really keen to limit the application of logic and evidence and consistency when it comes to this bill or to the Misuse of Drugs Act or drug policy as a whole.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic framing that imputes to the Minister a deliberate wish to keep logic and evidence out of drug policy — bad faith attributed to the person rather than a criticism of the policy. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil under the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We do require that there is a longer period of time for the select committee to receive this and ensure that the public, particularly Māori communities, get the valuable time that they need to be able to prepare the information and to prepare the stats—also, the medical fraternity, those pharmacists who are concerned with this, as we’ve seen and we’ve all been lobbied for.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — the length of the select committee period and who needs time to submit. Names the affected groups and the process at issue; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Labour Party is willing to support the bill to select committee; we just want the select committee to be long enough to ensure that this House gets the opportunity to hear the views, pro and against, so that we can make an informed decision at the second reading.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure and the process — the referral, the length of the committee stage, and the second reading. No characterisation of the other side.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I will give the Minister credit: at least he is giving us the opportunity to have a debate at select committee; that is not what we have seen, often, from this Government so far.
focus.explanation: A real process point (this bill does get a committee stage) wrapped in a general characterisation of the Government's conduct 'so far' — no named policy or instance is given for that second half.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: A proposed minor amendment to the Legal Services Act 2011 will exempt section 27 reports from the range of legal aid disbursements that can be made, without in any way limiting the independence of the commissioner with regard to the wider legal aid scheme.
focus.explanation: Purely about the mechanism of the measure before the House — which Act is amended, what is exempted, and what is deliberately left untouched. No reference to opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We do require that there is a longer period of time for the select committee to receive this and ensure that the public, particularly Māori communities, get the valuable time that they need to be able to prepare the information and to prepare the stats—also, the medical fraternity, those pharmacists who are concerned with this, as we’ve seen and we’ve all been lobbied for.
specificity.explanation: A clear direction (extend the period) but no duration, no proposed date and no figure. She calls one month 'way too short' without saying what would be long enough.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’ve tabled an amendment to the motion, to delay the report back to the House by one month, to 14 April.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument (an amendment to the motion), the change (one month) and the exact date (14 April). Fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Between 2018 and 2023, ram raids went up by 290 percent; robberies, 62 percent; victims of reported retail crime, 110 percent; family harm investigations, 34 percent; and acts intended to cause harm, 40 percent.
specificity.explanation: Five named crime categories, each with a percentage change and a stated window. Anyone could go and check every one of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A proposed minor amendment to the Legal Services Act 2011 will exempt section 27 reports from the range of legal aid disbursements that can be made, without in any way limiting the independence of the commissioner with regard to the wider legal aid scheme.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act, the provision, the exact legal effect (removing section 27 reports from claimable disbursements) and the limit of that effect. Missing only the commencement detail, which he supplies separately.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Again, I reiterate, I understand the concerns about keeping people well during the cold season, winter season, but there is no imminent solution to address the outstanding problem that we have in our communities with meth.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference against the urgency case: if no near-term solution exists, the winter deadline buys little. But the conclusion (so a longer period costs nothing) is left implicit and the premise is asserted rather than supported — a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: He himself has conceded that the official advice says that it probably actually won’t be in place till next year anyway. So what is the point in rushing too much?
rigor.explanation: A sound inference about the measure itself: if the Minister's own advice says the change will not bite until next year, the case for compressing the committee stage weakens. Premise and conclusion connect without a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Under the previous Government’s approach, where the only clearly articulated target in the justice sector was a 30 percent reduction in the prison population—irrespective of what is happening in our communities and on our streets—we saw an alarming increase in violent crime.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc: a stated prison-population target is placed alongside a rise in violent crime with nothing offered to connect them — no mechanism, no counterfactual, and no account of other drivers. The 'irrespective of what is happening' aside asserts the causal link rather than supporting it.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s popular. He’ll be the king of the chemist. Great. Good on him.
civility.explanation: Sarcasm and mockery aimed at the Minister personally — the 'king of the chemist' line imputes that he is motivated by popularity rather than the merits. Short of a direct insult, but it has left the substance and landed on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Under the previous Government’s approach, where the only clearly articulated target in the justice sector was a 30 percent reduction in the prison population—irrespective of what is happening in our communities and on our streets—we saw an alarming increase in violent crime.
civility.explanation: Hard criticism of a previous government's policy target and its results. No individual is attacked and no bad faith is imputed to a person — under the re-anchored scale this is the standard, not a deduction.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: He himself has conceded that the official advice says that it probably actually won’t be in place till next year anyway. So what is the point in rushing too much?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the responsible Minister has publicly acknowledged official advice that the pseudoephedrine change would not be operative until 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard, ministerial statements or contemporaneous media reporting from early 2024 on the Misuse of Drugs (Pseudoephedrine) Amendment Bill; true if the Minister publicly conceded advice that pseudoephedrine products would probably not be available until 2025, false if no such concession about the advice can be located.

veracity.statement: We’ve already had the vote at the first reading, and only one political party voted against it—as is their right.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that at the first reading of the Misuse of Drugs (Pseudoephedrine) Amendment Bill exactly one party cast its vote against.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The party-vote record in Hansard for the first reading of the Misuse of Drugs (Pseudoephedrine) Amendment Bill; true if exactly one party is recorded voting Noes, false if none or more than one did.

veracity.statement: It’s still, roughly, four months shorter than what a normal select committee length of time would be anyway.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a 14 April 2024 report-back is about four months earlier than the standard select committee report-back period would give.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Standing Orders of the House of Representatives on the default select committee report-back period (six months from referral); true if six months from the 20 February 2024 referral is approximately four months later than 14 April 2024, false if the default period makes the gap materially different.

veracity.statement: Between 2018 and 2023, ram raids went up by 290 percent; robberies, 62 percent; victims of reported retail crime, 110 percent; family harm investigations, 34 percent; and acts intended to cause harm, 40 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts five specific percentage increases in named offence and investigation categories over 2018–2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police recorded-crime and victimisation statistics and family harm investigation counts for calendar/financial years 2018 and 2023; true if each of the five stated percentage increases matches the published series within rounding, false if any is materially off or rests on a baseline other than 2018.

veracity.statement: The cost of all this to the taxpayer has grown from $40,000 in 2017 to approximately $7.5 million in the past financial year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that legal aid expenditure on section 27 cultural reports rose from about $40,000 in 2017 to roughly $7.5 million in the 2022/23 financial year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice legal aid disbursement figures for section 27 reports by financial year; true if the 2017 figure is about $40,000 and the most recent financial year about $7.5 million, false if either differs materially.

rigor.statement: These drivers of crime, if they go unaddressed, the likelihood of further reoffending is high. If a judge doesn’t know what factors contributed to an offender’s behaviour, they cannot address those factors at sentencing.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the mechanism: reports supply the drivers, judges need the drivers to address them at sentencing, so removing the reports removes that ability. The conclusion tracks the premises; the small gap is that it assumes judges have no other route to that information.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As if the justice system didn’t already have that bias, this legislation actually still allows those with the means and the networks and the resources to still be able to pull on more information for judges in the courts, thereby entrenching already unjust inequities, that you can have a better chance at justice if you have got the means.
rigor.explanation: A valid structure given its premises: if the ability to put material before a judge survives only for those who can pay for it, then access to that advantage tracks means. The gap is that it does not address the counter-claim that unpaid routes (whānau, employer testimony) remain open.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I rise somewhat astounded at the lack of faith in our judiciary and the way in which they have been discredited in their ability to understand the differential between an impassioned personal plea under a section 27 report from someone who actually has an association to the offender—whether it is whānau, iwi, hapū, friend, employer—and a pre-commissioned, rote report by someone who has absolutely no connection to the offender.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the opposing argument was that removing funding removes information from the court, not that judges cannot tell a genuine report from a rote one. The conclusion is drawn against a position nobody advanced, and it also assumes without support that judges weighting reports correctly makes the loss of them harmless.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I also stand in support of the victims, who I’m somewhat confused as to how they are adversely affected by this in a process that is part of the judiciary system—it’s part of the justice system.
rigor.explanation: Argument from personal incredulity and absence of evidence: the speaker's inability to see a mechanism of harm to victims is offered in place of a reason there is none, and the specific mechanism put by the other side (higher reoffending producing more victims) is left unanswered.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We know through written parliamentary questions that the Minister of Justice has not asked for or received any analysis of the impact of section 27 reports on reoffending, and so he has no understanding of the impacts of taking these away on the victims of crime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister of Justice, on the record of written parliamentary questions, has neither requested nor received any analysis of what section 27 reports do to reoffending rates.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The written parliamentary question responses from the Minister of Justice, on the Parliament WPQ register for late 2023/early 2024, asking what analysis he has sought or received on the effect of section 27 reports on reoffending. True if the answers record no such analysis sought or received; false if any commissioned or received analysis is disclosed.

veracity.statement: Māori are more likely to be apprehended, convicted, sentenced more harshly for doing the same thing—the same thing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a like-for-like disparity: for the same offending, Māori are apprehended, convicted and sentenced more harshly than others.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice and Department of Corrections research on ethnic disparity across the criminal justice pipeline (e.g. the Justice Sector Ethnic Disparity work and NZ Police apprehension data), where offence type and prior history are controlled for. True if Māori face materially higher rates of apprehension, conviction and sentence severity for comparable offending; false if the disparities disappear once offence and history are controlled.

veracity.statement: Now, we’re not seeking to remove section 27 from the Act, and the Minister made that very clear. That option will still be available to all offenders, and they can call people to speak on their behalf in court and actually have personal testimonies of things that may affect their sentencing and actually explain, potentially, their offending.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Bill removes only taxpayer funding, not the statutory right under section 27 for an offender to have people speak to their background at sentencing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Legal Services Amendment Bill (2024) against section 27 of the Sentencing Act 2002. True if the Bill amends only legal aid funding and leaves section 27's right to call persons to speak on the offender's cultural, whānau and community background intact; false if it repeals or narrows section 27 itself.

veracity.statement: Again, as was outlined by the Minister, under the last Labour Government, $25 million has been spent on these reports.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a cumulative legal aid spend of about $25 million on section 27 reports during the previous Labour Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / Legal Services Agency expenditure figures for legal aid grants for section 27 reports over the 2017–2023 parliamentary terms. True if cumulative spend is approximately $25 million; false if materially lower or if the figure covers a different period or category.

veracity.statement: But if you go and google cultural reports or section 27 reports, half a dozen websites will appear where you can just log on and ask for a report to be written.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a commercial market of report-writing websites is publicly findable and takes commissions on request.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: A web search for 'cultural reports' and 'section 27 reports' restricted to New Zealand providers, around February 2024. True if roughly six or more commercial sites offer to write such reports on request; false if only a handful of non-commercial or provider-vetted services appear.

focus.statement: We know through written parliamentary questions that the Minister of Justice has not asked for or received any analysis of the impact of section 27 reports on reoffending, and so he has no understanding of the impacts of taking these away on the victims of crime.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named decision-maker against a named policy instrument, sourced to a specific parliamentary record. This is an opposition MP holding a Minister to account on the measure before the House, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is just another example of a Government that is hooked on slogans, not solutions, and they have no interest in fixing the challenges that New Zealand now confronts.
focus.explanation: Characterises the Government's motives in general terms. Strip out the claim about what the other side is 'really like' and no policy, figure or measure is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: ACT and National are not interested in understanding the drivers of crime.
focus.explanation: Entirely a claim about two other parties' dispositions. No policy content survives once the party framing is removed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are so many avenues of—well, no surprise that this is the approach that this Government is taking to some serious issues that need grown up, enduring solutions and responses, not the dog-whistling approach; the dog-whistling to ill-informed emotion.
focus.explanation: Frames the Government's motive as dog-whistling. It gestures at the subject matter but names no clause, cost or outcome; the weight is on what the other side is like.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Were those members listening? Were they listening at all to that incredible research?
focus.explanation: About whether MPs opposite were paying attention at an event, not about the measure. No policy, figure or outcome is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What we are stopping is the taxpayer funding an industry which has sprung up as an unintended consequence of paying for these reports by the taxpayer.
focus.explanation: States precisely what the measure before the House does and the effect it is aimed at. Entirely on the policy, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: This bill, sadly, will mean there are more victims of crime, because the drivers of crime are not addressed and offenders reoffend.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that ending funded section 27 reports will raise reoffending and therefore the number of victims of crime.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice reoffending statistics (12-month reconviction and reimprisonment rates) for cohorts sentenced after the Legal Services Amendment Act's commencement, compared with the immediately preceding cohorts. True if reoffending rises materially above the pre-commencement trend; false if it is flat or falls.

specificity.statement: There are issues or problems with how these reports are doing, and let’s look into that. Let’s have a crack at fixing them.
specificity.explanation: Concedes a problem and proposes action, but names no problem, no mechanism, no alternative and no timeframe. Nobody could act on or check 'let's have a crack at fixing them'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Again, as was outlined by the Minister, under the last Labour Government, $25 million has been spent on these reports.
specificity.explanation: A named figure attached to a named category of spending over a defined period. Someone could go to the expenditure record and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Wāhine Māori make up 64 percent of the female prison population, and tāne make up 50 percent.
specificity.explanation: Two precise, named proportions attached to identifiable populations; anyone could check them against Corrections statistics.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It does not cancel section 27 reports; it removes the legal aid disbursement requirement.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact legal mechanism the bill operates on and distinguishes it from what it does not do; checkable directly against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Wāhine Māori make up 64 percent of the female prison population, and tāne make up 50 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori women are 64% of the women's prison muster and Māori men 50% of the men's.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections prison population statistics by ethnicity and gender for the quarter nearest February 2024; true if the wāhine Māori share is ~64% and the tāne Māori share ~50% within rounding, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: We know for a fact that when it comes to criminal justice systems, the case is that Māori are some of the worst over-incarcerated people on the planet.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori incarceration is among the highest in the world for any identifiable population group.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Māori imprisonment rate per 100,000 (Corrections/Stats NZ) compared with national and indigenous-population imprisonment rates internationally (e.g. World Prison Brief, Australian Bureau of Statistics for Aboriginal imprisonment); true if the Māori rate sits in the top handful of comparable populations, false if it is middling or lower.

veracity.statement: As part of their 100-day plan, this Government has pledged to end section 27 reports, which they’ve dubbed “cultural reports”—and I made comments to that earlier—but whatever language we’re using, words matter.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the coalition Government's published 100-day plan contained a commitment to end section 27 reports, as distinct from ending funding for them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the National-led coalition's published 100-day plan and the Legal Services Amendment Bill; true if the plan commits to ending the reports themselves, false if it commits only to stopping taxpayer/legal aid funding for them while the reports remain available.

veracity.statement: It does not cancel section 27 reports; it removes the legal aid disbursement requirement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill leaves section 27 of the Sentencing Act intact and alters only the legal aid disbursement for such reports.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Legal Services Amendment Bill as introduced and section 27 of the Sentencing Act 2002; true if the bill amends only the Legal Services Act's disbursement provisions and leaves section 27 unrepealed, false if it repeals or restricts section 27 itself.

veracity.statement: Members opposite speak a lot about Maōri overrepresentation in incarceration rates; not a single one has talked about Maōri overrepresentation as victims of crime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no opposition member in this debate has raised Māori over-representation among victims of crime.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of this first reading debate; true if no opposition speaker mentions Māori over-representation as victims, false if any does.

veracity.statement: Now, today we have heard them saying that we are saying on this side that we are getting rid of section 27 reports. I’ve listened to the debate. Not a single person said that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no Opposition speaker in this debate claimed the Government is getting rid of, ending or abolishing section 27 reports.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of this first reading debate; true if no Opposition speaker characterises the bill as ending or removing section 27 reports, false if any does (including formulations such as 'pledged to end section 27 reports').

veracity.statement: Then Te Hunga Rōia Māori O Aotearoa also put out a press statement saying they “strongly oppose the Government’s plans to withdraw funding for section 27 reports”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Māori Law Society issued a public statement in those terms opposing the withdrawal of funding.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements or media releases from Te Hunga Rōia Māori o Aotearoa dated between December 2023 and February 2024; true if one states strong opposition to withdrawing funding for section 27 reports, false if no such statement exists or its position differs.

veracity.statement: And so, without doing any analysis, without doing any consultation with anybody who knows anything about this, this Government has just decided to introduce this bill tonight.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no analysis and no consultation of any kind preceded the bill's introduction.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The departmental disclosure statement and regulatory impact material for the Legal Services Amendment Bill; true if it records no consultation and no analysis, false if it records consultation with any agency or body (for example Te Puni Kōkiri) or any policy analysis, however limited by time.

focus.statement: You cannot call tough on crime when you are insistent on being soft to poverty and blind to poverty and ignorant on critical analysis—critical cultural analysis—and out of touch with reality and, worst of all, indifferent to Māori, indifferent to whānau, indifferent to hapū, indifferent to the reality.
focus.explanation: A characterisation of what the Government is like — blind, ignorant, out of touch, indifferent — with no policy, measure, figure or outcome named. Strip out the description of the other side and nothing about section 27 reports remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Members opposite speak a lot about Maōri overrepresentation in incarceration rates; not a single one has talked about Maōri overrepresentation as victims of crime.
focus.explanation: Raises a real policy consideration — Māori as victims — but frames it as an accounting of what the other side has and has not said rather than engaging the funding change itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But, no. This Government doesn’t want to take any advice on this. They don’t want to do any analysis on this. They just want to punch down on those who use the section 27 reports.
focus.explanation: There is a real, named policy point underneath — the absence of analysis and consultation on this bill, which she had just read from the disclosure statement — but it is delivered as a claim about what the Government wants and what it is really like.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Unilaterally, removing funding means a greater risk of unfair and ineffective sentences, a higher rate of sentence appeals, and will create a situation where those who can afford to privately pay for these reports will be more advantaged—and we Māori will be disadvantaged yet again.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House with a stated mechanism: if the reports are no longer funded, only those able to pay privately will obtain them, so access varies with means. The step from there to 'a higher rate of sentence appeals' is asserted rather than supported, which is the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Members also appear not to be able to read the bill correctly because nothing in the section 27 of the Sentencing Act actually requires paid reports.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the statute, but a non sequitur: that section 27 does not *require* a paid report does not establish that removing funding leaves access unaffected, which is the objection being answered.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Unilaterally, removing funding means a greater risk of unfair and ineffective sentences, a higher rate of sentence appeals, and will create a situation where those who can afford to privately pay for these reports will be more advantaged—and we Māori will be disadvantaged yet again.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that removing legal aid funding will produce a measurable rise in sentence appeals and a widening access gap by ability to pay.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice sentencing and appeal statistics for the two years following the Act's commencement; true if the rate of sentence appeals rises measurably above the pre-change trend, false if it is flat or falls.

civility.statement: I didn’t intend to do that; I just can’t read clearly it seems tonight—much like many of the members who also can’t read the text of this bill, because it’s quite clear what the bill does.
civility.explanation: Turns an apology into a jibe at other members' comprehension. The target is their ability to read rather than their argument — condescension edging into a personal slight.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, we’ve got this intense cottage industry filled up with consultants and people feathering their nests, when actually all the intention of this section was was to allow accused the opportunity to bring their family, their background, their community, their whānau before the courts to give context and insight into their upbringing.
civility.explanation: 'Feathering their nests' imputes self-enrichment as the motive of the people who write these reports. Short of a direct insult, but it attributes bad faith to persons rather than contesting the work they do.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m getting plenty of commentary from the other side, and I’m sure members of the public will be able to assess that.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the conduct of the members opposite; no policy, mechanism, figure or outcome is named. This is the content-free party framing Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We said we were going to stop the funding for these cultural reports, we said we were going to end the cottage industry, and here we are, a couple of months after being in Government, and we’re doing it.
focus.explanation: Names the specific measure (ending funding for section 27 cultural reports) and ties it to a named commitment, though the framing is about delivery rather than the mechanism itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So if you want one of these reports professionally written and delivered in front of a judge, you have to pay for it. That absolutely rules out a large proportion of New Zealand society who cannot afford to pay.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: what removing legal-aid funding does mechanically and who it affects.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Once again, as with benefit cuts and as with increasing smoking, this is a Government that is focused on punching down, on finding those who are most vulnerable in our community and making sure that their lives are even worse than they are already.
focus.explanation: Two policies are gestured at, but the weight of the statement is a characterisation of what the Government is "really like" rather than engagement with any of them. No individual is attacked, so Civility is untouched; this is the party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because that would be better, and that wouldn’t have the impact of increasing reoffending, increasing the number of victims, and creating a two-tier justice system.
focus.explanation: Engages a named alternative option set out in the Bill's own regulatory impact statement — the accreditation scheme — and argues about its effects. This is engagement with the measure itself.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We said we were going to stop the funding for these cultural reports, we said we were going to end the cottage industry, and here we are, a couple of months after being in Government, and we’re doing it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the parties now in government campaigned on stopping taxpayer funding for section 27 cultural reports, and that this bill does that.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 law-and-order campaign material, the National–NZ First and National–ACT coalition agreements, and the Government's 100-day plan; true if ending taxpayer funding for section 27 reports appears as a stated commitment, false if no such commitment is recorded.

veracity.statement: So I think the first thing to clear up is that, for the record, at no point in time did any party on the Opposition benches at any stage ever say that this was going to be taken away.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no Opposition party ever claimed section 27 reports themselves (as opposed to their public funding) were being abolished.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard and press releases from Labour, Green and Te Pāti Māori MPs between December 2023 and 20 February 2024; false if any such statement claims the reports are being removed or abolished rather than defunded, true if all confine the claim to defunding.

veracity.statement: In the entire regulatory impact statement, we get three and a half lines about the impact on victims.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the regulatory impact statement devotes roughly three and a half lines to the effect on victims.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Justice regulatory impact statement for the Sentencing (Section 27 Reports) Amendment Bill; true if the victims entry in the stakeholder analysis runs to about three or four lines, false if victims are discussed substantially more extensively.

veracity.statement: So if, in this House, a member is going to stand and lecture on what’s right for victims, you might want to read your own regulatory impact statement, which clearly states that not one single victim has been involved or consulted on the impact of taking away legal funding for section 27 reports.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the regulatory impact statement records no consultation with any victim on the effect of removing funding for section 27 reports.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The consultation and stakeholder sections of the Ministry of Justice regulatory impact statement for the Bill; true if it records no victim consultation (e.g. states no information on victims' views), false if it documents consultation with victims or victim advocacy groups.

specificity.statement: That, I hope, will give New Zealanders and the people of this country confidence that this is a Government that will do what it says it’s going to do, and one of the critical things that this Government is going to achieve for this country is we’re going to restore law and order.
specificity.explanation: "Restore law and order" carries no figure, mechanism, target or timeframe — a slogan offered where a measurable objective was available.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the entire regulatory impact statement, we get three and a half lines about the impact on victims.
specificity.explanation: A named document and a countable quantity — someone can open the RIS and check it. Precision is high regardless of whether the count is right.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So if you want one of these reports professionally written and delivered in front of a judge, you have to pay for it. That absolutely rules out a large proportion of New Zealand society who cannot afford to pay.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the premise — if the report must be privately paid for, those who cannot pay are excluded. The gap is that "a large proportion" is asserted rather than shown, and legal aid coverage is not addressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The sad part about that is the savings that are made for that punching down go in the pockets of those middle-income New Zealanders who are going to receive a tax cut at the Budget.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a direct funding link between this bill's savings and the Budget tax cut. Nothing is offered to connect the two appropriations, and the inference treats fungible Crown revenue as an earmarked transfer — a non sequitur.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because that would be better, and that wouldn’t have the impact of increasing reoffending, increasing the number of victims, and creating a two-tier justice system.
rigor.explanation: The comparison is a genuine inference about a real option, but the three claimed harms of the chosen option are asserted rather than derived; the conclusion that the alternative is better rests on premises not established here.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So if, in this House, a member is going to stand and lecture on what’s right for victims, you might want to read your own regulatory impact statement, which clearly states that not one single victim has been involved or consulted on the impact of taking away legal funding for section 27 reports.
civility.explanation: The substance is real, but "you might want to read your own regulatory impact statement" is directed at a member and carries a note of condescension — pointed, and just past the line into the personal.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Guess what! One and a half million New Zealanders said, “Go to work on our law and order policies.” As a result, we have 68 MPs on this side of the House, and they have 55. So this is not something that some are trying to give the TV audience that this was landed on the Order Paper tonight. This was well consulted on and well supported.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to electoral mandate/popularity: the conclusion is that this specific bill was 'well consulted on', but the only support offered is the party-vote result of the general election. Winning a majority on a broad 'law and order' platform does not establish that this measure was consulted on, so the conclusion outruns the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What happened was a cottage industry was created, worth far more than this, that imposed these kinds of regulations on house owners, and those who were looking to rent or those who were renting, and were prejudiced through that particular process. If that side of the House wants to talk about cottage industries, they need only look in the mirror at what they’ve done to support cottage industries around this country.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque. Even granting that meth testing created a larger and more harmful cottage industry, that does not bear on whether section 27 report funding is itself justified. The premise is about a different policy of the other side and cannot support the conclusion about this one. Scored here rather than under Focus because it does engage a real, named policy and reasons from it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s, from my experience, not a common practice, not something that I’ve ever seen in my decade in the House—especially on the RIS, where the analysis is required in order to inform the House, inform the debate. So the question must be asked: what is that side of the House hiding?
rigor.explanation: The premise is an appeal to the speaker's own experience ('not something that I've ever seen'), and the conclusion — that something is being hidden — is an insinuation rather than an inference: a redaction is consistent with legal privilege or commercial sensitivity, and no ground is offered for preferring concealment. The observation about the RIS is real, which keeps this above the floor.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I guarantee that every member in the House has a whānau member like that. That’s why, on this side of the House, we are opposing the actions of this Government, and we will continue to oppose this as this bill proceeds through the House.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote, universalised without support ('I guarantee that every member'). Shared personal acquaintance with someone who went through the justice system is offered as the whole warrant for the conclusion that this funding should be retained; nothing connects the anecdote to whether the reports change sentencing outcomes.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would like to issue an apology to all the victims of rape, an apology to all the victims of violence, an apology to all the victims of aggravated robbery, for the $7.7 million of taxpayers’ money that was spent on those reports, trying to lessen the sentences of the perpetrators of those crimes against them.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to emotion built on a false dichotomy: the rhetorical apology treats money spent on sentencing background reports as a wrong done to victims, which only follows if funding the reports and serving victims are mutually exclusive. No link is offered between the reports and any harm to victims; the conclusion rests entirely on the emotive framing.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I have no doubt that if the people on this side of the House weren’t raising this issue through last year and the year before and pointing out the massive increase in spending, it would have continued on a trajectory towards $10 million and further, and that is money that could be spent, we think, more wisely in the legal aid system.
rigor.explanation: A counterfactual asserted by confident extrapolation: past growth is treated as guaranteeing continued growth to $10 million, and the speaker's own side is credited with having halted it, with no evidence offered for either link. The underlying spending trend is real, which keeps this off the floor, but 'I have no doubt' is doing the work an argument should.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Just as scrapping Labour’s prison reduction policies—that’s also been ticked off, I think, in the 100-day plan. Is that gone? That’s already been. Capping sentencing discounts to 40 percent—I think that’s coming as well. Getting tough on gangs—that’s also coming as part of this 100-day plan.
specificity.explanation: Names several distinct measures and one hard figure (a 40 percent cap on sentencing discounts), which is checkable content. But the status of each is hedged ('I think', 'that's coming') with no dates, mechanisms or amounts, so it sits in the middle of the scale rather than the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, it certainly does send a signal. It sends a signal that this Government is careful with its money; secondly, it is taxpayers’ money that we’re careful with; and, thirdly, we’re going to instil real consequences for crime.
specificity.explanation: A list of generic virtues — careful with money, careful with taxpayers' money, real consequences for crime — with no figure, mechanism, threshold or timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So the proposed minor amendment to the Legal Services Act exempts section 27 reports from the range of legal aid disbursements that can be approved, without limiting the independence of the Legal Services Commissioner. This bill doesn’t change section 27 of the Sentencing Act in any way, nor does it place any limits on the background information that offenders can provide to the court.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute amended, the exact mechanism (removing these reports from approvable legal aid disbursements), and what is expressly left untouched (section 27 of the Sentencing Act, the Commissioner's independence, what offenders may put before the court). Anyone can check this against the text of the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As the Minister of Justice, the Hon Paul Goldsmith, has said, this is an industry that went in 2017—that magical year; that was the last great year, wasn’t it, 2017—$40,000 spent. The previous Government then spent $25 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that spending on section 27 reports rose from $40,000 in 2017 to $25 million under the previous Government. The figure conflicts with the $7.5m/$7.7m cited by his own colleagues in the same debate; the criterion covers both the annual and cumulative readings.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / Legal Services Commissioner figures for legal aid disbursements on section 27 cultural reports. True if either the annual spend or the total spend under the 2017–2023 Labour government reaches approximately $25 million; false if the figures show materially less (the Minister in this same debate cites a rise from $40,000 in 2017 to $7.5 million a year, and Rima Nakhle cites $7.7 million).

veracity.statement: Well, let me remind that side of the House, when National were in power and they imposed meth testing on houses that set a standard that made sure that people had to test their houses for meth, it turned out to be bollocks—turned out to be an absolute farce.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the meth-testing standard imposed while National was in government was without foundation. The checkable core is whether the testing threshold then in force had an evidential basis for a health risk, not the colourful wording.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2018 report of the Prime Minister's Chief Science Advisor on methamphetamine contamination in residential properties, and the subsequent NZS 8510 / Housing New Zealand response. True if the contamination standard applied under the 2008–2017 National government is found to have had no health-risk basis at the levels used; false if the standard is found to have been evidence-based.

veracity.statement: Up and down the country as we campaigned last year and continued to talk to the population, the number one issue was the cost of living, and number two was restoring law and order, and people want to see that.
veracity.explanation: A claim about the ranking of public concerns during the 2023 campaign: cost of living first, law and order second. Checkable against published issue polling for that year rather than against the speaker's impressions on the campaign trail.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published New Zealand issues polling covering the 2023 election year (e.g. the Ipsos New Zealand Issues Monitor, or major published election-campaign polls). True if cost of living ranked first and crime/law and order ranked second among the issues facing New Zealand; false if a different issue (for example health or housing) held either of those two places.

focus.statement: It’s nothing new from this Government, because they do it on so many other things—they pull the ladder up when they’ve climbed it. Once many of the Ministers have climbed up a ladder, then they look back at everyone else and pull the ladder up. They’ve done it on benefits, they continue to do in the legal system, and they continue to do it in the justice system and in the corrections system.
focus.explanation: A general characterisation of what the governing parties are like, repeated across four policy areas without naming a measure, figure or outcome in any of them. The bare mention of 'benefits' is the only gesture at policy. Rigor is deliberately not scored: strip out the part about the other side and no argument remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What the other side doesn’t understand is that the victims are actually very important and should be the most important in this discussion. I have no shame about standing up for the rights of victims, and I’m sick and tired of people on the other side of the House making it out as if we don’t care.
focus.explanation: About what the other side supposedly fails to understand and about how the speaker feels being characterised by them. No policy, mechanism, figure or outcome is named once the party framing is removed.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I accept that there may not be unanimous support for this bill, but the Government remains convinced that bringing an end to taxpayer funding of the cottage industry of section 27 report writers is necessary to rebuild confidence in the justice system and public spending.
civility.explanation: Engages the contested question directly and concedes the disagreement without attacking anyone. 'Cottage industry of section 27 report writers' is dismissive of a group of practitioners, which is what holds it just below the standard rather than at it; no individual is impugned.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Information on the offenders’ background will continue to be presented to the court through other sources, such as their lawyer, the pre-sentence reports that the Department of Corrections prepares, or other reports that may be appropriate, such as alcohol and drug assessments or psychologists’ reports, and through letters of support from family and friends and letters from rehabilitation programme providers.
divination.explanation: Forecasts what will happen in sentencing courts once legal aid funding for section 27 reports is withdrawn: that the same background information reaches judges by other routes. This is a forecast about court practice, not a promise about the Government's own action, and it is the contested factual hinge of the debate.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Sentencing practice after the Act's commencement, as recorded in sentencing notes, Law Society or Ministry of Justice commentary, or published review of section 27 material. True if courts continued to receive offender background material through counsel submissions, Corrections pre-sentence reports, health assessments and letters of support at a comparable rate. False if the removal of legal aid funding is documented to have left sentencing courts without that background material in a substantial share of cases.

rigor.statement: On the one hand, the Government members are trying to say, “We’re tough on crime. We’re about the victims.”, but, actually, the ability to maintain section 27 reports is still there. It’s still there. So they’re not concerned about “tough on crime”. They’re concerned about removing the ability to access what only the rich are left to be able to access.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: because section 27 reports remain permissible and only the funding is withdrawn, the change cannot be about toughness on crime. The premise supports the narrower conclusion about access, but the leap to 'they're not concerned about tough on crime' is an inference to motive that the premise does not establish — a false dichotomy between the two possible aims.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Not once, in three years of sitting with victims, as a Minister, have I heard them ask to remove these cultural reports. Not once.
rigor.explanation: An argument from absence of evidence resting on personal anecdote: that she personally never heard victims request the change is offered as showing victims do not want it. Her own sample of consultations does not establish the population claim.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The problem as we see it is quite clear: in 2017, section 27 reports were costing $40,000; last financial year, $7.7 million. This has gone unchecked and it’s time to rein it in, and that is what we are doing.
rigor.explanation: The cost growth is offered as the reason to withdraw funding. The figures do support 'spending rose sharply', but the conclusion that it should be reined in assumes the growth is unwarranted without addressing whether the reports deliver value — a gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I know the power, in my very short time at the criminal bar, of actually having an employer turn up and speak on behalf of an offender and actually talk about how they can help that person actually stop their reoffending. That’s what was envisaged by section 27, actually having people with a personal connection, whether it’s whānau, an employer, other people in the community actually coming along, speaking on that person’s behalf at no cost and actually demonstrating to the court how they could help that offender.
rigor.explanation: Argues that unfunded personal testimony can do the work of a funded report, resting on the speaker's own brief courtroom anecdote plus an appeal to original legislative intent. Both are appeals — what section 27 'envisaged' does not show that the substitute is adequate in practice, and one recalled instance does not generalise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I can assure the House that I have held the victims after being raped, I have nursed the children who have been beaten, I have looked into the victim’s eyes, and I have retained a faith in the judiciary and the justice system to act appropriately.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that the justice system can be trusted to act appropriately — is supported only by the speaker's own experience and standing. An appeal to personal authority and anecdote; nothing about the system's performance is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is the judiciary who will weigh up the value of the information presented to them and they will know the difference between a well-coiled-up report written by professionals using special-speak and those impassioned pleas that are given by those who have genuine concern and connection to the offenders and want to see the very best outcomes.
rigor.explanation: A false dichotomy: professionally written reports are cast as jargon-laden artifice and unfunded testimony as genuine, with nothing offered to show the two categories are exclusive or that judges reliably prefer the latter. The conclusion that funding is unnecessary rests entirely on that constructed contrast.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: On the one hand, the Government members are trying to say, “We’re tough on crime. We’re about the victims.”, but, actually, the ability to maintain section 27 reports is still there. It’s still there. So they’re not concerned about “tough on crime”. They’re concerned about removing the ability to access what only the rich are left to be able to access.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual mechanism of the bill — that section 27 reports survive but the legal aid funding for them does not, and who that leaves able to obtain one. Some weight goes to characterising the Government's motives, which keeps it off a full 1.0.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So shame on this Government. Shame on them for trying to exploit rape—because using this racist legislation is trying to exploit rape and sexual violence.
civility.explanation: Goes past the legislation to impute a deliberate, contemptible motive — exploiting rape victims — to the members opposite. No individual is named, but 'shame on them' with an accusation of exploitation is sneering and bad-faith imputation rather than argument about the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I also was the chief panellist on the Owen Glenn inquiry into domestic violence and child abuse.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the speaker held the role of chief panellist on the Glenn Inquiry into Child Abuse and Domestic Violence (the privately funded inquiry backed by Owen Glenn).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Glenn Inquiry's published panel membership and contemporaneous media reporting of its expert panel; true if Davidson is recorded as chief/lead panellist, false if she held no such role or was an ordinary panel member only.

veracity.statement: The problem as we see it is quite clear: in 2017, section 27 reports were costing $40,000; last financial year, $7.7 million. This has gone unchecked and it’s time to rein it in, and that is what we are doing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that legal aid expenditure on section 27 cultural reports was $40,000 in 2017 and $7.7 million in the most recent financial year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / Legal Services Commissioner reported legal aid expenditure on section 27 cultural reports for 2016/17 (or 2017/18) and 2022/23; true if the two figures match to rounding, false if either is materially different.

divination.statement: They have written across social media and across media, and they have been very clear: all that removing the funding for cultural reports will do is entrench further discrimination in a justice system that already is trying to resolve its own discrimination.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that withdrawing legal aid funding for section 27 cultural reports will deepen existing ethnic disparity in sentencing outcomes rather than leave it unchanged or reduce it.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice sentencing and imprisonment statistics broken down by ethnicity, comparing the two years before and the two years after the funding change takes effect; true if the Māori share of custodial sentences, or the Māori/non-Māori gap in custodial sentencing rates for comparable offending, widens; false if it is flat or narrows.

specificity.statement: The problem as we see it is quite clear: in 2017, section 27 reports were costing $40,000; last financial year, $7.7 million. This has gone unchecked and it’s time to rein it in, and that is what we are doing.
specificity.explanation: Two dated figures for a named spending line, stated precisely enough that anyone could go to the legal aid expenditure records and check them.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Rather than insult the Opposition, as I normally do, I’ll give that a rest—as tempting as it is to insult some of them, and particularly with some of their nonsensical contributions.
civility.explanation: Declines to insult while simultaneously dismissing opponents' speeches as 'nonsensical' and framing them as tempting targets — sneering rather than a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: National, whether the other side like it or not, have played a major part in that too, and have been part of the strategies in terms of trying to redeem people.
civility.explanation: In a contested debate he credits the opposing party's contribution to rehabilitation policy; engages the record and attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: You know, you lot are a disgrace to their name—I knew I’d get to that. I mean, they would hang their heads in shame, looking at you lot over there.
civility.explanation: Direct attack on the character of the members opposite — calling them a disgrace and saying respected predecessors would be ashamed of them.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: These are good National people who believe in a strategy, and you lot have been duped by this useless right-wing fascist group over here: the ACT Party.
civility.explanation: Imputes gullibility to the members opposite ('duped'); the 'useless right-wing fascist' label lands on a party rather than an individual, so the personal cost here is the condescension.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I say tonight, Mr Meager, you showed so much promise in that maiden speech, but you’re going to the pack every other time you stand up.
civility.explanation: A personal judgement on a named member's conduct and trajectory in the House rather than on anything he argued.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And I’ve got to say to these Māori members—in particular, James, over there, and my good friend Tama Potaka—wake up and start standing up for your people, because, at the moment, you’re disappointing us.
civility.explanation: Condescending toward two named members and imputes that they are failing their own people — short of abuse, but aimed at the men rather than their argument.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: My mother, as Marama knows, was the longest-serving Parole Board member in this country—20 years, national Parole Board member.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that his mother (June Jackson) served 20 years on the NZ Parole Board and that this is the longest tenure of any member in the country.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Parole Board records / Department of Corrections annual reports and published obituaries of June Jackson: true if her board service ran ~20 years and no member is recorded as serving longer; false if her tenure was materially shorter or another member served longer.

veracity.statement: Willow-Jean Prime talked about the New Zealand Law Society, Māori Law Society, New Zealand Bar Association—all of them are saying that we need to tread carefully here.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that all three named legal bodies have publicly counselled caution on the sentencing/cultural-reports changes before the House.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published submissions and media statements from the New Zealand Law Society, Te Hunga Rōia Māori o Aotearoa and the New Zealand Bar Association on the 2024 sentencing reforms: true if all three urged caution, false if any of the three took no position or supported the change.

veracity.statement: That hard and fast ACT-type policy was never the National Party policy, but it has become now.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a hard-line sentencing approach of this kind was historically no part of National Party policy and has only been adopted under ACT's influence.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National Party sentencing policy documents, manifestos and legislative record before 2023 (e.g. the 2010 three-strikes regime and associated sentencing measures): true if no comparable hard-line sentencing policy was National policy previously, false if National had previously campaigned for or legislated equivalent measures.

rigor.statement: We’re talking about some of the best legal people in the business. Justice Joe Williams is the pride of te ao Māori. He’s saying this type of strategy should not be put in place because, in the end, Māori will be affected hugely by this type of strategy.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority: the case against the policy rests on the standing of the person objecting ('best legal people', 'the pride of te ao Māori') rather than on the reasoning behind the objection, which is only gestured at.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’re talking about some of the best legal people in the business. Justice Joe Williams is the pride of te ao Māori. He’s saying this type of strategy should not be put in place because, in the end, Māori will be affected hugely by this type of strategy.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the sentencing strategy before the House and the expert opposition to it, not the other party's character — high Focus even though the inference is weak.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It cannot just be a “put them in jail and throw the key away” strategy. It cannot be. It has to work on both sides—it has to be work on both sides.
focus.explanation: Directed at the substance of the sentencing approach itself rather than at the other party, even though it carries little detail.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: You know, you lot are a disgrace to their name—I knew I’d get to that. I mean, they would hang their heads in shame, looking at you lot over there.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the other side is like as a group; no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: These are good National people who believe in a strategy, and you lot have been duped by this useless right-wing fascist group over here: the ACT Party.
focus.explanation: Content-free party framing — who has captured whom — with no policy content once the characterisation of ACT and National is removed.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It cannot just be a “put them in jail and throw the key away” strategy. It cannot be. It has to work on both sides—it has to be work on both sides.
specificity.explanation: States a direction with no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named measure — 'work on both sides' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: At Tūrangawaewae, at least 20,000 people turned up to say what the Government was doing was just out the gate and needs some attention.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific attendance figure — at least 20,000 people — at the national hui held at Tūrangawaewae marae in January 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous crowd estimates for the Kīngitanga national hui at Tūrangawaewae on 20 January 2024 (police/organiser/RNZ and NZ Herald reporting); true if credible estimates are 20,000 or more, false if the reported turnout is materially below 20,000.

veracity.statement: Sixty thousand turned up at Waitangi and addressed Government across the paepae and said very clearly, in seven different ways—but in the language that only the Government can understand, which is the monolingual thing, English—so they could understand that they are letting whānau down.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 60,000 people attended Waitangi in February 2024 to address the Government from the paepae.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Reported attendance figures for the Waitangi Day 2024 commemorations (Waitangi National Trust, police estimates, RNZ/NZ Herald coverage); true if credible estimates reach approximately 60,000, false if the reported turnout is materially lower.

veracity.statement: This concerns me as well, given that the Minister on record has said, “On balance, colonisation is good for Māori.”—and he said it, so I’m not making that up.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a serving Minister is on record saying that colonisation was, on balance, good for Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: A published record — interview transcript, book, or Hansard — of the Minister referred to (in context, the Minister responsible for the bill) stating that colonisation was on balance good for Māori; true if such a record exists in substantially those terms, false if no such statement is on record.

veracity.statement: The document is dated 2021 and, of course, the Minister of Defence at the time was the Hon Peeni Henare.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the interim regulatory impact statement on establishing the Inspector-General of Defence is dated 2021, and that Peeni Henare held the Defence portfolio at that date.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The publication date on the interim regulatory impact statement 'Establishing the Inspector-General of Defence' on the Ministry of Defence/Treasury RIS register, checked against the ministerial list for the Defence portfolio on that date; true if the document is dated 2021 and Peeni Henare was then Minister of Defence, false on either count.

civility.statement: When any Minister says, “Colonisation was good for Māori, on balance.”, that is atrocious, disgusting, and needs to be challenged in every single way, and 60,000 people did—60,000 people did in Waitangi.
civility.explanation: Extremely harsh language — 'atrocious, disgusting' — but aimed at the remark and the position, not at the Minister's character, competence or worth. Under the re-anchored scale, fierce criticism of what was said is civil; it edges down only slightly because the remark is closely bound to one identifiable person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s interesting that the member opposite to me, jeering about the past Government, fails to recognise their own complicity, while in Opposition, in actually just calling for more harm for the communities that actually are served by these reports.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to a named individual member — 'complicity', 'calling for more harm' — which is short of a direct insult but no longer engages the substance. Scored against the speaker, since this is how he is conducting himself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m glad that members opposite have finally woken up to the idea of the fact that things cost.
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed at members opposite — 'finally woken up' treats them as belatedly grasping the obvious. A genuine civility failure under the re-anchored scale, though short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So when one of the previous speakers suggested that “We went to lots of community halls.”, it has to be a joke, really, because I didn’t hear him say “marae”; I didn’t hear him say “rūnanga”; I didn’t hear him say “whānau settings”.
rigor.explanation: An inference about the bill's consultation process, and a weak one: argument from absence of evidence. The conclusion that consultation excluded Māori settings rests entirely on words the previous speaker did not happen to use in one contribution, which does not establish where consultation occurred.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If they were really, really concerned about the costs of these reports, why haven’t they gone out and asked Harry Tam for his template and offered to do it for free?
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy, and a poor one: a false dichotomy dressed as a rhetorical question. It presupposes that the only sincere response to concern about cost is for opposition MPs to source and produce the reports unpaid, which does not follow from opposing the removal of legal aid funding.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I can tell you this with assurance: taking funding away—taking funding away—lessens opportunity; it lessens the access to fair and just decisions.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — the removal of legal aid funding — and on the mechanism by which it is said to affect access to justice. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s interesting that the member opposite to me, jeering about the past Government, fails to recognise their own complicity, while in Opposition, in actually just calling for more harm for the communities that actually are served by these reports.
focus.explanation: Almost entirely about the member opposite's conduct and consistency rather than the measure; the reference to 'communities served by these reports' is the only policy content, and it carries little of the weight.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In fact, for migrant and former refugee communities, these reports are critical—and were critical, actually—in being able to provide that broader context in terms of migrants’ and former refugees’ experiences with the justice system to understand that certain behaviours are caused by the trauma that people may be experiencing from fleeing war and persecution, and that is really important context that needs to be provided.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the measure directly: what the reports do and which groups are affected by their removal. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I stand with you today to recognise that the Government is continuing to push forward the agenda of mass incarceration, a colonial agenda that has just resulted in more violence, more indigenous people being incarcerated, and one that is, unfortunately, a global colonial product.
specificity.explanation: An attempt to convey substance, but it carries no figures, no named policy, no timeframe and no mechanism — 'agenda of mass incarceration' and 'global colonial product' are characterisations rather than checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’d like to quote Dean of Law at Auckland University of Technology Professor Khylee Quince, who talked about how cultural reports are not just about reducing sentences but also about providing relevant contextual information about offenders, including how they came to be the person before the decision maker, what they’ve done to address the harm, and this report that they have available to them that may provide the basis of the disposition.
specificity.explanation: Names the source and sets out what the reports actually contain and the function they serve at sentencing — checkable content — though without figures, costs or numbers of reports.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: This bill will only increase incarceration rates and will increase poverty and will increase violence by not being able to have in place systems that allow for healing and the involvement of the broader community within the operations of our justice system.
divination.explanation: Forecasts three future outcomes of the bill's enactment: higher incarceration rates, higher poverty and more violence. Not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections prison muster and sentencing statistics for the period following the Act's commencement, alongside Stats NZ material hardship figures; true if the prison population and average sentence lengths rise over the two years following commencement, false if they hold steady or fall.

veracity.statement: Six days ago, standing right here in this House, Efeso Collins delivered his maiden speech.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Collins gave his maiden speech in the House six days before this sitting (i.e. on or about 15 February 2024).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of Efeso Collins' maiden speech; true if it was delivered six days before 21 February 2024 (15 February 2024), false if the recorded date differs by more than a day.

veracity.statement: He spent three terms on the Auckland Council, serving as chair of the Ōtara-Papatoetoe Local Board and councillor for the Manukau ward.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific local-government record for Collins: three terms in Auckland Council structures, including the chairmanship of the Ōtara-Papatoetoe Local Board and a councillorship for the Manukau ward.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council election results and member records 2013–2022; true if Collins held Ōtara-Papatoetoe Local Board chair and Manukau ward councillor roles spanning three electoral terms, false if the count of terms or either role is wrong.

veracity.statement: It is a matter of record that he contested the Labour Party selection for the Manukau East seat in 2014 before going on to then run for the Auckland mayoralty.
