rigor.statement: Much of this is as a result of poor leadership and decision-making by the previous Government.
rigor.explanation: A causal conclusion — the system's poor performance is attributed to the prior Government's leadership — with no mechanism linking any identified decision to any identified outcome. Post hoc: the problems followed the previous administration, so the previous administration caused them.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: After 18 months in transition, under the guidance of a transition unit, before enablement in July 2022, and then given a further 18 months after that, this infant needed to be up on its feet and walking; despite the best efforts of staff, it was not.
rigor.explanation: The timeline is genuinely offered as a reason and does bear on the "still in its infancy" objection he is answering. But the conclusion — that the Authority was not performing — is asserted rather than evidenced, and the metaphor of walking carries weight that no stated criterion does. A real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is not clear to me that the Māori Health Authority was ever actually supported properly by the previous Government, who, in my view, were distracted by wider structural reforms to other parts of the health system.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy programme and a specific competing cause (the wider structural reforms), so it is a policy point rather than generic party-bashing — but the weight of the sentence is on what the other side's attention was on rather than on the mechanism or its effect.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It sure does, if that intent is indeed a regressive Māori policy agenda—and that’s what’s happening here today.
civility.explanation: Fierce criticism aimed at the coalition Government's policy agenda, not at any individual. No person's character, competence or motives are attacked, so this sits near the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There is no respect of this Government who actively silences the thousands of voices that contributed the establishment of Te Aka Whai Ora, further oppressing te Iwi Māori when it comes to our hauora solutions.
civility.explanation: Imputes deliberate bad faith — 'actively silences', 'further oppressing' — rather than confining the charge to the effect of the decision. It is aimed at the Government collectively and lands on no individual, so it stops short of a personal attack, but the ascription of motive is more than pointed.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We think that having a Government department predicated entirely on race is wrong, and it really is a simplistic way of looking at how we should deal with healthcare in this country.
civility.explanation: A blunt judgement on the structure and the thinking behind it, in a contested debate where the speaker had ample opportunity to turn on the people who built it. 'Simplistic' is directed at the approach, not at any member.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It sure does, if that intent is indeed a regressive Māori policy agenda—and that’s what’s happening here today.
focus.explanation: There is a policy claim here — the bill is characterised as part of an agenda — but no mechanism, figure or named provision is engaged. The weight of the sentence is a characterisation of the coalition as a whole rather than of what the bill does.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Where are the gentle hands in allowing the urgent claim before the Waitangi Tribunal, scheduled for this Thursday and Friday, to be heard—now undermined by this Government?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the process attaching to this specific measure: a named forum (the Waitangi Tribunal), a scheduled urgent hearing, and the claim that passing the bill under urgency pre-empts it. Legitimate scrutiny of a named commitment, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill also doesn’t remove the ability for Māori to be consulted, and we actually want to see more Māori health providers actually providing care at the coalface.
focus.explanation: Addresses what the bill before the House does and does not do, and states the intended alternative arrangement. Entirely on the measure, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Māori right up and down this country stood up to deliver during COVID-19 and, in fact, Te Whānau o Waipareira in West Auckland delivered over 70,000 vaccinations in Tāmaki-makau-rau alone.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that one named West Auckland Māori provider administered more than 70,000 COVID-19 vaccine doses in the Auckland region.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Whānau o Waipareira Trust's reported COVID-19 vaccination delivery totals for the 2021–22 Auckland rollout, or Ministry of Health/Health NZ provider dose data for that trust; true if the recorded doses administered by Waipareira exceed 70,000, false if materially fewer.

veracity.statement: It was opened in Tāmaki-makau-rau, Auckland, where the largest Māori population is in this country. It wasn’t run out of Wellington; in fact, it was put back into the hands of our people.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Auckland is the region with the largest Māori population in New Zealand, and that Te Aka Whai Ora was opened there.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ census figures by regional council for Māori descent/ethnicity; true if the Auckland region has the largest Māori population of any region in New Zealand at the 2018 or 2023 census, false if another region does.

veracity.statement: The review confirmed that Aotearoa has unacceptable Māori health inequities. We have institutional racism. The general health system has not improved Māori health outcomes, and approaches to design, purchasing, and contracting of health services have worsened these inequalities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the Health and Disability System Review (and the Wai 2575 inquiry it reinforced) concluded about Māori health inequities and the role of system design, purchasing and contracting.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Health and Disability System Review final report (June 2020) and the Waitangi Tribunal Wai 2575 stage one report; true if those documents find unacceptable Māori health inequities, institutional racism in the health system, and that design/purchasing/contracting approaches worsened inequities, false if the reports do not make those findings.

veracity.statement: I argue that Te Aka Whai Ora is a really small workforce—not even 300 kaimahi. And it’s not centrally driven as a bureaucracy but rather a group of committed health professionals connected to kāinga, based largely in the regions and in hospitals, who are focused on improving Māori health outcomes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Māori Health Authority employed fewer than 300 staff at the time of the debate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Aka Whai Ora / Māori Health Authority staff headcount or FTE as reported in its annual report or in Health New Zealand's disestablishment advice for early 2024; true if the workforce was under 300, false if materially more.

veracity.statement: The report also found that the authority was tracking behind the Government’s commitments, and under-delivering, resulting in, actually, Māori being underserved, not better served.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of a named review's findings about Te Aka Whai Ora's delivery against government commitments.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The performance/progress review of Te Aka Whai Ora referred to in the debate (the review of the authority's progress reported to the Minister of Health in 2023–24); true if that report finds the authority tracking behind the Government's commitments and under-delivering, false if it makes no such finding.

specificity.statement: Māori right up and down this country stood up to deliver during COVID-19 and, in fact, Te Whānau o Waipareira in West Auckland delivered over 70,000 vaccinations in Tāmaki-makau-rau alone.
specificity.explanation: Names the provider, the region and a hard figure; someone could go and check the delivery total. Missing only the period over which it was delivered.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We established the iwi-Māori partnership boards in order to make sure that we can fund and commission those outcomes directly in community.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete structure (iwi-Māori partnership boards) and the mechanism it was meant to serve (direct funding and commissioning in community), but supplies no amounts, coverage or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And guess what! Only 14 percent of those were to Māori. The rest of them were to everybody. This is the lesson I want that side of the House to remember: I want that side of the House to remember Te Aka Whai Ora was here not just for Māori but for the betterment of this entire nation.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy, with a real gap. The premise concerns the vaccination clientele of a single Māori health provider (Waipareira); the conclusion is about Te Aka Whai Ora, a different body. The step from one provider's reach to the authority's national purpose is not supplied — a hasty generalisation from a single case.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It was opened in Tāmaki-makau-rau, Auckland, where the largest Māori population is in this country. It wasn’t run out of Wellington; in fact, it was put back into the hands of our people.
rigor.explanation: A genuine rebuttal of the 'Wellington bureaucracy' characterisation, offering the location of the authority's opening and base as evidence. The inference is partial: where an agency was launched does not by itself establish that decision-making was decentralised, so the conclusion runs ahead of the evidence offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I argue that Te Aka Whai Ora is a really small workforce—not even 300 kaimahi. And it’s not centrally driven as a bureaucracy but rather a group of committed health professionals connected to kāinga, based largely in the regions and in hospitals, who are focused on improving Māori health outcomes.
rigor.explanation: A direct rebuttal of the Minister's 'Wellington bureaucracy' characterisation, resting on two offered premises — headcount and geographic distribution — that do bear on the conclusion. It leans partly on assertion (that staff are 'largely in the regions and in hospitals' is stated, not evidenced), leaving a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Dividing New Zealanders into two ethnic groups to receive public services does not help us deliver better public services, and, actually, it’s a poor analysis of the causes of poor health outcomes.
rigor.explanation: Engages the measure rather than the other party, so it is a genuine Rigor item — but the conclusion rests on nothing offered. It is bare assertion, and it also restates the authority's function as sorting service recipients into two ethnic groups, which is a strawman of a commissioning body: nothing is supplied to connect that characterisation to what Te Aka Whai Ora actually did.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The report also found that the authority was tracking behind the Government’s commitments, and under-delivering, resulting in, actually, Māori being underserved, not better served.
rigor.explanation: The report's findings are offered as premises, which is a real evidential base. The final step — 'resulting in Māori being underserved' — is a causal conclusion the cited finding about delivery timelines does not establish; a shortfall against commitments is not the same as service levels falling below what would otherwise have existed.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If you have a massive bureaucracy that is all about ideology, no health gain comes as a result.
civility.explanation: Blunt condemnation of bureaucratic structures and ideology; no individual is attacked, impugned or mocked. Harsh about the thing, civil about the people.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Let’s pick a moment in time and focus on what you want to focus the rest of Aotearoa, and that is you have gone on and you have conjured up a narrative that Māori deserve to die earlier; we deserve to be unwell; we deserve to have a system that’s designed by you all who have got no experience.
civility.explanation: Directly imputes bad faith to the members opposite — that they deliberately 'conjured up' a narrative that Māori deserve to die earlier — and closes on their personal lack of competence ('you all who have got no experience'). That lands on the people, not the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So not only have we had to endure a whole revolting campaign of you being so desperate to get into power that you created a narrative that Māori wanted different treatments in Aotearoa but you have continued to also sit there and offer no alternative, no option.
civility.explanation: Attributes a discreditable motive to the members opposite personally — 'so desperate to get into power' that they manufactured a racial narrative. Imputing bad faith of that kind is a civility failure even where the underlying criticism is fair.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is shameful, and, Dr Reti, my view is that your conduct in this is cowardly.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the named Minister's character rather than on his policy — 'cowardly' addresses the man, not the argument, and is delivered to him by name.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If you have a massive bureaucracy that is all about ideology, no health gain comes as a result.
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation stated as an absolute: nothing is offered connecting the size or ideological character of an agency to zero health gain, and the conclusion ('no health gain') is far stronger than anything supplied to support it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So we have comparatively a poor performance of life based on the fact that we have had to endure 180 years of a health system that has completely failed us.
rigor.explanation: A real inference from the mortality figures she has just cited, but it attributes the whole gap to a single cause. The premises (life expectancy differences) do not by themselves rule out the other determinants of health, so the causal conclusion outruns the evidence offered — a single-cause fallacy, though the direction of the inference is reasonable.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We were voted in by the people of New Zealand with a clear electoral mandate, and we are delivering on that mandate as part of our first 100 days in coalition agreements with coalition partners.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to mandate: the electoral result is offered as the reason the measure should pass. Winning an election establishes the authority to legislate but supplies nothing about whether disestablishing the agency will improve health outcomes, which is the proposition at issue. The conclusion does not follow from the premise given.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Māori health equity should be matrixed across the entire public health system, not ring-fenced, not put into a little box on the side, with bureaucratic capture.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the design question before the House — whether Māori health equity is delivered through a separate commissioning agency or embedded system-wide. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So not only have we had to endure a whole revolting campaign of you being so desperate to get into power that you created a narrative that Māori wanted different treatments in Aotearoa but you have continued to also sit there and offer no alternative, no option.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point here — that the Government has proposed no replacement mechanism for Te Aka Whai Ora — but most of the sentence's weight is on the other side's campaign conduct and motives rather than on the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I want to turn to the issue of how we could make substantial health gains for Māori and for non-Māori, and that is in community and primary care.
focus.explanation: Turns directly to the substantive policy question — where health gains are actually produced — rather than to the other party's character or record.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Māori health equity should be matrixed across the entire public health system, not ring-fenced, not put into a little box on the side, with bureaucratic capture.
specificity.explanation: States a direction ('matrixed across the entire system') with no mechanism, no funding, no accountability arrangement and no timeframe; 'matrixed' and 'little box on the side' are metaphors, not checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government is committed to lifting outcomes for Māori and non-Māori alike, and it’s not about the shape of the system; it’s about making sure that it actually delivers for all New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: A statement of commitment with no target, measure, mechanism, funding or timeframe. 'Lifting outcomes' and 'actually delivers' commit to nothing anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I want to turn to the issue of how we could make substantial health gains for Māori and for non-Māori, and that is in community and primary care.
specificity.explanation: Names a sector (community and primary care) but supplies no figures, funding, mechanism or timeframe; the surrounding sentences add localities and iwi-Māori partnership boards as the vehicle but still no how much or by when.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We don’t want a healthcare system that will deliver more bureaucracy than bandages, more paperwork than peripherally inserted central catheter lines, more heartbreak than heart health.
specificity.explanation: An alliterative slogan. No figure, no mechanism, no named policy and nothing that could be checked or acted on — it says only that bureaucracy is bad.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Currently, under the Pae Ora legislation, they do not have any commissioning powers but the future for them is to really come inside the health system and be that network provider down to the grassroots, where Māori health gain will be improved.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that, as the Pae Ora legislation stood in February 2024, iwi-Māori partnership boards held no commissioning powers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 as in force at February 2024, in the provisions setting out the functions of iwi-Māori partnership boards; true if those provisions confer no commissioning function on the boards, false if any commissioning power is conferred there.

veracity.statement: Māori die seven years earlier than everyone else.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a roughly seven-year life expectancy gap between Māori and the rest of the population.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ New Zealand Period Life Tables / Ministry of Health life expectancy at birth by ethnicity, most recent period published before February 2024; true if Māori life expectancy at birth is about seven years below the non-Māori or total-population figure, false if the gap is materially different.

veracity.statement: Now, let’s just remember non-Māori men are doing an average of 83 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that average life expectancy for non-Māori men is 83 years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ period life table life expectancy at birth for non-Māori males, most recent period published before February 2024; true if approximately 83 years, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: We have said that we campaigned clearly that we were going to disestablish the Māori Health Authority.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that disestablishing the Māori Health Authority was an explicit National Party commitment at the 2023 general election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National Party 2023 general election health policy documents and campaign announcements; true if disestablishing the Māori Health Authority appears as a stated campaign commitment before election day, false if it does not.

veracity.statement: What is so disappointing is that something which is the culmination of so much study and work and consultation in Aotearoa is now being removed by a Government who refuses to listen, under urgency, with no opportunity for select committee and no opportunity for the Waitangi Tribunal to be able to comment on this thing of critical importance to Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two procedural facts about this bill: that it is being progressed under urgency with no select committee stage, and that the Waitangi Tribunal has had no opportunity to comment on the disestablishment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The House's Hansard and order paper for the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill, plus the Waitangi Tribunal's register of inquiries and reports for late 2023 / early 2024; true only if the bill was taken under urgency with no referral to a select committee AND the Tribunal produced no report or hearing on the disestablishment before this reading, false if either limb fails.

civility.statement: Ko taku whanaunga te tangata arero rua.
civility.explanation: Calls the Minister "a two-faced man" — an attack on his character rather than on the bill or its effects. The disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora was genuinely contested, so there was a real opportunity to make the same criticism of the decision without labelling the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Nā te Minita i teka i tērā wiki.
civility.explanation: A direct accusation that the Minister lied — imputing deliberate dishonesty to a named individual rather than arguing that the consultation commitment was not honoured. Personal, not policy-directed.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Ko taku kōrero ki a koe, e taku whanaunga, e tino whakamā ana ahau i ō mahi.
civility.explanation: Says she is deeply ashamed of his actions ("ō mahi"), directed at conduct rather than the man himself. Pointed and personal in address but stops short of an attack on character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I roto i tēnei Whare, i whakautu ia i te pātai a Peeni Henare mehemea ka noho ia, ka kōrero ia, ka whakarongo ia ki ōna iwi Māori, ki ngā hapū, ki ngā iwi, ki te Taraipiunara.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in the House the previous week the Minister answered a question from Peeni Henare undertaking to sit with, discuss with and listen to Māori, hapū, iwi and the Waitangi Tribunal. The assertion is about what was said on the record, not about whether he meant it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for the sitting week preceding 2024-02-27: true if Peeni Henare put such a question to Hon Dr Shane Reti and Reti's reply gave an undertaking to sit with, listen to and consider the views of iwi, hapū and the Tribunal; false if no such exchange occurred or the reply gave no such undertaking.

veracity.statement: I recognise and venerate this and, in fact, have already moved from just those nice words to putting it into action with the announcement in December of a $50 million immunisation programme that utilises the special actions that Māori health providers can provide, and what mainstream cannot, or will not; their ability to reach into remote and vulnerable communities as part of the expertise that they have.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in December the Government announced a $50 million immunisation programme delivered through Māori health providers. The claim is about the existence, size and December timing of that announcement, not about its results.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Beehive.govt.nz / Ministry of Health announcements for December 2023: true if an immunisation funding package of approximately $50 million that funds Māori health providers was announced in that month; false if no such announcement exists, the amount is materially different, or it did not fund Māori health providers.

specificity.statement: I recognise and venerate this and, in fact, have already moved from just those nice words to putting it into action with the announcement in December of a $50 million immunisation programme that utilises the special actions that Māori health providers can provide, and what mainstream cannot, or will not; their ability to reach into remote and vulnerable communities as part of the expertise that they have.
specificity.explanation: Carries a dollar figure ($50 million), a month (December), a named programme type (immunisation) and the delivery channel (Māori health providers). Someone could go and check it or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have laid out a plan for Māori health in the context of an overarching strategy with priorities that include decentralisation, the importance of health workforce, and targets.
specificity.explanation: Names three priority headings but supplies no mechanism, figure, timeframe or target value — "decentralisation", "the importance of health workforce" and "targets" are categories, not commitments. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In that announcement, which at $50 million was not inconsequential, we funded Māori health providers to deliver to a universal audience. We backed them. These are tangible actions, not just words.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: one funding decision is offered as proof that the Government backs Māori health provision. It follows for the immunisation programme itself, but there is a gap between a single $50 million contract and the broader conclusion it is being used to support while the Authority is being disestablished — hasty generalisation from one instance.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: To conclude, briefly, I’ve described the changes that this bill brings about: (1) Māori Health Authority staff to repatriate to Health New Zealand and the Māori Health Authority; (2) uplifting of the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee; (3) uplifting of iwi-Māori partnership boards; (4) reconsideration of localities.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure before the House — the four structural changes the bill makes. No party framing and no reference to opponents at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Clause 6 of this particular bill that we are debating here tonight is clear subterfuge and straight-out play by this particular Government to make sure that they can continue to tinker with Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
focus.explanation: Names a specific provision of the measure before the House (clause 6) and what he says it does, so the charge is anchored to policy content rather than to the other party in general; the weight given to the Government's supposed motive keeps it below a 1.0.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That side of the House might choose to sit in ignorance and choose to sit there with blinkers on to the actual needs of Māori.
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of the other side's disposition. No policy, clause, figure or outcome is named, so nothing survives once the party-framing is removed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: He didn’t tell us how and how much we are going to lift the immunisation rates of our tamariki—in the House, on record, when asked about it, he talked about funding a data system.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny of a named commitment: it identifies the specific programme (immunisation rates), the missing element (target and quantum) and the answer actually given (a data system). Holding a Minister to account for a named policy is on-policy, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So with only one Māori board member, does the Minister believe that the governance of Te Whatu Ora have enough Māori capacity and capability?
focus.explanation: A precise accountability question tied to a named body, a specific consequence of the bill (loss of the Te Aka Whai Ora chair from the board) and a countable outcome. Entirely about the measure, not the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A known fact amongst our people: for those aged under 25, just over 50 percent of those people who are Māori are also Pacific.
specificity.explanation: Carries a numeric threshold and a defined age band, so a listener could go and look for the cross-tabulation; it names no source, period or dataset, which keeps it short of fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In this repeal bill, what it’s proposing is that the iwi-Māori partnership boards can only be constructed or approved by the Director-General of Health.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact mechanism the bill changes and the office in which the power would sit, which anyone could check against the bill's text. Falls short of 1.0 only because no clause is cited.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, if we look at the scrapping of Te Aka Whai Ora and shushing out community voice and te Iwi Māori voice, I reflect back on the submissions received on the Pae Ora legislation from November 2021 to August 2023—some 4,685 submissions.
specificity.explanation: Gives an exact submission count, the legislation it relates to and the window over which they were received — precise enough for someone to verify or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The status quo on steroids can only tell me one thing: that it’s going to go backwards even faster—the status quo on steroids tells me it is going to go backwards even faster.
rigor.explanation: An inference about the repeal's effect, but the conclusion rests on a metaphor and repetition rather than any offered mechanism: nothing connects returning to the previous arrangements with outcomes deteriorating at a faster rate. Non sequitur dressed as emphasis.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The system has failed to look after Māori, and we know this because Māori die at twice the rate of non-Māori from cardiovascular disease.
rigor.explanation: A real inference with evidence attached: a mortality disparity is offered as the reason for the conclusion, and it does support a claim of inequitable outcomes. The gap is generalising from a single disease-specific statistic to the failure of the whole system, which the premise alone does not establish.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Minister himself spoke about a $50 million fund to lift the rates of immunisation across the country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister of Health publicly referred to a $50 million fund for lifting national immunisation rates.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard and Government/Ministry of Health announcements up to 27 February 2024; true if the Minister of Health referred to an immunisation fund of approximately $50 million, false if no such figure or fund appears in his statements or announcements.

veracity.statement: Māori die, on average, seven years earlier than non-Māori in this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a life-expectancy gap of roughly seven years between Māori and non-Māori in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ period life tables / life expectancy at birth by ethnicity (most recent available before February 2024); true if the Māori vs non-Māori gap is approximately seven years, false if materially different (e.g. under five or over nine years).

veracity.statement: In 2019, the Waitangi Tribunal report for Wai 2575 confirmed the view and states that our primary healthcare legislation and policy breaches Te Tiriti and fails to care for Māori health and wellbeing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Waitangi Tribunal's 2019 Wai 2575 report found the primary health care legislative and policy framework to be in breach of Te Tiriti and failing Māori health.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal's Hauora: Report on Stage One of the Health Services and Outcomes Kaupapa Inquiry (Wai 2575); true if it was released in 2019 and found the primary health care legislative/policy framework breached Treaty principles, false if the finding or the year differs.

veracity.statement: There are currently two Māori members of Te Whatu Ora.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Te Whatu Ora board had two Māori members as at late February 2024, in a passage about board composition.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Whatu Ora / Health New Zealand board membership as published in February 2024; true if exactly two board members were Māori at that date, false if the count was one, three or more.

civility.statement: Now, while I respect the Director-General of Health—the current one and indeed the one that we worked with in order to establish Te Aka Whai Ora, Sir Ashley Bloomfield, who was hugely supportive of the work that we did for the health reform and of course for Te Aka Whai Ora—what we’re seeing here is a continual silencing of the Māori voice as we look towards things like the Iwi-Māori Partnership Board that the Minister and that side of the House pretend to commit themselves to and pretend to support.
civility.explanation: Accusing the Minister of pretending to support something imputes personal insincerity rather than disputing the policy; it lands on the person's good faith. Short of an outright insult, and softened by the genuine respect expressed for the Director-General, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Let’s be clear that successive Governments have breached Te Tiriti obligations through the generations by failing to protect the health and wellbeing of te Iwi Māori.
civility.explanation: A severe charge, but levelled at the record of governments over time, not at any individual. Attacks no one; this is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There have been many societies in history who have seen their citizens based on something as flat as race, and often they regret it as they lose sight of the beauty of each individual.
rigor.explanation: A loose historical analogy offered as the argument against the Māori Health Authority: unnamed historical societies that classified citizens by race came to regret it, therefore this agency should go. Nothing is offered to connect race-classification regimes to a health commissioning body, so the conclusion does not follow — a false analogy resting on an unstated equivalence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is an expert with 40 years of experience, with not a political bone in his body, who is really only worried about the wellbeing of our people.
rigor.explanation: A bare appeal to authority: the case for Te Aka Whai Ora rests entirely on the credentials and disinterestedness of the person cited, with no reasoning from what he actually found. The conclusion is carried by who said it, not by what was said.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Whether the other side wants to hear it or not, this Government isn’t creating division; it is trying to restore trust in the society which the last Government trashed.
focus.explanation: There is a policy-adjacent claim about the Government's intent, but the weight of the sentence is party framing — 'the other side', 'the last Government trashed' — with no measure, mechanism or outcome named. Not content-free tribalism, but close to it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’re doing this in a different way: as the Minister noted, decentralisation is a key way we’re focusing on this; absolute health targets where we ensure that the outcomes will be positive not just for Māori but Pasifika and all other communities as well, and also addressing the huge workforce pressures right across the health system.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy alternative — decentralisation, health targets, workforce — with no party-bashing content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How are the locality plans working, given that you have no data to say how they’re performing, no outcomes, and we haven’t seen any data outcomes since the DHBs were wound up?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny on a named mechanism — locality plans — and a named change (the winding up of the DHBs), asking for performance data. This is opposition holding the Government to account on the substance, which scores at the top.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I urge that we all work together, stand strong, and stand united as we continue to take this Government on with its anti-Māori agenda.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side's character and intent — an 'anti-Māori agenda' — with no policy, measure, figure or outcome named. No individual is insulted, so Civility passes it cleanly; this is the tribalism Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is appalling, it is shameful, it is a breach of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, and it is anti-Māori, frankly—as this Government expresses it wants to be.
focus.explanation: There is a substantive claim in here — that the measure breaches Te Tiriti — but it is carried by a run of condemnatory adjectives and closes on the Government's supposed intent rather than on the bill's effect. A real policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: For the benefit of Peeni Henare, I invite that member to finish his sentence on why he doesn’t have faith in the director-general.
civility.explanation: Pointed and personal in its target — it invites a named member to incriminate himself — but it does not insult him or impute bad faith outright. Edging toward the person without landing on them.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We’ve barely had our feet hit the ground, and, actually, we’re insulted by watching politicians stand up and speak for one to two minutes about kaupapa that are dear; not passionate.
civility.explanation: Imputes indifference and lack of care to other members personally — that their short contributions show they do not take the kaupapa seriously. Short of a direct insult, but it is a judgement about how colleagues are, not about the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So while Māori were out there, defending this nation and looking after everyone, we had a leader of this Government who was out making sure that he shared the Māori vaccination code.
civility.explanation: A direct accusation of misconduct aimed at an identifiable individual — a party leader in the coalition — rather than at a policy. It attacks the person's conduct and character, not the argument before the House.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This specious and gross double-speak which suggests that putting special focus on those in need of that focus is somehow a race-based privilege, is revolting—it is revolting double-speak.
civility.explanation: Targets the opposing argument rather than any individual, but 'double-speak' imputes deliberate deception rather than error, and the repeated 'revolting' is contemptuous of those making it. Below the standard, though no person is named or insulted.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is about removing duplicate, expensive bureaucracy, whether in Wellington or Auckland.
specificity.explanation: Names a rationale and gestures at where the duplication sits, but supplies no figure for the cost, no named function being removed, and no timeframe. A direction with very little checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Staff and structures will move to the Ministry of Health and Health New Zealand, and ACT supports this bill.
specificity.explanation: Names the two receiving agencies and what transfers to them, which is checkable against the bill, but gives no numbers, no transition date and no detail on which functions survive the move.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re doing this in a different way: as the Minister noted, decentralisation is a key way we’re focusing on this; absolute health targets where we ensure that the outcomes will be positive not just for Māori but Pasifika and all other communities as well, and also addressing the huge workforce pressures right across the health system.
specificity.explanation: Three named mechanisms (decentralisation, absolute health targets, workforce pressure), which is more than a slogan, but no target figures, no dates and no description of how any of them would operate.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, if I could draw his attention to Part 1, replacement section 15, inserted by clause 11, “Health New Zealand must support and engage with iwi-Māori partnership boards”.
specificity.explanation: Cites the Part, the replacement section, the inserting clause and the statutory wording. A reader can go to the bill and check it directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, in 1982, we had 55 doctors—55 Māori doctors. Now, we have 55 Māori doctors graduating a year, and, I guess, the hope that I have as I speak to our people is that if we were to put all our Māori health workers and authorities together, we would have a powerful vehicle for change.
specificity.explanation: A dated figure and a current annual rate, both concrete enough that someone could look them up — though the concluding hope is left undefined.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Māori die at twice the rate of non-Māori from cardiovascular disease. Māori tamariki have a mortality rate 1½ times the rate of non-Māori children.
specificity.explanation: Two named health measures with stated ratios against a named comparison group. Precise enough to be checked against published mortality statistics.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We believe that Te Aka Whai Ora—and if we go back to the report that was written, the high-level assessment of Te Aka Whai Ora, the progress against Cabinet expectations, just a small note here: overall there had been insufficient internal capacity and capability to deliver.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a named official document — the high-level assessment of Te Aka Whai Ora's progress against Cabinet expectations — concluded that the agency had insufficient internal capacity and capability to deliver.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the high-level assessment of Te Aka Whai Ora against Cabinet expectations (Ministry of Health / Te Whatu Ora review material released in 2023-24): true if the report states a finding of insufficient internal capacity and capability, false if it contains no such finding or reaches the opposite conclusion.

veracity.statement: Under the previous legislation, the iwi-Māori partnership boards were nothing more than a token gesture. They didn’t have any commissioning powers to deliver health services for Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that under the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 as originally enacted, iwi-Māori partnership boards held no commissioning powers for health services.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The functions of iwi-Māori partnership boards in the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 as enacted: true if the Act confers only engagement, priority-setting and monitoring functions on the boards with commissioning sitting elsewhere (Te Aka Whai Ora / Te Whatu Ora), false if the Act confers any commissioning or service-purchasing function on the boards.

veracity.statement: I guess my point is that with 16 pieces of legislation coming through urgency, it’s really hard to keep track of which one you’re actually doing, because in an 18-month run—in an 18-month run; let’s not forget and lose sight of this—the Government keeps carrying on as if it has evidence.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a count: sixteen pieces of legislation had been taken through urgency by the coalition Government at the point of speaking (27 February 2024).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard's record of urgency motions and bills progressed under urgency between the Government's formation in late November 2023 and 27 February 2024: true if the count of bills advanced under urgency is around sixteen, false if it is materially different.

veracity.statement: Eighty-three percent of Māori didn’t vote for this Government, which is why there is such a comfort in what is being rolled out.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 83 percent of Māori voters did not vote for any of the parties now in Government at the 2023 general election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission 2023 general election party-vote results for the seven Māori electorates (or Māori-roll party vote breakdown): true if the combined National/ACT/NZ First party vote share is about 17 percent, false if it is materially higher.

veracity.statement: So while Māori were out there, defending this nation and looking after everyone, we had a leader of this Government who was out making sure that he shared the Māori vaccination code.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a leader of one of the coalition parties passed on Māori COVID-19 vaccination data during the vaccination rollout.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous reporting and the Privacy Commissioner / Ministry of Health inquiry record from late 2021 into the leak of Māori vaccination data: true if a leader of a party now in Government received and passed on that data, false if no such transmission is recorded.

veracity.statement: So, in 1982, we had 55 doctors—55 Māori doctors. Now, we have 55 Māori doctors graduating a year, and, I guess, the hope that I have as I speak to our people is that if we were to put all our Māori health workers and authorities together, we would have a powerful vehicle for change.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two figures: that there were 55 Māori doctors in total in 1982, and that 55 Māori doctors now graduate each year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te ORA / Medical Council of New Zealand workforce data and university medical school graduate statistics: true if the 1982 Māori medical workforce was about 55 and the recent annual Māori medical graduate count is about 55, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: So, fresh in this loss that we experience as a party and as a House and as a nation, it is galling that in two days’ time, on the day that we will bury Efeso Collins, there is a Waitangi Tribunal being heard on this very question, and that this House and this Government is not willing to wait a mere two days.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a Waitangi Tribunal hearing into the disestablishment of the Māori Health Authority was scheduled two days after 27 February 2024, i.e. on or about 29 February 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal hearing schedule and the urgent inquiry record concerning the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora: true if an urgent hearing on that question was listed for on or about 29 February 2024, false if no hearing was scheduled in that window.

veracity.statement: The Waitangi Tribunal, in the hauora report, found that the legislative framework of the New Zealand primary healthcare system should recognise and provide for the Treaty of Waitangi and its principles.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific finding of the Waitangi Tribunal's hauora report on the health services and outcomes kaupapa inquiry — that the primary healthcare legislative framework should recognise and provide for the Treaty and its principles.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal's Hauora report (stage one, health services and outcomes kaupapa inquiry, Wai 2575): true if the report recommends that the primary health care legislative framework recognise and provide for the Treaty and its principles, false if it contains no such finding.

veracity.statement: Māori die at twice the rate of non-Māori from cardiovascular disease. Māori tamariki have a mortality rate 1½ times the rate of non-Māori children.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two mortality ratios: Māori cardiovascular mortality at twice the non-Māori rate, and Māori child mortality at one and a half times the non-Māori child rate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Stats NZ age-standardised mortality data by ethnicity: true if the Māori:non-Māori cardiovascular mortality ratio is about 2.0 and the child mortality ratio about 1.5, false if either ratio is materially different.

civility.statement: The reality is, under the last six years, the health outcomes for New Zealanders have gone backwards. New Zealanders haven’t been able to get the care they need. Our wait-lists and times have soared.
civility.explanation: Blunt criticism of the previous government's health record. No person is attacked, no bad faith imputed — this is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And I say to this doctor over here, you are ignoring exceptional people who know about this kaupapa much more than the people you have consulted, who seem to only be his mates in the National Party, the rednecks in the—I shouldn’t go that far—the right-wingers in the ACT Party, and the lost lot of New Zealand First.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to a named member — that he consulted only "his mates" — and reaches for "rednecks" and "the lost lot" about other members. Short of sustained abuse, but well past pointed.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The reality is, under the last six years, the health outcomes for New Zealanders have gone backwards. New Zealanders haven’t been able to get the care they need. Our wait-lists and times have soared.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that over the 2017-2023 Labour-led government, health waiting lists and waiting times increased substantially.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Whatu Ora / Ministry of Health planned care data comparing October 2017 with late 2023: the number of patients waiting beyond the four-month target for a first specialist assessment or elective surgery. True if that figure rose substantially over the period; false if it was flat or fell.

veracity.statement: Immunisation rates have plunged, and this Government is committed to lifting the health outcomes for New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that national immunisation coverage declined sharply over the preceding period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health national childhood immunisation coverage statistics for the eight-month milestone, comparing 2017 with 2023. True if coverage fell materially (several percentage points or more); false if coverage held steady or rose.

specificity.statement: And as part of doing that, we will disestablish the Māori Health Authority and merge the functions of the Māori Health Authority and transfer the rolls into the public health system.
specificity.explanation: Names the measure and the mechanism — disestablishment, merger of functions, transfer of roles into the public system — but gives no timeframe, cost, or account of how the transfer will work.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government is committed to finding more effective ways to work with all communities for better outcomes and to deliver solutions, as well as finding savings through disestablishment which may actually go to better health outcomes.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic goods — "more effective ways", "better outcomes", "solutions". The one concrete element, savings from disestablishment, carries no figure and is hedged to "may actually go to" better outcomes.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And as part of doing that, we will disestablish the Māori Health Authority and merge the functions of the Māori Health Authority and transfer the rolls into the public health system.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the measure before the House and what it does. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I ask Dr Reti: who are your people who you have consulted with? Give me two, three, one Māori professional who supports this.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny of the consultation behind this specific bill — who the responsible Minister took advice from before disestablishing the Authority. On-policy, not tribal.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I ask Dr Reti: who are your people who you have consulted with? Give me two, three, one Māori professional who supports this.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority combined with an argument from absence of evidence: that no named Māori health professional can be produced in support is offered as showing the policy is wrong. Expert opposition is real evidence, but the conclusion outruns it — no professional's reasoning is given, only their standing.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You can build whatever structures you like, but till you focus on outcomes, you’re going to have increasing health inequities, and patients will suffer.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: structures and a focus on outcomes are treated as alternatives, when the contested question is whether the structure delivers the outcomes. The consequence — rising inequities and patients suffering — is asserted with nothing offered to connect it to the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I think this serves as a precautionary tale to us. All these years later, we take that risk again.
rigor.explanation: An inference from a single anecdote about one woman deprived of rongoā knowledge a century after the Tohunga Suppression Act to the conclusion that disestablishing Te Aka Whai Ora repeats that risk. It engages the measure, but the connecting step is left unmade — argument from anecdote plus historical analogy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Māori Health Authority seemed like such a great idea and I held out such hope, as did so many of my health colleagues but, unfortunately, the causes of Māori health poor outcomes have got nothing to do with the health system; it’s to do with colonisation, it’s to do with the impacts of poor, it’s all about the fact that economic decisions and social policy have more impact than anything to do with the health system. So trying to restore and improve health outcomes for Māori through health policy is going to be useless.
rigor.explanation: The premises slide: 'economic decisions and social policy have more impact' is asserted, then upgraded to the causes having 'nothing to do with the health system', then to health policy being 'useless'. Greater impact elsewhere does not entail zero impact here — a false dichotomy carrying a non sequitur to the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I had every intention of coming into this calm and speaking about some of my family experiences, but I can’t help but sit here and feel insulted—insulted by that side of the House, who are telling us that they understand what’s best for us, they want what’s best for us.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point underneath — who holds authority over Māori health provision — but the weight of the statement is on the attitude of 'that side of the House' rather than on the bill's mechanism or effect. Party framing carries most of it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m furthermore insulted, such is the arrogance that when the Hon Willow-Jean Prime was making her case for hauora Māori—the wellbeing of Māori, in our language—barely half of that side put in their earpieces to hear what she was saying.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the conduct and character of the other side in the Chamber. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named, so there is nothing on-policy for the listener to check or act on.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is my great pleasure to do so, because one of the reasons that I came to this House was because of my incredible anger at the destruction of our wonderful health system, wrought upon us by the previous Labour Government.
focus.explanation: Directed at the previous Government's record in the most general terms — 'the destruction of our wonderful health system'. No reform, cost, service or outcome is named, so it functions as party framing rather than scrutiny of a specific commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Māori Health Authority seemed like such a great idea and I held out such hope, as did so many of my health colleagues but, unfortunately, the causes of Māori health poor outcomes have got nothing to do with the health system; it’s to do with colonisation, it’s to do with the impacts of poor, it’s all about the fact that economic decisions and social policy have more impact than anything to do with the health system. So trying to restore and improve health outcomes for Māori through health policy is going to be useless.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: it addresses what the Māori Health Authority was for, what drives Māori health outcomes, and why the speaker thinks the mechanism cannot deliver. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I’m furthermore insulted, such is the arrogance that when the Hon Willow-Jean Prime was making her case for hauora Māori—the wellbeing of Māori, in our language—barely half of that side put in their earpieces to hear what she was saying.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that barely half of the Government members present used interpretation earpieces during Willow-Jean Prime's speech. The claim is about a countable, recorded state of affairs, not about whether the inattention was justified.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament TV footage of the 27 February 2024 debate during Willow-Jean Prime's speech; true if fewer than half of the Government members present are visibly wearing translation earpieces during her te reo Māori passages, false if half or more are.

veracity.statement: The Māori Health Authority seemed like such a great idea and I held out such hope, as did so many of my health colleagues but, unfortunately, the causes of Māori health poor outcomes have got nothing to do with the health system; it’s to do with colonisation, it’s to do with the impacts of poor, it’s all about the fact that economic decisions and social policy have more impact than anything to do with the health system. So trying to restore and improve health outcomes for Māori through health policy is going to be useless.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the causes of poor Māori health outcomes have nothing to do with the health system itself, all of it lying in colonisation, economic decisions and social policy. The checkable part is the exclusion of health-system factors, not the ranking of causes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Peer-reviewed NZ health-services research and the Waitangi Tribunal Hauora report (WAI 2575) on whether health-system factors — differential access, referral and treatment rates, primary-care funding — contribute measurably to Māori health inequities; true if no health-system contribution is documented, false if documented differences in treatment or access by ethnicity exist.

specificity.statement: So I’m sad to say that this bill represents the dashing of hope, because it was something that was Māori-inspired, Māori-led, and all-inclusive.
specificity.explanation: Characterises Te Aka Whai Ora entirely through generic virtues — Māori-inspired, Māori-led, all-inclusive — with no funding figure, service, target or outcome attached. She had ample room to cite what the authority actually commissioned; nothing here is checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: How shameful that you would use her name.
civility.explanation: Aimed at the member personally rather than at her argument: it charges Weenink with acting shamefully in invoking Dr Marcia Walker, imputing bad faith rather than contesting the point about the partnership boards. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That has been met with incredibly disappointing speeches on the other side from practitioners, some of whom were previously practitioners in general practice and supposedly experts in health, who know that the status quo never worked for Māori and appreciate the deep inequities which have delivered health outcomes for Māori that would not be fixed by going back to that system.
civility.explanation: "supposedly experts in health" sneers at the professional standing of named-by-implication individual members opposite, and "who know that the status quo never worked" imputes that they are acting against knowledge they hold — a bad-faith imputation aimed at people rather than at the bill.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Māori die seven years earlier than any other group.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a roughly seven-year life-expectancy deficit for Māori relative to every other ethnic group in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ period life expectancy at birth by ethnicity, most recent release before February 2024. True if Māori life expectancy is roughly seven years below that of the other reported ethnic groups; false if the gap is materially smaller than seven years, or if any other reported group has a lower life expectancy than Māori.

veracity.statement: It’s important for the House to fully appreciate that the Crown’s own advice is that the introduction of this bill would, on the face of it, constitute a breach of the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Crown's own legal advice characterises the introduction of this bill as a breach of Treaty principles. Note the characterisation is slightly stronger than the text she read: Crown Law's wording is that a Tribunal finding of breach can be expected, which is a prediction about the Tribunal rather than a concession that a breach has occurred.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Crown Law memorandum to the Waitangi Tribunal dated 31 January 2024 concerning the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora. True if it states that proceeding without consultation can be expected to result in a Tribunal finding that Treaty principles have been breached and prejudice resulted; false if it contains no such assessment, or concludes the opposite.

focus.statement: The electoral mandate is there because it was won in a furore of his wrong-headed idea that Māori were getting special rights and special treatment, and, in fact, that debate was whipped up by members on the other side of this House.
focus.explanation: Answers the mandate argument by characterising how the other side campaigned rather than by engaging any provision of the bill. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named; the weight is on what members opposite are like.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think it’s really disappointing now that we are standing in this House and not only are we repealing the Māori Health Authority but there are also a number of changes in this bill, which I will be asking the Minister questions about in the committee stage, which take away the voice of iwi, of Māori, and of appointed experts in Māori health within the system and replace them with people who are appointed directly by the Minister and who can be dismissed by the Minister at any time.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the measure before the House does: the repeal and the appointment/dismissal changes it makes. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And so that localised system simply didn’t work for the entire population, because there was this deep need for Māori health services.
rigor.explanation: A real inference from the Counties Manukau example she has just laid out: concentrated high need under locality-based funding forces other services down, producing postcode disparities in eligibility. The step from that example to a general failure of localised funding is asserted rather than shown, and the causal attribution to Māori prevalence is offered without support — a hasty generalisation from a single case, but not a fallacious one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As a diabetes and cardio specialist, I can tell you that with self-responsibility and discipline, some of the health issues we’re facing in New Zealand can be prevented.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to the speaker's own authority: his clinical credentials are offered in place of evidence, and no mechanism or data connects individual discipline to the population-level inequities the debate is about. It does engage the policy question, so the defect is the inference, not the target.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: People in New Zealand want a health system based on needs, not race.
rigor.explanation: Two defects in one line: an appeal to popularity (what people want is offered as the reason the policy is right), resting on a false dichotomy that treats need-based and ethnicity-targeted provision as mutually exclusive, when the case put against him was that ethnicity is being used as a proxy for measured need.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I think it’s really disappointing now that we are standing in this House and not only are we repealing the Māori Health Authority but there are also a number of changes in this bill, which I will be asking the Minister questions about in the committee stage, which take away the voice of iwi, of Māori, and of appointed experts in Māori health within the system and replace them with people who are appointed directly by the Minister and who can be dismissed by the Minister at any time.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism — replacing iwi and expert appointees with ministerial appointees removable at will — which someone could check against the bill. Falls short of 1.0 because no clause, body or number is identified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government will continue to work together with our Māori community to deliver a solution.
specificity.explanation: No mechanism, no measure, no figure, no timeframe and no named body — "work together to deliver a solution" commits to nothing that could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For example, one of the principles here is, of course, the principle of partnership, yet we see later on, in clause 19, that section 35 is being amended, and with respect to the preparation of the Government Policy Statement (GPS), it removes a Māori voice.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific clause (19), the section it amends (35), the named document (the Government Policy Statement) and the concrete effect claimed. Someone could open the bill and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: For example, one of the principles here is, of course, the principle of partnership, yet we see later on, in clause 19, that section 35 is being amended, and with respect to the preparation of the Government Policy Statement (GPS), it removes a Māori voice.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that clause 19 of the bill amends section 35 so as to remove a Māori voice from the preparation of the Government Policy Statement on health.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Text of the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill as introduced in Feb 2024, clause 19, amending section 35 of the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022. True if that clause deletes a requirement for Māori input into GPS preparation (e.g. engagement with Te Aka Whai Ora or iwi-Māori partnership boards); false if section 35's Māori-input provisions survive the amendment unchanged.

veracity.statement: We can also go on to give another example here of clause 15, where section 30 is amended, and it goes down to the bottom there, to clause 15(5), which is: “Repeal section 30(1)(g).”, and that’s about iwi Māori getting to have a say on appointments.
veracity.explanation: Two joined factual assertions: that clause 15(5) repeals section 30(1)(g), and that the repealed paragraph is the one giving iwi Māori a say on appointments.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Clause 15(5) of the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill and section 30(1)(g) of the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022. True if clause 15(5) repeals section 30(1)(g) and that paragraph concerns iwi-Māori input into appointments; false if either the repeal or the description of what the paragraph covers is wrong.

veracity.statement: In fact, he took that case all the way to the High Court.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that John Tamihere litigated the question of timely release of health data for Māori communities as far as the High Court. 'All the way to' is loose in a New Zealand context, since the High Court is a first-instance court here; the checkable core is that the case reached the High Court.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Court records and contemporaneous reporting of litigation brought by John Tamihere, or the Whānau Ora commissioning agency he leads, against the Ministry of Health over release of Māori COVID-19 vaccination data. True if such a case was heard and decided in the High Court; false if it never proceeded past correspondence or was dealt with only in another forum.

rigor.statement: Now, when we think of the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi, it’s quite clear to me that (1) their voice isn’t being heard, so therefore one can argue here that that partnership isn’t being met there; and (2) it’s once again a clear breach of good faith as Māori are expected to only serve part of their consultation and part of their duty within this particular legislation and across the entire Pae Ora legislation, and yet are being silenced in other areas that are key to the successful execution of the Pae Ora legislation itself.
rigor.explanation: The first step is supported: he has cited specific repealed consultation provisions, so the inference from those to 'partnership isn't being met' tracks the evidence he offered. The second step does not — 'a clear breach of good faith' adds an intent claim that nothing offered establishes, so there is a real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What this sets out to do is give somewhat of a back-door exit, if you will, to give the Government a bit of a clause to escape out the back door when we look towards whether or not the engagement by Health New Zealand with Māori is appropriate and is timely.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the drafting — but it reads purpose into the ordinary qualifying language 'reasonable steps' without offering anything to connect the wording to the intent alleged. The conclusion about motive rests on suspicion rather than on the text he quoted.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, when we think of the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi, it’s quite clear to me that (1) their voice isn’t being heard, so therefore one can argue here that that partnership isn’t being met there; and (2) it’s once again a clear breach of good faith as Māori are expected to only serve part of their consultation and part of their duty within this particular legislation and across the entire Pae Ora legislation, and yet are being silenced in other areas that are key to the successful execution of the Pae Ora legislation itself.
focus.explanation: Argues from named clauses of the bill before the committee to a claim about its effect on Treaty principles. No party characterisation at all; this is scrutiny of a specific measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The other side of the House—and this is the question I put to the Minister—were rather dismissive of the COVID-19 pandemic that hit the world, and one of the key arguments for the case of Te Aka Whai Ora was made by Mr John Tamihere in the timely release of analytical data in order to serve our communities.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point here — the data-release rationale for Te Aka Whai Ora, which bears directly on the 'sufficient and timely information' clause he is questioning. But it is wrapped in a general characterisation of how the other side behaved during the pandemic, which carries no policy content of its own.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: For some of the newer members across the committee, they might not understand how the structure of good health policy in health legislation works.
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed at other members rather than at the substance — a remark about their grasp of the subject, not about the clause. Short of a direct insult and softened by 'might', but it lands on the people rather than the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This, in fact, represents a major centralisation of power here. It represents Ministers taking on a role that was previously devolved to representatives of local communities, who worked hand in glove with organisations like their local councils, their local providers, and their local people on the ground actually seeing and distributing these health services.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: the appointment power for the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee under the bill, and who previously held it. Names a specific mechanism and a specific consequence rather than characterising the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: IMPBs are at different levels of capacity, and we’ve looked at what that will entail to bring them up to a level where they are able to analyse, to collate, to take in local information, to do local analysis of it, to then institute local actions as to how to change it, and then pass it up further for aggregation at regional and other levels, where we can get a wider view across the whole sector.
focus.explanation: Entirely directed at the policy question put to him — the capacity of iwi-Māori partnership boards and how information is meant to move from local to regional level. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This, in fact, represents a major centralisation of power here. It represents Ministers taking on a role that was previously devolved to representatives of local communities, who worked hand in glove with organisations like their local councils, their local providers, and their local people on the ground actually seeing and distributing these health services.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real provision: if the Minister becomes the sole appointer of a body previously appointed in part by others, power has been centralised. The conclusion tracks the premise; the gap is that the 'previously devolved' premise is asserted rather than evidenced here.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Several things: first of all, the legislation clearly uplifts the voice of the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee (HMAC), so a very clear Māori voice there.
rigor.explanation: Circular: the conclusion ('a very clear Māori voice there') simply restates the premise ('the legislation clearly uplifts the voice of HMAC'). No provision, power or mechanism is offered to connect the two, and the question put was precisely how that voice operates once the appointment route through the boards is removed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Secondly, health service monitoring and decision making by iwi-Māori partnership boards (IMPBs) is mana motuhake almost by definition.
rigor.explanation: Definitional fiat — the conclusion is secured by relabelling rather than by argument. That a body monitors services does not by itself establish self-determination; the contested point was what decision-making powers the boards retain, and asserting it holds 'almost by definition' bypasses that rather than answering it.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: My third question to the Minister is about who he intends to appoint to the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee, because under the Minister’s new proposals, he would be the only appointer of eight new members of that committee.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable facts about the text of the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill: that the Minister is the sole appointer of the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee, and that the committee is to have eight members.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill as reported back from the Health Committee in February 2024, and the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 provisions it amends: true if the bill provides for the Minister alone to appoint HMAC members and sets the membership at eight; false if any other body has an appointment role under the bill or the membership number differs.

veracity.statement: Under the new model, there is no legislative backstop for the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee to be able to give proactive advice that the Minister doesn’t like.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the amended legislation contains no provision protecting or requiring the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee's ability to give the Minister unsolicited or unwelcome advice.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill and the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 as it would stand amended: false if any provision requires the Minister to seek, receive or have regard to HMAC advice, or protects HMAC's ability to advise or publish on its own initiative; true if the only statutory provisions are the Minister's power to establish the committee and appoint its members.

veracity.statement: I’d just point out that the process that the legislation talks to is the process now and has been for the past two years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the appointment process for the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee set out in the amendment bill is identical to the process that has operated since the Pae Ora reforms took effect two years earlier — i.e. that ministerial appointment is not a change.
veracity.subject: speaker
