focus.statement: The Minister hasn't answered my question regarding resourcing for localities up into the date of July 2029.
focus.explanation: Presses a named policy question — resourcing of localities out to July 2029 — rather than characterising the government. Legitimate scrutiny of a specific commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I’ve been advised that that terminology copies provisions of existing schedules and the consultation mirrors the Employment Relations Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 'reasonable consultation' wording in clause 43(2) (new Part 2 of Schedule 1) is copied from existing schedules and mirrors the consultation provisions of the Employment Relations Act 2000.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the text of clause 43(2) of the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill as introduced with the consultation provisions of the Employment Relations Act 2000 and with the equivalent schedules of the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022; true if the wording is substantially reproduced from those sources, false if the clause introduces a consultation test not found in them.

veracity.statement: I want to remind the Minister that, in clause 43, it says that Health New Zealand must undertake a reasonable consultation process before introducing any employment policy that is reasonably likely to have a material effect on that employee.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what clause 43 of the bill provides: a duty on Health New Zealand to run a reasonable consultation process before introducing employment policy likely to have a material effect on a transferring employee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Read clause 43 of new Part 2 inserted into Schedule 1 of the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill as introduced; true if it imposes the consultation duty in substantially those terms, false if the duty is absent or materially different.

civility.statement: So I do want to acknowledge the fact—and members opposite might not like the fact that people in electorates are unhappy with this process, and that’s exactly why we’re here tonight at the late hour on their behalf to ask the questions of the Government and to put these issues to the Minister, because they have not had an opportunity out in the community to actually put forward their views.
civility.explanation: Pointed and robust about the use of urgency, but it edges toward the people opposite by suggesting they would rather not hear that constituents are unhappy. Short of imputing bad faith outright, and no individual is attacked.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It doesn’t talk about changing the law—the Employment Relations Act. It talks very specifically about policies that have a material effect on that employee.
rigor.explanation: A valid distinction doing real work: the clause governs employment policy, not the statute, so pointing to the Employment Relations Act does not answer the question asked. The conclusion follows from the premise, though the conclusion is left implicit rather than stated.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So my question to the Minister is: did you talk to the unions? Did you talk to any of the kaimahi? Do you think that it would have been appropriate to talk to your kaimahi Māori who work for Te Aka Whai Ora, who work in the health system, who have the responsibility, the weight, of delivering these health services for our whānau?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: whether the consultation obligation was met before clause 40 transfers Te Aka Whai Ora employees. This is scrutiny of a named clause and a named process, not party-bashing, and it scores at the top.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So it is my proposal to the Minister that, actually, we don’t need this clause in the legislation and we could remove it, and she could be moved, and that we recognise the mana of this woman, and her hapū, her iwi, and her contributions to hauora Māori, and we put her in place as the co-CEO of Te Whatu Ora alongside Margie Apa.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure directly: identifies a specific clause, states what it does, and proposes deleting it and a concrete alternative arrangement. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So my question to the Minister is: did you talk to the unions? Did you talk to any of the kaimahi? Do you think that it would have been appropriate to talk to your kaimahi Māori who work for Te Aka Whai Ora, who work in the health system, who have the responsibility, the weight, of delivering these health services for our whānau?
specificity.explanation: Names the affected workforce, the union relationship and the body being abolished, but the substance is a repeated yes/no question about whether meetings happened — no dates, no numbers, no named consultation process is asked for.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What I’ll say to that is it’s consistent with all of Government data policies—that transfer of information that will accompany the Māori Health Authority.
specificity.explanation: An answer on data probity that names no policy, no safeguard, no agency and no process — 'consistent with all of Government data policies' commits to nothing a member could check or hold him to.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So it is my proposal to the Minister that, actually, we don’t need this clause in the legislation and we could remove it, and she could be moved, and that we recognise the mana of this woman, and her hapū, her iwi, and her contributions to hauora Māori, and we put her in place as the co-CEO of Te Whatu Ora alongside Margie Apa.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause to be removed, the person affected, the role proposed (co-CEO of Te Whatu Ora) and the incumbent she would sit alongside. Actionable as drafted; it lacks only how the co-CEO arrangement would be constituted.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Because it would appear, from the press release put out by the PSA, that that has not happened, and I think that is disgraceful.
civility.explanation: 'Disgraceful' is a hard judgement, but it lands on the Government's decision not to consult, not on the Minister as a person — no imputation about his character, competence or motives. Under the re-anchored scale, brutal criticism of a decision sits near the top.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: To the member who’s just taken her seat, the question she asked at 21.46 last night, questions of timing—already addressed that, thoroughly and multiple times during this debate, so I don’t envisage going there again.
civility.explanation: Pointed and dismissive — time-stamping the member's earlier question and declining to engage carries a note of condescension — but it stops at the conduct of the debate and does not attack her character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So it is my proposal to the Minister that, actually, we don’t need this clause in the legislation and we could remove it, and she could be moved, and that we recognise the mana of this woman, and her hapū, her iwi, and her contributions to hauora Māori, and we put her in place as the co-CEO of Te Whatu Ora alongside Margie Apa.
civility.explanation: Opposing the abolition of a body she supports, in an urgency debate, she attacks nobody — the criticism stays on the clause and the remainder is directed at what she proposes instead.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It turns out, in further discussion with officials, that there are certainly clear precedents for the five-year period. I won’t read through a range of legislation which has review periods of five years.
rigor.explanation: An argument about a real policy choice — the 2029 locality-plan date is justified because five-year review periods are precedented — but the support is an appeal to unnamed authority: officials said so, and the precedent legislation is explicitly not identified. civility.statement: It is bad enough that we are getting rid of the Māori Health Authority—or rather, the Minister, this Government, is getting rid of the Māori Health Authority—but let us not amplify the harm on those who are most vulnerable within that system, which includes that community of our tāngata whaikaha.
civility.explanation: Strong condemnation of the policy and a self-correction to attribute it to the Government rather than to 'we'. Attacks the decision, imputes nothing to any person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: “Te Aka Whai Ora”—doesn’t even have the guts to put it in the title.
civility.explanation: Moves off the drafting point onto the Minister's personal courage. Short of a sustained insult, but it is an attack on the man rather than on the decision.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Well, if you have a look at the 100-day plan, there’s 49 actions. In those actions, the word “introduce” is mentioned eight times and the word “begin” is mentioned 10 times.
veracity.explanation: Three countable assertions about the coalition Government's published 100-day plan: that it contains 49 actions, that 'introduce' appears eight times in them, and that 'begin' appears ten times.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National-led coalition Government's published 100-day plan (released December 2023): count the listed actions and the occurrences of the words 'introduce' and 'begin' within them. True if 49 actions with 8 and 10 occurrences respectively; false if the counts differ materially.

veracity.statement: It is saying that it’s OK for Māori to die seven years before non-Māori.
veracity.explanation: Rests on the factual premise that Māori life expectancy is about seven years shorter than non-Māori life expectancy in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ period life tables / Ministry of Health life expectancy at birth by ethnicity for the most recent published period: true if the Māori / non-Māori gap is approximately seven years, false if it differs materially (e.g. under five or over nine years).

rigor.statement: He could have introduced it through urgency to have its first reading, and sent it to the select committee, but he chose not to despite the 100-day plan saying “introduce” the legislation.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real procedural choice: the plan's own word is 'introduce', so passing all stages under urgency goes beyond what was committed. The gap is that 'introduce' does not on its own preclude proceeding further, so the conclusion is supported but not compelled.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It was a recommendation of the Waitangi Tribunal that we establish a Māori health authority.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a Waitangi Tribunal report recommended establishing a Māori health authority, offered as justification for the body being disestablished.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal's Hauora report (Wai 2575, stage one, 2019) and any subsequent stage findings: true if the Tribunal recommended establishment of a stand-alone Māori health authority/commissioning agency; false if no such recommendation appears in its reports.

veracity.statement: But, no, we’re rushing it through today, because, as I said last night, there’s something taking place, or should have been taking place, tomorrow: a planeload of the Minister’s relations are coming down to present to the Waitangi Tribunal their submissions—their opposition—on the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora—his own hapū, Te Kapotai, a named claimant in that urgency hearing to take place tomorrow.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three checkable facts: that a Waitangi Tribunal urgent hearing on the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora was scheduled for 28 February 2024, that Te Kapotai is a named claimant in it, and that Te Kapotai is the Minister's (Shane Reti's) own hapū.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal's urgent inquiry record into the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora (Wai 3307) — hearing schedule for late February 2024 and the register of named claimants; plus Shane Reti's stated hapū affiliations. True if a hearing was set for 28 February 2024 with Te Kapotai among the claimants and Reti affiliated to Te Kapotai; false if the hearing was not scheduled then, Te Kapotai was not a claimant, or Reti has no such affiliation.

veracity.statement: Just to speak to why Te Aka Whai Ora doesn’t appear in the title, it’s because it doesn’t appear in the Pae Ora legislation either and the amendment bill has to refer to the legal title in the statute.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the term 'Te Aka Whai Ora' does not appear anywhere in the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022, which establishes the body as the 'Māori Health Authority'.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 as enacted, on legislation.govt.nz: true if the string 'Te Aka Whai Ora' does not appear and the entity is named 'Māori Health Authority'; false if the te reo name appears in the Act.

veracity.statement: So I reflect on the 4,685 submitters to the Pae Ora legislation, who took the time to provide their local voice, their hapū, their whānau, their marae, their community voice, the health providers who contributed to the building blocks of Pae Ora.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count of submitters — 4,685 — on the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Bill during its select committee stage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Health Committee's report on the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Bill (2021–22) and the published submissions record: true if the number of submissions received is 4,685 or rounds to it, false if materially different.

specificity.statement: But when we look at the commencement date, this isn’t actually going to commence until 30 June.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise commencement date for the bill under debate; anyone could check it against the bill's commencement clause. Detail is carried by a scrutiny question, not an announcement.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That would have allowed ample time, in your rushed processes, to have a select committee process, to stop and do some consultation.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: if the Act does not take effect for four months, the interval was available for select committee scrutiny. The conclusion tracks the premise, though it treats available time as the only consideration bearing on urgency, leaving a modest gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It leaves us with no other conclusion except that this has been done deliberately to undermine the Waitangi Tribunal, to undermine the Minister’s own relations, who are named claimants in that claim.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy built on an argument from absence: because the Crown did not file notice, the speaker concludes there is 'no other conclusion' but deliberate undermining. Competing explanations (a 100-day plan timetable, ordinary legislative scheduling) are not ruled out, only unmentioned.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Just to speak to why Te Aka Whai Ora doesn’t appear in the title, it’s because it doesn’t appear in the Pae Ora legislation either and the amendment bill has to refer to the legal title in the statute.
rigor.explanation: Premise (the te reo name is not the statutory title) plus a drafting rule (an amendment bill must use the legal title) yield the conclusion directly. Whether the premise is true is a separate question.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It leaves us with no other conclusion except that this has been done deliberately to undermine the Waitangi Tribunal, to undermine the Minister’s own relations, who are named claimants in that claim.
civility.explanation: Imputes deliberate bad faith to the Minister — that he timed the bill to sabotage a tribunal hearing involving his own hapū. Short of a direct insult, but an accusation about motive rather than about the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Did you think that five minutes was a waste of time, Mr Bayly?
civility.explanation: A sneering rhetorical question aimed at a named member in response to his interjection. Not an insult to his character, but it turns from the bill to the person and is delivered as mockery.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So my plea is to the Government to consider the legislation that they are rushing through urgency for their 100-day plan, to give the people of New Zealand a chance.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism of the Government's use of urgency in a genuinely contested debate where she had every opportunity to attack the Minister personally, and does not. The target is the process, not any person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And I know the Minister will feel it in some sense; it’s a sensitive kaupapa that we are debating in this Chamber in urgency, and I know that he does have a heart and, as a health practitioner himself, he certainly will be looking with interest in this.
civility.explanation: In the middle of an opposed urgency debate, credits the Minister's good faith and professional background before pressing the disagreement. Engages the substance and attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Don’t use our reo when it suits; just go down the track that you’ve been going down—that the Government’s been going down—and call it what it is.
civility.explanation: Sneering and imputing bad faith to the Minister and the Government — that they invoke te reo only opportunistically. Short of a personal insult, but it is directed at motive rather than at the merits of the title, so it falls below the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: They are making changes everywhere; some of our Māori language speakers out there are not going to be compensated for their expertise in terms of te reo Māori, so they should be true to that and put a title up that encapsulates the philosophy of this Government at the moment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government has removed or is removing pay recognition for te reo Māori expertise among public sector staff.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public Service Commission guidance and public sector collective agreements from late 2023 to 2024: true if te reo Māori proficiency allowances or equivalent payments were withdrawn or ruled out for affected staff; false if those allowances remained in place unchanged.

veracity.statement: I was the Minister who appointed many of these tribunal members over the previous three years; many of them are good Pākehā people like Professor David Williams, who has been an advocate for kaupapa Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as Minister (Māori Development, 2020–2023) he was responsible for recommending the appointment of many sitting Waitangi Tribunal members, David Williams among them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Gazette appointment notices for Waitangi Tribunal members 2020–2023 and the portfolio responsible for recommending them: true if a substantial share of current members were appointed on the recommendation of the Minister for Māori Development while Jackson held the portfolio and David Williams is among the Tribunal's members; false if the appointments were made under a different Minister or Williams was not a member.

veracity.statement: Because we are pushing this through under urgency, we don’t have that select committee process, and there are matters that could normally be considered.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill is being passed under urgency and has therefore had no select committee stage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The House's order paper and Hansard record for the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill: true if urgency was accorded and the bill was not referred to a select committee; false if the bill received a select committee referral or was not taken under urgency.

focus.statement: So I ask the Minister: why the rush? Why couldn’t we wait a couple of days to show the due respect to a tribunal that has been very much a part of our people’s lives?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee — the 30 June commencement date — and names a concrete alternative (a delay of two days) tied to the Waitangi Tribunal's inquiry. No party-bashing content.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Yes, they’ll be doing it, but they’ll be doing it after the event.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Waitangi Tribunal's consideration of the disestablishment of the Māori Health Authority will be completed only after the legislation has taken effect, rather than in time to influence it.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The publication date of the Waitangi Tribunal's report on the disestablishment of the Māori Health Authority, compared with the commencement of the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Act: true if the report is released after that commencement date; false if the Tribunal reported before the Act took effect.

specificity.statement: My amendment would move the commencement date from 30 June 2024 to 30 June 2025.
specificity.explanation: A named mechanism (her Amendment Paper) with the exact provision changed and both dates stated. Anyone could check it against the Amendment Paper or act on it directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What that would do would allow health officials and others who assess it—like the Treasury, for example—to be able to look at that accountability documentation that providers are currently working on and assess it and determine if this bill actually needs to be put in place, or if there are other changes we would potentially like to make to it.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: providers are completing accountability documents now, so deferring commencement makes that evidence available before the decision is locked in. The step from 'officials could look at it' to 'the bill may prove unnecessary' is left implicit and assumes the assessment would be acted on, which is a genuine gap, but the conclusion largely tracks what was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill is taking away that right of self-determination for Māori in terms of their health.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the measure before the House and what it does, with no party framing or characterisation of opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I agree with the suggestion from the Hon Peeni Henare that the name should be changed to “Pae Mate”, and that Te Aka Whai Ora should be referenced in the title.
focus.explanation: Engages the amendment actually before the committee — the bill's title — and names the specific wording sought, rather than talking about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We can choose form or function; I choose function. We can choose activism or actions; I choose actions. We can choose outrage or outcomes; I choose outcomes.
focus.explanation: A closing flourish whose whole content is a contrast between his side and how he characterises the other — "activism", "outrage". No policy, figure or outcome is named; strip out the implied characterisation of opponents and nothing about the health system remains. Scored here and not under Rigor, because a rhetorical contrast is not an argument.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is what brings me to the suggestion of Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke that this should be called the “Tohunga Suppression Act 2.0”, because what it does is it fails to recognise that Māori have their own mātauranga, have their own knowledge and systems of understanding how best to apply health to their people. When they had free rein to do it, they had the most excellent health that could be observed.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that Māori health was excellent under self-determination rests entirely on a single 1770 observation by one European visitor — appeal to anecdote plus hasty generalisation from one datapoint to a general claim about a system of care.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One of the fundamental differences in approach is enabled by this legislation: this Government believes that decisions should be made closer to the home and hapū. Local circumstances require local solutions rather than national bureaucracies.
rigor.explanation: A false dichotomy: local delivery and a national body are presented as mutually exclusive when they are not, and no reason is offered for why local circumstances rule out a national agency. The premise is asserted rather than supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The context also for this, Mr Chair—and I realise you’ve asked me to keep it tight, so I will—is that underlying the logic behind the removal of the Māori Health Authority is the snake oil equality concept that for us to be more equal we have to take away the rights of another group, and the group from whom we’re taking the rights is the group who have the supposed privilege of dying seven years younger than non-Māori, of having twice the rate of cardiovascular disease of non-Māori; who have the privilege of having child health impacts at 1.5 times the rate of non-Māori.
veracity.explanation: Three quantified disparity claims: Māori die roughly seven years younger than non-Māori, have twice the rate of cardiovascular disease, and have child health impacts at 1.5 times the non-Māori rate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ period life-expectancy tables by ethnicity and Ministry of Health / Te Whatu Ora ethnicity-disaggregated cardiovascular and child-health indicator data for the period around February 2024; true if the life-expectancy gap is approximately seven years, the Māori cardiovascular rate is about double the non-Māori rate, and child health measures are about 1.5 times; false if any figure is materially off (e.g. a gap nearer three years, or CVD parity).

veracity.statement: As I’ve said before, when we focus on need, we very quickly find that it is Māori who have the greatest need in most areas of health.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that across most areas of health, Māori are the ethnic group with the greatest measured need in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Te Whatu Ora ethnicity-disaggregated indicator sets current at February 2024 (amenable mortality, life expectancy, chronic disease prevalence, unmet need, cancer and cardiovascular outcomes); true if Māori rank worst among ethnic groups on a majority of the major indicators, false if another group — most plausibly Pacific peoples — ranks worst on more of them.

specificity.statement: The context also for this, Mr Chair—and I realise you’ve asked me to keep it tight, so I will—is that underlying the logic behind the removal of the Māori Health Authority is the snake oil equality concept that for us to be more equal we have to take away the rights of another group, and the group from whom we’re taking the rights is the group who have the supposed privilege of dying seven years younger than non-Māori, of having twice the rate of cardiovascular disease of non-Māori; who have the privilege of having child health impacts at 1.5 times the rate of non-Māori.
specificity.explanation: Carries three checkable quantities — a seven-year life expectancy gap, a 2x cardiovascular rate, a 1.5x child health rate — each tied to a named comparison group.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We will be setting clear health targets to drive improved outcomes, but I want to be very clear that we will be setting ambitious targets that will take some time and resources to meet.
specificity.explanation: Announces targets while naming none: no measure, no number, no date, and the caveat about "some time and resources" removes even a rough timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I want to reiterate some of the key changes in this narrow bill: (1) Māori Health Authority staff are to transfer to Health New Zealand and the Ministry of Health—this will retain a focus on Māori health and retain organisational knowledge, including any gains that have been achieved—(2) uplifting of the Māori Health Advisory Committee into advisory and monitoring roles; (3) uplifting of iwi-Māori partnership boards, enhancing their relationship with local communities; and (4) pausing of the schedule for localities while we reconsider their place.
specificity.explanation: Four named mechanisms with named bodies and named destinations — staff transfer, committee role change, partnership board uplift, localities pause. Verifiable against the bill; short of full marks only for carrying no figures or dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I want to reiterate that I believe we all have the same dream for the health system: we all want to address health inequities, we all want to shorten waiting lists, and we all want a workforce that isn’t overstretched and that has the right skills to respond effectively to all our diverse populations.
civility.explanation: Closing a bitterly contested urgency debate in which his bill had just been called the "Tohunga Suppression Act 2.0", he attributes good motives to opponents and attacks nobody. A real opportunity to be uncivil, declined.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The authority’s progress report found that concerns were raised about staff transfers not being focused on skills and expertise but, instead, on taking Māori staff from Te Whatu Ora.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a specific document — the Māori Health Authority's own progress report — records concerns that staff transfers were driven by ethnicity rather than skills and expertise.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published Te Aka Whai Ora / Māori Health Authority progress or performance report current at February 2024; true if it records concerns that staff transfers from Te Whatu Ora were made on the basis of Māori staff rather than skills and expertise, false if it contains no such finding.

veracity.statement: Removing the authority did not remove provision for the Government to engage and consult with Māori on Māori matters.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Bill leaves the statutory engagement and consultation obligations toward Māori intact even though it disestablishes the authority.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 as amended by the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill; true if engagement/consultation mechanisms (iwi-Māori partnership boards, the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee, Te Tiriti obligations in the Act) survive the amendment, false if the Bill repeals them.

veracity.statement: My leader, the Rt Hon Winston Peters, has always, in fact, been an opponent of the Māori Health Authority as a separatist, bureaucratic behemoth.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a consistent public record: that Winston Peters has opposed the Māori Health Authority throughout its existence, not merely since the 2023 election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Winston Peters' recorded statements and NZ First policy documents from the authority's creation in 2022 onward; true if he opposed it publicly and continuously from its inception, false if there is a period in which he supported it or took no position.

veracity.statement: They won’t listen, and why would they listen when 83 percent of Māori did not support this Government?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure: that 83 percent of Māori did not vote for the parties now in government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: 2023 general election party-vote results for the seven Māori electorates / Māori electoral roll, published by the Electoral Commission; true if the combined party vote for National, ACT and NZ First among Māori roll voters is approximately 17 percent or less, false if materially higher.

veracity.statement: The beauty of it is that 70 percent of the population of Māori are under the age of 40, and you come from parties where your population aren’t procreating and you aren’t getting any younger.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a demographic figure: that 70 percent of the Māori population is aged under 40.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census / population estimates for the Māori ethnic group by age band; true if the share aged under 40 is approximately 70 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The Minister has guaranteed that the solution this Government promises will be better then what Māori designed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister of Health gave a guarantee — not merely an aspiration — that the replacement arrangements will outperform the Māori Health Authority.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard record of the Minister of Health's speeches on the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill; true if he gave an unqualified guarantee of better outcomes than the authority, false if his statements were aspirational or qualified.

civility.statement: But the Māori Health Authority provided another level of bureaucracy, another central government organisation that was failing to prove its worth.
civility.explanation: A blunt dismissal of an institution's value on genuinely contested legislation. It attacks no individual, imputes no bad faith, and stays on the organisation rather than the people who built it — the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Digest your racism well. Make sure it goes into your puku and sits heavy.
civility.explanation: Directed at a named member and imputing racism to him personally. This lands squarely on the person's character rather than on the bill or the Government's policy; the Speaker sought an apology for it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I want to thank the Minister of Health for nothing, actually.
civility.explanation: A sarcastic inversion of the customary thanks, aimed at the Minister personally rather than at the bill. Short of a direct insult, but it is mockery of a person and no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: ACT believes in localism and in empowering communities and that healthcare delivers on needs, not race.
specificity.explanation: A string of party principles — localism, empowerment, need not race — with no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named measure. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We will retain the iwi-Māori partnership boards, we want to empower them, we want to work with local communities, and we—as the Minister stated—believe local situations require local solutions.
specificity.explanation: One concrete commitment (retaining the iwi-Māori partnership boards) surrounded by wants and beliefs. No account of what 'empower' means in powers, funding or statute, and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Why would it not be struggling? When you have a previous Government, during a pandemic, with once-in-a-generation health reforms, of course it was going to be struggling.
rigor.explanation: A real causal inference about a real policy — large structural reforms attempted during a pandemic will strain the system. But the conclusion is carried by 'of course' rather than by any evidence linking the reforms to the current strain, and no alternative causes are addressed. A reasonable point with a gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This next layer of bureaucracy has actually failed to deliver Māori health gain. Where are the outcomes? We have not seen any from this.
rigor.explanation: Argument from absence of evidence: not having seen outcomes is offered as proof that none exist, with no account of what outcomes were promised, on what timetable, or whether an entity roughly eighteen months old could yet have produced them.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What we have is a Minister here who admits that the iwi-Māori partnership boards need to be powered up; there was no when, there was no how; that we have a mass of data to be collected; there was no when, there was no how; that we have locality plans that need to be worked on; there was no when, there was no how; that we have regional empowerment strategies, but there was no when, there was no how.
focus.explanation: Names four specific policy instruments the Minister has offered as replacements — iwi-Māori partnership boards, data collection, locality plans, regional empowerment strategies — and holds each to the same test of timing and mechanism. This is scrutiny of a named commitment, the job of an opposition MP, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: You are politicians on the eve of legacy parties, and you will not come back. You will not get a second chance at doing this.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the parties of the current coalition will not be returned to office at the next election and so will have no further opportunity to pursue this policy programme.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The result of the next New Zealand general election as declared by the Electoral Commission; true if National, ACT and NZ First do not together form the next Government, false if the coalition parties are returned to government.

civility.statement: In fact, the depth is so shallow that the dissatisfaction on this side of the House with the answers and the explanations given by the Minister and this Government shows that the depth of thinking in this action was not there.
civility.explanation: Moves off the bill's substance and onto the Minister's mind — 'the depth of thinking was not there' is condescension about his capacity rather than criticism of the policy. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It flies in the face of years and generations of work through the tribunal, good work through different shades of Government over decades, and it’s absolutely shameful, the handling of this bill.
civility.explanation: 'Absolutely shameful' is about as hard as criticism gets, and every word of it lands on the handling of the bill rather than on any member. Under the re-anchored scale, fierce condemnation of a process is the civil standard, not a deduction. He explicitly credits governments of all stripes, which pulls it further from the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Yet we have a Government that doesn’t care—it doesn’t care about the institution of Te Aka Whai Ora and this māreikura Riana Manuel who will lose her job, and where will she fit as the leader that she is in hauora Māori?
civility.explanation: The charge of indifference is levelled at 'a Government', not at any individual member; no person is insulted, sneered at or condescended to. Attacking the other side collectively is Focus's business, not Civility's, and the sentence is scored high here accordingly.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In fact, the depth is so shallow that the dissatisfaction on this side of the House with the answers and the explanations given by the Minister and this Government shows that the depth of thinking in this action was not there.
rigor.explanation: A stated inference with a real gap: that the Opposition is dissatisfied with the Minister's answers is offered as proof that the Government did not think. Opponents' dissatisfaction is close to guaranteed and is not evidence about the quality of the Government's reasoning — an appeal to his own side's disagreement. He is engaging the bill's passage, not merely characterising opponents, so this is a rigor item and not only a focus one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Dr Reti has said he is focused on priorities and targets. The statistics in health for Māori clearly state a case, then, that there will be increased funding from this Government for Māori health outcomes.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur, and an ought-to-is leap: from the Minister's stated focus on priorities plus disparity statistics, the conclusion drawn is that funding will in fact increase. The statistics may show funding ought to rise; nothing offered shows this Government will make it rise. Scored on the inference only — whether the underlying statistics are accurate is Veracity's question.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I heard from a cousin last night who works in Te Whatu Ora, and he shared how hard it was working in mainstream, being the one Māori in the team, and the battle it is for him to articulate ao Māori perspectives in a mainstream machine that really considers us all New Zealanders. Yet on our wards we need whānau who can care, and that’s why I think our kaimahi from Te Aka Whai Ora are so important.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote. A single second-hand account from one relative is the whole of the evidence offered for the general conclusion that Te Aka Whai Ora staff are needed on the wards; nothing is offered to show the experience is representative, and the anecdote concerns Te Whatu Ora rather than the agency being defended. It is a real inference about the measure before the House, badly supported — not a jibe at opponents.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Just because you campaigned on a kaupapa, doesn’t mean that te iwi Māori gives you the whakaae [permission] to go ahead and disestablish this institution of rangatiratanga hauora Māori nei [Māori health sovereignty].
rigor.explanation: A genuine rebuttal of the electoral-mandate argument: winning a general election on a platform is not the same as consent from a particular group, and the distinction holds. It falls short of the top because the further premise it needs — that Māori consent is separately required for this decision — is asserted rather than argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Dr Reti has said he is focused on priorities and targets. The statistics in health for Māori clearly state a case, then, that there will be increased funding from this Government for Māori health outcomes.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that this Government will increase funding directed at Māori health outcomes. A prediction about the Government's future budget decisions, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Vote Health estimates of appropriations for 2024/25 and 2025/26 compared with 2023/24: true if appropriations directed to Māori health outcomes rose in nominal terms under this Government, false if they were held flat or reduced.

veracity.statement: This House will be looking to the other side of the House, that Government, who are intent on austerity and cuts in the public sector and health services in order to make a tax cut for New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government is cutting public sector and health service spending, and that the purpose of those cuts is to fund a personal income tax reduction.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents and the Government's public sector savings targets: true if public sector and health service baselines were reduced and the identified savings were applied to the personal income tax package; false if health service funding rose in real terms or the tax package was funded from other sources.

veracity.statement: There is no privilege in dying seven years earlier—show me where that privilege is.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori die roughly seven years earlier than other New Zealanders — a life expectancy gap of about seven years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ period life tables (most recent available at February 2024) comparing life expectancy at birth for Māori and non-Māori: true if the gap is approximately seven years, false if materially smaller or larger.

veracity.statement: There is no privilege for a higher death rate of lung cancer by Māori women—there is no privilege in that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori women have a higher lung cancer death rate than other women in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Te Whatu Ora cancer mortality statistics by ethnicity and sex: true if the age-standardised lung cancer mortality rate for Māori women exceeds that for non-Māori women, false if it is equal or lower.

veracity.statement: The Minister and this Government gave the Māori Health Authority 18 months—18 months—to see whether or not they could turn around decades of inequities—decades of inequities—and I can guarantee that Minister and this Government that our people can’t wait.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Aka Whai Ora was given 18 months of operation before being wound up. The checkable element is the duration, measured from the authority's establishment to the disestablishment date set by this bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The commencement date for Te Aka Whai Ora under the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 (1 July 2022) against the disestablishment date set by this bill (30 June 2024): true if the interval is approximately 18 months, false if materially longer or shorter.

veracity.statement: And when I see a blatant disregard for the people of New Zealand and te iwi Māori, to shut us out, to have an opinion on such an important piece of legislation—4,685 submitters contributed towards Pae Ora, and now, within a matter of hours, maybe a day and a half, we see the end of half of what Pae Ora set out to do.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific submission count — 4,685 submitters — on the legislation that established Pae Ora, contrasted with the time taken to repeal part of it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Health Committee's report on the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Bill 2021: true if the number of submissions received was 4,685 or rounds to it, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The general health system has not improved Māori health outcomes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the mainstream health system has produced no improvement in Māori health outcomes. Read as a claim about absolute outcomes over time, not about the size of the gap with non-Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ and Ministry of Health Māori health indicators over the two decades to 2023 — Māori life expectancy at birth, Māori amenable mortality rate, Māori immunisation coverage: true if these show no improvement, false if they improved in absolute terms even where the gap with non-Māori persisted.

veracity.statement: They confirmed that their jurisdiction had now ended; that they could not hold the urgent inquiry into the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on the evening of 26 February 2024 the Waitangi Tribunal ruled it no longer had jurisdiction and vacated the urgent inquiry into the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal memoranda and directions on the Te Aka Whai Ora urgency application issued on or about 26 February 2024: true if the Tribunal vacated the urgent hearing on the ground that its jurisdiction had ended, false if the hearing was vacated on other grounds or not vacated.

veracity.statement: They are not a bureaucracy. Less than 300 kaimahi e tātou mā.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Aka Whai Ora employed fewer than 300 staff.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Aka Whai Ora's 2022/23 annual report or Public Service Commission workforce data: true if headcount or FTE is below 300, false if 300 or more.

specificity.statement: The Minister and this Government gave the Māori Health Authority 18 months—18 months—to see whether or not they could turn around decades of inequities—decades of inequities—and I can guarantee that Minister and this Government that our people can’t wait.
specificity.explanation: Names the body, gives a duration, and states what it was expected to achieve — enough for someone to check the timeframe. Loses the top of the scale because 'turn around decades of inequities' is not operationalised into any measure or target.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We will be holding this Government to account to make sure that their words around prioritising and focusing the spend and the energy of the health sector to where it’s needed the most will actually be delivered upon.
specificity.explanation: Genuinely trying to convey a commitment, but carries no checkable content: no measure, no figure, no mechanism for holding to account, and no date. 'Where it's needed the most' commits to nothing anyone could verify against.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Even when those around him seem intent on pulling him down, the ask is that he fights like a shark for our people.
focus.explanation: The substance here is a claim about the internal state of the governing side — that the Minister's own colleagues are undermining him. No provision, cost, timeframe or outcome of the bill is named. There is a sliver of policy direction in the appeal itself, so it is not a floor score, but the weight is on the other team's internal dynamics.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yet we have a Government that doesn’t care—it doesn’t care about the institution of Te Aka Whai Ora and this māreikura Riana Manuel who will lose her job, and where will she fit as the leader that she is in hauora Māori?
focus.explanation: Names a concrete consequence of the bill — the abolition of the agency and the chief executive losing her position — but the load-bearing claim is about the Government's character rather than about any provision, cost or outcome. A real policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m sorry, but I’m withdrawing Māori membership from those Māori members on the other side—you don’t deserve to be part of what we’re doing.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the identity and worth of named individuals opposite — purporting to strip them of their Māori membership and telling them they do not deserve to belong. Nothing here engages the bill; it goes at the persons.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They can get all the support from their Pākehā journalist friends, who think they do wonderful maiden speeches, but they have no standing—no standing—in te ao Māori.
civility.explanation: A personal attack on the standing and credibility of individual members, with a sneer at who supports them. Contested territory where he could have criticised their votes instead.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Dr Reti, like Peeni Henare, is someone who I’ve respected through the years, but he has let his whānau down and he has let his whakapapa down today.
civility.explanation: Tempered by genuine respect, but it lands on the person rather than the policy: a named Minister is said to have failed his family and his ancestry. Personal character, not the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We’re remodelling the COVID inquiry into an anti-vax circus for Winston’s crazy conspiracy mates.
civility.explanation: Names an individual and derides his associates as crazy conspiracists — mockery aimed at people rather than at the inquiry's revised terms of reference.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Need and race go together, and the reality is that that member has no idea what she’s talking about, as her leader has used the race argument to advance himself and his “Māori party”.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on an individual member's competence — 'no idea what she's talking about' — plus an imputation of self-serving motive to her leader. The underlying need-versus-race question could have been contested without either.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We have no options; we have to engage with these mongrels.
civility.explanation: Straightforward abuse of the members opposite. He withdrew it immediately when told it was unparliamentary, but the remark was made.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: National don’t want any scrutiny of public health vandalism, basically, because they’re cowards—there’s no doubt about it.
focus.explanation: No policy, figure or mechanism is named — the content is a characterisation of what National are like as a party. The insult is aimed at a party rather than an individual, so Civility passes it; this is precisely the tribalism Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’re remodelling the COVID inquiry into an anti-vax circus for Winston’s crazy conspiracy mates.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy referent (changes to the COVID-19 inquiry), but no term of reference, cost or mechanism is engaged; the weight of the sentence is on who the other side's allies are.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Māori Health Authority gave us the bureaucratic muscle to ensure Māori health outcomes mattered, but this new, reactionary Government has turned the whole debate into a health apartheid narrative.
focus.explanation: A genuine point about what the body before the House actually did, wrapped in party framing about what this 'reactionary Government' is like. Half substance, half characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There will be another day when this useless, pathetic Government has to stand down.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side's general worth and eventual removal; no policy, figure or outcome is named. The abuse is aimed at a government rather than a person, so Civility is untouched.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Regardless of organisational form, this remains, and it needs to be addressed to make sure we have better health outcomes for Māori, and also non-Māori.
focus.explanation: Directed at the substance of the measure — whether the organisational form is what determines outcomes — rather than at the other party. Vague, but on-policy; this is the Focus-high, Specificity-low pairing.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: There will be 8,000 deaths—8,000 deaths—from dumping smoke-free amendments.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a specific mortality outcome — 8,000 additional deaths — flowing from the repeal of the smokefree tobacco amendments. Not a promise about his own action, and not a claim about the present.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Peer-reviewed modelling and Ministry of Health / Stats NZ smoking-attributable mortality data following the repeal of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022; true if the additional deaths attributable to the repeal are estimated at or above roughly 8,000, false if materially lower (e.g. an order-of-magnitude or half that figure).

specificity.statement: There will be 8,000 deaths—8,000 deaths—from dumping smoke-free amendments.
specificity.explanation: Carries a hard figure and names the policy change it is attributed to, which is checkable against the published modelling. Docked for having no timeframe over which the deaths accrue and no source given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have an obligation as a Parliament to pass legislation that helps and enables our people.
specificity.explanation: A general standard with no measure, mechanism, threshold or outcome attached — nothing here could be checked or acted on. Squarely on the topic, but carrying almost no content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Regardless of organisational form, this remains, and it needs to be addressed to make sure we have better health outcomes for Māori, and also non-Māori.
specificity.explanation: A statement of desired outcome with no target, measure, timeframe or mechanism — 'better health outcomes' commits to nothing checkable, even though the sentence is genuinely trying to convey a position.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We have aspirin, which we have taken from the Greeks; we have quinine, which we have taken from the Peruvians; and we take the best to make sure our doctors and nurses can provide the best for their patients, regardless of where it’s coming from. Therefore, that’s why I commend this bill to the House.
rigor.explanation: An explicit inference — 'therefore' — from an analogy that does not carry it. That medicines were adopted from other cultures says nothing about whether a dedicated Māori commissioning agency should be disestablished; the premises and the conclusion are about different things. Non sequitur by false analogy.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We have aspirin, which we have taken from the Greeks; we have quinine, which we have taken from the Peruvians; and we take the best to make sure our doctors and nurses can provide the best for their patients, regardless of where it’s coming from. Therefore, that’s why I commend this bill to the House.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the historical origins of two medicines: that aspirin derives from Greek practice and quinine from Peru.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Standard history-of-medicine references on salicylate and cinchona; true if willow-bark salicylate use is attributed to ancient Greek medicine (Hippocratic writings) and quinine's source, cinchona bark, to Peru/the Andes, false if either origin is attributed elsewhere.

veracity.statement: Today, some in this House will have to go back to their marae to tell them that they are returning their whānau back to a system where our people die seven years earlier than their non-Māori counterparts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori die seven years earlier than non-Māori — a claim about the current life-expectancy gap by ethnicity.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / Ministry of Health life expectancy at birth by ethnicity for the most recent period published before February 2024; true if the Māori vs non-Māori gap is approximately seven years, false if materially smaller or larger.

civility.statement: The blood of their tūpuna will stain their hands for ever.
civility.explanation: Moves off the policy and onto the members who voted for it, imputing lasting personal moral guilt for deaths. Short of a direct insult but well past pointed.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I wonder if the doctors in this House who have supported the disestablishment of the Māori Health Authority today have abandoned their ethical principles that they were once asked to uphold as medical professionals—to act with integrity and in the best interests of their patients.
civility.explanation: Targets identifiable individuals (the doctors in the House) and imputes abandonment of professional ethics and indifference to Māori patients — an attack on their character rather than on the bill.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: How morally bankrupt do you have to become to sell out your own people and communities for a couple of trinkets and baubles of political office and a bit of a campaign clickbait?
civility.explanation: Direct attack on the character and motives of other members — 'morally bankrupt', 'sell out your own people' for personal advancement. Contemptuous, not merely robust.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is unfair, it is disgraceful, and every Māori on that side of the House, every member of this Government, should hang their heads in shame.
civility.explanation: Turns on named groups of members personally — calling their conduct disgraceful and demanding shame — rather than continuing the criticism of the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It should be a timely reminder for all people that it might be our health sovereignty and opportunities they are stealing today. But rest assured, they are coming for yours tomorrow.
rigor.explanation: Slippery slope: nothing is offered to connect the disestablishment of one agency to a general future removal of everyone else's rights. The inference rests entirely on the assertion itself.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We have seen outcomes—and tell me of a structural shift in this country’s history in Aotearoa New Zealand where we have measured the achievements and results within only 12 months, but we only do this to Māori.
rigor.explanation: A real argument — that a 12-month evaluation window is not the standard applied to other structural reforms, so judging this one on it is inconsistent. But the supporting premise is a rhetorical challenge rather than any cited comparison, leaving a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Te Aka Whai Ora—the Māori Health Authority—was never really equipped to undo the health inequities for Māori. Those gaps are huge, and the responsibility lies much further outside the health system.
rigor.explanation: The premise offered — that the determinants of Māori health inequity sit largely outside the health system — does bear on the conclusion, but nothing is offered to show the authority could not have moved the share that does sit inside health. The step from 'not sufficient' to 'never really equipped' is asserted.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I believe that this change is needed because the only symbolism that I remember was the two waka lashed together—really, those two lashed together.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the stated reason the change is needed is that the speaker only remembers a piece of symbolism. Nothing about the agency's function, cost or results is offered to support the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s a chance for Māori to make meaningful decisions about improving their health outcomes through commissioning the services they need, delivered in a way that they want rather than have the same stale ideas rammed down their throats by the greatest pack of bureaucrats that we have ever seen—the other side of the House.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point about the commissioning function of Te Aka Whai Ora, but the sentence resolves into a generalised jibe at the other side of the House rather than the mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We have seen outcomes—and tell me of a structural shift in this country’s history in Aotearoa New Zealand where we have measured the achievements and results within only 12 months, but we only do this to Māori.
focus.explanation: Engages the substantive question of how and when the agency's performance should be assessed, rather than the other party's general character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Te Aka Whai Ora—the Māori Health Authority—was never really equipped to undo the health inequities for Māori. Those gaps are huge, and the responsibility lies much further outside the health system.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House and what it could achieve; no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The strength of Te Aka Whai Ora lies in its independence from the Crown and its ability to provide coordinated and independent Māori-focused advice, policy, advocacy, and commission, and one year in we have seen incremental change.
specificity.explanation: Offered as the rebuttal to 'it didn't deliver anything', so it is trying to convey substance, but supplies only categories of activity and 'incremental change' — no programme, figure, service or outcome anyone could check.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s for the entire economy, and it’s for all of our Government to take note of those inequities because we can’t fix them within health alone; it has to be done across the board.
specificity.explanation: Offered as the alternative to the agency being abolished, but names no policy, agency, mechanism, funding or timeframe — 'across the board' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Those strong Māori health providers will still be working for Māori health, and everybody in the health system will be doing the same.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Māori health providers commissioned under Te Aka Whai Ora continue delivering Māori health services after the authority is disestablished.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Health NZ / Te Whatu Ora commissioning and contract records for providers formerly commissioned by Te Aka Whai Ora; true if those providers broadly retained contracts and continued delivering Māori health services after the disestablishment, false if a material share lost funding, had contracts discontinued, or closed.

civility.statement: Who are they to turn and support the assault upon the Māori people? It is Māori assaulting the Māori people.
civility.explanation: A third reading debate on a contested bill, so there was a real opportunity to be civil or not. This goes past the measure to the character of the Māori government members who support it, casting them as betraying their own people — imputed bad faith directed at persons rather than at the policy. Not sustained abuse, so above the floor. Scored against the speaker: an accusation aimed at others is still her own conduct.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: According to the statistics, the Māori people are dying earlier, seven years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori life expectancy is about seven years shorter than that of other New Zealanders. A claim about the present, sourced to published statistics, so it can be checked against the official series.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / Ministry of Health life expectancy at birth series comparing Māori and non-Māori as at 2024; true if the published gap is approximately seven years, false if it is materially different (e.g. under four or over ten years).

veracity.statement: The Māori Health Authority was established on the request of a group that carefully examined and carefully considered the research and the statistics in front of them, the Health and Disability Commission.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Aka Whai Ora was set up because an expert body that had examined the research recommended it, and identifies that body as the Health and Disability Commission. Both the existence of the recommendation and the identity of the body are checkable.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The final report of the Health and Disability System Review (2020) and the Health and Disability Commissioner's published recommendations; true if the named body recommended establishing a Māori health authority, false if no such recommendation was made by it.

veracity.statement: This House should know that the Minister didn’t speak to the Māori people about this.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the responsible Minister undertook no consultation with Māori before bringing forward the disestablishment bill. She asserts it herself rather than relaying it, so it sits against her own record.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's disclosure statement, regulatory impact material and Ministerial records of consultation prior to introduction on 27 February 2024; true if no consultation with iwi, Māori health providers or Māori health leadership is recorded before the bill was introduced, false if documented engagement occurred.

specificity.statement: According to the statistics, the Māori people are dying earlier, seven years.
specificity.explanation: Carries an actual figure — seven years — which makes it checkable, but names no source, no measure and no period. A direction with some detail rather than a fully pinned-down claim. Precision is judged here, not truth.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What I believe is that this is a preclusion of the authority of the tribunal, to cut off his relations that came to oppose his actions.
rigor.explanation: There is a genuine inference here about a real measure, not a jibe: the premises offered nearby are the bill's urgency and the consequent cancellation of the scheduled Waitangi Tribunal sitting, and the conclusion is that forestalling the tribunal was its purpose. The timing evidence is real, but inferring intent from sequence is post hoc — the same facts follow equally from an unrelated commencement deadline, which she herself supplies. A partial gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I sat and listened to his comments; what is his strategy? What is the plan? I didn’t hear at all a single thing come out of his mouth that is better than the Māori Health Authority.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy question before the House — what replaces the body being disestablished, and what the Minister's alternative strategy is. Legitimate scrutiny of a government decision, which is the job of an opposition MP and scores high. Marked down slightly because no specific policy, figure or mechanism is named, and it is framed around the Minister's performance in the debate rather than the substance of an alternative.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill removes the previous Government’s policies in three areas primarily: to cut by 90 percent the number of retailers that could sell smoked tobacco products, which was to happen later this year; introduce a low nicotine limit, which was to happen next year; and a policy to ban sales to all those born after 1 January 2009 that was planned to take effect in 2027.
specificity.explanation: Names each repealed measure, the percentage cut, the birth-date cut-off and the commencement timing for all three. Fully checkable against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government wants workable, practical policy that improves people’s lives and we are committed to our smoke-free future.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — workable, practical, improves lives — with no measure, figure, mechanism or date. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: To be clear, none of the measures being repealed are in place.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at February 2024 none of the three repealed smokefree measures (retailer reduction, denicotinisation, generation ban) had yet commenced.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The commencement provisions of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022; true if the retailer-reduction, low-nicotine and smokefree-generation provisions all had commencement dates after 27 February 2024, false if any was already in force.

veracity.statement: The New Zealand Health Survey results released in December last year showed that 6.8 percent of New Zealanders are smoking daily, down from 8.6 percent the previous year, and down from 16.4 percent when the survey began in 2011 and 2012.
veracity.explanation: Three specific figures attributed to a named source: daily smoking prevalence of 6.8%, 8.6% the prior year, and 16.4% at the survey's 2011/12 baseline.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence, 2022/23 release (published December 2023) and the 2011/12 baseline; true if the three rates match 6.8%, 8.6% and 16.4% within rounding, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: This is what is happening in the real world: our smoking rates have fallen drastically in recent times, better than in any other developed country.
veracity.explanation: A superlative comparative claim: that New Zealand's recent fall in smoking prevalence exceeds that of every other developed country.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD Health Statistics / WHO tobacco prevalence trend data on percentage-point and proportional falls in adult daily smoking over the comparable recent period; true if New Zealand's decline is the largest among OECD members, false if any comparable developed country recorded an equal or larger decline.

veracity.statement: My question to the members opposite is simple: what’s your excuse, because the evidence is now overwhelmingly clear—12 people a day in New Zealand die from smoking-related illness, and this Government wants to liberalise the sale of tobacco.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific mortality figure: twelve New Zealanders a day die from smoking-related illness.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Health Promotion Agency estimates of annual smoking-attributable deaths in New Zealand; true if the annual estimate divided by 365 is approximately 12 (roughly 4,000–4,800 deaths a year), false if materially outside that range.

veracity.statement: Why is it that you now believe that liberalising the sale of cigarettes is an appropriate way to raise half a billion dollars in revenue every year so that you can fund tax cuts that will disproportionately benefit the wealthiest New Zealanders?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the repeal produces about half a billion dollars of tobacco revenue annually, and that this revenue funds the Government's tax cuts.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury / Budget 2024 forecasts and the regulatory impact statement on the fiscal effect of repealing the smoked tobacco measures; true if the estimated annual excise revenue retained is approximately $500 million a year, false if materially lower (e.g. nearer $200–300 million a year) or if the revenue is not booked to the tax package.

divination.statement: If those trends continue without any additional measures, New Zealand will hit the headline smoke-free goal of less than 5 percent of the population smoking daily by 2025.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that adult daily smoking prevalence will fall below 5 percent by 2025 on the existing trajectory, with no further regulatory measures.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for the 2025 reporting year; true if below 5.0%, false if 5.0% or above.

focus.statement: Instead of that, they seemed obsessed with trying to prove they loved a good slogan.
focus.explanation: Characterises the other party's motives — a taste for slogans — with no policy, measure or figure named. Party framing rather than the substance of the repeal.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The last Government was moving towards an untested regime with a focus on prohibition that ignored how well quit-smoking initiatives were working, the potential downside of a prohibitionist approach for smokers, and also the impact on retailers and crime was being ignored or, at the very least, trivialised.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure at issue: names the regulatory approach and three specific claimed costs of it (cessation gains, harm to smokers, retailer and crime impacts). Criticism of a predecessor's policy, not of the party in general.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What is it that has happened between pre-election and post-election that has forced you to completely abandon the platform that you campaigned on?
focus.explanation: There is a real accountability point underneath — a reversal on a named policy area since the election — but it is put as a general charge about the other side's consistency rather than tied to a specific commitment or measure.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When dealing with an addiction of this nature, reduced supply does not remove demand and it presents a real risk of increasing demand and increasing desperation.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy, but a weak one: the claim that restricting supply would actually *increase* demand is asserted without evidence or mechanism — a bare assertion doing the work of an argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Why is it that you now believe that liberalising the sale of cigarettes is an appropriate way to raise half a billion dollars in revenue every year so that you can fund tax cuts that will disproportionately benefit the wealthiest New Zealanders?
rigor.explanation: A loaded question: it presupposes rather than establishes both the causal link between the repeal and the tax package and the motive behind it, so any answer concedes the premise. The conclusion is smuggled into the question rather than argued for.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In fact, I made it very clear that these were questions to the members opposite, but thank you for doing the Government’s bidding by interrupting my flow.
civility.explanation: Sarcasm aimed at the Speaker personally, imputing partisanship — that they were acting at the Government's behest. That is an attack on an individual's impartiality, not on any argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: No disrespect, but I won’t take any lectures from that member about that event. I was an employer of someone who lost an employee in that event, and I take that very seriously.
civility.explanation: Pointed and dismissive of the questioner ("I won't take any lectures from that member"), but it lands on the standing to ask rather than on the member's character or competence. Robust, edging toward the person without insulting them.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does the Prime Minister intend to ban coming to this House promising a bazooka but turning up with a pop gun?
civility.explanation: Mockery of the questioner's performance rather than engagement with anything said. Short of a direct insult, but it is sneering, which is a genuine civility failure on the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, the member either wants an answer or she doesn’t.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the questioner — that she is not actually interested in the answer. Aimed at the member's motives rather than at anything she argued, which is a failure on the re-anchored scale, though short of a personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why will he not rule out liberalising access to military-style semi-automatic weapons?
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy question (liberalising MSSA access) and presses the government on it. This is scrutiny of a named measure, not party framing, so it scores at the top.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does the Prime Minister intend to ban coming to this House promising a bazooka but turning up with a pop gun?
focus.explanation: Entirely about how the other side is performing. Strip the jibe at the Opposition and no policy, measure, figure or outcome remains.
focus.subject: speaker
