veracity.falsification_criterion: Corrections programme-participation data for sentenced prisoners in Corrections-run prisons as at approximately February/March 2023; true if the attendance rate was below 20%, false if it was 20% or higher.

veracity.statement: Programmes designed to turn around serious offenders—one such programme is the special treatment unit for violent offenders—reported a 54 percent completion rate for the year 2022-23.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 54% completion rate in 2022-23 for special treatment unit programmes for violent offenders.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Corrections reporting on Special Treatment Unit (violence) programme completions for the 2022/23 financial year; true if the completion rate was 54% (± rounding), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Another analysis also suggests—and this is from 2016—that Māori participants in these programmes do just as well, and in a lot of cases even better, than the non-Māori participants.
veracity.explanation: Claims a 2016 analysis found Māori participants in prison rehabilitation programmes achieve outcomes equal to or better than non-Māori participants.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2016 Corrections (or peer-reviewed) evaluation of rehabilitation programme outcomes by ethnicity; true if it reports Māori outcomes equal to or better than non-Māori, false if it reports worse outcomes for Māori or no such 2016 analysis exists.

veracity.statement: There has been some issue today raised that perhaps it wasn’t successful in Western Australia, but Police Commissioner Coster told the Justice Committee that the Western Australia example was working a treat and they are going to do their best to emulate it.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim attributed to Police Commissioner Andrew Coster about what he told the Justice Committee regarding the Western Australian gang-patch regime.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee transcript/evidence for Coster's appearance; true if he told the committee the Western Australian example was working well and that police intend to emulate it, false if he gave a qualified or contrary account.

veracity.statement: Justice and law and order make up a number of those 49 points that are in our law and order policies in the 100-day plan.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the coalition Government's 100-day plan comprises 49 points, of which a number are justice and law-and-order items.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published coalition Government 100-day plan; true if it contains 49 numbered actions and several are justice/law-and-order items, false if the plan contains a materially different number of points.

specificity.statement: As of 2023, around 56.5 percent of people with serious convictions are reconvicted within two years following release, and again another 35.8 percent are reimprisoned after two years following prison.
specificity.explanation: Two named rates to one decimal place, with a stated cohort, a stated year and a stated follow-up window — directly checkable against Corrections data.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We already are required to have management plans for prisoners under section 51 of the Corrections Act, so if a prisoner is sentenced for more than two months on remand or in custody or for a prison sentence of more than two months, then they do have to have one of these plans, and in that plan it actually identifies their specific needs, and then the programmes can be tailored to it.
specificity.explanation: Names the statutory provision, the threshold that triggers it and the mechanism by which the bill would attach to it — someone could go to the Act and check.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re not just about the stick; we want to do something practical.
specificity.explanation: Positioning language offered as substance but committing to nothing — no mechanism, no figure, no named step.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Just to reiterate its purpose, the policy objective of this bill is to provide a requirement for individuals in a corrections facility to complete skills and rehabilitation programmes prior to being considered for parole.
specificity.explanation: States the operative requirement and the point in the process it bites, but no thresholds, programme definitions or timeframes.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If you don’t have basic skills leaving prison, like reading, writing, arithmetic, the ability to open a bank account, and the ability to apply for a driver’s licence—and, obviously, over recent years, we’ve identified that even having an ID when you leave prison can be very difficult—it just makes it much, much harder to look for a job and do something productive. Often then, your only option is to go back to a life of crime—hence the circle continues.
rigor.explanation: The first step — no basic skills makes employment harder — is well supported by the literacy figures he has just given. The second step overreaches: 'your only option is to go back to a life of crime' is a false dichotomy, since nothing offered rules out the other options (benefits, family support, unskilled work). A real inference about the policy, with a real gap in it.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We’ve got the Hansard, Ginny Andersen; I’ll tell them about the success that the Western Australia model has had. I will send you the Hansard.
civility.explanation: A pointed, faintly condescending riposte to an interjecting member — the offer to 'send you the Hansard' implies she has not read it — but it stops at the evidence and does not attack her character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And rather than branding prisons as the “University of Crime” and focusing on reducing the prison population, regardless of how much crime is happening, this Government, this coalition Government, is confronting the real reasons behind crime and looking at rehabilitation as a key part of our success of overcoming repeated crime.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy contrast (prison-population reduction target versus rehabilitation) but the weight of the sentence is a characterisation of the other side's approach rather than the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We could go on about the crisis in the health sector and the crisis in the education sector that he left us and the economic fiscal cliffs and everything else, but we won’t; we’ll get back to the bill.
focus.explanation: A sweep across the previous government's record in general — no policy, measure, figure or outcome named, and nothing to do with the parole bill under debate.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So given these challenges to resources, I think it’s fair to say we have some concerns that parole could be denied due to Corrections resources rather than just the merits of the parole application.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the bill before the House and who it would affect — identifies a specific way the parole test could operate against prisoners for reasons unrelated to their case. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are not interested in reducing the prison population by 30 percent; that’s another action point that’s been delivered. We’re getting rid of that ridiculous goal.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific policy target with a figure (the 30 percent prison-population reduction goal) and states it is being removed, but supplies no mechanism or date for the removal.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And as the Minister of Justice presented today, his focus in the next few weeks and months is addressing the increasing violent crime in particular; in youth crime, getting on top of that; and of course the widespread delays in the court system.
specificity.explanation: Names three priority areas and a rough timeframe ("next few weeks and months") but no measures, figures or targets — a direction with some detail and no how or how much.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Looking at the main provisions of the bill, the clanger, I suppose, is clause 5, which inserts new section 24A in the principal Act, to require that an offender who has not completed a programme, indicated in their management plan under section 51 of the Corrections Act 2004, must not be considered for parole.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the new section inserted, the cross-referenced section and Act, and states the operative requirement — fully checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the briefing to the incoming Minister in 2023, Corrections stated that they have faced some pressures retaining and recruiting staff, and I don’t think that’s a situation that we’re unaware of.
specificity.explanation: Names the source document and its year and states what it said, so a listener can go and find it; falls short of 1.0 because the pressure itself is described qualitatively with no figures (vacancy rates, turnover).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I have since asked further questions, and resources are so constrained in Corrections that 12 out of the 18 prisons are not giving the legal entitlement of a visit a week.
specificity.explanation: A precise count against a precise denominator, tied to a named legal entitlement and to an identified evidence source (his own written questions). Directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Keep going. Skip the big words. Just do one more clause and then he will have filled it up.
civility.explanation: Mockery aimed at the member personally — "skip the big words" is a jibe at his command of the material, and the rest sneers that he is padding out his time. Short of a direct insult but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m not going to take quite so long as the member who’s has just resumed his seat, Cameron Brewer, unfortunately—unfortunately—and I know that pains you; I know.
civility.explanation: Teasing at the previous speaker's expense — the repeated "unfortunately" needles him for talking too long — but it is light banter that edges toward the person without landing on his character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: And with 6.5 percent cuts looming over the service, I don’t think it’s unreasonable for us to say that we certainly have some concerns as to how these pathways will continue to be funded sufficiently to support prisoners to be considered for parole, because it’s incredibly important that that process isn’t unduly interrupted.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Department of Corrections is facing a 6.5 percent cut to its baseline funding.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government's 2024 Budget baseline savings instruction to the Department of Corrections (Treasury Budget 2024 guidance / ministerial savings targets by agency): true if Corrections was set a 6.5% baseline savings target, false if it was set a different percentage or exempted.

veracity.statement: In the briefing to the incoming Minister in 2023, Corrections stated that they have faced some pressures retaining and recruiting staff, and I don’t think that’s a situation that we’re unaware of.
veracity.explanation: Attributes to the Department of Corrections' 2023 Briefing to the Incoming Minister a statement that the department faces staff recruitment and retention pressures.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published Department of Corrections Briefing to the Incoming Minister, 2023: true if it records recruitment and/or retention pressures for Corrections staff, false if it contains no such statement.

veracity.statement: I have since asked further questions, and resources are so constrained in Corrections that 12 out of the 18 prisons are not giving the legal entitlement of a visit a week.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 12 of New Zealand's 18 prisons are failing to provide the statutory weekly visit entitlement, on the basis of answers to his own parliamentary questions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections responses to written parliamentary questions (or OIA) on statutory prison visits, as at early 2024: true if the responses show 12 of 18 prisons not meeting the once-weekly statutory visit entitlement, false if the number of non-compliant prisons is materially different.

rigor.statement: And with 6.5 percent cuts looming over the service, I don’t think it’s unreasonable for us to say that we certainly have some concerns as to how these pathways will continue to be funded sufficiently to support prisoners to be considered for parole, because it’s incredibly important that that process isn’t unduly interrupted.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: if the funding line that pays for rehabilitation programmes is being cut while the bill makes completing those programmes a precondition of parole, the delivery question follows. The gap is that a baseline savings target does not automatically fall on programme delivery — the conclusion is stated as a concern rather than a consequence, which is appropriate to the strength of the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, if there are failings in our corrections system—and it’s clear there are some failings at the present time—those failings should not result in someone being denied parole.
rigor.explanation: A clean conditional: the premise (system failings exist) supports the conclusion (a prisoner should not bear the cost of them) via the unstated but uncontroversial principle that penalties should track the person's own conduct. No fallacy; the one soft spot is that "it's clear there are some failings" is asserted rather than argued here, though he evidences it in the preceding sentences.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: From New Zealand First’s point of view, we’re a party of common sense. It makes common sense that if you’re in that situation, you would take the opportunity to try to improve your life.
rigor.explanation: An inference about the policy (that prisoners will take up rehabilitation if offered) resting entirely on a bare appeal to self-evidence — 'common sense' — with nothing offered to connect the premise to the conclusion. On-policy, so Focus is unaffected.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In no way am I across the detail of all of the work that they do, except to say that I’ve seen and talked to many of the people who have been part of that programme, and it’s incredibly powerful and impressive and the results that they get are good for the whole community, not only those men and their families but everybody who then comes in to interact with somebody who’s been through it and who can then go and contribute to society, contribute to their own family, and have a much better sense of themselves.
rigor.explanation: Concludes that the programme's results are good for the whole community while expressly disclaiming knowledge of the detail; the support offered is personal impression from conversations — an appeal to anecdote rather than to outcome data.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Carpentry—something that this country has a deficit of, at the moment, in our building industry.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand had a shortage of carpenters in the building industry as at February 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Immigration NZ Green List / construction sector skill shortage listings and MBIE construction workforce reporting for 2023–24; true if carpenters are identified as in shortage at that time, false if the sector reported surplus or falling demand for carpenters.

veracity.statement: So the issue that we have is the proposed 6.5 percent cut to all Government departments, which includes Corrections. That is a real concern in terms of how this bill will deliver upon what it sets out to be able to do.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a 6.5 percent cut was proposed across all Government departments, Corrections included.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury / Ministerial directions for the 2024 baseline savings exercise; true if departments including Corrections were directed to find savings of about 6.5 percent, false if no such across-the-board target applied or Corrections was outside it.

veracity.statement: We’re proud that when we were in Government, we made mental health treatment, family violence counselling services, and alcohol and drug treatment all much more readily available right across prisons in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the previous Labour government mental health, family violence and AOD treatment became materially more available across New Zealand prisons.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections annual reports and Budget appropriations 2018–2023 for AOD, mental health and family violence programmes; true if participation numbers and availability rose materially across the prison network, false if flat or reduced.

veracity.statement: In 2016, Corrections estimated that around 65 percent of the prison population had literacy levels that were below NCEA level 1.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific 2016 estimate to Corrections: about 65 percent of prisoners with literacy below NCEA level 1.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections literacy and numeracy assessment data published around 2016; true if the estimate is approximately 65 percent below NCEA level 1, false if materially different or no such estimate exists.

veracity.statement: Corrections also found that 48 percent of Pākehā are below NCEA level 1 competency and 62 of Māori and Pasifika are below that level.
veracity.explanation: Attributes ethnicity-disaggregated literacy figures to Corrections: 48 percent of Pākehā and 62 percent of Māori and Pasifika prisoners below NCEA level 1. ('62' is plainly '62 percent' in spoken delivery.)
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The same Corrections literacy and numeracy assessment broken down by ethnicity; true if the figures are approximately 48 percent and 62 percent respectively, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: In the briefing to the incoming Minister, Corrections stated that they’re facing real pressures in recruiting and retaining staff.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Corrections Briefing to the Incoming Minister identified recruitment and retention pressures.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Department of Corrections Briefing to the Incoming Minister (published late 2023); true if it identifies staff recruitment and retention pressure, false if it does not.

specificity.statement: In this, it has, at subsection 3, that if people actually do these courses and upskill themselves, there’s an incentive—parole can actually be brought forward.
specificity.explanation: Points to a named provision of the bill and states the concrete mechanism it creates (earlier parole as an incentive for completing programmes). Someone could open the bill and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In 2016, Corrections estimated that around 65 percent of the prison population had literacy levels that were below NCEA level 1.
specificity.explanation: A dated figure attributed to a named source against a named benchmark — fully checkable and directly usable by the select committee.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: “Rehabilitative programmes” is defined in the Corrections Act 2004, so we don’t see it on the bill in front of us, but that means a programme designed to reduce reoffending by facilitating the rehabilitation of prisoners sentenced to imprisonment and their reintegration into society.
specificity.explanation: Names the governing statute and supplies the operative definition the bill relies on, so the scope of the obligation can be checked directly. Short of 1.0 only because no figures or timeframes attach.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So the issue that we have is the proposed 6.5 percent cut to all Government departments, which includes Corrections. That is a real concern in terms of how this bill will deliver upon what it sets out to be able to do.
focus.explanation: Names a specific fiscal measure and ties it to whether the bill before the House can be delivered. Scrutiny of a named government decision, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’re proud that when we were in Government, we made mental health treatment, family violence counselling services, and alcohol and drug treatment all much more readily available right across prisons in New Zealand.
focus.explanation: Real policy content — three named service types in prisons — but carried inside a claim of credit for the speaker's own party's time in office rather than the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I do note that the Hon Dr Duncan Webb, the Hon Ginny Andersen, the Hon Rachel Brooking, and the other colleagues I’ve already spoken about did point out some of the issues we may face, and I want to be upfront and acknowledge that.
civility.explanation: Closing a contested first-reading debate, where dismissing opposition criticism was readily available. Instead he names the opposing members and credits their points. Attacks no one; engages the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We actually heard today, when we were in the Justice Committee, about court delays that could play a part in this, because if prisoners aren’t getting their court dates, they’re spending time on remand, etc. There are a lot of issues.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the operation of the bill — the interaction between court scheduling, remand time and mandatory programme completion. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We actually heard today, when we were in the Justice Committee, about court delays that could play a part in this, because if prisoners aren’t getting their court dates, they’re spending time on remand, etc. There are a lot of issues.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a named mechanism (court delays pushing prisoners onto remand) and its source (the Justice Committee), but supplies no figures, scale or timeframe for the problem.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, look, I think we can address some of these concerns in the select committee. I think that we can have a robust and productive discussion, and let’s actually do something to, hopefully, enhance our criminal justice system, with all those caveats and concerns in place.
specificity.explanation: A closing appeal that commits to nothing checkable: no concern is named, no change to the bill is proposed, and 'enhance our criminal justice system' has no mechanism, amount or date attached. The only concrete element is the venue (select committee).
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I also totally accept what was said about Corrections. Again, it is, like many Government departments, one that is having trouble recruiting and retaining staff.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as present fact that the Department of Corrections is having difficulty recruiting and retaining staff, and that this is common across government departments.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections annual report and Public Service Commission workforce data for 2023/24: corrections officer vacancy rate and annual turnover rate. True if vacancies/turnover are materially elevated against the department's own establishment targets or prior-year baselines; false if the department was at or near full staffing with turnover in line with the wider public service.

specificity.statement: So the bill seeks to bring in, through clause 4, a definition of what a “rehabilitative programme” is. Through clause 5, it requires that offenders who have not done a rehabilitative programme be considered as ineligible for parole; but, conversely, for the Parole Board to then say to them that if they’re able to do a programme within the next 12 months, then that would be the best thing.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific clauses, the mechanism each creates (a statutory definition; an eligibility bar with a 12-month window), and the decision-maker. Someone could check this against the bill text. Falls short of 1.0 only because no figures or dates beyond the 12 months are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We want to be tough and crack down on the causes of crime, but, at the same time, we also want to have strong and thorough rehabilitative programmes in place for prisoners to prepare them for release.
specificity.explanation: A statement of aims made of generic virtues — 'tough', 'crack down', 'strong and thorough' — with no programme named, no mechanism, no cost and no timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on, in a debate where other speakers were describing the bill clause by clause.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In the Justice Committee, we have gone through an overview of the Ministry of Justice and the Department of Corrections, and the fact that the number of prisoners—whether in youth facilities or in Corrections facilities—are so many, and that the time that they spend there is considerable: over one year, sometimes close to two years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the time prisoners (in context, those on remand) spend in custody is typically over one year and sometimes close to two. A factual claim about current custodial durations, not an opinion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections / Ministry of Justice published statistics on time spent in custody on remand and in youth justice facilities for 2023–24: true if typical (median) durations exceed one year with a material tail approaching two years; false if typical durations are materially shorter, e.g. a few months, even if a small tail runs long.

veracity.statement: We know our prison population suffer a lot from illiteracy. They’re illiterate, often, and they’re also suffering from things like ADHD.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that literacy deficits and ADHD are markedly more prevalent in the New Zealand prison population than in the general population. A claim about present-day characteristics of a measured group.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections literacy and numeracy assessment data for prisoners, and published prevalence studies of ADHD/neurodisability among NZ prisoners: true if both rates are substantially above general-population rates, false if they are comparable to the general population.

veracity.statement: The paramount consideration of the Parole Board when considering someone for release is the safety of the community.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific point of law about the statutory test the Parole Board must apply — that community safety is the paramount consideration, ranking above all others.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Section 7 of the Parole Act 2002: true if the Act states that the paramount consideration in every parole decision is the safety of the community, false if the Act ranks some other consideration first or gives community safety no paramount status.

veracity.statement: I was actually lucky enough, earlier in the week, to talk to another great man who hails from Dunedin—he’s no longer there—Sir Ron Young, who’s actually the chair of the New Zealand Parole Board.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Sir Ron Young held the office of chairperson of the New Zealand Parole Board as at late February 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Parole Board's published membership listing and the relevant Ministry of Justice appointment notice as at February 2024: true if Sir Ron Young was then the Board's chairperson, false if the chair was someone else at that date.

focus.statement: For example, I’d love to see—and I’m not sure if it’s in scope—us look at the capacity to bring rehabilitation in as an offering to people on remand, because they sit on remand, at the present time, for far too long, lost and without those opportunities.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: proposes a specific extension of the bill's scope (rehabilitation for remand prisoners) and gives the reason. No party framing at all, despite an easy opening to attack the Government's corrections record.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This week has been a really hard one for the Labour Party in this House. We found the smoke-free legislation really difficult. It has been one of those things which really hurt a lot of people.
civility.explanation: Raises one of the most bitterly contested measures of the week — a real opportunity to attack the members who repealed it — and confines herself to the effect of the legislation. No person is impugned, no bad faith is imputed.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Prisoners, as we know, face many barriers to gaining employment post their release from prison, such as poor literacy, numeracy, and educational underachievement. This results in many offenders unfortunately falling back into criminal activity.
rigor.explanation: A real causal inference about the policy: employment barriers cause reoffending. The premise is stated and the conclusion tracks it, but the causal step is asserted rather than shown — 'as we know' does the work that evidence should, and no mechanism or study is offered to rule out the barriers and the reoffending sharing a common cause.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why has he broken his promise of no new taxes and no increases in fuel tax, given yesterday he announced a driver’s tax through hiking registration fees, plus a 22c per litre increase in fuel taxes, albeit on a delayed timetable?
focus.explanation: Names a specific announcement (registration fee increase, 22c per litre fuel tax) and a specific commitment it is said to breach. This is scrutiny of a named policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why isn’t he willing to defend the Government’s decision to break the promises the Prime Minister made before the election?
focus.explanation: A real accountability point about pre-election promises, but no specific policy, figure or commitment is named — the weight of the question is on the character of the Government rather than on a measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Who is correct: Nicola Willis, who said, “We’re not increasing taxes. We’re making an adjustment to a fee.”, or Nicola Willis, who said, “If it looks like a tax and it quacks like a tax, it’s a tax.”?
focus.explanation: The underlying question — whether the fee increase is a tax — is a real policy point, but it is framed as a personal inconsistency rather than argued on the substance of the charge.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How will an 18 percent decrease in funding to council subsidies to public transport services, a 34 percent decrease in funding for public transport infrastructure, and a 49 percent decrease in funding for walking and cycling improvements have a positive impact on meeting New Zealand’s climate change commitments?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: names three specific funding lines in a specific document and asks how they square with a named commitment. On-policy throughout, with no party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Has he seen evidence from the recent Programme for International Student Assessment study which shows dropping achievement can be explained by the number of students coming to school hungry?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy question — the link between food insecurity and educational achievement — with a named evidence source and no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why has he broken his promise of no new taxes and no increases in fuel tax, given yesterday he announced a driver’s tax through hiking registration fees, plus a 22c per litre increase in fuel taxes, albeit on a delayed timetable?
specificity.explanation: Carries a figure (22c per litre), a named instrument (registration fees) and a timing qualifier (delayed timetable). Someone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, this morning, Treasury released the Government’s financial statements for the seven months ending 31 January 2024. These show that core Crown tax revenue was $800 million below what was forecast in the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update (HYEFU) in December. Core Crown expenses were also lower than forecast in the HYEFU by a billion dollars. The OBEGAL deficit—the operating balance before gains and losses—was $400 million higher than forecast.
specificity.explanation: Named source, named period, and three separate figures with their direction against forecast. Fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Core Crown expenditure is forecast to be $140 billion over this financial year. That’s a lot of money, so I went back and I looked at what Government spending was in previous years, and to my horror I found that since 2018 Government spending has increased by a total of 73 percent. That is a 73 percent increase over only six years. Once again, this shows the financial mismanagement of the previous Government.
specificity.explanation: Gives a total ($140 billion), a base year (2018), a growth figure (73 percent) and a period (six years) — precise enough for anyone to reconstruct.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We said we were not going to increase the fuel excise duty (FED) and road-user charge (RUC), and that is what we have delivered in this GPS. We have not increased FED and RUC during this term of Government, but the reality is—the reality is—that we need to ensure that we set out the funding parameters to be able to deliver the infrastructure New Zealanders need, and that is why we have outlined FED and RUC increases from 2027.
specificity.explanation: Names the two instruments, the document they sit in, and the year the increases begin. Missing only the amounts.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How will an 18 percent decrease in funding to council subsidies to public transport services, a 34 percent decrease in funding for public transport infrastructure, and a 49 percent decrease in funding for walking and cycling improvements have a positive impact on meeting New Zealand’s climate change commitments?
specificity.explanation: Three separate percentage figures, each attached to a named funding category. Directly checkable against the GPS.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Why has he broken his promise of no new taxes and no increases in fuel tax, given yesterday he announced a driver’s tax through hiking registration fees, plus a 22c per litre increase in fuel taxes, albeit on a delayed timetable?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the announcement of the previous day contained both a registration fee increase and a 22c per litre fuel tax increase phased in later.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The draft Government Policy Statement on land transport 2024-34 released 4 March 2024, and Cabinet/Ministry of Transport announcements of the same date: true if it provides for motor vehicle registration fee increases and cumulative fuel excise duty increases totalling about 22c per litre; false if no such registration or FED increases are provided for.

veracity.statement: Who is correct: Nicola Willis, who said, “We’re not increasing taxes. We’re making an adjustment to a fee.”, or Nicola Willis, who said, “If it looks like a tax and it quacks like a tax, it’s a tax.”?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Nicola Willis made both of the quoted statements. The question's force depends entirely on the quotations being accurate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The public record of Nicola Willis's statements (Hansard, press conferences, media reports): true if she is on record with both quoted formulations as given; false if either quotation is not something she said or is materially altered.

veracity.statement: The law was fixed up in 2018-19, which led to the biggest fall in cigarette smoking in this country’s history.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that the relevant smokefree law was enacted in 2018-19 and that this enactment caused the largest fall in smoking in New Zealand's history.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Health Survey daily smoking prevalence series and the legislative record of smokefree amendments: true if a smokefree law change was enacted in 2018-19 and the largest recorded fall in smoking prevalence followed it; false if no such law was enacted in those years, or if the largest fall sits in a different period.

veracity.statement: On the second issue of calling the Prime Minister of this country squanderous, the Prime Minister on that score would be an amateur compared with what he inherited: hundreds of billions of dollars unaccounted for, over and over again.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a quantity that hundreds of billions of dollars were left unaccounted for by the previous Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury financial statements and Auditor-General reports for the 2017-2023 period: true if hundreds of billions of dollars of Crown expenditure are recorded as unaccounted for; false if the total of expenditure identified as unaccounted for is orders of magnitude smaller (total core Crown expenses in any single one of those years were under $140 billion).

veracity.statement: Well, this morning, Treasury released the Government’s financial statements for the seven months ending 31 January 2024. These show that core Crown tax revenue was $800 million below what was forecast in the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update (HYEFU) in December. Core Crown expenses were also lower than forecast in the HYEFU by a billion dollars. The OBEGAL deficit—the operating balance before gains and losses—was $400 million higher than forecast.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three specific variances between the January 2024 interim accounts and the HYEFU forecast.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's Interim Financial Statements of the Government of New Zealand for the seven months ended 31 January 2024, compared against the December 2023 HYEFU forecasts: true if tax revenue is about $800m below forecast, core Crown expenses about $1b below forecast, and the OBEGAL deficit about $400m worse than forecast; false if any of the three variances differ materially.

veracity.statement: Core Crown expenditure is forecast to be $140 billion over this financial year. That’s a lot of money, so I went back and I looked at what Government spending was in previous years, and to my horror I found that since 2018 Government spending has increased by a total of 73 percent. That is a 73 percent increase over only six years. Once again, this shows the financial mismanagement of the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $140 billion core Crown expenditure forecast and a 73 percent nominal increase in Government spending since 2018.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenses in the Financial Statements of the Government for the year ended 30 June 2018 compared with the forecast for the year ended 30 June 2024: true if the increase is approximately 73 percent and the 2023/24 forecast is around $140 billion; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: We said we were not going to increase the fuel excise duty (FED) and road-user charge (RUC), and that is what we have delivered in this GPS. We have not increased FED and RUC during this term of Government, but the reality is—the reality is—that we need to ensure that we set out the funding parameters to be able to deliver the infrastructure New Zealanders need, and that is why we have outlined FED and RUC increases from 2027.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no fuel excise duty or road-user charge increase has occurred during the current term, and that the increases set out in the GPS start in 2027.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The record of fuel excise duty and road-user charge rates from October 2023 to March 2024, and the draft GPS on land transport 2024-34: true if no FED or RUC increase took effect in that period and the draft GPS schedules increases beginning in 2027; false if either rate was raised in the term, or the GPS timetable differs.

veracity.statement: How will an 18 percent decrease in funding to council subsidies to public transport services, a 34 percent decrease in funding for public transport infrastructure, and a 49 percent decrease in funding for walking and cycling improvements have a positive impact on meeting New Zealand’s climate change commitments?
veracity.explanation: Asserts three specific percentage reductions across public transport and active-mode funding activity classes in the new GPS.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The funding ranges in the draft Government Policy Statement on land transport 2024-34 compared with the GPS 2021 (as amended): true if the midpoints show falls of about 18 percent for public transport services, 34 percent for public transport infrastructure and 49 percent for walking and cycling; false if the declines differ materially or the comparison baseline does not support them.

veracity.statement: Has he seen evidence from the recent Programme for International Student Assessment study which shows dropping achievement can be explained by the number of students coming to school hungry?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the PISA study shows falling achievement can be explained by the number of students coming to school hungry — a causal, explanatory claim about what the study found.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The PISA 2022 New Zealand results and OECD reporting on food insecurity: true if PISA reports that the decline in New Zealand achievement is explained by students attending school hungry; false if it reports only an association between food insecurity and lower scores, or does not attribute the decline to hunger.

veracity.statement: Again, the report that that member would have been aware of, commissioned by that former Government and reported on in 2023, under sections 24 and 25, does not find any such outcome in the way that member mistakenly is implying.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the named sections of the 2023 report contain no finding of an achievement gap for students in food poverty.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2023 report referred to, at the sections cited: true if those sections contain no finding that students in food poverty trail their peers in achievement; false if such a finding appears there.

civility.statement: Again, as the Acting Prime Minister, I stand by the things that I say, and I’m very happy to begin by giving that group a lesson in constitutional law in this country, about how this Parliament is properly run under the Standing Orders.
civility.explanation: Offering to give the Opposition "a lesson in constitutional law" is condescension aimed at the members rather than at any argument. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We’ll be paying for that over the next 10 years—a cost occasioned by that Minister, who threw money around like an eight-armed octopus.
civility.explanation: Mockery directed at a named member's personal conduct rather than at a decision or a policy. Ridicule of the person, not the spending choice.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: With the second one, he was pointing to what happens when you have 30 years of managerial neglect when it comes to Government properties—much of which was the responsibility of that Government over there—that sees millions and millions of dollars of assets wasted because of ideology, and I can recite all of the circumstances of that, which have now cost the taxpayer so much more money than looking after Ministers.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the question was how two contradictory statements can both stand, and the answer re-describes one of them as being about property neglect without showing that reading. The causal attribution to "ideology" is asserted, and the offer to "recite all of the circumstances" substitutes a promise of evidence for evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: On the second issue of calling the Prime Minister of this country squanderous, the Prime Minister on that score would be an amateur compared with what he inherited: hundreds of billions of dollars unaccounted for, over and over again.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque: the charge that the Prime Minister is wasteful is met by asserting that his predecessors were worse, which does not bear on whether the charge is true.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Core Crown expenditure is forecast to be $140 billion over this financial year. That’s a lot of money, so I went back and I looked at what Government spending was in previous years, and to my horror I found that since 2018 Government spending has increased by a total of 73 percent. That is a 73 percent increase over only six years. Once again, this shows the financial mismanagement of the previous Government.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion does not follow from what was offered: a raw nominal spending total, unadjusted for inflation, population or the COVID response, cannot by itself establish mismanagement. Growth in the aggregate is treated as identical to waste, with no premise connecting the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, on this side of the House, we are focusing the National Land Transport Fund on its core purpose, which is to build and maintain the roading network, and people who fill up their cars with petrol, who pay road-user charges, want to ensure that the money they’re paying is going back into building and maintaining the roading network, less potholes, and making sure we have the roads for the future to unlock economic growth and productivity across New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to popularity, and a premise asserted as definitional: that the fund's "core purpose" is roading is the very thing in dispute, and what motorists are said to want is offered as if it settled it. Nothing offered connects either premise to the climate commitments the question raised.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reasons why there is so much massive failure at school is to do with truancy and a whole lot of other reasons—for an education system that began, in 1877, making school attendance compulsory.
rigor.explanation: The evidence cited in the question is dismissed and replaced by an alternative cause asserted without support, and "a whole lot of other reasons" does no work. The 1877 reference is a non sequitur: the age of compulsory attendance law bears on neither hunger nor truancy as a cause of current achievement.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: As a result, the economy will almost certainly be in a weaker position this year than was anticipated before Christmas, and this has a direct flow-on to tax revenue.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the 2024 economy, and consequently tax revenue, will underperform the December 2023 HYEFU projection. This is a forecast about the economy, not a commitment to any action by the Minister.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ GDP releases and Treasury's Budget 2024 / Pre-election forecasts for calendar 2024, compared against the December 2023 HYEFU track: true if actual GDP growth and tax revenue for 2024 come in below the HYEFU forecast; false if they meet or exceed it.

focus.statement: Will he commit to improving student wellbeing and school achievement by keeping the healthy school lunches programme beyond 2025 and expanding it in the future to more learners struggling with food poverty?
focus.explanation: Names a specific programme (healthy school lunches), a specific horizon (beyond 2025) and a specific target group. Squarely on the policy, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, that side of the House thinks throwing more money is the solution to every single problem.
focus.explanation: Asked how people will get reliable services under his GPS, he characterises the other party's general disposition instead. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — strip out the part about the other side and nothing remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can people choose to avoid paying ETS prices and higher prices to use cars when his draft GPS cuts funding to public transport services, public transport infrastructure, walking, and cycling—basically every alternative to using a car?
focus.explanation: Names the measure at issue (the draft GPS), the specific activity classes affected and the consequence claimed. Scrutiny of a named policy, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What reports has the Minister seen, if any, in relation to advocacy by the former member of Parliament for Mt Albert—and, indeed, the current member of Parliament for Mt Albert—about Auckland light rail, and how did that project stack up against that advocacy?
focus.explanation: A named project and its delivery against a promise sit inside the question, so there is real policy content, but the framing is built around two individual opponents rather than the transport measure before the House. A policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So a very sensible, rational evaluation needs to be done now rather than a screaming reaction that says that every cent spent is spent well.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy built on a strawman: the alternative to evaluation is cast as the claim that 'every cent spent is spent well', which nobody advanced. The conclusion that evaluation is needed is reached by misdescribing the opposing position rather than by evidence. This engages the actual policy, so Focus is unaffected.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As the member knows, the emissions trading scheme (ETS) is the Government’s key tool to reduce emissions. As the member well knows, the transport sector is covered by the ETS and the ETS caps emissions.
rigor.explanation: Answers 'will the GPS contribute to emissions reduction' by pointing to a different instrument. Even granting both premises, that transport sits under a capped ETS does not establish that this GPS contributes anything to the reduction — the conclusion is about the GPS but the support is about the ETS. A real gap between what is shown and what is concluded, though the premises themselves are sound.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, the actual targets are slightly lower but we will get better outcomes because we’ll be focusing on making sure our public transport services are operating reliably.
rigor.explanation: Concedes lower funding targets and concludes better outcomes will follow, offering only the assertion that the focus will be on reliability. Nothing links a focus on reliability to outcomes improving despite reduced funding — the conclusion is asserted, not supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Go and ask the teachers, go and ask real Māori, who know down in the schools what’s going on. Ask somebody who’s been in a classroom, not somebody who’s forgotten what it’s like.
civility.explanation: Turns from the programme to the questioner: 'real Māori' implies the member is not one, and 'somebody who’s forgotten what it’s like' impugns her standing to ask. A personal jibe rather than criticism of the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This morning I announced that we intend to have a pilot for a military-style academy for youth offenders operating from the middle of this year.
specificity.explanation: Names the intervention (military-style academy pilot), the cohort (youth offenders) and a timeframe (middle of 2024). No cost or participant numbers, which keeps it short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There’s over $4.4 billion going into public transport services and public transport infrastructure.
specificity.explanation: A single figure attached to two named activity classes; anyone can take it to the draft GPS and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is he denying that, in the draft GPS, there is a specific provision that says local road funding, maintenance, and renewal cannot be used for multimodal improvements, and that includes bus lanes?
specificity.explanation: Points at a particular provision of a named document, the funding streams it governs and the concrete thing it is said to exclude. A precise question is as checkable as a precise answer; it stops short of quoting the clause.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The approach to serious and persistent youth offending over the past six years has clearly not been working, and something needs to change in how we respond to this group of young people to help them turn their lives around and break the cycle of offending.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the approach taken to serious and persistent youth offending across the six years to 2023 failed — i.e. that this offending did not decline over that period.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police recorded youth offending statistics and Oranga Tamariki reporting on serious and persistent youth offenders for 2017–2023: true if the rate of serious/repeat youth offending (including ram raids and repeat offender counts) rose or was flat over the period, false if it fell materially.

veracity.statement: An evaluation of this programme showed positive results, with improvements in the attitude and motivation of the young people to address their offending.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the published evaluation of the 2010–2016 Military-style Activity Camp programme recorded improvements in participants' attitude and motivation toward their offending.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Child, Youth and Family / Ministry of Social Development evaluation of the MAC programme: true if it reports improvements in participants' attitude and motivation, false if it reports no such improvement.

veracity.statement: This Government has delivered on its commitment to not raise fuel excise duties (FED) or road-user charges (RUC) in this term.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no increase to fuel excise duty or road-user charges had been made since the Government took office in late 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA and Ministry of Transport records of FED and RUC rate changes between October 2023 and 5 March 2024: true if no rate increase took effect or was legislated in that window, false if any increase did.

veracity.statement: There’s over $4.4 billion going into public transport services and public transport infrastructure.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the draft Government Policy Statement on land transport 2024 allocates more than $4.4 billion across the public transport services and public transport infrastructure activity classes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published draft GPS on land transport 2024 funding ranges: true if the combined public transport services and public transport infrastructure allocation exceeds $4.4 billion over the GPS period, false if it is below that.

veracity.statement: The last Government left the current state of our roads in a declining state.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the measured condition of New Zealand's roads deteriorated over the term of the previous government.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA/Waka Kotahi road condition metrics (e.g. percentage of state highway and local road network in poor condition, pavement renewal rates, pothole repair counts) for 2017–2023: true if condition measures deteriorated over the period, false if they held steady or improved.

veracity.statement: Well, they had six years and they spent $228 million on “Auckland Light Fail”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that approximately $228 million was spent on the Auckland light rail project across the previous government's two terms.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport and Auckland Light Rail Ltd reported expenditure on the Auckland light rail project from 2017 to 2023: true if total spend is around $228 million, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, I have seen reports of a former member for Mt Albert advocating for the Auckland light rail project prior to the 2017 election, saying it would be completed by 2021.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the then-member for Mt Albert publicly advocated Auckland light rail before the 2017 election and stated it would be finished by 2021.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: 2017 campaign statements and contemporaneous media reporting of the Labour leader and member for Mt Albert on Auckland light rail: true if a completion date of 2021 was publicly stated, false if no such timeframe was given.

veracity.statement: The number of people on remand has increased by 146 percent over the last 10 years, and remand now represents almost 45 percent of the entire prison population.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two statistics about the remand population: 146% growth over a decade, and remand at almost 45% of the total prison muster as at early March 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections prison population statistics (remand-accused plus remand-convicted vs sentenced) for early 2024 compared with early 2014; true if remand numbers rose by roughly 146% and remand is close to 45% of the total muster, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: But the good news is that Corrections has received 2,108 applications since the new recruitment ad started on 4 February 2024 to 21 February 2024. This is a huge increase—almost four times—compared with the 550 applications when the previous Government campaigned in February 2023.
veracity.explanation: Asserts 2,108 corrections officer applications between 4 and 21 February 2024, against 550 for a comparable February 2023 campaign — a near-fourfold increase.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections recruitment records / Official Information Act release of application counts for 4–21 February 2024 and for the February 2023 campaign; true if the counts are approximately 2,108 and 550 over comparable windows, false if the figures differ materially or the comparison periods are not comparable.

veracity.statement: There have been five studies in total commissioned by the Ministry of Education. None of them has done a robust, statistically significant comparison that has been able to find that the programme has increased attendance at school—those are the basic facts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Ministry of Education commissioned five evaluations of the Ka Ora, Ka Ako school lunch programme and that none of them found a statistically significant attendance effect.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The list of Ka Ora, Ka Ako evaluations commissioned by the Ministry of Education up to March 2024, and their reported attendance findings; true if there are five and none reports a statistically significant attendance improvement, false if a commissioned evaluation reports one or the count is wrong.

veracity.statement: Does he stand by his statement on Checkpoint: “The Treasury got on to that and also pointed out that they were wasting around 25 percent of the food that they had.”; and is he aware that it was never 25 percent, and that the Ministry of Education told the Education and Workforce Committee that food wastage had halved from 12 percent in the beginning to 6 percent?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 25 percent wastage figure was never accurate, and that the Ministry of Education told the Education and Workforce Committee that Ka Ora, Ka Ako food wastage fell from 12 percent to 6 percent.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Education and Workforce Committee evidence (transcripts / written answers) and Ministry of Education wastage reporting for Ka Ora, Ka Ako; true if the Ministry reported wastage falling from about 12 percent to about 6 percent and no official source supports a 25 percent figure, false if a Treasury or Ministry document supports 25 percent.

veracity.statement: Can the Minister confirm that the outgoing Government provided precisely zero dollars in funding for the next financial year for the school lunch programme, an enormous fiscal cliff; and can he also advise whether he has considered an approach to that problem, like that suggested by the member Tinetti, that he simply appropriate it because New Zealand doesn’t have a debt problem, as she told Mike Hosking.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government appropriated no funding at all for the school lunch programme for the 2024/25 financial year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2023 appropriations and the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update for Vote Education; true if no funding for Ka Ora, Ka Ako was appropriated beyond the 2023/24 financial year, false if any appropriation for 2024/25 existed.

specificity.statement: The number of people on remand has increased by 146 percent over the last 10 years, and remand now represents almost 45 percent of the entire prison population.
specificity.explanation: Two precise, checkable figures with a stated timeframe and a stated share of the prison population.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As part of the Amendment Paper which I’ve sent to the Justice Committee for consideration alongside the Corrections Amendment Bill, the proposed amendment sets out a clear expectation that remand-accused prisoners will be provided with reintegration and other non - offence-focused support while in prison.
specificity.explanation: Names the legislative vehicle (Amendment Paper to the Corrections Amendment Bill), the committee it went to, and the class of prisoner covered, but gives no figures, cost or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: However, what I will say, as Associate Minister of Education, is that our job is an education system where people feel they can go to school and be equipped to make a difference in their own lives—that’s what makes people happier.
specificity.explanation: A statement of general aspiration for the education system: no mechanism, no measure, no figure and nothing anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I think, when a study itself says that it couldn’t reach the conclusion asked, that is almost by definition not robust.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the evidence, but it overreaches: the evaluation said a larger group of schools was needed to assess longer-term attendance patterns, which is a stated limitation on one question, not a concession that the study as a whole was not robust. Hasty generalisation from a scope caveat to a verdict on the whole evaluation.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Unfortunately, in many places, 25 percent wastage would be an improvement.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion about wastage 'in many places' rests entirely on a single unnamed email from one high school read out immediately before — a hasty generalisation from anecdote, offered against the Ministry's aggregate wastage reporting.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I know that the former Minister probably thinks that she commissioned reports that are good enough for the taxpayer, but this Government is in favour of actually doing robust analysis when we go out and spend their money.
civility.explanation: Condescending speculation about what the former Minister 'probably thinks', with the implication that she is content with substandard work and careless with public money. Short of a direct insult, but it targets her rather than the evaluations.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That’s what this Government needs to do—that’s what anyone in finance needs to do—and that’s why Megan Woods didn’t get the job.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe at a named member's competence — the implication that she was passed over for the finance role because she cannot understand a budget. Aimed at the person, not the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Government is not making such a decision—the Government is having to make the most it possibly can in a range of policy areas because, after six years of this lot doing less and less with more and more taxpayers’ money, this Government now has to do more and more with less taxpayers’ money and try and pay down the debt besides.
focus.explanation: There is a real fiscal point about constrained spending and debt, but it is carried by a general characterisation of the other party's six years in office rather than by any named policy, figure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: You see, they’re leaving so many fiscal cliffs around that sometimes even I can’t keep up!
focus.explanation: A joke at the previous Government's general fiscal record. 'Fiscal cliffs' gestures at a policy problem but nothing specific is named — no programme, appropriation or figure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why does he think it is appropriate to prioritise tax breaks for landlords and property speculators above providing healthy and nutritious lunches to children in our poorest community?
focus.explanation: Names two specific policies — the restoration of interest deductibility for landlords and the school lunch programme — and puts them against each other. On-policy scrutiny, though the framing carries party colouring.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Could I ask the Minister, could he, in the interests of education, find a copy of the Andy Williams song “Lonely Street” and send a copy to that party over there so they can feel a bit more happy about life?
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mood of the party opposite. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named; the education framing is a joke wrapper.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We’re the largest exporter of strong wool, accounting for 20 percent of strong wool traded globally.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand is the world's largest exporter of strong (coarse) wool and that it supplies 20 percent of globally traded strong wool.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI/Stats NZ wool export statistics and international wool trade data (IWTO or Beef+Lamb NZ market reports) for the year to 2024: true if NZ ranks first among strong-wool exporters and its share of globally traded strong wool is approximately 20%, false if it ranks below first or the share is materially different from 20%.

veracity.statement: However, the value of New Zealand wool exports has shrunk from $750 million in 2004 to an estimated $390 million in 2024—a dire situation where it literally costs more to shear a sheep than the income received.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that NZ wool export value fell from about $750m (2004) to an estimated $390m (2024), and that shearing costs per sheep now exceed the wool income per sheep.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries wool export value series for the years ended 2004 and 2024: true if the two figures are within rounding of $750m and $390m. For the second claim, published shearing rates (NZ Shearing Contractors Association) versus average strong-wool clip value per sheep for 2023-24: true if the shearing cost exceeds the wool return per head.

veracity.statement: Why does she refuse to back the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill, a bill that is supported by the whole broadcasting industry?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill is supported by the entirety of the broadcasting industry — a universal claim, not merely a claim of majority support.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Written and oral submissions to the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee on the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill, plus public statements by NZ broadcasters (TVNZ, Warner Bros. Discovery/Three, MediaWorks, NZME, Stuff): true if no NZ broadcaster submitted or stated opposition to the bill, false if any broadcaster opposed it or sought material change.

veracity.statement: Why does the Minister refuse to take a position when the advice from her own officials suggests that the media is under pressure, revenue is declining, and, without intervention, the Government will be under pressure to fund public news content?
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of official advice to the Minister: that the sector is under pressure, revenue is falling, and that absent intervention the Government will face pressure to fund public news content.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry for Culture and Heritage briefings and aide-memoires to the Minister for Media and Communications released under the OIA or proactively published, up to March 2024: true if those papers state declining media revenue and a resulting fiscal risk of funding public news content, false if no such advice exists or it says otherwise.

veracity.statement: Having said that, the previous Government wasted $20 million on the failed merger of TVNZ and RNZ, which achieved fat zero.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific sum — $20 million — spent on the abandoned TVNZ/RNZ public media entity merger, and that it produced no result.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry for Culture and Heritage and Treasury reporting on total expenditure on the Aotearoa New Zealand Public Media entity programme before its cancellation in February 2023: true if total spend is approximately $20m, false if materially lower or higher; the 'achieved nothing' element is true if no legislation passed and no entity was established.

veracity.statement: Yesterday the Prime Minister and I released the draft Government policy statement (GPS) on land transport, announcing that we’re delivering on our campaign and coalition commitments to reintroduce the successful roads of national significance programme with 15 projects across the country to enable people and freight to move around quickly and safely.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the draft GPS on land transport released on 4 March 2024 reinstates the roads of national significance programme comprising 15 projects.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The draft Government Policy Statement on land transport 2024 as published by the Ministry of Transport: true if it lists a roads of national significance programme containing 15 projects, false if the count differs or no such programme is listed.

veracity.statement: We’ve listed two significant priorities in the Bay of Plenty, including Tauriko West State Highway 29 and Takitimu Northern Link stage 2, which was scaled back and delayed by the prior Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Takitimu Northern Link stage 2 was scaled back and delayed under the previous (2017-2023) Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Transport Agency board papers and National Land Transport Programme records for Takitimu Northern Link stage 2 between 2018 and 2023: true if the project's scope was reduced and its construction start pushed out in that period, false if scope and timing were maintained or advanced.

veracity.statement: Will the approximately 100 projects included in the listed pathway include projects for which consents have previously been declined or referred for reconsideration due to environmental risk, including the Te Kūhā coal mine and the Trans-Tasman Resources seabed mining project?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that consents for the Te Kūhā coal mine and the Trans-Tasman Resources seabed mining project were previously declined or referred back for reconsideration on environmental grounds.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Decision records for both projects: for Te Kūhā, the Buller District Council / Department of Conservation and Environment Court decisions on the access arrangement and consents; for Trans-Tasman Resources, the EPA decision-making committee grant and its subsequent treatment by the High Court, Court of Appeal and Supreme Court (2021). True if each was declined or remitted for reconsideration with environmental effects among the reasons, false if neither was.

veracity.statement: As the member will well know, it’s part of the Government’s 100-day plan of action, and I think we’re up to day 97, so the member does not have long to wait.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that fast-track consenting legislation was an item in the coalition Government's 100-day plan, and that 5 March 2024 was day 97 of that plan.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government's published 100-day plan (announced November 2023): true if it contains a commitment to introduce fast-track consenting legislation. For the day count, days elapsed from the swearing-in of the Government on 27 November 2023 to 5 March 2024: true if that count is 97, false if it differs materially.

specificity.statement: However, the value of New Zealand wool exports has shrunk from $750 million in 2004 to an estimated $390 million in 2024—a dire situation where it literally costs more to shear a sheep than the income received.
specificity.explanation: Two dated dollar figures for a named trade series plus a concrete cost-versus-income comparison; anyone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Minister of Agriculture has announced a woolshed tour, commencing in April, where we’ll be engaging with farmers from Northland to Southland to outline the opportunities and to seek their feedback.
specificity.explanation: A named activity with a start month and a stated geographic scope, but no number of events, no budget and no stated output from the feedback. Direction with some detail, short of a checkable commitment.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Having said that, the previous Government wasted $20 million on the failed merger of TVNZ and RNZ, which achieved fat zero.
specificity.explanation: A dollar figure attached to a named programme and a named outcome — precisely the kind of claim that can be checked against published spend.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yesterday the Prime Minister and I released the draft Government policy statement (GPS) on land transport, announcing that we’re delivering on our campaign and coalition commitments to reintroduce the successful roads of national significance programme with 15 projects across the country to enable people and freight to move around quickly and safely.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument (draft GPS on land transport), the programme, the release date and a project count. Concrete enough to check against the published document, though no costs or timeframes are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve listed two significant priorities in the Bay of Plenty, including Tauriko West State Highway 29 and Takitimu Northern Link stage 2, which was scaled back and delayed by the prior Government.
specificity.explanation: Two named road projects in a named region, tied to a published document. Checkable, though without cost or delivery dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How does he justify the proposal to have ministerial decision-making over complex environmental matters rather than having final decisions sitting with independent hearing panels who are able to robustly consider all the evidence?
specificity.explanation: Identifies the precise institutional choice at issue (Ministers versus independent hearing panels) but names no clause, threshold or project.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will the approximately 100 projects included in the listed pathway include projects for which consents have previously been declined or referred for reconsideration due to environmental risk, including the Te Kūhā coal mine and the Trans-Tasman Resources seabed mining project?
specificity.explanation: A project count, a named statutory pathway and two named projects — precise enough that the answer could be checked against the bill's schedule when it appears.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The fast-tracked consenting regime will allow Ministers to refer projects to panels to make conditions upon which those projects will take place, in accordance with the variety of statutes that the member has mentioned.
specificity.explanation: Sketches the mechanism — ministerial referral, panels setting conditions — but gives no threshold for referral, no composition of the panels, and no account of how the named Acts (Conservation, Wildlife, Reserves, EEZ) are actually engaged, which was the point of the question.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why does she refuse to back the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill, a bill that is supported by the whole broadcasting industry?
focus.explanation: Names a specific bill before a select committee and asks about the Minister's position on it. This is scrutiny directed at a named measure, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The honourable member, actually, and his Government had six years to solve the problem, including passing the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill that the member says the whole of media supports. He could have passed it. He failed to do it. It is still at select committee.
focus.explanation: There is real policy content — a named bill and its actual status — but the weight of the answer is the previous government's record rather than the measure or what the Minister will do about it. A policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: While the previous Government talked a big game about transport, we’re actually going to get on and deliver.
focus.explanation: Strip out the comparison with the other side and nothing remains: no project, no figure, no timeframe, no mechanism. A bare us-versus-them contrast on a day when the substance was available to him.
focus.subject: speaker
