focus.statement: How does he justify the proposal to have ministerial decision-making over complex environmental matters rather than having final decisions sitting with independent hearing panels who are able to robustly consider all the evidence?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the design of the proposed regime — who holds the decision right — rather than on the Government's character or record. Scrutiny of a named mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Why, at some of the darkest times in New Zealand media history, has this Minister disappeared from the media, refusing to be interviewed by National Radio, refusing to be interviewed by the Television New Zealand Breakfast show, refusing to be interviewed by the AM Show—why has this Minister disappeared from the national media?
civility.explanation: Turns from the policy onto the Minister herself: 'disappeared' repeated twice imputes hiding and evasion rather than putting a question about her media accountability neutrally. Short of a direct insult, but it is a sneer at the person rather than criticism of a decision.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Obviously, that honourable member isn’t reading the news or watching the news or reading The Spinoff.
civility.explanation: Condescension directed at the member himself — a jibe about his ignorance rather than a rebuttal of what he asked. Below a direct insult, but it is mockery of the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Broadly, yes. But the statement presupposes that the decision-making process will lack transparency, when our intention is that it be very transparent, and also presupposes that it will result in poor environmental outcomes, when our intention is that it result in good environmental outcomes.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested exchange on fast-track consenting where he could readily have gone after the questioner; instead he engages only the content of the quoted statement and attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Broadly, yes. But the statement presupposes that the decision-making process will lack transparency, when our intention is that it be very transparent, and also presupposes that it will result in poor environmental outcomes, when our intention is that it result in good environmental outcomes.
rigor.explanation: He correctly identifies that the quoted warning is conditional, which is a fair reading. But the rebuttal then rests entirely on stated intention: 'our intention is that it be very transparent' does not establish that the process as designed will be transparent, so the conclusion (that the judicial review risk does not arise) outruns what was offered. A real gap between premise and conclusion rather than a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In 2009, the previous National Government exempted electric vehicles (EVs) and plug-in hybrid vehicles from paying road-user charges (RUC), to encourage their uptake.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a 2009 National-led government created the RUC exemption for light EVs and plug-in hybrids, and that the purpose was to encourage uptake.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Road User Charges exemption order/legislation for light electric RUC vehicles and its accompanying Cabinet paper or regulatory impact statement; true if the exemption was made in 2009 under the Fifth National Government and covered EVs and plug-in hybrids with uptake as the stated purpose, false if the exemption originates from a different year, government, or vehicle scope.

veracity.statement: We’ve now passed the 2 percent mark for electric vehicles in the light vehicle fleet and it is only fair that those vehicles now start paying their fair share to contribute towards maintaining our roads and the upkeep of our roads.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that light electric vehicles now make up more than 2 percent of New Zealand's light vehicle fleet as at March 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA motor vehicle register / Ministry of Transport fleet statistics for early 2024; true if light EVs are above 2% of the registered light vehicle fleet, false if the share is at or below 2%.

veracity.statement: The last Government acknowledged it but did not make any preparations for this transition.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Labour government did no preparatory work for moving light EVs and plug-in hybrids into the road user charges system, beyond acknowledging the issue.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport consultation documents, Cabinet papers and the legislated expiry date of the light EV RUC exemption from the 2017–2023 term; true if no public consultation, policy work or legislated end date existed before the 2023 election, false if any such preparation is documented (for example a public consultation on a plug-in hybrid rate, or a statutory exemption end date already set).

specificity.statement: The Government has decided that the reduced rate should be set at $53 per 1,000 kilometres. The rate offers plug-in hybrid EV owners a 30 percent discount on the standard light vehicle rate of $76 per 1,000 kilometres, to account for the petrol consumption that they use.
specificity.explanation: Two exact rates, the discount percentage, the unit of measure and the class of vehicle each applies to. Anyone could check or act on this.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This transition is about fairness and equity, ensuring that all road users are contributing to the upkeep and maintenance of our roads, irrespective of the types of vehicles that they choose to drive.
specificity.explanation: Generic justification framing — 'fairness and equity', 'contributing to the upkeep'. It carries a direction (all vehicles pay regardless of fuel type) but no rate, mechanism or timeframe, in a speech where those were available.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We think it’s fair and equitable to increase that to 30 percent, acknowledging that the 20 percent was based on the average of those vehicles—on what the manufacturers estimate their fuel consumption to be. But when you look at what they actually use, we’ve taken a more conservative approach, and that is why we’ve increased that to a 30 percent reduction based on the light road-user charge rate.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: if manufacturer fuel-consumption estimates understate actual petrol use by plug-in hybrids, a larger discount is warranted to avoid double-charging. The conclusion tracks the premise, but the key premise ('when you look at what they actually use') is asserted with no source or figure offered, so there is a gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So this is an example of a piece of legislation that we’re bringing to the House due to the fact that the last Government did not deal with this problem.
focus.explanation: Blame framing aimed at the previous government, but it is tied to a specific, named policy gap — the expiry of the light EV road user charge exemption — rather than to the other party's character or record in general. Legitimate scrutiny of a policy omission, though the sentence itself leans on the party frame rather than the substance.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It has, effectively, waited for the clock to run down at the expense of members of the public and the community to be able to have an adequate say on the provisions contained within this bill, and so that is rather unfortunate in terms of the use of urgency.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named process failing on the specific bill before the House — the truncated consultation window and the use of urgency. No party-bashing; it names the measure and the mechanism it objects to.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But it also identifies that the submissions on this bill were rather mixed. I think that’s even more of a reason as to why a select committee process should allow for the full range of individuals and collectives to submit in and feed in to that process.
rigor.explanation: A real inference from a cited premise (the disclosure statement records mixed submissions) to a conclusion (a full select committee process is warranted). The link holds: disagreement among stakeholders is a reason to hear more of them. Minor gap in that mixed submissions could equally argue the matter is settled enough, but no fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Once people have the sunk cost of the car, they have an incentive to use it as much as possible. And what really makes the difference is the upfront purchase price of the car. So if we can provide a rebate at the point of purchase, then that has a much bigger impact not only on what consumers choose but on what is on the market here in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: A stated premise about purchase-price sensitivity and sunk costs supports the conclusion that a point-of-purchase rebate beats a running-cost incentive. The inference tracks the premises, and the premises are separately sourced earlier (Treasury advice, international evidence) rather than asserted bare. Whether the premises are true is Veracity's question, not this one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As someone who’s a diesel vehicle driver myself, I understand how streamlined the process is when you’re actually purchasing road-user charges, so I do not believe this will be a huge imposition on people who have previously not needed to deal with this because of the type of vehicle that they drive.
rigor.explanation: An argument about the policy, but the inference rests on a single anecdote: his own experience as an established diesel RUC payer is generalised to first-time users who have never dealt with the system. Appeal to personal anecdote, and the sample is unrepresentative of exactly the group in question.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But I really do start to question the motives of the Government when they, effectively, remove the Clean Car Discount, when they effectively remove other rebates, when they are not seeming to incentivise the uptake.
civility.explanation: Pointed — it questions motives rather than only decisions — but the target is the Government collectively, not a named person, and the charge is tied to specific policy removals rather than to anyone's character. Edges toward imputing bad faith without landing on an individual.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I heard the Minister say in his speech that the previous Government had done no work on this, and I have to say that is patently untrue because, obviously, they’d all gone out and done some consultation on it, firstly.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government carried out consultation on the road-user charge changes for EVs and plug-in hybrids, contrary to the Minister's claim that no work was done.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The departmental disclosure statement for the Road User Charges (Light Electric RUC Vehicles) Amendment Bill and Ministry of Transport consultation records; true if a consultation on RUC treatment of light electric vehicles was run under the 2017-2023 Government, false if no such consultation exists.

veracity.statement: We saw a huge transformation when the Clean Car Discount was brought in, massive increase in import registrations and use of pure electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids, and that has a positive consequence for our overall emissions as a country and the amount of oil we rely on to get around.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that registrations and use of pure EVs and plug-in hybrids rose sharply after the Clean Car Discount was introduced in July 2021. The 'huge'/'massive' framing is part of the claim and is checkable against the registration series.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA Motor Vehicle Register statistics for new and used light vehicle registrations by fuel type; true if EV and PHEV registrations rose substantially from 2021 relative to the pre-2021 baseline, false if the share was flat or fell over that period.

veracity.statement: This was a well-signalled policy. As the previous speaker, Julie Anne Genter, has just said, this was signalled by the previous Minister of Transport Simon Bridges, when he was in that role, that at 2 percent of the fleet this exemption would be removed, and that time has come.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the ending of the light EV road-user charge exemption at 2 percent of the light vehicle fleet was signalled when Simon Bridges was Minister of Transport, and that the 2 percent threshold has now been reached. Also attributes that account to Genter's preceding speech.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Road User Charges (Exemption Period for Light Electric RUC Vehicles) Amendment Act 2015/2016 and contemporaneous Ministry of Transport and ministerial statements, plus NZTA fleet statistics for EV share; true if the 2 percent fleet threshold was the stated trigger set under Bridges and the share has since reached 2 percent, false if the threshold or its origin differs. Genter's speech, quoted above, is the check on the attribution.

specificity.statement: So we have a pure EV and a plug-in hybrid Prius paying $98.80 for a trip, $94.78—nearly $100—and a conventional fossil fuel Prius would pay, in fuel excise duty, $42.92 for the exact same trip.
specificity.explanation: Three named vehicle types, a named route, and dollar figures to the cent, sourced to answers to written parliamentary questions. Fully checkable and actionable; nothing is left to inference about how much or on what basis.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Quickly, in 2009, the previous National Government exempted electric vehicles (EVs) and plug-in hybrid vehicles from paying road-user charges to encourage their uptake.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the road-user charge exemption for light EVs and plug-in hybrids was created by the National-led government in 2009, for the purpose of encouraging uptake.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The amending legislation to the road user charges regime that created the light electric/plug-in hybrid exemption: true if the exemption was enacted in 2009 under the fifth National Government, false if it was enacted in a different year or by a different government.

veracity.statement: This exemption was always planned to end when EVs hit around 2 percent of the light vehicle fleet, and, right now, New Zealand has reached that target.
veracity.explanation: Two linked assertions: that the exemption was designed from the outset to lapse at roughly 2 percent of the light vehicle fleet, and that the light EV share of the New Zealand fleet had reached that threshold as at March 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The original exemption legislation and its explanatory/regulatory impact material for the stated 2 percent trigger, plus Ministry of Transport light vehicle fleet statistics for early 2024: true if the 2 percent threshold appears as the stated end condition and the fleet share was at or about 2 percent, false if the threshold was not the stated condition or the fleet share was materially below 2 percent.

veracity.statement: They meant that New Zealand had one of the highest rates of increase of uptake in electric vehicles in our fleet in the world, and when we take away those options for people, it means that we will see an ongoing effect over several decades in terms of what is available not only in the primary vehicle purchasing market but also for the secondary vehicle purchases, which is most New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the RUC exemption and Clean Car Discount gave New Zealand one of the world's highest rates of growth in EV uptake. The second half of the sentence is a forecast and is not what is being checked here.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: International EV registration growth comparisons for the 2021-2023 period (IEA Global EV Outlook, or Ministry of Transport fleet statistics benchmarked against them): true if New Zealand's EV share growth rate ranked among the leading countries over that period, false if it sat mid-field or lower.

veracity.statement: The fact that we’re looking at moving this to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee—it’s absolutely appropriate that they do take calls of submissions from the public about the rate at which those particular vehicles pay—whether it be the $53 for the hybrids or the $73 per thousand kilometres for the electric vehicles.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the road user charge rates applying under the regime to plug-in hybrids ($53) and to light electric vehicles ($73) per thousand kilometres.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The road user charge rate schedule for light electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles as set out in the bill and the accompanying rates order: true if the rates are $53 and $73 per 1,000 km respectively, false if either figure differs materially from the gazetted rate.

specificity.statement: This exemption was always planned to end when EVs hit around 2 percent of the light vehicle fleet, and, right now, New Zealand has reached that target.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete threshold (2 percent of the light vehicle fleet) and asserts a current position against it — someone could check both against fleet statistics.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The fact that we’re looking at moving this to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee—it’s absolutely appropriate that they do take calls of submissions from the public about the rate at which those particular vehicles pay—whether it be the $53 for the hybrids or the $73 per thousand kilometres for the electric vehicles.
specificity.explanation: Names the committee, the mechanism (public submissions on the rate) and two concrete dollar figures per thousand kilometres. Checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: They are unlikely to be made available to the select committee in a four-week process.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the emissions-impact figures she says are missing will not be supplied to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee within the compressed report-back period.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Transport and Infrastructure Committee's report on the Road User Charges (Light Electric RUC Vehicles) Amendment Bill and the departmental advice published with it: false if modelling of the policy's effect on fleet emissions was provided to the committee before it reported back, true if no such figures were supplied.

focus.statement: So we need to give ourselves some assurance, as this House, that this isn’t having a long-run effect on our emissions profile over time, and those numbers aren’t available for the House today.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: names the specific gap in the evidence (fleet emissions modelling) that she says the committee process needs to fill. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If there was an appropriate amount of time given to these changes, then there would be no need to disregard those long-held Standing Orders, which allow members to conduct their electorate work—their important constituency work—alongside the work that they are expected to do in this House.
rigor.explanation: A valid conditional: the Standing Orders being set aside are the ones protecting electorate work, and they are only being set aside because of the compressed timetable, so a longer timetable removes the need. The conclusion tracks the premise; the unstated assumption is that the committee's workload is driven by the deadline rather than the volume of submissions.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But it’s also of no surprise to any of us that we think it’s only fair and reasonable that they actually now start to contribute to the cost of our roading itself.
rigor.explanation: The case for charging EVs rests on assumed universal agreement ("of no surprise to any of us", "only fair and reasonable") rather than on anything offered — an appeal to popularity and self-evidence. No premise connects EV road use to a cost share; the conclusion is asserted as obvious.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But she is being asked, as are my colleagues in the Labour Party, to give up what would otherwise be spent representing the constituency work when that is purely because the Government has not allowed enough time in its legislative agenda to progress these changes in the normal, democratic way.
civility.explanation: A hard criticism of the Government's handling of its legislative programme, including the charge that it is departing from normal democratic process. It lands entirely on the decision and the timetable, not on any individual — under the re-anchored scale that is near the top.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I took the opportunity to have a look at what the weight of EVs is, and even relatively small vehicles like a Fiat 500 electric vehicle are 1,400-plus kilograms.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the kerb weight of a Fiat 500 electric vehicle exceeds 1,400 kg, offered as evidence that few EVs would fall under the bill's 1,000 kg exclusion threshold.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Manufacturer/NZTA specification for the Fiat 500e kerb weight: true if the published kerb weight is 1,400 kg or above, false if materially below 1,400 kg.

veracity.statement: We will need to call for submissions immediately because the time frame that we’ve been given is to report back by 14 March—i.e., by next week.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, as committee chair, that the select committee's report-back deadline for this road-user charges bill is 14 March 2024 — a week after this debate. Another speaker in the same debate describes the committee period as four weeks.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The House's referral motion for the Land Transport (Road User Charges) Amendment Bill in the Journals of the House of Representatives: true if the reporting date set is 14 March 2024, false if a different date was set.

veracity.statement: For example, this Government has campaigned to build 15 new roads and are pledging $500 million to fix potholes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific Government transport commitments: a campaign pledge to build 15 new roads, and a $500 million pothole repair pledge.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 transport policy documents and post-election Government announcements: true if the roads-of-national-significance commitment numbers 15 and a $500m pothole fund was pledged; false if the counts or the dollar figure differ materially.

veracity.statement: The one pothole they cannot fix, however, is the $24 billion pothole in their budget.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $24 billion shortfall in the Government's budget — in context, the funding gap in its transport programme.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury fiscal forecasts and the Government Policy Statement on land transport / NZTA National Land Transport Fund revenue and expenditure projections: true if a shortfall of approximately $24 billion between the announced programme and funded revenue is documented, false if no such gap of that magnitude is identifiable.

veracity.statement: We heard the Minister who introduced this bill making wild claims that no work has been done on this in the previous Government and then in the next breath talking about the work the previous Government had been doing around road-user charges (RUCs) come 1 March 2024.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister, in the same speech, both denied that the previous Government had done work on road-user charges and referred to that Government's RUC work up to 1 March 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard transcript of the Minister's first reading speech on this bill: true if it contains both a denial that prior work was done and a reference to the previous Government's RUC work, false if it contains only one or neither.

veracity.statement: We know that 44 percent of our energy-related emissions in New Zealand comes from the transport sector and 20 percent of all of New Zealand’s greenhouse gas emissions come from transport, and the bulk of vehicle fleet, light-duty passenger vehicles are the vast majority.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two shares: transport as 44 percent of New Zealand's energy-related emissions, and 20 percent of total greenhouse gas emissions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE Energy in New Zealand / Ministry for the Environment greenhouse gas inventory for the year referenced: true if transport is ~44% of energy-related emissions and ~20% of gross emissions within rounding, false if either figure is materially different.

specificity.statement: I took the opportunity to have a look at what the weight of EVs is, and even relatively small vehicles like a Fiat 500 electric vehicle are 1,400-plus kilograms.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific vehicle model, gives a weight figure, and ties it to the bill's stated 1,000 kg exclusion threshold — someone could check or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our policy would see the use of both accessible and efficient free public transport: free for tamariki, free for students, free for community service cardholders, and made free for everyone within five years.
specificity.explanation: Names the groups covered and a five-year horizon for universal coverage, but supplies no cost, funding source or delivery mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As I’ve been driving around the roads of Northland, observing the state of those roads and observing the number of electric vehicles and hybrids, along with all the other users on the road, it’s become apparent to me that all people using the road should pay their fair share.
specificity.explanation: A statement of position with no figure, mechanism or timeframe; 'pay their fair share' and 'a fair transition' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We know that 44 percent of our energy-related emissions in New Zealand comes from the transport sector and 20 percent of all of New Zealand’s greenhouse gas emissions come from transport, and the bulk of vehicle fleet, light-duty passenger vehicles are the vast majority.
specificity.explanation: Two precise, sourced-in-kind percentages tied to the sector under debate, plus the breakdown by fleet type — directly checkable against published inventories.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, I don’t see that as being a fair question, because on this side of the House there is clearly an intention to roll out EV infrastructure right around the country. So that clearly says we want to see more people using EVs.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts a challenge to the Government's motive by citing the Government's own declared intention, then treats that declaration as establishing the motive. The conclusion rests on the assertion it was meant to test — close to circular, with no independent evidence (spending, timetable, targets) offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: By disincentivising electric vehicles while at the same time cutting public transport, this Government is fuelling climate change.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur by scale: two domestic transport measures are asserted to produce 'fuelling climate change' with nothing offered to connect them — no emissions estimate, no counterfactual uptake figure, no share of the transport budget.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As I’ve been driving around the roads of Northland, observing the state of those roads and observing the number of electric vehicles and hybrids, along with all the other users on the road, it’s become apparent to me that all people using the road should pay their fair share.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal anecdote: driving around and observing vehicles is offered as the whole basis for a general conclusion about who should pay road-user charges. No data on EV numbers, road wear or revenue is supplied to bridge the observation and the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, I don’t see that as being a fair question, because on this side of the House there is clearly an intention to roll out EV infrastructure right around the country. So that clearly says we want to see more people using EVs.
civility.explanation: Disagrees squarely with an opposing member's line of questioning without any imputation of bad faith or personal remark; the disagreement stays on the substance of the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We heard the Minister who introduced this bill making wild claims that no work has been done on this in the previous Government and then in the next breath talking about the work the previous Government had been doing around road-user charges (RUCs) come 1 March 2024.
civility.explanation: 'Wild claims' and 'in the next breath' are pointed and edge toward the Minister personally, but the charge is one of inconsistency in what he said rather than an attack on his character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: The cancelation of cycleway and walkway projects will contribute to road congestion, and, by extension, the increase of congestion charges at peak hour traffic.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that cancelling active-transport projects will raise road congestion and lead to peak-hour congestion charging being increased or introduced.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NZTA/Ministry of Transport congestion metrics for the main centres, plus the statute book on time-of-use charging: true if measured peak congestion rises over the period and a peak-hour congestion charge is enacted or raised; false if congestion is flat or falling and no congestion charging scheme is legislated.

focus.statement: As I’ve been driving around the roads of Northland, observing the state of those roads and observing the number of electric vehicles and hybrids, along with all the other users on the road, it’s become apparent to me that all people using the road should pay their fair share.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure before the House — the fairness of road-user charges — with no reference to another party or its record.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So that’s not a four-week select committee period; that’s less than a week. And it’s really difficult to see how the public who will be affected by these changes and also other technical experts will be able to develop a submission and submit to the select committee, and for the select committee to have enough time to deliberate and report back.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House: a stated premise (the interval to the report-back date) supports the conclusion that submitters and the committee cannot do the work. The premise is loosely stated in live speech ('less than a week' for a nine-day gap), but validity given the assumption holds; the weakness is that it leans partly on incredulity ('I don't see how') rather than on evidence about submission workloads.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The National Party that is leading this say that they’re on target to meet emissions budget 1 and emissions budget 2. If we’re going to make those claims, we have to hear from the experts.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure, not a swipe: if the Government asserts it is on track for the emissions budgets, then a change affecting the light vehicle fleet requires the supporting modelling before members vote. The step from 'they claim X' to 'therefore we need officials' evidence' is sound, though it stops short of showing that this particular bill materially moves the budgets — the gap between the claim made and the conclusion drawn.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And, while I fully support the Labour member Arena Williams’ suggestion for a normal select committee report back date, which would be six months, at the very least four weeks would give the public and the select committee more time—some time—to be able to properly consider what has been put forward.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete alternative with two explicit timeframes (six months, four weeks) and identifies whose proposal she is backing. Actionable and checkable; short of 1.0 only because no mechanism beyond the date is offered.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: One of the issues that I raised in my first reading speech was the significant discrepancy between what electric vehicle users and plug-in electric vehicle users will be paying on the same trip as a comparable car—that is, a fossil fuel car like a conventional Prius hybrid. According to the Minister’s data that he has given us, they’ll be paying more than twice as much.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that, on the Minister's own released figures, a plug-in hybrid driver will pay more than twice as much as a comparable petrol hybrid over the same trip under the new road-user charge regime.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport RUC rate material released with this bill: compute the per-kilometre cost for a plug-in hybrid (RUC rate for PHEVs plus fuel excise duty on the petrol actually consumed) against a comparable petrol hybrid such as a Prius paying fuel excise only. True if the PHEV total exceeds twice the hybrid's on an equivalent trip; false if it is materially less than double.

veracity.statement: One of the things that I am going to point the House’s attention to is in the departmental disclosure statement wherein it talks about the external consultation that happened on the policy document that underlies the legislation we’re examining today. There were over 3,000 submissions; they were far from unified.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the ministry-led consultation on the policy document underlying this bill drew more than 3,000 submissions, and that those submissions did not converge on a single view.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The departmental disclosure statement for this bill and the Ministry of Transport's published summary of submissions on the road-user charges consultation. True if the recorded submission count exceeds 3,000 and the summary reports divided views; false if the count is materially lower or the summary reports broad agreement.

veracity.statement: We had other measures in place that were driving the uptake of electric vehicles (EVs) and, arguably—well, actually, demonstrably; not arguably—were driving the uptake of EVs at a far greater rate than RUC exemption ever had.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Labour Government's other measures — principally the Clean Car Discount — drove electric vehicle uptake at a far greater rate than the road-user charge exemption did. The self-correction to 'demonstrably' raises the strength of the claim from arguable to established.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA light-vehicle registration data for battery and plug-in electric vehicles, comparing monthly new-EV registrations during the Clean Car Discount period (July 2021 to December 2023) against the preceding period when the RUC exemption applied without a purchase rebate. True if EV registration growth is materially higher under the discount; false if uptake tracks similarly across both periods.

civility.statement: I understand the Government may have set some time frames of its own that it wants to keep to but, given that the bill has only had its first reading today, to recommend a report-back date of next week seems completely farcical and unreasonable, and even though we didn’t support the bill at first reading, if it is going to go to a select committee, at the very least we should have four weeks to report it back.
civility.explanation: 'Farcical and unreasonable' is harsh, but it is aimed squarely at the proposed report-back date, not at the Minister. She even grants the Government's scheduling constraint before disagreeing. Fierce criticism of a decision is the expected standard, not a failure.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Often we have changes that are made to legislation—I haven’t gone back and done a calculation of it, but it is something that I may ask the Parliamentary Library to look into, which is the length of time spent at select committee and the shorter select committee processes and the likelihood of amendments coming up in the future, and I surmise that if you were to look into that, you would undoubtedly find that when legislation is not given its full process, then often there will need to be amendments and further House time taken up by fixing errors that are in legislation.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure at issue — short committee time causes later corrective amendments — but the speaker concedes she has done no analysis and then asserts the result as one you would 'undoubtedly find'. The conclusion rests on the speaker's own surmise offered as certainty; nothing is presented to connect the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’ve talked about the staff that it would impact, and I wanted to note that we are in a situation, an environment, where the Government has been looking for cost-cutting measures. We haven’t heard that Parliamentary Services is exempt to that. So placing extreme requirements by this House on staff members in that type of environment I think is very concerning.
rigor.explanation: An argument about the measure — compressed report-back time plus reduced staffing capacity produces an untenable workload — but the load-bearing premise is established from absence of evidence ('we haven't heard that Parliamentary Services is exempt') rather than from any showing that the cuts apply.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It actually has amendments to a primary Act—which is the Road User Charges Act 2012—and then it looks to change secondary legislation, and then my reading of this piece of legislation is that it inserts brand new schedules which would require scrutiny.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three structural facts about the road user charges amendment bill before the House on 5 March 2024: that it amends the Road User Charges Act 2012, that it alters secondary legislation, and that it inserts new schedules.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the road user charges amendment bill as introduced in 2024 (legislation.govt.nz / the bill as referred to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee): true if the bill amends the Road User Charges Act 2012, amends or provides for changes to secondary legislation, and inserts one or more new schedules; false if any of those three elements is absent.

veracity.statement: The main Standing Order, as I understand, in relation to report back, which isn’t mentioned, which I appreciate it’s not necessarily required by the motion, but the Minister, in a way, I feel should mention the Standing Order 303, which is the time for a report back. That is set at six months.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Standing Order 303 is the provision setting the time for a select committee report back, and that the period it sets is six months.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand House of Representatives Standing Orders in force in March 2024, Standing Order 303: true if that Standing Order governs the time for report back and sets it at six months from referral, false if it sets a different period or governs a different matter.

specificity.statement: The main Standing Order, as I understand, in relation to report back, which isn’t mentioned, which I appreciate it’s not necessarily required by the motion, but the Minister, in a way, I feel should mention the Standing Order 303, which is the time for a report back. That is set at six months.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific Standing Order governing report-back time and the exact default period it sets, against which the nine-day motion can be measured. Someone could look it up and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I would suggest that when the leader of the House, or Ministers in charge of legislation come to these select committee instructions, it would be appropriate not only to say, “We can include this” but also to rule out days such as Saturday, to rule out meeting after 6 p.m. on a non-sitting week, when people are in their constituencies, perhaps, and try and have some family time.
specificity.explanation: A concrete, actionable proposal with a named mechanism (wording in select committee instructions) and definite limits — no Saturday sittings, no meetings after 6 p.m. in a non-sitting week. Missing only who would enforce it.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I did listen to the Minister’s reasons and, to be fair, I wasn’t convinced at the need for this incredibly short report-back time, because we’re not talking about a report-back time which is half as long, three months.
civility.explanation: A contested motion where she could readily have impugned the Minister's motives; instead she credits that reasons were given, disagrees with the proposal itself, and attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I have never been to a select committee that met on a Saturday, but, then again, I’ve never been through a period of urgency such as this Government has imposed upon us.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism of the Government's use of urgency in a contested procedural debate, with no individual's character, competence or motives touched.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Whilst you might still set Sunday aside for a day of rest, it is my contention that given the fact that, for example, we’ll more likely than not be sitting to midnight on Wednesday night and sitting extensively on Thursday, the committee will then also quite likely be sitting on Friday, notwithstanding that it is a sitting week, and then quite possibly Saturday.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that, under the nine-day instruction, the Transport and Infrastructure Committee will end up meeting on a Friday and possibly a Saturday. Not a promise about his own action — a prediction about what the committee will do.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Transport and Infrastructure Committee's published meeting record for the nine-day report-back period on this bill (March 2024): true if the committee held a meeting on a Saturday, false if it held no Saturday meeting during that period.

rigor.statement: But by allowing a simple nine-day window for these matters to be addressed and actually for people to get organised and to submit to the process, I think, is shutting the door on these individuals.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House: short notice plus a nine-day window implies would-be submitters cannot organise in time. He supports it with the contrast that select committees usually take months and that the item only recently appeared on the Order Paper. The gap is that he offers no evidence of anyone actually shut out beyond a single constituent, so the conclusion runs slightly ahead of what was shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’ll tell you what will happen is that sentences will bear less relationship with the identity of the offender and the offending, because the judges won’t know, because it’s going to be harder for them to get that information.
rigor.explanation: A stated causal chain — defunding the reports makes the contextual information harder to obtain, judges therefore have less of it, sentences therefore track the offender's circumstances less closely. Each link follows from the last. It is weakened by his own concession that judges 'will still try and glean the information that they can from wherever they can', which he does not then account for.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The problem that we are addressing with this amendment is that if we take away some of that information that is made available to judges, then you narrow the scope of how the judge can weigh up what’s the best way to not only prevent this person from reoffending but also prevent more victims from being created within New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: A valid conditional: less information before the judge narrows the range of considerations the judge can weigh. The step from 'narrower scope' to worse outcomes for reoffending and future victims is asserted rather than shown, which is the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Government has named it the “Legal Services Amendment Bill” because it amends the Legal Services Act, and we think that’s appropriate.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered — the title follows the standard convention of naming an amendment bill after the Act it amends — so there is a genuine inference here. But it is an appeal to convention that does not engage the objection actually raised, which was that the convention leaves the title uninformative about what the bill does. The conclusion 'that's appropriate' therefore rests on restating the practice rather than defending it.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But by allowing a simple nine-day window for these matters to be addressed and actually for people to get organised and to submit to the process, I think, is shutting the door on these individuals.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the motion at issue — the length of the select committee referral and its effect on public submissions. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The problem that we are addressing with this amendment is that if we take away some of that information that is made available to judges, then you narrow the scope of how the judge can weigh up what’s the best way to not only prevent this person from reoffending but also prevent more victims from being created within New Zealand.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the mechanism of the bill — what information reaches judges at sentencing and what follows from removing it. No characterisation of the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The only explanation that we have heard in this House as to why the nine days is related to the 100-day plan for this Government. That is the only reason.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 100-day plan was the only justification the House was given for the nine-day referral period. Utikere himself refers a few sentences earlier to an argument that 'things were due to expire at the end of March', which bears on whether a second reason was in fact offered.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of this debate (5 March 2024) and the Minister's speeches on the referral motion; true if the 100-day plan is the sole justification offered for the nine-day referral period, false if any other reason was given in the House.

veracity.statement: The regulatory impact statement points out that, in fact, the likelihood is that this bill will have the exact opposite effect of the Government’s intention, in terms of sentencing being more effective and more efficient and more cost-effective.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill's own regulatory impact statement predicts an effect contrary to the Government's stated intention on sentencing effectiveness, efficiency and cost. The check is on what the RIS actually says, not on whether the RIS is right.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published regulatory impact statement for the Legal Services Amendment Bill (Ministry of Justice, 2024); true if the RIS assesses that removing funding for section 27 reports is likely to work against the objectives of more effective, efficient or cost-effective sentencing, false if it makes no such assessment or assesses the opposite.

veracity.statement: The other aspect of it is that if you put a person in prison for an extended period of time, you can almost guarantee they will emerge as more dangerous and more of a risk to public safety than they were beforehand.
veracity.explanation: Relaying Sir Kim Workman's claim that extended imprisonment near-certainly makes a person more dangerous on release. The empirical question is the direction and size of the sentence-length effect on reoffending risk; the near-certainty asserted is the checkable overstatement.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections recidivism statistics and peer-reviewed criminological research on the relationship between sentence length and post-release reoffending and violence; true if longer imprisonment is associated with a materially higher risk on release, false if the association is absent, negligible, or mixed. The strength of 'almost guarantee' is part of what is being tested.

civility.statement: This is a Government that has decided to leave it very, very late in the piece towards its 100th day—that’s what the Minister indicated in terms of his explanation earlier this afternoon.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the Government's handling and timing of the bill in a genuinely contested urgency debate. It targets a decision, not any member's character or competence, so it sits at the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So my tabled amendment, which is marked “B”, actually identifies that by inserting it in brackets: “this legal Act is the Legal Services (Making Sentences Harder for Judges) Amendment Act”.
specificity.explanation: Names the amendment paper by its marking and quotes the exact operative wording he proposes to insert. Anyone could look it up and act on it; the only missing detail is the clause reference.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is about legal aid, and legal aid is for poor people, and this is removing access to funding for reports from poor people.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — names legal aid funding and the specific effect of removing it. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I pointed to the fact that who will this disproportionately impact, and what we know from the regulatory impact statement and what we know from commentary regarding this is that this will disproportionately impact Māori, who are, sadly, disproportionately represented in the criminal justice system.
focus.explanation: Cites the bill's own regulatory impact statement and identifies who the change falls on. Named document, named impact — accountability, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I understand that there’s some political posturing going on in terms of saying you’re going to be able to save taxpayers a bunch of money, but, at the same time, if you’re chucking up their petrol taxes a whole heap, why don’t you just give Māori fair access to justice?
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point in here — the claimed fiscal saving — but it is carried on party framing ("political posturing") and a swipe about an unrelated tax.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’ll be quite frank, I find it a repugnant thing to do.
civility.explanation: Brutal about the decision, not the decision-maker. Under the re-anchored scale, condemning a policy in the strongest terms while attacking no one scores near the top.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: “Access” is a good word to use here because it ties in with the concept of access to justice, a concept that doesn’t seem to be one with which this particular Minister of Justice is particularly familiar with.
civility.explanation: Lands on the person: a sneer that the Minister of Justice is unfamiliar with access to justice is a jab at his competence in his own portfolio, not a criticism of the bill.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m sorry if I’m boring you, but this is important for us to discuss and debate this afternoon.
civility.explanation: Sarcasm directed at the Minister's demeanour rather than at his position — mockery of the person in the chamber, short of an insult but past civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We can use up an hour or two of time coming up with silly names on the other side of things, but if we want to debate the substance of the bill, we can move to clause 4, and I’m very happy to answer any questions on the bill at that point.
civility.explanation: Dismissive — "silly names" belittles the opposition's amendments and edges toward implying they are wasting the House's time, but the target is the proposals rather than any member.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But this is about poor people, because this is about payment for reports, and these reports cost between about $1,800 and $2,500 each.
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete costed range for a named item; someone could check the figure against legal aid billing data.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This goes to the point that if you want one of these section 27 reports going forward after this legislation has passed, then you have to pay for it.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific instrument (section 27 reports) and the mechanism the bill introduces — private payment — but supplies no amounts or thresholds.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But this is about poor people, because this is about payment for reports, and these reports cost between about $1,800 and $2,500 each.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a section 27 cultural report typically costs between roughly $1,800 and $2,500.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / Legal Services Agency data on amounts paid for section 27 cultural reports in 2023–24 (and provider fee schedules): true if the typical or average cost falls in the ~$1,800–$2,500 band, false if the typical cost sits materially outside it.

veracity.statement: I pointed to the fact that who will this disproportionately impact, and what we know from the regulatory impact statement and what we know from commentary regarding this is that this will disproportionately impact Māori, who are, sadly, disproportionately represented in the criminal justice system.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that the regulatory impact statement for this bill identifies a disproportionate impact on Māori, and that Māori are disproportionately represented in the criminal justice system.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published Regulatory Impact Statement for the Legal Services Amendment Bill 2024, plus Department of Corrections prison-population statistics against Stats NZ population share: true if the RIS records a disproportionate effect on Māori and the Māori share of the corrections population materially exceeds their population share; false if the RIS makes no such finding or the over-representation does not hold.

veracity.statement: To support that, I want to refer to an article where the Law Society said that the withdrawal of funding “will significantly limit access to justice”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the New Zealand Law Society publicly stated that withdrawing funding for these reports will significantly limit access to justice.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Law Society public statements and its submission/commentary on the Legal Services Amendment Bill 2024: true if the Law Society used that wording (or materially the same) about the withdrawal of funding, false if no such statement exists or the quotation misrepresents its position.

veracity.statement: As we do know, there is a disproportionate representation of Māori within the criminal justice system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori are over-represented in the New Zealand criminal justice system relative to their share of the population.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections prison and community-sentence population statistics by ethnicity compared with Stats NZ census population share: true if the Māori share of the justice population materially exceeds their population share, false if the shares are comparable.

rigor.statement: I understand that there’s some political posturing going on in terms of saying you’re going to be able to save taxpayers a bunch of money, but, at the same time, if you’re chucking up their petrol taxes a whole heap, why don’t you just give Māori fair access to justice?
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur / whataboutism: the level of fuel taxes has no bearing on whether the saving from cutting report funding is justified. The Government's conduct on an unrelated tax is offered as a reason to reverse this one, which does not connect.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The title that the Government has given the bill is the “Legal Services Amendment Bill”, and that is because it is a bill that amends the Legal Services Act, and that makes perfectly good sense.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows from the ordinary drafting convention he invokes, but it does not meet the objection actually put — that the convention leaves the title undescriptive — so there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I’m sure he knows his Magna Carta and the clause that’s still in force in New Zealand: that the courts will do right by all, rich and poor alike.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a clause of Magna Carta remains in force as New Zealand law, and characterises its content as a guarantee that the courts will do right by rich and poor alike.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Imperial Laws Application Act 1988, Schedule 1: true if Magna Carta (1297) chapter 29 is listed among the imperial enactments in force in New Zealand and its text bears the sense of not selling, denying or deferring right or justice to any person; false if no Magna Carta clause is retained or the retained clause says something materially different.

veracity.statement: In particular, I’d like to point out that we know, through written parliamentary questions, that the Ministry of Justice has not undertaken, commissioned, or received any research about the impact of section 27 reports on reoffending.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Ministry of Justice, answering written parliamentary questions, confirmed it holds no research of any kind — undertaken, commissioned or received — on the effect of section 27 reports on reoffending.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The written parliamentary question replies from the Minister of Justice / Ministry of Justice on the parliamentary WPQ register up to March 2024: true if a reply states no such research was undertaken, commissioned or received; false if a reply identifies any such research, or if no WPQ reply on the point exists.

veracity.statement: In terms of people being prepared, well, I’m sure all members of the House are conscious of the fact, when we talk about democracy, that this was something that was very well flagged during the election last year and throughout the year—widespread concern about the increase in money being spent on this, going from $40,000 to $7.5 million in a short period of time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific growth in expenditure on section 27 cultural reports — from $40,000 to $7.5 million over a short period. The claim is about the quantum of legal aid spending on these reports, not about whether the growth was justified.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / Legal Services Agency legal aid expenditure figures for section 27 cultural reports by financial year (as released in official information responses and cited in Budget and estimates material): true if annual spend rises from approximately $40,000 in the earlier year to approximately $7.5 million in a recent year; false if either endpoint is materially different, or if the growth spans a period that could not fairly be called short.

veracity.statement: They were supposed to be oral reports. At some point, around six years ago, a change occurred and they started to be funded out of legal aid. There was no select committee process or Government decision around that change—it just occurred—and the funding went up very, very substantially.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three things about the history of section 27 reports: that they were originally intended to be delivered orally, that legal aid funding for them began around six years before March 2024 (i.e. about 2018), and that this shift happened without any select committee process or Government decision.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Sentencing Act 2002 section 27 as enacted (whether it provides for a person to speak to the court rather than for a written report), together with Ministry of Justice / Legal Services records on when section 27 reports first became payable from legal aid and under what instrument: true if the section as enacted contemplates an oral address, legal aid funding began around 2018, and no Cabinet decision or select committee consideration preceded it; false if the section provided for written reports, if funding began materially earlier or later, or if an identifiable Government decision authorised the change.

rigor.statement: And certainly the papers that I’ve read from the department give that sense: let’s just slow this down a bit, because there are other options; there’s a whole lot of administrative abilities that the Minister and the Legal Services Commissioner have which could equally easily be used to ensure that quality reports are given by qualified people at reasonable prices, when they’re required.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: if existing administrative powers can already achieve the stated objective (quality reports, qualified authors, reasonable prices), legislation under urgency is not required. The premises support the conclusion; the gap is that the administrative powers are asserted rather than identified, so the 'equally easily' step is taken on the speaker's word.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s a sweeping change to access to justice, and that period of time after Royal assent for this to become law in New Zealand is just undemocratic. There is simply no opportunity for the people directly impacted by this bill to be able to have their voices heard.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion does not follow from the premise offered. The commencement period is the interval between Royal assent and the law taking effect; it is not a window in which affected people would be heard in any event. The absence of a hearing follows from the lack of a select committee stage, which is a different clause and a different objection — as stated, the inference is a non sequitur that attributes to clause 2 a defect belonging elsewhere.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Mr Webb suggests that we should never bring in the commencement of this legislation—and that doesn’t surprise me, in terms of a Government that was prepared just to sit on their hands while all this money was spent, and other legal aid meantime struggled.
rigor.explanation: Strawman. Webb proposed commencement by Order in Council conditional on a stated test, not that the Act should 'never' come into force; the reply argues against a position that was not advanced. The remainder is guilt-by-association with the previous Government's record rather than a reason bearing on the commencement clause.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I must say—putting it in within 14 days—I am a little concerned that this is just a little bit of posturing around getting stuff done and being able to say, “Look what I’ve delivered to you.”—a kick in the guts for the poor, because that’s what it is.
civility.explanation: Imputes a bad-faith motive to the Minister — that the commencement date is 'posturing' for the sake of appearing to deliver, rather than a policy judgement. That is the imputing-bad-faith band, though hedged ('a little bit of', 'I am a little concerned') and short of a personal insult. The 'kick in the guts for the poor' line attacks the effect of the clause, not the man, and does not itself cost anything.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It kind of looks like it’s just a tick box for the 100-day plan. It kind of just looks like this Government wants to look tough and say they’re doing some stuff.
focus.explanation: There is a policy anchor — the 100-day plan and the bill's place in it — but the weight of the passage is a characterisation of what the Government is 'really like' and what it wants to look like, rather than the measure's mechanism or effect. A real point wrapped in party framing. No individual is attacked, so Civility is untouched.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Mr Webb suggests that we should never bring in the commencement of this legislation—and that doesn’t surprise me, in terms of a Government that was prepared just to sit on their hands while all this money was spent, and other legal aid meantime struggled.
focus.explanation: There is a policy referent — legal aid spending and the pressure on other legal aid — but the passage is built around what the previous Government was disposed to do ('sit on their hands') rather than the commencement provision under debate. Partial policy content in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My question to the Minister, with respect to that, is: is there flexibility, or is the Minister and the department of a mind, where there are unforeseen circumstances within those two weeks, or, where there is a known backlog in a District Court, whether or not those who are affected by that backlog have some grace here to make sure that they get their application in in respect of the time line that the Minister has just described?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the operation of the clause under debate: whether the 14-day transitional window admits any flexibility for applicants caught by District Court backlogs. Names the mechanism, the affected group and the specific failure mode. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re debating the clause about when this Act would come into force, which will be 14 days after the bill is passed. That is to give people some notice and to have a process for applications or requests for approval for funding for these reports to be approved by the commissioner before the two weeks, so that people have some time to get the applications in, if they are currently under way, and they can be approved up until two weeks from when this bill is passed.
specificity.explanation: States the timeframe (14 days from passage), the actor (the commissioner), and the mechanism it is meant to enable (in-train applications lodged and approved before commencement). Someone could check the clause against this description and act on it. Short of 1.0 because no volume, cost or transitional-provision detail is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of people being prepared, well, I’m sure all members of the House are conscious of the fact, when we talk about democracy, that this was something that was very well flagged during the election last year and throughout the year—widespread concern about the increase in money being spent on this, going from $40,000 to $7.5 million in a short period of time.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete figures and a named cost driver, which makes the claim checkable against expenditure records. Not 1.0 because the years the two figures belong to are left unstated — 'a short period of time' carries the timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: What I want to focus on, in particular around the commencement date, is that this legislation is being rushed through under urgency; it hasn’t had the benefit of a select committee process.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two process facts about this bill: that it is being progressed under urgency, and that it was not referred to a select committee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record and Parliament's bill page for the sentencing/section 27 reports bill before the committee on 2024-03-05: true if the House had accorded urgency for its passage and the bill was passed without referral to a select committee; false if urgency was not in force or a select committee considered it.

veracity.statement: This is not good lawmaking, and I would just point out that the New Zealand Law Society, the Māori Law Society, the Bar Association, and several defence lawyers are all seriously criticising this move by the Government and the Minister.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that four named categories of legal body — the New Zealand Law Society, the Māori Law Society, the Bar Association and defence lawyers — publicly criticised the removal of section 27 cultural reports.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published statements, media releases or media comment from the New Zealand Law Society, Te Hunga Rōia Māori o Aotearoa and the New Zealand Bar Association dated around February–March 2024 on this bill: true if each publicly criticised it, false if any of the named bodies made no critical statement or supported the change.

civility.statement: This is not good lawmaking, and I would just point out that the New Zealand Law Society, the Māori Law Society, the Bar Association, and several defence lawyers are all seriously criticising this move by the Government and the Minister.
civility.explanation: Condemns the lawmaking process and the Government's move in strong terms while attacking no individual's character or competence — the expected standard under the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So is he expecting law and order to be restored to New Zealand 14 days after the commencement of this bill?
civility.explanation: Sarcasm aimed at the Government's stated rationale for the bill rather than at the Minister personally — pointed and needling, edging toward the person without landing on them.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My questions to the Minister are: is he confident that our prison system has the capacity and the resources to be able to deal with an increase, which is the likely effect of this decision that he is making today, and which this clause proposes is ready to go—up and running—in 14 days?
focus.explanation: Directed squarely at the clause before the committee — its commencement period and the prison-capacity consequence — rather than at the other party. Legitimate scrutiny of a named provision.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, one of the concerns I have is that it seems like we’re replacing a report, which is seen as expensive, with oral evidence. Oral evidence is not cheap. It is often something that is going to require costs on behalf of the witness—it may be an expert witness, which is going to really blow out the costs.
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism of the change and its cost consequences directly; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They anticipate the filing of Oranga Tamariki, medical, school, police, national intelligence application records to detail a defendant’s deprivation, harm, and disadvantage, and so they’ll have to engage cultural experts, psychologists, alcohol and drug therapists, as well as engage with whānau and family who may have literacy deficits and are intimidated by the courtroom.
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete record types and the specific professionals that would have to be engaged in place of a section 27 report — a checkable, actionable account of the mechanism, though without costs or volumes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m happy to tell the member that, yes, I am confident that the corrections system will be able to handle this change.
specificity.explanation: A bare assurance in answer to a question that put specific bed numbers (136, 120, 124) on the table; carries no figure, mechanism or timeframe of its own.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So has there been any consideration of running a trial in this, where you could just do this in one place and set it up against the other system and look at the consequences, so there weren’t unintended consequences.
specificity.explanation: Proposes an identifiable mechanism — a single-site pilot run against the existing system and measured for consequences — but supplies no site, duration, measures or threshold for judging it.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I am confident that in the 14 days after this bill is passed and before the Act comes into force, the—I cannot speak on behalf of the judiciary, of course, but what I can say is that they will continue to have many tools available to them to understand the background of offenders, and within 14 days. That is sufficient time for this change to be made.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that 14 days is sufficient — rests only on the premise that other tools remain available. That other tools exist does not bear on whether courts and counsel can adjust their processes within the window, so there is a real gap between what is offered and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, one of the concerns I have is that it seems like we’re replacing a report, which is seen as expensive, with oral evidence. Oral evidence is not cheap. It is often something that is going to require costs on behalf of the witness—it may be an expert witness, which is going to really blow out the costs.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: if the same information must still be put before the court, substituting oral evidence for a written report shifts cost rather than removing it, and she identifies the cost drivers (expert witnesses, judge and court time) that carry the conclusion. Supported, though no comparative figures are offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One of the concerns I raised is because I saw what happened when there were closing-down actions by this legislature of the role of various people in the Family Court. So, in that situation, what we saw when we closed down those avenues was others spring up that were way less efficient for the system.
rigor.explanation: An argument from precedent: because removing formal roles in the Family Court produced less efficient substitutes, removing funded written reports will do the same. The inference is a real one about the measure at hand, but the parallel between the two regimes is asserted rather than established, and no evidence of the earlier inefficiency is offered — a weak analogy rather than a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So the trajectory was clear: if we didn’t do something about it, we’d be heading for 10 million and then 15 million as the industry, the cottage industry, developed.
rigor.explanation: A straight-line extrapolation of a past spending curve into the future. The premises (a rising series) do partly support the conclusion, but nothing is offered to show the growth driver would persist — the inference leans on the trend alone.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, Minister, I would ask you to either revisit that and be clear to the committee, because I put it to you that you have no idea how many reports Harry Tam has provided or how much.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the premise offered: if the Ministry's own written answer says provider-level amounts are not held, the Minister cannot know how many reports that provider supplied. Valid inference from the cited record.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If somebody does an oral report, does that mean they’re bringing in a professional to do it, or does it mean they’re bringing in a whānau member to do it?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the policy before the committee — who would actually deliver the oral information that replaces a funded written report. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, in the previous Labour Government, that would have meant not doing very much, and maybe getting a report and thinking about it, and in 10 years’ time maybe considering it.
focus.explanation: A characterisation of how the other party generally behaves, with no policy, measure or outcome named. Strip out the swipe at Labour and nothing about section 27 reports remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So, Minister, I would ask you to either revisit that and be clear to the committee, because I put it to you that you have no idea how many reports Harry Tam has provided or how much.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named policy claim against the Minister's own written answer — an evidentiary challenge on the measure before the committee, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The options I refer to are: did he consider imposing a cap on the amount of legal aid funding available for section 27 reports? And option four: did he consider introducing an accreditation system for section 27 report writers? Also, did he consider option five: amend the Sentencing Act 2002 to introduce a threshold for provision of section 27 reports based on the seriousness of the offence?
focus.explanation: Entirely about the policy design — whether documented alternatives to scrapping the funding were weighed. No reference to the other party's character or record.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If somebody does an oral report, does that mean they’re bringing in a professional to do it, or does it mean they’re bringing in a whānau member to do it?
specificity.explanation: Names the replacement mechanism and two concrete alternatives for who would deliver it, but carries no figures, timeframe or process detail — a direction with some detail rather than something checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That sort of touting for business for these reports was something that has led over the last six years to a very steady and substantial increase in the outlays for these reports: starting off about 40,000 in 2017 and stepping up to a million and then to 2 million and then to 3 million, and by the time we got to 7.5 million last year and the graph was going up like that [gestures a steep incline].
specificity.explanation: A dated dollar series with a named cost line — a listener could go and check every figure in it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The options I refer to are: did he consider imposing a cap on the amount of legal aid funding available for section 27 reports? And option four: did he consider introducing an accreditation system for section 27 report writers?
