focus.statement: The reason Government are doing it is to save money. They don’t care about access to justice. They don’t care about a fair justice system. They don’t care about the tools that we have given to judges to perform their jobs. What they care about is saving money, and I think that that is abhorrent.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point buried here — cost saving traded against access to justice and judges' sentencing tools — but most of the passage is a repeated characterisation of what the other side does and does not care about rather than the effect of the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Because let’s be honest: this disproportionately affects Māori, and it is Māori who will see the real detriment from this bill when those factors are not able to be taken into account at sentencing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that removing legal-aid funding for section 27 reports will fall disproportionately on Māori — a factual claim about the composition of the affected population, not an opinion about whether the bill is desirable.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / Legal Services Agency data on the ethnicity of recipients of legal-aid-funded section 27 cultural reports, and Department of Corrections sentenced-population ethnicity data. True if Māori are represented among funded section 27 recipients at a materially higher rate than their share of the general population; false if their share is at or below population share.

veracity.statement: But it does stop the cottage industry that writing section 27 reports has become, costing the taxpayer millions—over $7.5 million last year, up from $40,000 in 2017—while doing nothing for the victims of crime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that legal aid expenditure on section 27 reports was over $7.5 million in the most recent year and $40,000 in 2017. The 'doing nothing for victims' clause is a value judgement and is not part of the checkable claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice legal aid expenditure figures for section 27 cultural reports, by financial year. True if the 2022/23 figure exceeds $7.5m and the 2017 figure is approximately $40,000; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: It was never envisioned for authors to be paid a whole lot of money which is raised from taxpayers—to be provided—even with no direct connection to the families or the offenders.
veracity.explanation: A claim about the original intent of section 27 of the Sentencing Act 2002: that publicly funded, professionally written reports by authors unconnected to the offender were not contemplated when the provision was enacted.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Section 27 of the Sentencing Act 2002 as enacted, its explanatory note and the 2002 select committee report. True if the provision as enacted contemplated only persons speaking on the offender's behalf and made no provision for paid external report authors; false if the enacting materials contemplated funded professional reports.

veracity.statement: In this own Government’s regulatory impact statement, it says, regarding these time frames, that the proposals in this paper have been assessed in a significantly truncated time frame, that it has had limited ability to test the assumptions underpinning the problem definition and proposed response, to investigate and understand the intended or unintended consequences, to undertake consultation with Māori and stakeholders, and to consider a broad range of options.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's own regulatory impact statement for this bill records that the analysis was done in a significantly truncated time frame with limited ability to test assumptions, consult Māori and stakeholders, or consider a broad range of options.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Justice Regulatory Impact Statement accompanying the Legal Services Amendment Bill (2023–24). True if it contains a limitations section stating a significantly truncated time frame and constrained consultation and option analysis; false if no such statement appears.

veracity.statement: In the departmental disclosure statement, it points out that there has been no consultation with Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the departmental disclosure statement for the Legal Services Amendment Bill records that no consultation with Māori was undertaken.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The departmental disclosure statement published for the Legal Services Amendment Bill. True if its consultation section records no consultation with Māori; false if it records consultation with Māori or iwi bodies.

divination.statement: Maybe one of those principles will be reviewed when we see the next bill come through the House on that one.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that a further bill dealing with the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi will be brought before the House. Not a promise about her own action — she is in opposition and predicting the Government's legislative programme.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Parliamentary bills register. True if a Government or member's bill whose subject is the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi is introduced and read in the House by the resolve-by date; false if no such bill is introduced.

civility.statement: So I congratulate the members opposite on ticking the 100-day box of the 100-day plan and I look forward to all the commentary that comes in the weeks and months that pass as this Government once again hypocritically rides roughshod over the rights of New Zealanders and democracy; of people having a voice and being able to say that this bill is just damn wrong.
civility.explanation: Mock congratulation plus an express charge of hypocrisy — sneering and an imputation of bad faith rather than engagement with the substance. No individual is named or insulted, so it stops short of a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Māori and Pasifika communities, Māori and Pasifika whānau, Māori and Pasifika offenders are not going to get the benefit of the section 27 legal funding when it is removed by this mean-spirited Government, who does not care about victims who require support.
civility.explanation: 'Mean-spirited' and 'does not care about victims' impute motive and indifference rather than contesting the policy. A genuine civility failure, though aimed at the Government collectively rather than at any named member.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And this Minister of Justice should hang his head in shame.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on a named individual's honour rather than on the decision — the Minister is told to be ashamed of himself, which is about the person, not the bill.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But it does stop the cottage industry that writing section 27 reports has become, costing the taxpayer millions—over $7.5 million last year, up from $40,000 in 2017—while doing nothing for the victims of crime.
specificity.explanation: Two dated figures and a named spending line: $7.5 million in the last year against $40,000 in 2017. Precise enough for anyone to go and check against the legal aid accounts.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But what the Legal Services Amendment Bill wishes to do is simply to bring back section 27 reports to what they were originally intended to do, which was to allow family members and friends, people who knew the offenders, to speak to the report and give them support.
specificity.explanation: Names the bill, the provision and who the mechanism is meant to cover, but supplies no figures, dates or operative detail of the amendment itself.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In this own Government’s regulatory impact statement, it says, regarding these time frames, that the proposals in this paper have been assessed in a significantly truncated time frame, that it has had limited ability to test the assumptions underpinning the problem definition and proposed response, to investigate and understand the intended or unintended consequences, to undertake consultation with Māori and stakeholders, and to consider a broad range of options.
specificity.explanation: Names the source document and reports its stated limitations in detail — truncated time frame, untested assumptions, no consultation, narrowed options. A listener could go to the regulatory impact statement and find the passage.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So to those that may be tuning in to this debate this morning, I would say this Government is saying that it’s tough on crime, that it’s saving money, that it’s shutting down a cottage industry, but their own analysis provided by officials in December says that this is likely to increase the costs on the justice system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official advice received in December 2023 on removing legal aid funding for section 27 reports concluded the change was likely to increase justice-system costs — contradicting the Government's stated saving.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Justice regulatory impact statement / departmental advice of December 2023 on the Legal Services Amendment Bill (removal of legal aid funding for s27 cultural reports); true if that advice states the change is likely to increase costs on the justice system, false if it projects net savings or is silent on cost increases.

veracity.statement: The Government’s own department, Te Puni Kōkiri, said it does not support these proposals.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Puni Kōkiri, as a government department consulted on the bill, recorded that it does not support the proposals to remove funding for section 27 reports.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Puni Kōkiri's departmental advice / agency comments recorded in the Ministry of Justice regulatory impact statement and disclosure statement for the Legal Services Amendment Bill 2024; true if TPK is recorded as not supporting the proposals, false if TPK supported them or gave no such position.

focus.statement: So to those that may be tuning in to this debate this morning, I would say this Government is saying that it’s tough on crime, that it’s saving money, that it’s shutting down a cottage industry, but their own analysis provided by officials in December says that this is likely to increase the costs on the justice system.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: names the policy, the source of the advice and the specific claimed effect (justice-system costs), which is scrutiny rather than party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is just politicking. This is just them and their arrogance, being absolutely determined to implement something within 100 days, with not even taking it through a proper process and inviting submissions from the experts from this.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine process point (the 100-day deadline, no select committee submissions), but it is carried by characterisation of the other side's motive and temperament rather than the content of the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What the last day of kōrero has shown me is the extent to which some people in this House will go to defend criminals. It’s been astounding.
focus.explanation: Characterises the motives of the other side and names no policy, mechanism, figure or outcome from the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So do not buy into their argument that this is a cost-saving exercise, that this has been unfair use of taxpayer money, when the evidence and the commentary provided from the legal profession—the experts, actually, in this field: the New Zealand Law Society, Māori Law Society, Bar Association, defence lawyers, former judges, and a Supreme Court judge—all say that they have grave concerns about the impact that this Government’s rushed policy to remove funding for section 27 reports will have on access to justice and on fair and appropriate sentences.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure, but the weight rests on an appeal to the authority of the legal profession: that experts hold grave concerns about access to justice does not by itself refute the cost-saving claim, which is a separate question about fiscal effect.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When I went through the practice part of the law component, I remember our lecturer saying that when it comes to sentencing, as a lawyer, you’ve got to put together a list of mitigating factors for the judge to consider when he or she is making a determination on sentence. So I don’t think it’s such a big ask for us to say, for our lawyers, let’s get back to the basics. Let’s put together that list of mitigating factors for our magistrates, for our judges to make their decisions.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote and to the authority of a remembered lecturer, with a gap between premise and conclusion: that counsel routinely list mitigating factors does not establish that funded section 27 reports add nothing, which is the proposition the bill turns on.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What the last day of kōrero has shown me is the extent to which some people in this House will go to defend criminals. It’s been astounding.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to other members personally — casting their opposition to the bill as a willingness to defend criminals rather than engaging their stated reasons.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The reason we are repealing this Act under urgency is that the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) is about to commit between $2 million to $3 million to develop an IT system to meet the requirements of the Act.
specificity.explanation: Names the agency, the spend band ($2-3m), the purpose (an IT system) and the reason for urgency. Someone could go and check the departmental estimate.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The other thing which we argued strongly with the Government at the time, as they railroaded this through the select committee, was that anyone, any small business, even an individual, and some of the members from across the way, if they so chose, could get on their phone, dial into a website, and go to one of the credit agencies—and there are four, but just to name one, such as Centrix—and they would be able to get that information on payment times in real time, not 10 months’ old, in real time, and actually much more comprehensively, and on the payment cycles of a particular firm for a mere sum of $35.
specificity.explanation: Names the alternative mechanism, the number of providers, a specific provider and a price point ($35). Concrete enough that a listener could act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The economy is being strangled by a spaghetti of regulations requirements that are tying businesses in knots.
specificity.explanation: A metaphor offered where a figure or a named regulation would do. No rule, cost, sector or count is identified, so nothing here can be checked or acted on — notable in a speech that is otherwise dense with figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I’m going to put out some amendments today, and I hope that the Minister will listen to them. They are amendments that are all about doing stuff that gives this more teeth, doing stuff that takes this seriously, because I want to see our small businesses thrive in this country, and we should be targeting those big businesses and holding them to account.
specificity.explanation: Amendments are announced but not described: 'doing stuff that gives this more teeth' names no clause, threshold, penalty or mechanism, and nothing here would let anyone tell what the amendments would change.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The reason we are repealing this Act under urgency is that the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) is about to commit between $2 million to $3 million to develop an IT system to meet the requirements of the Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that MBIE was, as at March 2024, about to commit $2-3 million to build an IT system required by the Business Payment Practices Act 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's regulatory impact statement / departmental cost advice for the Business Payment Practices Act 2023 implementation: true if it records planned IT build costs in the $2-3 million range, false if the documented figure is materially different or no such commitment was pending.

veracity.statement: The other aspect with the proposal in the Act was that the businesses, the large businesses, would be required to submit a return every six months, but they would then have four months after that to file their return. In essence, the information could at different periods of time be up to 10 months old when the small-business owner was actually trying to find out what is the current state of payment cycle for the large business.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Business Payment Practices Act 2023 required large businesses to report on a six-month disclosure period and allowed four months after the end of that period to file.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The disclosure-period and filing-deadline provisions of the Business Payment Practices Act 2023 and its regulations: true if the Act sets six-month disclosure periods with a four-month filing window, false if either the period or the deadline differs.

veracity.statement: The other thing which we argued strongly with the Government at the time, as they railroaded this through the select committee, was that anyone, any small business, even an individual, and some of the members from across the way, if they so chose, could get on their phone, dial into a website, and go to one of the credit agencies—and there are four, but just to name one, such as Centrix—and they would be able to get that information on payment times in real time, not 10 months’ old, in real time, and actually much more comprehensively, and on the payment cycles of a particular firm for a mere sum of $35.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that there are four credit reporting agencies in New Zealand and that a report on a particular firm's payment times can be bought from one of them, such as Centrix, for about $35.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Privacy Commissioner's list of credit reporters operating under the Credit Reporting Privacy Code, and Centrix's published price for a business credit/payment-behaviour report: true if there are four such agencies and a comparable report costs approximately $35, false if the count or the price is materially different.

veracity.statement: I would note that the Australian Government implemented a similar piece of legislation in 2020. There’s been a recent review of that. It’s found to be actually not working and, in some cases, has led to even worse outcomes for small businesses.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Australia passed comparable payment-times reporting legislation in 2020 and that a recent statutory review of it concluded the scheme was not working, and in some cases produced worse outcomes for small businesses.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Australian Payment Times Reporting Act 2020 and the statutory review of it reported to the Australian Government: true if the review concluded the scheme was not achieving its objectives and identified instances of detriment to small business, false if the review found the scheme working as intended or reported no such detriment.

veracity.statement: So a business like Fonterra delayed payment to its staff for three months.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Fonterra routinely withheld payment for about three months from people contracted to it — clarified in the immediately following exchange as sole traders and suppliers rather than employees.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Fonterra's supplier/contractor payment terms as reported in its own procurement policy and in contemporaneous reporting on New Zealand large-company payment terms: true if Fonterra imposed payment terms of around 90 days on sole traders or small suppliers, false if its standard terms over the period were materially shorter.

veracity.statement: And this emerged as an issue, and it got picked up, and it got picked up by The Spinoff in 2017, by one of the journalists, Cormack, who talked about it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that The Spinoff published coverage of late payment to small suppliers in 2017, written by a journalist named Cormack.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Spinoff's 2017 archive: true if an article on large-company payment delays to small businesses or contractors appears in 2017 under the byline Cormack, false if no such piece exists or the year or author is wrong.

veracity.statement: Our small ones are 97 percent of New Zealand businesses, and those people need a champion in this Government, and they haven’t got one.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that small businesses make up 97 percent of all New Zealand businesses.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Business Demography Statistics / MBIE small business factsheet for the year in question: true if enterprises meeting the standard small-business definition (fewer than 20 employees) are about 97% of all enterprises, false if the share is materially lower.

rigor.statement: However, many small businesses, particularly when you think about ones in Porirua or West Auckland or in parts of Tauranga, won’t even know who MBIE is. And the thought that they would go and search on an MBIE website—would know where to look on that MBIE website—to find the specific data is something that is not actually a very strong argument. This undermines the utility of the Act as the information disclosed is highly unlikely to be used by small businesses in their decision making as to who they should do business with.
rigor.explanation: The inference is sound in form — if small firms neither know of nor consult the register, published data cannot inform their decisions — but the premise about awareness rests on an unevidenced assertion about named localities rather than any survey or usage data. A real argument about the measure, with a gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The other aspect with the proposal in the Act was that the businesses, the large businesses, would be required to submit a return every six months, but they would then have four months after that to file their return. In essence, the information could at different periods of time be up to 10 months old when the small-business owner was actually trying to find out what is the current state of payment cycle for the large business.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion is straightforward arithmetic on the premise offered: a six-month reporting period plus a four-month filing window puts the oldest data ten months behind. Given the stated assumptions the inference holds; whether the timeframes are stated correctly is a separate question.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Small businesses won’t be impacted by this repeal, because the Act hasn’t come into effect yet.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure, with a genuine gap: it treats 'not yet in force' as equivalent to 'no effect forgone', which ignores the prospective benefit the Act was intended to deliver from the end of May. The conclusion only follows if the Act would have achieved nothing — the very point in dispute.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What they’ve got is a Minister who comes from the experience of being a fund manager, and that is all about financial markets. That’s big business. That’s very, very different from the small businesses I’m talking about.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion drawn in the preceding sentence — that small businesses have no champion — rests entirely on the Minister's former occupation. That is a circumstantial ad hominem: his career history is offered in place of any argument about what the repeal does or fails to do.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Start leading from the top—start leading from where Government sits rather than imposing costs on businesses, which is always the approach of the Labour Government when they thought about solutions.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point here — government agencies should meet payment standards before compliance costs are imposed on firms — but it is carried on a general characterisation of how the previous Government 'always' approached problems, with no measure or figure named on that side.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I have a great deal of time for Mr Bayly as a person—as he knows, we’ve sat on committees together, and I know him well—and I don’t intend to do anything but absolutely speak genuinely to the Government and to the Speaker about what I think about what is going on today.
civility.explanation: Opening a contested first-reading speech against the Minister's bill, she separates the person from the measure explicitly. Every opportunity to open on the man, taken on the argument instead.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What they’ve got is a Minister who comes from the experience of being a fund manager, and that is all about financial markets. That’s big business. That’s very, very different from the small businesses I’m talking about.
civility.explanation: Pointed and directed at the Minister personally, but it questions the relevance of his background rather than his character, competence or good faith, and it is delivered without sneering.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We have become used to the coalition Government’s desire to seek some fabled idyll where the lowly classes know their place.
focus.explanation: Characterises the coalition Government's motives in general terms; no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named. Pure party framing rather than engagement with the repeal before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Again, like so much that is undemocratic, this repeal is being pushed through under urgency which denies the voices of small businesses to be heard through the select committee process.
focus.explanation: Names the specific measure (this repeal), the specific mechanism (urgency) and the specific consequence (no select committee hearing). Legitimate procedural scrutiny of the bill actually before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill that we’re putting in place does repeal some unnecessary compliance costs—and in a relationship we don’t actually need to be interfering in.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the measure before the House and what it does — repeals reporting obligations — with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If anyone needed more proof that this Government has corporations in its pocket, they should look no further than this bill, the Business Payment Practices Act Repeal Bill.
focus.explanation: Names the specific bill, but the weight of the sentence is a general characterisation of whose interests the Government serves rather than what the repeal does.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is part of an economic agenda that values the profits of the tobacco industry over Māori lives.
focus.explanation: Leaves the payment practices repeal entirely to characterise the Government's motives across an unrelated policy area. No mechanism, cost or outcome of the bill under debate is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Again, like so much that is undemocratic, this repeal is being pushed through under urgency which denies the voices of small businesses to be heard through the select committee process.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that this particular repeal bill is being progressed under urgency and will therefore not go to a select committee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard and the Order Paper for the Business Payment Practices Act Repeal Bill in March 2024; true if the House was in urgency and the bill passed its stages without referral to a select committee, false if it was referred to select committee or taken outside urgency.

veracity.statement: Personally I would like to hear from those small businesses who are the backbone of our economy and are currently facing the harsh realities of high interest rates and soaring inflation that is being fuelled by this Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that inflation is currently soaring and that the present Government is fuelling it. Two checkable components: the direction of the inflation series, and attribution to this Government's policy.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation series for quarters from Q4 2023 through Q1 2024, plus RBNZ Monetary Policy Statement commentary on drivers; true if annual inflation rose after the coalition took office in November 2023 and the rise is attributed to government policy, false if annual inflation continued to fall over that period.

veracity.statement: Research from the Institute of Economic Research has shed light on the problem and suggests it’s $456 million annually—annually.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific estimate of the annual cost of late payments to New Zealand small business ($456 million) to NZIER research.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZIER research on the cost of late payments to New Zealand businesses; true if it estimates the annual cost at approximately $456 million, false if the figure, the scope or the attributed institution differ materially.

veracity.statement: The Commerce Commission concluded in 2020 that major supermarkets made a profit of $430 million, but now they can delay payment to those who are providing the goods and services to those particular organisations, without them being paid over a four-month period.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Commerce Commission reached a finding in 2020 that major supermarkets made $430 million in profit.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Commerce Commission market study into the retail grocery sector; true if the Commission concluded in 2020 that the major supermarkets made $430 million in profit, false if the year of the conclusion or the figure differ materially from the published report.

veracity.statement: The richest 10 percent now control 50 percent of the country’s wealth. The poorest half owns a mere 2 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific distribution of New Zealand household net worth: top decile holds half of all wealth, bottom half holds two percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Net Worth statistics from the Household Economic Survey; true if the wealthiest 10 percent of households hold approximately 50 percent of total net worth and the bottom 50 percent approximately 2 percent, false if either share differs materially.

veracity.statement: On top of that, average people of Aotearoa are paying 20.2 percent in tax while the wealthy are only paying 9.4 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific effective tax rates — 20.2 percent for average New Zealanders against 9.4 percent for the wealthy.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue's 2023 High-Wealth Individuals Research Project and the accompanying Treasury effective tax rate analysis; true if the published effective tax rate for the wealthiest group is approximately 9.4 percent and for middle-wealth New Zealanders approximately 20.2 percent on a comparable basis, false if either figure or the basis of comparison differs materially.

civility.statement: What is it that the Minister fears so much from small businesses? What is it that the Minister fears so much from public scrutiny?
civility.explanation: Rhetorical questions imputing fear of scrutiny to the Minister personally — a motive attack rather than an engagement with his reasons. Short of a direct insult, but it lands on the person rather than the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If they had listened to the speech from the Minister Andrew Bayly—clearly the Green member Scott Willis had not heard that or had chosen not to listen.
civility.explanation: Names an individual member and imputes either inattention or deliberate refusal to listen — a personal charge about how that member conducted himself, not a response to what he argued.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Helen White did actually do that, and I give her credit for that.
civility.explanation: In a contested debate where he has just criticised another member, he credits an opponent by name for engaging with the argument. Attacks no one and keeps the disagreement on the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Research from the Institute of Economic Research has shed light on the problem and suggests it’s $456 million annually—annually.
specificity.explanation: A named source and a precise annual figure for the cost of late payments — someone could go and check it or cite it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill that we’re putting in place does repeal some unnecessary compliance costs—and in a relationship we don’t actually need to be interfering in.
specificity.explanation: Asserts the compliance costs are 'unnecessary' without naming a cost, a reporting requirement or an affected class of firm. On-policy but carries almost no checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, if there is a six-month reporting period and then another four months after that, that is 10 months; whereas now there is information available.
specificity.explanation: Names the actual reporting cycle of the disclosure regime and works the timeframes through to a concrete lag figure. Missing the alternative's detail, but the mechanism claim is checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Commerce Commission concluded in 2020 that major supermarkets made a profit of $430 million, but now they can delay payment to those who are providing the goods and services to those particular organisations, without them being paid over a four-month period.
specificity.explanation: A named regulator, a year, a profit figure and a payment-delay period — concrete enough that each element can be checked against the source.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Minister pointed out that there will be a bill, which I predict will be called the “Bayly Bill”, which will actually address a lot of the issues that they raised, in a much more comprehensive way, in a much more cost-effective way, and bring all of the stories of woe that were brought before us under control.
specificity.explanation: The promised replacement is described only as more comprehensive and more cost-effective — a string of generic virtues with no mechanism, no timeframe and no content that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We actually do represent small business on this side of the House because we’ve been there.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal experience as authority: whose members have run small businesses does not establish whose policy serves small business. The conclusion (we represent them) rests entirely on biography rather than on anything about the measure.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But good business owners don’t make decisions based on 10 months of lapsed data.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the regime — stale data is less useful — but it leans on an unsupported generalisation about what 'good business owners' do, and the gap is that the regime's purpose was choosing whom to contract with, a decision for which ten-month-old payment history is still informative.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Our tax system is doing exactly what it was designed to do—take from the poor and give to the rich.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur from the preceding figures: a gap in effective tax rates, even if accurate, is evidence about outcomes and says nothing about design intent. The conclusion about what the system was 'designed to do' is asserted, not derived.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: The Minister pointed out that there will be a bill, which I predict will be called the “Bayly Bill”, which will actually address a lot of the issues that they raised, in a much more comprehensive way, in a much more cost-effective way, and bring all of the stories of woe that were brought before us under control.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that a further Government bill will be introduced that addresses late payment to small suppliers, replacing what the repealed Act would have done.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Parliament bills register; true if a Government bill dealing with business payment practices or late payment to small suppliers is introduced by the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs, false if no such bill is introduced by the resolve-by date.

veracity.statement: But, actually, that report did not say to repeal the system; it suggested some fundamental improvements that could make it work.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the Australian statutory review of the Payment Times Reporting Scheme actually recommended — reform of the scheme rather than its repeal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Australian Government's statutory review of the Payment Times Reporting Act 2020 (the Emerson review, reported 2023): true if its recommendations are for reform/redesign of the scheme and it does not recommend repeal; false if the review recommended abolishing the scheme.

veracity.statement: Well, in the first 100 days, we’ve got 49 actions, and our plans are very much focused on getting this economy back on track.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the incoming Government's published 100-day programme contained 49 actions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National-led coalition's published 100-day plan (beehive.govt.nz release, December 2023): true if the plan enumerates 49 actions, false if the published count is materially different.

veracity.statement: Now, the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment tells us—and other members of this House have been good enough to point this out—that there are more than half a million small businesses in New Zealand. That’s classed as a business with fewer than 20 employees—so that’s 97 percent of the businesses in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two MBIE figures: that New Zealand has more than 500,000 businesses with fewer than 20 employees, and that these make up 97 percent of all businesses.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE Small Business Factsheet / Stats NZ Business Demography Statistics for the year referenced: true if enterprises with fewer than 20 employees number above 500,000 and account for approximately 97% of all enterprises; false if either figure is materially different.

specificity.statement: We had the mitigation of increasing the cap from $10 million in revenue to $33 million. We made sure that the data that would be available would not be commercially sensitive. We made sure that there would be no prescriptive time frames for business, so we weren’t telling them what the time frames had to be; merely saying that they had to follow the rules that they set out for themselves.
specificity.explanation: Names the revenue threshold before and after (a $10m to $33m cap), the commercial-sensitivity carve-out and the no-prescribed-timeframes design — each of which could be checked against the Act and the select committee report.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment tells us—and other members of this House have been good enough to point this out—that there are more than half a million small businesses in New Zealand. That’s classed as a business with fewer than 20 employees—so that’s 97 percent of the businesses in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Gives a count, a defined threshold (fewer than 20 employees) and a percentage, with the source named — someone could look each of them up.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What businesses don’t need is for the Government to tell them to keep disclosing. What businesses need is smarter and more modern processes, so people can actually go on and pay faster.
specificity.explanation: A direction with no content attached: no figure, no named mechanism, no timeframe, and no description of what a 'smarter and more modern process' would consist of. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I also know, having worked in a large multinational organisation—the British Council—that it makes sense for big business to extend payment terms as long as possible because the incremental amount of interest that they get on holding on to those payments when they are aggregated upwards can amount to millions of dollars of profit for them.
rigor.explanation: Offers a stated mechanism — interest earned on aggregated withheld payments — and the conclusion that large firms are incentivised to stretch terms follows from it. Marked down only because the supporting warrant is her own workplace experience rather than data.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Another thing we know for sure is that late payments cripple cash flow and that that can and does kill small business. So, members, you don’t have to take my word for it, because in the heart of our electorate of Christchurch East is Kai Connoisseurs, proudly at home amongst the local businesses of Aranui, in Hampshire Street.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote: a general causal claim that late payment kills small businesses is offered as established, and the evidence explicitly presented in its support is a single constituent business. One case cannot carry the general conclusion, though the claim is at least about the policy's actual subject matter.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So it’s really disappointing today to see that he wants to sweep this out.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism aimed squarely at the Minister's decision to repeal, with no imputation of bad faith and no attack on the person. Contested debate, so there was a real opportunity to be uncivil.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We haven’t seen a lot of plans from this new Government.
focus.explanation: A general characterisation of the other side's competence rather than an engagement with the repeal before the House; no policy, measure or figure is named, though the surrounding remarks keep it tethered to the promised replacement bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: On that side of the House, they’d know nothing about innovation, productivity, aspiration for business, and that is why I commend this bill to the House.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the other side is like in general. No provision, cost, mechanism or outcome of the repeal bill is named — the only content is a characterisation of opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They borrowed a solution from Australia without thinking, and, I think, without the practical acumen to be able to work out whether, in fact, it was going to be a good scheme.
civility.explanation: Aimed at the previous Government rather than any individual, but it imputes thoughtlessness and a lack of competence rather than engaging only the merits of the scheme — condescension, short of a direct personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They borrowed a solution from Australia without thinking, and, I think, without the practical acumen to be able to work out whether, in fact, it was going to be a good scheme.
focus.explanation: A real policy point (the scheme was copied from the Australian reporting regime without testing its fit) carried inside a characterisation of the previous Government's judgement; a named policy is at issue, so this is well above tribalism but not purely on the mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That’s $51 billion of expenditure, which is, roughly, about a third of the economy, and we will report their outcomes in a transparent way.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the government agency expenditure covered by the 10-working-day payment commitment totals about $51 billion and that this is roughly one third of the New Zealand economy.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury / MBIE figures for annual central-government agency expenditure or procurement spend in 2023/24, and Stats NZ nominal GDP for the same period. True if agency spend is approximately $51bn AND that figure is close to a third of nominal GDP; false if either the dollar figure or the share of GDP is materially different.

veracity.statement: When you are talking about big businesses, the group that Kirk Hope is talking about at Business New Zealand represents about 65 percent of GDP in New Zealand—180 businesses—and making sure that they have clear code around when they do pay small businesses.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the BusinessNZ grouping of large firms comprises about 180 businesses and accounts for about 65 percent of New Zealand's GDP.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: BusinessNZ's own published description of its Major Companies Group (membership count and claimed share of GDP). True if the membership is around 180 firms and BusinessNZ/other published analysis puts their share of GDP near 65 percent; false if the membership count or the GDP share is materially different.

veracity.statement: It’s about improving those payment times, and the simple fact is that you can go and get this information at any one point in time for a mere cost of approximately $35.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the payment-practice information the repealed reporting regime would publish is already obtainable commercially for about $35 per enquiry.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published pricing from New Zealand credit bureaux (e.g. Centrix, Equifax, illion) for a single company credit/payment-behaviour report as at early 2024, and whether such a report contains payment-times data of the kind the Business Payment Practices Act required. True if a comparable report is available at roughly $35; false if no equivalent payment-times information is sold at that price.

veracity.statement: That is why we think this is a waste of time, and the reason this is being done in urgency—just to remind the House yet again for those who weren’t here for the first reading speech—is that the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment are about to commit at least $2 million to $3 million or possibly more on putting in a system that will mean that results are often 10 months out of date, and of course many large businesses are going to incur huge amounts of time putting in a system that at the end of the day, according to the Australian situation, will deliver no discernible benefits.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that MBIE is about to spend at least $2–3 million implementing the reporting system, and that the system would publish results up to about 10 months out of date.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's regulatory impact statement / departmental disclosure and Budget documentation for the Business Payment Practices Act implementation, plus the reporting-cycle timing set by the Act and its regulations. True if the documented implementation cost is $2m or more and the statutory reporting lag reaches roughly 10 months; false if the costed figure or the reporting lag is materially smaller.

specificity.statement: That’s why we’ll be asking Government agencies to put in place e-invoicing - capable systems—and some of them have, but many of them don’t—and, secondly, encouraging and incentivising, rather than requiring, small businesses to adopt e-invoicing, which is probably one of the biggest digital enhancements that we can achieve in New Zealand and it will drive some of the biggest productivity gains, and that is by making sure that if you use e-invoicing, particularly with the Government, you’ll get paid in an even shorter period of time of five working days.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (e-invoicing capability in agency systems, incentives rather than a mandate for small firms) and an exact payment timeframe of five working days; the productivity claim at the end is loose, but the operative content is checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is why we think this is a waste of time, and the reason this is being done in urgency—just to remind the House yet again for those who weren’t here for the first reading speech—is that the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment are about to commit at least $2 million to $3 million or possibly more on putting in a system that will mean that results are often 10 months out of date, and of course many large businesses are going to incur huge amounts of time putting in a system that at the end of the day, according to the Australian situation, will deliver no discernible benefits.
rigor.explanation: A real inference with premises supplied earlier in the speech: the Australian review found the equivalent scheme failed its stated object, the data would be up to 10 months stale, and implementation costs fall on MBIE and on reporting firms — therefore repeal before the spend. The gap is that the Australian finding concerned only the small-business-decision object, not the transparency object the reviewer called meritorious, so 'no discernible benefits' overreaches what the cited evidence established.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In fact, he accepts there is a problem and has said so openly, and yet what he is doing is he’s letting big business off the hook.
civility.explanation: Contested debate with a real opportunity to be uncivil. The criticism lands on the Minister's decision and its effect, not on his character or competence; 'letting big business off the hook' edges toward imputing indifference but stops short of a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It simply takes away the one thing that is there now and replaces it with zero.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the repeal bill before the House removes the existing payment-practices reporting obligation without substituting any replacement obligation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Business Payment Practices Act Repeal Bill as introduced (bills.parliament.nz) and the Act it repeals: true if the bill repeals the Business Payment Practices Act 2023 and contains no substitute reporting, disclosure or enforcement provision; false if it enacts any replacement obligation.

veracity.statement: It’s not good enough—absolutely not good enough—and what the Australian legislation review did was, actually, not talk about getting rid of a law like this, and, in fact, their threshold was higher.
veracity.explanation: Two factual claims about the Australian statutory review of its payment times reporting regime: that the review recommended strengthening rather than repealing the law, and that the Australian reporting threshold is higher than New Zealand's.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The statutory review of Australia's Payment Times Reporting Act 2020 (Emerson review, reported 2023) and the turnover thresholds in that Act versus the Business Payment Practices Act 2023: true if the review's recommendations were to retain and strengthen the regime and the Australian entry threshold is above the NZ one; false if the review recommended repeal or the Australian threshold is lower.

veracity.statement: We’ve had things like the trial periods for employees go out to our big companies, not our little ones.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the recent extension of employment trial periods benefited large employers specifically, because small employers already had access to them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Employment Relations (Extended Time for Personal Grievance for Sexual Harassment) / 90-day trial period amendment passed in the government's first 100 days, and the pre-existing s 67A of the Employment Relations Act: true if trial periods were previously available only to employers with fewer than 20 employees and the amendment extended them to employers of all sizes; false if the prior law already allowed all employers to use them.

rigor.statement: That to me seems a really good use of money by a big company, because what it’s doing is it’s holding itself to account.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the policy: the conclusion (the IT/reporting spend is worthwhile) rests on the stated reason that record-keeping produces self-accountability. The reason supports the conclusion in kind but not in degree — nothing is offered on the cost side that the 'waste of time' objection raised, so there is a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That has been going on, and it still is going on, but, actually, this legislation did make a change to the mentality of New Zealanders, because I think New Zealanders decided that wasn’t OK, and I think even the National Party’s statements on this, which say, “This is a problem we’ve got to fix.”—they’re influenced by this legislation and this discussion, which said that it was not OK.
rigor.explanation: A causal conclusion — the legislation shifted public attitudes and shaped the other party's statements — supported only by the speaker's own supposition ('I think') and the coincidence that both exist. Post hoc reasoning: the shared position is offered as proof of influence with nothing to rule out the reverse or a common cause.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I ask the Government to consider those amendments, because these 100 days just seem to have been about tearing everything down, and the focus has all been on supporting those big, big companies.
focus.explanation: Carries a real policy ask — consider the tabled amendments — but the weight of the sentence is a general characterisation of the government's 100-day programme as 'tearing everything down' and favouring big business, without naming a specific measure or outcome. A policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Let’s look at the amendments that we’ve made, and, instead of tearing down the house and burning everything that anyone’s ever done that’s constructive in this country, let’s make one of the actions in these 100 days be to build a better law, to build more protection around our small businesses, and to favour them for once over our big companies and actually change the dial in this country.
specificity.explanation: Trying to convey substance — it is a call to amend rather than repeal — but supplies no figure, threshold, mechanism or timeframe, and does not say what any amendment would actually do. 'A better law', 'more protection' and 'change the dial' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Perhaps it’s the major party’s partnerships that are pushing them in this direction, because it is clear that the Business Payment Practices Act was not perfect—that’s true—but does it need to simply be repealed and we’re being left with nothing because you haven’t got the ability to create something, to make something, to improve and to amend?
civility.explanation: Concedes the Act's flaws, but imputes a corrupt motive ('the major party's partnerships') and tells the members opposite they 'haven't got the ability to create something' — an imputation of bad faith plus a swipe at competence, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The problem is that the member doesn’t seem to have a clear idea about how we are going to support our small and medium enterprises in any meaningful way.
civility.explanation: Lands on the individual member rather than the bill — the claim is that the member personally lacks a clear idea. Policy-adjacent, but it is the member's grasp being impugned, not the measure being criticised.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: No one on this side wants to see late payment for small businesses or other solopreneurs out there who struggle with this.
civility.explanation: In a contested repeal debate where motives were being impugned on both sides, this addresses the substance of the disagreement and attacks nobody — the expected standard, met.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We can see the value, certainly, in ensuring Government agencies pay on time. That can be amended and that could be part of the Act.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: identifies a provision worth keeping (agency payment times) and proposes it be carried through by amendment. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ve heard the Government say that they want to save businesses money, but which businesses do you want to save money, really? Is it the businesses who might donate, because this is a real concern for us?
focus.explanation: Insinuation about who donates to the governing party. No policy mechanism, figure or named outcome survives once the suggestion about donors is removed — this is about the other team's motives, not the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Government isn’t looking after business; the Government is looking after corporates. That’s what this repeal is all about.
focus.explanation: The repeal is named, but the content is a characterisation of whom the governing parties really serve rather than any mechanism, cost or outcome of the repeal. Mostly party framing around a thin policy hook.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I don’t buy the argument that at the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, there’s going to be a blowout of costs. We do need IT and we do need data collection. There is no waste in ensuring we’re doing something better; there is a waste in the loss of income to our small and medium enterprises that continues with the repeal of this Act.
focus.explanation: Engages the administrative cost case for the Act directly — the MBIE cost estimate, the IT and data collection required, and the income loss the repeal leaves in place. On-policy throughout, even though the reasoning is weak.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: What we’re seeing with this backward approach is simply more of the same: simply supporting big business—the big corps—rather than the 97 percent of businesses in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that small and medium enterprises make up 97 percent of New Zealand businesses.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Business Demography Statistics / MBIE Small Business Factsheet for the year to 2023: the share of NZ enterprises with fewer than 20 employees. True if that share is approximately 97%; false if materially different (e.g. below 90%).

veracity.statement: I think the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment has it at $26 for a paper invoice, instead of encouraging people into e-invoicing for $10.
veracity.explanation: Attributes to MBIE a per-invoice processing cost of about $26 for a paper invoice against about $10 for an e-invoice.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's published e-invoicing cost estimates (e-invoicing business case / e-invoicing benefits material). True if MBIE puts the paper invoice cost at approximately $26 and the e-invoice cost at approximately $10; false if MBIE's figures are materially different or no such estimate exists.

rigor.statement: I don’t buy the argument that at the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, there’s going to be a blowout of costs. We do need IT and we do need data collection. There is no waste in ensuring we’re doing something better; there is a waste in the loss of income to our small and medium enterprises that continues with the repeal of this Act.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy, but the cost argument is rejected by bare assertion ('I don't buy it') and the conclusion that 'there is no waste' is simply stated, with no costing, offset or evidence offered against the departmental estimate it dismisses.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think medium and small businesses need to be looking at who they’re doing business with. It is something that everyone has to take responsibility for, and it doesn’t mean that you can’t already access information from your networks and from people you interact with about the business practices of the people whom you interact with.
rigor.explanation: An inference about the policy, and a weak one: from 'informal network information exists' it concludes a mandatory disclosure regime is unnecessary. That does not follow — the case for the register is that informal information is incomplete and unavailable to those without such networks, which the argument never addresses.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I know from speaking with many of my clients that what stresses them is compliance—things they don’t understand. They wouldn’t know how to interpret the data that is held by MBIE.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from her own coaching clients to small businesses at large, and to the conclusion that the MBIE payment data would go unused. Argument from anecdote: no survey, uptake figure or comparable scheme is offered to support the inference.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: New Zealand businesses are in a thicket of regulation: compliance, the different laws we have to go through—I mean, as a small-business owner, I think we all know how hard it is to keep track of all the different things that Government forces us to do.
specificity.explanation: Trying to convey substance about regulatory burden but naming none of it — no regulation, no compliance cost, no hours, no figure. 'A thicket of regulation' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I think the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment has it at $26 for a paper invoice, instead of encouraging people into e-invoicing for $10.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete figures attributed to a named source, directly checkable against MBIE's published estimates.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This piece of new legislation allows big businesses a four-month period to pay those bills.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill before the House permits large businesses 120 days to settle invoices.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Business Payment Practices Act Repeal Bill and of the Act it repeals; true if either sets or permits a 120-day payment term for large entities, false if the legislation concerns only disclosure/reporting of payment practices and fixes no payment terms.

veracity.statement: The between 2 percent to 10 percent that control 50 percent of this country’s wealth—that’s who they’re protecting in this particular legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a group between 2 and 10 percent of New Zealanders holds half the country's wealth.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Net Worth statistics (net worth distribution by decile); true if the wealthiest 2–10% hold approximately 50% of total net wealth, false if their share is materially different.

veracity.statement: We’ve got, in 2023—according to Centrix figures—35 percent of companies having filed for liquidation, year on year, with construction among the worst.
veracity.explanation: Attributes to Centrix a 2023 figure of 35 percent of companies filing for liquidation, with construction the worst-affected sector.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Centrix Credit Indicator reports for 2023; true if 35% of companies filed for liquidation that year, false if the 35% figure is instead a year-on-year increase in the number of liquidations or refers to some other base.

veracity.statement: At the time of the second reading debate on the previous bill, the Minister also talked about what he thought the biggest issue at the time for him was: “The biggest issue is its focus on large companies.”—so he said it himself.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for the second reading of the Business Payment Practices Bill; true if Bayly's speech contains the quoted words with that sense, false if the words do not appear or are materially different in wording or meaning.

veracity.statement: That information is actually available from four other entities, plus Centrix—which the Minister alluded to in his first reading speech—for a cost of $35.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the payment-practice information the repealed regime would disclose is already obtainable commercially from five providers for $35.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Centrix's published pricing for company credit/payment reports and the Minister's first reading speech; true if comparable late-payment information is available from Centrix and four other providers for about $35, false if no such commercial equivalent exists at that price or the count of providers is wrong.

focus.statement: This piece of new legislation allows big businesses a four-month period to pay those bills.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the content of the measure before the House — what payment period it allows — naming no party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But they will be impacted because that side of the House—the Government—want to ensure that they look after their corporate and rich mates.
focus.explanation: Strip out the characterisation of the Government's motives and no policy content remains — no mechanism, figure or provision is named, only who the other side is said to be serving.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I wonder if this Government ever gets tired of simping for the big corporates and the 1 percent, because assuming that getting rid of a disclosure regime on late payments will actually do anything but simply benefit those who are already creaming it at the top is an illusion.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point in here — the effect of removing the late-payment disclosure regime — but most of the sentence's weight is on who the Government is said to serve.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s interesting that the speakers on the Government side talk about how they really worry about all the additional costs and compliance mechanisms that they have to go through, but then they have to caveat it with all businesses, including big corporates, because, actually, this bill only added a disclosure regime to those at the very top.
focus.explanation: Engages the scope of the regime and the substance of the opposing argument, not the character or record of the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: He is going to bring forward seven initiatives that will go much further than this current bill does and in a much more efficient way that doesn’t add a whole lot of costs to businesses.
focus.explanation: Directed at what the Government intends to do on the same policy question, engaging the alternative rather than the opposition's character.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If you’ve got a company that has 20 people or less, they need to ensure that they can pay those whānau, because the trickle-down effect and the impact of not paying those bills means that people cannot pay the rent.
rigor.explanation: A real causal chain about the policy (late payment to a small firm flows through to its workers' ability to pay rent), but the links are asserted rather than shown; nothing is offered to connect the payment terms to the household outcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: He’s actually afraid of going through a select committee process and getting feedback from the smaller businesses and the workers, because if we look at the departmental disclosure statement, it’s so clear that there was no adequate stakeholder consultation as part of the creation of this repeal.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: thin consultation recorded in a disclosure statement is evidence about process, not about the Minister's state of mind; the conclusion about fear does not follow from the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s interesting that the speakers on the Government side talk about how they really worry about all the additional costs and compliance mechanisms that they have to go through, but then they have to caveat it with all businesses, including big corporates, because, actually, this bill only added a disclosure regime to those at the very top.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference with a stated premise: if the regime applied only to the largest entities, a compliance-burden objection framed around businesses generally is misdirected. The conclusion tracks the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve got, in 2023—according to Centrix figures—35 percent of companies having filed for liquidation, year on year, with construction among the worst.
specificity.explanation: Names a source, a year, a percentage and the worst-affected sector — someone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is about ensuring that small businesses have the mana and the dignity to be able to survive but also to be able to pay those who work for them.
specificity.explanation: An appeal to dignity and survival with no figure, mechanism, threshold or timeframe attached; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: He is going to bring forward seven initiatives that will go much further than this current bill does and in a much more efficient way that doesn’t add a whole lot of costs to businesses.
specificity.explanation: A count — seven — and a direction, but none of the initiatives are named and there is no timeframe or cost figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That information is actually available from four other entities, plus Centrix—which the Minister alluded to in his first reading speech—for a cost of $35.
specificity.explanation: A named provider, a provider count and a dollar figure — directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: He’s actually afraid of going through a select committee process and getting feedback from the smaller businesses and the workers, because if we look at the departmental disclosure statement, it’s so clear that there was no adequate stakeholder consultation as part of the creation of this repeal.
civility.explanation: Imputes a motive — fear of scrutiny — to the Minister personally, rather than confining the criticism to the process itself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But he could be presenting a bill rather than wasting our time in this place, simply simping for big businesses.
civility.explanation: Directed at the Minister personally — accuses him of wasting the House's time and of serving big business — rather than at the merits of the repeal.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Clearly, the member Ricardo Menéndez March did not hear what the Minister said in his first reading speech, and indeed in his second reading speech.
civility.explanation: Pointed and faintly condescending about the member's attentiveness, but it stops at what he failed to hear rather than at his character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So, coming back to a point that I made earlier and that other members on this side of the House have reiterated, ultimately, this repeal is of legislation that makes sure 3 percent of businesses provide information to make it easier, to make it more viable, and to make it sustainable for the 97 percent of small businesses to stay in business, and that’s in all of our interests.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Act being repealed imposed its disclosure obligation on only 3 percent of New Zealand businesses, and that the beneficiaries are the remaining 97 percent, who are small businesses.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Business Payment Practices Act 2023 disclosure threshold (large entities by total revenue) set against MBIE/Stats NZ business demography counts: true if entities in scope are approximately 3% of NZ businesses and approximately 97% of NZ businesses fall in the small-business category; false if the in-scope share is materially larger or the small-business share materially smaller.

specificity.statement: So, coming back to a point that I made earlier and that other members on this side of the House have reiterated, ultimately, this repeal is of legislation that makes sure 3 percent of businesses provide information to make it easier, to make it more viable, and to make it sustainable for the 97 percent of small businesses to stay in business, and that’s in all of our interests.
specificity.explanation: Names the measure at issue and gives a concrete split (3 percent / 97 percent) that someone could go and check against the Act's coverage threshold.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’d just like to read out some of the things that our Minister for Small Business and Manufacturing has already said in his speech—which, obviously, on that side of the House, you aren’t listening to—that we will be doing, and that’s reinforcing the requirement for Government agencies to pay ordinary creditors and ramping up the adoption of e-invoicing.
specificity.explanation: Two named mechanisms — the payment requirement on Government agencies and e-invoicing adoption — but no figures, no targets and no timeframe for either.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So, coming back to a point that I made earlier and that other members on this side of the House have reiterated, ultimately, this repeal is of legislation that makes sure 3 percent of businesses provide information to make it easier, to make it more viable, and to make it sustainable for the 97 percent of small businesses to stay in business, and that’s in all of our interests.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the bill before the House — who the disclosure obligation falls on and who benefits. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If there was a show of hands, I think that we would see that there are small-business owners and employers in every part of this House, and the argument constantly pushed from that side of the House that it’s some exclusive little club that only members of those parties in Government have ever been a part of is absolutely a hollow argument.
focus.explanation: Wholly about the other side's posture and who gets to claim small-business credentials. Names no clause, cost, figure or outcome of the repeal under debate.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’d just like to read out some of the things that our Minister for Small Business and Manufacturing has already said in his speech—which, obviously, on that side of the House, you aren’t listening to—that we will be doing, and that’s reinforcing the requirement for Government agencies to pay ordinary creditors and ramping up the adoption of e-invoicing.
focus.explanation: Directed at the substance: what the Government will do about payment times instead of the disclosure register. The jab at the other side is incidental to the policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That’s innovation, which we understand and which, obviously, on that side of the House, you don’t understand.
focus.explanation: No policy content once the claim about the other side is removed — it is entirely about which party is supposed to understand innovation.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The implication here, in my opinion, is that we’re suggesting—and one member reiterated this in their speech just now—that the people who own and run and are at the heart of our small businesses are somehow not smart enough or clever enough to be able to go online and look at a guide that tells them whether they’re going to be paid and whether their business will survive.
rigor.explanation: Strawman. The policy statement he has just quoted claims small businesses will not have the time to search the register and that the data would be unlikely to change their commercial decisions; he restates this as a claim that they are not intelligent enough to do so, then argues against that instead.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If you really believe in backing small business, why limit yourself to seven steps?
rigor.explanation: Loaded question resting on a false dichotomy: it treats the number of measures as the test of commitment, and so never engages the Government's actual stated reason for repeal (that the disclosure regime imposes compliance cost for little benefit). More steps is assumed to be better without argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But that is not done with more regulation and red tape being inflicted on business, which costs more and takes more time.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered (compliance cost and time), but the conclusion does not follow from it: that a measure has a cost says nothing about whether it fixes late payment. The trade-off is asserted rather than shown, and the word 'inflicted' does the work an argument should.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The fact that some of those members have been in small business and want to not do everything—to not take eight steps or nine steps but only seven steps—to support small businesses is, I think, pretty embarrassing.
civility.explanation: Pointed and edging past the policy onto the members themselves — calling their conduct embarrassing given their own background is closer to a reproach of the people than of the measure, though it stops short of an insult.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’ve heard that the Government is wanting to finish its block of work under its 100-day plan—its coalition agreement—but that is no justification to be using urgency to move bills that do not speak to what was campaigned on in the election.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real process: from 'the bill was not campaigned on' to 'urgency is not justified'. It works only if you grant the unstated premise that urgency is legitimate solely for manifesto items, which is asserted rather than argued — a genuine gap between what is shown and what is concluded, but not a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker
