specificity.explanation: A dollar figure, a test volume and a named revenue mechanism — concrete enough to check line by line.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We could be looking at general taxation policy to gather revenue for transport infrastructure projects, we could be looking at congestion pricing, and yet this Government isn’t brave enough to put progressive alternatives to commit funding for public transport infrastructure.
specificity.explanation: Names two concrete alternative revenue tools — general taxation and congestion pricing — but supplies no rate, yield, coverage or timeframe for either.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This Government campaigned to build 15 new roads and has pledged $500 million to fix potholes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific commitments: a campaign pledge to build 15 new roads, and a pledged $500 million for pothole repair.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 transport policy documents and the coalition Government's announced transport funding: true if the campaign commitment covers 15 named new roads (Roads of National Significance) and a pothole-repair fund of $500 million is on the record; false if the road count or the dollar figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: On top of road-user charges, they are putting up regos by $50. That money will go towards funding 50,000 roadside drug-tests, which they will be making back by increasing fines.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $50 increase in motor vehicle registration fees, that the proceeds fund a programme of 50,000 roadside drug tests, and that the cost is recovered through higher fines.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government's announced motor vehicle registration fee change (amount and phasing) and the stated funding source and test volume for roadside drug testing: true if the rego rises by $50 and the 50,000-test programme is funded from that increase; false if the increase is a different amount or the testing is funded from another appropriation.

veracity.statement: So, by having this bill in urgency, we’re preventing the campaigners—the young people who’ve been pushing for safe walking and cycling and infrastructure, on top of better public transport—from giving their thoughts on, actually, what should therefore replace this repeal if we’re going to have this being taken away from the Government’s ability to resource transport projects.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that taking the bill under urgency denies the public — specifically the safe-infrastructure campaigners — any opportunity to make submissions on it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's record for the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill: true if the bill was progressed under urgency with no select committee stage and so no call for public submissions; false if it was referred to a select committee that took submissions.

civility.statement: The repeal of the regional fuel tax leaves a gap when it comes to the ability to resource those projects, on top of a Minister of Transport that has actually waged a war on that safe infrastructure that would have enabled people to have those options.
civility.explanation: "Waged a war" is pointed and edges toward the Minister personally, but what it characterises is his policy record on safe walking and cycling infrastructure, not his character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But what I don’t like is when the Minister politicises an issue that should never have been political.
civility.explanation: Directed at the Minister personally rather than at the policy, imputing bad faith (playing politics with child road safety). Short of an insult, but it is a motive attribution about a person, so it sits at the failure end rather than the standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It has been pointed out he’s ring-fenced a project in his area that affects the people in his area.
civility.explanation: Implies the Minister allocated funding to his own patch — a self-interest imputation about a named person, though hedged as something others have pointed out rather than pressed as an accusation.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: When the Minister talks about speed bumps costing $500,000—knowing that that was retracted, because it’s been in the media that it wasn’t correct—there is a politicisation of an issue and a clouding of an issue that we surely have to see with much clearer vision than that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister used a figure of $500,000 for speed bumps, and that this figure was withdrawn after media reporting showed it was wrong.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous media reporting and Auckland Transport / ministerial statements from early 2024 on the cost of speed bumps or raised crossings: true if the Minister publicly used a $500,000 figure and it was subsequently corrected or withdrawn as inaccurate; false if no such figure was used, or if it stood uncorrected.

veracity.statement: It has been pointed out he’s ring-fenced a project in his area that affects the people in his area.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the list of transport projects protected from the regional fuel tax repeal includes a project located in the Transport Minister's own electorate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The list of Auckland projects ring-fenced or retained by the Government when the regional fuel tax was repealed (March 2024), cross-checked against the electorate boundaries of the then Minister of Transport: true if at least one retained project lies in his electorate, false if none does.

veracity.statement: This is money that was ring-fenced for Auckland, and it is an alternative to rate rises, and, instead, the Minister has taken away the specific ring-fenced tax to Auckland where Aucklanders pay for Auckland infrastructure, and instead he’s bringing in another tax which is actually through the driver’s licence system, and that goes to the whole of the country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the revenue removed with the Auckland regional fuel tax is being replaced by increased charges levied nationally through the driver licensing system.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government/NZTA announcements and the 2024 fee-review documents on driver licensing fee increases: true if increased driver licensing charges were announced as a revenue source alongside the regional fuel tax repeal and apply nationally, false if no such national licensing charge increase was proposed or if it was confined to Auckland.

veracity.statement: Removing the Auckland regional fuel tax will provide cost of living support, saving the driver of a Toyota Hilux around $9.20 every time they fill up in Auckland, while a Toyota Corolla driver will save around $5.75.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific per-fill savings from removing the Auckland regional fuel tax: about $9.20 for a Toyota Hilux and about $5.75 for a Toyota Corolla.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Auckland regional fuel tax rate (11.5c per litre including GST) multiplied by the standard fuel tank capacity of each named vehicle: true if the products come to approximately $9.20 and $5.75 respectively, false if either figure is materially off.

rigor.statement: When I look at the fuel prices that have been in the North and I compare them to the fuel prices once you’ve hit the area where the tax applies, you can’t see that that’s going to be a transparent drop in the price.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: regional price comparisons show Auckland pump prices are not higher by the amount of the tax, so removing it may not flow through. The observation supports the conclusion only weakly — it treats one cross-regional comparison as decisive about pass-through, with no account of competition or freight costs. A genuine argument with a gap between evidence and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is actually costing a lot, and we know now that if we can get people out of their cars—particularly in the inner city suburbs, because they can walk and they can cycle, and e-bikes make that possible—if we can encourage them out, and if we can have good busways, then it frees up the capacity for the roads to be used in a productive way.
rigor.explanation: A conditional argument that mode-shift in dense inner suburbs frees road capacity for productive use, with a stated mechanism (walking, cycling, e-bikes, busways). The chain is coherent, but the premise that congestion costs 'a lot' is asserted from personal experience of sitting in traffic rather than from any figure, so part of the conclusion rests on anecdote.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I also just want to tell them something that’s a bit of bad news, which is that if they expect to see the fuel come down 10c a litre every time they go to the pump, unfortunately that’s very unlikely to happen.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that removing the Auckland regional fuel tax will not produce a corresponding fall of about 10c a litre at Auckland pumps.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE weekly fuel price monitoring (and AA/Gaspy retail data) for Auckland versus the rest of the North Island either side of the regional fuel tax's removal on 30 June 2024: the prediction is true if the Auckland average fell materially less than the tax amount (11.5c/L including GST), false if the average fell by approximately the full amount.

focus.statement: I note that we’ve had a lot of people jump up on the other side and speak for their whole 30 seconds and they haven’t been from Auckland; we’ve had very few Aucklanders stand up on this one because it affects their constituents.
focus.explanation: Entirely about who on the other side has chosen to speak and why, not about the measure. Once the observation about the government benches is removed there is no policy content left — no mechanism, cost or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is money that was ring-fenced for Auckland, and it is an alternative to rate rises, and, instead, the Minister has taken away the specific ring-fenced tax to Auckland where Aucklanders pay for Auckland infrastructure, and instead he’s bringing in another tax which is actually through the driver’s licence system, and that goes to the whole of the country.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism on both sides — a region-specific hypothecated fuel tax replaced by nationwide driver licensing charges — and the incidence change from Auckland ratepayers to all motorists. No figures or dates, so short of fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Removing the Auckland regional fuel tax will provide cost of living support, saving the driver of a Toyota Hilux around $9.20 every time they fill up in Auckland, while a Toyota Corolla driver will save around $5.75.
specificity.explanation: Two named vehicles with dollar savings per fill, tied to a named tax. Anyone can check the arithmetic against the tax rate and tank capacity.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Every member of Parliament—this is absolutely in the bill—in this House should be reading this bill, thinking “I’m going to turn back up to my community and I need to front up and explain how we’re resolving congestion.”, because the plan that the Minister presented this week doesn’t provide a solution to addressing Auckland’s critical problem, which is congestion.
focus.explanation: Directed at the substance of the transport plan and the named problem it is said to leave unaddressed (Auckland congestion), not at the other party's character or record in general.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So it comes back to this Government and their absolutely false promise in the election. You haven’t provided cost of living relief to Aucklanders.
focus.explanation: There is a real accountability point in the second sentence (an election commitment on cost of living relief), but no specific measure, figure or outcome is named, and the weight of the passage is generalised blame of the Government.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, I think it would be helpful for the Minister to outline for the committee what the rationale is in terms of maintaining three of those projects within the bill, and what is the rationale for, effectively, dispensing with all the remaining projects that are outlined in the order.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the measure before the committee — the retention of three projects and the removal of the rest from the 2018 Auckland order. No party framing at all, in a debate where there was ample opportunity for it.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So it comes back to this Government and their absolutely false promise in the election. You haven’t provided cost of living relief to Aucklanders.
civility.explanation: Blunt about the Government's promise and record; no individual is attacked, no bad faith imputed to a person. Under the re-anchored scale, hard criticism aimed at a government's record sits near the top.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What was the process that the Minister went through in deciding how to deal with an issue where, in fact, he works and he is the elected MP in a particular area, and one of those projects is favoured in this situation?
civility.explanation: Raises a perceived conflict of interest — pointed and edging toward the Minister personally — but stops short of asserting bad faith, framing it as a question about the decision-making process rather than an accusation of corruption.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill has two parts. Part 1 deals with the purpose of the bill; the repeal of the statutory framework for establishing and operating the regional fuel tax; and it has some transitionary provisions, in particular clauses 6 and 7, which amend the current Auckland regional fuel tax order and reduce the list of capital projects in which revenue from the regional fuel tax scheme can be sent from 14 to three.
specificity.explanation: Names the clauses (6 and 7), the instrument amended, and the exact change to the project list (14 down to three). Anyone could go and check it against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My question to the Minister in relation to that is whether or not there was any thinking around whether a lower rate, and potentially a rate of zero, could have been applied, and, if so, why that, perhaps, was not an option that has been explored so that there is a framework for some point in the future.
specificity.explanation: Anchored to a named provision (the 10c/litre maximum rate under section 65C(3)) and puts a concrete alternative to the Minister — a reduced or zero rate with the framework retained. A precise question, and scored as such.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The answer to that was: we campaigned on removing the regional fuel tax, and we were elected with a mandate to do that, and this legislation is delivering on that mandate, so we did not consider any other change other than to remove the legislation in its entirety—which is what this is doing.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that no alternative (a lower or zero rate, retaining the framework) warranted consideration — rests solely on an appeal to electoral mandate. An election result establishes authority to act, not that every alternative design was unworkable, so the reason offered does not reach the conclusion drawn.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So what happens with that area, for example, and why would that not be given priority by a Government that says it wants intensification, and, in fact, has scrapped a whole lot of rules that meant there’d be more spread of intensification?
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: if the Government's stated goal is intensification, defunding transport works serving a large housing development is in tension with that goal. The inference is real but leaves a gap — it assumes the Carrington Road works are necessary to the development proceeding, which is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The answer to that was: we campaigned on removing the regional fuel tax, and we were elected with a mandate to do that, and this legislation is delivering on that mandate, so we did not consider any other change other than to remove the legislation in its entirety—which is what this is doing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that repealing the regional fuel tax was a policy the speaker's party campaigned on at the 2023 election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 general election transport/tax policy documents and campaign statements: true if repeal of the Auckland regional fuel tax was an explicit published campaign commitment; false if no such commitment appears.

veracity.statement: In regards to the question around different projects, the Eastern Busway is under construction, the City Rail Link trains are already under order, and the priority for the Government is to improve our roading network.
veracity.explanation: Two status claims offered as the reason these projects were retained: that Eastern Busway construction had begun and that the CRL trains were already on order.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Transport / NZTA project status for the Eastern Busway and City Rail Link procurement records as at March 2024: true if the Eastern Busway was in construction and the CRL train order had been placed by that date; false if either had not yet commenced.

veracity.statement: So what happens with that area, for example, and why would that not be given priority by a Government that says it wants intensification, and, in fact, has scrapped a whole lot of rules that meant there’d be more spread of intensification?
veracity.explanation: Asserts as established fact that the Government has already scrapped rules that would have produced wider intensification.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government housing policy announcements and legislation as at March 2024 on the medium density residential standards: true if the Government had by then removed or made optional the intensification rules enabling greater housing spread; false if those rules were still in force unamended and only a future intention had been signalled.

civility.statement: Miles Anderson looked very, very uncomfortable when that was spoken of from that side of the House, because the reality is that he’s a regional MP from the South Island, and his constituents are going to suffer from this stupid piece of legislation.
civility.explanation: Comments on a named member's demeanour and implies he is voting against his own constituents, which edges toward the person; but the weight of the remark is on the legislation's effect on regional voters, not on the member's character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But this Minister of Transport is one of the most cynical Ministers ever, who is trying to be seen to be giving with one hand but, at the same time, is actually taking with the other.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the Minister's character — naming him among the most cynical ever and imputing a deliberate intent to deceive. The criticism lands on the person, not on the policy design.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Every member of Parliament from Auckland that sits across that side of the House tonight, you should hang your head in shame, because while you campaigned on one thing, actually, this week, you have done another.
civility.explanation: Shaming named-by-seat members personally and imputing bad faith to them. There is a real accountability point underneath (campaign versus delivery), but it is delivered as a demand that individuals feel shame rather than as criticism of the decision.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The question for him is: which pedestrian crossing or transport project would he take away, because this regional fuel tax has invested in our community, and if he doesn’t know that, then he probably needs to do his research.
civility.explanation: The challenge itself is on the substance — name the project you would cut — but it closes with condescension about a named colleague's grasp of his own electorate. That final clause is directed at the member rather than at his argument.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We have a bunch of transport geniuses on the other side of the House here!
focus.explanation: Sarcasm directed at the other side of the House as a bloc. No policy, figure or measure is named; strip out the jibe at opponents and nothing remains. No individual is insulted, so Civility is untouched — this is the case Focus exists for. Nothing emitted for Rigor: a jibe is not an argument.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because Auckland and most Aucklanders—not the Remuera crew, not the crew that sit over there, the privileged, the people who think they’re entitled to a tax cut, entitled to pay less for their fuel.
focus.explanation: Characterises the people opposite as a privileged class rather than engaging the repeal. No policy, mechanism, cost or outcome is named; the content is entirely about what the other side is 'really like'.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because of them, Aucklanders are facing a drivers’ tax, adding a cost of $50 to Auckland families to register their car per year.
focus.explanation: Names a specific charge, a specific amount and who bears it. This is scrutiny of a government decision against a named cost — the job of an opposition MP — and is squarely on-policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: When they last came into Government in 2008-09, one of the first things they did in 2010, they increased the weight of trucks from 44 to 53 tonnes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a National-led government in 2010 raised the maximum permitted truck weight from 44 to 53 tonnes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2010 Vehicle Dimensions and Mass amendment / NZTA High Productivity Motor Vehicle permitting rules: true if the maximum gross vehicle mass available to heavy vehicles was raised from 44 tonnes to 53 tonnes in 2010, false if the year, the figures, or the fact of the change differ materially.

veracity.statement: It will come from safety investments that save lives across our country: $5 million is the estimated cost of every single fatal accident in our country, $900,000 for every serious accident in our country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts official estimates of the social cost of a fatal crash ($5 million) and of a serious injury crash ($900,000) in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport 'Social cost of road crashes and injuries' report current in March 2024: true if the per-fatality and per-serious-injury social cost figures round to roughly $5m and $900k, false if either departs materially from the published estimate.

veracity.statement: So they vary between $2.80, roughly, in Auckland; $2.90 in the West Coast; in Waikato, $2.70.
veracity.explanation: Asserts regional pump prices for petrol at the time of speaking — about $2.80 in Auckland, $2.90 on the West Coast, $2.70 in Waikato — as evidence that Aucklanders were paying less than the regions even with the regional fuel tax.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE weekly retail petrol price monitoring / regional pump price data for the week of 5 March 2024: true if regional 91-octane prices sit within a few cents of the three figures given and Auckland is not the dearest, false if Auckland was materially the most expensive or the spread differs by more than about 10c.

veracity.statement: They’ve made them believe, in an election, that they’re going to save, on average, $2 more a week or $100 a year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that National campaigned on an average saving to Aucklanders of about $2 a week or $100 a year from repealing the regional fuel tax.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 campaign transport/cost-of-living material and contemporaneous statements on the regional fuel tax repeal: true if a per-household saving of roughly $2 per week or $100 per year was publicly claimed, false if the claimed saving was materially different or no such figure was advanced.

veracity.statement: Because of them, Aucklanders are facing a drivers’ tax, adding a cost of $50 to Auckland families to register their car per year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government is increasing the annual motor vehicle licensing (registration) fee by $50 per vehicle per year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government/NZTA announcements on motor vehicle licensing fee changes announced in early 2024: true if the annual registration fee rises by about $50 per vehicle, false if the increase is materially smaller, larger, or not annual.

veracity.statement: In addition to that, they’re adding 12c a litre to petrol.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government is adding 12 cents per litre to the price of petrol, presented alongside the registration increase as offsetting the fuel tax repeal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The draft Government Policy Statement on land transport 2024 and Budget/excise announcements: true if a fuel excise duty increase totalling about 12c per litre was proposed or legislated, false if no such increase was signalled or the amount differs materially.

veracity.statement: National’s transport projects are estimated to cost twice the amount that they initially said. That’s a fiscal hole of $24 billion—$24 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the costed price of National's transport programme is double its stated figure, leaving a $24 billion shortfall. No source for the estimate is named in the statement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published costings of National's roading programme — Treasury/NZTA advice, the 2024 GPS funding tables, or the independent estimates circulating in March 2024 — set against National's own 2023 transport policy costings: true if the credible cost estimate is around twice the announced figure with a gap near $24bn, false if the gap is materially smaller or the doubling is not supported by any published costing.

veracity.statement: While, actually, we talk about what Aucklanders want, they are struggling with the cost of living, but what they said when Auckland Council commissioned a poll: 44 percent of Aucklanders actually, based on this discussion, wanted to keep the regional fuel tax; 26 percent were in favour of cancelling the regional fuel tax projects—that’s actually not that many.
veracity.explanation: Attributes two specific figures to a poll commissioned by Auckland Council: 44 percent wanting to retain the regional fuel tax and 26 percent favouring cancellation of the projects it funds.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Auckland Council commissioned polling on the regional fuel tax reported in 2023–24: true if the published results show roughly 44% for retention and 26% for cancelling the projects, false if the figures differ materially or no such council-commissioned poll exists.

specificity.statement: When they last came into Government in 2008-09, one of the first things they did in 2010, they increased the weight of trucks from 44 to 53 tonnes.
specificity.explanation: Names the years, the policy and both weight figures — a listener could go and check it or act on it. Scored on detail alone; whether the figures are right is Veracity's question.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The people of Northcote want a Government that will truly ease cost of living pressures; the people of Northcote want a Government that will actually end wasteful spending.
specificity.explanation: A pair of slogans offered as the case for the bill: no figure, no mechanism, no timeframe, and no identification of which spending is wasteful or how much relief the repeal delivers. Nothing here is checkable or actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The combination of that, quite frankly, as every regional and rural MP knows, has been the destruction of our roads since then.
rigor.explanation: A causal conclusion — that the 2010 weight increase plus the 2014 'sweat the assets' funding change destroyed the road network — carried entirely by an appeal to common knowledge ('as every regional and rural MP knows'). Appeal to popularity/authority standing in for evidence; the inference is about a real, named pair of policies, so it is eligible, but it is weakly supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: This is one more of those stupid pieces of legislation being passed through this House in urgency, where people don’t get a chance to scrutinise it, don’t get a chance to put up the counterargument and, indeed, I’d say to you, will be reversed in the future—will be reversed.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the repeal of the Auckland regional fuel tax will itself be reversed by a future Parliament. Not a promise about his own action in office — it is a claim about what the House will eventually do — and no timeframe is given, so the earliest fair resolution point is after two further electoral terms.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand statute book and Hansard: true if an Auckland regional fuel tax, or an equivalent regional fuel tax power for Auckland, is re-enacted and in force at any point before the resolve-by date; false if no such tax has been reinstated by then.

focus.statement: The next question is: I believe this Government is bringing in congestion charging at some point; why not wait until the congestion charging is ready before removing the regional fuel tax? I accept that congestion charging may be a fairer way of doing it.
focus.explanation: Names two specific instruments (congestion charging, the regional fuel tax) and engages the sequencing between them. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Dismantling the structure actually means that this is yet another step that this Government takes to repeal something with absolutely nothing to replace it with.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point — no replacement funding mechanism for the repealed tax — but the weight of the sentence is a characterisation of the Government's general pattern ('yet another step') rather than the measure before the House. A real point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No matter which party that we’re within, we know that we need to achieve certainty in the infrastructure sector and start to build a pipeline of at least 10 years, if not more.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy problem — investment certainty for the infrastructure sector — and explicitly disclaims party framing. No content about the other team at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The next question is: I believe this Government is bringing in congestion charging at some point; why not wait until the congestion charging is ready before removing the regional fuel tax? I accept that congestion charging may be a fairer way of doing it.
civility.explanation: Contested repeal under urgency, so there was a real opportunity to be uncivil; instead she presses the policy question and concedes the Government's alternative may be fairer. Attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I stated in my speech my concern of the Minister’s decision today to ram this through in urgency.
civility.explanation: 'Ram this through' is blunt, but it criticises a procedural decision, not the Minister as a person — no imputation of bad character or incompetence. Under the re-anchored scale, hard criticism of a decision sits near the top.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Then, finally, what consultation on the projects that should be dropped was there with health, ambulance, Cycle Auckland, Living Streets Aotearoa, or any of the other knowledgeable organisations?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific consultees she wants accounted for (health, ambulance, Cycle Auckland, Living Streets Aotearoa) and a specific decision (which projects were dropped), so the answer would be checkable. Loses ground only for 'any of the other knowledgeable organisations' and for setting no timeframe. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I know, also, that there have been arguments made over years based on, for example, an OECD report which was back in 2015 that showed that in lost productivity, just due to congestion in Auckland, we have lost productivity to the tune of $1.3 billion.
specificity.explanation: Names the source, the year and a dollar figure — someone could go and check it. Precision here is independent of whether the attribution holds up.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Looking just at the Order in Council, I mean, we know that this will lead to the fact that 14 projects that would have been funded through the Auckland regional fuel tax will now be reduced to three projects.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument (the Order in Council) and gives before-and-after project counts. Concrete and checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: No matter which party that we’re within, we know that we need to achieve certainty in the infrastructure sector and start to build a pipeline of at least 10 years, if not more.
specificity.explanation: A direction with one piece of detail (a pipeline of at least 10 years) but no mechanism, no funding amount and no named projects. High Focus, low Specificity — the two are answering different questions here.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I mean, ultimately, this bill focuses on the cost of living for New Zealanders, and we are reducing the regional fuel tax to address that issue.
specificity.explanation: Names the tax being reduced but supplies no figure for the saving, no timing and no mechanism connecting the reduction to household costs. Near-slogan level detail; the surrounding sentences add none.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I know, also, that there have been arguments made over years based on, for example, an OECD report which was back in 2015 that showed that in lost productivity, just due to congestion in Auckland, we have lost productivity to the tune of $1.3 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a 2015 OECD report quantified Auckland's congestion-related lost productivity at $1.3 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The OECD's 2015 publications on New Zealand (notably the 2015 OECD Economic Survey of New Zealand): true if a 2015 OECD document states a figure of about $1.3 billion in lost productivity from Auckland congestion; false if no 2015 OECD report contains that estimate, or if the $1.3 billion figure originates from a different body or a different year.

veracity.statement: We know, as I mentioned—actually, no, I didn’t mention previously—the cancellation of this tax will leave a shortfall in transport funding for Auckland of $1.2 billion over the next four years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific quantum for the transport funding shortfall created by repealing the Auckland regional fuel tax: $1.2 billion across the following four years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council / Auckland Transport and NZTA forecasts of regional fuel tax revenue for the four years from 2024, and Treasury or council statements on the repeal's fiscal effect: true if the forecast forgone transport funding over that window is approximately $1.2 billion, false if it is materially different (e.g. nearer $600 million on a revenue-only basis).

veracity.statement: Looking just at the Order in Council, I mean, we know that this will lead to the fact that 14 projects that would have been funded through the Auckland regional fuel tax will now be reduced to three projects.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Order in Council cuts the number of regional fuel tax funded projects from 14 to three.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Order in Council and accompanying ministerial announcement listing the retained regional fuel tax projects: true if 14 projects were previously funded and exactly three are retained, false if either count differs.

veracity.statement: Because I go back to quite a short and sharp media statement from Mayor Wayne Brown, which was straight to the thick of the cut and thrust of this piece of legislation, which is to put on hold 12 transport projects that were believed to be going ahead; that had tagged funding against them; that there was a means to an end to achieve a better transport system and infrastructure across walking and cycling, across active transport, across all modes of transport in Auckland; that created more options available for Aucklanders in that.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim about the content of Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown's media statement: that it put 12 transport projects on hold in response to this legislation. The speaker is reporting someone else's statement rather than asserting the underlying facts himself.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Wayne Brown's / Auckland Council's public statement of early March 2024 on the regional fuel tax repeal: true if it announces 12 transport projects being put on hold, false if the number stated is different or no such statement exists.

divination.statement: I believe that it does require consultation with Aucklanders over and beyond an election, because the greater question in front of us is actually: how do we invest in a modern transport infrastructure for a global city that will have a population of 2 million people come 2030?
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Auckland's population will reach 2 million by 2030. Not a promise about the speaker's own action; an outcome in the world.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates for the Auckland region: true if the estimated resident population of Auckland reaches 2,000,000 or more at any point up to 31 December 2030, false if it remains below that.

rigor.statement: I believe that it does require consultation with Aucklanders over and beyond an election, because the greater question in front of us is actually: how do we invest in a modern transport infrastructure for a global city that will have a population of 2 million people come 2030?
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: because the transport question spans decades, the mandate of a single election is insufficient authority for it. The premise supports the conclusion in direction but the gap is not closed — nothing is offered to establish why an electoral mandate cannot cover a long-horizon decision, so it leans on the appeal rather than demonstrating it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The issue in terms of what consultation was had with other organisations—I think that was Celia Wade-Brown again—ultimately, New Zealanders voted for this Government, and we are delivering on our campaign promises.
rigor.explanation: An inference about the policy question actually asked — what consultation occurred — and a non sequitur: an electoral mandate is offered as the answer to a question about consultation with named organisations. Winning an election establishes authority to act, not that any consultation happened, so the conclusion does not follow from the premise. Appeal to mandate substituting for evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I am disappointed to hear that the rationale for not looking at sections 65C and 65J is because of the campaign approach, whereas it appears—unless the Minister advises the committee otherwise—that the same outcome for Aucklanders could none the less have been achieved by engaging those two sections of the Land Transport Management Act.
specificity.explanation: Names two specific statutory provisions (ss 65C and 65J of the Land Transport Management Act) and the alternative route they would have provided; someone could go and read them and check the claim.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I invite the—well, I’m interested in the Minister’s response, and my question to the Minister is whether he still stands by the cost of living argument when the departmental disclosure statement very clearly indicates that in some cases, motorists will be around $1.87 better off a week, and the real difference that that would actually make to entertain the cost of living pressures.
specificity.explanation: Carries a precise figure ($1.87 a week), a named source (the departmental disclosure statement) and a defined population (motorists). Directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, in my earlier contribution today, I’d indicated that I’d had a look at what one could get for $1.87 at a supermarket in Auckland, and what you could get is a 227-gram tin of chunky pineapple.
specificity.explanation: A concrete, checkable illustration — a named amount, a named place and a named product at a stated weight — rather than a general assertion that the saving is small.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My other question is in relation to clause 20, and this is about whether or not there are provisions, or any either flexibility or proposed leeway in the Minister’s mind in approaching this clause, or whether the provision provides for some flexibility around that, particularly around the payment of tax that might be required post-disbursal.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause and the specific issue (flexibility over post-disbursal tax payment timeframes), but does not say what timeframe or what extenuating circumstances he has in mind, so there is a direction without the detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of the agency’s advice, in clause 18, all the advice that the New Zealand Transport Agency is required to provide the Minister currently, continues to be provided as the scheme is wound down. That relates to collection, auditing, administrating rebates, transferring net revenue, and monitoring revenue, cost, fuel prices, and volumes.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the agency, and enumerates the actual categories of advice — collection, auditing, rebate administration, net revenue transfer, and monitoring of revenue, cost, prices and volumes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of the question around passing on costs, there is a range of regulatory powers that MBIE have in terms of making sure that happens, and it’s very similar to what happened when the last Government reduced the fuel excise—those expectations remain.
specificity.explanation: Names the agency and an analogous precedent, but 'a range of regulatory powers' identifies no power, no monitoring mechanism and no consequence for non-compliance — which is precisely what the question asked for.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There will be 10c plus the corresponding 1.5c a litre in GST that will be reduced from people’s fuel bills; they’ll benefit through this saving.
specificity.explanation: Gives the exact per-litre amounts (10c plus 1.5c GST) and states where the saving lands (people's fuel bills).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now that the Minister is proposing these changes, how will he make sure that the savings that the bill seeks to provide to Aucklanders are passed on to drivers who would otherwise have been paying 10c extra that would have been collected by wholesale fuel distributors?
specificity.explanation: A precise question: names the amount (10c), the collection point (wholesale fuel distributors) and the group meant to benefit (Auckland drivers), so the Minister is asked for a specific enforcement mechanism rather than a general reassurance.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I am disappointed to hear that the rationale for not looking at sections 65C and 65J is because of the campaign approach, whereas it appears—unless the Minister advises the committee otherwise—that the same outcome for Aucklanders could none the less have been achieved by engaging those two sections of the Land Transport Management Act.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure — the Minister's stated rationale is inadequate because an alternative statutory mechanism would have achieved the same outcome — but the key premise is offered as bare assertion ('it appears') with nothing showing those sections would in fact deliver that outcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Are we, in fact, passing on costs that would otherwise not have been borne by people like my 90-year-old father who drives his car very little but needs to register it every year, and subsidising those people like me who drive great distances because of their work and to get around Auckland?
rigor.explanation: The inference tracks the mechanism it describes: swapping a per-litre charge for a flat annual registration fee does shift incidence from high-mileage to low-mileage drivers, and the conclusion about who cross-subsidises whom follows from that. The two personal examples illustrate the point rather than carrying it, so the anecdote is not load-bearing.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This relates to the Minister’s own electorate, and I do think that the committee does deserve a response around the perception of conflicts of interest, given that the Minister is the member for Pakuranga and this is a project that would obviously be of huge benefit at the expense of other Aucklanders if this was to proceed.
civility.explanation: Pointed and personal in direction — it raises the Minister's own interest in the outcome — but stays on 'the perception of conflicts of interest' and asks for a response rather than alleging corruption. Edges toward the person without landing on him.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This goes back a long time, when Trevor Mallard was Minister of Education—so I’m afraid, Minister, this might have been before you were born, or perhaps not; it’s hard to tell.
civility.explanation: A dig at the Minister's youth rather than at anything he has said or done. Light rather than abusive, but it is mockery directed at the person, which is a failure on the re-anchored scale where engaging the substance is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I invite the—well, I’m interested in the Minister’s response, and my question to the Minister is whether he still stands by the cost of living argument when the departmental disclosure statement very clearly indicates that in some cases, motorists will be around $1.87 better off a week, and the real difference that that would actually make to entertain the cost of living pressures.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill's departmental disclosure statement states that in some cases motorists will be around $1.87 a week better off.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The departmental disclosure statement for the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill; true if it states a weekly saving of about $1.87 for some motorists, false if it gives a materially different figure or contains no such estimate.

veracity.statement: There are 14 projects that are suggested to be either retained or dispensed with under this bill, and each in their own right is going to have a huge impact either way on the communities in Auckland.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill covers 14 projects that are to be either retained or discontinued.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The schedule of projects in the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill as it stood at the committee of the whole House stage; true if exactly 14 projects are listed for retention or discontinuation, false if a materially different number.

veracity.statement: And that should be read in the context of replacing some of the costs that were raised by the Government from the Auckland fuel tax with the $50 fee increase in drivers’ registrations of their vehicles.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government is raising the vehicle registration fee by $50, offsetting revenue lost from repealing the Auckland regional fuel tax.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government announcements and Cabinet/NZTA documents on motor vehicle registration fees in the first half of 2024; true if a $50 increase to the annual vehicle registration fee was announced, false if no such increase or a materially different amount.

divination.statement: So it’s all very sensible stuff, which I’m sure the Opposition is very happy to support.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Opposition will support the bill through its remaining stages.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The voting record for the remaining stages (committee of the whole House and third reading) of the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill; true if the Opposition parties supported the bill, false if any of them voted against it.

divination.statement: There will be 10c plus the corresponding 1.5c a litre in GST that will be reduced from people’s fuel bills; they’ll benefit through this saving.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the full 11.5c per litre will be passed through to Auckland motorists' fuel bills once the regional fuel tax ends — an outcome that depends on the pricing behaviour of fuel companies, not on the Minister's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE weekly fuel price monitoring comparing Auckland pump prices with the rest of New Zealand either side of the regional fuel tax's removal on 30 June 2024; true if the Auckland premium falls by approximately 11.5c per litre, false if the reduction is materially smaller.

specificity.statement: So just for those who are wondering about the purpose of the amendment that I’ve put forward—and I’m interested to know whether the Minister would support this—the project which is not going to go ahead is capital expenditure for downtown bus infrastructure, including a bus interchange in Lower Albert Street for the North Shore and western buses, a bus interchange in the Wynyard Quarter, a bus interchange in the Beach Road area, bus priority improvements, also capital expenditure for bus infrastructure in the city centre, also including bus priority improvements for passenger facilities, including bus stops and bus shelters on Wellesley St and Grafton Road, and a new learning quarter for the Grafton Gully bus interchange.
specificity.explanation: Names each individual capital item and its location — Lower Albert Street, Wynyard Quarter, Beach Road, Wellesley St, Grafton Road, Grafton Gully. Anyone could check this against the scheme schedule. Highly concrete.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There’s a range of tabled amendments which seek to—through various ways—reinsert others of those projects and, as I’ve outlined, the Government will not be supporting any of those tabled amendments.
specificity.explanation: States a clear position but carries no checkable content beyond it — no project named, no criterion for which amendments were rejected and no mechanism or figure, where the question asked for exactly that.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This specific project has allowed the streets to be redesigned and we have local roads that have reduced traffic for up to 30 percent—and that has been measured, Minister.
specificity.explanation: A quantified outcome (up to 30 percent traffic reduction) tied to a named local project and asserted to be measured, though the particular streets and measurement period are not given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill introduces a permanent change to the regime and, in fact, removes all of the Government’s taxing powers for cents per litre charge for fuel that can be used for local government transport projects that otherwise may not be fully funded.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the mechanism precisely — a permanent repeal of a cents-per-litre charging power hypothecated to local government transport — rather than asserting a general direction, though it gives no clause reference or figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If not, what can Aucklanders expect in relation to his plans for public transportation and also for bus infrastructure, specifically in the areas which I mentioned, which will now no longer be served as a result of this bill?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny directed entirely at the measure before the committee and its consequence for named services. No party framing, no characterisation of opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This specific project has allowed the streets to be redesigned and we have local roads that have reduced traffic for up to 30 percent—and that has been measured, Minister.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that measured traffic volumes on redesigned Māngere local roads fell by up to 30 percent as a result of the Te Ara Mua - Future Streets project.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published evaluation of the Te Ara Mua – Future Streets project in Māngere (NZTA / Auckland Council / research partners' traffic-count reporting): true if measured traffic volumes on the redesigned local roads fell by up to about 30 percent; false if the evaluations report no such reduction or a materially smaller one.

veracity.statement: This bill introduces a permanent change to the regime and, in fact, removes all of the Government’s taxing powers for cents per litre charge for fuel that can be used for local government transport projects that otherwise may not be fully funded.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the bill is not merely the end of Auckland's scheme but a permanent removal of the statutory power to levy any regional per-litre fuel charge for local government transport projects.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the bill as reported to the committee: true if it repeals the regional fuel tax provisions of the Land Transport Management Act in their entirety (removing the power to set any regional per-litre fuel charge hypothecated to local transport projects), false if it only ends the Auckland scheme while leaving the enabling power in place.

veracity.statement: Auckland Council is subject to a cap on the amount of money it can borrow.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Auckland Council's borrowing is constrained by a formal debt limit, which is the premise of the question about the repeal's effect on its books.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council's financial strategy and its Local Government Funding Agency lending covenants: true if a binding debt limit (debt-to-revenue ratio) applied to the council at the time of the statement, false if no such cap existed.

civility.statement: The repeal of this regional fuel tax does not benefit lower socio-economic communities like Māngere and others in South Auckland.
civility.explanation: A flat rejection of the Government's policy that attacks no person, imputes no bad faith and stays on the effect of the measure. This is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s relevant because this committee needs to understand who, within the system, is responsible for ensuring that the information is collected, so that the Minister can then be assured that consumers are enjoying the benefit of his bill.
rigor.explanation: A valid chain given its premise: if the bill's stated purpose is passing savings to consumers, verifying that requires price information, which requires a named agency accountable for collecting it. The conclusion follows; no fallacy or appeal is relied on.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What I want to understand is why we’ve lost that safety improvement out of the area in which I live and to what extent, Minister, you took it upon yourself to familiarise yourself with the details of the projects that were being lost and the impacts on the local communities.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: a named discontinued safety project and the process by which it was cut. Questioning whether the Minister informed himself about a specific project is scrutiny of a decision, not party-bashing, so it sits at the top of the scale.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But given that fuel tax is already being collected and the mechanism was in place to collect the regional fuel tax, did the Government give any consideration to the relative value of having something that is administratively simple and already in place to carry on with revenue so that infrastructure can carry on being funded until we have the congestion pricing or other mechanisms in place?
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism of the repeal directly — collection cost, revenue continuity, and the sequencing against congestion pricing. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m not sure if he’s had a conversation with his colleague Camilla Belich, because she has an identical tabled amendment where she doesn’t want to reinstate the road safety one but wants to reinstate active transport instead.
focus.explanation: There is genuine policy content — the tabled amendments are the measures before the committee, and the conflict between them is a real point about what the Opposition is asking the House to enact. But the weight of the remark is on the opponents' failure to coordinate rather than on the merits of reinstating either project, which is party framing around a substantive point.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The particular intersection that concerns me on these safety concerns—it was some safety improvements to the intersection of Blockhouse Bay Road and Chalmers Street.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact intersection and the exact class of work cut, tied to Project 8 identified in the surrounding text. Anyone could go and check what was in that project. No dollar figure or timeframe, which keeps it short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In discussions with the Mayor of Auckland, the priority projects are those main ones, which are the City Rail Link trains and stabling, which is critically important around the City Rail Link; the Eastern Busway and Reeves Road flyover, which is under construction; and local roading improvements.
specificity.explanation: Names the three projects the remaining funding will go to, which is checkable against the bill's schedule. Held back from the top because no amounts or dates are attached and 'local roading improvements' is an open category.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: But in the short term, there’s going to be a gap in revenue and then, in order for projects that were on the books in Auckland to continue being funded with a share from the council, it would have to come from some other source—probably rates or those projects simply won’t go ahead.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that repealing the Auckland regional fuel tax will leave a funding gap that Auckland Council must close either by raising rates or by dropping transport projects that were on the books.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council's 2024–2034 Long-term Plan and subsequent annual transport programme decisions: true if the Council either raises rates or defers/cancels previously programmed transport projects, with the regional fuel tax repeal cited as a cause of the shortfall; false if the affected projects proceed on schedule without a rates increase or an equivalent substitute revenue source.

veracity.statement: I said before: $5 million for every fatal accident.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the social/economic cost to New Zealand of a single fatal road crash is about $5 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport 'Social cost of road crashes and injuries' annual report (or Waka Kotahi's Monetised Benefits and Costs Manual value of statistical life) for the year current at March 2024: true if the stated average social cost per fatal crash is of the order of $5 million, false if materially different (e.g. under $2m or over $10m).

veracity.statement: We have a health and safety regime in this country that says if you identify a risk, you have a legal obligation to do something about that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand health and safety law imposes a legal duty to act on a risk once it has been identified.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Health and Safety at Work Act 2015, ss 22 and 30–36 (primary duty of care; duty to eliminate risks so far as is reasonably practicable, and otherwise to minimise them): true if the Act imposes a duty on a PCBU to eliminate or minimise identified risks, false if identification carries no accompanying legal duty.

veracity.statement: There is around $340 million of unspent regional fuel tax revenue.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific quantum of Auckland regional fuel tax revenue collected but not yet spent as at the time of the debate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council / Ministry of Transport reporting on the unspent Auckland regional fuel tax balance as at early 2024: true if the unspent balance is approximately $340 million (say within about $40m), false if materially different.

rigor.statement: Because if it was a workplace, and, indeed, as Minister of Transport, it is your workplace, Minister—how are you going to explain to the families of the people who are killed on rural roads because of insufficient infrastructure?
rigor.explanation: False analogy carrying the whole weight of the inference: the public road network is treated as the Minister's 'workplace' so that PCBU liability under the Health and Safety at Work Act follows, which is not what that Act covers. It is then closed with an appeal to emotion (explaining to bereaved families) in place of a link between the funding exclusion and specific deaths. The policy target is real, so this is a Rigor failure rather than a Focus one.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Deficiencies are areas in infrastructure that have been identified as faulty, and this is going to be excluded from funding in Auckland—this is outrageous.
civility.explanation: Blunt condemnation aimed entirely at the funding decision. No person is impugned, no bad faith imputed — under the re-anchored scale, fierce criticism of a decision is civil.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So, in essence, is the spending of the moneys for projects four, six, and 12 time bound; if so, could the Minister please point to the time-bound provision within clause 23, and, if not, why not?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: a named clause of the bill and three named projects. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, this is a fuel tax that has enabled public transport, it’s enabled walkable streets, it’s given the potential for light rail—and I can’t understand why anyone would want to stomp on local initiatives, on city initiatives, to do well by their communities.
focus.explanation: Engages what the regional fuel tax actually funded and what repealing it removes. It is about the measure and its effects, not about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is just a shocking, shocking indictment of the climate denialism that we face across the aisle.
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of what the other side is 'really like'. No policy, mechanism, figure or outcome is named, and nothing here bears on the bill. Rigor is deliberately omitted: strip out the part about the other side and no argument remains.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, in essence, is the spending of the moneys for projects four, six, and 12 time bound; if so, could the Minister please point to the time-bound provision within clause 23, and, if not, why not?
specificity.explanation: Names clause 23 and projects four, six and 12, and asks a precisely answerable question about whether a time bound exists and where. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In regards to clause 23, any incentive or disincentive to spend it, the legislation doesn’t make the spend time-bound, because obviously some of those projects are going to take two to three years, so there’s going to be no time-bounds on them.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, states the legislative position (no time bound) and gives a rough duration figure. Missing only the how-much and any dated milestone.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As you know, I come from Ōtepoti—Dunedin—and the Dunedin City Council has a zero-carbon target by 2030, and in that they aim to change modality in transport.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Dunedin City Council has adopted a zero-carbon target for 2030 and that transport mode-shift is part of how it intends to meet it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Dunedin City Council's adopted climate policy documents (Zero Carbon 2030 declaration / emissions management plan); true if the council has a formally adopted net-zero-by-2030 target that includes transport mode shift, false if it has no such target or the date is materially different.

veracity.statement: Now, this is a fuel tax that has enabled public transport, it’s enabled walkable streets, it’s given the potential for light rail—and I can’t understand why anyone would want to stomp on local initiatives, on city initiatives, to do well by their communities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Auckland regional fuel tax has in fact funded public transport and walking infrastructure, and has provided funding capacity toward light rail.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Transport / Auckland Council regional fuel tax expenditure and project reports 2018–2024; true if RFT revenue is recorded as funding public transport services or infrastructure and walking/streetscape projects, and includes any allocation toward light rail or rapid transit; false if the project list shows none of these.

veracity.statement: The Minister of Transport acknowledged that he had met with Mayor Wayne Brown, but my question was actually framed around what the current state of the relationship is and the impact of this piece of legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister of Transport, in this debate, acknowledged having met with the Mayor of Auckland, Wayne Brown.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard transcript of this committee stage on the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill; true if the Minister of Transport is recorded stating he met Mayor Wayne Brown, false if no such statement appears.

rigor.statement: In regards to clause 23, any incentive or disincentive to spend it, the legislation doesn’t make the spend time-bound, because obviously some of those projects are going to take two to three years, so there’s going to be no time-bounds on them.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy, but with a gap: that projects take two to three years is a reason not to set a *short* deadline, not a reason to set none at all. The conclusion overshoots the premise rather than following from it.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I respect the Minister, and I have enjoyed working with him in the transport space over the past few years, but I have openly called him cynical today in our speeches, on the basis that he has doubled down on pedestrian crossings in this particular discussion.
civility.explanation: Calling the Minister "cynical" imputes bad faith to the person, which is a real civility cost. It is tempered by an explicit statement of respect and is tied to a stated basis in the Minister's conduct on a policy question, so it sits above a bare sneer but below civil engagement with the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Given that he was not interested in responding about either the increased personal costs of injury and death nor the cost to the Government of increased health, I will focus on the very immediate cost of living question.
civility.explanation: "Not interested in responding" imputes indifference to injury and death to the Minister personally, rather than simply noting that the questions went unanswered. That is an attribution of bad faith, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Just saying that repeatedly, when we are raising concerns from our local communities, kind of does amount to going “Nyah nyah na-nyah nyah!”, so it would be helpful if we got some responses.
civility.explanation: Mocks the Minister by rendering his answers as a childish playground taunt. It targets his manner rather than his character or competence, but it is derision rather than engagement with what he said.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The question I had for the Minister is: in his second reading speech and first reading speech he continued to mention the amount of $500,000 as a cost for pedestrian crossings.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the Minister cited a $500,000 pedestrian-crossing cost in both his first and second reading speeches on this bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of Simeon Brown's first and second reading speeches on the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill; true if he cites $500,000 as a cost of a pedestrian crossing in both speeches, false if the figure does not appear or is materially different.

veracity.statement: My questions regarding pedestrian crossings are actually because, from what I’ve heard from the Minister, I worry that he has unfairly looked at those and used a poor example from the New Zealand Herald that has been withdrawn.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a New Zealand Herald item on pedestrian crossing costs, relied on by the Minister, has been withdrawn.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Herald's correction/retraction record for its reporting on pedestrian crossing costs in the period before 5 March 2024; true if the article or the cost figure it reported was withdrawn or corrected, false if the story stands uncorrected.

veracity.statement: I mean, ultimately, as I’ve outlined on a number of occasions, we took this policy to the election; Aucklanders voted for it—in fact, I think Auckland voted 57 percent for the coalition Government—and now we are delivering on that promise with this legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Auckland gave the coalition parties 57 percent of the vote at the 2023 general election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission 2023 general election party vote results aggregated across Auckland electorates; true if the combined National, ACT and New Zealand First party vote in Auckland is approximately 57%, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: I mean, ultimately what we’re doing here is removing the Auckland regional fuel tax, which removes 10c a litre plus GST off the cost of fuel in Auckland.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Auckland regional fuel tax was levied at 10 cents per litre plus GST.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Land Transport Management Act regional fuel tax scheme rate set for the Auckland scheme; true if the rate is 10 cents per litre exclusive of GST, false if a different rate or GST-inclusive.

veracity.statement: The median distance of travel to school in metro urban authorities is just over 2 kilometres.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a median school travel distance of just over 2 km in metropolitan urban territorial authorities.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport Household Travel Survey figures for median school journey distance in main urban areas; true if the median is between roughly 2 and 2.5 km, false if materially outside that.

specificity.statement: The question I had for the Minister is: in his second reading speech and first reading speech he continued to mention the amount of $500,000 as a cost for pedestrian crossings.
specificity.explanation: Names a figure, the item it is attached to, and the two specific speeches it was used in — someone could go to Hansard and check it directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m seeking an explanation from the Minister, because children’s safety, road safety, is a very important part of the decision that this legislation is making, and in my community we have very good examples where pedestrian crossings have been very effective: outside Birkdale Primary, Beach Haven Primary, Northcote Intermediate.
specificity.explanation: Names three specific sites, which is checkable, but "very effective" carries no measure — no injury figures, counts or costs are supplied to say in what respect they worked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I mean, ultimately what we’re doing here is removing the Auckland regional fuel tax, which removes 10c a litre plus GST off the cost of fuel in Auckland.
specificity.explanation: States the exact rate and its GST treatment and identifies the mechanism precisely; it stops short of top marks only because no date or dollar effect on households is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of the winding up of the scheme, this legislation effectively requires, from the time of Royal assent—we’ll get to that debate later—that the funds are required to be spent on these particular projects and then on 30 June that is when the tax ends.
specificity.explanation: Gives a mechanism and a hard end date for the tax, but leaves "these particular projects" and the amounts unnamed in an answer that was asked precisely about which projects and how much.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My first question is: how will the Minister ensure that the abolition of the regional fuel tax does not adversely affect the funding of current and future transport projects in Auckland, especially those that are critical to reducing and improving the public transportation system?
specificity.explanation: Identifies the policy and the area of concern but names no project, figure or funding gap; "current and future transport projects" and "critical" carry no detail that could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My fourth question, and this is in terms of clause 5, particularly the savings provisions of clause 5: how will the Minister ensure that the savings provisions protect the already committed funds and projects that were to be financed by the regional fuel tax and what measures will he put in place to ensure that these projects are completed as planned?
specificity.explanation: Pins the question to a named clause and a named legal mechanism (the savings provisions), which is checkable against the bill, but the funds and projects at issue are referred to only in the aggregate.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The median distance of travel to school in metro urban authorities is just over 2 kilometres.
specificity.explanation: A single precise statistic with a stated population and unit; anyone could go to the travel survey and confirm or refute it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Project 13 has dynamic lanes included, and there were to be dynamic lanes along Great North Road and around Patiki Road and around Blockhouse Bay Road.
specificity.explanation: Names the schedule item, the intervention type and the three specific roads affected — precise enough to check against the bill's schedule. No costs or timeframes, which keeps it just short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I mean, ultimately, as I’ve outlined on a number of occasions, we took this policy to the election; Aucklanders voted for it—in fact, I think Auckland voted 57 percent for the coalition Government—and now we are delivering on that promise with this legislation.
rigor.explanation: An appeal to electoral mandate offered as an answer to questions about what consultation and advice informed the decision. The vote share, even if accurate, does not bear on what advice was received, so the conclusion that the questions are not relevant to the bill does not follow from the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One of the things that the Minister says is “We won the election.” and so on, and “Therefore, we don’t need to discuss.” Indeed, that is quite clear, but that doesn’t mean that the Government is still not responsible for discussing these matters.
rigor.explanation: Grants the premise (the election result) and identifies precisely where the inference fails: winning an election settles the mandate to legislate, not the obligation to answer scrutiny of the legislation. Two distinct claims are correctly separated. The double negative is a spoken slip; the intended reading is plain.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There are a lot of businesses there and the traffic gets incredibly congested there. It is hard for businesses to operate there because the traffic is inadequate. Yet this project, which would have been so beneficial to them, has been taken off the drawing board.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House — congestion exists, the cut project addressed it, therefore the cut costs local businesses. The support is a personal anecdote about a dynamic lane on a different road (Vipond Road) plus an unquantified assertion of benefit; no traffic volumes or modelling connect the two corridors.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Ultimately, as I’ve outlined on a number of occasions, the Government has been very clear around which of these projects will require the remaining funding to support.
specificity.explanation: Answering a direct question about which Auckland projects keep funding, he names no project, no figure and no criterion — only an assertion that the Government has 'been very clear'. The opportunity for precision was squarely available and declined.
specificity.subject: speaker
