specificity.statement: By distributional assessment, I mean, for example, which population groups are the ones that the Minister expects to have most to gain as part of the repeal of the regional fuel tax.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete analytical instrument and defines it, and the surrounding text enumerates the groups he means (income-support recipients, ethnic groups, full- vs part-time workers, proximity to public transport). Checkable and actionable, though no figures are attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The one that I think most clearly illustrates that particular point is the project number 9, which I have suggested should be exempted, and one of the aspects of project number 9 was capital expenditure to support the City Centre Masterplan Access for Everyone programme.
specificity.explanation: Names the numbered project, the amendment she is moving on it, and the specific programme funded within it. Someone could go to the Schedule and the Amendment Paper and check it; what is missing is the dollar amount.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So what I’m interested to know is whether a child impact assessment has been done as part of the process of this bill, to actually evaluate the cost of living impacts on children, particularly on child poverty reduction, because, to me, I guess, this is one of the bills the Government intends to have cost of living impacts.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: asks what analysis was done of the bill's stated cost-of-living purpose. No party framing at all — this is scrutiny of a named policy process.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, the reason clause 7 keeps coming up, Madam Chair, as you’ll be aware, is clause 7, basically, gets rid of an entire Schedule within the primary Act, which lists a number of projects which the Minister, on the whole, has decided to defund for Aucklanders.
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism of the bill itself — a named clause, the Schedule it repeals, and the consequence for the projects in it. Textbook on-policy scrutiny with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think, again, if the Minister’s unable to substantiate his so-called cost of living impacts of this bill by backing it up with evidence and robust analysis, I just question, then, whether the cost of living argument for this bill is just based on vibes as opposed to actually robust evidence around who will benefit the most.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: no distributional or child-impact analysis produced, therefore the cost-of-living justification is unsubstantiated. That much follows. The step from 'unsubstantiated in this debate' to 'based on vibes' overreaches — absence of a published assessment is not absence of any basis — so it falls short of a clean conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’m not sure that simply saying, “I don’t want to” or “It’s not the one I picked” is a substantial enough or considered enough justification for the amount of projects which are being defunded, essentially, in Auckland.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the Minister's stated reason was that a fixed amount of remaining funding was prioritised to the projects listed in the bill. Rebutting a caricature ('I don't want to') rather than that reason means the conclusion — that the justification is inadequate — is not established by what was actually offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This will have a cost of living impact by reducing the cost of petrol for Aucklanders, and that is something which is, of course, good news to people in Auckland and I know has significant support from the people of Auckland.
rigor.explanation: Asked for the distributional and child-impact analysis behind the cost-of-living claim, he restates the claim and then supports it with an appeal to popularity ('significant support from the people of Auckland'). Public support is not evidence of the effect asserted, so the conclusion rests on nothing that was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think, again, if the Minister’s unable to substantiate his so-called cost of living impacts of this bill by backing it up with evidence and robust analysis, I just question, then, whether the cost of living argument for this bill is just based on vibes as opposed to actually robust evidence around who will benefit the most.
civility.explanation: 'So-called' and 'vibes' are dismissive of the Minister's argument, not of the Minister. Nothing is said about his character, competence or motives; the target throughout is the evidence base for the bill.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m not sure that simply saying, “I don’t want to” or “It’s not the one I picked” is a substantial enough or considered enough justification for the amount of projects which are being defunded, essentially, in Auckland.
civility.explanation: Pointed and edging toward the person: putting flippant words in the Minister's mouth imputes carelessness in how he has answered. It stops short of an attack on him as a person, and the complaint remains about the adequacy of his answers on the defunded projects.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I just had a look at the Standing Orders, and the Minister is required to answer all of our questions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Standing Orders of the House of Representatives impose a duty on the Minister in charge of a bill to answer every question put during the committee stage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Standing Orders of the House of Representatives in force in March 2024, plus Speakers'/Chairpersons' rulings collected in McGee, on the committee-of-the-whole stage: true if a Standing Order obliges the Minister in charge to answer all questions put; false if the Orders only require the Minister to be present and in charge of the bill, with the content and adequacy of answers not enforceable by the Chair.

veracity.statement: Now, for those of you who aren’t aware about the City Centre Masterplan Access for Everyone programme, I’m sure Auckland MPs, including the Minister, will be well aware of it, because it’s existed since 2012 and was, indeed, in 2019 consulted on and endorsed in 2020 by the Auckland planning committee.
veracity.explanation: Three dated assertions about the City Centre Masterplan / Access for Everyone: that it dates from 2012, that it was publicly consulted on in 2019, and that Auckland Council's Planning Committee endorsed it in 2020.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council records for the City Centre Masterplan and the Access for Everyone programme — the masterplan's original adoption date, the consultation record for the 2019 refresh, and the Planning Committee minutes/resolution adopting it: true if the plan dates from 2012, was consulted on during 2019 and was endorsed by the Planning Committee in 2020; false if any of the three dates or the endorsing body is materially wrong.

veracity.statement: Because ultimately we were elected to remove this tax, we’re removing it on 30 June this year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an electoral mandate for the repeal — that removing the Auckland regional fuel tax was a commitment the Government was elected on at the 2023 general election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 election transport policy documents and the National–ACT and National–NZ First coalition agreements: true if scrapping the Auckland regional fuel tax appears as a stated pre-election commitment or coalition commitment; false if no such commitment is recorded.

divination.statement: This will have a cost of living impact by reducing the cost of petrol for Aucklanders, and that is something which is, of course, good news to people in Auckland and I know has significant support from the people of Auckland.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that repealing the regional fuel tax will pass through to lower pump prices for Auckland motorists — an outcome in the market, not merely the repeal itself.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE weekly retail petrol price data comparing Auckland with the rest of New Zealand either side of the repeal date: true if Auckland's average 91-octane price falls relative to the national average by an amount approaching the regional fuel tax rate (11.5c/L plus GST) within three months of 30 June 2024; false if the Auckland–national gap is materially unchanged.

specificity.statement: So what this part does is it removes the legislative framework that allows new regional fuel taxes to be created, also from 1 July 2024, and the regulations relating to the proposals of new schemes and the conditions that must follow will also be revoked.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific legal effect of the clause under debate, the commencement date, and the revocation of the associated regulations. Concrete enough that a reader could check it against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So my question to the Minister is: I’m keen on Mill Road as a local roading upgrade—I want people to have access to that as a local project—but what I’m concerned about is that that project could balloon into, essentially, a road of national significance that we spend $3.5 billion on, and now, if it’s in that big pot and out of the instruments here in the small pot, which are being repealed by this bill, what assurance can the Minister give to the committee that there will be adequate controls over that sort of ballooning of costs in a project which should be an upgrade of a local road?
specificity.explanation: Carries a named project and a dollar figure, but the thing actually asked for — "adequate controls" — is left undefined, with no mechanism or threshold proposed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Death and serious injuries have increased by 70 percent between 2014 and 2017. That’s three times more than what the rest of the country has experienced.
specificity.explanation: A percentage, a date range, and a stated comparison against the national rate. Someone could go to the crash statistics and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, I get that we’re not delving into specific projects that are being removed by the dismantling of this structure through this particular repeal bill—I get that—but what I really want to ask the Minister about is the gaps, because, ultimately, what we’re talking about is 11 projects that will not go ahead, which, in its entirety, means that infrastructure that would have allowed children to be able, potentially, to cycle to schools or people to be able to get to their busiest local mall is not there.
specificity.explanation: Supplies a figure (11 projects) and a category of loss, but the question itself — what advice was received on "plugging the gaps" — carries no mechanism, cost or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So what this part does is it removes the legislative framework that allows new regional fuel taxes to be created, also from 1 July 2024, and the regulations relating to the proposals of new schemes and the conditions that must follow will also be revoked.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that clause 4 of the repeal bill removes the statutory framework for creating new regional fuel taxes, effective 1 July 2024, and revokes the associated regulations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The enacted text of the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill 2024, clause 4 and its commencement provision: true if the repeal of subpart 3 of Part 2 removes the mechanism for establishing new regional fuel tax schemes and takes effect 1 July 2024 with the related regulations revoked; false if the framework survives or the date differs.

veracity.statement: I would note, though, that the regional fuel tax was not proposing to spend any money on Mill Road because the last Government cancelled it.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that no Auckland regional fuel tax funding was allocated to Mill Road, and that the previous Labour-led government cancelled the Mill Road project.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Auckland regional fuel tax project schedule (Order in Council / Auckland Transport RFT programme documents current at March 2024) for whether Mill Road appears as a funded project, plus NZTA/Cabinet records on the 2022 decision on the Mill Road corridor: true if Mill Road drew no RFT allocation and was cancelled (not merely deferred or rescoped) under the previous government; false if Mill Road appears in the RFT programme or the previous government deferred rather than cancelled it.

veracity.statement: Those are particularly around, for example, bus improvements in areas like around Sylvia Park, which is the busiest shopping mall in the country and an area that deserves improvement so that people can get around.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Sylvia Park is the busiest shopping mall in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published visitor/foot-traffic figures for NZ shopping centres (Kiwi Property annual reports for Sylvia Park; comparable disclosures for Westfield Newmarket, St Lukes and Riccarton): true if Sylvia Park records the highest annual visitor numbers, false if another centre does.

veracity.statement: Death and serious injuries have increased by 70 percent between 2014 and 2017. That’s three times more than what the rest of the country has experienced.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that deaths and serious injuries on Auckland roads rose 70 percent between 2014 and 2017, and that this rate of increase was three times the increase experienced by the rest of New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA Crash Analysis System / Auckland Transport road safety reporting on deaths and serious injuries for Auckland and for the rest of New Zealand, 2014 to 2017: true if the Auckland increase is approximately 70% and roughly three times the non-Auckland increase; false if either figure is materially different.

focus.statement: So my question to the Minister is: I’m keen on Mill Road as a local roading upgrade—I want people to have access to that as a local project—but what I’m concerned about is that that project could balloon into, essentially, a road of national significance that we spend $3.5 billion on, and now, if it’s in that big pot and out of the instruments here in the small pot, which are being repealed by this bill, what assurance can the Minister give to the committee that there will be adequate controls over that sort of ballooning of costs in a project which should be an upgrade of a local road?
focus.explanation: Names a specific project (Mill Road), a specific funding mechanism change (out of the regional fuel tax, into the national land transport fund), and a specific risk (cost escalation to $3.5 billion). Entirely about the policy, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, I get that we’re not delving into specific projects that are being removed by the dismantling of this structure through this particular repeal bill—I get that—but what I really want to ask the Minister about is the gaps, because, ultimately, what we’re talking about is 11 projects that will not go ahead, which, in its entirety, means that infrastructure that would have allowed children to be able, potentially, to cycle to schools or people to be able to get to their busiest local mall is not there.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: the count of projects lost to the repeal and the concrete services those projects would have delivered. Scrutiny of a named consequence, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I mean, the first question from Arena Williams is not relevant to this bill. This bill is repealing the regional fuel tax. If the Government was to make other policy changes in regards to other types of funding and financing for infrastructure, that is something which would be done separately. So it’s not relevant to the bill which is in front of us.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: premise that the bill's scope is confined to repealing the regional fuel tax, conclusion that questions about other funding instruments fall outside it. The conclusion tracks the premise, but there is a gap — the question was precisely about whether repealing this framework forecloses or eases those other instruments, which the scope argument does not address.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I mean, the first question from Arena Williams is not relevant to this bill. This bill is repealing the regional fuel tax. If the Government was to make other policy changes in regards to other types of funding and financing for infrastructure, that is something which would be done separately. So it’s not relevant to the bill which is in front of us.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the question rather than the questioner. No imputation of bad faith, no mockery, despite a clear opportunity in a contested committee stage.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But is the Minister satisfied that those amendments capture all of the possibilities, and, in particular, what provision is there if particular projects—and at this stage it looks as though they will only be three of the projects—are either deferred or if they don’t proceed?
specificity.explanation: Names the consequential-amendment schedule and the three remaining projects, and asks a concrete contingency question (deferral or non-completion). Detailed enough to be answered or checked, though no figures or dates are supplied.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And when I look at what is proposed here, my amendment is, effectively, to delete the words “Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax)” and to replace it with “Land Transport Management (Instructions to Auckland Council Regarding the Regional Fuel Tax)”.
specificity.explanation: States the exact words to be deleted and the exact replacement wording. Fully actionable — the House could vote on it as read.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On 1 July 2024, the Act will come into place. This is when the regional fuel tax will be lifted, and the fuel distributed in Auckland region will no longer be subject to the extra 10c per litre plus 1.5c of GST—11.5c per litre.
specificity.explanation: A commencement date, the per-litre rate, the GST component and the combined total, tied to a named region. Precise and directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But is the Minister satisfied that those amendments capture all of the possibilities, and, in particular, what provision is there if particular projects—and at this stage it looks as though they will only be three of the projects—are either deferred or if they don’t proceed?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee — the coverage of the consequential amendments and what happens to the retained projects. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Perhaps this is something that should say: “227g Dole Pineapple Chunk” because that is the cost of living sort of measure that this Government is going to provide as part of this piece of legislation.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy referent underneath — the size of the household saving from lifting the fuel tax — but it is carried entirely by ridicule of the Government's cost-of-living framing rather than by any named figure or mechanism. A policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And so your suggestion, Minister, that, well, it’s called what is suggested because it is a repeal bill; well, this House is the author of its own destiny, and it can determine what it wishes.
rigor.explanation: A genuine rebuttal: the Minister's implied premise is that the title follows necessarily from the bill being a repeal bill, and Utikere correctly points out the House is not so constrained. Valid as far as it goes, but it only defeats the constraint claim — it offers no support for the positive premise that the bill is better described as instructions to Auckland Council, which is what the conclusion actually needs.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Leaving a year allows some activity to continue, so that’s issuing refunds, and it will allow the NZTA to continue its auditing process to ensure the tax has been correctly paid.
rigor.explanation: A conclusion (the year-long delay before the savings provisions end is warranted) supported by two specific mechanisms that require the scheme to remain on the books — refunds and NZTA auditing. The reason genuinely supports the design choice; no fallacy or gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, we haven’t got anything from you, so many people will be waiting for quite some time.
civility.explanation: A retort to Andy Foster's interjection that lands on the member rather than on any argument — a sneer at his output as an MP. Short of a direct insult, but it engages no substance and belittles a named colleague.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: On 1 July 2024, the Act will come into place. This is when the regional fuel tax will be lifted, and the fuel distributed in Auckland region will no longer be subject to the extra 10c per litre plus 1.5c of GST—11.5c per litre.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Auckland regional fuel tax was levied at 10c per litre plus 1.5c GST, totalling 11.5c per litre at the pump, and that it ceases on 1 July 2024. The rate component is the checkable part.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The rate set by the Regional Fuel Tax (Auckland) Order 2018 / Land Transport Management Act regional fuel tax provisions: true if the Auckland regional fuel tax was 10 cents per litre exclusive of GST, i.e. 11.5 cents per litre inclusive of GST; false if the statutory rate or the GST-inclusive total differs materially.

veracity.statement: The regional fuel tax order from 2018 contained a list of 14 projects, and this legislation will constrain that remaining revenue and funds which have accumulated to be spent on the remaining three projects, as outlined in earlier parts of this debate.
veracity.explanation: A count claim about the 2018 order — that it specified 14 eligible projects — set against the three the repeal bill retains.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The schedule of the Regional Fuel Tax (Auckland) Order 2018: true if the order lists 14 projects eligible for regional fuel tax revenue, false if the count in the order as made is materially different.

civility.statement: Mr Foster, we’re still waiting for a contribution that’s meaningful from him.
civility.explanation: A sneering aside dismissing another member's contributions as not meaningful. It targets the member rather than any argument he made, so it falls short of civil, though it stops well short of direct abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: With all due respect, I would point out to the Minister that the campaign wasn’t on the infrastructure projects—the 11 projects, that would be scrapped as a result of this bill going through—it was just on the repeal of the tax, which sounds great, but what people might not have known, because it wasn’t campaigned on, was the indirect costs to Aucklanders as a result of this.
civility.explanation: Hard criticism of the bill and of what was and was not put to voters, directed entirely at the policy and the campaign. Nothing is said about the Minister as a person; on the re-anchored scale this is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Because they’d take money from Northland, or they’ll take money from Otago, or they’ll take money from South Canterbury because none of those members of Parliament are standing up for their own regions.
civility.explanation: Imputes dereliction to the government's regional MPs — that they are not standing up for the places they represent. It is aimed at those members rather than at the funding decision, which is a real civility failure even though no individual is named.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And I’m interested in the Minister’s thoughts around this because being able to provide a bit of a buffer in terms of a delay to the commencement would mean that some of those transitional provisions could actually be looked at.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: the commencement clause and what a one-year delay would allow. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: With all due respect, I would point out to the Minister that the campaign wasn’t on the infrastructure projects—the 11 projects, that would be scrapped as a result of this bill going through—it was just on the repeal of the tax, which sounds great, but what people might not have known, because it wasn’t campaigned on, was the indirect costs to Aucklanders as a result of this.
focus.explanation: Names a specific consequence of the measure — 11 infrastructure projects lost and indirect costs to Aucklanders — rather than characterising the governing parties. Legitimate scrutiny of a named policy outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But my question is about the amendment restricting which capital projects will be supported from the Auckland regional fuel tax revenue, because that comes into force the day after the bill receives Royal assent.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of clause 2 and the effect of a staggered commencement. Scrutiny of the drafting before the committee, with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because they’d take money from Northland, or they’ll take money from Otago, or they’ll take money from South Canterbury because none of those members of Parliament are standing up for their own regions.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point here — that regional road funding may be diverted to backfill Auckland — but its weight rests on a characterisation of the other side's members rather than on the funding mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I’d ask the Minister to give an assurance—an absolute assurance—that from commencement date, there will be no shift in funding from projects or commitments and safety around the rest of the country just to fund the shortfall that this bill will create for Auckland.
focus.explanation: Directly on the consequence of the commencement clause for the national land transport fund and regional road safety spending. A policy question put to the Minister, not a party attack.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And I’m interested in the Minister’s thoughts around this because being able to provide a bit of a buffer in terms of a delay to the commencement would mean that some of those transitional provisions could actually be looked at.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the clause — delayed commencement yields time to work through transitional provisions — and the conclusion follows. It is weakened only by the absence of any account of which transitional provisions are defective, so the need for the buffer is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The only response that we’ve had from the Minister to date is that his party’s won an election.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that across the passage of the bill the Minister has offered no justification for commencing the repeal other than the election result.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill 2024 debates up to 5 March 2024: true if the Minister's answers on why the repeal proceeds cite only the election mandate; false if he advanced any substantive reason (cost of living, fuel prices, Auckland Council budget alignment).

veracity.statement: There was a long-term programme of initiatives to improve bus services from the likes of New Lynn, Mount Roskill, Onehunga, right through to the airport. Now that’s been scrapped as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a long-term bus service improvement programme covering New Lynn, Mount Roskill, Onehunga and the airport was funded under the Auckland regional fuel tax and has been cancelled as a consequence of the repeal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Auckland regional fuel tax project schedule (Auckland Transport / Auckland Council RLTP documents) and Auckland Transport's post-repeal reprioritisation reporting: true if a bus-improvement programme covering those localities and airport access appears on the RFT-funded list and was dropped after the repeal; false if no such programme was RFT-funded or if it continued under other funding.

veracity.statement: We were elected to remove the Auckland regional fuel tax; we are delivering on that commitment, which Aucklanders overwhelmingly voted for.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Aucklanders voted for the repeal of the regional fuel tax by an overwhelming margin at the 2023 general election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission 2023 general election party vote results aggregated across Auckland electorates: true if the parties campaigning on repeal (National, ACT, NZ First) took a clear majority of the Auckland party vote — say 60% or more, matching 'overwhelmingly'; false if their combined Auckland share was at or near half. There was no referendum on the tax, so the party vote is the only available measure.

veracity.statement: Now, there are remaining funds in the Auckland Council coffers—over $340 million—and there’ll be remaining funding which will be received between now and 1 July, and as I’ve outlined publicly, 1 July was the date chosen because that aligns with the Auckland Council’s annual budget year and that’s the right time to make that change.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than $340 million of Auckland regional fuel tax revenue remained unspent in Auckland Council's hands as at early March 2024, and that 1 July aligns with the council's annual budget year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council / Auckland Transport regional fuel tax financial reporting for the 2023/24 year: true if unspent RFT funds exceeded $340m at around March 2024 and the council's financial year begins 1 July; false if the unspent balance was materially below $340m.

veracity.statement: Because my questions—and the Minister and his colleagues voted down my amendment relating to road safety and the ongoing need for that funding.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an amendment he tabled to this bill concerning road safety funding was put and defeated by the government parties earlier in the committee stage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard committee-stage record for the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill 2024 on 5 March 2024: true if an O'Connor amendment relating to road safety funding was put and negatived on the government's votes; false if no such amendment was moved or if it was not voted down.

specificity.statement: There was a long-term programme of initiatives to improve bus services from the likes of New Lynn, Mount Roskill, Onehunga, right through to the airport. Now that’s been scrapped as well.
specificity.explanation: Names the corridor and the specific localities served by the programme she says is lost. Someone could go to the project list and check it; it stops short of 1.0 only because no dollar figure, timeframe or project name is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But my question is about the amendment restricting which capital projects will be supported from the Auckland regional fuel tax revenue, because that comes into force the day after the bill receives Royal assent.
specificity.explanation: Identifies exactly which limb of the commencement clause is at issue and the precise trigger — the day after Royal assent — rather than the 1 July date. Precise enough that the Minister can only answer it or refuse to.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, there are remaining funds in the Auckland Council coffers—over $340 million—and there’ll be remaining funding which will be received between now and 1 July, and as I’ve outlined publicly, 1 July was the date chosen because that aligns with the Auckland Council’s annual budget year and that’s the right time to make that change.
specificity.explanation: A figure, a date, and the stated reason for that date. It answers the question asked with checkable content rather than a direction of travel.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I’d ask the Minister to give an assurance—an absolute assurance—that from commencement date, there will be no shift in funding from projects or commitments and safety around the rest of the country just to fund the shortfall that this bill will create for Auckland.
specificity.explanation: A clear direction — no diversion of funding from regional and safety projects — but no named projects, no amounts and no mechanism by which the assurance would be tested.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, “Palmy” is not in Auckland, Mr Costley, in case you didn’t know, all right?
civility.explanation: A retort to an interjection that is pointed and lightly condescending — "in case you didn't know" implies the member is ignorant — but it stops short of a personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The other one is the member for Pakuranga, the Minister who is responsible—his own project seems to be funded.
civility.explanation: Insinuates that the responsible Minister has steered funding to a project in his own electorate — an imputation of self-interest aimed at a named individual rather than at the merits of the funding decision.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But of the three, there were two of them that managed to make the cut, and it’s interesting that with regard to project No. 12, which is the Glenvar Road - East Coast Road, Erica Stanford has put a petition up and, lo and behold, it’s suddenly one of the projects that is still able to attract the funding.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable facts: that Erica Stanford ran a petition on the Glenvar Road - East Coast Road project, and that this project is among the small number retaining funding under the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's petitions register and Erica Stanford's public campaign material for whether she ran a petition on the Glenvar Road - East Coast Road project, plus the project schedule attached to this bill / the NZTA-Auckland Transport funded project list; true if such a petition exists and project No. 12 (Glenvar Road - East Coast Road) remains funded after the repeal, false if either the petition or the project's continued funding cannot be established.

veracity.statement: This is a Government that is signalling to Auckland that they know best when it comes to projects in Auckland, and they didn’t even support one of the amendments which was to ensure that there was ongoing dialogue and consultation with Auckland’s mayor.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an amendment requiring ongoing consultation with Auckland's mayor was put and not supported by the Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The committee of the whole House record for this bill; true if an amendment (SOP) requiring ongoing consultation with Auckland's mayor was moved and defeated with Government members voting against, false if no such amendment was put or the Government supported it.

veracity.statement: This is a bill where it really is a shame that the Parliament has progressed this piece of legislation without any select committee process.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that this bill was passed with no select committee stage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's progress record on legislation.govt.nz / Parliament's bills page; true if the bill had no select committee stage, false if it was referred to a select committee at any point.

focus.statement: Mr Speaker, they get a bit tetchy over there when they get challenged, and isn’t that interesting?
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of how the other side is behaving; no policy, project, figure or outcome is named. Nobody individually is insulted, so this is the tribalism case Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What is wrong with putting in this piece of legislation a provision that would require there to be some consultation with Auckland so that the transport needs of the future for Auckland were considered and were put into the mix and that the mayor and the council were part of that particular process as well?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: a named legislative provision, who it would bind and what it would require. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: However, capital expenditure for charging infrastructure for electric ferries, among other things, will not happen as a result of this bill.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that removing the regional fuel tax revenue stream will stop capital spending on electric ferry charging infrastructure in Auckland.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Auckland Transport / Auckland Council capital programme and annual reports on electric ferry charging infrastructure at the downtown ferry terminal; true if that charging capital expenditure is cancelled or left unfunded following the repeal, false if the charging infrastructure is funded and delivered from another source.

rigor.statement: This is a Government that is signalling to Auckland that they know best when it comes to projects in Auckland, and they didn’t even support one of the amendments which was to ensure that there was ongoing dialogue and consultation with Auckland’s mayor.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure — from one procedural vote to a general attitude that the Government "knows best" — but the gap is wide: declining a statutory consultation clause is offered as sufficient evidence of the wider disposition. Hasty generalisation from a single vote.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What is wrong with putting in this piece of legislation a provision that would require there to be some consultation with Auckland so that the transport needs of the future for Auckland were considered and were put into the mix and that the mayor and the council were part of that particular process as well?
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (a statutory consultation provision) and the parties to it (the mayor and council), but supplies no drafting, trigger, timing or threshold for what the consultation would require.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill will remove the previous Labour Government’s 11.5c per litre Auckland regional fuel tax, and this bill will do so on 1 July 2024.
specificity.explanation: Names the measure, the rate (11.5c per litre) and the commencement date. Fully checkable and actionable; a minister introducing a repeal could easily have spoken in generalities instead.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Aucklanders overwhelmingly voted—over 55 percent of Aucklanders—for the coalition Government, and here we are today delivering on our promises.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than 55 percent of Auckland voters supported the three coalition parties at the 2023 general election. The word 'overwhelmingly' is also a quantitative overstatement claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission official party-vote results for the 2023 general election, aggregated across Auckland general electorates: true if the combined National + ACT + New Zealand First party vote exceeds 55%, false if it is materially below that.

veracity.statement: There is over $340 million of unspent revenue.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than $340 million of regional fuel tax revenue collected to date remained unspent at the time of the debate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council / Auckland Transport regional fuel tax financial reporting as at early 2024, or the departmental disclosure statement for the repeal bill: true if the unspent balance exceeds $340 million, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: This is an appalling use of the House’s time and urgency, and it will come as no surprise to members of this House that we in the Labour Party will be opposing this terrible piece of legislation that is being rushed through without any select committee process and with no public scrutiny, and it is a real indictment on the ability of this Government to engage with communities, because it simply does not know how to.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the bill is being passed with no select committee stage and no public submissions process.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The parliamentary record for the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill: true if the bill was passed under urgency with no select committee referral and no call for public submissions, false if it was referred to a select committee.

veracity.statement: They have no credibility, they are wanting to whack folk with a 22 percent increase to fuel excise, and they are wishing to, effectively, introduce a drivers’ tax on folk.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government intends to raise fuel excise duty by 22 percent. The checkable core is the size of the announced or signalled increase relative to the current excise rate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government Policy Statement on land transport 2024 and any announced fuel excise duty schedule: true if the signalled cumulative increase equals approximately 22% of the fuel excise rate prevailing in March 2024, false if the announced increase is materially different (e.g. a ~12c increase on a ~70c rate, about 17%).

veracity.statement: But when we have a look at what is contained in that departmental disclosure statement, in the absence of any regulatory impact statement, it simply says that when it comes to the focus on the cost of living, removing this regional fuel tax “will result in modest savings for households and businesses, between $5-$10 per tank”—and we seem to hear that from Minister Simeon Brown frequently—but also that the actual savings, based on the average distances that are travelled in Auckland City and not collecting that RFT out to 2028, will equate to around $1.85 for a motorist, all right—$1.85.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the bill's departmental disclosure statement says: both a $5–$10 per tank saving and an average saving of around $1.85 per motorist, and that no regulatory impact statement was produced.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The departmental disclosure statement published for the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill, and the Ministry of Transport's RIS register: true if the document contains both quoted figures on the basis he describes and no regulatory impact statement was prepared; false if the $1.85 figure is stated on a different basis (e.g. per week) than he represents, or if a RIS exists.

divination.statement: There are a number of reasons why we are removing the regional fuel tax: firstly, because it will save Aucklanders money as they fill up their cars from 1 July this year: $5 to $10 per tank.
divination.explanation: Forecasts the consumer effect of the repeal: a per-tank saving of $5 to $10 for Auckland motorists from 1 July 2024. This is an outcome in the world (whether pump prices fall by the tax amount), not merely a promise to pass the bill.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE weekly petrol price monitoring comparing Auckland pump prices against the rest of New Zealand before and after 1 July 2024: true if the Auckland-specific price falls by approximately 11.5c per litre, yielding $5–$10 on a typical 45–90 litre tank; false if retailers absorb the cut and the Auckland differential does not close.

divination.statement: This will result in cuts to critical transportation projects in Auckland, projects that will make a huge difference.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that repealing the regional fuel tax will cause Auckland transport projects to be cut, not merely deferred in name. The forecast concerns Auckland Council and Auckland Transport decisions, not the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Auckland Transport's Regional Land Transport Plan 2024-34 and Auckland Council's 2024 Long-term Plan: true if projects previously funded from regional fuel tax revenue are cancelled or deferred and the councils attribute this to the repeal, false if the affected programme is funded from other sources with no project cancellations.

rigor.statement: They thought that we should tax Aucklanders more to build speed bumps. Speed bumps—$490,000 speed bumps—that’s why they wanted to tax Aucklanders more, and red light cameras: they wanted to take another 11.5c a litre off Aucklanders to put red light cameras in.
rigor.explanation: Cherry-picking amounting to a strawman: he concludes the entire tax existed for speed bumps and red light cameras, having himself named the Eastern Busway, electric trains and stabling as projects it funds two sentences earlier. The conclusion about the previous government's purpose does not follow from two selected line items.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’ve done a little bit of a calculation and a little bit of online shopping, and I know members opposite don’t like to hear this, but what will that get Aucklanders? It will get them a 227-gram can of Dole pineapple chunks—not a large tin; a small one.
rigor.explanation: Equivocation between two different bases. He sets a single $1.85 figure — drawn from an averaging out to 2028 — against the per-tank saving quoted from the same document, and prices it as one grocery item, as though $1.85 were the whole benefit to a household. The conclusion that the saving is trivial needs the two figures reconciled, and they are not. Scored here rather than under Focus because the statement genuinely engages the policy's costed effect; the defect is in the inference.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They thought that we should tax Aucklanders more to build speed bumps. Speed bumps—$490,000 speed bumps—that’s why they wanted to tax Aucklanders more, and red light cameras: they wanted to take another 11.5c a litre off Aucklanders to put red light cameras in.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual spending programme with named categories and a dollar figure rather than generic party-bashing, so it stays largely on-policy — but a real share of the weight is characterising what the other side 'thought' and 'wanted', which pulls it off the top of the scale.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is a Government that clearly has no eye on the future. It is a Government that has no new ideas, it has no new funding, and, in particular, it has no replacement for this legislation—there is no replacement whatsoever.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point buried here — that the repeal leaves no replacement revenue mechanism — but it is wrapped in general characterisation of the other side ('no eye on the future', 'no new ideas') that names no measure, figure or outcome. A real point in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The best thing about that contribution was when the member sat down.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe at the previous speaker rather than anything he said. It engages no part of the argument and exists only to belittle the member — a clear personal attack, though not sustained abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This is an appalling use of the House’s time and urgency, and it will come as no surprise to members of this House that we in the Labour Party will be opposing this terrible piece of legislation that is being rushed through without any select committee process and with no public scrutiny, and it is a real indictment on the ability of this Government to engage with communities, because it simply does not know how to.
civility.explanation: Harsh language ('appalling', 'terrible') but every word of it lands on the bill and the process, and the competence criticism is aimed at a Government collectively rather than any individual. Under the re-anchored scale, fierce criticism of a measure is civil; it sits just below the top only because 'it simply does not know how to' edges toward sneering.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What a coincidence, and when questioned as part of the committee of the whole stage, one of the issues that came out was the perception of conflicts of interest.
civility.explanation: Sneering insinuation aimed at a named individual: 'What a coincidence' imputes that the responsible Minister preserved funding for a project in his own electorate. It stops short of a direct accusation of corruption, but imputing bad faith to a person is a civility failure under the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Again, that’s another education session, which we might, if we bothered, provide.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic offer to "educate" members opposite about Te Tiriti — condescension and sneering directed at other members rather than at the substance of the bill. Not a direct insult, so above 0.25, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Minister’s brazen confidence in pushing a bill through without actually substantiating the cost of living impacts it will have, despite the general policy statement focusing on the cost of living relief that the repeal of the regional fuel tax will have, is, quite frankly, admirable.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic "admirable" plus "brazen" turns a real procedural complaint into mockery of the Minister personally. The underlying point about unsubstantiated cost-of-living claims could have been made without the sneer.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This will be the third time in a span of 30 years that a National-led Government has repealed such a tax.
specificity.explanation: A countable, checkable claim with a number and a timeframe — three repeals, 30 years, a named class of government and a named tax. Someone could go and verify it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Minister is leading a generation of the Americanisation of our towns and our cities, which is not exactly the kind of urban planning that I think we should be going towards.
specificity.explanation: "Americanisation" carries no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named planning instrument, and "not exactly the kind of urban planning" commits to no alternative. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This will be the third time in a span of 30 years that a National-led Government has repealed such a tax.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a National-led Government has repealed a regional fuel tax (or equivalent) on three separate occasions in the last three decades — this being the third.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative record of regional fuel tax / regional petrol tax measures in New Zealand since roughly 1994 and which governments repealed them: true if three separate repeals by National-led governments can be identified in that window (including the 2024 repeal), false if fewer.

veracity.statement: It is not the top 1 percent of Aotearoa who utilise public transport—our buses, our trains, our cycleways—it is largely those who cannot afford private transport who rely on transport infrastructure and who rely on us in Parliament to ensure we can provide for them at least their basic needs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that public transport use in New Zealand is concentrated among lower-income people who cannot afford private vehicles, rather than the highest earners.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport New Zealand Household Travel Survey (and Auckland Transport patronage surveys) broken down by household income: true if public transport mode share is materially higher in the lower income deciles than the top, false if usage is flat across income or skews to higher-income commuters.

veracity.statement: The Minister should be ashamed that he was not able during the committee of the whole House to substantiate—he couldn’t even confirm to us about whether he had done a child impact assessment, despite parading the cost of living impacts that this bill would have.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that, during the committee of the whole House on this bill, the Minister was unable to confirm whether a child impact assessment had been carried out.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of the committee of the whole House stage on the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill: true if the Minister was asked about a child impact assessment and did not confirm one had been done, false if he confirmed one or was never asked.

rigor.statement: With this bill, there was no clear vision, at least not beyond this coalition’s three-year term. A lack of vision beyond three years is, in essence, a lack of direction for all of Aotearoa.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur by equivocation: an absence of stated long-term planning in one transport bill is redefined as "a lack of direction for all of Aotearoa". Nothing is offered to bridge the gap between the particular measure and the national conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There are going to be more people locked in traffic because this guy thinks that all we need is one more lane and that that will actually fix transport.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the Minister's transport position is reduced to "one more lane" and the congestion conclusion is then drawn from that caricature rather than from anything the Minister argued. The statement is on-policy (road capacity vs public transport), so the defect is the inference, not the subject matter.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is not the top 1 percent of Aotearoa who utilise public transport—our buses, our trains, our cycleways—it is largely those who cannot afford private transport who rely on transport infrastructure and who rely on us in Parliament to ensure we can provide for them at least their basic needs.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the distributional question the bill raises — who uses the infrastructure the repealed tax funds. Names the affected group and the services at issue; no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They are determined to demonstrate their conceit and arrogance, and I could not possibly commend this to the House.
focus.explanation: Characterises the governing parties' motives and temperament rather than the measure before the House. No policy, figure or outcome is named — the only substantive content is the refusal to commend the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Minister couldn’t substantiate whether this bill will lift some of those 7,000 children out of poverty.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny tied to the measure before the House and to a specific figure — whether the bill's claimed cost-of-living benefit reaches a named group. Holding a minister to a stated benefit is on-policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill reflects the very “short-termism” of the coalition Government, and particularly the National Party Minister of Transport, Simeon Brown. The whole way that they approach the problems and solutions is incredibly short term.
focus.explanation: It names the bill before the House, but the weight of the remark is a general characterisation of how the Government and the Minister think, rather than the measure's mechanism or effect.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why we’re not supporting this bill is because it is very much central government dictating to local government and local communities about what they can do and how they can solve their local problems, and it’s the exact opposite of the rhetoric the exact same Minister used in all of the speeches around the repeal of the three waters.
focus.explanation: Names the measure, states the specific objection (removal of a local funding tool), and points to a named comparator policy (three waters repeal). Entirely on the substance.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But that’s the kind of Donald Trump environment that we are now facing in New Zealand thanks to the National Party in Opposition, who were totally irresponsible.
focus.explanation: No policy, figure or measure is named — it is a characterisation of what the other party is like. No individual is insulted, so Civility is untouched; this is exactly the party-directed content Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In the first 100 days, this Government has repealed Act after Act and not replaced them, and if they have been replaced, then it has been to the detriment of our people and, in actual fact, to the detriment of their so-called one New Zealand, which is the preferred rhetoric.
focus.explanation: A general indictment of the Government's legislative record with no measure, figure or outcome named in this sentence — the weight sits on the Government's rhetoric rather than on any policy's content or effect.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Despite the groaning in the corner, we have endured and continue to endure—only naming a few—the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora, a Māori institution.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy decision and its effect — the disestablishment of the Māori Health Authority. Legitimate scrutiny of a named government action, not party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I think we heard that the official advice from the Ministry of Transport was that it is about $1 or maybe $2 a week.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official Ministry of Transport advice put the per-household weekly saving from repealing the Auckland regional fuel tax at roughly $1–$2 a week.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport advice / regulatory impact statement accompanying the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill; true if the departmental estimate of the average household weekly fuel saving is in the $1–$2 range, false if it is materially higher or lower.

veracity.statement: They ripped out the electrified, light rail public transport that had existed in the beginning of the 20th century in many parts of New Zealand, and that’s why New Zealand now has the highest car-ownership rate in the entire world.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand has the highest rate of car ownership per head of any country in the world.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: International vehicle-ownership statistics (Ministry of Transport fleet statistics; World Bank / OICA motor vehicles per 1,000 people); true if New Zealand ranks first globally on vehicles per capita, false if any other country ranks above it.

veracity.statement: Transport is usually the second- or third-highest category of expense for a household, and for low-income households in New Zealand, it is much higher.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (a) transport is typically the second or third largest household expenditure category, and (b) transport takes a materially larger share for low-income households.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Economic Survey expenditure shares by category and by income decile; true if transport ranks second or third by average household spend and its share of expenditure is higher in the lowest deciles, false if it ranks lower or the low-income share is not higher.

veracity.statement: The only piece of evidence he cited was a New Zealand Herald article about this one project, and in subsequent New Zealand Herald articles where they kept referring to the cost of raised pedestrian crossings as $500,000, they had to retract it and print a correction because it’s just not true.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the New Zealand Herald published a retraction/correction of its reporting that raised pedestrian crossings cost $500,000 each.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Herald published corrections/retractions from late 2023–early 2024 relating to raised pedestrian crossing costs; true if a correction to the $500,000 figure was printed, false if no such correction exists.

veracity.statement: But even if that were the case, why is it that on the one hand, putting in infrastructure that enables elderly people and young children to safely cross the road in urban areas where there are schools and markets and shops and homes—like why are we focusing on these trivial, tiny costs when the Government of the day is looking at building a highway in Auckland that’s going to cost $500 million per kilometre?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a highway the Government is planning to build in Auckland will cost $500 million per kilometre.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA/Treasury published cost estimates for the Auckland roading project referenced, divided by route length; true if the per-kilometre estimate is around $500 million, false if it is materially lower.

veracity.statement: Now, the problem is that in Opposition, they did not have access to the kinds of tools to carry out a proper democratic process to properly cost things, and that’s why, of course, there is a $24 billion hole between the money they actually have and the projects they’ve promised to deliver.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $24 billion shortfall between available transport funding and the projects the Government has committed to deliver.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government Policy Statement on land transport, NLTF revenue forecasts and NZTA project cost estimates for the 2024–27 period; true if the gap between committed project costs and forecast available funding is around $24 billion, false if it is materially smaller.

veracity.statement: All it will mean is that at the moment, Auckland gets about $130 million a year from this tax. It also gets about $1.5 billion from the National Land Transport Fund (NLTF), so any good project that meets the criteria of the NLTF can get funded; it might take a little bit longer.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two funding figures: roughly $130 million a year to Auckland from the regional fuel tax, and roughly $1.5 billion a year to Auckland from the National Land Transport Fund.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council regional fuel tax revenue reports and NZTA National Land Transport Programme allocations to the Auckland region; true if both figures are within rounding of the published totals, false if either is materially off.

veracity.statement: The last Labour Government was quite emphatic that there were going to be no more regional taxes across the country as a whole—no more. That was Jacinda Ardern who said that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Jacinda Ardern, as Prime Minister, stated there would be no further regional fuel taxes elsewhere in the country.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, press conferences and Hansard records attributed to Jacinda Ardern on regional fuel taxes; true if she ruled out further regional fuel taxes beyond Auckland, false if no such statement exists or she left the option open.

veracity.statement: So this is meeting the coalition agreement. It is meeting the commitments that the National Party made to the country in the election campaign.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that repealing the Auckland regional fuel tax is a commitment contained in the coalition agreement and in National's 2023 election campaign platform.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published National–ACT and National–NZ First coalition agreements and National's 2023 transport policy documents; true if repeal of the Auckland regional fuel tax appears in both, false if it appears in neither or only one.

rigor.statement: The reason why New Zealanders have such high transport costs is because subsequent Governments over many decades—even more than half a century, I would say—have failed to provide for cost-effective transport solutions.
rigor.explanation: A causal conclusion offered with supporting premises in the following sentences (motorway prioritisation, planning rules, underfunded public transport, asset sales). The support is real but the account is monocausal — no alternative driver of transport costs is considered or ruled out.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They ripped out the electrified, light rail public transport that had existed in the beginning of the 20th century in many parts of New Zealand, and that’s why New Zealand now has the highest car-ownership rate in the entire world.
rigor.explanation: 'That's why' attributes the whole car-ownership outcome to a single historical cause (removal of tram/light rail systems) with nothing offered to exclude the other drivers she herself lists moments earlier. Single-cause reasoning.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Why we’re not supporting this bill is because it is very much central government dictating to local government and local communities about what they can do and how they can solve their local problems, and it’s the exact opposite of the rhetoric the exact same Minister used in all of the speeches around the repeal of the three waters.
rigor.explanation: A consistency argument: the same Minister invoked localism on one measure and centralism on this one. The inference is real and supported, though it does not address whether the two cases are relevantly alike.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Their children are much healthier and their people are much healthier because it’s normalised to be able to walk and ride bikes and take public transport.
rigor.explanation: A causal conclusion (walkability causes better health) drawn from an unspecified set of countries members may have visited. Appeal to anecdote, and correlation treated as cause; no evidence or comparison offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: All it will mean is that at the moment, Auckland gets about $130 million a year from this tax. It also gets about $1.5 billion from the National Land Transport Fund (NLTF), so any good project that meets the criteria of the NLTF can get funded; it might take a little bit longer.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that any good project can still be funded from the NLTF — rests on the premise that NLTF criteria are neutral as to project type, which is precisely what the new Government Policy Statement is disputed to have changed. A real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: So we’re going to save a tiny amount of money for people in the short term, but in the medium term and long term, we’re going to keep having this same problem of households having to own more cars.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that household car ownership will continue to rise rather than fall following the repeal of the regional fuel tax and the withdrawal of funding from alternatives.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport annual fleet statistics and Stats NZ census/household data on vehicles per household; true if vehicles per household in New Zealand is the same or higher five years after the statement, false if it has fallen.

civility.statement: Finally, in this debate, the Minister has repeatedly used misinformation to exaggerate.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to a named individual — not that the Minister is mistaken, but that he has repeatedly deployed misinformation deliberately. Short of a direct insult, but it lands on the person rather than the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, I know math is not everybody’s thing, but, like, that’s a thousand times more per kilometre.
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed at the members she is addressing — a suggestion that they cannot do arithmetic. Mild, and not sustained, but it edges past the argument onto the people opposite.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, the problem is that in Opposition, they did not have access to the kinds of tools to carry out a proper democratic process to properly cost things, and that’s why, of course, there is a $24 billion hole between the money they actually have and the projects they’ve promised to deliver.
specificity.explanation: Puts a single named figure on the claimed funding gap, which makes it something an opponent could contest or an official could check — though the composition of the $24 billion is not broken down.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s now abundantly evident to every New Zealander who follows these issues that the National Party said anything to get elected.
focus.explanation: A characterisation of the other party's general honesty. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — the content is entirely about what the other team is like. (Nothing is emitted for Rigor: strip out the part about the other side and no argument remains.)
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Cambridge to Piarere: the National Party told New Zealanders it would cost $721 million. Present budgeted cost just a month or two later: between $1.3 billion and $1.7 billion.
focus.explanation: Names a specific project, a specific pre-election commitment and a specific outcome. This is scrutiny of a named policy costing — the constitutional job of an opposition MP — not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There is so much to say following a lecture like that from David Parker, but what I actually want to say—as Ronan Keating sang—is that you say it best when you say nothing at all. So I commend this bill to the House.
focus.explanation: The entire contribution on a bill before the House is a jibe at the previous speaker. No mechanism, cost, figure, timeframe or outcome is touched — there is no policy content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There is so much noise from that side, they’ve finally decided to wake up.
focus.explanation: Purely about the other side's conduct in the Chamber. No individual is insulted, so Civility passes it cleanly; nothing of the measure before the House is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That was made clear most recently in a media article reporting on advice that has been given by ministries to the Minister that their “Roads of National Party Significance” are between $6 billion and $22 billion more than the amounts that they told the electorate at the time of the election.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official advice to the Minister of Transport puts the cost of the Roads of National Significance programme $6bn–$22bn above the figures National published before the 2023 election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Transport / NZTA advice to the Minister referred to in early March 2024 (obtainable under the OIA or as reported), compared against National's published 2023 transport policy costings: true if the advised cost range exceeds the pre-election costings by roughly $6bn–$22bn, false if the gap is materially smaller or no such advice exists.

veracity.statement: Cambridge to Piarere: the National Party told New Zealanders it would cost $721 million. Present budgeted cost just a month or two later: between $1.3 billion and $1.7 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts National costed the Cambridge to Piarere project at $721 million before the election and that the current budgeted range is $1.3bn–$1.7bn.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 transport policy costings for Cambridge to Piarere versus the NZTA/Ministry of Transport cost estimate current in March 2024: true if the pre-election figure is ~$721m and the current estimate is ~$1.3bn–$1.7bn, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: It’s being pushed through with no regulatory impact statement to judge the Minister’s errant comments that this will reduce the cost of living for Aucklanders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no regulatory impact statement accompanied the bill repealing the Auckland regional fuel tax.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's disclosure statement and the Ministry of Transport / Treasury regulatory impact statement register for the regional fuel tax repeal bill: true if no RIS was prepared or published, false if one exists.

veracity.statement: The cost of Auckland’s congestion is around $1.3 billion a year in lost productivity.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific annual economic cost of Auckland congestion in lost productivity.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published Auckland congestion cost estimates (NZIER/Ministry of Transport 'The Congestion Question' and predecessors): true if a credible published estimate puts the annual cost at approximately $1.3 billion, false if the accepted range is materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: We increased State highway maintenance funding by 65 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Labour-led government raised State highway maintenance funding by 65 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA National Land Transport Programme state highway maintenance, operations and renewals allocations for the 2018–21 and 2021–24 NLTPs against the 2015–18 baseline: true if the increase is approximately 65%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: They say they’re going to fill it in with congestion charging; they opposed that legislation. They say, “We want road tolls”; they blocked tolling for Penlink.
veracity.explanation: Two record claims about National in opposition: that it opposed the congestion charging legislation, and that it blocked tolling for the Penlink project.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard division records and party statements on the congestion-charging (time of use charging) legislation of the 53rd Parliament, and the public record of decisions on Penlink tolling: true if National voted against or publicly opposed both, false if it supported either — in particular, false if the removal of Penlink tolling was a decision of the Labour-led government rather than National.

veracity.statement: The reduction of traffic speed has enabled more lives to be saved because people understand that it’s an actual local road and not a highway.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that speed reductions on the local streets treated under the Te Ara Mua / Future Streets programme in Māngere have reduced deaths.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waka Kotahi Crash Analysis System death and serious injury counts for the treated Māngere streets before and after the speed reductions, and the published Te Ara Mua Future Streets evaluations: true if the post-treatment fatality/DSI rate fell beyond normal variation, false if it did not change or rose.

specificity.statement: Take the one that was referred to in just the last couple of days: Tākitimu stage two. What did the National Party tell the public that was going to cost: $627 million. What’s its current funding projection: between $900 million and $1,400 million.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific project and gives both the claimed and the current cost figures. Fully checkable and actionable; whether the figures are right is Veracity's question, not this one.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In many communities, the haves are fine, the have-nots will not be fine, and this will limit the choices of transport.
specificity.explanation: A general distributional sentiment. No community, project, figure, mechanism or timeframe is given — nothing here could be checked or acted on, even though the direction of the concern is clear.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Here we go, the reference to speed bumps. What puerile comments we have from the other side.
civility.explanation: Calling the other side's contributions 'puerile' is mockery and condescension aimed at the members rather than at any argument. Short of a direct insult to a named person, but a real failure on the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Simeon Brown pretends that he’s interested in the issues, but he really is not interested in serious answers to serious and difficult problems.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on a named member's sincerity and seriousness — imputing that he only pretends to care. The target is the person, not the transport policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There is so much to say following a lecture like that from David Parker, but what I actually want to say—as Ronan Keating sang—is that you say it best when you say nothing at all. So I commend this bill to the House.
civility.explanation: A pointed personal jibe at a named member — that his contribution would be improved by silence. It engages nothing he said; the target is the man, not the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So what happens if you don’t resurface the roads? The water gets in. What happens when the water gets in? You get potholes.
rigor.explanation: A genuine causal chain offered to link a maintenance funding freeze to pothole formation, and the mechanism is a real one that supports the conclusion. Marked down slightly because it treats resurfacing rates as the sole driver of road condition, ignoring traffic volumes and weather, which the speaker elsewhere concedes matter.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We oppose it, because if you visit the Auckland international airport or if you visit the Auckland domestic airport, be prepared because you are going to be in gridlock.
rigor.explanation: A conclusion (oppose the repeal) offered with a reason (airport gridlock), but the inference is a non sequitur as stated: the gridlock described is the present condition under the fuel tax, and nothing is offered to connect the repeal to it. The premise, if anything, cuts the other way until the missing link is supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We won it on a mandate of easing cost of living pressures, of getting this country back on track, and of cutting back waste. This bill does it all, so I commend this bill to the House.
