rigor.explanation: An appeal to electoral mandate is offered as the reason the bill should pass, and the conclusion that this single repeal bill 'does it all' — cost of living, national direction and waste — does not follow from anything offered. Nothing connects the measure to the three outcomes.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But in this process, as with anyone who wins an election, it doesn’t mean you’re above this House. If you win an election, it doesn’t mean that you can bypass parliamentary process.
rigor.explanation: A valid rebuttal to the mandate argument: it separates the authority to govern from the obligation to follow process, so an election win cannot by itself license skipping scrutiny. Marked short of the top because the premise linking it to what was actually bypassed sits in adjacent sentences rather than here.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But that’s not the only broken promise to cost of living, because Aucklanders also face a 23 percent increase in water rates because those members also repealed the affordable water reforms.
rigor.explanation: The causal step is asserted, not shown: the water price rise is attributed wholly to the repeal without any account of what the reforms would have changed about Watercare's revenue path in that year. A post hoc inference from sequence to cause.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Last year, people in Mt Roskill elected a National MP for the first time, because they believed in National’s 100-day plan to get New Zealand back on track.
rigor.explanation: The stated reason for the result — that voters believed in the 100-day plan — is read straight off the fact of the win, with no polling or other evidence about voter motivation. An unsupported causal attribution.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We have all noticed the increase in gang-related violence, public intimidation, and crimes involving illegally held firearms. We’ve seen it increase significantly since 2017, where the data and the evidence tell a horrid story.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on 'we have all noticed' and on 'the data and the evidence' that are never named or quantified — an appeal to shared perception and to unspecified authority in place of the figures that would carry the claim.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There hasn’t been a regulatory impact statement. They’ve pushed this legislation through the House. There haven’t been public submissions. There hasn’t even been a contribution from Auckland Council themselves.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three specific process facts about the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill: that no regulatory impact statement was produced, that there was no public submission process, and that Auckland Council made no contribution.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Transport / Treasury regulatory impact statement register for the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill, and the Parliament bill page for its select committee stage. True if no RIS was published and the bill passed without a select committee submission process; false if either a RIS exists or public submissions were taken.

veracity.statement: I then asked what was the nature of the relationship, knowing that both of those organisations—both Mayor Wayne Brown and Dean Kempton, CEO of Auckland Transport—do not agree with this particular piece of legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Auckland's mayor and the chief executive of Auckland Transport both oppose the repeal bill, and that Dean Kempton holds that role.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, council/AT correspondence or media reporting from Wayne Brown and Auckland Transport in the period Nov 2023 – Mar 2024 on the repeal of the regional fuel tax, plus Auckland Transport's record of who was CEO at the time. True if both are on record opposing the repeal; false if either supported it or took no position.

veracity.statement: But what they got hoodwinked with was not cost of living relief, as promised; they got slapped with a $50 drivers’ tax, and if you count that up, that’s already impacting on Aucklanders. On top of that, they’re adding another 22c to fuel excise.
veracity.explanation: Two numeric claims about government charges: a $50 motorist charge already imposed, and a further 22 cents per litre being added to fuel excise duty.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government announcements and the draft Government Policy Statement on land transport 2024 for (a) the announced increase in the annual motor vehicle licensing fee and (b) the scheduled fuel excise duty increases. True if a $50 vehicle charge was announced and the signalled excise rise totals about 22c/litre; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: But that’s not the only broken promise to cost of living, because Aucklanders also face a 23 percent increase in water rates because those members also repealed the affordable water reforms.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Auckland water charges are rising 23 percent, and that this rise follows from the repeal of the Three Waters / affordable water reforms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council / Watercare long-term plan consultation documents for 2024/25 on the proposed water price increase. True if the proposed increase is approximately 23 percent; false if materially different.

veracity.statement: I’m calling them out on their broken promises to Aucklanders, because all we’ve seen in 16 out of 17 bills come through this House in urgency is that they are only repealing bills, and not putting up new plans.
veracity.explanation: A countable claim that 16 of the 17 bills taken under urgency by this government to date were repeal bills with no replacement measure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard and legislation records of bills taken under urgency between the government's formation in November 2023 and 5 March 2024, classified as repeal or not. True if 16 of 17 are repeals; false if the count or ratio is materially different.

veracity.statement: The Auckland regional fuel tax has disproportionally hurt those on the lowest incomes in my electorate, who often drive the oldest and most un - fuel-efficient cars.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the regional fuel tax fell hardest on the lowest-income Aucklanders, on the stated basis that they drive older, less fuel-efficient vehicles.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Distributional/incidence analysis of the Auckland regional fuel tax by household income decile (Ministry of Transport or Auckland Council advice, or Stats NZ Household Economic Survey fuel spend as a share of income), plus fleet age by income. True if fuel spend is a materially higher share of income for the lowest deciles; false if the burden is flat or progressive.

veracity.statement: Last year, people in Mt Roskill elected a National MP for the first time, because they believed in National’s 100-day plan to get New Zealand back on track.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2023 election returned the first National MP ever elected in the Mt Roskill electorate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission results for the Mt Roskill electorate for every general election since the seat was created in 1996. True if no National candidate won it before 2023; false if one did.

veracity.statement: We have all noticed the increase in gang-related violence, public intimidation, and crimes involving illegally held firearms. We’ve seen it increase significantly since 2017, where the data and the evidence tell a horrid story.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a significant increase since 2017 in gang-related violence and in offending involving illegally held firearms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police recorded crime statistics for firearms offences and gang-related violent offending, and the National Gang List membership series, comparing 2017 with 2023. True if both show a significant rise; false if flat or falling.

specificity.statement: There hasn’t been a regulatory impact statement. They’ve pushed this legislation through the House. There haven’t been public submissions. There hasn’t even been a contribution from Auckland Council themselves.
specificity.explanation: Names four concrete, checkable procedural omissions — RIS, urgency, submissions, council input — rather than a general complaint about process. No figures or dates, so short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But what they got hoodwinked with was not cost of living relief, as promised; they got slapped with a $50 drivers’ tax, and if you count that up, that’s already impacting on Aucklanders. On top of that, they’re adding another 22c to fuel excise.
specificity.explanation: Carries two named charges with dollar and cent figures, so the claim can be checked against announced policy. No dates attached to either, which is what keeps it below the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill will amend the Arms Act 1983, the Search and Surveillance Act 2012, and the Sentencing Act 2002 to reform the firearms prohibition orders regime.
specificity.explanation: Names the three statutes amended and the regime being changed, so anyone can go and check what the bill actually does. Short of the top only because no thresholds or figures are attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They’ve heckled from over there. The member for Upper Harbour has heckled. The member for Northcote has heckled.
focus.explanation: Once the roll-call of who heckled is removed there is no policy content left — it is about the conduct of members opposite, not the fuel tax repeal. It carries a thread of a real point about Auckland representation in the debate, which keeps it off the floor.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Auckland regional fuel tax has disproportionally hurt those on the lowest incomes in my electorate, who often drive the oldest and most un - fuel-efficient cars.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: it names the tax and argues about who bears its cost, which is exactly the substance at issue.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They’ve heckled from over there. The member for Upper Harbour has heckled. The member for Northcote has heckled.
civility.explanation: Names individual members to characterise their behaviour in the chamber rather than their argument, but stops at reporting the heckling without insult or imputation of motive.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But they got hoodwinked—they got hoodwinked. They got gaslit by this Minister.
civility.explanation: 'Gaslit' imputes deliberate psychological deception to the Minister personally rather than criticising the policy. This is an attack on the person's honesty, not on the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And I am quite surprised to hear from the member across the way asking me what the criteria is, seeing as it was his Government that actually brought it in in the first place and didn’t do the job correctly, so we’ve got to come back here and fix it up.
civility.explanation: Pointed and faintly needling toward the member personally ("quite surprised to hear" he does not know), but the criticism lands on his Government's legislative work rather than on him as a person. Robust, edging toward the person without landing on him.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, that was quite a press release, but not much else, frankly.
civility.explanation: Sneering dismissal of the Minister's speech as empty publicity. It stops short of a direct insult but imputes that she was performing rather than legislating, which is a genuine civility failure under the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But this is simply virtue signalling. It does nothing to make our communities safer at all.
civility.explanation: "Virtue signalling" imputes insincere motive rather than engaging the bill's terms — a claim that the Government is posturing, not legislating. It is aimed at the Government collectively rather than at a named individual, which keeps it above a personal attack, but imputing bad faith is a genuine failure on the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: And I am quite surprised to hear from the member across the way asking me what the criteria is, seeing as it was his Government that actually brought it in in the first place and didn’t do the job correctly, so we’ve got to come back here and fix it up.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the existing firearms prohibition order regime was created by the previous Labour government, of which Duncan Webb was a member.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Enactment history of the Firearms Prohibition Orders Legislation Act 2022: true if the FPO regime was introduced and passed under the Labour-led Government (2020–2023), the party of the member addressed; false if it originated under a different government.

veracity.statement: Until now, FPOs could only be issued to people convicted of certain specific violent offences, like murder, serious assault, sexual violence, and aggravated robbery.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the pre-amendment scope of the FPO qualifying criteria was limited to a list of specified serious violent offences.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The qualifying-offence provisions of the Firearms Prohibition Orders Legislation Act 2022 as in force on 5 March 2024: true if eligibility was confined to a schedule of specified serious violent offences including murder, serious assault, sexual violation and aggravated robbery; false if the Act already extended to drug or general firearms offending.

veracity.statement: In 1765, that question was closed, because it was said that no one should be subject to arbitrary search.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the English case he has just described (Entick v Carrington) was decided in 1765 and settled the principle against arbitrary search.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The law report of Entick v Carrington: true if the case was decided in 1765 and held that general warrants to search a house were unlawful at common law; false if the date or the holding are materially different.

veracity.statement: The bill before the House says that this can be done without any reasonable suspicion that any offence or breach has occurred.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill's new search power carries no reasonable-suspicion threshold of any kind — not a characterisation of intent but a claim about what the drafted clause says.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The search-power clauses of the Firearms Prohibition Orders Legislation Amendment Bill as introduced: true if a constable may search an FPO subject, their vehicle or premises without a warrant and without any requirement of reasonable grounds to suspect an offence or a breach of the order; false if the clause requires reasonable grounds.

veracity.statement: The Chief Science Advisor to the Prime Minister said that the reason that people join gangs is because of poverty—that a majority of people are in gangs because they experience abuse at the hands of the State.
veracity.explanation: Relays two attributed findings — poverty as the reason people join gangs, and a majority of gang members having suffered State-inflicted abuse. She is reporting the Chief Science Advisor's claim rather than asserting it from her own knowledge.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.subject_name: Chief Science Advisor to the Prime Minister
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published advice from the Office of the Prime Minister's Chief Science Advisor on gangs and gang membership: true if it identifies poverty as a driver of gang membership AND states that a majority of gang members experienced abuse while in the care of the State; false if it makes no such finding, or if it reports state-care abuse for a minority rather than a majority.

specificity.statement: So any crime committed that has a penalty of one year or more under the Arms Act 1983, the Crimes Act 1961, the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, or the Psychoactive Substances Act 2013 meets the current FPO Act’s criteria of being necessary, reasonable, and appropriate to managing the risk that the offender poses to public safety will be allowed.
specificity.explanation: A named penalty threshold and four named statutes, plus the statutory test being applied. Anyone could go to the Acts and check exactly what the expanded criteria cover.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill provides police with the practical tools that they need to enforce FPOs, and it also sends a strong message to criminals and gangs that we are absolutely committed to addressing gang crime and to enforcing consequences for criminals, and we are taking back our communities.
specificity.explanation: A closing summary carrying no figures, mechanisms or timeframes — "practical tools", "strong message", "taking back our communities". Nothing here could be checked or acted on, in contrast to the clause-level detail she gave earlier.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There is no point placing an FPO on a criminal if the police don’t have the legislation that allows them to verify compliance with that order.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: unverifiable orders are ineffective, therefore search powers are needed. But "no point" is a false dichotomy — it treats the new at-any-time search power as the only possible verification mechanism, when existing warrant and search-on-suspicion powers also verify compliance. The conclusion overshoots the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But what we know about the bills that are going through the House this week is that they’re not going to do that, because they’re targeting such a minority group in society and placing the blame squarely on that minority group in society.
rigor.explanation: An argument about the measure itself, so it is properly assessed here, but there is a real gap between premise and conclusion: that a law targets a small group does not itself establish that it will fail to reduce harm. The inference is asserted rather than shown — no mechanism connects narrow targeting to ineffectiveness.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, that was quite a press release, but not much else, frankly.
focus.explanation: A bill with concrete provisions is before the House and this engages none of them — it characterises the Minister's contribution rather than naming any policy, mechanism, figure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is what this bill does: a warrantless, without cause search on the suspicion that someone might have a firearms protection order of them, their car, and anyone in the car.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: the search power, its threshold, and who it reaches. This is scrutiny of a named provision rather than commentary on the other party, and scores at the top even though the characterisation is contested.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If you look at the reasons, which this Government has not been doing at all—they love to talk about gangs all day long, but they never even seek to understand why it is that people join gangs in the first place.
focus.explanation: Characterises the Government's general disposition — what they talk about, what they never bother to understand — without naming a provision, figure or outcome in the bill under debate. Party framing with almost no policy content, in contrast to her later citation of the Chief Science Advisor.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I don’t understand what this Government is up to when they are going to make assault-style firearms more accessible in our communities, and then, on the other hand, they are trying to do things like this bill represents.
focus.explanation: Names two specific firearms policies — the Government's loosening of assault-style firearm rules and this bill — and puts them against each other. Policy content, not party character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But the most important part is the third part of the bill, and it’s around our police. It’s around the police being able to search, and being able to search people who are a high risk to the public.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure before the House directly — identifies which limb of the bill matters and what it does. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So what this means is that police will be able to invade our homes—our homes—and conduct searches without reasonable grounds to suspect that any offence has been, is being, or will be committed.
focus.explanation: Directed at the operative content of the bill — the search power, where it can be exercised, and the evidential threshold it removes. A specific consequence of a specific provision.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We tried six police Ministers in six years, and all we saw was failure and all we saw was soaring crime.
focus.explanation: About the previous government's ministerial churn rather than any policy, measure or provision. The countable detail is personnel turnover, not a named commitment or outcome the bill bears on — party record framing with no policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I don’t understand what this Government is up to when they are going to make assault-style firearms more accessible in our communities, and then, on the other hand, they are trying to do things like this bill represents.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government is making assault-style firearms more accessible.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The coalition agreements and the Government's announced Arms Act reform programme as at March 2024: true if a Government policy or bill loosens restrictions on assault-style / military-style semi-automatic firearms relative to the Arms (Prohibited Firearms, Magazines, and Parts) Amendment Act 2019; false if no such loosening is proposed or enacted.

veracity.statement: Māori women—Māori women—a group which that member is part of, are the most highly incarcerated indigenous people in the world—in the world.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori women have the highest incarceration rate of any indigenous population worldwide.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Comparative incarceration rates for indigenous women (NZ Department of Corrections prison population by ethnicity and sex against Australian Bureau of Statistics figures for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women, and equivalent Canadian/US data): true if the Māori women's rate per 100,000 is the highest of the comparable indigenous groups, false if another group's rate is higher.

veracity.statement: When Moana Jackson wrote his amazing report in the 1980s, He Whaipaanga Hou, Māori women represented only 6 percent of the prison population. How is it that in only four decades, we represent more than 60 percent of the prison population?
veracity.explanation: Two figures: Māori women at 6 percent of the prison population at the time of He Whaipaanga Hou (1987–88), and above 60 percent now.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: He Whaipaanga Hou (Jackson, 1987–88) and Department of Corrections prison population statistics by ethnicity and sex: true if the late-1980s figure is ~6% and the current figure exceeds 60% on the same denominator, false if either figure is materially different or the two use different denominators (e.g. share of the female prison population vs share of the whole prison population).

veracity.statement: When the pad in Washdyke was demolished by the council, firearms were present.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that firearms were found at the gang pad in Washdyke, Timaru, when it was demolished by the council.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police statements and contemporaneous news reporting on the demolition of the Washdyke gang pad: true if firearms were recovered or reported present at the site during the demolition, false if no firearms were found or no such demolition occurred.

veracity.statement: Next week, on March 15th, it will be the fifth anniversary of the Christchurch mosque attacks that targeted our Muslim community and claimed the lives of 51 innocent people.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the date of the fifth anniversary of the Christchurch mosque attacks and the death toll of 51.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The date of the attacks (15 March 2019) and the official death toll recorded by the Royal Commission of Inquiry and the coronial record: true if the anniversary falls on 15 March 2024 and the toll is 51, false if either differs.

veracity.statement: It was Labour who originally introduced laws in response to the attacks in Christchurch as a means to justify the implementation of Operation Tauwhiro and Operation Cobalt.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that the post-Christchurch firearms laws were introduced by Labour, and that they were introduced in order to justify Operations Tauwhiro and Cobalt.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative record for the Arms (Prohibited Firearms, Magazines, and Parts) Amendment Act 2019 and the Arms Legislation Act 2020, plus NZ Police statements establishing Operation Tauwhiro (2021) and Operation Cobalt (2022): true if those Acts were introduced by the Labour government AND the operations were established under or justified by reference to them; false if the operations rest on separate legal authority or predate the laws.

veracity.statement: This Act will give police the power to conduct warrantless searches without cause.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill's amendments to the Search and Surveillance Act permit police searches with no warrant and no required cause.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Firearms Prohibition Orders Legislation Amendment Bill as introduced, specifically its amendments to the Search and Surveillance Act 2012: true if a search power is conferred that requires neither a warrant nor any statutory precondition; false if the power is confined to persons already subject to an FPO or otherwise conditioned on a stated trigger.

veracity.statement: The gang numbers are through the roof, and if we look at some of the stats out of police districts: gang numbers in Auckland City Police District, up 87 percent in six years; Waitematā, up 74 percent; Wellington, up 124 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts percentage growth in gang membership over six years in three named police districts.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police National Gang List figures by police district for the six years to 2023: true if the Auckland City, Waitematā and Wellington districts rose by approximately 87%, 74% and 124% respectively over that window; false if the figures differ materially or cover a different period.

civility.statement: Congratulations, because that member’s bill is going to contribute to more incarceration of indigenous peoples. What a legacy to have—what a legacy to have.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic congratulation aimed at a named member personally, immediately after invoking her ethnicity — mockery of the person rather than criticism of the bill.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Unlike other members in this House, I care about the people of Rangitata.
civility.explanation: Imputes indifference to the safety of constituents to other members — a claim about their motives rather than their arguments. Short of a direct insult, but it is bad faith attributed to opponents.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s because of bills that have gone through this House that seek to target small groups of people, without understanding those drivers of crime, that we have that overrepresentation.
rigor.explanation: A single-cause causal claim: the rise in Māori women's imprisonment is attributed wholly to targeted legislation. No mechanism or evidence links the specific bills to the specific increase, and other candidate causes are not addressed — a post hoc inference from a trend to one cause.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If you read the report that the Chief Science Advisor to the Prime Minister wrote about gang membership and why people are joining gangs in the first place, it is all of those contributing factors that matter.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the root-causes claim in a named, topic-relevant evidence source rather than assertion. It leans on the authority of the report without reciting its findings, so there is a gap between the citation and the conclusion, but citing the relevant expert review is a legitimate move.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When the pad in Washdyke was demolished by the council, firearms were present. There is no doubt that this bill goes some way to making sure that no longer happens.
rigor.explanation: One local incident is offered and a categorical conclusion about the bill's effect is drawn from it — generalisation from a single anecdote, with 'there is no doubt' standing in for the missing link between the FPO regime and that outcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because of the actions inspired by white supremacy, the Government, with this law, targets gang members, aka Māori and their associates, ultimately targeting Māori, which, no doubt, will lead to the increased incarceration of our people, continuing the cycle of trauma in our communities.
rigor.explanation: The chain turns on an equivocation — 'gang members' is redefined mid-sentence as 'Māori and their associates', so a measure aimed at one group is treated as aimed at another — and the incarceration outcome is asserted with 'no doubt' rather than supported. The conclusion does not follow from what is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We believe that safer communities can be achieved when we address the root causes of crime and gang membership, which this House has no interest in doing. Those things include a healthy, affordable home, livable incomes, meaningful mahi opportunities, good education, and high quality access to healthcare.
specificity.explanation: A list of generic social goods — homes, incomes, work, education, health — with no figures, mechanisms, thresholds or timeframes. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But the most important part is the third part of the bill, and it’s around our police. It’s around the police being able to search, and being able to search people who are a high risk to the public.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (police search powers over people subject to an FPO) but supplies no thresholds, safeguards or scope — the how-far and under-what-conditions are absent.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So what this means is that police will be able to invade our homes—our homes—and conduct searches without reasonable grounds to suspect that any offence has been, is being, or will be committed.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the provision and the exact legal threshold said to be dispensed with ('reasonable grounds to suspect'), but gives no scope, limits or numbers.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The gang numbers are through the roof, and if we look at some of the stats out of police districts: gang numbers in Auckland City Police District, up 87 percent in six years; Waitematā, up 74 percent; Wellington, up 124 percent.
specificity.explanation: Three named police districts, three percentage changes, and a stated period. Precisely checkable against the source data.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So Police say, “We do not know whether the previous regime is working because it’s too early” and, furthermore, the only evidence we have is a “perception” expressed in the National Party election manifesto, and that is the basis of the law change that we are here tonight debating.
rigor.explanation: A real inference from the tabled Police advice to the conclusion that the bill lacks an evidence base, and the premises she has quoted do support it. Marked down only for the leap in “the only evidence we have” — the report describing a manifesto perception does not establish that nothing else was before the House.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is unbelievable that you can try and trumpet that you’re doing a tough-on-crime approach by bringing in something but, at the same time, you’re making available semi-automatic weapons, which will find their way into the hands of the criminal underworld whether you like it or not.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inconsistency argument between two of the government's own policies, which is a valid form. But the load-bearing causal step — that newly available firearms will reach the criminal underworld — is asserted with “whether you like it or not” rather than supported, so the conclusion outruns what was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Before coming down to the House, I listened to my colleague the Hon Dr Duncan Webb, who is a professor of law, talk about the history of—I think it was way back in the 1700s and there was some story about a particular man who, and I don’t profess to have the legal intellect that that Dr Webb has, but I know that it was really important that not since that time have we thought about engaging these measures. So that goes to show what a potentially ill-conceived and ill-thought-out piece of legislation this is.
rigor.explanation: Bare appeal to authority plus an anecdote the speaker concedes she cannot recount. Nothing about the 1700s precedent is actually stated, so no premise connects to the conclusion that the bill is ill-conceived — a non sequitur resting on a colleague's credentials.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, ACT is putting our police in harm’s way, and I don’t say that lightly, but I think that that’s actually quite justified. The police have already got a dangerous job, as we know, without the risk of having assault weapons pulled on them during circumstances where these FPO orders are being amended.
rigor.explanation: A real argument about a policy consequence, but with the middle of the chain missing: that police work is dangerous does not establish that this bill or ACT's firearms position raises the number of encounters with assault weapons. The conclusion is asserted, then defended by insisting it is justified.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Too often, senior gang members have been getting away with their peddling of misery while the young recruits—those that are often lured to the gang lifestyle for the reasons mentioned by my colleague Tamatha Paul, which I acknowledge—are the ones that are usually dealing with the stronger sentences. So this bill helps rectify this imbalance, and it will help people in Takanini, in Mount Roskill, in West Auckland, in South Auckland, and around New Zealand feel much safer.
rigor.explanation: Premise and conclusion are both present, but nothing links them: no provision of the bill is identified that would shift enforcement from young recruits to senior members, so “this bill helps rectify this imbalance” does not follow from the sentencing disparity asserted.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So Police say, “We do not know whether the previous regime is working because it’s too early” and, furthermore, the only evidence we have is a “perception” expressed in the National Party election manifesto, and that is the basis of the law change that we are here tonight debating.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: the named regulatory impact document, the FPO regime's commencement date, and the evidentiary basis for the amendment. Holding the government to the advice it received is scrutiny, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So there’s a couple of just practical things that we have to think about. How will a person be identified as a gang member? What is the process for demonstrating that they’re no longer a gang member or they’re no longer affiliated to that gang? And what does good behaviour mean with regard to actually getting off an FPO earlier?
focus.explanation: Three questions about the operating mechanism of the measure itself — the gang-membership test, the exit process, and the good-behaviour threshold for revocation. Precise scrutiny of how the bill would work, with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We knew the “coalition of cuts” would cut services, and we’ve talked about that throughout the evening in various other ways, but now we’re actually talking about cutting safety and cutting protections from our communities.
focus.explanation: Built on a party nickname and a general characterisation of the government's programme. There is a gesture at policy — “cutting safety and protections” — but no measure, provision, figure or outcome is named, so the weight of the sentence is party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Police consider it is too early to properly assess and, in addition, the reason why it’s too early to assess it is that the majority of those individuals who now have an FPO placed upon them are in prison; so we don’t know how that will impact upon them, because they’re presently incarcerated.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that a majority of people currently subject to a firearms prohibition order are in prison, and that this is the reason Police give for the regime being unassessable.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Police supplementary analysis report on firearm prohibition orders tabled with the Firearms Prohibition Orders Legislation Amendment Bill (March 2024), plus Police FPO issuance data: true if the report records that a majority of current FPO subjects are incarcerated; false if the report gives no such figure or gives a minority.

veracity.statement: Then, on top of that, we have a coalition Government who’s making semi-automatic weapons more readily available to the general public.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a present fact that the coalition Government is widening general public access to semi-automatic firearms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Coalition agreements, Cabinet papers and any Arms Act amendment or regulation in force as at 5 March 2024: true if a decision had been taken that loosens who may lawfully obtain military-style semi-automatic or centrefire semi-automatic firearms; false if the announced firearms work programme (Arms Act rewrite, registry review) left the post-2019 prohibition on general access intact.

veracity.statement: So the FPO laws are already in place, and they work—they work well—and the Government is really, really planning to make military style semi-automatic weapons more widely available.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the existing firearms prohibition order regime is working well — a claim about the present state of an evaluated policy, made in a debate where the tabled Police advice was quoted as saying the opposite.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Police supplementary analysis report on FPOs and any Police evaluation or issuance/outcome data as at March 2024: true if there is evidence that the regime is achieving its public-safety objective; false if Police advise it is too early to evaluate and there is little baseline evidence, which would make “they work well” unsupported.

veracity.statement: And I just want to finish my contribution by saying that Nicola Willis made a commitment that National would continue to support a ban on those weapons after the 15 March attack.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific past commitment by a named MP: that Nicola Willis said National would continue to support the ban on military-style semi-automatic weapons following the 15 March 2019 Christchurch attack.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard and contemporaneous media records of Nicola Willis's statements after 15 March 2019, plus National's position on the Arms (Prohibited Firearms, Magazines, and Parts) Amendment Act: true if she is on record committing National to continued support for the ban; false if no such statement exists or her statements were qualified.

civility.statement: So you’re introducing new powers on controlling gun control while bringing back semi-automatic weapons: loopy, pretty damn loopy, I say.
civility.explanation: “Pretty damn loopy” is blunt, but it is aimed at the combination of two policies, not at any member's character or competence. Harsh criticism of a decision is the expected standard, not a failure.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It is a bill that clearly sends the message that gun crime will not be tolerated and confirms our commitment to all our local communities that we take their safety seriously.
specificity.explanation: A message and a commitment, with no clause, threshold, figure, timeframe or mechanism, in a speech on a bill that has three concrete amendments available to describe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The first one amends the Arms Act 1983 to extend the group of persons against whom a firearms prohibition order (FPO) may be made; amends the Arms Act 1983 to establish a new review process that enables persons subject to an FPO to apply to the court to have that order varied, perhaps modified, or even revoked; and it amends the Search and Surveillance Act 2012 to introduce a new, without cause, search power that enables police to conduct searches in respect of a person who the police suspect on reasonable grounds may be subject to an FPO.
specificity.explanation: Names the two statutes amended, the year of each, and the precise operative effect of all three changes, including the legal test for the new search power. Directly checkable against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Last week, ANZ released its business outlook report and its consumer confidence report, both of which come out monthly. These show that consumer confidence continues to rise, albeit off a very low base, and business confidence is on a strong upward trend, despite levelling out in February.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the February 2024 ANZ-Roy Morgan consumer confidence survey and ANZ Business Outlook survey showed: consumer confidence rising from a low base, business confidence on an upward trend but flat in February.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: ANZ-Roy Morgan Consumer Confidence index and ANZ Business Outlook business confidence series, readings to February 2024. True if consumer confidence rose over recent months from historically low levels and business confidence trended up across late 2023 with February 2024 roughly flat or slightly down; false if either series was falling over that period.

veracity.statement: Landowners are already voluntarily protecting areas of native biodiversity—over 180,000 hectares are already protected through QEII National Trust. Put together, that would be our fifth-largest national park, all voluntarily.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (a) that more than 180,000 hectares are protected under QEII National Trust open space covenants, and (b) that this area would rank fifth among New Zealand's national parks by size.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: QEII National Trust's published covenanted-area total as at March 2024, and DOC's national park areas. True if the covenanted total exceeds 180,000 ha and that area sits fifth in the ordered list of national park areas; false if the total is materially below 180,000 ha, or if 180,000 ha would rank other than fifth (e.g. fourth, ahead of Rakiura).

veracity.statement: To the member, is he aware of the EU’s requirement to prove that there is no deforestation taking place in areas that are supplying the EU market, and that, in fact, the protection of SNAs will assist farmers to access that high-value market?
veracity.explanation: The checkable half of the question is the assertion that the EU requires proof that products entering its market come from land free of deforestation. (The second half — that SNAs will assist market access — is a forward-looking opinion and is not part of this claim.)
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: EU Regulation 2023/1115 (the EU Deforestation Regulation) and its scope as at March 2024. True if the EU requires operators placing covered commodities on the EU market to demonstrate they are deforestation-free via due diligence; false if no such EU requirement existed or it did not apply to goods supplied from New Zealand.

veracity.statement: Can I ask the Minister as to whether or not he’s received any reports that say his task now to solve this problem has been massively exacerbated by bringing in 148,000 immigrants as at December last year?
veracity.explanation: Asserts, within the question, a specific migration figure: that 148,000 immigrants were brought in as at December 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration estimates for the year ended December 2023 (provisional figures as published early 2024). True if either annual net migration or the relevant arrivals measure was approximately 148,000; false if the published figures are materially different (net migration was reported around 126,000-133,000 at the time, and migrant arrivals far higher).

rigor.statement: The Business Outlook survey saw lifts in most forward-looking indicators, such as businesses’ own activity, investment intentions, employment intentions, and profit expectations. Together with the consumer results, this reinforces that New Zealanders are more optimistic about their future under this coalition Government.
rigor.explanation: Evidence is offered and the move from rising forward-looking indicators to 'more optimistic' is fair, but two gaps: a business survey is generalised to 'New Zealanders', and the causal attribution to the coalition Government rests on temporal coincidence alone (post hoc). Judged on the inference only, not on whether the survey figures are accurate.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Apart from being at a disincentive to voluntarily conserve areas of indigenous biodiversity, farmers know well what happens when the ability to actively manage land is restricted. If SNAs are applied to areas with low biodiversity value, then without the landowner managing pest and weed - control, it will just go to gorse, broom, and wilding pines.
rigor.explanation: A real causal argument about the policy, but the load-bearing premise — that an SNA designation actually prevents landowners doing pest and weed control — is asserted rather than shown, and 'farmers know well' is an appeal to common knowledge standing in for evidence. The conclusion is plausible but does not follow from what was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does he agree with the previous Minister for social development and Minister for Social Housing who introduced the emergency housing special needs grant, Paula Bennett, who stated, “This is the first time any Government has committed ongoing dedicated funding for emergency housing, because we recognise that not everyone has access to a safe and stable home.”; if yes, why is he looking to reduce access to that support, and pushing more New Zealanders back to sleeping in cars?
rigor.explanation: A complex (loaded) question: the 'why' clause presupposes both that access is being reduced and that the reduction causes people to sleep in cars, neither of which is established. There is also an implicit appeal to authority — that a former National Minister's endorsement settles the merits. The policy target is real, so this is scored here rather than skipped, but the inference is not supported by what was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Landowners are already voluntarily protecting areas of native biodiversity—over 180,000 hectares are already protected through QEII National Trust. Put together, that would be our fifth-largest national park, all voluntarily.
specificity.explanation: A named body, a hectare figure and a concrete comparison; anyone could go and check it or act on it. Scored on precision only — whether the figure and the ranking are right is a separate question.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The way to protect biodiversity on private land is to work collaboratively with landowners, including farmers, foresters, and iwi, to incentivise the sustainable use of land, and to show them that their work to protect the biodiversity is valued and then they will want to do more.
specificity.explanation: Answers a question about long-term action with a direction and no content: no mechanism for the incentives, no funding, no timeframe, no instrument to replace SNAs. 'Work collaboratively' and 'incentivise sustainable use' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We receive advice on housing matters on a regular basis, and the advice that we’ve received is that we will continue to focus on ending the large-scale use of emergency housing and getting whānau and tamariki into homes faster.
specificity.explanation: Asked about advice on a specific policy change, the reply carries no checkable content: no document, no date, no numbers, no criteria. 'Regular basis' and 'faster' commit to nothing anyone could verify or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need bold and radical solutions to end the housing crisis that has been exacerbated under the previous Government. We need to get the country back on track, and particularly with housing, and we will do that through a wide series of responses and steps, one of which is prioritising the tamariki and whānau who have been sleeping in emergency accommodation for 12 consecutive weeks or more.
specificity.explanation: Opens with slogans ('bold and radical solutions', 'back on track', 'a wide series of responses and steps') but lands on one concrete, checkable criterion — prioritising families in emergency accommodation for 12 consecutive weeks or more. A direction with one real mechanism and no costs, targets or dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Has he received advice or evidence showing that New Zealanders who will no longer be able to access emergency housing special needs grants under this Government’s new approach will all find housing and not end up living on the streets?
focus.explanation: Names a specific instrument (emergency housing special needs grants), a specific change in access, and the specific outcome it asks the Minister to account for. This is scrutiny of a named policy, not party framing — the opposition doing its job.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is it now this Government’s strategy to make it harder to access emergency housing grants so as to reduce the number of New Zealanders in emergency housing on their books at the expense of more New Zealanders sleeping rough outside our businesses, in our carparks, and in our parks?
civility.explanation: No individual is attacked, but the question imputes a bad-faith motive — massaging the numbers 'on their books' knowing people will sleep rough. That is short of a personal insult and above a sneer, but it is an imputation of motive rather than an engagement with the reasoning, so it sits below the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he agree with the Minister for Social Development and Employment that “I am not saying that it is going perfect; what I am saying is that we will have fewer children in motels, and that is what we are out to achieve.”, and, if so, is living on the streets more perfect than living in a motel?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the emergency housing policy — it names the motel/emergency housing regime and presses on a specific consequence (people ending up on the street). Legitimate scrutiny of a named commitment, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In terms of the comment, I think, as I said previously, it is ironic to watch this member ask this question, given his previous interview on Q + A.
focus.explanation: No policy content survives once the tu quoque is removed — it is entirely about the questioner's own past conduct, not about media sustainability or editorial independence.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Certain expenditure is always warranted, but none of it will amount to the $1.2 billion that vanished on three waters.
focus.explanation: Asked about the cost of mitigating failed fast-track projects, the answer pivots to the previous Government's programme. There is a figure attached, but it is not about the measure at issue.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I agree with my learned colleague the Minister for Social Development and Employment, the member for Taupō, in that we do need absolute radical and bold solutions for our housing crisis, and it is tough for those folks, and no one in this House wants to see whānau, tamariki, and mokopuna living in emergency housing for an extended period of time, but that is what we have seen over the last six years.
specificity.explanation: "Absolute radical and bold solutions" commits to no mechanism, figure or timeframe; the only concrete content is the retrospective claim about the last six years.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That expert panel will apply relevant consent and permit conditions. Panels will have a maximum of six months to do so. The projects will then be sent back to joint Ministers to either approve it or decline it, and they’ll be able to refer the project back to the panel if the consent conditions are too onerous.
specificity.explanation: Names the decision-maker at each step, a hard statutory timeframe (six months), and the referral-back mechanism. Someone could check this against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government is committed to working with the sector on ways to ensure sustainability. As I have previously stated, the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill is currently before select committee, and I’m awaiting the committee’s report. I’m working with officials to modernise the media system in New Zealand to level the playing field for our local broadcasters. I want to encourage more private and international investment in our local content.
specificity.explanation: One named measure at a known stage (the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill before select committee); the rest is direction-of-travel language — "modernise", "level the playing field", "encourage investment" — with no mechanism, amount or date.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is he not able to guarantee that his policies will lead to more people being homeless, because the policies will actually create more reasons for front-line Ministry of Social Development (MSD) staff to deny special needs grants to enable people to be in emergency housing?
specificity.explanation: Names the actual mechanism — MSD front-line discretion over special needs grants for emergency housing — rather than asserting harm in the abstract. Checkable against the grant criteria; missing only figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I can guarantee that this Government is committed to getting New Zealanders—tamariki and whānau—out of emergency housing and into homes faster. And I can also guarantee that our officials will work hard to ensure that whānau do not end up in emergency housing and end up in alternative housing before they get there.
specificity.explanation: Guarantees a commitment and that officials will "work hard" — no number of houses, no criteria, no date. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will we see homelessness situations like that of West Auckland tetraplegic woman Tracey Penney, who was living in her van in January 2017—it was widely reported on—arise again because of the changes to the treatment of homeless Ministry of Social Development clients?
specificity.explanation: Names an individual, a location, a month and year, and the specific policy change at issue. Concrete enough for the Minister to answer or rebut directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I agree with my learned colleague the Minister for Social Development and Employment, the member for Taupō, in that we do need absolute radical and bold solutions for our housing crisis, and it is tough for those folks, and no one in this House wants to see whānau, tamariki, and mokopuna living in emergency housing for an extended period of time, but that is what we have seen over the last six years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that over the six years to 2024 households, including children, were living in emergency housing for extended periods.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD emergency housing special needs grant data 2017/18–2023/24 on the number of households and children in emergency housing and their length of stay; true if long-duration placements (e.g. 6+ months) were common and rose over that period, false if placements were predominantly short or the population was negligible.

veracity.statement: Can I please reiterate that we will support those with genuine need to have emergency housing, but our aspiration is to end the large-scale use of emergency housing, particularly in places like Hamilton and Waikato, where there are over 500 kids living in emergency housing right now.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than 500 children were living in emergency housing in the Hamilton/Waikato area as at March 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD emergency housing special needs grant quarterly data broken down by region and by number of children, for the quarter to March 2024; true if the Waikato/Hamilton figure exceeds 500 children, false if materially below.

veracity.statement: All the projects considered under the new fast-track regime will be considered by an expert panel. And, of course, the expert panel process is not a new one, because that process was set up by the last Government when it came to their own COVID-19 fast-track regime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the expert-panel consenting mechanism originated with the previous Government's COVID-19 fast-track consenting regime.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The COVID-19 Recovery (Fast-track Consenting) Act 2020; true if that Act established expert consenting panels to set consent conditions, false if it used a different decision mechanism or predates the previous Government.

veracity.statement: That member does not even know that that photo was taken at the New Zealand Open, and I was there as the Minister responsible for funding the Major Events Fund.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the photograph in question was taken at the New Zealand Open golf tournament and that she attended in her official capacity as the Minister responsible for the Major Events Fund.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial diary disclosures for Melissa Lee for February–March 2024 and MBIE Major Events Fund records; true if the diary records attendance at the New Zealand Open in a ministerial capacity and the Fund supported that event, false if the photo was taken at another event or the attendance was not official.

veracity.statement: What impression does the Minister think she gives out to those who’ll be losing their jobs at Television New Zealand and Newshub that, at the exact time she was refusing to do media, she was attending a luxury resort on the taxpayers’ dollar—what is the impression she gives out to the public and to all the poor people who’ve been losing their jobs?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a conjunction: that Lee was declining media interviews at the same time she was attending a luxury resort, and that the attendance was publicly funded.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Media reports and ministerial diary entries for the days of the Newshub/TVNZ announcements in Feb–Mar 2024, plus MBIE/ministerial expense records; true if Lee declined interview requests on the same day she attended a resort event paid for from public funds, false if the attendance was on another date, was an official Major Events Fund engagement rather than a personal stay, or she did not decline media at that time.

veracity.statement: Certain expenditure is always warranted, but none of it will amount to the $1.2 billion that vanished on three waters.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that $1.2 billion was spent on the Three Waters reform programme with nothing to show for it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DIA and Treasury reporting on total Crown expenditure on the Three Waters/Affordable Water reform programme to early 2024; true if total spend was approximately $1.2 billion, false if materially different. The stronger claim that it "vanished" resolves against whether the spend produced identifiable assets or transfers (e.g. the better-off funding paid to councils).

veracity.statement: Will we see homelessness situations like that of West Auckland tetraplegic woman Tracey Penney, who was living in her van in January 2017—it was widely reported on—arise again because of the changes to the treatment of homeless Ministry of Social Development clients?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a tetraplegic woman named Tracey Penney in West Auckland was living in a van in January 2017 and that the case received wide media coverage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand news archives for January 2017; true if reports exist of a West Auckland tetraplegic woman of that name living in a van, false if no such reporting exists or the details (location, disability, date) differ materially.

civility.statement: I’ve just answered the question about the Treaty. You really need to listen.
civility.explanation: Turns from the substance to the members opposite. "You really need to listen" is condescension aimed at people rather than an argument — short of an insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In terms of the comment, I think, as I said previously, it is ironic to watch this member ask this question, given his previous interview on Q + A.
civility.explanation: Imputes hypocrisy to the member personally rather than engaging the point; a sneer at the questioner, though short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What impression does the Minister think she gives out to those who’ll be losing their jobs at Television New Zealand and Newshub that, at the exact time she was refusing to do media, she was attending a luxury resort on the taxpayers’ dollar—what is the impression she gives out to the public and to all the poor people who’ve been losing their jobs?
civility.explanation: Goes past the Minister's decisions to her personal indulgence — "a luxury resort on the taxpayers' dollar" imputes self-serving motive rather than criticising a policy or a decision.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The fact is that that exclusion will have a very positive outcome for Māori because now things will be based on merit and not just elitism and racism, which ordinary Māori never asked for in the first place.
civility.explanation: Harsh about a set of arrangements and about "elitism", but no individual is attacked. Under the re-anchored scale, fierce criticism aimed at no one is civil.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If he can’t guarantee that his policies won’t leave more people in the street and without safe shelter, why is he going ahead with them?
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy, and a weak one: it treats the absence of a guarantee as a reason not to proceed — an argument from absence of evidence, and a demand for certainty no policy could meet.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The fact is that that exclusion will have a very positive outcome for Māori because now things will be based on merit and not just elitism and racism, which ordinary Māori never asked for in the first place.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: the Treaty clause's removal is presented as a straight swap of "elitism and racism" for "merit", with nothing offered to connect the removal of the clause to any outcome for Māori. The conclusion is asserted, not supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: The Government’s creation of the priority one category will prioritise getting families with children out of emergency housing, under stable social housing, sooner.
divination.explanation: Forecasts an outcome of the priority one category: that families with children will move out of emergency housing into social housing faster than before. This is a claim about an effect in the world, not merely a promise to act.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: HUD/MSD emergency housing reporting on households with children in emergency housing and median length of stay; true if the number of families with children in emergency housing and their median stay fall after the priority one category takes effect (April 2024), false if they are unchanged or higher.

veracity.statement: The member will note that the previous Government left a fiscal cliff of funding for social housing, so any future funding is subject to Budget decisions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that funding for social housing places was appropriated only to a fixed end point by the previous Government, with no ongoing baseline beyond it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Vote Housing and Urban Development appropriations and Treasury forecasts as at Budget 2023 for public housing places (IRRS and supply funding); true if funding for new public housing places drops away after the committed delivery period with no baseline provided beyond it, false if ongoing funding for new places was appropriated across the forecast period.

veracity.statement: The Budget 2023 increased social housing places by 3,000.
veracity.explanation: A specific claim that Budget 2023 funded an additional 3,000 public housing places.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2023 Vote Housing and Urban Development documents and the HUD Public Housing Plan; true if Budget 2023 funded 3,000 additional public housing places, false if the figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: It is true that the National Government from 2008 to 2017—which, by the way, I’m not responsible for, but I’m happy to comment extensively on—transferred ownership of some social housing in Tauranga to Accessible Properties.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a National-led government transferred ownership of Tauranga social housing stock to the community housing provider Accessible Properties.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Housing New Zealand Corporation / Crown transaction records and HUD social housing transfer documentation for Tauranga; true if ownership of the Tauranga stock was transferred to Accessible Properties under the 2008–2017 government, false if no such transfer took place or the recipient was a different entity.

veracity.statement: Under the funding track we inherited, in writing Kāinga Ora was planning to sell 10,000 State houses.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the existence of a written Kāinga Ora plan to sell about 10,000 state houses under the inherited funding track.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora board papers, its asset/portfolio strategy and the briefing to the incoming Minister (2023–24); true if a written plan projects the sale or disposal of approximately 10,000 state houses, false if no such figure appears or the documented figure is materially smaller.

veracity.statement: I plan on being a better Minister responsible for homelessness than the last one, the Hon Marama Davidson, who saw homelessness skyrocket to record levels and couldn’t even spend the money that Megan Woods allocated to her.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that homelessness reached record levels during the named Minister's tenure, and that allocated homelessness funding went unspent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ severe housing deprivation estimates and the 2018/2023 Census homelessness measures, plus Vote Housing and Urban Development end-of-year appropriation reports for the Homelessness Action Plan and Housing First; true if homelessness measures reached record highs over 2020–2023 and the allocated homelessness appropriations were materially underspent, false if either measure fell or the funding was substantially spent.

veracity.statement: Well, 57.8 percent of Aucklanders voted for the coalition Government at the last election, and our draft Government policy statement prioritises the projects that we campaigned on: Mill Road, a project that that member of Parliament campaigned on very, very hard.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a precise Auckland-wide vote share for the three coalition parties at the 2023 general election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission 2023 general election official party-vote results aggregated across Auckland general electorates; true if the combined National, ACT and NZ First party vote is 57.8% (± rounding), false if materially different or if the figure only holds for a narrower subset of seats.

veracity.statement: We’ve actually modelled the new law on the old regime introduced by the last Labour Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the new fast-track consenting bill was modelled on the COVID-19 fast-track consenting regime enacted under the previous government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Fast-track Approvals Bill 2024, its explanatory note and regulatory impact statement, compared against the COVID-19 Recovery (Fast-track Consenting) Act 2020; true if the official documents state the bill is based on or derived from that Act, false if they identify a different basis or the structures differ on the point at issue (who makes the decision).

focus.statement: But the key thing is we’re not going to sit by like the last Government did and ignore it.
focus.explanation: Names no policy, figure or measure — the content is a comparison with the other party's general disposition. Contrasted with the rest of the answer, which does engage the policy, this sentence is party framing only.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Unlike the last Government, we do not have an obsession with the idea that the Government should do everything in housing.
focus.explanation: Characterises the other party's mindset rather than naming a mechanism, cost or measure. There is a faint policy position underneath (state versus mixed provision), but the weight is party contrast.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why, then, did the Government make an emergency housing announcement without committing to funding more additional social housing?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named policy announcement and a specific gap in it — additional social housing funding. This is the accountability question an opposition MP is there to ask; no party-bashing content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why should economic Ministers decide what is worthy of proceeding, rather than an expert panel, as suggested in the new fast-tracking legislation?
focus.explanation: Goes straight at a specific decision-making mechanism in a named bill. Entirely on the policy, with no party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So between 18 months ago and two years, up until June 2025, there are 6,000 new social housing places, delivered both by Kāinga Ora and by the community housing sector.
specificity.explanation: Carries a number, a time window with an end date, and names the two delivery agencies. Someone could go and check it against the public housing plan.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We back communities, we back the private sector, and we back housing for Kiwis.
specificity.explanation: A slogan: no figures, mechanisms, timeframes or named policies. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If they can’t stay in emergency housing and the Government won’t commit to funding more social housing, transitional housing, or rental places, where are they supposed to go?
specificity.explanation: Names the three housing categories at issue and the condition, but supplies no figures, dates or scale of the group affected.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s great news: the Government is investing up to $4.4 billion on public transport infrastructure and services.
specificity.explanation: A dollar figure attached to a named spending category; checkable against the draft Government Policy Statement. Marked down slightly for "up to", which leaves the actual commitment open.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The fastest way to increase homelessness would have been for the Government to continue with the funding track we inherited, which would have seen 10,000 State houses sold off by Kāinga Ora because of that member’s party’s woeful mismanagement of one of the biggest companies in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Real inference about a real policy, but with a large unbridged gap: the causal chain from funding track to sales to homelessness is asserted rather than shown, and the speaker had argued moments earlier that transferring ownership leaves tenants housed — so sales do not entail homelessness on his own account.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because the whole purpose of the fast-track consenting regime that we are introducing is to fast track economic development projects.
rigor.explanation: Question-begging: the question asked why economic Ministers rather than an expert panel should decide, and the answer restates the regime's purpose. Nothing offered connects the purpose of the regime to who holds the decision.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I plan on being a better Minister responsible for homelessness than the last one, the Hon Marama Davidson, who saw homelessness skyrocket to record levels and couldn’t even spend the money that Megan Woods allocated to her.
civility.explanation: Names an individual member and attacks her personal competence — "couldn't even spend the money" is mockery of the person rather than criticism of a policy.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: On Tuesday, we introduced and have now passed legislation to stop taxpayer funding of section 27 cultural reports that proliferated under the former regime, consuming more than $7 million out of the legal aid budget.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that section 27 cultural reports consumed more than $7 million of the legal aid budget, and that legislation ending that funding was introduced and passed in the week of 7 March 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice legal aid expenditure figures for section 27 cultural reports (annual spend, most recent full year before March 2024); true if the reported spend exceeds $7 million, false if materially lower. Plus the Hansard record for the Criminal Procedure (Section 27 Reports) Amendment Bill; true if it passed the week beginning 4 March 2024.

veracity.statement: Why is the Minister pushing his wasteful gang insignia ban when his own department and the Chief Science Adviser has said, “A challenge of this suppression strategy is that there is no strong evidence it works to reduce long-term offending behaviours or eliminate gangs”? It’s science.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Ministry of Justice and the Chief Science Adviser have both stated, in the quoted words, that there is no strong evidence gang-insignia suppression reduces long-term offending or eliminates gangs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Prime Minister's Chief Science Advisor's published report on gangs and the Ministry of Justice advice/regulatory impact statement on the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill; true if the quoted sentence (or its substance) appears in either, false if neither document contains such a finding.

veracity.statement: Because the gangs have been recruiting faster than the police over the past six years, from 6,000-odd in 2018, to 9,000 at present—a 50 percent increase.
veracity.explanation: Asserts gang membership rose from roughly 6,000 in 2018 to about 9,000 by March 2024 — a 50 percent increase — and that this outpaced growth in police numbers over the same six years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police National Gang List headcount for 2018 and for the most recent month before March 2024, and sworn police FTE over the same period; true if the gang list figures are close to 6,000 and 9,000 and the percentage growth in gang membership exceeds that in police numbers, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, indeed, I listen to a wide range of evidence, and, of course, one of the strongest issues around gang insignia has been the success of the previous bill introduced by the Hon Todd McClay, which banned gang patches from schools, hospitals, and public buildings, which has been very successful.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Todd McClay introduced a bill banning gang patches from schools, hospitals and public buildings, and that it has been very successful.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Act 2013 — its sponsor and the premises it covers — and any published evaluation or prosecution/enforcement statistics under it; true if McClay was the sponsor, the coverage is as described, and evaluation shows a measurable effect; false if the sponsorship or coverage is wrong or no evidence of effect exists.

veracity.statement: Why is he pressing on with his insignia ban, given the advice he received from the Ministry of Justice that the reduction in visibility of gangs experienced by Queensland and Western Australia is simply the product of gangs relocating to other jurisdictions that impose fewer restrictions, and New Zealand’s unitary nature means there is no alternate jurisdiction to which gangs can relocate?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Ministry of Justice advice to the Minister attributed the drop in gang visibility in Queensland and Western Australia to relocation between jurisdictions, and noted New Zealand has no equivalent alternative jurisdiction.
veracity.subject: speaker
