rigor.explanation: Strawman: the bill's rationale is restated as squeamish avoidance rather than as anything its supporters argued, and the rest of the point is then built against that caricature. The reasoning targets a position nobody advanced, so the conclusion does not follow.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When I met with those liaison officers, the area commanders and the district commanders all talked about how quickly crime was resolved when we had open communication and we understood things more.
rigor.explanation: An argument that engagement with gangs produces better policing outcomes, resting entirely on recalled testimony from officers she met — an appeal to anecdote and to the authority of those commanders. The evidence is on-point and from people positioned to know, but no data, evaluation or comparison is offered for a claim about what works.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are already the highest incarcerated peoples in this country: 50 percent of the male prison population are Māori, 64 percent of the female prison population are Māori.
specificity.explanation: Two precise, sourceable proportions attached to named populations. Anyone could go and check it — which is what this attribute asks, independently of whether the figures are right.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It is a social investment approach that will eliminate those factors. It’s an approach that this Government will take, eliminating poverty, abuse, substance abuse, welfare dependency, lack of access to good education, good healthcare, and good jobs.
specificity.explanation: A list of ills to be eliminated with no mechanism, no funding figure, no timeframe and no named programme. 'Social investment approach' is a label, not a described action; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I lay down a challenge—that any member speaking on the second reading read 13 pages, the abridged version, just 13 pages, of Towards an understanding of Aotearoa New Zealand’s adult gang environment.
specificity.explanation: Names the document, the exact edition, the page count and the point in the legislative process by which it should be read. The requested action is precise enough that compliance could be checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We are already the highest incarcerated peoples in this country: 50 percent of the male prison population are Māori, 64 percent of the female prison population are Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori are the most-incarcerated population group in New Zealand and that Māori make up 50% of the male and 64% of the female prison population at the time of speaking (March 2024).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections prison population statistics for the quarter around March 2024, broken down by ethnicity and sex: true if the Māori share of the male muster is ~50% and of the female muster ~64% (within a couple of percentage points), false if either is materially different; the 'highest incarcerated' claim is settled by Corrections/Stats NZ imprisonment rates per 100,000 by ethnicity.

veracity.statement: There are 5.1 million people in this country, yet there are, according to your statistics, 8,000 gang members.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: New Zealand's population is 5.1 million, and the Government's own gang statistics record about 8,000 gang members.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ national population estimate for March 2024 (true if ~5.1m, false if materially higher) and the Police National Gang List headcount cited by the Government at that date (true if ~8,000, false if materially different).

veracity.statement: Of the whānau in gangs, 80 percent to 90 percent have come out of State care.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that between 80% and 90% of gang members have a history of State care.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published research on the NZ adult gang environment and Oranga Tamariki/Royal Commission (Abuse in Care) findings on the proportion of gang members with a State care history: true if credible studies put the figure in the 80–90% band, false if the best available estimates are materially lower or apply only to one gang.

veracity.statement: When I worked in Police—Police under a National Government—police were instructed to not even talk to gangs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that during her employment at NZ Police, under a National-led government, officers were under an instruction not to engage or communicate with gangs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police operational policy, gang-strategy documents or ministerial/commissioner directives from the 2008–2017 period: true if a policy or standing instruction against engaging with gangs can be identified, false if the record shows no such instruction or shows engagement was permitted throughout.

civility.statement: The gravity of the problem is the challenge to us that we must not dog-whistle; we must actually do what makes a difference here.
civility.explanation: A contested gangs debate where she had a real opportunity to turn on opponents. 'Dog-whistle' edges toward imputing bad faith, but it is framed inclusively ('us') as a caution to the whole House rather than landing on any person or naming anyone.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Pushing them out, excluding them, making it difficult to communicate with them, isn’t actually going to help a situation; it’s going to hinder it in terms of bringing those people back within the fold of a functional family and support system.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the bill's own machinery — the statutory definition of whānau and the consorting provisions — and who it would exclude. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Pushing them out, excluding them, making it difficult to communicate with them, isn’t actually going to help a situation; it’s going to hinder it in terms of bringing those people back within the fold of a functional family and support system.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real provision: the definition is too narrow to cover people acting as family, therefore the consorting rules will exclude the very people most at risk and hinder reintegration. The premise is drawn only from personal acquaintance and the causal step to 'will hinder' is asserted rather than shown — an argument from anecdote, but a coherent one about the measure itself.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In 2024, we’re living in a virtual world where audio and video technology is part of daily life. This bill has the potential to increase access to justice and the efficiency of our courts, as well as providing a safe option for victims to participate in court processes.
rigor.explanation: The premise — technology is ubiquitous in daily life — does not support the conclusion about access to justice and court efficiency; that technology is familiar says nothing about whether its use in court reduces delay or widens access. An appeal to the spirit of the times with a gap between what is offered and what is concluded. Softened by the hedge 'has the potential', which is why this is not lower.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: One of the things I noticed was that there was a serious misgiving about some of the provisions, because other alternatives that might not have breached as many rights had not been examined fully.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fact about the content of the Attorney-General's BORA vet of this bill — that it recorded serious misgivings about some provisions, on the ground that less rights-restrictive alternatives had not been fully examined.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Attorney-General's report to the House under s 7 of the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990 on the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill (tabled early 2024). True if that report identifies provisions as an unjustified limit on protected rights and gives, among its reasons, that less rights-limiting alternatives were not adequately assessed; false if the report raises no such misgiving or rests on entirely different reasoning.

veracity.statement: The court system is currently experiencing significant delays, particularly in the criminal and the family jurisdictions of our busiest court, the District Court.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that court delays are significant at the time of speaking, that they are worst in the District Court's criminal and family jurisdictions, and that the District Court is the busiest court.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice court timeliness/case-flow statistics for 2023–24: median and mean time-to-disposal and active case volumes by jurisdiction. True if District Court criminal and family disposal times were materially elevated against pre-2020 levels and the District Court carried the largest caseload of any court; false if delays were not elevated or were concentrated outside those jurisdictions.

veracity.statement: This bill contributes towards the fulfilment of one of the Government’s 100-day plan commitments: to enable more virtual participation in court proceedings.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that enabling more virtual participation in court proceedings was a listed item on the Government's published 100-day plan.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National-led coalition Government's published 100-day plan (released late 2023). True if that document contains a commitment to enable more virtual/remote participation in court proceedings; false if no such item appears in it.

specificity.statement: The bill allows the use of audio links such as teleconferences for appropriate court proceedings, and it will be making permanent what was a temporary change to the law made during the pandemic that clarified remote participation in criminal proceedings is consistent with open justice.
specificity.explanation: Names the actual mechanisms — audio links for specified proceedings, and making permanent a named temporary pandemic-era amendment on open justice. Someone could go to the bill and check both. Short of 1.0 only because no figures or dates are attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The enthusiasm with which the Minister for Courts congratulated herself for having the last piece of the 100-day plan tabled a little under two hours ago is a little concerning.
civility.explanation: Contested first-reading debate where he could have engaged the tabling timeline alone. Instead he characterises the Minister personally as self-congratulatory — restrained sneering rather than an insult, so short of a personal attack but no longer clean.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m standing here having to express my party’s view on the Courts (Remote Participation) Amendment Bill, having had only less than two hours to look at it, and this isn’t something that should be rushed.
focus.explanation: Names the measure before the House and objects to a specific feature of its handling — the time available to scrutinise it. Legitimate process scrutiny of a named bill, not party-bashing; slightly short of 1.0 because it engages the handling rather than the bill's content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think, just to wrap up, this bill is good because it shows that that side of the House is capable of thinking about and implementing justice policies and laws that centre humanity and empathy. I just wish they would do it a little bit more often.
focus.explanation: Nominally endorses the bill, but the weight of both sentences is a verdict on the other side's general character and legislative habits rather than on anything the bill does. A policy peg carrying party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It means sitting in a little cubicle with a screen in front of you, where the camera is pointed, usually, at the person who’s speaking.
specificity.explanation: Concrete description of the actual arrangement — cubicle, screen, camera pointed at the current speaker — drawn from a site he names elsewhere. Checkable detail rather than a general concern about video links; no figures or timeframes keeps it off the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: To me, this bill goes a way to centring those rights of survivors and their safety and their experiences within the justice system.
specificity.explanation: Trying to convey why the bill is worth supporting, but supplies no mechanism, no provision and no measure of effect — 'centring rights, safety and experiences' would fit almost any justice bill. The surrounding sentences add no detail to credit.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You can see the Crown lawyer raise an eyebrow in disbelief at an argument that’s being made, and that’s important because it enables you to understand what’s going on. You can hear the sigh of a judge whilst the Crown prosecutor is speaking, and it tells you what is going on in the courtroom.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: a single fixed camera excludes courtroom cues, therefore a remote defendant loses information a present one has. The premises support the conclusion, but they rest on his own observation rather than any evidence about how remote participants actually fare.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We all realise there are delays in our court systems at the moment, and when we have delays, we have costs. And those costs are something that this Government wants to be more efficient on. Allowing participation by virtual means is a way of delaying delays, and it’s also reducing the cost of court proceedings.
rigor.explanation: The premises establish only that delay is costly; the conclusion that remote participation reduces delay and cost is asserted, with nothing offered to connect the mechanism to the outcome. A real gap between what was shown and what was concluded, though the argument is about the policy rather than the other side.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, i roto i tēnei pire, ae e tautoko ana Te Pāti Māori [yes, this bill is supported by Te Pāti Māori], but when we look at the whakapapa of this bill, I think the issue, though, is that, yes, this Government is going to need a faster system—to its victims, but more so that they can lock Māori up.
rigor.explanation: An inference about the measure itself, not merely a swipe: from laws that fall heavily on Māori to the claim that speeding the courts is intended to imprison Māori faster. The step from disparate impact to purpose is unsupported — a motive attributed without evidence connecting the bill's mechanism to the alleged aim.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The bill wishes to provide an avenue of safety to witnesses and victims so they may be present, even if they’re not actually face to face. That, undoubtedly, will facilitate more readiness and willingness to come into the court process.
rigor.explanation: A plausible mechanism — removing face-to-face contact lowers a known barrier — but the causal conclusion is asserted as beyond doubt with no evidence for the size or existence of the effect. Reasonable point, real gap between premise and 'undoubtedly'.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Because justice delayed is justice denied, and justice at the present time is absolutely and most certainly delayed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as present fact that the New Zealand courts are running materially late — a claim about case timeliness and backlog as at March 2024, not a prediction or an opinion about whether delay is bad.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice court statistics for 2023–24: median time from first appearance to disposal in the District Court and the Family Court, and the size of the active caseload. True if those measures are materially above pre-2020 levels; false if timeliness and caseload are at or better than historic norms.

veracity.statement: Just this morning, at the Justice Committee, we heard from survivors about how traumatising it can be going through the justice system and having to prove the harm that has already been caused to them and that contributes to that harm.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific past event: that survivors gave evidence to the Justice Committee on the morning of 7 March 2024 describing re-traumatisation by the court process.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's record of oral submissions for the morning of 7 March 2024. True if survivors appeared and gave evidence to that effect; false if the committee did not sit, or heard no such evidence.

rigor.statement: But I even became aware of it when we moved to mediation that was remote. It did exactly what Duncan Webb has talked about. It was very difficult to read the signals of people. It meant that it was easy to be dismissive when you were trying to move people, and they needed to trust each other.
rigor.explanation: An inference about the bill's subject matter drawn from a single strand of personal professional experience: remote mediation was harder, therefore remote court participation has limits. The mechanism offered (signals are hard to read on screen) is at least stated rather than asserted bare, but the generalisation from her own employment-law practice to criminal proceedings rests on anecdote and is not evidenced.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So with victims of crime that do have to go through this process—and we want it to be a fair process—this helps to alleviate some of those feelings of anxiety that they do find themselves in when they’re going through the court process.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that this bill will alleviate anxiety for victims — is carried entirely by her recollection of witnesses in a Sydney Magistrates Court while she was a law student. Argument from a single unquantified anecdote in another jurisdiction, and the causal step from 'attendance caused dread' to 'remote participation reduces it' is asserted, not shown. The statement does engage the measure, so this is a Rigor gap, not a Focus one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That has affected behaviour of a new generation of criminals coming through who are never called to account by standing in court.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc causal inference: pre-charge warnings were introduced, therefore a generation's offending behaviour changed. Nothing is offered connecting the two — no reoffending data, no comparison group, no measure of the behaviour said to have shifted. The premise about the policy is engaged (so this is a reasoning failure, not a Focus one), but the conclusion outruns the evidence supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So it’s a very different thing if you’re in a salubrious house in Devonport with a pool if you’re being put on home detention, from if you are in a very small space, sharing with others.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance of the measure — how remote and home-based participation lands differently depending on a defendant's actual living conditions. No party framing at all; it names a concrete consequence of the policy for a class of affected people.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’d love to see victims given a very special place in that process, because the harm that has been done often means that they are quiet; they don’t necessarily even want to participate.
specificity.explanation: A direction with a reason attached, but no mechanism, no threshold and no proposal: 'a very special place in that process' names no procedure, no entitlement and no test by which anyone could check whether it had been delivered. She is trying to convey substance here, so the low score is earned rather than an artefact of the statement being a courtesy.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There’s three main changes that we want to make, which we’re proposing, and as a Government we agree about these.
specificity.explanation: Announces a count and nothing else. The three changes are neither named nor described, and she had every opportunity to list them — a listener is left unable to check or act on anything the sentence contains.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In about 2012, the then National Government instructed the police to reduce the number of entries into the criminal justice system by 19 percent over 12 months.
specificity.explanation: A year, a named actor, a named mechanism, a percentage and a period — fully checkable against the Police record. Whether the figure is right is Veracity's question; on detail carried, this is near the top of the scale.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill makes targeted legislative changes, designed to boost remote participation in court proceedings, including the ability for victims to observe a criminal trial and sentencing remotely.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy and one concrete change within it — victims observing trial and sentencing remotely — which is checkable against the bill. But 'targeted legislative changes' does the rest of the work: no clauses, no thresholds, no scope for who else may appear remotely and under what test.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In about 2012, the then National Government instructed the police to reduce the number of entries into the criminal justice system by 19 percent over 12 months.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific instruction from the National-led Government to Police around 2012 setting a target of a 19 percent reduction in criminal justice system entries within 12 months. At issue is whether such a target existed, whether its figure was 19 percent, whether the timeframe was 12 months, and whether it was a ministerial instruction rather than a Police-set operational goal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police 'Policing Excellence' programme documents, the relevant Police Statement of Intent / annual report for 2011-2013, and any Ministerial letter of expectation to the Commissioner from that period. True if a target of a ~19% reduction in criminal justice system entries over 12 months, set by or at the direction of the Government, is documented; false if the documented target is materially different in size, period or origin (e.g. a Police-initiated goal, a different percentage, or a multi-year horizon).

divination.statement: So I know this bill is going to be about enabling more work to be done remotely, but I just say: be very careful, because it will work fine for about one or two years, but, all of a sudden, in five years, like we did with the tag and release, we will actually start to regret this.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that expanded remote participation in courts will appear to work for one to two years and then, at about the five-year mark, produce consequences serious enough that the decision is regretted — explicitly modelled on the reversal of sentiment about pre-charge warnings. This is a forecast about outcomes in the world, not a promise about his own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The status of the Courts (Remote Participation) Amendment Bill's provisions as at March 2029: an official review, Ministry of Justice evaluation, Law Commission report or select committee inquiry finding adverse effects from expanded remote participation, or legislative amendment/rollback narrowing those provisions. True if such a review or rollback exists by the resolve-by date; false if the provisions remain in force with no official finding of adverse effect.

veracity.statement: As Derek Cheng from the New Zealand Herald said not so long ago in an interview: 500 days for a jury trial, 18 months for victims of serious crime before they get their day in court.
veracity.explanation: Relays two figures on court delay: that a jury trial takes about 500 days, and that victims of serious crime wait about 18 months to get to court.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice court timeliness statistics for 2023/24 (and the cited NZ Herald reporting by Derek Cheng): true if the average time to disposal for jury trials is around 500 days and the median wait for serious-crime cases is around 18 months; false if either figure is materially different from the published series.

veracity.statement: This sits amongst six law and order priorities in the 100-day plan.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the coalition Government's published 100-day plan contains six law-and-order items, of which court delays is one.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government's published 100-day plan as released in November 2023: true if it lists six items under law and order (including court delays); false if the count of law-and-order items differs.

specificity.statement: So this Government is very, very focused on addressing the court delays.
specificity.explanation: A statement of priority with no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named measure attached — it commits to nothing checkable on its own.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re introducing legislation to crack down on serious youth offending, and we are now introducing legislation to enable more digital participation, remote participation, in court proceedings.
specificity.explanation: Names the actions and the general mechanism (remote participation in court proceedings), but supplies no figures, thresholds or timeframes.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And I know that you’re always keen for me to keep focusing back to the bill, so as well as the Courts (Remote Participation) Amendment Bill, this Government has introduced legislation to ban gang patches as one of its law and order priorities.
civility.explanation: A contested first-reading debate with opposition interjections, so there was room to turn on someone; instead he answers with a light, self-directed aside about staying on the bill and attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’re introducing legislation to crack down on serious youth offending, and we are now introducing legislation to enable more digital participation, remote participation, in court proceedings.
focus.explanation: Entirely about named legislative measures, including the bill before the House. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s the anniversary of the earthquake that took 185 lives and changed the future for everyone in Christchurch.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 22 February 2011 Christchurch earthquake killed 185 people.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The official death toll for the 22 February 2011 Christchurch earthquake as recorded by NZ Police and the Canterbury Earthquakes Royal Commission; true if the recorded toll is 185, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: In Christchurch East, we lost eight schools, thousands of homes—thousands.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count of schools lost in the Christchurch East electorate following the earthquakes, plus the loss of thousands of homes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education records of school closures and mergers in the Christchurch schools renewal programme, filtered to the Christchurch East electorate; true if eight schools closed or were merged out of existence, false if materially fewer. Home loss checkable against the residential red zone property counts for the eastern suburbs.

specificity.statement: The actions taken in your first 100 days means that there are already people in New Zealand who will now need good luck to make it through the day—good luck to make it through the day.
specificity.explanation: Refers to "the actions taken" without naming a single policy, figure, mechanism or affected group; "need good luck to make it through the day" commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A team that understands the immediate challenges, like how we ensure local media survives the current crisis so that democracy thrives—and so they can report on our plans to deepen our commitment to Te Tiriti, act with pace on the climate crisis, ensure fairer tax, deliver better health and education outcomes, and look after workers and people that can’t work.
specificity.explanation: A list of policy directions — media, Te Tiriti, climate, tax, health, education, workers — carrying no mechanism, amount or timeframe for any of them; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The actions taken in your first 100 days means that there are already people in New Zealand who will now need good luck to make it through the day—good luck to make it through the day.
focus.explanation: Directed at the coalition Government's 100 days as a bloc rather than at any named measure; there is a real policy-consequence claim underneath, but nothing specific is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We shouldn’t be making cuts to our social services—the scars will outlive the cuts.
focus.explanation: Squarely about a policy question — cuts to social services — rather than about the other party's character or record, though no particular service or budget line is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because people don’t fall into poverty; they’re pushed there—and you are pushing.
focus.explanation: An accusation about the other side's culpability for poverty with no policy, programme or figure named — the content is who is to blame rather than what the measure does.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Because people don’t fall into poverty; they’re pushed there—and you are pushing.
civility.explanation: A hard accusation aimed at the Government collectively over the effect of its decisions; no individual's character, competence or motives are attacked.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Recently, a few misguided souls have sought to appropriate Tā Apirana’s thoughts on the Treaty of Waitangi a hundred years ago—mischief-making.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested point (the current use of Ngata's Treaty writings) where she had a real opportunity to engage the substance. Instead of addressing the interpretation, she characterises the unnamed people making it as 'misguided souls' engaged in 'mischief-making' — imputing bad faith and condescension. No individual is directly insulted, so this is a mid-scale failure rather than a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I framed my campaign on the whakatauākī of Tā Apirana Ngata’s “E tipu e rea”, and I’m so proud to have brought the hou, the seat home to te Riu o Waiapu for the first time since he held it 80 years ago.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no MP from the Waiapu valley (te Riu o Waiapu) has held this Māori electorate — Ikaroa-Rāwhiti and its predecessor Eastern Maori — in the roughly 80 years since Apirana Ngata held it. A concrete historical claim about the seat's succession, not an opinion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary/electoral records for Eastern Maori and Ikaroa-Rāwhiti listing every MP since Ngata lost the seat in 1943, together with each MP's home rohe. True if none of the intervening members (e.g. Tiaki Omana, Parekura Horomia, Meka Whaitiri) was from the Waiapu valley and the gap is approximately 80 years; false if any intervening member came from te Riu o Waiapu or if the interval is materially different from 80 years.

veracity.statement: “Nek minnit”, I’m attending the New Zealand Rugby Union AGM as CEO of Ngāti Porou East Coast Rugby, the only female CEO or chair in New Zealand Rugby at that time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that when she attended the NZ Rugby AGM as CEO of Ngāti Porou East Coast (circa 2012–13), no other provincial union in New Zealand Rugby had a woman as either chief executive or chair.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Rugby annual reports and provincial union records for the relevant year listing the CEO and chair of each provincial union; true if she was the only woman holding either role, false if any other union had a female CEO or chair at that time.

veracity.statement: In 1971, she made her Covent Garden debut as the Countess in Mozart’s Marriage of Figaro.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific year (1971), venue (Covent Garden / Royal Opera House) and role (the Countess, Le nozze di Figaro) for Kiri Te Kanawa's debut there.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Royal Opera House performance archive and Kiri Te Kanawa's documented career chronology; true if her Covent Garden debut was in 1971 in the role of the Countess in Le nozze di Figaro, false if the year, venue or role differs.

veracity.statement: When Charles and Diana married in 1981, before a global audience of 600 million, the royal family turned to Kiri Te Kanawa to sing Handel’s Let the bright Seraphim—the seraphim is a form of angel, Willie.
veracity.explanation: Three assertions bundled: the wedding year (1981), that she sang Handel's 'Let the Bright Seraphim' at it, and that the global viewing audience was 600 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporary broadcast records and the order of service for the 29 July 1981 Charles–Diana wedding; true if she performed 'Let the Bright Seraphim' at that ceremony and the reported global audience is around 600 million, false if the piece differs or the widely-documented audience figure is materially different from 600 million (commonly cited figures run higher).

veracity.statement: Twenty years ago, her Kiri Te Kanawa Foundation, as King Charles noticed, was established and has helped more than 40 singers succeed globally as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Kiri Te Kanawa Foundation was established around 2004 (twenty years before this March 2024 statement) and has supported more than 40 singers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Kiri Te Kanawa Foundation's own incorporation/registration record and its published list of award recipients; true if founded circa 2004 and the cumulative recipient count exceeds 40, false if the founding year is materially different or the recipient count is below 40.

veracity.statement: You also went on, in terms of music and your career, receiving New Zealand’s first ever gold disc for music sales—what an achievement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a priority claim: that Kiri Te Kanawa received the first gold disc ever awarded in New Zealand for music sales.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Recorded Music NZ / former NZ Federation of Phonographic Industry certification records; true if no gold disc was certified in New Zealand before the one awarded to Kiri Te Kanawa, false if an earlier New Zealand gold disc certification exists for another artist.

veracity.statement: As one of the world’s greatest opera singers, the iconic New Zealander of the Year in 2012, you never forgot where you came from.
veracity.explanation: Embedded factual assertion that Kiri Te Kanawa held the New Zealander of the Year title for 2012. The surrounding praise is opinion; only the award claim is checkable.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published roll of New Zealander of the Year recipients (Kiwibank New Zealander of the Year Awards); true if Kiri Te Kanawa is listed as the 2012 recipient, false if the 2012 award went to someone else or if the honour she received that year was a differently-named award.

focus.statement: Our Government believes in rights and responsibilities, so if you contribute to a culture of intimidation and abuse, it’s time to change your behaviour, and if you don’t, you may not keep your taxpayer-funded State house.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named policy — the announced Kāinga Ora tenancy sanctions — stating the mechanism and who it applies to. No party-bashing content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, I can tell you I’m not going to take any lectures from that member about economic management. That was a Government that was characterised by spending more, taxing more, borrowing more, and we heard from the new finance spokesperson they want to continue to do more of it.
focus.explanation: Asked about a specific $5.6b shortfall, the reply names no policy, measure or figure — it is a general characterisation of the other party, past and future.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is the IRD correct that his Government’s proposed tax on offshore online casino operators will raise $155 million over four years, or are the “rock-solid” costings that he and Nicola Willis produced correct, suggesting the change will bring $716 million of revenue over the same period—a difference of over $500 million?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named policy against a named official estimate. Holding the government to a specific costing is the opposition's job and is squarely on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that the fiscal impact of the mortgage interest deductibility changes is greater than the estimate of one party and closer to the estimate of another party in the coalition, because this Government is actually a coalition of three partners working together for a better New Zealand, and does he have any advice for the guy on the other side who has no friends?
focus.explanation: Opens on a real policy question (the interest deductibility costing) but the weight of the question is coalition self-promotion and a swipe at the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our Government believes in rights and responsibilities, so if you contribute to a culture of intimidation and abuse, it’s time to change your behaviour, and if you don’t, you may not keep your taxpayer-funded State house.
specificity.explanation: Names a real mechanism (loss of a state tenancy for abusive behaviour) but gives no threshold, no process, no timeframe and no numbers.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re not going to increase Government spending by 84 percent. We’re not going to hire 16,000 more public servants. We’re not going to increase Government debt from $5 billion to $100 billion and actually have nothing to show for it.
specificity.explanation: Three concrete, checkable quantities — a percentage, a headcount and two debt levels. Whether they are right is a separate question.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is the IRD correct that his Government’s proposed tax on offshore online casino operators will raise $155 million over four years, or are the “rock-solid” costings that he and Nicola Willis produced correct, suggesting the change will bring $716 million of revenue over the same period—a difference of over $500 million?
specificity.explanation: Names the measure, the source of the competing estimate, both figures, the period and the gap between them. Fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The result is that net core Crown debt increased from around $59 billion in 2017 to $183 billion this year, an increase of more than $100 billion in six short years.
specificity.explanation: Named debt measure, two dated levels, and the change between them. Directly checkable against published fiscal data.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I can tell you I’m not going to take any lectures from that member about economic management. That was a Government that was characterised by spending more, taxing more, borrowing more, and we heard from the new finance spokesperson they want to continue to do more of it.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the member's standing to ask rather than the substance of the question, but stops short of an insult to the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, look, I can tell you it is ironic that you are trying to lecture me on economics after six years of being in Government, of actually causing huge damage to our books, having had economic mismanagement and vandalism on a scale we’ve never seen before, an 84 percent increase in Government spending.
civility.explanation: 'Vandalism', addressed directly at the member, imputes wilful destructiveness rather than error — bad faith attributed to the person, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Why did he claim on 11 March that he hadn’t seen the advice that his Government’s tax cuts for landlords had blown out by $800 million, given his finance Minister had already publicly confirmed that that was the case, or has he just given up on trying to keep track of all of his Government’s Budget blowouts?
civility.explanation: The closing 'has he just given up on trying to keep track' is a sneering imputation about the Prime Minister personally rather than a question about the policy — a real failure, though short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that the fiscal impact of the mortgage interest deductibility changes is greater than the estimate of one party and closer to the estimate of another party in the coalition, because this Government is actually a coalition of three partners working together for a better New Zealand, and does he have any advice for the guy on the other side who has no friends?
civility.explanation: 'The guy on the other side who has no friends' is a direct personal jibe about the Leader of the Opposition's standing, not about any argument he made.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We’re not going to increase Government spending by 84 percent. We’re not going to hire 16,000 more public servants. We’re not going to increase Government debt from $5 billion to $100 billion and actually have nothing to show for it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the previous government core Crown spending rose 84 percent, the public service grew by 16,000 staff, and government debt rose from $5 billion to $100 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenses 2017 vs 2023 (true if the increase is ≈84%); Public Service Commission workforce data 2017 vs 2023 (true if the rise is ≈16,000 FTE); Treasury net core Crown debt levels for those years (true if debt was ≈$5b in 2017 and ≈$100b in 2023). False if any of the three is materially different from the figure given.

veracity.statement: Under that Government, average rents went up $170 a week.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that average weekly rents rose by $170 over the term of the previous Labour government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE tenancy bond data, national median/mean weekly rent, October 2017 vs October 2023; true if the increase is ≈$170 per week, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: You drove up domestic inflation, you drove up interest rates, the last three quarters of the last year’s economic growth went down, and you’ve got rising unemployment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, among the causal claims, two checkable facts: that GDP growth was negative in each of the last three quarters of 2023, and that unemployment was rising.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP for Q2, Q3 and Q4 2023 — true only if all three quarters recorded negative growth; and Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate over 2023 — true if it rose. False if any of those three quarters was positive.

veracity.statement: Does he agree with Christopher Luxon, “I can tell you in the National Party we understand the economy and we are rock solid in our numbers.”, given his tax promises were $800 million out on interest deductibility, more than $500 million out on gambling, and $1.3 billion out on benefit indexation?
veracity.explanation: Asserts three specific discrepancies between National's pre-election costings and later official advice: $800m on interest deductibility, over $500m on online gambling duty, $1.3b on benefit indexation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's pre-election fiscal plan figures against Treasury/IRD/MSD advice released by March 2024 for each of the three items; true if each discrepancy is of the magnitude stated, false if any is materially smaller or does not exist.

veracity.statement: The result is that net core Crown debt increased from around $59 billion in 2017 to $183 billion this year, an increase of more than $100 billion in six short years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts net core Crown debt was about $59 billion in 2017 and $183 billion in the current year, a rise of more than $100 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury financial statements / HYEFU 2023 net core Crown debt for the years ended June 2017 and the 2023/24 year; true if the levels are ≈$59b and ≈$183b on a consistent definition, false if the two figures use different debt measures or differ materially.

rigor.statement: What we will be doing is increasing the supply of rental property and putting downward pressure on rent, as he has received in formal advice before in Government.
rigor.explanation: Engages the policy but the supply-to-lower-rents link rests entirely on an appeal to unnamed 'formal advice' — the authority is asserted, never shown or cited.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, COVID-19 was a big reason that net core Crown debt increased so quickly, but Government spending outside of COVID has also increased significantly, with Treasury advising me that the previous Government left us with a structural operating deficit of around 2 percent of GDP.
rigor.explanation: Concedes the largest competing explanation (COVID) rather than ignoring it, and offers cited evidence (Treasury advice on a structural deficit) for the residual. The gap: a 2%-of-GDP structural deficit is not shown to account for the scale of the debt increase claimed — the inference from the one to the other is left implicit.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would invite members to engage in a little thought experiment, where we went through the GFC and COVID with a starting point for net debt of 50 percent of GDP rather than 5 percent; so Governments should always be thinking about the next shock that’s around the corner, not just maxing out the credit card today.
rigor.explanation: A real inference offered with support: if shocks ratchet debt upward, then a lower starting point leaves more fiscal room, therefore keep debt low in good times. The counterfactual is stated rather than asserted, and the conclusion tracks the premises. No fallacy; the main gap is that no magnitude is given for the buffer required.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The previous Government and their friends in the Green Party promoted a policy that facilitated a culture of intimidation and abuse, and I’m very proud that our Government is going to deliver change.
rigor.explanation: An argument about a policy, and a weak one: it generalises from a single tenant's account to the conclusion that a policy produced 'a culture of intimidation and abuse' across the whole tenancy stock. Argument from anecdote, with no rate, comparison or counterfactual connecting the policy to the outcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Can I ask the Prime Minister as to whether he’s seen or heard of any policy, either here or anywhere in the world, where a tenant can have absolute contempt for the landlord, whether it be State or whether it be private, and yet be the beneficiary of the largess being suggested by that questioner?
rigor.explanation: Strawman. The question Swarbrick asked was whether children would be made homeless; it did not propose that tenants who hold their landlord in 'absolute contempt' should keep their houses. The argument defeats a position nobody advanced, and it is an argument about the housing policy rather than merely a swipe, so it is assessable here.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And here’s the thing: when you’re actually careful about eliminating waste in the back office, when you actually drive down the amount wasted on consultants and contractors and ridiculous processes and low-value programmes, that frees up more cash for front-line services that New Zealanders rely on.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about a real policy — back-office savings fund front-line services — but with a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded. Nothing is offered on whether the identified savings are of the same order as the front-line commitments being questioned, and the premise that the spending is 'waste' is assumed rather than established. A reasonable point that does not carry the weight placed on it.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I have seen a report saying that a future Government would consider taking on more debt, despite New Zealand’s debt being the highest for 30 years, despite us having little to show for it, and despite interest costs rising to $8.8 billion this year.
veracity.explanation: Two checkable factual assertions about the present: that NZ public debt is at its highest level in 30 years, and that Crown finance costs reach $8.8 billion in the 2023/24 year. ('Little to show for it' is opinion and is not part of the claim being checked.)
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown net debt as a share of GDP series back to 1994 — true if the 2023/24 figure is the highest in that window, false if any year since 1994 was higher. And Treasury's Crown accounts / HYEFU 2023 forecast for core Crown finance costs in 2023/24 — true if approximately $8.8 billion, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The problem today is that there are 24,000 people on a State house wait-list, which went up four or five times under the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a present level of the social housing register (about 24,000 applicants) and a past multiple (a four- to fivefold rise over the 2017–2023 government).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD Housing Register quarterly statistics: true if the register stood at approximately 24,000 applicants at the March 2024 release, and if the December 2017 figure multiplied by four to five approximates the 2023 figure; false if the level is materially different or the increase falls outside that multiple.

veracity.statement: Does she agree with the Prime Minister when he committed to no new taxes or increasing existing taxes; if so, how does she reconcile that with breaking her promise to axe the app tax, increasing petrol taxes by 22c a litre, and introducing an additional $50 tax on every New Zealanders’ vehicle?
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the Government is increasing fuel excise by 22c a litre, is introducing an additional $50 charge on every vehicle, and did not repeal the GST change on app-based services ('the app tax').
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2024 draft Government Policy Statement on land transport and the associated Cabinet papers for the scheduled fuel excise duty increases and the motor vehicle registration fee change: true if the announced excise increases total approximately 22c per litre and the annual registration increase is approximately $50, false if the announced figures or their scope differ materially. For the app tax, the Taxation (Annual Rates 2023–24) legislation and Budget 2024 documents: true if the GST platform-economy rules remained in force, false if repealed.

veracity.statement: This is a Government that wants to continue the school lunch programme that the other Government didn’t leave any budgeted funding for, so we’re prioritising it in our upcoming Budget.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the outgoing government left no appropriated funding for the school lunch programme (Ka Ora, Ka Ako) beyond the current year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2023 Estimates and forecast appropriations for Ka Ora, Ka Ako Healthy School Lunches: true if the appropriation ends at the close of the 2023/24 financial year with no funding in the outyears, false if the forward estimates carry funding into 2024/25 or beyond.

veracity.statement: And I’d just reassure the member that we will be delivering tax relief to the hard-working Kiwis who missed out on her Government’s watch and who haven’t had a tax reduction since 2010.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that New Zealand personal income taxpayers have received no tax reduction since 2010.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The statutory personal income tax rates and thresholds in the Income Tax Act from 1 October 2010 to March 2024: true if neither the rates nor the thresholds were reduced or shifted in favour of taxpayers over that period, false if any general personal income tax reduction (rate cut or threshold shift) took effect. Note that a new 39% top rate was added in 2021, which cuts against 'reduction' only for that bracket.

civility.statement: I’m disappointed to hear that coming from a member of this House, Barbara Edmonds.
civility.explanation: Pointed and personalised — it names an individual member and expresses disappointment in her rather than in her argument — but it stops well short of an insult or an imputation of bad faith. Robust, edging toward the person without landing on them.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does he care at all about the evidence that his Government’s policies will increase homelessness, poverty, and inequality, or is he intent on running this Government on vibes?
civility.explanation: Goes past the policy to the Prime Minister himself: 'does he care at all' imputes indifference, and 'running this Government on vibes' is a jibe at his personal seriousness rather than at the decision. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil under the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Why is she introducing at least three new taxes she promised not to, cutting funding for wheelchair servicing, refusing to commit to funding school lunches as set out in her fiscal plan, and is she worried she will run out of election commitments to break?
civility.explanation: The first three-quarters is legitimate scrutiny of named commitments, but the closing clause — will she 'run out of election commitments to break' — is mockery directed at the Minister personally rather than a further point about the policies. Sneering, though mild, so a real failure rather than merely pointed.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’ll give the member a little instruction on coalition Government, because the Government’s tax and fiscal plans reflect coalition negotiations which resulted in a number of amendments to the proposals that National and other parties campaigned on.
civility.explanation: Condescension. Offering 'a little instruction' casts a fellow member — herself a former tax official — as needing to be taught the basics, which is directed at her standing rather than at the substance of her question. Under the re-anchored scale, condescension is a genuine failure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Look, the member can list a bunch of assertions that are completely incorrect but it doesn’t reflect well on her.
civility.explanation: The first half rebuts the claims, which is fine; the second half turns to the person — what listing them says about her — rather than to why the claims are wrong. Imputes poor judgement to the member instead of answering, which is a genuine civility failure rather than robustness.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What I question is whether New Zealanders can see $123 billion worth of value generated by that Government for the $123 billion worth of debt that they have saddled this and future generations with.
focus.explanation: Names a specific figure and a specific outcome (debt incurred versus value delivered), which is accountability rather than tribalism. Marked down slightly because the frame is 'that Government' as an actor rather than any named programme or spending line.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The previous Government and their friends in the Green Party promoted a policy that facilitated a culture of intimidation and abuse, and I’m very proud that our Government is going to deliver change.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy claim underneath — that a sustaining-tenancies approach had a consequence for neighbours — but the policy is never named, and the weight of the sentence falls on who promoted it ('the previous Government and their friends in the Green Party'). A real policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because a taxpayer has woken up this morning—a low and middle income worker that the Labour Party used to care about, who’s actually paying their taxes, going to work, giving it to the Government—to actually subsidise the living of some other fellow Kiwi.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point here — that State housing is taxpayer-subsidised and that carries obligations — but it is delivered through a claim about who the Labour Party 'used to care about', which is about the other team rather than the housing policy. Policy content wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does she see front-line services when she looks at Customs staff, police officers, firefighters, free school lunches, and carers funded through Whaikaha, and, if so, why is her Government cutting the support for these front-line services?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy: it tests a stated commitment against named, specific spending decisions. This is scrutiny of a government's own promise, which is the job of an opposition MP, and it names the measures rather than characterising the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I particularly stand by my commitment to give tax relief to hard-working New Zealanders in the upcoming Budget in May.
specificity.explanation: A direction with a timeframe — tax relief, delivered at the May Budget — but no rate, threshold, amount or mechanism, so nobody could check what counts as delivery. Mid-scale: the 'by when' is supplied, the 'how much' is not.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The problem today is that there are 24,000 people on a State house wait-list, which went up four or five times under the previous Government.
specificity.explanation: A concrete, checkable figure and a stated rate of change on a named measure (the State house wait-list). Someone could go and verify it directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The plan here is to give people a shot of getting a State house—who deserve a shot at getting a State house and are going to appreciate it and value it, and actually make sure that they can actually get their shot at the Kiwi Dream.
specificity.explanation: Offered as a description of a plan, so it is trying to convey substance, but it carries none: no mechanism, no numbers, no timeframe and no criterion for who 'deserves' a house. 'A shot at the Kiwi Dream' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are wanting to grow this economy so we can drive more prosperity in this economy and lift wages and incomes for everybody.
specificity.explanation: A slogan. Growth, prosperity, wages and incomes are named as goals with no policy, figure, mechanism or date attached to any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does she see front-line services when she looks at Customs staff, police officers, firefighters, free school lunches, and carers funded through Whaikaha, and, if so, why is her Government cutting the support for these front-line services?
specificity.explanation: Names five concrete services and a named agency (Whaikaha) rather than gesturing at 'the front line'. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer. Held below the top only because no dollar figures or headcounts are attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does she agree with the Prime Minister when he committed to no new taxes or increasing existing taxes; if so, how does she reconcile that with breaking her promise to axe the app tax, increasing petrol taxes by 22c a litre, and introducing an additional $50 tax on every New Zealanders’ vehicle?
specificity.explanation: Three named revenue measures with two exact figures — 22c a litre and $50 per vehicle — plus a named commitment they are being tested against. Fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Does he care at all about the evidence that his Government’s policies will increase homelessness, poverty, and inequality, or is he intent on running this Government on vibes?
divination.explanation: Embedded in the question is a forecast that the Government's housing and welfare policies will drive measured increases in homelessness, poverty and inequality. The forecast, not the rhetoric, is what is extracted here.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ child poverty statistics (material hardship measure) and the Stats NZ/HUD severe housing deprivation and emergency-housing series for the years following March 2024: true if material hardship and measured homelessness both rise beyond sampling error over the period; false if either holds steady or falls.

civility.statement: Oh, well, yesterday, the Minister of Finance and I, as shareholding Minister, sent an interim letter of expectation to the board of Kāinga Ora - Homes and Communities (KO), instructing them to end their Sustaining Tenancies Framework, the policy of the last Government that enabled intimidation, abuse, and destruction in communities up and down this country.
civility.explanation: Condemns a previous government's policy in strong terms — 'enabled intimidation, abuse, and destruction' — but attacks no individual. Under the re-anchored scale, brutal criticism of a policy is civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I respect the role of the president of the Police Association and he respects our role. The police and the Police Association are engaged in good-faith negotiations, and they carry on.
civility.explanation: Invited to respond to a named person's 'slap in the face' attack — a real opportunity to be uncivil — and he engages the role rather than the man, imputing no bad faith.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have directed Kāinga Ora to make better use of tools in the Residential Tenancies Act 1986, including formal warning notices, relocations, and, in severe and persistent cases, terminating tenancies.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute and three concrete mechanisms, with the condition under which the strongest applies. Someone could check whether these tools are being used. No figures or deadline, which is why it is not at the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: To give you the exact numbers, in 2017, tenants’ rent debt was $1 million; six years later, it has ballooned to $21 million.
specificity.explanation: Two dated figures for a named quantity — precisely checkable, which is exactly what this attribute rewards, independently of whether the numbers are right.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Completely appropriate, but what I’d say to you: the purpose of fast-track consenting is it’s taking too long to get anything done in this country. We have built an obstruction economy. We are here to get things done. That’s why we’re taking fast track, introduced by David Parker, beefed it up, put it on steroids, and are actually going to get some outcomes for some people.
specificity.explanation: Metaphors ('obstruction economy', 'on steroids', 'outcomes for some people') carrying no figure, timeframe or mechanism, in answer to a question that asked what advice he had received.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are introducing five key targets that clearly spell out faster cancer treatment, improved immunisation for children, shorter stays in emergency departments, and shorter wait times for both first specialist assessments and planned care.
specificity.explanation: Names the five domains being targeted, so the direction is concrete, but supplies no threshold percentages, no baseline and no date by which any target must be met.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In 2015, when targets were still at the forefront of Government policy, the immunisation rates for children stood at just over 93 percent. Today, that number is worrisome, at 83 percent.
specificity.explanation: Two dated coverage percentages for a named measure — precise enough for anyone to look up and contest.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Despite this, only three people were evicted last year for bad behaviour.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Kāinga Ora ended only three tenancies on antisocial-behaviour grounds in the preceding year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora tenancy-termination data (annual report or OIA release) for 2023: true if terminations on antisocial-behaviour/disruptive-behaviour grounds number about three, false if materially higher.

veracity.statement: To give you the exact numbers, in 2017, tenants’ rent debt was $1 million; six years later, it has ballooned to $21 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Kāinga Ora tenant rent arrears totalled about $1 million in 2017 and about $21 million six years later.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora / Housing New Zealand annual reports or OIA releases on total tenant rent arrears at 2017 and 2023: true if the two figures are approximately $1m and $21m, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, we’ve been very clear that the coalition agreement says that we will deliver 500 additional police officers in two years, and the Prime Minister is absolutely right in restating that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the coalition agreement's text says about police numbers and the timeframe attached to it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published National–NZ First coalition agreement: true if it commits to 500 additional police within two years, false if it contains no such number or no two-year timeframe.

veracity.statement: We want to actually deliver on our climate goals, something that I think the Green Party would want to identify and align with us around, but you can’t take eight years to consent a wind farm and two years to build it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a factual characterisation that consenting a New Zealand wind farm takes around eight years against roughly two years to build.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Consent lodgement-to-decision durations for New Zealand wind farm applications (EPA/council records, MBIE or Electricity Authority project timelines): true if typical or leading cases run to about eight years, false if typical consenting durations are materially shorter.

veracity.statement: In 2015, when targets were still at the forefront of Government policy, the immunisation rates for children stood at just over 93 percent. Today, that number is worrisome, at 83 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts childhood immunisation coverage of just over 93 percent in 2015 and 83 percent at the time of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health national childhood immunisation coverage series (the 24-month milestone): true if coverage was about 93% in 2015 and about 83% in late 2023/early 2024, false if either figure is materially different.

rigor.statement: Well, we’ve all seen the stories of the kind of misery that the last Government’s policy enabled, which is why we have directed Kāinga Ora to stop it.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote: media stories are offered as the ground for a nationwide policy reversal, with no link shown between the framework and the incidents. He does engage the actual policy, so this is a genuine (weak) inference rather than a jibe.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Is the real reason the police pay offer is not backdated and contains three significant clawbacks due to funding now going to tax cuts for landlords?
rigor.explanation: A complex question that presupposes a causal link between the interest-deductibility change and the pay offer with nothing offered to connect them. The failing is the inference about the policy, not the fact that it targets opponents.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Completely appropriate, but what I’d say to you: the purpose of fast-track consenting is it’s taking too long to get anything done in this country. We have built an obstruction economy. We are here to get things done. That’s why we’re taking fast track, introduced by David Parker, beefed it up, put it on steroids, and are actually going to get some outcomes for some people.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the conclusion asserted is that a post-select-committee insertion of projects is constitutionally appropriate, and the only support offered is that consenting is slow. Speed of process says nothing about the propriety of the procedure.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This Government believes that health targets help direct attention and resources and sets a clear agenda for where our health system should be heading. That is why it is important to have targets at the forefront of decision making.
rigor.explanation: Circular: the conclusion (targets should be at the forefront) restates the premise (targets set a clear agenda) with nothing external offered — no evidence that target-setting changed outcomes.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is the real reason the police pay offer is not backdated and contains three significant clawbacks due to funding now going to tax cuts for landlords?
focus.explanation: Names specific features of a specific offer — backdating, three clawbacks — and a specific fiscal policy. Scrutiny of a named government decision, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Which is correct: the coalition agreement that promises 500 new police in two years, or Christopher Luxon’s statement that it’s “a clear goal that we are heading towards”?
focus.explanation: Holds the government to a named commitment with a named number and timeframe, contrasted against a specific quoted statement. Textbook accountability, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What advice, if any, has he received on the constitutional appropriateness of adding a list of projects into the legislation after the select committee stage, and the ways in which this could undermine public input, scrutiny, and transparency?
focus.explanation: Squarely on a procedural mechanism of the bill before the House — when projects are inserted, and its effect on submissions. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he agree with former chief press secretary for the National Party Janet Wilson that “the fast-track consenting bill is not an act of political alliance so much as pork barrelling at its finest, providing a new golden age for National and New Zealand First’s backers”, and, if not, why not?
focus.explanation: A named bill is at issue, but the weight of the question is on the motives and backers of two parties rather than on any provision, cost or outcome of the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I also stand by my statement last week that there has been no change to statutory or regulatory obligations on councils. Those obligations continue to apply until they are amended.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at 19 March 2024 no statutory or regulatory obligation on councils under the NPS-IB had actually changed, the Cabinet decision notwithstanding.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NPS for Indigenous Biodiversity as gazetted and the NZ Legislation/Gazette record as at 19 March 2024: true if no amending or suspending instrument had legal effect by that date, false if one was already in force.

veracity.statement: The biodiversity collaborative stakeholder group did not actually reach a consensus in the end. There was a minority statement, by a number of groups, so there was no consensus on an outcome.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the Biodiversity Collaborative Group's work ended without consensus and that a minority statement was filed by several member groups.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Biodiversity Collaborative Group's 2018 report to the Minister for the Environment: true if the report records a minority or dissenting statement from one or more member organisations, false if all members endorsed a single agreed position.

veracity.statement: No consultation has been undertaken in this.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no consultation preceded the decision to suspend the SNA requirements.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cabinet papers and Ministry for the Environment records for the SNA suspension decision: true if no public or targeted consultation process (including with Māori landowners) was run before the decision, false if documented engagement exists.

veracity.statement: The execution of 39 search warrants saw 29 firearms seized and 25 arrests made. Additionally, police seized more than 80 grams of methamphetamine, over $7,000 in cash, two stolen vehicles, and a stolen motorbike. During the operation, 11,372 cannabis plants were destroyed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific operational results for the recent five-day Bay of Plenty police operation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police media release / operational reporting for the Bay of Plenty Operation Emerald action of March 2024: true if the warrant, firearm, arrest, methamphetamine, cash, vehicle and plant figures match those stated, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Police destroyed over 35,000 cannabis plants and prevented $128 million going into the pockets of gangs through Operation Emerald. Based on the drug harm index, the estimated social harm prevented by Operation Emerald last year was $127 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a plant count and two dollar figures — revenue denied to gangs and social harm averted — for Operation Emerald over the previous year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police Operation Emerald reporting for 2023 and the NZ drug harm index methodology: true if published figures show ~35,000 plants destroyed with ~$128m denied revenue and ~$127m social harm prevented, false if the published figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: The fund for the equipment and modification of services has been increased by 10 percent. So the misleading statements from the Opposition about funding cuts is completely incorrect.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 10 percent increase in the equipment and modification services fund.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The appropriation for Whaikaha equipment and modification services, 2023/24 against the prior year (Estimates/Supplementary Estimates): true if it rose by about 10 percent, false if it was flat or reduced.

veracity.statement: So the priority has been that the funding must be spent on the person with the disability, when, in the past, the previous Government allowed such flexibility for carers to be able to spend on such things for themselves as pedicures, as massages, as overseas travel.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the previous settings carers were permitted to spend disability funding on pedicures, massages and overseas travel for themselves.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Whaikaha flexible-funding purchasing rules and approved-purchase records in force before 18 March 2024: true if such purchases were permitted and made, false if the guidance excluded them or no such approvals are documented.

specificity.statement: Cabinet has agreed to amend the NPS for Indigenous Biodiversity through a legislative vehicle, and suspend the NPS requirements for councils to adopt new SNAs into their plans.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument, the decision-maker and the mechanism (amendment via a legislative vehicle plus suspension of the SNA adoption requirement), but gives no timeframe or vehicle name.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What, according to his own ministry’s reporting, is the proportion of native species in Aotearoa that are threatened or at risk of extinction?
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable question: names the evidence source (the Minister's own ministry's reporting) and asks for a single quantity. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How we will encourage this is by encouraging the behaviour that has already been happening.
specificity.explanation: Answers "how will you protect biodiversity on private land" with a restatement of the question — no instrument, funding, target or timeframe. Nobody could check or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The execution of 39 search warrants saw 29 firearms seized and 25 arrests made. Additionally, police seized more than 80 grams of methamphetamine, over $7,000 in cash, two stolen vehicles, and a stolen motorbike. During the operation, 11,372 cannabis plants were destroyed.
specificity.explanation: Counts for warrants, firearms, arrests, drug weight, cash, vehicles and plants — every element is checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: These changes are happening from 18 March 2024 and are in place while we complete work on the long-term settings for the use of flexible funding. Whaikaha is working to manage a forecast overspend in the disability support system in this financial year.
specificity.explanation: Gives a start date and a stated reason (a forecast overspend), but no amount, no criteria for the new settings and no end date for the "temporary" period the question asked about.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because the current use of SNAs are an unjustified intrusion on private property rights, and they are a barrier to the great work that landowners have already been doing on their farms.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the measure itself — what SNAs do to property rights and to landowner activity. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What is the effect on people in rural New Zealand when they hear statements from urbanites such as “they want to kill the birds faster”, as the Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick just heckled while he was answering questions about a serious topic?
focus.explanation: Entirely about a member opposite's heckle and how it makes rural people feel; no policy, figure or outcome is named. The question exists to attack the other side, not to engage the SNA decision.
focus.subject: speaker
