rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We have heard, in opposition to this bill, that it would create a lot of bureaucracy, but I will just point out this is like any controlled medication that a pharmacist needs to distribute: they need to have that face-to-face contact, and there’s paperwork and prescriptions to go along with it.
rigor.explanation: Answers the bureaucracy objection by analogy to existing controlled medicines, which is a genuine inference about the policy. The analogy is imprecise on its own terms — it leans on prescriptions, which the very next sentence concedes this product would not require — so it under-supports the conclusion that no new burden is created.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But, of course, that level of supply coming into the country has meant the price of meth has dropped a lot, so any supply from pseudoephedrine would be at a fairly low level.
rigor.explanation: A real economic inference with a real gap: cheap imported supply lowers the incentive for domestic manufacture, but a falling price does not by itself establish that pseudoephedrine-derived production would stay small, and the premise is the disputed 400-tonne figure.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We supported National—what they did in 2011.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that her party backed the National-led government's 2011 reclassification of pseudoephedrine as a Class B controlled drug.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard and voting record for the 2011 reclassification of pseudoephedrine (Misuse of Drugs Amendment Bill / the associated classification instrument); true if the Māori Party voted in support of that change, false if it opposed or abstained.

veracity.statement: Typically, we probably will experience two or four colds a year, and that probably equates to about 14 to 40 days of feeling like absolute rubbish, each year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that adults typically get two to four colds a year, each lasting roughly a week, totalling 14–40 symptomatic days annually.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published public-health estimates of adult common-cold incidence and duration (e.g. US CDC, NHS, NZ Ministry of Health); true if the accepted adult range is about 2–4 colds a year lasting roughly 7–10 days each, false if the accepted incidence or duration is materially different.

veracity.statement: But, of course, I will just point out, these medications are still available in Australia, the UK, the US, and most of Europe.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that pseudoephedrine-containing cold medicines remain purchasable in Australia, the UK, the US and most of Europe, in contrast to New Zealand's restriction.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The medicines schedules of the named jurisdictions as at March 2024 — Australia's Poisons Standard (Schedule 3), UK MHRA pharmacy-medicine classification, and the US Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act behind-the-counter regime, plus major EU member states; true if pseudoephedrine decongestants can be bought from a pharmacy in each, false if any of those has banned the substance outright.

veracity.statement: I will just once again point out that it takes 2,430 packets of pseudoephedrine medication to make 1 kilogram of meth.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific conversion ratio: 2,430 retail packets of pseudoephedrine medication are required to produce one kilogram of methamphetamine.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The pseudoephedrine content of a standard NZ retail pack combined with the conversion yield used in Police/Ministry of Health or ESR advice; true if the implied requirement is approximately 2,430 packets per kilogram, false if the figure is out by a factor of two or more.

veracity.statement: I think one of the members already has alluded to a shipment of in the vicinity of 400 tonnes was intercepted before coming to Australia and New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Relays another member's claim that a methamphetamine (or precursor) shipment of roughly 400 tonnes bound for Australia and New Zealand was intercepted.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police, NZ Customs and international (AFP/UNODC) seizure records for 2023–24; true if an interception of approximately 400 tonnes of methamphetamine or its precursors destined for Australia/New Zealand is on record, false if the largest such seizure in the period was smaller by an order of magnitude.

specificity.statement: Again, I just want to put on the side that we still haven’t addressed the massive addiction issue, predominantly in our vulnerable communities, and for us, as Māori.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a gap but carries no checkable content: no service, funding figure, mechanism or timeframe for the addiction support she says is missing.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yet I think where the gap lies—and I want to acknowledge submitters who raised issues of this nature—is around ensuring that we have adequate addiction support services, making sure that we actually address some of the social determinants of health that continue being completely not addressed, such as good incomes, good housing, connected communities.
specificity.explanation: A direction with no checkable content — 'adequate' support services and a list of general goods (good incomes, good housing, connected communities) with no figure, named programme, mechanism or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Typically, we probably will experience two or four colds a year, and that probably equates to about 14 to 40 days of feeling like absolute rubbish, each year.
specificity.explanation: Gives a numeric incidence and a derived duration range; someone could check both figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I will just once again point out that it takes 2,430 packets of pseudoephedrine medication to make 1 kilogram of meth.
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable conversion figure tied to a named unit — exactly the kind of content someone else could verify or dispute.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: But, of course, that level of supply coming into the country has meant the price of meth has dropped a lot, so any supply from pseudoephedrine would be at a fairly low level.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that after the reclassification, methamphetamine manufactured from retail pseudoephedrine will remain a marginal share of supply.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NZ Police clandestine laboratory detection statistics and wastewater methamphetamine data following the Act's commencement; true if pseudoephedrine-based domestic manufacture stays near post-2011 levels, false if clan lab detections or pseudoephedrine-linked seizures rise materially toward pre-2011 levels.

veracity.statement: Secondly, I also support this bill because it’s actually very straightforward: it’s just restoring the settings, and matches a range of other countries—such as the UK, US, Canada, and Australia.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that over-the-counter/pharmacy availability of pseudoephedrine as proposed by the bill matches the regulatory settings in the UK, US, Canada and Australia.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Medicines-classification records in each named jurisdiction as at March 2024 (UK MHRA P-medicine list, US Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act behind-the-counter rules, Health Canada schedule, Australian TGA Poisons Standard Schedule 3); true if pseudoephedrine-containing products are purchasable from a pharmacist without prescription in all four, false if any of them require a prescription.

veracity.statement: What we’ve heard instead is that it was a very rushed process. They missed the chance to hear valuable evidence and there was a very small number of pharmacy representatives involved in that conversation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the select committee process on the Misuse of Drugs (Pseudoephedrine) Amendment Bill was truncated and heard from only a very small number of pharmacy-sector submitters.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Health Committee's report and submission record for the Misuse of Drugs (Pseudoephedrine) Amendment Bill (2024): the length of the submission period compared with the standard period, and the count of pharmacy-sector submitters heard; true if the period was materially shortened and pharmacy submitters heard number in the low single figures, false if the process ran to standard length with a normal range of pharmacy submitters.

veracity.statement: So this is the only medication that has ever been shown to be effective in adults at reducing that risk, and the thing that prevents complete rupture of the tympanic membrane—that’s been shown on systematic review.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that pseudoephedrine is the sole medication with demonstrated efficacy in adults for preventing aerotitis/barotrauma of the eardrum, and that this is established by systematic review.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published systematic reviews on drug prophylaxis for aircraft-flight ear barotrauma (e.g. the Cochrane review of interventions for preventing ear barotrauma); true if pseudoephedrine is the only agent found effective in adults, false if the reviews find no adult benefit or find another agent (e.g. an intranasal decongestant or antihistamine) also effective.

veracity.statement: That being said, this is a very sensible approach to something that hadn’t made any difference to that scourge, and I commend the bill to the House.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the existing restriction on pseudoephedrine made no difference to methamphetamine harm in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police/ESR national wastewater methamphetamine consumption data and border seizure and use statistics spanning the 2011 reclassification; true if consumption and availability show no sustained decline attributable to the restriction, false if the series show a sustained fall following it.

focus.statement: It’s very straightforward because, ultimately, it is still the pharmacies who have the ultimate choice to stock or not to stock this product.
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism of the measure itself — that stocking remains a pharmacy decision — with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think our local pharmacies need to be looked after and protected, and I think that taking this action without having the conversations with the appropriate representative agencies and organisations places them at greater risk.
focus.explanation: Directed at the measure and its consultation process and at a named affected group (pharmacies); no party-versus-party content.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And my third reason to support this bill is there is evidence that we’ve seen that it has limited scale of risk, even if the products are made available over the counter.
rigor.explanation: Bare appeal to unidentified authority/evidence: the conclusion that risk is limited rests entirely on 'evidence that we've seen' with nothing offered about what it is or what it showed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But do people find that out when they pop in to purchase some pseudoephedrine, or do they find that out halfway through a ram raid when they’ve already done the damage to the store, they’ve already smashed in the window, and they do even more damage looking for the product that they’re there to get?
rigor.explanation: A real counter-inference to the 'pharmacies can choose not to stock' defence — an opt-out is unknown to an offender before the break-in, so it cannot prevent the targeting. Sound as far as it goes, but the force is carried by a vivid scenario rather than by any evidence that targeting follows availability.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So it’s fine to say that those businesses don’t get support, but if they don’t get support, then they place themselves at greater risk by not being able to have pseudoephedrine in safe storage inside their premises.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the absence of a Government security subsidy is treated as entailing that pharmacies cannot store the product safely, with nothing offered to show that safe storage depends on public funding.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And my third reason to support this bill is there is evidence that we’ve seen that it has limited scale of risk, even if the products are made available over the counter.
specificity.explanation: No source, figure, mechanism or measure of what 'limited scale of risk' means; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So my plea would be: take the time to get it right, to ensure the benefits outweigh the potential harm, make sure there are some constructive policies in the pipeline that actually address the very real concerns of pseudoephedrine and meth addiction.
specificity.explanation: A general exhortation — 'get it right', 'constructive policies in the pipeline' — with no named measure, mechanism, figure or timeframe attached to any of it.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think our local pharmacies need to be looked after and protected, and I think that taking this action without having the conversations with the appropriate representative agencies and organisations places them at greater risk.
civility.explanation: Criticises the Government's handling of the bill squarely, without any imputation against a person, in a passage where an attack on the responsible Ministers was readily available.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: As a result of this slowing in demand, the IMF expects inflation to come back into the Reserve Bank’s 1 percent to 3 percent target range in the third quarter of 2024.
divination.explanation: Relays a dated forecast that New Zealand annual CPI inflation will re-enter the 1–3 percent target band by the September 2024 quarter.
divination.subject: other
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index, annual inflation for the September 2024 quarter; true if the annual rate is between 1.0% and 3.0%, false if it is above 3.0% (or below 1.0%) in that quarter.

veracity.statement: Well, as I outlined to this House yesterday, New Zealand’s debt levels are now at a level that we haven’t seen since the late 80s, mid-1990s.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the current level of government debt is the highest since the late 1980s/mid-1990s — a claim about where today's ratio sits in the historical series.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's historical fiscal series for net core Crown debt as a percentage of GDP; true if the 2023/24 ratio is higher than every year since the mid-1990s, false if any intervening year (e.g. the early 2020s or 2010s) sits at or above it on the same measure.

veracity.statement: And I have to say, I agree with that member when he said that he didn’t do enough on unruly tenants in six years, and that’s quite obvious, because there are 335 serious complaints every month over the last three months and, in particular, there are three evicted tenants in the last year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two figures: an average of 335 serious complaints per month over the preceding three months, and three tenants evicted in the past year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora's own reporting on serious/severe disruptive-behaviour complaints for the December 2023–February 2024 months, and its count of tenancy terminations for disruptive behaviour over the preceding twelve months; true if the monthly average is about 335 and the eviction count is three, false if either figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: What I’d say on that is that there has been no change to the disability services support budget from the budget that was set in your last Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the appropriation for disability support services is unchanged from the level set in Budget 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Vote Health/Vote Whaikaha appropriations for disability support services in Budget 2023 compared with the current 2023/24 appropriation and any subsequent baseline adjustment; true if the appropriated total is unchanged, false if it was reduced.

veracity.statement: The ministry made the decision to tighten up the criteria for modifications and equipment, which is a piece of the total disability services budget.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the March 2024 tightening of purchasing rules for equipment and modifications was decided by the ministry, not by a Minister or Cabinet.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Whaikaha – Ministry of Disabled People's documentation of the 18 March 2024 purchasing-rules change and the subsequent official review of that decision; true if the change was made by officials without ministerial or Cabinet decision, false if a Minister or Cabinet directed or approved it.

civility.statement: How do these levels of debt fit within wider time frames over several decades or even as long as the Deputy Prime Minister’s lifetime?
civility.explanation: The substantive question is about debt over long horizons, but it carries a jab at a named colleague's age. Pointed and personal in flavour without landing an insult on his character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And I have to say, I agree with that member when he said that he didn’t do enough on unruly tenants in six years, and that’s quite obvious, because there are 335 serious complaints every month over the last three months and, in particular, there are three evicted tenants in the last year.
focus.explanation: Half the weight is a jab at the predecessor's record in general, but it names a specific policy area and supplies specific outcome figures, which pulls it toward accountability rather than tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why can Cabinet agree on tax cuts for landlords prior to the Budget, as announced on 10 March and as indicated in the statement that he’s just made, but not on boosting disability support funding and instead cutting entitlements for the families who receive them?
focus.explanation: Names two specific government decisions — the interest deductibility announcement of 10 March and the disability entitlement criteria change — and asks about the trade-off between them. Scrutiny of named policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What’s the estimated annual cost of reinstating interest deductibility for landlords once that policy is fully implemented?
focus.explanation: Entirely about a named government policy and its fiscal cost; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why can Cabinet agree on tax cuts for landlords prior to the Budget, as announced on 10 March and as indicated in the statement that he’s just made, but not on boosting disability support funding and instead cutting entitlements for the families who receive them?
specificity.explanation: Names both policies and dates one of them, but carries no figures for either the tax cost or the disability shortfall it alleges.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What’s the estimated annual cost of reinstating interest deductibility for landlords once that policy is fully implemented?
specificity.explanation: A precisely framed question: a named policy, a defined measure (annual cost) and a defined point in time (full implementation). Someone could go and check the answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That target aims for 90 percent of patients to receive cancer management within 31 days of a decision to treat.
specificity.explanation: A named target with a percentage and a defined clinical timeframe; a reader could check performance against it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m informed an additional 22 lives could be saved every year on the current uptake and 65 with full uptake.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete modelled figures tied to explicit uptake conditions, rather than a general claim that lives will be saved.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What does she see as a greater priority for her Budget allowance: respite care for Debbie, the parent of two adults who have disabilities in my electorate of Mana, who has been a caregiver for 36 years and a sole caregiver for 30 years, or meeting the $800 million blowout in the cost of tax cuts for landlords?
specificity.explanation: Carries a named electorate, a specific caregiving history in years, and a dollar figure for the competing fiscal item — a precise question, which counts as fully as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why are Government’s coffers an open pit for landlords but not for disabled communities?
specificity.explanation: A metaphor with no figure, no named measure and no mechanism — the substance of the contrast is left entirely implicit.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Last Thursday, I declared drought conditions for the top of the South, as a medium-scale adverse event, to give farmers certainty.
specificity.explanation: A dated action with the exact classification used and the region it applies to; checkable against the ministerial declaration.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, last week, I announced a partnership which will help New Zealand’s pastoral farmers save $332 million per year in productivity losses, by eliminating the significant impact of facial eczema.
specificity.explanation: A dollar figure, an annual basis, and a named animal-health cause tied to the mechanism by which the saving is claimed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he agree with police advice released under the Official Information Act regarding police employees that these corporate functions will be an important and necessary enabler to support the Government’s priority of recruiting an additional 500 new front-line police over the next two years; if not, why not?
specificity.explanation: Names the evidence source (advice released under the OIA), the target figure (500 additional front-line police) and the timeframe (two years).
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The extension of breast cancer screening means that around 120,000 additional women will be eligible for screening every two years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the announced age extension to the breast screening programme adds roughly 120,000 women to the eligible population per two-year screening cycle.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Health New Zealand advice on the BreastScreen Aotearoa age extension: true if the officially estimated additional eligible population is approximately 120,000 women per screening round, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The Government recently announced that Health New Zealand has approved funding for an updated set of criteria that will allow for about 1,000 more publicly funded PET/CT scans per year in the South Island.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Health New Zealand approved funding and revised access criteria yielding roughly 1,000 extra publicly funded PET/CT scans annually in the South Island.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand's announcement and PET/CT access criteria of early 2024: true if funding was approved and the stated volume increase is about 1,000 scans per year for the South Island, false if no such approval or a materially different volume.

veracity.statement: The coalition agreement between New Zealand First and the National Party commits to the establishment of a fuel security plan to safeguard transport, logistics, and emergency services from any domestic or international disruption.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of a published document — that the NZ First–National coalition agreement contains a commitment to a fuel security plan in these terms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the National–New Zealand First coalition agreement (November 2023): true if it contains a commitment to establish a fuel security plan covering transport, logistics and emergency services, false if no such commitment appears.

veracity.statement: It was also, we should remember, the majority producer of jet fuel.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Marsden Point refinery supplied the majority of New Zealand's jet fuel prior to its closure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE oil and refining statistics for the years before the 2022 conversion: true if Marsden Point supplied more than half of New Zealand's jet fuel, false if its share was 50 percent or less.

veracity.statement: But not only has it put fuel security at risk, it has endangered cardon dioxide supplies for beer and food.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a causal supply consequence: that closing the refinery has jeopardised New Zealand's carbon dioxide supply for beverage and food use.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE / industry records on domestic CO2 supply after the 2022 refinery conversion: true if the refinery was a major domestic CO2 source and documented shortages followed its closure, false if CO2 supply was unaffected or sourced elsewhere.

veracity.statement: I particularly stand by my statement from yesterday’s question time asking whether New Zealanders can see $123 billion worth of value generated for the $123 billion worth of Government debt racked up since 2017.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific quantum of Government debt accumulated since 2017, namely $123 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury / NZ Debt Management figures on the increase in Crown borrowing between 2017 and early 2024: true if the increase on the measure used is approximately $123 billion, false if materially different on every standard debt measure.

veracity.statement: In a rare breaking out of bilateral consensus across the House, National, in its fiscal plan, had the same quantum of cost pressure funding for health as the Labour Party, and I agree that that was a good amount.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that National's published fiscal plan allowed the same amount of health cost-pressure funding as Labour's.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 fiscal plan and Labour's Budget/PREFU health cost-pressure allowances: true if the health cost-pressure quanta are the same, false if the two allowances differ materially.

veracity.statement: Well, I reject that entirely, and I would note and caution the member that the ministry for disability services is operating on the appropriation that the previous Labour Government gave it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the disability services ministry's current operating funding is the appropriation set by the previous Labour Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2023 appropriations for Whaikaha — Ministry of Disabled People and any subsequent adjustment: true if the 2023/24 operating appropriation was set by the previous Government and unchanged since, false if the current Government has altered it.

veracity.statement: Does she stand by her commitment to not cut front-line public services; if so, how does she reconcile that with the Police Association’s comments today that the indefinite freeze on hiring non-sworn officers is already causing backlogs and delays, and that this policy would take police officers off the street?
veracity.explanation: Relays a third party's claim: that the Police Association stated today that the non-sworn hiring freeze is already causing backlogs and delays and would take officers off the street.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Police Association public statements and media reporting of 20 March 2024: true if the Association made comments to that effect on that day, false if no such comments were made or they were materially different.

veracity.statement: What does she see as a greater priority for her Budget allowance: respite care for Debbie, the parent of two adults who have disabilities in my electorate of Mana, who has been a caregiver for 36 years and a sole caregiver for 30 years, or meeting the $800 million blowout in the cost of tax cuts for landlords?
veracity.explanation: Asserts an $800 million increase in the fiscal cost of restoring interest deductibility for residential landlords relative to what was budgeted.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury / IRD costings for the restoration of interest deductibility compared with the pre-election costing: true if the revised cost is approximately $800 million higher, false if the revision is materially smaller or absent.

rigor.statement: We share a desire that Kiwis should be free of reliance on fossil fuels in the near future. That stuff, however, belongs in an Enid Blyton storybook.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to ridicule: the position is dismissed by comparison to a children's storybook rather than by any offered reason. The subject matter is the energy policy itself, not the other party, so the defect belongs here.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This is a stark reminder to the people who sit under a rock, not appreciating the genuine complexity of energy resilience.
civility.explanation: Condescension directed at the people holding the opposing view — they 'sit under a rock' and lack appreciation — rather than at the argument they make.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The situation is grossly worsened by the closure of our refinery, reflective of the shallow thinking behind that decision maker.
civility.explanation: Moves from the decision to the decision maker, characterising their thinking as shallow — an attack on a person's competence rather than on the reasoning offered.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, I reject that entirely, and I would note and caution the member that the ministry for disability services is operating on the appropriation that the previous Labour Government gave it.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point — the appropriation Whaikaha is currently operating on — but the weight of the answer is placed on which party set it rather than on what the funding does.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does she stand by her commitment to not cut front-line public services; if so, how does she reconcile that with the Police Association’s comments today that the indefinite freeze on hiring non-sworn officers is already causing backlogs and delays, and that this policy would take police officers off the street?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named commitment against a named policy (the non-sworn hiring freeze) and a specific claimed consequence. Holding a minister to a stated commitment is on-policy accountability, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why are Government’s coffers an open pit for landlords but not for disabled communities?
focus.explanation: A genuine policy contrast between two spending areas sits underneath, but it is delivered as a general characterisation of the Government's motives rather than as a named policy or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he agree with police advice released under the Official Information Act regarding police employees that these corporate functions will be an important and necessary enabler to support the Government’s priority of recruiting an additional 500 new front-line police over the next two years; if not, why not?
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named Government commitment and the departmental advice bearing on whether it can be delivered — accountability for a specific policy, with no party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Conditions on the ground across Marlborough, Tasman, and Nelson districts are extremely dry and likely to get worse in the coming months.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that dry conditions in Marlborough, Tasman and Nelson will deepen over the months following March 2024.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NIWA soil moisture deficit / New Zealand Drought Index readings for Marlborough, Tasman and Nelson: true if deficits deepen relative to their March 2024 levels during the following months, false if conditions ease.

specificity.statement: Well, what I can guarantee the public of New Zealand is that they have got a Government that is serious about reducing violent crime.
specificity.explanation: Answering a question about 111 wait times, this offers only a statement of seriousness of intent — no measure, figure, mechanism or timeframe that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will he guarantee that uniformed officers will not be pulled off the front line into support-staff work as a result of this freeze on police employees?
specificity.explanation: Names a specific policy (the freeze on police employees), a specific mechanism (redeployment of uniformed officers to support-staff roles) and asks for a guarantee that could be checked against staffing records. A precise question, precisely put.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have removed the Auckland regional fuel tax. We have actually ensured that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand is focused on reducing inflation. There are many things that we are doing to actually grow this economy, reduce the cost of living, and lower inflation.
specificity.explanation: Two named, identifiable actions (the regional fuel tax repeal, the Reserve Bank mandate change) followed by an undifferentiated "many things". Concrete enough to check at the front, a platitude at the back; no amounts or dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What we’re doing very clearly is we want to double the amount of renewable electricity in this country. How are we doing that? We’ve actually got fast-track consenting provisions in place to get renewable energy projects built faster.
specificity.explanation: Names a quantified goal (doubling renewable electricity) and a named mechanism (fast-track consenting), but supplies no timeframe, no baseline and no amounts.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A significant number, and they deserve their shot at a State house, as well.
specificity.explanation: Asked for a count out of 25,000 on the social housing register, the answer supplies no figure, no proportion and no source — "a significant number" commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What actions prior to 18 March did she take to seek additional funding for Whaikaha since she first found out about the forecast overspend in December last year?
specificity.explanation: Names the agency, the two dates that bound the period in question, and the specific event (the forecast overspend) — an answer could be checked against the record. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, again, what I will guarantee is this Government is going to support our police with legislation that will allow them to go out and police gangs properly so they don’t take over rural provincial towns like they did under the previous Government, and they get on top of the violent retail crime, which grew at over 500 percent under the previous six years of the Labour Government.
focus.explanation: There is real policy content — gang legislation and a named crime trend with a figure — but the weight of the sentence is a comparison with the previous Government rather than the police-staffing question at issue.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yes, I do agree with Mark Mitchell, and the fact of the matter is our police had six years of weak political leadership, where they didn’t back them.
focus.explanation: A characterisation of the previous Government's leadership in general terms. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named, so there is nothing here that could be checked as accountability rather than party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will he guarantee that uniformed officers will not be pulled off the front line into support-staff work as a result of this freeze on police employees?
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named government policy and its operational consequence — scrutiny of a specific measure, with no party-directed content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, you’ll have to wait till the Budget. But we are very clear: we are going to deliver tax relief for low and middle income workers. Those are the people that the people of the Labour Party and the Green Party used to care about.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy commitment (tax relief for low and middle income earners), but a substantial part of the answer is about what the opposing parties supposedly no longer care about rather than about who benefits from the cuts, which is what was asked.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What we’re doing very clearly is we want to double the amount of renewable electricity in this country. How are we doing that? We’ve actually got fast-track consenting provisions in place to get renewable energy projects built faster.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the policy instruments — consenting, generation build rates, emissions. No content about the other parties beyond an invitation to support the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can I ask the Prime Minister: has he, in the interest of the Greens and Labour Party, and in the cost of living, reduced the cost of lemons?
focus.explanation: Framed as a cost-of-living question but carries no policy content whatsoever; its whole purpose is a jibe at the two opposing parties. Nothing is named that could be checked or acted on.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Well, again, what I will guarantee is this Government is going to support our police with legislation that will allow them to go out and police gangs properly so they don’t take over rural provincial towns like they did under the previous Government, and they get on top of the violent retail crime, which grew at over 500 percent under the previous six years of the Labour Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that violent retail crime grew by more than 500 percent over the six years of the previous Labour Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police retail crime victimisation statistics for the six years to 2023 (the sixth Labour Government, Oct 2017 – Nov 2023): true if a published series for violent retail crime shows growth exceeding 500% over that period, false if the increase is materially smaller or if no such series supports the figure.

veracity.statement: We have removed the Auckland regional fuel tax. We have actually ensured that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand is focused on reducing inflation. There are many things that we are doing to actually grow this economy, reduce the cost of living, and lower inflation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts in the past tense that the Auckland regional fuel tax has already been removed, offered as an action already taken to reduce the cost of living.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The commencement date of the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Act and Auckland Council/NZTA records of when the 11.5c/litre levy stopped being charged: true if the tax had ceased to apply on or before 20 March 2024, false if it was still being collected at that date.

veracity.statement: But what I’d say to that member is what has been exciting to see and good to see is that fresh fruit and vegetables are down 9.3 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific 9.3 percent fall in fresh fruit and vegetable prices, cited as evidence that cost-of-living pressure is easing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Food Price Index for the month most recently published before 20 March 2024 (February 2024): true if the fruit and vegetables subgroup shows an annual fall of about 9.3%, false if the figure is materially different or refers to a different period or basket.

veracity.statement: It is that they are struggling with the cost of living crisis, and the reason is very simple: the previous administration—the previous Labour Government—increased Government spending by 84 percent. It lifted domestic inflation, it raised interest rates, it supressed economic growth, and it has created rising unemployment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Labour Government increased government spending by 84 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenditure figures for the fiscal years spanning the sixth Labour Government (2017/18 to 2023/24): true if total spending rose by approximately 84% between the stated endpoints, false if the increase is materially different or if the figure depends on endpoints not fairly described as "the previous administration".

civility.statement: Does he agree with Mark Mitchell that “The police need to get a sense that there’s some strong political leadership and some strong political leadership coming within their own organisation to actually back them and allow them to get out there and do their job at the moment”, and if so, will he finally show some leadership and actually give the police the support and the pay that they deserve?
civility.explanation: The quotation and the pay question are substantive, but "will he finally show some leadership" lands on the Minister personally, implying he has so far failed to. Pointed and edging onto the person without becoming an outright insult.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, I’m sorry, but today, there are children waking up in scungy motel rooms. Today, there are children waking up on living room floors of friends’ and families’ houses. Those families are desperate to get a State house, and they deserve their go at that.
rigor.explanation: An appeal to emotion standing in for an inference: the hardship of families on the wait-list is offered as grounds for the eviction policy, but it does not bear at all on the question of what becomes of the tenants who are evicted. The premise and the conclusion are about different people.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is that they are struggling with the cost of living crisis, and the reason is very simple: the previous administration—the previous Labour Government—increased Government spending by 84 percent. It lifted domestic inflation, it raised interest rates, it supressed economic growth, and it has created rising unemployment.
rigor.explanation: A real causal argument about a real policy record, but a chain of four consequences is asserted from one figure with nothing offered to connect them, and "that is the story of economics" substitutes an appeal to self-evidence for the missing support.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: No, because it would be administratively complex.
rigor.explanation: A reason is genuinely offered for the refusal, which is more than a bare no. But administrative complexity alone does not establish the conclusion without weighing it against the claimed benefit, and no support for the complexity claim is given.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The situation that Whaikaha are dealing with is a funding envelope that was given to them by the previous Government—the Labour Government—and then a situation where they had no regulations, no rules, and no settings around the individual funding flexibility.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Whaikaha was established with no regulations, rules or settings governing flexible individualised funding.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Whaikaha — Ministry of Disabled People purchasing guidelines and the Cabinet papers/establishment documents for the ministry (2022) and the flexible/individualised funding settings in force before December 2023; true if no published rules or guidelines governed flexible individualised funding, false if such guidelines existed.

veracity.statement: The question also assumes that the way to clear the social housing wait-list—which I note went up 500 percent in the last six years—is to build Kāinga Ora public homes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the social housing wait-list grew fivefold over the six years to early 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD Housing Register applicant numbers, quarter ending March 2018 compared with quarter ending March 2024 (or December 2017 vs December 2023); true if the register rose by about 500 percent (roughly sixfold), false if the increase is materially smaller.

veracity.statement: It is true that a failure to build enough houses has ultimately made rents more unaffordable—that is why our failure to build enough houses over the last six years saw rents increase by $170 per week under the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that weekly rents rose by $170 over the six years of the previous Government. (The possessive "our failure" is a live-speech slip; the claim under test is the $170 figure.)
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE tenancy bond data / Stats NZ rental price series, national median weekly rent for new tenancies late 2017 compared with late 2023; true if the increase is about $170 per week, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: It’s already a matter of law that building consents and code compliance certificates—or CCCs—must be completed within 20 working days.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a statutory 20-working-day limit applies to both building consents and code compliance certificates.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Building Act 2004 and the Building (Forms) Regulations — the statutory processing periods for building consents and for code compliance certificates; true if both are set at 20 working days, false if either has a different or no statutory period.

veracity.statement: Unbelievably, there is currently no consistent nationwide data on building consent time frames.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at March 2024 no consistent national dataset existed on how long building consent authorities take to process consents.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE and Stats NZ published building-consent datasets as at March 2024; true if no nationwide, consistently-collected series on BCA processing time frames was published, false if such a series existed (e.g. an MBIE building consent authority accreditation or performance dataset covering processing times).

rigor.statement: There is a Budget process that is in place, but the most prudent thing was for us first of all to get discipline and settings in place for the funding that was already there, which was not put in place by the previous Government.
rigor.explanation: An inference is offered — settings must precede more money because the existing funding lacks rules — but nothing connects the absence of rules to an inability to seek additional funding in parallel; the conclusion outruns the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There is no more bureaucracy involved, because this data is already collected.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference from a stated premise, but with a gap: that authorities hold the information internally does not establish that standardising and reporting it quarterly adds no administrative burden.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There is a Budget process that is in place, but the most prudent thing was for us first of all to get discipline and settings in place for the funding that was already there, which was not put in place by the previous Government.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual mechanism at issue (funding settings and the Budget process) rather than the other party in general, though the closing clause is party blame.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I regret enormously that the disabled sector is having to work through what Whaikaha are having to deal with, which is the mess that was left by the previous Government in setting up a ministry without the right settings and rules in place for them to be able to administer their funding.
focus.explanation: Asked to apologise, she redirects to the other party's record; it does name a specific failing (ministry set up without funding rules), so there is real policy content wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does she accept that parents and carers require respite to enable them to have the capacity to care for a disabled person?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance of the funding change — the respite entitlement and who it affects — with no party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We are far more about supporting the community housing sector on this side of the House than members opposite in the past, who think that Kāinga Ora is the answer to everything.
focus.explanation: A comparison of the two sides' attitudes with no policy named — no measure, figure, mechanism or outcome. Strip out the characterisation of the other party and nothing remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What steps will the Minister be taking to ensure that building consent authorities have the appropriate resources to meet these new requirements?
focus.explanation: Directly on the announced measure and its implementation cost to the bodies that must carry it out; no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As the Minister of Finance has said in her answer, there will be more funding for the disabled sector, but it is absolutely imperative that we get the settings, the policies, the regulations, and the rules in place for the funding as it is now, before anything additional has to be done.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic nouns — settings, policies, regulations, rules — with no amount, no named change and no timeframe; "more funding" is unquantified and undated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We absolutely accept that there does need to be support for our disabled community, and so no disabled person will lose access to funding for essential services, equipment, or support.
specificity.explanation: Names the categories covered (essential services, equipment, support) and makes a categorical, checkable guarantee, but supplies no mechanism, threshold or timeframe for how it will be honoured.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have a comprehensive programme of work in conjunction with our New Zealand First coalition partners, where we’re committed to making it easier to build 60-square-metre granny flats on land; and alongside our coalition partners in the ACT Party, making the Medium Density Residential Standards optional but at the same time making sure we explore the idea of GST-sharing with councils to make sure that councils go for housing growth.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete measures with a figure (60-square-metre dwellings, making the Medium Density Residential Standards optional, GST-sharing with councils); no dates or amounts, and the last is only "explore".
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What advice, if any, has he seen on how a net decrease of public housing places over the past 40 years has impacted rental affordability at the same time as total households renting have more than doubled?
specificity.explanation: Carries a defined period, a direction of change in public housing stock and a quantified change in renting households — checkable content, though no figures for the stock itself.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: However, starting next month, building consent authorities will be required to report time frames for building consents and CCC applications, with this data being published on the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment website every quarter.
specificity.explanation: Names who must report, what they must report, when it starts, the publication venue and the frequency — actionable and checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I regret enormously that the disabled sector is having to work through what Whaikaha are having to deal with, which is the mess that was left by the previous Government in setting up a ministry without the right settings and rules in place for them to be able to administer their funding.
civility.explanation: Harsh about a previous Government's record — "the mess that was left" — but it lands on a decision and an institution, not on any person's character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: When will she apologise to our disability communities for the callous accusations she made about parents and carers; the changes themselves, that will significantly affect the wellbeing of carers; and the appalling way in which they were communicated?
civility.explanation: "Callous accusations" imputes indifference to the Minister personally rather than criticising the decision; "appalling" is aimed at her handling. Pointed enough to be a personal charge, short of sustained abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Remember the rock-solid reassurance that Christopher Luxon, Nicola Willis, and all of their MPs gave before the election that there would be no cuts to front-line public services—no cuts to front-line public services.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that National, and Luxon and Willis specifically, gave a pre-election commitment that there would be no cuts to front-line public services.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 campaign material and recorded statements by Christopher Luxon and Nicola Willis on public service savings; true if they publicly committed to protecting front-line services from cuts (e.g. savings limited to back-office/contractors), false if no such commitment is on the record.

veracity.statement: More evidence of exactly that happening, police hiring freezes in place because they can’t be assured that they’re going to get the funding from the Government that they need to be able to do the job that they have in front of them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a hiring freeze was in place at New Zealand Police as at March 2024, and that funding uncertainty was the cause.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police and Police Association statements, internal communications or OIA responses covering February–March 2024; true if a freeze or pause on police hiring was in effect in that period and attributed to budget/funding uncertainty, false if no such freeze existed or it had another stated cause.

veracity.statement: Because what we’ve seen in the last few days is a Government penny-pinching when it comes to the support for some of the most vulnerable in our communities whilst dishing out literally billions of dollars to the country’s landlords.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's landlord tax changes are worth billions of dollars. The 'penny-pinching' characterisation is opinion; the quantum is the checkable part.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD costings for the restoration of interest deductibility for residential rental property announced in early 2024; true if the fiscal cost to the Crown is $1 billion or more over the forecast period, false if it is materially under $1 billion.

veracity.statement: And let’s look at the examples that the Minister gave yesterday of parents supposedly getting massages and pedicures using the funding provided for disability support.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister for Disability Issues cited massages and pedicures as examples of how disability support funding was being spent, in the House on 19 March 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for 19 March 2024 and contemporaneous reporting of Penny Simmonds' remarks; true if she named massages and pedicures as examples of flexible disability funding use, false if she did not.

veracity.statement: We repealed the Auckland regional fuel tax, We killed Let’s Get Wellington Moving, which delivered a set of traffic lights on Cobham Drive and nothing else.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Let's Get Wellington Moving produced only a signalised crossing on Cobham Drive over its lifetime.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: LGWM programme delivery records and Waka Kotahi/Wellington City Council reporting 2018–2023; true if the Cobham Drive crossing was the only completed physical work delivered under the programme, false if other physical works (e.g. Thorndon Quay/Hutt Road improvements, Golden Mile early works) were also delivered.

veracity.statement: There are 49 actions—we accomplished every single one of them in those first 100 days.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the coalition Government's 100-day plan contained 49 actions and that all 49 were completed within the 100 days ending March 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published coalition 100-day plan action list and the Government's own 100-day progress statement, checked item by item; true if the plan listed 49 actions and each was completed by the 100-day mark, false if the count differs or any listed action was incomplete at that date.

veracity.statement: Actually, we did it really quickly and it’s working remarkably well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, as at 20 March 2024, that the school cellphone ban was already in force and already producing good results.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The commencement date of the cellphone ban requirement for New Zealand schools and any evaluation evidence available before 20 March 2024; true if the ban was operative in schools and evidence of its effect existed by that date, false if it had not yet taken effect (e.g. if it applied only from the start of Term 2, 29 April 2024).

veracity.statement: The last Government’s policy of, basically, walking away and making sure that no one could ever be evicted from a State house caused mayhem.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the previous Government's tenancy policy no Kāinga Ora tenant could be evicted.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora tenancy termination and eviction figures for 2018–2023 and the text of the sustaining tenancies framework; true if the policy barred evictions and no tenancies were terminated for behaviour, false if terminations continued to occur under the framework.

focus.statement: They decided that tax breaks for landlords were so important that they needed to be decided before the Budget process had even begun, but those who have real issues around disability support on a day-to-day basis now are going to have to wait for longer and, in fact, in the meantime they are having support cut off from them.
focus.explanation: Names two specific Government decisions — the landlord tax change and the disability support funding changes — and their timing and effect. Policy scrutiny, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The fact that we changed the funding criteria when we were in Government to give those parents the ability to access respite was not a mistake. It was totally and utterly justified.
focus.explanation: Squarely about a named policy change — the flexible funding criteria for disability respite — and defends it on its merits rather than attacking the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I actually reckon Chlöe outdid Mr Hipkins, and that doesn’t speak well about his prospects.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the opposition's leadership dynamics. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: A hundred days of invisibility for them, and a hundred days of action for this Government.
focus.explanation: A content-free contrast between the two parties' general standing. Nothing about the other side's position on any measure, and no policy named on his own side either.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What we learnt over the last six years is it’s all very well to talk about kindness, it’s all very well to talk about the things you want to do about child poverty and making New Zealand better; actually, what matters is good public policy and action and moving with a sense of purpose and speed.
focus.explanation: Gestures at a real policy area (child poverty) and a real critique (intentions versus delivery), but the weight of the statement is a characterisation of the previous government's disposition rather than any measure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They decided that tax breaks for landlords were so important that they needed to be decided before the Budget process had even begun, but those who have real issues around disability support on a day-to-day basis now are going to have to wait for longer and, in fact, in the meantime they are having support cut off from them.
rigor.explanation: Infers wrong priorities from the juxtaposition of two unrelated fiscal decisions; the argument treats them as a single trade-off (an implied false dichotomy) without showing the landlord package displaced the disability funding. A real inference about real policies, but a leaky one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, I want to talk to the Minister about what those pedicures actually help to prevent: ingrown toenails, fungal nail infections, corns and calluses, athlete’s foot; people who are dealing with disability support face those very ailments.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: if these conditions are prevalent among the group and pedicures prevent them, the spending is defensible. The gap is that no evidence is offered that the particular claimants the Minister cited had those needs — the general case is asserted, not the specific one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You only need to google “Kāinga Ora tenants disruptive behaviour” or “antisocial behaviour” to hear some of the horror stories out there, and I have a list, which, in the interest of time, I won’t read out to the House, but every member of this House knows that there are gang members causing mayhem in Kāinga Ora properties, there are people who are engaged in acts of violence, intimidation, and harassment.
rigor.explanation: The evidence offered for a policy conclusion is a search engine, an undisclosed list, and 'every member of this House knows' — appeal to anecdote plus appeal to common knowledge. The argument engages a real policy, so it is scored here, but the inference rests on nothing that was actually produced.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The last Government’s policy of, basically, walking away and making sure that no one could ever be evicted from a State house caused mayhem.
rigor.explanation: Restates the previous policy in its most extreme form ('no one could ever be evicted') and then attributes 'mayhem' to it — a strawman carrying a causal claim with no evidence linking the policy to the outcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, I want to talk to the Minister about what those pedicures actually help to prevent: ingrown toenails, fungal nail infections, corns and calluses, athlete’s foot; people who are dealing with disability support face those very ailments.
specificity.explanation: Names four concrete conditions and a concrete mechanism by which the funded service addresses them; checkable content, though no figures or thresholds.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We repealed the Auckland regional fuel tax, We killed Let’s Get Wellington Moving, which delivered a set of traffic lights on Cobham Drive and nothing else.
specificity.explanation: Two named policies and a named, checkable output. Concrete enough that anyone could go and verify it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are 49 actions—we accomplished every single one of them in those first 100 days.
specificity.explanation: A precise count and a precise completion claim against a defined window; directly checkable against the published plan.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: You only need to google “Kāinga Ora tenants disruptive behaviour” or “antisocial behaviour” to hear some of the horror stories out there, and I have a list, which, in the interest of time, I won’t read out to the House, but every member of this House knows that there are gang members causing mayhem in Kāinga Ora properties, there are people who are engaged in acts of violence, intimidation, and harassment.
specificity.explanation: Explicitly withholds the list that would carry the content. No figures, no case counts, no proportion of tenancies — only categories of alleged behaviour.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They are giving up their lives, in many cases, to supporting people with disabilities and to see the Minister who is supposed to be their champion belittling them in the way that she was in the House yesterday is absolutely shameful.
civility.explanation: Goes past criticising what the Minister said and characterises her conduct as shameful and a betrayal of the people she is meant to champion — imputing bad faith to a named person rather than attacking the position.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I actually reckon Chlöe outdid Mr Hipkins, and that doesn’t speak well about his prospects.
civility.explanation: A personal put-down of a named member — mocking Hipkins' standing and political future rather than engaging anything he argued.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m talking about a former commander—and this is one example I want to impress upon the House—a member of the SAS no less, with 32 years of active service, three postings in the NZSAS as a commanding officer no less, retired as a colonel, with two years in the Royal New Zealand Infantry Regiment in Singapore, and four years as an adviser in Kuala Lumpur.
specificity.explanation: A concrete, checkable case: years of service, rank, unit, postings and locations. Someone could verify each detail and test it against the qualifying-service rules. Falls short of 1.0 only because the rule the case is meant to bear on is not itself cited.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re going to back our police and make sure there’s 500 extra front-line police on our streets in the next two years.
specificity.explanation: A number (500), a defined cohort (front-line police) and a timeframe (two years). Directly checkable against future police headcount. No mechanism or funding source given, which keeps it just below the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have started to reduce the bloated bureaucracy in Wellington, and we’re axing wasteful projects.
specificity.explanation: No agency, headcount, project name, saving or date. 'Bloated bureaucracy' and 'wasteful projects' are evaluative labels rather than checkable content; nobody could verify or act on this as stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So the consultation, the discussions, and the solutions, directly with disabled people and their carers and advocates, has to be a priority in any funding changes.
specificity.explanation: A clear direction with no how, how much or by when: no consultation mechanism, timeframe, or funding figure. Genuinely policy-directed but not checkable or actionable as stated — the high-Focus, low-Specificity case.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In 2019, the Veterans’ Advisory Board recommended that all those that served be recognised, considered veterans; a reflection, perhaps, of the many sacrifices so many had made, from peacekeepers in Tonga or Papua New Guinea, or in the multiple humanitarian missions that were the face of deployment to assist in natural disasters.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in 2019 the Veterans' Advisory Board recommended that all who served be recognised as veterans — i.e. that the Board proposed removing the qualifying-service restriction.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Veterans' Advisory Board's published advice/minutes to the Minister for Veterans in 2019 (and Veterans' Affairs NZ records of it); true if the Board recommended that all those who served be treated as veterans, false if it made no such recommendation or recommended a narrower definition.

veracity.statement: We have abolished the prisoner reduction target.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the target for reducing the prison population, set under the previous government, has been formally removed by this government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cabinet/Corrections and Ministry of Justice policy records and ministerial announcements from late 2023 to March 2024; true if the prison-population reduction target was formally revoked, false if it remained in force at the time of the statement.

veracity.statement: We’ve taken the regional fuel tax off, that will save hard-working New Zealanders money at the pump.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as an accomplished fact, on 20 March 2024, that the Auckland regional fuel tax has been removed — i.e. that motorists were no longer paying it at that date.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Land Transport Management Act regional fuel tax provisions and the repeal legislation's commencement date; true if collection of the Auckland regional fuel tax had ceased on or before 20 March 2024, false if the tax was still being charged at the pump on that date.

rigor.statement: If we don’t recognise and protect those people in our history, how can we truly invest in our future and the surety that must surely follow?
rigor.explanation: A rhetorical question standing in for an inference: that failing to recognise past service prevents investment in the future. Nothing connects the two — a non sequitur resting on appeal to sentiment rather than any stated mechanism. It is a genuine (if weak) argument about the policy at issue, not a swipe at opponents.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We will grow the economy, and our finance Minister’s already articulated a great plan to actually boost growth in our economy, because that’s how, ultimately, growing comes: grow the tax base in this country and make all of our communities better off.
rigor.explanation: The support offered for growth being achievable is that the finance Minister has a 'great plan' — an appeal to authority with no content — and the stated reasoning ('that's how growing comes: grow the tax base') is close to circular, since growing the tax base is a consequence of growth rather than a means to it. The argument is about the government's own economic policy, so it is scorable here rather than being a swipe at opponents.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As a former prevention of violence Minister, I know firsthand what it is like for the sector to not believe that you are doing things to them instead of with them, for the community to not believe that you are doing things to them instead of with them.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion about what happens when a Minister does not work with a sector is supported by the speaker's own past ministerial experience — an appeal to personal authority and anecdote. It is a relevant and plausible inference about the policy process, but the evidence offered is the speaker's say-so rather than anything a listener could weigh.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s been 112 days since the coalition Government was formed, 112 days since change came to our communities and our country, 112 days since we left the frustration of the leaky boat of the six years of the previous Labour Government and we can focus on a better and brighter future for our country.
focus.explanation: No policy, measure or figure is engaged — the content is the other party's era characterised as a 'leaky boat' and the speaker's side as 'better and brighter'. The 112-day count is framing, not a policy outcome. Party-versus-party, so Focus is low; no individual is insulted, so Civility is untouched.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We have started to reduce the bloated bureaucracy in Wellington, and we’re axing wasteful projects.
focus.explanation: Squarely about a government policy programme (public service reductions and project cancellations) rather than about the other party. On-policy even though it carries no detail — that omission is Specificity's concern.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So the consultation, the discussions, and the solutions, directly with disabled people and their carers and advocates, has to be a priority in any funding changes.
focus.explanation: Directly engages how the disability support funding changes should be made — the process attached to the measure at issue, not the other party's character or record.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is simply not good enough for a Minister who has the responsibility right now to not have asked and ensured that more funding is taken into account when it comes to disabled people, who are continuously—continuously—at the end of the line when it comes to funding, acknowledgment, value, and support.
civility.explanation: Severe criticism of a Minister's decision and of a funding record, but it lands on the decision, not the person — no imputation of bad character, competence or motive. Under the re-anchored scale, blunt condemnation of a choice is civil.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is a Government with a grab bag and a mishmash of random ideas which have been promoted by lobbyists and vested interests on the campaign, and do not reflect the kind of Aotearoa New Zealand that we could have now and could have for the future of our children.
focus.explanation: Characterises the Government's programme as a whole — no bill, measure, figure or outcome is named, so there is nothing on-policy to engage. Not zero, because it does at least gesture at the legislative programme rather than purely at the other party's character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I won’t wax lyrical about the last 100-day programme, or the 49 projects which we were both committed to and achieved, although it was very good, and the community is certainly relieved to see the meaningful progress after six years of well-meaning ideology, fantasy, unicorns, and, frankly, hot air.
focus.explanation: Names a real programme and a countable deliverable (the 100-day plan, 49 actions), but the weight of the sentence is a characterisation of the previous government's six years rather than any policy of theirs.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No commensurate social investment or rehabilitation programme or key performance indicators or rationale to figure it was good; let’s just empty the prisons, because it seems like a good idea.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named policy — the prison population reduction target and what did or did not accompany it. The reasoning is weak, but weak reasoning about a real measure is still on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In fact, since we have been in this Government, I have heard the Opposition use the word “outcomes” more than ever; it was a shame they didn’t use it in the last six years.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's vocabulary and past conduct. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — this is the content-free party framing Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Things like keeping unemployment below 4 percent for nine consecutive quarters is the kind of legacy that as a finance Minister one can be proud of.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the unemployment rate stayed below 4 percent for nine consecutive quarters during Grant Robertson's tenure as Minister of Finance.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate series; true if there is a run of nine or more consecutive quarters printing under 4.0% within Robertson's term as Finance Minister (Oct 2017 – Nov 2023), false if the longest such run is shorter.

veracity.statement: The 2021 welfare package undid the damage that the “mother of all Budgets” did in 1991 by restoring welfare to the level it was then in real terms.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2021 Budget's main benefit increases returned benefit rates, in real terms, to their pre-1991-cut levels.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD main benefit rate tables deflated by CPI, compared with the equivalent rates immediately before the 1991 benefit cuts; true if the post-2021 real rates match or exceed the 1990 rates across the main benefit categories, false if they remain materially below for the main categories.

veracity.statement: I won’t wax lyrical about the last 100-day programme, or the 49 projects which we were both committed to and achieved, although it was very good, and the community is certainly relieved to see the meaningful progress after six years of well-meaning ideology, fantasy, unicorns, and, frankly, hot air.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the coalition's 100-day plan contained 49 actions and that all of them were completed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published coalition 100-day action plan and the Government's completion statement of March 2024; true if the plan listed 49 actions and each was recorded as delivered within the 100 days, false if the count differs or any listed action was not completed in that window.

veracity.statement: Last year in New Zealand, 12,383 retail crimes occurred, on average, every month—that’s one retail crime every 3½ minutes in little, old New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that retail crimes recorded in New Zealand in 2023 averaged 12,383 per month.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police retail crime / victimisations data for calendar 2023; true if the monthly average of recorded retail offences is approximately 12,383 (annual total around 148,600), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: We recently abolished Labour’s prison reduction target of 30 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that the previous Labour government held a target of reducing the prison population by 30 percent, and that the present government has removed it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Corrections/ministerial announcements and the Hōkai Rangi–era target documents; true if a 30% prison population reduction target was official policy under the previous government and has since been formally dropped, false if no such target existed or it remains in place.
