civility.statement: I just want to call out the Minister of Revenue, the Hon Simon Watts, who previously was speaking to some of these points in the Tax Working Group report, because he loves to cherry-pick the fact that the Tax Working Group went through this policy and said that it wouldn’t work and it wouldn’t do what it said on the tin, but what he doesn’t want to put the microscope on is the fact that the Tax Working Group recommended a comprehensive capital gains tax, which would have gone some way to fixing our tax system and some of those fundamental inequities that I opened my speech with.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to a named member — 'loves to cherry-pick' and 'doesn't want to put the microscope on' allege deliberate selective quotation rather than disagreement. It is tethered to a specific evidentiary point about the same report, which keeps it above a bare sneer, but it is an accusation about the person's honesty.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We also know, as a result of that independent advice, that a policy like this, unfortunately, will disproportionately benefit the wealthy, who will buy more of those goods at the supermarket.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion is supported both by cited independent advice and by a stated mechanism (higher-spending households capture more of a consumption-tax exemption in absolute terms), so it does not rest on the appeal to authority alone. It stops short of 1.0 because 'disproportionately' is left ambiguous between absolute and proportional benefit, and that ambiguity is doing some of the work.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I also want to say thank you to our colleagues and friends in Te Pāti Māori for expanding the tax debate from the austerity, trickle-down nonsense that we have heard thus far from the three-headed taniwha that is this coalition Government.
focus.explanation: There is a thread of policy content — a characterisation of the government's tax and spending direction — but no measure, figure or outcome is named, and the weight of the sentence is a label for the coalition itself ('three-headed taniwha') rather than an engagement with what it has done.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We built more State houses than any Government since the 1970s.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the sixth Labour Government's public housing build exceeded that of every government since the 1970s.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: HUD / Kāinga Ora public housing stock and new-build completion series by government term; true if net new state/public houses delivered 2017-2023 exceeds every term since 1979, false if any intervening government delivered more.

veracity.statement: We built more school classrooms than any previous Government.
veracity.explanation: A superlative claim about the number of new school classrooms delivered under his government relative to all previous governments.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education school property programme figures on new teaching spaces delivered per parliamentary term; true if 2017-2023 exceeds every prior term on the same count, false if any earlier term delivered more.

veracity.statement: We supported thousands of apprentices, and we lifted the pay of nurses by more than 20 percent and the pay of teachers by a similar amount.
veracity.explanation: Claims cumulative pay increases of over 20 percent for nurses and a comparable rise for teachers during 2017-2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Whatu Ora / NZNO multi-employer collective agreement rates and PPTA/NZEI settlement rates, comparing base scales in 2017 with 2023; true if the cumulative increase exceeds 20 percent for nurses and is comparable for teachers, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: In the end, across the lockdowns, the wage subsidy paid out $19 billion and protected more than 1.8 million jobs.
veracity.explanation: Two figures: total wage subsidy expenditure of $19 billion, and more than 1.8 million jobs covered across all lockdown rounds.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD COVID-19 wage subsidy scheme final payment data and Treasury COVID Response and Recovery Fund reporting; true if total paid is approximately $19bn and jobs covered exceed 1.8 million, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: New Zealand was one of only a handful of countries to have its credit rating upgraded during the pandemic by the international ratings agencies, and it’s worth noting that those credit ratings have been maintained throughout our time in Government.
veracity.explanation: Claims a sovereign credit rating upgrade during the pandemic, rare internationally, and no downgrade over the 2017-2023 period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: S&P Global and Fitch sovereign rating actions on New Zealand 2020-2023, plus counts of sovereign upgrades globally over the same window; true if NZ was upgraded and among a small number of sovereigns upgraded, false if no upgrade occurred or upgrades were common.

veracity.statement: When we entered Government in 2017, Government spending was 27 percent of GDP.
veracity.explanation: A specific figure for core Crown expenditure as a share of GDP at the point the government took office in 2017.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Financial Statements of the Government / core Crown expenses as a percentage of GDP for the 2016/17 and 2017/18 fiscal years; true if approximately 27 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: In my first two Budgets, we posted a surplus and kept net debt below our self-imposed limit of 20 percent of GDP.
veracity.explanation: Claims operating surpluses in the years covered by Budgets 2018 and 2019 and net core Crown debt held under the government's stated 20 percent of GDP ceiling.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Financial Statements of the Government for years ended June 2018 and June 2019: OBEGAL and net core Crown debt as a percentage of GDP; true if both years show an OBEGAL surplus and net debt under 20 percent, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: Treasury were forecasting 13.5 percent unemployment and mass business failures.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific unemployment forecast of 13.5 percent to the Treasury during the early COVID-19 period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's April 2020 COVID-19 economic scenarios and the 2020 Budget Economic and Fiscal Update; true if a published Treasury scenario projects unemployment reaching about 13.5 percent, false if no such figure appears.

veracity.statement: On that measure, New Zealand stood head and shoulders above others, with lower death rates than in normal years.
veracity.explanation: Claims New Zealand recorded negative excess mortality during the pandemic — fewer deaths than a normal-year baseline — and led international comparisons on that measure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / OECD excess mortality estimates for New Zealand covering 2020-2022 against the pre-pandemic baseline; true if cumulative excess mortality is negative and among the lowest internationally, false if positive or middling.

veracity.statement: We are almost alone in the OECD in terms of not properly taxing assets and wealth in some form.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand is one of very few OECD members without a comprehensive tax on capital assets or wealth.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD Revenue Statistics and country tax profiles on the presence of a general capital gains tax, net wealth tax, estate/inheritance tax or land tax; true if only one or two OECD members besides New Zealand lack all of these, false if a substantial group does.

veracity.statement: To see how far we had come less than 10 years later was remarkable, and to win the marriage equality vote 77 to 44 was a strong vindication.
veracity.explanation: States the division numbers on the third reading of the marriage equality legislation as 77 in favour to 44 against.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard division record for the third reading of the Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Bill, 17 April 2013; true if the vote was 77-44, false if the recorded numbers differ.

divination.statement: The scheme will be fully operational next year, funded via industry levies. It will protect the first $100,000 of a deposit.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the depositor compensation scheme will be fully operational during 2025, levy-funded, covering deposits up to $100,000. The scheme's commencement rests with the Reserve Bank and the incoming government, not the speaker.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Reserve Bank of New Zealand announcements and the Deposit Takers Act commencement orders; true if the Depositor Compensation Scheme is in force during 2025 with a $100,000 per-depositor cap funded by levies on deposit takers, false if it has not commenced by the end of 2025 or commences on materially different terms.

specificity.statement: The scheme will be fully operational next year, funded via industry levies. It will protect the first $100,000 of a deposit.
specificity.explanation: Names the coverage cap, the funding mechanism and the timeframe — enough for someone to check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s not my place any longer to say specifically what the answer is here, but I do know that the answers are out there, and this is not a message for my party alone.
specificity.explanation: Follows a substantive claim that the tax system is unfair and unbalanced, but supplies no tax, rate, threshold, mechanism or timeframe — the speaker explicitly declines to name a remedy and gestures at unspecified 'answers'. Nothing here is checkable or actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s not enough. It’s the reason why we had sewage running down the wall of hospitals, it’s why nurses and doctors were so underpaid, and it’s why we saw a growth in homelessness and more kids in poverty.
rigor.explanation: Takes a single aggregate ratio — spending at 27 percent of GDP — as the cause of four distinct outcomes, with no mechanism, comparison or evidence linking the ratio to any of them. Single-cause attribution and post hoc reasoning; other candidate causes (allocation, population growth, sector-specific decisions) are not addressed. It is a real argument about a real policy setting, just a weakly supported one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But one thing I have learnt from my contact with hapū and iwi across the motu: if Māori are doing well, if Māori are supported and enabled, if Māori are given their rangatiratanga, we are all better off.
rigor.explanation: A general conclusion about national outcomes drawn from the speaker's personal contacts. Appeal to anecdote and personal experience; no data or mechanism connects the premise to the universal conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: People with absolutely no care for women’s sport suddenly became warriors for safety in pursuit of an imagined enemy.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to opponents in the debate over trans participation in sport — asserting their stated concern for women's sport is insincere rather than engaging the argument. No individual is named, so this falls short of a personal attack, but ascribing dishonest motive is a genuine civility failure on the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Opening the floodgates next to what else could be GST-exempt—once you exempt GST on a few items, what next? Dental treatment? Wheelchairs? There’s no longer a justification against any further campaigns to remove GST from items on the basis of necessity.
rigor.explanation: Slippery slope: nothing is offered to connect a food exemption to the collapse of any principled line, and the conclusion that 'there's no longer a justification against any further campaigns' does not follow from a single carve-out. The reasoning is about the policy, so Focus is unaffected.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, in the month of April, I will be returning back to Tai Tokerau, and the thick end of a quarter of an acre of not only kūmara but native peruperu potatoes—a number of names that I won’t repeat in the Whare because they could be misconstrued, but that’s a small example of how there’s a practical response to relying on convenience food.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote: a single personal gardening example is offered as the practical response to national food costs, with nothing connecting one quarter-acre of kūmara to the affordability problem the bill addresses. The inference is about the policy question, so this is a Rigor failing rather than a Focus one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But a decile 8 household would get $46 a week, and a decile 9 household would get $53 a week, and a decile 10 household would get $68 a week. The benefits of this change would flow primarily to high-income households.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the evidence offered: the decile figures cited immediately before and here show benefits rising with household income, which is exactly what 'flows primarily to high-income households' asserts. No gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I didn’t realise people ate live animals at the place of consumption, but maybe they will if your bill was to pass.
civility.explanation: Sarcasm aimed at a drafting definition in the bill rather than at Waititi himself — pointed and mocking in tone, addressed directly to the member, but the target remains the measure, not the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Some people who desire to be stars are better staying behind the stable door.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe about the mover's motives — that he is a would-be celebrity who should stay out of sight. It lands on the individual rather than on the bill, which is a clear personal attack even though it is delivered obliquely.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So because the benefit-flows from this bill, alas, go mostly to higher-income households, and because the way of helping lower-income households could best be achieved through targeted measures, the Labour Party does not support this bill.
civility.explanation: Opposes a contested bill purely on its distributional effect and on a policy alternative. Nobody's motives, competence or character is touched, in a debate where several other speakers did.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Did the Speaker know that if you wanted to get a resource consent for a supermarket down the road, you would have to prove that your new supermarket, Mr Speaker, would not interfere with the business of the existing supermarket?
veracity.explanation: Asserts, in question form, that resource consent for a new supermarket requires the applicant to demonstrate no interference with an incumbent supermarket's business.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Resource Management Act 1991 (notably s104(3)(a)(i) and the trade-competition provisions in ss 308A–308I) and representative district plan rules for large-format retail; true if consent authorities are required to consider effects on an existing operator's business, false if the Act directs them not to have regard to trade competition effects.

veracity.statement: In 2009, France reduced their VAT rate on restaurant service from 19.6 to 5.5 percent, but only 45 percent of that rate cut ended up being passed through to lower consumer prices. In 2010, in Germany, the VAT on hotels, guest houses, and campsites was reduced from 19 to 7 percent, but only 28.4 percent of those savings were passed through to consumers.
veracity.explanation: Two distinct factual assertions: the French 2009 restaurant VAT cut from 19.6% to 5.5% passed 45% through to consumer prices, and the German 2010 accommodation VAT cut from 19% to 7% passed 28.4% through.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The French Loi de finances 2009 and German Wachstumsbeschleunigungsgesetz for the rate changes, plus published pass-through studies (e.g. Benzarti & Carloni on French restaurants, ifo/DIW analyses of the German hotel VAT cut) and the OECD/IMF summaries of them; true if the headline rate changes match and estimated consumer pass-through is within a few points of 45% and 28.4% respectively, false if the rates or the estimated pass-through differ materially.

veracity.statement: A decile 1 household—so that’s the lowest-wealth 10 percent of our households—would, in today’s terms, get maybe about $19 a week benefit from taking GST off kai; a decile 2 household would actually get $18 a week; and a decile 3 household would get $23 a week.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Tax Working Group's 2018 GST background paper estimated weekly benefits of roughly $19, $18 and $23 for decile 1, 2 and 3 households once uprated by about 28 percent food price inflation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Tax Working Group 2018 background paper on GST and its table of estimated household benefit by decile from exempting food, uprated by the Stats NZ food price index from 2018 to March 2024; true if the recomputed decile 1–3 figures land within a dollar or two of $19/$18/$23, false if they differ materially or the paper contains no such decile estimates.

focus.statement: One way we might address competition issues is through reform of the Resource Management Act to remove some of the economic tests that would currently apply if you wanted to open a new supermarket down the road where there’s an existing supermarket.
focus.explanation: Squarely on policy: names a specific statute and a specific mechanism (removing economic tests from consenting) as an alternative route to the cost-of-food problem before the House. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This policy, Mr Waititi, Mr Speaker, is nothing but an act of desperation from a visionless, TikTok-driven party—absolutely empty of ideas, no idea how to deliver real value to New Zealanders.
focus.explanation: Once the characterisation of Te Pāti Māori as visionless, desperate and TikTok-driven is removed there is no policy content left — no mechanism, cost, figure or outcome. This is the party-directed case Focus exists to catch; the insult is at a party, not a person, so Civility is untouched, and there is no inference here to assess for Rigor.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Please highlight that the Māori Party, like magpies, have sought to take shiny items from the New Zealand First manifesto.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party — an accusation of borrowing from New Zealand First's manifesto — with no policy mechanism, cost or outcome named. Attacks a party rather than a person, so Civility passes it; there is no argument left once the party characterisation is removed, so nothing for Rigor.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think this is where the Māori Party is woefully short of anything that can be contributed, other than the predictable narrative that it’s all the fault of Captain Cook.
focus.explanation: A general characterisation of what Te Pāti Māori is like as a party rather than engagement with any measure; no policy, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One way we might address competition issues is through reform of the Resource Management Act to remove some of the economic tests that would currently apply if you wanted to open a new supermarket down the road where there’s an existing supermarket.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act and the class of provision to change, but supplies no figures, no timeframe, and no detail on which tests would go.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In 2009, France reduced their VAT rate on restaurant service from 19.6 to 5.5 percent, but only 45 percent of that rate cut ended up being passed through to lower consumer prices. In 2010, in Germany, the VAT on hotels, guest houses, and campsites was reduced from 19 to 7 percent, but only 28.4 percent of those savings were passed through to consumers.
specificity.explanation: Named countries, years, sectors, before-and-after rates and pass-through percentages to one decimal place. Fully checkable regardless of whether the figures turn out to be right.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Regulation, tax system, and Parliament will never address or never replace the sense of responsibility.
specificity.explanation: A broad statement of principle offered as the alternative to the bill, with no mechanism, no figures and nothing anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A decile 1 household—so that’s the lowest-wealth 10 percent of our households—would, in today’s terms, get maybe about $19 a week benefit from taking GST off kai; a decile 2 household would actually get $18 a week; and a decile 3 household would get $23 a week.
specificity.explanation: Per-decile weekly dollar benefits, a named source period and an explicit inflation adjustment. Precise enough that anyone could go and recompute it.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: In the animal kingdom, a mayfly is an insect that lasts for one day; it is born, and then it perishes, and that will be the outcome for this bill—it will be addressed, it will be voted upon, and it will go the way of the mayfly.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the GST-off-food member's bill will be voted down at the reading before the House rather than proceeding. This is a prediction about the House's decision, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The division record for the first reading of Rawiri Waititi's Goods and Services Tax (Removing GST from Food) Amendment Bill; true if the bill is defeated at that reading, false if it passes and is referred to select committee.

focus.statement: On that side of the House, they have used hard-working New Zealanders as a bottomless ATM.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the other party is like as a party — no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named. This is the party-level jibe Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I have here a proposal that Labour members seek to work on with members of the Government, with all parties around this House, on a select committee inquiry into food pricing, because every member of this House has given a speech tonight which has identified a huge problem and a weakness, a structural weakness, in our economy about the price of food.
focus.explanation: Names a specific proposed mechanism — a select committee inquiry into food pricing — and addresses the substance of the problem rather than the other parties.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: On that side of the House, they have used hard-working New Zealanders as a bottomless ATM.
civility.explanation: Heated, but aimed at a party rather than any individual; no person's character, competence or worth is attacked, so it passes Civility cleanly. Focus carries the tribalism.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have put a stop to that, already making announcements to get rid of the ute tax, the fuel tax, and we’re bringing back the brightline test back to two years and restoring interest deductibility, because these are practical solutions, practical policies that are going to get this economy back on track by focusing on less tax and more productivity to strengthen our economy.
specificity.explanation: Four named measures and one figure (brightline back to two years). No dollar amounts or dates for the effects claimed, which keeps it short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Taking GST off food will cost the Crown about $2.6 billion, it is estimated out there.
specificity.explanation: A single precise, checkable figure attached to the measure before the House. Whether the figure is right is Veracity's question, not this one.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But the way to bring food prices down is to get on top of inflation, strengthen the economy, and make it easier for the businesses to produce the food—that is, less red tape, less regulation, so that we can actually bring the cost of food down.
specificity.explanation: A direction with no mechanism, amount or timeframe: 'less red tape, less regulation' names no regulation, and 'strengthen the economy' commits to nothing checkable. Squarely on-policy, but a platitude.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I have here a proposal that Labour members seek to work on with members of the Government, with all parties around this House, on a select committee inquiry into food pricing, because every member of this House has given a speech tonight which has identified a huge problem and a weakness, a structural weakness, in our economy about the price of food.
specificity.explanation: A named, actionable step (a select committee inquiry with a stated subject), but no terms of reference, timeframe or scope.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need to be having a conversation around why it is possible for super-profits to be made in our grocery and food sector, that New Zealand has one of the least effective markets for consumers of groceries in the world, that our supermarkets—which are, in fact, Australian supermarkets—are 20 times more profitable than their European counterparts, which exist in a much more competitive market.
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete comparative figure and a named ownership claim about an identified sector — checkable content, whatever its accuracy.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Taking GST off food will cost the Crown about $2.6 billion, it is estimated out there.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the annual cost to the Crown of zero-rating food for GST is approximately $2.6 billion, attributed to existing estimates.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published fiscal costings of removing GST from food (Treasury/IRD costings, or the costing attached to the Te Pāti Māori member's bill): true if credible estimates of the annual revenue forgone cluster around $2.6 billion, false if they are materially different (e.g. under $2b or over $3.5b).

veracity.statement: But this particular one did make some quite interesting comments around GST. Basically, they said that it was a bad idea.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Tax Working Group advised against removing GST from food.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Tax Working Group's Final Report (February 2019) and its interim report, section on GST: true if the Group recommended against GST exceptions/exemptions for food, false if it endorsed or was neutral on removing GST from food.

veracity.statement: At the moment, we are seeing inflation high, but we need to bring that down.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that inflation was high as at the date of the speech.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ consumers price index, annual inflation rate for the quarter current at March 2024: true if the rate is above the Reserve Bank's 1–3 percent target band, false if it is within or below it.

veracity.statement: We need to be having a conversation around why it is possible for super-profits to be made in our grocery and food sector, that New Zealand has one of the least effective markets for consumers of groceries in the world, that our supermarkets—which are, in fact, Australian supermarkets—are 20 times more profitable than their European counterparts, which exist in a much more competitive market.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that NZ supermarkets are Australian, and that they are twenty times more profitable than European counterparts. Foodstuffs is a New Zealand-owned cooperative, and reported NZ grocery margins are a small multiple of, not twenty times, European ones.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Commerce Commission retail grocery market study (2022) and published accounts for Foodstuffs North Island/South Island and Woolworths NZ, compared with European grocery retailers' reported margins/returns: true if NZ supermarket profitability is roughly 20 times the European comparators and NZ's major grocery retailers are Australian-owned, false if the multiple is materially smaller (e.g. low single digits) or if a major NZ grocery retailer is not Australian.

rigor.statement: When we look at this, it’s not actually the ones that are the most deprived that are going to get the most benefit out of this bill, because the research has proven that the administrative costs and the complexity means that it could be that the supermarkets are going to be the ones that, basically, benefit from this—and not directly going into the consumers’ pockets, where it needs to be going.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to unnamed authority ('the research has proven') and a gap between what is offered and what is concluded: the premise is hedged to 'it could be' that supermarkets benefit, which cannot support the flat conclusion that the most deprived will not benefit most.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We should be looking at that and taking that advice, because it is a bad idea, where we would see more administrative costs, more complexity, and that money not actually going into the pockets of the people who really need it, because the ones that would benefit more are the ones that are going to be spending more on groceries at the supermarket, not the ones that aren’t going to be spending as much.
rigor.explanation: Opens circularly — we should take the advice because it is a bad idea, which is the advice — but then supplies a genuine distributional inference: a proportional tax cut returns more to those who spend more, so the benefit is not concentrated on the poorest. The second half follows; the framing does not.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The answer is not that the Government shouldn’t take its share of food, that we should not pay our way as part of a goods and services tax that is levied very cheaply across everyone, and includes people like tourists and visitors to this country who wouldn’t otherwise pay tax.
rigor.explanation: A real reason is offered for the conclusion — a broad-based GST captures non-residents who pay no other NZ tax, so exempting food narrows the base — and the inference tracks it. It does not address whether the revenue loss could be recovered elsewhere, which leaves a gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s not the solution to the problem to take tax off things like food and grocery; it’s the solution to actually look at why the duopoly and luxurious market conditions that the supermarkets enjoy have been able to go on for so long.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: the two courses are presented as alternatives with nothing offered to show they are mutually exclusive, and no support is given for why market-structure reform would deliver where the tax change would not.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Labour began this work; if we had been able to finish that work, we would be in a different situation than we are today.
rigor.explanation: A bare counterfactual: the conclusion that things would be different rests on nothing beyond the assertion that the work was started. No evidence about the work's likely effect is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What it says is that if a person thinks that she or he is at serious risk of mental or physical harm, then she or he can, after swearing a statutory affidavit to that effect—so there’s a statutory declaration to that effect; there’s a test in there—then that person can apply to the Companies Office to have their physical address removed from the records, and they must provide an alternate address for service.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the operative mechanism of the bill: the threshold (serious risk of mental or physical harm), the procedural step (statutory declaration), the body applied to (Companies Office), and the required substitute (an alternate address for service). Someone could act on this description. Short of 1.0 only because no timeframe or figures attach to it.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So, in fact, with a little bit of effort, if you know someone who is a company director, and you know that person’s legal name, then it is perfectly possible to go and type in the person’s legal name, and come up with their address in a matter of moments—seconds even.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the online NZ Companies Register lets anyone retrieve a company director's residential address by searching their legal name, in seconds.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Companies Office register search at companies-register.companiesoffice.govt.nz: true if a name search returns director records including a residential address without login, payment or manual request; false if director addresses are withheld, require an application, or are not searchable by personal name.

veracity.statement: Of course, I have read out the example which Sarah Pallett gave, and one of the obvious groups of people that this applies to is women, that women are more likely to be stalked or subject to violence.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that women are more likely than men to be stalked or subjected to violence.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Crime and Victims Survey (and NZ Police family harm statistics) victimisation rates by sex for stalking/harassment and for intimate partner and sexual violence: true if women's rates materially exceed men's, false if they are equal or lower.

rigor.statement: As I was writing about this bill being pulled from the ballot on my social media, I had my old friend contact me to say he’d been out in public on some issue, someone had tracked him down through his personal address, and then had managed to turn up outside his kid’s school to harass him, because he was able to trace him.
rigor.explanation: A single anecdote, but the conclusion it is offered for is existential — that men as well as women are affected — and one case is logically sufficient for that. Marked down from the top because the anecdote is second-hand and unverified, and it does nothing to establish scale, but the inference drawn does not overreach what an anecdote can support.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But we’re not going to support the bill, and the reason why is not because we don’t find the bill is worthy; we do.
civility.explanation: Announcing opposition to a colleague's member's bill is the genuinely contested moment in this debate and a real opportunity for incivility. He declines the bill while attributing no bad motive to the sponsor and disparaging nobody — he separates the merits of the measure from his vote explicitly.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I must put out loud and clear—and, eventually, in black and white in the Hansard—that this member’s proposal to amend our current effective, fair Goods and Services Tax Act is ambitious; however, it is very dangerous to New Zealand’s tax system, not only just now but also in the long run.
civility.explanation: A hard, unqualified verdict on the member's bill — 'very dangerous' — aimed entirely at the proposal, not at the member. Under the re-anchored scale, brutal criticism of a policy is the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I do want to acknowledge the Government over the last few speeches—you’ve gone all the way through to the end of them!
civility.explanation: Mock congratulation of members for using their allotted speaking time. It is condescension rather than an insult, and directed at a bench rather than a named person, so it sits just below the pointed-but-civil band.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What is clear to Te Pāti Māori, and our whānau living in poverty, is that everybody against this bill is blinded by their privilege.
civility.explanation: Imputes a discreditable motive to every member who voted the other way, rather than engaging their stated reasons. Short of a direct insult to a named person, but it is an attack on the opponents themselves.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is precisely because they’ve lost hope for the last Government, who had tried for six years—six years—to do something for New Zealand, but they didn’t.
focus.explanation: A speech on a GST bill turns to the previous government's general record. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — 'they didn't' is party framing with no content once the target is removed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Let me ask who in this House—members and Speaker—needs a new definition of what “food” is. We know what food is. We don’t need a separate tax definition to tell us what food means, so I am opposed to this overhaul of word game that the member is proposing.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the bill's actual mechanism — whether the Act would need a statutory definition of food. This is the substance of the measure, not the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What is clear to Te Pāti Māori, and our whānau living in poverty, is that everybody against this bill is blinded by their privilege.
focus.explanation: Strip out the characterisation of opponents and nothing about the measure remains. The bill is mentioned only to identify who is being condemned; no mechanism, cost or outcome is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Let me ask who in this House—members and Speaker—needs a new definition of what “food” is. We know what food is. We don’t need a separate tax definition to tell us what food means, so I am opposed to this overhaul of word game that the member is proposing.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to obviousness: from the premise that ordinary speakers know what food means, she concludes tax legislation needs no definition of it. The premise is about common usage, the conclusion is about statutory drafting, and nothing offered bridges them.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We are talking about better technologies, so that our people, our tradies, and our companies can have higher profit return, and, therefore, pay higher wages for their employees.
rigor.explanation: An explicit 'therefore' chain from technology to profit to wages. The second link — that higher profits are passed through to employees — is asserted rather than supported; the conclusion outruns the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We did a questionnaire on one of my social media pages, where we asked people how much they were paying for GST—what was the average cost that they were paying in a supermarket. The average was $400; $80 a week on GST. That’s $320 a month. That’s $3,840 per year that they would keep in their pocket.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a self-selected poll of the speaker's own social media followers to what households would save, and then assumes the whole of the GST would be handed back at the checkout rather than partly retained by retailers. Unrepresentative sample plus an unstated pass-through premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If you were to put more effort into chasing down tax evaders who are costing this country $7 billion a year, you’d make a hell of a lot more money than on regressive tax like GST on kai.
rigor.explanation: Infers that enforcement would raise more than the GST forgone, which requires that a large share of an estimated evasion figure is actually recoverable by additional effort. Nothing is offered on recovery rates or enforcement cost, so the conclusion assumes the gap equals the yield.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re encouraging people to look into baking a bigger cake so that every single New Zealander can have more to share.
specificity.explanation: Offered as the government's alternative to the bill, so it is trying to convey substance, but it carries only a metaphor — no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named programme that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I heard from this side of the House that $2.6 billion will be lost if we were to take GST off food, but you want to give $3 billion in tax cuts to landlords—absolutely makes no sense to me.
specificity.explanation: Two named fiscal quantities attached to two named policies. Someone could go to the costings and check both numbers; that is what this attribute rewards, independent of whether they are right.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I heard from this side of the House that $2.6 billion will be lost if we were to take GST off food, but you want to give $3 billion in tax cuts to landlords—absolutely makes no sense to me.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the fiscal cost of restoring landlords' interest deductibility is about $3 billion, set against a $2.6 billion cost for removing GST from food. What is being compared — annual versus forecast-period totals — is left unstated and is what a check must settle.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published Treasury/IRD fiscal costings current at March 2024 for (a) revenue forgone from zero-rating food for GST and (b) the cost of restoring interest deductibility for residential rental property. True if the official figures are approximately $2.6b and $3b on comparable bases; false if either is materially different, or if a multi-year total is being set against an annual figure.

veracity.statement: Just remember that New Zealand wouldn’t be an isolated case to take GST off food; Canada, Australia, Mexico, Ireland, and the UK have all done it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Canada, Australia, Mexico, Ireland and the United Kingdom all remove their consumption tax from food. The claim is about basic food generally, not about every food item — prepared and restaurant food is treated differently in several of these systems.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The consumption-tax legislation and revenue-authority guidance of each of the five named countries as at March 2024, on whether basic food or groceries are zero-rated or exempt from GST/VAT. True if all five exclude basic food from the standard rate; false if any one applies the standard rate to basic groceries.

veracity.statement: If you were to put more effort into chasing down tax evaders who are costing this country $7 billion a year, you’d make a hell of a lot more money than on regressive tax like GST on kai.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific annual cost of tax evasion to New Zealand of $7 billion. What must be checked is whether an official estimate of that magnitude exists, and whether it measures evasion rather than the broader tax gap including avoidance and error.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IRD's published tax gap and hidden-economy estimates for the most recent period before March 2024. True if an official estimate puts annual tax evasion at approximately $7 billion; false if the published estimates are materially lower or if no official estimate supports a figure of that size.

civility.statement: Interesting, I’ve just been interjected by the former Minister of commerce, and I’ve just got to say that I find it staggering that the previous Government didn’t take the opportunity to progress this issue when it was in Government, and particularly that Minister who progressed many things—and, in fact, I’m having to tidy up some of them at the moment.
civility.explanation: Not a direct insult, but the aside that the former Minister 'progressed many things' which Bayly is now 'having to tidy up' is a sarcastic dig at that individual's competence rather than at the policy. Pointed and edging onto the person.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Interesting, I’ve just been interjected by the former Minister of commerce, and I’ve just got to say that I find it staggering that the previous Government didn’t take the opportunity to progress this issue when it was in Government, and particularly that Minister who progressed many things—and, in fact, I’m having to tidy up some of them at the moment.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point underneath — the previous government did not act on director address disclosure — but no measure, figure or outcome is named, and the weight of the remark is on the other side's record and Bayly's own clean-up work.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Look, I agree with the member—it is an important issue—but the reason we are going to oppose it is that we will be introducing a revised Companies Act, which will include amendments to it, which will address this issue, in particular.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure and the legislative alternative to it; states a reason for the position that turns on policy rather than on the party proposing it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As a true Marxist, I’m not really one to stand up for the petite bourgeoisie, but I think what this bill is trying to do is address structural issues relating to violence that may occur as a result of the way we have created a disclosure regime that does put people at risk of violence because of how easy, as the previous speaker actually demonstrated, it is to find some of that information.
focus.explanation: Engages the purpose of the bill before the House and the disclosure regime it would change, and takes the opposing speaker's demonstration on its merits rather than attacking his party.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So clause 4 of the bill, amending section 215 of the Companies Act, allows replacing a director’s residential address with a service address in public records, provided new section 360D conditions are met.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the section amended, the parent Act, the mechanism and the gating provision. Anyone could pull the bill and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So just before I came to the House, I went to the Companies Office and I put in “Brian Smith”—and, by the way, I think it went to 51 pages, but I’ve just printed off a few of them.
specificity.explanation: Names the source (the Companies Office), the exact search term and a figure for the result volume — a checkable, reproducible demonstration rather than an assertion.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Look, I agree with the member—it is an important issue—but the reason we are going to oppose it is that we will be introducing a revised Companies Act, which will include amendments to it, which will address this issue, in particular.
specificity.explanation: Names a vehicle (a revised Companies Act) and the issue it will cover, but supplies no timeframe, no drafting detail and no indication of what the amendments would actually do.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As a true Marxist, I’m not really one to stand up for the petite bourgeoisie, but I think what this bill is trying to do is address structural issues relating to violence that may occur as a result of the way we have created a disclosure regime that does put people at risk of violence because of how easy, as the previous speaker actually demonstrated, it is to find some of that information.
specificity.explanation: Policy-directed but carries almost no checkable content: 'structural issues relating to violence' and 'a disclosure regime' name no provision, mechanism, figure or affected group. High focus, low specificity.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The lack of logic is: if we accepted this solution to this important issue and we allowed people to strike off their residential address, the lack of logic is that if they are a shareholder—and for many smaller entities, the directors are also the shareholder of those companies—the shareholder residential address would not be changed under the provisions in this bill, and that is rather much of a glaring issue.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure: if director-and-shareholder overlap is common in small companies and the bill touches only the director entry, the protection is defeated by the shareholder entry. The conclusion follows from the premises offered; no fallacy or appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, news flash: they already do. Because if you open a business or a company via an accountant, the accountant’s office is there—which I can tell you our business was.
rigor.explanation: A real inference answering a real objection: if the concealment the objectors fear is already available, the objection does not count against the bill. The conclusion follows, though the supporting premise rests on a single instance — her own business.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So this bill actually allows for an alternative address, but, really, what is the benefit from having any address publicly available? I really, honestly don’t see the benefits.
rigor.explanation: Argument from personal incredulity and absence of evidence: the conclusion that public addresses have no benefit rests only on the speaker not being able to think of one, and it does not engage the accountability rationale other speakers in the same debate had just given.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The lack of logic is: if we accepted this solution to this important issue and we allowed people to strike off their residential address, the lack of logic is that if they are a shareholder—and for many smaller entities, the directors are also the shareholder of those companies—the shareholder residential address would not be changed under the provisions in this bill, and that is rather much of a glaring issue.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill, as drafted, leaves a shareholder's residential address publicly visible even where the same person's director address has been suppressed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Companies (Address Information) Amendment Bill as introduced. True if its amendments reach only the director address entries (s 215 and new s 360D) and leave the shareholder register's residential address requirement (s 87 of the Companies Act 1993) untouched; false if the bill also provides for suppressing a shareholder's residential address.

veracity.statement: So just before I came to the House, I went to the Companies Office and I put in “Brian Smith”—and, by the way, I think it went to 51 pages, but I’ve just printed off a few of them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a name search of the public register for "Brian Smith" returned about 51 pages of results, offered as evidence that names alone do not uniquely identify directors.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: A Companies Office companies-register search on the director/officer name "Brian Smith" as at March 2024. True if the result set runs to approximately 51 pages at the register's default page size; false if it returns materially fewer (or the search cannot return anything like that volume).

veracity.statement: Well, news flash: they already do. Because if you open a business or a company via an accountant, the accountant’s office is there—which I can tell you our business was.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that companies registered through an accountant already show the accountant's office rather than the individual's address, so larger companies' directors can already keep their addresses off the register.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The registration and register-disclosure requirements of the Companies Act 1993 and a sample of register entries for accountant-registered companies. True if a director's address shown on the public register may be the accountant's office; false if s 214 requires each director's actual residential address to be entered and displayed regardless of who registered the company or where the registered office and address for service are.

rigor.statement: New Zealand First is not going to support this bill, and that is, basically, on the basis that we think there is other legislation, which has been talked about already in this House, which is going to be more comprehensive, and we don’t want to take too much of the House’s time—valuable time—to consider one bill when a more comprehensive approach is planned to be taken.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: oppose this bill because a broader alternative is coming. The gap is that the alternative is asserted rather than shown — nothing is offered about its content or timing, so the conclusion rests on an appeal to unseen forthcoming work.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think we are a little concerned about that concept of the “mental safety”, because that could be—you know, physical safety is one thing, but mental safety is something which we could see some fairly long bows drawn, and what we don’t want to see is people hiding behind those sort of things and it being too hard to administer.
rigor.explanation: Argues from the breadth of the term 'mental safety' to predicted misuse and unworkability, but nothing connects the two — a slippery-slope move with no example, no administrative evidence and no comparison to how similar tests are applied.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We have something concrete in front of us now that is going to keep people safe. That is why we need to be voting in support of this.
rigor.explanation: The certain-now versus uncertain-later comparison is a legitimate inference and supports acting on the bill. But the premise doing the work — that this bill will keep people safe — is assumed rather than argued, so the conclusion runs ahead of what was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reason you want to be able to find a director is because the director in many circumstances is liable for the operations of the company—legally liable. So you need to be able to go and track them down for legal purposes to serve a notice on the company or for shareholders to serve notices on the director for similar purposes.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the premise: directors carry personal legal liability, therefore a means of serving notice on them is needed. A stated legal mechanism supports a stated purpose, and it rebuts the media-doorstepping rationale on its own terms rather than by characterising whoever advanced it.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: New Zealand First is not going to support this bill, and that is, basically, on the basis that we think there is other legislation, which has been talked about already in this House, which is going to be more comprehensive, and we don’t want to take too much of the House’s time—valuable time—to consider one bill when a more comprehensive approach is planned to be taken.
specificity.explanation: A reason is given and, read with his later reference to Andrew Bayly's holistic approach, a source for the alternative is named — but no bill, no scope, no timeframe and no indication of what the broader approach would contain.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So finding the balance, here, between the safety of the business person and their responsibility to the people who are their clients is a really, really important one.
specificity.explanation: States only that a balance matters. No threshold, no mechanism, no test for where the balance should sit and nothing anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think we are a little concerned about that concept of the “mental safety”, because that could be—you know, physical safety is one thing, but mental safety is something which we could see some fairly long bows drawn, and what we don’t want to see is people hiding behind those sort of things and it being too hard to administer.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the bill's own test — what counts as a safety ground and whether it can be administered. No party framing at all; the objection is to the mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And we’re hearing work’s coming, but we don’t know when that is or when those discussions will actually take place.
focus.explanation: Engages the substantive question actually in dispute — the timing and certainty of the Government's promised wider Companies Act work versus the bill in front of the House. No party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Institute of Directors have been calling for this change for quite some time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Institute of Directors has been a long-standing public advocate for removing directors' home addresses from the public Companies Office register — a claim about the organisation's past public position, not about the bill's merits.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Institute of Directors NZ public submissions, media statements and policy papers on the Companies Office register; true if the IoD has publicly advocated allowing directors to keep residential addresses off the public register over a period of years before March 2024, false if no such advocacy predates the bill.

veracity.statement: But the one issue that I really started to get a bit antsy about when I was reading it was in November of last year when there was an article that was put up about an Auckland company director who felt forced to break the law to keep her home address off the Companies Office register when she was persecuted by a man with a history of violence towards her.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific, dated media report: November 2023, an Auckland company director, breaking the register's address requirement to escape an identified violent individual.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand news archives for November 2023; true if an article was published that month reporting an Auckland company director who gave a false or non-residential address on the Companies Office register to keep her home address from a man with a history of violence toward her, false if no such November 2023 article exists.

veracity.statement: In fact, New Zealand is on a grey list for that reason because it’s not possible to see who owns what and where funds are going because of the ability to hide shareholdings.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as present fact that New Zealand is grey-listed by some international body because beneficial ownership of companies cannot be traced. The claim is about listing status, not about whether ownership is hard to trace.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The FATF list of Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring (the 'grey list') as at March 2024, and any comparable named international 'grey list' on beneficial-ownership transparency (e.g. EU or OECD listings); true if New Zealand appears on such a list, false if New Zealand appears on none of them.

civility.statement: And, I mean, it beggared belief to me that Andrew Bayly would come into the House and talk about a bill that touches on privacy and start reading out people’s home addresses. It shows how out of touch he is, that the very thing that Deborah Russell has brought this bill to the House to protect, he sits there and violates.
civility.explanation: Starts from a specific act but lands on the person: 'shows how out of touch he is' is a judgement on a named member's character rather than on the argument, delivered with a sneer ('beggared belief', 'he sits there and violates'). Short of sustained abuse, but past pointed-and-robust.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As a journalist, I actually did uncover quite a large story. It was actually an exclusive story and I did about three or four kind of exposés on this specific company that was fraudulently ripping a lot of its clients off. So that was not on, and that company was not doing a good thing. So I suppose what I’m trying to get to here is that, you know, that information on the Companies Office website actually can be very beneficial in some cases.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote: a single personal experience is generalised into a conclusion about the value of the register. The inference also misses its target — her story turned on identifying who the directors and shareholders were, which the bill does not touch; it withholds residential addresses. Nothing offered connects the anecdote to the provision being opposed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s not available to the hairdressers and the tradies that Laura Trask spoke about tonight, and that’s why we should make this urgent change, even if there is further change coming later, which I welcome.
rigor.explanation: A parity argument that tracks: if large operators can already withhold addresses through an alternative structure and small operators cannot, an unequal protection follows and the remedy follows from it. The 'even if further change is coming' clause pre-empts the delay objection rather than dodging it. Small gap — it assumes equal need for the protection rather than showing it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is a sensible thing. I hope members in all parties can listen to this debate and change their minds here and now, because there is nothing in this bill which would create harm, there is nothing in this bill which would put the directors in a worse position than they were before, and there’s certainly nothing in this bill that would put shareholders in a worse position than they were before.
rigor.explanation: Proof by repetition: the same 'no harm' assertion is restated three times with nothing offered to support any of them. It also fails to engage the counter-consideration she herself set out earlier — that limited liability is granted on the condition that people can find you to settle debts — which is precisely the harm a critic would allege.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But how to move forward is not this specific bill. We just need to make sure that we don’t have people who are manipulating the system and potentially, you know, who could evade fraud or other serious legal matters.
civility.explanation: Rejects the bill squarely on its substance in a genuinely contested debate. No person is attacked, no bad faith is imputed to the sponsor — the expected standard, met.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But how to move forward is not this specific bill. We just need to make sure that we don’t have people who are manipulating the system and potentially, you know, who could evade fraud or other serious legal matters.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure before the House and the risk she says it carries. No party framing, no reference to the other team's record. Vague, but vagueness is Specificity's problem, not Focus's.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, what I was saying about the commerce Minister coming down here and telling us he’s reviewing the Companies Act—that is good news. I’m really interested in that. When? When will the Companies Act be reviewed?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny of a named commitment: the Minister has said he will review a specific statute, and she presses for the date. Names the policy and the missing element, with no party-bashing content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But how to move forward is not this specific bill. We just need to make sure that we don’t have people who are manipulating the system and potentially, you know, who could evade fraud or other serious legal matters.
specificity.explanation: States a direction with no content: no mechanism for how the system would be manipulated, no alternative route named, no threshold or safeguard proposed. 'Make sure we don't have people manipulating the system' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They can use things that already enjoy the protections of limited liability, but still allow directors to not have their addresses published—things like limited partnerships which allow them to have all of their address details withheld from public view.
specificity.explanation: Names the actual mechanism — limited liability without published director addresses, via limited partnerships — rather than gesturing at 'corporate structuring'. Someone could go and check the register. No figures or dates, which is what keeps it off 1.0.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: They can use things that already enjoy the protections of limited liability, but still allow directors to not have their addresses published—things like limited partnerships which allow them to have all of their address details withheld from public view.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that limited partnerships permit all address details to be withheld from public view, which is offered as the reason large operators already have the protection the bill would extend. The load-bearing word is 'all' — limited partner details are restricted, but general partner details are recorded on the public register.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Limited Partnerships Act 2008 and the public Limited Partnerships Register on the Companies Office site: true if a limited partnership can be registered with no partner address details visible on public search; false if the register publicly displays address details for general partners (or for any partner class) in the same way the Companies Register does for directors.

veracity.statement: We want to make sure that small-business owners, who make up the majority of business owners in New Zealand, have the ability to enjoy the same kinds of protections that their big-business - owning counterparts have.
veracity.explanation: The embedded factual claim is that small-business owners are the majority of business owners in New Zealand. It is the premise doing the work in her fairness argument, and it is checkable against the official business-count series.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Business Demography Statistics / MBIE Small Business Factsheet for the year of the statement: true if enterprises meeting the standard small-business definition (fewer than 20 employees) are more than 50% of all NZ enterprises; false if they are 50% or fewer.

veracity.statement: If I can refer to the latest transparency.org.nz recent review on New Zealand’s latest corruption performance index, CPI, ranked in 2023, about conducting businesses in New Zealand, we are ranked top three in the world.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand placed in the top three of Transparency International's 2023 Corruption Perceptions Index.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index for 2023 (published January 2024): true if New Zealand is ranked 1st, 2nd or 3rd; false if ranked 4th or lower.

veracity.statement: Secondly, I also do not support this bill to the House because we, as New Zealand—and this is according to the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment official information, that in New Zealand, small and micro-business, including the self-employed, make up 97 percent of all companies registered in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, sourced to MBIE, that small and micro businesses including the self-employed account for 97 percent of all companies registered in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's published small business statistics (Small Business Factsheet / business demography data) for the year referenced: true if the small-and-micro share of registered businesses is 97% ± 2 points, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: But it did only take about 30 seconds to find the Minister of commerce’s home address.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a sitting Minister's residential address was retrievable from the public Companies Register in roughly half a minute — i.e. that directors' residential addresses are published and name-searchable there.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Companies Office register (companiesoffice.govt.nz) director search: true if a director's residential address is displayed publicly and retrievable by a name search in under a minute, false if residential addresses are withheld, require an account, or are not name-searchable.

specificity.statement: Secondly, I also do not support this bill to the House because we, as New Zealand—and this is according to the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment official information, that in New Zealand, small and micro-business, including the self-employed, make up 97 percent of all companies registered in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Carries a named source (MBIE), a defined category (small and micro business including self-employed) and a figure (97 percent) — checkable as stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But, of course, this bill does not seek to enable all directors to use different addresses; it is just in the case where a director has serious fears for their own safety or for the safety of someone who lives with them, and they sign a statutory declaration to that effect, and then they can apply to have their name removed from the register and a different address used instead.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the actual mechanism: an eligibility threshold (serious fears for the director's or a co-resident's safety), the procedural gate (a statutory declaration), and the remedy (application to substitute a different address). Someone could check this against the bill's text.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I don’t understand how substituting the address for a director address on the company’s website will be helpful, when you can literally go to the next page, look at the shareholder, and identify the same person with her or his address.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: given her premise that director and shareholder are the same person in 97% of registrations, suppressing only the director address would not conceal it. The conclusion largely follows, but there is a gap — the bill applies only to directors with a declared safety fear, so the overlap rate for that subset is not established.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But that is precisely the sort of problem that can be ironed out at the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee.
rigor.explanation: Engages the substantive objection that shareholder records defeat the bill's purpose, but answers it by deferral rather than argument: nothing is offered to show the defect is fixable within the bill's scope, so the conclusion that the objection is no barrier to a first reading rests on an assertion about process.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In principle, I do acknowledge there is a need to protect the privacy and safety of our own people, but I do not support this bill, because it’s just simply not good enough.
civility.explanation: Blunt rejection of the bill in a contested first reading, aimed entirely at the measure's adequacy; concedes the sponsor's underlying concern and attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The last speaker, Nancy Lu, did raise an interesting point about transparency, pointing out that New Zealand does have very transparent businesses, and it’s a very good point.
civility.explanation: Replying to an opponent who has just moved to kill her bill — ample opportunity to sneer — she instead credits the opposing argument on its merits before answering it.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I’d like to begin this final speech by saying, well, I’m pretty sad that this bill looks like it won’t make it through the first reading.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Companies (Address Information) Amendment Bill will not pass its first reading in the vote taken at the conclusion of the debate.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The division record for the question that the Companies (Address Information) Amendment Bill be now read a first time: the forecast is true if the noes exceed the ayes and the bill is defeated, false if the ayes prevail and the bill proceeds to select committee.

specificity.statement: Section 24 of the Local Electoral Act 2001 qualifies individuals that own property outside the area they reside in to vote in that area in addition to their place of residence.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact statutory provision and states precisely what it does — a listener could go and read section 24 and check the description.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Theoretically, with 78 local authorities representing all areas in New Zealand, including the 110 community boards and 21 local boards, an individual could vote 209 times if they owned property in each.
specificity.explanation: Three counts and a derived total, all checkable against published local government structures.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Theoretically, with 78 local authorities representing all areas in New Zealand, including the 110 community boards and 21 local boards, an individual could vote 209 times if they owned property in each.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the number of separately-elected local bodies in New Zealand and hence the theoretical maximum number of ballots one property owner could cast.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Internal Affairs / Local Government NZ published counts of local authorities, community boards and local boards as at 2024; true if there are 78 local authorities, 110 community boards and 21 local boards (summing to 209), false if the counts differ materially.

veracity.statement: Although the number of individuals enrolled on the ratepayer roll is relatively low—7,277 in the 2022 local body election—unfortunately, so is the turnout at local body elections, thus the potential for a well-organised group to influence an election is a very real possibility.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific national enrolment figure for the ratepayer roll at the 2022 local body elections.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral officers' returns / DIA local authority election statistics for the 2022 local body elections; true if the national total of ratepayer-roll enrolments was 7,277, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Perhaps a better example of that is the Thames-Coromandel District Council, where 8.42 percent of voters are ratepayer electors.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the share of the Thames-Coromandel electoral roll made up of non-resident ratepayer electors.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Thames-Coromandel District Council electoral officer's roll figures for the most recent local body election; true if ratepayer electors were 8.42% of enrolled voters, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: I’ll give an example: in the Wellington mayoral election 2019, my good friend Andy Foster, now a member in this House, won the chains by 62 votes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the winning margin in the 2019 Wellington mayoralty.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Wellington City Council's declared final result for the 2019 mayoral election; true if Andy Foster's winning margin was 62 votes, false if the declared margin differs.

rigor.statement: In that election, there were 219 ratepayer electors, and I’m sure Mr Foster will be happy to vote for my bill to ensure no accusation would ever be made that out-of-towners influenced an election—obviously, that’s absolutely no aspersion on Mr Foster or the merits of his victory; the point being that it does highlight this anomaly.
rigor.explanation: The inference is that because the ratepayer-elector pool (219) exceeded the winning margin (62), the roll is capable of deciding a race. That much follows arithmetically, and he is careful to claim only a potential rather than an actual effect. The gap is that it assumes those electors could vote as a bloc, which is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: To those who would argue no taxation without representation, then that argument would take us back to the 1800s, where that logic would mean anyone who owned a business in a general electorate anywhere other than where they reside should be entitled to vote in that electorate as well.
rigor.explanation: A reductio ad absurdum against the taxation-without-representation objection, extending it to parliamentary electorates. The move is a real inference about the policy, but the analogy is imperfect — rates are levied on the property itself by the very body being elected, which is the disanalogy the reductio does not address.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: He had an ally in the current Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon, who told Newsroom in 2023, in explaining why he would not work with Te Pāti Māori after the election, that it was because his party stands for one person, one vote.
focus.explanation: The one-person-one-vote principle is the substance of the bill, so citing an opponent's stated position on it is on-policy. It is discounted because the citation is routed through coalition-formation politics rather than the ratepayer roll itself.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Given those statements by both leaders, I’ll be disappointed if those parties don’t support my bill.
civility.explanation: He holds two opposing leaders to their own recorded words on the very principle at issue — a place where it would be easy to sneer or impute hypocrisy — and instead states only that he would be disappointed. Pressure entirely on the position, none on the people.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The member opposite discussed turnout in local elections and how it was so low, and his answer for low turnout was to reduce the number of eligible voters, which doesn’t make any sense at all.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: it identifies a tension between the stated concern (low turnout) and the mechanism (fewer eligible voters). The conclusion tracks, though it treats the bill's purpose as turnout-raising when the proponent's case was about franchise principle, which is a partial strawman.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: First and foremost is the removal of property owners’ ability to vote in local elections. This is the core concept of taxation without representation, and it flies in the face of natural justice.
rigor.explanation: An argument from principle with a real gap: it asserts the "taxation without representation" label rather than establishing that a property charge in a jurisdiction one does not live in is the relevant kind of taxation. "Flies in the face of natural justice" is assertion, not support.
rigor.subject: speaker
