focus.explanation: Engages a specific decision in the bill — the extended deadline for the tax treatment of North Island flood victims — and asks whether the timeframe is adequate. Names the measure and the affected group; no reference to the other party at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, by reverting to the old practice of allowing the full deduction—well, it’s going to be 80 percent in the next tax year and then a full deduction in the following tax year—in fact, the Government is reverting to the practice of giving a really concessionary treatment with respect to interest in comparison to other sort of regular expenses that people incur with respect to a residential rental property, such as insurance or rates and so on.
specificity.explanation: Carries the phase-in percentage (80 percent), the tax years involved, and names the comparator expenses (insurance, rates). Checkable against the Amendment Paper; short of 1.0 only because no amounts or revenue figures are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And on this side of the House, we are focused on making life easier for people to be productive in our economy, to earn more income, to hire more people, and to ensure that that flows to those that need it most.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic goals — productivity, income, hiring — with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named measure. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, by reverting to the old practice of allowing the full deduction—well, it’s going to be 80 percent in the next tax year and then a full deduction in the following tax year—in fact, the Government is reverting to the practice of giving a really concessionary treatment with respect to interest in comparison to other sort of regular expenses that people incur with respect to a residential rental property, such as insurance or rates and so on.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the measure before the committee — the interest deductibility phase-in and how it compares with the treatment of other rental expenses. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In light of the advice that’s here in the information that’s provided in front of us that says Treasury recommends a brightline test of 20 years and outlining the benefits not only for our house affordability but other reasons as well, why on earth is he not only going in the other direction but absolutely dismissing the advice that Treasury, their own department, who presumably played a massive role in the development of this bill, has put in this document?
focus.explanation: Names the specific measure (the brightline period), the specific document (Treasury's advice) and the specific outcome at issue (house affordability). Textbook scrutiny of a named policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Except the interesting thing is that if a person was caught by the brightline test—so they paid tax on the capital gains—then they could claim the interest deductions as part of that tax calculation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the previous Government's interest limitation rules, interest that was otherwise denied could be claimed against a brightline-taxable disposal of the property.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The interest limitation provisions of the Income Tax Act 2007 as enacted in 2022 (and Inland Revenue guidance on them); true if denied interest was deductible against income from a brightline-taxed sale of the property, false if interest remained denied on such a sale.

veracity.statement: I think it is also important to note that in regards to the ability to take that interest deduction, under the prior Government’s rules, the deduction for interest in regards to residential property, even in circumstances where the property did not achieve or obtain a capital gain, was denied.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government's interest limitation rules denied interest deductions on residential rental property irrespective of whether the property produced a capital gain.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The interest limitation rules in the Income Tax Act 2007 as enacted in 2022; true if denial of interest deductibility applied without any test of whether a capital gain arose, false if the rules made deductibility contingent on a gain.

veracity.statement: And my question is specifically around the advice that he’s receiving, given that even in their own documentation that’s provided here, Treasury not only suggests that doing what the Government’s proposing is the wrong idea; Treasury proposes that they push it out—they push it out to 20 years, because what they recognise is, as is intended with a brightline test, it discourages speculation in the market.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Treasury's published advice on this bill both advised against shortening the brightline test and recommended extending it to 20 years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Treasury regulatory impact statement / departmental advice published with the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023–24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill; true if Treasury's advice recommends a 20-year brightline period, false if it recommends no extension or a different period.

rigor.statement: I’d like to submit that, actually, the previous Government’s treatment of it by allowing the tax deductions when the person paid a tax on the capital gain was actually a rather more consistent treatment of interest; and, in fact, was the better treatment.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows from premises she actually laid out: deductions require a nexus with taxable income, rental interest partly funds untaxed capital gain, so allowing the deduction only where the gain is taxed matches the general rule. No fallacy; the inference tracks the stated principle.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In regards to the member’s question around the capital gains aspect in regards to the interest deduction—I mean, in effect, what we’re doing here, in regards to allowing an interest deduction on residential property, is no different to what is allowed by someone that undertakes an interest deduction on a commercial property, which was allowed under the previous rules, or likewise for a farm, for example, that is a similar entity that may be funded proportionately by debt and equity.
rigor.explanation: An argument from analogy with commercial property and farms, which does bear on the consistency point. But it leaves a real gap: the question asked was whether apportionment between taxed rent and untaxed gain was considered, and the analogy is asserted rather than shown to dispose of it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You don’t have to travel too far to get feedback from a number of experts within the tax field that acknowledge that a 10-year brightline versus a two-year derives significantly more compliance costs.
rigor.explanation: Bare appeal to unnamed authority: the compliance-cost conclusion rests entirely on unidentified 'experts' with no figure, study or mechanism offered to connect brightline length to compliance cost.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: But, specifically, we’re talking here about affordability of homes, and in doing what the Government is proposing, it will do the reverse of what the justification was and the rationale behind bringing it in in the first place—even albeit for two years—right when the housing crisis was really getting going, to try and discourage speculation within the market.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that shortening the brightline test will increase property speculation rather than discourage it — the opposite of the test's stated purpose.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: CoreLogic / REINZ buyer-classification data on the investor share of residential purchases, and Inland Revenue or CoreLogic data on properties resold within two years, comparing the two years after the 1 July 2024 change with the two years before; true if investor share and short-hold resale activity rise materially, false if they are flat or fall.

civility.statement: In light of the advice that’s here in the information that’s provided in front of us that says Treasury recommends a brightline test of 20 years and outlining the benefits not only for our house affordability but other reasons as well, why on earth is he not only going in the other direction but absolutely dismissing the advice that Treasury, their own department, who presumably played a massive role in the development of this bill, has put in this document?
civility.explanation: Sharp — 'why on earth', 'absolutely dismissing' — but the target throughout is the Minister's decision and his handling of departmental advice, not his character or competence as a person.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, the trustee tax rate at the moment is 33 percent but in the bill as drafted, the trustee tax rate—applying from 1 April next year, provided the bill goes through in time—will change to 39 percent.
specificity.explanation: Two exact rates, the commencement date, and the instrument that carries the change; fully checkable against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It seemed like a quite a complex web of trustees and beneficiaries but, quite simply, the definition in regards to what is qualifying within a disabled beneficiary trust is that the person must be disabled and there is a definition in regards to that, within the fact they need to be in receipt of a child disability allowance, a supported living payment, disability allowance or a jobseeker health conditions and disabilities allowance for longer than six months.
specificity.explanation: Names the four qualifying benefits and the six-month receipt period — a test someone could apply to a case.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I do note here that there’s a proposed new section CZ 26B of the Income Tax Act, which is to be inserted by new clause 18C, which would ensure that the brightline and other time-related tests don’t apply to properties that have been affected by one of the North Island adverse weather events, and I do just want to seek that certainty that that is both of those North Island events.
specificity.explanation: Cites the inserting clause, the new section, the affected tests and the class of property — precise enough for the Minister to answer without clarification.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Given that 84 percent of estates have trustee income below $10,000, does this bill as amended reduce the administration costs of deceased estates, and then, if it does, does it do that over the three-year period discussed by the Finance and Expenditure Committee for the administration of those estates?
specificity.explanation: A figure, a threshold and a named timeframe from the committee report; a precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Now, the trustee tax rate at the moment is 33 percent but in the bill as drafted, the trustee tax rate—applying from 1 April next year, provided the bill goes through in time—will change to 39 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the existing trustee tax rate, the rate the bill substitutes, and when the new rate takes effect.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023–24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill as reported back from the Finance and Expenditure Committee: true if the current trustee rate is 33% and the bill sets it at 39% commencing on the 1 April she names; false if either rate differs or the commencement falls on a different 1 April.

veracity.statement: But in regards to the points raised by the member, there is no fiscal cost to the rollover relief, in the context that these aspects have already been considered as part of the broader baselines and therefore there’s no additional appropriation required.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the rollover relief provisions carry no fiscal cost because they are already inside existing baselines and need no new appropriation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's departmental disclosure statement and regulatory impact statement, plus the Finance and Expenditure Committee commentary on the North Island weather event rollover relief: true if they record no forecast revenue impact or additional appropriation attributable to the relief; false if any foregone or deferred revenue is quantified against it.

veracity.statement: Given that 84 percent of estates have trustee income below $10,000, does this bill as amended reduce the administration costs of deceased estates, and then, if it does, does it do that over the three-year period discussed by the Finance and Expenditure Committee for the administration of those estates?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a distributional statistic about deceased estates — that 84 percent earn under $10,000 of trustee income — as the premise of the question.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue's regulatory impact statement and the Finance and Expenditure Committee report on the trustee tax rate changes: true if they state that approximately 84% of estates have trustee income below $10,000; false if the proportion or the income threshold materially differs.

rigor.statement: I hope the Minister can see the question I’m asking, and it is: if we’re trying to ensure that a person with disabilities is taxed at an appropriate rate—done through a disability beneficiary trust—then why not for other trusts of which they happen to be a beneficiary as well, just because they’re not disabled beneficiary trusts.
rigor.explanation: An argument from consistency of purpose: if the concession exists because a disabled person should face a lower rate, the same reason reaches income they receive from other trusts. The inference tracks the stated purpose, but leaves a gap — it does not address that those other trusts also have non-disabled beneficiaries, which is what would make apportionment hard.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The simple reason—to the member’s question around, in effect, the ability for someone who is not disabled and why they can and can’t be in that—is that the rules are set up to ensure that non-disabled persons don’t, in effect, benefit from the exemption that we have provided.
rigor.explanation: The anti-leakage rationale does support excluding non-disabled beneficiaries where the whole trust is treated alike, so it is not merely circular. But it assumes the concession cannot be apportioned within a mixed trust, which is precisely the premise the question put in issue — a real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But in regards to the points raised by the member, there is no fiscal cost to the rollover relief, in the context that these aspects have already been considered as part of the broader baselines and therefore there’s no additional appropriation required.
rigor.explanation: Equivocates between two different things: that no further appropriation is needed supports 'no new spending decision', not 'no fiscal cost'. Deferred revenue recognition is a cost to the Crown whether or not it sits inside an existing baseline, so the conclusion overreaches the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I just want to ask the Minister: how does the rollover relief provisions which apply for a 10-year brightline, which are covered in the Amendment Paper that was introduced last year in 2023, which is now in the revised track version of the bill, align with the brightline test which is now in the Minister’s name in the Amendment Paper?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: the interaction between a named Amendment Paper's rollover relief and the new brightline period. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I hope that the Minister of Revenue might, please, explain why the Government is prioritising these late changes to Government tax cuts for landlords and other relatively minor amendments instead of addressing more ways that tax amendments could prioritise more productive investment.
focus.explanation: About the substance of what the bill does and what it omits — the tax treatment of property against investment elsewhere. "Tax cuts for landlords" is partisan characterisation rather than the measure's own terms, which pulls it below 1.0, but the point is a policy-priority point, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I just want to ask the Minister: how does the rollover relief provisions which apply for a 10-year brightline, which are covered in the Amendment Paper that was introduced last year in 2023, which is now in the revised track version of the bill, align with the brightline test which is now in the Minister’s name in the Amendment Paper?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific instrument (the 2023 Amendment Paper), the specific provisions (rollover relief), the two brightline periods, and asks for start dates. Checkable and actionable; short of 1.0 only because no dates or figures are supplied by the speaker.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, it’s sitting in clause 39, which inserts new section HC 39, and, in particular, in section HC 39(3), “A ‘disabled beneficiary’, for an income year,” is a person who receives some various sorts of benefits under the Social Security Act.
specificity.explanation: Cites the clause, the inserted section, the subsection and the statute the definition depends on. Anyone could turn to the page and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The decision that has been made is that for those trusts, the amendments that we’ve tabled would provide that a deceased estate would be subject to a 33 percent tax rate on trustee income for the incoming year of death and the following three income years.
specificity.explanation: A rate, a base and a duration: 33 percent on trustee income for the year of death plus three income years. Directly checkable against the tabled amendment.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The third question I have for the Minister in this contribution is whether a trust can be both a de minimis trust—and that is dealt with in the Finance and Expenditure Committee’s report—and a deceased estate. I’m asking that because, if so, the question is: could it continue to get the lower rate if the trustee income was below $10,000?
specificity.explanation: A precise question: names the two trust categories at issue, the source that deals with one of them, and the $10,000 trustee-income threshold that would decide the answer. A precise question counts as fully as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have a very high level of investment in property, largely driven by untaxed capital gains, and there could be some more low-impact, job-rich aspects encouraged by a more imaginative tax regime.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a target (untaxed capital gains) but proposes nothing concrete: no tax named, no rate, no threshold, no timeframe. "Low-impact, job-rich aspects" and "a more imaginative tax regime" commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I’d just like it if the Minister could clearly step it out, because the brightline test has, over the years, changed from two, to five, to 10, and it’s gone back to two.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the sequence of statutory brightline periods for residential land in New Zealand: introduced at two years, extended to five, extended to ten, and now reduced back to two.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The amending Acts to the Income Tax Act 2007 setting the brightline period: true if the successive statutory periods were 2 years (Taxation (Bright-line Test for Residential Land) Act 2015), then 5 years (2018), then 10 years (2021), then 2 years (2024); false if any step in that sequence differs.

veracity.statement: The Productivity Commission—or should I say the late Productivity Commission—did criticise the fact that such a high proportion of this country’s wealth, whether it’s investment funds, whether it’s private individuals, is hugely based on property and land.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that the New Zealand Productivity Commission published criticism of the concentration of national wealth in property and land, and (by "late") that the Commission no longer exists.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published New Zealand Productivity Commission inquiry reports (e.g. its housing affordability and urban land work) plus the legislation disestablishing it; true if at least one Commission report criticises the share of national wealth held in property and land and the Commission had been disestablished before 26 March 2024, false if no such report exists or the Commission was still operating on that date.

civility.statement: And the member can interject as much as they like around the 10 years, but the member should know that, when you have to basically litigate this, if you are a lawyer for a taxpayer who has been possibly consequentially punished because of the change in the brightline, the test dates are really important around the start dates.
civility.explanation: A live interjection gave a real opportunity to turn on the interjector. She dismisses the interjection and the phrase "the member should know" is faintly condescending, but she immediately returns to the substantive point about commencement dates and attacks nobody.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As a child, he was in receipt of an ORS grant—an Ongoing Resourcing Scheme grant—but, of course, that’s an educational thing. It’s not something under the Social Security Act. So here we have what is actually a problem, and I’m not sure we can resolve it right now, but it is something we do need to have a think about.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: if the concessionary rate is keyed to Social Security Act payments, and a demonstrably disabled trust beneficiary was supported instead through an education-system grant, then the definition can exclude people it was meant to cover. A single counterexample is logically sufficient to show a definition under-inclusive, so the conclusion follows. Marked down slightly because the further step to "there must be other people" generalises from one anecdote without any estimate of how large that class is.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I can’t speak for the individual, in fact, but, as I said, the child disability allowance is the mechanism in which the Finance and Expenditure Committee assessed as the appropriate mechanism in order to deal with that.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority. The gap raised was that some disabled beneficiaries receive no Social Security Act payment at all; answering that the select committee assessed the child disability allowance as the appropriate mechanism asserts who decided, not why the excluded class is in fact covered. The conclusion does not engage the premise it is offered against.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We have a very high level of investment in property, largely driven by untaxed capital gains, and there could be some more low-impact, job-rich aspects encouraged by a more imaginative tax regime.
rigor.explanation: The causal premise (property investment is driven by untaxed capital gains) is stated rather than shown, and the leap from it to "a more imaginative tax regime" producing low-impact, job-rich investment skips the whole mechanism — nothing connects a change in tax treatment to the claimed employment outcome. The subsequent Productivity Commission reference is an appeal to authority supporting only the first half.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In some cases, it can take up to 18 months, I believe, but, in this case, it seems that this particular charity—the Emergency Alliance—has been granted overseas donee status very quickly; in fact, quite soon after the election on 26 October 2023.
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete comparator (up to 18 months for normal processing), a named organisation and a date, so the contrast she is drawing could be checked. Short of full precision because the timeframe is hedged with 'I believe' and no source is named.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So we now have a situation where a New Zealand taxpayer could be fined a sum up to $100,000 for not complying with rules that are being set by the OECD.
specificity.explanation: Names the penalty ceiling, who is liable, the triggering failure and the body that authors the rules being incorporated — concrete enough that a reader could check it against the clause. Not 1.0 because the clause and reporting requirement are identified in adjacent sentences rather than this one.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In some cases, it can take up to 18 months, I believe, but, in this case, it seems that this particular charity—the Emergency Alliance—has been granted overseas donee status very quickly; in fact, quite soon after the election on 26 October 2023.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named measure — the grant of overseas donee status to a specific organisation under the bill — rather than on the other party. The mention of the election is scene-setting for the process question, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So we now have a situation where a New Zealand taxpayer could be fined a sum up to $100,000 for not complying with rules that are being set by the OECD.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the mechanism of the measure before the committee — the penalty in clause 74's new section 139AAB and the incorporation of OECD GLoBE rules by reference. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s great to be able to respond quickly to these types of events, but we know that when there are a discretionary types of decisions and when due process is not followed, it can also lead to uncertainty and a sense of unfairness for other charities.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: discretionary decision-making without due process produces uncertainty and perceived unfairness for comparable applicants. The conclusion broadly tracks the premise, but the premise that due process was not followed here is assumed rather than established, and the harm is asserted from general principle rather than evidence — a real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Just quite quickly for the member, the Emergency Alliance is a group of existing charities, and, therefore, all of the individual members of that Emergency Alliance are already charities and, therefore, already have the status.
rigor.explanation: Equivocation, plus a circular first step. The first 'therefore' restates the premise (a group of existing charities is composed of charities); the second slides from 'are already charities' to 'already have the status', where the status at issue is overseas donee status under schedule 32, which registered charities do not automatically hold. That is the very question asked, so the conclusion assumes what it needed to show.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I just wonder if the Minister could comment, then—you know, the suggestion was proposed that the way for that potential overtaxing of a person who was a disabled person that was not in receipt of one of these particular social security allowances, was to allocate the trust income so it was taxed at the beneficiary’s own rate, but, of course, for a child, that does, then, fall foul of the minor beneficiaries’ rule.
rigor.explanation: A valid counter-example. Premise: the proposed remedy is to allocate trust income so it is taxed at the beneficiary's rate. Premise: the minor beneficiary rule taxes allocated income of a child at the trustee rate. Conclusion: the remedy fails for a beneficiary who was disabled as a child. The conclusion follows from the two rules as stated; it stops short of 1.0 only because the interaction is asserted rather than worked through against the specific exemptions in the rule.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: If we look at the recommendation from the select committee, which I did not sit on—and that’s why this has peaked my interest, because I don’t have the background to it— they recommended inserting clause 2(14C) into the bill so that the Emergency Alliance would be deemed to have had overseas donee status beginning on 26 October 2023.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the select committee recommended a specific new clause, 2(14C), deeming the Emergency Alliance to hold overseas donee status backdated to 26 October 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Finance and Expenditure Committee's report on the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023–24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill: true if the committee recommended inserting clause 2(14C) deeming the Emergency Alliance to have overseas donee status from 26 October 2023; false if no such recommendation exists, or the clause number, organisation or effective date differ materially.

veracity.statement: Again, the Finance and Expenditure Committee, in its deliberations, did look at this matter as part of their considerations, and the amount of $100,000 has been set in the context of what is applicable to other penalties for other similar sized entities.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions about the record: that the select committee considered the GLoBE country-by-country reporting penalty, and that the $100,000 maximum was set by reference to existing penalties applying to comparably sized entities.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Finance and Expenditure Committee report and the officials'/departmental report on the bill: true if they record the committee considering this penalty and justify the $100,000 figure by comparison with penalties for entities of similar size; false if the papers show the matter was not considered, or give a materially different basis for the figure.

rigor.statement: Having worked with many of the fine officials at Inland Revenue, I doubt that they would issue the assessment one day and expect the penalty to be paid the next.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real drafting question: the conclusion (the discretion will not be abused) rests on the speaker's personal acquaintance with IRD officials rather than on anything in the clause. An appeal to personal experience — mild, and she goes on to seek the assurance rather than treat it as settled, so a genuine gap but not a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The other aspect to acknowledge is that, actually, these penalties, alongside any other penalties, can be disputed by a taxpayer, like any other assessment of tax. On that basis, we’re comfortable with the amendments.
rigor.explanation: Premise and conclusion are both present and on the policy: because the penalties are disputable like any other assessment, the amendments are acceptable. The inference is not fallacious, but there is a real gap — the question asked was what the dispute procedure actually is for an ultimate owner under new section 94BB(2), and asserting that a route exists does not establish that it is adequate.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But then, looking at Part 3, which deals with the administration of tax, I want to direct the Minister’s attention to clause 69, inserting new sections 78H to 78J into the Tax Administration Act, and that’s on pages 76 through 79 of this rather dense and long bill that is in front of us.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the new sections, the parent Act and the exact pages. Anyone could turn to the provision and check what she is asking about.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So my particular question is in relation to clause 72 C, which inserts new sections 94BB to 94BD.
specificity.explanation: Pins the question to a named clause and a named range of new sections, and the surrounding passage quotes the provision and identifies the parent section (139AAB). A precise question is as checkable as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: One of the issues there was that the GloBE rules were being incorporated in our law by reference to the OECD rules, so not directly incorporated into our law but, actually, our law is going to direct multinational enterprises, and the like, to go to the OECD website in order to work out how the law applies.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fact about the drafting technique used in Part 2 of the bill: that the GloBE rules are brought into NZ law by reference to the OECD material rather than reproduced in the statute, so that taxpayers must consult the OECD rules themselves.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of Part 2 of the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023–24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill and the departmental commentary: true if the multinational top-up tax provisions apply the OECD GloBE rules by incorporation by reference to OECD-published material; false if the GloBE rules are set out in full in the NZ statute.

veracity.statement: I think it’s important to recognise that we are talking about 20 to 25 entities specifically under the global anti-base erosion rules.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a factual figure: that only about 20 to 25 entities fall within the scope of the global anti-base erosion (GloBE) rules as enacted in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue's regulatory impact statement and departmental commentary on the multinational top-up tax: true if the official estimate of in-scope groups is in the 20–25 range, false if the estimate is materially outside it (e.g. single digits or well over 50).

veracity.statement: The commissioner can use their powers to impose a penalty, but it has to be at a date that is later or further beyond the 30-day period, so just to cover that aspect.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the bill provides: that where the Commissioner specifies a due date for a penalty instead of the default, that date must fall no earlier than 30 days after the notice of assessment — i.e. 30 days is a floor, not merely a default.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the due-date provisions in clauses 74 and 75 (new sections 139AAB and the applied-GloBE penalty section) as enacted: true if the Commissioner-specified date is constrained to be no earlier than 30 days after the notice of assessment, false if the provision lets the Commissioner specify any date, including an earlier one.

civility.statement: I admire the enthusiasm from the Government members, and I’m hoping they’re going to offer some calls on this rather important part of the bill.
civility.explanation: Ironic praise aimed at Government members for staying silent — a sneer about their engagement rather than about any argument. Short of a personal insult, but it is directed at the members rather than the substance, so below the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And, again, the member on the other side may mock this particular element of interest and penalties, but we are dealing with large multinational entities who have complex tax affairs, and if the Commissioner of Inland Revenue says to a person, “You owe X amount of tax because it’s my opinion that you have sought this amount.”, we need to be clear that there is a way for those taxpayers to be able to dispute it, because, if not, I don’t think that’s a laughing matter.
civility.explanation: Pushes back on an interjection by characterising the member opposite as mocking and not taking the matter seriously. Pointed and edging toward the person's conduct, but it does not impute bad faith or attack character, and the bulk of the sentence returns to the substance of dispute rights.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And if I look at the particular features of those two—of what’s actually in the bill in relation to the backdating—it says that for ACC, “the lump-sum payment would be taxed at the recipient’s average tax rate for the four years prior”.

specificity.statement: So, just to contextualise this, what this section does is speak to the Child Support Amendment Act 2021, which gave a four-year time frame in which to assess child support, and it was designed to provide more certainty, so parents knew that child support would be needed from them or payable to them for four years.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute, the exact period (four years), the mechanism (a time bar on assessment) and the policy rationale — checkable detail rather than a general concern about child support.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The member is right to highlight the retrospective element of this, but, in this area and in these circumstances, we’re comfortable that the balance is in the right space in regards to providing the exemptions that are necessary for people to be able to ensure that they meet their obligations under the law.
specificity.explanation: Answering a question about a dated retrospective look-back with 'the balance is in the right space' — no criterion for the balance, no limit on the retrospectivity, no date, no mechanism. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’re speaking about people’s liabilities here, and to apply a retrospective liability by removing an exemption is worrying because, for a start, it is retrospective—and so we all know the perils about that—but equally it goes back to a fairly considerable amount of time, 2021.
rigor.explanation: Half the inference is circular — retrospective liability is worrying because it is retrospective, resting on an appeal to shared assumption ('we all know the perils about that') rather than an argument. The second limb, the length of the look-back to 2021, is a genuine reason offered in support. A real but partly unsupported inference about the measure.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And so while I acknowledge the member wasn’t on that committee, other members in this Chamber were, and that was considered.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority/process: the conclusion that the concern is answered rests only on the fact that a committee looked at the provision, which does not bear on whether the retrospectivity objection is sound. Nothing is offered about the substance of the objection.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If the Minister accepts that online casinos would have, to some degree, attracted some turnover that would have otherwise gone through class 4 operators, the Minister must also, therefore, acknowledge that, in making this change at the proposed 12 percent, without accounting for the turnover that would have otherwise gone to class 4 operators, there is actually a change in the intent that has been set by this Parliament as to what to do with the revenue that is extracted from that activity.
rigor.explanation: A structured conditional argument, but the 'must also, therefore' overreaches: that online operators captured some turnover which would otherwise have flowed through class 4 does not by itself entail that setting the duty at 12 percent changes Parliament's intent about where gambling revenue goes. A real gap between the premise granted and the conclusion drawn.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I don’t see checks and balances as to the powers that the commissioner may be able to use to apply that retrospectivity.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: a named power (the Commissioner's ability to apply the exemption retrospectively) and a named deficiency (absence of checks on it). No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If the Minister accepts that online casinos would have, to some degree, attracted some turnover that would have otherwise gone through class 4 operators, the Minister must also, therefore, acknowledge that, in making this change at the proposed 12 percent, without accounting for the turnover that would have otherwise gone to class 4 operators, there is actually a change in the intent that has been set by this Parliament as to what to do with the revenue that is extracted from that activity.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure directly — the proposed 12 percent rate, the displacement of class 4 turnover, and the community-redistribution consequence. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I haven’t been able to see any submissions on that, but I wonder if the Minister has turned his mind to that, and can he give us an opinion about whether he thinks that those victims should remain exempt from this legislative power?
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested committee exchange where the Minister could easily have been accused of negligence. Instead the pressure stays entirely on whether the policy question has been considered; nothing is imputed to the Minister personally.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And so while I acknowledge the member wasn’t on that committee, other members in this Chamber were, and that was considered.
civility.explanation: Pointed rather than substantive — noting the member's absence from the committee goes to her standing to ask rather than to her argument, but it stops short of a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: The broader points that are raised by the member are part of the broader gambling system, and I think what I can say is that the introduction of this gambling duty component to those offshore gambling operators will potentially look to increase the amount of gambling activity from offshore back through to those domestic providers, whether they’re gambling operators in pubs or clubs, Lotto, the TAB in New Zealand, or other aspects such as that.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a market outcome — that imposing the new offshore gambling duty will shift gambling activity from offshore operators back to New Zealand domestic providers (pubs/clubs gaming machines, Lotto, the TAB). Not a promise about his own action; the action is the duty, the forecast is the market response to it.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Department of Internal Affairs gambling expenditure statistics and TAB NZ / Lotto NZ annual turnover for the first full year after the offshore gambling duty commenced (1 July 2024), compared with the preceding year. True if domestic operator turnover in these categories rises after commencement; false if it is flat or falls.

specificity.statement: So I think that with the increase in the amount of regulation and licensing in the offshore domain, the proxy in terms of whether that will flow through to domestic aspects is probable, but in terms of the exact elements around that, it’s a highly complex area in terms of that.
specificity.explanation: A Minister answering a committee-stage question on his own bill, with the regulatory impact statement's figures available to him, offers no rate, no quantum, no timeframe and no mechanism — only that a flow-through is 'probable' and the area is 'highly complex'. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So the commentary directs us in that particular way, and that’s pretty useful for the commissioner to be able to do that, but, of course, the amendment as put in place right through this doesn’t allow just the commissioner to communicate to KiwiSaver providers; the effect of the amendment is to allow KiwiSaver providers to communicate back to the commissioner as well.
specificity.explanation: Anchored to a named clause and section (clause 86 of the bill as reported back, amending section 220B of the KiwiSaver Act), quotes the operative words, and identifies a precise, checkable discrepancy: the commentary describes a one-way disclosure from the Commissioner, the enacted words permit two-way disclosure. Anyone can go to the bill and the commentary and verify it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Of the different options, option 1 was in relation to status quo, which is, basically, allowing them to tax just with GST; option 2 was to tax consistently with New Zealand casinos, and that’s because for casinos based in New Zealand their tax is GST, they have a 4 percent casino duty on gross betting revenue, and 28 percent on income tax profits; then option 3 was taxing consistently with gaming machines, which the Hon Kieran McAnulty has touched upon; and then option 4 was to align with tax rates imposed in other countries.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates the four options the officials' advice considered, with the actual rates attaching to each comparator — 4 percent casino duty on gross betting revenue, 28 percent income tax on profits, GST. Precise enough that the Minister's choice can be located against a named alternative.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As a result of that, we may expect to see some movement of gambling activity from those individuals that deal with offshore entities to domestic entities, because of that levelling up and the fact that the implication of the gaming duty on offshore operators, in effect, will, in part, allow domestic operators to be more competitive.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House: a cost imposed on one side of a market shifts relative competitiveness, so demand moves. The direction follows. But the reason offered for the conclusion largely restates it — activity will move because the duty will 'allow domestic operators to be more competitive' — so the load-bearing step (that a 12 percent duty is large enough relative to offshore operators' other advantages to change consumer behaviour) is asserted rather than supported. Mildly circular, with the magnitude gap unaddressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So it’s quite clear, because the Minister has gone with option 4, that it means that this particular option which the Minister has brought to the House is not consistent with previous statements made by members of Parliament.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure — if the pre-election position was income tax on profits and the bill adopts option 4 (aligning with overseas duty rates), the two do differ. But the conclusion is announced as 'quite clear' when the premise it rests on was offered a sentence earlier as 'if I remember correctly', and it then generalises from one member's campaign remark to 'previous statements made by members of Parliament'. The step outruns what was shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Could he please indicate to the committee how that response then correlates with the advice through the regulatory impact statement, which actually suggests that the duty being placed on some operators may actually lead to turnover being transferred from those registered operators that would be hit by the duty on to operators that are unlikely to comply?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Inland Revenue's regulatory impact statement for this proposal advises that the duty may transfer turnover from registered, duty-paying operators to operators unlikely to comply — i.e. that the official advice contains a leakage-to-non-compliers risk that cuts against the Minister's answer.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The IRD Regulatory Impact Statement accompanying the offshore gambling duty in the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023–24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill. True if the RIS states that the duty may cause turnover to shift from compliant registered operators to operators unlikely to comply; false if the RIS contains no such analysis.

veracity.statement: So the commentary directs us in that particular way, and that’s pretty useful for the commissioner to be able to do that, but, of course, the amendment as put in place right through this doesn’t allow just the commissioner to communicate to KiwiSaver providers; the effect of the amendment is to allow KiwiSaver providers to communicate back to the commissioner as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill commentary describes the amendment as allowing the Commissioner of Inland Revenue to communicate deceased-member estate information to KiwiSaver providers, while the amendment as drafted is wider, also permitting providers to communicate back to the Commissioner.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The departmental commentary on the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023–24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill as introduced, read against clause 86 and the new information-sharing provision in section 220B of the KiwiSaver Act 2006. True if the commentary describes only Commissioner-to-provider disclosure while the clause permits disclosure in both directions; false if the clause is one-directional or the commentary already describes both directions.

veracity.statement: Of the different options, option 1 was in relation to status quo, which is, basically, allowing them to tax just with GST; option 2 was to tax consistently with New Zealand casinos, and that’s because for casinos based in New Zealand their tax is GST, they have a 4 percent casino duty on gross betting revenue, and 28 percent on income tax profits; then option 3 was taxing consistently with gaming machines, which the Hon Kieran McAnulty has touched upon; and then option 4 was to align with tax rates imposed in other countries.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (a) that the IRD regulatory impact statement set out these four options for taxing offshore casino websites, and (b) that New Zealand-based casinos currently pay GST, a 4 percent casino duty on gross betting revenue, and 28 percent income tax on profits.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The IRD Regulatory Impact Statement for the offshore gambling duty (options analysis section), plus the casino duty rate set under the Gambling Act / Gambling (Duties) regulations and the company income tax rate in the Income Tax Act 2007. True if the RIS lists these four options and the casino duty is 4 percent of gross betting revenue with a 28 percent company tax rate; false if the options differ materially or either rate is wrong.

veracity.statement: Now, if I remember correctly, the Hon Nicola Willis, during the campaign, said that she would be looking at income tax on the profits of these offshore gaming providers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that during the 2023 election campaign Nicola Willis said she would look at applying income tax to the profits of offshore online gambling operators — as distinct from the gaming duty on turnover that the bill in fact imposes. The claim is hedged ('if I remember correctly') but is a definite assertion about what was said.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 campaign tax and fiscal plan documents and Willis's contemporaneous public statements on taxing offshore online gambling. True if she proposed taxing the profits/income of offshore gambling operators; false if her stated proposal was a duty on turnover or gross betting revenue rather than income tax on profits.

focus.statement: Could he please indicate to the committee how that response then correlates with the advice through the regulatory impact statement, which actually suggests that the duty being placed on some operators may actually lead to turnover being transferred from those registered operators that would be hit by the duty on to operators that are unlikely to comply?
focus.explanation: Textbook scrutiny: names the specific advice document, states the specific finding in it, and asks the Minister to reconcile it with the answer he has just given. No party framing at all — the question is entirely about the measure and the evidence base behind it.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So I’d find it interesting to know whether anyone else spoke to that operator.
civility.explanation: A pointed insinuation that the Minister's consultation may have run through a single named operator. It edges toward imputing favouritism but never lands on the person and stops short of alleging bad faith outright.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I want to know what information the commissioner is able to get. Is it just the names of the administrator of the estate, or will the commissioner have access to the actual will of that deceased estate? Will the commissioner be able to access the bank accounts of that deceased estate?
specificity.explanation: Names the exact categories of information at issue — administrator's name, the will, the bank accounts of the estate — so the Minister's answer would be checkable against the clause. A precise question, scored as such rather than discounted for not being an announcement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And as the member would have seen when he reviewed the regulatory impact statement for this bill, that 25 percent in New Zealand is higher than Italy at 20 percent, Belgium at 11, UK at 21, Sweden at 22, and I could go on.
specificity.explanation: Four named jurisdictions with a rate attached to each, tied to a numbered section of the regulatory impact statement. Anyone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If you look at the duty that is applied to profit on casinos, it’s 4 percent—that’s onshore, of course. If you look at the duty that’s applied to onshore pokie machines or gaming machines, that’s 20 percent. And so the proposed rate of 12 percent is inconsistent with either of the two online gambling areas that this proposed duty would cover.
specificity.explanation: Three rates, each attached to a named gambling category, distinguishing onshore from offshore. The comparison could be checked or acted on directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So we needed a critical mass of countries to adopt an income inclusion rule and a critical mass of countries to adopt an under-taxed profits rule. So that’s a pretty open-ended statement—what is meant by “a critical mass of countries”.
specificity.explanation: Names the two specific OECD GloBE mechanisms — the income inclusion rule and the under-taxed profits rule — which is concrete, but the commencement trigger she is asking about has no threshold, number or date attached, a gap she identifies herself.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because, while Dr Deborah Russell says that there’s an intention that is mentioned in the report and that it seems to be going in a particular direction, we cannot rely on the application of this to be done in the way the report provides; it needs to be applied in the way that the words of the legislation allow.
rigor.explanation: A valid inference: from the premise that a select committee report states intention but the statute governs application, the conclusion that the report's assurance cannot be relied on follows. No fallacy; the reasoning tracks how statutory interpretation actually works.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I don’t think anyone thinks that that isn’t a sensible thing. This was discussed by the select committee. The select committee didn’t propose any amendments in that regard.
rigor.explanation: Answers a substantive privacy question with an appeal to consensus ("I don't think anyone thinks") plus an appeal to authority and to the absence of objection — that the select committee proposed no amendment does not establish that the clause raises no privacy issue. The inference is about the policy, so it is a Rigor failure rather than a Focus one, but nothing was offered to connect the committee's silence to the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If you look at the duty that is applied to profit on casinos, it’s 4 percent—that’s onshore, of course. If you look at the duty that’s applied to onshore pokie machines or gaming machines, that’s 20 percent. And so the proposed rate of 12 percent is inconsistent with either of the two online gambling areas that this proposed duty would cover.
rigor.explanation: Two figures are offered and the conclusion tracks them: if the comparable onshore rates are 4 and 20 percent, a 12 percent rate does match neither, which undercuts the "level the playing field, keep things consistent" rationale he is answering. The inference is sound given its premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: And as the member would have seen when he reviewed the regulatory impact statement for this bill, that 25 percent in New Zealand is higher than Italy at 20 percent, Belgium at 11, UK at 21, Sweden at 22, and I could go on.
veracity.explanation: Asserts four specific foreign duty rates and that New Zealand's combined 25 percent sits above all of them. UK remote gaming duty at 21 percent and Belgium at 11 percent are as I understand them; Sweden's rate was 18 percent of GGR until a rise to 22 percent later in 2024, so the Swedish figure may be prospective rather than current at the date of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The comparative table at section 44 of the regulatory impact statement for the Taxation (Annual Rates 2023-24) bill, checked against each jurisdiction's published online-gambling duty rate as at March 2024: Italy's remote gaming tax, Belgium's online gaming tax on GGR, UK remote gaming duty, and Sweden's gambling tax. True if each of the four named rates matches the rate in force (or in the RIS table) within a percentage point; false if any named figure is materially wrong or the New Zealand 25 percent combined figure exceeds them only selectively.

veracity.statement: If you look at the duty that is applied to profit on casinos, it’s 4 percent—that’s onshore, of course. If you look at the duty that’s applied to onshore pokie machines or gaming machines, that’s 20 percent. And so the proposed rate of 12 percent is inconsistent with either of the two online gambling areas that this proposed duty would cover.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the two existing onshore gambling duty rates — 4 percent on casino profit and 20 percent on gaming machines. Both are, to my knowledge, the statutory rates, but the claim stands or falls on the published rates rather than on my recollection.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand's Gambling Duties Act 1971 and Inland Revenue's published rates as at March 2024: casino duty as a percentage of casino wins, and gaming machine duty as a percentage of gaming machine profits. True if casino duty is 4 percent and gaming machine duty 20 percent; false if either differs.

veracity.statement: And it wasn’t something that went through select committee, it wasn’t something that the public were consulted on; it was something that was introduced in this Chamber in the committee of the whole House stage and therefore avoided all of the sort of process which is fundamental to our lawmaking about taxation, because taxation is something that we treat in a way which is consultative.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the substantive amendment (the interest deductibility change) was not considered by select committee or public consultation, but was introduced at the committee of the whole House stage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee report on the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023-24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill and the Amendment Paper record: true if the interest-deductibility provisions appear only in an Amendment Paper moved at the committee of the whole House and are absent from the bill as reported back by the Finance and Expenditure Committee; false if they were before the committee and open to submissions.

veracity.statement: Look, I appreciate the energy in regards to that contribution, but when the select committee reviewed the title of the bill, which actually was the title that was put on the bill by the prior Government, which we didn’t look to seek to change: the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023-24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill's title was set by the previous (Labour) Government at introduction and left unchanged by the current Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill as introduced on legislation.govt.nz: true if the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023-24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill was introduced under the previous Government with that title and the title is unamended in the version reported back; false if the title was assigned or altered after the change of government.

veracity.statement: While most of that was out of scope, the aspect in regards to the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act (BORA) vet that was noted by the member Ingrid Leary, I can assure the member—and I note that she wasn’t on the Finance and Expenditure Committee—there was a BORA vet undertaken for this bill and introduced as part of that, and there were no concerns that were raised in regards to that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a Bill of Rights Act vet was carried out for this bill and tabled with it, and that it raised no concerns.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Justice / Attorney-General BORA advice published for the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023-24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill: true if a vet exists for this bill and identifies no inconsistency with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act; false if no vet was produced or if it flagged concerns.

veracity.statement: It is absolutely clear that when that change was made by the prior Government, the marginal price paid for existing homes moved from being paid by landlords leveraging their property to purchase yet another property to add to their property portfolio, and moved instead to first-home buyers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2021 removal of interest deductibility shifted the marginal buyer of existing homes from investors to first-home buyers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: CoreLogic buyer-classification series on the share of residential purchases by multiple-property owners versus first-home buyers, before and after October 2021: true if the investor share falls and the first-home buyer share rises around that date; false if the shares are flat or move the other way.

veracity.statement: Rents actually did not go up by further than inflation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that rent increases following the interest deductibility change did not exceed general consumer price inflation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ rental price index (and/or MBIE bond data mean rents) compared with the CPI over the period from October 2021: true if annual rent growth is at or below annual CPI inflation across that period; false if rent growth exceeds CPI.

veracity.statement: Indeed, the Amendment Paper to the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023-24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill—the Amendment Paper from the Minister or the department—runs to 55 pages long.
veracity.explanation: A precise claim about the length of the Amendment Paper tabled for this bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published Amendment Paper (Supplementary Order Paper) for the named bill on the Parliament website: true if it runs to approximately 55 pages, false if materially shorter or longer.

focus.statement: And it wasn’t something that went through select committee, it wasn’t something that the public were consulted on; it was something that was introduced in this Chamber in the committee of the whole House stage and therefore avoided all of the sort of process which is fundamental to our lawmaking about taxation, because taxation is something that we treat in a way which is consultative.
focus.explanation: Engages the legislative process for a named measure — what was and was not consulted on — rather than characterising the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So this bill should change its name to the “Taxation (Punishment for First-home Buyers at the Expense of Landlords) Bill 2023”, because this bill goes to the heart of the way that we design an economy which provides for first-home buyers to get into the market.
civility.explanation: A scathing characterisation of the bill's effect, aimed entirely at the measure and its economic consequences. No individual is impugned.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: While most of that was out of scope, the aspect in regards to the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act (BORA) vet that was noted by the member Ingrid Leary, I can assure the member—and I note that she wasn’t on the Finance and Expenditure Committee—there was a BORA vet undertaken for this bill and introduced as part of that, and there were no concerns that were raised in regards to that.
civility.explanation: The parenthetical that the member 'wasn't on the Finance and Expenditure Committee' is aimed at her standing to ask rather than at the question; a condescending aside short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We will return to a home-buying market where first-home buyers are systematically—because of the way this is regulated—locked out of the market.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that restoring interest deductibility for landlords will push first-home buyers out of the residential purchase market. Not a promise about her own action — a prediction about market outcomes.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: CoreLogic (or REINZ) buyer-classification data on first-home buyers' share of residential property purchases: true if the first-home buyer share falls materially below its early-2024 level (~26%) and the investor share correspondingly rises over the two years following the change; false if the first-home buyer share holds at or above that level.

specificity.statement: The question specifically around the date of commencement is in clause 2(19), and I so acknowledge there are three pages of commencement dates, but that is not inconsistent with tax legislation.
specificity.explanation: Points to a named clause and quantifies the extent of the commencement provisions — a reader could go to clause 2(19) and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Can the Minister confirm that in respect of these revisions to interest deductibility, the full nominal amount of an interest payment is going to be deductible, not just the real interest component.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact mechanism at issue — nominal versus real interest deductibility — precisely enough that the answer is checkable against the bill's text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But if I look at the title and commencement date and then I look at Schedule 7, it’s got very sweeping language around the sections to do with child payments and the deductibility and the exemptions coming into force on, before, or after the date of 26 October 2021.
specificity.explanation: Names the schedule, the subject matter and the retrospective commencement date, so the provision can be located and checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When the previous Government introduced the taxation principles bill, one of the biggest outcries from the then Opposition was that this was going to provide far too much power for the Commissioner of Inland Revenue and, ultimately, for politicians to be able to see information relating to the tax affairs of its citizens. And yet that is what this provision does.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real provision, but the conclusion rests on asserting an equivalence rather than showing it: the earlier objection is offered in place of any demonstration that section 220B confers the same power. Argument by parallel with a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But my question is: is the Minister aware that in the situation where the regulatory framework has not been set up before such taxes have been introduced, other OECD countries have shown that, actually, that very small gap between the regulatory framework being set up and the implementation of the new tax has shown that there’s been a lot of black-market operations in between that very small gap.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: the 1 July 2024 application date for the offshore gambling duty, the sequencing of the harm-minimisation regulatory framework, and comparative evidence about what happens in the gap. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Depriving landlords of the ability to be able to claim mortgage interest deductions has made residential property less attractive as an investment, and this is simply a matter of supply and demand, as with more landlords offering properties, upward pressure on rents will resolve.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure: the interest limitation rules, their effect on investor behaviour and the flow-through to rents. No characterisation of the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But my question is: is the Minister aware that in the situation where the regulatory framework has not been set up before such taxes have been introduced, other OECD countries have shown that, actually, that very small gap between the regulatory framework being set up and the implementation of the new tax has shown that there’s been a lot of black-market operations in between that very small gap.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy: if other jurisdictions saw black-market activity when the tax preceded the regulatory framework, the same sequencing risk applies here. The gap is that the comparative evidence is asserted rather than sourced — no country, no measure, 'a lot of black-market operations' is unquantified — so the analogy to New Zealand's case is left unargued.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Depriving landlords of the ability to be able to claim mortgage interest deductions has made residential property less attractive as an investment, and this is simply a matter of supply and demand, as with more landlords offering properties, upward pressure on rents will resolve.
rigor.explanation: The chain — restore deductibility, more landlords enter, rent pressure resolves — is asserted rather than supported, and 'this is simply a matter of supply and demand' does the work an argument should. It skips whether rental supply actually responds, and whether a cost reduction to landlords is passed to tenants rather than retained; a real gap between what is offered and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But my question is: is the Minister aware that in the situation where the regulatory framework has not been set up before such taxes have been introduced, other OECD countries have shown that, actually, that very small gap between the regulatory framework being set up and the implementation of the new tax has shown that there’s been a lot of black-market operations in between that very small gap.

veracity.statement: And the regulatory impact statement does make reference to offshore gambling providers about their ability to be able to be ready in time to collect those taxes by 1 July 2024.
