veracity.statement: Does he then agree with the Climate Change Commission, who said on Monday, and I quote, “there has not be an important or notable change in the understanding of the physical science on methane and how it warms the atmosphere”; or is he to extend his logic also to reopen the science on, say, gravity?
veracity.explanation: Relays a direct quotation attributed to the Climate Change Commission on the state of methane science.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Climate Change Commission's April 2024 statement or draft advice on biogenic methane; true if it contains wording to the effect that there has been no important or notable change in the understanding of the physical science of methane's warming effect, false if no such statement was made.

civility.statement: He may not like it, but he should listen to the fact, because today that wage earner pays 20.6 percent of their income in tax, as compared to 15.5 percent in 2011.
civility.explanation: The substance is entirely a tax figure, but 'he may not like it, but he should listen' is a mild personal admonishment of the member rather than pure engagement with the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does he then agree with the Climate Change Commission, who said on Monday, and I quote, “there has not be an important or notable change in the understanding of the physical science on methane and how it warms the atmosphere”; or is he to extend his logic also to reopen the science on, say, gravity?
civility.explanation: The gravity comparison is a reductio aimed at the Prime Minister's reasoning rather than an attack on him personally, but it edges into mockery rather than straight engagement.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Sure. Well, the fiscal drag I have described affects people at all levels of income. As the years go by, they find themselves paying an increasing share of their earnings in income tax, and this can affect people's perceptions of fairness in the tax system and as a result have a negative impact on compliance. Also, as people move into higher tax brackets, they face higher marginal tax rates, which can be a disincentive to work.
rigor.explanation: A coherent chain — unindexed thresholds raise average tax rates, which affect perceived fairness and marginal incentives — with the causal steps appropriately hedged ('can'), though the compliance link is asserted without evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Tax relief will be funded by reducing Government consumption and increasing revenue elsewhere, all sitting within the Budget 2024 operating allowance. Furthermore, that allowance will be lower than the allowance set by the previous Government. This means that tax relief is affordable, we will not be borrowing extra to pay for it, and tax relief will not add to inflationary pressures.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that no extra borrowing is required follows from the stated funding premises, but the further step to 'will not add to inflationary pressures' is a leap: fiscally neutral packages can still shift demand between households and government.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I don't know how to answer the last part of that question, but what I would just say is that we are determined to make sure that we update the science base on methane. It has changed over the last five years. It's changed over the last 10 years. It will change in the next five years and in the next 10 years. It's important that we get a common base of understanding of science knowledge so we can set the right targets.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that targets must be reviewed rests on a bare, unsupported assertion that the science has changed — offered against a directly contrary expert finding just put to him, with nothing cited to bridge the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Tax relief will be funded by reducing Government consumption and increasing revenue elsewhere, all sitting within the Budget 2024 operating allowance. Furthermore, that allowance will be lower than the allowance set by the previous Government. This means that tax relief is affordable, we will not be borrowing extra to pay for it, and tax relief will not add to inflationary pressures.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Budget 2024 personal tax relief will not add to inflationary pressure and will not require extra borrowing.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Treasury Budget 2024 Economic and Fiscal Update and subsequent RBNZ Monetary Policy Statements; true if the Budget 2024 tax package was assessed as fiscally neutral with no material addition to inflation and annual CPI continued to decline through 2024–25, false if Treasury or RBNZ attributed additional inflationary pressure to the package or if it was funded by additional borrowing.

specificity.statement: This target aims to see 95 percent of people wait less than four months for their elective treatments.

specificity.statement: They have taken me through it and showed, with the change proposal, the proposal is actually to go from 5.5 fulltime-equivalents (FTE) in the Suicide Prevention Office, which it currently is, to 6.5 in the change proposal, which is only a proposal but it will increase capacity and capability in that office that will remain open.
specificity.explanation: Gives exact FTE figures before and after, names the document he saw and when he saw it.

veracity.statement: They have taken me through it and showed, with the change proposal, the proposal is actually to go from 5.5 fulltime-equivalents (FTE) in the Suicide Prevention Office, which it currently is, to 6.5 in the change proposal, which is only a proposal but it will increase capacity and capability in that office that will remain open.

veracity.statement: It has been misleading: the Public Service Association put out a press release that it was to close; I was never informed of that, and it was not to close.

veracity.explanation: Relays a claim attributed to the Prime Minister about average duration on benefit for adults (13 years) and for under-25s (24 years). The claim being checked is the Prime Minister's, not the questioner's own.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Social Development benefit-duration statistics and the actuarial valuation of the benefit system: true if the average total years an adult spends on benefit is approximately 13 years and approximately 24 years for those starting under 25; false if the official figures differ materially or refer to projected future lifetime years rather than time already spent, as the phrasing implies.

rigor.statement: We last achieved 95 percent between early 2015 and the end of 2017, so we know it’s possible.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: past attainment is offered as evidence of feasibility. It supports the conclusion in principle, but leans on the assumption that conditions (demand, workforce, population) are comparable, which is not established — a modest gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, that’s very simple, because the fiscal sustainability programme clearly states to find savings while still delivering quality public services, and delivering a Suicide Prevention Office is a quality public service.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the question asked why officials were apologising, and the offered premises (the savings programme requires quality services; this office is a quality service) do not entail any explanation of the apology. The conclusion does not follow from what was supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’ve been very clear—and I was even interviewed by Jack Tame on Q+A—that I’ve been disappointed by the Suicide Prevention Office; I think it’s lacked real leadership.
civility.explanation: Blunt criticism directed at an office's performance and leadership as an institution, not at any named person. Harsh about the record, civil toward individuals.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Prime Minister was referring to independent evidence produced by Taylor Fry in 2022, which reported that someone on the jobseeker benefit is expected to spend 13 years on benefit throughout their lifetime. The same evidence shows someone on a youth benefit is expected to spend 24 years on benefits throughout their lifetime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2022 Taylor Fry benefit system valuation reports an expected lifetime duration on benefit of 13 years for jobseeker recipients and 24 years for youth benefit recipients.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Taylor Fry 2022 valuation of the MSD benefit system (released under the OIA): true if it states an average/expected future lifetime duration on benefit of ~13 years for jobseeker clients and ~24 years for youth benefit clients; false if those figures apply to a small sub-group rather than the stated client categories, or differ materially.

veracity.statement: Is she aware that the Taylor Fry report she just quoted actually says that only 0.5 percent of people on the benefit are expected to spend 24 years on a benefit throughout their lifetime?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Taylor Fry report attributes the 24-year figure to only 0.5 percent of benefit recipients, not to the average recipient.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The same Taylor Fry 2022 valuation report: true if it shows the 24-year expected lifetime duration applies to roughly 0.5% of the benefit population; false if the report attributes 24 years to a whole client category (e.g. all youth payment recipients).

veracity.statement: As I said in my primary answer, the context in which that was given was a discussion about long-term welfare dependency—the horrendous change that we have seen under the last six years with a significant increase in young people going on to welfare and staying on it—and the Taylor Fry report was one piece of the evidence that shows why we must prioritise this group.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that over the six years to 2024 there was a significant increase in young people going onto welfare and remaining on it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets / quarterly benefit statistics for 18–24 year olds, 2017/18 to 2023/24: true if both the number of young people on main benefits and the proportion in continuous receipt over 12 months rose materially; false if either was flat or fell.

veracity.statement: It’s estimated that around 185,000 Kiwis or 4.4 percent of the population are victims of an assault, robbery, or sexual assault, and we don’t regard that as normal or acceptable.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a victimisation count of about 185,000 people, or 4.4 percent of the population, for assault, robbery or sexual assault.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZ Crime and Victims Survey (Ministry of Justice) cycle current in early 2024: true if the estimated number of adults victimised by assault, robbery or sexual assault is ~185,000 / ~4.4%; false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The previous Government targeted reducing the prison population while violent crime increased.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that the previous government had a prison-population reduction target and that violent crime rose over the same period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Labour's stated 2017–2023 justice target (the 30% prison population reduction goal) plus NZ Crime and Victims Survey / Police victimisation data for violent offences over that period: true if the target existed and violent offending/victimisation rose; false if either element is absent.

veracity.statement: How will his gang patch legislation assist in achieving those targets when advice provided to him by the Ministry of Justice on 27 November states clearly that there’s no strong evidence to show that such actions work to reduce long-term offending and, in fact, risks making it more difficult to change offending behaviours and may drive an increase in gang numbers?
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of dated Ministry of Justice advice — that there is no strong evidence gang patch bans reduce long-term offending, and that they risk entrenching offending and increasing gang numbers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Justice regulatory impact statement / departmental advice dated 27 November 2023 on the gang patch legislation: true if it states there is no strong evidence such measures reduce long-term offending and flags the risks described; false if it contains no such assessment.

veracity.statement: I think it was the mixed attitude towards gangs over the past six years that led—a contributor, no doubt—to a 50 percent increase in gang membership in our community.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 50 percent increase in gang membership over the six years to 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police National Gang List membership numbers, 2017/18 compared with 2023/24: true if the increase is approximately 50% or more; false if materially smaller.

veracity.statement: I certainly received the briefing on 22 February that these were initiatives that Whaikaha was considering, and then they confirmed on 14 March that they would be implementing those changes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific sequence of dates for receiving and signing off Whaikaha's proposed changes — and differs from the 23 February date she gave moments earlier.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Whaikaha briefing documents released under the OIA and the Minister's answers to written parliamentary questions: true if a briefing on the proposed initiatives was received on 22 February 2024 and confirmation of implementation on 14 March 2024; false if the documented dates differ.

veracity.statement: Why did she only formally advise the finance Minister of eligibility changes that resulted from Whaikaha’s funding shortfall on 20 March, two days after the announcement was made and implemented, as she has confirmed in written parliamentary questions No. 3593 and 3599?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister formally advised the Minister of Finance on 20 March, two days after the 18 March announcement and implementation, citing two numbered written questions as the source.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Written parliamentary questions 3593 and 3599 (2024): true if the answers confirm the finance Minister was formally advised on 20 March and the changes were announced/implemented on 18 March; false if the dates given there differ.

veracity.statement: Why, given she was first aware of the proposed changes on 22 or 23 February, did it take her till 25 March to first go to Cabinet, considering over 26,000 carers have been impacted by these changes?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than 26,000 carers were affected by the Whaikaha equipment/flexible funding eligibility changes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Whaikaha – Ministry of Disabled People figures on the number of carers/clients using flexible funding affected by the 18 March 2024 purchasing rule changes: true if over 26,000; false if materially fewer.

specificity.statement: The Prime Minister was referring to independent evidence produced by Taylor Fry in 2022, which reported that someone on the jobseeker benefit is expected to spend 13 years on benefit throughout their lifetime. The same evidence shows someone on a youth benefit is expected to spend 24 years on benefits throughout their lifetime.
specificity.explanation: Names the source, the year, the two benefit categories and precise year figures — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is she aware that for that tiny 0.5 percent proportion of people, the modelling has taken into account seven additional risk factors, including acute unplanned care from a public hospital, interaction with Oranga Tamariki, and exclusion from school, and, if so, why didn’t she create a target to reduce those risk factors, as opposed to just getting 50,000 people off the benefit?
specificity.explanation: Names the number of risk factors, three of them by name, and the government's 50,000 target — a precise, checkable question.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Prime Minister announced on Monday that the Government has set a target to see a reduction in the number of people who are the victims of an assault, robbery, or sexual assault by 20,000.
specificity.explanation: Names the offence categories, the numeric target and when it was announced; directly checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re restoring the three-strikes legislation that the previous Government repealed, showing that we will not tolerate repeat violent offending in our communities. We’ll give judges additional tools to deal with serious repeat youth offenders, including military-style academies. We’ll also limit excessive sentencing discounts so penalties actually fit the crime.
specificity.explanation: Three named measures with identifiable mechanisms, but no figures, thresholds or timeframes attached to any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How will his gang patch legislation assist in achieving those targets when advice provided to him by the Ministry of Justice on 27 November states clearly that there’s no strong evidence to show that such actions work to reduce long-term offending and, in fact, risks making it more difficult to change offending behaviours and may drive an increase in gang numbers?
specificity.explanation: Names the legislation, the advising agency, the date of the advice and its specific findings — someone could pull the document and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why did she only formally advise the finance Minister of eligibility changes that resulted from Whaikaha’s funding shortfall on 20 March, two days after the announcement was made and implemented, as she has confirmed in written parliamentary questions No. 3593 and 3599?
specificity.explanation: Names the dates, the interval, and the exact written questions from which the facts are drawn.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Whether it’s one person, whether it’s 100, or whether it’s 100,000, every one of those people counts, to me, and I am unwilling to sit by and let them get stuck.
rigor.explanation: Offered as a reason why the scale of the affected group does not matter; it is a bare appeal to emotion that does not engage the question of whether the modelling supports the claimed magnitude, so the conclusion does not follow from anything shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And so I think everybody acknowledges the negative impact that gang membership and intimidation in our communities have on our towns and our communities. And so that bill is designed to give the police extra powers to deal with gang intimidation, and that will help.
rigor.explanation: Answers a question about evidence of effectiveness with an appeal to common acceptance of the harm, then concludes the bill 'will help' — the conclusion does not follow from the premise offered, which establishes that a problem exists rather than that this measure addresses it.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is she confident in the accuracy of her and the Prime Minister’s comments that the average young person is spending 24 years on a benefit?
civility.explanation: A pointed challenge in a genuinely contested exchange, but directed entirely at the accuracy of the statements made rather than at the Minister personally.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The previous Government targeted reducing the prison population while violent crime increased.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy target of the previous government and a specific measurable outcome rather than making a general claim about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I received the briefing on 23 February 2024. I noted that Whaikaha was making changes which were needed to reduce its forecast deficit as recommended, and, as I have said multiple times, these issues are inherited from the previous Labour Government, and I am taking urgent steps to address the situation with a review.
focus.explanation: Answers the substantive question about the briefing and names concrete responses (extra funding, a review), but a material part of the answer is attributing the problem to the previous government rather than engaging the decision at issue.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The current approach puts the cart before the horse, designing assessments before having a curriculum in place, and it is not best practice to design assessment before knowing what is to be assessed.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about sequencing: the premise (assessment design depends on knowing what is assessed) does support the conclusion that curriculum should come first. It leans partly on an unevidenced 'best practice' appeal, which caps it below the top.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They think the tenants should be grateful for the fact that the landlords are getting the tax break, and, in many cases, they won’t see a cent of that extra money.
rigor.explanation: The second clause is a real policy claim about pass-through to tenants, but the conclusion is fronted by a strawman characterisation of the Government's stated position ('tenants should be grateful') that is not supported by anything offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That 5 percent is the number that makes people a little less hopeful each week, because the pay packet gets stretched thinner and thinner and the idea of saving some disappears.
rigor.explanation: An appeal to emotion doing the work of an inference: nothing connects the roughly five-percentage-point rise in effective tax to the asserted loss of hope or savings, and the argument also relies on an unsupported leap from a rate change to household behaviour.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, no, because all the while when they were spending New Zealanders’ hard-earned wages, the wait-lists grew, the education standards declined, violent crime rose, and dairies were ram-raided.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: the outcomes are placed alongside the spending increase and treated as showing the spending achieved nothing, with no causal link offered and no counterfactual considered.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The current approach puts the cart before the horse, designing assessments before having a curriculum in place, and it is not best practice to design assessment before knowing what is to be assessed.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the design sequencing of the NCEA Change Programme and the curriculum refresh; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They made the decision to prioritise that nearly $3 billion in tax breaks for landlords whilst considering cutting school lunches, whilst cutting our defences at the border with cuts to the Ministry for Primary Industries and Customs, whilst cutting funding for the Ministry of Health, whilst cutting support for those with disabilities, whilst cutting support for the conservation estate—the list could go on.
focus.explanation: Names a specific fiscal measure and a list of specific agencies and programmes affected. This is scrutiny of named government decisions, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Unfortunately, though, I’m not going to hold my breath, because we’ve got a Government with no vision, a Government that has the wrong priorities and that is focused on taking New Zealand backwards rather than leading New Zealand forward, and a Government that is focused on managing New Zealand’s decline, rather than actually leading the country forward.
focus.explanation: No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — it is a general characterisation of the other side as visionless and backward-looking.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The current Leader of the Opposition decided to begin his speech talking about choices, and is it any surprise when everyone behind him was sitting there thinking about choices: thinking first about a choice the New Zealand people made so definitively to boot them out, and then thinking about the choice they need to make in the coming months about who, in fact, should lead them into the future.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's internal state — election defeat and a supposed leadership question. No policy, measure or outcome named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I came here to give a more serious speech: a requiem for the worker’s party, because, not content with delivering an intergenerational cost of living crisis to the working people of New Zealand, we now have a Labour Party whose reason for being, whose very reason for getting up in the morning, is to rail against tax relief for working people.
focus.explanation: Tax relief is touched on, but the weight of the passage is a characterisation of what the Labour Party fundamentally is and exists for, rather than any mechanism, cost or effect.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The members opposite have a special talent, actually—let’s give them that—of spending more and delivering less.
focus.explanation: A general characterisation of the other side's competence; no specific programme, figure or outcome is named in the statement itself.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And to achieve better public services, I will be delaying the NCEA Change Programme by two years while we complete the curriculum.
specificity.explanation: Names the programme, the action (delay) and the duration (two years). Checkable and actionable, though no dated milestones for the curriculum work.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In addition to teaching the basics brilliantly in our primary and intermediate schools, this Government has a laser focus on delivering a knowledge-rich curriculum to all students, right up to year 13.
specificity.explanation: Attempts to convey substance but supplies only a direction plus generic descriptors ('brilliantly', 'laser focus', 'knowledge-rich'); the only concrete element is the year 13 endpoint. No mechanism, cost or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In 2011, a median-wage earner paid 15.5 percent of their average income in tax.
specificity.explanation: A precise, dated, checkable figure tied to a defined income reference point.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We will match that with targets, with accountability for the performance of our public services, with more police, and with rescuing the school lunch programme that they didn’t leave a dollar for.
specificity.explanation: Names four directions of travel (targets, accountability, more police, school lunches) but attaches no figures, mechanisms or dates to any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The report shows that teachers want a more explicit curriculum with more off the shelf material and resources.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Education Review Office report into the Aotearoa New Zealand histories curriculum found teachers wanting a more explicit curriculum and more ready-made teaching materials.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The ERO 2024 report on the Aotearoa New Zealand histories curriculum; true if its findings record teacher demand for greater explicitness and more supplied resources/materials, false if the report contains no such finding or reports the opposite.

veracity.statement: One of the first decisions this Government took—not only took but actually found the money to do—was $2.9 billion worth of tax breaks for the country’s landlords.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the restoration of interest deductibility for residential rental property was costed at $2.9 billion and was among the coalition Government's earliest decisions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD costings for the reinstatement of interest deductibility (Budget 2024 and pre-Budget fiscal documents); true if the forecast revenue foregone is approximately $2.9b over the forecast period, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, here is an example of where the Government’s priorities are simply wrong: for the price of the tax cuts that they have given landlords, you could more than double the size of the free and healthy school lunches programme.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the fiscal cost of the interest deductibility change exceeds twice the annual cost of the Ka Ora, Ka Ako healthy school lunches programme.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare Treasury costings for interest deductibility restoration with Vote Education appropriations for Ka Ora, Ka Ako on a like-for-like annual basis; true if the tax measure exceeds double the programme's annual cost, false if it does not.

veracity.statement: We focused on elimination, and all evidence to date suggests that we have succeeded in doing that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Mycoplasma bovis eradication programme pursued under the previous government has, on the evidence to April 2024, succeeded.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI/Biosecurity New Zealand M. bovis programme status reports as at April 2024; true if the programme had moved to provisional absence with no active confirmed properties, false if active infected properties or ongoing detections remained.

veracity.statement: I was interested in looking at what that might mean: universal free school lunches for every child attending school in Estonia; a light rail system in their largest city, in Estonia; heavily subsidised kindergarten education in Estonia; and teachers focused on not just the basics but digital skills, on coding, and on other skills that their learners are going to need for the 21st century.
veracity.explanation: Asserts four factual features of Estonian policy: universal free school meals, a light rail/tram system in Tallinn, heavily subsidised kindergarten, and a curriculum emphasis on digital skills.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Estonian Ministry of Education and Research and Tallinn city documentation; true if free school meals are provided universally in basic and upper-secondary education, Tallinn operates a tram network, kindergarten fees are substantially state/municipally subsidised, and digital competence is a curriculum priority; false if any is materially misstated.

veracity.statement: Now, New Zealanders have had no change in tax rates or thresholds since 2010.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no personal income tax rate or threshold has been altered in New Zealand between 2010 and April 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IRD/Treasury record of personal income tax rates and thresholds 2010–2024; true if no rate or threshold changed, false if any did — e.g. the introduction of a 39% top rate on income over $180,000 from 1 April 2021.

veracity.statement: In 2011, a median-wage earner paid 15.5 percent of their average income in tax.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific average effective personal tax rate of 15.5% for a median-wage earner in 2011.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD average effective tax rate calculations for a median full-time wage earner in 2011; true if approximately 15.5%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, no, because all the while when they were spending New Zealanders’ hard-earned wages, the wait-lists grew, the education standards declined, violent crime rose, and dairies were ram-raided.
veracity.explanation: Asserts four measurable deteriorations over the 2017–2023 period: longer health wait-lists, falling education standards, rising violent crime, and increased ram raids.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Whatu Ora/Ministry of Health elective wait-list series, PISA and NCEA/curriculum achievement data, NZ Police victimisation statistics for violent offences, and Police ram-raid offence counts across 2017–2023; true if each rose/declined as stated, false if any moved the other way.

veracity.statement: An 80 percent increase in spending in six short years, an outstandingly bad cost of living crisis, and what do we have to show for it?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that government spending rose by about 80 percent over the six years of the previous government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenses, 2017/18 to 2023/24 (Budget and Financial Statements of the Government); true if nominal growth is approximately 80%, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: But don’t worry, because what we also got was 18,500 more public servants—so that really made the difference!—and sky-high inflation, and who paid for it all?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a net increase of 18,500 in the public service workforce under the previous government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Kawa Mataaho Public Service Commission workforce data, 2017 to 2023; true if the increase in public service FTEs/headcount is approximately 18,500, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: We will match that with targets, with accountability for the performance of our public services, with more police, and with rescuing the school lunch programme that they didn’t leave a dollar for.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous government left no funding allocated for the school lunch programme beyond its term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2023 Vote Education appropriations for Ka Ora, Ka Ako; true if no funding was appropriated beyond the 2023/24 year, false if funding was appropriated into later years.

civility.statement: But I did note that the Prime Minister finally has found a bit of a vision.
civility.explanation: Not an insult, but the 'finally' is a personal jibe about the Prime Minister's capacity for vision rather than a criticism of any policy — condescension aimed at the individual.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The current Leader of the Opposition decided to begin his speech talking about choices, and is it any surprise when everyone behind him was sitting there thinking about choices: thinking first about a choice the New Zealand people made so definitively to boot them out, and then thinking about the choice they need to make in the coming months about who, in fact, should lead them into the future.
civility.explanation: Turns on the individual rather than any argument: it tells the Leader of the Opposition his own caucus is contemplating replacing him, a personal jibe about his standing rather than his policy.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So, over the next month, we’ll hear a lot of wailing from the Labour Party about how terrible it is to allow people to keep more of their own income, and that’ll be the message of the day.
focus.explanation: The weight of the sentence is a caricature of how the other party will react, not the mechanism, cost or effect of the tax package. It gestures at 'keeping more of their own income' but names no rate, threshold or figure.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So, over the next month, we’ll hear a lot of wailing from the Labour Party about how terrible it is to allow people to keep more of their own income, and that’ll be the message of the day.
civility.explanation: Derisive ('wailing'), but the target is a party, not any individual; no person's character, competence or motives are impugned. Under the re-anchored scale that is close to the standard, with the tribalism captured by Focus instead.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That was the most horrendous public policy failure that we’ve seen in recent times, and so that’s why we’re really focused on addressing that.
civility.explanation: A brutal verdict on a policy — motels used as emergency housing — with no individual named, blamed or belittled. Hard criticism of a decision is the expected standard, not a failing.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We’ve all seen in our communities the trauma that’s caused by violent crime, by the massive increase in retail crime that we’ve seen in our communities, and particularly by that small group of serious young offenders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that retail crime has increased massively in the period leading up to April 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police retail-sector victimisation statistics (retail crime / burglary and theft from retail premises) for the years preceding April 2024; true if recorded retail offences show a large rise over the preceding two to three years, false if the series is flat or falling.

veracity.statement: That’s why Christopher Luxon announced amongst the nine focused targets for this Government a couple in the justice space, reducing the number of victims of crime by 20,000.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the existence and content of a specific announced government target.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government targets announced by the Prime Minister in April 2024; true if there were nine targets and one of them was a reduction of 20,000 in the number of victims of (violent) crime, false if the count of targets or the 20,000 figure differs.

veracity.statement: Remember, the previous Government had a goal of reducing the prison numbers, irrespective of what was going on.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous government held a stated goal of reducing prison numbers, unconditioned on crime trends. Relays the opponent's own policy position.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published Labour Government policy statements and Corrections/Justice documents 2017–2023; true if a stated target to reduce the prison population (e.g. a percentage reduction by a stated year) existed, false if no such goal was adopted. The 'irrespective of what was going on' qualifier is true only if the target was expressed without reference to crime levels.

veracity.statement: It’s about ensuring that we deal with not having 3,000 or 4,000 waking up every morning in emergency accommodation in hotels in places like Rotorua.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a numeric count of (evidently) children living in motel emergency accommodation. The elided noun is plain from context and is not scored as a false claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD emergency housing special needs grant data on the number of children in emergency housing motels around 2023–24; true if the count is in the 3,000–4,000 range, false if materially lower or higher.

specificity.statement: That’s why Christopher Luxon announced amongst the nine focused targets for this Government a couple in the justice space, reducing the number of victims of crime by 20,000.
specificity.explanation: Names the target-setting exercise, the number of targets, the policy area and a numeric goal (20,000 fewer victims) — all checkable against the published target list.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We want to reduce the number of serious repeat youth offenders, and that partly is about giving judges extra tools with which to deal with that small cohort. Having military academies are part of the mix, and also having a new category of young serious offenders.
specificity.explanation: Names two concrete mechanisms — military-style academies and a new 'young serious offender' category — but supplies no numbers, thresholds or timeframe for either.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If crime was going up, they still wanted to reduce prison numbers. Well, that is not actually how you keep the community safe.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (that this is not how you keep communities safe) is asserted rather than argued — no evidence or mechanism linking prison numbers to community safety is offered, and the premise restates the opponent's target in its most unfavourable form, so it leans on a bare assertion plus a strawman.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Winston Peters was the only politician to walk amongst those who asked simply to be heard—Winston Peters was the only politician to walk amongst those who wanted to be heard.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Winston Peters was the only politician who went among the protesters occupying Parliament grounds in early 2022.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous news reporting and video from the February–March 2022 Parliament grounds occupation: true if no other sitting MP is recorded going out among the protesters; false if any other MP (e.g. ACT or Green MPs, or other party figures) is documented doing so.

veracity.statement: Very importantly, amongst those promises, the coalition committed to establishing a complete, full-scale, wide-ranging, independent inquiry conducted publicly with local and international experts into how the COVID-19 pandemic was handled in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the National–NZ First coalition agreement contains a commitment to a full-scale, wide-ranging, public, independent COVID-19 inquiry with local and international experts.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the National–New Zealand First coalition agreement (November 2023): true if it contains a commitment in those terms, false if no such commitment appears or its wording materially differs.

veracity.statement: We welcome the first steps made to expand these terms of reference of this inquiry, and we applaud the 11,000 New Zealanders who made their submissions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that about 11,000 New Zealanders made submissions to the public consultation on expanding the COVID-19 royal commission's terms of reference.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Internal Affairs / Government reporting on the number of public submissions received on the COVID-19 inquiry terms of reference consultation (early 2024): true if approximately 11,000, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: It has killed more than 4,800 civilians.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Myanmar military regime had killed more than 4,800 civilians as at April 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Assistance Association for Political Prisoners (Burma) and UN OHCHR civilian death tolls for the period since the February 2021 coup up to April 2024: true if the recorded toll exceeds 4,800, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: Two and a half million people are displaced in the country at the moment because of this regime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts roughly 2.5 million people were internally displaced in Myanmar as at April 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: UN OCHA Myanmar humanitarian updates for April 2024 reporting internally displaced person numbers: true if approximately 2.5 million, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: The National Unity Government, the Government in exile, and the ethnic resistance organisations that are such a significant part of the resistance have had a string of military successes, and 43 percent of the territory of Myanmar is controlled by the democratic opposition, not by the military regime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at April 2024 resistance forces controlled 43 percent of Myanmar's territory.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Territorial-control assessments for Myanmar around April 2024 (e.g. Special Advisory Council for Myanmar, ISP-Myanmar, BNI): true if credible assessments put opposition-controlled territory at about 43 percent, false if they put it materially lower or classify most of that area as contested rather than controlled.

veracity.statement: They recently introduced conscription. Young people between the ages of 18 and 35 are now being press-ganged into military service because the military is so desperate.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Myanmar junta had recently activated conscription covering people aged 18 to 35.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Myanmar State Administration Council's February 2024 activation of the People's Military Service Law and its stated age ranges: true if conscription was activated shortly before April 2024 covering men aged 18–35, false if no such activation occurred or the ages differ materially.

veracity.statement: If we look back over the past six years, debt went from $5 billion to $100 billion under the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific increase in Crown debt from $5 billion to $100 billion over the six years of the previous Government.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Financial Statements of the Government: net core Crown debt (and gross sovereign-issued debt) for 2017/18 compared with 2023/24. True if a standard Treasury debt measure was about $5 billion in 2017/18 and about $100 billion by 2023/24; false if the starting figure on every standard measure was materially higher (net core Crown debt was tens of billions in 2017/18).

veracity.statement: We had inflation, the economy ground to a halt so that we were in a recession, and all New Zealanders—all New Zealanders—have faced higher taxes, and so they’re seeing greater opportunities offshore.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that every New Zealander faced higher taxes under the previous Government, alongside recession and inflation.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue personal income tax rates and thresholds 2017–2023 plus Treasury/IRD analysis of fiscal drag: true if average tax rates rose for essentially all income earners; false if statutory rates were unchanged for all but top earners and any rise in average rates did not apply across the board. Recession claim checkable against Stats NZ quarterly GDP.

veracity.statement: It’s actually what you achieve and what you do that counts, and what the Government did is they managed to spend 80 percent more—nearly doubled Government spending over six years—and actually had worse outcomes just about everywhere you looked: longer waiting times, higher crime, fewer houses, and a real mess everywhere.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an 80 percent rise in government spending over six years, together with longer health waiting times, higher crime and fewer houses.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenses for 2017/18 vs 2023/24 (true if the increase is about 80 percent, false if materially lower); Stats NZ new dwelling consents/completions 2017 vs 2023 for 'fewer houses'; Ministry of Health elective wait times and NZ Police recorded crime/victimisation statistics for the other two.

specificity.statement: Now, New Zealand First were very specific in our commitments, and there were four important areas that we wanted to cover: firstly, the use of multiple lockdowns; secondly, the procurement and the efficacy of the vaccines; thirdly, the social and economic impacts, both regionally and nationally, on the people of New Zealand; and, finally, whether the decisions made and the steps taken were justified.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates four named subject areas the inquiry is to cover; concrete enough that the eventual terms of reference could be checked against them, though no dates or mechanisms are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I say to the Minister of Foreign Affairs, the Rt Hon Winston Peters, to do the right thing. Refuse the visas, and keep the butchers of Myanmar out of our country.
specificity.explanation: Names the decision-maker and the exact action sought (refusing visas for the named delegation), but supplies no mechanism, conditions or further detail beyond the ask.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If the Government is more disciplined with its spending and it’s not stoking the fires of inflation, that will help New Zealanders with the cost of living.
specificity.explanation: A direction of travel with no figures, no named spending reductions, no timeframe and no stated size of the cost-of-living effect.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now is the very time that we should be isolating that regime, not inviting them to New Zealand to take part in talks.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows loosely from the premises he laid out (resistance gains, military weakness, prior New Zealand policy), but nothing offered connects the regime's battlefield position to the effect of a visa decision, so there is a real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: How they managed to do it was they turbocharged spending during COVID, and then when COVID ended and people got back to their lives, they didn’t stop. They just kept on spending as if we were in the middle of COVID, and that’s how the damage was created.
rigor.explanation: A single-cause post hoc attribution: continued spending is asserted to be how 'the damage was created', with nothing offered to rule out other contributors (global inflation, supply shocks, monetary policy) or to link the spending path to the specific outcomes claimed.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now is the very time that we should be isolating that regime, not inviting them to New Zealand to take part in talks.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a specific government decision — whether to grant visas for junta representatives to attend the ASEAN dialogue meeting — rather than on the other party in general.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When you think about that, you think about Jacinda Ardern and her legacy, and Chris Hipkins. I often thought if they were to come up with a billboard that they should have run in the election, it would have been “It’s the thought that counts”, and that sums up Jacinda Arden’s whole approach—it’s the thought that counts.
focus.explanation: Content is entirely a characterisation of two opponents' general approach; no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named in the passage.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: When you think about that, you think about Jacinda Ardern and her legacy, and Chris Hipkins. I often thought if they were to come up with a billboard that they should have run in the election, it would have been “It’s the thought that counts”, and that sums up Jacinda Arden’s whole approach—it’s the thought that counts.
civility.explanation: Mockery aimed at two named individuals — an invented billboard slogan used to characterise a former Prime Minister's whole approach as well-meaning but empty. Short of a direct insult, but it sneers at the person rather than engaging the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Ivory towers—that’s all I say to them. Wake up.
focus.explanation: Purely a characterisation of 'the left' as detached; no policy, mechanism, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’re a plant-based pastoral system, for goodness sake, and yet I hear the boffins say, “Use boluses”. Well, I’m a farmer that’s got five or six broken bones from drenching animals. What a nonsense!
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the mitigation technology at issue in the methane debate rather than the opposing party, even though the inference offered is weak.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I know that that side of the House may struggle to comprehend that logic, but, then again, farm logic is beneath them; not this Government.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the Opposition is supposedly like; no policy, figure or measure is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s been tough for many communities as they’ve had to deal with the torrent of unpopular and damaging Government policy.
focus.explanation: A blanket characterisation of the previous government's policy programme; no specific policy, cost or outcome is named for the claim to be tested against.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’re a plant-based pastoral system, for goodness sake, and yet I hear the boffins say, “Use boluses”. Well, I’m a farmer that’s got five or six broken bones from drenching animals. What a nonsense!
rigor.explanation: Rejects a specific mitigation option (methane-inhibiting boluses) on the basis of one personal anecdote about drenching injuries — an appeal to anecdote; the conclusion that the approach is unworkable does not follow from the speaker's own injury history.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And the member can dispute that, but this is what people are telling me from their firsthand experiences.
rigor.explanation: Offers second-hand personal anecdotes (a taxi driver, a nurse's mother) as the evidential basis for the effectiveness of the pandemic response — an appeal to anecdote; the conclusion about policy efficacy does not follow from individual testimony.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Public servants are being stripped out and are losing their jobs purely to pay for tax cuts—tax cuts that will provide lower-income earners with the equivalent of two lollipops in their back pocket.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a sole causal link ('purely') between public sector job losses and funding tax cuts with nothing offered to establish the connection — a bare causal attribution.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They navigated the global financial crisis well because they have a mineral sector that backs their country.
rigor.explanation: A single-cause explanation of Australia's GFC performance attributed wholly to mining, with nothing offered to rule out the fiscal stimulus, banking regulation or Chinese demand that also plausibly explain it — the conclusion outruns the evidence given.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Government has announced GE as part of our future, moving forward.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the coalition Government has announced a policy of enabling gene technology / genetic engineering.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government announcements and coalition agreement text prior to 10 April 2024 on ending the effective ban on gene technology. True if a ministerial announcement or coalition commitment to liberalise GE/gene technology rules exists; false if no such announcement had been made.

veracity.statement: This current Government, as he mentioned, is choosing to give a $2.9 billion tax cut to landlords.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Government's restoration of interest deductibility for residential rental property is worth $2.9 billion to landlords.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury / IRD costings of the restoration of interest deductibility for residential rental property over the forecast period. True if the published cost is approximately $2.9 billion; false if materially different (e.g. under $2b or over $4b).

veracity.statement: We’ve heard this Government’s laser-sharp focus on the cost of living crisis, and yet their early childhood policy is simply going to create more bureaucracy for parents when early childhood is one of the most expensive in the world, here in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that early childhood education/care in New Zealand is among the most expensive in the world.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD net childcare cost data as a percentage of household income (Family Database / Tax-Benefit models). True if New Zealand sits in the most expensive group of OECD countries on that measure; false if it sits around or below the OECD median.

veracity.statement: On top of the consequences in the aftermath of closed borders, which has left New Zealand with massive supply chain issues and massive staffing challenges, the cost of living has gone through the roof, and it’s being fuelled largely by domestic inflation and many businesses are struggling to climb out of that hole.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's inflation at this time was driven largely by domestic (non-tradable) rather than imported factors.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI decomposition into tradable and non-tradable inflation for the quarters preceding April 2024. True if non-tradable inflation contributed the larger share of the annual CPI increase; false if tradable inflation dominated.

veracity.statement: Now, this system was extremely well tested after Cyclone Gita, when some temporary legislation went in place, but it only lasted five years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that temporary legislation enabling recovery of storm-damaged timber was enacted after Cyclone Gita (2018) and expired after five years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand statute/regulation enacted following Cyclone Gita in February 2018 permitting harvesting of weather-damaged trees on conservation land, and its stated expiry. True if such an instrument existed with a five-year duration; false if no such instrument existed or its term differed materially.

civility.statement: Quite frankly, I found some of her comments absolutely sickening.
civility.explanation: Directed at a named member's remarks rather than at her as a person, but 'sickening' is a visceral denunciation that edges past robust disagreement into condemnation of the member herself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But for someone to brag when it’s only going to be the equivalent of a couple of Chupa Chups for some people, and yet a far higher amount for people like us here, in Parliament, as MPs—we don’t need the tax cuts that the Government is proposing or wanting to put in place.
civility.explanation: 'Brag' is a pointed characterisation of how the Minister presented the policy, but the criticism stays largely on the distributional substance rather than landing on her as a person.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, I would argue with Mr Goldsmith that that turbocharged spending saved businesses, saved lives, and saved livelihoods, and we make no apology on this side of the House for doing so by putting people first.
specificity.explanation: A defence of COVID spending with no amounts, programmes, timeframes or outcome measures attached — three general verbs and a statement of principle.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This current Government, as he mentioned, is choosing to give a $2.9 billion tax cut to landlords.
specificity.explanation: Names a dollar figure, a beneficiary group and a specific policy choice — directly checkable against fiscal costings.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But, never fear: our new Government is here. Common sense is back and we’re going to get the economy thriving again—back on track, as we say.
specificity.explanation: Slogans only — 'common sense is back', 'back on track' — with no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named policy.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It just makes another demonstration of economic common sense, and that’s my member’s bill, which has gone into the ballot today: the Adverse Weather-affected Timber Recovery on Conservation Lands Bill, which will enable the Director-General of Conservation to decide on the harvesting of parts of trees irreversibly damaged in weather events.
specificity.explanation: Names the bill, the decision-maker it empowers and the precise scope of the power; missing only quantities or expected economic value.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Within our court justice system, this Government has removed section 27 of the Sentencing Act, which experts have stated will lead to further discrimination of Māori in the criminal justice system, higher rates of offending, and higher rates of Māori in prison, when we, as Māori, are already the most incarcerated indigenous people on the planet—or within our health sector, which has seen Te Aka Whai Ora be completely abolished.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three checkable facts as of April 2024: that the Government has removed section 27 of the Sentencing Act 2002; that Māori are the most incarcerated indigenous people in the world; and that Te Aka Whai Ora (the Māori Health Authority) has been abolished.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: (a) NZ legislation database / Hansard: whether an enacted amendment had removed or repealed s27 of the Sentencing Act 2002 by 10 April 2024 — true if enacted, false if only announced or before the House; (b) Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Act 2024 — true if enacted and the entity wound up; (c) comparative imprisonment-rate data (Corrections/Statistics NZ vs Australian and Canadian indigenous imprisonment rates) — true if Māori rates are the highest reported for any indigenous population.

veracity.statement: We’ve launched an additional mobile breast screening unit, which will take the national fleet to 13, further increasing access for up to 6,000 people in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a further mobile breast-screening unit has been launched, that the national fleet now numbers 13, and that this extends access to up to 6,000 people.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand / BreastScreen Aotearoa records and the Minister of Health's announcements as at April 2024: true if a new mobile unit was in service bringing the fleet to 13 and the official estimate of additional women screened is around 6,000; false if the fleet total or the access figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: The healthcare system went backwards under the previous Government and it failed to drive targets.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous (Labour) Government did not operate health targets; the 'went backwards' clause is judged only through that operational claim about targets and published performance.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Health NZ published health-target reporting 2017–2023: true if the national health targets were discontinued or not publicly reported under that Government and headline measures (ED six-hour, elective wait times, immunisation coverage) deteriorated over the period; false if targets were maintained and publicly reported with stable or improving performance.

veracity.statement: Methane decays back to carbon dioxide—it decays back to carbon dioxide in 10 or 12 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that atmospheric methane oxidises to carbon dioxide over a period of roughly 10 to 12 years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IPCC AR6 / atmospheric chemistry literature on the perturbation and atmospheric lifetime of CH4: true if the accepted atmospheric lifetime is approximately 10–12 years and the principal sink is oxidation ending in CO2; false if the lifetime or the decay product is materially different.

veracity.statement: New Zealand used to have over 70 million sheep—70 million. It’s now less than 25 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a historical peak NZ sheep flock above 70 million and a current flock below 25 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Agricultural Production Statistics sheep numbers: true if the recorded peak exceeded 70 million and the most recent published count as at 2024 was below 25 million; false if either figure is materially outside that.

veracity.statement: Peak herd was in 2005 and 2006. Ruminant numbers have been falling ever since.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's ruminant livestock numbers peaked in 2005–2006 and have declined continuously since then.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Agricultural Production Statistics series for dairy cattle, beef cattle, sheep and deer: true if total ruminant numbers (and the dairy herd) peaked in 2005–06 and fell in every subsequent period; false if any major class — notably dairy cattle — continued rising after 2006.

focus.statement: I mean, there’s literally nothing left you can take away from us: section 27 in the court justice system, section 27AA in Oranga Tamariki, ministerial alienation of te reo Māori, disestablishment of the Māori Health Authority, the fast-tracking bill, the repeal of smoke-free laws, and the Treaty principles bill—what a list.
focus.explanation: Names seven specific measures of the Government's programme and holds the Government to account for each. This is scrutiny of named policy, not party-bashing, so it scores at the top.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I know the other side is shouting because they don’t want better health outcomes, but I do just want to close and thank all the hard work of our healthcare staff, who work across the country to deliver better health outcomes for all New Zealanders.
focus.explanation: The contested part of the statement is purely about what the other side supposedly wants; no policy, figure or mechanism is at issue in it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is why oral questions raised yesterday by the left highlighted their blatant ignorance of farming and on-farm practices. What—did you all fail third-form science?
focus.explanation: Nominally about methane questions, but the content is entirely a characterisation of opponents as ignorant; no mechanism, figure or provision is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I mean, there’s literally nothing left you can take away from us: section 27 in the court justice system, section 27AA in Oranga Tamariki, ministerial alienation of te reo Māori, disestablishment of the Māori Health Authority, the fast-tracking bill, the repeal of smoke-free laws, and the Treaty principles bill—what a list.
specificity.explanation: Names identifiable statutory provisions, bills and repeals that a reader could look up, but supplies no figures, dates or mechanisms — a checkable list rather than a precise account.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, I’ve talked about faster cancer treatments, but our targets also include improving immunisation for kids: we want 95 percent of children to be immunised by the age of 24 months.
specificity.explanation: A named target with a precise threshold (95 percent) and an age point (24 months) that anyone could check performance against.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This has to go down as the worst plan towards Māori and indigenous people since 1863.
civility.explanation: An extremely harsh judgement, but aimed entirely at the Government's 100-day plan. No person is attacked, no bad faith is imputed to any individual. Under the re-anchored scale, brutal criticism of a policy is civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I know the other side is shouting because they don’t want better health outcomes, but I do just want to close and thank all the hard work of our healthcare staff, who work across the country to deliver better health outcomes for all New Zealanders.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to opposing members — that they actively do not want better health outcomes. Short of a direct insult, but it ascribes malice rather than engaging their position.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What of Megan Woods or Chlöe Swarbrick yesterday and today offering evangelical sermons of what farmers should do to farmers?
civility.explanation: Names two members and mocks them personally — casting their contributions as 'evangelical sermons' rather than engaging what they actually argued about methane.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That is why oral questions raised yesterday by the left highlighted their blatant ignorance of farming and on-farm practices. What—did you all fail third-form science?
civility.explanation: Directly derides members' intelligence and education ('did you all fail third-form science?'), a personal jibe aimed across the House rather than at any argument.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What, would you have us slaughter all our animals? If not, how many—how many should we slaughter?
rigor.explanation: A strawman and false dichotomy: it recasts a position on methane pricing/targets as a demand to slaughter the national herd, and offers nothing connecting the opposing policy to that conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In fact, about 80 percent of countries around the world already recognise this right in their domestic legal systems.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 80% of the world's countries already recognise a right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment in domestic law.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: UN Special Rapporteur / UNEP global surveys of constitutional, legislative and treaty recognition of the right to a healthy environment (e.g. the ~155-of-193-states count); true if the share recognising it domestically is approximately 80% as at 2024, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: But it is a right that we have recognised internationally, because in 2022 it was the subject of a historic UN resolution, and New Zealand voted in favour of that resolution.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a UN resolution recognising the right to a healthy environment was adopted in 2022 and that New Zealand voted in favour of it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: UN General Assembly voting record for resolution A/RES/76/300 (28 July 2022); true if the resolution recognises the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment and New Zealand is recorded as voting in favour, false if New Zealand abstained, voted against, or no such 2022 resolution exists.

veracity.statement: I may be shepherding it through the House, but it was originally proposed by Lawyers for Climate Action NZ back in 2019 and supported by 59 then Queens Counsel in an open letter.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the origin of the proposal (Lawyers for Climate Action NZ, 2019) and that 59 Queen's Counsel signed an open letter in support.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Lawyers for Climate Action NZ's 2019 publications and the open letter itself; true if the proposal dates from 2019 and the letter carries 59 QC signatories, false if the year or signatory count is materially different.

veracity.statement: Ten years ago, Patrick Gower, the former Newshub political editor, pilloried my maiden speech as a call for human rights for snails, because in that speech I had pointed out that, in my lifetime, fully half of all of the planet’s wildlife has been extinguished.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that Patrick Gower characterised Shaw's maiden speech that way, and that half the planet's wildlife has been lost within Shaw's lifetime.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Newshub archive of Gower's commentary on Shaw's 2014 maiden speech, and the WWF/ZSL Living Planet Index for declines in monitored vertebrate populations since the early 1970s; true if Gower made that characterisation and the standard index shows losses of the order of half or more, false if either is contradicted.

rigor.statement: It is simply a statement of fact that each and every one of us depends on clean air, fresh water, healthy soils, and a stable climate for our very survival. You take any one of those away and our own human rights become untenable.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: environmental preconditions underpin the exercise of other rights, therefore environmental protection is a rights question. The step from dependence to 'untenable' is somewhat stronger than what is offered, but the reasoning largely tracks the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, some will argue, no doubt, that creating this new right will enable the courts to interfere with parliamentary sovereignty. It does no such thing, any more than the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act does today.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts an anticipated objection by analogy to the existing operation of NZBORA, and the surrounding sentences supply the mechanism (ss 6 and 7 interpretation and vetting). The analogy carries most of the weight but is grounded rather than asserted.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If you witness the current drive to repeal, unwind, and override nearly 40 years of environmental legislation, regulation, and jurisprudence, it appears to me that, in the current moment, there is actually less political consensus on even the most basic environmental protections than there has been for most of my lifetime.
focus.explanation: Directed at a body of policy — the repeal programme for environmental legislation and regulation — rather than at the other party's character, but it stays at the level of a general legislative direction without naming a specific measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’re hearing about the respect that the members of the Government have for the courts and for the judicial system, and they’re heckling.
focus.explanation: An aside entirely about the conduct and supposed hypocrisy of members opposite; no policy, measure or figure is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We’re hearing about the respect that the members of the Government have for the courts and for the judicial system, and they’re heckling.
civility.explanation: A sarcastic aside imputing insincerity to Government members over their professed respect for the courts; it sneers rather than engaging any argument they made.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Instead, this Government is proposing to concentrate power in an unprecedented way—into the hands of three Ministers—yet they’re trying to make it look like they’re going to have some level of independent consideration with some pretend panels that are going to have some sort of opinion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the fast-track bill gives final decision-making power to three Ministers, with expert panels holding only an advisory role.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Fast-track Approvals Bill as introduced (March 2024): true if the Bill vests joint final approval in three named Ministers and makes the expert panel's role advisory/recommendatory only; false if the decision sits with the panel or with a wider set of decision-makers.

veracity.statement: The United Kingdom passed similar legislation in 2020, and New South Wales in 2022.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the enactment dates of comparable 'no body, no parole' laws in the UK and New South Wales.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: UK and NSW statute books: true if a UK Act requiring parole boards to consider non-disclosure of a victim's remains received Royal Assent in 2020 and an equivalent NSW Act was passed in 2022; false if either date is wrong.

veracity.statement: Similarly, New South Wales became the fifth state in Australia to introduce the legislation colloquially known as “Lyn’s Law”, after former Sydney teacher Chris Dawson was convicted in 2022 of murdering his 33-year-old wife, Lynette, who disappeared from their northern beaches home over 40 years ago.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that NSW was the fifth Australian state to enact 'no body, no parole' legislation and that Chris Dawson was convicted in 2022 of murdering Lynette Dawson.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Australian state parole legislation records and the NSW Supreme Court judgment in R v Dawson: true if four other Australian states had already enacted such laws before NSW and Dawson's murder conviction was entered in 2022; false if the ordinal count or the conviction year is wrong.

veracity.statement: Both laws in the United Kingdom and New South Wales have successfully acted as incentives for those who conceal the remains of victims to front up about their whereabouts, and have prevented those who refuse to do so from being released on parole.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a demonstrated effect of the UK and NSW laws: that they have induced disclosures and blocked parole for non-disclosing offenders.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: UK Parole Board and NSW State Parole Authority reporting, plus published reviews of Helen's Law and Lyn's Law up to April 2024: true if documented cases exist of offenders disclosing remains after the laws or being refused parole under them; false if no such cases are recorded.

veracity.statement: Mr Benbow was sentenced to life with a minimum non-parole period of 17 years in March of this year for the murder.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the sentence and minimum non-parole period imposed on David Benbow in March 2024 for the murder of Michael McGrath.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Christchurch High Court sentencing decision for David Benbow: true if sentenced in March 2024 to life imprisonment with a minimum period of 17 years; false if the date or the minimum period differs.

focus.statement: Instead, this Government is proposing to concentrate power in an unprecedented way—into the hands of three Ministers—yet they’re trying to make it look like they’re going to have some level of independent consideration with some pretend panels that are going to have some sort of opinion.

focus.explanation: Squarely engages the measure before the House and the reason for opposing it; no party-bashing content.
