focus.statement: I would just say, if you want to create a human right to property, you’d want to be very careful what you wish for, because you might have to hand back all the land that was stolen and swindled and confiscated.
focus.explanation: Directly engages the substantive objection raised in debate — that entrenching a new right in the Bill of Rights invites a right to property — and answers it on its merits rather than turning on the parties opposite.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There was the fantastic speech by Simon Court. Of course, he said, “Here’s a reckon”—and it’s probably true, hence outlining how this Government makes its decisions: pub talk translated into Government policy!
focus.explanation: Once the jibe about how the Government supposedly makes decisions is removed there is no policy content left — no mechanism, cost, or provision of the bill is named.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would just say, if you want to create a human right to property, you’d want to be very careful what you wish for, because you might have to hand back all the land that was stolen and swindled and confiscated.
rigor.explanation: A real consequence-based inference: an entrenched property right would collide with historical confiscations. But the legal mechanism connecting a BORA property right to restitution of confiscated land is asserted rather than shown, so there is a gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I also want to thank the 59 King’s Counsels who supported the amendment—and if David Parker wants a debate about what the appropriate place is, I can find him 59 King’s Counsels to have that argument with—as well as organisations like World Wide Fund for Nature, who are supporting it.
rigor.explanation: Answers a legal objection about whether the Bill of Rights Act is the appropriate vehicle by counting supportive senior lawyers rather than giving a reason. A bare appeal to authority — the number of KCs does not itself establish the constitutional point.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And he looked at me and he said, “Well, it’s a very interesting area of law.”, and then walked off. In other words, I suspect they had no idea what was in it.
rigor.explanation: Concludes that a whole Cabinet did not understand the Whanganui settlement from a single remembered brush-off in a 2011 election debate. Argument from anecdote, with nothing offered to bridge one evasive reply and collective ignorance.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: People pollute the atmosphere. They destroy rivers and species and ecosystems for the very same reasons that they used slave labour or seized land that once belonged to a people that they considered to be inferior.
rigor.explanation: Rests the case for the bill on an analogy between environmental degradation and slavery/land confiscation, asserting the motives are "the very same" without offering anything to establish the parallel. The conclusion rides on the emotional force of the comparison rather than on a demonstrated similarity.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There was the fantastic speech by Simon Court. Of course, he said, “Here’s a reckon”—and it’s probably true, hence outlining how this Government makes its decisions: pub talk translated into Government policy!
civility.explanation: Sarcastic framing of a named member's speech ("fantastic") used as a springboard for mockery — sneering rather than engaging what was said. Short of a direct insult but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I also want to thank the 59 King’s Counsels who supported the amendment—and if David Parker wants a debate about what the appropriate place is, I can find him 59 King’s Counsels to have that argument with—as well as organisations like World Wide Fund for Nature, who are supporting it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 59 King's Counsel publicly supported the proposed right-to-a-sustainable-environment amendment, and that WWF is among the supporting organisations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Lawyers for Climate Action NZ's published open letter/submission on the sustainable environment BORA amendment and its signatory list; true if 59 King's Counsel are recorded as signatories/supporters, false if the count is materially different or no such list exists. WWF-NZ's own statements would settle the second limb.

veracity.statement: Now, sadly, Polly died of lung cancer in 2019, which is the same year that Lawyers for Climate Action first proposed the bill.
veracity.explanation: Two joined factual claims: that barrister Polly Higgins died of lung cancer in 2019, and that Lawyers for Climate Action NZ first proposed this amendment in that same year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published obituaries and Stop Ecocide/legal press reports of Polly Higgins' death (cause and year), plus Lawyers for Climate Action NZ's own publication record for when the sustainable-environment BORA amendment was first proposed; true if both the 2019 death from lung cancer and a 2019 first proposal are documented, false if either year or the cause differs.

specificity.statement: This bill will address this injustice in two ways. It will repeal the Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act, remove it from the statute book; and the people who lost citizenship in 1982 will be entitled to apply for and receive citizenship by a grant under the Citizenship Act 1977.
specificity.explanation: Names the two operative mechanisms of the bill, the statutes involved (Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act, Citizenship Act 1977) and the affected cohort (those who lost citizenship in 1982). Fully checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill will address this injustice in two ways. It will repeal the Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act, remove it from the statute book; and the people who lost citizenship in 1982 will be entitled to apply for and receive citizenship by a grant under the Citizenship Act 1977.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure before the House — what it repeals and what entitlement it creates. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But our point is that the Governments of the past, of many stripes, of many different colours—red, blue, green, Te Pāti Māori, others—have not taken this up, and we would argue it’s because legally the arguments have been exhausted over a 42-year period.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of why the bill should not proceed — the forum, the history of the issue and the state of the legal arguments — rather than characterising the sponsor's party. The roll-call of party colours is descriptive, not tribal.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We had a group of New Zealand citizens who had their citizenship recognised and then had that citizenship removed by statute. That is unfair—plain and simple. States should not be able to remove citizenship wholesale like that. It is unjust.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: recognised citizenship was stripped wholesale by statute, therefore unjust. The conclusion follows from the stated premise plus an explicit normative principle about states removing citizenship, though the principle itself is asserted rather than argued for.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But our point is that the Governments of the past, of many stripes, of many different colours—red, blue, green, Te Pāti Māori, others—have not taken this up, and we would argue it’s because legally the arguments have been exhausted over a 42-year period.
rigor.explanation: Infers from the fact that no government has legislated on the issue that the legal arguments must be exhausted. That is an argument from inaction — successive governments' failure to act is equally consistent with lack of political priority, and no legal analysis is offered to support the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The New Zealand administration was so appalling and so bad that Prime Minister Helen Clark had to apologise in 2002.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a New Zealand Prime Minister, Helen Clark, delivered an apology to Samoa in 2002 over New Zealand's colonial administration.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporary records of the Prime Minister's speeches and NZ/Samoan news reporting from 2002; true if Helen Clark delivered a formal apology to Samoa for New Zealand's administration during 2002, false if no such apology occurred or it was made by another person or in a different year.

veracity.statement: What a lot of New Zealanders don’t know is that New Zealand administered Samoa for 48 years as part of the World War I effort, on behalf of Britain from the then German colonial rule.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 48-year duration for New Zealand's administration of Samoa, beginning with the World War I seizure of the territory from German colonial rule on Britain's behalf.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Historical record of the New Zealand occupation/administration of Samoa (seizure in 1914 through to Samoan independence in 1962); true if the administration spanned approximately 48 years and began as a WWI action against German colonial rule on Britain's behalf, false if the span is materially different or the origin is misdescribed.

veracity.statement: It was in 1982 that the Privy Council ruled that all Samoans born between 1924 and 1948 were British subjects and, because of that, from 1949 onwards, they were New Zealand citizens.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the year (1982), the body (Privy Council) and the birth-year range (1924–1948) of the ruling that conferred British subject and subsequently New Zealand citizenship status on a cohort of Samoans.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Privy Council judgment in Lesa v Attorney-General (New Zealand) and its reported date and reasoning; true if decided in 1982 and covering Samoans born between 1924 and 1948 with the citizenship consequence described, false if the year, tribunal or birth-year range differs materially.

veracity.statement: Over 9,000 people signed that petition.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the signature count of the 2003 petition to Parliament on the Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act, referenced immediately beforehand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliamentary petition record and select committee report for the 2003 petition on the Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act 1982; true if the recorded number of signatories exceeds 9,000, false if materially fewer.

veracity.statement: If we look back since 1982 and that Muldoon administration, that National Government, we’ve had three Labour Governments since—the fourth, the fifth, and the sixth—we’ve had 10 Prime Ministers, we’ve had an array of wonderful representation from our Pasifika community and from our Samoan community, and we’ve had an apology from a previous Prime Minister, Jacinda Ardern, on the Dawn Raids, in 2021.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three checkable historical facts: three Labour Governments since 1982, a count of 10 Prime Ministers over that period, and a Dawn Raids apology delivered by Jacinda Ardern in 2021.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The list of New Zealand Prime Ministers and Governments from 1982 to 2024, and reporting of the Dawn Raids apology; true if there have been three Labour Governments (fourth, fifth, sixth) and about 10 Prime Ministers in that span and Ardern apologised for the Dawn Raids in 2021, false if the counts are materially wrong (e.g. the true number of PMs since 1982 differs) or the apology's author or year is wrong.

civility.statement: We in the National Party are opposing this Restoring Citizenship Removed By Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act 1982 Bill, and I just want to take you through some of our thinking.
civility.explanation: States opposition to a contested bill, in front of an affected community, without any disparagement of the sponsor or of those affected — the substance only.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So our concern is that it does create a number of unprecedented measures, and it also creates a situation where we have got a focus at the moment on managing the immigration settings and adopting them accordingly to fit today’s demands, and 173,000 non - New Zealand citizens migrated here in 2023.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 173,000 non-New Zealand citizens migrated to New Zealand in the 2023 calendar year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration statistics for calendar year 2023, non-NZ-citizen migrant arrivals (and/or net migration of non-NZ citizens); true if a published series gives approximately 173,000, false if the relevant figures are materially different.

veracity.statement: The members opposite say, “Oh well, you’re in charge now.” Well, can I just remind them that they were in charge, with the biggest majority in MMP history, six months ago. They were in charge, with a single-party majority, just six months ago.
veracity.explanation: Claims Labour held the largest majority in MMP history, a single-party majority, and was in government six months before 10 April 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission final results for the 2020 general election compared with all MMP-era elections (1996 onward); true if Labour's 2020 seat share was the largest single-party majority of the MMP era and the change of government followed the October 2023 election roughly six months before this debate, false if another MMP-era party held a larger majority or the timing is materially wrong.

veracity.statement: They were one or many of the 90,000 people that signed the petition at the time and have been fighting for this change for decades.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2003 petition to Parliament on Samoan citizenship carried 90,000 signatures.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary petition records and contemporaneous reporting on the 2003 Samoan citizenship petition; true if the recorded signature count is approximately 90,000, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: However, beyond the Dawn Raids, the Muldoon-led National Government continued on their trajectory with the 1982 retrospective removal of the right to citizenship for those Samoans born between 1924 to 1948.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act 1982, passed under the Muldoon National Government, retrospectively removed New Zealand citizenship from Samoans born between 1924 and 1948.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act 1982 and the Privy Council decision in Lesa v Attorney-General; true if the Act retrospectively deprived that birth cohort of citizenship and was enacted under the Muldoon government, false if the cohort, effect or government is materially misstated.

veracity.statement: As part of the apology, we provided educational scholarships, access to the Manaaki New Zealand Short Term Scholarship training courses, support for Pacific artists and historians to develop a comprehensive written and oral account of the Dawn Raids, but no one at that time implied that the work required by New Zealand Governments to demonstrate a genuine understanding of the discrimination and trauma the Pacific community had endured was complete.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the specific content of the 2021 Dawn Raids apology package: educational scholarships, Manaaki New Zealand Short Term Scholarship training courses, and support for Pacific artists and historians to record the Dawn Raids.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The August 2021 Dawn Raids apology announcement and associated Ministry for Pacific Peoples / MFAT documentation; true if those three components were part of the announced package, false if they were not.

veracity.statement: Turning my mind back to the bill in front of us, Teanau Tuiono has stated clearly we are talking about 3,000 to 5,000 people, not all of whom would want to take the opportunity up.
veracity.explanation: Relays Teanau Tuiono's claim that the bill would affect 3,000 to 5,000 people.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's explanatory note, departmental advice or Tuiono's first reading speech on the number of people affected; true if the stated range is 3,000-5,000, false if the sponsor's or officials' estimate is materially different.

veracity.statement: And when we look at that historic matter—this is my view—which, obviously, we want to explore in the select committee process, at the time, the citizenship of those people was revoked because those people acquired Samoan citizenship.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the operative reason New Zealand citizenship was removed by the 1982 Act was that the affected people had acquired Samoan citizenship.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act 1982 and the Privy Council judgment in Lesa v Attorney-General (1982); true if the Act's deprivation provisions turned on acquisition of Samoan citizenship, false if it deprived citizenship of a birth cohort recognised as NZ citizens by the Privy Council regardless of Samoan citizenship (with an exception only for those present in NZ at the specified date).

specificity.statement: You would have seen our immigration Minister, Erica Stanford, unveil a range of changes to the likes of the Accredited Employer Work Visa scheme, and also, at the weekend, she put in a number of measures that will address migrant worker exploitation.
specificity.explanation: Names a real scheme (Accredited Employer Work Visa) and a rough timeframe ('at the weekend'), but describes the content only as 'a range of changes' and 'a number of measures' — no mechanism, figure or detail of what was actually announced.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Turning my mind back to the bill in front of us, Teanau Tuiono has stated clearly we are talking about 3,000 to 5,000 people, not all of whom would want to take the opportunity up.
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete, checkable magnitude for the bill's effect (3,000-5,000 people) with the caveat that not all would take it up, though it gives no breakdown or source.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Everyone has looked at this. Successive Prime Ministers have looked at this. Successive Governments have looked at this. We on this side of the House have also looked closely at it. We have also been talking to friends like our friend Arthur Anae. We have also been lobbied hard. We have also taken legal advice. But, on the balance of it, National will oppose this bill.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (oppose the bill) rests on an appeal to tradition and authority — that previous Prime Ministers and Governments considered the matter and did not act, and that legal advice was taken — without stating any of the reasons or grounds. That others declined to act does not entail that acting is wrong.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Off the back of the significant contributions Samoans have made to Aotearoa, it is the right thing to do; on behalf of the nearly 200,000 Samoans who have made New Zealand their home, it is the right thing to do; in the spirit of the 1962 Treaty of Friendship between Samoa, where we pledged the two countries would be governed by a spirit of close friendship, it is the right thing to do; and with the acknowledgement of the discriminatory immigration policy our Samoan community endured before and during the period that this legislation was passed, it is the right thing to do.
rigor.explanation: An anaphoric appeal to sentiment and community standing: past contributions, population size and a treaty's 'spirit' are offered as grounds, but none of them entail that this particular legislative remedy is warranted. The final clause (past discrimination by this Act) is a real premise; the rest is rhetorical repetition.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There is no precedent being set when it is only being considered at select committee. That is where we get to consider the advice, the submissions from the community, and to hear from the legal experts.
rigor.explanation: Directly rebuts the precedent objection with a valid procedural point — referral to select committee is not enactment, and is the stage at which advice and submissions are tested. The inference holds, though it slightly understates that a first reading vote is itself a signal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We want to say that we do not see that that 1982 Act was about being racist, because if it was about being racist then we know that even in 1982 there were people from so many different parts of the world; the citizenships of all those people would have been revoked if it was based on race.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the conclusion assumes racial discrimination must apply to every non-European group at once, so that singling out one group cannot be racially motivated. Discrimination directed at a single ethnic group is not excluded by the absence of a universal revocation.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The members opposite say, “Oh well, you’re in charge now.” Well, can I just remind them that they were in charge, with the biggest majority in MMP history, six months ago. They were in charge, with a single-party majority, just six months ago.
focus.explanation: Answers an interjection by pointing at the previous government's majority and inaction rather than at the bill's provisions. There is a thread of accountability (Labour did not do this when it could have), but no policy, figure or mechanism is named — the weight is party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There is no precedent being set when it is only being considered at select committee. That is where we get to consider the advice, the submissions from the community, and to hear from the legal experts.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the question before the House — what a select committee referral does and does not decide — with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Labour is represented by our Samoan community. Labour is here to support the Samoan community. We stand by our Green Party brother in supporting this bill today.
focus.explanation: Party positioning — who stands with whom — rather than the content of the bill. It names the bill only as the thing being supported, with no mechanism, figure or effect.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So I do find it very interesting that the member Cameron Brewer says that he doesn’t want to retroactively reinstate citizenship for Samoans when it was retrospectively taken away from them.
civility.explanation: Pointed, mildly barbed framing ('I do find it very interesting') aimed at a named member, but the substance engages his stated position on retrospectivity rather than his character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We don’t need to hear from the people who think they are legal experts in the House today.
civility.explanation: A sneer at other members' pretension to expertise — it disparages who they think they are rather than engaging what they argued.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We want to say that we do not see that that 1982 Act was about being racist, because if it was about being racist then we know that even in 1982 there were people from so many different parts of the world; the citizenships of all those people would have been revoked if it was based on race.
civility.explanation: Contests the sponsor's characterisation of the 1982 Act with a stated reason and no reflection on the member himself.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It will mean that approximately 5,000 people who lost citizenship in 1982 will be able to apply for and receive citizenship by grant. We acknowledge this doesn’t confer citizenship directly but creates automatic eligibility to apply for and receive citizenship.
specificity.explanation: Gives a number affected, the year, and the precise legal mechanism (automatic eligibility to apply, not direct conferral) — checkable against the bill's explanatory note.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It was 1976 when Dawn Raids began targeting Pacific households accused of harbouring overstayers, despite it being those of European ethnicity who made up two-thirds of all overstayers in New Zealand at the time.
specificity.explanation: Names a year, the targeted group, and a proportion — precise enough that someone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We know there’s been numerous attempts to repeal this Act, and I acknowledge the petition in 2003, and, again, the former MP Arthur Anae for his work.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a petition seeking repeal of the Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act 1982 was presented in 2003 and that former MP Arthur Anae worked on the repeal effort.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary petition records / select committee reports for 2003 on the Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act 1982; true if a repeal petition was received that year and Arthur Anae is recorded as promoting repeal, false if no such petition exists in that period.

veracity.statement: It was 1976 when Dawn Raids began targeting Pacific households accused of harbouring overstayers, despite it being those of European ethnicity who made up two-thirds of all overstayers in New Zealand at the time.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that the Dawn Raids started in 1976, and that roughly two-thirds of overstayers at the time were of European ethnicity.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Historical record (NZHistory/Te Ara, Immigration Division statistics of the era) on the start date of the Dawn Raids and the ethnic breakdown of overstayers; true if raids are dated to 1976 and contemporary overstayer figures show ~two-thirds European, false if raids began materially earlier (e.g. 1973-74) or the European share was materially different.

veracity.statement: The bill will restore the right of citizenship to our Samoan community born between 1924 and 1949 that was stripped away with the introduction of the Citizen (Western Samoa) Act of 1982.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the birth-date range of the cohort affected by the 1982 Act and that the bill restores their citizenship right.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Text and explanatory note of the Restoring Citizenship Removed By Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act 1982 Bill and the 1982 Act itself; true if the covered cohort is those born in the stated window (c. 1924-1949) and the bill restores the citizenship entitlement, false if the dates or the effect (eligibility to apply rather than restoration) are materially different.

veracity.statement: Today is a historical day because we have seen the Labour Party support the Greens, we have seen Te Pāti Māori support the Greens, we have seen the ACT Party support the Greens—never thought I’d see this day—and I’ve seen New Zealand First support the Greens, support the bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Labour, Te Pāti Māori, ACT and New Zealand First all supported the Green member's bill at its first reading on this day.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard first reading vote record for the Restoring Citizenship Removed By Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act 1982 Bill of 10 April 2024; true if all four named parties are recorded as voting in favour, false if any voted against or abstained.

veracity.statement: We are proud that we are the third most spoken language in this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Samoan is the third most spoken language in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ census language data (most recent census at the time of speaking); true if Samoan ranks third by number of speakers, false if another language (e.g. Northern Chinese/Mandarin or Hindi) ranks above it.

veracity.statement: We are proud that we are the fastest growing Pacific population in Aotearoa New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Samoan population is the fastest growing Pacific ethnic group in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ census ethnic group counts across the two most recent censuses; true if the Samoan ethnic group shows the highest percentage growth among Pacific ethnic groups, false if another Pacific group (e.g. Fijian) grew faster.

focus.statement: The whakapapa of this bill takes us back in time to an era not so long ago, in the time of the Polynesian Panthers, of the Dawn Raids, and, you know, the picture that comes to mind right now is Hone Harawira, and many of those of our whānau nō Te Tai Tokerau, he Māori katoa ka tautoko i ēnei whānau [family from Northland, they are all Māori who support these families]; and the time where Māori and Pasifika joined together to fight back against the relentless infringement of our rights as Pasifika and Māori that a Muldoon or National Government—not too dissimilar to our current one—inflicted upon us.
focus.explanation: Genuine historical context for the bill, but the weight of the aside is a party comparison ("not too dissimilar to our current one") that names no policy or measure of the present government.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We should have a select committee on this—if we don’t, we are still saying we know what’s best for you.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the process for this bill, but it rests on a false dichotomy: select committee referral is treated as the only alternative to paternalism, with nothing offered to rule out other means of consulting affected communities.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, the unfortunate thing for me is I did not learn about our New Zealand history until I chose to learn it at university, and that is something wrong with our country, that something as remarkable as the stripping of citizenship rights for Samoan people who were born during a period where New Zealand administered them, was their Government, was removed through an Act of this House.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single personal anecdote about her own schooling to a conclusion about a national failing — an appeal to anecdote, though the underlying point about the curriculum is coherent.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s very simple: we had a group of New Zealand citizens who had their citizenship recognised, and then they had their citizenship removed by statute.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a group of people were recognised as New Zealand citizens and then had that citizenship stripped by an Act of Parliament — the historical premise for the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Privy Council decision in Lesa v Attorney-General (NZ) [1982] and the text of the Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act 1982; true if the Privy Council recognised Western Samoans born in the relevant period as New Zealand citizens and the 1982 Act subsequently removed that status for that group, false if no such recognition or no such statutory removal occurred.

veracity.statement: One of the points that she said, and that I agreed with, is perhaps it would have been better if the National Party and the Labour Party both did the ifoga, because during that time period the Dawn Raids happened through both Governments as well.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim attributed to Judith Collins during the Dawn Raids apology debate, together with the embedded factual claim that the Dawn Raids occurred under both National and Labour governments.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for the 2021 Dawn Raids apology debate for whether Judith Collins made a remark to the effect that both National and Labour should perform the ifoga; and historical records of the Dawn Raids (1973–1979) for whether they were conducted under both the Kirk/Rowling Labour and Muldoon National governments. True if both check out, false if either the attributed remark or the two-government span is not supported.

civility.statement: I just wanted to address some of the comments from the National Party. I hope that when this comes to the select committee, they will engage with it in an open mind—that they will engage with this topic in a way that the community needs those stories to be heard.
civility.explanation: Responding to the party that voted the bill down, he addresses their position and invites engagement without any imputation of bad faith or attack on any member — a real opportunity to be uncivil that he declines.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I do also want to emphasise that this is automatic eligibility for a citizenship by grant, which we could and we should talk about.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the measure before the House — what the bill actually confers (automatic eligibility for citizenship by grant) rather than anything about opposing parties.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I do also want to emphasise that this is automatic eligibility for a citizenship by grant, which we could and we should talk about.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific legal mechanism the bill uses, but supplies no parameters, numbers or eligibility criteria — he explicitly leaves those to be discussed.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There are tensions here, political tensions in the Pacific, and we can navigate that well when we do relationship diplomacy. This bill is relationship diplomacy. If we treat the elders of Samoa with respect and dignity, and offer a pathway of citizenship back here to Aotearoa New Zealand, that is good for Aotearoa and good for Samoa and, ultimately, good for our region.
rigor.explanation: A syllogism whose middle term is asserted rather than shown: 'relationship diplomacy works' plus the bare stipulation that 'this bill is relationship diplomacy' is used to conclude regional benefit. Definitional assertion with no evidence linking this particular citizenship pathway to the diplomatic outcome claimed.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But I do want to acknowledge what is glaringly obvious, that the bill has the support of the wider House.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a majority/most parties in the House support the Restoring Citizenship Removed By Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act 1982 Repeal Bill at its first reading.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard division record for the first reading of the Restoring Citizenship Removed By Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act 1982 Repeal Bill (April 2024); true if the bill passed with support from parties beyond the sponsor's own (a clear majority), false if it was opposed by a majority or passed only narrowly on a single bloc.

veracity.statement: That particular day, 11 Samoans died, including the independent leader, Paramount Chief Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III, on Saturday, 28 December 1929.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a death toll of 11 Samoans, including Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III, on Black Saturday, dated Saturday 28 December 1929.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Standard histories of the Mau movement and NZ government/Te Ara historical records of 'Black Saturday'; true if the date is 28 December 1929 and the recorded Samoan death toll is 11 including Tamasese, false if the date or the toll is materially different.

veracity.statement: Many New Zealanders do not know or do not understand that New Zealand administered Samoa for 48 years, from 1914 to 1962.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Historical record of New Zealand's occupation (August 1914), League of Nations mandate, and UN trusteeship ending with Samoan independence on 1 January 1962; true if the administration ran 1914–1962, false if the start or end date is materially different.

veracity.falsification_criterion: (a) Historical record of German Samoa's dates (1900–1914) and mainstream historiography comparing the two administrations, including the 1918 influenza epidemic and Black Saturday; (b) the record of the apology delivered to the Samoan parliament — true if Helen Clark as Prime Minister made a formal apology in 2002, false if the apology was made by another person, in another year, or not at all.

veracity.statement: And yet, it was also done when New Zealand went in, in 1914, as was just mentioned—it was done without firing a shot; it was completely peaceful.

veracity.statement: I note that what this bill does is restore citizenship not to those in more recent times from Samoa, not to those who were living in New Zealand—because they always had it, and even in 1982 their citizenship was, of course, protected if they were living in New Zealand.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act 1982, in particular the provision preserving citizenship for persons in New Zealand on the specified 1982 date; true if those resident in New Zealand at that date retained citizenship, false if the Act removed citizenship from that group as well.

veracity.statement: But the specific date period is nothing actually to do with New Zealand’s colonial trusteeship, as it was known at the time of Samoa, but it’s actually around being a British subject; it’s not about New Zealand.

rigor.statement: And so I think we do need to think through this thing. We’re giving New Zealand citizenship in response to British citizenship. So it’s actually not quite as simple as maybe some of the emotive arguments bring out.

divination.statement: And isn’t it appropriate that we can have this discussion and, as it no doubt moves through to select committee and wherever it may go from there, that we can bring different perspectives, that we can have these conversations, but we don’t have to be firing shots at each other.

specificity.statement: My bill as it’s reported back requires offenders to advise the police of the names of the countries they will stay in for more than 48 hours, the addresses they intend to stay in in that country, the date they intend to travel to and leave that country, and, if they do not intend to return to New Zealand, provide the details of the country they intend to reside in.

veracity.statement: The vast majority of sex offenders know their victim, the victim knows them, and certainly, more ominously, the offender often knows the family and the caregivers of the family. That’s where we need to direct our protection, direct our laws, to prevent further offending.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police / Ministry of Justice victimisation data and peer-reviewed research on offender–victim relationship in child sexual offending; true if a clear majority of recorded child sexual offences involve an offender known to the victim, false if strangers account for the majority.

veracity.statement: In 2016, the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) Act was passed.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand legislation record for the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) Act; true if it received Royal assent in 2016, false if in another year.

veracity.statement: The Attorney-General was concerned about section 7 of the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act.

veracity.statement: I can say that most of the Australian states have similar legislation.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Australian state and territory child protection offender registration statutes (e.g. NSW Child Protection (Offenders Registration) Act 2000 and equivalents); true if more than half impose reporting obligations for intended overseas travel, false if fewer do.

veracity.statement: They’ve got a very low recidivism rate—again, as I talked about before—because they do the programmes and also they don’t want to go back.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections reimprisonment/reconviction statistics for child sex offenders (and Te Piriti / Kia Marama programme evaluations); true if their sexual reoffending rate is materially below the general reoffending rate, false if comparable or higher.

rigor.statement: The vast majority of sex offenders know their victim, the victim knows them, and certainly, more ominously, the offender often knows the family and the caregivers of the family. That’s where we need to direct our protection, direct our laws, to prevent further offending.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that protection and law should be aimed at known offenders — follows directly from the stated premise about where offending predominantly comes from. No fallacy; the inference tracks the premise, though the premise itself is asserted without a cited source.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They’ve got a very low recidivism rate—again, as I talked about before—because they do the programmes and also they don’t want to go back.
rigor.explanation: The causal explanation — that the low rate is because offenders complete programmes and do not want to return to prison — is asserted from personal experience with nothing offered to connect cause to effect. An appeal to anecdote in place of evidence for the causal step.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It requires registered child sex offenders to provide additional information when they are travelling overseas for more than 48 hours, and it actually struck me as quite interesting that we didn’t require this already.

veracity.statement: It requires registered child sex offenders to provide additional information when they are travelling overseas for more than 48 hours, and it actually struck me as quite interesting that we didn’t require this already.

veracity.statement: I think there were about 10 written submissions, eight of which were in favour, one, I think, was neutral, and maybe one or two more were opposed.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's report on the bill, which records the number of written submissions received: true if roughly 10 written submissions were received with about eight supportive, one neutral and one or two opposed; false if the submission count or the balance of positions differs materially.

rigor.statement: But I have a view on this, which is that this legislation has been before the House in 2015, again in 2017, in 2021 with amendments, and now, in 2024, it is, hopefully, passing through the House with support, and at some point we must recognise that what does qualify—putting the Hansen test aside—as being demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society should at some point be able to be endorsed by the Parliament itself.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (that these limits on rights are demonstrably justified) is inferred from the fact that Parliament has repeatedly legislated in this area — an appeal to repetition/tradition. Repeated enactment of similar limits is not evidence that the limits are proportionate; the premise about legislative history does not support the normative conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So we felt, as a committee, that any issues around enforceability could be addressed and could be solved through operational processes and that that should not get in the way of supporting a bill like that through the committee and into the House today.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: because the same enforceability gap already exists domestically, the offshore gap is treated as no barrier. That is a tu quoque-shaped move — the existence of a parallel weakness does not show the objection is answered — and 'operational processes' is offered as the solution without anything to show it works.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But I have a view on this, which is that this legislation has been before the House in 2015, again in 2017, in 2021 with amendments, and now, in 2024, it is, hopefully, passing through the House with support, and at some point we must recognise that what does qualify—putting the Hansen test aside—as being demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society should at some point be able to be endorsed by the Parliament itself.

civility.statement: After discussions with the member in charge of the bill, I understand that it wasn’t signalled to the member, which is a breach of courtesy, if nothing else.

civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: After discussions with the member in charge of the bill, I understand that it wasn’t signalled to the member, which is a breach of courtesy, if nothing else.

focus.statement: The way I get around that, I guess, is to say, well, it may have that effect, but, certainly, its dominant purpose is to protect potential victims, if you like, and that, in terms of proportionality, the burden on the offender is quite low. focus.explanation: Engages directly with the mechanism of the bill's notification provision and its effect on offenders; no party framing at all.

rigor.statement: The chair of the Justice Committee was perhaps a little dismissive of the Attorney-General’s report, and I can see why, but I do think we need to take statements from the Attorney-General—after all, she is, she is a King’s Counsel, if you hadn’t been told already.

rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The way I get around that, I guess, is to say, well, it may have that effect, but, certainly, its dominant purpose is to protect potential victims, if you like, and that, in terms of proportionality, the burden on the offender is quite low. Because we’re not refusing the ability to travel, we’re just requiring certain notification provisions.
rigor.explanation: A genuine proportionality inference: the conclusion (retrospectivity is tolerable) is supported by two stated premises — protective dominant purpose and a low burden evidenced by the fact that travel itself is not restricted. The step from 'dominant purpose' to 'not punishment' is asserted rather than argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: And anyone who reads the select committee report will see that there are some substantial changes, including the removal of some clauses, such as clause 4, where an amendment to section 21 was removed, where the kind of detail that perhaps was needed was actually watered down a bit so that you didn’t need to know every element of the person’s travel.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's report as reported back on the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) (Overseas Travel Reporting) Amendment Bill: true if the report recommends removing clause 4 / the amendment to section 21 and narrowing the required travel detail; false if clause 4 was retained unchanged or no such narrowing was recommended.

specificity.statement: And anyone who reads the select committee report will see that there are some substantial changes, including the removal of some clauses, such as clause 4, where an amendment to section 21 was removed, where the kind of detail that perhaps was needed was actually watered down a bit so that you didn’t need to know every element of the person’s travel.

specificity.statement: The penalties for failure to report will also be comparable: failing to comply with reporting obligations, a fine of up to $2,000 or imprisonment for one year; and providing false or misleading information, a fine of up to $4,000.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact penalty amounts and the maximum term of imprisonment attached to each reporting offence — fully checkable against the bill text.

veracity.statement: Under the country’s first ever Minister for the prevention of violence, Marama Davidson, Marama Davidson was able to pull together the country’s first ever 25-year nationwide strategy to eliminate family violence and sexual violence—eliminate.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Marama Davidson was New Zealand's first Minister for the prevention of family and sexual violence, and that under her a first-ever 25-year national strategy to eliminate family and sexual violence was produced.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial warrant records for the portfolio 'Prevention of Family and Sexual Violence' (created 2020) and the publication record of Te Aorerekura; true if Davidson was the first holder of that portfolio and Te Aorerekura is a 25-year national strategy to eliminate family and sexual violence published during her tenure, false if the portfolio predates her, or if the strategy is not 25-year/not the first of its kind.

rigor.statement: Any inconsistencies with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act would have to be conditional on a proven, effective reason for public good. rigor.explanation: A genuine proportionality argument — a stated standard (BORA breaches must be justified by proven public benefit) applied to a stated premise (insufficient evidence of effectiveness). The inference tracks, but it leans on an argument from absence of evidence, and the closing clause about shared intent does no work for the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: At best, registers like this do nothing in and of themselves to reduce offending and, at worst, undermine rehabilitation efforts and safe integration into community. We have that evidence very clearly.

rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: At best, registers like this do nothing in and of themselves to reduce offending and, at worst, undermine rehabilitation efforts and safe integration into community. We have that evidence very clearly.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the measure before the House — what offender registers do and do not achieve. No party framing at all.

focus.statement: This is an example of flawed legislation that will make politicians feel better about themselves and look tough on crime while there is no substance behind this action.

civility.statement: This is an example of flawed legislation that will make politicians feel better about themselves and look tough on crime while there is no substance behind this action.

rigor.statement: Some offenders may still choose to travel overseas for shorter periods to avoid detection. Therefore, I urge the Government to consider extending these requirements to all registered sex offenders travelling overseas, regardless of the duration of their visit.

rigor.statement: What if, however, these additional requirements were, in fact, a deterrent for the sex offender?
rigor.explanation: Offered as a reason to support the bill, but it is bare conjecture: no evidence, study or mechanism is given to connect pre-travel reporting requirements to deterrence, and the point is left as a rhetorical question rather than an argued premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Some offenders may still choose to travel overseas for shorter periods to avoid detection. Therefore, I urge the Government to consider extending these requirements to all registered sex offenders travelling overseas, regardless of the duration of their visit.

specificity.statement: It proposes amendments to the existing legislation to require registrable offenders to provide additional information to the authorities before they travel overseas for more than 48 hours.

specificity.statement: New Zealand First upholds the principles of protecting vulnerable individuals, safeguarding public safety, and ensuring the effective enforcement of laws.

veracity.statement: The World Health Organization reports that one in 13 men and one in five women are sexually abused globally.

veracity.statement: In New Zealand, one in seven children are estimated to experience sexual abuse—one in seven children in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a New Zealand child sexual abuse prevalence estimate of one in seven children.
veracity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It is alarming to note that child sex tourism is actually a significant component of the sex tourism industry in certain regions such as Thailand, where hundreds of thousands of children are estimated to be working in the sex trade.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published estimates from ECPAT International, UNICEF, the ILO or the US State Department Trafficking in Persons reports on the number of children in Thailand's sex trade; true if credible published estimates are in the hundreds of thousands, false if the accepted estimates are an order of magnitude lower or no such estimate exists.

veracity.statement: It proposes amendments to the existing legislation to require registrable offenders to provide additional information to the authorities before they travel overseas for more than 48 hours.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill's additional overseas-travel reporting obligation is triggered by travel of more than 48 hours.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) (Overseas Travel Reporting) Amendment Bill as reported back from the Justice Committee; true if the reporting trigger is travel exceeding 48 hours, false if the bill sets a different threshold or no duration threshold.

focus.statement: As a party that stands firm against crime, especially crimes against the most vulnerable, we must support measures that restrict the freedom of those who seek to harm our children.

focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: So, in summary, New Zealand First believes that public safety concerns and the safety of children, who are our most vulnerable and defenceless, far outweighs the privacy or equal protection claims of the sex offender, and it is why we believe that this bill will be well received.

divination.falsification_criterion: The division records for the remaining readings of the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) (Overseas Travel Reporting) Amendment Bill; true if the bill passes its third reading with support from a large cross-party majority, false if it is defeated, lapses, or passes only narrowly with substantial opposition.

veracity.statement: Established back in around 2016 was New Zealand’s first ever sex offender register, which required those sex offenders, when travelling within New Zealand, if travelling away from their primary residence, to make sure it was recorded where they were staying and for the length of time they’re staying, within New Zealand.

veracity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So that means that if a New Zealand citizen goes to another country and commits a sex offence against a child, then that offender can also be charged and convicted back in New Zealand.

veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific NZ prosecution: an offender who travelled to Moscow in 2007 and photographed and exploited children was sentenced in the High Court in 2008 to seven years' imprisonment on four charges of sexual violation.

veracity.statement: The child sex offender situation is on a constant escalation path.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that child sex offending is continuously increasing — a claim about a trend, not a prediction.

veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police recorded victimisations / charges for child sexual offences and internationally reported child sexual abuse material figures over the decade to 2024; true if the series show sustained year-on-year increases, false if the trend is flat, declining, or mixed.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) (Overseas Travel Reporting) Amendment Bill as reported back from the Justice Committee; true if it amends s 21 of the 2016 principal Act, false if it amends a different section or a different Act.

focus.statement: So what this bill really does is bring the overseas requirements for child sex offenders in line with the requirement which already exists when offenders travel domestically.

rigor.statement: Typically, I’m not a big fan of policies that are based on the idea of deterring someone from committing a crime because most of the research demonstrates that deterrence in itself doesn’t really work in terms of preventing crime from happening. specificity.statement: We know that there’s been instances in the past where someone travelled to Moscow in 2007 where he photographed and exploited young children. That person was then sentenced at the High Court in 2008 and received a seven-year imprisonment on four charges of sexual violation.

specificity.statement: The Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) (Overseas Travel Reporting) Amendment Bill seeks to amend section 21 of the principal Act, which is the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) Act of 2016.

veracity.statement: As mentioned before, we had 72 submissions; 12 of them appeared in person.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the submission counts for the select committee's consideration of the Sale and Supply of Alcohol (Cellar Door Tasting) Amendment Bill: 72 written submissions received, 12 heard in person.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's report on the Sale and Supply of Alcohol (Cellar Door Tasting) Amendment Bill, submissions section; true if it records 72 submissions received and 12 submitters heard, false if the recorded numbers differ materially.

civility.statement: I was curious as to why she was supporting this, because there’s been some, I think, quite reasonable apprehension from the Greens in the past around alcohol legislation, and the harm minimisation requirements need to be in that. Then I looked at the back page of the departmental report and saw that the Waiheke Wine Growers Association had made a very powerful submission.

divination.statement: It may well be the first time that the class of 2023 needs to see a personal vote in a couple of weeks, so I’m very much looking forward to that.

divination.falsification_criterion: Hansard's division record for the second reading of the Sale and Supply of Alcohol (Winery Cellar Door Tasting) Amendment Bill; true if that reading was decided by a personal vote and no earlier personal vote had been held in the 54th Parliament, false if it was a party vote or a personal vote had already occurred in this Parliament.

veracity.statement: We talk now of a $3 billion industry—this is an industry that has put New Zealand and places like Marlborough on the map—a $3 billion industry that is growing, and out of a $3 billion industry, that’s created a massive amount of tourism.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the New Zealand wine industry is worth approximately $3 billion and is growing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Winegrowers annual report / Stats NZ export figures for 2023-24; true if total wine industry value (exports plus domestic sales) is around $3 billion and rising year on year, false if materially lower or declining.

veracity.statement: In Marlborough, for instance, we’ve got over 80 percent of the wine industry, and that’s something we are really, really proud of and something we want to promote.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than 80 percent of New Zealand's wine industry is located in Marlborough.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Winegrowers vineyard-area and production statistics by region; true if Marlborough accounts for over 80% of national producing area or production, false if the share is materially below 80%.

veracity.statement: I think, originally in the bill, it was a 40-millilitre pour, and through hearing about that and through maybe the views of some members on the other side of the House, it has been reduced to 35 millilitres.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the bill as introduced specified a 40ml tasting sample and that the Justice Committee reduced it to 35ml.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Sale and Supply of Alcohol (Cellar Door Tasting) Amendment Bill as introduced versus the Justice Committee's reported-back version; true if the sample size changed from 40ml to 35ml, false if either figure differs.

specificity.statement: And the most ironic thing was that—and we heard this through the submissions—businesses—and for one particular submission, they said their bottles of wine were worth between $70 to $90 and they were giving away eight of them a day.
specificity.explanation: Carries concrete, checkable detail — a per-bottle price range and a daily quantity — sourced to a named committee's submissions, though the submitter is not named.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What we are trying to stop, here, is a free-for-all, so to anybody who would want to vote against this, I would say to you: why would you want to vote for a free-for-all, because that’s actually what you’ve got at the moment.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy framed as a loaded question: opposing this particular bill is equated with endorsing the status quo 'free-for-all', excluding any alternative amendment or regulatory approach.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s actually going to make a situation where when you turn up, you’re actually going to think a lot more about what you are purchasing and what you are tasting, because you are going to be charged for it.
