rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The provision of snacks and water actually create a protective factor as well for the front-line staff who will be working at these wineries.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable causal chain — food and water slow intoxication, and less intoxication means fewer difficult patrons for staff — but the intermediate step is left implicit and no evidence is offered for the size of the effect.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: He’d put this in as a member’s bill, and it had been pulled out, and I must say that even while I was campaigning at that stage against Mr Smith, this was well-received.
civility.explanation: Speaking about an electoral opponent in a contested setting where a jibe was easily available, he engages only with the merits of the opponent's bill and attacks nothing personal.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The provision of snacks and water actually create a protective factor as well for the front-line staff who will be working at these wineries.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific amendment made to the bill (the requirement to provide snacks and water) and identifies who it affects and how; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Yesterday, I saw that the Reserve Bank’s monetary policy committee agreed to leave the official cash rate at 5.5 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the RBNZ Monetary Policy Committee held the OCR at 5.5 percent at its review the day before 11 April 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ Monetary Policy Review statement dated 10 April 2024; true if the OCR was left unchanged at 5.5%, false if it was moved or set at another level.

veracity.statement: New Zealand has had a cost of living crisis in recent years, with inflation being over 7 percent for most of 2022.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that annual CPI inflation exceeded 7 percent through the majority of 2022.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation for the four quarters of 2022; true if three or more quarterly annual rates exceeded 7.0%, false if two or fewer did.

veracity.statement: This Government has set a clear goal of having net core Crown debt reduce as a proportion of GDP, in stark contrast with other members in this House, including the one who just asked a question, who said that she would be comfortable with debt increasing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Barbara Edmonds has publicly said she would be comfortable with debt increasing.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: On-the-record statements by Barbara Edmonds (media interviews, Hansard, RNZ reporting) before 11 April 2024; true if she said she would accept or be comfortable with higher debt, false if no such statement exists.

veracity.statement: I can also say—[Interruption] I am trying to help the member with the answer to the question—that we have committed to a lower operating allowance than that committed to by the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the current Government's Budget operating allowance is lower than the allowance set by the previous Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget Policy Statement 2024 and the previous Government's Budget 2023/HYEFU operating allowance figures; true if the announced allowance is lower in dollar terms, false if equal or higher.

veracity.statement: I have seen the ANZ’s response to the Budget policy update, in which it identified that the fiscal track and the approach being taken by the incoming Government is more restrictive on spending than the last Government.
veracity.explanation: Relays ANZ's published assessment that the new Government's fiscal track is more spending-restrictive than its predecessor's.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: ANZ economic commentary on the March 2024 Budget Policy Statement; true if it characterises the fiscal track as more restrictive on spending than the previous Government's, false if it says otherwise or is silent.

veracity.statement: Well, I have seen a report from Radio New Zealand that said that Labour’s finance spokesperson, Barbara Edmonds, said a future Labour Government would consider taking on more debt.
veracity.explanation: Relays an RNZ report attributing to Barbara Edmonds the statement that a future Labour Government would consider more debt.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: RNZ reporting prior to 11 April 2024 quoting Barbara Edmonds; true if such a report exists with that substance, false if no RNZ item carries the attribution.

veracity.statement: This is the first time, actually, that New Zealand wool has been specifically featured at the IWTO—it is quite a big deal.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2024 IWTO Congress is the first at which New Zealand wool has been specifically featured.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IWTO Congress programmes and archives; true if no prior congress featured a dedicated New Zealand wool segment, false if an earlier congress did.

divination.statement: Inflation has been falling since then, and the monetary policy committee is confident that inflation will return to within the 1 to 3 percent band in this calendar year.
divination.explanation: Relays the MPC's forecast that annual CPI inflation returns inside the 1-3 percent target band during calendar 2024.
divination.subject: other
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation prints for the June, September and December 2024 quarters; true if any 2024 quarterly annual rate falls within 1-3%, false if all four remain above 3%.

civility.statement: No, I did not say that. I checked the transcripts, and, as has become a habit from this member, she’s paraphrased me in a way that is inaccurate. When we read the transcript, we find that the reason that she may not have heard my actual words is that she was interrupting continuously.
civility.explanation: Denies the claim but attaches a personal characterisation of the questioner — a habitual misquoter who interrupts continuously — which impugns her conduct rather than only correcting the record.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Not only do I agree that we will keep our commitments, what I also agree is that it is a very good thing that this Government was elected, because if it wasn’t, we would be continuing as a country down a path of deepening structural deficit, of escalating debt, of wasteful spending, and of high inflation, and I am so glad that the adults are back in charge.
civility.explanation: "The adults are back in charge" is a sneer implying the members opposite are not adults; it stops short of naming an individual but is condescending rather than substantive.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does she agree with Nicola Willis, who promised to achieve a surplus in 2026-27, reduce Government debt by $3.4 billion compared with the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update, not borrow for tax cuts, not cut front-line services, and introduce no new taxes, and are there any promises she doesn’t intend to break?
civility.explanation: The listed commitments are substantive, but the closing sting — asking whether there are any promises she does not intend to break — imputes bad faith to the Minister personally.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And the deal we did with New Zealanders was this: we said we’re going to spend their money more effectively, we’re going to reduce the amount of money on back-office bureaucracy, we’re going to stop subsidies for private firms to decarbonise, and we’re going to take those savings and we’re going to invest them in tax relief.
specificity.explanation: Names identifiable mechanisms (back-office reductions, ending decarbonisation subsidies, recycling savings into tax relief) but supplies no amounts or timeframes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does she accept that if she did not restore interest deductibility or pursue tax cuts, debt would be at least $11 billion lower, with all things being equal?
specificity.explanation: Names two specific policies and attaches a precise dollar figure to their fiscal effect, making the question checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does she agree with Nicola Willis, who promised to achieve a surplus in 2026-27, reduce Government debt by $3.4 billion compared with the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update, not borrow for tax cuts, not cut front-line services, and introduce no new taxes, and are there any promises she doesn’t intend to break?
specificity.explanation: Enumerates five named commitments with a dated surplus target and a dollar figure benchmarked to PREFU.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government is actually committed to listening to our farmers, primary sector, and rural communities.
specificity.explanation: A statement of commitment with no mechanism, measure or timeframe attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Over the next few months, we will be undertaking over 20 of these meetings, from Northland through to Southland.
specificity.explanation: Gives a count and a geographic spread with a rough timeframe, though no dates or locations.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Actually, if she’s saying that Labour’s suddenly woken up and thinks savings are a good idea, then what a great revelation that is!
focus.explanation: Entirely about the opposing party's supposed conversion; names no policy, figure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Not only do I agree that we will keep our commitments, what I also agree is that it is a very good thing that this Government was elected, because if it wasn’t, we would be continuing as a country down a path of deepening structural deficit, of escalating debt, of wasteful spending, and of high inflation, and I am so glad that the adults are back in charge.
focus.explanation: Gestures at deficits, debt and inflation but the weight of the answer is a counterfactual celebration of the election result rather than engagement with the borrowing question asked.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does she accept that if she did not restore interest deductibility or pursue tax cuts, debt would be at least $11 billion lower, with all things being equal?
focus.explanation: Squarely on named fiscal policies and their quantified debt consequence — accountability scrutiny, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: To the Minister and his colleagues: why was there a recent announcement that ministerial oversight of the Overseas Investment Office would be removed, which means more farms will be sold to foreigners to be planted in pine trees?
focus.explanation: Names a specific decision — removing ministerial oversight of the Overseas Investment Office — and a specific claimed consequence for farmland.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: To the Minister and his colleagues: why was there a recent announcement that ministerial oversight of the Overseas Investment Office would be removed, which means more farms will be sold to foreigners to be planted in pine trees?
rigor.explanation: The inference from removing ministerial oversight to more farm sales converted to pine plantations is asserted with nothing connecting the two steps — a non sequitur presented as settled.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As a Government, we are absolutely committed to protecting the resources, and this simply shows that we have a range of Ministers that are interested in environmental factors.
rigor.explanation: The question was whether having the Environment Minister outside Cabinet and no environmental Cabinet committee weakens environmental weight in decisions. The reply concludes the opposite — that the arrangement 'simply shows' broad ministerial interest — without offering any connecting premise. A non sequitur: the absence of a dedicated committee is offered as evidence of wider engagement.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We know that waging a war on landlords just ends in pain for tenants—part of the reason why rents have gone up by $170 a week in the last few years.
rigor.explanation: A causal conclusion — landlord-directed regulation caused rent increases — asserted with nothing offered to connect the two beyond sequence. Post hoc reasoning; no mechanism, counterfactual or evidence supplied, and the many other drivers of rent are simply not addressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, over the last few years, we have heard from many landlords that without the backstop of 90-day no-cause terminations, they’re just unwilling to take a chance on tenants who might have otherwise missed out on the rental market—people leaving prison, for example; people with criminal records; or people at the edges of the rental property market.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that restoring no-cause terminations will help marginal tenants rests entirely on reported anecdote — what 'many landlords' have said — with no data on actual tenancy outcomes for those groups. An appeal to anecdote, though the inference from the reported premise is at least coherent.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Instead, landlords decided it was all too hard, and instead those properties ended on Airbnb, actually, which has contributed to people sleeping in tents down by the foreshore in Queenstown, and other cases of hardship.
rigor.explanation: A three-link causal chain — 2020 tenancy law change caused landlords to exit, which moved stock to Airbnb, which caused rough sleeping in Queenstown — with no evidence offered for any link. Post hoc reasoning; Queenstown's short-stay market and housing shortage long predate the 2020 amendments.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is she concerned that extractive industries will soon be able to bypass the environmental protections in New Zealand law, including the Resource Management Act, the Wildlife Act, the Conservation Act, and the exclusive economic zone Act through the Government’s proposed fast-track process?
focus.explanation: Names a specific Government measure (the fast-track consenting process) and the four named statutes it is said to override. Legitimate scrutiny of a policy mechanism, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will the reduction of 50,000 beneficiaries be purely based on those who exit into work, or will they also include those who exit because they go to prison, move overseas, change relationship status, reach age of eligibility for superannuation, or, sadly, die, and, if all of the above, why does she keep saying the target is about supporting people into work?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measurement design of a named Government target — which exit categories count toward the 50,000. Scrutiny of a specific commitment, not party attack.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Today, I’ve announced changes to the Residential Tenancies Act to encourage landlords back into the rental property market. We are reintroducing 90-day no-cause terminations for periodic tenancies, returning landlords’ notice periods for ending a tenancy to 42 days in certain circumstances, and we are reintroducing landlords’ ability to give notice to end a fixed-term tenancy at the end of a term without giving a reason.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the content of a named legislative change and its intended effect on the rental market; no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can he guarantee that whānau won’t be kicked out of rental homes and the neighbourhoods that they’re connected to as a result of the policies that he has announced today?
focus.explanation: Directed at the consequences of the specific tenancy changes announced that day and who they affect. On-policy scrutiny; slightly below the top only because the effect asked about is put in general terms rather than tied to a named mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why, given that statement and the unfolding crisis in the media sector, is there nothing for the media sector in the Government’s full second-quarter action plan?
focus.explanation: Holds the Government to a specific published document — the second-quarter action plan — and its contents on a named sector. Textbook opposition scrutiny of a named commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does the Minister think she has the confidence of the media sector, and, if so, what does she say to former TVNZ boss and TV3 political editor Bill Ralston, who, I quote, said, “The Minister has no idea what she is doing”?
focus.explanation: Almost nothing about the policy; the question is about whether the Minister personally commands confidence, and what a commentator thinks of her. A sliver of policy relevance survives in the reference to the sector's state, but the weight is on the individual's standing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is it the case that, actually, the Minister has no plan, no one supports or believes her, and she has to wait until Winston Peters gets back to do her job for her?
focus.explanation: No policy, mechanism, figure or named commitment is engaged. The content is entirely about the Minister's supposed incapacity and internal Government dynamics.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is she concerned that extractive industries will soon be able to bypass the environmental protections in New Zealand law, including the Resource Management Act, the Wildlife Act, the Conservation Act, and the exclusive economic zone Act through the Government’s proposed fast-track process?
specificity.explanation: Four named Acts and a named consenting process; a listener could check exactly which protections are at issue. Missing only the particular clauses or projects.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: All job seekers deserve the same opportunities to get support and service to focus them on the rewards that work provides. We don’t discriminate. We want to use every single day that is available to support people towards work.
specificity.explanation: Asked whether jobseekers with a health condition or disability are inside the 50,000 target, the reply offers only generic statements of intent — 'same opportunities', 'we don't discriminate', 'every single day'. No mechanism, category, figure or timeframe that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is about those who are currently on the jobseeker support benefit—not main benefits; jobseeker support. We want to see 50,000 fewer people receiving the jobseeker benefit support by the year 2030.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact benefit category (jobseeker support, expressly not all main benefits), the numeric size of the reduction, and the target year. Checkable and actionable; stops short of 1.0 because it still does not define how an exit is counted, which was the question.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will the reduction of 50,000 beneficiaries be purely based on those who exit into work, or will they also include those who exit because they go to prison, move overseas, change relationship status, reach age of eligibility for superannuation, or, sadly, die, and, if all of the above, why does she keep saying the target is about supporting people into work?
specificity.explanation: Enumerates the precise exit categories at issue and ties them to a named numeric target; a precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Today, I’ve announced changes to the Residential Tenancies Act to encourage landlords back into the rental property market. We are reintroducing 90-day no-cause terminations for periodic tenancies, returning landlords’ notice periods for ending a tenancy to 42 days in certain circumstances, and we are reintroducing landlords’ ability to give notice to end a fixed-term tenancy at the end of a term without giving a reason.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute, three distinct mechanisms and two concrete notice periods (90 days, 42 days). Fully checkable against the announced amendments.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need improvements to the rental market to make it easier to be a landlord and to be a tenant, but most fundamentally we need to smash the urban limits that are holding our cities back, fix infrastructure settings, and introduce incentives for cities and regions to go for growth.
specificity.explanation: Names real policy directions (urban limits, infrastructure settings, growth incentives) but supplies no instrument, cost, quantum or timeframe for any of them — a direction of travel rather than something checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m focused on helping the industry modernise and innovate so the industry can be more profitable going forward. There is no silver bullet to fix the current situation that TVNZ and Warner Bros. Discovery are facing at the moment. There is a process under way, and I’ll have more to say when that process has concluded.
specificity.explanation: Asked what the Government is doing for the media sector, the answer offers 'modernise and innovate' and an unnamed 'process' with no timeframe, no instrument and no funding. Beyond naming two broadcasters, there is nothing a listener could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We have nearly 190,000 people today on the jobseeker benefit.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the current jobseeker support caseload is close to 190,000 as at April 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets / Benefit System quarterly data for the March or June 2024 quarter: true if jobseeker support recipients are within a few thousand of 190,000, false if materially different (e.g. under 175,000 or over 205,000).

veracity.statement: We know that waging a war on landlords just ends in pain for tenants—part of the reason why rents have gone up by $170 a week in the last few years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts weekly rents have risen by $170 over the last few years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE tenancy bond data / Stats NZ rental price index: true if national median weekly rent rose by approximately $170 between roughly 2017–2020 and early 2024, false if the increase over any reasonable reading of 'the last few years' is materially smaller.

veracity.statement: Why, given that statement and the unfolding crisis in the media sector, is there nothing for the media sector in the Government’s full second-quarter action plan?
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Government's second-quarter 2024 action plan contains no items relating to the media sector.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published Government Quarterly Action Plan for April–June 2024: true if no listed action relates to media, broadcasting or the media sector, false if any such action appears.

divination.statement: How does she intend to reduce the amount of people on jobseeker support - work ready by nearly 50 percent at a time when unemployment is expected to rise?
divination.explanation: Carries the forecast, adopted as the premise of the question, that unemployment will rise in the period following April 2024.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate: true if the rate rises materially above the March 2024 quarter level (4.3%) over the following four quarters, false if it holds flat or falls.

civility.statement: Does the Minister think she has the confidence of the media sector, and, if so, what does she say to former TVNZ boss and TV3 political editor Bill Ralston, who, I quote, said, “The Minister has no idea what she is doing”?
civility.explanation: Quoting a commentator does not launder the attack: the question is built to put an assault on the Minister's personal competence — 'no idea what she is doing' — into the House. A clear personal attack, delivered by proxy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is it the case that, actually, the Minister has no plan, no one supports or believes her, and she has to wait until Winston Peters gets back to do her job for her?
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the Minister's personal competence and standing — that nobody believes her and that a colleague must do her job for her. It targets the person, not the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The target is deliberately ambitious. We want whānau and tamariki to have safe, warm, and nice homes. Emergency housing should be a last resort, for a short period of time, for those who genuinely need it.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational framing about what emergency housing 'should' be, with no figure, mechanism, or timeframe attached to the target being discussed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And the Kāwanatanga has announced a priority one category for whānau with tamariki who have been in emergency housing for 12 weeks or more, prioritising them on the social housing register.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific mechanism (a priority one category on the social housing register), a specific cohort (families with children) and a specific threshold (12 weeks or more).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As my learned sentinel the Hon Chris Bishop has most recently said, to end New Zealand’s cataclysmic housing crisis, we need to use many tools to increase housing supply and to enable more homes and houses for all New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: A general statement that 'many tools' are needed to increase supply; no tool, figure, mechanism or timeframe is named.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of funding, the veterans at the moment receive about $131 million for covering pension costs, and there’s another $30 million for administering the schemes, including the VIP scheme that the member talks about.
specificity.explanation: Two named funding lines with dollar figures, split between pension costs and scheme administration.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: And the Kāwanatanga has announced a priority one category for whānau with tamariki who have been in emergency housing for 12 weeks or more, prioritising them on the social housing register.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government has announced a priority one social housing register category for families with children who have spent 12 or more weeks in emergency housing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD/HUD announcements and social housing register policy documents from 2024; true if a priority one category with a 12-week emergency housing threshold for households with children was announced, false if no such category exists or the threshold/cohort differs materially.

veracity.statement: Well, first of all, I dispute the premise of that question. What has happened is that all those who have served—the Chief of Defence has reallocated the staff to process the unacceptable backlog of health claims for those veterans with medical conditions associated with their service. And the reason he has done that is the dreadful legacy that the previous Government has left us to deal with, because it’s taking up to 361 days to process these medical claims, and it is an outrageous situation for New Zealand veterans.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that processing a veteran's medical claim is currently taking up to 361 days.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Veterans' Affairs New Zealand claims processing statistics / ministerial or OIA reporting for early 2024; true if maximum or reported processing times of around 361 days are documented, false if the reported maximum is materially lower.

veracity.statement: In terms of funding, the veterans at the moment receive about $131 million for covering pension costs, and there’s another $30 million for administering the schemes, including the VIP scheme that the member talks about.
veracity.explanation: Asserts approximately $131 million of veterans' pension funding and a further approximately $30 million for administering veterans' schemes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Vote Defence Force / Veterans' Affairs appropriations in the 2023/24 Estimates; true if the pension-related appropriation is around $131m and administration around $30m, false if either figure is materially different.

focus.statement: What will the Minister, given that it is two weeks until Anzac Day, be telling those veterans who have been removed from the waiting list for Veterans’ Independence Programme (VIP) services?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny directed at a named programme (the Veterans' Independence Programme) and a specific claimed administrative action; no party-directed content.

focus.statement: Well, first of all, I dispute the premise of that question. What has happened is that all those who have served—the Chief of Defence has reallocated the staff to process the unacceptable backlog of health claims for those veterans with medical conditions associated with their service. And the reason he has done that is the dreadful legacy that the previous Government has left us to deal with, because it’s taking up to 361 days to process these medical claims, and it is an outrageous situation for New Zealand veterans.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance — staff reallocation, claims backlog, processing times — but a substantial part of the weight is placed on characterising the previous Government's legacy rather than the mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, first of all, I dispute the premise of that question. What has happened is that all those who have served—the Chief of Defence has reallocated the staff to process the unacceptable backlog of health claims for those veterans with medical conditions associated with their service. And the reason he has done that is the dreadful legacy that the previous Government has left us to deal with, because it’s taking up to 361 days to process these medical claims, and it is an outrageous situation for New Zealand veterans.
rigor.explanation: The reallocation-because-of-backlog step is supported by the processing-time figure offered, but the causal attribution of that backlog to the previous Government is asserted rather than argued — a gap between what is shown (a long processing time now) and what is concluded (whose doing it is).
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does the Minister really have confidence in continuing in the job, given the fact that she has confessed to being “boring”, “inarticulate”, and “not a magician”?
civility.explanation: The question is aimed at the Minister's personal qualities and fitness for the job rather than any aspect of the school lunch policy; quoting self-deprecating remarks back at her to suggest she is unfit is a personal jibe, not engagement with the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Both those statements are correct. But the way that the member has asked the question, I think he needs to go and have a look at the difference between the endorsements and prohibited licences, because, yes, there are 328 pest controllers out there, but there’s also a large number of members of the licensed firearms community that can still use those prohibited firearms. Now, there is a difference between what Brenton Tarrant used and what is a centre-fire semi-automatic, and I suggest, if the member would like, I can give him some education in differing and understanding what they both are.
civility.explanation: Offering the questioner "some education" and telling him he needs to go and look things up is condescension directed at the member rather than at his argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I did see a comment from Mr Cahill that read “she is using these figures to try and suggest that semi-automatic firearms are already widely available when they’re not”. I would suggest that Mr Cahill cease trying to mislead the public. After working adjacent to the firearms community for many years, he will be well aware that semi-automatic firearms can be owned on a number of licence types and licence endorsements.
civility.explanation: Accuses a named individual of deliberately misleading the public — an imputation of bad faith aimed at the person rather than a rebuttal of what he said.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does she agree with Tom Mauser, whose son was killed in the Columbine school shooting, when speaking of semi-automatics being used for sport shooting: “I understand that there are people who have fun firing these weapons … But, we have to get beyond fun and we really have to consider the danger.”; if so, why is she distracting from the debate on the danger of semi-automatics by suggesting they’re more widely available than they really are?
civility.explanation: The second half imputes a deliberate motive — that the Minister is distracting from the debate — rather than simply contesting her figures, which tips a substantive challenge into an allegation about her conduct.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: On behalf of the Minister, the Government is committed to looking at the evidence and improving the cost-effectiveness of the taxpayer-funded school lunch programme after the previous Government left it unfunded from 2024.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Labour government provided no funding for the Ka Ora, Ka Ako school lunch programme beyond 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2023 appropriations and forward estimates for Ka Ora, Ka Ako / Free and Healthy School Lunches (Vote Education); true if no funding was appropriated for the programme past the end of 2024, false if ongoing baseline funding beyond 2024 was appropriated.

veracity.statement: On Tuesday, I announced that the New Zealand Transport Agency has proposed to increase speed limits on the Mackays to Peka Peka and Peka Peka to Ōtaki sections of the Kāpiti Expressway to 110 kilometres per hour, with consultation on these changes beginning 22 April.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that NZTA has proposed a 110 km/h limit on the two named Kāpiti Expressway sections with consultation opening 22 April 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA/Waka Kotahi consultation notices and April 2024 ministerial press releases; true if a 110 km/h proposal for the Mackays–Peka Peka and Peka Peka–Ōtaki sections opened for consultation on 22 April 2024, false if no such proposal or a different date/limit.

veracity.statement: Since the expressway opened, no one has died in a crash on this expressway, and there’s been a 70 percent reduction in roads in the Kāpiti district.
veracity.explanation: Asserts there have been no fatal crashes on the Kāpiti Expressway since it opened, and a 70 percent reduction (the trailing words are a spoken slip for road deaths/serious injuries) in the Kāpiti district.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA Crash Analysis System records for the Mackays to Peka Peka / Peka Peka to Ōtaki expressway sections from opening to April 2024; true if zero fatalities are recorded on those sections and district road-death figures show a fall of about 70 percent, false if any fatal crash is recorded on the expressway or the district reduction is materially smaller.

veracity.statement: Yes, especially my statement regarding the fact that semi-automatic firearms were never banned under his Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous government's firearms reforms did not ban semi-automatic firearms as a class.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Arms (Prohibited Firearms, Magazines, and Parts) Amendment Act 2019; true if categories of semi-automatic firearms (e.g. rimfire semi-automatics with small magazines, semi-automatic shotguns of limited capacity) remained lawfully possessable on standard licences, false if all semi-automatic firearms were prohibited.

veracity.statement: The fact of the matter is that there are over 6,600 licensed firearm owners in New Zealand who have licence endorsements which can allow them to possess a semi-automatic firearm.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a figure of more than 6,600 licence holders in New Zealand whose endorsements permit possession of a semi-automatic firearm.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police / Te Tari Pūreke firearms licence endorsement statistics as at early 2024; true if the count of holders of endorsements permitting possession of a semi-automatic firearm exceeds 6,600, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: I’m very confused by that question. For one, there’s no such thing as a high-powered semi-automatic—we have rim-fire; we’ve got centre-fire.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that "high-powered semi-automatic" is not a real firearms category in New Zealand, the recognised distinction being rimfire versus centrefire.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Arms Act 1983 and its amendments, and NZ Police firearms classification guidance; true if no statutory or regulatory category of "high-powered semi-automatic" exists and the classification turns on rimfire/centrefire and prohibited status, false if such a category appears in the legislation or official classification.

veracity.statement: In the 2018-19 year, there were 2,076 conviction charges for firearm-related offences, but in the 2022-2023 year, this has increased to 2,588. This is a 24 percent increase. New Zealanders have not been made safer by the rushed firearm laws, and this Government is wholly committed to righting the wrongs for the past for the benefit of public safety and practical regulation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts firearm-related conviction charges rose from 2,076 in 2018-19 to 2,588 in 2022-23, a 24 percent increase.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice conviction and sentencing statistics for firearm-related offences by fiscal year; true if the two figures match for 2018-19 and 2022-23 within rounding, false if materially different.

rigor.statement: I think a lot of people see Ka Ora, Ka Ako as a way of achieving other social goals, like improving nutrition. That may well be the case, but we don’t fund the Ministry of Education for health reasons, just like we don’t fund health for education reasons.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that nutrition benefits should not count in assessing the programme — rests on an assumed clean separation of portfolio purposes, offered as an analogy rather than an argument; it is a false dichotomy, since a programme delivered through education can legitimately be justified by more than one outcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think it’s common sense, and multiple international evaluations tell us, that students benefit from receiving food at school. But for the Ka Ora, Ka Ako programme itself, we have limited evidence of its impact on attendance and achievement, and it’s very important for us as a Government that we are focusing on attendance and achievement at the heart of our education policies.
rigor.explanation: Concedes international evidence of benefit, then leans on absence of local evidence about attendance and achievement to justify narrowing the programme — an argument from absence of evidence, and the first clause partly undercuts the second.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Both those statements are correct. But the way that the member has asked the question, I think he needs to go and have a look at the difference between the endorsements and prohibited licences, because, yes, there are 328 pest controllers out there, but there’s also a large number of members of the licensed firearms community that can still use those prohibited firearms. Now, there is a difference between what Brenton Tarrant used and what is a centre-fire semi-automatic, and I suggest, if the member would like, I can give him some education in differing and understanding what they both are.
rigor.explanation: The reconciliation is sound in form: the two figures count different categories (pest-control authorisations versus endorsements generally), so both can hold; the gap is that the size of the second category is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I did see a comment from Mr Cahill that read “she is using these figures to try and suggest that semi-automatic firearms are already widely available when they’re not”. I would suggest that Mr Cahill cease trying to mislead the public. After working adjacent to the firearms community for many years, he will be well aware that semi-automatic firearms can be owned on a number of licence types and licence endorsements.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that he is misleading rests on an inference from his presumed knowledge to his intent; nothing is offered to close the gap between "he should know better" and "he is deliberately deceiving".
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In the 2018-19 year, there were 2,076 conviction charges for firearm-related offences, but in the 2022-2023 year, this has increased to 2,588. This is a 24 percent increase. New Zealanders have not been made safer by the rushed firearm laws, and this Government is wholly committed to righting the wrongs for the past for the benefit of public safety and practical regulation.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: a rise in firearm-related conviction charges over four years is attributed to the 2019 law changes with no attempt to exclude other causes, and rising charges could equally reflect increased enforcement of the new offences.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: My sympathies go out to all of the families that have been affected by the Columbine shooting, but it is of an important note that we are not America, we do not have their laws, and our laws and legislation will be relative to what we have here in New Zealand and the use of those firearms.
rigor.explanation: The point put was about the danger of semi-automatics in sport shooting; the reply establishes only that New Zealand's legal regime differs from America's, which does not bear on whether the danger claim holds — a non sequitur.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think it’s common sense, and multiple international evaluations tell us, that students benefit from receiving food at school. But for the Ka Ora, Ka Ako programme itself, we have limited evidence of its impact on attendance and achievement, and it’s very important for us as a Government that we are focusing on attendance and achievement at the heart of our education policies.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the named programme, the evidence base for it, and the outcome measures the Government says it prioritises; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Who is correct in relation to high-powered semi-automatic rifles: the police Minister when he said, in response to written questions, “As [of] 1 March 2024 there are 328 persons authorised to possess and use (including firing live ammunition) a prohibited firearm for the purposes of pest control”, or the Minister when she said, “we have 6,600 people who have endorsements to be in possession of those firearms”?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: it tests a specific numerical claim about firearms authorisations against the police Minister's own written answer, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On behalf of the Minister, what I would say to those people who have corresponded with that member is that this Government is committed to the Ka Ora, Ka Ako programme; however, what we’re committed to is cost-effectiveness of the programme. We shouldn’t be looking at extending how much money we are spending, but we should be looking at making sure it’s going to the right places.
specificity.explanation: Names the programme and a direction (no extra spending, better targeting) but supplies no figures, no mechanism for targeting, and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On Tuesday, I announced that the New Zealand Transport Agency has proposed to increase speed limits on the Mackays to Peka Peka and Peka Peka to Ōtaki sections of the Kāpiti Expressway to 110 kilometres per hour, with consultation on these changes beginning 22 April.
specificity.explanation: Names the two exact road sections, the proposed speed limit, and the date consultation opens — fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Rather than forcing people to slow down, our plan ensures that, when speed limits are set, economic impacts, including travel times and the views of road users and local communities, are taken into account alongside safety.
specificity.explanation: Names the factors that will be weighed in speed-limit setting, but gives no instrument, threshold or timeframe for how they are weighed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Who is correct in relation to high-powered semi-automatic rifles: the police Minister when he said, in response to written questions, “As [of] 1 March 2024 there are 328 persons authorised to possess and use (including firing live ammunition) a prohibited firearm for the purposes of pest control”, or the Minister when she said, “we have 6,600 people who have endorsements to be in possession of those firearms”?
specificity.explanation: Cites two named sources, an exact date and two precise figures, setting up a discrepancy anyone could go and check.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the 2018-19 year, there were 2,076 conviction charges for firearm-related offences, but in the 2022-2023 year, this has increased to 2,588. This is a 24 percent increase. New Zealanders have not been made safer by the rushed firearm laws, and this Government is wholly committed to righting the wrongs for the past for the benefit of public safety and practical regulation.
specificity.explanation: Two dated figures, a stated percentage change and a named class of offence — precisely checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It is calamitous to see so many whānau in emergency housing, and we’ve recently announced a target of 75 percent reduction of the number of households in emergency housing by 2030.
specificity.explanation: States a named target with a precise percentage, a defined measure (households in emergency housing) and a date.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The first one was actually negotiated by Ngāti Apa. In any settlement, that was the first one ever done. This one is six times bigger, and I congratulate Te Korowai o Wainuiārua for getting that amount of cultural revitalisation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the cultural revitalisation instrument was first negotiated in the Ngāti Apa settlement, that it was the first such provision in any Treaty settlement, and that the Te Korowai o Wainuiārua cultural revitalisation provision is six times larger.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the cultural revitalisation fund provisions in the Ngāti Apa (North Island) deed of settlement with those in the Te Korowai o Wainuiārua deed of settlement (Te Arawhiti / Office for Māori Crown Relations deed summaries); true if Ngāti Apa is the earliest settlement containing such a fund and the Te Korowai o Wainuiārua amount is approximately six times the Ngāti Apa amount, false if an earlier settlement contained one or the ratio is materially different.

veracity.statement: This bill acknowledges that by the signing of Te Tiriti o Waitangi in Whanganui in May 1840, the ancestors of Te Korowai o Wainuiārua sought to build a partnership based on fairness, justice, and honour.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Tiriti o Waitangi was signed at Whanganui in May 1840 and that the bill's historical account characterises the ancestors' intent in those terms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Check the Treaty signing records (Archives NZ / NZ History Treaty signatory sheets) for the date of the Whanganui signings, and the historical account and Crown acknowledgements in the Te Korowai o Wainuiārua Claims Settlement Bill; true if the Whanganui signings occurred in May 1840 and the bill contains that acknowledgement, false if the date or the bill's text differs materially.

veracity.statement: Both situations breached the agreement that the iwi made with the Crown and eventually led to the rushed purchasing of some 411,196 acres, in which the Crown has acknowledged they moved with—and I quote—“unreasonable haste”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific acreage (411,196 acres) purchased by the Crown and that the Crown's apology/acknowledgements use the phrase 'unreasonable haste'.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Check the Crown acknowledgements and apology in the Te Korowai o Wainuiārua Claims Settlement Bill / deed of settlement; true if the acreage figure of 411,196 acres and the phrase 'unreasonable haste' appear as described, false if the figure or wording differs materially.

veracity.statement: Contrary to popular belief, ACT has always supported the Treaty settlement process.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the ACT Party has consistently supported the Treaty settlement process throughout its history.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Check the Hansard division records and party votes on Treaty settlement bills since ACT entered Parliament in 1996, plus ACT's published positions on the settlement process; true if ACT has voted for settlement legislation without recorded opposition, false if ACT voted against or publicly opposed the settlement process at any point.

specificity.statement: Both situations breached the agreement that the iwi made with the Crown and eventually led to the rushed purchasing of some 411,196 acres, in which the Crown has acknowledged they moved with—and I quote—“unreasonable haste”.
specificity.explanation: Carries a precise acreage figure and a directly quoted phrase from the Crown's acknowledgement, both of which a reader could look up in the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The settlement includes financial and commercial redress valued at $21.7 million and cultural redress funding of $6.85 million; the return of sites of cultural significance, including three sites that will be jointly vested in Te Korowai o Wainuiārua and neighbouring iwi; 12 commercial properties, including Crown Forestry land at Erua and the former prison site at Waikune; recognition of the vision of Te Korowai o Wainuiārua to establish an eco-sanctuary at Pokaka to reinvigorate native flora and fauna, including an overlay classification and conservation management redress; the right to nominate a member of Te Korowai o Wainuiārua to the Tongariro Taupō Conservation Board and the establishment of a strategic advisory committee to ensure that they have governance-level engagement on conservation issues; relationship redress with a range of Crown agencies including the National Emergency Management Agency—a first in Treaty settlements.
specificity.explanation: Names dollar figures for both redress streams, counts of properties, named sites (Erua, Waikune, Pokaka), a named board and a named agency. Every element is checkable against the deed and the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Pākohe is actually included in this legislation under one of the mechanisms, as part of this legislation allows the post-settlement entity to be able to go and collect pākohe from the riverbeds in certain agreed areas, along with a number of other cultural materials that are important to this iwi.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific material, the entity that may collect it and where, but gives no clause reference, quantities or limits on the agreed areas.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The settlement includes financial and commercial redress valued at $21.7 million and cultural redress funding of $6.85 million; the return of sites of cultural significance, including three sites that will be jointly vested in Te Korowai o Wainuiārua and neighbouring iwi; 12 commercial properties, including Crown Forestry land at Erua and the former prison site at Waikune; recognition of the vision of Te Korowai o Wainuiārua to establish an eco-sanctuary at Pokaka to reinvigorate native flora and fauna, including an overlay classification and conservation management redress; the right to nominate a member of Te Korowai o Wainuiārua to the Tongariro Taupō Conservation Board and the establishment of a strategic advisory committee to ensure that they have governance-level engagement on conservation issues; relationship redress with a range of Crown agencies including the National Emergency Management Agency—a first in Treaty settlements.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the specific quantum and contents of the redress package, and that relationship redress with the National Emergency Management Agency is a first in Treaty settlements.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Te Korowai o Wainuiārua deed of settlement and the Te Korowai o Wainuiārua Claims Settlement Bill as introduced: true if financial and commercial redress is $21.7m, cultural redress funding $6.85m, 12 commercial properties are transferred including Erua Crown Forestry land and the former Waikune prison site, and NEMA relationship redress appears (and is the first such in a Treaty settlement); false if the figures or listed items differ materially.

veracity.statement: In May 1840, 15 rangatira signed the Raukawa Moana Treaty sheet at Whanganui, including Te Peehi Tūroa and his son Te Peehi Pākoro Tūroa.
veracity.explanation: A specific historical claim about the number, place and date of signatories to a named Treaty sheet.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Archives NZ / Waitangi Treaty signatory records for the Cook Strait (Raukawa Moana) sheet: true if 15 rangatira signed at Whanganui in May 1840 and the two named Tūroa signatories appear; false if the count, place, month or names differ.

veracity.statement: Large tracts of their land were purchased or taken for public works, including for the North Island main trunk railway line to create scenic reserves, for defence purposes, for electricity generation, and for two of New Zealand’s national parks.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the specific purposes for which Te Korowai o Wainuiārua land was purchased or taken by the Crown.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The historical account and Crown acknowledgements in the Te Korowai o Wainuiārua deed of settlement, plus Waitangi Tribunal reports on the Whanganui/National Park district: true if Crown purchase and public works takings for the main trunk line, scenic reserves, defence, electricity generation and the two national parks are recorded; false if those categories of taking are not attested.

veracity.statement: On 29 July 2023, Te Korowai o Wainuiārua deed of settlement, Te Tihi o te Rae, was signed at Raetihi Marae following a ratification process by Te Korowai o Wainuiārua claimant community.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the date, name and place of signing of the deed of settlement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Arawhiti / Office for Māori Crown Relations deed of settlement record: true if the deed named Te Tihi o te Rae was signed at Raetihi Marae on 29 July 2023 after a ratification vote; false if the date, name or location differ.

veracity.statement: In 2015, the Crown recognised the mandate of Uenuku Charitable Trust to represent the people of Te Korowai o Wainuiārua to negotiate a comprehensive historical Treaty of Waitangi settlement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the year in which the Crown recognised the negotiating mandate and the entity that held it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Arawhiti mandate recognition records for Uenuku Charitable Trust: true if Crown mandate recognition was granted in 2015; false if granted in a different year or to a different entity.

veracity.statement: My whakapapa to this iwi is through my grandmother Iriaka Rātana, who was a member of this House as well, from 1949 to 1969.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the speaker's grandmother served in the House across the stated twenty-year period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary records of members for Western Māori: true if Iriaka Rātana served as an MP from 1949 to 1969; false if the dates of service differ materially.

veracity.statement: Pākohe is actually included in this legislation under one of the mechanisms, as part of this legislation allows the post-settlement entity to be able to go and collect pākohe from the riverbeds in certain agreed areas, along with a number of other cultural materials that are important to this iwi.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill contains a mechanism permitting the post-settlement entity to collect pākohe and other cultural materials from agreed riverbed areas.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Text of the Te Korowai o Wainuiārua Claims Settlement Bill and its deed: true if a cultural materials / pākohe (argillite) collection mechanism for the post-settlement governance entity appears; false if no such provision exists.

veracity.statement: Dozens of iwi before this iwi, Te Korowai o Wainuiārua, have made that decision to do it, and so we come today for this.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that dozens of iwi had already completed this settlement process before this one.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Arawhiti's register of completed historical Treaty settlements as at April 2024: true if at least about two dozen iwi/claimant groups had signed deeds of settlement before Te Korowai o Wainuiārua; false if the number is under roughly 24.

veracity.statement: This is the 101st settlement that comes before this House.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that this Treaty settlement bill is the 101st settlement to be brought before the House.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Office for Māori Crown Relations – Te Arawhiti / Parliament's record of Treaty of Waitangi claims settlement bills introduced; true if Te Korowai o Wainuiārua Claims Settlement Bill is the 101st such settlement introduced, false if the count is materially different.

veracity.statement: The land in question is over 600,000 hectares—and that is the same, actually, with all settlements that have gone before this House in that no settlement can really address the actions that the Crown has made.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the land at issue in the Te Korowai o Wainuiārua settlement exceeds 600,000 hectares.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Te Korowai o Wainuiārua deed of settlement / historical account and Waitangi Tribunal Whanganui district reports on the area of the iwi's rohe and land alienated; true if the stated area exceeds 600,000 ha, false if materially smaller.

veracity.statement: As myself and the Hon Peeni Henare know, and we know this process as well as anyone up there, you went into this process 35 years ago—35 years ago our people went into this process.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the iwi began the settlement/claims process approximately 35 years before April 2024, i.e. around 1989.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal claim register lodgement dates for the Uenuku, Tamahaki and Tamakana claims; true if the first claims were lodged around 1989 (±a few years), false if materially later or earlier.

veracity.statement: I pay tribute to the kuia and kaumātua who are no longer here, who also fought hard, and who were among the first to submit claims to the Waitangi Tribunal in the 1980s.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that claimants for these iwi were among the earliest to lodge claims with the Waitangi Tribunal, during the 1980s.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal Wai claim register: lodgement dates of claims by Uenuku/Tamahaki/Tamakana claimants; true if claims were registered in the 1980s, false if first registered in the 1990s or later.

veracity.statement: When the Uenuku Charitable Trust, representing Te Korowai o Wainuiārua, and the Crown signed an agreement in principle in July 2023, trust chair Aiden Gilbert, who is here today, recounted a story of old.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Uenuku Charitable Trust and the Crown signed an agreement in principle in July 2023, and that Aiden Gilbert was trust chair.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Arawhiti / Office for Māori Crown Relations settlement documents for Te Korowai o Wainuiārua; true if an agreement in principle was signed in July 2023 with Aiden Gilbert as trust chair, false if the date or signatory differs.

specificity.statement: Treaty settlements are not just a gravy train for Māori; they honour redress for Māori, but they also provide huge economic, social, and wellbeing benefits for all, across communities, and, in this case, across the mighty Rangitīkei.
specificity.explanation: A broad assertion of 'huge economic, social, and wellbeing benefits' with no figures, mechanisms, timeframes or named programmes — nothing a listener could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I’ve said in our reo that a number of us have been involved in this journey—in my case, since 1986, as the translator for Matiu Rata’s lawyer David Baragwanath in the original Muriwhenua fisheries claims that kicked off in 1986, along with Sir Graham Latimer and the Maunganui claim.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the speaker worked as translator for David Baragwanath, counsel to Matiu Rata, in the Muriwhenua fisheries claim beginning in 1986.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal record for the Muriwhenua fisheries claim (Wai 22) and its 1988 report: true if the claim proceedings began in 1986 with Matiu Rata as claimant and David Baragwanath as counsel, and contemporaneous records/biographies place Shane Jones as translator on that claim; false if the dates, counsel or Jones's role are materially different.

veracity.statement: In the 1980s, it was Baye Riddell and Manos Nathan, the son of the famous Māori Battalion leader Uncle Ned Nathan, who was captured in Crete and was nursed back to life by his wife’s people.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Manos Nathan was the son of Māori Battalion soldier Ned Nathan, that Ned Nathan was captured in Crete, and that he was nursed by the family of the woman he married.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published biographies/obituaries of Manos Nathan and Ned Nathan (e.g. Te Ara, 28 Māori Battalion records, NZ Herald obituaries): true if Manos Nathan is recorded as Ned Nathan's son and Ned Nathan is recorded as wounded/captured in Crete and sheltered by the Cretan family into which he married; false if the parentage or the Crete capture is contradicted by those records.

veracity.statement: From the Crown’s strategic land grabs without consultation in the 1870s to the confiscation of the North Island main trunk railway without consent in the 1880s and the resulting land losses for public works throughout the late 19th and early 20th centuries, the impacts have been profound and enduring.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific historical Crown actions against these iwi: land purchases without consultation in the 1870s, taking of land for the North Island main trunk railway without consent in the 1880s, and further public works takings into the early 20th century.
veracity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Only a very small minority of OECD countries have decided not to provide personal income tax relief since 2010, and, in fact, have raised taxes. Those countries include Portugal, Greece, and New Zealand.

veracity.statement: Well, there are no projects that have been approved.

veracity.statement: Does he agree with Tama Potaka on 26 July 2023, regarding the repeal of section 7AA, that “It would be contradictory of us to dismiss this provision entirely, which is intended to be a genuine option to address and meet the best interests of the child in State care.”?

civility.statement: Well, he had six years and he ignored working people and made no adjustment.

focus.statement: But what I'd just say is that that's the same leader who was a Prime Minister, along with Grant Robertson, his former Minister of Finance, who actually got advice about the problems in that department, agency, and their management of their money and their budget and did nothing about it. There is a thread of policy content — advice about the department's budget management — but the weight of the passage is party characterisation rather than the issue put to him.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Look, I have to say the sanctimony from that member is quite outrageous, because it took him longer to sack Michael Wood than it will take for the backbench to sack him.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the opposing leader's character and his party's internal state. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Again, what I'd say is that we have a great fast-track process. It's designed to get things built in this country, but a key component of it is an independent expert panel that will weigh up considerations economically, environmentally, and socially, and inform Ministers.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure at issue directly, describing the mechanism of the fast-track process and the role of the expert panel rather than turning on the questioner's party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can the public have confidence in this Government's Cabinet overseeing the decisions of the hundred projects in the Fast-track Approvals Bill when Ministers are not disclosing their conflicts of interest?
focus.explanation: Names the specific measure (the Fast-track Approvals Bill), the number of projects, and the decision-making body — legitimate scrutiny of a named policy rather than general party criticism.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: A recent study published by the Norwegian Institute of Public Health wrote that banning smart phones significantly reduced bullying, improved the grades of students, and significantly decreased the number of visits students made to see mental health specialists.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a named institution's study found three specific effects of school smartphone bans: reduced bullying, improved grades, and fewer mental-health specialist visits.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Norwegian Institute of Public Health / Sara Abrahamsson working paper on smartphone bans in Norwegian middle schools; true if it reports statistically significant reductions in bullying, improvements in student grades and reductions in psychological-consultation visits; false if it reports null results, or if no such NIPH study exists, or if the reported effects were confined to a subgroup in a way that makes the blanket claim inaccurate.

veracity.statement: It’s been 14 long years. It’s been a 40 percent increase in the cost of goods through inflation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that consumer prices have risen about 40 percent over the 14 years since tax thresholds were last adjusted (2010 to 2024).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index, cumulative change from the 2010 quarter of the last threshold adjustment to Q1 2024; true if the cumulative rise is approximately 40 percent, false if materially different (e.g. under 30 or over 55 percent).

veracity.statement: When, if ever, will the $2.9 billion landlord tax cut trickle down to the 1.5 million renters in this country?
veracity.explanation: Asserts, as the premise of the question, that restoring interest deductibility for landlords is worth $2.9 billion and that there are 1.5 million renters in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD costing of the interest deductibility restoration published with Budget 2024 or the enacting legislation's regulatory impact statement; and Stats NZ 2023 Census counts of people living in rented dwellings. True if the fiscal cost is around $2.9b over the forecast period and the renter population is about 1.5 million; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Is it good judgment for the Department of Internal Affairs to make cuts to the child exploitation team, cuts to care or support funded through Whaikaha—Ministry of Disabled People, and Customs cutting its border services?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that DIA proposed cuts affecting its child exploitation team, that Whaikaha reduced care and support funding, and that Customs cut border services.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DIA's 2024 change/consultation documents on the Digital Child Exploitation team, Whaikaha's March 2024 announcement on disability support purchasing rules, and NZ Customs Service 2024 restructuring proposals; true if each agency proposed or made reductions in the area named, false if any of the three did not.

veracity.statement: How can it be true that front-line services aren’t being reduced when hospitals are under instruction from Health New Zealand leadership to reduce the use of casual nurses who cover roster gaps across a range of services?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Health New Zealand leadership has instructed hospitals to reduce the use of casual nurses used to cover roster gaps.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand internal communications or district guidance issued in early-to-mid 2024 on casual/bureau nursing and overtime; true if hospitals were directed to reduce casual nurse usage, false if no such instruction was issued.

veracity.statement: Why did he deny in a statement to Radio New Zealand that there is a hiring freeze in public hospitals when Health New Zealand wrote to health unions on 17 April to say that all unfilled roles were being reviewed and considered for removal?
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that the Minister denied a hospital hiring freeze in an RNZ statement, and that Health New Zealand wrote to health unions on 17 April 2024 saying all unfilled roles were being reviewed and considered for removal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RNZ reporting carrying the Minister's denial, and the 17 April 2024 Health New Zealand letter to health sector unions; true if the denial was made and the letter contains that wording about unfilled roles, false if either element is absent or materially misdescribed.

veracity.statement: This is a reflection that in the calendar year 2023, I am informed that 2,500 nurses entered the workforce. As a consequence of that, we are needing to acquire less penal time and less overtime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 2,500 nurses entered the New Zealand health workforce during calendar year 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Nursing Council of New Zealand annual registration data and/or Te Whatu Ora workforce reporting for calendar 2023; true if net or new nurse entries to the workforce were approximately 2,500, false if materially different.

rigor.statement: The study also found that schools that implemented a policy removing phones for the whole day—not just class time—experienced a larger increase in student educational performance. That is why it is our expectation that cellphones are off and away all day, so we can get back to basics and ensure our kids are literate, numerate, and aspirational about their futures.
rigor.explanation: A clean inference: the cited finding (whole-day removal produced larger gains than class-time-only) directly supports the design choice being defended (an all-day rather than lesson-time ban). The evidence and the conclusion match in scope.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yes, and especially this Government’s action to bring back three strikes. Communities across New Zealand are sick and tired of seeing what happens when a Government spends years embedding a “soft on crime” approach that prioritises offenders over victims, and that’s why we’re making the changes, because New Zealanders expect this Government to restore law and order.
rigor.explanation: The justification offered for three strikes is entirely that the public wants it — an appeal to popularity ('communities are sick and tired', 'New Zealanders expect'). Nothing is offered about whether the law reduces offending.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is a reflection that in the calendar year 2023, I am informed that 2,500 nurses entered the workforce. As a consequence of that, we are needing to acquire less penal time and less overtime.
rigor.explanation: The inference — more permanent nurses means less need for casual cover and overtime — is coherent, but there is a real gap: nothing is offered on whether 2,500 entrants exceeded departures or matched the roster gaps the question was actually about.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is a globally tight market for specialists, and I am informed that 200 fulltime-equivalent specialists joined the health workforce in the calendar year 2023. rigor.explanation: The conclusion that services are safe rests on a bare appeal to authority — 'I am reassured by Health New Zealand' — and the supporting example (consumables procurement savings) does not bear on the question of unfilled specialist roles.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I said that when agencies were putting forward savings proposals, they should apply good judgment and be careful that proposals should not put front-line services at risk.
specificity.explanation: Asked what directions she gives to avoid front-line cuts, she describes the direction only as 'apply good judgment' and 'be careful'. No threshold, no definition of front line, no enforcement mechanism, no document named.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.explanation: Three named mechanisms (interest deductibility, the brightline test, tenancy law changes), which is real content, but no figure for the expected effect on rents and no timeframe by which it should show up.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When, if ever, will the $2.9 billion landlord tax cut trickle down to the 1.5 million renters in this country?
specificity.explanation: Carries a costing ($2.9 billion), a named measure (the restoration of interest deductibility, framed as a landlord tax cut) and an affected population (1.5 million renters). Checkable as asked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why did he deny in a statement to Radio New Zealand that there is a hiring freeze in public hospitals when Health New Zealand wrote to health unions on 17 April to say that all unfilled roles were being reviewed and considered for removal?
specificity.explanation: Names the outlet, a dated document (17 April), the recipients (health unions) and the exact content alleged — all of which someone could go and check.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It is a globally tight market for specialists, and I am informed that 200 fulltime-equivalent specialists joined the health workforce in the calendar year 2023. Having said that, I am reassured by Health New Zealand that health services are safe and they are simply looking for efficiencies, such as the $2.75 million that they found in one hospital in the past three months for more efficient procurement of consumables.
specificity.explanation: Two hard figures (200 FTE specialists, $2.75 million in procurement savings over three months) plus the mechanism they came from, though the hospital is not named.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In what has become a habit from that member, she tends to paraphrase and summarise a series of loosely connected facts and make assertions about them.
civility.explanation: Rather than engaging the three named cuts, she characterises the questioner's habitual conduct — a sneering aside about the member's honesty with facts. It lands on the person, not the argument.

But I am pleased that the member opposite is obviously as excited as I am about the 2024 Budget. You’ll have to wait until 30 May when I deliver it, and, I’m sorry, you’re not going to get first dibs on the content.
civility.explanation: Mild mockery of the questioner ('as excited as I am', 'first dibs') in place of an answer. Teasing rather than abusive, but it plays the questioner rather than the substance.

civility.statement: Will the Prime Minister, then, commit to rent prices coming down under his Government, or is that all hot air?

focus.statement: Yes, and especially this Government’s action to bring back three strikes. Communities across New Zealand are sick and tired of seeing what happens when a Government spends years embedding a “soft on crime” approach that prioritises offenders over victims, and that’s why we’re making the changes, because New Zealanders expect this Government to restore law and order.
focus.explanation: A named policy (three strikes) is the anchor, but the supporting content is a characterisation of the previous government as 'soft on crime' rather than any mechanism, cost or expected effect.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What is the cost of a two-zone fare on the bus for a teenager in Auckland today, and what will it be tomorrow when the Government cancels half-price public transport fares?
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named policy change (the end of half-price public transport fares) and its concrete effect on a specific group of users. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is it good judgment for the Department of Internal Affairs to make cuts to the child exploitation team, cuts to care or support funded through Whaikaha—Ministry of Disabled People, and Customs cutting its border services?
focus.explanation: Names three specific agencies and three specific service areas and tests them against the Minister's own stated standard. This is exactly the named-outcome scrutiny an opposition finance spokesperson should be doing.
