veracity.falsification_criterion: The published set of Government targets for the public service announced in 2024: true if none of the targets is expressed in terms of productivity; false if any target measures productivity or output per worker.

veracity.statement: We also heard in terms of emissions budget 2 and emissions budget 3 that it’s very difficult to introduce new initiatives to achieve savings in those Budget periods, and given the hole that has been left in the emissions budgets by the mini-Budget in the year under review—3 megatonnes by the Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry Fund alone in emissions budget 2; 4 megatonnes in emissions budget 3; not to mention the cancelling of the Clean Car Discount and other transport initiatives—there’s quite a gap there that needs to be made up.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific quantified emissions shortfalls attributable to the cancellation of the GIDI fund across two emissions budget periods.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry for the Environment or Treasury estimates of the emissions impact of cancelling the Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry Fund: true if the estimated foregone abatement is approximately 3 Mt CO2-e in emissions budget 2 and approximately 4 Mt in emissions budget 3; false if official estimates differ materially from those figures.

veracity.statement: Emissions budget 1 is pretty much in order and on track.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's first emissions budget is on track to be met.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry for the Environment / Climate Change Commission emissions budget tracking published around 2024: true if projected net emissions for emissions budget 1 (2022-2025) sit at or below the budgeted allocation; false if the tracking shows the budget being exceeded.

specificity.statement: They had $2 billion they started with, then they came back to the Government for another $1.2 billion, and they used it to go out and bid up the price of building materials, of land, of project managers, of builders.

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So the question is about productivity, and I am pleased to inform the member that the Treasury will actually very shortly be publishing a working paper on productivity and its analysis of what’s been going so badly wrong with productivity in the New Zealand economy in recent years.
specificity.explanation: Names the agency and the output (a Treasury working paper on productivity), but 'very shortly' supplies no date and nothing is said about the paper's scope or measures, which was what the question asked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We also heard in terms of emissions budget 2 and emissions budget 3 that it’s very difficult to introduce new initiatives to achieve savings in those Budget periods, and given the hole that has been left in the emissions budgets by the mini-Budget in the year under review—3 megatonnes by the Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry Fund alone in emissions budget 2; 4 megatonnes in emissions budget 3; not to mention the cancelling of the Clean Car Discount and other transport initiatives—there’s quite a gap there that needs to be made up.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific budget periods, the specific cancelled programmes (GIDI, Clean Car Discount) and quantified emissions consequences in megatonnes for each budget period. Directly checkable against departmental estimates.

specificity.statement: There will be an opportunity to provide information around exactly those mechanisms in the months to come, and that is a work programme that is currently under way.

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But the overall programme of initiatives in order to ensure that we do meet those targets—which is a commitment of this Government, under the Prime Minister’s statements commitment No. 9—is in regard to the pathways that will be included in regards to our emissions reduction plan two, which we will begin to consult on in June and will finalise at the end of this year.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument (emissions reduction plan two), cites the specific commitment it sits under, and gives both a consultation month and a completion timeframe. Falls short of 1.0 because the pathways themselves — the actual content — are not described.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But that’s the thing about Chlöe Swarbrick: she’s going to get an Oscar pretty soon for her starring role as the woman who wasn’t there.
civility.explanation: A sustained piece of mockery aimed at a named member personally — her presence and seriousness — rather than at anything she has argued. Nothing in it engages a position.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Then there’s the suggestion—and I think the member Chlöe Swarbrick needs to know that if you could tax your way to prosperity, her side would’ve won the Cold War, but, unfortunately, you can’t tax your way to prosperity, and a capital gains tax is not going to make housing more affordable, for the very simple reason, as Chris Bishop will tell you, housing is about supply and demand.
civility.explanation: Condescension toward a named member ('needs to know') combined with aligning her with the losing side of the Cold War. It edges past robust disagreement into sneering at the person, though it stops short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: For a bit there, I thought she was going to follow her leader’s lead and let Chlöe Swarbrick do all the talking—but a question, none the less.
civility.explanation: A sneer at the questioner and at her leader — implying they are letting another party's MP speak for them — with a grudging aside about the question itself. It targets the members rather than any position they hold.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: So the question is about productivity, and I am pleased to inform the member that the Treasury will actually very shortly be publishing a working paper on productivity and its analysis of what’s been going so badly wrong with productivity in the New Zealand economy in recent years.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Treasury — a body other than the speaker — will publish a productivity working paper very shortly.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Treasury's published papers list: true if the Treasury publishes a working paper or analytical note on New Zealand productivity within roughly eight months of 30 April 2024; false if no such paper appears in that period.

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The key element for us is to actually ensure that we are progressing an acceleration of implementation of those renewable generation projects, and our primary focus in that space is around consenting Resource Management Act reform and the fast-track legislation.

veracity.explanation: Asserts that CERF money was recovered centrally and used to fund tax relief for landlords, and that decarbonising-freight funding was among what was cut.

veracity.statement: In the year under review, a plan was made that could have increased the number of nurses in training placements in New Zealand by a thousand.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The health workforce plan published in 2023: true if it identifies an option or target to lift domestic nurse training placements by approximately 1,000, false if no such figure appears.

civility.statement: In taking the Climate Emergency Response Fund back to centre to pay for tax cuts for landlords, whether or not that will be there and what hole will be left in our emissions budgets as a consequence of not doing that work around decarbonising freight.

veracity.statement: But there were significant constraints placed upon Iwi-Māori Partnership Boards within the rohe who were unable to access locality funding to start the journey to establish and hear that very important whānau voice.

veracity.statement: I had a couple of questions for the Minister of Health, and one was around the growing wait-list for first specialist assessments and how can he explain that.

rigor.statement: We do need to have some caution here now around several areas: first of all, that the internationally qualified nurses that we bring in are qualified to actually meet some of the positions that we have. civility.explanation: Criticises a former Prime Minister's policy decision rather than the person; regretful in tone and aimed at the decision not to continue the fund, though the coy 'a certain Prime Minister' edges slightly toward the individual.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The return is delivered by people who know what they’re doing, and they’ve demonstrated that; it is not delivered by us making political decisions about where investments should go.
civility.explanation: Directly disputes another member's position on directing the fund, and does so entirely on the substance — the disagreement is with the idea ('a very, very dangerous thing'), with no reflection on the member himself.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The New Zealand Superannuation Fund is very important, and New Zealand First has always believed that and believed in building our economic capability, and we can’t do that if we don’t save and don’t invest.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy proposition about the fund and national saving, but the weight of the sentence is party positioning — what New Zealand First has 'always believed' — rather than a mechanism, figure or measure.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In particular, I stand by the Government’s “phone away for the day” policy, which is so popular with parents and students and schools—and with great feedback from people like the Hornby High School head boy, Khush Patel, who said the ban “has helped students focus more academically”.
rigor.explanation: The case for the policy working rests entirely on testimonial anecdote — a head boy and a principal — plus an assertion of popularity. Appeal to anecdote and appeal to popularity; no outcome data connects the ban to the claimed benefit.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Ministry of Justice has previously produced an evidence brief suggesting that reintroducing the three-strikes legislation in New Zealand has the potential to reduce crime. US studies on similar laws have shown reductions in both minor and serious violent crimes, along with decreased arrest rates among offenders with previous strikes.
rigor.explanation: Evidence is offered and the conclusion tracks it in form, but it leans on the authority of an unnamed departmental brief and generalises from US jurisdictions to New Zealand without establishing comparability; the incapacitation conclusion ("keep offenders off the street") does follow from longer sentences.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I remember that meeting vividly because what I saw in the eyes of their officials was what I felt, which was abject horror at the situation the previous Government was prepared to leave Pharmac in.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion about the previous Government's intent is carried by the speaker's recollection of officials' expressions and her own emotional reaction — an appeal to emotion and personal anecdote rather than anything about the funding decision itself.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In particular, I stand by the Government’s “phone away for the day” policy, which is so popular with parents and students and schools—and with great feedback from people like the Hornby High School head boy, Khush Patel, who said the ban “has helped students focus more academically”.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named government policy and its claimed effects in named schools; no party framing in this passage.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, look, I thank the member for their concern about that constituent, but what I’d say is that help is on the way, because we are going to deliver low and middle income tax relief to hard-working Kiwis. These are the people that the Labour Party used to care about but have long forgotten.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy referent (low and middle income tax relief), but it is unelaborated and the answer's weight falls on a general characterisation of what the Labour Party cares about rather than on the transport cost asked about.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’d just say to that member, again, help is on the way to low and middle income New Zealanders doing it tough in a cost of living crisis created by that member’s previous Government.
focus.explanation: No mechanism, measure or figure engages the school transport and lunch costs asked about; the content is a slogan plus attribution of the cost of living crisis to the previous Government.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Could I ask the Prime Minister as to whether people in Auckland would be catching the bus each day if light rail had been built as Labour promised?
focus.explanation: Names a specific undelivered commitment (Auckland light rail), which is legitimate scrutiny, but it is deployed as a counterfactual jab rather than engaging the public transport cost question before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What does he think best reflects his promised laser-like commitment to tackling the cost of living: higher public transport costs, his Government’s new drivers tax, higher costs for prescriptions, higher rents, higher fuel prices, higher rates, lower pay increases, or higher unemployment?
focus.explanation: Holds the Government to a named commitment and lists eight specific cost areas rather than trading in general party characterisation — accountability against a stated promise.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s very disappointing to see representatives from Te Pāti Māori not even speaking about the victims of crime but more about cuddling and cotton-wooling those criminals instead.
focus.explanation: Names no policy, mechanism or figure; the content is entirely a characterisation of what the other party is really like.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Personally, I would reserve the term “fiscal jiggery-pokery” to describe the practice of funding medicines for one year only and then taking it away again. I think that is being highly misleading to New Zealand, and I would expect much better from the Labour health spokesperson, Ayesha Verrall.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point about single-year medicines funding, but the answer is framed around rebuking a named opposition spokesperson's commentary rather than the funding mechanism itself.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why isn’t he aware that, using the National Party’s own tax cut calculator, someone in their early 20s that takes the bus each day and earns the average wage could be worse off by more than $70 a fortnight as a result of that change?
specificity.explanation: Names the source (National's own tax calculator), a defined household type (early 20s, average wage, daily bus user) and a figure ($70 a fortnight). Checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, look, I thank the member for their concern about that constituent, but what I’d say is that help is on the way, because we are going to deliver low and middle income tax relief to hard-working Kiwis. These are the people that the Labour Party used to care about but have long forgotten.
specificity.explanation: "Help is on the way" and "tax relief" with no amount, no threshold, no date — no answer to the fortnightly cost put to him.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is he aware that parents will now need to pay more to get their under-13s to school as a result of that change, while his Government is also threatening to cut the school lunch programme that could see those same parents $33 a week, per child, worse off?
specificity.explanation: Names two specific measures (under-13 fare concessions, the school lunch programme) and attaches a per-child weekly figure, though the $33 is presented without its derivation.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will the $2.9 billion of tax cuts for landlords result in lower rents, given Trade Me reporting that rents have surged 8.3 percent since last year?
specificity.explanation: A costed measure ($2.9 billion), a named data source (Trade Me) and a percentage change — anyone could go and check both halves.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government is committed to putting downward pressure on rents, and we are bringing the brightline test back from 10 to two years; we’re making sure we restore interest deductibility and we get the balance of laws right between tenants and landlords. But what I’d say to that member is we are not going to see a $170 per week increase in rents, as we saw under his administration.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete levers, one with figures (brightline from 10 years to two), and a quantified comparison; the third lever ("the balance of laws right") is undefined.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What does he think best reflects his promised laser-like commitment to tackling the cost of living: higher public transport costs, his Government’s new drivers tax, higher costs for prescriptions, higher rents, higher fuel prices, higher rates, lower pay increases, or higher unemployment?
specificity.explanation: Eight named cost categories, but every one is a direction of travel with no magnitude, period or source attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve got the Reserve Bank focused on a single target of fighting inflation, we’ve actually made sure we’ve introduced our Family Boost policy to give families that are struggling with childcare costs some support and subsidy, and we’re making sure that we’re going to give tax relief in this Budget for low and middle income working New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Three named actions — the single-mandate change to the Reserve Bank remit, the Family Boost childcare rebate, and Budget tax relief — but no rates, thresholds or dollar amounts for any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As I pointed out in the Budget Policy Statement, one of the biggest challenges for this year’s Budget is that the previous Government left behind multiple initiatives with time-limited funding that was about to expire. At the half-year update in December, Treasury identified nine instances of these fiscal cliffs where, in each case, the costs of continuing funding were $100 million more over the forecast period.
specificity.explanation: Names the document, the date, the source agency, a count (nine) and a dollar threshold ($100 million over the forecast period) — checkable against the published update.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The previous Government gave Pharmac additional funding of $350 million for the 2023-24 fiscal year to purchase new medicines and widen access to some that were already funded, but this expires on 30 June and there was no funding set aside for future years.
specificity.explanation: Amount, agency, fiscal year, expiry date and purpose are all stated; directly checkable against the appropriations.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Why isn’t he aware that, using the National Party’s own tax cut calculator, someone in their early 20s that takes the bus each day and earns the average wage could be worse off by more than $70 a fortnight as a result of that change?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that National's own tax cut calculator, combined with the end of half-price public transport for under-25s, leaves an average-wage 20-something daily bus commuter more than $70 a fortnight worse off.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Run the National Party 2023 tax calculator for a single earner on the Stats NZ average ordinary-time wage as at April 2024, and net the fortnightly tax cut against the fortnightly increase in adult public transport fares from the loss of the under-25 half-price concession (Auckland Transport/Metlink published fare tables). True if the net position is worse by more than $70 a fortnight; false if the shortfall is materially smaller or the person is better off.

veracity.statement: Will the $2.9 billion of tax cuts for landlords result in lower rents, given Trade Me reporting that rents have surged 8.3 percent since last year?
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that the interest deductibility restoration for landlords is worth $2.9 billion, and that Trade Me has reported rents rising 8.3 percent year on year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD costings published with Budget 2024 for the restoration of interest deductibility on residential rental property — true if the fiscal cost is around $2.9 billion over the forecast period; and the Trade Me Property Rental Price Index release for the month preceding 1 May 2024 — true if it reports a national year-on-year median rent increase of 8.3%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: This Government is committed to putting downward pressure on rents, and we are bringing the brightline test back from 10 to two years; we’re making sure we restore interest deductibility and we get the balance of laws right between tenants and landlords. But what I’d say to that member is we are not going to see a $170 per week increase in rents, as we saw under his administration.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that rents rose by $170 per week during the previous Labour-led Government's time in office.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE Tenancy Services bond data on national median weekly rent, comparing the figure for late 2017 with that for late 2023. True if the increase is approximately $170 per week; false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: We’re serious about lowering inflation, and isn’t it good that inflation hit 4 percent—the lowest it’s been for three years—we’re on our way.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the latest inflation reading was 4 percent and that this was the lowest annual inflation rate in three years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index release for the March 2024 quarter. True if annual CPI inflation is 4.0% and no quarterly annual reading in the preceding three years was lower; false if the rate differs materially or a lower annual reading occurred within that window.

veracity.statement: The Ministry of Justice has previously produced an evidence brief suggesting that reintroducing the three-strikes legislation in New Zealand has the potential to reduce crime. US studies on similar laws have shown reductions in both minor and serious violent crimes, along with decreased arrest rates among offenders with previous strikes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a Ministry of Justice evidence brief concluded reinstating three strikes has potential to reduce crime, and that US studies of comparable laws found reductions in minor and serious violent crime and lower arrest rates among prior-strike offenders.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Justice evidence brief / regulatory impact statement on the three-strikes reinstatement, released under the Official Information Act or published on justice.govt.nz. True if it states the regime has potential to reduce crime and cites US studies to that effect; false if the brief's stated conclusion is that the evidence of a crime-reduction effect is weak or absent.

veracity.statement: What is the response to the 2018 report by then Prime Minister Bill English which called out Aotearoa’s high rates of incarceration for being based on dogma, not evidence, and criticised policies such as three strikes for being a retributive rather than restorative approach to crime based on unsupported claims that prisons can solve the problem of crime?
veracity.explanation: Relays the content and provenance of a 2018 report attributed to Bill English as then Prime Minister, said to describe New Zealand's incarceration rates as based on dogma rather than evidence and to criticise three strikes as retributive.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Locate the report attributed to Bill English on imprisonment. True if a 2018 report authored by him characterises high incarceration as based on 'dogma, not evidence' and criticises three strikes as retributive; false if no such report exists, if it is not from 2018, or if English was not Prime Minister at the time of its release.

veracity.statement: Does she accept the findings from research from the United States in 2022, where this law was modelled from, that showed three strikes has no measurable deterrent effect, that it disproportionately locked up African Americans, and that it had no impact on lowering crime rates at all?
veracity.explanation: Relays findings said to come from 2022 US research: that three-strikes laws produce no measurable deterrent effect, disproportionately imprison African Americans, and have no effect on crime rates.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Identify peer-reviewed US research published in 2022 evaluating three-strikes laws. True if such a study reports no measurable deterrent effect, racially disproportionate incarceration of African Americans, and no crime-rate impact; false if no 2022 study makes these findings or if the weight of the 2022 literature reports a deterrent or incapacitation effect.

veracity.statement: Well, yes, we have. Since Labour came into power, we have seen a 33 percent increase in violent crime, resulting in an increased number of victimisations.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 33 percent increase in violent crime dating from Labour taking office in 2017.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey (cycles 1 to 6) measure of violent interpersonal offence victimisations, and/or Police recorded victimisations for violent offences, comparing 2017/18 with 2022/23. True if either series shows an increase of about 33 percent; false if the increase is materially smaller or the series shows no increase.

veracity.statement: As I pointed out in the Budget Policy Statement, one of the biggest challenges for this year’s Budget is that the previous Government left behind multiple initiatives with time-limited funding that was about to expire. At the half-year update in December, Treasury identified nine instances of these fiscal cliffs where, in each case, the costs of continuing funding were $100 million more over the forecast period.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Treasury, at the December half-year fiscal update, identified nine fiscal cliffs each costing over $100 million across the forecast period to continue funding.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update, December 2023, and its accompanying specific fiscal risks schedule. True if it identifies nine time-limited funding cliffs each with a continuation cost above $100 million over the forecast period; false if the count or threshold differs materially.

veracity.statement: The previous Government gave Pharmac additional funding of $350 million for the 2023-24 fiscal year to purchase new medicines and widen access to some that were already funded, but this expires on 30 June and there was no funding set aside for future years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $350 million one-year Pharmac top-up for 2023-24, expiring 30 June, with no out-year funding provided.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2023 Vote Health appropriations for Pharmac combined medicines funding. True if the additional appropriation is around $350 million confined to the 2023/24 year with no baseline funding in 2024/25 onwards; false if the amount differs materially or out-year funding was appropriated.

civility.statement: It’s very disappointing to see representatives from Te Pāti Māori not even speaking about the victims of crime but more about cuddling and cotton-wooling those criminals instead.
civility.explanation: Not a policy criticism but an imputation of motive to the members opposite — that they do not care about victims — delivered with the mocking "cuddling and cotton-wooling". Sneering and bad-faith imputation rather than engagement with their argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Personally, I would reserve the term “fiscal jiggery-pokery” to describe the practice of funding medicines for one year only and then taking it away again. I think that is being highly misleading to New Zealand, and I would expect much better from the Labour health spokesperson, Ayesha Verrall.
civility.explanation: The turnaround on the phrase engages the substance, but it closes by naming an individual member and delivering a condescending judgement on her — "I would expect much better from" — which lands on the person rather than the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Last week, the coalition Government announced we’re delivering on our commitment to improve resource management laws and give certainty to consent applications, with a bill being introduced to Parliament next month, the bill we’re calling the Resource Management Amendment Bill (No 1).
specificity.explanation: Names the specific bill, the policy area and a timeframe for introduction; checkable against the parliamentary order paper.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re proposing to remove the problematic and contentious low slope map, and for regional councils and farmers to determine where stock needs to be excluded based on risk. The focus is on farm-level and regionally suitable solutions.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete instrument (the low slope map) and the replacement mechanism, though without figures or dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Across the coalition documents making up this multiparty Government, there are 20 different commitments relating to the RMA that we are responsible for delivering.
specificity.explanation: Gives a countable figure tied to a named source (the coalition agreements), though not what the commitments are.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How does prioritising Government policies that removes te reo Māori from Government departments, removes the Treaty provisions in the Oranga Tamariki Act, and repeals the Māori Health Authority contribute to Māori success?
specificity.explanation: Identifies particular statutory changes (Oranga Tamariki Act Treaty provisions, Māori Health Authority repeal, departmental te reo policy), though without figures or dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Can I ask how he can claim he is a strong advocate for Māori success when all Māori are seeing is cuts, repeals, and the undermining of kaupapa Māori initiatives?
specificity.explanation: Generalised references to 'cuts, repeals, and the undermining of kaupapa Māori initiatives' with no named programme, figure or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Late last year, we saw a number of Māori, particularly whānau Māori, who lost their jobs at Juken, at Gisborne’s timber mill, and Te Puni Kōkiri and others got behind and rallied behind those people and gave them support to retrain and transition out of an unemployment situation into horticulture and construction.
specificity.explanation: Names a particular employer, location and the sectors workers moved into, but gives no numbers of people supported or programme detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: These priorities will support the Government to be laser-focused on ensuring that at least 80 percent of our kids are at curriculum by 2030.
specificity.explanation: A numeric target with a deadline, checkable against future curriculum-achievement reporting.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The equity gap is stubbornly wide; 20 percent of our tamariki Māori are at curriculum for maths at the end of year 8, and in 2022, almost 10,000 kids left school with no qualifications at all.
specificity.explanation: Two precise, sourced-style statistics with a year and a year level attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Under this Government, education and a social investment lens will deliver greater social mobility, support breaking intergenerational cycles of poverty, and build the pathways that allow every child to fulfil their potential and to be ambitious about their future.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic aspirations — social mobility, breaking poverty cycles, pathways — with no mechanism, funding, measure or date.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The latest advice that I received from police in relation to front-line safety is that there was a 45.5 percent increase in assaults on police since 2018.
specificity.explanation: A precise percentage against a stated baseline year, attributed to a named source.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I’m proud to say this coalition Government is ending the war on farmers. The last Government loaded on the regulations, putting unnecessary costs on farmers and growers.
civility.explanation: Robust criticism aimed at a previous government's regulatory record; no individual is attacked.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Can I ask how he can claim he is a strong advocate for Māori success when all Māori are seeing is cuts, repeals, and the undermining of kaupapa Māori initiatives?
civility.explanation: Pointed challenge to the Minister's own claim about himself; edges toward the person but stays on his stated record rather than his character.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does the Minister consider that the question’s phraseology is more understandable to 95 percent of New Zealanders than it’s ever been in the past?
civility.explanation: A sneering aside at the way the previous questioner phrased his question in te reo, rather than engagement with the substance; mockery short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, I’m proud to say this coalition Government is ending the war on farmers. The last Government loaded on the regulations, putting unnecessary costs on farmers and growers.
focus.explanation: A gesture at regulation, but the weight is party framing ('war on farmers', 'the last Government') with no named measure or figure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’re proposing to remove the problematic and contentious low slope map, and for regional councils and farmers to determine where stock needs to be excluded based on risk. The focus is on farm-level and regionally suitable solutions.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the regulation being changed and who decides under it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How does prioritising Government policies that removes te reo Māori from Government departments, removes the Treaty provisions in the Oranga Tamariki Act, and repeals the Māori Health Authority contribute to Māori success?
focus.explanation: Names three specific measures and tests them against the Minister's own stated objective — scrutiny of named policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does the Minister consider that the question’s phraseology is more understandable to 95 percent of New Zealanders than it’s ever been in the past?
focus.explanation: A policy question about Te Puni Kōkiri cuts was before the House; this engages no policy, mechanism or figure at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: However, we’ve heard the concerns of Kiwis that less significant areas are being captured, and this can place too much restriction on how land is used.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the SNA criteria, but the justification for suspending them rests on unquantified reported concerns — an appeal to anecdote rather than evidence of over-capture.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: One thing that I would say is that under the last Government where some of these outcomes went haywire, we saw an increase of 98,000 through to 130,000 Māori on main benefits, and we are committed to supporting Minister Upston and others to get this country back on track.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the number of Māori receiving a main benefit rose from about 98,000 to about 130,000 during the previous Labour-led government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Social Development benefit fact sheets / quarterly main benefit statistics broken down by ethnicity; true if the Māori main-benefit count rose from roughly 98,000 (around 2017) to roughly 130,000 (around 2023), false if the start and end figures differ materially from those numbers.

veracity.statement: I agree with Minister Seymour, who has observed that having one out of three Māori kids going to school is an absolute failure and we need to get more Māori children back to school.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim attributed to David Seymour that only about one in three Māori students attends school (in context, attends regularly).
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education attendance statistics for the relevant term/year; true if roughly one third of Māori students met the regular-attendance threshold, false if the published share is materially different.

veracity.statement: The equity gap is stubbornly wide; 20 percent of our tamariki Māori are at curriculum for maths at the end of year 8, and in 2022, almost 10,000 kids left school with no qualifications at all.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that 20 percent of Māori students are at curriculum level in maths at the end of year 8, and that close to 10,000 students left school in 2022 with no qualification.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education / NMSSA curriculum-achievement data for year 8 maths by ethnicity, and Education Counts school-leaver attainment statistics for 2022; true if the Māori year-8 maths figure is about 20 percent and 2022 leavers with no qualification number close to 10,000, false if either departs materially from those values.

veracity.statement: The latest advice that I received from police in relation to front-line safety is that there was a 45.5 percent increase in assaults on police since 2018.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that police advice records a 45.5 percent rise in assaults on police officers since 2018.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police assault-on-police statistics (or the Police advice released under OIA) comparing 2018 with the most recent year at May 2024; true if the increase is about 45.5 percent, false if materially different.

focus.statement: Can she assure the House, given her outrage over what she describes as “fiscal cliffs”, that all items in her Budget will be baselined?
focus.explanation: Squarely on a fiscal-management question — whether Budget items will be baselined rather than time-limited. No party-bashing content; it presses a named budgetary mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There will be no hidden fiscal cliffs established for a future Government to deal with, and there will never be, under this Government’s watch, a fiscal cliff left for essential medicines—shame on you.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual policy question (time-limited versus baselined funding, and medicines funding specifically), though wrapped in a jab at the other side.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And I would point that member to the colleagues either side of her on that front bench, who actively chose not to adjust tax thresholds, even while inflation ate away at people’s incomes, who actively chose to pour fuel on the inflation fire while a cost of living crisis surged, who actively chose to spend money on a TVNZ and RNZ merger when New Zealanders couldn’t pay for their groceries.
focus.explanation: Directed at the previous government's record, but names specific decisions — tax threshold settings and spending on the public media merger — rather than generic party abuse.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can I ask the Minister—not to be speculative in this case—is it a fact that no member or Minister or party in the Government has taken $350,000 illegally from a charity, as is the fact publicly known now?
focus.explanation: Contains no reference to the fast-track bill or any policy at issue; it exists entirely to insinuate wrongdoing by another party during a question about consenting legislation.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There will be no hidden fiscal cliffs established for a future Government to deal with, and there will never be, under this Government’s watch, a fiscal cliff left for essential medicines—shame on you.
civility.explanation: The substantive part is about budgeting for medicines, but it closes with 'shame on you' — a moral rebuke flung across the chamber rather than an engagement with the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Will she be the only New Zealander better off by saving her own job ahead of the jobs of front-line workers?
civility.explanation: Moves off the policy and onto the Minister personally, imputing self-interested motive — that she is protecting her own position at the expense of others' jobs.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m surprised by that question. I’ve actually been giving the Opposition member the benefit of the doubt. That question was well beneath her and I’m not going to honour it with an answer.
civility.explanation: Condescending toward the questioner — 'giving her the benefit of the doubt' and 'well beneath her' address the member's standing rather than the substance, though it stops short of an insult.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There will be important cases where we will ensure that a review is undertaken before we commit to baseline funding—for the very good reason that, as I’ve said to this House many times, we are a Government that is committed to fiscal discipline on value for money and ensuring that where we commit New Zealand taxpayer money permanently into the future, we can first assure New Zealanders that we know that dollar is going to its best purpose.
specificity.explanation: Names one real mechanism — a review before baselining — but supplies no figures, no criteria for the review and no timeframe; the remainder is generic fiscal-discipline language.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How will the additional 12,000 New Zealanders who are now unemployed, according to today’s unemployment figures, benefit from the tax cuts and be better off in Budget 2024?
specificity.explanation: Carries a precise figure, a named data release and a named Budget — the answer could be checked against the same source.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, Mr Speaker, it is the position of our Government that the best thing that we can do is allow people to keep more of their own money so that they can make choices about how they spend that money.
specificity.explanation: A general statement of principle — no amounts, thresholds, dates or mechanisms that could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Was he made aware of a conflict of interest by Minister Jones which disclosed $50,000 was donated to New Zealand First from entities with a connection to Kings Quarry before he sent the 3 April letter inviting Kings Quarry to apply for the fast-track process?
specificity.explanation: Names the Minister, the donor entity, the amount and the exact date of the letter — every element is independently checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: How will the additional 12,000 New Zealanders who are now unemployed, according to today’s unemployment figures, benefit from the tax cuts and be better off in Budget 2024?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the unemployment statistics released that day show an additional 12,000 unemployed New Zealanders.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey for the March 2024 quarter, released 1 May 2024: true if the number of unemployed people rose by approximately 12,000 over the quarter; false if the increase was materially different or if the series fell.

veracity.statement: All New Zealanders benefit from a strong economy, and we as a Government are embarking on a significant project to rebuild an economy that has been drastically weakened by a period of prolonged, very high inflation that has eroded people’s real incomes and purchasing power, that has led to a significant increase in interest rates, that is in turn leading to four of the past five quarters having been in recession and very challenging economic conditions.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP series as published at the date of the statement (latest print December 2023 quarter): true if four of the five quarters to December 2023 recorded a fall in real GDP; false if fewer than four were negative.

veracity.statement: And I would point that member to the colleagues either side of her on that front bench, who actively chose not to adjust tax thresholds, even while inflation ate away at people’s incomes, who actively chose to pour fuel on the inflation fire while a cost of living crisis surged, who actively chose to spend money on a TVNZ and RNZ merger when New Zealanders couldn’t pay for their groceries.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget appropriations and Ministry for Culture and Heritage / Treasury records for the Aotearoa New Zealand Public Media (TVNZ-RNZ merger) programme: true if public money was appropriated and spent on the merger project; false if no expenditure was incurred.

veracity.statement: The member might be interested to know we have based the process on the COVID-19 fast-track legislation introduced by the previous Government, in which Cabinet delegated to David Parker decision making for what projects were to be listed in the bill upon introduction. veracity.falsification_criterion: Cabinet papers and minutes for the COVID-19 Recovery (Fast-track Consenting) Bill 2020 and the bill as introduced: true if Cabinet delegated project-listing decisions to Minister David Parker and no public consultation preceded introduction; false if the listing decision sat elsewhere or was publicly consulted on.

veracity.statement: Was he made aware of a conflict of interest by Minister Jones which disclosed $50,000 was donated to New Zealand First from entities with a connection to Kings Quarry before he sent the 3 April letter inviting Kings Quarry to apply for the fast-track process?

veracity.statement: Will he commit to reducing the concentration of powers in Ministers under the bill after concerns were raised by the Auditor-General and the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment about the proposed decision-making approach?

veracity.statement: Mr Speaker, the member, like others in her party, has made much of a courtesy form letter that went to 200 organisations, some of whom are interested in fast-track, some of whom are not interested in fast-track. veracity.falsification_criterion: The Minister's released correspondence or an OIA/parliamentary response listing recipients of the 3 April 2024 fast-track letter: true if approximately 200 organisations received an identical form letter; false if the distribution was materially smaller or the letters were individually targeted.

veracity.statement: For example, during the COVID era, a bill was introduced which advanced 17 projects included upon introduction, added by Cabinet without any public consultation, without anyone even knowing what the projects were until they were dropped in the Parliament.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The COVID-19 Recovery (Fast-track Consenting) Bill as introduced in 2020: true if its schedule of listed projects contained 17 projects at introduction; false if the count was materially different.

rigor.statement: This is a novel new policy from the Labour Party today. They’re going to be subsidising everyone’s insurance bill, I see.
rigor.explanation: Straw man: the question asked whether people facing higher insurance premiums would be better off, which does not entail any commitment to subsidise premiums. The rebuttal is aimed at a position the questioner did not take.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Mr Speaker, the member, like others in her party, has made much of a courtesy form letter that went to 200 organisations, some of whom are interested in fast-track, some of whom are not interested in fast-track. So writing a letter to someone which is, essentially, a press release letting them know that the fast-track process is open does not raise any concerns like the member is raising.
rigor.explanation: The inference — that a mass form letter cannot raise concerns — follows only if the concern were about the letter's contents. It does not answer the premise actually put, which was about who received it and what interests they held; the volume of recipients does not establish the absence of a conflict.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I think that we’re in a terrible situation as a country where, under the previous Government, we’ve seen a massive increase in violent crime: a 33 percent increase.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Police recorded victimisations / NZ Crime and Victims Survey data for violent offences, comparing 2017 with 2023; true if the increase is approximately 33%, false if materially different or if no series supports that figure.

veracity.statement: We’ve seen a 76 percent increase in gang members.

veracity.statement: The current earthquake-prone building system was put in place in 2017 in good faith and required buildings considered to be earthquake-prone to be remediated before set dates. Nearly 500 deadlines are set to expire over the next four years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the current earthquake-prone building regime dates from 2017 and that close to 500 remediation deadlines fall due within four years of the statement.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Commencement date of the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Act regime and the MBIE EPB register count of remediation deadlines falling between 2024 and 2028; true if the regime began in 2017 and the deadline count is close to 500, false if either is materially wrong.

specificity.statement: I think that we’re in a terrible situation as a country where, under the previous Government, we’ve seen a massive increase in violent crime: a 33 percent increase.

specificity.statement: Well, what I’d say to that is that this Government is committed to making sure that our police have got all the intelligence, all the tools, all the resources that they need to go out there and keep the public safe.

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, there’s nothing incompatible at all about the approach to law and order and public safety by this coalition Government. We have committed to an additional 500 police officers. We are bringing new legislation and that will deal with violent gangs.

specificity.statement: Is he confident that front-line police officers will be able to access up-to-date intelligence on firearms if the Firearms Safety Authority is removed from police and located within another Government department such as the Department of Internal Affairs?

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.explanation: Quotes the source advice directly and identifies the two instruments said to conflict.

specificity.statement: The programme that this Government is working on will have a military-style component with a rehabilitative and trauma - informed care approach.

specificity.explanation: Points to a named source of advice and a specific evidential claim, though without naming the reports or dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government is bringing forward a review of earthquake-prone buildings to provide greater certainty for Kiwis. While this review is under way, all current remediation deadlines will be extended by four years.
specificity.explanation: Names the action, the affected regime, and the exact length of the deadline extension.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, there’s nothing incompatible at all about the approach to law and order and public safety by this coalition Government. We have committed to an additional 500 police officers. We are bringing new legislation and that will deal with violent gangs.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the conclusion that nothing is incompatible is supported by a list of unrelated commitments (police numbers, gang legislation), none of which bear on the alleged timing conflict between the Arms Act and the coalition agreement.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, I can say that public safety is important to this Government, because that’s what we’re about as a coalition.
rigor.explanation: Circular reasoning: the claim that public safety is a priority is justified by asserting that being about public safety is what the coalition is.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What the evidence does show us is what we are doing now is not working. We can’t accept the status quo.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: that the status quo is failing does not support the specific intervention asked about, and no evidence for the proposed programme is offered in answer to a question demanding exactly that.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And police safety—if the Minister had read my letter of expectation to the commissioner, which we had to release to get us back on track and focused again on the things that matter, she would see that police safety is a priority for this Government.
civility.explanation: Edges onto the questioner personally by implying she has not read the relevant document, rather than simply answering; condescending but short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: First of all, I’d like to say I disagree with the member’s interpretation of the advice, as asked in the question.
civility.explanation: Contests the member's reading of the evidence without any imputation about the member herself.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is he confident that front-line police officers will be able to access up-to-date intelligence on firearms if the Firearms Safety Authority is removed from police and located within another Government department such as the Department of Internal Affairs?
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named machinery-of-government change and its operational consequence; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can he say that front-line safety is his priority when police themselves have raised real concerns directly with him regarding taking the Firearms Safety Authority out of police?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny of a named proposal and the advice attached to it; no content-free party attack.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government has an ambitious target to double the value of exports over the next decade, continue to support major events, increase foreign direct investment, and improve the Government procurement system by reducing red tape and bureaucracy.
specificity.explanation: One genuinely checkable commitment (double export value over a decade) attached to a timeframe, but the remaining items are directional generalities with no amounts, mechanisms or dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What does she say to members of the tech sector, who contribute $13 billion to the New Zealand economy, like NZTech, who have publicly asked the Minister to—and I quote—“please retain the industry led, Government supported framework to enable collaboration and alignment across this rapidly growing part of the economy.”?
specificity.explanation: Carries a named organisation, a dollar figure and a directly quoted request — a reader could go and check each element.

specificity.statement: There are many decisions that this Government makes and one of the things that we are actually trying to do is grow the economy, and some of the decisions that that Government put through were actually a bad idea and we cancelled them.

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The tech industry is very well supported by this Government, and one of the great Ministers—Judith Collins—is actually very focused on that.
specificity.explanation: A general assurance of support plus a named Minister; no programme, funding, mechanism or timeframe that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Investment will go where it’s needed: into our schools, into our hospitals, into our police, and we will also put it in in the most important place: the back pockets of working New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Three sectors named but no amounts, no programmes and no dates; 'the back pockets of working New Zealanders' commits to nothing checkable ahead of the Budget.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: From 1842 to today, almost 70 percent of children in care are Māori, a number which has only ever gone up.
specificity.explanation: A precise proportion, a defined population (children in care) and a stated historical trend — checkable against agency statistics.

focus.statement: Why did she allow the cancellation of Industry Transformation Plans, given it was a tool to work alongside industry to accelerate the growth and success of New Zealand businesses?

focus.explanation: Ascribes a motive to another party and its voters; names no clause, cost, timeframe or outcome of the repeal being debated.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Waitangi Tribunal’s interim report, and so take heed of this, and indeed, the Minister’s own officials in their regulatory impact statement, echo concerns over the lack of express rationale—I’ll pause there—behind this repeal, truthfully, because it isn’t there.
focus.explanation: Cites two specific official documents on the specific measure before the House and states what they concluded about it.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.explanation: Asserts that the New Zealand tech sector contributes $13 billion to the economy, and that NZTech publicly made the quoted request to the Minister.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTech / MBIE published figures on the technology sector's contribution to GDP or export earnings around 2023-24; true if a $13b contribution figure is supported, false if the published figure is materially different. veracity.statement: It is almost three years since inflation went above 3 percent and gave rise to a cost of living crisis that was prolonged and has now gone on for some years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's annual CPI inflation rate first rose above 3 percent roughly three years before this May 2024 statement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index annual inflation series; true if the first print above 3.0% falls in mid-2021 (about three years before 1 May 2024), false if it falls materially later or earlier.

veracity.statement: All of that means that today we saw the unemployment numbers climb up.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that unemployment figures released on the day of the statement (1 May 2024) showed a rise.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey for the March 2024 quarter, released 1 May 2024; true if the unemployment rate rose on the previous quarter, false if it was flat or fell.

veracity.statement: From 1842 to today, almost 70 percent of children in care are Māori, a number which has only ever gone up.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki published care-population statistics for 2023-24 on the proportion of tamariki in care who are Māori; true if close to 70%, false if materially lower. veracity.statement: The Waitangi Tribunal’s interim report, and so take heed of this, and indeed, the Minister’s own officials in their regulatory impact statement, echo concerns over the lack of express rationale—I’ll pause there—behind this repeal, truthfully, because it isn’t there.

civility.statement: One of the things that I can tell that member is that I have been travelling up and down the country, including to his electorate of New Plymouth—well, actually, he’s a list member, so it’s not his electorate—last week to hear their concerns and find ways to support them to achieve their economic success.

civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: E te Minita, ka aroha ki a koe kua karetaohia e tō pāti. Kia kaha rā.
civility.explanation: Addresses the Minister directly to call her a puppet of her party — pitying condescension aimed at the person's autonomy rather than at the repeal.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Interest rates have risen very high to try and fight that inflation—higher than they would have had to if there had been a Government that was doing its bit to take the fuel off the inflation fire.
rigor.explanation: A counterfactual conclusion — rates would have been lower under different fiscal policy — asserted with nothing offered to support the link. No modelling, magnitude or mechanism is given, so the conclusion outruns the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We understand that the lifting of the unemployment rate this week is not the consequence of a decision taken yesterday or the week before. It is the build-up of successive decisions that were made over many years, over six years, where the economy was second on the list.
rigor.explanation: Concludes that the rise in unemployment is caused by six years of the predecessor's decisions, but the only support offered is the assertion that 'the economy was second on the list'. No decision, channel or lag is identified — the causal conclusion does not follow from what was given.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The theory of the Minister is that Oranga Tamariki’s governing principles should be colour-blind, which is just another word for white supremacy, because to say we are all one people is really to say we should all be white people, erasing the very hue of our identity and culture that makes us whole as tangata Māori, tamariki Māori, mokopuna Māori.
rigor.explanation: Equivocation: 'colour-blind' is redefined as 'we should all be white people' and the conclusion of white supremacy is drawn from that substitution rather than from anything in the Minister's stated position.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Mark my words: regardless of the likely inevitable removal of section 7AA, Te Pāti Māori will one day build a mokopuna Māori authority which will outshine this shameful moment in history, just like we did with Whānau Ora, by Māori for Māori and of Māori.

divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand statute book and Parliament's bills record; true if a Bill repealing section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 passes third reading and receives Royal assent, false if the repeal is abandoned, defeated or still unenacted by the resolve-by date.

veracity.statement: They cannot say that they are concerned about the 4.3 percent unemployment that was announced today and then say that it has got nothing to do with the 3,000 positions that have been disestablished in the public sector.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey release of 1 May 2024 (March 2024 quarter) — true if the headline unemployment rate is 4.3%, false if materially different; and Public Service Commission / published tallies of public sector role disestablishments to 1 May 2024 — true if approximately 3,000 positions had been disestablished, false if the figure is far lower.

veracity.statement: One of those things is getting rid of free and half-price public transport. This affects 1.6 million New Zealanders—a huge number of New Zealanders will be paying more because of this Government’s decision.

veracity.statement: The cuts that this Government has made to working people—and I just think it’s really important to note this—have mainly affected women, kaimahi Māori, and Pacific people.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that public sector job cuts to date have fallen disproportionately on women, Māori and Pacific workers.

veracity.statement: So we saw the Government repeal fair pay agreements; we saw Government, effectively, institute a wage decrease with the cuts to the minimum wage, which was less than inflation; and we’ve seen them introduce 90-day trials again for the whole of the country, meaning that people at work are more likely to get sacked.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Act and its enactment date; the 1 April 2024 minimum wage order rate compared with the annual CPI figure for the same period (true if the percentage increase was below CPI inflation); and the Employment Relations Amendment provisions extending 90-day trials beyond employers with fewer than 20 staff — false if any of the three did not occur as described.

veracity.statement: Unfortunately, the project blew out in cost by 300 percent—300 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the cost of the Marlborough colleges rebuild project rose to roughly four times its original estimate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education project documentation and reporting on the Marlborough Boys'/Girls' Colleges rebuild — true if the revised cost estimate is approximately 300 percent above the original budget, false if the escalation is materially smaller.

veracity.statement: Unfortunately, the then education Minister knew about this going on and, in fact, didn’t inform his Cabinet.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous education Minister was aware of the cost escalation on the Marlborough colleges project and withheld it from Cabinet.

civility.explanation: A sharp, sarcastic hit at the previous government's record and results; it targets a record and an administration, not any individual's character or competence.
