rigor.statement: In my opinion, the single greatest thing the Government can do to break intergenerational welfare dependency and poverty is to provide every child with a world-class education, allowing them the opportunity of employment, allowing them purpose and independence rather than becoming dependent on the State, because no one wins from State dependency.
rigor.explanation: A causal chain is offered (education → employment → independence), but the superlative conclusion that education is the single greatest lever is asserted rather than supported; nothing is offered to rank it against other interventions, and 'no one wins from State dependency' is a bare assertion doing the work of a premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And it’s working—it’s working. Just this week, we’ve banned cellphones in school, and the feedback I’ve had from parents in my electorate is great.
rigor.explanation: Argument from anecdote: the conclusion that the plan 'is working' rests on informal parental feedback about a measure introduced days earlier, which cannot yet bear on attendance or achievement outcomes.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So, in the period in review, we not only saw an increase in the number of people on the jobseeker benefit in the 5½ years up to that point—an increase in 50,000 people—but we saw more people staying on welfare for longer.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that jobseeker benefit recipient numbers rose by about 50,000 over the roughly 5½ years to 30 June 2023, and that average duration on welfare also lengthened.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets / Statistical Report: jobseeker support recipient counts at approximately December 2017 and at 30 June 2023. True if the increase is close to 50,000; false if materially different (e.g. under 30,000 or over 80,000). Duration claim checkable against MSD continuous-duration-on-benefit series.

veracity.statement: So jobseeker support across all categories: in September 2017, the estimate was 9.3 years—it went up to 12.7 years. For jobseeker support under 25 years, it was 12.12 years—went up to 18.9 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific values of the Taylor Fry actuarial estimate of average future years on main benefit for jobseeker support (all categories, and under-25s) in September 2017 versus the year to 30 June 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Taylor Fry actuarial valuation of the benefit system as at 30 June 2023 and the 2017 valuation: average estimated future years on main benefit to age 65 by benefit category. True if the four figures (9.3, 12.7, 12.12, 18.9) match the published tables within rounding; false if materially different.

veracity.statement: There is a direct correlation and the data tells us job seeker numbers went up when sanctions went down—pretty clear.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an observed inverse relationship in the data between the number of benefit sanctions imposed and jobseeker recipient numbers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD quarterly data on sanctions/obligation failures imposed alongside jobseeker support recipient numbers, 2017–2023. True if the two series move inversely over the period; false if jobseeker numbers rose or fell independently of sanction volumes.

veracity.statement: They are not now languishing 24 years on the benefit.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 24-year figure from the Taylor Fry report is a forward-looking estimate of future lifetime years on benefit, not a measure of time young beneficiaries have already spent on welfare, so the claim that they 'are now languishing' 24 years is a misreading.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Taylor Fry actuarial valuation as at 30 June 2023: whether the 24-year figure for youth payment / young parent payment recipients is defined as 'average estimated future years on main benefit to age 65'. True if it is a projection of future years; false if the report reports it as years already spent on benefit.

veracity.statement: We’ve seen an increase of not just the total debt but the average repayments during the period that we’re reviewing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that both total debt owed to MSD by clients and the average repayment amount rose over the review period (year to 30 June 2023).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD debt statistics (total client debt outstanding and average weekly repayment) for the year to 30 June 2023 versus the prior year. True if both measures rose; false if either fell or was flat.

veracity.statement: And also, if you look at the period of time that we are referring to and the years before that, we have seen—just let me get my figures right—in terms of the number of hardship assistance, that the number of hardship assistance provided nearly doubled, and the value of the hardship assistance nearly trebled.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the number of hardship assistance grants nearly doubled and their total value nearly trebled over the review period and preceding years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD hardship assistance data (number of special needs grants / hardship payments and their total value) comparing roughly 2017 with the year to 30 June 2023. True if volumes roughly doubled and value roughly trebled; false if either multiple is materially off.

veracity.statement: We’ve seen that more than 70 percent of children successfully completing those programmes are not re-referred or don’t go on to be referred to those programmes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a non-re-referral rate above 70 percent for children completing the multi-agency youth programmes in South and West Auckland.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD / multi-agency team programme evaluation or reporting for Kotahi te Whakaaro and the West Auckland Multi-Disciplinary Cross Agency Team: proportion of completing participants not subsequently re-referred. True if the reported rate exceeds 70 percent; false if materially lower or if no such measure is reported.

specificity.statement: So, in the period in review, we not only saw an increase in the number of people on the jobseeker benefit in the 5½ years up to that point—an increase in 50,000 people—but we saw more people staying on welfare for longer.
specificity.explanation: Carries a named benefit, a numeric increase and a defined period, so the claim is directly checkable against MSD data.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So jobseeker support across all categories: in September 2017, the estimate was 9.3 years—it went up to 12.7 years. For jobseeker support under 25 years, it was 12.12 years—went up to 18.9 years.
specificity.explanation: Named indicator (average estimated future years on main benefit to age 65), named cohorts, named baseline date and precise figures — someone could look each of these up in the actuarial valuation.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And also, if you look at the period of time that we are referring to and the years before that, we have seen—just let me get my figures right—in terms of the number of hardship assistance, that the number of hardship assistance provided nearly doubled, and the value of the hardship assistance nearly trebled.
specificity.explanation: Gives a direction and rough multiples ('nearly doubled', 'nearly trebled') for named measures, but no dollar figures, baseline or precise period.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve seen that more than 70 percent of children successfully completing those programmes are not re-referred or don’t go on to be referred to those programmes.
specificity.explanation: A numeric outcome measure tied to named programmes, though the cohort size and measurement window are not given.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There is a direct correlation and the data tells us job seeker numbers went up when sanctions went down—pretty clear.
rigor.explanation: Answering a request for evidence that sanctions work, the conclusion that sanctions cause employment outcomes is drawn from a bare co-movement of two series — a correlation-implies-causation inference with no control for the labour market conditions (including COVID-era settings) that plausibly drove both.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because employers go to meet job seekers at work expos and work seminars, and they end up in a job. That’s a win, to me.
rigor.explanation: Asked how she knows the seminars work, and having just conceded no cumulative outcome data is collected, she concludes they work from an anecdotal description of the process — an appeal to anecdote, with the conclusion resting on the mechanism being plausible rather than on any measured outcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I know that member may not want to see more Kiwis in work, but I definitely do.
civility.explanation: Imputes to a named opponent the motive of not wanting New Zealanders in work — an attack on the member's good faith rather than on his argument about the evidence for work seminars.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I really appreciate the Minister’s hot takes on sanctions, but she didn’t present any research or empirical evidence about whether they work, so I’ll ask my question again succinctly.
civility.explanation: The substantive point — that no evidence was offered — is squarely on the argument, but 'hot takes' is a dismissive characterisation of the Minister personally rather than of her case.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I really appreciate the Minister’s hot takes on sanctions, but she didn’t present any research or empirical evidence about whether they work, so I’ll ask my question again succinctly.
focus.explanation: Directed entirely at the evidential basis for the sanctions regime, a specific policy under review; no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They are not now languishing 24 years on the benefit.
focus.explanation: Engages a named report, a named figure and the specific way it has been used in public statements — accountability scrutiny with concrete content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In particular, the multi-agency teams in South Auckland have run programmes such as Kotahi te Whakaaro, and also in West Auckland, the West Auckland Multi-Disciplinary Cross Agency Team, where we’re seeing really good outcomes from there.
focus.explanation: Names specific programmes and asks about their funding continuation into the next financial year; entirely about the policy, with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In the six months of this coalition Government, we have seen this Government introduce policies that will put more children in poverty, that will cut school lunches, that will repeal world-leading smoke-free legislation which would have seen a smoke-free generation for our tamariki.
focus.explanation: Names specific measures — school lunch funding, the smoke-free legislation repeal — rather than generalised party-bashing; this is policy-directed scrutiny.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I implore the Prime Minister, who the report was addressed to, to take pause to listen to what the Waitangi Tribunal has said, to stop the repeal of section 7AA—and that there are other options to look at these areas where they may have concerns.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named legislative provision and the alternative courses available; no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This organisation is being told to find 6.5 percent savings. Why is that? It’s so that they can pay for tax cuts for landlords. That’s what this is about.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual fiscal mechanism — a named savings percentage set against a named tax measure — rather than the other party's character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Also, to the Minister, will she commit to the ongoing funding for Mana in Mahi, which has been successful in keeping people from long-term benefit dependency and also has been stated as a major priority for this Government?
focus.explanation: A precise question about a named employment programme and its funding — accountability on policy, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This was a piece of policy introduced by the National Government, because they recognised that for generations there have been disproportionate numbers of tamariki Māori taken into care and that there are huge disparities within the child protection organisation and system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act was originally enacted under a National-led Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Legislative history of section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989: which Act inserted it and which Government was in office when it passed. True if inserted by the Children, Young Persons, and Their Families (Oranga Tamariki) Legislation Act 2017 passed under a National-led Government; false if enacted under a different Government.

veracity.statement: It was been said in the Waitangi Tribunal’s interim report that there is no—no—empirical evidence to support that there is any conflict between section 7AA and the best interests of the child, and, in fact, the evidence presented says it is to the contrary.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of the Waitangi Tribunal's 2024 interim report on the section 7AA repeal — that it found no empirical evidence of conflict between s7AA and the child's best interests.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Waitangi Tribunal's 2024 urgent-inquiry interim report on the repeal of section 7AA. True if the report states there is no empirical evidence of conflict between s7AA and the best interests of the child; false if it makes no such finding or finds otherwise.

veracity.statement: They are making a choice here, and so, in looking for savings within the department, Oranga Tamariki has identified over 600 roles, and 447 of those are going to be cut; almost 9 percent of the organisation is being cut at the direction of this Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Oranga Tamariki identified over 600 roles and is cutting 447 of them, close to 9 percent of the organisation.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki's 2024 change proposal / final decision documents and contemporaneous reporting. True if the proposal identified 600+ roles with 447 to be disestablished (~9% of staff); false if the numbers materially differ.

veracity.statement: In 2022-23, the ministry’s non-departmental expenditure was $37.88 billion; that’s compared to $38.24 billion in the year preceding that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts MSD non-departmental expenditure of $37.88b in 2022/23 against $38.24b in 2021/22.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Social Development Annual Report 2022/23 non-departmental expenditure totals. True if the figures match within rounding; false if materially different.

veracity.statement: For example, the ministry’s core payment system, SWIFTT, is over 40 years old and was introduced before both the internet and EFTPOS.
veracity.explanation: Asserts MSD's core payment system SWIFTT is more than 40 years old and predates the internet and EFTPOS in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD documentation / select committee evidence on SWIFTT's introduction date, and the dates of EFTPOS rollout in NZ (late 1980s). True if SWIFTT was introduced before ~1984 and predates NZ EFTPOS; false if introduced materially later.

veracity.statement: Of course, given that in the time in review we, unfortunately, did see an explosion of the jobseeker benefits, we want to see programmes that are getting outcomes to support people into employment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that jobseeker support numbers rose sharply (an 'explosion') during the 2022/23 financial year under review.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets, jobseeker support recipient numbers at June 2022 versus June 2023. True if numbers rose substantially over that year; false if flat or falling, or if the rise was marginal such that 'explosion' overstates it.

civility.statement: I implore the Prime Minister, who the report was addressed to, to take pause to listen to what the Waitangi Tribunal has said, to stop the repeal of section 7AA—and that there are other options to look at these areas where they may have concerns.
civility.explanation: Addresses the Prime Minister directly on a contested repeal but attacks no person — the appeal is entirely about the measure and the Tribunal's evidence.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This organisation is being told to find 6.5 percent savings. Why is that? It’s so that they can pay for tax cuts for landlords. That’s what this is about.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a causal link between Oranga Tamariki's savings target and interest-deductibility changes for landlords with nothing offered to connect them — an unsupported causal attribution presented as self-evident.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, firstly, because this is a debate on the annual review for the financial year 2022-23, it is to the year 30 June 2023. So I won’t be answering any questions that take a forward view or indicate what future funding might look like.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows from the stated premise about the debate's scope, but the scope premise does all the work and is asserted rather than established — a reasonable inference leaning on an appeal to procedure.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They are making a choice here, and so, in looking for savings within the department, Oranga Tamariki has identified over 600 roles, and 447 of those are going to be cut; almost 9 percent of the organisation is being cut at the direction of this Government.
specificity.explanation: Gives a role count, a proposed cut figure and a percentage of the organisation — precise enough for anyone to check against the change proposal.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In 2022-23, the ministry’s non-departmental expenditure was $37.88 billion; that’s compared to $38.24 billion in the year preceding that.
specificity.explanation: Two exact expenditure figures for named years, directly checkable against the ministry's annual report.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The ministry has so far allocated $183 million to cover the first two years of the programme. We noted that the overall cost of the programme is projected to cost somewhere between $2.1 and $2.6 billion.
specificity.explanation: Names an allocated amount, the period it covers, and a costed range for the whole programme.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Also, to the Minister, will she commit to the ongoing funding for Mana in Mahi, which has been successful in keeping people from long-term benefit dependency and also has been stated as a major priority for this Government?
specificity.explanation: Names the programme and the decision sought, but supplies no figures, numbers served, or funding amounts.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That is underpinned by Te Aorerekura, with the six shifts that are specified in that plan.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the national strategy Te Aorerekura specifies six 'shifts' in its action plan.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of Te Aorerekura, the National Strategy to Eliminate Family Violence and Sexual Violence (2021), and its action plan; true if the plan is structured around six named shifts, false if it specifies a different number or no such structure.

veracity.statement: We know that they have done initial reports on monitoring—three experience of care reports and two in-depth review reports have also been produced.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a count of publications by the Independent Children's Monitor Aroturuki Tamariki as at May 2024: three experience of care reports and two in-depth review reports.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Independent Children's Monitor's published report list as at 1 May 2024; true if three 'experiences of care in Aotearoa' reports and two in-depth reviews had been published by that date, false if the counts differ.

veracity.statement: The last Government invested over $27 million to help Pacific people gain employment, and I have a specific question around the Toloa Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, and Maths programme; Tupu Aotearoa; and the Pacific Work Connect service: will the Government continue to invest?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous (Labour) Government invested over $27 million in Pacific employment initiatives.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry for Pacific Peoples / Budget appropriations for Pacific employment programmes (Tupu Aotearoa, Toloa, Pacific Work Connect) under the 2017–2023 Government; true if the total committed exceeds $27 million, false if materially less.

veracity.statement: Because when I was employment Minister, I picked up He Poutama Rangatahi, which was actually a National Party initiative that was put on hold back around 2017.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that He Poutama Rangatahi originated as a National Party initiative dating from around 2017 which was then paused, and that Jackson as Employment Minister revived it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2017 documents and MSD/MBIE records on the origin and funding history of He Poutama Rangatahi (Youth Employment Pathways); true if the programme was established under the National-led Government around 2017 and subsequently paused before being resumed, false if it originated under the 2017–2023 Government.

veracity.statement: And I do want to ask the question about He Poutama Rangatahi that saw over 12,000 young people engaged in the programme, resulting in 77 percent of those young people—77 percent, Minister—engaging in employment, education, or training.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that over 12,000 young people participated in He Poutama Rangatahi and that 77 percent of them moved into employment, education or training.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD/MBIE He Poutama Rangatahi outcome reporting; true if participant numbers exceed 12,000 and the reported employment/education/training rate is approximately 77 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: And we committed over $95 million for the fund which delivered 63 Māori-lead projects and will support over 4,000 Māori across Aotearoa.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government committed over $95 million to the fund, that it delivered 63 Māori-led projects, and that it will support over 4,000 Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Puni Kōkiri / MSD funding announcements and reporting for the Māori trades training fund; true if the appropriation exceeds $95 million and 63 Māori-led projects were funded, false if the figures differ materially.

specificity.explanation: A dollar figure plus three named programmes and a clear question about their continuation.

rigor.statement: But we know, as the previous Government, that specific programmes were able to do that, and so that’s why we’ve asked the questions about Mana in Mahi.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable inference — if named programmes demonstrably produced the outcomes, asking about those specific programmes rather than general principles follows — but the premise is asserted from the speaker's own experience rather than evidenced at this point in the argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Of course, we had the priorities of the education sector, but just to let those listening know, the agencies and organisations that we heard from were: the Ministry of Education, the Tertiary Education Commission, the Education Review Office, the New Zealand Qualifications Authority, Education New Zealand, Education Payroll Ltd, and Network for Learning—some in-depth, some in a standard review format, some in a review briefing format, and some pro forma.
specificity.explanation: Names every agency reviewed and distinguishes the review format applied to each, rather than summarising vaguely as 'a range of education agencies'. Checkable against the committee's report; no figures or dates, so short of the top.

specificity.statement: I’m just really wanting to know when the public is likely to hear a report back from the ministerial advisory group on curriculum, and if they’re making significant recommendations, which I’m sure that they will be, having read some blog pieces by some of those members recently around changes, what work is the Minister thinking about to ensure that there is sector consultation that will happen, given that some of those peak bodies are complaining that they feel that they are not being consulted in recent times?

specificity.explanation: Names the learning area and the exact deficiency alleged (absence of year-by-year progressions), which someone could verify against the published documents. No dates or quantities, so not top of scale.

focus.statement: So the work that was started, unfortunately not completed or well-completed over that six-year period, but I think we’re on the same track, which is we have to have a knowledge-rich curriculum that lays out year by year what the key core content is that must be taught so it doesn’t matter where you go to school in this country and what your family circumstances are, you get access to the same knowledge, skills, and competencies.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the curriculum policy — what a knowledge-rich, year-by-year curriculum would do and why consistency across schools matters — rather than the other party's character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I just really want to focus on the fact around why, when there were expert groups that have been putting together the curriculum and working through that and making certain that the sector is on board, does the Minister feel that a new group was needed of alternate experts and whether they had so-called better expertise than the experts that were already there?
focus.explanation: Directed at a specific decision — the establishment of a new ministerial advisory group alongside existing expert groups — and at sector buy-in. Legitimate scrutiny with no party-versus-party content.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So the work that was started, unfortunately not completed or well-completed over that six-year period, but I think we’re on the same track, which is we have to have a knowledge-rich curriculum that lays out year by year what the key core content is that must be taught so it doesn’t matter where you go to school in this country and what your family circumstances are, you get access to the same knowledge, skills, and competencies.

civility.statement: I just really want to focus on the fact around why, when there were expert groups that have been putting together the curriculum and working through that and making certain that the sector is on board, does the Minister feel that a new group was needed of alternate experts and whether they had so-called better expertise than the experts that were already there?
civility.explanation: Pointed and robust: 'so-called better expertise' casts light doubt on the credentials of the new advisers, edging toward the people rather than the appointment decision, but stops well short of an insult or an imputation of bad faith.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: From my perspective, looking back, the fact that we have had a curriculum that has been very vague, high-level, and devoid of knowledge has been a real problem for New Zealand. I think our decline in our standards started from 2007 when we introduced that curriculum.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: the causal link between the 2007 curriculum and a national decline in standards rests solely on the coincidence of dates. No mechanism, comparison or evidence is offered to exclude other causes, and the curriculum's characterisation is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’ll just point out that it is within the parameters of this debate because the Minister did bring it up herself within the annual review hearing that she had with the select committee.
rigor.explanation: A clean inference: if the Minister raised the topic in the annual review hearing, it falls within the scope of the annual review debate. The conclusion follows from the premise offered; it depends on the premise being accurate, which is a separate question.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I think our decline in our standards started from 2007 when we introduced that curriculum.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the measurable decline in New Zealand student achievement began in 2007, coinciding with the introduction of the New Zealand Curriculum.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: International and national achievement trend series for New Zealand — PISA (2000 onward), TIMSS and PIRLS, and NMSSA. True if those series show flat or rising achievement to 2007 and a decline commencing around that year; false if a sustained decline is already visible in the cycles before 2007 (e.g. PISA reading/maths falling between 2000 and 2006).

veracity.statement: If we look at English, there have been no year-by-year progressions done; we look at other learning areas and the progressions aren’t there year by year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the curriculum refresh documents released for English, and for other learning areas, contain no progressions specified year by year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published Te Mātaiaho / curriculum refresh learning-area documents for English and other learning areas as at April 2024. True if progressions are expressed only in multi-year phases or bands rather than per year level; false if year-by-year progressions are published for English.

veracity.statement: We know that about 90 percent of kids learn to read using structured literacy.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 90 percent of children successfully learn to read when taught by a structured literacy (systematic phonics-based) approach.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Reading-science literature and Ministry of Education advice on structured literacy efficacy (e.g. National Reading Panel, Castles/Rastle/Nation 2018, BSLA evaluations); true if the commonly cited proportion of children who learn to read under systematic structured literacy instruction is around 90 percent, false if the literature supports a materially different figure or no such estimate.

veracity.statement: I was just looking at the Better Start Literacy Approach, it’s seen an 87 to 96 percent success rate of students reaching the expected level for their year group.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Better Start Literacy Approach produces an 87–96 percent rate of students reaching the expected reading level for their year group.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published Better Start Literacy Approach evaluation data (University of Canterbury / Ministry of Education reports); true if reported success rates fall in the 87–96 percent band for students reaching expected year-level, false if the reported rates are materially different.

veracity.statement: To be fair to the previous Government, I think they started to acknowledge that and did invest in structured literacy, and I want to give credit to them for doing that, because the Better Start Literacy Approach (BSLA) was brought in under the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Better Start Literacy Approach was introduced under the previous (Labour-led) Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education / Budget records on when BSLA was funded and rolled out; true if it was introduced and funded during the 2017–2023 Labour-led Government, false if it originated under a different administration.

veracity.statement: I’d put some written questions to the Minister around the level of support in her office for Pacific communities, but the information was withheld on the context of personal identification.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that written parliamentary questions he lodged about Pacific-community support resourcing in the Minister's office were answered with the information withheld on privacy/personal-identification grounds.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliament written questions register for 2024 under Utikere's name to the Minister of Education; true if the answers withhold the requested information citing personal identification/privacy, false if no such questions or no such withholding appears.

specificity.statement: I was just looking at the Better Start Literacy Approach, it’s seen an 87 to 96 percent success rate of students reaching the expected level for their year group.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific programme and gives a precise, checkable performance range against a defined benchmark.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I want to give you the example of the Māori students at Maramarua School, because, in 2021, 37 percent of Māori learners were at or above the curriculum level for reading, but by the end of 2023, 68 percent were.
specificity.explanation: Named school, named cohort, two dated percentages against a defined curriculum benchmark — checkable in principle against the school's achievement data.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So it is my intention to bring that all together and make sure that we are investing in our aspiring teachers who want to go on to leadership, that we are making sure that they have the skills, the knowledge, and the experience that they need to take on that role, and also, once they’re in that role, that those in-service principals get the support that they need.
specificity.explanation: A direction of travel on principal-leadership pipelines with no mechanism, funding figure, programme name or timeframe attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I want to sort of take a little bit of a change now to go to learning support, and I’m quite interested to know what the progress has been of the Highest Needs Review to date, particularly over the 2023 year, and what changes have been seen for learning support delivery from the beginning of 2024 as a result.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific review and the specific periods (2023, from the start of 2024) being asked about, though it does not specify which measures or outputs would count as progress.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: To be fair to the previous Government, I think they started to acknowledge that and did invest in structured literacy, and I want to give credit to them for doing that, because the Better Start Literacy Approach (BSLA) was brought in under the previous Government.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested partisan point where an attack was available; instead she credits opponents on the substance and attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We know that the greatest results will be for those kids who come from homes where they have no resources to help, because wealthy homes will do after-school reading—their parents, educated parents, will read to them after school because they don’t hold down three jobs each.
rigor.explanation: The premise (wealthier households supplement reading at home) supports the idea that low-income children have less home support, but the leap to 'greatest results' from the intervention requires an additional step about differential response to instruction that is asserted rather than shown — a real gap between what is offered and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is where we really missed a trick in the last six years: embedding structured literacy in every single classroom in this country from year one.
focus.explanation: Criticism of the past six years that names a specific pedagogical policy and the specific omission — accountability with policy content, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I want to sort of take a little bit of a change now to go to learning support, and I’m quite interested to know what the progress has been of the Highest Needs Review to date, particularly over the 2023 year, and what changes have been seen for learning support delivery from the beginning of 2024 as a result.
focus.explanation: Squarely scrutinises a named policy workstream (the Highest Needs Review) and its delivery effects; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’ve made comments in the past about the previous iterations of the common practice model that I saw. It was incoherent, it was based on competing ideologies, it was not based on what the latest research and evidence in science and cognitive research says, which is the science of learning and how the brain learns to acquire knowledge.
civility.explanation: Harsh criticism aimed entirely at a policy document (the common practice model), naming no person and imputing no bad faith. Under the re-anchored scale, brutal criticism of a policy is the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And if the member’s opposed to profit, then next time he goes to an early childhood education centre, he should ask himself where everything from the food to the carpet came from and figure out how, in his communist utopia, any of those things would be provided without profit.
civility.explanation: Mockery directed at the member personally, attributing to him a 'communist utopia' he did not advocate. Goes past robust disagreement into sneering at the individual.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Oh no, we’ve gone from anti-business sentiment to outright xenophobia.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the questioner's character — labelling him xenophobic for asking about offshore profit-shifting rather than engaging the accountability question.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And you won’t be surprised to hear that we need to make sure it’s based on the science of learning, that it’s year by year, that all of the core content is there in a structured way, especially in things like mathematics and literacy, which are so important that we do things in the right order.
specificity.explanation: A direction with some named content (science of learning, year-by-year, maths and literacy) but no figures, no timeframe and no mechanism for how the curriculum material will be produced.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The network approval was something that was introduced in February 2023 as part of the Early Learning Action Plan, and objective 5.1 states that early learning services are part of a planned and coherent education ecosystem that is supported, accountable, and sustainable.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy, the month it commenced and the numbered objective, with its wording — precise enough that anyone could go to the document and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As I said, the year-by-year literacy progressions were not done, so we have to do them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the curriculum work inherited by the Minister did not include year-by-year literacy progressions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education curriculum refresh documentation (Te Mātaiaho / the English learning area and literacy progressions as published up to early 2024); true if no year-by-year literacy progressions had been produced by the time of this statement, false if such year-by-year progressions had already been published.

veracity.statement: The network approval was something that was introduced in February 2023 as part of the Early Learning Action Plan, and objective 5.1 states that early learning services are part of a planned and coherent education ecosystem that is supported, accountable, and sustainable.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that ECE network approval began in February 2023 under the Early Learning Action Plan, and quotes objective 5.1 of that plan.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Early Learning Action Plan (He Taonga te Tamaiti, 2019) objective 5.1 text and the Education and Training Act network approval commencement date; true if network approval requirements took effect in February 2023 and objective 5.1 reads substantially as quoted, false if either the date or the objective wording is materially different.

veracity.statement: What the survey told me is that one of the concerns—if not the greatest—of unionised teachers in the ECE sector was actually the red tape and regulation that the Government puts on them when they’re trying to do their job.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an NZEI survey of its ECE members identified regulation and red tape as one of, if not the, greatest concern of unionised ECE teachers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZEI Te Riu Roa member survey provided to the Associate Minister around 2024 (or NZEI's published ECE workforce survey results); true if regulatory compliance/red tape ranks at or near the top of members' stated concerns, false if pay, staffing ratios or workload rank materially above it.

rigor.statement: It’s not really obvious why the member has a problem with profit in early childhood education, because if he went into any centres, he’d be surrounded by the products of for-profit entities.
rigor.explanation: Equivocation: the presence of for-profit suppliers of carpet and furniture does not bear on whether the publicly funded provision of the education service itself should be for profit. The conclusion does not follow from the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And what was discovered—long and painfully, I might add—was that Governments generally don’t know exactly where to invest. They don’t know the best places for people to do business. They don’t understand community demand as well as the people who are involved in running the businesses. So we’re getting rid of network management because it creates an additional burden on the people managing the centres.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: if central planners have worse information about demand than operators, planning approval adds cost without benefit. But the premises are asserted as general historical lessons rather than evidenced for the ECE case, and the stated conclusion (burden) is only loosely connected to the information argument that precedes it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, no, not really, because they’re not the ones that are making decisions about when to expand or when to open or when to close a centre, so it would be unusual to consult people that aren’t really affected by a regulation on the regulation.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on an unsupported premise smuggled in mid-sentence — that teachers are 'not really affected' by a regulation governing where and whether centres open, which is precisely what is contested. Assumes what needs establishing.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, once again, this is why the member’s side lost the Cold War.
focus.explanation: Content-free party framing — situates the questioner's 'side' in a global ideological defeat without naming any policy, figure or mechanism at issue in the ECE network management question.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The wait times have increased, the numbers have increased, and, as we all know, the worst thing for a child is to be on a wait-list.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that both waiting times and the number of children waiting for learning support rose over the period under review (the previous parliamentary term).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education learning support data (e.g. Early Intervention Service / ORS referral wait times and numbers on wait-lists) for roughly 2017–2023; true if both average wait time and the number of children waiting rose over that period, false if either was flat or fell.

veracity.statement: One of the things, though, that I noticed coming into this role was that we spend an awful amount of money on learning sport; well—well—over a billion dollars and potentially a lot more once we start collecting up all the things we spend money on.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that annual Crown spending on learning support exceeds $1 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Vote Education appropriations / Ministry of Education learning support expenditure for 2023/24; true if identifiable learning support spend exceeds $1 billion a year, false if materially below that.

veracity.statement: As I said in my previous contribution as well, there were a lot of strategies written by the last Government; not a lot of action. Actually, you can see the results. Learning support—much worse. Academic achievement—much worse. Kids going to school—much worse. A lot of glossy documents; not a lot of doing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that learning support, academic achievement and school attendance all deteriorated markedly under the previous government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education regular attendance statistics and NCEA/PISA/curriculum achievement series for 2017–2023; true if attendance and achievement measures declined materially over that period, false if they were stable or improved.

specificity.statement: So it will be my focus, with the backing of the ministry, to make sure that we are evaluating and monitoring all of the things that we do so that we can shift money into things that are working and stop doing things that are not working.
specificity.explanation: A clear direction (evaluate programmes, reallocate funding) but no named programmes, no evaluation measures, no amounts and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Also, how would the Minister and the ministry plan to achieve our Learning Support Action Plan 2019-2025 when expert roles directly supporting neurodivergent and disabled students and teachers and schools will be lost in the Ministry of Education cuts?
specificity.explanation: Names the Learning Support Action Plan 2019-2025, the affected roles and the mechanism (ministry cuts); lacks figures on how many roles.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: First of all, I can tell the member that, along with Minister Stanford and Cabinet colleagues, we’ve been working very quickly to get the basic ideas around policy decisions around charter schools made. And we’re doing that in order that we can pass legislation and have the first charter schools open in term 1, 2025.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (Cabinet policy decisions, then legislation) and a dated milestone (first charter schools open in term 1, 2025); no numbers of schools or funding.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As I said in my previous contribution as well, there were a lot of strategies written by the last Government; not a lot of action. Actually, you can see the results. Learning support—much worse. Academic achievement—much worse. Kids going to school—much worse. A lot of glossy documents; not a lot of doing.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc inference: a list of deteriorating outcomes is offered as proof that the previous government's strategies produced no action, with nothing linking the documents to the outcomes and no alternative causes considered.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As I said in my previous contribution as well, there were a lot of strategies written by the last Government; not a lot of action. Actually, you can see the results. Learning support—much worse. Academic achievement—much worse. Kids going to school—much worse. A lot of glossy documents; not a lot of doing.
focus.explanation: Names real outcome areas (learning support, achievement, attendance), but the weight of the passage is a general characterisation of the last Government as producers of glossy documents rather than engagement with any named measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Also, how would the Minister and the ministry plan to achieve our Learning Support Action Plan 2019-2025 when expert roles directly supporting neurodivergent and disabled students and teachers and schools will be lost in the Ministry of Education cuts?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: names a specific plan, a specific cohort and a specific policy action (ministry cuts) and asks how the commitment will still be met.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m quite keen to understand from the Minister how that work programme to bring in charter schools is looking, what progress has been made so far, and what makes the Minister so confident about charter schools—that charter schools will be able to help students that are at risk.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named policy — the charter school work programme, its progress and its evidence base for at-risk students — with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In many respects, you could say in recent years we have got the balance wrong with New Zealand education policy: enormous amounts of micro-management of what shape classroom they have and how they operate under the Common Practice Model, but almost no accountability for whether students actually attend and actually achieve.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of education policy — names the Common Practice Model and contrasts prescription of practice with absence of accountability for attendance and achievement — rather than characterising an opposing party.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: First of all, I would like to reject the Associate Minister’s claim before. I was asking a valid question—“can he ensure”—and I get called xenophobic. But that’s OK; I forgive that member.
civility.explanation: Rebuts a personal accusation while staying on the substance of his own question; the closing "I forgive that member" is faintly condescending, which keeps it below the standard, but no attack on the person is made.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: New Zealand has the highest species extinction rate in the world.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's rate of species extinction is the highest of any country in the world.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DOC / Ministry for the Environment 'Environment Aotearoa' and IUCN comparative data on extinction rates and proportions of threatened species by country; true if a recognised source ranks New Zealand first on species extinction rate, false if the ranking is materially different or if the commonly cited statistic is about the proportion of threatened species rather than an extinction rate.

veracity.statement: Sixty-three percent of our ecosystems are threatened. Those ecosystems are the home of our native species, of which 4,000 are either at risk or threatened with extinction. That includes 90 percent of our seabirds, 82 percent of our native birds, 94 percent of our reptiles, and 72 percent of our native freshwater fish.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific figures for threatened ecosystems and for the proportion of seabirds, native birds, reptiles and freshwater fish that are at risk or threatened with extinction.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DOC New Zealand Threat Classification System summaries and Stats NZ / MfE 'Environment Aotearoa 2022' indicators for threatened species and ecosystems; true if each figure matches the published percentages within rounding, false if any is materially different.

veracity.statement: One of the times when I really burnt a chunk of my political capital was to secure the $1.3 billion for Jobs for Nature in Budget 2020.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Jobs for Nature received $1.3 billion in Budget 2020.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2020 documents and Treasury appropriations for the Jobs for Nature / environmental jobs package; true if the announced allocation is $1.3 billion (within rounding), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Now, New Zealand was the first country in the world to introduce that measure, and for that, the Hon Kris Faafoi and Hon David Clark can take a bow.
veracity.explanation: Asserts New Zealand was the first country in the world to introduce mandatory climate-related financial disclosures.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Legislative record for the Financial Sector (Climate-related Disclosures and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2021 and comparative dates for equivalent mandatory regimes elsewhere (e.g. UK); true if New Zealand's mandatory regime was legislated first, false if another jurisdiction legislated a mandatory regime earlier.

veracity.statement: Our vote went up at the 2020 election, and we became the first support party to increase our support after a term in Government.
veracity.explanation: Two claims: that the Green Party's party vote rose between 2017 and 2020, and that no previous MMP support party had increased its vote after a term supporting a government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission official party vote results for 2017 and 2020, plus the vote share of every prior MMP support party (NZ First, ACT, United Future, Māori Party, Progressives) before and after their terms in support; true if the Green vote rose and no earlier support party did so, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: The Greens now have more members of Parliament than we have ever had before, including three electorate seats, which we have never had before.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Green caucus after the 2023 election is the party's largest ever and that it holds three electorate seats, a first.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission results: Green caucus size after each election since 1996 and the number of Green electorate seats held; true if the post-2023 caucus exceeds every earlier one and three electorates are held, false if an earlier Parliament had as many or more.

veracity.statement: Last week—I’ll just let you recover from that for a moment—we got the news that New Zealand’s emissions fell for the third year in a row.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the greenhouse gas inventory released in April 2024 showed a third consecutive annual fall in New Zealand's emissions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry for the Environment's New Zealand Greenhouse Gas Inventory published April 2024; true if gross emissions declined in each of the three most recent reported years, false if any of those years shows an increase.

specificity.statement: Sixty-three percent of our ecosystems are threatened. Those ecosystems are the home of our native species, of which 4,000 are either at risk or threatened with extinction. That includes 90 percent of our seabirds, 82 percent of our native birds, 94 percent of our reptiles, and 72 percent of our native freshwater fish.
specificity.explanation: Four separate percentages by taxon plus an absolute count of at-risk species — precise and checkable against the published conservation status series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One of the times when I really burnt a chunk of my political capital was to secure the $1.3 billion for Jobs for Nature in Budget 2020.
specificity.explanation: Named programme, named Budget, exact appropriation figure — directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I am a Star Trek fan, so I am giving myself a five-year mission to boldly reduce or remove 150 million tonnes of climate pollution from global emissions by 2030.
specificity.explanation: A quantified target with a deadline — 150 million tonnes by 2030 — though no mechanism or means is given for how it would be achieved.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are some in the new Government who seem to want to put these endangered species on the fast track to oblivion. So those numbers may well go up.
focus.explanation: Alludes to fast-track consenting policy, but names no measure or provision; the weight of the sentence is a characterisation of what unnamed members of the new Government want.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I know that the current Minister is more interested in the quid than the quo, but, Christopher, if you let them unwind the National Policy Statement for Indigenous Biodiversity, I will haunt you!
focus.explanation: Names a specific instrument, the National Policy Statement for Indigenous Biodiversity, and the specific action at issue (unwinding it).
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Pressure is building and the consensus is fraying and some of those partisans sit in this House and some of them are now Government Ministers. The framework is being quietly sabotaged and subtly undermined, and there is an increasing risk that New Zealand will collapse into the climate culture wars that we see in the United States or Britain or Canada or Australia and elsewhere.
focus.explanation: Refers to the climate framework he has just described, so there is real policy content, but the claim of sabotage is directed at unnamed partisan Ministers rather than at any named decision or provision.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So my message to this House is that if you take positions that are lateral to that tug of war and to those entrenched debates, and you build alliances across them, then you can actually radically shift the political centre in your own direction because there’s no one resisting you. And where I did, it worked: the zero carbon Act, the Climate Change Commission, the emissions targets and our five-year emissions budgets, our 2030 target under the Paris Agreement, and our 2050 net zero targets all seem to have largely survived the change of Government when very little else has.
focus.explanation: Names six specific instruments and the outcome claimed for each; entirely about mechanism and results rather than party.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I know that the current Minister is more interested in the quid than the quo, but, Christopher, if you let them unwind the National Policy Statement for Indigenous Biodiversity, I will haunt you!
civility.explanation: Jocular, but imputes a motive to a named Minister — that he cares about the payment and not the obligation — rather than engaging his stated reasons. Pointed, edging toward the person.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One of the reasons, I believe, that successive Governments had never really dealt with climate change is they’re so busy dealing with the fiasco du jour, and then they kick the long-term, really big challenges down the road.
rigor.explanation: A causal explanation supported by the preceding list of crises faced by three governments — the anecdotal survey is consistent with the conclusion, but nothing rules out competing explanations, so the inference outruns the evidence offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So my message to this House is that if you take positions that are lateral to that tug of war and to those entrenched debates, and you build alliances across them, then you can actually radically shift the political centre in your own direction because there’s no one resisting you. And where I did, it worked: the zero carbon Act, the Climate Change Commission, the emissions targets and our five-year emissions budgets, our 2030 target under the Paris Agreement, and our 2050 net zero targets all seem to have largely survived the change of Government when very little else has.
rigor.explanation: A general claim supported by evidence — the durability of a named set of instruments through a change of government. The evidence tracks the conclusion, but it is a single case generalised into a rule, and the survival of those instruments has other candidate explanations.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They’re saying we’re investing about 5 to 6 percent of GDP in infrastructure, but if we were to get what we need to get out of it, with the way we do it currently, we’d need to invest about 10 percent, so about 4 percent of GDP, essentially, being wasted in our processes.
specificity.explanation: Carries concrete, checkable magnitudes — current infrastructure investment at 5–6 percent of GDP, a notional requirement of 10 percent, and an implied ~4 percent of GDP lost in process inefficiency.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They said that, roughly speaking, we should be investing about 60 percent in maintenance, 40 percent in new, but we are investing probably about 30 percent in maintenance.
specificity.explanation: Gives a numeric benchmark split (60/40) and an actual figure (about 30 percent) that someone could go and check against agency spending data.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One of the things which is absolute music to my ears—because I’ve been saying this for 40 years—is that we need a population strategy and we need an immigration strategy, and we haven’t had one of those worthy of the name for all of those 40-odd years.
specificity.explanation: Names two desired strategies but supplies no content, mechanism, target or timeframe for either — a direction with nothing checkable or actionable attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s why our Government’s priorities are to boost economic growth and productivity, increase maintenance and resilience, improve safety, and achieve value for money.
specificity.explanation: A list of four generic policy virtues with no figures, mechanisms, funding levels or timeframes; nothing in it could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They’re saying we’re investing about 5 to 6 percent of GDP in infrastructure, but if we were to get what we need to get out of it, with the way we do it currently, we’d need to invest about 10 percent, so about 4 percent of GDP, essentially, being wasted in our processes.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance of infrastructure investment quality and delivery efficiency; no party framing at all in a debate where he could easily have reached for it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Our State highways have been peppered with 62,000 potholes in the last year, and the last Government was focused on trying to tell people to get out of their cars and trying to tell them to drive really, really slowly, rather than actually trying to stay focused on the basics.
focus.explanation: Opens with a specific, checkable maintenance figure, but the weight of the sentence is a general characterisation of what the previous government was 'focused on' rather than a named policy or measure.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: They’re saying we’re investing about 5 to 6 percent of GDP in infrastructure, but if we were to get what we need to get out of it, with the way we do it currently, we’d need to invest about 10 percent, so about 4 percent of GDP, essentially, being wasted in our processes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, as relayed from the Infrastructure Commission, both the current level of infrastructure investment as a share of GDP and the level that would be needed at present efficiency.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Waihanga / New Zealand Infrastructure Commission published evidence base and strategy documents on infrastructure investment as a share of GDP; true if the Commission's material puts current investment at roughly 5–6% of GDP and states that around 10% would be required at current delivery efficiency, false if its figures are materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, they said that the quantum investment is sufficient, but the quality of that investment is poor and New Zealand ranks in the bottom 10 percent of high-income countries in terms of the amount of infrastructure we deliver per unit of capital invested.
veracity.explanation: Relays a specific comparative ranking attributed to the Infrastructure Commission: New Zealand in the bottom 10 percent of high-income countries for infrastructure delivered per unit of capital invested.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Infrastructure Commission (Te Waihanga) international benchmarking work on infrastructure delivered per dollar invested; true if it places New Zealand in the bottom decile of high-income countries on that measure, false if it places New Zealand elsewhere or makes no such ranking.

veracity.statement: They said that, roughly speaking, we should be investing about 60 percent in maintenance, 40 percent in new, but we are investing probably about 30 percent in maintenance.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a recommended maintenance-to-new-build investment ratio and New Zealand's actual maintenance share, as relayed from the Commission.
veracity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s also pleasing to hear that he’s certainly not pushing back on the fiscal hole of between $8 billion and $22 billion for him to deliver his National Party roads of significance there—so that’s interesting to hear.

veracity.statement: The last Government spent an awful lot of time talking about things, talking about Auckland light rail, spending $227 million on business case reports and consultancy reports and glossy documents and no delivery—absolutely no delivery.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The draft GPS on land transport 2024 (Ministry of Transport), specifically its named projects and roads of national significance list: true if no or almost no South Island projects appear, false if it names multiple South Island projects.

rigor.statement: Does the Minister understand that the best way to move more people and goods now is to invest in better public transport, and walking and cycling in our urban areas, and inter-city rail and buses and ferries in the rest of our country, so that the people using the roads don’t have to compete with so many other cars and trucks?
rigor.explanation: A real mechanism is offered — mode shift frees road capacity for those who must drive — and the conclusion tracks it. But 'the best way' is a comparative claim, and nothing is offered to rule out the alternative (road capacity) or to address induced demand, so there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.

rigor.statement: Well, what Aucklanders want and what Aucklanders voted for is delivery, and that is what this Government is focused on.

rigor.statement: When you call something the “National Land Transport Fund”, you sort of think the “Land” part could be quite important—so the clue’s in the name.

rigor.statement: Instead of people getting Mill Road, every time they filled up their car, they thought they were filling up their car and they’d get Mill Road built a bit faster, actually they get a speed bump.

rigor.statement: It’s also pleasing to hear that he’s certainly not pushing back on the fiscal hole of between $8 billion and $22 billion for him to deliver his National Party roads of significance there—so that’s interesting to hear.

veracity.statement: Interestingly, as was recounted in the House a couple of weeks ago by, I think, Barbara Edmonds, who was telling a story of how Grant Robertson, when he was Minister of Finance, put this bill together and, initially, had checked in with Sir Michael Cullen about it, and Sir Michael did feel that it was around about appropriate for the Cullen fund to move into this sort of position now.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for the earlier reading of the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests) Amendment Bill in April 2024; true if Edmonds recounted Robertson consulting Cullen and Cullen endorsing the change, false if no such account appears in the record.

specificity.statement: It’s not necessarily 51 percent, as people might think; it could be quite a bit smaller than that. Because of the way company shareholdings work, it could be as little as 20 percent, or even less in some diverse shareholding companies, which is quite common in equity markets.

rigor.statement: Investing in strategic infrastructure—yes, I think the problem we run into when we start prescribing what you can and can’t invest in is that you’re then limiting choices. Limiting choices means probably—almost certainly—limiting returns.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: restricting the investable universe narrows choice, and narrower choice tends to reduce the efficient frontier. The step from 'limiting choices' to 'almost certainly limiting returns' is asserted rather than shown — no evidence or modelling offered — so there is a gap between premise and the strength of the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So we have to make a decision of do we have a superannuation fund that is something we want to achieve political ends with, or is it something we want to secure superannuation with, and I’d argue strongly that it should be the latter.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: the choice is framed as either a politically-directed fund or a returns-focused fund, excluding the middle case actually proposed (a returns-focused fund operating within ethical exclusions).

rigor.statement: That’s the sort of thing that happens when you start prescribing what you can and what you can’t invest in, and I think it’s so short-sighted.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single anecdote about a Western Australian farmer's tractor loan and bank emissions reporting to a conclusion about statutory investment mandates for the Super Fund — a hasty generalisation resting on a weak analogy between bank lending rules and a fund's investment exclusions.

rigor.statement: So the founder of the fund thought that it was the right sort of move, and I know that across the House that is supported now because we do want that fund to have some good returns.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority: the fund's founder approving is offered as the reason the change is right, with no argument about the merits of allowing controlling interests.

rigor.statement: I think we need to be careful, and we need to be careful because we actually don’t want politicians interfering too closely in the investment decisions of the Superannuation Fund. We actually need to leave the managers to use their expertise in that area.

focus.statement: This is positive because it’s removing the control restriction, which will enable the New Zealand Superannuation Fund to access a wider group of viable investment partners and opportunities, particularly here in New Zealand, which is where we want to see more investment and more capital, because that’s what’s going to help grow our economy.

rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure, but with a gap: removing an ownership restriction widens the pool of possible partners, yet nothing offered connects that to investment landing domestically rather than offshore, or to economic growth. rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s sitting at about $70 billion and is projected to reach $110 billion by the end of the decade.
