civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We inherited a cost of living crisis and a state of the economy that was going so far backwards, businesses everywhere were losing staff.
focus.explanation: General characterisation of the previous government's economic legacy; no specific policy, measure or figure is named, so it is party framing rather than policy engagement.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is the former leader of the ACT Party, the Hon Richard Prebble, nothing more than a Chinese puppet for writing his recent article entitled “It is lunacy to join a military alliance aimed at our biggest trading partner”?
focus.explanation: Names a specific published critique of AUKUS, but the thrust is testing the Minister's name-calling rather than engaging the substance of the AUKUS decision.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yes, particularly those comments that highlighted the fact that critics don’t know what they don’t know regarding the strategic challenges New Zealand faces; that they malign the agencies of State charged with collecting and analysing, for their Government, intelligence that informs our view about the challenging strategic environment in the Pacific; that Pillar 2 is a technology-sharing mechanism and not a military alliance; that the critics were silent like lambs ever since October 2021, when that member’s Government started considering New Zealand’s involvement with AUKUS—the same Labour Government that sanctioned officials to initiate discussions with AUKUS partners in 2023 but who now act like lions, following the change of Government.
focus.explanation: Contains a real policy claim (that Pillar 2 is technology-sharing, not a military alliance) with a dated allegation about the previous government's engagement, but much of the weight is on characterising critics and the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But in Mr Prebble’s case, he did write a book called I’ve Been Thinking—and I wish you would do that now.
focus.explanation: Contains no policy content at all; it is entirely a swipe at the member opposite.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The former leader of the National Party—due to his colleagues being here, I have to say he has many, many skills, and they’re quite exceptional in some cases. But they aren’t in foreign policy.
civility.explanation: Faint praise used to dismiss Don Brash's competence in the very domain at issue, rather than engaging the argument in his article. Sneering/condescending toward the person, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, can I just say that I’m not certain who wrote those questions, but it doesn’t sound like the member did.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe suggesting the member did not write and does not understand his own questions; it engages nothing in the question itself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Was that not noticed last December, or do people just want to run their own convenient argument all the time, followed by so many people up there [Points to the press gallery] who began that in the first place?
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith — that critics and the press gallery knowingly run a 'convenient argument' — rather than contesting the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And just in answer to a rebuttal that came from the other side there, we do not use military-style semi-automatics for duck shooting, so perhaps you would like to educate yourself on what’s actually being used.
civility.explanation: The factual correction is fine, but 'perhaps you would like to educate yourself' is condescension directed at the interjecting member rather than at the point made.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In short, Mr Keating is making comments that his own Labor Party in Parliament, in the Senate, and in the House of Commons in Canberra don’t in any way or shape support; nor do I suspect does the Hon Penny Wong, the Foreign Minister.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Paul Keating's criticism of AUKUS is not supported by the Australian Labor Party in the federal Parliament, nor by Foreign Minister Penny Wong. (The reference to a 'House of Commons in Canberra' is an evident slip for the House of Representatives and is not the claim being assessed.)
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements and policy positions of the Australian Labor government and its parliamentarians on AUKUS as at May 2024, including Penny Wong's on-record remarks; true if the ALP parliamentary party and Wong publicly back AUKUS against Keating's criticism, false if significant ALP parliamentary support for Keating's position is on record.

veracity.statement: Why can’t the Minister understand New Zealanders’ concerns about the promotion of AUKUS when, less than two weeks ago, he upped the ante by saying he saw “powerful reasons for New Zealand engaging practically with [AUKUS]”?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that within the previous fortnight Winston Peters publicly said he saw 'powerful reasons for New Zealand engaging practically with' AUKUS.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of Peters' foreign policy speeches/statements in the two weeks before 2 May 2024; true if that wording (or its unambiguous equivalent) appears in an April 2024 speech, false if no such statement exists in that window.

veracity.statement: We set out very clearly last night that we haven’t even had a chance to consider the matters that they began their discussion on or conclude them, or have even been asked by the AUKUS partners to be a part of it, and if that request comes, then we’ll have to examine here—and, hopefully, across party political lines—whether we should or not.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at 2 May 2024 New Zealand had not been asked by the AUKUS partners to join (Pillar Two of) the arrangement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official statements from MFAT, the Minister of Foreign Affairs and the AUKUS partners about whether a formal invitation to New Zealand had been issued by May 2024; true if no invitation had been extended, false if a formal request to participate is on record before that date.

veracity.statement: For a start, the first thing we did about the tobacco controls was put the tax up on cigarettes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the coalition Government's first action on tobacco was to raise tobacco tax, in December (of 2023).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Customs Service / legislative record of tobacco excise changes from November 2023 onward; true if a government-initiated excise increase took effect around December 2023 before other tobacco measures, false if the only change was the pre-existing automatic CPI indexation or if the smokefree repeal came first.

veracity.statement: Every day, an estimated five Kiwi kids are born with FASD.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an incidence of roughly five New Zealand babies born with fetal alcohol spectrum disorder each day (about 1,800 a year).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Health New Zealand published FASD prevalence estimates against Stats NZ annual live births; true if the official estimate is around 1,800 births a year, false if the accepted estimate is materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: I have been advised that there is no proposal to disestablish the international child protection and intercountry and domestic adoption services teams. What is proposed is to bring both teams together under one manager for adoptions and international case work, and it’s my expectation that the best interests of the children and young people will be at the forefront of any final decision in the future structure. This work will continue.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Oranga Tamariki change proposal does not disestablish the international child protection and adoption teams but merges them under a single manager.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Oranga Tamariki chief executive's 2024 change/restructure proposal document; true if it retains both teams under one manager, false if it proposes disestablishing either team or its functions.

veracity.statement: I am advised that front-line staff roles are not to be considered for cuts, and lawyers are not classed as front-line staff. I am advised that front-line staff roles that are considered to be children’s workers are defined in section 23 of the Children’s Act, and lawyers are not front-line workers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 'children's workers' — the basis for her front-line definition — are defined in section 23 of the Children's Act, and that lawyers fall outside that definition.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of section 23 of the Children's Act 2014 (formerly Vulnerable Children Act); true if it defines 'children's worker' and that definition excludes Oranga Tamariki legal staff, false if the definition sits elsewhere in the Act or captures those lawyers.

veracity.statement: Is there any evidence that the considerable and unprecedented build-up in back-office staff at Oranga Tamariki under the previous Government led to children being any safer?
veracity.explanation: The premise asserts that back-office staffing at Oranga Tamariki grew considerably and to an unprecedented level under the previous Labour Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki annual reports / Public Service Commission workforce data for corporate and non-front-line FTE from 2017 to 2023; true if corporate FTE rose substantially and to a historic high over that period, false if growth was modest or concentrated in front-line roles.

veracity.statement: It shows that bigger Government departments may not necessarily mean better results for young people. I will refer you to the Safety of Children in Care report, that during July 2022 and June 2023, 519 children in care experienced harm, even though we had bigger Government departments.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Safety of Children in Care report records 519 children in care experiencing harm between July 2022 and June 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Oranga Tamariki 'Safety of Children in Care' annual report for 2022/23; true if it records 519 children in care found to have experienced harm in that period, false if the figure differs materially or covers a different cohort.

veracity.statement: For an estimated 60,000 New Zealanders, the opening weekend of duck-shooting season is an eagerly awaited occasion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that about 60,000 New Zealanders take part in the opening weekend of the game bird hunting season.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Fish & Game New Zealand game bird licence sales for the 2024 season; true if licences/participants are around 60,000, false if materially fewer (e.g. in the 30,000–45,000 range typically reported).

veracity.statement: And just in answer to a rebuttal that came from the other side there, we do not use military-style semi-automatics for duck shooting, so perhaps you would like to educate yourself on what’s actually being used.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that military-style semi-automatic firearms are not used for duck shooting in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Arms Act 1983 as amended in 2019 (prohibited firearms), Fish & Game regulations on shotgun magazine capacity, and Wildlife Act hunting rules; true if MSSAs are prohibited/not lawfully usable for game bird hunting, false if such firearms are lawfully and commonly used.

focus.statement: Why can’t the Minister understand New Zealanders’ concerns about the promotion of AUKUS when, less than two weeks ago, he upped the ante by saying he saw “powerful reasons for New Zealand engaging practically with [AUKUS]”?
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the Government's AUKUS position and quotes a specific recent ministerial statement rather than trading in party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why is the Minister blind to the fact that Kiwis saw this as yet another lurch from this National-led Government while they’re still reeling from other surprises like the reversal of tobacco controls to fund tax cuts, using fast track to override environmental laws by ministerial fiat, and multibillion-dollar tax cuts for landlords?
focus.explanation: Names three specific measures (smokefree repeal, fast-track consenting, interest deductibility for landlords) so it carries real policy content, but the weight of the question is generalised framing about the Government's direction.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The truth is that there’s no lurch. We were left with a massive fiscal disaster—borrowing like there’s no tomorrow, like an eight-armed octopus with no restraint—and we’re going to bring this country back to control. We’re going to bring our economy, as some leader has said, back on track, and, as a more profound leader said, take back our country.
focus.explanation: Shifts from the AUKUS question to a generalised characterisation of the previous government's borrowing, without naming a policy, figure or programme.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How is disestablishing the International Child Protection Unit, which investigates cases on cross-border child sexual and labour exploitation, protecting our children?
focus.explanation: Names a specific unit and its specific function and tests a specific proposed change against the Minister's stated objective — scrutiny with concrete policy content, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Can I tell that member that one of the parts about having a legal training is you make sure you put the rider on it, and that very paragraph closes with the words “when the parties mutually agree that the time is appropriate”.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts a selective quotation by citing the qualifying clause that closes the same paragraph; the conclusion (the quoted remark was conditional) follows from the evidence offered, though it rests on the accuracy of his own recollection of the text.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It shows that bigger Government departments may not necessarily mean better results for young people. I will refer you to the Safety of Children in Care report, that during July 2022 and June 2023, 519 children in care experienced harm, even though we had bigger Government departments.
rigor.explanation: Draws a conclusion about departmental size from a single year's harm count with no comparison period, no baseline and no link between corporate headcount and harm outcomes — the inference outruns the evidence offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The truth is that there’s no lurch. We were left with a massive fiscal disaster—borrowing like there’s no tomorrow, like an eight-armed octopus with no restraint—and we’re going to bring this country back to control. We’re going to bring our economy, as some leader has said, back on track, and, as a more profound leader said, take back our country.
specificity.explanation: Metaphor and slogans — 'back to control', 'back on track', 'take back our country' — with no figures, mechanisms or named measures despite the topic being fiscal policy.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Last week at Papakura Marae, I announced that the coalition Government is taking action on fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD). This announcement means that hundreds of New Zealand families affected by fetal alcohol spectrum disorder will benefit from a new focus on prevention and treatment. FASD is a condition which has been under-recognised and under-supported for too long. This announcement changes that.
specificity.explanation: Gives a place and a date for the announcement and a rough scale ('hundreds of families'), but no funding, mechanism or timeframe for the action itself.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Five new initiatives are being introduced as part of this work. These include publishing new FASD clinical diagnostic guidelines and offering training to health professionals on how to use these new guidelines, with an aim to have 30 trained by the end of the year.
specificity.explanation: Counts the initiatives, names a concrete deliverable (clinical diagnostic guidelines plus training) and attaches a number and a deadline (30 trained by year end).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yes. I’d like to see a system where every child and young person that is brought to the attention of Oranga Tamariki is assessed and has the help based on their needs, not on everyone else’s needs. Oranga Tamariki has grown, it has become too broad in its focus, and we need to get back to its core purpose, which is the care and protection of children and young people. I want to see a system where children and young people come first.
specificity.explanation: A statement of direction — narrower focus, needs-based assessment — with no mechanism, no measure of what falls outside the 'core purpose', and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I have been advised that there is no proposal to disestablish the international child protection and intercountry and domestic adoption services teams. What is proposed is to bring both teams together under one manager for adoptions and international case work, and it’s my expectation that the best interests of the children and young people will be at the forefront of any final decision in the future structure. This work will continue.
specificity.explanation: Describes the actual proposed structural change (two named teams brought under one manager for adoptions and international case work), though it gives no timing or staffing numbers.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It is normal to review contracts in an annual process, and I expect that these reviews will prioritise the outcomes for children. Some of these decisions are still Budget-sensitive, and we will find out more when the Budget is announced.
specificity.explanation: Points to a real process and a real decision point (the Budget) but supplies no funding figures, no list of affected contracts and no date.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: New data from Stats New Zealand, released in April, shows that it takes around 569 days on average for a home to be built after it receives a building consent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a Stats NZ release in April gives an average of about 569 days from building consent issue to completion of a home.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ building activity / consent-to-code-compliance duration release of April 2024; true if the published average time from consent to completion for a standalone house is approximately 569 days, false if materially different or if no such figure was published.

veracity.statement: Te Pūkenga were not meeting milestones. They had student numbers declining, they had staff leaving, and they did not have a credible pathway back to being financially viable.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Pūkenga missed milestones, had falling enrolments and staff departures, and lacked a viable financial pathway as at the period referred to.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga annual report / TEC monitoring reports for 2023; true if enrolment (EFTS) declined year on year, staff numbers fell, deficits were reported and milestones in the TEC investment plan were recorded as unmet; false if enrolments and finances were stable or improving.

veracity.statement: What, if anything, is she doing to address Māori unemployment which has increased by 1.4 percent to 8.2 percent in the last quarter, at a rate that is nearly five times worse than the national average?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori unemployment rose 1.4 percentage points to 8.2 percent in the latest quarter, and that this increase was nearly five times the national increase.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey, March 2024 quarter (released 1 May 2024); true if the Māori unemployment rate is 8.2% having risen 1.4 percentage points, and the national rate rose by roughly one-fifth of that, false if the published figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: I just do want to correct: there have been no job cuts at MSD. There has been a round of voluntary redundancies, which are under way and the responsibility of the chief executive.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at 2 May 2024 the Ministry of Social Development had made no job cuts, only a voluntary redundancy round run by the chief executive.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD公 change proposals and public statements up to 2 May 2024; true if only a voluntary redundancy round had been initiated with no compulsory role disestablishments proposed or announced, false if a proposal to disestablish roles at MSD had been announced by that date.

veracity.statement: Unlike the other side, this Government will not see the number of Māori on the jobseeker benefit explode by 57 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the number of Māori jobseeker beneficiaries rose 57 percent under the previous Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets, Māori jobseeker support recipients, comparing the count at the start and end of the 2017–2023 Labour-led government; true if the increase is approximately 57 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: In addition to that, it has been made known to me that the Australian pension fund will invest $75 million in the Snowy River gold mining project near Reefton—jobs and wealth coming to Te Tai Poutini.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $75 million investment commitment by an Australian pension fund into the Snowy River gold project near Reefton.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Company/investor announcements and West Coast news reporting from April–May 2024; true if an Australian pension fund committed approximately NZ$75m to the Reefton (Snowy River) gold project, false if no such commitment or a materially different sum.

veracity.statement: In addition to that, Santana Minerals has raised $31 million for a project in the Otago region, and TiGa Minerals and Metals has been given the go-ahead by an independent commissioner for their proposed mine at Barrytown Flats on the West Coast.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: a $31m capital raise by Santana Minerals for an Otago project, and consent granted by an independent commissioner to TiGa Minerals and Metals for a mine at Barrytown Flats.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: ASX/NZX announcements by Santana Minerals in early 2024 and the West Coast Regional Council / Grey District commissioner decision on the TiGa Barrytown mineral sands application; true if both the raise (~$31m) and the consent grant are on the record by May 2024, false if either did not occur or differs materially.

specificity.statement: New data from Stats New Zealand, released in April, shows that it takes around 569 days on average for a home to be built after it receives a building consent.
specificity.explanation: Names the source, the month of release, and a precise figure — directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the last couple of months alone, we have advised the removal of artificial barriers to the use of overseas building products, brought forward a review of the earthquake-prone buildings regime and extending remediation deadlines while the review is under way, exempted small building projects under $65,000 value from paying the building levy, required councils to submit time frames for building consent applications, and, finally, raised the height thresholds for dam safety regulations from 1 to 4 metres.
specificity.explanation: Five named measures with dollar and metre thresholds; each is individually checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I have sent a new letter of expectation in December 2023, setting out my desire that Te Pūkenga cease its centralisation programme of work and focus on achieving greater regional decision making.
specificity.explanation: A named instrument, a date, and the substantive direction it conveyed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is one of the meetings she referred to in response to oral question No. 8 on 19 December 2023—the meeting that an attendee described to Newshub as “a total s٭٭tshow”?
specificity.explanation: Pins the question to an identified meeting, a date, an attributed source and a quoted characterisation — precisely checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: At the meeting referred to in response to oral question No. 8 on 19 December 2023, with the CEO and the chair of Te Pūkenga, did she direct the then CEO of Te Pūkenga to cease the restructuring of vocational education?
specificity.explanation: Names the meeting, the date, the participants and the precise instruction alleged.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What, if anything, is she doing to address Māori unemployment which has increased by 1.4 percent to 8.2 percent in the last quarter, at a rate that is nearly five times worse than the national average?
specificity.explanation: Two precise rates, the change, the period and a stated comparison to the national figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It is of course concerning to see the continued increases in Māori unemployment, and the Government’s plan to reduce the number of people on the jobseeker benefit will, of course, proportionately, or disproportionately in a positive way, impact on Māori.
specificity.explanation: Refers to a 'plan' with no named measure, target, figure or timeframe; the substantive content is a direction of hoped-for effect only.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In addition to that, it has been made known to me that the Australian pension fund will invest $75 million in the Snowy River gold mining project near Reefton—jobs and wealth coming to Te Tai Poutini.
specificity.explanation: Named investor type, named project, named location and a dollar figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, unclear regulations add unnecessary delays to building. For example, Kiwis who need to swap out comparable building products in the event of a shortage will often have to submit a completely new building consent application or wait for that specific product to become available.
rigor.explanation: The general claim (unclear regulation causes delay) is supported by a concrete mechanism — product substitution triggering a fresh consent — so the conclusion tracks the example given. It rests on a single illustrative case rather than data, hence not top marks.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Coal mining is a legitimate part of the economy, and if we do not recover our gas reserves in New Zealand, we’ll be powering our energy system with coal.
rigor.explanation: A substitution argument — less domestic gas means more coal in the generation mix — which is a real inference about a real policy, but offered bare, with nothing on demand, renewables build or import options to connect the premise to the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Certainly it has left a legacy in the vocational education sector that is a disaster, with student numbers falling, financials getting worse, staff leaving, and generally industry feeling that they are not being supported in supplying a workforce.
civility.explanation: Extremely harsh about an institution and a policy model, but attacks no individual — this is the standard the re-anchored scale expects.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I can assure the member that I have very many clues about what we need to do to get rid of the disaster that is Te Pūkenga.
civility.explanation: A pointed comeback that stays on the institution rather than on the questioner personally.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is it the case that she simply doesn’t have a clue what she is going to do in the vocational education sector?
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the Minister's personal competence rather than on the policy or its absence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does she agree that Te Pūkenga model set up by the previous Government is in fact an “s٭٭t show”?
civility.explanation: Vulgar and sneering, but aimed at a policy model and a previous government, not at any individual.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Recently, our Government corrected an egregious oversight left behind by a former Minister that relates to Resource Management Act changes and streamlining the treatment of coal mining, so it is not treated as a leper.
civility.explanation: Attributes an 'egregious oversight' to a former Minister personally rather than criticising the drafting or the policy on its merits; imputes carelessness to an individual, though unnamed.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Certainly it has left a legacy in the vocational education sector that is a disaster, with student numbers falling, financials getting worse, staff leaving, and generally industry feeling that they are not being supported in supplying a workforce.
focus.explanation: Names a specific reform and four specific outcomes (enrolments, finances, staffing, industry support) rather than simply characterising the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I can assure the member that I have very many clues about what we need to do to get rid of the disaster that is Te Pūkenga.
focus.explanation: A riposte that turns the questioner's wording back on her; beyond naming Te Pūkenga it carries no policy content — no mechanism, timeframe or measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: At the meeting referred to in response to oral question No. 8 on 19 December 2023, with the CEO and the chair of Te Pūkenga, did she direct the then CEO of Te Pūkenga to cease the restructuring of vocational education?
focus.explanation: Squarely on a specific ministerial action affecting a named reform programme; textbook scrutiny.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does she agree that Te Pūkenga model set up by the previous Government is in fact an “s٭٭t show”?
focus.explanation: Names a policy model, but the weight of the question is a crude characterisation aimed at the previous Government rather than any mechanism, cost or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is it her view that Te Pūkenga has lived up to the wild aspirations that were held for it as a transformative initiative, or is it more likely that it has missed all of its key milestones and is another episode of centralisation that has failed?
focus.explanation: Refers to a named policy and to milestone performance, but is framed as a loaded either/or about the other side's record rather than an examination of the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I note that some of them are Associate Ministers who seem to be leading resource management reforms, and she may want to comment on that—the first round of resource management reforms, amendments to the Act that are all regulations, and that the press release that came out last week did not have her name on it.
civility.explanation: Pointed — it implies the Minister has been sidelined from her own portfolio — but it stops at the allocation of responsibilities and the press release rather than landing on her competence or character.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There was a huge work programme at the time of this annual review period to overhaul or rewrite the Waste Minimisation Act as being out of date and not good enough for the compliance monitoring and enforcement functions, but also for product stewardship, and also the very old Litter Act.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy: names the Waste Minimisation Act, the Litter Act, and the specific functions (compliance monitoring and enforcement, product stewardship) at issue. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And the wider point on that is the Government’s been here now for over five months and surely that work could have been done via the normal regulatory process rather than needing primary legislation.
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism of the reform itself (regulation versus primary legislation) rather than the character of the governing parties.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We also will, in due course, make our own changes to the National Policy Statement for Highly Productive Land (NPS-HPL), because it is not enabling enough of development capacity and infrastructure, in particular.
focus.explanation: Names the specific instrument to be changed and the specific ground for changing it — development capacity and infrastructure. Entirely policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There was a huge work programme at the time of this annual review period to overhaul or rewrite the Waste Minimisation Act as being out of date and not good enough for the compliance monitoring and enforcement functions, but also for product stewardship, and also the very old Litter Act.
specificity.explanation: Names the statutes and the functional areas, and cites the transcript page elsewhere, but gives no figures, timeframes or a description of what the work programme actually contained.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I was very pleased, I think in February of this year, to be able to announce the $6.6 million of investment to the local authorities to address those sites in Tai Rāwhiti, in Nelson, in South Canterbury, and also in Southland.
specificity.explanation: Carries a dollar figure, an approximate date, the class of recipient and four named regions — someone could go and check or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And the wider point on that is the Government’s been here now for over five months and surely that work could have been done via the normal regulatory process rather than needing primary legislation.
rigor.explanation: The inference — that elapsed time shows the changes could have gone through regulation instead of statute — rests on 'surely' rather than on any account of which changes require primary legislation. A real gap between what is shown (five months) and what is concluded (regulation would have sufficed).
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There is a process where written comments will be sought from the Minister for the Environment, where they are the relevant portfolio Minister, and I am confident that the environmental considerations across many stages will be considered by approving Ministers—in addition to the environmental protection that will be given through the expert panel stage of any fast-track consenting.
rigor.explanation: An inference from the existence of a consultation step to the substantive conclusion that environmental considerations will in fact be weighed; the load is carried by the speaker's own confidence rather than by anything about how the Ministers' group must treat those comments.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We also will, in due course, make our own changes to the National Policy Statement for Highly Productive Land (NPS-HPL), because it is not enabling enough of development capacity and infrastructure, in particular.

rigor.statement: Take, for example, Maramarua School, which has seen incredible results for their Māori students with structured literacy. In 2021, only 37 percent of their students were at or above curriculum level for reading. By the end of 2023, as a result of adopting structured literacy, it was 68 percent. That is evidence-based results for children who need it most.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single school and attributes the entire improvement to structured literacy ('as a result of'), with no comparison group or control for other changes: appeal to anecdote plus post hoc reasoning, then labelled 'evidence-based'.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: On behalf of the Minister, I can't comment specifically about that programme, but what I would say is the single best thing we can do for underachieving Māori and Pasifika students in our school system is develop a knowledge-rich curriculum and go back to the basics and end the 30-year experiment on our children that has involved experiential learning, play-based learning, and other such activity that has failed a generation of children when it comes to literacy.
rigor.explanation: Concludes that a knowledge-rich curriculum is 'the single best thing we can do' from an unsupported causal premise that experiential and play-based learning caused a generation's literacy failure; no evidence links the pedagogy to the outcome, and no alternative cause is considered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If there was a connection between student achievement and the number of bureaucrats in the Ministry of Education, we would have seen better results over the last six years. In fact, we hired hundreds of extra staff at the ministry, including in the specific areas the member talks about, and children's results went backwards.
rigor.explanation: A real inference — staffing rose while results fell, therefore staffing is not the driver — but it treats a single uncontrolled correlation as decisive and assumes any connection would have to show up as an aggregate improvement over six years.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is a Minister who gets out and about and does the job and is committed to lifting educational achievement because the single best thing we can do for Pasifika children in this country is have aspiration for them rather than have a poverty of ambition and decide that because they are Pasifika, they are condemned to failure.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy built on a strawman: the question was about resourcing to understand Pacific learners' needs, and the answer poses a choice between 'aspiration' and believing Pasifika children are 'condemned to failure' — a position nobody advanced.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The bill follows a series of different reviews, including by the Law Commission in 1998—1998; I just want to reflect on that—to improve insurance law in New Zealand and will bring our law into line with international best practice.

veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Law Commission publication record: true if the Commission published a report or study paper reviewing insurance contract law in 1998; false if no such 1998 Law Commission insurance work exists.

veracity.statement: It brings together five separate pieces of insurance legislation into one—some of it over 100 years old.

rigor.statement: Let me give you a real-life example: a wife tried to make a life insurance claim when her husband was killed by a truck driver. rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is important because increased risk means increased insurance costs and premiums. This ultimately hurts Kiwi households, and in a cost of living crisis, the Government is acutely aware of the need to keep insurance premiums to a minimum.
rigor.explanation: The risk-to-premium-to-household-cost chain is coherent, but the step that matters — that this bill's certainty provisions actually lower insurers' risk enough to restrain premiums — is asserted rather than shown, leaving a gap between the evidence offered and the conclusion drawn.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For example, if an insurer would have charged higher premiums if the consumer had disclosed the truth, the bill provides that the insurer can reduce what it pays the consumer for the consumer’s claim.

veracity.statement: Currently, insurance contracts are governed by the number of pieces of legislation and case law, and, as already mentioned, some of them are as old as 100 years.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZ statute book and the Contracts of Insurance Bill's explanatory note / regulatory impact statement: true if insurance contract law is governed by several separate Acts and at least one of them dates from around 1924 or earlier (e.g. the Marine Insurance Act 1908 or Life Insurance Act 1908); false if the law sits in a single modern statute or the oldest relevant Act is materially more recent.

rigor.statement: So amending the law pertaining to disclosure will simplify the insurance process and remove the scope for miscommunication, which can disadvantage many people in the sector.

rigor.statement: And let’s face it, if they don’t protect that and they pay out money unnecessarily, that will be reflected in other people’s premiums further down the track.

veracity.statement: I think, in this case, what we’ll also mention is—and particularly us from Tāmaki-makau-rau Auckland will already know that people are still working through their insurance policies and have still not yet fully received the claims of the insurances as a result of the extreme weather that we saw at the beginning of last year, which is, I would say, more than a year ago and definitely more than 14 months ago, still working through those policy claims and insurance claims as a result of those extreme weather patterns caused by the acceleration of climate change.

veracity.statement: So looking at the various legislation that this bill is going to bring the insurance components from, it is the Life Insurance Act 1908—yep, 1908; very old legislation—the Law Reform Act 1936, the Insurance Law Reform Act 1977 and 1985, and the Insurance Intermediaries Act 1994.

focus.statement: I’m surprised you didn’t mention the fact that this bill was worked on by me, and, before me, by David Clark, and before that by Kris Faafoi.
