veracity.explanation: Asserts that Budget 2024 allocates $67 million to support the structured literacy rollout, covering both English and te reo Māori medium.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Education appropriation documents and the associated Ministry of Education press release; true if a structured-literacy allocation of approximately $67m appears, false if the figure or purpose is materially different.

veracity.statement: Just yesterday, the OECD Economic Survey of New Zealand 2024 made recommendations for a clearer curriculum—something I’m pleased to say this Government is already actioning.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the OECD Economic Survey of New Zealand 2024, released the previous day, recommended a clearer curriculum.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The OECD Economic Survey of New Zealand 2024 text and its publication date; true if the survey was published on or about 6 May 2024 and contains a recommendation for a clearer/more specific curriculum, false if no such recommendation appears.

veracity.statement: Recent data shows that just 56 percent of year 8 students are at the expected level for reading, and 35 percent for writing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific national achievement figures for year 8 reading (56%) and writing (35%) against curriculum expectation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NMSSA (National Monitoring Study of Student Achievement) year 8 English results for the most recent cycle; true if the at-or-above-curriculum proportions are approximately 56% reading and 35% writing, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: What I’d just say to that member is there are 450 beds in that prison at Waikeria today, there are 600 that will come on-stream next year, and there are a further 810 beds to be added under the announcement from yesterday that will lead to over 1,800 beds at Waikeria Prison.
veracity.explanation: Asserts current capacity of 450 beds at Waikeria, 600 more coming on-stream next year, and 810 announced, totalling over 1,800.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections capacity figures for Waikeria Prison and the Government's May 2024 prison capacity announcement; true if the 450/600/810 figures and the ~1,800 total match, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, under the previous administration, the only goal on law and order was a reduction in the prison population.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Labour-led government's sole law and order objective was reducing the prison population.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The previous government's stated justice-sector targets and strategies (e.g. Hāpaitia te Oranga Tangata, the 30% prison population reduction target, Budget justice-sector priorities); true if prison population reduction was the only stated goal, false if other law and order goals (e.g. reducing violent crime or reoffending) were also stated.

veracity.statement: Māori are sadly overrepresented in the prison population, but they’re also overrepresented as victims of crime too.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Māori are overrepresented both among prisoners and among victims of crime, relative to population share.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections prison population ethnicity statistics and the NZ Crime and Victims Survey victimisation rates by ethnicity; true if the Māori share in both exceeds the Māori share of the general population, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: Are the number of victimisations from incidents involving a stabbing or cutting weapon in the Waitematā Police District up by 25 percent since he took office?
veracity.explanation: Asserts, in question form, that victimisations involving a stabbing or cutting weapon in the Waitematā Police District rose 25 percent since the Minister took office in late 2023.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police victimisation time-series data for Waitematā District, offences involving a stabbing or cutting weapon, comparing the period since November 2023 with the equivalent prior period; true if the increase is approximately 25%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: In terms of the Auckland CBD, we have increased by over 50 percent the amount of beat patrols and foot patrols now.
veracity.explanation: Asserts beat and foot patrols in the Auckland CBD have increased by more than 50 percent under this Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police reporting on beat/foot patrol hours or deployments in the Auckland City CBD before and after the change of government; true if the increase exceeds 50%, false if materially lower.

rigor.statement: I’ve received strong support—overwhelmingly strong support—from the sector.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the sector overwhelmingly supports the policy is supported only by a handful of selected favourable messages — an appeal to anecdote, with no sampling or sector-wide evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’re now seeing in Australia an increased use of knife crime, and this is probably going to arrive on our shores too, and this Government’s going to get ahead of the problem and make sure that we actually deal with it.
rigor.explanation: Infers a coming New Zealand knife-crime wave purely from trends in two other countries — a weak analogy with nothing offered to connect the overseas trend to domestic conditions.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yes, I do agree with the Prime Minister because just about every day he’s committed to making sure that we’ve got a safer country and that we’re moving in the right direction.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the question was whether it is for the chief executive or Commissioner to determine who counts as front line, and the reason given (the PM's daily commitment to safety) has no bearing on that proposition.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What qualifies a fast-track project as having significant regional or national benefits, and how are these economic benefits weighted against environmental costs?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the fast-track legislation — the qualifying threshold and how competing considerations are weighted. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that, regrettably, Māori are more often victims of crime and, unlike this line of questioning he’s just been addressing, our coalition Government is focused on the Māori victims of crime before we worry about the welfare of criminals, and, actually, that goes to people of all ethnic backgrounds?
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point (victimisation of Māori, prioritisation within justice policy), but it is wrapped in a framing that characterises the opposing questioner's motives rather than engaging the overcrowding question actually asked.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Absolutely we stand by that statement, because we’ve come off the back of six years of a soft-on-crime Government and we’re having to fix and repair the enormous amount of damage that they did.
focus.explanation: Answers a question about a specific victimisation statistic entirely with a characterisation of the previous government; no policy, measure or figure is named.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that, regrettably, Māori are more often victims of crime and, unlike this line of questioning he’s just been addressing, our coalition Government is focused on the Māori victims of crime before we worry about the welfare of criminals, and, actually, that goes to people of all ethnic backgrounds?
civility.explanation: Imputes to the questioner a concern for 'the welfare of criminals' over victims — a bad-faith characterisation aimed at the member asking, though stopping short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We’re now seeing in Australia an increased use of knife crime, and this is probably going to arrive on our shores too, and this Government’s going to get ahead of the problem and make sure that we actually deal with it.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the rise in knife crime observed in the UK and Australia will also occur in New Zealand.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NZ Police victimisation statistics for offences involving a knife or other cutting weapon; true if national counts rise materially above the 2023-24 baseline by the resolve-by date, false if flat or falling.

veracity.statement: For example, the operating allowance for Budget 2023 was originally set at $2.6 billion, then was successively raised to $2.7 billion, $4 billion, and, finally, $4.5 billion. The actual new spending in Budget 2023 was $4.8 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific sequence of operating allowance settings for Budget 2023 and the final new spending figure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Budget Policy Statements, Budget Economic and Fiscal Updates and Budget 2023 documents; true if the operating allowance was set at $2.6b and successively revised to $2.7b, $4b and $4.5b with $4.8b of actual new operating spending, false if the published series differs materially.

veracity.statement: Yes, and especially last week’s announcement that beginning in term 1, 2025, all State schools will be teaching reading using the proven structured literacy approach. Currently, only 56 percent of our year 8 students are at the expected level for reading and writing, and that is unacceptable—all part of our plan to improve educational outcomes so young Kiwis gain the skills that they need to succeed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that only 56 percent of year 8 students are at the expected level for reading and writing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NMSSA / Curriculum Insights and Progress Study achievement data for year 8 reading and writing current at May 2024; true if the proportion at or above the expected curriculum level is about 56 percent, false if the published proportion differs materially or applies to a different year level or subject.

veracity.statement: Does he agree with submitters such as the New Zealand Planning Institute, which said the current fast-track legislation “risks overloading the system and slowing it down, contrary to the intent of creating a fast process.”?
veracity.explanation: Relays a quotation attributed to the New Zealand Planning Institute's submission on the fast-track bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZ Planning Institute's written submission to the Environment Committee on the Fast-track Approvals Bill; true if it contains this wording or substantively this claim, false if absent or materially misquoted.

veracity.statement: Is he concerned that seven out of eight regional councils who submitted on the bill oppose it in its current form?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that of the eight regional councils that made submissions on the Fast-track Approvals Bill, seven opposed the bill in its current form.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Environment Committee's published submissions on the Fast-track Approvals Bill; true if exactly eight regional councils submitted and seven of them opposed the bill as drafted, false if the counts differ materially.

veracity.statement: Will the Prime Minister allow public scrutiny of the list of projects intended for fast tracking at select committee, given the multitude of concerns raised about environmental protections, lack of transparency, executive oversight, free-trade agreements, and the 27,000 submissions on the bill?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Fast-track Approvals Bill attracted 27,000 submissions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Environment Committee's submission count for the Fast-track Approvals Bill as at May 2024; true if approximately 27,000 submissions were received, false if the official count is materially different.

veracity.statement: On Sunday, I joined Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown to announce that the Government has delivered on our election promise to provide a financially sustainable water services model for Auckland under our Local Water Done Well plan. Our plan was unanimously endorsed by Auckland Council’s governing body, and Watercare’s more financially sustainable model will ensure water rates for Aucklanders remain affordable, both now and into the future.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Auckland water plan was unanimously endorsed by Auckland Council's governing body.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council governing body minutes and voting record for the relevant resolution (April–May 2024); true if the resolution passed unanimously, false if any member voted against or abstained, or if no such endorsement was made.

veracity.statement: Under the Local Water Done Well solution we announced on Sunday, Aucklanders will avoid the 25.8 percent water rate hike previously proposed by Watercare; $1.2 billion was spent over the last six years by the last Government on water reform, which took away local control and was divisive.
veracity.explanation: Two checkable claims: that Watercare had proposed a 25.8 percent water rate increase, and that $1.2 billion was spent on water reform over the last six years by the previous Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Watercare's proposed price path in Auckland Council's draft long-term plan (for the 25.8 percent figure) and Treasury/DIA reporting on Three Waters reform programme expenditure 2018–2023 (for the $1.2 billion); true if both figures match the published record, false if either is materially different.

veracity.statement: Some said that our Government’s Local Water Done Well plan would not work, but in just six months we have delivered a financially sustainable water services model for Auckland, and we spent only $300,000 on that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the cost to Government of delivering the Auckland Local Water Done Well arrangement was $300,000.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DIA/Treasury cost figures or a written parliamentary question answer on expenditure to date on the Local Water Done Well Auckland arrangement; true if the total is about $300,000, false if the published figure is materially higher or covers a different scope.

veracity.statement: Is it responsible fiscal management to continue with her tax cuts when her Budget Policy Statement shows that tax revenue will be down $13.9 billion over the forecast period, and she has confirmed she will be borrowing for everyday costs; if so, which economists support her tax cuts in the current economic climate?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister's Budget Policy Statement shows tax revenue down $13.9 billion across the forecast period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Budget Policy Statement 2024 / HYEFU 2023 revenue forecasts against the preceding forecast; true if the downward revision to tax revenue over the forecast period is about $13.9 billion, false if the documents show a materially different figure.

veracity.statement: Can the average earner expect to be $50 better off, as per the coalition agreements, or $10 to $20 per week better off, as announced by David Seymour last week in the media?
veracity.explanation: Relays two figures: a $50 benefit for the average earner said to be in the coalition agreements, and a $10–$20 per week figure attributed to David Seymour in the media the previous week.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National–ACT and National–NZ First coalition agreements (for the $50 figure) and media reporting of David Seymour's remarks in the week to 7 May 2024 (for the $10–$20 per week figure); true if both are accurately reported, false if either figure or its attribution is materially wrong.

specificity.statement: For example, the operating allowance for Budget 2023 was originally set at $2.6 billion, then was successively raised to $2.7 billion, $4 billion, and, finally, $4.5 billion. The actual new spending in Budget 2023 was $4.8 billion.
specificity.explanation: Four named figures, a named Budget and a named fiscal aggregate; entirely checkable against Budget documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yes, and especially last week’s announcement that beginning in term 1, 2025, all State schools will be teaching reading using the proven structured literacy approach. Currently, only 56 percent of our year 8 students are at the expected level for reading and writing, and that is unacceptable—all part of our plan to improve educational outcomes so young Kiwis gain the skills that they need to succeed.
specificity.explanation: Names a dated implementation (term 1, 2025), the schools covered, the named method (structured literacy) and a numeric baseline.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: No; we are going to build things in this country. We have to get things done. It does not need to take eight years to consent an onshore wind farm in this country. It can take one year. We can build it in two and we can get the climate change benefits of it. That’s why I look forward to that member’s support, as the leader of the Green Party, to support this legislation.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete timeframes (eight years now, one year to consent, two to build) for a named class of project, but no mechanism or source.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Under the Local Water Done Well solution we announced on Sunday, Aucklanders will avoid the 25.8 percent water rate hike previously proposed by Watercare; $1.2 billion was spent over the last six years by the last Government on water reform, which took away local control and was divisive.
specificity.explanation: Two named figures, a named entity and a named programme; both are checkable against council and departmental records.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I will just invite the member opposite to consider the counterfactual. So if the counterfactual was to have a $3.5 billion operating allowance and spend it, as was her party’s stated alternative, then our Budget package, including tax relief for working people, requires less borrowing.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete counterfactual operating allowance ($3.5 billion) and the comparison being drawn, but gives no figure for the borrowing difference.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We’ve not shared any details of the Budget with the OECD, but it is safe to say that after 30 May, they will find that the Budget is entirely consistent with this advice.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Budget 2024, delivered 30 May 2024, will match the OECD's advice that the deficit continue to fall as planned and that any tax cuts be fully funded by offsetting revenue or expenditure measures.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents (BEFU 2024) and subsequent OECD commentary; true if the Budget's tax package is fully funded by offsetting savings/revenue and the deficit track continues to narrow as previously planned, false if the tax package is debt-funded or the forecast deficit path deteriorates against the plan the OECD endorsed.

rigor.statement: No, the complete opposite is going to happen. We are going to speed up the building of infrastructure in this country, and I seriously hope that I get the support of the Greens for this legislation, because if you want serious delivery on our climate change goals, we need to build renewable energy projects much faster. Faster consenting—the better that is for everybody.
rigor.explanation: The Planning Institute's point was that the bill could overload and slow the system; the reply asserts the contrary outcome without engaging the mechanism, and substitutes the desirability of faster consenting for evidence that this bill delivers it — a bare assertion plus a non sequitur.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: No; we are going to build things in this country. We have to get things done. It does not need to take eight years to consent an onshore wind farm in this country. It can take one year. We can build it in two and we can get the climate change benefits of it. That’s why I look forward to that member’s support, as the leader of the Green Party, to support this legislation.
rigor.explanation: Asked about seven of eight regional councils opposing the bill, the reply does not address the objection and offers consenting timeframes as assertions with nothing connecting the bill to the one-year figure.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, this legislation, as I’ve been explaining to the member, is about accelerating towards our climate change goals and commitments. This is enabling us to build more renewable energy. That surely is a good thing. That is what I would expect that member to be supporting.
rigor.explanation: Asked about publishing the project list for scrutiny, the conclusion that the member should support the bill rests on the general desirability of renewable energy; the transparency premise is never engaged — a non sequitur.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I will just invite the member opposite to consider the counterfactual. So if the counterfactual was to have a $3.5 billion operating allowance and spend it, as was her party’s stated alternative, then our Budget package, including tax relief for working people, requires less borrowing.
rigor.explanation: A genuine comparative argument: against a stated alternative allowance, the package requires less borrowing. Valid on its own terms, but it answers a different question from the one asked (whether borrowing for everyday costs while cutting tax is responsible) by shifting the baseline.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, that’s a very long question from that member, but what I would say is that the legislation is before a select committee, and, importantly, as you’ve heard from the Minister, he’s very comfortable with taking on feedback from that process.
civility.explanation: Opens with a small dig at the questioner's manner rather than her argument, before turning to substance; pointed at the person but very mild.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I look forward to when that member explains to working people why they should be yet again denied the opportunity to keep more of their own hard-earned money.
civility.explanation: Casts the questioner personally as wanting to deny workers their own money — a sneering imputation of motive rather than engagement with her question about how the cuts are funded.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he agree with submitters such as the New Zealand Planning Institute, which said the current fast-track legislation “risks overloading the system and slowing it down, contrary to the intent of creating a fast process.”?
focus.explanation: Names the bill, a named submitter and a specific mechanism of failure; scrutiny of a measure before the House with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I look forward to when that member explains to working people why they should be yet again denied the opportunity to keep more of their own hard-earned money.
focus.explanation: No mechanism, figure or measure; the content is a characterisation of what the opposing member would have to justify.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Only 22 sleeps to go. I tell this to every worker listening to question time today: you will get precisely zero dollars of tax relief from a Labour-led Government, and from our Government you’ll be getting a lot, lot more than that.
focus.explanation: Asked for a specific number, the reply is a contrast between the two parties with no policy detail on either side — party framing rather than the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is it responsible fiscal management to continue with her tax cuts when her Budget Policy Statement shows that tax revenue will be down $13.9 billion over the forecast period, and she has confirmed she will be borrowing for everyday costs; if so, which economists support her tax cuts in the current economic climate?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny anchored to a named document, a named figure and a named policy; asks about the fiscal mechanism, not the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So as of June 2023, Kāinga Ora’s total debt was $12.3 billion, more than four times its debt level in 2018, which was $2.7 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Kāinga Ora's total debt at June 2023 was $12.3 billion and that this is more than four times the 2018 figure of $2.7 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora annual reports for FY2018 and FY2022-23 (total borrowings/debt): true if the June 2023 debt is ~$12.3bn and the 2018 figure ~$2.7bn, false if either figure is materially different or the multiple is below four.

veracity.statement: And Kāinga Ora advised that in the 2022-23 financial year, they built 2,893 new public and supported homes against a target of 3,400 homes.
veracity.explanation: Relays that Kāinga Ora delivered 2,893 new public and supported homes in 2022-23 against a target of 3,400.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora 2022-23 annual report delivery figures and its stated target: true if delivery was 2,893 against a 3,400 target, false if either number differs materially.

veracity.statement: I’m really interested to understand a bit more about complaints in the previous year, and the fact that 45 percent of those households where there have been complaints have had children, and I’m really interested to know how those children benefited from the Sustaining Tenancies Framework being in place, because obviously that is about to be removed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 45 percent of households subject to tenancy complaints in the previous year contained children.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora tenancy/antisocial-behaviour complaint data for 2022-23 (annual review evidence to the Social Services and Community Committee): true if ~45% of complaint-affected households included children, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: It’s a matter of public record that the information that came to Ministers upon this coalition Government taking office is that the latest forecast from Kāinga Ora was that over the forecast period—so, in other words, from this year onwards—Kāinga Ora was forecasting the sale of over 10,000 State houses.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that briefing material provided to incoming Ministers contained a Kāinga Ora forecast of more than 10,000 State house sales over the forecast period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Treasury/Kāinga Ora briefing to incoming Ministers (late 2023), as released or cited in the House: true if it forecasts sales exceeding 10,000 houses over the forecast period, false if the documented forecast is materially lower or absent.

veracity.statement: Kāinga Ora has on average, until now, been selling anywhere between 50 and 150 houses per year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Kāinga Ora's historical annual State house sales have run at roughly 50 to 150 per year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora annual reports / HUD disposal data on state house sales per year: true if annual sales fall within roughly 50–150 across recent years, false if they routinely exceed or fall below that band.

veracity.statement: Again, it is a matter of public record that future income-related rent—or IRRS, as we call it—subsidies for social housing places finish on 30 June 2025.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that funding for future income-related rent subsidy places is appropriated only up to 30 June 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget appropriations for Vote Housing and Urban Development / IRRS place funding: true if funding for new IRRS places is time-limited to 30 June 2025, false if appropriations extend beyond that date.

specificity.statement: So as of June 2023, Kāinga Ora’s total debt was $12.3 billion, more than four times its debt level in 2018, which was $2.7 billion.
specificity.explanation: Two dated dollar figures and a stated ratio between them; directly checkable against published accounts.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m really interested to understand a bit more about complaints in the previous year, and the fact that 45 percent of those households where there have been complaints have had children, and I’m really interested to know how those children benefited from the Sustaining Tenancies Framework being in place, because obviously that is about to be removed.
specificity.explanation: Carries a named framework and a precise percentage, though the period and the source of the 45 percent are not stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So her question was specifically about who will build new public houses in New Zealand, and the answer is, as is always the case, both the community housing sector, which does an excellent job around the country, and also Kāinga Ora, which plays a very important role in our housing system.
specificity.explanation: Names two categories of builder but supplies no volumes, funding amounts or timeframes, which is what the question about future IRRS places asked for.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Its debt is forecast to peak at $28.9 billion in 2033.
divination.explanation: Relays Kāinga Ora's forecast that its debt reaches a maximum of $28.9 billion in the 2033 year and declines thereafter.
divination.subject: other
divination.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora annual reports and Treasury forecasts through 2033: true if reported total debt peaks in 2033 at approximately $28.9bn, false if the peak occurs in a different year or at a materially different level.

focus.statement: I’m really interested to understand a bit more about complaints in the previous year, and the fact that 45 percent of those households where there have been complaints have had children, and I’m really interested to know how those children benefited from the Sustaining Tenancies Framework being in place, because obviously that is about to be removed.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy instrument (the Sustaining Tenancies Framework), a specific data point about complaints, and asks about the effect of its removal. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We make no apologies for striking a different balance, because the social licence for Kāinga Ora to operate has been eroded over the last few years by repeated and wilful bad behaviour by a small group of tenants who the public see as very—no consequences or responsibility for that behaviour.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (change the sustaining-tenancies balance) rests on an appeal to public perception and generalises from an acknowledged 'small group of tenants' to erosion of the agency's overall social licence; no evidence is offered to connect the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That is clearly something that the member finds alarming.
civility.explanation: Mildly dismissive characterisation of the questioner's reaction rather than engagement with her point, but it stops well short of any attack on her.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Yes, and especially our announcement on the weekend which will save Aucklanders, including those in that member’s electorate, from a predicted rates increase of 26 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a 26 percent rates increase for Auckland had been predicted, and that the Government's water announcement averts it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council / Watercare 2024 long-term plan consultation documents and Watercare price-path forecasts; true if a rates or water-charge increase of about 26 percent was forecast for Auckland absent the Government's water reform, false if the published forecast figure is materially different or no such forecast exists.

veracity.statement: The previous Government’s divisive, ineffective approach wasted $1.2 billion and achieved absolutely nothing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government spent $1.2 billion on the Three Waters programme and that it produced no result at all.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Internal Affairs and Treasury reporting on total appropriated and actual spend on the Three Waters / Affordable Water Reforms programme to December 2023; true if total spend is about $1.2 billion and no delivered assets or services can be identified, false if the spend figure is materially different or documented outputs (entity establishment, transition work, funding transferred to councils) exist.

veracity.statement: Look, what I agree with is that low and middle income working New Zealanders—the very people that the Labour Party and the Green Party used to profess they cared about—actually deserve tax relief. It’s been 14 long years; there’s been a 40 percent growth in inflation. They’re going to get it at this Budget.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that inflation has grown 40 percent over the 14 years since tax thresholds were last adjusted.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index; true if cumulative CPI growth from 2010 to Q1 2024 is approximately 40 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Does he agree with the OECD’s findings, some of which his Minister of Finance was just referring to, that, I quote, “New Zealand’s tax settings remain an outlier internationally.”, and that shares, land, and owner-occupied residential property are tax favoured?
veracity.explanation: Relays, as a direct quotation, findings attributed to the OECD about New Zealand's tax settings being an international outlier and shares, land and owner-occupied housing being tax favoured.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The OECD Economic Survey of New Zealand published in 2024; true if it contains the quoted wording and the finding that shares, land and owner-occupied residential property are tax favoured, false if the wording or findings are not in the document.

veracity.statement: This announcement will take Waikeria’s total capacity when complete to 1,865 prisoners, making it New Zealand’s largest prison.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a completed capacity figure of 1,865 for Waikeria and that this would make it the largest prison in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections published prison capacity/bed numbers for Waikeria and for other facilities (e.g. Auckland South, Rimutaka, Mount Eden); true if Waikeria's stated completed capacity is about 1,865 and exceeds every other facility, false if the figure or the ranking is wrong.

veracity.statement: One of my priorities as the incoming Minister was around corrections officer safety, because we’ve seen an alarming rise, under the previous Government, of assaults on our corrections officers. The good news is that assaults on corrections officers are starting to reduce.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that assaults on corrections officers rose under the previous Government, and that they have begun to fall since.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections annual reports and prisoner-on-staff assault statistics; true if recorded assaults on staff rose over 2017–2023 and the most recent reported period shows a decline, false if the trend series does not show a rise, or shows no decline in the latest period.

specificity.statement: What I would say is what they got right is that we need to invest more in education; we need to invest more in competition and deregulation; and we need to make sure that we’re investing in science, technology, innovation, and international trade and investment.
specificity.explanation: A list of broad investment areas with no figures, mechanisms, programmes or timeframes; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Alongside the Prime Minister, I announced $1.9 billion of investment in Corrections to meet their workforce requirements for a growing prison population as well as capital investment to build a new 810-bed facility at Waikeria Prison.
specificity.explanation: Names a dollar figure, the purposes of the spend, the bed count and the named site — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, we’ve said that the first 500 will be delivered in the middle of next year. Then, the additional 810 will be delivered towards the end of 2028.
specificity.explanation: Gives both bed counts and delivery dates for each tranche; a precise answer to a 'when' question, though without cost detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Look, what I agree with is that low and middle income working New Zealanders—the very people that the Labour Party and the Green Party used to profess they cared about—actually deserve tax relief. It’s been 14 long years; there’s been a 40 percent growth in inflation. They’re going to get it at this Budget.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point (tax relief for low and middle income earners at the coming Budget), but a substantial part of the weight is party framing about what Labour and the Greens 'used to profess'.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can the Minister confirm that the fiscal approach of the previous Government when it came to corrections funding was to believe that all the money came from Treasure Island?
focus.explanation: A patsy jibe about the other party's general character as fiscal managers; it gestures at corrections funding but names no figure, mechanism or decision, so there is nothing to engage with.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Are the additional 810 new prison beds part of this Government’s approach to Māori housing?
focus.explanation: Names the specific measure (the 810 beds) and juxtaposes it with a named policy area, but the framing is rhetorical rather than an engagement with cost, mechanism or effect.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does the Prime Minister agree that our tax settings incentivise property speculation and disincentivise productivity, or does he disagree with the Treasury, the IMF, the OECD, and pretty much every credible economist in the country?
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy layered on an appeal to authority: the question offers only agreement with her characterisation or disagreement with a list of institutions, and the weight of the argument rests on who holds the view rather than on the mechanism by which the settings would incentivise speculation.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does the Prime Minister agree that our tax settings incentivise property speculation and disincentivise productivity, or does he disagree with the Treasury, the IMF, the OECD, and pretty much every credible economist in the country?
civility.explanation: Pointed and designed to corner the Prime Minister, but the challenge is to his policy position and to the evidence, not to him personally.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, if you give me a second, I will answer it. You seem very excited and keen to hear the answer; why don’t you just let me say it?
civility.explanation: Turns from the substance to mock the questioner's manner — condescension aimed at the person rather than the argument, though short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Well, this Government has clearly said that we’re putting public safety at the heart of what we’re doing. That means that we anticipate that there probably will be an increase in numbers coming into our corrections system, and that’s why we made this announcement around capacity.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the number of people entering the corrections system will rise as a consequence of the Government's public safety settings.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections quarterly prison population (muster) statistics; true if the total prison muster is higher in mid-2025 than at May 2024, false if it is flat or lower.

specificity.statement: Lastly, can I ask what is the total number of homes approved and contracted for delivery in Te Tai Tokerau, Tāmaki-makau-rau, Waikato, Tainui, Ikaroa-Rāwhiti, Te Tai Hauāuru, and Te Wai Pounamu in the last 12 months?
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable question: a named programme's delivery, a named set of electorates/regions, and a defined 12-month window. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m interested to hear the Minister’s comments that when they came to office, they were presented with Treasury advice—this is consistent with the statement that he made on 18 February on Facebook and that the Prime Minister made in the state of the nation speech. I ask how he can rectify that, when considering response to written question 7084, that the advice in question was actually commissioned by the Minister of Finance later in December.
specificity.explanation: Names a dated Facebook statement (18 February), a specific written question number, and a specific commissioning body and month — all checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m not sure what’s inconsistent about that. The Minister of Finance and I are both responsible Ministers for Kāinga Ora. I’d have to go back and check the exact specifics. It was either a joint memo or piece of advice to the two of us, or it was a piece of advice to the Minister forwarded to me.
specificity.explanation: Gives a relevant fact (joint ministerial responsibility) but offers only alternatives about the document's provenance and defers on specifics — no dates, titles or content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In some locations, over 70 percent of those residents of emergency housing arrangements are Māori, such as in Rotorua and near to Hamilton.
specificity.explanation: A figure, a threshold and two named locations — checkable against published emergency housing data.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So there is a definite intent to look at how we can encourage and work more closely with those operating within the Whai Kāinga Whai Oranga strategy to ensure greater efficiency and expeditious delivery of housing.
specificity.explanation: An intent to 'look at how we can encourage' greater efficiency: no mechanism, no funding figure, no timeframe, in answer to a question about whether the programme's support continues.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I can reflect that that mahi has actually resulted in some really good outcomes for people living in homes that have had a few challenges, getting them back up to scratch and up to speed, and I can come back with specifics on numbers for both that and the question around Te Pouahi up in Te Taitokerau, which is one of the iwi housing prototypes, which has just got started, and it started a little bit later than the other three housing prototypes.
specificity.explanation: Responds to a question asking how many whānau had homes repaired with qualitative description and an undertaking to supply numbers later; the only concrete content is naming the Te Pouahi prototype and its relative start.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, 2018: only 31 percent of Māori were in a position of home ownership compared to 57.9 percent of Pākehā countrywide.
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures with a year and a national scope, offered as the basis for the question that follows.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Housing First, in their last quarterly findings, reported that of all people who access their services, 59 percent were Māori, based on the primary applicant from the participating household.
specificity.explanation: Names the source, the reporting period, the figure and the measurement basis (primary applicant per household).
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Lastly, can I ask what is the total number of homes approved and contracted for delivery in Te Tai Tokerau, Tāmaki-makau-rau, Waikato, Tainui, Ikaroa-Rāwhiti, Te Tai Hauāuru, and Te Wai Pounamu in the last 12 months?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the delivery record of a named housing programme; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m interested to hear the Minister’s comments that when they came to office, they were presented with Treasury advice—this is consistent with the statement that he made on 18 February on Facebook and that the Prime Minister made in the state of the nation speech. I ask how he can rectify that, when considering response to written question 7084, that the advice in question was actually commissioned by the Minister of Finance later in December.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny of a named ministerial claim and a named document; no tribal framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Proposed changes to the Residential Tenancies Act encourage landlords, mostly Pākehā, back into the rental property market. What assurance can the Minister provide for Māori who are, perversely, tenants on their own whenua, that the Government will protect their rights against the greed of landlords?
focus.explanation: Engages a named measure before the House — the proposed Residential Tenancies Act changes — and asks about a specific effect on tenants' rights.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How will the Minister ensure forced eviction of unruly tenants utilising Kāinga Ora services is not a measure used to disguise racist attacks and removal of whānau and tamariki from their kāinga?
focus.explanation: Directed at a specific named policy — eviction of disruptive tenants from Kāinga Ora housing — rather than at the other party in general.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I’m interested to hear the Minister’s comments that when they came to office, they were presented with Treasury advice—this is consistent with the statement that he made on 18 February on Facebook and that the Prime Minister made in the state of the nation speech. I ask how he can rectify that, when considering response to written question 7084, that the advice in question was actually commissioned by the Minister of Finance later in December.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Treasury advice the Minister said he was presented with on coming to office was in fact commissioned by the Minister of Finance later in December, citing the answer to written question 7084.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published answer to parliamentary written question 7084 (2024) and the Treasury advice's commissioning date: true if that record shows the advice was commissioned by the Minister of Finance in December 2023; false if it shows the advice pre-dated or was presented at the change of government.

veracity.statement: We took office on 27 November, so three or four weeks later is, I would argue, “upon coming to office”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the current Government took office on 27 November (2023).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Executive Council/Governor-General swearing-in record for the Sixth National-led Government: true if ministers were sworn in on 27 November 2023, false if on a materially different date.

veracity.statement: It is a matter of fact and now public record that at the end of last year, Kāinga Ora was forecasting a significant surge in State house sales over the forecast period.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Kāinga Ora's own forecasts, as at late 2023, projected a large increase in State house sales over the forecast period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora's internal financial forecasts / the Treasury advice referred to (including the 10,200 figure) as released publicly: true if those documents show a materially increased projection of State house sales over the forecast period as at late 2023, false if they do not.

veracity.statement: But I would venture to suggest that the member goes and talks to his colleagues who’ve been previous Ministers of Housing. They would not have found a situation at any time in the last 6.5 years in which Kāinga Ora was forecasting such a significant upsurge in State house sales.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that at no point in the previous 6.5 years did Kāinga Ora (or its predecessor Housing New Zealand) forecast a comparable surge in State house sales.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora / Housing New Zealand forecast and annual report documents for 2017-2023: true if none project a comparable scale of State house sales, false if any such forecast exists in that period.

veracity.statement: In some locations, over 70 percent of those residents of emergency housing arrangements are Māori, such as in Rotorua and near to Hamilton.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori make up over 70 percent of emergency housing residents in some locations, naming Rotorua and the Hamilton area.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD emergency housing special needs grant / motel placement data by ethnicity and region around 2023-24: true if Māori exceed 70% of emergency housing residents in Rotorua or the Waikato/Hamilton area, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: So, 2018: only 31 percent of Māori were in a position of home ownership compared to 57.9 percent of Pākehā countrywide.
veracity.explanation: Asserts 2018 home ownership rates of 31 percent for Māori and 57.9 percent for Pākehā/European nationally.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2018 Census home ownership rates by ethnicity: true if the Māori and European/Pākehā figures are approximately 31% and 57.9%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Māori report higher moving rates between homes, at 8.7 percent compared to 5 percent for Pākehā.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a residential mobility rate of 8.7 percent for Māori against 5 percent for Pākehā, sourced to a 2021 report on Māori housing and wellbeing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2021 Māori housing and wellbeing report referred to (and Stats NZ residential mobility data by ethnicity): true if it reports rates of approximately 8.7% for Māori and 5% for Pākehā, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Housing First, in their last quarterly findings, reported that of all people who access their services, 59 percent were Māori, based on the primary applicant from the participating household.
veracity.explanation: Relays a Housing First quarterly figure that 59 percent of primary applicants accessing its services were Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The most recent Housing First quarterly reporting available in early 2024: true if it records approximately 59% of primary applicants as Māori, false if materially different.

rigor.statement: We took office on 27 November, so three or four weeks later is, I would argue, “upon coming to office”.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: from the swearing-in date he concludes that advice three or four weeks later falls within 'upon coming to office'. The conclusion follows, though the boundary of the phrase is asserted rather than argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Proposed changes to the Residential Tenancies Act encourage landlords, mostly Pākehā, back into the rental property market. What assurance can the Minister provide for Māori who are, perversely, tenants on their own whenua, that the Government will protect their rights against the greed of landlords?
civility.explanation: Robust, and imputes 'greed' to landlords as a class, but attacks no member; the criticism is directed at the policy and its effects rather than at a person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: How will the Minister ensure forced eviction of unruly tenants utilising Kāinga Ora services is not a measure used to disguise racist attacks and removal of whānau and tamariki from their kāinga?
civility.explanation: Frames the Minister's tenancy policy as a possible cover for racist attacks — an imputation of bad faith, though stopping short of a direct personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: She’s doing well when she asks sensible questions rather than talk about some of the things she was talking about in the general debate last week.
civility.explanation: Condescending praise of a named member — grading her questions as 'sensible' by contrast with her earlier contribution is directed at the member rather than at any argument she made.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In 2018, which is the latest figure we have stats for, homeownership was down to 63 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the most recent available home-ownership figure, from 2018, was 63 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2018 Census home-ownership statistics: true if the headline ownership rate cited for 2018 is approximately 63 percent (within rounding); false if the official figure is materially different (e.g. the household tenure rate of ~64.5% or the individual rate of ~51.8% would need to be reconciled with the 63% claim).

veracity.statement: The member will have seen the TradeMe data out last week that rents are at record highs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Trade Me rental data released in the week before 7 May 2024 showed rents at record highs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Trade Me Rental Price Index release of late April / early May 2024: true if it reported a record national median weekly rent; false if it reported no record or if no such release occurred in that window.

veracity.statement: As the member well knows herself, if she looks at the evidence from the Auckland Unitary Plan that was adopted in 2016, which has led to a big house-building boom in Auckland, particularly around apartments and terraced housing and other housing typologies that Auckland didn’t have enough of, there’s a wealth of evidence now available—and I refer the member to Stuart Donovan’s research and some other research by other urban economists that Auckland has experienced an increase in rents far less than other housing markets with inflexible land supply and restrictive land policy.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Auckland Unitary Plan was adopted in 2016, that it produced a construction boom concentrated in apartments and terraced housing, and that published research (including Stuart Donovan's) finds Auckland rents rose less than in comparable restrictive-supply markets.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council records for the date the Unitary Plan became operative; Stats NZ/Auckland Council consent data on dwelling typologies post-2016; and the published work of Stuart Donovan and Greenaway-McGrevy et al. on Auckland rents. True if the plan was adopted in 2016, consents shifted toward attached typologies, and that literature reports relatively lower rent growth; false if any of those is contradicted.

veracity.statement: And the second thing they almost universally agree on, with the exception of a few crank economists out there, is that rent controls are counterproductive and stupid policy, and that’s why we won’t be adopting them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that economists almost universally agree rent controls are counterproductive.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published surveys of academic economists, notably the IGM Forum/Chicago Booth panel questions on rent control: true if a large supermajority agree rent controls reduce housing quality/quantity; false if opinion is materially divided.

veracity.statement: Kāinga Ora owns 70,000 houses around the country, and it’s $45 billion company.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Kāinga Ora's portfolio size (about 70,000 homes) and balance-sheet scale (about $45 billion).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora Annual Report for the year to 30 June 2023 or 2024: true if homes owned/managed is approximately 70,000 and total assets approximately $45 billion; false if either figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: And I can confirm that no such advice was ever received by any Minister from the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no Minister in the previous (Labour) Government received advice that Kāinga Ora would sell 10,200 homes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora / HUD briefings and advice to Ministers before October 2023, obtainable via OIA or proactive release: true if no pre-election advice to Labour Ministers proposed or forecast the sale of ~10,200 homes; false if such advice is produced.

veracity.statement: We’ve seen community housing providers, like the Salvation Army, indicate that they have cancelled projects.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that community housing providers, specifically the Salvation Army, have publicly indicated they cancelled planned housing projects.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Salvation Army public statements and media reporting from late 2023 to May 2024: true if the Salvation Army stated it had cancelled or shelved planned housing developments; false if no such statement exists.

specificity.statement: The centrepiece of that is the Going for Housing Growth plan, which is about unlocking land inside our cities and at the edge of our cities and sorting the infrastructure constraints that stop that land from being developed, and also working alongside councils to develop incentives for them to grow.
specificity.explanation: Names an actual policy programme and three mechanisms (land release, infrastructure constraints, council incentives), but supplies no figures, targets or timeframes by which delivery could be checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Actually, the New Zealand housing system would fall apart without private sector landlords, because they do a lot of the heavy lifting when it comes to providing accommodation to people.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered (private landlords supply much rental accommodation), but the conclusion — the system 'would fall apart' — is far stronger than the premise supports; nothing connects a large share of supply to total collapse in their absence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I invite the member to go to Sydney and Melbourne and London and all the other countries and places that have, in some cases, quite punitive capital gains taxes, where you will find housing markets that are utterly out of control.
rigor.explanation: Cherry-picked correlation offered as refutation: naming three expensive cities that have capital gains taxes does nothing to isolate the effect of CGT, and the conclusion that tax settings 'don't affect it' does not follow from the examples.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As the member well knows herself, if she looks at the evidence from the Auckland Unitary Plan that was adopted in 2016, which has led to a big house-building boom in Auckland, particularly around apartments and terraced housing and other housing typologies that Auckland didn’t have enough of, there’s a wealth of evidence now available—and I refer the member to Stuart Donovan’s research and some other research by other urban economists that Auckland has experienced an increase in rents far less than other housing markets with inflexible land supply and restrictive land policy.
rigor.explanation: Names a specific natural experiment and cites identified empirical research to support the supply-side conclusion; the inference from upzoning to slower rent growth tracks the evidence offered, though it is presented as settled rather than contested.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And the second thing they almost universally agree on, with the exception of a few crank economists out there, is that rent controls are counterproductive and stupid policy, and that’s why we won’t be adopting them.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority: the policy conclusion rests entirely on asserted professional consensus, and dissenters are defined away as 'crank economists' rather than answered — the argument is made unfalsifiable by construction.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We have rejected the last Government’s policies when it comes to interest deductibility and restored a principled approach to tax policy which taxes profit, not revenue, and so that will be wound back and that will put downward pressure on rents.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that restoring interest deductibility for landlords will exert downward pressure on rents.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ rental price index (and Trade Me median weekly rent series): true if annual rent inflation over the 12 months to April 2026, after deductibility is fully restored, is materially lower than the 12 months to April 2024; false if annual rent growth is the same or higher.

focus.statement: The proposals often put about by the Greens—and I’m pretty sure the Māori Party has been on board this illogical train as well.
focus.explanation: No policy, figure or mechanism is named in the sentence — it characterises two opposing parties as riding an 'illogical train'. Content-free party framing rather than engagement with the rent-control question he is discussing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The annual-review appearance at select committee was useful, and it enabled us to put some context in the claim that the Prime Minister made in his state of the nation speech, the story that, presumably, they lined up before that, which indicated that there was advice sitting on their desk when they got under Government that said that Kāinga Ora was going to sell 10,200 homes, because the appearance at select committee clarified that that was contingent on this Government not providing funding post-2025—a pretty important piece of context.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny anchored in specifics: a named speech, a named figure (10,200 homes), a named forum (annual review select committee) and the precise qualification he says the evidence added.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I mean, to give one notable example, there is Porirua East, which was announced with great fanfare in 2021, or perhaps even a touch earlier than that, which has been massively downscaled, which was done very quietly in mid-2023 without many public pronouncements—I suspect because the Government wasn’t very keen on it, but that’s what happened.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Porirua East development, announced around 2021, was substantially downscaled quietly in mid-2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora / HUD announcements and board papers on the Porirua East large-scale development: true if the announced scope (dwelling numbers/programme) was materially reduced during mid-2023 without a public announcement; false if no such reduction occurred in that period or it was publicly announced.

veracity.statement: Kāinga Ora did its budget in December 2023, based on the settings not from the current Government but from the outgoing Government. So it was right on the precipice of the change in Government, and Ministers had barely been sworn in and had not taken any policy decisions whatsoever.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Kāinga Ora completed its budget in December 2023 on settings inherited from the previous Government, with no policy decisions yet taken by incoming Ministers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora board minutes/budget documents and Ministerial decisions register: true if the budget was finalised in December 2023 on funding settings set before the November 2023 change of Government and no incoming-Government policy decision had altered them; false if the budget was struck under new settings or after decisions by incoming Ministers.

veracity.statement: And it was actually very pleasing to see that some of the changes in the approaches of police towards the end of the last term of Government have actually led to a bit of a down-tick in some of those ram-raiding offences.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that ram-raid offending declined toward the end of the 2020-23 parliamentary term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police monthly retail crime / ram-raid offence counts: true if recorded ram-raid incidents fell over roughly mid-to-late 2023 relative to the 2022 peak; false if counts were flat or rising over that period.

veracity.statement: The committee covered off topics around youth offending, we looked at increases in cyber-crime, and also an interesting stat that came through during the select committee stage was that a good 25 percent of what police deal with now is family harm.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 25 percent of current police demand/workload is family harm, citing evidence given at the select committee review.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police demand statistics and the Justice Committee's 2022-23 annual review transcript: true if Police report family harm at approximately 25% of demand/call-outs; false if the published proportion is materially different (e.g. under 15% or over 40%).

veracity.statement: The key challenge that was sort of identified is that Police—with a $2.2 billion budget, $1.7 billion of which is in staff—is that they’re facing into a 6.5 percent budget cut, so that’s really looking at personnel.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a Police budget of $2.2 billion with $1.7 billion in personnel, and a 6.5 percent budget cut requirement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Vote Police estimates 2023/24 and the Government's baseline savings instructions to agencies: true if Police appropriation is approximately $2.2b with roughly $1.7b personnel and Police were required to find 6.5% savings; false if the appropriation, the personnel share or the savings percentage differ materially.

veracity.statement: Today, we established that it’s for the commissioner to determine what is front line or not, but also the Minister today said that 111 call responders were not front-line staff.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister stated earlier that day that 111 call responders are not front-line staff.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard record of oral questions for 7 May 2024: true if the Police Minister said 111 call responders are not front-line staff; false if no such statement appears or he said the opposite.

veracity.statement: Without a doubt they’re doing an outstanding job protecting and serving our communities, and they’ve done it under a fairly difficult set of circumstances, certainly in 2022-23, because we have seen a massive increase—an ongoing massive increase—in violent retail crime, we’ve seen an increase in family harm incidents, and we’ve seen an increase in mental health call-outs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts increases across three measures in 2022-23 and ongoing: violent retail crime, family harm incidents and mental health call-outs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police recorded victimisations / retail crime series, family harm investigations, and 1M/mental-health call-out counts for 2022-23: true if all three rose relative to prior years; false if any of the three was flat or declining over that period.

veracity.statement: She’s right in that under the previous Government, in the 2022-23 year, there’s been a big investment in numbers but their core funding has not increased; in fact, quite the opposite. They were asked to fund from baseline the competency service increment payment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in 2022-23 Police received investment in staff numbers while core funding did not increase, and that Police were required to fund the competency service increment payment from their existing baseline.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Vote Police estimates and supplementary estimates 2022/23 and Police annual report: true if the competency service increment was met from baseline rather than new appropriation and non-headcount core funding did not rise; false if a separate appropriation covered the CSI payment or core funding was increased.

focus.statement: I mean, to give one notable example, there is Porirua East, which was announced with great fanfare in 2021, or perhaps even a touch earlier than that, which has been massively downscaled, which was done very quietly in mid-2023 without many public pronouncements—I suspect because the Government wasn’t very keen on it, but that’s what happened.
focus.explanation: Rebuts by naming a specific housing development, its announcement date and the change to it, rather than characterising the other party in general.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Kāinga Ora did its budget in December 2023, based on the settings not from the current Government but from the outgoing Government. So it was right on the precipice of the change in Government, and Ministers had barely been sworn in and had not taken any policy decisions whatsoever.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Recorded interviews/Hansard for Willie Jackson as Minister for Māori Development; true if he is on record saying 'democracy has changed' (or that phrase in context), false if no such statement exists.

veracity.statement: Well, Moko is not elected as the mayor of the Far North on a Māori ward; he is elected as the Mayor of the Far North District Council in an open contest against every single other person who decides to put their name forward for elected office.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Far North mayor was elected in an at-large open contest rather than via a Māori ward.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Far North District Council 2022 election results and the Local Electoral Act provisions for mayoral elections; true if the mayoralty is elected at large by all voters, false if the mayor was returned through a Māori ward.

veracity.statement: Dave Gawn, Chief Executive of the National Emergency Management Agency, recently spoke to us and said that the New Zealand Emergency Management System has been set up to manage small events, generally weather events—not big catastrophes like the Hikurangi subduction or the Alpine Fault, which could be level 8 and almost unimaginable.
veracity.explanation: Relays evidence the NEMA Chief Executive is said to have given the Governance and Administration Committee about the limits of the emergency management system.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Governance and Administration Committee transcript/evidence from Dave Gawn's appearance; true if he made substantially this statement about the system being built for small events rather than catastrophic ones, false if the record shows otherwise.

veracity.statement: However, smaller councils do not employ any specialised civil defence and emergency staff, and, in addition, Fire and Emergency New Zealand have not extended their local advisory committees to all of New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that smaller councils employ no dedicated civil defence staff, and that FENZ local advisory committees do not cover all of New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: FENZ's published list of established local advisory committees against its full set of local areas, plus council staffing records/CDEM group reports for small territorial authorities; true if LAC coverage is incomplete and small councils lack dedicated CDEM staff, false if coverage is complete or such staff are commonly employed.

veracity.statement: They were appointed on 9 February 2021 through to the elections in October in 2022, to align them back to the local government elections, and then their appointment was extended to July 2024.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific appointment and extension dates for the Tauranga City Council commissioners.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Gazette notices and DIA records of the appointment of commissioners to Tauranga City Council; true if appointed 9 February 2021 and extended to July 2024, false if the dates differ.

veracity.statement: But they’re also keen to ensure we’ve got representatives sitting at that council with future direction, future forward thinking, so we can take our city—the fifth-largest in New Zealand—forward and have the prosperous city that we want to have.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Tauranga is New Zealand's fifth-largest city.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ urban area / territorial authority population estimates for 2024; true if Tauranga ranks fifth, false if it ranks otherwise on the standard measure.

veracity.statement: Now we’re seeing record numbers.
veracity.explanation: In context, asserts that record numbers of Māori have been elected to local councils following the introduction of Māori wards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DIA/LGNZ data on Māori elected members after the 2022 local elections compared with prior elections; true if the 2022 count is the highest recorded, false if earlier elections returned as many or more.

veracity.statement: But I do have a question that I would love to hear you expound on, and that is, Minister: what do you think about what the commissioners, in their time as the leaders of Tauranga City Council—what do you make of the decision the commissioners took to ignore a petition which was submitted to council with the required amount of votes to have a referendum on a Māori ward?
veracity.explanation: Asserts, within the question, that a petition meeting the signature threshold for a poll on a Māori ward was submitted to Tauranga City Council and disregarded by the commissioners.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tauranga City Council records and electoral officer determinations on any Māori ward poll petition 2021–2024; true if a petition met the statutory threshold and no poll was held, false if no valid petition reached the threshold.

veracity.statement: I’d like to also note that we are going to be having a Māori ward established in Tauranga, where there has never been one before, due to the decisions made by this commission.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Tauranga City Council has never previously had a Māori ward and that the commissioners established the first one.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tauranga City Council representation review records and DIA's history of Māori ward establishment; true if no Māori ward existed before the commissioners' decision, false if one existed earlier.

specificity.statement: Obviously, we’ve taken a very different approach from the last Government in terms of water; the last Government had a one-size-fits-all approach to water, and that ultimately ended up with them spending, I think, $1.2 billion in the last six years, mandating co-governed mega-entities or local councils across the country.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy approach, a dollar figure and a time period, though the mechanism of the replacement is only named, not detailed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s really important that councils do play that role, and ultimately that’s why my message to local government is to focus on the must-haves, not the “nice-to-haves”.
specificity.explanation: Answers a detailed question about civil defence resourcing with a slogan; no funding figure, mechanism, or definition of what counts as a must-have.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When it comes to the issue of Māori wards, we are going to reverse the position to ensure that local communities can make those decisions as to whether there is a Māori ward on a particular council—that is about letting local voters actually make decisions.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy and its mechanism (local polls on Māori wards) but gives no timeframe, legislative vehicle or process detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: However, smaller councils do not employ any specialised civil defence and emergency staff, and, in addition, Fire and Emergency New Zealand have not extended their local advisory committees to all of New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete gap and a named agency's committee structure, but gives no count of affected councils or areas.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They were appointed on 9 February 2021 through to the elections in October in 2022, to align them back to the local government elections, and then their appointment was extended to July 2024.
specificity.explanation: Exact appointment date, original end point and extension date — fully checkable against the appointment record.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I note this is the former Minister who once famously said “democracy has changed”. Well, I’m not quite sure what he means by “democracy”, but on this side of the House, democracy has not changed, because we actually believe in people of this country being able to decide who represents them.
civility.explanation: Turns from the question to the questioner, implying by contrast that the member and his side do not believe in people deciding who represents them — imputed bad faith rather than engagement with the representation question asked.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When it comes to the issue of Māori wards, we are going to reverse the position to ensure that local communities can make those decisions as to whether there is a Māori ward on a particular council—that is about letting local voters actually make decisions.
focus.explanation: Directly answers the question about Māori representation by naming the policy change the Government intends and the decision rule it restores.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: In some councils around New Zealand, I expect they will vote to retain those Māori wards, and in other councils they may not.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a mixed outcome from the binding polls on Māori wards to be held with the next local elections.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Official results of the Māori ward polls held alongside the 2025 local body elections; true if at least one council's voters vote to retain and at least one votes to remove, false if the results are uniform in one direction.
