divination.statement: Whether a council retains its Māori ward because the voters in that community decide they want it, or they don’t, I am confident that more and more Māori will get elected to local councils up and down this country.
divination.explanation: Forecasts an increase in the number of Māori elected to local councils regardless of the Māori ward poll outcomes.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: DIA/LGNZ counts of Māori elected members after the 2025 local elections compared with 2022; true if the number rises, false if it falls or is flat.

rigor.statement: Well, Moko is not elected as the mayor of the Far North on a Māori ward; he is elected as the Mayor of the Far North District Council in an open contest against every single other person who decides to put their name forward for elected office.
rigor.explanation: A valid rebuttal: if the mayoralty is contested at large, the example cannot support the claim that Māori wards produced it. The conclusion tracks the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Surely Māori have a right to be a part and play a part in New Zealand’s democracy today, because there’s been so few who’ve been afforded an opportunity.
rigor.explanation: The stated reason does not establish the conclusion: past under-representation is evidence of a problem, but a right to participate does not follow from the scarcity of past opportunity — the premise and conclusion are about different things.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries is correct in saying that he wants Māori to be able to progress their interests in developing their fisheries rights and sharing that with iwi who benefit from settlements, then isn’t the first version of the bill which came to this House, which had cross-partisan support, and will be enduring, a better option than what has come back and has been proposed, essentially, by Te Ohu Kaimoana to suit their interests in the status quo?
focus.explanation: Engages the substance directly: compares two named versions of a fisheries bill and the interests behind the change. No party-bashing content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ll try third time lucky. We still haven’t had an answer from the Minister to industry transformation plans and the time frame for the taihoa on cameras on boats. Perhaps he’s still looking through his mammoth heap of paper there to find the answer.
focus.explanation: Names two specific policy items (industry transformation plans, the timeframe for the pause on cameras on boats) and holds the Minister to account for not answering on them.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’d like to put to the Minister: what has motivated him to, essentially, disestablish the Oceans Secretariat and how does he expect that to impact the fishing industry and the health of New Zealand’s oceans, respectively.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named administrative decision (disestablishing the Oceans Secretariat) and its consequences; no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Minister, can I, for the sake of the question, help you illuminate—or you might be able to illuminate this further—the difference between the coastal commercial fleet fishing and the deepwater fleet, the disparities in technology.
focus.explanation: Directed at a concrete operational policy question — fleet differences and the technology gap relevant to camera roll-out — rather than at the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Sadly, the cameras issue was conceived without true appreciation of costs, but it’s driven and propelled by an ideology which is very hostile to the flourishing of the fishing industry. Sadly, that was allowed to carry on uncontested. But wait, taihoa, help is on the way.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point (the cameras programme underestimated costs), but the weight of the passage is framing opponents' motives rather than the mechanism or the numbers.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What has been the direction of travel for the three types of fishers—the commercial, customary, and recreational fishers—and whether or not we can expect, with him as Minister, to see any changes regarding stock but also allocation?
focus.explanation: A substantive policy question about stock and allocation across the three named fisher categories; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My question to the Minister: could he inform the Chamber as to what is the response to the roll-out of the camera programme? What is the response from many of the skippers on the boats that have these cameras?
focus.explanation: Directed at a named programme (cameras on boats) and the affected group (skippers), though it invites a general impression rather than probing a mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: If the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries is correct in saying that he wants Māori to be able to progress their interests in developing their fisheries rights and sharing that with iwi who benefit from settlements, then isn’t the first version of the bill which came to this House, which had cross-partisan support, and will be enduring, a better option than what has come back and has been proposed, essentially, by Te Ohu Kaimoana to suit their interests in the status quo?
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the first version of the fisheries bill introduced to the House had cross-partisan support.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The first reading division record in Hansard for the fisheries/Māori commercial fisheries bill referred to; true if parties from both government and opposition voted in favour at first reading, false if the vote split on government/opposition lines.

veracity.statement: In 2023, the New Zealand orange roughy fisheries ORH 3B, responsible for 80 percent of the catch, lost our Marine Stewardship Council certification—an important marking point to the United States and EU consumers.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that ORH 3B accounts for about 80 percent of the NZ orange roughy catch, and that it lost MSC certification in 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Marine Stewardship Council certification register / MSC public announcements for the New Zealand orange roughy fishery, plus Fisheries NZ catch data by quota management area; true if MSC certification for ORH 3B ended during 2023 and ORH 3B is ~80% of the national orange roughy catch, false if certification was retained through 2023 or the share is materially different.

veracity.statement: On the question of orange roughy, I’m advised by the officials, on searching for the answer in this mammoth midden heap of paper, that in 2023-24, orange roughy 3B was reduced by 40 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the orange roughy 3B catch limit was cut by 40 percent in the 2023-24 fishing year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Fisheries New Zealand sustainability round decisions / TACC schedule for ORH 3B for the 2023-24 fishing year; true if the total allowable commercial catch was reduced by approximately 40 percent, false if the reduction was materially different or no reduction was made.

specificity.statement: In 2023, the New Zealand orange roughy fisheries ORH 3B, responsible for 80 percent of the catch, lost our Marine Stewardship Council certification—an important marking point to the United States and EU consumers.
specificity.explanation: Names the stock (ORH 3B), a year, a percentage share of catch and a named certification body — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: To that end, four meetings a year are happening between the key leaders. They are finding common ground that will include—that will include—options not to increase levies during the next two or three years, and to learn to live within a shortened piece of cloth.
specificity.explanation: Gives a cadence (four meetings a year) and a named mechanism (options to hold levies flat over two to three years), but no amounts, no decision point and no commitment.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Minister, given the recent article in the Sunday-Star Times this weekend of the footage of the efficacy or otherwise of the SLEDs, the sea lion exclusion devices, will you release that footage or instruct that that footage is released for public scrutiny so that we can indeed assess the efficacy of the SLEDs?
specificity.explanation: Names a specific piece of evidence (the SLED footage referenced in a named newspaper), a named device, and a specific requested action — releasing it for scrutiny.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Evidence showed that the fishers were having to trawl for longer yet still not catching more fish, suggesting depletion and spawning aggregations had disappeared or were severely reduced on seamount areas and had been heavily trawled. The only seamount that showed some positive signs for the fish was one that is closed to trawling. The implication is that the extent of the exploitation was meaning that there would be no sustainable orange roughy, because we’d fished it to oblivion.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: declining catch per unit effort plus the contrast with a closed seamount is offered as evidence of depletion. The conclusion broadly tracks the premises, though 'fished it to oblivion' overreaches what falling CPUE alone establishes.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And, in that regard, I wanted to repeat my question: why remove the bycatch kill limit for sea lions, if indeed the SLEDs are working? Surely there is no need to remove the limit, because it won’t be reached.
rigor.explanation: A clean conditional argument: if the exclusion devices work, the bycatch limit is not binding, so removing it is unnecessary — and the removal therefore implies doubt about the devices. The conclusion follows from the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Just before we wind up, there is no great threat to sea lions. I trust the quality of advice coming from our officials. They are not driven by politics, ideology, such as the member who’s just resumed his seat.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion ('no great threat to sea lions') rests entirely on a bare appeal to the authority of officials, buttressed by an ad hominem contrast with the questioner. No evidence is offered for the substantive claim.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The system works in this very simple way: scientists establish—and I’m talking about robust, genuine science, not these lib pen-pushers—genuine enforceable justiciable figures, and the politicians, like myself, act on that. But we have no time for these lib pen-pushers who write all this green diatribe.
civility.explanation: Sneering dismissal of a class of people as 'lib pen-pushers' writing 'green diatribe' — contempt directed at people rather than at any argument they make.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We’ll try third time lucky. We still haven’t had an answer from the Minister to industry transformation plans and the time frame for the taihoa on cameras on boats. Perhaps he’s still looking through his mammoth heap of paper there to find the answer.
civility.explanation: Pointed and lightly mocking of the Minister's disorganisation, but the jibe is glancing and the substance — an unanswered question — carries most of the weight.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Sadly, the cameras issue was conceived without true appreciation of costs, but it’s driven and propelled by an ideology which is very hostile to the flourishing of the fishing industry. Sadly, that was allowed to carry on uncontested. But wait, taihoa, help is on the way.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith — that the policy was driven by an ideology hostile to the industry — rather than engaging the policy's design on its merits.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Just before we wind up, there is no great threat to sea lions. I trust the quality of advice coming from our officials. They are not driven by politics, ideology, such as the member who’s just resumed his seat.
civility.explanation: Turns on the questioner personally, characterising him as ideologically driven, rather than answering the point about sea lion bycatch.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And I’m not interested in the wittering of that lady from the Otago university—irrelevant to me.
civility.explanation: Dismisses an identifiable researcher as 'that lady' who 'witters' — a belittling personal put-down that engages nothing she actually said.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I guess I’ll repeat the question: will you release the footage that proves, or otherwise, the efficacy of those seal protection devices? What are you afraid of showing; what is the industry afraid of showing?
civility.explanation: 'What are you afraid of showing' imputes concealment and bad faith to the Minister personally, though it stops short of an insult and stays tethered to the request for the footage.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But let no one think in this session that that footage is going to be surrendered to people who have as their motivation the delegitimisation of fisheries. That’s just not happening.
civility.explanation: Justifies withholding evidence by ascribing a discrediting motive to those who requested it, rather than engaging the case for release.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: So I understand that our seafood exports are going to increase, hopefully, to around $2.3 billion by 2024.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that New Zealand seafood export earnings will rise to about $2.3 billion by 2024.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries seafood export revenue figures for the year to 2024; true if seafood export earnings reach approximately $2.3 billion, false if materially below that.

divination.statement: So the question to my right was a very clever question, and given that we will be addressing the uncertainty around the permits associated with aquaculture, you will find there will be a greater level, percentage-wise, of wealth coming from aquaculture over the next 5 to 10 years.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that aquaculture will account for a larger percentage share of seafood sector revenue over the following five to ten years.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Aquaculture NZ / MPI seafood export revenue breakdown; true if aquaculture's share of total New Zealand seafood export revenue is higher in the 2029-2034 window than in 2024, false if its share is flat or lower.

veracity.statement: Minister, after the industry fought for so long against cameras on boats, we found that when the data came in on the 127 vessels with cameras, there was significant under-reporting: a sevenfold increase in dolphin interactions, a 350 percent increase in albatross interactions, and an almost 50 percent increase in discarded fish volume.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that camera data from 127 vessels showed a sevenfold rise in reported dolphin interactions, a 350% rise in albatross interactions and an almost 50% rise in discarded fish volume relative to pre-camera self-reporting.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Fisheries New Zealand / MPI onboard-camera programme reporting data for the vessels fitted with cameras: true if reported dolphin interactions rose roughly sevenfold, albatross interactions ~350% and discard volume ~50% after cameras were fitted, and the fitted fleet numbered about 127 vessels; false if the published figures are materially different.

veracity.statement: Despite our nation, New Zealand, having put through a proposal for a 70 percent protection of vulnerable marine ecosystems, including seamounts—which was actually a descent in the proposal of the whole body, for 100 percent protection; we reduced it to 70—after the change of Government, we refused to submit that proposal and in fact Australia had to submit it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts New Zealand had developed a 70% seamount/VME protection proposal for SPRFMO, declined to submit it after the change of government, and that Australia submitted it instead.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: SPRFMO Commission meeting papers and proposal records for 2023–2024: true if a 70% VME protection proposal originating with New Zealand was tabled by Australia rather than New Zealand; false if New Zealand tabled it or no such proposal exists in the record.

veracity.statement: New Zealand backing out from this was a cause of some significant annoyance to the United States and to Australia—to the extent that Australia considers it should now treat New Zealand as an opponent when it comes to managing fisheries in the South Pacific.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that US and Australian officials were annoyed by New Zealand's withdrawal of the proposal, and that Australia now regards New Zealand as an adversary in South Pacific fisheries management.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Australian and US government statements, diplomatic correspondence or contemporaneous reporting around the 2024 SPRFMO meeting: true if Australian officials characterised New Zealand as an opponent or expressed formal displeasure; false if no such statements exist or officials described continued alignment.

veracity.statement: Moving to industry transformation plans (ITPs) and what he sees as the state of those ITPs: what learnings can be taken forward as a result of that exercise of pulling all of that information and people—not just the info but the people—together to put in place an industry transformation plan; and whether he agrees or not with David Wilson, New Zealand First’s Upper Harbour candidate, who said at the pre-election World Wildlife Foundation debate that he agreed and celebrated what the ITP was for the sector?
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim about what David Wilson, a New Zealand First candidate, said at a pre-election WWF debate — that he agreed with and celebrated the fisheries industry transformation plan.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Recording, transcript or contemporaneous reporting of the pre-election WWF/environment debate: true if Wilson expressed support for the fisheries ITP there; false if he did not or made no such comment.

veracity.statement: I campaigned against cameras, but that was unsuccessful, sadly.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the speaker campaigned publicly against onboard cameras on fishing vessels and did not succeed in stopping them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ First and Shane Jones campaign material and public statements from the 2023 election period, plus the record of the camera roll-out proceeding: true if he publicly opposed cameras on boats and the roll-out went ahead anyway; false if no such opposition is on record.

specificity.statement: Minister, after the industry fought for so long against cameras on boats, we found that when the data came in on the 127 vessels with cameras, there was significant under-reporting: a sevenfold increase in dolphin interactions, a 350 percent increase in albatross interactions, and an almost 50 percent increase in discarded fish volume.
specificity.explanation: Three quantified comparisons plus the number of camera-equipped vessels — fully checkable against the published camera programme data.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On the question as to what the future of the camera roll-out is, a number of boats will be focused on and the cameras will be affixed to them, and at that point we’re going to have a taihoa and ascertain who’s going to pay for this, and, if it’s a public good, then how the public is going to pay for it.
specificity.explanation: Indicates a direction (pause the roll-out, review funding) but gives no vessel numbers, no date for the pause or review, and no funding mechanism — 'a number of boats' and 'at that point' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Indeed, four times a year we are engaging with the senior figures of the fishing industry to effect better outcomes between the civil service, myself, and them.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete frequency and named participants, but no detail on what the engagements cover or what outcomes they are meant to produce.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And the final thing I’d say about Māori fisheries: the member makes a very good point: I have no interest in disfiguring the progress forward for Māori fisheries but neither do I want to set up a host of opportunities for Māori and for them to argue with each other; I’d rather see them mend a net, catch some fish, and make some money.
specificity.explanation: Asked why he is proposing to change a specific bill, he names no clause, no change and no timeframe — a general sentiment about disputes and fishing in place of any checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: My question is: if, as the industry claims, the sealion exclusion devices are working, surely, then, there is no need to remove the limit, because it won’t be reached?
rigor.explanation: A valid conditional: if the exclusion devices work, a binding mortality cap would never bind, so removal is unnecessary. The gap is that a limit can carry compliance and monitoring costs independent of whether it is reached, which the inference does not consider.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’re not going to have this commercial sector continually burdened down with a host of compliance costs preventing it from generating the necessary economic dividend to pay for our schoolteachers, our police men and women, and to meet the costs of our schools and hospitals.
rigor.explanation: A long causal chain — camera compliance costs to lost sector earnings to unfunded schools, police and hospitals — asserted with nothing offered to link the steps or size the effect. The appeal is to the emotive end-point rather than to any evidence on compliance cost.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Go and talk to the Spanish about their own fishing outcomes before you lecture the matua.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque: the implied conclusion is that the criticism of New Zealand's SPRFMO stance need not be answered because other fishing nations behave worse. Another party's conduct does not bear on whether the criticism is sound.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I wanted to repeat the question to the Minister: have you given any instructions to the Ministry for Primary Industries on marine protected areas?
focus.explanation: A direct scrutiny question about a named agency and a named policy area, with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I just wanted to touch on this issue of the South Pacific Regional Fisheries Management Organisation and ask the Minister what the current position is regarding the proposed bottom fishing management boundaries—but, in particular, the role that New Zealand scientists were involved in in developing those boundaries and what might be seen by some as world leading, and whether or not the Minister supports them as scientists in their approach or not?
focus.explanation: Names a specific international body, a specific measure (bottom fishing management boundaries) and the scientific advice behind it; no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Perhaps the Minister could enlighten the committee a little bit further on the technology that, especially, the coastal commercial fleet has implemented over the last few years and speak to, if he’d be so kind, the changes in net technology—the fact that it has gone from a four to a five to a six, from a diamond to a square—especially in the mid-water fish space, and, by virtue, the technology that has embraced, taking into consideration the bycatch limits and how onerous it is.
focus.explanation: Entirely about a technical policy matter — net mesh technology in the coastal commercial fleet and its relationship to bycatch limits.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Minister, if I make a statement—and I’m pleased with a yes or no—do you agree: do you agree that the coastal commercial sector has innovated significantly over the last 10 years to try and alleviate bycatch? And what does innovation look like, to try and nullify some of the concerns on the political left?
focus.explanation: A genuine policy question about bycatch innovation, but framed around answering 'the political left' rather than the substance of the concerns themselves.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Maōri fisheries are really important and I want to ask the Minister why he is proposing to change what is a bill that was supported by iwi Māori, worked on by the Māori Affairs Committee that used a cross-partisan approach, that dealt with stakeholders for a number of months and engaged deeply with those stakeholders, and is it because the Minister is only taking advice from Te Ohu Kaimoana? And is the Minister acting in the interests of Te Ohu Kaimoana?
focus.explanation: Names a specific bill, its select committee process and the stakeholders involved, and asks about a specific proposed change — scrutiny with policy content throughout.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So to be very, very clear, I’m not going to continue with the perfidy of the last regime.
focus.explanation: Names no policy, mechanism or figure — a bare characterisation of the previous government as treacherous, offered in place of the camera policy detail being asked for.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Maōri fisheries are really important and I want to ask the Minister why he is proposing to change what is a bill that was supported by iwi Māori, worked on by the Māori Affairs Committee that used a cross-partisan approach, that dealt with stakeholders for a number of months and engaged deeply with those stakeholders, and is it because the Minister is only taking advice from Te Ohu Kaimoana? And is the Minister acting in the interests of Te Ohu Kaimoana?
civility.explanation: Squarely on the bill and its process, but the closing questions impute to the Minister personally that he is serving one organisation's interests rather than the public's — pointed and edging into bad-faith imputation.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It grieves me to hear—in fact, it reminds me of the milky flesh disease when I listen to the member from the Green Party suggesting that the industry, number one, is not telling the truth.
civility.explanation: Likens listening to a named colleague's contribution to a fish disease — mockery directed at the member rather than engagement with the under-reporting data he cited.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Neither are we going to have a situation where the footage associated with the cameras is continually chased up by these busybodies, these meddlesome third-party interests who want to further stigmatise the existence of a proud industry.
civility.explanation: Characterises those who request camera footage as 'busybodies' and 'meddlesome', and imputes to them a motive of stigmatising the industry, rather than addressing the access question on its merits.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Neither will we pay any attention to MPs standing up here invoking provisions from overseas trade deals as if it’s some type of bludgeon to undermine the democracy and the sovereignty of our legitimately elected Government.
civility.explanation: Attributes to the questioning members an intent to undermine democracy and sovereignty — an imputation of bad faith aimed at the MPs rather than a response to the point about international obligations.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Although there is a low likelihood of mass arrivals to New Zealand, we’re living in a fool’s paradise to assume that it won’t occur. Quite simply, a failure to plan is a plan to fail.
rigor.explanation: A precautionary inference (low probability still warrants planning) that is coherent in shape, but the only support offered for the conclusion is an aphorism — 'a failure to plan is a plan to fail' — rather than any evidence about risk or consequence. Appeal to maxim/slogan doing the work of a premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We all know our district courts are under significant case load pressure, and allowing more time will reduce the risk of additional pressure if any mass arrival group was to arrive on our shores.
rigor.explanation: The premise is asserted by appeal to common knowledge ('we all know') with no caseload evidence offered, but the conclusion drawn from it — longer statutory timeframes ease pressure on the courts — is modest and does broadly follow from the stated premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We have limited capacity of appropriately qualified lawyers capable of representing any such group. Currently, there are only around 40.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at May 2024 only about 40 lawyers in New Zealand are appropriately qualified to represent a mass-arrival group.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Immigration New Zealand / Ministry of Justice (Legal Services) records of the number of lawyers approved or qualified to provide legal aid representation in immigration/mass-arrival detention matters as at May 2024, or the departmental advice and regulatory impact statement accompanying the Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Bill; true if the figure is approximately 40, false if materially different (e.g. an order of magnitude higher or lower).

veracity.statement: We are a nation of immigrants. Our arrival to this beautiful country started some 800 years ago and continues to this day.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that human arrival in New Zealand began approximately 800 years ago.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Archaeological and radiocarbon consensus on the date of first human (Polynesian) settlement of New Zealand, e.g. Te Ara / Royal Society NZ syntheses; true if first settlement is dated to roughly 800 years before 2024 (i.e. c. 1200–1300 CE), false if the accepted date is materially outside that range.

specificity.statement: We have limited capacity of appropriately qualified lawyers capable of representing any such group. Currently, there are only around 40.
specificity.explanation: Supplies a concrete, checkable figure (around 40 qualified lawyers) tied to a named constraint, though the qualifying criterion for 'appropriately qualified' is left undefined and no source is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But, rest assured, not only are we adult enough to reconsider our previously held position on this amendment bill; we will actually do something that will seem refreshingly original, given the previous administration’s record of non-delivery.
focus.explanation: After a substantive speech, this closing turns to generalised party framing: the other side's 'record of non-delivery' and the implication they were not 'adult enough'. No specific policy, figure or outcome is named — the weight is on characterising the previous administration rather than on the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Secondly, the legislation must require an immigration officer to establish, in making an application for a group warrant of commitment, the following: why the proposed detention is necessary, that the detention sought is for the least amount of time and is the least restrictive necessary to achieve the outcomes of detention, how the proposed location of detention meets the Government’s obligations under the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act, and how the proposed location of detention meets New Zealand’s obligations under the 1951 Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, which is the piece of international law that governs the rights of asylum seekers.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact statutory test to be inserted, the four matters an immigration officer would have to establish, and the two named instruments (NZ Bill of Rights Act, 1951 Refugee Convention). Fully checkable against a drafted amendment.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One of them, which I think is worth considering, and which I hope the Government will consider, is the idea of this legislation specifying that in the event of a mass arrival, the Government will undertake with an independent organisation—that could be the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC); it could be the Ombudsman—to put in place a memorandum of understanding that would deploy someone from one of those independent organisations to regularly inspect the conditions and the treatment of the detainees.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (a memorandum of understanding written into the legislation), two named candidate bodies and the function they would perform (regular inspection of conditions), though no timeframe or thresholds are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, currently, we’re looking to change the rules so that if an application is made within 96 hours of the initial arrest and detention, the court must then determine this application as soon as reasonably practical and within seven days. If the court considers that this is not reasonably practical to determine the application—the number of people we’ve got to deal with—then they can extend it out to 28 days.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the operative mechanism with exact figures: a 96-hour application window, a seven-day determination requirement, and a 28-day extension where determination is not reasonably practicable.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Secondly, the legislation must require an immigration officer to establish, in making an application for a group warrant of commitment, the following: why the proposed detention is necessary, that the detention sought is for the least amount of time and is the least restrictive necessary to achieve the outcomes of detention, how the proposed location of detention meets the Government’s obligations under the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act, and how the proposed location of detention meets New Zealand’s obligations under the 1951 Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, which is the piece of international law that governs the rights of asylum seekers.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of the bill before the House — what an amendment would require and why — with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yes, it’s very low, but we just have to look at the history of this great nation of ours and the original settlers, whether they’d be Māori or European, arrived here by boat. They travelled for very long distances in themselves. You can extrapolate that out, where people could come from many parts of the world to come here.
focus.explanation: Weak as reasoning, but squarely engaged with the rationale for the measure before the House — the probability of a mass arrival — rather than with the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So it just shows that we are a Government that can be pragmatic and sensible, and we are prepared to work with an idea that we need, and with policy and legislation that the country needs.
focus.explanation: Party framing rather than policy content: the point is what kind of government his side is, with no measure, figure or outcome named.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It was our Government that commissioned Victoria Casey KC to investigate the practice of detaining asylum seekers in criminal justice facilities and in corrections facilities, and found that to be contrary to New Zealand’s international obligations under international law for the treatment of asylum seekers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that (a) the previous Labour government commissioned Victoria Casey KC to review the detention of asylum seekers in prisons/police cells, and (b) that review concluded the practice was contrary to New Zealand's international obligations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published Casey review of immigration detention (MBIE/Immigration New Zealand commissioning documents and the report itself): true if the review was commissioned during the 2017–2023 Labour government and its findings state the detention of asylum seekers in corrections/police facilities is inconsistent with New Zealand's international obligations; false if it was commissioned under another government or reached no such finding.

veracity.statement: There are precedents in Canada of steel-hulled ships being used to transport, by people smugglers, a mass group of would-be asylum seekers across the ocean that landed in Canada.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Canada has experienced mass arrivals of asylum seekers brought across the ocean by people smugglers aboard ships.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Canadian government and contemporaneous news records of maritime mass arrivals (e.g. the Ocean Lady in 2009 and the MV Sun Sea in 2010): true if at least one vessel organised by smugglers landed a large group of asylum seekers in Canada; false if no such arrival is documented.

veracity.statement: So, currently, we’re looking to change the rules so that if an application is made within 96 hours of the initial arrest and detention, the court must then determine this application as soon as reasonably practical and within seven days. If the court considers that this is not reasonably practical to determine the application—the number of people we’ve got to deal with—then they can extend it out to 28 days.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Bill provides for an application within 96 hours of arrest and detention, court determination within seven days, extendable to 28 days.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Bill as reported back from the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee: true if the group warrant provisions contain the 96-hour, seven-day and 28-day periods as described; false if the periods in the bill differ materially.

veracity.statement: It’s been noted by many that, in the country, there are only currently around 40 lawyers who are qualified to deal with this.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 40 lawyers in New Zealand are qualified to act in refugee and protection / immigration detention matters.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice legal aid provider approval lists for refugee and protection work, or select committee evidence on the bill: true if the number of approved practitioners is approximately 40; false if it is materially higher or lower.

veracity.statement: There’s been concern about holding people in prison, and let’s make this very, very clear: there is no expectation and there has never been any expectation that ordinary members of a mass arrival would be held in a prison.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that detention of ordinary mass-arrival asylum seekers in prison has never been contemplated, either in the bill or in official expectations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's text and departmental disclosure statement, plus Immigration New Zealand's documented detention practice (including the Casey review findings): true if neither the bill nor official advice contemplates holding ordinary mass-arrival members in a prison; false if the legislation permits, or officials' advice or past practice records, detention of asylum seekers in corrections facilities.

rigor.statement: Yes, it’s very low, but we just have to look at the history of this great nation of ours and the original settlers, whether they’d be Māori or European, arrived here by boat. They travelled for very long distances in themselves. You can extrapolate that out, where people could come from many parts of the world to come here.
rigor.explanation: False analogy / non sequitur: historic settlement voyages by Māori and European settlers are offered as grounds for the likelihood of a modern smuggler-organised mass arrival. Nothing connects the two, and the speaker explicitly labels the move an extrapolation without supplying the link.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And I note the comments from a member across the House who highlighted this issue—and he’s right to highlight the issue.
civility.explanation: On a contested point in a contested bill, the speaker credits an opposition member's argument rather than disparaging him. Engages the substance, attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This change updates clauses 9, 11, and 15 of the bill, to revert the term labelled “Pacific person” in the defined terms of the Pacific Education Foundation Act, rather than proceed with the previous Government’s proposal to use the term label of “Aotearoa Pacific person”.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact clauses (9, 11, 15), the Act, and the precise textual change being made — fully checkable against the bill and the Amendment Paper.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Clause 11, again, deletes the word “Aotearoa” in section 5(a); clause 15 deletes it from clause 15(1), page 6, line 6.
specificity.explanation: Clause, section, page and line references — as concrete and directly checkable as a statement in committee can be.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Look, I just want to know, now that we’re considering it all in one question, whether or not, with the section that we have talked about—the Ngarimu VC fund—with the proposed amendments, the Minister in the chair, Simeon Brown, considers that there are any great changes that we can see long term, or whether this is sort of a fairly minor amendment?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific fund at issue, but the question itself is framed loosely — 'any great changes', 'fairly minor' — with no figure, mechanism or timeframe to test an answer against.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is just a clarification in terms of subclause (2) of new clause 35: “An order made under this section is secondary legislation”.
specificity.explanation: Pinpoints the exact subclause and quotes the operative wording, so the clarification sought is unambiguous and answerable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The reason for this legislation is to make sure that they are legally able to use the emblems of the 28th Māori Battalion, because there has been some question in their new form, their new entity, whether or not they have the legal right to use those, and this just clarifies that they do.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the concrete problem the provision addresses (legal uncertainty over emblem use by the successor entity) and the mechanism — clarification of the right — though without reference to the schedule or scope.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I just want to understand if the Minister has any idea on the number of companies that passing this amendment would enable the Superannuation Fund to expand its investment into as part of the Government’s focus on ensuring that we can grow a more productive and value-adding New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: The thing asked for — a count of companies opened up by the amendment — is concrete, but it is wrapped in generic growth language and no figure, threshold or definition of the relevant company set is offered.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Effectively, what the previous Government was doing by creating a new term “Aotearoa Pacific person” was creating a new definition which, of course, isn’t used in other legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the term “Aotearoa Pacific person”, proposed by the previous Government, does not appear anywhere else in New Zealand legislation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: A search of the NZ statute book (legislation.govt.nz) for the defined term “Aotearoa Pacific person”: true if the term appears in no other Act or set of regulations at the time of the statement, false if it is already used in other legislation.

veracity.statement: A very quick call Mr Chair, just to point out that this bill came back from the select committee unchanged and with unanimous support from the select committee. So there is very little to debate and the objective of the bill is not something where the Government should be telling companies what to do, but it just gives the New Zealand Superannuation Fund a little bit more scope to make more investment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable facts about the committee stage: that the bill was reported back unamended, and that the committee's support was unanimous.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee report on the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Amendment Bill: true if the committee recommended the bill be passed without amendment and recorded no minority or differing view, false if amendments were recommended or any party dissented.

rigor.statement: So we’re asking questions on this bill to enable the New Zealand Superannuation Fund to invest a larger portion of the ownership of particular businesses, and we recognise that the New Zealand market is a small market and that the Superannuation Fund has grown substantively over a reasonable period of time and is now in a position where it is unable to take minority positions in sufficient numbers of companies to fully utilise all of its funds.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: a small domestic market plus a substantially grown fund implies too few available minority stakes to deploy the capital. The conclusion tracks the premises, though 'grown substantively' and 'sufficient numbers' are left unquantified, so the step to 'unable' is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: A very quick call Mr Chair, just to point out that this bill came back from the select committee unchanged and with unanimous support from the select committee. So there is very little to debate and the objective of the bill is not something where the Government should be telling companies what to do, but it just gives the New Zealand Superannuation Fund a little bit more scope to make more investment.
rigor.explanation: Infers from unanimous select committee support that 'there is very little to debate'. That is an appeal to prior consensus — agreement at select committee bears on the bill's contentiousness, not on whether the committee-stage questions being asked (how many companies, what economic effect) have answers.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think it’s important, when we’re asking questions about this bill at this stage, that we have that sort of clarity so that we can assure the public that the Government’s agenda of delivering on growth in this economy and growth in productivity will be achieved through increasing the Superannuation Fund’s mandate to take these majority stakes.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point — the mandate change and whether it delivers — but the weight of the sentence is on advertising the Government's agenda rather than on the mechanism or its effects.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s great to stand up here and look at this bill, and we really enjoyed the second reading, where we did see cross-party support for this very, very important issue of the Superannuation Fund in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the second reading of the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests) Amendment Bill attracted support from across the parties, not just the governing side.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard division/vote record for the second reading of the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests) Amendment Bill: true if parties from both Government and Opposition benches voted in favour, false if support came only from the Government parties.

veracity.statement: More generally, beyond agriculture, it is obvious that when we look at New Zealand, we’ve actually seen a reducing proportion of the Super Fund’s investments being in New Zealand over time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand-domiciled assets have fallen as a share of the New Zealand Superannuation Fund's total portfolio over recent years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Super Fund / Guardians of New Zealand Superannuation annual reports and portfolio disclosures: true if the New Zealand share of total fund assets shows a declining trend over the years preceding May 2024, false if that share was flat or rising.

focus.statement: But I was particularly interested in amended section 49A(b), inserted by clause 5, “an entity that is formed or controlled by the Guardians for the purpose of holding, facilitating, or managing the investments of the Fund”, and just around, I suppose, the implications of that moving forward when we are looking at investment around New Zealand.
focus.explanation: Directs the question at a named clause of the bill before the committee and its practical implications; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If an investor is investing in something seeing long-term potential, sometimes what that will require is changes to the way that a business is operating—recapitalisation in different ways, new personnel, new approaches—which necessarily require a controlling interest in order to exercise those changes.
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism the bill enables — controlling stakes — and why an investor would need one. Entirely on the substance.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think it’s important to point out the section because while my colleagues on this side of the Chamber are following me clearly, my colleagues on the other side of the Chamber are finding it difficult to follow.
focus.explanation: Nominally about citing a section of the Act, but the weight of the sentence is a jibe at the comprehension of members opposite rather than any content of the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I want to have certainty for my constituents that the Minister assures this committee that there won’t be political influence in any form enabled through this bill being enacted through this House.
focus.explanation: Puts a substantive question about the bill's effect — whether it opens a channel for political influence over the Fund's investee companies — to the Minister in charge.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But I was particularly interested in amended section 49A(b), inserted by clause 5, “an entity that is formed or controlled by the Guardians for the purpose of holding, facilitating, or managing the investments of the Fund”, and just around, I suppose, the implications of that moving forward when we are looking at investment around New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision (amended section 49A(b), inserted by clause 5) and quotes its text, but the concern raised — 'the implications moving forward' — is left unquantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I would put to members that by allowing this change, this controlling stake, we’re opening up a whole new range of investments for the Super Fund, medium and long term assets, and there could be some significant economic benefit from having another investor at scale investing in growth industries and businesses in our own country.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (permitting a controlling stake) and the asset class (medium- and long-term), but the payoff is 'some significant economic benefit' with no figure, no scale and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I want to have certainty for my constituents that the Minister assures this committee that there won’t be political influence in any form enabled through this bill being enacted through this House.
specificity.explanation: Anchored to the political-influence provisions he has just cited, but the risk itself is put as 'political influence in any form' with no mechanism, threshold or scenario identified.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If an investor is investing in something seeing long-term potential, sometimes what that will require is changes to the way that a business is operating—recapitalisation in different ways, new personnel, new approaches—which necessarily require a controlling interest in order to exercise those changes.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: long-term investing sometimes requires operational change, and operational change requires control, therefore a controlling interest is warranted. The chain holds, though 'necessarily require' overstates the link — influence short of control can also drive change, so there is a modest gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In fact, what we’re seeing, as I’m sure the Minister will be aware, is entities such as BlackRock Investment, which are the champions and the global leaders in ESG investments, have been losing funds. Their returns are down, and they’ve been losing investment from the private sector putting money into that, because of those poorer returns that they’ve had.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that BlackRock, presented as the global leader in ESG investing, has suffered fund outflows and declining returns, and that private-sector money has been withdrawn as a result.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: BlackRock's published fund-flow and performance reporting and Morningstar sustainable-fund flow data for 2023–24: true if BlackRock's ESG/sustainable funds show net outflows and underperformance over that period; false if flows and returns were flat or positive.

veracity.statement: So I simply draw members’ attention to section 58 of the Act, which requires the Guardians to “invest on a prudent commercial basis” and requires them to apply “best-practice portfolio management;” and to “[maximise] return without undue risk to the Fund as a whole;”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that section 58 of the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001 imposes those three specific investment duties on the Guardians.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of section 58 of the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001 on legislation.govt.nz: true if it requires investment on a prudent commercial basis consistent with best-practice portfolio management and maximising return without undue risk to the Fund as a whole; false if those words are not in that section.

veracity.statement: I would note that the Minister is not able to give a direction that is inconsistent with the Guardians’ duty to invest the fund on a prudent commercial basis.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a legal limit on the Minister's power of direction over the Guardians of New Zealand Superannuation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The ministerial-direction provisions of the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001 (s 64 and related): true if a direction inconsistent with the duty to invest on a prudent commercial basis is prohibited; false if the Act permits such a direction.

veracity.statement: And in terms of this particular thing, there has been no amendment—there has been no new amendment tabled.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no amendment paper was tabled for the committee-of-the-whole stage of the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests) Amendment Bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's Amendment Paper (SOP) record and the committee-stage Hansard for that bill on 7 May 2024: true if no amendment paper was lodged for the committee stage; false if one was.

rigor.statement: In fact, what we’re seeing, as I’m sure the Minister will be aware, is entities such as BlackRock Investment, which are the champions and the global leaders in ESG investments, have been losing funds. Their returns are down, and they’ve been losing investment from the private sector putting money into that, because of those poorer returns that they’ve had.
rigor.explanation: Causal inference: ESG focus → poorer returns → outflows, supported by a single firm cited as representative. Hasty generalisation from one example, and the causal link between ESG mandates and the returns is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Super Fund, if it is to be free to make investments, also has to be free to make investments that fail, without the expectation that the Crown would be bailing it out.
rigor.explanation: A valid conditional: genuine investment freedom entails bearing downside risk, so a bail-out expectation would undercut the independence the Act creates. The link between an implicit bail-out expectation and constrained investment is asserted rather than demonstrated, but the inference broadly holds.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I simply draw members’ attention to section 58 of the Act, which requires the Guardians to “invest on a prudent commercial basis” and requires them to apply “best-practice portfolio management;” and to “[maximise] return without undue risk to the Fund as a whole;”.
specificity.explanation: Names the statutory section and quotes the operative duties, so the answer can be checked directly against the Act.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That is what has given rise to some of the technical and consequential amendments in the bill, which include amending sections of the Income Tax Act and the Ombudsmen Act to make it very clear that any controlled entities are not subject to the same requirements as Crown entities.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the named statutes amended and the precise legal effect intended, which a reader could verify against the bill's consequential amendments.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Good to see members on the opposite side being so engaged and involved with the debate.
civility.explanation: Sarcasm at Opposition members prompted by an interjection — mockery of their engagement rather than of any argument, though it stops short of a direct personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Good to see members on the opposite side being so engaged and involved with the debate.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the behaviour of the other side in the Chamber; names no provision, figure or outcome of the bill before the committee.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Just very quickly, as I read through this piece of legislation, and going on from what my colleague has just mentioned around Māori accessing the New Zealand Superannuation Fund, and due to our mortality rates—dying seven to 10 years earlier than everybody else—it seems to me that this particular fund has built up its funds due to those who maybe don’t have access to it, including Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori die seven to 10 years earlier than the rest of the population.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ period life tables / Ministry of Health life-expectancy statistics comparing Māori and non-Māori life expectancy at birth around 2024; true if the gap falls within roughly 7-10 years, false if materially smaller or larger.

veracity.statement: New Zealand investment represents only around 14 percent of the Super Fund’s current total portfolio.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the share of the NZ Superannuation Fund's total portfolio that is invested in New Zealand assets is about 14 percent at the time of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Superannuation Fund annual report / portfolio disclosures for FY2023-24 showing the proportion of the total portfolio held in New Zealand assets; true if approximately 14%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The Superannuation Fund made clear to me that they are both looking forward to and prepared for its passage.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the NZ Superannuation Fund (its board) told the Minister it welcomed and was ready for the Controlling Interests Amendment Bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Guardians of New Zealand Superannuation's public submission and statements on the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests) Amendment Bill, and any released ministerial meeting records; true if the Fund is on record supporting and preparing for the bill, false if it opposed or raised readiness concerns.

rigor.statement: Just very quickly, as I read through this piece of legislation, and going on from what my colleague has just mentioned around Māori accessing the New Zealand Superannuation Fund, and due to our mortality rates—dying seven to 10 years earlier than everybody else—it seems to me that this particular fund has built up its funds due to those who maybe don’t have access to it, including Māori.
rigor.explanation: Infers from earlier Māori mortality that the Super Fund's balance has been built up by those who do not live to access it; the connecting step between individual mortality and accumulation in a Crown-contributed sovereign wealth fund is asserted rather than shown — a gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So the point that I would simply make is if we want the Super Fund to be more invested in activities that create prosperity for New Zealanders and that create commercial return for New Zealanders, then we should be broadening out the scope.
rigor.explanation: Conditional argument from a stated goal to the bill's mechanism; broadening the permitted scope plausibly enables more such investment, but the conclusion that it will produce more New Zealand-focused prosperity is not established — the Guardians' commercial mandate is left to do unexamined work.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One thing also to mention: Australia has great investment in transport and infrastructure businesses through this very protocol, and so I’m really excited to see what this will do for our superannuation scheme, for investment, for people getting involved in KiwiSaver as well, obviously resulting in the outcome of better investment and what that contributes to New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Argument by analogy from Australian superannuation practice to a claimed New Zealand outcome, with 'obviously resulting in the outcome of better investment' asserted rather than supported; nothing offered to connect the Australian case to the effect of this bill.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Many of them don’t own homes—we’re renters—and so the investment into housing, the investment into better health outcomes, I think, would be a better spend for the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act.
specificity.explanation: Names two broad investment directions (housing, health outcomes) and the relevant Act, but supplies no mechanism, amount, target or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The member is bright, he is bright-eyed, he is bushy-tailed, he’s enthusiastic, and he’s full of ideas.
civility.explanation: Good-humoured but faintly patronising characterisation of another member rather than engagement with his suggestion; teasing rather than an attack.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I think back to the Rt Hon Bill English, who as finance Minister directed the Super Fund to conduct a higher level of investment in New Zealand markets.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Bill English, as Minister of Finance, issued a ministerial direction to the Guardians of the NZ Superannuation Fund concerning greater investment in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury / NZ Super Fund published record of ministerial directions issued under section 64 of the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001; true if a direction from Bill English as Minister of Finance addressing New Zealand investment exists, false if no such direction was issued by him.

veracity.statement: That currently forms a very small portion of the fund’s overall investment portfolio.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand infrastructure makes up only a very small share of the NZ Superannuation Fund's total portfolio as at May 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Super Fund annual report / portfolio disclosures for 2023-24 showing the proportion of total fund assets held in New Zealand infrastructure; true if that share is a low single-digit percentage, false if it is a substantial share (say above 10%).

veracity.statement: We die seven to 10 years earlier than non-Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a Māori / non-Māori life expectancy gap of seven to ten years in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ period life tables (most recent to 2024) comparing Māori and non-Māori life expectancy at birth; true if the gap falls in the 7-10 year range for either sex, false if materially smaller or larger.

specificity.statement: However, the Official Information Act—by way of, I understand, sections 9(2)(b), 9(2)(i)—does allow entities to withhold the release of information on a number of grounds relating to commercial sensitivity.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific statutory withholding grounds by section number and ties them to the commercial-sensitivity concern raised, so the answer can be checked against the Act.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For members’ interest, the Super Fund does already have a number of direct investments in New Zealand in which it doesn’t have a controlling interest but which it does have a direct investment. This includes: Kaingaroa Timberlands, which obviously owns a large forest; Longroad; Datacom; Awanui; Kaha Ake; Fidelity Life; and NZ Gourmet—alongside significant property investments in hotels and land development.
specificity.explanation: Names seven individual holdings plus asset classes, all of which can be checked against the fund's disclosed portfolio.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The problem we have and the issue we have for Māori is we don’t get access to the Superannuation Fund. We die seven to 10 years earlier than non-Māori. If you follow the science and the data, it tells us that. So what we need is legislation and policy that aligns to be able to adjust the inequalities of superannuation so that we can get access to it sooner, earlier, so that Māori get access to their right and to what they’ve contributed to in their years of life.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy area and the direction of change (earlier access to superannuation for Māori) but supplies no age, no mechanism and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But I want to turn to clause 6 of the bill: sections 59 to 59B of the principal legislation are being replaced with section 59, “Status of certain entities”, which the Minister covered.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the exact clause and the exact sections of the principal Act being replaced, so the point is anchored to checkable text.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The point that I am simply making is that the Super Fund has been able to make investments of this nature while being subject to the OIA previously, and that gives me confidence that when it later takes controlling interests in entities that could be similar to those it already holds, this will not be prejudicial to its commercial performance in the way that the member raises.
rigor.explanation: An inductive inference from past non-controlling investments to future controlling ones, but it glides over the disanalogy the questioner actually raised: a controlling interest brings a different volume and kind of company information into the Guardians' hands, so past experience under the OIA does not straightforwardly carry over. Real reasoning, with a gap between evidence and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The problem we have and the issue we have for Māori is we don’t get access to the Superannuation Fund. We die seven to 10 years earlier than non-Māori. If you follow the science and the data, it tells us that. So what we need is legislation and policy that aligns to be able to adjust the inequalities of superannuation so that we can get access to it sooner, earlier, so that Māori get access to their right and to what they’ve contributed to in their years of life.
rigor.explanation: A genuine premise-to-conclusion argument: a shorter life expectancy means fewer years of drawing a contributed-to entitlement, therefore the eligibility settings should change. The inference is reasonable but incomplete — it appeals to the data without connecting the population-average gap to the individual eligibility rule, and offers nothing on why an age adjustment rather than another remedy follows.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If I was a company that was looking for an investment, large capital raised in some way, and a New Zealand Superannuation Fund was one of the options, if I knew that any information that I had about my company could be accessible via the Official Information Act (OIA), I’d be reticent. If I’ve got two offers on the table, one from the New Zealand Super Fund and one, say, from an overseas investment firm, and one of them I know will not be subject to the OIA and the other will be, I’d be quite concerned.
rigor.explanation: A clean conditional argument from a stated mechanism: if disclosure risk attaches to one bidder and not the other, a company choosing between them is disadvantaged by taking the Super Fund's money, which cuts against the bill's stated purpose. The conclusion follows from the premises; the weakness is that it assumes without argument that the withholding grounds would not cover commercially sensitive material.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The cumulative effect of the Crown’s actions and omissions had a devastating effect on the economic, social, and cultural development of Ngāti Tara Tokanui, leaving the iwi virtually landless by the 1920s.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Crown land purchasing and Native Land Court operation left Ngāti Tara Tokanui effectively landless by the 1920s.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The historical account and Crown acknowledgements in the Ngāti Tara Tokanui deed of settlement (signed July 2022) and the Waitangi Tribunal's Hauraki Report (2006); true if those records state the iwi was left virtually landless by the 1920s, false if they record substantial retained landholdings at that date.

veracity.statement: The Waitangi Tribunal heard the Hauraki claims, including the Ngāti Tara Tokanui Wai 714 claim lodged by the late Hone Tewaewae Williams, from 1998 to 2002. The tribunal heard 24 hearings and completed its report in 2006.
veracity.explanation: Three checkable assertions: the Wai 714 claimant's identity, the 1998–2002 hearing period with 24 hearings, and a 2006 report completion date.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal records for the Hauraki inquiry (Wai 686) and the Hauraki Report; true if the hearings ran 1998–2002 across 24 hearings, the report is dated 2006, and Wai 714 was lodged by Hone Tewaewae Williams; false if any of those dates, the hearing count, or the claimant differ.

veracity.statement: The bill was referred to the Māori Affairs Committee on 29 June 2023. The committee received and considered 15 submissions on the bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a referral date to select committee and a submission count.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliament bill record and the Māori Affairs Committee report on the Ngāti Tara Tokanui Claims Settlement Bill; true if the referral date is 29 June 2023 and 15 submissions were received, false if either differs.

veracity.statement: The negotiations with Ngāti Tara Tokanui began at Ngahutoitoi Marae in 2011.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a start date and venue for direct negotiations between the Crown and Ngāti Tara Tokanui.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ngāti Tara Tokanui deed of settlement summary and Te Arawhiti / Office for Māori Crown Relations negotiation timeline; true if direct negotiations commenced in 2011 at Ngahutoitoi Marae, false if the recorded commencement year or venue differs.

specificity.statement: The Waitangi Tribunal heard the Hauraki claims, including the Ngāti Tara Tokanui Wai 714 claim lodged by the late Hone Tewaewae Williams, from 1998 to 2002. The tribunal heard 24 hearings and completed its report in 2006.
specificity.explanation: Named claim number, named claimant, a date range, a hearing count and a report year — all directly checkable, where a vague 'long journey' framing was equally available.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: There are members who have contributed to this piece of legislation who will be proud today to have reached the second stage in the legislation, and who will be looking forward to the third reading, when it will pass into law.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Ngāti Tara Tokanui Claims Settlement Bill will complete its third reading and become law.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand legislation register and Hansard third-reading record; true if the Ngāti Tara Tokanui Claims Settlement Bill receives Royal assent, false if it lapses, is voted down or remains unpassed by the resolve-by date.

veracity.statement: In the years between 1909 and 1917 alone, the remains of kahikatea were reduced by 63 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific quantified loss of remaining kahikatea stands over an eight-year period early last century.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Forest Service / royal commission and historical forestry statistics on kahikatea (white pine) stand area or millable volume for 1909 and 1917; true if the recorded reduction is about 63%, false if materially different or unsupported by any such series.

veracity.statement: The kahikatea is the largest native tree—not the kauri, but the kahikatea—and, for context, these trees are so ancient ecologically, they are 160 to 180 million years old, which is to say the kahikatea tree came into existence before there were even birds on Planet Earth.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that kahikatea rather than kauri is New Zealand's largest native tree, and that the species/lineage dates to 160–180 million years ago, predating birds.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DOC / NZ Plant Conservation Network descriptions of tree size (kahikatea is the tallest at ~60 m; kauri is the largest by trunk volume/girth) and palaeobotanical dating of Podocarpaceae versus the ~150 Ma first appearance of birds in the fossil record; true if kahikatea is correctly described as largest and the dating stands, false if kauri holds the 'largest' designation or the dating is unsupported.

veracity.statement: I note that Andrew Little said that the Crown will apologise for confiscating large tracts of land, as well as for the policies and laws that were designed to dislocate Ngāti Tara Tokanui from their land, to erode their tribal structure—and, rightly, that is a just apology for a terrible loss—and, also, I would add, to destroy the ecological basis of the society and the culture of the livelihood of those people.
veracity.explanation: Relays what Andrew Little stated about the content of the Crown apology to Ngāti Tara Tokanui.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard record of Andrew Little's statements on the Ngāti Tara Tokanui settlement and the apology text in the deed of settlement / the bill; true if the apology covers confiscation of large tracts of land and policies designed to dislocate the iwi and erode tribal structure, false if the apology text or Little's remarks say otherwise.

veracity.statement: In fact, the historical account indicates that after having land confiscated, and after selling a large amount of land—although it’s not made clear, it appears that that was to pay bills—they were left with only 232 acres of land by 1995.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, citing the settlement's historical account, that Ngāti Tara Tokanui retained only 232 acres by 1995.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The historical account in the Ngāti Tara Tokanui deed of settlement / the bill's schedule; true if it records approximately 232 acres remaining in iwi ownership by 1995, false if it gives a materially different figure or date.

veracity.statement: But in terms of the actual response to the legislation, or to getting a settlement process under way, it’s been a good 25 years, and 13 years since the negotiations began.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two elapsed periods: roughly 25 years since the settlement process began and 13 years since negotiations for Ngāti Tara Tokanui commenced.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Office for Māori Crown Relations (Te Arawhiti) settlement timeline and the deed of settlement for Ngāti Tara Tokanui, giving the dates of the initial claim/settlement process and the start of formal negotiations; true if those dates are about 25 and 13 years before May 2024, false if materially different.

focus.statement: We do not, as Te Pāti Kākāriki—as we have articulated before—support the idea of full and final settlements.
focus.explanation: States a position on a specific feature of Treaty settlement policy — the full-and-final settlement mechanism — rather than characterising another party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It restores the property rights and provides compensation for an iwi which had their property taken in an unjust way, and it was in breach of the Treaty of Waitangi.
focus.explanation: Engages what the bill before the House actually does — restoration of property rights and compensation — with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In fact, the historical account indicates that after having land confiscated, and after selling a large amount of land—although it’s not made clear, it appears that that was to pay bills—they were left with only 232 acres of land by 1995.
specificity.explanation: Carries a precise acreage, a date and a named source document, so the claim can be checked directly against the historical account.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But it appears that the iwi never got to benefit from it, because some of the commercial arrangements that they entered into were all cost and no reward.
