focus.statement: There’s no need to be a cellar with a “c”, because all you are being through this bill is a seller with an “s”. There’s no geographical proximity to the origin. The definition of a cellar door with a “c” is that manufacturers and producers offer alcohol for sale from their premises.
focus.explanation: Engages the drafting of the measure before the House — whether the bill's coverage is tied to producers' own premises.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What the bill seeks to be able to address is to make it easier for cellar door operators to get through what used to be quite a hurdle of red tape in terms of licensing their cellar door and their cellar restaurants.
focus.explanation: Directly describes the purpose and mechanism of the measure before the House — licensing requirements for cellar door operators — with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have things in our law that are getting in the way of a manufacturer of a product that will actually help our population kick a really dangerous habit, and we have not taken the time to address that issue in this Parliament.
specificity.explanation: Refers to unnamed 'things in our law' with no statute, provision, mechanism or remedy identified; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So does the bill explicitly prevent an operator, a seller with an “s”, putting a bottle on the table, setting out some 35 millilitre glasses and advising people that they can taste the wine? It doesn’t sound much like a cellar door experience to me.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete scenario and the 35 millilitre measure, identifying a checkable gap (number of pours, not just size); stops short of citing the clause or proposing a fix.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The wine industry is, in export, over $2 billion of earnings to our New Zealand economy. In the local market, it is in excess of $1 billion already.
specificity.explanation: Two named magnitudes attached to named markets (export and local); lacks a source or reference year, which is what keeps it off the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So what I would ask is that this Parliament, when it puts in yet another very narrow bill that looks at one area which might suit a particular group in its constituency, thinks wider—think wider next time there’s a member’s bill and put in one that will help this problem.
civility.explanation: Pointed — hints that the bill serves a sponsor's constituency interest — but the criticism stays on the bill's narrowness and names no one; she elsewhere congratulates the sponsor.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So, because of those reasons and because I don’t think that we should take it as lightly as some other members of the House are this evening, I don’t think we should take our responsibility lightly around minimising alcohol harm and taking very seriously anything we do to roll back legislation that is put there to protect communities and to manage the responsible consumption of alcohol—I think we need to be far more cautious, and we need to have much better legislation than this before we move forward with it.
civility.explanation: Suggests other members are treating alcohol harm lightly, which edges toward the people rather than the argument, but it is unnamed, mild and immediately returned to the substance of the legislation.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There’s no need to be a cellar with a “c”, because all you are being through this bill is a seller with an “s”. There’s no geographical proximity to the origin. The definition of a cellar door with a “c” is that manufacturers and producers offer alcohol for sale from their premises.
rigor.explanation: Rests the conclusion that the bill is 'inaccurate' on an appeal to definition and a spelling pun; the underlying point (no proximity-to-producer requirement) is real, but the inference from 'the dictionary sense of cellar door differs' to 'the bill is defective' is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Because of the economic vandalism of the last Government, we saw public expenditure go up by 80 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that public (core Crown) expenditure rose by 80 percent under the previous Labour-led Government.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenses series (Financial Statements of the Government / Budget documents) comparing the last full year before the 2017 change of government with 2023/24; true if the increase is approximately 80%, false if materially lower (e.g. under ~65%) or higher.

veracity.statement: The economy is in a recession, we have a budget deficit of over $9.4 billion, and we know we’re going to be in deficit until 2027.
veracity.explanation: Two present-tense assertions: that New Zealand is in recession as at May 2024, and that the Crown's budget deficit exceeds $9.4 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP releases up to March 2024 (true if two or more consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth had been recorded), and Treasury OBEGAL for 2023/24 in HYEFU 2023 / Budget 2024 (true if the deficit is above $9.4b, false if below).

veracity.statement: Because of people like Willie Jackson, our grandkids are going to inherit debt that has ballooned over $100 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Crown debt has grown to over $100 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Financial Statements of the Government, net core Crown debt and gross sovereign-issued debt as at 30 June 2023/2024; true if the relevant debt measure exceeds $100 billion, false if below.

veracity.statement: The reason I bring that point up is because, on this side of the House, we know tourism and hospitality is our second-biggest export earner in this country—tourism is the second-biggest export earner in this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that tourism is New Zealand's second-largest export earner as at May 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / MBIE tourism satellite account and merchandise export rankings for the year to March 2024; true if tourism export earnings rank second behind dairy, false if another category (e.g. meat, wood, or non-dairy food) exceeded tourism.

veracity.statement: That’s because Mr Smith was actually the chair of the board of New Zealand Wine Growers for over six years before he came into politics, and he was responsible for taking New Zealand wine sales offshore to over the $1 billion export mark.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Stuart Smith chaired the New Zealand Winegrowers board for more than six years prior to entering Parliament, and that wine exports passed $1 billion under his chairmanship.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Winegrowers annual reports and board records for the dates and length of Smith's chairmanship, and NZ Winegrowers/Stats NZ export data for the year wine exports first exceeded $1 billion; true if the tenure exceeds six years and the $1b threshold was crossed during it, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: There will be no surprise that “Stewie” Smith has won his seat in four general elections now, because the people he knows, the people that he represents know that when he comes to Wellington, he brings their voice to this Parliament and he makes a difference.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Stuart Smith has won his electorate seat at four general elections as at May 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission official results for the Kaikōura electorate at the 2014, 2017, 2020 and 2023 general elections; true if Smith won the electorate at four elections, false if fewer or more.

veracity.statement: The prohibition of synthetic urine bill that I brought to this House that was voted down—a very important bill that I wasn’t taking the piss on, but I wasn’t able to get it through.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the speaker introduced a member's bill prohibiting synthetic urine and that the House voted it down.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bills register and the Hansard division record for a Doocey member's bill on synthetic urine; true if such a bill was introduced in his name and defeated at a reading, false if no such bill exists or it was not voted down.

veracity.statement: I stand here tonight as also the Minister for hospitality—New Zealand’s first Minister for hospitality.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the speaker holds a hospitality portfolio and is the first New Zealand minister to do so.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DPMC ministerial list for the 2023 coalition Government and the historical record of ministerial portfolio titles; true if 'Hospitality' appears in Doocey's portfolio title and in no earlier minister's title, false if an earlier hospitality portfolio existed.

divination.statement: The economy is in a recession, we have a budget deficit of over $9.4 billion, and we know we’re going to be in deficit until 2027.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Crown's operating balance will remain in deficit through to 2027.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Treasury Financial Statements of the Government OBEGAL out-turns for the fiscal years to 2026/27; true if every year to and including 2026/27 records a deficit, false if a surplus is recorded in any of those years.

specificity.statement: The economy is in a recession, we have a budget deficit of over $9.4 billion, and we know we’re going to be in deficit until 2027.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete fiscal figure ($9.4 billion), a named economic condition and a dated horizon — all checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So whatever we can do to support tourism and hospitality in this country is going to bring people jobs; it’s going to bring them better incomes.
specificity.explanation: 'Whatever we can do' names no measure, cost, timeframe or job number; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Because of people like Willie Jackson, our grandkids are going to inherit debt that has ballooned over $100 billion.
civility.explanation: Singles out a named individual member as personally responsible for the national debt. Not a direct insult, but it attributes blame to the person rather than engaging a decision or policy.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So whatever we can do to support tourism and hospitality in this country is going to bring people jobs; it’s going to bring them better incomes.
rigor.explanation: Infers from the sector's export ranking that any support for it will produce jobs and higher incomes. The conclusion is plausible but the leap from sector size to employment and income outcomes is asserted, with no mechanism or evidence offered — a gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Let’s not forget when we talk of a sector like tourism and hospitality, that’s a sector where people can go to the smaller regions of New Zealand, the smaller rural towns—only places Labour MPs have seen on a map—they’re the places that we represent on the side of the House, because we represent hard-working New Zealanders on the side of the House.
focus.explanation: Starts on a real policy point about tourism in smaller regions, but the weight of the sentence is party framing — a jibe that Labour MPs have only seen rural towns on a map, and a claim about which side represents 'hard-working New Zealanders'. No measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: On this side of the House, we know that businesses employ people—unlike that side, who think Government employs people.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the other party supposedly believes. No policy, mechanism, figure or outcome is engaged once the characterisation of the opposition is removed.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It allows cellar door wineries to charge people for tasting their wine, for tasting 35 millilitres of their wine at a time.
specificity.explanation: States the concrete mechanism of the bill (permitting charging for tastings) and the exact sample volume, 35 millilitres; checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As we’ve mentioned, areas like the Marlborough region produce over 80 percent of New Zealand’s wine, and, over there, tourism accounts for 6 percent of the gross domestic product.
specificity.explanation: Two named regions/figures with percentages attached — precise enough that a reader could go and check both numbers.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: By allowing flexibility with licensing, where cellar door wineries can hold both an on-licence and an off-licence under the same legal entity, this bill will reduce unnecessary costs on the businesses, therefore, once again, cutting red tape and pulling back regulations.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific licensing change (holding an on-licence and off-licence under one legal entity) and the intended effect, though no cost figure or timeframe is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s about stripping back unnecessary regulation as much as possible so businesses can just do what they love doing, work the mahi they enjoy to do.
specificity.explanation: A general statement of philosophy — no regulation named, no mechanism, no measure or timeframe; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As we’ve mentioned, areas like the Marlborough region produce over 80 percent of New Zealand’s wine, and, over there, tourism accounts for 6 percent of the gross domestic product.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that Marlborough produces more than 80 percent of New Zealand's wine, and that tourism accounts for 6 percent of GDP (in Marlborough, on the natural reading).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Winegrowers annual report vintage/production statistics for the seasons around 2024: true if Marlborough's share of national wine production exceeds 80%, false if materially below. For the second limb, Stats NZ / Marlborough regional tourism GDP figures: true if tourism's share of GDP is about 6%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The Lebanese community established the second winery in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the winery founded by the Lebanese Corban family was the second winery established in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Documented founding dates of New Zealand wineries (e.g. Te Papa / NZ History records, Mission Estate 1851, Corbans 1902): true if no more than one winery predates Corbans, false if several New Zealand wineries were established before 1902.

rigor.statement: Also, what it means is that by charging for these samples of wine, we’re also giving that message to the public that “Hey, we encourage responsible drinking.” So these two points indicate the Government’s commitment to responsible alcohol consumption.
rigor.explanation: The inference is that permitting wineries to charge for samples signals, and produces, responsible drinking. Nothing is offered to connect price to consumption behaviour, and the conclusion about a 'commitment to responsible alcohol consumption' is asserted rather than shown — a non sequitur resting on an assumed price effect.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And I think in the absence of established definitions for these other alcohols—for example, craft beer, gin, etc.—and what component of alcohol is acceptable, what would make a sample at this stage? And we said this in our report—the majority of the committee said this—that, at this stage, we just want to stick to just wine.
rigor.explanation: Argues from a stated premise (no settled statutory definition of 'craft beer' or an agreed sample measure for spirits, confirmed by a submitter) to the conclusion that the bill should stay limited to wine for now. The inference tracks the premise, though it leans on a single submitter's answer as evidence that no definition exists.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: By allowing flexibility with licensing, where cellar door wineries can hold both an on-licence and an off-licence under the same legal entity, this bill will reduce unnecessary costs on the businesses, therefore, once again, cutting red tape and pulling back regulations.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure before the House — the licensing mechanism and its effect on winery costs. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I hear the concerns by some people across the House; I really do. But I was surprised that the concerns were so strong when, in fact, this amendment bill, as I said, promotes responsible alcohol consumption, and it does this, as I mentioned earlier, by stipulating the sample size.
civility.explanation: Addresses opponents' objections directly and disagrees on the substance of the bill without imputing motive, sneering or attacking anyone personally, in a debate where alcohol-harm objections invited a dismissive reply.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As the OECD survey released earlier this week confirmed, the economy is ailing and there has been a substantial deterioration in New Zealand’s fiscal position in recent years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an OECD survey published in the week to 9 May 2024 found the New Zealand economy weak and the fiscal position substantially deteriorated in recent years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The OECD Economic Survey of New Zealand published in early May 2024: true if it characterises the economy as weak/slowing and describes a substantial deterioration in the fiscal position over recent years; false if the survey contains no such findings or was not released in that week.

veracity.statement: The Government currently invests more than $70 billion a year in social services. But despite that investment, many people are not getting the help they need when they need it, and we see evidence of that in increasing welfare dependency, declining school attendance and achievement, poorer health outcomes, and rising rates of youth and violent crime. What this demonstrates is that good intentions are not sufficient to change outcomes. Just chucking money at problems doesn’t work.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: annual government spend on social services exceeds $70 billion, and that welfare dependency, school attendance/achievement, health outcomes and youth/violent crime have all been moving in the stated directions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Budget 2024 expenditure tables for social services/social sector spend (true if the aggregate exceeds $70bn/yr), plus MSD benefit-recipient series, Ministry of Education regular-attendance series, and Police victimisation statistics for 2018-2024; false if the spend figure is materially below $70bn or if the named indicators do not show the stated direction of travel.

veracity.statement: Will she look to increase the funding for food support, given organisations like the Salvation Army are reporting increased demand as a direct result of declines for hardship support through the Ministry of Social Development (MSD)?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Salvation Army and comparable organisations have reported rising demand, and attributes that rise directly to reduced MSD hardship assistance.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Salvation Army State of the Nation / foodbank demand reporting for 2023-24 and MSD hardship-assistance grant statistics: true if the Salvation Army reported increased demand and MSD hardship grants declined over the same period with the organisation itself drawing that link; false if demand reporting shows no increase or hardship-assistance volumes did not fall.

veracity.statement: Of about 188,000 people who are currently receiving the jobseeker support benefit, only 53 of them have employment case managers at any given time, so this early intervention is crucial for making sure that all job seekers are taking the steps they need to find work.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that approximately 188,000 people were receiving jobseeker support at the time of speaking (May 2024).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets / quarterly benefit statistics for the March or June 2024 quarter: true if jobseeker support recipients number approximately 188,000; false if materially different from that figure.

specificity.statement: There is no country in the world in which I would rather live and raise my family. But the fundamentals need to be sorted: getting Government spending under control; delivering better value for money; and creating an environment in which businesses want to invest, innovate, take risks, hire people, build things, and make things.
specificity.explanation: A list of broad directions — control spending, better value, a good business environment — with no figures, mechanisms or timeframes. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government currently invests more than $70 billion a year in social services. But despite that investment, many people are not getting the help they need when they need it, and we see evidence of that in increasing welfare dependency, declining school attendance and achievement, poorer health outcomes, and rising rates of youth and violent crime. What this demonstrates is that good intentions are not sufficient to change outcomes. Just chucking money at problems doesn’t work.
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete spending figure ($70 billion a year) and names five specific outcome indicators, all of which someone could go and check.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Social investment will use an evidence and analytical approach to invest in those services which will have the biggest impact for dollar spent.
specificity.explanation: Asked whether specific struggling services would be funded, the reply names no service, no criterion, no amount and no date — a statement of general method that commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I want to be very clear about the fact that financial capability services will continue to be provided, as they have been, at the level they were funded to. There is a procurement process under way, which will mean that some providers that were providing a service will be different. But services will continue to be provided.
specificity.explanation: Names the service class (financial capability services) and the mechanism (a procurement process), and is clear that providers may change — but supplies no funding figure, no timeline for the procurement, and no detail on which providers are affected.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What I can commit to is that this Government will prioritise addressing the cost of living crisis, providing tax relief, supporting more New Zealanders into employment and out of the hardship.
specificity.explanation: Four broad priorities with no amounts, no mechanisms and no dates. 'Tax relief' is the only near-concrete item and it is unquantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Only by grappling with the long-term drivers of hardship will we be able to reduce the demand for hardship. The Government is committed to doing this, consistent with its coalition commitments, whether through improving school attendance, supporting more people off welfare and into work, or grappling with the complex drivers of dysfunction. We are committed to taking action to reduce hardship, rather than just setting up working groups and talkfests.
specificity.explanation: Policy areas are named but nothing is quantified — no targets, no funding, no dates, and 'the complex drivers of dysfunction' carries no operational content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: All new jobseeker beneficiaries who have work obligations must now meet with the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) within two weeks of starting their benefit to determine their next steps towards finding work.
specificity.explanation: States exactly who is covered, what they must do, with which agency, and within what timeframe. Fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Of about 188,000 people who are currently receiving the jobseeker support benefit, only 53 of them have employment case managers at any given time, so this early intervention is crucial for making sure that all job seekers are taking the steps they need to find work.
specificity.explanation: Gives a recipient count and a case-manager count and links both to the rationale for the new requirement — precise enough that anyone could check it against MSD statistics.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Government currently invests more than $70 billion a year in social services. But despite that investment, many people are not getting the help they need when they need it, and we see evidence of that in increasing welfare dependency, declining school attendance and achievement, poorer health outcomes, and rising rates of youth and violent crime. What this demonstrates is that good intentions are not sufficient to change outcomes. Just chucking money at problems doesn’t work.
rigor.explanation: From high spending co-occurring with worsening indicators it concludes that spending money 'doesn't work'. The observation is consistent with the conclusion but does not establish it — no counterfactual is offered, and worsening indicators could equally be why spending rose. A gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In answer to the first part of the question, yes. Social investment is about doing the right thing. I would encourage that member to ask herself: who wouldn’t, if they could, invest to give a young child the opportunity to live a productive, rewarding life rather than a life of dependency and, potentially, crime? Data matters.
rigor.explanation: The defence of the approach rests on a rhetorical question inviting agreement that helping children is good — a bare appeal to emotion and to unanimity. It also answers a question about deficit-based data by substituting the uncontested premise that intervention is desirable, which nobody disputed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I reject the assertion that’s been made in that comment about the service that MSD provide. But I do accept, as I said before, that there is genuine hardship in our communities, which in most cases has been caused by the previous Government’s inactions, which has led to an economic crisis, and families everywhere are doing it incredibly tough.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a two-step causal chain — the previous government's 'inactions' caused an economic crisis, which caused 'most' current hardship — with no mechanism, no evidence and no policy identified. The conclusion about causation is simply announced, not derived.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will her social investment approach overlay data with people’s lived experience and what works to build resilience, or will it revert back to what National did before: deficit-based data that treats people as numbers?
focus.explanation: A genuine policy question about the methodology of social investment — lived experience versus deficit-based data — but the second limb is framed as a return to what the other party 'did before' rather than to a named policy or programme.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will she look to increase the funding for food support, given organisations like the Salvation Army are reporting increased demand as a direct result of declines for hardship support through the Ministry of Social Development (MSD)?
focus.explanation: Names a specific funding line (food support), a specific agency (MSD) and a specific reported outcome from a named organisation. Textbook scrutiny of an identified policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will she prioritise support for social services at this year’s Budget, given forecasted increases in unemployment, incomes for our poorest New Zealanders not keeping up with the cost of living, and cuts to policies that did help to alleviate the pressure for many families?
focus.explanation: Directs the question at a specific decision (Budget 2024 social services funding) and grounds it in three named conditions — unemployment forecasts, real incomes at the bottom, and policy cuts. Policy content throughout, no party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Only by grappling with the long-term drivers of hardship will we be able to reduce the demand for hardship. The Government is committed to doing this, consistent with its coalition commitments, whether through improving school attendance, supporting more people off welfare and into work, or grappling with the complex drivers of dysfunction. We are committed to taking action to reduce hardship, rather than just setting up working groups and talkfests.
focus.explanation: Names three genuine policy directions (school attendance, welfare-to-work, drivers of hardship), but closes on a contrast with 'working groups and talkfests' that characterises the other side's approach rather than naming a measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Has she received feedback that, as a result of her Government’s cuts, Vaiola Pacific Island Budgeting Service Trust, Māngere, which provides critical services for Māngere working families, will have less money to work with these struggling families?
focus.explanation: Names a specific provider, a specific community and a specific claimed consequence of a funding decision. Scrutiny anchored to an identifiable case rather than general party criticism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How will the commitment in the coalition agreement between National and the ACT Party to provide opportunity for all in education, health, and employment reduce hardship in the long term?
focus.explanation: Points at a named document (the National–ACT coalition agreement) and three named policy areas, asking about the causal link to hardship. Party names appear only to identify the agreement, not as an attack.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: My statements included: that workers have endured 14 years without any adjustment to tax brackets; that Government spending went up 80 percent; that even with this increase in spending, health waiting lists have grown, educational achievement has fallen, and violent crime has soared; that this year’s Budget won’t be an instant fix but that, instead, it will lay the ground for steady progress for today, tomorrow, and the longer term.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two dated quantitative claims: that personal income tax thresholds have been unchanged for 14 years, and that government spending rose 80 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IRD/Treasury record of the last change to personal income tax thresholds (true if the last adjustment was in 2010, false if thresholds were adjusted after 2010); and Treasury core Crown expenditure series (true if core Crown spending rose approximately 80% over the period she refers to, false if materially lower).

veracity.statement: Are the 17 percent of New Zealanders that are going to see no direct benefit from her tax cuts immune from the cost of living crisis?
veracity.explanation: Embedded factual premise that 17 percent of New Zealanders receive no direct benefit from the Government's 2024 tax package.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD distributional analysis of the 2024 personal income tax package; true if approximately 17% of the adult population/New Zealanders receive no direct gain, false if the share is materially different.

veracity.statement: I have advice from the New Zealand Treasury that our proposals will put downward pressure on rents.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Treasury has advised the Government that its tax proposals (restoring interest deductibility for landlords) will put downward pressure on rents.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published Treasury advice or regulatory impact statement on the restoration of interest deductibility; true if it states the change will put downward pressure on rents, false if Treasury advice contains no such conclusion or reaches the opposite view.

veracity.statement: Does the Minister agree with Te Uru Kahika, the collective of regional and unitary councils, that “local views risk being bypassed for expedience” in the granting of fast-track consents, and, if not, why not?
veracity.explanation: Relays a quoted position attributed to Te Uru Kahika, the collective of regional and unitary councils, about the Fast-track Approvals Bill.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Uru Kahika's public submission or statement on the Fast-track Approvals Bill; true if it contains the quoted phrase 'local views risk being bypassed for expedience' or an unambiguous equivalent, false if no such statement exists or the words are from another body.

veracity.statement: There is one dedicated gas storage facility, but only 6 petajoules of the 12 petajoules it can store can be used, as the rest is needed to maintain reservoir pressure. Six petajoules is around 15 days of gas supply for the New Zealand market.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific technical figures for New Zealand's single gas storage facility (Ahuroa): 12 PJ nominal capacity, 6 PJ usable, equating to roughly 15 days of national gas supply.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE gas statistics and the operator's (Firstgas/Ahuroa) published storage capacity figures, plus annual NZ gas consumption; true if usable working volume is approximately 6 PJ of a ~12 PJ total and 6 PJ equals roughly 15 days of demand, false if the capacity or the implied daily demand is materially different.

veracity.statement: So, yes, the money was returned, because we’re not going to waste taxpayers’ money like the last Government did on ghost projects like Lake Onslow, which weren’t going to come until 2040, when we have information such as this [holds up graph], where the number of low residual notices from Transpower have increased dramatically from zero up to 15 per year since that last Government cancelled oil and gas exploration.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Transpower low residual notices rose from zero to 15 per year following the 2018 oil and gas exploration decision.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Transpower's published record of low residual situation/notice issuances by year; true if the count rose from zero pre-2018 to approximately 15 in a recent year, false if notices were issued before 2018 or the recent annual count is materially different from 15.

veracity.statement: What’s happened because of the oil and gas exploration is we are having more and more coal being burnt at Huntly, which has twice the carbon intensity. That party on the other side of the House, their policies are pro-coal.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that coal burning at Huntly has increased and that coal has twice the carbon intensity of gas for electricity generation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE electricity generation fuel statistics for Huntly coal use over recent years, and standard emissions factors for coal versus natural gas generation; true if coal use has risen and coal's CO2 per unit of generation is roughly double that of gas, false if coal use has not increased or the intensity ratio is materially different.

specificity.statement: My statements included: that workers have endured 14 years without any adjustment to tax brackets; that Government spending went up 80 percent; that even with this increase in spending, health waiting lists have grown, educational achievement has fallen, and violent crime has soared; that this year’s Budget won’t be an instant fix but that, instead, it will lay the ground for steady progress for today, tomorrow, and the longer term.

rigor.statement: They banned oil and gas exploration and then they spent the last number of years on pumped hydro down the bottom of the South Island, a project that wasn’t even going to come on stream until 2040. focus.statement: Looking back in terms of the annual review, I am mindful of the fact that we’ve had, over the last year, $19.6 million spent by the previous Minister on his failed merger of TV and RNZ, and so we’re mindful of that, and we don’t want to be making those sorts of mistakes further down the line.
focus.explanation: Names a specific programme, a specific dollar figure and a specific outcome in the context of the annual review — scrutiny of a spending decision, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is not only a great committee, as Chlöe Swarbrick says, but it is also important that we tackle and address that fundamental question of the funding and the financing and who pays and have that advice as we tackle the work around climate adaptation.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance of the inquiry — the funding and cost-allocation question the committee should examine. No party framing, no characterisation of opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, mother Nature has just told them they put in one that was too small to start with. So why are we creating this cost and making this barrier to people doing the right thing and putting in correct and sensible infrastructure?
focus.explanation: Entirely on the regulatory mechanism and its effect on landowners; no reference to any other party or its record.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It is not only a great committee, as Chlöe Swarbrick says, but it is also important that we tackle and address that fundamental question of the funding and the financing and who pays and have that advice as we tackle the work around climate adaptation.
specificity.explanation: Names a topic ('who pays', funding and financing) but supplies no mechanism, no options, no figures and no timeframe. A direction rather than checkable content; nothing nearby in her speech adds detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As we’ve seen, climate change - charged weather events also amplify inequities that are already baked into the way that our economic system works, so we need to be having these really critical discussions about the interface with Te Tiriti o Waitangi, about the interface with whether we’re going to take the same approach to those who have baches or those marae that are on coastlines, for example.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete cases the terms of reference would have to distinguish — coastal baches versus coastal marae — and the Te Tiriti interface, but offers no mechanism, criteria or figures for how they would be treated differently.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When the farmer goes to replace that culvert, the challenge is they have to get a resource consent if they want to put in a bigger culvert.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a named regulatory instrument (resource consent), a specific piece of infrastructure (culverts) and the exact trigger (upsizing after a washout); checkable against the rules, though no cost figure or plan rule is cited.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: At the moment, there’s so many rules and regulations getting in the way of people just being able to do sensible extraction, being able to keep the gravel banks low in many areas against their properties, and this is going to just create more of an opportunity for floodwaters to extend into farmland, to housing, to everything else.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete activity (gravel extraction from the riverbed, staying out of the waterway) and the harm claimed, but no rule, consent pathway, region or quantity is identified — 'so many rules and regulations' carries no checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But if we’re to reflect on why it is that this is so fundamentally important to New Zealanders, just over a year ago we were hammered in the North Island by deadly and devastating climate change - charged weather events, and this followed so-called unprecedented, so-called one-in-100-year weather events that had battered Northland, the East Coast, the West Coast, and the top of the North Island every single year in recent living history.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that events characterised as 'one-in-100-year' struck Northland, the East Coast, the West Coast and the top of the North Island in every single year of recent years, preceding the early-2023 North Island events.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NIWA / MetService severe weather event records and central- or local-government state-of-emergency declarations for 2018–2022; true if each of those years contains at least one event in the named regions officially described as a one-in-100-year (1% AEP) event, false if one or more of those years has no such event.

veracity.statement: When the farmer goes to replace that culvert, the challenge is they have to get a resource consent if they want to put in a bigger culvert.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that replacing a blown-out farm culvert with a larger one triggers a resource consent requirement, rather than being a permitted activity.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Regional plan permitted-activity rules for culverts and the National Environmental Standards for Freshwater (2020) regs 70–71 on culvert installation; true if upsizing a culvert beyond the permitted diameter/hydraulic-capacity thresholds requires resource consent, false if like-for-larger replacement is permitted without consent under the standard rules.

veracity.statement: One of the things that the select committee did in the 52nd Parliament was travel to the United Kingdom to hear about their climate legislation, which by that stage had been 10 years in the making.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that the Environment Committee of the 52nd Parliament (2017–2020) travelled to the UK to study UK climate legislation, and that the UK legislation was about ten years old at that point.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary committee travel records / Hansard and committee reports on the Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Bill for evidence of a UK visit; and the enactment date of the UK Climate Change Act 2008 against the year of the visit. True if a UK trip is recorded and the Act was roughly a decade old then, false if no such travel occurred.

veracity.statement: Adaptation has been a focus of the work that Minister Shane Jones was doing as part of the Provincial Growth Fund, and I’ll raise an example here. He put money into the Taradale stop bank.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Provincial Growth Fund, under Shane Jones as the responsible Minister, funded work on the Taradale stopbank in Hawke's Bay.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Provincial Growth Fund / Kānoa investment announcements and the PGF project register; true if a PGF grant or loan to the Taradale (Hawke's Bay) stopbank or flood-protection scheme is recorded, false if no such allocation appears.

rigor.statement: To that effect, we also need to outline that getting a new bucket—that is, to adapt to the changing climate—doesn’t actually mean all too much if you’re not also focused on stopping the increased leakage.
rigor.explanation: An argument by analogy: adaptation without mitigation is a replacement bucket with the leak unfixed. The analogy maps onto the underlying claim reasonably (adaptation capacity is exceeded if emissions keep rising), but the conclusion rests on the metaphor rather than on any offered evidence about the limits of adaptation.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As we’ve seen, climate change - charged weather events also amplify inequities that are already baked into the way that our economic system works, so we need to be having these really critical discussions about the interface with Te Tiriti o Waitangi, about the interface with whether we’re going to take the same approach to those who have baches or those marae that are on coastlines, for example.
rigor.explanation: Premise (weather events amplify existing inequities) supports the conclusion (the inquiry must address distributional and Treaty questions) without a large gap; the premise itself is asserted rather than evidenced, but the inference from it is sound.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, mother Nature has just told them they put in one that was too small to start with. So why are we creating this cost and making this barrier to people doing the right thing and putting in correct and sensible infrastructure?
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real rule: the flood demonstrated the original culvert was undersized, therefore consenting the larger replacement imposes cost for no gain. It follows loosely, but it treats the consent process as having no purpose other than obstruction — the possible downstream effects a consent exists to assess are assumed away rather than addressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: At the moment, there’s so many rules and regulations getting in the way of people just being able to do sensible extraction, being able to keep the gravel banks low in many areas against their properties, and this is going to just create more of an opportunity for floodwaters to extend into farmland, to housing, to everything else.
rigor.explanation: A causal chain — restrictions on gravel extraction lead to raised riverbeds, which lead to greater flood spread. The chain is coherent, but nothing is offered to connect the steps (no evidence of aggradation rates or of flooding attributable to the rules), so the conclusion outruns what was shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, if that piece of adaptation work hadn’t happened, when the cyclone went through there would have been even greater damage happen because of the floodwaters—from the banks, obviously, if they hadn’t been rebuilt.
rigor.explanation: A counterfactual inferred from the stopbank's purpose: had it not been rebuilt, cyclone damage would have been worse. The inference is plausible on its face but rests on an unstated assumption that the works held during Gabrielle; no engineering assessment or damage comparison is offered to support the counterfactual.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And I think that it’s really disappointing that the Government wasn’t able to move faster, wasn’t able to engage, wasn’t able to address those concerns.
focus.explanation: Directed at the Government's response to the Newshub closure — a real event and a real accountability point — but no specific policy, mechanism or measure is named, so the weight sits on generalised criticism of the Government rather than on a policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And in some instances, in fact, coalition partners—some members of the Government—made really insensitive comments about that very fact, and I think that’s pretty disappointing.
focus.explanation: Once the characterisation of coalition partners' remarks is removed there is no policy content — no measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Just quickly, can the Minister comment on the roll-out of ultra-fast broadband, and I ask how he has seen the uptake of it has been, the number of homes and businesses that this is projected to affect, and how that looks for New Zealand going forward.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named programme and its measurable outcomes (uptake, homes and businesses reached), with no party framing at all, though it carries no figures of its own.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And in some instances, in fact, coalition partners—some members of the Government—made really insensitive comments about that very fact, and I think that’s pretty disappointing.
civility.explanation: Imputes insensitivity to unnamed Government members. Pointed and edging toward the person, but no individual is named and no attack on character or competence is made.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So it would just be good if the Minister could answer maybe just one question today.
civility.explanation: A sarcastic dig at the Minister personally rather than at his policy — mocking his willingness to answer. Short of a direct insult but no longer purely on the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Those gatekeepers have shifted from being local media platforms—in many cases locally and independently owned media platforms—and it has shifted instead to some of the largest and most powerful media entities; in fact, the largest and most powerful companies we have seen in history. And so it is our responsibility in this House to ensure that we can guarantee and secure a plurality of media for New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: A premise about a shift in distribution gatekeepers is offered, and the conclusion about Parliament's responsibility to secure media plurality broadly tracks it, but the step from 'gatekeepers have changed' to 'we must guarantee plurality' is asserted rather than shown — nothing connects concentration of platforms to a loss of plurality that legislation could remedy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, if someone thinks it was well handled, I’d like to hear where and how, because you had a Minister who was replaced along the way.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the Government's response to the Newshub closure was badly handled rests on the single fact of a ministerial change. That is a non sequitur — a reshuffle can have many causes, and nothing is offered linking it to the quality of the response.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’m sure he realises that He Poutama Rangatahi is co-designed with the community provider, which is what, in many ways, makes it successful, because it is locally led and locally delivered.
rigor.explanation: A causal claim that co-design makes the programme successful, supported only by restating the same feature ('because it is locally led and locally delivered'). Effectively circular; no evaluation or outcome evidence is offered to connect the design feature to the result.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So my questions, in finishing, are: what industry feedback has the Minister seen in the last year from New Zealand’s major news media players about the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill?
specificity.explanation: Names a specific bill, a specific class of respondent and a defined period, so the answer sought is concrete and checkable; it stops short of asking for particular submissions or figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The ministry has been conducting a review of the Broadcasting Act to strengthen the media system in New Zealand. Where is the review currently at, and are we on track for planned consultation to begin?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific review and the specific milestone (commencement of planned consultation) being asked about, so the answer would be checkable; no dates or figures are supplied.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Of course, they were in Government for six years, and they did manage to spend $19,604,000 on a programme to merge Radio New Zealand and TVNZ, which was nixed—nixed—by the previous Prime Minister, Mr Hipkins, I think, on 8 February.
specificity.explanation: Gives an exact dollar figure to the dollar, names the programme, the entities to be merged, the person who cancelled it and the date — entirely checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the 2022-23 year, 2,710 young people participated in the programmes, which I think is a great result.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise participation count tied to a named year and programme; someone could check it directly. Slightly diluted by the unquantified 'great result'.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: He never answered one of our questions, so I’ll repeat the questions for the Minister.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister answered none of the questions put to him in the preceding portion of the annual review.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard transcript of Paul Goldsmith's immediately preceding contribution in this annual review debate; false if he gave a substantive answer to any question put by Opposition members in that contribution, true if none of the questions received an answer.

veracity.statement: Also, $117 million was reprioritised over four years—over four years—to New Zealand On Air to address priority challenges.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific reprioritisation of $117 million over four years to New Zealand On Air.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget appropriation documents and NZ On Air / Ministry for Culture and Heritage funding records; true if a reprioritisation of approximately $117 million over a four-year period to NZ On Air is recorded, false if the figure or the recipient agency differs materially.

veracity.statement: Of course, they were in Government for six years, and they did manage to spend $19,604,000 on a programme to merge Radio New Zealand and TVNZ, which was nixed—nixed—by the previous Prime Minister, Mr Hipkins, I think, on 8 February.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that $19,604,000 was spent on the Strong Public Media (RNZ–TVNZ merger) programme and that Chris Hipkins cancelled it on 8 February.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry for Culture and Heritage / Treasury figures for total spend on the Strong Public Media programme, and the Government announcement record for the cancellation of the RNZ–TVNZ merger; true if the spend is approximately $19.6 million and the cancellation was announced by Hipkins on 8 February 2023, false if either figure or date is materially different.

veracity.statement: Just a 10-second answer to that question: it was one of the greatest investments in infrastructure in our recent history so that 87 percent of the country now has access to ultra-fast broadband and New Zealanders as a whole are very well equipped to engage in the modern world of media and communications.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 87 percent of the country now has access to ultra-fast broadband.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Crown Infrastructure Partners / MBIE ultra-fast broadband coverage reporting as at mid-2024; true if UFB availability was around 87 percent of the population, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: I want to correct a statement he made in saying that it was a National Party initiative that was put on hold around 2017. That’s not correct; it was launched in 2017.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that He Poutama Rangatahi was launched in 2017 rather than put on hold in that year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE and Ministry of Social Development records and 2017 ministerial announcements for He Poutama Rangatahi; true if the programme was launched in 2017, false if it was announced but suspended or not commenced that year.

veracity.statement: In the 2022-23 year, 2,710 young people participated in the programmes, which I think is a great result.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a participation figure of 2,710 young people in He Poutama Rangatahi programmes in 2022-23.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD / MBIE annual report or He Poutama Rangatahi programme reporting for the 2022-23 year; true if participation is recorded at approximately 2,710, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: There are a number of employment programmes that have been invested in over recent years that have proven to be effective, and actually there’s the reporting to show that they are effective: Mana in Mahi, Flexi-wage, He Poutama Rangatahi, Apprenticeship Boost are a few of them, just to name a few.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that four named MSD employment programmes (Mana in Mahi, Flexi-wage, He Poutama Rangatahi, Apprenticeship Boost) have been shown to be effective, and that published reporting demonstrates this.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD evaluation/outcome reports and the MSD employment programme effectiveness series for the named programmes; true if published evaluations report positive employment outcomes for these programmes, false if evaluations are absent or report no/negative effect.

veracity.statement: Over recent years, the Government previously had worked hard to always beat their forecasts of unemployment and the numbers of beneficiaries anticipated to come on to benefit, and I think, when we look back, that is very evident.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the previous (Labour) Government actual unemployment and benefit numbers consistently came in better than the official forecasts.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare Treasury BEFU/HYEFU unemployment and benefit-recipient forecasts issued 2018–2023 with Stats NZ HLFS outturns and MSD benefit fact sheets; true if outturns were consistently better than forecast across that period, false if outturns matched or exceeded forecast levels in material periods.

veracity.statement: Well, of course, it’s very unfortunate that we are in a position and we have a set of economic conditions that means Treasury has forecast unemployment to grow.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Treasury's current forecasts (as at May 2024) project a rising unemployment rate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's most recent published economic forecasts as at May 2024 (HYEFU 2023 / BEFU 2024); true if the unemployment rate track rises from its then-current level, false if the forecast track is flat or falling.

veracity.statement: It was actually the Minister before me, the member who’s resumed her seat, who ensured that the programme was for five years, and early last year the indication and the decision was communicated to the community that it would not continue past the five-year mark.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Kaiwhakaoranga programme was established with a fixed five-year term under the previous Minister, and that its end was communicated to the affected community in early 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD/Cabinet records establishing the Kaiwhakaoranga programme's funding term and MSD correspondence to the Christchurch Muslim community; true if the programme was time-limited to five years and cessation was communicated in early 2023, false if it was open-ended or no such communication occurred.

veracity.statement: One of the reasons that it’s been very important that the Ministry of Social Development has focused on ensuring that people have access to anything they might be eligible to through the welfare system is because we are legally required to, through the Social Security Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Social Security Act imposes a legal duty on MSD to ensure people receive the assistance they are eligible for.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Text of the Social Security Act 2018 (in particular the provisions on the purpose of the Act and MSD's duties to inform and assist applicants); true if a statutory obligation to ensure eligible people receive their entitlements is present, false if the Act imposes no such duty.

veracity.statement: Information from the 2023-24 Estimates process also tells us that an additional $863.6 million over four years was required to respond to the then emerging cost pressures.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a precise figure of $863.6 million over four years identified in the 2023-24 Estimates as needed to meet Whaikaha cost pressures.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2023-24 Estimates of Appropriations and Vote Social Development / Whaikaha supporting material; true if the $863.6m over four years figure appears as the cost-pressure requirement, false if the documented figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: Since 2018, the population receiving disability support services has increased from about 32,000 to almost 50,000 people.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a growth in the number of people receiving disability support services from roughly 32,000 in 2018 to nearly 50,000 in 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health Disability Directorate and Whaikaha client-count statistics for 2018 and 2023-24; true if the counts are approximately 32,000 and approximately 50,000 respectively, false if they differ materially.

veracity.statement: Crown expenditure on disability support services adjusted for inflation has roughly doubled from 2005-06 to now.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that real (inflation-adjusted) Crown spending on disability support services has approximately doubled between 2005-06 and 2023-24.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Vote Health / Vote Disability Issues appropriations for disability support services in 2005-06 and 2023-24, deflated by CPI or the Treasury GDP deflator; true if the real increase is close to 100%, false if materially less or more.

veracity.statement: Now, as we all know, and we’ve determined in the House over the past month and a half or so that the former Minister knew about the funding shortfall within Whaikaha back in December last year and did nothing to address that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Minister for Disability Issues was aware of the Whaikaha funding shortfall in December 2023 and took no action in response.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Whaikaha/Ministerial briefings and OIA-released advice dated December 2023, plus the record of ministerial decisions between December 2023 and 18 March 2024; true if the Minister was briefed in December 2023 and no responsive action was taken, false if no such briefing exists or action was taken.

specificity.statement: There are a number of employment programmes that have been invested in over recent years that have proven to be effective, and actually there’s the reporting to show that they are effective: Mana in Mahi, Flexi-wage, He Poutama Rangatahi, Apprenticeship Boost are a few of them, just to name a few.
specificity.explanation: Names four specific programmes, which makes the claim locatable, but supplies no figures, outcome measures or evaluation citations.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m not going to cover off questions that I replied to in the previous session, but what I will say is that we will continue to ensure that programmes that are delivered—assessment is undertaken to ensure that they are effective, and if they are not effective, funding won’t continue.
specificity.explanation: States a general decision rule (assess, defund if ineffective) but names no programme, no assessment framework, no threshold and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Madam Chair, of course, as part of the hearing we talked about the ambitious jobseeker target, to reduce the number on jobseeker benefits by 50,000.
specificity.explanation: Cites a named target with a concrete figure (50,000 fewer on jobseeker support), though without the date or the mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The first priority of this Government is to address the cost of living crisis so that families aren’t under the level of pressure they are under, and, of course, I will always be responding to and listening to any pressure that organisations are under.
specificity.explanation: Asked about additional investment in social services, the answer offers a stated priority and a promise to listen — no amount, mechanism or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Information from the 2023-24 Estimates process also tells us that an additional $863.6 million over four years was required to respond to the then emerging cost pressures.
specificity.explanation: Gives an exact dollar figure, a period, and the document the figure comes from — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’d really like to know what the Minister can tell us in terms of the total number of people who have been impacted by the changes that were announced and implemented on 18 March, and that would be everyone who was accessing the different funding support pools that were impacted.
specificity.explanation: Asks a precisely bounded question — a headcount, tied to a dated policy change and to a defined set of funding pools — that could be answered with a single figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Madam Chair, I did say in the answer to the last question, if the member had bothered to listen, that we will continue to assess programmes for their effectiveness.
civility.explanation: 'if the member had bothered to listen' is a condescending jab at the questioner personally rather than at her argument; short of a direct insult but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Given that the Kaiwhakaoranga programme has been running for a number of years and the feedback from our Muslim community in Christchurch has been positive with respect to the case management service that they have received through this programme, why is the Minister now deciding to cut funding to that programme? What advice did she receive? And what response has she received from the community?
focus.explanation: Names a specific programme, the community it serves and the decision at issue, and asks for the advice behind it — squarely on the policy rather than the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: The review will report back within six weeks on the short-term measures required to stabilise the system, with the second phase of the review making recommendations on longer-term policy and funding settings.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the independent review of the disability support system, announced 30 April 2024, will deliver its first-phase report on short-term stabilisation measures within six weeks.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Date of delivery of the first-phase report of the independent review of the disability support system (Ministerial announcements / Whaikaha publications); true if the first-phase report was delivered by roughly mid-June 2024, false if it was delivered materially later or not at all.

focus.statement: The bill proposed by the previous Government was tokenistic and does not go far enough to address the very real issues that those living with disabilities face.
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure (the Accessibility for New Zealanders Bill) and the substantive complaint about it, rather than attacking the other party generally.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This was another example, like the creation of the Ministry for Disabled People, where expectations were enormous and, then, what was delivered has been a massive disappointment.
focus.explanation: Two named policies are cited, but the weight of the sentence is a general characterisation of the previous government's delivery rather than an engagement with the measures' content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I would like to know—this is a question in the public interest; many have asked me about it—what are the savings that will be realised as a result of the changes that were made on 18 March, given that they were done in response to Whaikaha’s funding shortfall, as the previous Minister outlined.
focus.explanation: Direct scrutiny of a named change on a named date by a named agency; asks for the fiscal consequence rather than characterising the government.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So disabled people now have been saying to me that while they can move around within their community to access services, many have family who live in a different region, for example, and now there is no access to the funding that they had prior to 18 March to be able to go and visit their own family that lives in a different part or in a different region, which is then leading to them becoming more isolated as a result of this. How, then, does the Minister reconcile the two? This is clearly a cut to funding that doesn’t allow a disabled person to travel to see their own family.
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism of the 18 March purchasing-rule change and its concrete effect on a named category of spending (domestic travel).
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The bill proposed by the previous Government was tokenistic and does not go far enough to address the very real issues that those living with disabilities face.

civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The challenge we have now is that the bill is so fundamentally flawed, and I don’t recall actually many, if any, submitters that were in favour of the bill when it was before the select committee.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that few or no submitters to the select committee supported the Accessibility for New Zealanders Bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The submissions received by the Social Services and Community Committee on the Accessibility for New Zealanders Bill, and the committee's report summarising them; true if the great majority of submissions opposed or sought fundamental change and essentially none supported the bill as drafted, false if a substantial body of submissions supported it.

veracity.statement: I refer to a press release that was put out on 20 March, where the former Minister for Disability Issues said that no disabled person will lose access to funding for essential services, equipment, or support.
veracity.explanation: Relays that a 20 March press release from the then Minister for Disability Issues contained an assurance that no disabled person would lose access to funding for essential services, equipment or support.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The beehive.govt.nz release dated 20 March 2024 from the Minister for Disability Issues; true if it contains that assurance in substantially those terms, false if no such release exists or it carries no such assurance.

veracity.statement: What I can say—and I was hoping not to quote this; the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet stocktake of Whaikaha, which identifies significant risks that were in this financial period that absolutely directly contribute to changes that were necessary earlier this year: financial risks, operational risks, legal risks, people leadership risks, high stakeholder expectations.

rigor.statement: The challenge we have now is that the bill is so fundamentally flawed, and I don’t recall actually many, if any, submitters that were in favour of the bill when it was before the select committee.

rigor.statement: So disabled people now have been saying to me that while they can move around within their community to access services, many have family who live in a different region, for example, and now there is no access to the funding that they had prior to 18 March to be able to go and visit their own family that lives in a different part or in a different region, which is then leading to them becoming more isolated as a result of this. rigor.explanation: The inference from 'travel funding withdrawn' to 'access to a support has been lost, contradicting the assurance' is sound on its own terms; the gap is that it leans on constituent report and assumes travel counts as an 'essential support', which is the contested term.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But I will come back and address the issue of the accessibility bill, because the underlying problems of access that you spoke about in your contribution still exist and they create real challenges for the quality of disabled people’s lives.

focus.statement: The annual review report and supporting documents highlighted various engagement structures within Whaikaha, such as the transformation management board, the strategic advisory group, and nōku te kainga noho, nōku te whakatau steering groups. veracity.statement: Māori experience disability at a higher rate than any other population group in Aotearoa. One in three Māori have some form of disability, yet we have the least access to support in health and disability services.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Disability Survey / Household Disability Survey prevalence rates by ethnicity: true if the Māori rate is the highest of the reported ethnic groups and is approximately 33%, false if materially lower or if another group's rate is higher. rigor.statement: Our tāngata hauā community feel they are being systematically targeted by Government organisations and Crown agencies and treated as economic burdens. specificity.statement: So my commitment to you in terms of the review that’s under way is that before any decisions are taken, there will be consultation with the disabled community.
specificity.explanation: A concrete sequencing commitment (consultation precedes decisions) tied to a named review, but with no form, scope, timeframe or participants specified.

rigor.statement: Today, the fund has matured and I would reflect, over successive Governments, has demonstrated its independence, and we see a different story now. The Guardians’ governance has evolved to provide effective oversight of complex investment strategy and, at the same time, direct investment globally is now a much more common feature of best-practice portfolio management and the New Zealand Super Fund is now considered a mature fund. In this new environment and this changed context, a prohibition on taking controlling interests in companies is no longer needed; it is obsolete—and that is why this bill is in the House.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: the premises offered (the fund's maturity, evolved governance, and the now-common global practice of direct investment) are the same conditions she earlier identified as the original rationale for the prohibition, so the conclusion that the restriction is obsolete tracks the premises. It is not airtight — the politicisation concern she names is only partly addressed by the maturity premise — but no fallacy carries the argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I entered the first reading of this bill with some concern about the potential for this to lead to less independence for the fund and the potential to have impact on competition with other market investors in New Zealand. I’m satisfied from our deliberations that the bill will have limited impact on competition with other market investors due to the size and scale of the fund’s direct investments and that the existing measures which exist in the super Act will preclude the kind of inappropriate influence that we have discussed.
rigor.explanation: A stated concern is resolved with two reasons — the scale of the fund's direct investments, and existing statutory safeguards — so the conclusion is supported rather than asserted. But the weight rests partly on an appeal to the select committee's deliberations rather than on evidence presented here, and no threshold is given for what counts as 'limited impact' on competition.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The New Zealand Super Fund prohibition from taking controlling interests in companies formed has been in place since establishment.

The sentence is a live-speech slip in word order; the assertion being checked is the date of origin of the prohibition.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001 as enacted (s 59 and related investment restrictions): true if the prohibition on the Guardians taking a controlling interest in companies was present from the Act's commencement in 2001, false if it was inserted by a later amendment.

veracity.statement: I will thank the previous Government for introducing the bill and I’m pleased to see our Government support the bill through its remaining time in the House.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bill record for the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests) Amendment Bill: true if the bill was introduced to the House before the change of government in late 2023 (i.e. by the sixth Labour Government), false if it was introduced by the current Government.

specificity.statement: The bill removes the prohibition on the New Zealand Super Fund taking a controlling interest in companies. This will ensure that the Guardians in future have the tools to manage direct investment and therefore the ability to seek out a much wider range of investment opportunity, including in New Zealand.

specificity.statement: It requires the board of the Guardians to include in the statement of investment policies, standards, and procedures the details of a governance framework for the implementation and operation of controlled entities.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a named instrument (the statement of investment policies, standards and procedures), the body obliged (the Guardians' board) and the content required (a governance framework for controlled entities). Someone could check the clause and see whether the requirement exists.

veracity.statement: We really need that financial discipline, ensuring that investment opportunities are well thought through and are actually providing for Kiwis’ futures and continuing to deliver excellent returns of something like just under 10 percent over the life of the fund.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the New Zealand Superannuation Fund has returned a little under 10 percent per annum since its inception.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Guardians of New Zealand Superannuation annual report / monthly performance disclosure of the Fund's since-inception annualised return as at mid-2024; true if that figure is close to but below 10% p.a., false if materially different (e.g. below 8% or above 10.5%).

veracity.statement: I was actually just reflecting, as I was sitting here, that one of the things I’ve got a real interest in is Pharmac, which is our medicines procurement and funding body, and that actually hasn’t had an update and a look at probably in 33 years.
