veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Pharmac's founding date (Pharmaceutical Management Agency established 1993) and the record of reviews/legislative changes affecting it since — e.g. the 2021–22 independent Pharmac Review and the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022; true if no substantive review or statutory update has occurred since establishment and the interval is about 33 years, false if reviews or statutory updates are on the record or the interval is materially shorter.

veracity.statement: The last thing I want to reflect on, and the member Ingrid Leary did mention Michael Cullen—I did also enjoy, in the second reading, people might remember the former finance Minister Grant Robertson also said he had spoken to Michael Cullen about these changes and got his endorsement.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of the second reading of the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests) Amendment Bill; true if Grant Robertson's speech states he spoke to Michael Cullen about the changes and had his endorsement, false if no such statement appears.

veracity.statement: They actually have a network of 30 Age Concern groupings throughout 40 locations across the country, and they did do a submission in relation to this bill.

veracity.statement: So, once again, that speaks to New Zealand’s very high—usually number one; sometimes number two—placing by Transparency International around how we do business, what our money flows are, the ability of not only New Zealanders to trust the fund but also for foreign investors to know that New Zealand is a safe and stable place to do business.

rigor.statement: Particularly, I think that in this case, when we’re looking at—as was addressed previously—certain populations where their scientifically proven age and also life expectancy does not go too far beyond the age of 65, we do see, particularly in this case, that Māori and Pasifika populations are not receiving the full benefit of the New Zealand Superannuation Fund that they deserve.

veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Budget 2022 operating allowance was $5.9 billion with over $6 billion of additional out-of-allowance spending across the forecast period, and that the Budget 2023 allowance was $4.8 billion.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2022 and Budget 2023 documents (Fiscal Strategy Report / Budget Economic and Fiscal Update): true if the stated operating allowances are $5.9 billion and $4.8 billion respectively and out-of-allowance spending in Budget 2022 exceeded $6 billion over the forecast period; false if the published figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: Well, I can tell you what we’re not going to do is we’re not planning to sell off 10,000 State houses, because your Government—that member’s Government—borrowed $10 billion more, and loaded that up on Kāinga Ora (KO), and they quadrupled the social house wait-list, and they had more children growing up in motels.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous government added $10 billion of borrowing onto Kāinga Ora, that the social housing wait-list quadrupled under it, and that more children were living in motels.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora annual reports on borrowings 2017-2023 (true if the increase is around $10 billion), MSD Public Housing Register counts for the same period (true if the register roughly quadrupled), and MSD emergency housing data on children in motels: false if any of the three figures is materially different.

veracity.statement: But I can tell you, under that member, and the way that he left Kāinga Ora, they are faced with a sell-off of 10,200 houses in order to make the finances work because of the mess that you loaded them up with.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Kāinga Ora, on the settings inherited from the previous government, faced having to sell 10,200 state houses to make its finances work.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora board papers, statements of performance expectations and advice to Ministers (including the 2024 independent review of Kāinga Ora): true if documents show a planned or forecast disposal of approximately 10,200 homes arising from the inherited financial settings; false if no such plan or advice exists.

veracity.statement: Does he agree with the then National Party housing spokesperson, Nicola Willis, who said, in 2020, “The Government needs to build state houses, and what I would like to see is the Government continuing to build state houses. That’s absolutely a policy that either Labour or National needs to continue in the years ahead”; if so, how many additional State houses will he commit to building?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Nicola Willis, as National's housing spokesperson, made this statement in 2020.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Media reports, transcripts or Hansard from 2020 recording Nicola Willis's remarks on state house building: true if she is recorded saying substantially these words in 2020 while housing spokesperson; false if the quote is misattributed, misdated or materially altered.

focus.statement: Having loaded KO up with billions of dollars in debt and wasted time on broken policies like KiwiBuild, rents soared, social housing wait-lists exploded, and we have more children in motels on their watch.
focus.explanation: Names specific policies and outcomes — Kāinga Ora debt, KiwiBuild, rents, the social housing wait-list, children in motels — and pairs them with his own government's actions, so it is substantive scrutiny rather than content-free party framing, though the 'on their watch' framing carries some of the weight.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can he guarantee no one will be made homeless by his Government’s decision to reinstate no-cause evictions?
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named government decision (reinstating no-cause evictions) and its consequence for a named outcome; no party characterisation at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What I am willing to say is that we have a housing crisis in New Zealand, and—unlike the Labour and the Green Government that did nothing about it, and outcomes got a lot worse—we are working each and every aspect to increase the supply of houses available, houses available to rent, and social housing supply, as well.
focus.explanation: A real policy direction (housing supply, rentals, social housing) but the central move is a characterisation of the opposing parties as having 'did nothing about it', with no named measure or figure on either side.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will he guarantee that there will be at least as many State houses at the end of this parliamentary term as there were at the start of it?
focus.explanation: Seeks a specific, measurable commitment on a named policy outcome over a defined period — squarely on the substance with no party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is he aware Auckland Council have identified five lead indicators that his Government has direct control over, including the return of no-cause evictions, which are likely to increase homelessness in our largest city?
specificity.explanation: Cites a named source, a specific count of indicators, and a named policy lever (no-cause evictions) — checkable against the council's own material.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is the Prime Minister proud of his decision to hand $2.9 billion in tax cuts to landlords on the one hand, but on the other hand, making decisions that will by all accounts increase homelessness in this country?
specificity.explanation: Carries a precise dollar figure attached to a specific, identifiable policy change; someone could check the costing.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I said in the Budget Policy Statement that the operating allowance for Budget 2024 will be less than $3.5 billion—$3.5 billion, members may recall, was the operating allowance for Budget 2024 set by the previous Government.
specificity.explanation: A named document, a named budget, and a precise fiscal threshold that can be checked and acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The allowance in that Budget was $5.9 billion, plus more than $6 billion over the forecast period for the cost of living payment and other spending outside allowances. The allowance for Budget 2023 was relatively modest by comparison, at only $4.8 billion.
specificity.explanation: Three separate, dated fiscal figures tied to identified Budgets — fully checkable against published Budget documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What I can guarantee is that there will be an increase in the number of social houses in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: A bare direction of travel in answer to a question about numbers: no figure, no baseline and no timeframe, when all three were available to give.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he agree with the then National Party housing spokesperson, Nicola Willis, who said, in 2020, “The Government needs to build state houses, and what I would like to see is the Government continuing to build state houses. That’s absolutely a policy that either Labour or National needs to continue in the years ahead”; if so, how many additional State houses will he commit to building?
specificity.explanation: Quotes a dated, attributed statement in full and asks for a number against it — precise on both the evidence cited and what is being sought.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is the Prime Minister unwilling or unable to say that his Government’s policies will increase homelessness in this country?
civility.explanation: A pointed 'unwilling or unable' dilemma that edges toward the Prime Minister's candour and competence rather than staying purely on the policy, without landing a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, what is important is we are getting the balance right in our tenancy laws so that we encourage landlords to put more houses up and make them available to more tenants so we avoid homelessness.
rigor.explanation: Offers a causal chain — rebalanced tenancy law leads landlords to supply more rentals, which avoids homelessness — with nothing offered to connect the links; the conclusion that homelessness is avoided is asserted rather than supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So the allowance in Budget 2024 of less than $3.5 billion, no matter how less than, is a lot more fiscally responsible than those delivered in the last few irresponsible Budgets.
rigor.explanation: Concludes fiscal responsibility from the size of the operating allowance alone; nothing is offered linking a smaller allowance to responsible fiscal management, and the 'no matter how less than' concedes the magnitude is unknown, so the conclusion outruns the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, the member has made a very serious accusation and one only has to look at the information and facts that are in the public domain to understand that it is correct.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (the accusation is correct) rests entirely on a gesture at unspecified 'information and facts that are in the public domain'. No premise is actually supplied, so nothing connects the assertion to its support — a bare appeal to unstated evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, I could equally ask that member why the previous Government did not confirm funding beyond 2025 in the last Budget, when the last Government had the opportunity to confirm the funding track for the next four years. Instead, they only confirmed it for two years so that Mr Robertson could run a fake surplus in 2026-27.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque: the question asked why this Government has not confirmed post-2025 funding, and the answer offered is that the previous Government also did not. The predecessor's conduct does not bear on whether the current decision is justified.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: To make it simpler for the House, our tax relief won’t require additional borrowing, and our tax cuts will reduce inflationary pressures.
rigor.explanation: The ANZ passage she quoted says the net fiscal impact is 'broadly neutral' and 'marginally contractionary'; she translates that into an affirmative claim that the cuts will reduce inflationary pressure and require no borrowing. The inference overshoots the quoted premise, though it runs in the same direction.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I happen to believe that one of the greatest things we can do for productivity is send New Zealanders the message that there will be reward for their hard work. And that is what tax relief will do.
rigor.explanation: Asked what will raise productivity, the answer asserts that 'sending a message' about reward for hard work is among the greatest productivity levers, with no mechanism, evidence or causal chain offered. The conclusion rests on a bare assertion of belief.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will he commit to keeping the same criteria for someone to be placed on the social housing wait-list, or will he reduce the wait-list by changing the criteria, as the previous National Government did?
focus.explanation: Names a specific mechanism (social housing wait-list eligibility criteria) and asks for a commitment on it. Legitimate scrutiny of a named policy lever, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is the first job that we have to do to clean up the mess that that member and his Government left us.
focus.explanation: Tethered loosely to the Kāinga Ora work just described, but the content of this sentence is generalised blame of the previous Government's 'mess' with no policy, figure or outcome named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why has he refused to confirm funding for the income-related rent subsidy post-2025, given community housing providers like the Salvation Army are cancelling housing developments due to funding uncertainty?
focus.explanation: Names a specific funding instrument (the income-related rent subsidy), a specific timeframe (post-2025) and a specific claimed consequence for named providers. Textbook scrutiny of a policy decision.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why do community housing providers have to wait for the Budget before knowing if they can build new houses, given the Government was happy to announce a $2.9 billion tax cut for landlords weeks ago?
focus.explanation: Names two specific measures — community housing build decisions pending the Budget, and a costed tax change — and contrasts them. The 'tax cut for landlords' framing is partisan, but the policy content is real and specific.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Under Labour, it may be that workers are always the last to get served, but under this Government, we’re making sure they get what they deserve.
focus.explanation: A pure party contrast: no policy, figure, mechanism or outcome is named on either side of the comparison. It is about which team treats workers better, not about what either did.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why is she choosing tax cuts over the livelihoods of the 4,500 Kiwis that have lost their jobs because of her Budget?
focus.explanation: Puts a specific number and a specific claimed consequence of the Government's fiscal programme against a named policy choice. The 'choosing X over livelihoods' framing is rhetorical, but the underlying point is a costed policy trade-off.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But the first thing to do is, rather than putting good money after bad, we’re going to take stock of the KO organisation, make sure that it actually has a board refresh, make sure it has a turnaround plan in place by November, and make sure it gets on a financially sustainable footing.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete actions (board refresh, turnaround plan) and a deadline (November) for a named agency, but gives no figures, no savings target and no detail on what the plan must contain.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: He steps into the role on 4 June, where he’ll be tasked with leading a refreshed board which we expect to be in place in July.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete dates attached to a named appointment and a named governance change; checkable and actionable, though it does not say who the refreshed board members will be.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I happen to believe that one of the greatest things we can do for productivity is send New Zealanders the message that there will be reward for their hard work. And that is what tax relief will do.
specificity.explanation: Offers no figure, mechanism or timeframe for the productivity effect claimed — 'send New Zealanders the message that there will be reward for their hard work' is not something anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: They’ve made seven major recommendations which propose significant changes to Kāinga Ora and the system, and we’ve agreed to immediately adopt four of those recommendations.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the independent review of Kāinga Ora made seven major recommendations and that the Government has agreed to adopt four of them immediately.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published Independent Review of Kāinga Ora (Sir Bill English et al., 2024) and the Government's 20 May 2024 response: true if the review contains seven recommendations and the Government's announced response adopts four of them immediately; false if the counts differ.

veracity.statement: Why has he refused to confirm funding for the income-related rent subsidy post-2025, given community housing providers like the Salvation Army are cancelling housing developments due to funding uncertainty?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that community housing providers, the Salvation Army among them, are cancelling housing developments because income-related rent subsidy funding beyond 2025 is unconfirmed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements and reporting from the Salvation Army and Community Housing Aotearoa in the first half of 2024: true if a provider is on record cancelling or halting developments citing post-2025 IRRS funding uncertainty; false if no such cancellation is documented.

veracity.statement: The last Government allocated 6,000 social housing places in Budget 2023.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Budget 2023 allocated funding for 6,000 additional social/public housing places.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2023 documents and the associated housing package announcement: true if the public housing places funded number approximately 6,000; false if the figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Why do community housing providers have to wait for the Budget before knowing if they can build new houses, given the Government was happy to announce a $2.9 billion tax cut for landlords weeks ago?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government announced a tax change worth $2.9 billion benefiting landlords (the restoration of interest deductibility for residential rental property).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD costings for the restoration of interest deductibility as announced in 2024: true if the fiscal cost over the forecast period is approximately $2.9 billion; false if materially different.

veracity.statement: We are in a situation where there have been no adjustments to personal income tax rates or thresholds for 14 years, other than a new rate being added at the top.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's personal income tax rates and thresholds were last adjusted 14 years before May 2024, with the sole exception of a new top rate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IRD's record of personal income tax rate and threshold changes: true if the last threshold change was the October 2010 adjustment and the only subsequent change was the 39% top rate introduced in 2021; false if any other rate or threshold change occurred in that period.

veracity.statement: And we are a country where someone working full time on the minimum wage is now facing a marginal tax rate of 30 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a full-time minimum wage earner's annual income in May 2024 exceeds the threshold at which the 30% marginal rate begins.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The adult minimum wage from 1 April 2024 multiplied by 40 hours × 52 weeks, compared with the $48,000 threshold at which the 30% rate applies: true if annual earnings exceed $48,000; false if below.

veracity.statement: Why is she choosing tax cuts over the livelihoods of the 4,500 Kiwis that have lost their jobs because of her Budget?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 4,500 New Zealanders have lost their jobs as a result of the Government's Budget/fiscal savings programme.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public Service Commission and agency-by-agency reporting on public sector role reductions to May 2024: true if approximately 4,500 filled positions were disestablished with people losing employment; false if the tally is substantially composed of unfilled vacancies or is materially smaller.

veracity.statement: I’d note that the number that she is referring to is one that includes job vacancies that have been closed, which is not the same as someone losing their job.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 4,500 figure cited by Barbara Edmonds counts disestablished vacant positions rather than only people made redundant.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The composition of the public sector job-reduction tally circulating in May 2024 (Public Service Commission data and agency change proposals): true if a material share of the 4,500 are vacancies never filled; false if the figure counts only filled roles disestablished.

civility.statement: Well, I could equally ask that member why the previous Government did not confirm funding beyond 2025 in the last Budget, when the last Government had the opportunity to confirm the funding track for the next four years. Instead, they only confirmed it for two years so that Mr Robertson could run a fake surplus in 2026-27.
civility.explanation: Imputes deliberate bad faith to a named individual — that Grant Robertson set the funding track to manufacture a 'fake surplus'. Short of a direct insult, but it attributes dishonest motive to the person rather than criticising the decision.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I would first warn the member that she’s once again doing what she has done several times in this House, which is making a statement of fact where she doesn’t actually have evidence to support it.
civility.explanation: Goes beyond disputing the figure to characterise the member as repeatedly asserting things without evidence — a claim about her conduct and reliability rather than about the number itself. Not an insult, but no longer engaging only the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: To the Minister for Children: does she agree with the official advice that the repeal of section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act could cripple trust built up with Māori communities and put vulnerable children at greater risk?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official advice on the repeal of s7AA warned it could 'cripple' trust with Māori communities and put vulnerable children at greater risk.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement and departmental advice to the Minister for Children on repealing s7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989; true if the advice warns in substance that the repeal risks damaging trust with Māori communities and increasing risk to vulnerable children, false if the advice contains no such warning.

veracity.statement: No, I do not agree with reports that have stated this. I assume the member is referring to an article with that headline. What that was referring to was a regulatory impact statement that actually said, “a repeal of section 7AA may undo some of the progress that Oranga Tamariki has made in building trust, relationships, and accountability in the communities we work with.” However, the regulatory impact statement also says that the repeal “may increase levels of confidence in the Department’s decision-making for some members of the public”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the regulatory impact statement contains both of the quoted passages, in those words.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Oranga Tamariki s7AA repeal regulatory impact statement; true if both quoted sentences appear in it substantially as quoted, false if either is absent or materially misquoted.

veracity.statement: Does she agree with official advice that stripping Treaty provisions “may worsen the safety, stability, and well-being of our children with the greatest needs.”, and, if not, what counter evidence does she have?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official advice contains the quoted warning about removing the Treaty provisions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official advice/regulatory impact statement on the repeal of s7AA; true if it contains that quoted wording or its substantive equivalent, false if no such passage exists.

veracity.statement: Does she agree with Tama Potaka and the National Party, who voted down her member’s bill making the same repeal of 7AA, that “It would be contradictory of us to dismiss this provision entirely, which is intended to be a genuine option to address and meet the best interests of the child in State care.”?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that National, including Tama Potaka, voted against Chhour's member's bill repealing s7AA and that Potaka spoke the quoted words.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard first-reading debate and division record for Karen Chhour's Oranga Tamariki (Repeal of Section 7AA) Amendment Bill; true if National voted against it and Potaka's speech contains the quoted sentence, false if National voted for it or the quote does not appear.

veracity.statement: The Government has announced roads of regional significance to sit alongside roads of national significance as part of our plan to get transport back on track. Two roads of national significance and 10 roads of regional significance will replace roading projects in the New Zealand Upgrade Programme. The New Zealand Upgrade Programme’s roading projects were subject to significant cost blowouts that resulted in project cancellations and delays across the country. These changes get these roading projects back on track.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific replacement count (2 RoNS and 10 RoRS) for NZUP roading projects and that NZUP roading projects suffered cost blowouts causing cancellations and delays.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government/NZTA announcement of May 2024 on roads of regional significance and Treasury/NZTA reporting on the New Zealand Upgrade Programme; true if the announcement lists two roads of national significance and ten of regional significance replacing NZUP projects and NZUP costs rose enough to force cancellations/deferrals, false if the counts differ or NZUP projects were not cancelled or delayed on cost grounds.

veracity.statement: Yes. Preparatory work started on this consent in 1999. A range of assessments had to be undertaken so they could submit a consent application; have a reasonable chance if granted a workable consent. The work was not optional. The final decision to grant the consent was made by the Environment Court in July 2007—eight years after the work began on the consent from the applicant. West Wind took two years to construct, so the total time, end to end, in developing it into a wind farm was 10 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that preparatory consenting work on the West Wind wind farm began in 1999, that the Environment Court granted consent in July 2007, and that construction took a further two years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Environment Court decision record for the West Wind (Makara) wind farm and Meridian's project history; true if the Court's decision dates to July 2007 and documented preparatory consent work began around 1999 with roughly two years' construction, false if the consenting work began materially later or the decision date differs.

veracity.statement: Is it not correct that although the land was purchased in the 1990s, as the Minister said, no consent was lodged for building a wind farm on that land till it was transferred to Meridian—in fact, it was lodged on 1 July 2005; a final decision was made on 20 July 2007—and, if this is what this party is hanging its Resource Management Act reform on, it’s pretty thin?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the West Wind consent application was lodged on 1 July 2005 and finally decided on 20 July 2007, i.e. a consenting period of about two years rather than eight.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The consent application record and Environment Court decision for the West Wind wind farm; true if lodgement was 1 July 2005 and the final decision 20 July 2007, false if either date is materially different.

veracity.statement: I just point the member, further—without litigating something that happened in the early 2000s, I would just point the member to the comments from almost every major electricity generator in the last couple of years when it comes to the Resource Management Act. I quote Contact Energy, for example: the single biggest barrier to the decarbonisation of the New Zealand economy is our planning system—which is the Resource Management Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Contact Energy has publicly described the planning system/RMA as the single biggest barrier to decarbonising the New Zealand economy.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contact Energy's public submissions and statements on the RMA in the two years to May 2024; true if a Contact Energy statement identifies the planning system/RMA as the single biggest barrier to decarbonisation, false if no such statement exists.

veracity.statement: Does the Minister recall the supermarket look-in that took 28 years to get consent, and is his fast-track aligned—to use the Prime Minister’s words—with the 17 precedent set by the Labour Party when last in Government?
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that there was a supermarket development that took 28 years to obtain resource consent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Council/Environment Court consenting records or contemporaneous reporting on a New Zealand supermarket development; true if an identifiable supermarket consent process ran approximately 28 years, false if no such case can be identified.

veracity.statement: The classic that I like—which I’ve got to admit I was unaware about until about half an hour ago—is the reconsenting of the 100-year-old 0.5 megawatt Raetihi hydro power station, which took 19 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that reconsenting of the Raetihi hydro power station, a 0.5 MW century-old scheme, took 19 years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Horizons Regional Council / Environment Court consenting records for the Raetihi hydro power station; true if the reconsenting process ran about 19 years for a ~0.5 MW station, false if the duration or capacity is materially different.

veracity.statement: Has the Minister received advice that under the COVID fast-track consenting process, where Ministers referred projects and independent experts made the decisions, the renewable energy projects referred had a combined generating capacity of 1,630 megawatts—that’s the equivalent of nearly four Clyde Dams’ worth of electricity—and that one of those was Te Rere Hau Wind Farm, which obtained approval in way under 18 months?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that renewable projects referred under the COVID-19 fast-track consenting regime totalled 1,630 MW of generating capacity and that Te Rere Hau Wind Farm was approved in well under 18 months.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MfE records of projects referred under the COVID-19 Recovery (Fast-track Consenting) Act and the expert panel decision for Te Rere Hau; true if the referred renewable projects sum to about 1,630 MW and Te Rere Hau's approval took well under 18 months, false if the total is materially different or the approval took longer.

veracity.statement: Will the Minister commit to changing the bill, given the majority of the major electricity generators—under the Electricity Sector Environment Group—in their submission to the select committee have recommended that decisions on whether to approve or decline approvals for eligible projects are made by independent expert panels rather than by the joint Ministers as proposed under the bill as is currently drafted—i.e., they are proposing a very similar scheme to the regime that Labour had?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Electricity Sector Environment Group's select committee submission, representing most major generators, recommends decisions be made by independent expert panels rather than joint Ministers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Electricity Sector Environment Group submission to the Environment Committee on the Fast-track Approvals Bill; true if it recommends independent expert panels rather than joint Ministers as decision-makers, false if it makes no such recommendation.

focus.statement: To the Minister for Children: does she agree with the official advice that the repeal of section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act could cripple trust built up with Māori communities and put vulnerable children at greater risk?
focus.explanation: Names a specific statutory provision, a specific repeal and the specific harm identified in official advice; this is scrutiny of a named measure, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Oh, well, the member is surprisingly complimentary about the troika of Ministers alongside Matua Shane and Mr Brown. As the member knows, the bill is before select committee. focus.statement: Under his Government’s bill that is before select committee, has he lifted and shifted the fact that it is independent experts who make decisions and not three wise men of Ministers?

specificity.explanation: Identifies the source document and quotes two specific passages from it, so the answer can be checked directly against the RIS.

specificity.statement: I have stood here and made it very clear time and time again that the best interests and the safety of our children should be first and foremost in all decision making of our young people, not based on their race.
specificity.explanation: A statement of general principle offered in place of any figure, mechanism or timeframe; nothing here could be checked or acted on.

specificity.statement: Yes. Preparatory work started on this consent in 1999. The final decision to grant the consent was made by the Environment Court in July 2007—eight years after the work began on the consent from the applicant. West Wind took two years to construct, so the total time, end to end, in developing it into a wind farm was 10 years.
specificity.explanation: Named project, named decision-maker, specific years for each stage and a total elapsed time — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is it not correct that although the land was purchased in the 1990s, as the Minister said, no consent was lodged for building a wind farm on that land till it was transferred to Meridian—in fact, it was lodged on 1 July 2005; a final decision was made on 20 July 2007—and, if this is what this party is hanging its Resource Management Act reform on, it’s pretty thin?
specificity.explanation: Supplies exact lodgement and decision dates against which the Minister's eight-year claim can be tested.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The classic that I like—which I’ve got to admit I was unaware about until about half an hour ago—is the reconsenting of the 100-year-old 0.5 megawatt Raetihi hydro power station, which took 19 years.

specificity.statement: Has the Minister received advice that under the COVID fast-track consenting process, where Ministers referred projects and independent experts made the decisions, the renewable energy projects referred had a combined generating capacity of 1,630 megawatts—that’s the equivalent of nearly four Clyde Dams’ worth of electricity—and that one of those was Te Rere Hau Wind Farm, which obtained approval in way under 18 months?

specificity.statement: Will the Minister commit to changing the bill, given the majority of the major electricity generators—under the Electricity Sector Environment Group—in their submission to the select committee have recommended that decisions on whether to approve or decline approvals for eligible projects are made by independent expert panels rather than by the joint Ministers as proposed under the bill as is currently drafted—i.e., they are proposing a very similar scheme to the regime that Labour had?

civility.statement: We’re nine days out from the Budget and apparently we’re litigating on exactly what time frame an energy company submitted a resource consent application.

civility.statement: Under his Government’s bill that is before select committee, has he lifted and shifted the fact that it is independent experts who make decisions and not three wise men of Ministers?

rigor.statement: I just point the member, further—without litigating something that happened in the early 2000s, I would just point the member to the comments from almost every major electricity generator in the last couple of years when it comes to the Resource Management Act. I quote Contact Energy, for example: the single biggest barrier to the decarbonisation of the New Zealand economy is our planning system—which is the Resource Management Act.

rigor.statement: Oh, well, the member is surprisingly complimentary about the troika of Ministers alongside Matua Shane and Mr Brown. As the member knows, the bill is before select committee. We are committed to a one-stop-shop, fast-track regime, which, as the record of the previous Government acknowledges—with the exception of the Luddites and the Green Party—every mainstream political party recognises this as a problem holding New Zealand back. divination.statement: There are very few bills that go to Parliament that go to a select committee that don’t come back with sensible refinements to improve the legislation. I’m sure that will be true of the fast-track bill.

divination.falsification_criterion: The Environment Committee's report back on the Fast-track Approvals Bill; true if the committee recommends amendments to the bill as introduced, false if it recommends the bill proceed unamended or does not report back.

veracity.statement: The Police Commissioner has announced the formation of a national gang unit and district level gang disruption units made up of both new and reprioritised resources.

veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police media releases / Commissioner's public statements in May 2024; true if a national gang unit and district gang disruption units were announced with mixed new and reprioritised resourcing, false if no such announcement exists or the structure announced differs materially.

veracity.statement: Does he agree with the Dairy and Business Owners Group spokesperson, Sunny Kaushal, who said, “While the new Government was elected with high hopes, it is yet to meet our expectations”?

veracity.falsification_criterion: Media reporting or press statements from the Dairy and Business Owners Group around May 2024; true if Kaushal is on record with that wording or a close variant, false if the quote cannot be traced to him or is materially altered.

veracity.statement: Those roles that the member is speaking of are still a proposal, still under consideration, and still out for consultation.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki change proposal and consultation documents / Public Service Commission records for May 2024; true if the roles were still in consultation on that date, false if decisions to disestablish them had already been confirmed.

veracity.statement: Does she remain “unapologetic for putting the children first” when her ministry’s regulatory impact statement indicates that there is a lack of robust evidence that section 7AA does anything at all to harm children, and that repealing section 7AA may worsen the safety, stability, and wellbeing of our children with the greatest needs, on page 24, at paragraph 44?

veracity.falsification_criterion: The Oranga Tamariki regulatory impact statement on repealing section 7AA, page 24 paragraph 44; true if that passage states both propositions in substance, false if it does not or says the opposite.

veracity.statement: How will Oranga Tamariki meet her expectation to establish more partnerships with Māori and continue current strategic partnerships, despite repealing section 7AA, when she is slashing 21 Māori roles at Oranga Tamariki, including the very roles that support engagement—such as the regional Māori practice coaches and senior iwi and Māori engagement advisers—as well as the Treaty response unit and the Māori practice advisers?

veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki restructuring/change proposal documents of May 2024; true if 21 such roles are listed for disestablishment covering those named positions, false if the number or the roles differ materially.

veracity.statement: What they find is that a kid in a charter school in America, at the end of each year, has learnt 16 days more reading—imagine if Rawiri Waititi had been there—than in a State school.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Stanford CREDO study found US charter school students gain 16 additional days of reading learning per year relative to matched public school students.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Stanford CREDO national charter school study (2023); true if it reports approximately 16 additional days of reading growth per year for charter students versus virtual twins, false if the figure or direction differs materially.

veracity.statement: After years of denial, where the Labour Minister of Education, for example, was absolved from responsibility for misleading the House because she didn’t know where the educational data on attendance was, we are now fronting up, we’re publishing the data, and we’re creating new options so that kids can be engaged by people with insights in their community about what will get them to school and get them engaged.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a Labour Minister of Education was cleared of responsibility for misleading the House on school attendance data on the basis that she did not know where the data was.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The Privileges Committee report on the question of privilege concerning Hon Jan Tinetti (2023) and the House's response; true if the committee's finding turned on her lack of knowledge and relieved her of responsibility, false if she was found in contempt or the reasoning differed.

veracity.statement: One commentator said, “When you look at the success this alternative-style educational model has had for Māori, then it gets an A every day.”, and “Our staff tell us they have seen the change in our tamariki, especially those who have been failed by mainstream schooling.” Another commentator has said, “I support that particular charter school, and the reason I do so is that I’ve seen kaupapa grow from the fetal stages all the way that they have today and I’ve seen the outcomes they’ve achieved, and that’s why I support that particular kaupapa.” I would like to thank Willie Jackson and Peeni Henare for those quotes.

specificity.statement: The Government has announced several new powers for police, including the banning of patches and insignia in public, dispersal notices, consorting prohibition notices, and strengthened firearms prohibition orders with warrantless search powers.

specificity.statement: This is a strong step in the right direction and sends a clear message to gangs and organised crime groups that they are no longer operating in a permissive environment or above the law. Restoring law and order is a key priority for this coalition Government.

specificity.statement: Does she remain “unapologetic for putting the children first” when her ministry’s regulatory impact statement indicates that there is a lack of robust evidence that section 7AA does anything at all to harm children, and that repealing section 7AA may worsen the safety, stability, and wellbeing of our children with the greatest needs, on page 24, at paragraph 44?

focus.statement: Well, I agree a lot with Sunny Kaushal, and I was very pleased to be with him on the weekend at a public meeting in Hamilton, where he said that he is very happy with the work that this Government is doing and he is looking forward to working even more closely with us.

focus.statement: For the people at home, the thing about the Opposition—there’s an old saying “They don’t like it up ‘em”.

civility.statement: And any member on the other side of the House that can argue that putting the safety and the best interests of our kids first—[Interruption] needs to take a good, long, hard look in the mirror.

civility.statement: What they find is that a kid in a charter school in America, at the end of each year, has learnt 16 days more reading—imagine if Rawiri Waititi had been there—than in a State school.

civility.statement: That’s what the data and evidence says about charters, and the people that say otherwise are flat-earthers.

rigor.statement: At the end of the day, this is a coalition agreement, something that I campaigned on, an issue that I promised to fix while I went around the country and heard the horrific stories of how our young people were put at risk because it was based on their race, not their safety.

civility.statement: It’s not true. Stop talking bunkum. Yeah, you’d believe that because you’re so naïve.

civility.statement: I would expect that member, if he cared, actually, about people who are in homeless situations, if he cared about people who can’t get access to rental properties, and if he cared about people who are in emergency housing and the 3,000 kids that woke up in motels today—he’d actually want to do something about increasing the supply of houses available, houses available to rent, and houses available in social housing.

civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to two named Ministers — that they were 'looking for every possible excuse' to undermine the agency — rather than contesting what they actually said.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.explanation: Imputes contempt for the public to Ministers and characterises the Prime Minister as evading rather than engaging with what he actually said.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There are a few things that the member Kieran McAnulty—who I realise is new to the housing portfolio—needs to realise about Kāinga Ora and the financial situation that this Government has inherited.
civility.explanation: Opens by framing the opponent as inexperienced and in need of instruction — condescension aimed at the member rather than at his argument, though short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he agree with his own Government that no-cause evictions and the return of interest deductibility are pro-renter policies, and, if so, can he explain why not a single renters advocacy group agrees that these policies are pro-renter?
focus.explanation: Names two specific measures (no-cause evictions, return of interest deductibility) and asks about their effect on a named group; squarely on the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can I ask the Prime Minister: when he experiences those sort of nasty allegations in the House, does he not sort of think of Michael Cullen and his famous quote, “We won. You lost. Eat that!”?
focus.explanation: During an exchange on housing and children in State care, this raises no policy, measure, figure or outcome at all — it is purely about the other side losing an election.

focus.statement: When it comes to social housing, the National Party are all talk. They’ve always been all talk and they always will be all talk, and there’s no better example than the response to the review into Kāinga Ora that occurred yesterday, as the Prime Minister and the housing Minister stood there in front of the media and looked for every possible excuse they could to undermine Kāinga Ora and the provision of State houses in this country.

veracity.statement: Does he agree with his own Government that no-cause evictions and the return of interest deductibility are pro-renter policies, and, if so, can he explain why not a single renters advocacy group agrees that these policies are pro-renter?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no renters advocacy group in New Zealand endorses no-cause evictions or the restoration of interest deductibility as pro-renter policies.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Public submissions and statements from NZ renter advocacy organisations (Renters United, Tenants Protection Association, ActionStation) on the Residential Tenancies Amendment Bill 2024 and the restoration of interest deductibility; true if none endorsed either as pro-renter, false if any such group publicly supported either measure as benefiting renters.
