veracity.falsification_criterion: Christopher Luxon's entry in the Register of Pecuniary and Other Specified Interests of Members of Parliament for 2024; true if seven residential properties are listed, false if the number is materially different.

veracity.statement: I would expect that member, if he cared, actually, about people who are in homeless situations, if he cared about people who can’t get access to rental properties, and if he cared about people who are in emergency housing and the 3,000 kids that woke up in motels today—he’d actually want to do something about increasing the supply of houses available, houses available to rent, and houses available in social housing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that approximately 3,000 children were living in emergency housing motels in New Zealand on the day of the statement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD emergency housing special needs grant data on the number of children in emergency housing motels for the quarter covering May 2024; true if the figure is around 3,000, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: In the nine years that they governed, the number of State houses went backwards by 1,500, and the bloke that oversaw that was the bloke that oversaw the review that the Prime Minister and the housing Minister used to justify their agenda.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the net number of State houses fell by about 1,500 across the 2008–2017 National-led Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Housing New Zealand Corporation annual report stock figures for 30 June 2008 versus 30 June 2017; true if net stock fell by approximately 1,500 dwellings, false if it rose or fell by a materially different amount.

veracity.statement: On numerous occasions, the Prime Minister mentioned that debt had gone up from $3 billion to $12 billion. At no point did the Prime Minister mention the asset value that had been accumulated in that time, that had gone from roughly $20 billion to roughly $45 billion in six years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Kāinga Ora's asset value rose from roughly $20 billion to roughly $45 billion over six years, alongside the debt rise from $3 billion to $12 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora / Housing New Zealand annual report total assets and borrowings for 2017-18 and 2023-24; true if total assets moved from about $20b to about $45b over that span, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: What amazed me was it seemed like the Prime Minister and the housing Minister only realised that it costs money to build houses, and a lot of houses—14,000 is the number that public houses increased by in the last six years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the stock of public houses increased by 14,000 over the six years to 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: HUD Public Housing Quarterly Report net public housing places, June 2018 versus March/June 2024; true if the net increase is approximately 14,000, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: That advice was commissioned by the Minister of Finance as a result of a conversation she had with the Secretary to the Treasury.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Kāinga Ora advice about potential house sales was commissioned by the Minister of Finance following a conversation with the Secretary to the Treasury, rather than arriving unsolicited on Ministers' desks.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Answers to written parliamentary questions and Treasury/Kāinga Ora documents on who commissioned the 2023-24 advice on Kāinga Ora asset sales; true if the Minister of Finance commissioned it after a discussion with the Secretary to the Treasury, false if it was produced independently before the Government took office.

veracity.statement: We housed families; we housed disabled people, who, incidentally, make up 70 percent of Kāinga Ora’s tenants.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that disabled people constitute 70 percent of Kāinga Ora's tenants.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora / HUD tenant statistics on the proportion of tenants or tenancy households that include a disabled person; true if around 70 percent, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: They have reintroduced interest deductibility for landlords, a $2.9 billion tax cut.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that restoring interest deductibility for residential landlords costs $2.9 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/Budget 2024 costing of the restoration of interest deductibility for residential rental property over the forecast period; true if approximately $2.9 billion, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: It’s like they think New Zealanders are thick, but they’re not thick and they know what to expect from this Government, when they see their Prime Minister unable this morning on Breakfast to answer a simple question: “How many State houses will you sell?” He refused to answer.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Prime Minister, interviewed on TVNZ's Breakfast that morning, declined to say how many State houses would be sold.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The TVNZ Breakfast interview with Christopher Luxon broadcast on 21 May 2024; true if he was asked how many State houses would be sold and gave no number, false if he answered with a figure or was not asked.

veracity.statement: Of all the European examples to follow on housing policy, the UK is the last one. The number of social houses has gone down; the number of homeless has gone up.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in the United Kingdom the stock of social housing has declined while homelessness has risen.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: UK Department for Levelling Up/MHCLG dwelling stock statistics for social rented housing and statutory homelessness statistics over the past decade; true if social housing stock fell and homelessness rose, false if either moved the other way.

rigor.statement: There is a reason why I didn’t refer to its full name—this so-called independent report—because I do not accept that placing Sir Bill English, the man who oversaw the wholesale of our State houses while he was finance Minister, is anywhere near independent.
rigor.explanation: Circumstantial ad hominem: the report's independence is rejected entirely on the reviewer's prior record, with nothing offered about the report's method, evidence or findings.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: On numerous occasions, the Prime Minister mentioned that debt had gone up from $3 billion to $12 billion. At no point did the Prime Minister mention the asset value that had been accumulated in that time, that had gone from roughly $20 billion to roughly $45 billion in six years.
rigor.explanation: A sound inference on its own terms: citing debt growth without the matching asset growth gives an incomplete picture of the balance sheet, which supports the conclusion that the presentation was selective.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So the reverse is true: by them bringing it back, there won’t be new builds; there will be competition on existing stock, house prices will go up, new homebuyers will be locked out, and rents will go up.
rigor.explanation: Assumes the effect of a policy runs symmetrically in reverse when repealed, with nothing offered to show the market responds identically in both directions.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is the very thing they will do, because it’s the very thing they did last time.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests solely on precedent — they did it before, therefore they will do it again — with no evidence offered about the current Government's stated intentions or settings.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: So the reverse is true: by them bringing it back, there won’t be new builds; there will be competition on existing stock, house prices will go up, new homebuyers will be locked out, and rents will go up.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that restoring interest deductibility will suppress new builds, push up house prices and push up rents.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ residential building consents, REINZ House Price Index and Stats NZ rental price index for the two years after May 2024; true if new-build activity falls while house prices and rents rise, false if house prices and rents are flat or falling over that period.

divination.statement: It is the very thing they will do, because it’s the very thing they did last time.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that this Government will carry out a mass transfer of State-owned houses to community housing providers or similar bodies.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora and HUD announcements and annual reports before the 2026 general election; true if more than around 1,000 State houses are transferred or sold to community housing providers or comparable organisations, false if no such large-scale transfer programme occurs.

rigor.statement: The previous Government was donkey-deep in the situation that this Government has inherited, because even the profligate previous Government realised that what was going on at Kāinga Ora was not acceptable.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a policy: the previous Government commissioned the funding and financing review, therefore it recognised the problem and shares responsibility. The premise does support the conclusion that they saw a problem, though 'donkey-deep in the situation' overreaches what commissioning a review establishes about culpability.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s because they pretended that after that time there’d be no more additional social housing funding so that the 2025-26 books could look better, so that they could pretend that around that time, and the year after that, they would deliver a surplus.
rigor.explanation: The observed fact (funding scheduled only to 2025) is used to conclude a deliberate deception about the surplus track. Nothing is offered connecting the funding profile to intent; the motive is asserted, not inferred — mind-reading presented as established cause.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, it’s Groundhog Day today and history is repeating itself, because before us we have another National-led Government trying to create the social licence to sell off tens of thousands of public houses that are owned by the people—a move straight out of the playbook of John Key and Bill English’s National-led Government.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that the current review is groundwork for selling tens of thousands of public houses — rests entirely on an analogy with a previous government's actions. No feature of the review itself is offered to support the inferred intent; it is argument by historical parallel.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Desperately needed homes in urban centres and in the regions are being cancelled because this Government does not have the courage to actually face the housing crisis.
rigor.explanation: The stated cause of the cancellations is a character trait of the Government ('does not have the courage'), not any funding decision or mechanism. The conclusion does not follow from anything offered — the causal step is replaced by an attribution of motive.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I hate to break it to the other side of the House, but some things are more important than turning a profit, such as making sure that people have a stable roof over their head, being able to pay the rent, being able to continue to send your kids to school in the same neighbourhood that they’ve grown up in—not displacing and gentrifying our communities by only building houses that rich people and property investors can afford.
rigor.explanation: Strawman and false dichotomy: the opposing position is recast as caring only about profit and building only for the wealthy, and the conclusion follows only against that recast version, not against the argument actually made about financial viability.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: One of the outcomes of that review was a report that landed on the new Government’s desk in December 2023 that said, on the budget approved by the board in December 2023, that Kāinga Ora was forecast to sell, over the next four years, 10,200 houses—that is fact.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a report arising from the Treasury/MHUD funding and financing review, reflecting the Kāinga Ora board's December 2023 budget, forecast the sale of 10,200 houses over four years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Treasury/Ministry of Housing and Urban Development funding and financing review report and the Kāinga Ora board-approved December 2023 budget (obtainable via the review documents or OIA); true if a four-year forecast disposal figure of about 10,200 dwellings appears, false if the document contains no such forecast or a materially different number.

veracity.statement: In 2022-23, it ran at a loss of $520 million, which is forecast, on the current track, to increase to $700 million by 2026-27.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Kāinga Ora recorded a $520 million operating loss in the 2022-23 financial year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora Annual Report 2022/23 (and the Independent Review of Kāinga Ora, April 2024); true if the reported net deficit for 2022/23 is approximately $520 million, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: It has added 2,000 staff since 2017-18.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Kāinga Ora's headcount grew by about 2,000 between 2017-18 and the present.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora / Housing New Zealand annual report staff numbers (FTE or headcount) for 2017/18 compared with 2022/23; true if the increase is approximately 2,000, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The review that we are responding to in this urgent debate finds that the cash cost over the next four years is $21 billion for Kāinga Ora.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the independent review of Kāinga Ora found a four-year cash cost of $21 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Independent Review of Kāinga Ora (English review, released May 2024); true if it states a four-year cash requirement/cost of about $21 billion, false if no such figure appears or the figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: To give you a sense of it, they funded 6,000 more social houses in Budget 2023 over the next two years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Budget 2023 funded 6,000 additional social/public housing places over a two-year period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2023 housing package documents (Vote Housing and Urban Development estimates and the Budget 2023 announcements); true if the additional public/social housing places funded total about 6,000 over two years, false if the announced figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Here’s the facts: the last National Government transferred, at market rates, houses owned by Housing New Zealand to accessible properties.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the transfer of Housing New Zealand stock to Accessible Properties (Tauranga) was a transfer at market rates, not a sell-off.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2016 Housing New Zealand / Accessible Properties Tauranga transaction documents and Treasury social housing transfer reporting; true if the properties were transferred to Accessible Properties at an assessed market value, false if transferred at a discount or to a non-social-housing purchaser.

veracity.statement: Well, here are the facts: social housing wait-lists quadrupled to 25,000 families.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the public housing register roughly quadrupled over the previous Government's term, reaching about 25,000 applicants.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD Housing Register quarterly series; true if the register rose from roughly a quarter of ~25,000 (about 6,000) in 2017 to about 25,000 by late 2023, false if the multiple or the endpoint is materially different.

veracity.statement: The New Zealand Government, as of today, spends a million dollars a day housing people in emergency housing motels.
veracity.explanation: Asserts current Crown spending on emergency housing motel accommodation is about $1 million per day.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD Emergency Housing Special Needs Grant expenditure reporting for the quarter containing May 2024; true if annualised spend is around $350–400 million (≈$1m/day), false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: In fact, I learnt recently that if we had the same amount of State housing that we had in 1991, we would have enough public housing to clear the public housing wait-list and have an additional 10,000 houses in our country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 1991 State housing stock, if held today, would exceed current stock by enough to house the entire public housing register plus 10,000 more households.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Housing New Zealand/Kāinga Ora stock figures for 1991 versus 2024, compared against the MSD Housing Register; true if (1991 stock − current stock) exceeds the register by approximately 10,000 dwellings, false if the difference is materially smaller or negative.

veracity.statement: That is why thousands of build projects are being cancelled and delayed across the country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that thousands of housing build projects nationally have been cancelled or delayed as a consequence of funding uncertainty.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora and Community Housing Aotearoa reporting on paused, cancelled or deferred developments during 2024; true if cancelled/delayed dwellings number in the thousands, false if the documented total is in the hundreds or fewer.

specificity.statement: The review that we are responding to in this urgent debate finds that the cash cost over the next four years is $21 billion for Kāinga Ora.
specificity.explanation: Names the source document, the quantity, the timeframe and the entity — a reader can go to the review and check the $21 billion four-year figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We will, under this Government, build more social houses.
specificity.explanation: A directional commitment with no number, no timeframe and no mechanism; the surrounding sentences add 'more Kāinga Ora houses' and 'facilitate' without supplying any figures either.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In fact, I learnt recently that if we had the same amount of State housing that we had in 1991, we would have enough public housing to clear the public housing wait-list and have an additional 10,000 houses in our country.
specificity.explanation: Names a baseline year, a comparison quantity and a surplus figure of 10,000 houses — the arithmetic can be reconstructed and checked, though the underlying stock number is not stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need to stop trying to micromanage Kāinga Ora and get out of their way and actually allow them to build the housing that our people desperately need.
specificity.explanation: A clear direction with no content behind it: no indication of which controls should be lifted, what build volume is sought, or over what period.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The member who led off this debate, the leader of the—well, maybe the leader in the future of the Labour Party, but the leader when it comes to housing talked a lot about the 2025 social housing places and how the Government hasn’t confirmed funding beyond that.
civility.explanation: A needle at a named member's supposed leadership ambitions inserted into an otherwise accurate summary of his argument. Pointed and personal in flavour, but light and it does not attack his character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Here’s the difference: unlike the socialists opposite, who care about who owns things, on this side of the House, we are agnostic as to ownership; we care about the tenants and the services that they are receiving.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy contrast here (ownership of housing stock versus tenant outcomes), but it is delivered as a characterisation of what the other party is 'really like' — a real policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We need to stop trying to micromanage Kāinga Ora and get out of their way and actually allow them to build the housing that our people desperately need.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the policy question in the debate — the Crown's operating relationship with Kāinga Ora and its build programme. No party framing, no reference to opponents' character.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And then I watched Kieran McAnulty’s demeanour and his attempt at faux crescendos rising up and down in his body position, and I thought: that guy wants to be leader. That’s why he did it.
civility.explanation: Mocks a named member's physical delivery as 'faux' and imputes a self-serving leadership motive to him personally, rather than engaging the argument he made. A clear personal attack, though short of sustained abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And yet somehow, through decades of policy neglect, we have made it too hard to build a house—too hard to get the resource consent, too hard to fund and finance the infrastructure, too hard to get the building materials, and too hard to get the building consent.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy question before the House: it names the specific bottlenecks (consenting, infrastructure financing, materials, building consents) and blames a multi-decade policy failure rather than the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It took them 58 months from go to woe to build a house, on average.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific average end-to-end duration for Kāinga Ora to deliver a completed house.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Independent Review of Kāinga Ora (English/Duncan/Wilson, 2024) and Kāinga Ora's own build-programme data on average elapsed time from project initiation to house completion; true if the reported average is approximately 58 months, false if materially different (e.g. under 40 months).

veracity.statement: Not only were they terrible as a builder, so inefficient that they are losing half a billion dollars a year—you know, every day, today, Kāinga Ora will lose $1.5 million dollars.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Kāinga Ora is running an annual loss of about half a billion dollars, restated as a daily loss of $1.5 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora annual report / Crown financial statements for the most recent reported year; true if the reported net operating deficit is approximately $500 million a year (roughly $1.4–1.5 million per day), false if materially smaller.

veracity.statement: The report talks about saying that the average KO house costs $35 million—sorry, $35,000. It’s not $35 million—that would be getting a bit excessive. But it costs $35,000 more than the equivalent average that was built by somebody else.
veracity.explanation: Relays the review's finding that a Kāinga Ora house costs about $35,000 more than an equivalent house built by another provider. The '$35 million' is an immediately self-corrected mis-speak, not a claim.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.subject_name: Independent Review of Kāinga Ora (Sir Bill English and others)
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Independent Review of Kāinga Ora report's comparison of Kāinga Ora build costs against comparable non-KO builds; true if the report states a gap of approximately $35,000 per dwelling, false if it states a materially different figure or makes no such comparison.

veracity.statement: What we see in the report too is that the expectation is that they will be spending $23 billion more over the next four years—$23 billion more.
veracity.explanation: Relays a figure from the review for Kāinga Ora's projected additional spending over four years.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.subject_name: Independent Review of Kāinga Ora (Sir Bill English and others)
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Independent Review of Kāinga Ora report's forecast of Kāinga Ora's additional funding/borrowing requirement over the coming four years; true if it projects approximately $23 billion, false if the projected figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: But I want to talk to you about security, because how can you have security when you have the neighbours from hell and their landlord won’t do something about it, and they didn’t do something about it on the instructions—the explicit instructions—of the previous Government?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Kāinga Ora's non-action on disruptive tenants followed explicit instructions from the previous Government, rather than agency policy.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial letters of expectations to Kāinga Ora and the Sustaining Tenancies Framework 2018–2023; true if a direction from the previous Government explicitly instructed Kāinga Ora not to end tenancies of disruptive tenants, false if no such instruction exists and the policy was set by the agency itself.

specificity.statement: It took them 58 months from go to woe to build a house, on average.
specificity.explanation: A single precise, checkable figure with a stated basis (average, whole build process). Someone could go to the review or KO data and test it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re going to fix the resource management law. We’re going to do city and regional deals to coordinate infrastructure funding with city planning. We’re going to do infrastructure funding and financing so the pipes and the roads and the bus stops show up when you build new homes. And we’re going to make it easier to bring in the building materials that the rest of the world uses at lower costs, so we can build homes more efficiently.
specificity.explanation: Names four distinct workstreams and the mechanism each is meant to fix, which is more than a slogan, but supplies no amounts, no legislative vehicles and no dates by which any of them happen.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You look at the financial track record, and that doesn’t look particularly spectacular. You look at the cost of building houses that they were doing, and that doesn’t look particularly spectacular. If you look at their record as a neighbour, that doesn’t look very good either. So, it’s not particularly hard to undermine KO, which we were being accused of, because they simply are not performing.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion ('they simply are not performing') rests on three bare assertions that unspecified records 'don't look spectacular'; no figure, comparison or source is offered to bridge premise and conclusion. Effectively assertion-as-evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Secondly, it’s pushed interest rates up much higher than they were, so everybody that is paying a mortgage, everybody that is paying a debt on a business, they are paying for that profligacy as well.
rigor.explanation: A causal chain from one agency's overspending to nationwide interest rates to every mortgage-holder's costs, with nothing offered to connect the links and no acknowledgement of other drivers of rates. The inference outruns what was shown (post hoc / single-cause attribution).
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What he said in the mighty Northland was simply that the change of approach that this Government has taken to that has changed some of those bad tenant behaviours, and that is a great thing.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the policy change is working rests entirely on what one unnamed Kāinga Ora manager told the speaker in one region — an appeal to anecdote, with no data offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: All whānau have a right to warm, leak-free, secure homes, yet 30,000 tamariki are hospitalised every year in this country because of substandard housing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an annual figure of 30,000 child hospitalisations in New Zealand attributable to substandard housing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published NZ research/Ministry of Health data on annual child hospitalisations for housing-sensitive conditions (e.g. the He Kāinga Oranga / University of Otago estimates); true if the annual figure is around 30,000, false if materially lower or if no such attribution exists in the data.

veracity.statement: Further, over 100,000 people are homeless in Aotearoa and 60 percent of them are Māori.
veracity.explanation: Two claims: a homeless population above 100,000, and a Māori share of 60 percent of that population.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ severe housing deprivation estimates (2018 census-based, ~102,000) and their ethnicity breakdown; true if the total exceeds 100,000 and Māori are around 60% of it, false if the Māori share is materially below that.

veracity.statement: I can say that as it is, Māori make up of half of the social housing wait list.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Māori are about half of applicants on the social housing register.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD Housing Register quarterly report ethnicity breakdown for the quarter nearest May 2024; true if Māori are approximately 50% of main applicants, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: So I would like to start by thanking the people who put their lives into making Kāinga Ora a fantastic organisation that has delivered more State houses in New Zealand’s history than any Government since the 1950s.
veracity.explanation: Claims the public housing delivery under the organisation/government referred to exceeds that of any government since the 1950s.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: HUD Public Housing Quarterly Reports and historical state housing build records; true if net/gross state house delivery 2017-2023 exceeds every government term since the 1950s, false if any later government (e.g. the 1990s or 2008-2017) delivered more.

veracity.statement: But I absolutely remember putting out a press release during the election saying there is funding for income-related rent subsidy to 2025.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the speaker issued a public statement during the 2023 election campaign stating IRRS was funded through to 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Labour Party / Beehive press releases attributed to the speaker between August and October 2023; true if one states income-related rent subsidy funding runs to 2025, false if no such release exists.

veracity.statement: This so-called need to sell off 10,000 houses was the result of advice commissioned in December in 2023 by the Minister of Finance after a discussion with her Treasury officials, no doubt about the fact there would be no further funding for income-related rent subsidy, and there are written questions to Kieran McAnulty with the Minister herself telling him this, that she commissioned that advice.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Minister of Finance commissioned advice in December 2023 that produced the 10,000-house sale figure, and that she confirmed commissioning it in answers to written parliamentary questions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Written parliamentary question answers from the Minister of Finance to Kieran McAnulty in 2024, plus Treasury/HUD advice release dates; true if advice was commissioned by the Minister in December 2023 as described, false if it was commissioned by another party or at another time.

veracity.statement: And the evidence is that under our Government, CHPs added 7,255 new places; Kāinga Ora built 7,777.
veracity.explanation: Asserts community housing providers added 7,255 places and Kāinga Ora built 7,777 during the 2017-2023 government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: HUD Public Housing Quarterly Reports covering Oct 2017 to Nov 2023; true if the net additions by CHPs and Kāinga Ora match the stated figures within rounding, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Rental debt in Kāinga Ora going from $1 million in 2017 to $21 million in 2023.
veracity.explanation: Asserts tenant rent arrears held by Kāinga Ora rose from $1 million in 2017 to $21 million in 2023.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora / Housing New Zealand annual reports and OIA-released rent arrears figures for 2017 and 2023; true if arrears match roughly $1m and $21m, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Kāinga Ora houses thousands—tens of thousands, nay—of people in very hard situations—over 70,000 homes in our country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Kāinga Ora's portfolio exceeds 70,000 homes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora annual report 2023/24 stated number of homes owned/managed; true if above 70,000, false if below.

specificity.statement: Our solution to the historical oppression of our people through housing—or, rather, lack thereof—would be to build papa kāinga [original homes], a cost estimated to be $600 million.
specificity.explanation: Names a defined policy (papa kāinga build programme) with a costing of $600 million, though no number of homes or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We would introduce rent controls with higher incomes, end property speculation, and allocate 50 percent of new social housing to Māori—given we make up the majority of those who utilise these services.
specificity.explanation: Three named policy mechanisms and one quantified allocation target, but no cost, timeframe or design detail for rent controls or the speculation measure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And the evidence is that under our Government, CHPs added 7,255 new places; Kāinga Ora built 7,777.
specificity.explanation: Two exact delivery figures split by provider type — directly checkable against public housing reporting.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The recommendations of the independent review are even more pressing—for example, consolidating the Government funding for housing outcomes under the Minister of Housing, my learned sentinel Christopher Bishop, supported by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development; the Ministry of Housing directing Housing and Urban Development to take a social investment approach to social housing; and responsible Ministers to set an expectation that the Kāinga Ora board will have a credible plan to improve financial performance.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete recommended mechanisms and the agencies and office-holders responsible, though without costs or deadlines.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We want better for our people, for our mokopuna, and this Government threatens our very existence unless we assimilate, conform, and keep ourselves from sharing what they consider our unhelpful comments.
focus.explanation: In a debate on a specific housing review, this sentence names no policy, measure or figure; it characterises the other side's general intent toward Māori.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But where the Government and where choices that Governments make come in is what funding is put in in the form of income-related rent subsidy funding; that’s what turns a building into a public house, a State house, or a social house.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the funding mechanism at issue — how income-related rent subsidy converts a build into public housing — with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That’s quite a novel idea for some people in this room, but not for us in this party or this Government.
focus.explanation: A contrast drawn purely between 'us' and the other side; no policy, figure or mechanism is named in the sentence.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: But there is one thing that you cannot get away from in this report, and that is the elephant in the report: this is nothing more than priming the public up for the fact that (a) next week there will be no new income-related rent subsidy for housing in the Budget, and (2) it is a softening up for once again the sell-off of State houses in New Zealand.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Budget 2024, delivered the following week, will contain no new income-related rent subsidy funding, and that state house sell-offs will follow.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 (30 May 2024) Vote Housing and Urban Development documents; true if no new income-related rent subsidy places are funded, false if the Budget funds additional IRRS-supported social housing places.

civility.statement: Now, we have Chris Bishop saying that he was presented with a fiscal cliff that they didn’t know about because the bad Labour Government did not fund what he knew he wouldn’t be able to get through a National Party Cabinet.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to a named member — that he knowingly misrepresented a fiscal cliff he understood the true cause of. Short of a direct insult, but it attacks his honesty rather than his argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I rise to scaffold the articulate and agile kōrero of my learned colleague and sentinel the Minister of Housing, Christopher Bishop, and to respond, respectfully, to the king of hyperbole from Wairarapa and the Nostradamus of housing from Christchurch, who have demonstrated—demonstrated—some of the sheepish guilt that they must feel—sheepish because some of the lowlights of the last six years by a Government that’s been misguided, and devoting energy and wasteful spending on housing support for needy New Zealanders.
civility.explanation: Mocking epithets aimed at two identifiable members ('king of hyperbole from Wairarapa', 'the Nostradamus of housing from Christchurch') plus an imputation of 'sheepish guilt' — the target is the people, not their argument.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And what did we hear from Kāinga Ora when they came to the select committee? That if there was more Government funding to add new State houses, new income-related rent subsidy, they wouldn’t have to sell any off. This was advice prepared for a Government that was gearing up to do what it always does and back away from its commitments.
rigor.explanation: The select committee evidence supports the narrow point that sales are funding-contingent, but the leap to the advice having been prepared for a government intending to withdraw commitments rests on 'what it always does' — an appeal to past pattern rather than anything shown here.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Let me be clear that in that history of the Northcote housing development, there were no houses built under the last National Government. Zero. In fact, across New Zealand, they ended up with fewer overall State houses than what they started with.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions about the 2008-2017 National government: that it built no houses in the Northcote development, and that the national State house stock was smaller when it left office than when it took office.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora/Housing New Zealand build records for the Northcote redevelopment area 2008-2017 (true if zero new State houses completed there in that period); and HNZC/MSD public housing stock figures for 2008 and 2017 (true if the total State house count was lower in 2017 than 2008, false if equal or higher).

veracity.statement: We’ve got 150 hospital beds waiting to open because this Government hasn’t funded it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 150 built hospital beds remain unopened, and attributes that to the current government not funding their operation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Whatu Ora / Health NZ statements or OIA material on unopened bed capacity at the North Shore / Auckland facilities referred to; true if roughly 150 completed beds were unopened as at May 2024 pending operating funding, false if the number is materially different or the beds were funded and opened.

veracity.statement: The Minister will be well aware that New Zealand has twice the workplace fatality rate of Australia, and, as noted in a recent briefing, six times the rate of the UK.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific international comparisons of workplace fatality rates: NZ at twice Australia's rate and six times the UK's.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Comparable per-100,000-worker fatality rates from WorkSafe NZ, Safe Work Australia and the UK HSE for the most recent common years; true if the NZ rate is approximately double Australia's and around six times the UK's, false if the ratios are materially different.

veracity.statement: I’m also keen for her to expand around the changes that WorkSafe has made since the SageBush report on the Strategic Baseline Review, which found that WorkSafe was failing to intervene in key areas.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of a named review — that the Strategic Baseline Review of WorkSafe found the agency was failing to intervene in key areas.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published Strategic Baseline Review of WorkSafe (the report referred to as 'SageBush'); true if it contains findings that WorkSafe was not intervening in key harm areas, false if it contains no such finding or reaches the opposite conclusion.

focus.statement: Let me be clear that in that history of the Northcote housing development, there were no houses built under the last National Government. Zero. In fact, across New Zealand, they ended up with fewer overall State houses than what they started with.
focus.explanation: Names a specific development, a specific government's record and a specific measurable outcome (State house numbers). Legitimate scrutiny of a housing record, not content-free party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: All they have wanted to do, pre-election and post-election, is put the boot in to Kāinga Ora.
focus.explanation: Characterises the other side's motives and general disposition rather than engaging any policy, mechanism, figure or outcome; strip out the claim about what 'they' want and nothing about housing policy remains.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think it’s in large part associated with very high levels of inward migration as policy settings were loosened as the country came out of COVID and faced intense skills shortages, and a great deal of pressure was there from industries who were desperate to get workers.

A mechanism is offered and the claim is appropriately hedged ("associated with"), but the link between migration volume and exploitation rates is asserted rather than evidenced — a plausible but unsupported correlation-to-cause step.

rigor.statement: So touching on the labour inspectorate as to how it is involved in migrant exploitation, due to the question from Phil Twyford, I can tell the member that 35 percent of all labour inspectorate investigations completed in the year that we’re reviewing of 2022-23 involved migrant exploitation, which shows the seriousness of the breaches that are involved in our country.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion ("shows the seriousness of the breaches") does not follow from the premise offered: the share of investigations involving migrant exploitation is a measure of prevalence or of inspectorate focus, not of the severity of individual breaches. veracity.statement: But research commissioned by the Treasury in 2016 found no evidence that the ability to use trial periods significantly increases firms’ overall hiring, and no evidence that the policy increased the probability that a new hire by a firm was a disadvantaged job seeker.

veracity.statement: Fair pay agreements—our pātai: how will the removal of fair pay agreements support Māori workers when the median hourly wage for Māori is $24.98, compared to $28.01 for Pākehā, and when Māori are overrepresented in jobs where low pay, job security, health and safety, and upskilling are significant issues?

veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE annual report / labour inspectorate performance reporting for the review year; true if interventions are reported as 3,174 with a ~39% increase on 2021-22 and a 2,200 target, false if the reported figures differ materially.

specificity.statement: It’s important that I make it very clear that this bill does not prevent Oranga Tamariki from retaining its current strategic partnership or from entering into new partnerships with iwi, hapū, and Māori organisations.

focus.statement: While its original aim was well intentioned, I believe that section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act has been able to be used to influence care decisions that have put vulnerable children in harm’s way by prioritising cultural considerations over safety and wellbeing.

focus.statement: I have heard a lot about Treaty obligations, rights of iwi, Māori rights, and racism. But where is this same level of outrage when a Māori child takes their last breath in this world because the people who are supposed to love them and care for them do not?
focus.explanation: Turns from the provision before the House to the supposed selective outrage of those making the opposing case; there is a gesture at child deaths but no policy, figure or mechanism named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If the other side of the House will try to paint this as racist or try to paint me as some kind of traitor to my race, I know New Zealanders will hear the empty, hollow words for what they really are.

rigor.statement: While its original aim was well intentioned, I believe that section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act has been able to be used to influence care decisions that have put vulnerable children in harm’s way by prioritising cultural considerations over safety and wellbeing.

It is a real inference about the measure, but the support is thin relative to the conclusion.

rigor.statement: Quite frankly, anyone who argues that the safety and wellbeing of a child should not be the most important consideration needs to take a good hard look at themselves.

civility.statement: Quite frankly, anyone who argues that the safety and wellbeing of a child should not be the most important consideration needs to take a good hard look at themselves.

civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We believe that cultural considerations, whilst important, should not impede a process and possibly put a child’s safety and security at jeopardy.

civility.statement: What many don’t have the cultural intellect—despite any other intellect—to understand is that a Māori person is different to a Pākehā.

civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I am doubtful, however, the Minister or any of the Government have taken the time to read that seminal report, otherwise we wouldn’t be discussing this repeal.

civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Unfortunately, there have been some words that I think have been said in the heat of emotion and passion that aren’t actually connected to the reality of what we’re doing here and what this Government is doing, which is aiming to focus Oranga Tamariki on the wellbeing of children.

civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There has been a concern around section 7AA addressing a child’s cultural needs ahead of their immediate safety, stability, and wellbeing.

focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m just to ignore the nonsense on the left—they can’t help themselves.

focus.statement: The Independent Children’s Monitor will still report on the strategic partnerships that Oranga Tamariki has with iwi and Māori organisations as part of their broader reporting on outcomes for Māori children, young people, and their whānau, so that will still be happening.

rigor.statement: There is a genuine concern that section 7AA, when executed, is simply too traumatic for the young child; hence, removing this provision from the Oranga Tamariki Act, which puts an obligation on the chief executive around abiding by the Treaty of Waitangi in decision making when it comes to caring for our young people.

specificity.statement: The repeal of section 7AA is a targeted extermination of our babies—hold tight: don’t have feelings yet—exterminating any ounce of culture, identity, and any sense of their Māori selves.

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: While this bill repeals references to cultural consideration in section 7AA, it does not remove existing provisions in other parts of the Act which require decision makers to consider cultural factors in care decisions.

veracity.statement: The Minister’s own officials advised against the repeal, in sync with the Waitangi Tribunal.

veracity.statement: When section 7AA was introduced, the Human Rights Commission applauded the provision. It recommended the duty be strengthened to a direct obligation to form strategic partnerships with iwi.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The Human Rights Commission's submission on the Children, Young Persons, and Their Families (Oranga Tamariki) Legislation Bill (2016–17) and its contemporaneous statements. veracity.statement: While this bill repeals references to cultural consideration in section 7AA, it does not remove existing provisions in other parts of the Act which require decision makers to consider cultural factors in care decisions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that provisions elsewhere in the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 requiring decision makers to consider cultural factors survive this bill untouched.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Oranga Tamariki (Repeal of Section 7AA) Amendment Bill as introduced, read against the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989. specificity.statement: On 13 December, I asked the Minister to explain what that conflict was, and I asked her how she can claim that there is a conflict in upholding the best interests of the child, when section 4 of the same legislation says that in all decisions of Oranga Tamariki, the best interests of the child is the primary consideration.
specificity.explanation: Names a date, a named questioning of the Minister, a specific statutory provision and what it provides — concrete and checkable rather than a general complaint.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If this Government was serious about evidence-based policy making, it would wake up to the hard evidence presented to it by officials time and time again that the ratio of Māori to non-Māori in State care has reduced because of 7AA, that Māori children in State care have reduced because of 7AA, that children and young people in care are telling us 7AA is working.
specificity.explanation: Names the provision and three specific claimed effects (ratio, absolute numbers, reported experience of children in care), but gives no figures, periods or source documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Instead of repealing a bill which is protecting children from a State that was harming them, we need to be looking at more solutions, because there is so much more that we need to do.
specificity.explanation: Calls for 'more solutions' and 'so much more' without naming a single alternative measure, mechanism, cost or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m sorry, but I’ve dealt with cases as an electorate MP of constituents when exactly this has happened. So you might want to deny it. I know it would be really nice to deny it doesn’t happen, but it does. It is happening.
specificity.explanation: Refers to constituent cases without number, date, circumstance or any detail that would let anyone check or act on the claim.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But, actually, in some cases, the application of the law has shown that this change is required to ensure that we protect the most vulnerable children in this country.
specificity.explanation: Asserts that 'some cases' justify the change without identifying the cases, the number affected, or which part of the law's application produced the problem.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: What they have said to those claims that we heard tonight is that there is a lack of robust evidence to support the view that section 7AA causes harmful changes to long-term care arrangements.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the regulatory impact statement for the repeal and the Waitangi Tribunal's final report both found insufficient evidence that section 7AA causes harmful changes to long-term care arrangements.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published regulatory impact statement for the Oranga Tamariki (Repeal of Section 7AA) Amendment Bill and the Waitangi Tribunal's final report on the repeal of section 7AA; true if either document states there is a lack of robust/empirical evidence that 7AA drove harmful changes to care arrangements, false if neither does.

veracity.statement: I will finish on the fact that she was not prepared to present to the Waitangi Tribunal and answer these very questions so that we could all understand what the problem is and what the possible solutions could be to this issue.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister for Children declined or refused to appear and give evidence before the Waitangi Tribunal's urgent inquiry into the repeal of section 7AA.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal record of the urgent inquiry into the repeal of section 7AA (Wai 3350) and contemporaneous court records; true if the Minister did not appear/give evidence before the Tribunal, false if she did appear.

veracity.statement: If this Government was serious about evidence-based policy making, it would wake up to the hard evidence presented to it by officials time and time again that the ratio of Māori to non-Māori in State care has reduced because of 7AA, that Māori children in State care have reduced because of 7AA, that children and young people in care are telling us 7AA is working.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official advice records that both the Māori/non-Māori ratio in State care and the absolute number of Māori children in State care have fallen as a result of section 7AA.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki published care statistics and the departmental advice/regulatory impact statement on the 7AA repeal; true if officials' advice attributes the reduction in Māori children in care and in the Māori/non-Māori ratio to section 7AA, false if the advice records the reductions without that causal attribution or records no such reductions.

veracity.statement: All of the names the Minister for Children has just mentioned, those tragic cases were all before 7AA came out.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that every case the Minister named in her speech occurred before section 7AA came into force on 1 July 2019.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of the Minister's immediately preceding speech listing the named children, checked against the date of each case and the 1 July 2019 commencement of section 7AA; true if every named case predates commencement, false if any postdates it.

veracity.statement: Seven out of 10 children in care were Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that around 70 percent of children in State care were Māori at the time section 7AA was introduced.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki / Ministry for Children published statistics on the ethnicity of children in State care around 2018-2019; true if the Māori share is approximately 70 percent, false if materially different.

focus.statement: What they have said to those claims that we heard tonight is that there is a lack of robust evidence to support the view that section 7AA causes harmful changes to long-term care arrangements.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: the named section, the stated rationale for repeal, and what the official advice documents say about it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What is actually driving this is political ideology. They are anti-Māori, they are anti - Te Tiriti o Waitangi; that is what is driving this.

focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’re talking about a Government who is making decisions based on their own anti-Tiriti vibes, not evidence.
focus.explanation: A claim about the other side's motives and disposition; no mechanism, cost, figure or named outcome of the repeal is engaged in this sentence.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No. You are completely distorting what this debate is about. It’s really unfortunate that the members opposite aren’t listening to what the heart of this debate is about.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the conduct of the members opposite; no aspect of the repeal, its mechanism or its effects is addressed.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: She says she’s proud. Well, I don’t think she should be proud of condemning future generations to having issues with their whakapapa, their connections, and their whanaungatanga.
civility.explanation: Pointed and personalised around the Minister's stated pride, but the criticism lands on the consequences of her decision rather than on her character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And anyone in this House who denies that we are not still harming children is in La-La Land, absolute La-La Land.
civility.explanation: Mockery: characterises other members as detached from reality rather than engaging what they actually argued, though it is aimed at an unnamed class of members rather than one person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: No. You are completely distorting what this debate is about. It’s really unfortunate that the members opposite aren’t listening to what the heart of this debate is about.
civility.explanation: Directly accuses the interjecting member of distortion and the Opposition of wilfully not listening — an imputation of bad faith rather than a rebuttal of the point made.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’m sorry, but I’ve dealt with cases as an electorate MP of constituents when exactly this has happened. So you might want to deny it. I know it would be really nice to deny it doesn’t happen, but it does. It is happening.
rigor.explanation: Answers a claim about the absence of empirical evidence with unspecified personal casework — an appeal to anecdote, which cannot establish the systemic pattern in dispute.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What this repeal bill does is it doesn’t compel the Government, nor does it hold the Government to account, when it comes to the care of tamariki Māori.

focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I expect it from the ACT Party. I do. I’m not surprised by that. That’s their ideology. That’s their dogma.

focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The removing of section 7AA does not restrict the engagement and specialised relationship that iwi, hapū, and Māori organisations offer. It does not strip that.

focus.statement: So how frustrating it must be for these National Party MPs to be championing an amendment to a law that was written and passed by the National Government in 2017, which had support from ACT’s David Seymour, which the ACT Party have now made into a political football which has chased votes of exactly the type of people who have rarked up a divisive debate in Aotearoa New Zealand that we did not have before this election campaign that ACT have drawn on for votes.

focus.statement: This is a divisive piece of legislation, designed to drum up divisive, ugly politics. They’re ugly politics for political end and they have no place in this House.

focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, the evidence is quite clear that repealing section 7AA, in the Oranga Tamariki amendment bill this evening, isn’t evidence-based. rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I wonder—and our people are asking the question—did the Minister for Whānau Ora stick up for our whānau? Did other Māori Ministers in that Cabinet discussion stick up for our whānau? Quite clearly, they did not.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the conclusion 'quite clearly, they did not' is drawn about confidential Cabinet discussions from nothing but the bill's existence. Nothing is offered that bears on what any Minister said.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s the whole object, because it is possible that, in the way the law is there, it can be abused.

rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So not only is this Minister coming to the House and presenting this bill as if it is the only solution, she also commissioned the advice in a way that did not let her officials propose any other solutions to care for children.

rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, the evidence is quite clear that repealing section 7AA, in the Oranga Tamariki amendment bill this evening, isn’t evidence-based. It needs to consider the years and years of evidence, the many reviews that have been undertaken under the previous National Government and under the time when Labour was Government, to make the system better.

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Love does not call out by race. Love is called out by the kind of values that the care environment provides to the children, or seeks to provide the children.

civility.statement: I wonder—and our people are asking the question—did the Minister for Whānau Ora stick up for our whānau? Did other Māori Ministers in that Cabinet discussion stick up for our whānau? Quite clearly, they did not.

civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m ashamed when I think of all the times that I’ve heard members, in particular on that side of the House, use that quote and misquote it.

civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In fact, the New Zealand First speaker tonight repeated those claims and said that cultural considerations were getting in the way of proper care and protection. That is verging on misinformation, which is misleading to the public.

civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So not only is this Minister coming to the House and presenting this bill as if it is the only solution, she also commissioned the advice in a way that did not let her officials propose any other solutions to care for children.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the Minister personally — that she deliberately framed the commissioning to suppress alternatives — rather than confining the criticism to the narrowness of the advice.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: They’re quoting my and Mariameno Kapa-Kingi’s tupuna Meri Ngaruto.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the whakataukī 'He aha te mea nui o te ao? He tangata, he tangata, he tangata' originates with the tupuna named, and that she is an ancestor of the speaker and of Mariameno Kapa-Kingi.

veracity.statement: The removing of section 7AA does not restrict the engagement and specialised relationship that iwi, hapū, and Māori organisations offer. It does not strip that.

veracity.statement: So how frustrating it must be for these National Party MPs to be championing an amendment to a law that was written and passed by the National Government in 2017, which had support from ACT’s David Seymour, which the ACT Party have now made into a political football which has chased votes of exactly the type of people who have rarked up a divisive debate in Aotearoa New Zealand that we did not have before this election campaign that ACT have drawn on for votes.

veracity.statement: The Minister for Children now, Karen Chhour, has claimed that race-based factors set out in section 7AA create a conflict for the best interests of the child, but the official advice—as you’ve heard from my colleague the Hon Willow-Jean Prime—says exactly the opposite.

veracity.statement: Yes, seven out of 10.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that seven in ten children in Oranga Tamariki care are Māori, offered as the proportion behind the speaker's 'greater percentage is Māori'.
veracity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But then came the lady from the Green Party, who’s been here for five minutes—I don’t know who she is; I don’t much care, because she’ll probably be gone in a scandal next week anyway.
civility.explanation: Turns from the argument to the member herself — dismissing her as unknown and not worth knowing, and predicting she will be removed by scandal. That is contempt directed at a person, not criticism of a position.

civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is really what betrays the motivation of people on this other side of the House who oppose this bill. They are race fanatics. They believe that a person’s race is more than all the other attributes that make up a person.
focus.explanation: Strip out the characterisation of the other side's motives and nothing about section 7AA, its mechanism or its effects remains. It names no policy detail, only what the opposing parties are supposedly 'really like'.
