rigor.statement: Well, actually, then we heard from Willow-Jean Prime, and if there was ever a failure of logic, it was this: Willow-Jean Prime repeatedly said that there was no evidence that section 7AA made any difference because section 4 actually says that the rights of the child always come first anyway. Now, if she’s right, then she wouldn’t care about section 7AA because it doesn’t make any difference.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure before the House: if 7AA is inert, opposing its repeal is inconsistent. But it is a false dichotomy — a provision can be judged to add no operative difference while its repeal still carries signalling or interpretive consequences, so the conclusion overreaches the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is an important bill that proposes sensible, much-needed changes to the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 which will remove barriers to increasing private rental housing supply as well as introducing pet bond provisions—which is part of the National-ACT coalition agreement and has generated a lot of excitement amongst many people, particularly pet owners.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute amended and one concrete mechanism (pet bonds), and locates it in the coalition agreement, but the rest is direction-of-travel language with no figures, thresholds or dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Rents increased rapidly under the last Government; the social housing wait-list that we’ve been talking about a bit in the House over the last couple of days increased by around 20,000 families; and of course we have, very sadly, many families in New Zealand living in emergency housing motels.
specificity.explanation: Carries one checkable magnitude (an increase of around 20,000 families on the wait-list) tied to a named period, though 'rents increased rapidly' and 'many families' are left unquantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Rents increased rapidly under the last Government; the social housing wait-list that we’ve been talking about a bit in the House over the last couple of days increased by around 20,000 families; and of course we have, very sadly, many families in New Zealand living in emergency housing motels.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the social housing register grew by roughly 20,000 applicants over the 2017–2023 Labour government, and that rents rose rapidly across the same period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD Housing Register quarterly applicant counts, September 2017 vs the last quarter before the 2023 change of government: true if the net increase is approximately 20,000 applicants (say 17,000–23,000), false if materially outside that. Rent claim checked against Stats NZ rental price index / MBIE tenancy bond median rents over the same period.

divination.statement: So, ultimately, when it comes to fixed-term tenancies and the 90-day notices, we are incentivising landlords back into the market to put downward pressure on rents—that’s a good thing.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that reinstating 90-day no-cause terminations and restoring fixed-term tenancy expiry will increase rental supply and push rents down.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ rental price index (and MBIE tenancy bond median rents) for the 12 months following commencement of these provisions in early 2025: true if annual rent growth is materially lower than in the 12 months before commencement, false if rent growth is flat or accelerates.

civility.statement: I mean, the Greens are yet to join the fun on this—the Greens, sadly, still propose economically insane policies like rent controls, so the Greens are yet to kind of join the mainstream of the of the Parliament when it comes to housing supply.
civility.explanation: The pejorative ('economically insane') is aimed at a policy, rent controls, and at a party position — no individual is attacked. Hard criticism of a policy is the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Typical—typical National MP. He’s asked a question, gets presented with evidence, doesn’t like the answer, and so changes the subject.
civility.explanation: Turns from the argument to the interjector's conduct and motives, imputing bad faith — he is said to dodge because he 'doesn't like the answer'. Short of a direct insult, but no longer engaging the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What they have done is they have packaged this up with the nice and fluffy bits, like the pet bonds—and did you notice how the Minister focused on that for much of his speech?
civility.explanation: Attributes a concealment motive to the Minister personally — that he dwelt on pet bonds in order to distract from the rest of the bill. Imputing bad faith to a named individual rather than contesting the provisions.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I mean, the Greens are yet to join the fun on this—the Greens, sadly, still propose economically insane policies like rent controls, so the Greens are yet to kind of join the mainstream of the of the Parliament when it comes to housing supply.
focus.explanation: A real policy is named (rent controls, housing supply), but the weight of the sentence is a characterisation of where the Green Party sits relative to 'the mainstream' rather than engagement with the mechanism or evidence.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Right throughout every single debate, every announcement, and every policy debate, this Government has not been upfront with New Zealand when it comes to housing.
focus.explanation: A sweeping characterisation of the Government's honesty across all debates and announcements. No specific policy, measure, figure or outcome is named, so there is nothing on-policy to engage with.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But the core of this bill is that it is easier for landlords to dismiss tenants and make them homeless than it would be otherwise, and that is simply why we cannot support this bill.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: identifies the provision he objects to (easier termination of tenancies) and ties his party's vote directly to it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: For the Minister to stand up in the House when introducing this bill and say that there is a consensus on increasing the supply, yet in seven months they have not made a single announcement that will lead to the increase in supply, or—i.e., in simple terms—the building of new houses.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: takes a specific claim the Minister made in the same debate and tests it against a named outcome (announcements leading to new houses being built) over a stated period.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Typical—typical National MP. He’s asked a question, gets presented with evidence, doesn’t like the answer, and so changes the subject.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what a National MP is 'typically' like. No policy, figure or outcome survives once the characterisation of the other side is removed.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because, as I said in a debate—I think it was last week in the House—economists don’t agree on much, but they agree on two things: one, free trade is good and it lifts incomes and raises economic growth; and the second thing they agree on is that rent controls are nuts.
rigor.explanation: Bare appeal to authority: the conclusion that rent controls are bad policy rests entirely on asserted expert consensus, with no mechanism, data or reasoning about the New Zealand rental market offered to connect premise to conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: By changing that, what they’ve done is they’re going to move investment away from new builds and increase speculation on existing stock.
rigor.explanation: The inference tracks its premise: if the tax advantage of new builds came from deductibility being denied on existing stock, restoring that deductibility does remove the relative incentive. The gap is that no magnitude is offered — the direction follows, the claimed size of the effect does not.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Because, as I said in a debate—I think it was last week in the House—economists don’t agree on much, but they agree on two things: one, free trade is good and it lifts incomes and raises economic growth; and the second thing they agree on is that rent controls are nuts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that professional economists hold a near-universal consensus on two propositions: that free trade raises incomes and growth, and that rent controls are harmful.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published surveys of economists (e.g. the IGM Forum / Chicago Booth expert panel questions on rent control and on trade liberalisation); true if a large majority of surveyed economists agree rent controls reduce the quality and availability of rental housing and that free trade raises incomes, false if opinion among surveyed economists is materially divided on either.

veracity.statement: It also confirms the long-held understanding that a landlord may prohibit a tenant from smoking indoors, which clarifies the law after some recent Tenancy Tribunal decisions to the contrary.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that recent Tenancy Tribunal decisions have held, contrary to prior understanding, that a landlord may not prohibit indoor smoking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tenancy Tribunal decisions issued before 21 May 2024 on the enforceability of no-smoking-indoors clauses; true if one or more decisions held such a prohibition ineffective or unenforceable, false if no such decisions exist.

veracity.statement: There’s massive delays in the Tenancy Tribunal right now.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at May 2024 the Tenancy Tribunal had unusually long waiting times for hearings.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE / Tenancy Services published Tenancy Tribunal waiting-time statistics for 2023–24; true if median time from application to hearing was materially longer than the Tribunal's target and its historic norm, false if within normal range.

veracity.statement: For the Minister to stand up in the House when introducing this bill and say that there is a consensus on increasing the supply, yet in seven months they have not made a single announcement that will lead to the increase in supply, or—i.e., in simple terms—the building of new houses.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in its first seven months in office the Government made no announcement capable of increasing housing supply.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government housing announcements between 27 November 2023 and 21 May 2024 (Beehive releases, Cabinet papers); false if any announced measure was directed at increasing dwelling supply — e.g. granny-flat consenting exemptions, changes to intensification/MDRS rules, city and regional deals or housing infrastructure funding — true if no such announcement can be identified.

veracity.statement: As a result of moving that, we saw an increase in new builds and an increase in new homebuyers in the market.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that after interest deductibility was removed for existing rental properties (leaving new builds exempt), both new-build activity and first-home-buyer participation rose.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ new dwelling consents and RBNZ C31 / CoreLogic first-home-buyer share of purchases for the period following the March 2021 interest deductibility change; true if both new dwelling consents and the first-home-buyer share rose over that period, false if either did not.

veracity.statement: They can holler, they can bicker, they can shout, and they can heckle, but they actually have nothing to refute the fact that their policies last time increased homelessness and increased house prices, and we saw a drop in the build of new builds, of affordable builds, and of social housing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the previous National-led government homelessness and house prices rose while new builds, affordable builds and social housing stock fell.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: For 2008–2017: Stats NZ severe housing deprivation estimates and MSD emergency housing grant numbers; REINZ House Price Index; Stats NZ new dwelling consents; and Housing New Zealand / social housing stock counts. True if all four move in the direction claimed, false if any — notably new dwelling consents, which are readily checkable — moved the opposite way.

specificity.statement: So what we are doing is enabling landlords to require a pet bond if they have agreed to the tenant keeping a pet up to the equivalent of two weeks’ rent.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact mechanism (a pet bond conditional on landlord agreement) and quantifies the cap at two weeks' rent — checkable against the bill as drafted.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: In fact, what is clear is that the policy changes that this Government has made will decrease and disincentivise and lead to fewer houses being built.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Government's housing and tax policy changes will result in fewer new dwellings being built than would otherwise have been the case.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ new dwelling consents series; true if annual new dwelling consents in the two years after May 2024 fall below the year-to-May-2024 level, false if they hold steady or rise.

focus.statement: Because regardless of whether you have been the best tenant in the world, regardless of the value you have added to your home by maintaining it or even improving it, and regardless of whether your whānau has settled into the communities that you have built roots in, your landlord can kick you out for no reason at all.
focus.explanation: Engages the specific mechanism before the House — no-cause termination of periodic tenancies — and its effect on tenants. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Oh, you wish you had this level of social media engagement.
focus.explanation: A retort to an interjector about social media popularity. Names no policy, figure or outcome; strip the personal jab and nothing about the bill remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How many of them were from Green Party members?
focus.explanation: Insinuates the eviction stories were partisan submissions. It is entirely about the other party's supporters and names no policy, measure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is a rejection of the Opposition’s cheap campaign to pit landlords and tenants against each other.
focus.explanation: Nominally about the bill, but the content is a characterisation of the Opposition's motives rather than any mechanism, cost or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I look across the House there and say that you guys should try that, because it would have done you a lot better than some of the things that you did actually do when there were a lot of hidden agendas that you didn’t tell the public about and you then proceeded to embark upon.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the previous Government's alleged "hidden agendas" in general. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — remove the party characterisation and nothing is left.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: And this is on top of the billions of dollars of tax cuts that this Government is giving to landlords.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's tax changes benefiting landlords amount to billions of dollars.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/Budget 2024 costing of the restoration of interest deductibility on residential rental property (and related landlord tax changes); true if the fiscal cost to the Crown is in the billions of dollars over the forecast period, false if it is materially under $1 billion.

veracity.statement: What else do you expect when you elect a leader of a Government who owns seven houses at a time where people can’t even make their rent?
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Prime Minister owned seven houses as at May 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Register of Pecuniary and Other Specified Interests of Members of Parliament for 2024 (Christopher Luxon's real property entries); true if seven properties are listed, false if a materially different number is listed.

veracity.statement: And this is a statement by a Minister that is so deeply out of touch with the reality for average New Zealanders, because I put out a call asking good tenants to share times when they had been unfairly evicted, and I received over 500 responses in less than 24 hours.
veracity.explanation: Asserts she received over 500 responses to a public call for unfair-eviction stories in under 24 hours.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tamatha Paul's public call-out post of May 2024 and contemporaneous reporting or her office's records of responses received; true if 500 or more responses were received within 24 hours, false if the number or timeframe is materially smaller.

veracity.statement: This bill reinstates the 90-day no-cause termination for periodic tenancies, and returning landlords notice period to 42 days in specific circumstances.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the specific notice periods the bill establishes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Residential Tenancies Amendment Bill 2024 as reported back; true if it reinstates 90-day no-cause termination notices for periodic tenancies and sets a 42-day landlord notice period for specified circumstances, false if either period differs.

veracity.statement: Approximately 64 percent of New Zealand households own at least one pet, and more than half of those remaining would like to get a pet.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a national pet-ownership rate and a further claim about the aspirations of non-owning households.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Companion Animals New Zealand's national companion animal survey; true if the reported share of households owning at least one pet is about 64 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: This is something which was signalled quite clearly in the campaign and signalled quite clearly in the coalition agreement that this was the thing that the Government was going to do, and the Government is doing exactly what it said.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the tenancy changes in the bill were pre-announced in the election campaign and written into the coalition agreement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's published 2023 election housing/tenancy policy and the National–ACT and National–NZ First coalition agreements of November 2023; true if reinstating 90-day no-cause terminations appears in both the campaign policy and a coalition agreement, false if it appears in neither.

civility.statement: What else do you expect when you elect a leader of a Government who owns seven houses at a time where people can’t even make their rent?
civility.explanation: Turns from the policy to the Prime Minister's personal property holdings, using them to impute self-interest to him personally rather than contesting the bill.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And this is a statement by a Minister that is so deeply out of touch with the reality for average New Zealanders, because I put out a call asking good tenants to share times when they had been unfairly evicted, and I received over 500 responses in less than 24 hours.
civility.explanation: "So deeply out of touch with the reality" moves from the Minister's claim to the Minister's personal grasp of reality — condescension aimed at the man rather than at his argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Oh, you wish you had this level of social media engagement.
civility.explanation: Mockery directed at another member personally — short of an insult, but it belittles rather than engages.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I’ll close by saying this: renters deserve better and I have no doubt that they will rise up and kick this Government out in two years’ time for these actions.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the incumbent coalition Government will be voted out at the next general election, roughly two years from May 2024.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Official Electoral Commission result of the next New Zealand general election; true if the National-ACT-NZ First coalition loses office (i.e. does not form the next Government), false if it is returned to government.

rigor.statement: We live in a country which is sparsely populated. The only reason we have got a shortage of housing is because of decisions made by Government that make it harder to build and provide housing to each other.
rigor.explanation: Single-cause fallacy: low population density is offered as grounds for concluding that regulation is the sole cause of housing shortage, when nothing connects the premise to the exclusion of every other cause (construction costs, land supply, migration, finance).
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The previous Government sought to increase hurdles in the housing sector, causing many of our landlords to exit the market. The amendments made today are sensible changes that work to fix that.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc causal claim: landlord exits are attributed to the previous Government's rules with no evidence offered, and the conclusion that these amendments "fix that" rests entirely on that unsupported attribution.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Look, we’ve heard quite a lot of hyperbole already in this debate and how radical this discussion that we’re having is, but the reality is that we’ve actually had this discussion before in this House, probably not that long ago, when the roles were reversed and the direction of the legislation was reversed, so it’s not particularly radical.
rigor.explanation: A valid symmetry argument — if the House recently legislated in the opposite direction, reversing it is not unprecedented — but it establishes only that the change is familiar, not that it is unradical in effect, so there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The coalition is committed to easing access to housing for over 1.7 million New Zealanders by removing barriers to rental supply and incentivising landlords to get back into providing to the rental market.
specificity.explanation: Carries one checkable figure (1.7 million renters) but the mechanisms — "removing barriers" and "incentivising landlords" — have no amounts, instruments or timeframes attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill reinstates the 90-day no-cause termination for periodic tenancies, and returning landlords notice period to 42 days in specific circumstances.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact mechanisms and the exact notice periods in the bill — anyone could check this against the text of the amendment.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This is exactly what we said we were going to do and it’s exactly what we are doing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Residential Tenancies Amendment Bill (reinstating 90-day no-cause terminations for periodic tenancies) matches what the governing parties campaigned on and agreed to before the 2023 election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 housing/rental policy documents and the National–ACT and National–NZ First coalition agreements; true if they contain a commitment to reinstate no-cause (90-day) terminations for periodic tenancies, false if no such commitment appears or if the bill goes materially beyond it.

veracity.statement: The research shows that Māori report higher rates of movement between homes, at 8.7 percent compared to 5 percent of New Zealanders. The reality of this is Māori moving five times within five years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific comparative residential-mobility statistic: 8.7 percent for Māori against 5 percent for New Zealanders overall.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / Census or HUD residential mobility data on the share of Māori versus all New Zealanders who moved dwelling in the reference period; true if the figures are 8.7% and 5% on a comparable basis, false if the published rates differ materially or are not comparably defined.

veracity.statement: Only 31 percent of Māori were in a position of homeownership, compared to 57.9 percent of New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts 2018 home-ownership rates of 31 percent for Māori against 57.9 percent for New Zealanders overall.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2018 Census home-ownership figures by ethnicity; true if Māori home ownership is ~31% and the national/European figure ~57.9% on the stated basis, false if the published rates differ materially.

veracity.statement: There are 1.7 million renters in New Zealand; 80 percent of those renting rent from the private market—not from the Government—from the private market.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the total number of renters in New Zealand (1.7 million people) and that 80 percent of renters rent privately rather than from the State.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census dwelling/tenure data and HUD rental-stock figures; true if the number of people in rented dwellings is ~1.7 million and the private (non-Kāinga Ora/community-provider) share of renting households is ~80%, false if either figure is materially different.

rigor.statement: We heard over there from the Green Party that so often, tenants are kicked out for no reason. But as a landlord, why would you kick a good tenant out? What is the purpose of doing that? If they’re a good tenant, they’re paying their rent, they’re not damaging your property, why would you kick them out? That is completely stupid and is against your best interest.
rigor.explanation: Answers an empirical claim (that tenants are in fact terminated without cause) with an argument about what would be irrational for a landlord — an assumption of perfect rational self-interest, offered via rhetorical question with no evidence, and it ignores the common non-'bad tenant' reasons for termination (selling, moving family in, raising rent).
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You know, the funny thing is that what landlords are doing is they’ve responded to that and they have withdrawn from the market. The funny thing is that what that has done is it has driven up rental costs, so it has actually not been in the best interests of the tenants.
rigor.explanation: A two-step post hoc causal chain — policy caused landlord exit, exit caused rent rises — asserted with nothing offered to connect the links or to exclude the obvious alternative drivers of rent (interest rates, migration, construction costs).
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reason that house building has dropped off is a very simple one. It’s the economy—the cost of building has gone up like that. The value of houses went down like that. What do you expect to happen? Lots of developers have pulled out of the market simply because they cannot make the numbers work.
rigor.explanation: The inference is coherent: rising build costs plus falling house values squeeze development margins, so developers exit. Weakened by the insistence that the cause is 'a very simple one' — a single-cause claim that excludes financing, consenting and demand factors without argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The changes would, for one, reintroduce 90-day, no-cause terminations for periodic tenancies. This supports landlords’ power to end a tenancy without requiring a specific reason. This is dangerous for our people, given that there is a higher proportion of Māori who reside in rental properties and social housing.
rigor.explanation: Valid as far as it goes — greater exposure to renting plus weaker tenure protection implies greater exposure to the change — but the step from 'less security' to 'dangerous' is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The research shows that Māori report higher rates of movement between homes, at 8.7 percent compared to 5 percent of New Zealanders. The reality of this is Māori moving five times within five years.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: an 8.7 percent mobility rate does not entail 'moving five times within five years' — the conclusion is a far stronger claim than the cited statistic supports.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The regulatory environment needs to be structured in such a way that people are willing to rent their houses, and the no-cause termination—or the periodic tenancies—that we’ve seen have had an impact that has been quite extraordinary in my own region in Queenstown, as well as other places in the country. Literally, it became a crisis where people were unable to find a house. People were sleeping in their vans, sleeping in cars, sleeping in all sorts of places around the region that were literally unsafe.
rigor.explanation: Attributes the Queenstown rental shortage to the removal of no-cause terminations on the strength of temporal coincidence and local anecdote — post hoc reasoning, with no attempt to weigh Queenstown's well-known tourism-driven demand, short-term letting and land-supply constraints.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We heard over there from the Green Party that so often, tenants are kicked out for no reason. But as a landlord, why would you kick a good tenant out? What is the purpose of doing that? If they’re a good tenant, they’re paying their rent, they’re not damaging your property, why would you kick them out? That is completely stupid and is against your best interest.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of no-cause terminations and how landlords would use it, not on the other party's character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Look, we know that the Labour Party didn’t set out to demonise landlords, but the reality is you look at the kind of legislation they’ve passed, you look at the approach they’ve taken, and time and time again from that side of the House, we’re hearing the arguments against the deduction of interest against the cost of running a business. Every other business is able to do that, but poor landlords, they’re not able to do it, according to that side of the House—there’s something wrong with that.
focus.explanation: Contains a genuine policy point (interest deductibility and the treatment of rental property versus other businesses), but the weight of the passage is a characterisation of the other party's attitude toward landlords rather than the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The changes would, for one, reintroduce 90-day, no-cause terminations for periodic tenancies. This supports landlords’ power to end a tenancy without requiring a specific reason. This is dangerous for our people, given that there is a higher proportion of Māori who reside in rental properties and social housing.
focus.explanation: Names the specific provision in the bill and identifies the mechanism and the affected group; entirely on the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What the Government illustrates to us is that we are not worth a single bill, a single amendment or repeal, unless our failure is their financial success.
focus.explanation: A general characterisation of the Government's motives with no policy, figure or measure named; the content is entirely about what the other side is 'really like'.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The regulatory environment needs to be structured in such a way that people are willing to rent their houses, and the no-cause termination—or the periodic tenancies—that we’ve seen have had an impact that has been quite extraordinary in my own region in Queenstown, as well as other places in the country. Literally, it became a crisis where people were unable to find a house. People were sleeping in their vans, sleeping in cars, sleeping in all sorts of places around the region that were literally unsafe.
focus.explanation: Engages the specific provision at issue and its claimed effect on rental supply in a named place; no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: The Minister of Housing, Chris Bishop, claims that the changes to the Act will encourage landlords back into the rental property market.
divination.explanation: Relays the Minister's forecast that reinstating no-cause terminations will bring landlords back into the private rental market.
divination.subject: other
divination.falsification_criterion: Tenancy Services bond-lodgement data and MBIE active-bond/rental-stock series for the private rental market; true if the number of active private rental bonds/tenancies rises after the amendments take effect, false if the stock is flat or continues to decline.

civility.statement: I must then question whether the Minister understands the obligation as a partner of the Te Tiriti o Waitangi, when he continuously supports choices that he knows will negatively impact on Māori communities.
civility.explanation: Moves from the policy to the named Minister personally — questioning his comprehension of his Treaty obligations and imputing that he knowingly acts to harm Māori. That is an attribution of bad faith to an individual, not criticism of a decision.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This reverses changes made by the last Government, which were no doubt well intentioned and trying to assist renters, but actually had quite the opposite effect; a classic example of the unintended consequences principle, which is often seen in this House, and the implications flow out into our country from well-meaning decisions that unfortunately aren’t well considered, and don’t take into account all factors, and, in some cases, have effects that can’t be foreseen by anyone.
civility.explanation: Criticises the previous Government's law squarely while expressly crediting its good intentions; the disagreement lands on the policy and on no person.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Only 31 percent of Māori were in a position of homeownership, compared to 57.9 percent of New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Two precise percentages, a named comparison group and a stated reference year — directly checkable against the census.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because of this change to the legislation, they are unable to do that. That meant that a lot of people who would otherwise have had access to the house throughout the year, and many of them—people who worked a seasonal job were unable to have those houses. That means that people were literally living in their vans as a consequence.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — the removal of no-cause terminations and its claimed effect on the supply of rental housing in a named region. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The reality is we need a lot more houses, and that is something that the Government is doing with the fast-track legislation, which I know that the Opposition is also opposing.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point about housing supply and named legislation, but the closing clause pivots to what the Opposition is doing rather than to the mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What is the answer? It’s putting more funding into Kāinga Ora and the ability to build more houses.
focus.explanation: Directed at the policy question — a named agency and a named remedy (state house building) offered as the alternative to the bill.

rigor.statement: I simply make the point that I don’t know when my house might burn down by fire, but I’m going to get insurance anyway. veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD advice to Ministers on the removal and restoration of interest deductibility for residential rental property (2021 and 2023-24 papers): true if officials advised that interest deductibility settings affect rents in the direction stated and comparable advice went to the previous Government, false if the advice was silent, contrary or materially different.

veracity.statement: I thank the member for their question, because we inherited a situation where house prices had gone up 50 percent, rental prices had gone up $180 per week, and the social housing register had quadrupled.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three figures for the period of the previous Labour government: house prices +50%, weekly rents +$180, and a fourfold increase in the social housing register.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: REINZ/Stats NZ house price index, MBIE tenancy bond median weekly rents, and the MSD social housing register, each compared between late 2017 and late 2023: true if each figure is within rounding of 50%, $180/week and a fourfold rise; false if any is materially overstated.

veracity.statement: They’ll have gone down because of the economic cycle, because of the market, but I would say to you that this is a Government that is going to open up more greenfields.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that building consents for new houses have fallen since he became Prime Minister in November 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ building consents issued for new dwellings: compare the months from November 2023 to April 2024 against the equivalent prior-year months; true if consents fell, false if they rose or were flat.

veracity.statement: Does the Prime Minister agree with the Ombudsman on the Fast-track Approvals Bill that “When you get a bill like this that creates enormous executive power, there is ever more need to have a check and a balance unless it’s matched by oversight and accountability. I think democracy itself is the loser.”?
veracity.explanation: Relays a quoted statement attributed to the Ombudsman about the Fast-track Approvals Bill; the checkable claim is that he said this.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Chief Ombudsman Peter Boshier's public comments and submission on the Fast-track Approvals Bill (May 2024): true if the quoted words appear in his reported remarks or submission, false if no such statement exists or the quotation materially misstates it.

focus.statement: If the purpose of scrapping First Home Grants, as his Government announced today, is to increase social housing, why is the Government spending less on new social housing places than it’s saving by scrapping the grants?
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named policy change and its fiscal consequence — textbook scrutiny of a specific government commitment, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The choice that we’re making is to invest in 1,500 new social housing places for Kiwi families, and that will mean that some of those families are out of Labour’s motels.
focus.explanation: Engages the housing measure and names a specific number of places, with a light party tag on the end.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, you had your go, and they didn’t actually achieve any outcomes.
focus.explanation: Pure party framing — no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named; strip out 'the other side had their turn' and nothing remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If house prices were going up by a massive 50-plus percent, wouldn’t a saver seeking to buying a house have to be saving that way as well, and does he know anybody who can do that, including anybody in the Labour Party who can do that over there?
focus.explanation: A real affordability point, but half the question is a jibe about whether anyone in the Labour Party could manage it; the party framing carries most of the weight.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Labour Government had six years to deal with it and failed to achieve anything.
focus.explanation: A blanket verdict on the other party's term with no policy, target or figure named — the sentence has no policy content to check.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The track record from the last Labour-Greens Government was abysmal: billions of dollars spent only to peddle misery with more children growing up in motels and sleeping in cars.
focus.explanation: Gestures at an outcome (children in motels) but the sentence is mainly a characterisation of the previous Government's record; no measure, target or figure is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is it correct that the announcement made today regarding money for social housing places continues on into the out-years, so it is correct to say that every single dollar saved by discontinuing First Home Grants funds social housing?
focus.explanation: Engages the fiscal mechanism of the announcement — out-year funding and the destination of the savings — without party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does the Prime Minister agree with the Ombudsman on the Fast-track Approvals Bill that “When you get a bill like this that creates enormous executive power, there is ever more need to have a check and a balance unless it’s matched by oversight and accountability. I think democracy itself is the loser.”?
focus.explanation: Directly on the bill before the House and on a specific structural objection to it — executive power without matching oversight.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: So, actually, unwinding interest deductibility, lowering the brightline test, making sure that we get the balance right are good things—it will put downward pressure on rents.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that restoring interest deductibility, shortening the brightline test and rebalancing tenancy law will lower rents.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ rental price index and MBIE tenancy bond median weekly rents: true if national rent growth falls materially below its pre-2024 trend (or rents fall) in the two years after the changes take effect; false if rent growth continues at or above that trend.

rigor.statement: They’ll have gone down because of the economic cycle, because of the market, but I would say to you that this is a Government that is going to open up more greenfields.
rigor.explanation: A real causal claim about a real policy outcome, but the cause is simply asserted: consents fell, therefore the economic cycle did it. No mechanism or evidence is offered to rule out policy effects — bare post hoc attribution.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If house prices were going up by a massive 50-plus percent, wouldn’t a saver seeking to buying a house have to be saving that way as well, and does he know anybody who can do that, including anybody in the Labour Party who can do that over there?
rigor.explanation: There is a genuine inference here about deposit affordability, but it does not follow: a 50% rise in prices requires a deposit to grow 50%, not savings to grow 'at 50-plus percent' as a rate — the two rates of change are conflated.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What I don’t understand is how the masterminds that brought us KiwiBuild ended up increasing house prices 15 percent, added $180 to average weekly rents, and four times more people on the social house waiting list.
civility.explanation: 'the masterminds that brought us KiwiBuild' is sarcasm at the competence of the people who designed the policy rather than criticism of the policy itself — mockery, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What I would say is we have proposed an independent expert panel that will judge conditions including the environment, including social benefits and economic benefits, the whole lot, and we’ve actually proposed that in the select committee.
specificity.explanation: Names a mechanism (an independent expert panel) and the forum (select committee), but no membership, criteria, thresholds or timing — a direction with partial detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will the Prime Minister undertake, here and now, to have regard to all the comments on the 17 precedented fast-track projects of the last Government when he’s considering the fast-track process in this Government—remember what the Greens said back then—and will he have regard to it when he’s going forward?
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete figure (17 prior fast-track projects) and a named process, but the ask itself — 'have regard to all the comments' — is undefined in scope or mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will he, in light of his request for the Green Party’s support, commit to no new coal mines, not reopening oil and gas drilling, protecting the conservation estate from mining, and no extinction of native species through his Fast-track Approvals Bill?
specificity.explanation: Four concrete, checkable conditions attached to a named bill; the Prime Minister could answer yes or no to each.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The operating balance excluding gains and losses—commonly known as the OBEGAL—is the difference between total Crown revenue and total Crown expenses, before gains and losses.
specificity.explanation: A precise definition naming the components and the exclusion; anyone could check it against the Crown accounts' stated basis.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, after stripping out large, one-off expenses, and adjusting for the economic cycle, the Treasury estimates a structural operating deficit of around 1.5 percent of GDP in the current financial year.
specificity.explanation: Names the source, the adjustment method, the magnitude and the period — directly checkable against Treasury's published cyclically-adjusted balance.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But what I can tell the House is that in the current economic circumstances, if we continued with the future Budget operating allowances in the half-year update, which was set by the previous Government, there might not be a surplus posted in New Zealand until 2030-31.
specificity.explanation: Names the counterfactual policy setting (half-year update operating allowances) and a dated consequence (2030-31), though hedged with 'might'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have chosen to support renters because we don’t want to see the acceleration in rents they faced under that Government, and we are taking policy actions to put downward pressure on rents.
specificity.explanation: 'Taking policy actions to put downward pressure on rents' names no action, no amount and no timeframe; only the contrast with past rent growth carries any content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why has she chosen to support landlords with a $2.9 billion tax break but cut the funding to help first-home buyers?
specificity.explanation: A named figure attached to a named beneficiary group and a named offsetting cut; the trade-off asserted is checkable against Budget documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Budget 2024 will allocate $140 million in new funding for 1,500 new social housing places to be provided by community housing providers, not Kāinga Ora, thanks to savings found by ending the First Home Grant.
specificity.explanation: Dollar figure, number of places, named provider type and the named funding source — fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And I’d just say to the member, again, please support the bill. If you care about the environment, if you care about climate change, you’d back our fast-track legislation.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy / non sequitur: caring about the environment is asserted to entail supporting this particular bill, with nothing offered to connect the premise to the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because there was a banning of an oil and gas ban from the Labour-Greens. There was no follow-up plan to it. It was a bunch of bumper stickers, headlines, and Post-it notes, and, actually, what was needed is we need gas as a transitory energy source so we can keep our energy security in place.
rigor.explanation: An inference is offered (the exploration ban without a replacement plan produced energy security risk, therefore gas is needed as a transition fuel), but the causal link between the ban and current security risk is asserted rather than evidenced, and the 'bumper stickers' characterisation does no argumentative work.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: A structural deficit, members, is not sustainable in the long term, as it requires continual borrowing to cover expenses, leading to a never-ending accumulation of public debt—a debt spiral. That is the mess our Government is cleaning up.
rigor.explanation: The step from 'structural deficit' to 'never-ending accumulation' and a 'debt spiral' is a slippery slope: nothing is offered to show the deficit persists indefinitely rather than being closed, which the very next answer says the Government intends to do.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The second point is that the evidence suggests that it brings forward the purchase of a home because it provides money towards the deposit, but it doesn’t actually make the difference for most people between buying a house or not buying a house and that is one of the reasons why we have reprioritised it to higher-value expenditure.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (reprioritise the grant) does follow from the stated premise about marginal effect on purchase decisions, but 'the evidence suggests' is an unnamed appeal to authority — no study, agency or figure is identified to support the key premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And I’d just say to the member, again, please support the bill. If you care about the environment, if you care about climate change, you’d back our fast-track legislation.
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure before the House (the fast-track legislation) and ties it to climate goals rather than to the other party's character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because there was a banning of an oil and gas ban from the Labour-Greens. There was no follow-up plan to it. It was a bunch of bumper stickers, headlines, and Post-it notes, and, actually, what was needed is we need gas as a transitory energy source so we can keep our energy security in place.
focus.explanation: A genuine energy-policy point about security of supply and transition fuel, but a substantial share of the answer is dismissive framing of the opposing parties rather than the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Modesty prevents me saying anything, Mr Speaker. Can I ask the Minister: could he possibly deal with the question that came by way of objection but is the specialty of the member who shouted it out, Rachel Boyack, when she shouted out “Rubbish”?
focus.explanation: A housing measure was under discussion, but the question carries no policy content at all: it is entirely about another member's conduct.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will he, in light of his request for the Green Party’s support, commit to no new coal mines, not reopening oil and gas drilling, protecting the conservation estate from mining, and no extinction of native species through his Fast-track Approvals Bill?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the named measure before the House and the specific environmental outcomes it would govern.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he stand by his statement on 8 May, “support our reversal of the oil and gas ban, support our fast-track legislation, and let’s go get renewable energy built in this country.”, and, if so, is he confused about the difference between oil and gas and renewable energy?
focus.explanation: Anchored to a dated statement and two named policies (the oil and gas ban reversal, the fast-track bill), though the closing clause shifts to the man rather than the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: A structural deficit, members, is not sustainable in the long term, as it requires continual borrowing to cover expenses, leading to a never-ending accumulation of public debt—a debt spiral. That is the mess our Government is cleaning up.
focus.explanation: A real fiscal argument about the structural balance, but closed with 'the mess our Government is cleaning up' — party framing appended to the substance.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We have chosen to support renters because we don’t want to see the acceleration in rents they faced under that Government, and we are taking policy actions to put downward pressure on rents.
focus.explanation: A housing-policy answer in substance, but it turns on a comparison with the previous Government rather than on the first-home buyer funding actually asked about.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does she stand by her statement “These savings and revenue initiatives are the same as those in the National Party’s tax plan, with some adjustment to reflect coalition agreements.”; if so, where in the coalition agreement does it say that first-home grants will be scrapped?
focus.explanation: Textbook scrutiny: quotes a specific ministerial statement and tests it against a specific named policy change (scrapping first-home grants).
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I thank the member because, again, it was inspired thinking from David Parker, who invented a fast-track process. We’ve taken that, we’ve put it on steroids so that we can get things built.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that David Parker originated a fast-track consenting process which the current bill builds on.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Legislative record for the COVID-19 Recovery (Fast-track Consenting) Act 2020: true if David Parker was the responsible Minister who introduced/sponsored a fast-track consenting regime; false if no such fast-track process was created under him.

veracity.statement: The OBEGAL is in deficit and has been since 2019.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an unbroken run of OBEGAL deficits in the Crown accounts beginning in 2019.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Financial Statements of the Government of New Zealand, OBEGAL line, financial years 2018/19 to 2023/24: true if every year from 2019 onward records a deficit; false if any intervening year posted an OBEGAL surplus.

veracity.statement: So, after stripping out large, one-off expenses, and adjusting for the economic cycle, the Treasury estimates a structural operating deficit of around 1.5 percent of GDP in the current financial year.
veracity.explanation: Attributes to Treasury a structural operating deficit estimate of about 1.5 percent of GDP for the 2023/24 financial year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's cyclically-adjusted/structural balance estimates published in the Budget 2024 or Half Year Update documents: true if the structural operating deficit for the current financial year is stated at roughly 1.5% of GDP; false if materially different or if Treasury published no such estimate.

veracity.statement: I can tell the House that the forecasts have continued to deteriorate even since the Budget Policy Statement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that economic and fiscal forecasts worsened between the Budget Policy Statement and the time of speaking (May 2024).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare Treasury's Budget Policy Statement 2024 forecasts with the Budget Economic and Fiscal Update 2024 (30 May 2024): true if key forecasts (GDP growth, tax revenue, OBEGAL track) are revised down; false if revised up or materially unchanged.

veracity.statement: Why has she chosen to support landlords with a $2.9 billion tax break but cut the funding to help first-home buyers?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's restoration of interest deductibility for landlords is worth $2.9 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD costings for the restoration of residential rental interest deductibility as published in Budget 2024 or the coalition tax plan: true if the fiscal cost is around $2.9 billion over the forecast period; false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Budget 2024 will allocate $140 million in new funding for 1,500 new social housing places to be provided by community housing providers, not Kāinga Ora, thanks to savings found by ending the First Home Grant.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a Budget 2024 allocation of $140 million for 1,500 social housing places delivered by community housing providers, funded by ending the First Home Grant.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 (30 May 2024) Vote Housing and Urban Development appropriations and the associated Government press release: true if $140m for 1,500 CHP places, funded from First Home Grant savings, appears; false if the figures or funding source differ.

veracity.statement: As the House has discussed previously, funding for new social housing places under the previous Government ends in June 2025—another fiscal cliff we’ve had to confront.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government's appropriation for new social housing places was time-limited and expires in June 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Vote Housing and Urban Development appropriations set in Budgets 2020–2023 for new public housing places: true if the funding track terminates at the end of the 2024/25 financial year; false if funding continues beyond June 2025.

veracity.statement: Well, as the House discussed yesterday and as I announced on Monday, the independent review into Kāinga Ora reveals that it’s not financially sustainable in its current form.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the independent review of Kāinga Ora concluded the agency is not financially sustainable in its current form.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The independent review of Kāinga Ora released in May 2024 (chaired by Sir Bill English): true if it finds the agency's financial position unsustainable in its current form; false if it makes no such finding.

veracity.statement: At a time when the wait-list for social housing is over 25,000 applicants, we have made the tough call to prioritise support for them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the social housing register stood at more than 25,000 applicants in May 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD Housing Register quarterly statistics for the March 2024 quarter: true if applicants on the register exceed 25,000; false if below.

veracity.statement: Does the Minister agree that many first-home buyers have relied on the First Home Grant to purchase their first home, including 10,000 last year?
veracity.explanation: Asserts approximately 10,000 people received a First Home Grant in the previous year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora First Home Grant recipient statistics for the 2023 calendar year (or 2022/23 financial year): true if around 10,000 grants were paid; false if materially fewer.

veracity.statement: No, actually, last year—the member’s wrong—7,800 people received the First Home Grant, so the member’s wrong on that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 7,800 people, not 10,000, received the First Home Grant in the previous year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora First Home Grant recipient statistics for the 2023 calendar year (or 2022/23 financial year): true if the count is approximately 7,800; false if materially different.

civility.statement: Modesty prevents me saying anything, Mr Speaker. Can I ask the Minister: could he possibly deal with the question that came by way of objection but is the specialty of the member who shouted it out, Rachel Boyack, when she shouted out “Rubbish”?
civility.explanation: Singles out a named member and makes her the object of mockery — 'the specialty of the member' — rather than engaging anything she argued.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does he stand by his statement on 8 May, “support our reversal of the oil and gas ban, support our fast-track legislation, and let’s go get renewable energy built in this country.”, and, if so, is he confused about the difference between oil and gas and renewable energy?
civility.explanation: The second limb drops the policy point and asks whether the Prime Minister is 'confused' — a jab at his personal grasp of the subject rather than at the position itself.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The advice may see that an increase in reporting could be seen as an improvement, when, actually, it just means more people are reporting—doesn’t mean that we’ve made successes in that space.
rigor.explanation: A valid inference about a measurement proxy: a rise in reporting is consistent with either better detection or worse outcomes, so it does not by itself establish improvement. The conclusion tracks the premise; no fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As I’ve travelled around the country the last couple of months, talking to NGOs and community organisations on where they see the gaps and where they see the Government can help them in this space, I realise there is a lot of work to do and we have to make sure that we’re actually listening to the people on the ground and making a real positive difference in this space rather than reactionary legislation and targets that don’t make a damn bit of difference.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote: the evidence offered is the speaker's own travel and conversations, and the conclusion that targets 'don’t make a damn bit of difference' is asserted rather than supported by anything she has set out.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What I do believe, as I’ve heard from many landlords and many people out there who work with vulnerable tenants, is that bringing back no-cause evictions will enable landlords to take a chance on often quite vulnerable tenants who are trying to access rental properties.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote set directly against the departmental evidence just cited: the support offered for the causal claim is what he has 'heard from many landlords', with nothing connecting the removal of cause requirements to landlords accepting riskier tenants.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The member needs to appreciate that the policy intent is positive not negative.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the objection put was about the outcome for evicted tenants, and the stated intent of the policy does not bear on whether that outcome occurs. Intent is offered where effect was asked about.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does she think it’s acceptable to only develop targets that are easy to measure and easy to achieve, and, if so, where does this leave victims of family and sexual violence?
civility.explanation: Pointed and loaded — it presupposes the Minister is deliberately choosing soft targets — but the imputation attaches to the target-setting decision rather than to her character. Robust, edging toward the person without landing on them.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is it the Minister’s leadership style to see the staff that work for her department as capable and worth backing, rather than running them down before a review is even complete?
civility.explanation: Framed as a question about the Minister's personal 'leadership style' and carrying the imputation that she runs down her own staff before a review concludes. The target is the person's conduct and character rather than the restructuring proposal itself.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As I’ve travelled around the country the last couple of months, talking to NGOs and community organisations on where they see the gaps and where they see the Government can help them in this space, I realise there is a lot of work to do and we have to make sure that we’re actually listening to the people on the ground and making a real positive difference in this space rather than reactionary legislation and targets that don’t make a damn bit of difference.
specificity.explanation: No figures, mechanisms, named programmes or timeframes; 'a lot of work to do', 'listening to the people on the ground' and 'a real positive difference' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yes, I believe everyone should be able to access a warm and dry home to live in. The intent of our tenancy policy changes is to encourage more landlords into the market so that people can access those homes.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy area and states a causal intent (more landlords into the market), but supplies no mechanism detail, no numbers and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he accept the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development’s (HUD) advice that evidence is uncertain that no-cause evictions will put downward pressures on rents but that the evidence is clear that security of tenancy for renters will be negatively impacted?
specificity.explanation: Names the source (HUD advice), the policy (no-cause evictions) and the two specific findings attributed to it, so the assertion can be checked against the published advice.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are fixing the underlying issues in our housing market that have caused that to be the case.
specificity.explanation: A bare assertion of remedial action: no named measure, mechanism, figure or timeframe, and 'the underlying issues' is left undefined.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Last Friday, I announced with the Prime Minister and Minister of Transport, the Hon Simeon Brown, that through Budget 2024 the Government would be providing an additional $63.6 million over four years to fund Coastguard New Zealand and Surf Lifesaving New Zealand so that these NGOs can continue to deliver their essential front-line water safety and rescue and prevention services across New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Exact amount, period, named recipients, named funding vehicle and the date of the announcement — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How is it in the best interests of children and young people to add specialist legal work to Oranga Tamariki social workers, work that they are not trained for, and in an organisation where they are already 160 social workers short?
specificity.explanation: Names the agency, the specific proposal (shifting legal work to social workers) and a hard figure for the vacancy shortfall, all of which can be checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: No, I don’t agree, because “front line” has been defined—the advice is that front-line staff roles are considered to be children’s workers, as defined in section 23 of the Children’s Act, and the definition of “front-line service” is an operational matter for Oranga Tamariki.
specificity.explanation: Cites a named statutory provision (section 23 of the Children's Act) as the operative definition and identifies where responsibility for the operational definition sits — checkable against the Act.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are many departments that the work will still continue, they’re just being consolidated under less managers so that the managers can get out of the way so they can make better decision-making.
specificity.explanation: No named function, no numbers, no reporting-line detail and no timeframe; 'consolidated under less managers' and 'better decision-making' leave the actual change unstated.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Does he accept the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development’s (HUD) advice that evidence is uncertain that no-cause evictions will put downward pressures on rents but that the evidence is clear that security of tenancy for renters will be negatively impacted?
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of HUD's departmental advice on the Residential Tenancies Amendment: that the rent-reduction evidence is uncertain while the tenure-security harm is clear.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Regulatory Impact Statement / departmental advice from the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development on the 2024 Residential Tenancies Amendment reinstating 90-day no-cause terminations; true if that advice characterises the downward-pressure-on-rents evidence as uncertain and the negative impact on tenure security as clear, false if it makes no such characterisation or the reverse.

veracity.statement: It is also illegal to do that on the grounds of what the member is talking about.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that terminating a tenancy because the tenant filed a healthy homes complaint is unlawful in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 retaliatory-notice provisions (s 54) and Tenancy Tribunal practice; true if a termination notice given in response to a tenant exercising a right such as a healthy homes complaint can be declared of no effect and attract exemplary damages, false if no such prohibition exists.

veracity.statement: Last Friday, I announced with the Prime Minister and Minister of Transport, the Hon Simeon Brown, that through Budget 2024 the Government would be providing an additional $63.6 million over four years to fund Coastguard New Zealand and Surf Lifesaving New Zealand so that these NGOs can continue to deliver their essential front-line water safety and rescue and prevention services across New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Budget 2024 allocates an additional $63.6 million over four years to Coastguard New Zealand and Surf Life Saving New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Transport appropriations and the Government's 17 May 2024 announcement; true if the water-safety allocation to those two organisations totals $63.6m over four years, false if the figure or the four-year period differs materially.

veracity.statement: Coastguard New Zealand will receive $19.5 million over four years, while Surf Lifesaving New Zealand will receive $44 million over the same period.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the split of the Budget 2024 water-safety funding between the two organisations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 appropriation detail and the Ministry of Transport's funding announcement; true if Coastguard NZ receives $19.5m and Surf Life Saving NZ $44m over four years, false if either figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: Surf Lifesaving and the Coastguard are both experiencing increased demand for services at a time when costs are increasing due to the cost of living crisis.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a present-tense rise in demand for both organisations' services alongside rising operating costs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Annual reports and incident statistics of Coastguard New Zealand and Surf Life Saving New Zealand for the years to 2023–24; true if callout/patrol demand and reported operating costs both rose over that period, false if demand was flat or falling.

veracity.statement: How is it in the best interests of children and young people to add specialist legal work to Oranga Tamariki social workers, work that they are not trained for, and in an organisation where they are already 160 social workers short?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Oranga Tamariki was 160 social workers short at the time of the statement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki social worker vacancy/establishment figures for mid-2024, as reported in its annual report or in answers to written questions; true if the shortfall against establishment was about 160, false if materially different.

divination.statement: This funding will ensure that our current levels of services are maintained and ensures that they can meet the increasing levels of demand.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Budget 2024 allocation will be sufficient for both organisations to hold current service levels and absorb rising demand over the four-year funding period.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Coastguard NZ and Surf Life Saving NZ annual reports for the years to 2028; true if neither organisation reduces patrol hours, station coverage or rescue capability over the funding period and both report meeting demand, false if either cuts services or publicly reports being unable to meet demand on this funding.

focus.statement: Could I ask the Minister as to whether he’s received accolades and congratulations for this policy, belatedly so, because it was part of the coalition negotiations which failed at the time, but which they’ve now come around to seeing as a brilliant idea?
focus.explanation: A real policy referent (the coastguard and surf lifesaving funding) but the weight of the question is credit-claiming and needling the coalition partners over who wanted it first, rather than the funding's substance.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How is it in the best interests of children to slash the Safety of Children in Care team, which reports on children abused while they are in care?
focus.explanation: Names a specific team within a specific agency and a specific proposed change, and asks about its consequence for a named group. Straightforward scrutiny of a government proposal, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Absolutely, which is why we have a comprehensive five-point plan to fix our housing crisis. I’m happy to detail it for the member in response to that patsy, but the member’s heard it before, which is about opening up land supply at the edge of our cities and going up inside our cities; fixing our infrastructure funding and financing system; actually doing what Phil Twyford promised to do five years ago, which is smash the metropolitan urban limit in Auckland; focusing on building and construction changes being led by Chris Penk; fixing the Resource Management Act; delivering better social housing; and fixing the private rental market.
specificity.explanation: Names seven distinct workstreams, a named policy (the metropolitan urban limit), a named statute and a responsible Minister, but supplies no figures, costs or timeframes for any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Are first-home buyers, therefore, justified in feeling like they’ve been kicked in the guts when the Government has given landlords a $2.9 billion tax cut, but he won’t keep a $60 million scheme that helped them buy their first home?
specificity.explanation: Two precise, checkable figures attached to two identifiable measures — the interest-deductibility restoration and the first-home grant scheme.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Oranga Tamariki currently have 10 strategic partnerships, and I have directed officials to continue with these and enter into new partnerships when and where there are good reasons to do so.
specificity.explanation: Gives a count of existing partnerships and a concrete ministerial action (a direction to officials); stops short of naming the partners or any timeframe for new agreements.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: After a number of years with her foster family and being in a safe environment for the first time, Oranga Tamariki suddenly decided to uplift Moana, because her foster parents were Pākehā and Oranga Tamariki didn’t think they could provide for her cultural needs.
specificity.explanation: A concrete, checkable account of an identified case — the placement, its duration, the decision to remove and the stated reason — rather than a general assertion about practice.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is why we have a series of targets that will focus the public sector on achieving improved results in this area, including reducing crime, with a target of 20,000 fewer people as victims of assaults, robberies, and sexual assaults by 2029.
specificity.explanation: A numeric target, the offence categories it covers and a date by which it is to be met — checkable as stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does she agree with the advice of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet that developing a specific target for family violence was not suitable as “family violence victimisations are unlikely to change over a three- to six-month period and therefore it is not specific enough to drive delivery.”; if not, why not?
specificity.explanation: Cites a named source and quotes the specific wording of the advice being put to the Minister, so the premise of the question can be checked directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Absolutely, which is why we have a comprehensive five-point plan to fix our housing crisis. I’m happy to detail it for the member in response to that patsy, but the member’s heard it before, which is about opening up land supply at the edge of our cities and going up inside our cities; fixing our infrastructure funding and financing system; actually doing what Phil Twyford promised to do five years ago, which is smash the metropolitan urban limit in Auckland; focusing on building and construction changes being led by Chris Penk; fixing the Resource Management Act; delivering better social housing; and fixing the private rental market.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Phil Twyford, as the previous Government's Housing Minister, promised about five years earlier to abolish Auckland's metropolitan urban limit.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public record of Twyford's statements as Minister of Housing and Urban Development (2017-2019) — speeches, the Urban Growth Agenda, media reports; true if he publicly committed to removing/abolishing the Auckland urban growth boundary or rural-urban boundary, false if no such commitment is on record.

veracity.statement: Homeownership in New Zealand is at record lows. It is down to 63 percent.
veracity.explanation: Two linked assertions: that the New Zealand home-ownership rate stands at 63 percent, and that this is the lowest level on record.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Census / Household Economic Survey home-ownership series; true if the most recent published rate as at May 2024 is approximately 63 percent and is the lowest in the series, false if the published rate is materially different or if lower rates appear earlier in the series.

veracity.statement: Are first-home buyers, therefore, justified in feeling like they’ve been kicked in the guts when the Government has given landlords a $2.9 billion tax cut, but he won’t keep a $60 million scheme that helped them buy their first home?
