veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's restoration of interest deductibility for landlords is worth $2.9 billion, and that the first-home grant scheme being discontinued costs $60 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/Budget 2024 costings for restoring interest deductibility on residential rental property and the appropriation for the First Home Grant; true if the published fiscal costs are approximately $2.9 billion and $60 million respectively, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Oranga Tamariki currently have 10 strategic partnerships, and I have directed officials to continue with these and enter into new partnerships when and where there are good reasons to do so.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Oranga Tamariki had ten section 7AA strategic partnerships in place as at May 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki published records or ministerial/OIA statements of section 7AA strategic partnerships as at May 2024; true if the count is ten, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: After a number of years with her foster family and being in a safe environment for the first time, Oranga Tamariki suddenly decided to uplift Moana, because her foster parents were Pākehā and Oranga Tamariki didn’t think they could provide for her cultural needs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Oranga Tamariki moved to remove the child known as 'Moana' from a long-standing foster placement, and that the reason was that the caregivers were Pākehā and could not meet her cultural needs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Family Court judgment in the 'Moana' case (Judge Callinicos, 2020) and the subsequent independent review; true if the record shows Oranga Tamariki sought to move the child from Pākehā caregivers after several years on cultural-connection grounds, false if the record shows the removal was sought for other reasons or did not occur as described.

veracity.statement: No, because family violence is not omitted from the Government’s nine targets—it is part of the “Reducing violent crime” target.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that family violence is captured within the Government's 'reducing violent crime' public service target rather than being left out of the nine targets.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published definition and measurement basis of the Government's violent crime target (victims of assault, robbery and sexual assault, measured via the NZ Crime and Victims Survey); true if family violence victimisations are counted within that measure, false if the measure excludes them.

veracity.statement: Does she agree with the advice of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet that developing a specific target for family violence was not suitable as “family violence victimisations are unlikely to change over a three- to six-month period and therefore it is not specific enough to drive delivery.”; if not, why not?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet advised that a specific family violence target was unsuitable, in the words quoted.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The DPMC advice on the Government's public service targets (proactively released or released under the OIA); true if it contains the quoted reasoning about family violence victimisations and three- to six-month change, false if no such advice or wording exists.

civility.statement: Well, I mean, look, I can’t believe the member is now literally—literally—stating truisms in the House.
civility.explanation: Mockery aimed at the questioner rather than the question's substance — sneering at the member for asking something obvious. Short of a direct insult, but it belittles the person rather than engaging the point.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That is what I announced today; the member needs to listen up.
civility.explanation: Pointed and a little condescending toward the interjecting member, but the jab is about not listening rather than an attack on the person's character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: No, I don’t. As I’ve said consistently, this is about ensuring Oranga Tamariki puts the safety, wellbeing, and the best interests of children, not race, at the forefront of social-work practice and decision making.
civility.explanation: Asked to respond to an accusation that her bill is a 'targeted extermination', she rejects it and restates the policy rationale without turning on the person who said it.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I appreciate that this will not please everybody, but, actually, government is about doing the right thing, and the last Government lapsed far too easily into thinking that the solution to every problem was to throw money at it.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy contention underneath (spending versus supply-side reform), but it is delivered as a generalised characterisation of the previous Government's habits rather than by naming a measure, a figure or an outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does she accept that the repeal of section 7AA is a repeal of the relationships Oranga Tamariki have made with iwi, hapū, and kaupapa Māori organisations, and, if not, what will her approach be when “entering into further strategic partnership agreements with iwi or Māori organisations”?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: names the statutory provision being repealed and presses on a specific consequence for strategic partnership agreements. Legitimate scrutiny with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Repealing section 7AA is not about disregarding the whakapapa of Māori children; section 7AA places duties on the chief executive that are at odds with the agency’s primary purpose, which is to support the wellbeing of our most vulnerable and at-risk children.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (repeal is warranted and does not disregard whakapapa) rests entirely on an asserted conflict between the section 7AA duties and the agency's primary purpose; no mechanism, case or provision is offered to show the two are actually incompatible. A real inference about the measure, but a bare assertion carries the weight.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We run a structural deficit that is the second-worst in the developed world, and we heard today that that’s expected to be 1.5 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts New Zealand has the second-largest structural deficit among developed economies, and that it is forecast at 1.5 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IMF Fiscal Monitor / OECD structural (cyclically-adjusted) balance estimates for 2024 for advanced economies; true if NZ ranks second-largest structural deficit and the figure is ~1.5% of potential GDP, false if NZ is materially outside the top two or the figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: We have the official cash rate (OCR)—which was confirmed again today—at 5.5 percent, which drives interest rates, which is a significant impost on household incomes, or disposable incomes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Reserve Bank's official cash rate stood at 5.5 percent and was reconfirmed on the day of the speech (22 May 2024).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ Monetary Policy Statement / OCR decision of 22 May 2024; true if the OCR was held at 5.50%, false if the rate was any other figure or no decision was released that day.

veracity.statement: So inflation has driven rents up, as we’ve heard today, to an increase of $170 a week from 2017.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that average rents have risen by $170 a week since 2017.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE tenancy bond rent data / Stats NZ rental price index comparing mean weekly rent in 2017 with 2024; true if the increase is approximately $170 per week, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: When she was asked about whether we had a tax problem and that perhaps we weren’t raising enough tax, she pointed out that in 2011, the median-income earner was paying 15.5 percent of their salary in tax, and today, that figure is 20.6 percent.
veracity.explanation: Relays the Minister of Finance's select committee claim about the average tax rate on the median income earner rising from 15.5 percent in 2011 to 20.6 percent now.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Finance and Expenditure Committee transcript/evidence for the Budget Policy Statement 2024 hearing plus IRD/Treasury effective average tax rate calculations for a median-income earner in 2011 and 2024; true if both figures match, false if either is materially different or the Minister did not say this.

veracity.statement: So we don’t have a tax problem. What we have is an expenditure problem, and we have to bear in mind that only 40 percent of taxpayers pay net tax.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that only 40 percent of taxpayers are net contributors once transfers are netted off.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD analysis of net tax paid by household or individual (tax paid minus transfers received); true if approximately 40 percent are net payers, false if the published share is materially different or the measure is households rather than taxpayers.

veracity.statement: The Minister of Finance also committed to keeping the operating allowance to less than $3.5 billion, and she confirmed that yesterday, in question time, and here, today.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Minister of Finance publicly committed to a Budget 2024 operating allowance below $3.5 billion and repeated that on 21 and 22 May 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget Policy Statement 2024 and Hansard for question time on 21 May 2024 and the FEC hearing; true if the sub-$3.5b allowance commitment appears in those records, false if the stated allowance figure differs or no such confirmation was given.

veracity.statement: However, the previous Government had locked in $2.3 billion of that spending, so it’s very little to come and go on.
veracity.explanation: Asserts $2.3 billion of the Budget 2024 operating allowance was already pre-committed by decisions of the previous government.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Budget Policy Statement 2024 / Budget Economic and Fiscal Update tables on pre-committed operating allowance; true if approximately $2.3b of the allowance is recorded as pre-committed from prior-government decisions, false if the figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: That is a saving of $104 million, and it’s still going to feed, actually, more than the same number of children. It’s going to feed 10,000 additional children between the ages of two and five.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the school lunches pre-Budget announcement saves $104 million while extending coverage to 10,000 more children aged two to five.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 pre-Budget announcement documents on the Ka Ora, Ka Ako school lunch programme; true if the stated saving is ~$104m and the extension covers ~10,000 additional 2-5 year olds, false if either figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: Then, of course, there is the Pharmac announcement, with the largest ever Budget of $6.294 billion, and we do know—we canvassed this well—of the fiscal cliff that was left by the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Budget 2024 gives Pharmac its largest-ever budget at $6.294 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Health appropriations and Pharmac's historical combined pharmaceutical budget series; true if the figure is $6.294b and exceeds all prior Pharmac budgets on the same basis, false if the figure differs or a previous budget was larger on a comparable basis.

specificity.statement: We run a structural deficit that is the second-worst in the developed world, and we heard today that that’s expected to be 1.5 percent.
specificity.explanation: Carries a ranking and a numeric figure that someone could check against published fiscal comparisons.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That is a saving of $104 million, and it’s still going to feed, actually, more than the same number of children. It’s going to feed 10,000 additional children between the ages of two and five.
specificity.explanation: Names the saving, the beneficiary group, the age band and the number of additional children — all checkable against the announcement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have to trust and give an opportunity to those in the private sector to deliver services, and I’m sure that they are able to do that in a cost-effective way.
specificity.explanation: A general statement of principle with no mechanism, target, cost comparison or measure of what cost-effective delivery would look like.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We are in a significantly difficult position, and that’s thanks to the mismanagement of the previous Government, quite frankly.
focus.explanation: Attributes the fiscal position to the other side's 'mismanagement' in general terms without naming a specific policy, programme, decision or figure; the weight is party blame rather than substance.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is, effectively, making it cheaper, on the one hand, for banks to lend money, and, on the other hand, trying to make it more expensive for banks to lend and drive interest rates up.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about policy mechanism: if the Funding for Lending programme lowers bank funding costs while OCR rises raise them, the two settings work against each other. The conclusion of contradiction follows from the described mechanisms, though the relative magnitudes are asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So we don’t have a tax problem. What we have is an expenditure problem, and we have to bear in mind that only 40 percent of taxpayers pay net tax.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy plus a gap in the inference: a rising average tax rate on one earner shows tax take per person has grown, but it does not by itself establish that revenue is adequate and therefore that the problem must lie entirely on the expenditure side.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, some pundits call for a much higher level of debt, but that is not actually suitable for New Zealand, because we suffer from quite regular shocks, be they natural disasters or other things, so we need to have that buffer to move on.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered and the conclusion tracks it: exposure to frequent shocks supports holding fiscal headroom. The gap is that no evidence is given for why 20-40 percent specifically is the right buffer.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It just shows how you can find wasteful spending right across the Public Service, I’m sure, just by looking at doing things in a different way, and I think that’s a great start for our Budget.
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation: one programme redesign is offered as showing that comparable waste exists 'right across the Public Service', with nothing connecting the single case to the general claim.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Mr Speaker, I don’t know about you, but it certainly didn’t do me any harm at school—having sandwiches and a piece of fruit, rather than butter chicken—and there are many more savings to be made in other places.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal anecdote: the speaker's own childhood lunches are offered as grounds for the adequacy of a national school food programme.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We have to trust and give an opportunity to those in the private sector to deliver services, and I’m sure that they are able to do that in a cost-effective way.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on a bare assertion of confidence ('I'm sure') — no evidence, comparison or delivery record is offered for private-sector cost-effectiveness.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’m really looking forward to seeing those take off, because I know what difference they make, and, actually, often they take on the children with the most difficult learning situations and get fantastic results.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal knowledge and unsourced assertion: charter school results are asserted from what the speaker 'knows' rather than from any evidence about outcomes.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: They have removed the free public transport fares. They were free for those who were 12 and under, we made them half price for those under 25, and they’ve removed them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the current Government removed free public transport for under-13s and half-price fares for under-25s, both introduced by the previous Labour government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport / NZTA and Budget 2024 announcements on the Community Connect scheme: true if free fares for under-13s and half-price fares for under-25s were discontinued by decision of the coalition Government; false if either concession remained in place.

veracity.statement: They’ve also introduced a new car tax, an additional $50 with road-user charges to Kiwis.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Government has imposed an additional $50 charge on motorists connected with road user charges.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government Policy Statement on land transport 2024 and NZTA fee schedules: true if a $50 increase in annual vehicle licensing/RUC-related charges was announced or in force as at May 2024; false if no such $50 impost exists.

veracity.statement: It’s very similar to a situation that we saw in previous years under a National Government, when the training incentive allowance was removed by stealth as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a previous National-led government removed the training incentive allowance without announcing it in its Budget publicity.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2009 documents and MSD records on the Training Incentive Allowance: true if the allowance was withdrawn for level 4+ study by the National-led government and the change did not appear in the Budget's announced highlights; false if it was not removed or was announced up front.

veracity.statement: And yet if you actually go on to the National Party tax calculator—because they keep saying, basically, the tax cuts are going to help—well, some of our lowest-paid Kiwis are probably only going to get $2 in the hand, according to their calculator—$2 in the hand each week.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that National's own published tax calculator returns a weekly gain of about $2 for some of the lowest-paid workers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National Party tax calculator as published in 2024, run at low-wage income levels: true if a plausible low-income earner returns roughly $2 per week; false if the minimum output for such earners is materially higher.

veracity.statement: There we found that the top 311 families in Aotearoa hold more wealth combined than the bottom 2.5 million New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific wealth-concentration finding drawn from IRD's high-wealth individuals research and associated Treasury papers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IRD High-Wealth Individuals Research Project (2023) and the accompanying Treasury wealth-distribution papers: true if they show 311 families holding combined wealth exceeding that of the bottom 2.5 million New Zealanders; false if the figures differ materially or no such comparison is supported.

veracity.statement: And, in fact, as I’ve just alluded to, climate change is not mentioned once in this Budget Policy Statement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the phrase 'climate change' appears nowhere in the Government's Budget Policy Statement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Text search of the Budget Policy Statement 2024 as published by the Treasury: true if the term does not appear; false if it appears at any point.

veracity.statement: We also saw that one of the first things out the door from this Government, under its first 100 days, was a repeal of smoke-free legislation, which no one had asked for and no one had campaigned on except for the tobacco lobby.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that the smokefree legislation was repealed within the Government's first 100 days, and that no party had campaigned on doing so.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard/legislation record for the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment repeal date, plus the 2023 election policy documents and coalition agreements of National, ACT and NZ First: true if the repeal passed within the first 100 days and no party's published election policy proposed it; false if the repeal fell outside that window or any party campaigned on it.

specificity.statement: They have removed the free public transport fares. They were free for those who were 12 and under, we made them half price for those under 25, and they’ve removed them.
specificity.explanation: Names the concession, the two age bands affected and who did what — directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’ve heard 33 percent up in Northland, we’ve got 17 percent in Porirua, and then it’s 8 percent the next year.
specificity.explanation: Gives three concrete rates-rise percentages and two locations, but attributes them to hearsay and does not name the councils or the years precisely.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There we found that the top 311 families in Aotearoa hold more wealth combined than the bottom 2.5 million New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Precise numbers on both sides of the comparison, sourced to a named report — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Interest deductibility—so, straight away, landlords—$2.9 billion—will be able to outbid them at auction because they will be able to have that tax break behind them.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages a named tax measure, its cost and the group it affects.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But on that point of productivity—and we’ve had a lot of debate about this, back and forth, in the likes of question time and other debates over the last few months—we have had not only Treasury officials in many hearings in front of the Finance and Expenditure Committee but also the likes of the International Monetary Fund and the OECD saying to the Government that one of the most important things that it could do, if it really cared about the productivity of this economy, is to fix the tax system.
focus.explanation: Engages the productivity objective in the Budget Policy Statement and names the specific policy lever and the institutional advice on it, rather than characterising the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Interest deductibility—so, straight away, landlords—$2.9 billion—will be able to outbid them at auction because they will be able to have that tax break behind them.
rigor.explanation: The mechanism (restored deductibility improves landlords' bidding capacity) is coherent, but the conclusion that first-home buyers will therefore be outbid is asserted without any evidence on magnitude or on the offsetting removal effects; a real inference, but a gappy one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And if we are solely, as a Government or as a Parliament, talking about funding mental health treatment while not talking about addressing the causes of mental ill health, then we are missing a massive trick and putting far too many New Zealanders in pain and suffering that they do not need to go through.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows reasonably from the premise she has just laid out (He Ara Oranga and the international literature on environmental determinants); the weak point is the unsupported jump from 'determinants matter' to a claimed quantum of avoidable suffering.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When it comes to climate change, well, my many parliamentary written questions to the Minister for climate show that he’s not even asking, so we can only conclude that he doesn’t care.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur resting on absence of evidence: the answers to written questions could at most show what advice was sought, and the leap from that to a claim about the Minister's inner motivation is unsupported.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We have seen over the last 24 hours this Government using smoke and mirrors to basically disguise their cuts and we will hold them to account in eight days’ time.
civility.explanation: Imputes deliberate concealment rather than disagreeing with a decision, though the imputation is aimed at the Government collectively and no individual is named or insulted.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: When it comes to climate change, well, my many parliamentary written questions to the Minister for climate show that he’s not even asking, so we can only conclude that he doesn’t care.
civility.explanation: Moves from the Minister's conduct to an assertion about his character — that he 'doesn't care' — which imputes indifference to the person rather than criticising the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I also just wanted to pull through some of these pre-Budget announcements that the Government has put out there, because, frankly, this Government is gaslighting New Zealanders with all the more oil, coal, and gas.
civility.explanation: 'Gaslighting' imputes deliberate psychological manipulation rather than disagreeing with the decisions; aimed at the Government collectively, so no individual is attacked.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: More people are losing their jobs and will under the economic track that this Government has decided to pursue.
divination.explanation: Forecasts continued and rising job losses in New Zealand under the current Government's economic settings.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey and filled-jobs series: true if the unemployment rate rises and filled jobs fall over the twelve months following May 2024; false if unemployment falls or is flat and employment grows.

divination.statement: So, for all of the hot air that we hear in here, for all of the rhetoric that we hear from the Government—that they care about people, that they care about the planet—there’s the evidence that bears out completely the contrary of that—that their decisions will increase inequality, they will increase house prices, and they will increase homelessness.
divination.explanation: Forecasts three outcomes from the Government's decisions: rising inequality, rising house prices and rising homelessness.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: REINZ/CoreLogic house price indices and Stats NZ severe housing deprivation / MSD emergency and transitional housing data to mid-2026: true if house prices and measured homelessness both rise over the period; false if house prices are flat or falling and homelessness measures do not rise.

civility.statement: I would give some responses to what Barbara Edmonds said, but, to be honest, I can’t remember any of it already!
civility.explanation: A dismissive jibe at a named member — it engages nothing she said and instead mocks her as forgettable. Short of sustained abuse, but it lands on the person rather than the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I was interested in some of the things that Chlöe Swarbrick said, and I know it’s unparliamentary to refer to a member’s absence, but you’ve got someone who is actually doing her best impression of the woman who wasn’t there.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe at a named member, knowingly skirting the standing order on referring to absence; the target is her presence and credibility as a person, not her policy position.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Things out there are grim, and they’re grim for New Zealanders because, fundamentally, while New Zealanders were tightening their belts, Grant Robertson, the former finance Minister, was loosening his endlessly.
civility.explanation: Pointed and personalised — it names the former Minister and casts his fiscal management as self-indulgent — but the criticism remains tied to his conduct in office rather than his character.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, actually, to the people on that side of the House, over with Labour and the Greens and Te Pāti Māori, when you’re earning $160,000, it might not mean much to you.
civility.explanation: Imputes indifference to the hardship of low earners to the members opposite on the basis of their salaries — a sneer at their motives rather than an engagement with their argument about the tax cut.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: She was part of a Government where the average house price went up $250,000, or 30 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the average New Zealand house price rose by about $250,000, or 30 percent, over the term of the 2017–2023 Labour-led Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: REINZ/QV/CoreLogic average or median dwelling value series for October 2017 versus October 2023; true if the increase is approximately $250,000 and approximately 30 percent, false if materially different on either figure.

veracity.statement: She backed a Government where the average rent went up $200 a week.
veracity.explanation: Asserts average weekly rent rose by $200 over the 2017–2023 Labour-led Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE tenancy bond lodgement data, national mean/median weekly rent, late 2017 versus late 2023; true if the increase is about $200 per week, false if materially lower (e.g. nearer $150).

veracity.statement: Where it got us is that we’ve got a Government inheriting an extra $100 billion worth of debt.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the incoming government inherited an additional $100 billion of government debt accumulated under the previous government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury net core Crown debt (or gross sovereign-issued debt) figures for June 2017 versus June 2023/2024; true if the increase is approximately $100 billion, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: We’ve got a Government that is inheriting inflation that is 5.8 percent domestically, even as tradable inflation from the rest of the world falls.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that non-tradables (domestic) inflation was 5.8 percent at the time of the statement while tradables inflation was falling.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI release for the March 2024 quarter: annual non-tradeable inflation rate and annual tradeable inflation rate; true if non-tradeables is 5.8% and tradeables is declining, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: A classic is the $50 million on designing a bike bridge they didn’t actually build.
veracity.explanation: Asserts approximately $50 million was spent on design work for a cycle bridge (the Auckland Harbour crossing) that was never constructed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waka Kotahi/NZTA and Treasury reporting on expenditure for the Northern Pathway / Auckland Harbour cycling bridge before cancellation; true if the sunk cost is around $50 million with no bridge built, false if materially lower or if a bridge was built.

veracity.statement: These guys over there—Kieran McAnulty and Arena Williams and all of them—supported and were part of a Government that actually decided to set up Kāinga Ora in such a way that it loses half a billion dollars a year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Kāinga Ora is running an annual operating loss of about half a billion dollars, attributed to how the previous government structured it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora annual report / the 2024 independent review (Bill English) operating deficit figure for the relevant year; true if the annual loss is approximately $500 million, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The result of all of that is that the amount of money spent per person after inflation—let’s not even talk about that for now—was 30 percent more in 2023 than in 2017.
veracity.explanation: Asserts real (inflation-adjusted) government spending per person was 30 percent higher in 2023 than in 2017.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenditure series deflated by CPI and divided by Stats NZ population estimates, 2017 versus 2023; true if the real per-capita increase is around 30 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The Healthy School Lunches Programme wasn’t funded past the end of this school year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the school lunch programme (Ka Ora, Ka Ako) had no appropriated funding beyond the end of the 2024 school year under the previous government's Budget forecasts.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2023 Estimates/forecast appropriations for Ka Ora, Ka Ako; true if funding lapsed at the end of the 2024 school year, false if baseline funding continued into 2025.

veracity.statement: Do you know what we’ve actually done? A little bit of option 3, but we’ve also made the scheme $104 million cheaper while feeding more children at the same time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the redesigned school lunch programme costs $104 million less than before while serving a larger number of children.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 appropriations and Ministry of Education programme documents for Ka Ora, Ka Ako; true if the announced saving is about $104 million and the number of students served is greater than before, false if the saving differs materially or student numbers fall.

focus.statement: And no amounts of catnip clips on Instagram are going to make your rent cheaper.
focus.explanation: Directed at another party's social-media style rather than any measure, mechanism or figure; the reference to rent is a rhetorical hook, not a policy claim.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: These guys over there—Kieran McAnulty and Arena Williams and all of them—supported and were part of a Government that actually decided to set up Kāinga Ora in such a way that it loses half a billion dollars a year.
focus.explanation: Names a specific agency, a specific financial outcome and the decision that produced it — scrutiny of a named policy vehicle rather than generic party-bashing, though it is framed by naming opposing members.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s actually difficult to exaggerate how clownish that Government was in its execution.
focus.explanation: A general characterisation of the previous government's competence with no policy, figure or mechanism attached — party framing rather than engagement with a measure.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve got a Government that is inheriting inflation that is 5.8 percent domestically, even as tradable inflation from the rest of the world falls.
specificity.explanation: Gives a named measure and a precise figure, and distinguishes domestic from tradable inflation — directly checkable against the CPI release.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We had to either borrow another $340 million, tax another $340 million, or find $340 million of savings elsewhere to make it happen next year.
specificity.explanation: Names the programme, the exact sum at stake and the three concrete fiscal mechanisms, with a timeframe — checkable against the Budget documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: After years and years of Labour doing less and less with more and more, this Government is doing more and more with less and less—just as households and firms and employers and farmers have had to do for the last three years of the cost of living crisis.
specificity.explanation: A rhetorical antithesis with no figure, mechanism, programme or timeframe — nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yes, there was a pandemic, but the rest of the world had moved on by 2022-23.
rigor.explanation: Offered as a rebuttal to the pandemic explanation for poor outcomes, but the inference relies on a bare assertion about 'the rest of the world' with no comparator data, and does not connect the timing to the New Zealand outcomes he attributes to policy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’ve spoken to real estate agents who tell me the number one reason people are selling is because of relationship breakdown because of years of financial stress through the COVID period and the inflation period and everything else that the previous Government did for us.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote: unnamed agents' impressions are used to establish both a national 'number one reason' for house sales and a causal chain running back to the previous government's policy, with no data supporting either link.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We had to either borrow another $340 million, tax another $340 million, or find $340 million of savings elsewhere to make it happen next year.
rigor.explanation: The three options offered (borrow, tax, reprioritise) are genuinely exhaustive for funding an unfunded appropriation, so the constraint he draws follows from the premise rather than being a false trilemma.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I predict that, in 2026, Labour will still be blaming things on COVID!
divination.explanation: Forecasts that during 2026 Labour will still publicly attribute current problems to the COVID-19 pandemic.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Public statements by Labour MPs during calendar year 2026 (Hansard, press releases, media interviews); true if Labour MPs are documented attributing current economic or public-service problems to the COVID-19 pandemic, false if no such attribution can be found.

veracity.statement: The level of GDP in this document, the economic scenario is showing a $42.8 billion lower forecast in the forecast period—that’s $42.8 billion less in the nominal GDP.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Budget Policy Statement 2024 economic scenario revises nominal GDP down by $42.8 billion across the forecast period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's Budget Policy Statement 2024 / associated economic and fiscal forecasts: true if the cumulative downward revision to nominal GDP over the forecast period is stated as approximately $42.8 billion; false if the document shows a materially different figure.

veracity.statement: The difference between the Government’s revenue and the Government’s spending has been in deficit since 2019-20 and it has been driven by an increase in the core Crown expenses.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an unbroken operating deficit from the 2019-20 fiscal year onward, attributed to growth in core Crown expenses.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's Financial Statements of the Government (OBEGAL) for 2019/20 onward: true if every year from 2019/20 records a deficit and core Crown expenses rose materially over that period; false if any of those years recorded a surplus or if the deficit is not associated with rising core Crown expenses.

veracity.statement: We’ve had those announcements around the Coastguard and the Surf Life Saving, around that $63 million; the Defence Force spending, around $571 million; Gumboot Friday, $24 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three specific pre-Budget funding announcements at $63 million (Coastguard and Surf Life Saving), $571 million (Defence Force) and $24 million (Gumboot Friday).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government pre-Budget 2024 press releases and Budget 2024 vote documents: true if each of the three announcements matches the stated amount within rounding; false if any announced figure differs materially or was not announced.

veracity.statement: What I would like to highlight in this document was the multi-year allowance that has been increased to $7 billion, and infrastructure in this country is something that we need to make sure we’re putting more investment in.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Budget Policy Statement 2024 increased the multi-year capital allowance to $7 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget Policy Statement 2024 (Treasury): true if the multi-year capital allowance is set/increased to $7.0 billion; false if the document states a different figure.

specificity.statement: The level of GDP in this document, the economic scenario is showing a $42.8 billion lower forecast in the forecast period—that’s $42.8 billion less in the nominal GDP.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise dollar figure, the variable (nominal GDP) and the source document, so it can be checked directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve had those announcements around the Coastguard and the Surf Life Saving, around that $63 million; the Defence Force spending, around $571 million; Gumboot Friday, $24 million.
specificity.explanation: Three named funding commitments each with a dollar amount attached; directly checkable against the announcements.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are going to make sure that that service is more effective and more efficient.
specificity.explanation: A commitment framed entirely in generic virtues — no mechanism, no target, no funding, no timeframe for the health service being discussed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Most importantly, it’s setting us up to take back our country, and that’s what New Zealand First has set out to do.
specificity.explanation: A closing slogan committing to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What I would like to say is it’s a bit like running a household. Once you realise your expenditure is exceeding your income, you’ve got to adjust—and the last Government was far too slow in doing that. This Government will get our spending back under control.
rigor.explanation: False analogy: the conclusion about required fiscal adjustment rests on treating a sovereign government's balance sheet as equivalent to a household budget, ignoring the differences (currency issuance, borrowing capacity, counter-cyclical role) that the speaker himself acknowledges elsewhere in the speech.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What I would like to say is it’s a bit like running a household. Once you realise your expenditure is exceeding your income, you’ve got to adjust—and the last Government was far too slow in doing that. This Government will get our spending back under control.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the fiscal position (revenue versus expenditure, the need to adjust), but the point is wrapped in a general characterisation of the previous Government rather than a named measure or figure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ve had those announcements around the Coastguard and the Surf Life Saving, around that $63 million; the Defence Force spending, around $571 million; Gumboot Friday, $24 million.
focus.explanation: Entirely about named spending decisions and their amounts, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We will cut wasteful spending, get money out of the back office and into the front office, invest in infrastructure, and deliver tax relief for hard-working New Zealanders, who haven’t had any tax relief for the past 14 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealanders have received no tax relief in the 14 years to May 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue / Treasury records of personal income tax rates and thresholds and of tax-credit changes between 2010 and 2024; true if no reduction in personal income tax rates, thresholds or tax credits took effect in that period, false if any personal tax rate/threshold reduction or new tax credit (e.g. Families Package tax credits, IETC changes) took effect.

veracity.statement: Our tax relief package will increase the taxed take-home income of 83 percent of New Zealanders 15 and over, and 94 percent of households across this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the coverage of the Government's tax package: 83% of New Zealanders aged 15+ and 94% of households receive higher take-home income.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/Budget 2024 tax package documentation and Minister of Finance costings; true if the official figures state 83% of those aged 15+ and 94% of households benefit, false if the official figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: It’s early days, but inflation has come back to 4 percent from its peak of more than 7 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts annual CPI inflation was around 4 percent at the time of speaking, down from a peak above 7 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation series; true if the most recent print before 22 May 2024 was approximately 4.0% and the series peak exceeded 7%, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Food inflation has dropped to just 0.8 percent, with fruit and vegetable prices falling from this time last year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts annual food price inflation of 0.8 percent and an annual fall in fruit and vegetable prices.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Food Price Index for the month preceding 22 May 2024; true if annual food price inflation was ~0.8% and the fruit and vegetables subgroup fell year-on-year, false if either differs materially.

veracity.statement: We’ve announced $1.9 billion in investment to enhance safety and rehabilitate offenders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $1.9 billion government announcement for corrections safety and offender rehabilitation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 / Vote Corrections announcements; true if a package of approximately $1.9 billion for prison safety and rehabilitation was announced, false if the announced figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: And also, as we’ve already heard, we’ve invested in education—$67 million into structured literacy, because we know if we’re going to drive this country forward, we need to invest in education, in our children, and lift performance in the classroom.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $67 million government investment in structured literacy.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education / Budget 2024 announcements on structured literacy funding; true if approximately $67m was committed, false if the committed figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: Our Government has just announced today a boosting fund for Surf Lifesaving New Zealand, and Coastguard, as we’ve heard earlier—$63.64 million over the next four years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a same-day announcement of $63.64 million over four years for Surf Life Saving NZ and Coastguard.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government press releases / Budget 2024 documents dated on or about 22 May 2024; true if approximately $63.6m over four years was announced for Surf Life Saving NZ and Coastguard, false if no such announcement or a materially different figure.

veracity.statement: We’ve already heard about our housing crisis in the House today; we have seen rents go up by $170 a week in the past six years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts weekly rents rose by $170 over the six years to 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE tenancy bond data on national median weekly rent for 2018 and 2024; true if the increase is approximately $170 per week, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Interest on that is more than we spend on education.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Crown debt-servicing (finance) costs exceed government spending on education.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 / Treasury core Crown expense tables; true if core Crown finance costs for the forecast year exceed core Crown education expenses, false if education expenses are the larger.

specificity.statement: Our tax relief package will increase the taxed take-home income of 83 percent of New Zealanders 15 and over, and 94 percent of households across this country.
specificity.explanation: Two precise, checkable coverage percentages tied to a named policy package and defined populations.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We want our country to be a better place to do business, to invest, to innovate, to take risks, to build things, to make things, to hire people, to grow, and to raise our children.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic aspirations with no figures, mechanisms, named measures or timeframes; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is time for them to keep more of what they earn, and spend it how they want to spend it, not see it wastefully frittered away by bureaucrats who think they know best.
civility.explanation: Goes beyond criticising spending decisions to impute arrogance and waste to public servants as people ('think they know best'), which is sneering rather than substantive.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Our actions so far are already restoring business confidence, and confidence on the farm, where inflation has been at record highs. I’ve been out talking to businesses across my electorate, and talking to farmers, and there is aspiration, once again.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that government actions are restoring confidence rests on an appeal to personal anecdote from conversations in her own electorate; no confidence data or causal link is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That’s where we are investing in practical solutions, like restoring interest deductibility, and bringing the brightline test back to two years.
focus.explanation: Names two specific tax measures as the response to the rent/housing issue under discussion; entirely on the policy, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: These actions are significant for my home region of Hawke’s Bay, which is a huge export region, and will play a big part in helping us double the value of our exports in the next ten years.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the value of New Zealand's exports will double within ten years of May 2024.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ total goods and services export value for the year to mid-2034 compared with the year to mid-2024; true if at least double in nominal terms, false if less.

veracity.statement: We’ve seen an increase in unemployment, we’ve seen a decrease in people employed by the Public Service, and so we’re seeing just cuts, cuts, cuts everywhere, and we’re haemorrhaging everywhere, and this is what this Budget is showing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two measurable trends at the time of speaking (May 2024): that unemployment has risen, and that headcount employed by the Public Service has fallen.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate series to Q1 2024 — true if the rate rose over the preceding quarters, false if flat or falling; and Public Service Commission workforce data / agency announcements for 2023-24 — true if total public service headcount fell, false if it rose.

veracity.statement: Those who are on $30,000 or less—that’s 2.2 million people in this country who are paying tax on $30,000 earnings.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 2.2 million New Zealanders have taxable income of $30,000 or less and pay income tax on it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IRD / Stats NZ taxable income distribution for the most recent tax year — true if the count of individuals with taxable income at or below $30,000 is approximately 2.2 million, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: There’s no increase in take-home pay for 98 percent of the whānau.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 98 percent of families receive no increase in take-home pay under the Government's fiscal plan as set out in the Budget Policy Statement 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD distributional analysis of the Government's 2024 personal income tax changes — true if 98% or more of households/earners see no increase in take-home pay, false if a substantial majority receive an increase.

veracity.statement: Many are paying between 24 and 30 percent tax; 2 percent of this country are paying 9.4 percent but they control 50 percent of this country’s wealth, and that is not reflected in the Budget Policy Statement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an effective tax rate of 9.4 percent for the wealthiest 2 percent of New Zealanders, and that that group controls 50 percent of national wealth, against effective rates of 24-30 percent for others.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IRD High-Wealth Individuals Research Project (2023) for the 9.4% effective rate and the population it covers, and Stats NZ Household Economic Survey net worth distribution — true if the 9.4% rate applies to roughly the top 2% and that group holds about half of total household wealth, false if the rate applies to a far narrower group or the wealth share is materially different.

veracity.statement: We’ve got 50 percent of the social housing waiting list are Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori make up about half of applicants on the public/social housing register.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD Housing Register quarterly reports, ethnicity breakdown of main applicants at the time of the statement — true if the Māori share is approximately 50%, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: We only own 31 percent of homes here in Aotearoa—31 percent of our people own their own home, and they’re intergenerational houses.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a Māori home-ownership rate of 31 percent (self-corrected mid-sentence from share of all homes to share of Māori who own their home).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Census / Housing in Aotearoa home-ownership rate for Māori adults — true if approximately 31%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Political choice is about what we value—whether we are going to value those who have been doing it tough the most, for generation after generation; whether we are going to continue to allow for those who have been given more support than they will ever need, and whether they are going to continue to see more support, like landlords receiving $2.9 billion worth of tax cuts when they do not need them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's tax changes deliver $2.9 billion to landlords — a reference to the fiscal cost of restoring interest deductibility on residential rental property.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/Budget 2024 fiscal costings for the restoration of interest deductibility for residential rental property over the forecast period — true if the costed figure is approximately $2.9 billion, false if materially different.

focus.statement: So my three - bullet point contribution to this Budget is: the first bullet point is that this Budget Policy Statement 2024 is in breach of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, once again, article 1, as Māori have been excluded from developing and managing our own Māori budgets.
focus.explanation: Directed at the measure before the House — names the Budget Policy Statement 2024 and a specific article of Te Tiriti, with a stated reason (exclusion from developing Māori budgets), rather than at the other party in general.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is what this National Government is choosing to prioritise instead of massively, massively ramping up and scaling up public housing—public housing.
focus.explanation: Contains a genuine policy contrast (housing as capital investment versus public housing supply), but it is carried mostly by party framing about what 'this National Government' is like, with no named programme, figure or target.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, if the Minister would read Te Tiriti o Waitangi, he would know that those two bullet points have been breached.
civility.explanation: Rather than arguing the breach, it implies the Minister has not read the founding document — condescension aimed at the individual, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That is what this National Government is choosing to prioritise instead of massively, massively ramping up and scaling up public housing—public housing.
civility.explanation: Hard criticism of the Government's spending priorities that attacks no individual and stays on the substance of the choice being made.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Those who are on $30,000 or less—that’s 2.2 million people in this country who are paying tax on $30,000 earnings.
specificity.explanation: Carries a precise, checkable figure and an income threshold — someone could go to the taxpayer distribution data and test it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have, in Aotearoa, everything—let me say that again: everything—that we need to ensure that everyone lives good lives; to ensure that we are protecting our environment for generations to come; to ensure that we are taking the strongest action for a stable climate, for mokopuna, that we possibly can.
specificity.explanation: A string of general aspirations with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named measure; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, we can actually clear the public housing register in five years—clear the public housing register—if we choose to scale up and invest in public housing—in public housing—and actually clear the public housing register.
specificity.explanation: Gives a named outcome and a timeframe (clear the public housing register in five years) but no build numbers, cost, or delivery mechanism beyond 'scale up and invest'.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: And on this, I must share the shocking, shocking financial data again, which I repeatedly shared during the Finance and Expenditure Committee and also to many of the constituents that I met in the community—that the New Zealand Government now pays $1 billion more this year than the spending that we give to Defence, Police, Corrections, and Customs combined.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that core Crown finance costs (debt servicing) in the current fiscal year exceed the combined spending on Defence, Police, Corrections and Customs by $1 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Budget 2024 / Crown financial statements for 2023/24: compare core Crown finance costs against the combined appropriations for Defence, Police, Corrections and Customs. True if finance costs exceed the four combined by approximately $1 billion; false if finance costs are below the combined figure or the gap is materially different.

veracity.statement: Tax thresholds have not been adjusted for 14 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's personal income tax thresholds were last changed 14 years before May 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IRD/Treasury record of personal income tax threshold changes. True if the last adjustment to the thresholds took effect in 2010; false if any threshold was altered between 2010 and 2024.

veracity.statement: We also need to rebuild New Zealand’s economy because special economic and tax forecasts prepared by the Treasury for the BPS showed that Treasury has downgraded the expectations of economic growth for New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Treasury forecasts prepared for the Budget Policy Statement revised New Zealand's economic growth expectations downward relative to the previous set of forecasts.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's economic and tax forecasts published with the March 2024 Budget Policy Statement, compared against the preceding (HYEFU 2023) forecasts. True if real GDP growth projections were revised down; false if they were unchanged or revised up.

specificity.statement: And on this, I must share the shocking, shocking financial data again, which I repeatedly shared during the Finance and Expenditure Committee and also to many of the constituents that I met in the community—that the New Zealand Government now pays $1 billion more this year than the spending that we give to Defence, Police, Corrections, and Customs combined.
specificity.explanation: A named dollar figure, a named fiscal year and four named spending areas — precisely checkable against Treasury documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So our economy is not good—period. Our state of the nation is not good—period. Our Kiwis are suffering—period.
specificity.explanation: Three assertions offered as substance about the economy but carrying no figure, indicator, timeframe or mechanism; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So the National-led Government is laser-focused on rebuilding our economy by cutting down wasteful Government spending, enhancing revenue, investing in growth, and implementing structural reforms.
specificity.explanation: A list of generic fiscal directions — cut waste, raise revenue, invest, reform — with no amounts, named programmes, mechanisms or dates attached to any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It doesn’t need economists or experts or data analysts to tell us that our economy is suffering. Just simply talk to people around us in our community up and down the country and ask about how they feel about the economy, about their living, and about their cost of living in New Zealand right now.
rigor.explanation: Explicitly sets aside expert and statistical evidence in favour of how people 'feel' — an appeal to anecdote and popular sentiment offered as the basis for a macroeconomic conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It also means, for the members opposite, for you to understand, that our Government’s ability to respond to future crises is limited because we have committed spending to our country but we have less fiscal headroom to address the unforeseen events such as economic downturns, such as natural disasters, such as public health emergencies without further increasing debt.
rigor.explanation: The inference is sound on its own terms: committed spending reduces fiscal headroom, which in turn constrains the capacity to respond to shocks without more borrowing. The conclusion tracks the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Kiwis voted for the National-led Government to fix the economy because they are suffering and they know it will have to be a National-led Government to be prudent with the taxes that they pay and a National-led Government to reconnect New Zealand with our existing trading partners around the world, and also connect with new regions and new countries to create new revenue opportunities for Kiwis.
rigor.explanation: Argues from the election result to the correctness of the policy programme — an appeal to popularity — and attributes specific beliefs about trade and prudence to voters as though the vote itself established them.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It also means, for the members opposite, for you to understand, that our Government’s ability to respond to future crises is limited because we have committed spending to our country but we have less fiscal headroom to address the unforeseen events such as economic downturns, such as natural disasters, such as public health emergencies without further increasing debt.
civility.explanation: The aside 'for the members opposite, for you to understand' is condescension directed at other members — implying they need the concept spelled out for them. Short of a direct insult but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Thirdly, the mess that the last six years of Labour Government created for New Zealand will take more than one Budget to fix.
focus.explanation: Frames the fiscal task entirely as the other party's 'mess' over six years without naming a policy, programme, figure or outcome; the only policy content is the generic reference to Budgets.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Tax relief will be funded from within a new operating allowance for Budget 2024, and we won’t be borrowing extra for tax relief and will not be adding to inflationary pressures.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Budget 2024 tax package will be funded inside the operating allowance without additional borrowing and will not add to inflationary pressure in the economy.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents (30 May 2024) plus the subsequent Treasury and Reserve Bank assessments. True if the tax package was funded within the announced operating allowance with no additional borrowing attributed to it and the RBNZ's following Monetary Policy Statements did not identify it as adding to inflationary pressure; false if borrowing was increased to fund it or official assessments attributed added inflationary pressure to the package.

veracity.statement: We had Bill English in 2008, in the midst of the global financial crisis, issue a Budget Policy Statement and an operating allowance.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as incoming Finance Minister after the 2008 election, Bill English issued a Budget Policy Statement that included a stated operating allowance.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Budget Policy Statement published by the Treasury in December 2008 under Minister of Finance Bill English; true if that document exists and states an operating allowance for the forthcoming Budget, false if no BPS was issued for that Budget round or it contained no operating allowance.

veracity.statement: We saw the incoming Government in 2017, formed very late in the year, not only deliver a Budget Policy Statement with a stated operating allowance but also a mini-Budget in that period.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Labour-led government formed in October 2017 published both a Budget Policy Statement containing an operating allowance and a mini-Budget before the end of that year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury publications from December 2017: the Budget Policy Statement 2018 and the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update / mini-Budget released by Grant Robertson; true if a BPS with a stated operating allowance and a mini-Budget were both released, false if either is absent.

veracity.statement: We see a transition to a low-emissions economy gone—not a mention of decarbonisation or climate change.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's Budget Policy Statement contains no mention at all of decarbonisation or climate change, and drops the low-emissions transition as a priority.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Text search of the Budget Policy Statement released by the Minister of Finance in March 2024 for the terms 'climate change', 'decarbonisation', 'emissions' and 'low-emissions'; true if none of those terms appear, false if any appear in the document.

veracity.statement: In fact, there are big gaping holes—in emissions budget two, a 4 million tonne hole left by scrapping the Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry Fund, and a further hole in emissions budget three, and a Government that has absolutely no plan, no vision, and no idea of how it will achieve closing the gaps on it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that cancelling the GIDI fund leaves a 4 million tonne shortfall against emissions budget two, and that a further shortfall exists in emissions budget three.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry for the Environment / Climate Change Commission emissions projections and the official advice on the abolition of the GIDI fund; true if the published estimate of the abatement lost is around 4 Mt CO2-e against emissions budget two and a projected shortfall exists for emissions budget three, false if the estimated abatement is materially different or no shortfall is projected.

veracity.statement: We discussed the analysis that had been carried out by Westpac and the economists at Westpac, which outlines that the Government will need to borrow up to $15 billion over the next four years, and that is close to the publicised cost of the tax cut programme outlined by this Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Westpac economists published analysis finding the Government will need to borrow up to $15 billion over four years, an amount close to the announced cost of its tax package.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Westpac NZ economics commentary published in the first half of 2024; true if it projects additional borrowing of about $15 billion over a four-year forecast period and the announced tax package cost is of a similar magnitude, false if Westpac's figure or timeframe is materially different or no such analysis exists.

veracity.statement: This is a Government that says, out of one side of its mouth, it wants to pay down debt, but yet its actions are showing that it is going to borrow $15 billion over four years to pay for tax cuts, and this is in addition to the $2.9 billion it will be delivering to landlords while making sure that first-home buyers are locked out of the market.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fiscal cost of $2.9 billion for the restoration of interest deductibility for residential landlords, on top of $15 billion of borrowing over four years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury / Inland Revenue costings for the restoration of interest deductibility published with the 2024 tax package; true if the forecast revenue cost over the forecast period is about $2.9 billion, false if the published costing is materially different.

rigor.statement: It spells out the strategic intent to make sure that they do rip out and cut the funding for any climate measures that were in place.
rigor.explanation: Infers a positively stated strategic intent to cut all climate funding from what she has just described as the document's silence on climate. Argument from silence: absence of a mention does not establish a spelt-out intent, and the conclusion (defunding 'any climate measures') is far stronger than the premise supports.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is not radical economics to say that if you weren’t spending 15 billion bucks on tax cuts, you wouldn’t need to borrow $15 billion.
rigor.explanation: Given the premises (a $15b tax package and $15b of extra borrowing) the arithmetic conclusion broadly follows, but it assumes borrowing is attributable to one line item and ignores other revenue and spending choices that could equally account for the gap — a real but modest gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That member, if she was paying attention at the committee would have heard a number of submitters, including a discussion with the Minister about how we are indeed not on track to deliver on emissions budgets.
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed at a named colleague: the point about the emissions budgets is wrapped in a suggestion that Catherine Wedd was not paying attention in committee, which targets the member rather than her argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But, no, what we have is a Minister and her minions that trot out that what we will see is by bringing back interest deductibility, we will see a lowering of rents for renters.
civility.explanation: 'Minions' belittles the Minister's colleagues personally as unthinking followers, and 'trot out' sneers at them rather than engaging the interest-deductibility argument itself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We have an opportunity in the Budget Policy Statement to have good and constructive debates about operating allowances and we will, across different parties, have different views on what they should be, but in order for that to happen, we need a Government that is transparent enough, with a finance Minister that is transparent enough to actually tell the public how much that operating allowance is.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the Minister's disclosure decision, but it stays on the conduct in question and imputes no bad character; it explicitly allows that parties may legitimately differ on the allowance itself.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In fact, there are big gaping holes—in emissions budget two, a 4 million tonne hole left by scrapping the Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry Fund, and a further hole in emissions budget three, and a Government that has absolutely no plan, no vision, and no idea of how it will achieve closing the gaps on it.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific quantum (4 million tonnes), the specific emissions budget periods (two and three) and the specific programme cancelled (the Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry Fund) — checkable against emissions budget projections.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The sophisticated economic modelling that sits behind the National Party’s backwards thinking—it depends.
focus.explanation: Gestures at a real policy gap (no quantified rent effect from interest deductibility) but the sentence itself is a sarcastic characterisation of the other party's thinking rather than engagement with the mechanism or the numbers.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In the midst of this housing crisis of slashing the number of State houses that would have otherwise been built and making sure that they are prioritising investors over renters, what are they doing? They’re bringing back the ability of landlords to kick tenants out for no reason, with bringing back no-cause evictions.
focus.explanation: Names specific measures — the reduced State house build programme and the restoration of no-cause tenancy terminations — and who they affect, rather than characterising the other party in general.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We have an opportunity in the Budget Policy Statement to have good and constructive debates about operating allowances and we will, across different parties, have different views on what they should be, but in order for that to happen, we need a Government that is transparent enough, with a finance Minister that is transparent enough to actually tell the public how much that operating allowance is.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure at issue: what a Budget Policy Statement should disclose, and the specific missing item (the operating allowance).
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Most New Zealanders are expecting $250 a fortnight in tax cuts, so I guess, in eight sleeps, New Zealanders will know whether or not the National Government is going to deliver on that election promise of up to $250 a week—not the few cents that many of them will get while they are paying more for rents, while they are paying more for insurance, while they are paying more for so many other things.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the tax package in the Budget to be delivered eight days later will give many New Zealanders only a token amount, well short of the headline figure campaigned on.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The tax package published in Budget 2024 (30 May 2024) and Treasury/IRD distributional tables; true if the great majority of households receive substantially less than the headline $250 per fortnight, false if the advertised amount is delivered broadly across households.

veracity.statement: If ever there’s one day that summarises the lack of empathy for all New Zealanders, it’s today, because, on this day, $60 million that was a little bit of help to first-home buyers has been taken off the table, because it has to pay for a $2.9 billion subsidy, tax cut, tax break, for the landlords and the people who they will have to rent from.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two figures announced on that day: $60 million of first-home buyer support removed, and a $2.9 billion cost of restoring interest deductibility for residential landlords.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 / Treasury and Housing Minister announcements of 22 May 2024: true if the First Home Grant scheme scrapped released approximately $60m and the interest deductibility restoration is costed at approximately $2.9bn over the forecast period; false if the figures are materially different.

veracity.statement: That $2.9 billion is on top of the $2.8 billion that taxpayers pay to landlords in accommodation supplement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that annual accommodation supplement expenditure paid to (via tenants, to) landlords is $2.8 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD / Treasury Vote Social Development expenditure on the Accommodation Supplement for 2023/24: true if approximately $2.8bn, false if materially different (e.g. below $2.5bn or above $3.1bn).

veracity.statement: A lot of New Zealanders might have voted for National, because they were promised a $250-a-fortnight tax cut, $250-a-week tax cut.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that National's election campaign promised voters a $250-a-fortnight tax cut.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 'Back Pocket Boost' tax plan documents and campaign material: true if a $250-a-fortnight figure was promised as stated; false if the figure was materially different or was framed as a capped maximum for a narrow household type rather than a general promise.

veracity.statement: You do that through tax relief, and it has not been done for 14 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no income tax relief (threshold adjustment) has occurred in New Zealand for 14 years prior to May 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IRD/Treasury record of personal income tax rate and threshold changes: true if the last change to personal income tax thresholds took effect in 2010; false if any threshold or rate reduction took effect after 2010.
