veracity.statement: Other countries around the world, their tax rate adjusts with inflation, unlike ours, and we’re going to do something about it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that other countries index personal income tax thresholds to inflation while New Zealand does not.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD tax policy sources on automatic indexation of personal income tax brackets: true if multiple comparable countries (e.g. US, Canada, Netherlands) index brackets and New Zealand has no statutory indexation; false if New Zealand indexes, or if indexation is not used elsewhere.

specificity.statement: If ever there’s one day that summarises the lack of empathy for all New Zealanders, it’s today, because, on this day, $60 million that was a little bit of help to first-home buyers has been taken off the table, because it has to pay for a $2.9 billion subsidy, tax cut, tax break, for the landlords and the people who they will have to rent from.
specificity.explanation: Names two specific fiscal measures with dollar figures and a date, all checkable against Budget documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need to make sure we are focusing on what gets return on investment; what is going to help Kiwis the most, and that is doing the basics right: healthcare, education, law and order, fix the cost of living.
specificity.explanation: A list of broad portfolio areas and generic virtues — no figures, mechanisms, timeframes or named measures that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because on that side of the House, it’s full of people who have rental properties.
rigor.explanation: Explains the policy's existence by the personal property holdings of government members — a genetic/ad hominem inference: even if many members own rentals, that does not establish the policy's rationale or effect. The conclusion rests on who holds the interest rather than on the merits of the measure.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But if we look at the number of landlords in this country and we take $2.9 billion and spread it among them, it’s a hell of a lot more than $250 per fortnight.
rigor.explanation: An arithmetic inference that is valid in form, but it compares a multi-year aggregate spread across landlords with a per-fortnight household figure without stating the period or the number of landlords — a real gap between what is offered and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: No one’s going to come and invest in New Zealand if we don’t show that we’ve got a plan for 30 years.
rigor.explanation: A sweeping conditional offered without support — an absolute claim ('no one') derived from the general desirability of an infrastructure pipeline; the conclusion far exceeds the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Subsidising his landlord mates is what this Government, this National-led Government, is doing.
civility.explanation: Directed at an individual member ("his ... mates"), imputing cronyism and self-interested motive rather than engaging the merits of the tax change.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Unlike the member who’s just sat down, the Hon Damien O’Connor, I have in fact actually read this document, and it outlines some quite amazing things, like goals and priorities.
civility.explanation: A named personal jibe asserting the previous speaker did not read the document — an attack on the member's diligence rather than on his argument.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Subsidising his landlord mates is what this Government, this National-led Government, is doing.
focus.explanation: A real policy (the landlord tax change) sits underneath, but the weight of the remark is on the motives of members opposite rather than the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There has been some outrageous crystal ball - gazing from the other side of the House. It is remarkable how many things they think they know when it is not possibly true.
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of the other side's speeches; no policy, figure or measure is named or engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I can tell you that after six years of letting this country go down the tubes, it is not going to be fixed in one Budget.
focus.explanation: General condemnation of the previous government's record with no named policy, measure or outcome; the only concrete element is the party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You know, they can guffaw, but the first thing they did was to take the mandate away from the Reserve Bank to consider employment. And what do we have? Rising unemployment.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: the removal of the Reserve Bank's employment mandate is placed immediately before rising unemployment and the causal link is left to inference. Nothing is offered to connect the policy change to the labour-market outcome — no transmission mechanism, no timeframe, no counterfactual.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The idea, the suggestion, that giving people tax cuts in this economy isn’t inflationary is madness. It cuts across everything we know about how the economy works.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to incredulity and to unnamed consensus: the conclusion rests on calling the opposing view 'madness' and on an unspecified body of received knowledge, with no mechanism, modelling or source offered to show the tax cuts would be inflationary.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Only last night, I was talking to a scion of the infrastructure industry who said, “There is no confidence.”, that their projects have been ditched and nothing new has been started.
rigor.explanation: Argument from anecdote: a single unnamed industry figure's remark is offered as evidence for a sector-wide collapse in confidence and investment. One conversation cannot support the general conclusion drawn from it.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: You know, they can guffaw, but the first thing they did was to take the mandate away from the Reserve Bank to consider employment. And what do we have? Rising unemployment.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that the Government's first action was to remove the Reserve Bank's employment objective, and that unemployment is rising.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Economic Objective) Amendment Act 2023 — true if it removed the maximum sustainable employment objective from the Bank's monetary policy remit and was among the coalition's first legislative acts in December 2023; and Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey — true if the unemployment rate rose across the quarters to March 2024, false if flat or falling.

veracity.statement: This is a Government that saw minimum wage New Zealanders go backwards by giving them a 1.5 percent pay rise in the face of 5 percent inflation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the April 2024 minimum wage increase was 1.5 percent and that inflation at the time was 5 percent, so real minimum wages fell.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE published adult minimum wage rates for 1 April 2023 and 1 April 2024 (percentage increase), against Stats NZ CPI annual inflation for the March 2024 quarter. True if the rise was ~1.5% and inflation ~5%; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: She said she will deliver the tax cuts that she promised in the election—$9.6 billion of tax cuts is what she promised in the election.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the tax package Nicola Willis promised at the 2023 election was worth $9.6 billion.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's published 2023 election tax plan and its costings document, plus Treasury/independent costings of the package. True if the headline cost of the promised tax relief is ~$9.6 billion on the basis stated; false if the figure is materially different or refers to a different measure.

veracity.statement: There is no economist—there is no economist—who says that this is a good idea.
veracity.explanation: A universal claim that no economist supports delivering the tax cuts in the current economic conditions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public commentary by named New Zealand economists (bank chief economists, NZIER, academic economists) in the period around May 2024. False if any identifiable economist publicly endorsed the tax package as sound policy at that time; true only if no such endorsement can be found.

veracity.statement: So far, 4,500 jobs have been slashed—people who look after New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 4,500 public sector jobs had been cut by 22 May 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public Service Commission figures and contemporaneous tallies of announced public sector role reductions as at May 2024. True if the confirmed total was approximately 4,500; false if materially lower or higher.

divination.statement: The projections are out: we’ll see another 26,000 people on the dole.
divination.explanation: Forecasts, on the basis of published projections, that the number of people receiving unemployment-related benefit will rise by roughly 26,000.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit statistics for Jobseeker Support recipients: true if the number of recipients rises by approximately 26,000 (within a few thousand) from the May 2024 level over the projection period; false if the increase is materially smaller or numbers fall.

specificity.statement: This is a Government that saw minimum wage New Zealanders go backwards by giving them a 1.5 percent pay rise in the face of 5 percent inflation.
specificity.explanation: Two named percentages attached to a named policy decision and an identified group; anyone could look up the minimum wage rise and the CPI print and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That’s what this Government is interested in: looking after their mates.
focus.explanation: No policy, figure or measure is named — a bare characterisation of the other side's motives. The surrounding speech engages the Budget, but this sentence is purely about what the other team is 'really like'.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We saw the excise tax frozen—a coalition promise so that the New Zealand First Party could look after big tobacco.
focus.explanation: A real, named policy (the tobacco excise freeze in the coalition agreement) but the point is delivered as an imputation of whose interests a coalition partner serves rather than an account of the policy's cost or effect.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is exactly what happened last time National was in Government. They turned off the New Zealand economy, and all of that top talent left the country.
focus.explanation: A sweeping characterisation of the other party's past record with no named policy, programme or figure attached — the weight is on what National is generally like rather than on any measure in the Budget Policy Statement.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I can hear Cameron Brewer yapping away there. He really should go on a holiday to the Gold Coast. I hear he likes them—google that one.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe at a named member — 'yapping' likens him to a dog, and the invitation to 'google that one' insinuates something discreditable about him personally. Nothing here engages any argument he made.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, that last speaker, Katie Nimon, just rabbited out the usual lines.
civility.explanation: Dismissive mockery of a named member — 'rabbited out' casts her as reciting scripted lines rather than thinking. Short of a direct insult, but it belittles the person rather than answering the substance of her speech.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The committee received and considered 112 submissions on the bill and heard oral evidence from 40 submitters.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two precise counts about the Māori Affairs Committee's consideration of the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill: 112 written submissions received and 40 submitters heard orally.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Māori Affairs Committee's report on the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill (presented 2024) and the committee's submission records; true if the report states 112 submissions received and 40 submitters heard, false if the figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: Te Whakatōhea first petitioned this House in 1914 for the Crown to honour its commitments under the Treaty of Waitangi and to recognise its breaches regarding the confiscation of Whakatōhea lands.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Whakatōhea's first petition to Parliament over the land confiscations was made in 1914.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary petition records and the Waitangi Tribunal Whakatōhea report / deed of settlement historical account; true if a Whakatōhea petition to the House concerning confiscation is recorded in 1914 and none earlier, false if the first recorded petition is a different year.

veracity.statement: In the 1990s, Te Whakatōhea were amongst the first iwi to enter settlement negotiations with the Crown and, in 1996, initialled a deed of settlement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Whakatōhea were among the earliest iwi into Treaty settlement negotiations and initialled a deed of settlement in 1996.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Office for Māori Crown Relations – Te Arawhiti settlement records and the Whakatōhea deed of settlement summary; true if a Whakatōhea deed was initialled in 1996 (and negotiations began in the early 1990s), false if the initialling occurred in another year or did not occur.

veracity.statement: This piece of legislation will disestablish the Whakatōhea Māori Trust, and Te Tāwharau o Te Whakatōhea will take over that role.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill dissolves the Whakatōhea Māori Trust Board and transfers its role to Te Tāwharau o Te Whakatōhea as post-settlement governance entity.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill/Act as reported back from the Māori Affairs Committee; true if it provides for the dissolution of the Whakatōhea Māori Trust Board and vesting of its role/assets in Te Tāwharau o Te Whakatōhea, false if the board is retained or another entity is named.

specificity.statement: The committee received and considered 112 submissions on the bill and heard oral evidence from 40 submitters.
specificity.explanation: Two exact figures attached to a named committee process; directly checkable against the select committee report.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I acknowledge the strong views of those from Te Ūpokorehe and Ngāti Ira who seek their own settlements. However, I support the committee’s decision. Te Whakatōhea has worked hard towards settlement for many years, and moving into the post-settlement space will provide opportunities for all hapū.
rigor.explanation: The reasons offered — long effort and unspecified future opportunities — do not bear on the objection raised (that two hapū want to be withdrawn and settle separately). The conclusion is supported by an assertion of benefit rather than by anything addressing the premise of the dissent; effectively begging the question at issue.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But I’ve heard from colleagues who were very impressed—I’ve read for myself; I can see that. I also attended the Ahuwhenua awards last Friday and I could see that demonstrated as well, that the Whakatōhea Māori Trust Board has done an amazing job.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion about the trust board's performance rests on second-hand impressions from colleagues and a single event attended — appeal to anecdote and hearsay, with no asset, financial or performance evidence offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: This reading today is another important step in the settlement process, before the third reading, which will result in the full and final settlement of the historic Treaty of Waitangi claims for Whakatōhea.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the bill will reach and pass a third reading, delivering full and final settlement of Whakatōhea's historic Treaty claims.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The parliamentary record for the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill; true if the bill passed its third reading and received royal assent as a settlement Act, false if it lapsed, was defeated, or was not enacted.

civility.statement: I raise that issue because it would seem to me that some of the submitters—I’ll be kind and say “may have been misled” as to what the role of the committee was.
civility.explanation: Pointed and mildly condescending toward submitters — the parenthetical 'I'll be kind and say' implies a harsher word was available — but it engages the substantive question of the committee's role and attacks no individual.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’ve sat through all 13 speeches, listening to the different members, and I felt like I was in a bit of an Orwellian novel there as I saw history being revised by former Government members, as they went through all of the things that are wrong with New Zealand like the last six years didn’t happen; like they had no part to play in the pain and misery that they have inflicted on New Zealand businesses, on New Zealand households.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the members opposite — that they are deliberately rewriting history and disowning harm they caused — rather than engaging what they argued. Short of a direct insult, but sneering.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’ve sat through all 13 speeches, listening to the different members, and I felt like I was in a bit of an Orwellian novel there as I saw history being revised by former Government members, as they went through all of the things that are wrong with New Zealand like the last six years didn’t happen; like they had no part to play in the pain and misery that they have inflicted on New Zealand businesses, on New Zealand households.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the character of the previous Government's contributions to the debate; no measure, figure or policy is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, you did have something to do with it, you had a huge amount to do with it, and you had six years to try and make a better New Zealand and you made a significantly worse New Zealand.
focus.explanation: Blanket blame of the other side's six years in office; no specific policy, programme or outcome is named for the claim to attach to.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Through your inability to run a country, you oversaw a vast transfer in wealth from the lower and middle income segments of New Zealanders to capital-rich households in this country.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine distributional policy claim (wealth shifting to asset-holders), but it is wrapped in general 'inability to run a country' framing rather than a named policy or figure.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We come into Government in a situation where structural deficit is at 1.5 percent. We have the second-worst structural deficit in the developed world.
veracity.explanation: Asserts New Zealand's structural (cyclically-adjusted) fiscal deficit was about 1.5 percent of GDP on taking office, and that this was the second-largest among developed economies.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IMF Fiscal Monitor / OECD cyclically-adjusted general government balance series for New Zealand for 2023-24 compared with other advanced economies; true if NZ's structural balance is around -1.5% of GDP and ranked second-worst among advanced economies, false if the figure or the ranking is materially different.

veracity.statement: We look at the official cash rate; we inherited this at 5.5 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Reserve Bank's Official Cash Rate stood at 5.5 percent when the Government took office in late 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ Official Cash Rate history for November-December 2023; true if the OCR was 5.5%, false if it was any other level.

veracity.statement: And we have a little walk down memory lane to 2011 when tax relief was last delivered, and we had people paying 15.5 percent of their income—around that—in tax. We look at that today; it’s up at 20.6 percent, as Stuart Smith, chair of the Finance and Expenditure Committee, pointed out in his opening speech.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the average effective personal income tax rate rose from about 15.5 percent in 2011 to 20.6 percent by 2024, with no threshold adjustment in between.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD average effective personal income tax rate series (or the figures cited in the Finance and Expenditure Committee's Budget Policy Statement report) for 2011 and 2024; true if the rates are approximately 15.5% and 20.6%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: We saw the announcement today around community housing providers and social housing where we’re going to provide $140 million into that to provide 1,500 new social housing places.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an announcement made on 22 May 2024 of $140 million for community housing providers to deliver 1,500 new social housing places.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government's housing announcement of 22 May 2024 / Budget 2024 documents; true if $140 million is allocated for about 1,500 social housing places through community housing providers, false if the figures differ materially.

divination.statement: We have interest payments that will be up at around $10 billion per annum.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Crown debt-servicing costs will reach approximately $10 billion a year.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Treasury's Financial Statements of the Government / Budget Economic and Fiscal Update core Crown finance costs; true if annual finance costs reach approximately $10 billion (within about 10%) in a fiscal year up to 2026/27, false if they remain materially below that.

rigor.statement: I walk around and I talk to construction, I talk to businesses, and I get the same stories all the time that the revenue they are getting is down significantly, that the construction sector is coming to a halt and they are worried that all of their workers are going to disappear to Australia and when things come back online they are not going to have the workers there.
rigor.explanation: Argument from anecdote: a sector-wide conclusion ('the construction sector is coming to a halt') rests solely on conversations the speaker has had, with no data offered to connect the sample to the whole.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We don’t have a tax problem in New Zealand; we have a spending problem.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: revenue and expenditure are presented as mutually exclusive explanations of the fiscal position, and nothing is offered to rule out the first.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And we have a little walk down memory lane to 2011 when tax relief was last delivered, and we had people paying 15.5 percent of their income—around that—in tax. We look at that today; it’s up at 20.6 percent, as Stuart Smith, chair of the Finance and Expenditure Committee, pointed out in his opening speech.
specificity.explanation: Two dated, checkable percentages with a named source for the comparison.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are going to reduce debt. We want to reduce debt below 40 percent.
specificity.explanation: A numerical target is given but the measure (which debt indicator, of what) and the date by which it is to be met are both absent.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are focused on rebuilding our economy, we are focused on restoring law and order, and we are focused on delivering better public services.
specificity.explanation: A string of slogan-level priorities with no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named measure.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As part of the Treaty settlement process, this bill gives effect to the deed of settlement signed between the Crown and members of Whakatōhea in May 2023.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Whakatōhea deed of settlement was signed between the Crown and Whakatōhea in May 2023, and that the bill before the House gives effect to it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Arawhiti / Office for Māori Crown Relations record of the Whakatōhea deed of settlement signing date, and the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill's explanatory note; true if the deed was signed in May 2023 and the bill implements it, false if the signing date is a different month/year or the bill implements a different deed.

veracity.statement: With a population of about 17,000, Whakatōhea’s area of interest spans about 200,000 hectares.
veracity.explanation: Two quantitative claims: the Whakatōhea population is around 17,000 and the iwi's area of interest covers around 200,000 hectares.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Deed of settlement / bill schedules defining the Whakatōhea area of interest (hectares) and Stats NZ census iwi affiliation counts for Whakatōhea; true if both figures are within rounding of the official numbers, false if either is materially different.

veracity.statement: Whakatōhea joined the 800-strong Tairāwhiti taua, a combined force drawn from East Coast iwi and hapū.
veracity.explanation: Historical claim that a Whakatōhea contingent joined a combined East Coast taua of about 800 fighters (the force engaged at Kaokaoroa in 1864).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal Whakatōhea district reports, the deed of settlement historical account, and standard NZ Wars histories of the 1864 Kaokaoroa engagement; true if the combined Tairāwhiti taua is recorded at roughly 800 with Whakatōhea participation, false if the recorded size or composition is materially different.

veracity.statement: I too recognise all the descendants of those who fought at the siege on Te Tarata, the Whakatōhea casualties during that pakanga cost 10 percent of the Whakatōhea population at that time—a tremendous loss for their iwi too great to put into words.
veracity.explanation: Quantitative historical claim that Whakatōhea casualties at the siege of Te Tarata amounted to 10 percent of the iwi's population at the time.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal / deed of settlement historical account of the Te Tarata engagement, giving casualty numbers and contemporary Whakatōhea population estimates; true if casualties are recorded at approximately one tenth of the iwi population, false if the recorded proportion is materially lower or higher.

specificity.statement: With a population of about 17,000, Whakatōhea’s area of interest spans about 200,000 hectares.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete, checkable figures (population and land area) rather than a general description of the iwi.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This settlement deed and this bill will acknowledge the wrongs of the past, recognise the sufferings inflicted by the Crown, and provide financial, cultural, and commercial redress to the people of Whakatōhea for the benefit of those people who are most important to them: their mokopuna.
specificity.explanation: Names the three categories of redress (financial, cultural, commercial) and the acknowledgement of Crown wrongs, but supplies no quantum, no mechanism and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This process of the Crown in the Treaty settlements is a breach of Te Tiriti. The process of this House still continues to divide and conquer te iwi Māori in this process. We must make Waitangi Tribunal recommendations binding on the Crown and implement all unaddressed Wai claim recommendations. We must also abolish full and final settlements, which is outlined in our mana motuhake policy.
specificity.explanation: Names three identifiable mechanisms — binding Waitangi Tribunal recommendations, implementing unaddressed Wai claim recommendations, abolishing full and final settlements — and the party policy they sit in, but gives no legislative vehicle, cost or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I acknowledge the support that this bill received in the submission process, and I also respectfully acknowledge the opposition to this bill as well, but we can’t let perfection be the enemy of good.
civility.explanation: Explicitly acknowledges opponents of the bill with respect where she had an obvious opening to disparage them; nothing is directed at any person.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I acknowledge the support that this bill received in the submission process, and I also respectfully acknowledge the opposition to this bill as well, but we can’t let perfection be the enemy of good.
rigor.explanation: The reason offered for proceeding over the objections is a bare aphorism, which sets up a false dichotomy between passing this bill as drafted and holding out for perfection; the substance of the submitters' objections is never engaged, so the conclusion is not supported by anything offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This process of the Crown in the Treaty settlements is a breach of Te Tiriti. The process of this House still continues to divide and conquer te iwi Māori in this process. We must make Waitangi Tribunal recommendations binding on the Crown and implement all unaddressed Wai claim recommendations. We must also abolish full and final settlements, which is outlined in our mana motuhake policy.
rigor.explanation: The premise (the settlement process breaches Te Tiriti and divides iwi) is asserted rather than evidenced, and there is a real gap between it and the three prescriptions: nothing offered connects the alleged breach specifically to non-binding Tribunal recommendations or to finality clauses, so the conclusions outrun the support.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This process of the Crown in the Treaty settlements is a breach of Te Tiriti. The process of this House still continues to divide and conquer te iwi Māori in this process. We must make Waitangi Tribunal recommendations binding on the Crown and implement all unaddressed Wai claim recommendations. We must also abolish full and final settlements, which is outlined in our mana motuhake policy.
focus.explanation: Engages the settlement process itself and names concrete alternative measures (binding Tribunal recommendations, ending full and final settlements) rather than characterising another party.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We cannot expect that mahi to be able to happen without, firstly, an ongoing acknowledgment of the way that Crown processes have continued to breach Te Tiriti and the way that Crown processes expect things to be settled, as opposed to having an enduring, positive relationship between people, including between iwi and the Crown, and between hapū.
civility.explanation: A sharp criticism of Crown settlement processes with no person targeted; the attack is entirely on the process, which is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Crown went way beyond what was necessary or appropriate—to understate the matter.
civility.explanation: Blunt condemnation of Crown conduct with no individual targeted — hard criticism of a record, which is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: You’ve got this convoluted situation of iwi lands being used by the Crown to settle another iwi’s grievances.
focus.explanation: Engages a concrete feature of the settlement mechanism — the use of one iwi's land to settle another's claims — rather than any party or opponent.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We have to be able to support Whakatōhea to validly pick up those concerns and those kōrero in whatever way Whakatōhea knows is best in order to validly pick up those concerns to ensure that Ūpokorehe and Ngāti Ira are cared for and are worked with.
focus.explanation: Squarely about what should follow from the bill for the named hapū; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill returns cultural sites of importance, and I grant that it’s not enough but, with your goodwill, I hope we can move forward to a brighter and better community together, where I can come down and fish around the mussel farms, maybe launch my boat, and go out through the cut.
focus.explanation: Opens on what the bill actually does — returning cultural sites — and concedes its limits, but the second half drifts into personal aspiration rather than the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have to be able to support Whakatōhea to validly pick up those concerns and those kōrero in whatever way Whakatōhea knows is best in order to validly pick up those concerns to ensure that Ūpokorehe and Ngāti Ira are cared for and are worked with.
specificity.explanation: Names the hapū but commits to no mechanism, no agency, no funding and no timeframe — 'in whatever way Whakatōhea knows is best' leaves nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Pākōwhai settlement was bombarded by a Crown warship, and at least 35 bodies were left desecrated and, afterwards, buried by the Crown forces in a mass grave.
specificity.explanation: Names the settlement, the means of attack, a numeric floor for the casualties and what was done with the bodies — all checkable against the historical record.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Crown confiscated productive land and established the Ōpape Native Reserve, causing the displacement and subsequent loss of connection and economic stability for the iwi and the future of Whakatōhea.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific instrument (the Ōpape Native Reserve) and the confiscation, but gives no dates, acreage or figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill returns cultural sites of importance, and I grant that it’s not enough but, with your goodwill, I hope we can move forward to a brighter and better community together, where I can come down and fish around the mussel farms, maybe launch my boat, and go out through the cut.
specificity.explanation: 'Returns cultural sites of importance' names a category of redress but no sites, no quantum and no timeframe; the rest is anecdote.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So I did focus intentionally in the majority of my contribution—this is my first contribution on Whakatōhea, because the fantastic former Green MP Jan Logie did our first reading speech.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Jan Logie gave the Green Party's first reading speech on this bill and that this is Davidson's first speech on it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard record of the first reading of the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill: true if Jan Logie delivered the Green Party call at that reading and Davidson made no earlier speech on the bill; false if the Green call was taken by another member or Davidson had spoken on it before.

veracity.statement: Pākōwhai settlement was bombarded by a Crown warship, and at least 35 bodies were left desecrated and, afterwards, buried by the Crown forces in a mass grave.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a naval bombardment of Pākōwhai and a specific minimum number of desecrated bodies buried in a mass grave.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The historical account in the Whakatōhea deed of settlement and the Waitangi Tribunal's Bay of Plenty/Ōpōtiki reports: true if they record a naval bombardment of Pākōwhai and at least 35 bodies desecrated and buried in a mass grave by Crown forces; false if the recorded number is materially lower or no bombardment/mass grave is recorded.

veracity.statement: The Governor-General granted Mokomoko a free pardon in 1992, but it didn’t help as much as it should have if the descendants had had a part in working that through.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the year and the granting authority of Mokomoko's pardon.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Gazette and the Mokomoko pardon legislation: true if a free pardon for Mokomoko was granted by the Governor-General in 1992; false if the pardon was granted in a different year or by a different instrument.

veracity.statement: The Crown confiscated productive land and established the Ōpape Native Reserve, causing the displacement and subsequent loss of connection and economic stability for the iwi and the future of Whakatōhea.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Crown confiscation of Whakatōhea land and the establishment of the Ōpape Native Reserve with displacement following.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Whakatōhea deed of settlement historical account and Waitangi Tribunal findings on the Ōpōtiki confiscation: true if the Crown confiscated Whakatōhea land and created the Ōpape Native Reserve to which the iwi were relocated; false if no such reserve was created or the confiscation is not attributed to the Crown.

veracity.statement: In the context of a people defending their land, a man by the name of Mokomoko was wrongly accused of murdering a missionary and taken to Mt Eden Prison, and he was hanged.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Mokomoko was wrongly convicted of the murder of a missionary, imprisoned at Mt Eden and executed there.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Historical record of the 1866 trial and execution of Mokomoko for the killing of the missionary Carl Völkner, plus the statutory pardon (Mokomoko (Restoration of Character, Mana, and Reputation) Act 1992); true if he was convicted of a missionary's murder, hanged at Mt Eden, and later officially recognised as wrongly convicted, false if any of those is not borne out.

veracity.statement: Because it occurs in the strictures of the red book, it offers a fractional 1 to 2 percent of what has been lost in a physical sense, let alone can it amend for the human social livelihood and cultural impact of colonisation—and the ecological loss, because nature is invariably irreversibly destroyed and desecrated in that act of colonisation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Treaty settlements, conducted under the Office of Treaty Settlements' 'Red Book' framework, deliver only 1 to 2 percent of the material value that was lost.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published estimates comparing Treaty settlement quantum to the assessed value of land and resources confiscated (e.g. Waitangi Tribunal reports, Office of Treaty Settlements/Te Arawhiti figures, or peer-reviewed economic estimates); true if the ratio of settlement redress to assessed loss falls in the 1–2% range, false if it is materially higher or lower.

veracity.statement: The effect of the current process is that those hapū who do not feel represented by a settlement nevertheless have their own claims extinguished by that settlement. Where a hapū wants the right to withdraw from a settlement to pursue their own path, there should be a means for that to happen.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the current settlement process, hapū who oppose a settlement have their historical claims extinguished by it regardless.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The settlement/jurisdiction clauses of the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill and comparable settlement Acts, and the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975 provisions removing Tribunal jurisdiction over settled historical claims; true if those provisions extinguish all historical claims of the settling group's members including dissenting hapū, false if dissenting hapū retain the ability to pursue their claims.

specificity.statement: Because it occurs in the strictures of the red book, it offers a fractional 1 to 2 percent of what has been lost in a physical sense, let alone can it amend for the human social livelihood and cultural impact of colonisation—and the ecological loss, because nature is invariably irreversibly destroyed and desecrated in that act of colonisation.
specificity.explanation: Carries a checkable figure (1 to 2 percent) and names the governing framework (the red book), but the remainder — social, cultural and ecological loss — is asserted without measure or mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The effect of the current process is that those hapū who do not feel represented by a settlement nevertheless have their own claims extinguished by that settlement. Where a hapū wants the right to withdraw from a settlement to pursue their own path, there should be a means for that to happen.
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism of the bill before the House — the extinguishment of historical claims across all hapū of the settling group — and proposes a specific change to it. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The effect of the current process is that those hapū who do not feel represented by a settlement nevertheless have their own claims extinguished by that settlement. Where a hapū wants the right to withdraw from a settlement to pursue their own path, there should be a means for that to happen.
rigor.explanation: A stated defect in the settlement mechanism leads directly to the proposed remedy; the inference from 'claims are extinguished without consent' to 'there should be a withdrawal mechanism' follows, though no reason is offered for why a withdrawal right would not itself undermine finality.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But let us say it’s important that we simplify the process so we avoid what we call in Māori the kongakonga principle—crumbs being left rather than a robust or singular body.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the substance of the settlement question — the fragmentation of hapū interests and the case for a single settlement body — rather than characterising another party.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But let us say it’s important that we simplify the process so we avoid what we call in Māori the kongakonga principle—crumbs being left rather than a robust or singular body.
specificity.explanation: Names a concept (kongakonga) and a direction (simplify the process, one robust body) but supplies no mechanism, no clause of the bill, no figure and no timeframe, so there is nothing here to check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But it’s an endowment also that has been augmented and added to by the efforts of myself and my leader, and indeed the late Parekura Horomia, who took us to Whakatōhea in about 2006-07 to talk about the development of an aquaculture industry off the coast of that part of Mataatua country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific historical event: that Parekura Horomia took Jones and Winston Peters to Whakatōhea around 2006–07 to discuss developing an aquaculture industry off the Eastern Bay of Plenty coast, and that this contributed to the settlement's marine endowment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous records of a 2006–07 visit by Jones and Peters to Whakatōhea with Minister Parekura Horomia concerning aquaculture development — ministerial diaries, Hansard, Ministry of Fisheries/Te Puni Kōkiri records, or Eastern Bay of Plenty media reports; true if such a visit and aquaculture discussion is documented in that period, false if no record exists or the visit occurred in a materially different period or context.

rigor.statement: It may sound trite when I say it like this, but no society prospers by continually looking backwards, continually raking up the coals of discontent. I, as a member of the Ngāpuhi tribe, know that better than any other single whānau in Aotearoa.
rigor.explanation: A sweeping generalisation about all societies is supported only by an appeal to the speaker's own tribal membership and personal insight — an appeal to personal authority and anecdote, with nothing offered to connect Ngāpuhi's experience to the universal claim.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Ehara i te hāhi whakapāhongia ai pēnei me tērā whanaunga o tātou a Bishop Tāmaki, kahore.
civility.explanation: Uses a named individual (Brian Tamaki) as a dismissive foil to praise the Ringatū church, and pairs it with mockery of 'the ravings of some' heard on the radio. Not a direct insult, but it is sneering at a person rather than engaging any substance, which under the re-anchored scale is a genuine failure.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Public Works Act was also at force for Whakatōhea, with significant lands listed here in this bill that were taken under the Public Works Act. Moutohora Quarry was one of those that was taken, and is included in this apology.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Whakatōhea settlement bill lists lands taken under the Public Works Act, and specifically that Moutohora Quarry was one of them and features in the Crown apology.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill (2024) as introduced/reported back: true if the bill's historical account or apology/schedules record land takings under the Public Works Act including Moutohora Quarry; false if the Public Works Act takings or the Moutohora Quarry reference are absent from the bill.

civility.statement: I acknowledge that the Crown’s policy of large natural groups is brutal and unkind; it does not suit the natural formations of hapū and iwi.
civility.explanation: Harsh language ('brutal and unkind') aimed squarely at a Crown settlement policy, not at any person; no bad faith imputed to anyone.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I acknowledge that the Crown’s policy of large natural groups is brutal and unkind; it does not suit the natural formations of hapū and iwi.
focus.explanation: Names a specific Crown policy (the large natural groups negotiation policy) and states its effect on hapū and iwi structures; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s on the record that this settlement contains financial and commercial redress and cultural funds of around $100 million, and I’d like to just point out to Whakatōhea that my own iwi, Ngāi Tahu, back in 1997, themselves had a settlement of around $170 million and have now accrued an asset base of over $2 billion, so I’d just like to say that with this, there is a pathway forward.
veracity.explanation: Three checkable quantities are asserted: the Whakatōhea settlement package is around $100 million; the 1997 Ngāi Tahu settlement was around $170 million; and Ngāi Tahu's asset base now exceeds $2 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Whakatōhea deed of settlement summary (Te Arawhiti / Office for Māori Crown Relations) for the total financial, commercial and cultural redress quantum; the Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act 1998 / 1997 deed for the $170 million quantum; Ngāi Tahu Holdings' most recent published annual report for total assets. True if each figure matches within ordinary rounding of 'around'/'over'; false if any is materially different (e.g. settlement quantum well under $100m, or net assets below $2b).

veracity.statement: It was the State that established native reserves confiscated from Ngāti Rua, forcing members of other Whakatōhea hapū to relocate there.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific historical mechanism: native reserves were created out of land confiscated from Ngāti Rua, and members of other Whakatōhea hapū were compelled to relocate onto those reserves.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The historical account in the Whakatōhea deed of settlement and the Waitangi Tribunal's Ōpōtiki/eastern Bay of Plenty confiscation reports. True if those records describe reserves created from Ngāti Rua confiscated land onto which other Whakatōhea hapū were relocated; false if the reserves are recorded as drawn from other hapū's land or if no such compelled relocation is recorded.

specificity.statement: It’s on the record that this settlement contains financial and commercial redress and cultural funds of around $100 million, and I’d like to just point out to Whakatōhea that my own iwi, Ngāi Tahu, back in 1997, themselves had a settlement of around $170 million and have now accrued an asset base of over $2 billion, so I’d just like to say that with this, there is a pathway forward.
specificity.explanation: Carries three named figures, a named iwi, a named year and a comparison anyone could look up; the only vague element is the closing 'pathway forward'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Whakatōhea has an area of interest covering around 200,000 hectares in the Eastern Bay of Plenty and is a proud iwi with over 16,000 members comprising six hapū: Ngāi Tamahaua, Ngāti Ira, Ngāti Ngahere, Ngāti Patumoana, Ngāti Ruatākena, and Ūpokorehe.
specificity.explanation: Gives a land area, a membership figure and names all six hapū — concrete, checkable detail rather than generalities about the iwi.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But I did want to ask whether the Minister had, for example, done any consultation around the health needs of people arriving by sea that actually could be quite different from perhaps those arriving via the airport—people with disabilities or people who may have health conditions—and whether he actually sought any advice around the potential impacts of how that could be addressed.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete group (arrivals by sea, including disabled people and those with health conditions) and a concrete action (consultation and advice), but carries no figures, mechanism or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Whakatōhea has an area of interest covering around 200,000 hectares in the Eastern Bay of Plenty and is a proud iwi with over 16,000 members comprising six hapū: Ngāi Tamahaua, Ngāti Ira, Ngāti Ngahere, Ngāti Patumoana, Ngāti Ruatākena, and Ūpokorehe.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Whakatōhea's area of interest is approximately 200,000 hectares, that the iwi has more than 16,000 registered members, and that it comprises the six named hapū.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Whakatōhea deed of settlement and Te Tāwharau o Te Whakatōhea / Te Arawhiti documentation: true if the deed's area of interest is c.200,000 ha, registered membership exceeds 16,000, and the six hapū listed match those named; false if the area, membership figure or hapū list materially differs.

veracity.statement: In 1946, Whakatōhea received a small amount of compensation for those confiscations: £20,000.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Crown paid Whakatōhea £20,000 in compensation for the raupatu in 1946.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The historical account in the Whakatōhea deed of settlement and Waitangi Tribunal reports on the Whakatōhea raupatu: true if a compensation payment of £20,000 was made in or about 1946, false if the amount or year materially differs or no such payment is recorded.

focus.statement: Not everyone’s in favour of the settlement, and the hapū of Ngāti Ira and Ūpokorehe spoke at length about their desire to have the settlement delayed so they could work through issues in the Waitangi Tribunal. rigor.explanation: Concedes the premise of the objection (the manual is amendable) and answers it with a distinct reason — that the safeguards also rest on statutory and treaty instruments with higher change costs. The conclusion follows from what is offered; the layered-safeguard step is stated rather than assumed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’m tempted to make the point that the least suitable possible facilities for children would be a rust bucket of a vessel at sea trying to make its way illegally across the vast expanse of the Pacific Ocean, even the Tasman Sea.
rigor.explanation: A relevance shift: the question was whether the detention facilities are suitable for children, and the answer's comparison is to the sea voyage, which does not bear on the suitability of the facilities. He partly repairs it by disclaiming the inference immediately afterwards, so it stops short of a full false dichotomy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As for MIQ-style arrangements, I don’t imagine that any assurances that I would seek in May 2024 would be particularly meaningful in a future month or year or decade. Of course, we don’t know when it might be, if at all that this bill would be—or Act, as it will be; if it’s being applied, it would be an Act at that point. We simply can’t know what the future would hold.
rigor.explanation: Valid inference from a stated premise: because the Act's trigger point is indefinitely distant, present-day capacity assurances would have decayed by the time they were relied on, so seeking them now carries little information. The gap is that it does not address whether an assurance regime could be required at the time of use rather than now.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I’m pleased to advise the member—or perhaps remind him and advise the committee—he might well already be aware that there are facilities within that centre that provide education for children.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Māngere Refugee Resettlement Centre contains on-site facilities providing education for children (he goes on to call it a school), as a matter of present fact.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Immigration New Zealand / MBIE and Ministry of Education descriptions of the Māngere Refugee Resettlement Centre's on-site services; true if an on-site school or education programme for children is documented as operating at the centre at May 2024, false if the centre has no education facility for children on site.

rigor.statement: The reality is that if you don’t put something in law and you tell us, “Don’t worry; the rights of children will be safeguarded in the operational manual.”, one is relying on the operational manual to ensure that the rights of children are upheld, and this is the reason that it is being used to justify not voting for amendments that would, for example, exclude children and their accompanying parents or guardians in a mass arrivals group from being detained, as proposed by myself.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: if a protection is not in statute and the assurance offered points to the manual, then the assurance rests on the manual. The conclusion follows from the premise offered; the only gap is that other statutory protections might also bear on it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When we have members to my left literally making fun of the debate, the issue, and saying the contributions are boring, I would not have any trust that the operational manual would be robust enough.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the conduct of members during debate is offered as the reason to distrust the robustness of an operational document. Nothing connects the heckling to the manual's contents.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I can’t guarantee that it won’t be changed. I can’t guarantee that the sun will rise in the East and set in the West tomorrow.
rigor.explanation: False analogy: the contents of an operational manual are within the Government's own control, whereas the movement of the sun is not, so the inability to guarantee the second says nothing about the first.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Finally, in relation to the guarantee sought that there will be no public health emergencies that might impact on the capacity of these facilities, of course I can’t.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the question asked was whether he had advice that the facilities relied on would remain available during a public health emergency, not whether he could guarantee no such emergency would occur. The easier claim is refuted in place of the one made.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Minister kind of proved the point, right? He said, “I cannot guarantee what will be in the operational manual.” But this is why those amendments really matter. rigor.explanation: The inference tracks: if the manual can be altered by any future Minister and no guarantee is available, putting the protection in statute removes that dependency. The conclusion follows from the Minister's own concession.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I almost think New Zealand First is in support of this by the looks of it, because it seems like security is one of the key concerns and why not just make it more specific.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur from an interjection: a member shouting 'Security' during debate is offered as evidence that his party would support narrowing the bill's detention grounds to security risks alone.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The reality is that if you don’t put something in law and you tell us, “Don’t worry; the rights of children will be safeguarded in the operational manual.”, one is relying on the operational manual to ensure that the rights of children are upheld, and this is the reason that it is being used to justify not voting for amendments that would, for example, exclude children and their accompanying parents or guardians in a mass arrivals group from being detained, as proposed by myself.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of the committee of the whole House stage on the Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Bill, 21–22 May 2024; true if Chris Penk declined or avoided giving such an undertaking when asked, false if he gave the commitment.

civility.statement: But to sort of take the remarks in bad faith and to suggest that there is necessarily a thing to happen upon which I am supposed to give a guarantee about the future, I think is, frankly, not reasonable.

civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But, anyway, going to one of my other amendments, particularly drawing on the submission from the New Zealand Council for Civil Liberties, one of the things that they suggested, and that I put forward as an amendment, was around narrowing the reasons for a mass arrivals group to be detained to only be to manage security risks, instead of it disrupting the operations of the District Courts, or that it is challenging for the immigration system to manage the mass arrivals group.

rigor.statement: I can answer very simply the reason that we do not think it appropriate to narrow the scope of this bill, effectively, to just national security considerations, important as those may be in many situations. rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the amendment before the committee: if the warrant's purpose is defined solely by reference to national security, the other statutory purposes recorded in the bill are displaced. The conclusion tracks the premise; no fallacy.

rigor.statement: I’m just confused that any member of this House would suggest that we shouldn’t aim to effectively manage an arrival and to uphold the integrity of the system.

rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s also, by the way, while I’m at it, appropriate that the commencement date be the day after Royal assent, because we don’t know when and if this bill might be required, but we cannot afford to take the chance that we have a regime not in place, whereby we’d have a system overwhelmed and without a good capacity to deal with it.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered and the conclusion follows from it: if the triggering event is unpredictable, immediate commencement avoids a gap. The premise that the consequence would be an overwhelmed system is asserted rather than shown, which is the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Obviously, my officials did engage, but at the end of the day, judgment has to be exercised. rigor.explanation: A stated reason (avoiding reopening the iwi/urban Māori dispute) does support the decision not to amend, but it leans on the speaker's own position and preference rather than on anything offered as evidence that amendment would produce that discord.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I can answer very simply the reason that we do not think it appropriate to narrow the scope of this bill, effectively, to just national security considerations, important as those may be in many situations. focus.explanation: Engages a specific clause of the bill — the commencement provision — and the rationale for it.

focus.statement: I know that this debate may feel like a joke for the members of New Zealand First, who have made a career of fearmongering the public when it comes to migrants, but the reality is, this bill is a load of rubbish. focus.explanation: There is a real policy claim (the bill diminishes asylum seekers' rights), but the weight of the passage is characterising another party's record and motives rather than the measure.

focus.statement: I want to ask the Minister whether that is because this legislation was drafted around the time—2015, I believe—when the independent review was conducted. And perhaps the Minister could comment on why it has taken this long for the legislation to reach the House, given that the independent review was conducted in 2015?

focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The National Party differing view sought changes to those two clauses, and so my question to the Minister is: what has changed in his mind where there are no amendments that have been tabled or seem to be willing to be progressed at committee stage in light of that?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny anchored to two identified clauses and a documented select committee differing view — a named measure and a named position, not party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m just confused that any member of this House would suggest that we shouldn’t aim to effectively manage an arrival and to uphold the integrity of the system.
civility.explanation: Pointed and faintly condescending toward unnamed members ('I'm just confused that any member would suggest'), but it does not land on any individual's character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I know that this debate may feel like a joke for the members of New Zealand First, who have made a career of fearmongering the public when it comes to migrants, but the reality is, this bill is a load of rubbish. It simply diminishes the rights of those asylum seekers, and any member of this House should be ashamed of supporting this bill, instead of focusing on the issues that matter to those communities.

civility.statement: So my question to the Minister is whether or not that engagement with stakeholders took place or whether those were words that Ministers were able to say but weren’t able to fulfil; if so, what is the nature of the engagement with specific stakeholders that has led to the path of not seeking any change to clauses 25 and 37?

veracity.statement: During the period of time 2017, 2020, this bill did not enjoy a level of urgency or priority. It, obviously, fell to the recently departed Government that it should be expedited. I have inherited that role and I am moving it forward.
