rigor.statement: Will he maintain the standards that New Zealanders expect of their Government and stand down Mr Stephenson from his role, or is he unwilling to challenge David Seymour’s exploitation of a loophole which allows a pharmaceutical industry plant to assist the Minister responsible for Pharmac?
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: the question offers only 'stand down Stephenson' or 'unwilling to challenge Seymour', excluding any other basis for the appointment standing.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Alcohol and drugs are the number one contributing factor in fatal road crashes in New Zealand. In 2022 alone, alcohol and drugs were contributors to 200 fatal crashes on our roads.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that alcohol and drugs are the leading contributing factor in fatal crashes, and specifically that they contributed to 200 fatal crashes in calendar/CY 2022.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport / NZTA Crash Analysis System annual road-safety statistics for 2022: true if alcohol/drugs are recorded as the top contributing factor in fatal crashes and the count of fatal crashes with alcohol or drugs as a contributing factor is ~200; false if the figure is materially different or another factor (e.g. speed) ranks first.

veracity.statement: I have seen reports that despite legislation being passed in 2022 to enable roadside drug testing, roadside testing has not been rolled out as the legislation required the test to be suitable for evidentiary purposes and not just for a screening intent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (a) drug-driving legislation passed in 2022, (b) roadside oral fluid testing had not been rolled out as at May 2024, and (c) the cause was the statutory requirement that the roadside device meet an evidentiary standard.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Land Transport (Drug Driving) Amendment Act 2022 and its enactment date; NZ Police/Ministry of Transport statements on whether roadside oral fluid testing had commenced by May 2024 and the stated reason. True if the Act passed in 2022, no roll-out had occurred, and officials attribute this to the evidentiary-standard requirement; false if testing had begun or the stated cause is not supported.

veracity.statement: They cancelled the last tax relief in 2017 that was last legislated.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the incoming 2017 Labour-led Government repealed or cancelled tax reductions that had already been legislated by the previous Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Taxation (Budget Measures) Act 2017 tax threshold changes and the Taxation (Budget Measures: Family Incomes Package) Act 2017 / Families Package (Income Tax and Benefits) Act 2017: true if the legislated April 2018 threshold changes were repealed before taking effect, false if no such legislated tax reduction was cancelled.

veracity.statement: On behalf of the Minister of Housing, the review of Kāinga Ora was funded by a forecast underspend of transitional housing for the current financial year, and there is no impact by this decision to transfer an underspend of transitional housing on transitional housing numbers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (a) the Bill English review of Kāinga Ora was paid for from a forecast transitional housing underspend in the 2023/24 year, and (b) that transfer had no effect on the number of transitional housing places.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: HUD/MHUD Budget and appropriation transfer documents and Written Question answers on the funding source for the Kāinga Ora review, plus HUD transitional housing place counts before and after the transfer: true if the review was funded from a forecast transitional housing underspend and contracted place numbers were unchanged; false if funded elsewhere or if place numbers fell as a result.

veracity.statement: We’re not going to get into the mathematics of transitioning places, but what we can say is that there was an underspend on transitional housing over the last year—unlike the serious overspend that the previous Government has made, leaving 3,000-plus kids in emergency housing and 25,000 households on the social housing register.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two figures inherited from the previous Government: more than 3,000 children living in emergency housing, and about 25,000 households on the social housing register.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD Housing Register quarterly data and MSD/HUD emergency housing statistics for the quarters around the change of government in late 2023: true if children in emergency housing exceeded 3,000 and the social housing register was around 25,000 households; false if either figure is materially different.

specificity.statement: Our roadside drug-testing regime will use oral fluid testing devices at the roadside, for screening purposes. If two oral fluid tests are positive, then an oral fluid sample will be tested in a laboratory for evidentiary purposes.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the actual mechanism — device type, two positive screening tests, then laboratory confirmation — which is concrete enough to be checked against the bill when introduced. Falls short of 1.0 only in giving no timing or thresholds.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re proposing to remove the problematic and ineffective low-slope map, which imposes a significant cost for minimal environmental benefits, especially for low-stock farms.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific regulatory instrument being removed (the low-slope map) and who it affects, but supplies no figures for the 'significant cost' or the 'minimal environmental benefits', and no date.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ll also be repealing ineffective intensive winter grazing regulations in time for the 2025 season.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact regulations to be repealed and a deadline tied to the 2025 winter grazing season — concrete and checkable — though it gives no mechanism or cost figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does she agree with Treasury advice that a revenue package that is fiscally neutral “may still have an inflationary impact given lower-income individuals are likely to have a higher marginal propensity to consume out of additional income”; if not, why not?
specificity.explanation: Quotes a named source verbatim and identifies the precise economic mechanism at issue (marginal propensity to consume among lower-income earners), so the Minister and any reader can check exactly what is being put. A precise question, not merely a general challenge.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why was he willing to sacrifice up to 83 transitional housing places to pay for Bill English’s review, when that funding could have come from any other allocation?
specificity.explanation: Carries a specific number of places, a named piece of expenditure (the Bill English review) and an identified trade-off, making the claim checkable against the funding transfer.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I wouldn’t want to overstate the impact, but since tax relief will be fully paid for, it should, at the margin, take a bit of pressure off inflation, given that households may save some of their tax relief rather than spend it all.
rigor.explanation: A real inference with stated premises: fiscal neutrality plus a saving propensity below one implies a marginally contractionary effect. The conclusion tracks the premises, but the step rests on an unstated assumption that the offsetting spending cuts fall on higher-propensity-to-consume expenditure, which is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’re proposing to remove the problematic and ineffective low-slope map, which imposes a significant cost for minimal environmental benefits, especially for low-stock farms.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (remove the map) rests on a cost-benefit claim that is simply asserted — 'significant cost', 'minimal environmental benefits' — with no evidence, modelling or source offered to connect the premise to the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: By improving primary sector efficiency, we can boost our largest export sector and deliver for all New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: The step from sector efficiency to 'deliver for all New Zealanders' is a non sequitur: nothing is offered to connect gains at the farm gate to a benefit distributed across the whole population.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I don’t know whether the member has read the Monetary Policy Statement.
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed at the questioner rather than her argument — implies she has not done her reading. Short of a direct insult, but it targets the member rather than the substance of the point about the Reserve Bank's forecast.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But what I just want to point out to the House is that that party on the other side of the House hate tax cuts and will always vote against them.
focus.explanation: Pivots from a Treasury-advice question to a characterisation of the opposition party's general disposition. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named; it is party framing with no substance to check.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But what I would just say to members on the other side: they will say and do anything to oppose tax relief for working New Zealanders.
focus.explanation: Answers a question about interest rates and the Monetary Policy Statement with an assertion about the opposition's motives. Nothing about the mechanism, cost or effect of any policy; it is entirely about the other team.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why was he willing to sacrifice up to 83 transitional housing places to pay for Bill English’s review, when that funding could have come from any other allocation?
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named spending decision and its quantified consequence for a specific programme — accountability for a policy choice, with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Research shows that for every $1 invested in flood protection, it is estimated between $5 and $8 in direct losses is avoided.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a benefit-cost ratio from research: $1 spent on flood protection avoids $5-$8 of direct losses.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published flood-protection benefit-cost research cited in NZ (e.g. NIWA / Local Government NZ / Deloitte Access Economics or MBIE-Kānoa business cases); true if a recognised study reports avoided direct losses of roughly $5-$8 per $1 invested, false if the cited literature reports a materially different ratio or no such figure exists.

veracity.statement: More good news: since 2018, through previous funds, such as the Provincial Growth Fund, central government has invested $174 million in 177 Otago-based projects, including $24 million into manufacturing and engineering sectors.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific cumulative PGF/regional fund investment figures for Otago since 2018: $174m across 177 projects, $24m to manufacturing and engineering.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kānoa - Regional Economic Development & Investment Unit project database / PGF investment reporting for Otago from 2018; true if totals match approximately $174m over 177 projects with ~$24m in manufacturing and engineering, false if the published totals differ materially.

veracity.statement: Mr Speaker, you will be delighted to hear that Abiotic Factor has risen to fifth place on the global gaming platform Steam over the weekend.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the game Abiotic Factor reached fifth place on Steam over the weekend before 23 May 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Steam global top-sellers chart records / SteamDB rankings for the weekend of 18-19 May 2024; true if Abiotic Factor appeared at rank 5, false if it did not reach that position.

veracity.statement: I understand the genesis for the investment in the Hillside workshops was the Provincial Growth Fund, which was a key policy that the New Zealand First Party took into the 2017 election.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Provincial Growth Fund originated as a New Zealand First policy taken into the 2017 general election, and that it funded Hillside.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ First's 2017 election policy material and the 2017 Labour-NZ First coalition agreement; true if a regional development fund of this kind was NZ First 2017 policy and formed part of the coalition agreement, false if the PGF originated elsewhere.

veracity.statement: Australian customers of major banks can get a new home mortgage online within 10 minutes; meanwhile, Kiwi customers of the same banks still have to go through that lengthy manual process to get a loan.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a concrete trans-Tasman contrast: Australian customers of the same banks can obtain an online home mortgage within 10 minutes while NZ customers cannot.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Australian bank product documentation and Australian consumer data right / open banking reporting on digital mortgage approval times; true if major Australian banks offered online home-loan approval in about 10 minutes in 2024 while their NZ arms did not, false if approval times are materially longer or the NZ/AU difference does not hold.

veracity.statement: Given that the Minister’s Contracts of Insurance Bill picked up a Labour member’s bill and that this consumer data rights bill picked up Arena Williams’ member’s bill, are there any other Labour members’ bills the Minister is intending to pick up?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Customer and Product Data Bill takes up the substance of Arena Williams' member's bill and that the Contracts of Insurance Bill took up a Labour member's bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's members' bill ballot records and the texts of the Customer and Product Data Bill and Contracts of Insurance Bill; true if Arena Williams had a consumer data right member's bill materially overlapping the Government bill and a Labour member's bill covered insurance contract law, false if no such member's bills existed or the subject matter differs materially.

veracity.statement: Is the Minister aware of a report by The Education Hub released recently that said there are a growing number of neurodivergent children at schools but that inadequate resourcing, lack of knowledge, and training about how best to support neurodivergent children is taking a substantial toll, and, if so, how can she then justify cutting what little support these children currently have to be able to cope with school?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a recently released Education Hub report found growing numbers of neurodivergent children in schools alongside inadequate resourcing, knowledge and training.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education Hub's published 2024 report on neurodiversity/learning support in NZ schools; true if it reports growing numbers of neurodivergent students and inadequate resourcing, knowledge and training taking a substantial toll, false if no such report exists or its findings differ materially.

specificity.statement: Research shows that for every $1 invested in flood protection, it is estimated between $5 and $8 in direct losses is avoided.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete, checkable numeric ratio attached to a named policy area rather than a general claim that flood protection is worthwhile.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One such investment is in the beating heart of South Dunedin, which is the Hillside railway workshops, which will open again very shortly. This project has received $20 million from the PGF and will provide heavy manufacturing and service capacity for KiwiRail.
specificity.explanation: Names the project, the fund, the dollar amount and the intended function — someone could check the PGF allocation and the facility's purpose.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill will first apply to the banking sector, followed by the electricity sector. These are two areas right now where New Zealanders are hurting with high costs. In time, we will look to apply the bill to the telecommunications sector.
specificity.explanation: Names the sequence of sectors the framework will apply to, but supplies no dates, thresholds or mechanism for when each phase begins.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Multiple Government agencies have responsibilities for funding disability support, including the Ministry of Disabled People - Whaikaha, and the Ministry of Education through its learning supports. The recent changes to the purchasing guidelines reflected the Ministry of Disabled People’s view that the Ministry of Education is responsible for funding support during school hours.
specificity.explanation: Names the agencies, the instrument changed (purchasing guidelines) and the demarcation applied, though without dates or the funding amounts involved.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: One such investment is in the beating heart of South Dunedin, which is the Hillside railway workshops, which will open again very shortly. This project has received $20 million from the PGF and will provide heavy manufacturing and service capacity for KiwiRail.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the rebuilt KiwiRail Hillside workshops in Dunedin will open in the near future.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: KiwiRail / Government announcements and media reporting on the opening of the Hillside workshops; true if the facility formally opened within roughly a year of 23 May 2024, false if the opening had not occurred by then.

focus.statement: Could the Minister explain who was responsible for the revival of the Hillside workshops in Dunedin, as opposed to who took credit for it?
focus.explanation: Names a specific project, but the point of the question is about which party deserves political credit rather than the substance of the investment.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Did the Minister report back to his ministerial colleagues, following his intrepid southern journeys, that New Zealand exists beyond the Cook Strait, given so many of their recent decisions?
focus.explanation: Gestures at 'so many of their recent decisions' without naming any policy, decision or figure; the content is a characterisation of the Government rather than a policy point.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Given that the Minister’s Contracts of Insurance Bill picked up a Labour member’s bill and that this consumer data rights bill picked up Arena Williams’ member’s bill, are there any other Labour members’ bills the Minister is intending to pick up?
focus.explanation: Names two specific bills and a specific member's bill, but the thrust is a point about political credit for legislation rather than about what the measure does.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think it’s a far cry to say that this bill picks up Arena Williams’ bill. I do acknowledge that this bill had its genesis under the previous Parliament, but I’ve got to say that the industry were just at pains to say to me, “Why the hell did it take so long to get this bill in the House?” They’re so happy that this coalition Government has done it within six months, and they couldn’t believe the previous Government.
focus.explanation: Engages the bill's history and delivery timeline, but much of the weight is comparative party framing about the previous Government.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What does she say to the mum whose 11-year-old daughter diagnosed with autism and ADHD and chronic health challenges, who relies on a special one-to-one gymnastic therapy class to help improve her muscle tone and regulate her anxiety levels, will no longer be able to access support because of this new change?
focus.explanation: Directs the question squarely at the consequences of the named funding change for a specific type of support, rather than at the Government's character or record generally.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is the Minister aware of a report by The Education Hub released recently that said there are a growing number of neurodivergent children at schools but that inadequate resourcing, lack of knowledge, and training about how best to support neurodivergent children is taking a substantial toll, and, if so, how can she then justify cutting what little support these children currently have to be able to cope with school?
focus.explanation: Cites named evidence and ties it directly to the specific funding change under scrutiny — accountability on a named policy, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Did the Minister report back to his ministerial colleagues, following his intrepid southern journeys, that New Zealand exists beyond the Cook Strait, given so many of their recent decisions?
civility.explanation: Mockery aimed at the Minister personally — 'intrepid southern journeys' and the suggestion he needs to inform colleagues the South Island exists is sneering rather than substantive.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, I think, from my extensive answers, you can hear that the Government is focused very much, and certainly Kānoa and the regional development agency, on a number of projects in the South Island.
rigor.explanation: Rests the conclusion on his own preceding answers ('from my extensive answers') — a self-referential appeal; listing some southern projects does not establish the broader claim about the Government's overall regional focus.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think it’s a far cry to say that this bill picks up Arena Williams’ bill. I do acknowledge that this bill had its genesis under the previous Parliament, but I’ve got to say that the industry were just at pains to say to me, “Why the hell did it take so long to get this bill in the House?” They’re so happy that this coalition Government has done it within six months, and they couldn’t believe the previous Government.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts the claim by reporting unattributed industry reaction — an appeal to anecdote and unnamed authority that does not address whether the bill's content derives from the earlier member's bill.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is unfortunate that important services like this are operating during school hours when we actually want children to be in school and get the support for their education at school.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: treats a therapy service delivered during school hours as necessarily competing with schooling, and assumes without support that school-based learning support substitutes for the specialist service withdrawn.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My responsibility, and what the review will look at, is how to ensure that the Disability Support Services is sustainable; that it delivers for disabled children, people, their families, and their carers; but that it is not substituting funding that is available in other Government agencies that are providing disability support.
specificity.explanation: Names the review and its purpose and identifies one concrete test (funding not substituting for other agencies' disability support), but gives no terms of reference, figures, or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government’s objective is to give communities the final decision about whether their district or region will have Māori wards rather than councillors. The Waitangi Tribunal report will be available for the select committee to consider alongside the bill. We look forward to viewing the select committee’s recommendations. This Government is restoring local democracy.
specificity.explanation: States the mechanism (decision moves from councillors to communities) and the select committee process, but no dates, thresholds or detail on how the polls would work.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, I thank the former Her Worship for the patsy question. Ultimately, we trust local communities to make these decisions. We agree local communities, through the ballot box, should be able to make decisions. We are going to entrust local communities to be able to vote on whether or not they should retain—or not—Māori wards in their communities. What’s wrong with some democracy?
specificity.explanation: Three restatements of the same general sentiment about trusting local communities; no mechanism, threshold, timing or figure beyond the bare fact of a vote.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How many other representation decisions will he require compulsory referendums for—for the number of councillors, for rural wards, for the boundaries, or is it only Māori wards?
specificity.explanation: Names the exact class of decisions at issue — councillor numbers, rural wards, boundaries — so the question can be answered concretely, though it carries no figures itself.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As the member knows, what we’re doing here is we’re requiring those councils which put in place these wards without a referendum to have a referendum. Following that, if a council wishes to put in place a Māori ward, petitioners can petition for a referendum. But, ultimately, councils, when they’re setting up other wards—their checks and balances are in place with the Local Government Commission having those checks and balances. And I would encourage local councils, if there are issues that they also wish to put to referendum, put them to referendum.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the operative mechanism: which councils are caught (those that established wards without a poll), what happens afterwards (petition-triggered referendum), and where other wards' safeguards sit; missing thresholds and dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: What is his response to the Waitangi Tribunal’s finding regarding his bill to reinstate binding polls on Māori wards that “the Crown has breached the Treaty principle of partnership by prioritising coalition agreement commitments and completely failing to consult with its Treaty partner or any other stakeholders”?
veracity.explanation: Relays, as a direct quotation, a specific finding attributed to the Waitangi Tribunal about the Māori wards bill.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal's 2024 urgent inquiry report on the Māori wards / local government electoral changes; true if the report contains a finding in those terms (breach of the principle of partnership through prioritising coalition commitments and failure to consult), false if the report contains no such finding or is materially misquoted.

veracity.statement: Well, I make this very clear point: when it comes to the rural wards, which seems to be the only argument that some people have against our policy, the Local Government Commission can take appeals on those wards. And, by the way, the Local Government Commission has the final say on those wards. What we’re saying when it comes to Māori wards is that the last Government took away the ability for any appeal rights, not even to the Local Government Commission, and we are giving the right to local communities to make that decision for their community.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government removed all appeal rights, including appeals to the Local Government Commission, in respect of Māori ward decisions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2021 and the Local Electoral Act 2001 appeal/objection provisions; true if the 2021 amendment removed rights of appeal or objection (including to the Local Government Commission) over Māori ward decisions, false if such appeal or objection rights remained available.

veracity.statement: Is he concerned that over 50 of the country’s mayors and regional council chairpeople have signed an open letter opposing mandatory referendums for Māori wards; if so, why is he introducing legislation that directly overrides local government?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than 50 mayors and regional council chairpeople signed an open letter opposing mandatory referendums on Māori wards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The open letter from mayors and regional council chairs circulated in May 2024 and its published signatory list; true if signatories who are mayors or regional council chairpeople number more than 50 and the letter opposes mandatory Māori ward referendums, false if the count is materially lower or the letter's subject differs.

veracity.statement: Is he aware that the advice he received on this bill from the Department of Internal Affairs stated that the polls proved to be an almost insurmountable barrier to establishing Māori wards, and, if so, is this a deliberate tactic to reduce Māori representation in local government?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that departmental advice from the Department of Internal Affairs on this bill described the polls as an almost insurmountable barrier to establishing Māori wards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Department of Internal Affairs advice and regulatory impact statement for the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill; true if the documents describe binding polls as an almost insurmountable barrier to establishing Māori wards, false if no such assessment appears.

veracity.statement: Does he believe that consulting with affected parties is crucial when developing legislation and, if so, why was this not done with local government representatives as indicated in the regulatory impact statement?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the regulatory impact statement for this bill records that local government representatives were not consulted during its development.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement published with the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill; true if it records that consultation with local government representatives did not occur, false if it records that such consultation was undertaken.

veracity.statement: There was a thing on 14 October called an election, and the parties on this side of the House went out and campaigned on this policy, and the public, all 5.5 million New Zealanders—or not all of them could have a vote—but all 5.5 million New Zealanders were able to be part of a national conversation. They’ll all be able to have their say one day. And, ultimately, they decided on 14 October to elect the Government. And what we’re doing is implementing the policy that we were elected to do and then giving local communities the ability to have their say.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the governing parties campaigned at the 14 October general election on this policy of requiring referendums on Māori wards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2023 published election policy documents and campaign statements of National, ACT and New Zealand First; true if each of the governing parties publicly campaigned before 14 October 2023 on restoring binding polls/referendums for Māori wards, false if the commitment first appears only in the post-election coalition agreements.

rigor.statement: Well, I say to those mayors who wrote to this Government that they should focus on those core issues, and I also say to them: why should they be afraid of what the public have to say about Māori wards? What is wrong with local democracy? Ultimately, they come into my office and they write letters to me and say, “We believe in localism.” Well, the ultimate localism is giving local people the right to have their say through the ballot box.
rigor.explanation: Contains one real inference — mayors profess localism, therefore they should accept a local poll — but it rests on a loaded rhetorical question ("why should they be afraid") that presumes the objection is fear, and it does not engage the mayors' actual argument that the bill overrides local decision-making.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, I make this very clear point: when it comes to the rural wards, which seems to be the only argument that some people have against our policy, the Local Government Commission can take appeals on those wards. And, by the way, the Local Government Commission has the final say on those wards. What we’re saying when it comes to Māori wards is that the last Government took away the ability for any appeal rights, not even to the Local Government Commission, and we are giving the right to local communities to make that decision for their community.
rigor.explanation: Answers the rural-wards analogy with a stated mechanism (appeal rights to the Local Government Commission exist for rural wards but not, on his account, for Māori wards); given that premise the disanalogy conclusion follows.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I wonder whether the Minister will explain to the questioner that all sorts of people, including Māori, live in the rural wards, but everybody who’s not a Māori does not live in a Māori ward?
rigor.explanation: Advances a real inference — rural wards are open to all residents whereas Māori ward representation turns on the Māori roll, so the two are not analogous — though the connection between roll-based eligibility and the poll requirement is left implicit.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Ultimately this is about local democracy, local communities making a decision on whether or not to have a ward based upon ethnicity. That is a major constitutional change for a council and, ultimately, on this side of the House, we’re of the view that communities should make those significant decisions rather than the council. And what’s wrong with a little bit of democracy? Those councils should be right behind this, actually supporting their communities being able to have their say.
rigor.explanation: There is an inference — the change is constitutionally significant, therefore the community rather than the council should decide — but the significance premise is asserted rather than supported, and the closing rhetorical question substitutes an appeal to the word "democracy" for a response to the departmental advice raised.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There was a thing on 14 October called an election, and the parties on this side of the House went out and campaigned on this policy, and the public, all 5.5 million New Zealanders—or not all of them could have a vote—but all 5.5 million New Zealanders were able to be part of a national conversation. They’ll all be able to have their say one day. And, ultimately, they decided on 14 October to elect the Government. And what we’re doing is implementing the policy that we were elected to do and then giving local communities the ability to have their say.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the question was why affected parties were not consulted during the bill's development, and an electoral mandate does not entail that statutory or departmental consultation occurred or was unnecessary. The general election is treated as a substitute for consultation on a specific bill.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is a very clear difference between Māori wards and rural wards—that all voters who reside within that geographical boundary are able to vote for the person or their councillor, whereas Māori wards are basing the decision on ethnicity. It is this Government’s view that those decisions should be made by local communities. And I say to people on the other side of the House: why are you so afraid of the public being able to have their say? It’s called democracy.
focus.explanation: Opens with a substantive distinction between the two ward types, then pivots to characterising the other side of the House as afraid of democracy — a real policy point half-swallowed by party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, this Government will be ensuring that councils can have those referendums at the same time as the next election for local councils. And so the voters will be able to vote for their mayor and their councillors at the same time as voting for whether or not they want to retain those mayors. And I say once again to members on the other side of the House: what’s wrong with some democracy? Because clearly they don’t believe in that on the other side of the House.
focus.explanation: Gives concrete policy content on timing (referendums held alongside the next local body elections), then closes on a content-free claim about what the other side of the House believes.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I thank the former Her Worship for the patsy question. Ultimately, we trust local communities to make these decisions. We agree local communities, through the ballot box, should be able to make decisions. We are going to entrust local communities to be able to vote on whether or not they should retain—or not—Māori wards in their communities. What’s wrong with some democracy?
civility.explanation: Mocks the questioner personally — the sarcastic "former Her Worship" and the "patsy question" jibe dismiss an opposition MP's question as insincere rather than engaging it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is he aware that the advice he received on this bill from the Department of Internal Affairs stated that the polls proved to be an almost insurmountable barrier to establishing Māori wards, and, if so, is this a deliberate tactic to reduce Māori representation in local government?
civility.explanation: The evidentiary half of the question is squarely on the policy, but the second half imputes a covert bad-faith motive to the Minister personally ("a deliberate tactic to reduce Māori representation") rather than arguing the effect.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In 2021, the previous Government removed the binding polls that councils had to hold if they received a valid petition to decide on whether Māori wards would be established in their constituencies.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a 2021 legislative change removed the binding-poll mechanism that allowed electors to petition against a council's decision to establish Māori wards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2021 as enacted; true if it repealed the poll/petition provisions in the Local Electoral Act 2001 relating to Māori wards, false if those provisions were retained or removed by some other instrument.

veracity.statement: Since removing the binding poll mechanism in 2021, 45 councils have decided to establish a Māori ward without having a poll.
veracity.explanation: A specific count: 45 councils established Māori wards or constituencies after the 2021 change without holding a binding poll.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Internal Affairs / Local Government NZ records of councils that resolved to establish Māori wards or constituencies between the 2021 amendment and May 2024; true if the number is 45 (or the stated count within rounding of the official list), false if materially different or if a material number of those councils did hold polls.

veracity.statement: The exception to this is Tauranga City Council, which is holding their local elections on 20 July, which is less than two months away and before this bill will be passed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Tauranga City Council's local election is scheduled for 20 July 2024, ahead of the bill's passage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tauranga City Council / DIA published election timetable for the 2024 Tauranga elections; true if polling day was 20 July 2024, false if a different date.

veracity.statement: In fact, members may recall that the Kaikōura District Council unanimously voted no to establishing a Māori ward and instead decided to continue to work in partnership with mana whenua to investigate other options of greater inclusion and council decision-making.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Kaikōura District Council voted unanimously against establishing a Māori ward and resolved instead to pursue partnership arrangements with mana whenua.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kaikōura District Council meeting minutes/resolution on Māori wards (2021–2023); true if the vote was unanimous against establishing a ward with an accompanying partnership resolution, false if the vote was not unanimous, was in favour, or no such resolution exists.

veracity.statement: He went around the country and promised local government that if National were elected, they would help them pay for their water.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Simon Watts, campaigning before the 2023 election, promised councils that a National government would provide financial assistance for water infrastructure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 Local Water Done Well policy documents and reported campaign statements by Simon Watts to councils/LGNZ; true if a commitment to central government financial contribution to council water infrastructure was made, false if the policy offered only balance-sheet separation, borrowing capacity and regulatory change without central funding.

specificity.statement: Binding polls will be restored with the same policy settings as they were prior to 2021, including that a petition from 5 percent of electors on a council’s roll at the last local elections will require the council to hold a binding poll.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism, the threshold (5 percent of electors on the roll at the last local elections) and the consequence (a binding poll); checkable against the bill's text.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But there are some decisions which, ultimately, we leave to voters to be able to make and to decide upon, and generally those decisions are constitutional decisions. Whether it’s a parliamentary term or whether it’s the type of voting system, we allow the voters of New Zealand to have their say on those matters, and it’s the same when it comes to local councils.
rigor.explanation: An argument from analogy: because term length and voting system go to referendum, Māori wards should too. The analogy is offered rather than established — it assumes without support that establishing a ward is constitutional in the same sense as changing the electoral system, and that national referendum practice transfers to council representation arrangements.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: New Zealand Post has informed the Government that it would take up to two weeks to complete nationwide delivery of voting papers for the 2025 local elections and beyond, and as this creates a risk that some voters will not have a reasonable opportunity to have their voices heard, I propose to adjust the statutory time frames for how long voting papers can be sent out in order to allow for that.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the premises: if delivery now takes up to two weeks and the statute allows six days, the statutory window is inadequate and adjusting it follows directly. No gap between what is offered and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Minister’s defence of the Government’s position that rural wards are different because there is a provision to go to the Local Government Commission was pitiful—absolutely pitiful. If they wanted a level playing field, simply make Māori wards have the same provision, and then you’ve got what you say you’re after.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: if the stated justification for treating rural wards differently is the Local Government Commission appeal route, then extending that same route to Māori wards would satisfy the stated principle. The conclusion follows from the Government's own premise; it stops short of showing the two ward types are otherwise alike.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If there was a member’s bill in Parliament today proposing that what they are putting forward for Māori wards applied to rural wards or urban wards or any other form of wards—but especially rural wards—they would vote against it because they would argue that there’s a very good chance that the much higher-population urban areas in those districts would not vote in the rural people’s interests, and because rural people vote for them.
rigor.explanation: The argument rests entirely on a counterfactual about how members would vote on a bill that does not exist, and on an attributed electoral motive. Nothing is offered to support either; the inference cannot be tested against anything the members have actually done.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I say again to the people on the other side of this House: what should they be afraid of when it comes to democracy in this country? This side of the House supports democracy. They clearly do not.
focus.explanation: No policy content: no mechanism, figure or provision is named. It is a characterisation of what the other side of the House is 'really like' on democracy, framed as team-versus-team.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Minister’s defence of the Government’s position that rural wards are different because there is a provision to go to the Local Government Commission was pitiful—absolutely pitiful. If they wanted a level playing field, simply make Māori wards have the same provision, and then you’ve got what you say you’re after.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual mechanism at issue — the Local Government Commission provision and the asymmetry between rural and Māori wards — and proposes a concrete alternative.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This bill is nothing short of appalling. The speech made by the Minister was nothing short of disingenuous, and the entire rationale behind this bill is racially motivated.
civility.explanation: Calling the bill appalling is fierce criticism of a measure and costs nothing, but 'disingenuous' imputes bad faith to the Minister personally — the speaker is charged with knowingly misleading the House.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Simeon Brown should be ashamed—be ashamed—for giving in to extreme elements for the sake of a cheap vote.
civility.explanation: A direct personal attack that names the Minister and attributes a corrupt motive — capitulating to extremists for electoral gain — rather than engaging the bill's provisions.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Just like the homosexual law reform or marriage equality—and Simon Watts scoffs. He probably voted No. Maybe that’s why he’s scoffing.
civility.explanation: Speculates about another named member's private voting record on marriage equality in order to disparage him; a personal jibe with no bearing on the bill's substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: An appalling Minister—no one likes him, because he never turns up, and when he does turn up, he lectures them just like he did then.
civility.explanation: Sustained attack on the Minister as a person — his likeability, his attendance and his manner — with no engagement of the bill at all.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I predict that in 20 years, 30 years, Māori wards will be normal. They will be universally adopted and people will wonder what the argument was all about.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Māori wards will become uncontroversial and universally adopted across New Zealand councils within 20–30 years.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: DIA / Local Government NZ records of territorial and regional authorities with Māori wards or constituencies in 2044; true if the large majority of councils have them and no party is campaigning to abolish them, false if a substantial share of councils have none or abolition remains an active political contest.

civility.statement: The aforementioned group of activist mayors that are going against what the community want because they are afraid of the community which they represent having a say, in case they go against what they want, are on a highway to nothing.
civility.explanation: Imputes motive — fear of their own communities — to a group of named-in-kind opponents ('activist mayors') and dismisses them as 'on a highway to nothing'. Short of a direct personal insult, but it attributes bad faith to people rather than engaging their stated reasons.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So maybe the Hon Kieran McAnulty should be a little bit careful, when he’s in glass houses, about throwing stones.
civility.explanation: A hypocrisy jibe aimed at a named member rather than at his argument. Mild and idiomatic rather than abusive, but it targets the person's standing to speak instead of what he said.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Te Tiriti was created so the Queen of England could control her unruly Pākehā in Aotearoa, and I support the recent letter of our whanaunga Margaret Mutu for the British Crown to rein in these unruly Pākehā sitting across from me now.
civility.explanation: Characterises the members opposite personally as 'unruly' people needing to be reined in, an attack on the members themselves rather than on the bill or the arguments for it.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The fact is that Māori have been doing a fantastic job at local government level at being elected: 13.5 percent of local government representatives are Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori make up 13.5 percent of elected local government representatives in New Zealand at the time of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Local Government New Zealand / Department of Internal Affairs elected-member demographic data following the 2022 local elections; true if the Māori share of elected local government representatives is approximately 13.5%, false if materially different (e.g. around 22%).

veracity.statement: There is a requirement in all other wards to be plus or minus 10 percent population. There are some times when you’re able to be given an exemption by the Local Government Commission. That requirement is not there for Māori wards.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the statutory fair-representation rule requiring ward populations per member to fall within ±10 percent, subject to Local Government Commission exemption, does not apply to Māori wards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The fair representation provisions of the Local Electoral Act 2001 (s 19V and the Māori ward provisions); true if the ±10% per-member rule and its exemption process apply to general wards but not in the same form to Māori wards, false if the Act applies the same requirement to both.

veracity.statement: The problem was that the population in the general ward was about three times the size, if I remember correctly, of the population of the Māori ward.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the arrangements in the Rotorua District Council (Representation Arrangements) Bill the general ward population was roughly three times that of the Māori ward, each electing three councillors.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The general and Māori electoral roll populations for Rotorua district used in the Rotorua District Council (Representation Arrangements) Bill and the Attorney-General's s 7 report on it; true if the general ward population was approximately three times the Māori ward population, false if the ratio was materially different (e.g. closer to 2.5:1 or lower).

veracity.statement: The rohe alone covers 6,000 square kilometres, a whenua home to a population which makes up 46 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, of the Far North District, a land area of about 6,000 square kilometres and a Māori share of the population of 46 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census usual resident population by Māori ethnicity/descent for Far North District, and the district's official land area; true if the Māori share is approximately 46% and the area approximately 6,000 km², false if either is materially different.

specificity.statement: The fact is that Māori have been doing a fantastic job at local government level at being elected: 13.5 percent of local government representatives are Māori.
specificity.explanation: Carries a named figure for a named population that someone could go and check against local-government representation data; only the source is missing.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There is a requirement in all other wards to be plus or minus 10 percent population. There are some times when you’re able to be given an exemption by the Local Government Commission. That requirement is not there for Māori wards.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise statutory threshold, the exempting body, and the class of wards to which it does not apply.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The establishment of Māori wards in the Far North gave the 13 iwi entities, the 252 hapū, and 100-plus Māori social services, reo, and local trust organisations greater confidence in their local government—a confidence resulting from Māori representation.
specificity.explanation: Names counts of iwi entities, hapū and organisations in a named district; the effect claimed ('greater confidence') is not itself quantified or evidenced, which keeps it below the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill gives effect to the coalition Government’s commitment to restore the right to a local referendum on the establishment or ongoing use of Māori wards.
focus.explanation: States the measure before the House and the mechanism it introduces — a local referendum on establishment or continued use of Māori wards. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s a rushed piece of legislation that undermines the ability for Māori to determine representation.
focus.explanation: Directed squarely at the bill before the House — its process and its effect on Māori representation — rather than at the other party in general, though it names no figure or clause.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Furthermore, this Government and the races it represents blindly ignore the truly undemocratic historical actions imposed by this Pākehā Government over tangata whenua: stealing our land, wrongfully seizing political power, cleansing our identity, our knowledge, and creating violent laws that demote us to second-class citizens.
focus.explanation: Characterises the Government and those it represents in general terms rather than engaging the referendum mechanism, the representation review process, or any figure or clause in the bill; the historical grievance is asserted at large, with no specific measure or outcome named.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Very, very few of them will survive a referendum.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that when the binding polls required by this bill are held, only a small minority of existing Māori wards will be retained by voters.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Official results of the Māori ward polls held with the 2025 local body elections; true if a large majority of the councils polling voted to disestablish their Māori ward, false if most wards were retained.

rigor.statement: But if you have the situation where you only require a ward to have a little over 50 percent of the population of another ward, that means that those votes, effectively, count for twice as much, and that is a problem.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the premise: if a ward electing the same number of members has roughly half the population, each vote does carry roughly double weight. The stated principle of equal vote value is supplied earlier in the same passage, so the inference is not left hanging.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: All three Government parties campaigned on this, leading up to the last election, and were voted in accordingly—in quite a contrast, perhaps, to 2021, where we saw the first changes to representation and Māori wards not campaigned on at all in 2020.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that National, ACT and NZ First all campaigned in 2023 on changing the Māori wards rules, and that the 2021 change to Māori ward polling provisions was not part of any 2020 campaign platform.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: 2023 general election policy documents/manifestos of National, ACT and NZ First: true if all three publicly committed before the 2023 election to restoring binding polls on Māori wards, false if any of the three had no such published commitment; and 2020 Labour manifesto/campaign material on removing the poll provisions of the Local Electoral Act — true if absent, false if present.

veracity.statement: In my electorate of Ōtaki, in both the Horowhenua and Kāpiti councils, Māori councillors fill general ward seats at a higher rate than the general population.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the proportion of Horowhenua District Council and Kāpiti Coast District Council general-ward councillors who are Māori exceeds the Māori share of those districts' populations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Elected member records for Horowhenua DC and Kāpiti Coast DC (2022 triennium) with councillors' self-identified Māori descent, compared to Stats NZ 2023 Census Māori ethnicity/descent share for each district: true if the councillor share exceeds the population share in both councils, false if it does not in either.

veracity.statement: This is about not just putting it through a 17-day process, as the last Government did in 2021—17-day process in 2021, rushed through without any consultation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government's 2021 amendment to the Māori wards provisions was passed in a 17-day process with no public consultation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary record for the Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill 2021: introduction date, dates of each reading, and whether it was referred to a select committee for submissions. True if elapsed time from introduction to Royal assent is about 17 days and no select committee/public submission stage occurred; false if the elapsed period differs materially or public submissions were taken.

specificity.statement: In my electorate of Ōtaki, in both the Horowhenua and Kāpiti councils, Māori councillors fill general ward seats at a higher rate than the general population.
specificity.explanation: Names two specific councils and makes a checkable comparative claim about representation, though it supplies no actual figures or percentages.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is about not just putting it through a 17-day process, as the last Government did in 2021—17-day process in 2021, rushed through without any consultation.
specificity.explanation: Gives a specific duration, a specific year and a specific procedural claim (no consultation) that can be checked against the parliamentary record, though it does not name the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, in my experience in local government, local government is the best example of Māori relationships, of engagement, of enactment, of enablement. So they have nothing to fear about losing voice in local government because local government, I would argue, are at best practice with local Māori relationships.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — engagement, enactment, enablement, 'best practice' — with no council, programme, figure or mechanism attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They are already represented. Moving them from a general seat to a Māori ward doesn’t change their impact around the council table.
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation: from an observation about two councils in his own electorate he concludes that ward type makes no difference to Māori influence anywhere, and the conclusion also assumes what is contested (that the seat's basis of election is irrelevant to representation).
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s very hard to be inspired by that word “democracy”, when we are in fact the minority in our own country as Māori.
rigor.explanation: A genuine counter to the majoritarian-mandate argument — that a poll of a majority population cannot settle minority representation — but the inference is left implicit and no link is drawn between minority status and the specific polling mechanism in the bill.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If promises were kept, we would not have needed to establish Māori wards.
rigor.explanation: A counterfactual asserted rather than argued: nothing is offered connecting the specific Treaty obligations she invokes to the conclusion that Māori wards would have been unnecessary, so the step from premise to conclusion is unsupported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, in my experience in local government, local government is the best example of Māori relationships, of engagement, of enactment, of enablement. So they have nothing to fear about losing voice in local government because local government, I would argue, are at best practice with local Māori relationships.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal anecdote and authority, and near-circular: the conclusion that Māori have nothing to fear rests solely on his own assertion that local government is 'best practice', restated as its own supporting premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Those are the same people that voted for MMP, and that was a referendum, wasn’t it? They were the same people that voted for euthanasia, and that wasn’t a conservative issue. They are the same voters that voted in and around cannabis for recreational use at referendum and that nearly got through.
rigor.explanation: Equivocation plus non sequitur: the 1993 MMP electorate and the 2020 referendum electorate are not 'the same people', and how voters behaved on electoral system, euthanasia and cannabis gives no support to a conclusion about how they would vote on Māori ward polls.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Aue te moumou taima me te moumou moni o tēnei pire.
civility.explanation: Blunt, dismissive condemnation of the bill as a waste of time and money on a genuinely contested measure; the target is the legislation, not any member.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because I know they’ve been throwing it out to middle New Zealand—an insinuation that perhaps the hurdle was insurmountable, which is an insinuation for the rest of middle New Zealand, ratepayer New Zealand, as somewhat conservative and potentially racist.
focus.explanation: Almost entirely about what the other side is supposedly insinuating about voters; the poll threshold is gestured at but no aspect of the measure — the threshold, the timing, the cost — is actually engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The speech from the previous member, Cameron Brewer, when he tries to claim that National MPs who have contributed to this debate want more Māori representation at local bodies and want more expertise around the local council table when it comes to iwi relationships, is pretty rich, when that member sat on a local board, I believe it was the Rodney local board, in a year where I, as the general counsel for Ngāti Whātua o Kaipara, was seeking to establish with that board a relationship agreement between the board and the iwi, and it was blocked over and over.
civility.explanation: "Pretty rich" imputes bad faith to a named member personally, casting his contribution as hypocrisy rather than engaging the argument he made. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: At the same time as they think that they’re championing democracy, they’re also using their parliamentary privilege to sledge every mayor who dared to have an opinion about democracy in their local area.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the members opposite — that they abuse privilege to sledge critics while pretending to champion democracy — rather than contesting what they said.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The other challenge that I put to the Minister is that in the four and a bit weeks that have been afforded to this particular process there is a long weekend and for members there is a scrutiny week; I must ask the question: will the committee and will the membership of that committee have enough time to be able to make sure that they can give this bill the due recognition and also the public the opportunity to find their voice on this very important matter?
civility.explanation: In a debate where others turned on individuals, this presses the Minister hard on the timetable without any imputation about him personally.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The speech from the previous member, Cameron Brewer, when he tries to claim that National MPs who have contributed to this debate want more Māori representation at local bodies and want more expertise around the local council table when it comes to iwi relationships, is pretty rich, when that member sat on a local board, I believe it was the Rodney local board, in a year where I, as the general counsel for Ngāti Whātua o Kaipara, was seeking to establish with that board a relationship agreement between the board and the iwi, and it was blocked over and over.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque: the conclusion that National members' stated support for Māori representation is insincere rests on one member's conduct on one local board, which does not establish the position of the MPs who spoke in the debate.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’m raising this with the House because the Justice Committee is the wrong committee to consider this. The Māori Affairs Committee has, in the previous Parliament, considered the original bill which amended the legislation to remove the barrier for locally elected councils to make a decision about the way that they conduct their representation inquiries and to decide on Māori ward representative structures.
rigor.explanation: A precedent-based inference — the same committee considered the predecessor legislation, so it should consider this — which supports the conclusion but leaves a gap, since prior consideration does not by itself establish the Justice Committee is unsuitable.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think it’s far too short given that even with this rush, we’ve already had over 50 mayors sign a letter saying they don’t agree.
rigor.explanation: Infers that the timeframe is inadequate from the volume of mayors already objecting; the volume of submitters expected is relevant to time needed, but opposition to the bill is not itself evidence about how long consideration requires.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But it really is simple that, in 2021, Labour removed the barrier to democratically elected councils to determine whether or not, around the council table, they saw fit to establish Māori wards.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a Labour-led change in 2021 removed the mechanism that previously prevented councils from deciding for themselves to establish Māori wards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2021 and its passage record: true if it was enacted in 2021 under the Labour Government and removed the elector-initiated poll/veto mechanism over council decisions to establish Māori wards; false if no such 2021 enactment exists or it did not remove that barrier.

veracity.statement: Since that law was enacted, 45 councils have elected to have a Māori ward.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count of councils that resolved to establish Māori wards or constituencies following the 2021 law change.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Local Government New Zealand / Department of Internal Affairs records of councils with Māori wards or constituencies as at May 2024; true if the number that resolved to establish them since the 2021 Act is 45 (or rounds to it), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Instead, the ACT Party members have come to this House today and called those mayors “activist mayors”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that ACT members used the phrase "activist mayors" about mayors opposing the bill during this debate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of the first reading debate on the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill, 23 May 2024; true if an ACT member used the phrase "activist mayors", false if no such usage appears.

veracity.statement: The bill will restore the ability for communities to have a direct influence on the establishment of Māori wards and Māori constituencies by restoring the ability for 5 percent of councils’ electors to call for a binding poll on Māori wards - establishment decisions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill reinstates an elector-initiated binding poll on Māori ward decisions triggered by 5 percent of a council's electors.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill as introduced; true if it reinstates a poll demandable by 5 percent of electors, false if the threshold or mechanism differs.

veracity.statement: Restoring the right to local referendums on Māori wards is a commitment under both the ACT and New Zealand First coalition agreements.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that both the National–ACT and National–NZ First coalition agreements contain a commitment to restore local referendums on Māori wards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published National–ACT and National–New Zealand First coalition agreements of November 2023; true if both contain a commitment to restore the right to a local referendum on Māori wards, false if either does not.

veracity.statement: All three parties campaigned on reversing the previous Labour Government’s changes to local electoral law and, today, we are delivering on that commitment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that National, ACT and New Zealand First all campaigned at the 2023 election on reversing Labour's 2021 local electoral law change on Māori wards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2023 election policy documents/manifestos of National, ACT and New Zealand First; true if all three published a commitment to reverse the 2021 Māori wards local electoral changes, false if any of the three did not.

veracity.statement: I take the Minister’s point that next year is the local body election. He didn’t seem to expand any further on exactly why that particular date has been chosen, only giving ourselves one month instead of what would normally be a six-month process.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the select committee period allowed for this bill is about one month against a normal six-month process.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Standing Orders of the House of Representatives on the default select committee report-back period, and the report-back date set for this bill on 23 May 2024; true if the default is six months and the date set is roughly one month away, false if either differs materially.

veracity.statement: I’m raising this with the House because the Justice Committee is the wrong committee to consider this. The Māori Affairs Committee has, in the previous Parliament, considered the original bill which amended the legislation to remove the barrier for locally elected councils to make a decision about the way that they conduct their representation inquiries and to decide on Māori ward representative structures.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Māori Affairs Committee considered the earlier bill that removed the poll barrier to councils establishing Māori wards.
veracity.subject: speaker

veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous records — Hansard, press reports or biographies of the fourth Labour Government: true if Lange is documented describing agriculture or the primary sector as a 'sunset industry'; false if the phrase is not attributable to him (e.g. it belongs to another minister or is unsourced).

veracity.statement: We gave them extraordinary powers to amalgamate what was then two major cooperatives, New Zealand Dairy Group and Kiwi Dairies, and merge them with the Dairy Board, which was the exporter—the single exporter—at the time as that was being disestablished.

veracity.statement: So the Ministry for the Environment duly invested a lot of time—many, many hours of work by staff from the Ministry for the Environment, an agency that in the last six years of the last Government had quadrupled its number of employees—and they presented a very big, fulsome report to the select committee.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry for the Environment annual reports, FTE/staff numbers for 2017 and 2023: true if the 2023 figure is approximately four times the 2017 figure; false if the growth multiple is materially lower (e.g. roughly doubled or tripled).

rigor.statement: What we need to do—and what ACT and this coalition Government with National and New Zealand First are doing—is focus on replacing the Resource Management Act with a system based on property rights, because it’s only with true property rights that you can create wealth in a society, and it is only with wealth in a society that you can secure a healthy, prosperous, and sustainable environment.
rigor.explanation: A two-step causal chain asserted rather than supported: 'only' property rights create wealth and 'only' wealth secures a good environment. Both premises are bare assertions and the chain excludes every alternative route by stipulation — a false dichotomy carrying the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The amount of highly productive land is shrinking, and it’s shrinking dramatically in areas where we used to grow a lot of our high-quality crops.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the stock of highly productive land in New Zealand is declining, and sharply so in traditional cropping districts.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / Ministry for the Environment 'Our land' reporting and MPI land-use change data on the area of Land Use Capability class 1-3 (highly productive) land, including Pukekohe/Horowhenua/Canterbury cropping areas; true if the series shows a measurable decline in highly productive land available for production over the last two decades, false if the area is stable or rising.

veracity.statement: We’ve got over 290 catchment groups.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of DPMC's national security long-term insights briefing; true if it states that climate change will drive competition for scarce resources and increased migration to New Zealand, false if it contains no such assessment.

veracity.statement: Tens of thousands of people were displaced in the middle of a cost of living crisis.

veracity.falsification_criterion: NEMA / regional civil defence and Government recovery reporting on evacuations and displacement from Cyclone Gabrielle (February 2023); true if the count of people evacuated or displaced from their homes reached 20,000 or more, false if it was in the low thousands.

veracity.statement: We saw urupā desecrated and whānau having to dig up tūpāpaku so that they could be moved to safety.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Cyclone Gabrielle damaged urupā (Māori burial grounds) to the point that whānau exhumed and relocated remains.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous news reporting and iwi/Te Puni Kōkiri accounts of Cyclone Gabrielle damage to urupā in Tairāwhiti and Hawke's Bay; true if documented cases exist of urupā being flooded/washed out and tūpāpaku being disinterred and reburied, false if no such case is recorded.

rigor.statement: As land is being taken up for housing, that high-quality food production land is being taken away.
rigor.explanation: A direct inference: if housing expands onto productive land, that land ceases to be available for food production. The conclusion follows from the premise, though it is close to a restatement and offers nothing on scale.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Aotearoa cannot continue to treat climate change as a distant threat, because it is a very real part of our present day reality.

rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But first, we’ve got to get the policy and the legislation effectiveness, and we’ve got to get the right legislation, the right policies, and we’ve got to get the buy-in, and we’ve got to get people empowering our communities.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic requirements — 'the right legislation', 'the right policies', 'buy-in' — with no named statute, mechanism, figure or timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.

specificity.statement: We’ve got to find, through innovation, better ways for getting rid of forestry slash, like biochar and looking at those type of opportunities.

specificity.statement: The solution to climate change is through sustainable, resilient indigenous thinking, action, and modelling.

specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I did hear from the other side of the House around Jobs for Nature. That’s something New Zealand First is proud of and was proud of in 2017-2020.

civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We can improve that by having higher standards for our public housing, our council housing, to meet universal design standards. That is going to go a long way to addressing stable homes for seniors and people with disabilities.

specificity.statement: We can improve that by having higher standards for our public housing, our council housing, to meet universal design standards. That is going to go a long way to addressing stable homes for seniors and people with disabilities.
specificity.explanation: Names a mechanism (universal design standards) and the housing tenures it would apply to, but supplies no figures, no cost, no timeframe and no legislative vehicle.

specificity.statement: So Autism New Zealand, they have indicated that 2 percent of people in New Zealand suffer from autism, which is around 93,000 individuals.

specificity.statement: In 1986, as the report says, 79 percent of Europeans and Asians owned their own home; it’s now 51 percent.

veracity.statement: That report by academics completely backs up what this briefing says about declining homeownership rates and increasing renting within Māori populations.
