veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Read the named report (Māori housing/homeownership research by NZ academics) alongside HUD's long-term insights briefing: true if the report documents declining Māori homeownership and rising Māori rental tenure consistent with the briefing; false if it reports no such trend or contradicts the briefing.

veracity.statement: So Autism New Zealand, they have indicated that 2 percent of people in New Zealand suffer from autism, which is around 93,000 individuals.
veracity.explanation: Relays Autism New Zealand's stated prevalence figure of 2 percent of the NZ population, and converts it to roughly 93,000 people.

Also check the arithmetic against Stats NZ population (2 percent of ~5.2 million is ~104,000).

veracity.statement: In fact, you look at the number of nought to four-year-olds as a proportion of the population, it’s half what it was in 1961—half what it was.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ census/population estimates for the 0-4 age group as a percentage of total population in 1961 versus the most recent year: true if the current share is approximately half the 1961 share, false if it is materially more or less than half.

veracity.explanation: Asserts specific New Zealand life expectancy at birth figures for 1948: 66.7 years for men and 68.5 years for women.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ New Zealand period life tables for the late 1940s: true if life expectancy at birth around 1948 is approximately 66.7 (male) and 68.5 (female), false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: In 1986, as the report says, 79 percent of Europeans and Asians owned their own home; it’s now 51 percent.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Housing and Urban Development long-term insights briefing on housing, plus Stats NZ census homeownership rates by ethnicity: true if the 1986 and current figures for European/Asian homeownership are approximately 79 and 51 percent, false if materially different.

rigor.statement: When houses are really expensive, we do see, in fact, the birth rate going down, which is quite evident at the moment.
rigor.explanation: Treats a co-occurrence as an established causal relationship ('we do see, in fact') with nothing offered to link house prices to fertility — correlation presented as causation, supported only by an appeal to what is 'evident'.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is a great example of what we can see when you bind a community together to solve the issues that they have.
rigor.explanation: Generalises a broad conclusion about community-led housing from a single unexamined instance — an appeal to anecdote, with no evidence that the example's outcomes hold more widely.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’ve got a housing crisis and we want to build more houses, but, of course, what people did is say, “Well, actually, there is no money in building houses because the house prices are falling, the cost of building is going up.”, and people stopped building houses.
rigor.explanation: Offers a real causal mechanism — falling prices against rising build costs squeeze developer margins, so building stops — which does support the conclusion that price falls alone don't fix supply. But the post-COVID slowdown is attributed to that single cause with no data offered, so the inference leans on a plausible story rather than evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It projects an increase from 17 percent of the population being over the age of 65 in 2023 to 24 percent of the population by 2053.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: REINZ / Stats NZ median residential sale price for Auckland (the area covered by the Tāmaki Makaurau Māori electorate) for the months around May 2024; true if the median is above $1,000,000, false if materially below. Plus the text of Treasury's He Tirohanga Mokopuna 2021 for a discussion of declining first-home-buyer affordability.

veracity.statement: It means that tonight 100,000 people in Aotearoa will be sleeping rough on streets, in tents, in cars, in garages, or in unlivable houses that are making them sick.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a current figure of roughly 100,000 people in New Zealand without adequate shelter on any given night, described as rough sleeping, cars, garages or uninhabitable housing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / University of Otago severe housing deprivation estimates and MSD/HUD homelessness statistics for 2023-24; true if the count of people in the categories named (rough sleeping, cars, garages, uninhabitable dwellings) approximates 100,000, false if the 100,000 figure only holds when broader categories such as temporary accommodation and sharing others' housing are included, or if the total is materially lower.

veracity.statement: It means that 30,000 tamariki will be hospitalised this year because of substandard housing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that around 30,000 New Zealand children are hospitalised annually for illnesses caused by poor-quality housing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Te Whatu Ora hospitalisation data and published child-poverty or housing-and-health research (e.g. NZ Child and Youth Epidemiology Service) on housing-sensitive hospitalisations for children; true if annual admissions attributed to housing conditions are of the order of 30,000, false if materially lower or if no such attribution exists in the data.

veracity.statement: There are currently 94,000 unoccupied houses in this country doing nothing but collecting dust.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that there are currently about 94,000 empty dwellings in New Zealand sitting unused.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census dwelling occupancy counts and published 'empty homes' analyses; true if the count of long-term unoccupied dwellings (excluding dwellings whose residents were merely away on census night) is about 94,000, false if the figure is materially different or if 94,000 conflates census-night absentees with genuinely vacant homes.

veracity.statement: Māori make up 60 percent of homelessness in Aotearoa.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 60 percent of homeless people in New Zealand are Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ severe housing deprivation estimates and HUD/MSD emergency-housing and Housing First ethnicity breakdowns; true if the Māori share of the homeless population is approximately 60 percent, false if materially different (e.g. nearer half).

veracity.statement: Our people are being forced to pay over half their income to feed their landlord’s whānau when they can barely afford to feed their own, and, just yesterday, this Government confirmed it will be scrapping first-home grants, further locking Māori, Pasifika, and rangatahi out of homeownership.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that on 22 May 2024 the Government confirmed the abolition of the First Home Grant scheme.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Beehive press releases and news reports dated 22 May 2024; true if the Government announced on that date that the First Home Grant would be scrapped, false if no such announcement was made then or if the scheme was retained.

veracity.statement: This would save the Crown $245 million over four years, which is about 8 percent of the $3 billion handout they’re giving to landlords.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two fiscal figures: a $245 million four-year saving from ending the First Home Grant, and roughly $3 billion of four-year fiscal cost from the restoration of interest deductibility for residential landlords.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 fiscal documents and Treasury costings; true if the First Home Grant abolition is costed at about $245m over the forecast period and the interest-deductibility restoration at about $3 billion over four years, false if either figure is materially different.

rigor.statement: That is enough empty houses to put roofs over the heads of every single person who’s experiencing homelessness in Aotearoa right now, yet in Aotearoa, we’re happy to allow tamariki to sleep in cars.
rigor.explanation: Infers from 94,000 empty dwellings and roughly 100,000 homeless people that the empty stock would house everyone. Given multiple occupants per dwelling the arithmetic broadly holds, so the conclusion follows from the premises offered, but the inference silently assumes the empty houses are in the right places, habitable and available — a real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Our people are being forced to pay over half their income to feed their landlord’s whānau when they can barely afford to feed their own, and, just yesterday, this Government confirmed it will be scrapping first-home grants, further locking Māori, Pasifika, and rangatahi out of homeownership.
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure — the scrapping of first-home grants — and the specific group it is said to affect, rather than attacking the other party in general. Legitimate scrutiny of a named government decision.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This would save the Crown $245 million over four years, which is about 8 percent of the $3 billion handout they’re giving to landlords.
specificity.explanation: Carries two named dollar figures, a four-year timeframe and a stated ratio between them — someone could go to the Budget documents and check every element.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This would save the Crown $245 million over four years, which is about 8 percent of the $3 billion handout they’re giving to landlords.
civility.explanation: Sharply critical framing ('handout they're giving to landlords') but aimed entirely at a fiscal policy choice; no individual is impugned.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When overseas markets and our trade agreements are demanding that New Zealand live up to our PR brand of being clean and green, backtracking would be dangerous to our nature and our prosperity as a country.
focus.explanation: Squarely on climate policy and its trade/economic consequences rather than on the other party's character; the target is the substance of backtracking on climate settings.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: To be blunt: if members opposite shatter the Shawist legacy of working across the aisle to achieve wins for climate, then they’ll make climate another front in our culture wars, and—I promise—that’s not a war that they’ll win, but it’s not a war that we will win either.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point (the cross-party climate consensus established around the zero carbon framework), but much of the weight is party framing about what the other side will do.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The lack of a consistent national framework and resourcing on adaptation, and the chopping and changing of policies makes the task of climate-proofing our communities even harder.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the substance of climate adaptation policy — the missing national framework, funding and policy stability — with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When overseas markets and our trade agreements are demanding that New Zealand live up to our PR brand of being clean and green, backtracking would be dangerous to our nature and our prosperity as a country.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: premise (trading partners demand green credentials) supports conclusion (retreat damages prosperity). The link is plausible but asserted rather than evidenced — a gap between the premise and the strength of the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: To be blunt: if members opposite shatter the Shawist legacy of working across the aisle to achieve wins for climate, then they’ll make climate another front in our culture wars, and—I promise—that’s not a war that they’ll win, but it’s not a war that we will win either.
rigor.explanation: A conditional whose consequent — abandoning bipartisanship turns climate into a culture war neither side wins — is asserted with nothing offered to connect the two steps; a mild slippery-slope supported by an extended war analogy rather than evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The climate movement didn’t get everything we wanted from the zero carbon Act—just look at Russel Norman’s tweets about the Greens over the past six years, if you want proof—but neither did Federated Farmers.
rigor.explanation: Argues that the zero carbon Act was a balanced compromise because both flanks are unhappy; the only evidence offered for one side of that is one individual's tweets — an appeal to anecdote, and the 'both sides complain therefore it is balanced' step does not follow on its own.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: How can a country that prides itself on a fair go for all sleep soundly while tens of thousands of kids go hungry and cold, while their landlords reap the benefit of billion-dollar tax cuts?
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes hungry children with a tax change to imply the one causes or is traded off against the other, without offering any link between them; the persuasive work is done by an appeal to emotion in rhetorical-question form.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: To be blunt: if members opposite shatter the Shawist legacy of working across the aisle to achieve wins for climate, then they’ll make climate another front in our culture wars, and—I promise—that’s not a war that they’ll win, but it’s not a war that we will win either.
civility.explanation: A contested, pointed warning aimed at 'members opposite' as a bloc and at their handling of climate policy; no individual's character, competence or motives are attacked.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The lack of a consistent national framework and resourcing on adaptation, and the chopping and changing of policies makes the task of climate-proofing our communities even harder.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete policy gap (a national adaptation framework and resourcing for councils), but supplies no figures, no mechanism and no timeframe for what would replace it.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: How can a country that prides itself on a fair go for all sleep soundly while tens of thousands of kids go hungry and cold, while their landlords reap the benefit of billion-dollar tax cuts?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that landlords are receiving tax cuts worth billions of dollars — in context, the restoration of interest deductibility for residential rental property announced in Budget 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD fiscal costings published with Budget 2024 for the restoration of interest deductibility on residential rental property (and associated changes to the bright-line test); true if the forecast revenue foregone to landlords totals $1 billion or more over the forecast period, false if materially under $1 billion.

veracity.statement: I am here as a cog in the Green machine, the 42nd Green MP to be sworn into Parliament, a tribune for the environmental and social movements that this party exercises power on behalf of and with.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an ordinal fact: that he is the forty-second Green Party MP ever sworn in to the New Zealand Parliament.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary and Green Party records of every Green MP sworn in (from the party's first MPs in the 1990s to May 2024), counted in order; true if Hernandez is the 42nd, false if the count gives a different number.

veracity.statement: I pay tribute to the Filipinos who have blazed a path in New Zealand: Kookie Samin, the first ever Filipino candidate for Parliament; Dennis Maga, the first Filipino and first Asian to helm a major trade union in Aotearoa; Thelma Bell, the first Filipino elected to public office; and my colleague Paulo Garcia, the first Filipino ever elected to Parliament.
veracity.explanation: Asserts four 'first Filipino' claims, the most checkable being that Paulo Garcia was the first Filipino elected to the New Zealand Parliament and that Dennis Maga was the first Filipino and first Asian to lead a major NZ trade union.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary records of MPs' birthplace/ethnicity (Garcia entered as a National list MP in 2013) and union leadership records for FIRST Union/E tū and other major NZ unions; true if no earlier Filipino MP and no earlier Filipino or Asian major-union head can be identified, false if an earlier holder exists in either case.

veracity.statement: The free breakfast programme still exists to this very day, and the scarfie shuttles branched off into a very successful local business called Airport Shuttles Dunedin, still run by the taxi driver Divesh, whom we partnered with many years ago.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the OUSA free breakfast programme begun during his term was still operating in 2024, and that the student shuttle initiative became the ongoing business Airport Shuttles Dunedin under the same operator.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OUSA published student services/programme listings for 2024 and NZ Companies Office / business records and website for Airport Shuttles Dunedin; true if the breakfast programme was running in 2024 and the shuttle business exists under the named operator, false if either has ceased or cannot be traced to the student scheme.

veracity.statement: The tragic reality of the previous administration was Government spending went up 84 percent, inflation hit an all-time high, interest rates hit an all-time high, the economy’s in recession, and rising unemployment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific 84 percent rise in government spending under the 2017-2023 government, plus claims that inflation and interest rates reached all-time highs and that the economy is in recession.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenditure series 2017/18 to 2022/23 (is the increase about 84%?); Stats NZ CPI annual inflation series (was the 2022 peak an all-time high, versus the 1970s-80s?); RBNZ OCR and mortgage rate series (were 2023-24 rates an all-time high?); Stats NZ GDP for two consecutive quarters of contraction. True only if each stated indicator holds; false if inflation or interest rates were higher in an earlier period.

veracity.statement: Is he aware that that very speech he’s referencing of the Hon Shane Jones where he repeated the International Energy Agency’s assessment that the world needs six times more rare minerals for green transition is premised on a rapid phase-out of fossil fuels and an end to coalmining?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the IEA 'six times more minerals' figure quoted in Shane Jones's speech comes from a scenario that assumes a rapid fossil fuel phase-out and an end to coalmining.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Shane Jones's May 2024 resources speech and the IEA critical minerals/net-zero publication it cites. True if the 'six times' estimate is drawn from a scenario premised on rapid fossil fuel phase-out including no new unabated coal; false if the figure comes from a scenario carrying no such assumption.

veracity.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware, in terms of the setting of future policy, that the latest records show that the Green MPs have the highest aviation expenditure record of every party in Parliament?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that published expenditure records show Green MPs top every party on aviation spending.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary Service quarterly members' expenses disclosures for air travel by party, for the most recent published period before 28 May 2024. True if the Green Party ranks first on the party aviation expenditure measure; false if another party ranks higher on that measure.

veracity.statement: Last week, I was proud to announce that Budget 2024 allocates $140 million to funding 1,500 new social homes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Budget 2024 allocates $140 million for 1,500 new social housing places.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Housing and Urban Development appropriations and the associated ministerial press release. True if $140m is allocated to fund 1,500 new social housing places; false if the amount or the number of places differs materially.

veracity.statement: They do an outstanding job housing people in need, currently providing over 13,000 social houses around New Zealand, and they have the capability, expertise, and desire to grow further.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that community housing providers currently supply more than 13,000 social houses nationally.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: HUD social housing stock / Housing Register statistics as at mid-2024 for places supplied by registered community housing providers. True if the figure exceeds 13,000; false if it is materially below.

veracity.statement: The first is we are a Government that was left with a massive hole where funding for the Pharmac budget should have been—they left massive fiscal cliffs so that we have already announced our commitment to a $1.8 billion boost for Pharmac.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous government left no ongoing Pharmac funding provision and that this Government had already announced a $1.8 billion Pharmac uplift as at 28 May 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2023 Vote Health baselines for Pharmac's combined pharmaceutical budget, and Government announcements dated before 28 May 2024. True if Pharmac's out-year funding was unappropriated and a roughly $1.8b uplift had already been announced by that date; false if the baseline was funded or no such announcement predates the statement.

veracity.statement: I’d also like to point out that in the last week to Friday 24, 90.8 percent of schools reported their data voluntarily, and this is a fabulous development.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific voluntary reporting rate of 90.8 percent of schools for the week ending Friday 24 May 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education daily attendance dashboard data for the week ending 24 May 2024. True if the voluntary school reporting rate was 90.8%; false if materially different.

specificity.statement: The tragic reality of the previous administration was Government spending went up 84 percent, inflation hit an all-time high, interest rates hit an all-time high, the economy’s in recession, and rising unemployment.
specificity.explanation: Carries one hard figure (84 percent) and names five distinct economic indicators, all checkable, though the comparison periods are left implicit.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Can the Prime Minister assure the country that despite the economic crisis we inherited and despite the targeted expenditure and changes we’ve made, we, nevertheless, are looking forward to a period where New Zealand will have more money in the economy than ever before but in the right places?
specificity.explanation: Attempts to convey substance about the Budget but supplies no figure, mechanism or timeframe; 'more money in the economy than ever before but in the right places' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is he aware that that very speech he’s referencing of the Hon Shane Jones where he repeated the International Energy Agency’s assessment that the world needs six times more rare minerals for green transition is premised on a rapid phase-out of fossil fuels and an end to coalmining?
specificity.explanation: Names the speech, the source organisation and the multiplier, so the claim can be located and checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Last week, I was proud to announce that Budget 2024 allocates $140 million to funding 1,500 new social homes.
specificity.explanation: A named budget, a dollar figure and a unit count — directly checkable against the Budget documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What we have said is that around 500 new homes of the 1,500 will be allocated quickly, using the existing pipeline of community housing provider opportunities, with three objectives in mind: firstly, value for money from Government investment; secondly, contributing towards our target of getting people out of emergency housing motels; and a balanced approach between achievability and building capability in historically underserved regions.
specificity.explanation: Gives a number, the procurement mechanism and three stated allocation criteria, though 'quickly' leaves the timing loose.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Has she taken down the tax calculator because she knows New Zealanders will not receive the $250 per fortnight in tax cuts that they had promised?
specificity.explanation: Names the tax calculator and the exact promised figure ($250 per fortnight), making the underlying charge checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There will be an official Government tax calculator. It will be hosted on the Treasury website, it will be available from 2 p.m. on Thursday, and you should go and check it out.
specificity.explanation: Names the host site and an exact time and day for availability — precise and immediately verifiable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’d also like to point out that in the last week to Friday 24, 90.8 percent of schools reported their data voluntarily, and this is a fabulous development.
specificity.explanation: A precise percentage tied to a named week and a named data source.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The tragic reality of the previous administration was Government spending went up 84 percent, inflation hit an all-time high, interest rates hit an all-time high, the economy’s in recession, and rising unemployment.
focus.explanation: Criticism of the previous government but anchored to named economic outcomes and a figure rather than generic party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, look, I think the member would understand that actually mining is very important for helping us actually adopt EVs, to use smartphones, to adopt solar panels, and to make sure we get wind farms. We need minerals for that process and that transition.
focus.explanation: Squarely about mining policy and its role in the energy transition, not about the opposing party, even though the inference is weak.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does the Prime Minister have any advice for people who say they are opposed to mining but live a luxuriant lifestyle thanks to the benefit of it every single day of their life?
focus.explanation: The mining-dependence point is a thin wrapper around an attack on opponents' consistency; no policy, figure or measure is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does the Prime Minister think that sacrificing the habitat of the great spotted kiwi at the altar of coalmines is an accurate representation of his Government’s economic and environmental policies?
focus.explanation: Names a concrete consequence (great spotted kiwi habitat) and ties it to the Government's mining policy, though the framing is more rhetorical than evidential.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that the ability to hold up colour laser-printed images all day, every day, in Parliament is reliant on a vast array of materials, from printer toner to the metal in the printer to the fibre-optic cables that transmitted the signal—you name it, it all comes from mining—and would the words “hypocritical actions” come to the Prime Minister’s mind?
focus.explanation: Entirely directed at an opponent's conduct in the Chamber; no policy, cost or measure is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware, in terms of the setting of future policy, that the latest records show that the Green MPs have the highest aviation expenditure record of every party in Parliament?
focus.explanation: The 'setting of future policy' preamble is decorative; the substance is about another party's expense record, with no policy or measure at issue.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Where in the coalition agreement does it say that the international visitor levy will increase?
focus.explanation: Tests a specific named measure (the international visitor levy) against a specific named document; textbook scrutiny rather than party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And I also appreciate the opportunity to help the member understand economics, which is when you increase spending, you increase domestic inflation; that lifts interest rates, that slows the economy down, and that raises unemployment.
civility.explanation: Offering to 'help the member understand economics' is condescension aimed at the questioner personally rather than at his argument, though it stops well short of an insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does the Prime Minister have any advice for people who say they are opposed to mining but live a luxuriant lifestyle thanks to the benefit of it every single day of their life?
civility.explanation: Imputes hypocrisy and a 'luxuriant lifestyle' to those opposing the policy; pointed and sneering but aimed at a class of people rather than a named member.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does the Prime Minister think that sacrificing the habitat of the great spotted kiwi at the altar of coalmines is an accurate representation of his Government’s economic and environmental policies?
civility.explanation: Rhetorically fierce about the Government's policy ('at the altar of coalmines') while attacking no person; hard criticism of a policy is the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that the ability to hold up colour laser-printed images all day, every day, in Parliament is reliant on a vast array of materials, from printer toner to the metal in the printer to the fibre-optic cables that transmitted the signal—you name it, it all comes from mining—and would the words “hypocritical actions” come to the Prime Minister’s mind?
civility.explanation: Directly invites the label 'hypocritical' for the member holding up the props; the target is the member's character rather than her argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: No, in the next two years—you should listen up, mate; I answered that last week.
civility.explanation: 'You should listen up, mate' is a condescending rebuke of the interjecting member rather than an engagement with anything he said.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Has she taken down the tax calculator because she knows New Zealanders will not receive the $250 per fortnight in tax cuts that they had promised?
civility.explanation: The 'because she knows' construction imputes deliberate concealment to the Minister personally, which is an allegation of bad faith rather than of error.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Mr Speaker, I’m sure that you should have gone to Specsavers.
civility.explanation: A jibe at the Speaker's eyesight; light in tone but directed at a person rather than any argument.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And I also appreciate the opportunity to help the member understand economics, which is when you increase spending, you increase domestic inflation; that lifts interest rates, that slows the economy down, and that raises unemployment.
rigor.explanation: A genuine causal chain (spending to inflation to rates to unemployment) whose conclusion follows from its premises, but presented as automatic with no conditions or magnitudes offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, look, I think the member would understand that actually mining is very important for helping us actually adopt EVs, to use smartphones, to adopt solar panels, and to make sure we get wind farms. We need minerals for that process and that transition.
rigor.explanation: Equivocation: the question concerned coalmining and oil and gas, and the answer substitutes critical minerals for EVs and solar panels, so the conclusion does not reach the policy actually at issue.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’ve also seen a gradual decline in attendance over the last four weeks, which we might attribute to the winter season where more and more people have been calling in sick.
rigor.explanation: Infers a cause (winter illness) from a seasonal correlation with no supporting data offered, but hedges appropriately with 'might attribute', so the claim does not outrun the evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: After 14 years, this is a Government that is finally delivering income tax relief to hard-working New Zealanders in the Budget.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no income tax relief has been delivered to New Zealanders in the 14 years preceding Budget 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IRD/Treasury record of personal income tax rate and threshold changes since 2010; true if the last reduction in personal income tax (rates or thresholds) took effect around 2010 and none occurred between then and Budget 2024, false if any personal income tax reduction took effect in that period.

veracity.statement: The last Government’s response to inflation was more spending, more taxes, and more debt.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that core Crown spending, tax take/tax rates and Crown debt all rose under the 2017–2023 Labour government's handling of inflation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Financial Statements of the Government: core Crown expenses, core Crown tax revenue and net core Crown debt for 2020–2023, plus the record of new tax measures (e.g. the 39% top personal rate); true if all three rose over that period, false if spending, tax or debt did not increase.

veracity.statement: How is removing references to Treaty principles from over 40 pieces of legislation meeting his Tiriti obligations?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government is removing Treaty-principles references from more than 40 statutes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The coalition agreement commitment on Treaty principles references and a legislation.govt.nz search for Acts containing 'principles of the Treaty of Waitangi'; true if the review/removal programme covers more than 40 Acts, false if the number is materially lower (e.g. the commonly cited ~28).

veracity.statement: What actions will his Government be taking to uphold his obligations to the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in response to Israel’s continued assault on civilians and children in Rafah, including the murder of over 50 people last night?
veracity.explanation: Embeds a factual claim that more than 50 people were killed in Rafah on the night of 27–28 May 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous casualty reporting for the 26–27 May 2024 Rafah strike (Gaza health ministry figures, UN OCHA situation reports); true if the reported death toll exceeded 50, false if it was materially lower.

veracity.statement: Well, I think you heard us declare in February—and we partnered with both Australia and Canada at the time—that we did not want to see Israel undertake military operations in Rafah, because it would have catastrophic implications and impact on people.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in February 2024 New Zealand issued a joint declaration with Australia and Canada opposing an Israeli military operation in Rafah.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The record of joint statements by the New Zealand, Australian and Canadian leaders in February 2024; true if such a joint statement opposing a Rafah offensive exists, false if no joint February 2024 statement with both countries can be found.

veracity.statement: As I said yesterday, this line-by-line process has uncovered more than 240 individual saving initiatives for inclusion in Budget 2024.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the savings exercise produced more than 240 individual savings initiatives for Budget 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 savings documentation published by Treasury/the Minister of Finance (the savings initiative schedule); true if 240 or more distinct initiatives are listed, false if materially fewer.

veracity.statement: This includes finding $442 million in savings at Corrections so we can reinvest in our prisons and front-line corrections officers; finding $99 million from within the New Zealand Defence Force to reinvest in defence personnel and equipment; stopping work on the income insurance scheme, another name for a job tax; stopping work on so-called industry transformation plans; stopping work on Lake Onslow; repealing the Clean Car Discount; exiting the Crown’s contribution to Let’s Get Wellington Moving, otherwise known as “Let’s Slow Wellington Down”; and continuing the school lunch programme left unfunded by the outgoing Government, and delivering it in a way that saves taxpayers approximately $107 million a year.
veracity.explanation: Among other claims, asserts the school lunch programme was left unfunded by the previous Government and that the new delivery model saves about $107 million a year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2023 appropriations for Ka Ora, Ka Ako (whether ongoing funding extended beyond 2024) and Budget 2024 documents for the stated annual saving; true if the programme had no baseline funding beyond the outgoing Government's term and the announced saving is about $107m a year, false if ongoing funding was appropriated or the saving figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: According to the most recent advice I have received, the Government’s baseline savings exercise will remove around 2,250 roles from Government departments, as well as closing around 1,150 vacancies.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that departmental advice as at late May 2024 put role reductions at about 2,250 plus about 1,150 vacancies closed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public Service Commission / departmental change-proposal tallies for the 2024 baseline savings exercise as reported in May–June 2024; true if the figures are approximately 2,250 roles and 1,150 vacancies, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Does he agree with the then Leader of the Opposition, Christopher Luxon, who stated on 19 September 2023, regarding the National Party’s proposed tax cuts, that “for an average household income family with young kids, that would mean $250 a fortnight”?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Luxon made that specific $250-a-fortnight claim on 19 September 2023 about National's proposed tax cuts.
veracity.subject: speaker

rigor.explanation: The justification for abolition rests on a bare assertion of belief with no evidence, data or evaluation offered — an unsupported premise doing all the inferential work.

divination.statement: And like him—though I don’t agree with Labour’s tax policy at the election; he’s already flip-flopped on capital gains tax, and my bet is he’s going to flip-flop on GST too.

specificity.statement: Would it be fair to say that Kāinga Ora’s perception of itself and its unblemished excellence is somewhat different from the perception that communities have of Kāinga Ora’s approach to stakeholder engagement, is somewhat different from the approach harassed tenants have of the way Kāinga Ora deals with those matters, is somewhat different from the perception that those in the building and construction industry have from Kāinga Ora’s gold-plated approach to development, and is it in fact the case that the only people defending Kāinga Ora are the Labour Party?

specificity.statement: Was a process for managing perceived or real conflicts of interest used in relation to the previously undisclosed dinner Minister Jones had with coalmining executives, including those from Te Kuha coalmine project, and, if not, why not?

specificity.statement: Well, I reject the premise of the question. We have processes in place to manage conflicts. veracity.statement: This Government has set a goal that by 2030, 80 percent of students will be attending school at least 90 percent of the time.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government's published attendance action plan / Ministry of Education target statements from 2024; true if the official target is 80% of students attending 90%+ of the time by 2030, false if the threshold, share or date differ materially.

veracity.statement: How is it thorough when the organisation under review has stated, “There was relatively limited engagement with our organisation, leading to some review conclusions appearing to be based on analysis informed by anecdotes rather than independently considering the performance of the organisation.”?

veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora's written response to the independent review of Kāinga Ora (as released with the Cabinet paper or under the OIA); true if that wording appears in the response, false if no such passage exists or the wording materially differs.

veracity.statement: How is it thorough when he in paragraph 56 of the relevant Cabinet paper omitted that there were serious and credible concerns raised in Kāinga Ora’s response, instead stating, “the Board is broadly comfortable with the review recommendations”?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that paragraph 56 of the Cabinet paper characterised the Board as 'broadly comfortable with the review recommendations' while omitting the serious concerns Kāinga Ora raised.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The proactively released Cabinet paper on the Kāinga Ora review, paragraph 56; true if it contains the quoted phrase and does not record Kāinga Ora's substantive objections, false if the paragraph does relay those concerns or the quoted phrase is absent.

veracity.statement: The reviewers did talk to Kāinga Ora.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the independent reviewers engaged directly with Kāinga Ora during the review.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The independent review of Kāinga Ora's terms of reference and its record of engagements/meetings; true if meetings with Kāinga Ora are documented, false if the review records no engagement with the agency.

veracity.statement: Was a process for managing perceived or real conflicts of interest used in relation to the previously undisclosed dinner Minister Jones had with coalmining executives, including those from Te Kuha coalmine project, and, if not, why not?

veracity.statement: But we make no apologies for adapting something that David Parker brought in the previous Government to actually fast-track and get things done in this country.

rigor.statement: When you have 80 percent of students attending 90 percent of the time, you actually require a daily rate of approximately 94 percent.

rigor.statement: And in relation to the first part of his question, the concerns that the member relays as apparently or purportedly credible and serious are not credible and serious. focus.statement: How is it thorough when he in paragraph 56 of the relevant Cabinet paper omitted that there were serious and credible concerns raised in Kāinga Ora’s response, instead stating, “the Board is broadly comfortable with the review recommendations”?

focus.statement: And in relation to the first part of his question, the concerns that the member relays as apparently or purportedly credible and serious are not credible and serious. focus.statement: We’ve been in office for six months; you really want to talk about your six years—good grief!

specificity.statement: This funding includes 1,200 new on-site teacher-training places, a stipend for the trainees, contribution towards their tuition fees, and funding to support host schools.
