veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard, speeches or media records of Jan Tinetti's public statements on structured literacy; true if she is on record praising it in substantially those terms, false if no such statement can be found.

veracity.statement: A report by the Auditor-General earlier this year found that despite a $1.9 billion investment into mental health by the previous Government, young people in need of mental health support are waiting longer to access care.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 2024 Auditor-General finding that, despite $1.9 billion of mental health investment by the previous government, young people's waits for care lengthened.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Office of the Auditor-General's 2024 report on mental health and addiction services; true if it reports the $1.9b figure and lengthening waits for young people, false if the figure or the waiting-time finding is materially misstated.

veracity.statement: A 2023 ImpactLab assessment found that every $1 invested in I Am Hope results in a social return to New Zealand of $5.70.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific 2023 ImpactLab social-return-on-investment figure of $5.70 per $1 invested in I Am Hope.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2023 ImpactLab Gumboot Friday / I Am Hope assessment; true if it states an SROI of about $5.70 per dollar, false if the published ratio differs materially or no such assessment exists.

focus.statement: Is the Minister aware of the Government’s own report that found that children who partake in the reading recovery programme made double the normal progress expected; if so, why is she cutting the successful programme?
focus.explanation: Names a specific programme, a specific reported outcome, and a specific decision — textbook scrutiny of a policy rather than party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does the structured literacy method teach children, for example, to sound out and say the sentence “Shooting fish in a barrel.”?
focus.explanation: Framed as a question about the policy but carries no policy content — the point is entirely that the Opposition's line of questioning is easy to knock over.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: A report by the Auditor-General earlier this year found that despite a $1.9 billion investment into mental health by the previous Government, young people in need of mental health support are waiting longer to access care.
focus.explanation: Criticism of the previous government is anchored to a named report, a named spending figure and a named outcome measure (waiting times), which is accountability rather than tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Did any other mental health charities have the opportunity to bid for the $24 million contract?
focus.explanation: Goes straight to the procurement mechanism behind a named, costed contract — a precise policy question with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I will not continue to fund a programme that, at the core of its philosophy, believes in teaching children the habits of poor readers. That research that that member is quoting is taking a look at reading recovery compared to what they’re doing now, which is a little sprinkling of structured literacy. So what we know is when you do structured literacy, you get better results. So how about we just do structured literacy and see what happens, because we know the evidence backs that up.
rigor.explanation: The comparator objection is a real methodological point, but the conclusion then rests on a bare assertion that 'the evidence backs that up' with no evidence identified, and 'let's just do it and see what happens' does not follow from the premises offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In year 8, he was reading between a year 1 and year 2 level. With a structured literacy intervention, he gained that entire primary school—six years of reading—so that he was ready to start high school, using a structured literacy intervention. That is the result I want to see for all Kiwi kids who are falling behind in their reading—evidence-based structured literacy approaches that are proven to work.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single second-hand anecdote met at an airport to a claim about what works for all children — an appeal to anecdote, with no comparison or base rate offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I will not continue to fund a programme that, at the core of its philosophy, believes in teaching children the habits of poor readers. That research that that member is quoting is taking a look at reading recovery compared to what they’re doing now, which is a little sprinkling of structured literacy. So what we know is when you do structured literacy, you get better results. So how about we just do structured literacy and see what happens, because we know the evidence backs that up.
civility.explanation: Hard, dismissive criticism of the programme and of the research cited, but nothing is aimed at the member personally.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I would also like to quote a very learned person, in fact a very learned teacher, who said that structured literacy was one of the best things that she had seen in her lifetime of teaching. And that person was Jan Tinetti.
civility.explanation: A set-up-and-reveal gotcha whose sarcastic build ('a very learned person, in fact a very learned teacher') mocks the questioner personally rather than addressing her argument, though it stops short of an insult.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Did any other mental health charities have the opportunity to bid for the $24 million contract?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named procurement — a specific $24 million mental health contract and whether it was contestable. Names a specific measure and figure rather than attacking the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I implore this House to make sure that when it’s considering legislation on any issue to do with Te Tiriti o Waitangi—whether it is removing clauses from legislation, minimising the value of those clauses, minimising the value of Te Tiriti o Waitangi—they think twice about doing that and they remember this day that they voted for the third reading of the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill and they know that that is in that bill.
focus.explanation: Directed at a live policy question — the removal or weakening of Treaty clauses in legislation — and ties it to the bill before the House. No party is named or characterised; the weight is on the legislative practice, not on opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Did any other mental health charities have the opportunity to bid for the $24 million contract?
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable question: a named dollar value, a named sector, and a specific procurement process. Missing only the contract's name or date.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I implore this House to make sure that when it’s considering legislation on any issue to do with Te Tiriti o Waitangi—whether it is removing clauses from legislation, minimising the value of those clauses, minimising the value of Te Tiriti o Waitangi—they think twice about doing that and they remember this day that they voted for the third reading of the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill and they know that that is in that bill.
specificity.explanation: Names a category of legislative action (removing or minimising Treaty clauses) and the bill at hand, but identifies no particular statute, clause, timeframe or figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s 138 years since the Crown confiscated 144,000 acres of Whakatōhea land and moved its people to the Ōpape Native Reserve.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two facts: the elapsed time since the Whakatōhea land confiscation, and its extent in acres, together with the relocation of the people to Ōpape.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal / Te Arawhiti historical account and the Whakatōhea deed of settlement historical background: the date of the Whakatōhea raupatu and the acreage confiscated. True if the confiscation occurred approximately 138 years before May 2024 (i.e. c.1886) and covered about 144,000 acres; false if the elapsed interval or the acreage is materially different.

veracity.statement: Today marks 184 years since rangatira of Te Whakatōhea signed Te Tiriti o Waitangi in Ōpōtiki on 27 and 28 May 1840, and one year since Te Whakatōhea signed their deed of settlement with my predecessor the Hon Andrew Little.
veracity.explanation: Two datable assertions: the 1840 Ōpōtiki signing dates of Te Tiriti, and that the Whakatōhea deed of settlement was signed one year earlier with Andrew Little.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Archives NZ / Te Tiriti o Waitangi signing records for the Ōpōtiki signing dates in 1840, and the Te Arawhiti record of the date the Whakatōhea deed of settlement was signed and by which Minister. True if the Ōpōtiki signings were on 27–28 May 1840 and the deed was signed with Andrew Little as Minister in about May 2023; false if either date or the Minister named is wrong.

veracity.statement: This settlement provides financial, commercial, and cultural redress funds totalling $100 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the total monetary value of redress provided under the Whakatōhea settlement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Whakatōhea deed of settlement and the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill as passed: the stated total of financial, commercial and cultural redress. True if the combined redress totals about $100 million; false if the total is materially different.

rigor.statement: That apology only means something for Whakatōhea if this House upholds its obligation to this apology.
rigor.explanation: A conditional inference: the value of a formal apology depends on subsequent conduct by the body that gave it. The link is reasonable but asserted rather than supported — no evidence offered that legislative conduct is what gives an apology its force, so there is a gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: And then iwi members raised concerns that the negotiators had gone beyond their mandate and the settlement package was insufficient.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the early-1990s Whakatōhea comprehensive settlement attempt broke down because iwi members objected that the negotiators exceeded their mandate and that the package was inadequate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal reports on Whakatōhea mandate/settlement (and the historical background section of the Whakatōhea deed of settlement); true if those records show iwi members in the early 1990s objected that negotiators acted beyond their mandate and that the package was insufficient, false if the record shows the 1990s process ended for other reasons or that no such mandate objections were raised.

rigor.statement: It is and has always been in the vision of all of our tūpuna that it is about an enduring relationship, where the Crown—as Mr Adrian Rurawhe has already said—must continue to honour its partnership agreement, and at the centre uphold the mana motuhake and the tino rangatiratanga of Whakatōhea over its lands and peoples.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that the Crown must keep honouring partnership beyond the settlement — rests on an appeal to ancestral intent and on a citation of another member, rather than on anything offered in support; the premise that all tūpuna held this single vision is asserted, not established. Appeal to tradition/authority, though the inference from that premise to the conclusion is coherent.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That really does mean that a side takes ownership of what had happened—that the Crown agrees about what had happened and the responsibility that the Crown had for these historical travesties that took place.
rigor.explanation: Infers Crown ownership of the historical wrongs from the fact that an apology is written into statute. The inference is reasonable — enacting an apology does formally commit the Crown to the narrative it contains — but nothing is offered to bridge the gap between a written statement and genuine acceptance of responsibility, which is the stronger sense the word 'ownership' carries here.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It was Parekura Horomia and Michael Cullen who, in 2005-06, took us to Ōpōtiki, where it became evident that one day we would have infrastructure built in Ōpōtiki.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that ministers Parekura Horomia and Michael Cullen led a visit to Ōpōtiki in 2005-06 at which the case for infrastructure (the harbour/aquaculture development) became apparent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporary records of ministerial visits — Beehive releases, Hansard, NZ Herald/Whakatāne Beacon reporting, or Whakatōhea/Ōpōtiki District Council records — showing Horomia and Cullen visiting Ōpōtiki in 2005 or 2006 in connection with harbour/aquaculture development; true if such a visit is documented, false if no such visit occurred in that period.

divination.statement: I am very confident that once the dust settles around this settlement, there’ll be the inevitable smoothing-out processes, you will seize the opportunity and work and build on the collaborative nature of the mahi that has been carried out over the last three to five years and create New Zealand’s largest and most profitable and most desirable new platform of marine, blue ocean growth, otherwise known as mātaitai, ngā kūtai, ngā kuku, ngā porohe—koia tēnā te kupu i ‘hakatupungia ai mātou mō te kūtai i a mātou i te nohinohi i roto i ō mātou kāinga me ō mātou kuikuia.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Whakatōhea will build out of this settlement New Zealand's largest and most profitable marine aquaculture (mussel/shellfish) operation.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Aquaculture NZ / MPI industry production and revenue data plus Whakatōhea Mussels (Ōpōtiki) reported output; true if the Whakatōhea/Ōpōtiki offshore marine farm is by then the largest NZ marine aquaculture operation by area or volume and reporting profitable operation, false if it is neither the largest nor profitable.

rigor.statement: But if you live on an isolated part of this country, as is the case where I hail from in the very Far North, or are Whakatōhea, we need to be strategic and work collaboratively with the Crown and other private sector investors to make the resources that we have at our doorstep more valuable and turn them into a flow of goods and services.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (isolated iwi must partner with the Crown and private investors) follows from the stated premise that Treaty settlements are largely confined to mana whenua boundaries, so iwi outside the wealthy regions have a thinner asset base. The inference is reasonable though the step from 'confined boundaries' to 'therefore private-sector partnership' is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But if you live on an isolated part of this country, as is the case where I hail from in the very Far North, or are Whakatōhea, we need to be strategic and work collaboratively with the Crown and other private sector investors to make the resources that we have at our doorstep more valuable and turn them into a flow of goods and services.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the Treaty settlement model — how settlement redress is bounded and what iwi in isolated rohe must do with it — rather than characterising another party.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill gives effect to the deed of settlement signed between the members of Whakatōhea and the Crown in May 2023.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the deed of settlement underpinning this bill was signed by Whakatōhea and the Crown in May 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Arawhiti / Office for Māori Crown Relations record of the Whakatōhea deed of settlement signing date; true if the deed was signed in May 2023, false if signed in a different month or year.

veracity.statement: With a population of about 17,000, the Whakatōhea iwi is based on the Eastern Bay of Plenty—and I would like to acknowledge the MP here, Dana Kirkpatrick for East Coast, and, of course, Cushla Tangaere-Manuel—with a land interest of about 200,000 hectares, and comprises of six hapū.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three checkable facts about Whakatōhea: a population of about 17,000, a land interest of about 200,000 hectares, and six constituent hapū.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Whakatōhea deed of settlement summary and Stats NZ iwi affiliation data; true if population is ~17,000, area of interest ~200,000 ha and the iwi comprises six hapū, false if any figure is materially different (e.g. a different hapū count).

veracity.statement: This settlement, in particular, is a trailblazer—in two ways: first, that it confers 5,000 hectares of marine space to go to Whakatōhea for aquaculture endeavours; and two, that it allows for the Waitangi Tribunal to continue its Waitangi Tribunal district inquiry Wai 1750 pertaining to Whakatōhea, and to make findings, but not recommendations; two firsts of its kind in a Treaty settlement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the settlement grants 5,000 hectares of marine space for aquaculture and permits the Wai 1750 inquiry to continue and make findings but not recommendations, and that both provisions are firsts in a Treaty settlement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Act and the deed of settlement, plus Te Arawhiti's list of prior settlements; true if both provisions appear as described and no earlier settlement contained either, false if the marine space figure differs, the Tribunal provision differs, or a precedent settlement exists.

veracity.statement: They enacted the only cavalry attack in New Zealand’s history, and the lives of 45 men and women were tragically stolen as a result at Te Tarata Pā.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Crown's forces carried out the only cavalry attack in New Zealand's history and that 45 men and women were killed at Te Tarata Pā.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The agreed historical account in the Whakatōhea deed of settlement and Waitangi Tribunal / NZ History records of the Te Tarata engagement; true if the death toll is recorded as about 45 and the attack is documented as the sole cavalry charge in NZ, false if the toll is materially different or other cavalry actions are recorded.

veracity.statement: The Whakatōhea story spans over 180 years, beginning with the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi on this day, May 28, in 1840.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Whakatōhea signatories signed the Treaty of Waitangi on 28 May 1840.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Archives NZ Treaty signatory sheets and the deed of settlement's historical account for the Ōpōtiki/Eastern Bay of Plenty signing date; true if a Whakatōhea signing is recorded on 28 May 1840, false if the recorded date differs.

specificity.statement: This settlement, in particular, is a trailblazer—in two ways: first, that it confers 5,000 hectares of marine space to go to Whakatōhea for aquaculture endeavours; and two, that it allows for the Waitangi Tribunal to continue its Waitangi Tribunal district inquiry Wai 1750 pertaining to Whakatōhea, and to make findings, but not recommendations; two firsts of its kind in a Treaty settlement.
specificity.explanation: Names two concrete mechanisms of the settlement with a figure (5,000 hectares of marine space) and a named inquiry (Wai 1750), including the precise limitation to findings but not recommendations.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This settlement, in particular, is a trailblazer—in two ways: first, that it confers 5,000 hectares of marine space to go to Whakatōhea for aquaculture endeavours; and two, that it allows for the Waitangi Tribunal to continue its Waitangi Tribunal district inquiry Wai 1750 pertaining to Whakatōhea, and to make findings, but not recommendations; two firsts of its kind in a Treaty settlement.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the measure before the House — what redress the settlement confers and how it treats the Tribunal inquiry — with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In the context of the people defending their land, a man by the name of Mokomoko was wrongly accused of murdering the missionary Völkner, and he was taken to Mt Eden Prison and he was hanged.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Mokomoko was wrongly accused of Völkner's murder, imprisoned at Mt Eden and hanged there.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Historical record — the Mokomoko (Restoration of Character, Mana, and Reputation) Act 1992, Waitangi Tribunal Whakatōhea reporting, and Dictionary of New Zealand Biography. True if Mokomoko was convicted over Völkner's death, hanged at Mt Eden Prison, and the conviction has since been officially recognised as wrongful; false if he was not hanged at Mt Eden, or if no official finding of wrongful conviction exists.

veracity.statement: But I think it’s worth noting that in May 1840, seven Whakatōhea rangatira signed Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the Treaty of Waitangi, and by 1864 had developed a thriving agricultural economy, constructing a shipping fleet and trading extensively with the growing Auckland settlement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific number of Whakatōhea signatories (seven) in May 1840 and a thriving agricultural and shipping economy trading with Auckland by 1864.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Whakatōhea deed of settlement historical account and the Treaty signatory record (Archives NZ / Waitangi Tribunal Whakatōhea report). True if seven Whakatōhea rangatira signed te Tiriti in May 1840 and the historical account records Whakatōhea shipping and trade with Auckland by 1864; false if the signatory count or dates differ materially.

veracity.statement: And then Carl Völkner of the Church Missionary Society was hanged at Ōpōtiki in March 1865 after a meeting called by visiting Pai Mārire missionaries, who demanded his death.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the manner, place, date and instigators of Völkner's killing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Dictionary of New Zealand Biography entry for Carl Sylvius Völkner and the Waitangi Tribunal Whakatōhea report. True if Völkner was hanged at Ōpōtiki in March 1865 following a meeting called by Pai Mārire emissaries who demanded his death; false if the date, location, or instigating party differ materially.

veracity.statement: And I was fortunate recently to visit Taiwan and just get some perspective on the broad connection that has to our region, actually, because te reo Māori is part of the Austronesian languages.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that te reo Māori belongs to the Austronesian language family.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Standard linguistic classification (Ethnologue, Glottolog, and comparative Austronesian scholarship). True if te reo Māori is classified within the Austronesian family; false if it is classified outside it.

divination.statement: The ongoing taking of land, denying of resources, denying of customary entitlement, denying of the mana motuhake and the tino rangatiratanga is, rightly, to some extent, acknowledged and laid out in this very bill, in this deed of settlement, in the bill that will pass its third reading tonight.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill will complete its third reading that same evening — an outcome depending on the House, not on the speaker's own action alone.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Hansard and the Parliament bills record for 28 May 2024. True if the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill passed its third reading that sitting evening; false if the third reading was not completed that night or the bill was defeated.

specificity.statement: But I think it’s worth noting that in May 1840, seven Whakatōhea rangatira signed Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the Treaty of Waitangi, and by 1864 had developed a thriving agricultural economy, constructing a shipping fleet and trading extensively with the growing Auckland settlement.
specificity.explanation: Carries a date, a count of signatories, a second date, and named economic activity — all checkable against the settlement's historical account.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Your settlement process started as far back as the 1990s.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Whakatōhea Treaty settlement process (claims/negotiations) began in the 1990s.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Office of Treaty Settlements / Te Arawhiti record and the Whakatōhea deed of settlement background, plus Waitangi Tribunal Wai 87 filing and mandate dates; true if Whakatōhea's settlement/negotiation process demonstrably began during the 1990s, false if it began materially later (e.g. only in the 2000s).

veracity.statement: I note there are 33 vesting sites as well as part of the cultural redress.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count of 33 sites vested in Whakatōhea as cultural redress under the settlement bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The cultural redress schedules of the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill/Act 2024; true if the number of vesting sites is 33, false if the schedules list a materially different number.

veracity.statement: The fact that there are 5,000 hectares of space in the coastal marine area and that only Whakatōhea may apply for those permits, I think that is a great opportunity.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the settlement sets aside 5,000 hectares of coastal marine area in which only Whakatōhea may apply for aquaculture permits.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The aquaculture provisions of the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill/Act 2024 and the deed of settlement; true if approximately 5,000 ha is reserved with an exclusive Whakatōhea right to apply for permits, false if the area or the exclusivity differs materially.

specificity.statement: I note there are 33 vesting sites as well as part of the cultural redress.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise, checkable figure tied to a named component of the settlement (cultural redress vesting sites), though nothing about which sites.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The fact that there are 5,000 hectares of space in the coastal marine area and that only Whakatōhea may apply for those permits, I think that is a great opportunity.
specificity.explanation: Names an area figure, the location (coastal marine area) and the mechanism (exclusive right to apply for permits).
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There’s no good having aquaculture if we don’t have a water system that takes our paru water away and keeps our clean water clean.
rigor.explanation: A conditional argument: the value of the aquaculture redress depends on water quality, which depends on wastewater infrastructure. The dependency is real and the conclusion follows, though the link between the settlement's aquaculture rights and the wider water system is asserted rather than evidenced.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I guess I would like to say that I saw firsthand how damaging and difficult that policy could be, and that Whakatōhea saw that up close and continues to feel the pain of that policy.
focus.explanation: Criticism aimed at a named Crown settlement policy (the preference to negotiate only with large natural groups) and its effect on a named iwi, not at another party.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I guess I would like to say that I saw firsthand how damaging and difficult that policy could be, and that Whakatōhea saw that up close and continues to feel the pain of that policy.
civility.explanation: Hard criticism of a Crown negotiating policy; no person is attacked, and the related anecdote about her former boss is reported without imputing bad faith to anyone.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’ve seen firsthand the impact of Treaty settlements, the ability they bring for iwi to build homes, to start businesses, to fashion schools, to deliver medical services, to directly assist their whānau, and to see language and tikanga flourish anew; the ability, the space, the resources to genuinely pursue tino rangatiratanga.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that Treaty settlements deliver this range of outcomes rests entirely on the speaker's personal observation — an appeal to anecdote, with no data, evaluation or named settlement offered to support the generalisation.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What is, I believe, incredibly clear is that tino rangatiratanga was the very essence of what was agreed to and that tino rangatiratanga, the ability and the authority for every iwi to pursue its own flourishing, to care and provide for its own people, remains, as it was then, the very best hope of those communities today.
rigor.explanation: The historical premise is supported only by an appeal to the authority of the cited scholars (Fletcher, Carpenter) rather than their arguments, and the second half — that tino rangatiratanga is 'the very best hope' for iwi today — is a normative leap that does not follow from a textual finding about 1840.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In last week’s second reading, Shane Jones spoke of the centrality of your Ringatū faith to the strength and identity of Whakatōhea.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Shane Jones, in his second reading speech on the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill the previous sitting week, addressed the Ringatū faith as central to Whakatōhea identity.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of the second reading debate on the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill (May 2024); true if Shane Jones's speech there refers to the Ringatū faith as central to Whakatōhea's strength/identity, false if he made no such reference or did not speak in that debate.

veracity.statement: I was reading the bill here, and the part that stuck out to me the most says, on page 4, “In our view, delaying the bill would frustrate the will of [Te] Whakatōhea”, so I don’t wish to continue any longer—I’d hate for my relations to be frustrated even further—but I will finish and conclude my contribution with the words I said in the second reading, and I’ll say it in Māori and I’ll translate it: tēnei mea te whakapapa e kore e taea te karo [our genealogy can never be cast aside]—the beauty of our genealogy is it can never be cast aside.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the printed bill as reported back (page 4, select committee commentary) contains the words 'In our view, delaying the bill would frustrate the will of Whakatōhea'.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill as reported from the Māori Affairs Committee, page 4 of the commentary; true if that wording appears substantially as quoted, false if no such statement appears there.

veracity.statement: At inception, Whakatōhea owned just under 10 percent of shares in the aquaculture entity, and now, as part of this settlement, the Crown Regional Holdings Limited shares will transfer to the iwi, increasing its shareholding to just under 48 percent and, as a result, increasing the return on investment for you as the people of Whakatōhea.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two figures about the Whakatōhea shareholding in the aquaculture company: just under 10 percent at inception, and just under 48 percent after the Crown Regional Holdings Limited share transfer effected by the settlement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill / deed of settlement and Crown Regional Holdings Limited disclosures on the transfer of its shareholding in the Ōpōtiki aquaculture entity (Whakatōhea Mussels Ōpōtiki Ltd); true if the post-transfer iwi shareholding is approximately 48 percent and the founding stake was approximately 10 percent, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: The share transfer in the settlement arrangement, with them having sole access to 5,000 hectares of seabed for aquaculture, is a game-changer.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Whakatōhea has sole access to 5,000 hectares of seabed consented for aquaculture.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Bay of Plenty Regional Council marine farming consents and the Ōpōtiki open-ocean aquaculture area records; true if the consented area held exclusively by the Whakatōhea entity is approximately 5,000 hectares, false if the consented area is materially smaller (e.g. the commonly cited 3,800 ha) or is not exclusively held.

specificity.statement: At inception, Whakatōhea owned just under 10 percent of shares in the aquaculture entity, and now, as part of this settlement, the Crown Regional Holdings Limited shares will transfer to the iwi, increasing its shareholding to just under 48 percent and, as a result, increasing the return on investment for you as the people of Whakatōhea.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific asset transferred (Crown Regional Holdings Limited shares), the mechanism (transfer under the settlement) and both before-and-after percentage figures — someone could check it against the deed.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: By 2034, the next 10 years, it expects to be employing in the order of 320 people, be operating out of the new harbour entrance, have many more vessels in the ocean, and will fair be pumping along.
divination.explanation: Relays the aquaculture entity's forecast that by 2034 it will employ around 320 people, operate from the new Ōpōtiki harbour entrance, and run a larger fleet.
divination.subject: other
divination.falsification_criterion: Whakatōhea Mussels Ōpōtiki / Te Tāwharau o Te Whakatōhea annual reporting and Ōpōtiki District employment data as at 2034; true if reported headcount is around 320 and operations are based at the new harbour entrance, false if headcount is materially below that or operations have not moved to the new harbour entrance.

veracity.statement: I'm talking about 1995, when our good friend Ranginui Walker said no—he said no to this process.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the academic Ranginui Walker publicly refused to take part in the Crown's Treaty settlement negotiation process in 1995, in the Whakatōhea context.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporary records (Waitangi Tribunal reports on Whakatōhea, OTS/Crown records, 1990s news archives, Walker's published writing) of Ranginui Walker rejecting or refusing the Crown settlement negotiation process around 1995; true if such a documented refusal exists in or about that year, false if no such refusal is recorded or it occurred in a materially different context or period.

veracity.statement: It was the same Shane Jones who keeps rubbishing the Waitangi Tribunal, and they want us to shut the tribunal down.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Shane Jones repeatedly disparages the Waitangi Tribunal and that his party wants the Tribunal abolished.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements by Shane Jones and NZ First policy/coalition documents as at May 2024; true if Jones is on record repeatedly criticising the Tribunal and NZ First has advocated abolishing or shutting it down, false if no such record of repeated criticism exists or the party's stated position is only to review/narrow rather than close the Tribunal.

civility.statement: Don't listen to Shane Jones—he'll just waffle on with Winston's carry on, you know.
civility.explanation: Dismisses a named colleague personally — that he 'waffles on' and merely parrots another member — rather than engaging what he has argued about the Tribunal. A personal put-down, though not sustained abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It might be the start of another one because we have Māori rights under threat and we have the tribunal being attacked every second or third day by two Ministers who should know better—particularly Mr Jones.
civility.explanation: 'Ministers who should know better', with one named, is condescension directed at the individuals rather than a criticism of what they have proposed. Short of an outright insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The tribunal should be alive for ever and a day. It does not shut down just because we complete Treaty settlements.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy question at issue — the continuing role of the Waitangi Tribunal once historical settlements conclude. No party framing, though it carries little detail (a Specificity matter, not a Focus one).
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Are these the same people whom I'm listening to, going “Here's some great kōrero from ACT, great kōrero from National.”, and yet we have Māori rights under threat.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy grievance underneath (rights being eroded alongside settlements), but no measure, figure or outcome is named — the weight of the sentence is on the inconsistency of the parties opposite.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If we shut if the tribunal down, are we saying we're going to trust the Crown for ever and a day? That's not what the tribunal was about.
rigor.explanation: A false dichotomy put as a rhetorical question: closing the Tribunal is treated as equivalent to a decision to trust the Crown permanently, with nothing offered to rule out other oversight mechanisms or to connect the two propositions.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I see that on Thursday, Te Pāti Māori is running their protests, and good on them, I say.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Te Pāti Māori will hold protest action on the Thursday following this 28 May 2024 speech — an action by another party, not by the speaker.
divination.subject: other
divination.falsification_criterion: News reporting and Te Pāti Māori communications for Thursday 30 May 2024; true if Te Pāti Māori-organised protest action took place that day, false if no such action occurred or it was held on a materially different date.

specificity.statement: Getting Wellington out of farming is an important part of our plan to get the economy back on track.
specificity.explanation: A slogan-style framing of the plan: no mechanism, no figure, no timeframe, and 'getting Wellington out of farming' names no instrument, even though the surrounding speech does contain detail elsewhere.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Fifthly, the bill suspends for three years the requirements under the National Policy Statement for Indigenous Biodiversity for councils to identify new significant natural areas—SNAs—and include them in district plans.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument (NPS for Indigenous Biodiversity), the mechanism (suspension of the SNA identification requirement for district plans) and a duration (three years). Directly checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Regional councils tell us there’s been a significant improvement in winter grazing practices around the country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that regional councils have reported to the Government a significant nationwide improvement in intensive winter grazing practice, offered as the evidential basis for repealing the winter grazing regulations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Regional council and MfE/MPI intensive winter grazing monitoring reports for 2022–2024 (e.g. Environment Southland, Otago Regional Council compliance and aerial monitoring surveys) plus MfE advice on the bill: true if council monitoring records show a material improvement in winter grazing practice/compliance across multiple regions, false if council monitoring shows flat or worsening practice or no such advice exists.

veracity.statement: It’s typically a two-year process to amend items of national direction, as other members in the House will know.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that amending an item of national direction (an NPS or NES) under the Resource Management Act typically takes about two years from start to gazettal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry for the Environment guidance on the national direction development process and the elapsed time between board-of-inquiry/consultation start and gazettal for recent NPS/NES amendments: true if the typical elapsed time is around two years, false if amendments typically complete materially faster (under about a year) or take substantially longer.

veracity.statement: This is why economies that are poor tend to be the worst environmental vandals. Economies that are wealthy and prosperous tend to look after the environment, and there’s a direct correlation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that there is a direct correlation between national wealth and environmental performance, with poor economies being the worst environmental performers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cross-country comparison of GDP per capita against environmental performance measures (Yale Environmental Performance Index, per-capita greenhouse gas emissions, consumption-based footprint data): true if wealth correlates positively with environmental performance across the main measures, false if the relationship reverses or disappears on key measures such as per-capita emissions or consumption footprint.

rigor.statement: If it’s not mined domestically, all we do is import coal and steel with potential flow-on costs—increasing greenhouse gas emissions.
rigor.explanation: A substitution argument about a real policy, but the inference has a gap: it assumes demand is entirely fixed and that imported coal/steel is necessarily more emissions-intensive, neither of which is offered any support. False dichotomy between domestic mining and importing.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is why economies that are poor tend to be the worst environmental vandals. Economies that are wealthy and prosperous tend to look after the environment, and there’s a direct correlation.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a bare correlation and treats it as establishing the causal claim that growth produces environmental protection. No evidence is offered for the correlation, and the direction of causation is assumed rather than argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I hear the member over the other side going on simplistically and tritely about destroying the environment.
civility.explanation: Dismisses another member with sneering characterisation ('simplistically and tritely') rather than engaging what they said. Short of a direct insult, but it lands on the member rather than the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: No, no chance of that, Mr Bennett. The electorate for which Mr Bennett used to be the representative will discover that many of the projects and many of the benefits of the fast-track bill apply to the great electorate of New Plymouth, as will other electorates around the House.
civility.explanation: Pointed reminder that the interjector lost his seat, aimed at the member personally rather than at his interjection, though it is folded into a substantive point about the fast-track bill.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Just like all the advice you’re given. Maybe you want to look at the supplementary analysis report.
civility.explanation: Imputes that the Minister habitually ignores official advice — a jab at his conduct rather than at the merits of the bill, though it does gesture at a real document.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So members opposite want to have a trite debate about the economy versus the environment. We have a more sophisticated and nuanced approach on this side of the House.
focus.explanation: Frames the disagreement as one side being trite and the other sophisticated. There is a faint policy premise (economy versus environment), but the weight is on characterising the other side rather than on any measure, figure or mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: No, no chance of that, Mr Bennett. The electorate for which Mr Bennett used to be the representative will discover that many of the projects and many of the benefits of the fast-track bill apply to the great electorate of New Plymouth, as will other electorates around the House.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the New Plymouth electorate will turn out to host many of the projects and benefits under the fast-track approvals regime.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The schedule of listed projects in the Fast-track Approvals Act as enacted, plus subsequent referred-project decisions: true if multiple listed or referred projects sit within the New Plymouth electorate, false if none or only an isolated one does.

civility.statement: I can assure the Minister responsible for RMA Reform that I’m not interested in having trite discussions, but what I have heard a lot of here has been trite.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the Minister's contributions as "trite" — a sneering characterisation aimed at what the person opposite has been saying rather than at the substance of the argument, though short of a direct personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is going to primary production, and I have nominated the Environment Committee. I think that is where this bill should go to, because, of course, it is about amending the Resource Management Act (RMA), and what committee has always considered things to do with the Resource Management Act? Oh, that would be, of course, the Environment Committee that should be considering this, because the regulations that are being amended by this bill are to do with protecting the environment and improving the environment by stopping pollution.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a procedural-policy question about the bill before the House — which select committee should scrutinise an RMA amendment — naming the committee, the Act, and the subject matter of the regulations. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can there be any discussion of rebalancing that hierarchy unless you intend for profit to come over the environment and to come over people?
focus.explanation: Engages the specific measure at issue — the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy and proposals to rebalance it — rather than the other party's general record.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I don’t know where to start with this aspect of the bill, other than to say the science is crystal clear that if we want to prevent a future filled with climate catastrophe and extreme weather, then fossil fuels need to stay in the ground.
focus.explanation: Addresses the coalmining provisions of the bill and the reason for opposing them, not the other party's record or character, though the reasoning is pitched at a general level.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is going to primary production, and I have nominated the Environment Committee. I think that is where this bill should go to, because, of course, it is about amending the Resource Management Act (RMA), and what committee has always considered things to do with the Resource Management Act? Oh, that would be, of course, the Environment Committee that should be considering this, because the regulations that are being amended by this bill are to do with protecting the environment and improving the environment by stopping pollution.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: the bill amends the RMA and environmental regulations, therefore the specialist Environment Committee should consider it. The subject-matter premise supports the conclusion, but the supporting arm ("what committee has always considered" RMA matters) is an appeal to precedent/tradition rather than a reason why that committee is better placed, leaving a gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: How can there be any discussion of rebalancing that hierarchy unless you intend for profit to come over the environment and to come over people?
rigor.explanation: A false dichotomy posed as a rhetorical question: any adjustment to the hierarchy's ordering is treated as necessarily entailing an intent to rank profit above both environment and people, with no intermediate possibility (e.g. changing how the hierarchy applies to consents rather than inverting it) admitted or ruled out.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I don’t know where to start with this aspect of the bill, other than to say the science is crystal clear that if we want to prevent a future filled with climate catastrophe and extreme weather, then fossil fuels need to stay in the ground.
rigor.explanation: A bare appeal to authority ("the science is crystal clear") carrying the whole weight, plus a gap between the general premise about global fossil fuel use and the specific conclusion about this bill's coalmining consent pathway; no step is offered connecting the consenting change to the climate outcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Of those six, five of them are amendments to regulations. There is no need for primary legislation to make these changes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that of the six main changes the Minister identified in the Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Bill, five are amendments to regulations (national policy statements / national environmental standards) rather than to primary legislation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Bill as introduced (May 2024), its explanatory note and departmental disclosure statement: true if five of the six main changes described operate on regulations/national direction instruments and only one requires amendment of the Act itself; false if two or more of the six require primary-legislative amendment.

veracity.statement: In terms of fast-track, that is totally wrong, because, of course, the fast-track bill that we have before us at the Environment Committee has nothing about the environment in its purpose.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the purpose provision of the Fast-track Approvals Bill (then before the Environment Committee) contains no reference to the environment, being confined to facilitating development.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Clause 3 (purpose) of the Fast-track Approvals Bill as introduced in March 2024: true if the purpose clause refers only to facilitating the delivery of infrastructure and development projects with significant regional or national benefits and makes no reference to environmental protection; false if the purpose clause includes an environmental object.

veracity.statement: I note that the Minister for the Environment was not even involved in the press release about these changes, which is mind blowing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister for the Environment was not a party to (not named or quoted in) the Government press release announcing these RMA/freshwater changes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Beehive.govt.nz press release announcing the Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Bill / the associated changes (May 2024): true if the Minister for the Environment is not listed as an issuing Minister and is not quoted; false if she is named as an issuing Minister or quoted in it.

veracity.statement: We see in the documents supplied with the bill that the officials have said we don’t even know if this is a problem.
veracity.explanation: Relays official advice accompanying the bill as saying it is not known whether the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy is in fact obstructing consents — i.e. that the problem the amendment addresses is unevidenced.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The supplementary analysis report / regulatory impact material published with the Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Bill on the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy and consenting: true if officials record that the extent of the problem is unquantified or unknown; false if officials quantify a demonstrated consenting problem.

veracity.statement: There was official advice that said there was no time for consultation, none with iwi Māori, no assessment of the Treaty impacts, including on the Crown’s Treaty settlements or commitments.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the official advice on the coalmining consenting provisions of the bill records that there was no time for consultation, no consultation with iwi Māori, and no assessment of Treaty impacts including on Treaty settlements.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The supplementary analysis report published with the Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Bill covering the coalmining consenting pathway: true if it states consultation was not undertaken for want of time, that iwi Māori were not consulted, and that Treaty impacts were not assessed; false if it records consultation with iwi Māori or a Treaty impact assessment.

veracity.statement: Because when these changes were first announced, 50 of Aotearoa’s top freshwater experts and leaders were so concerned about it that they actually organised and wrote a letter to the Prime Minister and Ministers, clearly and concisely stating their concerns.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 50 leading New Zealand freshwater scientists and leaders signed and sent an open letter to the Prime Minister and Ministers opposing the announced freshwater changes, after they were announced.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Media reporting and the text of the open letter to the Prime Minister on freshwater policy in early 2024: true if such a letter exists with approximately 50 freshwater scientist/leader signatories; false if no such letter exists or the signatory count is materially different.

specificity.statement: It is, first, the quality of the water body that comes first. Second comes the ability for humans to use that water—so things like drinking water; that’s important. Third is the consumptive use—that’s the ability to make money from the water.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the actual three-tier mechanism of the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy in order, with what each tier covers. Concrete and checkable against the national policy statement, rather than a general appeal to freshwater protection.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There was official advice that said there was no time for consultation, none with iwi Māori, no assessment of the Treaty impacts, including on the Crown’s Treaty settlements or commitments.
specificity.explanation: Names the source (official advice on the bill), and three distinct, checkable omissions — no consultation time, no iwi Māori consultation, no Treaty impact assessment — rather than a general complaint about process.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, before I do, we’ve heard a bit about how this is going to be the end of nature in New Zealand from the other side, despite these people previously protesting and getting all aggrieved about being accused of being at war with farming, yet these words clearly demonstrate they’re still at war with farming.
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of the Opposition's attitude and past grievances; no policy, mechanism, figure or outcome is named. Once the party framing is removed nothing about the bill remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: All the current and soon-to-be previous regime did was add cost by forcing a regulatory burden on councils and farmers.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the regulatory regime being replaced and its claimed effect (compliance cost on councils and farmers), not about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is the fact that the Environment Committee stuffed it up so badly the first time around because there weren’t enough farmers or people that understood the implications of the things they were signing off that we’re in this place now.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine process point about which select committee should scrutinise the bill, but the weight of the sentence is blame directed at the previous committee rather than the substance of the legislation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It was a vague, catch-all term that could have meant anything. It could have shut down any farming operation for any reason.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific provision of the legislation before the House — the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy — rather than the other party. Weak reasoning, but squarely on the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Since 2003, 25,000 kilometres of riparian margins have been fenced off.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 25,000 km of riparian margin has been fenced in New Zealand since 2003 (clarified in the following sentence as dairy-sector fencing).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DairyNZ / Ministry for the Environment reporting on kilometres of dairy waterway/riparian fencing since 2003; true if the reported cumulative figure is about 25,000 km, false if materially lower or if no such measured figure exists.

veracity.statement: “The end of [the] war on farming” is how Federated Farmers have responded to this piece of legislation getting introduced to the House.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Federated Farmers publicly characterised this bill's introduction as the end of the war on farming.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Federated Farmers media releases/statements from around late May 2024 responding to the Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Bill; true if they used that phrase or a direct equivalent, false if no such statement exists.

veracity.statement: There are 290 catchment groups now in this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a count of 290 catchment groups operating in New Zealand as at May 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Aotearoa New Zealand Catchment Communities / NZ Landcare Trust published counts of catchment groups for 2024; true if approximately 290, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, Simon Upton, has just come out with a report on this, and he has said that the catchment-level solution is the only way forward here, that regulations that work within farm boundaries, catchments, and ecological systems do not.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim about what a recent Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment report concluded — specifically that catchment-level management is the only workable approach and farm-boundary regulation is not.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The PCE report published around May 2024 on freshwater/land management; true if it concludes that catchment-scale management is the necessary approach and criticises farm-boundary-based regulation, false if no such report exists in that period or if its conclusions differ materially from the characterisation.

veracity.statement: We have fly-overs in Otago and in many parts of the country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that aerial monitoring of farm practice (notably intensive winter grazing) is carried out in Otago and other regions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Otago Regional Council and other regional councils' published compliance-monitoring programmes for intensive winter grazing; true if aerial surveillance flights are documented, false if no such programme exists.

veracity.statement: There are hundreds of thousands of hectares of native vegetation, particularly on our sheep and beef land, much of it in QEII Trust, much of it preserved for perpetuity.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that hundreds of thousands of hectares of native vegetation sit on privately owned farmland, much of it under QEII National Trust covenant in perpetuity.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: QEII National Trust reported covenanted area and Beef + Lamb New Zealand estimates of native vegetation on sheep and beef farms; true if the covenanted/native area on such land is at least in the hundreds of thousands of hectares, false if materially lower.

rigor.statement: If you added that all in, I am sure you would probably double that number.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that unmeasured sheep and beef fencing would double the dairy figure rests on nothing but the speaker's own impression — an appeal to personal anecdote with no data connecting premise to conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Think of all the farms you see on Country Calendar. These are the sort of farms that would be put out of business by having to do all this.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote and televised imagery: an evocative image of a farm type is offered in place of any costing or evidence linking the fencing requirement to business failure.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The previous stock exclusions, low-slope map, and its various evolutions have proven once again that one-size-fits-all from Wellington isn’t the solution.
rigor.explanation: A sweeping general conclusion about centralised regulation is drawn from a single instrument, with the intermediate step — that the low-slope map failed because it was uniform rather than for other reasons — asserted rather than shown. Hasty generalisation, though a real inference about a real policy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is the fact that the Environment Committee stuffed it up so badly the first time around because there weren’t enough farmers or people that understood the implications of the things they were signing off that we’re in this place now.
rigor.explanation: Causal claim that the committee's occupational composition produced the defective legislation; the link is asserted with no evidence about the committee's membership or its deliberations, and it assumes the conclusion (that the law was badly made) as its own proof.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It was a vague, catch-all term that could have meant anything. It could have shut down any farming operation for any reason.
rigor.explanation: Slippery slope: from the premise that Te Mana o te Wai is broadly worded, the conclusion leaps to shutting down any farm for any reason, with nothing offered about how the provision operates or has been applied.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That wasn’t an attack on property rights. We are a property-rights Government across this side of the House.
rigor.explanation: Circular: the denial that the SNA work attacked property rights is supported only by the Government's self-description as pro-property-rights, which presupposes the very point at issue.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Going forward, we need better definitions of what “significant” is and we also need a much better carrot-type approach to improving biodiversity on private land as opposed to the Opposition’s favoured “go to stick” method.
specificity.explanation: Names a direction — a revised definition of 'significant' and incentive-based biodiversity support — but supplies no definition, no instrument, no funding and no timeframe. Nobody could check or act on it as stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government is committed to ensuring we have a fit for purpose system that doesn’t create duplication of paperwork and that provides farmers with good knowledge and plans on how they can make a difference in their catchments.
specificity.explanation: A statement of intent built from generic virtues — 'fit for purpose', 'no duplication', 'good knowledge and plans' — with no mechanism, cost or date attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, farmers: we are freeing them from the tyranny of one-size-fits-all regulation being imposed on them by Wellington, and we are fulfilling those promises of getting Wellington out of farmers.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-level framing: no regulation is named, no provision cited, no promise identified, nothing quantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They thought that shiny, painted people sitting in front of computer screens looking at Google Maps of landscapes and slopes and things like that, they thought that those people had a better understanding of land, of catchment areas, of resource, of land slopes and all those sorts of things than the farmers and people who worked that land.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the previous regime's national freshwater rules are recast as a claim that desk-bound officials understand individual paddocks better than farmers do, and the caricature is then treated as the position being refuted. Nothing is offered to show anyone actually held that view.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because without a thriving, growing economy, none of that other good stuff that we need for our environment can occur.
rigor.explanation: Offered as the reason environmental protection depends on growth, but it is an unsupported absolute ('none of that other good stuff can occur') presented as if it settled the question. No evidence or mechanism connects growth to environmental outcomes.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is why we are able to sell our product to the world: because of our clean, green image.
rigor.explanation: Single-cause reasoning: export success is attributed wholly to the clean, green image, with no evidence offered and no consideration of price, trade access, quality or supply as alternative explanations.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: However, whether it be in agriculture, whether it be in the corporate world, there are always going to be those laggards who let everybody else down who is doing the right thing. The purpose behind the regulations that were introduced by the previous Government was to help to pull those laggards into line because they were dragging the rest of the sector down.
rigor.explanation: A coherent inference: if a minority underperforms and imposes costs on the rest, a rule aimed at that minority follows. The gap is that nothing is offered to show the regulations were targeted at laggards rather than applying uniformly.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Let’s be clear: we didn’t need regulation or law for our farmers to want to do this.
rigor.explanation: Draws a general conclusion from listed examples (fencing, covenants, catchment groups) while ignoring that some of those results were driven by industry accords or regional rules — the examples do not establish that the outcomes were independent of regulation.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They thought that shiny, painted people sitting in front of computer screens looking at Google Maps of landscapes and slopes and things like that, they thought that those people had a better understanding of land, of catchment areas, of resource, of land slopes and all those sorts of things than the farmers and people who worked that land.
civility.explanation: Not a named target, but 'shiny, painted people sitting in front of computer screens looking at Google Maps' is mockery of the people involved rather than engagement with the rule they wrote — sneering, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: He has said, without any hesitation in his very good report, that actually a catchment-by-catchment approach is entirely the right approach.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment's report, released the week before 28 May 2024, endorses without qualification a catchment-by-catchment approach to land and resource management.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The PCE report by Simon Upton released in May 2024; true if it recommends or endorses managing land use at catchment scale, false if it recommends a national/uniform approach, or endorses catchment management only with substantial qualifications that contradict 'without any hesitation'.

veracity.statement: One of the things that I did notice in the regulatory impact statement is that they felt that the engagement process has been inadequate for reasons including insufficient information, lack of time, and that decisions appeared to have already been taken, which was in reference to a letter from the Minister Responsible for RMA Reform to support this view.
veracity.explanation: Relays what the regulatory impact statement for this freshwater bill records about engagement: that it was inadequate for insufficient information and lack of time, and that decisions appeared already taken, referencing a letter from the Minister Responsible for RMA Reform.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.subject_name: officials' regulatory impact statement for the bill
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published regulatory impact statement accompanying the Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Bill 2024; true if it records those engagement concerns in substantially those terms, false if it does not contain such an assessment or characterises engagement as adequate.

veracity.statement: The reality is we need you now more than ever, given the near $100 billion debt that we’ve been left with by those same members over there.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Labour-led Government left a debt of nearly $100 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury fiscal data (Budget 2024 / Crown financial statements); true if either the net core Crown debt level at the 2023 change of government or the increase in it across the 2017–2023 term is close to $100 billion, false if the relevant figure is materially different (e.g. under ~$80b or well over ~$120b) on both readings.

veracity.statement: The 25,000 kilometres of waterways already fenced off—almost 100 percent of all waterways on dairy farms are fenced off.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two figures: roughly 25,000 km of waterways fenced on farms, and that close to 100 percent of waterways on dairy farms are fenced.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DairyNZ / Ministry for the Environment reporting on stock exclusion under the Sustainable Dairying Water Accord and subsequent monitoring; true if fenced length is about 25,000 km and the share of dairy waterways excluded from stock is around 95–100%, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: The 5,000th QEII covenant was registered in the Wairarapa very recently.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Queen Elizabeth II National Trust's 5,000th registered covenant was in the Wairarapa and occurred shortly before May 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: QEII National Trust announcements and annual reports; true if the trust recorded its 5,000th registered covenant in the Wairarapa within roughly the year before 28 May 2024, false if the milestone was elsewhere, at a different count, or much earlier.

specificity.statement: We think that actually there is a potential for us as a smart nation with clever people who have a regard and concern for our natural environment, to also be able to protect, maintain, and enhance that natural environment while at the same time encouraging a development, encouraging proper and appropriate land use that encourages the wealth and prosperity of our entire nation to give us the economic performance and strength that we need to provide for that maintenance, protection, and enhancement of our natural environment.
specificity.explanation: A long string of generic aspirations — 'smart nation', 'clever people', 'proper and appropriate land use' — with no mechanism, figure, threshold or timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The second step is of course to introduce the fast-track consenting system so that we can get things done in New Zealand, and that is currently before my select committee and we’re working our way through that.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific measure (the fast-track consenting regime), its place in a stated three-phase sequence, and its current stage at select committee — but gives no timeframe, thresholds or content of the regime.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One of the things that I did notice in the regulatory impact statement is that they felt that the engagement process has been inadequate for reasons including insufficient information, lack of time, and that decisions appeared to have already been taken, which was in reference to a letter from the Minister Responsible for RMA Reform to support this view.
specificity.explanation: Cites a named document, three enumerated reasons, and the specific correspondence relied on — enough for someone else to go and look it up.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The 25,000 kilometres of waterways already fenced off—almost 100 percent of all waterways on dairy farms are fenced off.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete, sourceable quantities — a kilometre total and a percentage of dairy waterways — that someone could check directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We trust our farmers. We back our farmers. We can grow our economy. We can get Wellington out of farming.
