specificity.explanation: Carries a figure (62,000 potholes), named instruments (30-year pipeline, 10-year city and regional deals, a national infrastructure agency) but no funding amounts or dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he stand by his statement, “I want all New Zealanders to be able to flourish in this country. I want everybody to be able to realise their potential”, and, if so, does he think that it is fair that the average New Zealander pays double the effective tax rate of the wealthiest 311 families in this country?
specificity.explanation: Names a precise comparison (double the effective tax rate) and a precisely defined group (the wealthiest 311 families), both checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, what I’d say to that member is that’s why we come to politics. We want every New Zealand child to have a great future; we want them to be able to realise their potential and realise their version of the Kiwi Dream, whatever that may be.
specificity.explanation: Pure aspiration — no figure, mechanism, policy or timeframe, and nothing anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, that’s why we’ve got to make sure we rebuild the economy: so that we can actually afford the public services so that we can deal with issues of inequality across New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: A direction of travel ('rebuild the economy' to fund public services) with no named measure, amount or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How tough was the choice to make changes to benefit indexation that his official advice says will put 13,000 more New Zealand children in poverty?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific policy change (benefit indexation), the source (official advice) and a precise quantified effect (13,000 more children).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How tough was the choice to roll back smoke-free protections, which will result, ultimately, in more New Zealanders dying from smoking than otherwise would have, in order to generate half a billion dollars more in Government revenue?
specificity.explanation: Names the policy repeal and a revenue figure (half a billion dollars), though the health effect is left unquantified and undated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Tomorrow at 2 p.m., I will be announcing the Budget itself. Alongside my Budget speech, there are a number of documents that provide information on the Budget, ranging from high-level summaries to very detailed, line-by-line descriptions of changes to appropriations. These include the Estimates documents, the summary of initiatives, Treasury’s Budget Economic and Fiscal Update, the Fiscal Strategy Report, the child poverty report, and the Budget At a Glance pamphlet. Compared to recent years, there will be less verbiage, fewer pretty pictures, and a lot more substance.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise time and enumerates each Budget document by name; only the closing comparison is unquantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Recent Budgets have tended to be long lists of spending increases. Tomorrow’s Budget will include new targeted discretionary spending, but it will also contain lots of savings, lots of reprioritisation, and—spoiler alert—it will contain tax relief.
specificity.explanation: Names the categories the Budget will contain (savings, reprioritisation, tax relief) but attaches no amounts, thresholds or dates to any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does she accept advice from the Ministry of Social Development that “Increases in public housing supply need to be at a very large scale to result in significant movement of child poverty rates.”, and, if so, can we expect to see a large increase in the Kāinga Ora build programme?
specificity.explanation: Quotes named departmental advice and names the specific programme at issue (Kāinga Ora build programme), but 'large increase' is left unquantified and undated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will her Budget be a success if families do not get the $250 per fortnight as outlined in the fiscal plan and if it causes inflation to stay higher for longer?
specificity.explanation: Pins the question to a precise promised figure ($250 per fortnight) from a named document (the fiscal plan) plus a named macroeconomic consequence.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Low-income workers will be far, far better off with this Government’s economic management than they were under six years of Labour’s big-spending, big-inflation ways.
specificity.explanation: 'Far, far better off' carries no amount, threshold or date; the only concrete element is the label attached to the previous government.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We are determined to deliver on the Smokefree 2025 goals. What’s been impressive is, under the legislation that we’ve put back in place, daily smoking rates have fallen from 8.6 percent to 6.8 percent. We’re well on our way to 5 percent—that’s our goal.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc attribution: the fall in smoking rates is credited to legislation the government reinstated, but the measured decline necessarily precedes that legislation taking effect. The conclusion does not follow from the data offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s important that we increase the supply of rental property and that renters don’t end up being slugged with more costs. That’s why we’re actually delivering interest deductibility, revisiting the brightline test, and balancing the laws between landlords and tenants: because we care about renters. And I’d hope that member would do the same.
rigor.explanation: Names real mechanisms but the link from restoring interest deductibility to lower rents is asserted, not shown, and the load-bearing reason offered is an appeal to motive ('because we care about renters').
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Of course, that depends on how that member defines “conservation land”, because stewardship land most certainly is not conservation land.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that stewardship land falls outside the category of conservation land.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Conservation Act 1987 definitions (s2 'conservation area', s25 stewardship area) and DOC's published classification of the public conservation estate; true if stewardship land is legally distinct from and outside 'conservation land', false if stewardship areas are held and administered as conservation areas under the Act.

veracity.statement: The second thing is that we need to respect the property rights of investors who already have enterprises on conservation land, including the conservation department’s allocation to Rua Minerals for a new permit in the Coromandel bush last week.
veracity.explanation: Asserts DOC granted/allocated a new permit to Rua Minerals for Coromandel conservation land in the week before 29 May 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DOC access-arrangement records and NZ Petroleum & Minerals permit register for May 2024; true if a permit or access arrangement involving Rua Minerals in the Coromandel was granted in the week to 29 May 2024, false if no such grant exists in that period.

veracity.statement: Does the Minister accept that the International Energy Agency’s World Energy Outlook from 2021 states that the pathway for less than 1.5 degrees of warming needs “no new oil and gas fields approved for development” and “no new coal mines or mines extensions”, and, if not, why not?
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim about what the IEA's 2021 World Energy Outlook says regarding the 1.5 degree pathway.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the IEA World Energy Outlook 2021 (and its 1.5C/net-zero pathway section); true if it states that the pathway requires no new oil and gas fields approved for development and no new coal mines or mine extensions, false if that wording appears only in a different IEA publication or not at all.

veracity.statement: Stuff reported that with 42 percent of gang members linked to reported crimes as a suspect or offender and 18 of percent of serious crimes committed by gang members, it’s clear New Zealand has a gang problem.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two statistics about gang members' share of reported crime and of serious crime, attributed to a Stuff report.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Stuff article referenced and the underlying NZ Police gang-list/crime data; true if the reported figures are 42% of gang members linked to reported crime as suspect or offender and ~18% of serious crime committed by gang members, false if the source gives materially different figures.

veracity.statement: Police have also conducted 1,668 search warrants; 926 warrantless searches; entered 80,102 charges, warnings, and infringement notices; and seized 661 firearms.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific police activity counts for the roughly six months since the change of government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police operational reporting / OIA release covering the period referenced (approximately Dec 2023 – May 2024); true if the counts of search warrants, warrantless searches, charges/warnings/infringements and firearms seized match within rounding, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: I don’t have that exact number, but I can assure the member of this—that under the previous Government we saw an over 50 percent increase in gang members in this country. We saw a 33 percent increase in violent crime in this country, and this Government has come in, and we’ve been very clear about the fact that we are not going to tolerate that. And that is why you’re seeing the police being so effective over the last six months in starting to suppress gang members in this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two quantified trends over the previous government's term: gang membership up more than 50 percent and violent crime up 33 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police National Gang List figures for 2017 and 2023, and the NZ Crime and Victims Survey / Police victimisation data for violent offences over the same period; true if gang list membership rose by more than 50% and violent crime by about 33%, false if either series shows a materially different change.

veracity.statement: What does she say in response to the submission on the Fast-track Approvals Bill by the Auditor-General that “Ministers of course have a broad discretion to make decisions, however that power comes, in my view, with an obligation to be transparent to the public about how and why they made those decisions, particularly where those decisions differ from official advice.”?
veracity.explanation: Relays a quotation attributed to the Auditor-General's submission on the Fast-track Approvals Bill.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Auditor-General's written submission to the Environment Committee on the Fast-track Approvals Bill (2024); true if it contains the quoted wording about ministerial discretion and transparency, false if the wording does not appear or is from a different submitter.

veracity.statement: What I can tell the member is that I, as Minister, am responsible for the procurement framework—which the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) is actually responsible for. But in terms of the procurement for the mental health issue that he is actually talking about, it is part of our Budget 2024, where we commit to the mental health services for our young people. That is not a lesson or a lecture that I am prepared to take from that member or that party, who actually wasted $1.9 billion of taxpayer money for mental health and actually did not deliver very much.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous government spent $1.9 billion on mental health and did not deliver much from it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2019 mental health and addiction package documents (Treasury/Vote Health) plus Ministry of Health and Auditor-General reporting on delivery; true if the package was $1.9b and independent reporting found substantial under-delivery, false if the figure is materially different or the reporting shows the funded services were largely delivered.

specificity.statement: The second thing is that we need to respect the property rights of investors who already have enterprises on conservation land, including the conservation department’s allocation to Rua Minerals for a new permit in the Coromandel bush last week.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific company, a specific decision (a new permit), the granting agency, a location and a timeframe — all checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does the Minister accept that the International Energy Agency’s World Energy Outlook from 2021 states that the pathway for less than 1.5 degrees of warming needs “no new oil and gas fields approved for development” and “no new coal mines or mines extensions”, and, if not, why not?
specificity.explanation: Names the issuing body, the publication, the year and quotes the wording verbatim — fully checkable against a document.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Stuff reported that with 42 percent of gang members linked to reported crimes as a suspect or offender and 18 of percent of serious crimes committed by gang members, it’s clear New Zealand has a gang problem.
specificity.explanation: Two precise percentages with a named source and a defined measure (gang members as suspects/offenders in reported crime).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Police have also conducted 1,668 search warrants; 926 warrantless searches; entered 80,102 charges, warnings, and infringement notices; and seized 661 firearms.

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How many individuals are recorded as gang members on the National Gang List as of February 2024, and does this represent an increase of 176 individuals since he took office?
specificity.explanation: Names the exact register, an exact date and an exact number — a precise, answerable question.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What does she say in response to the submission on the Fast-track Approvals Bill by the Auditor-General that “Ministers of course have a broad discretion to make decisions, however that power comes, in my view, with an obligation to be transparent to the public about how and why they made those decisions, particularly where those decisions differ from official advice.”?
specificity.explanation: Names the bill and the submitter and quotes the submission verbatim, making the basis of the question fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I am aware of those aspirations. They will be taken into account and given appropriate importance as we secure energy resilience in New Zealand, and as the member and the person sitting next to her ride their bikes, know that coal is keeping the lights on.
civility.explanation: Mocks the questioner and a named colleague personally ("ride their bikes") rather than engaging the IEA pathway put to him; sneering rather than a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That is a ridiculous statement. This is a piece of wardrobe that creates drive-by shootings and gang conflicts, and markets to and targets young men for gang recruitment, and to earn the right to wear one, you have to show that you have the propensity to commit violent crime. There is a trail of tears and victims sitting behind every one of those gang patches. This Government is banning that part of the wardrobe that is clearly designed to intimidate and inflicts misery and violence on communities.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the proposition ("that is a ridiculous statement") rather than the person, and the rest engages the patch ban itself; robust but not personal.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What I can tell the member is that I, as Minister, am responsible for the procurement framework—which the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) is actually responsible for. But in terms of the procurement for the mental health issue that he is actually talking about, it is part of our Budget 2024, where we commit to the mental health services for our young people. That is not a lesson or a lecture that I am prepared to take from that member or that party, who actually wasted $1.9 billion of taxpayer money for mental health and actually did not deliver very much.
civility.explanation: Ends by refusing to take "a lesson or a lecture" from the questioner and imputing waste to him and his party — dismissive of the member personally rather than only of the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I am aware of those aspirations. They will be taken into account and given appropriate importance as we secure energy resilience in New Zealand, and as the member and the person sitting next to her ride their bikes, know that coal is keeping the lights on.

This is a piece of wardrobe that creates drive-by shootings and gang conflicts, and markets to and targets young men for gang recruitment, and to earn the right to wear one, you have to show that you have the propensity to commit violent crime. We saw a 33 percent increase in violent crime in this country, and this Government has come in, and we’ve been very clear about the fact that we are not going to tolerate that. focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What I can tell the member is that I, as Minister, am responsible for the procurement framework—which the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) is actually responsible for. But in terms of the procurement for the mental health issue that he is actually talking about, it is part of our Budget 2024, where we commit to the mental health services for our young people. rigor.statement: Absolutely not. New Zealand has a world-class police force, and I have full confidence that the men and women that go to work every day to keep Kiwis safe without fear or favour have the skills, training, capability, and, very soon, the tools to target, disrupt, and suppress the gangs and the misery that they cause in our communities.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that gangs will not ignore police rests entirely on the speaker's own expressed confidence and a laudatory characterisation of the force — a bare appeal to assertion/authority, with no evidence offered connecting the new powers to gang compliance.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is a ridiculous statement. This is a piece of wardrobe that creates drive-by shootings and gang conflicts, and markets to and targets young men for gang recruitment, and to earn the right to wear one, you have to show that you have the propensity to commit violent crime. There is a trail of tears and victims sitting behind every one of those gang patches. This Government is banning that part of the wardrobe that is clearly designed to intimidate and inflicts misery and violence on communities.
rigor.explanation: Attributes direct causation to an item of clothing ("a piece of wardrobe that creates drive-by shootings") and supports the ban with emotive imagery ("a trail of tears"); the causal step from patch to shooting is asserted rather than shown, and the appeal to emotion carries the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It identified that of the 4 percent of New Zealanders who are highly victimised, Māori are disproportionately represented, comprising 30 percent of that group. This is twice the rate of the rest of the population.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Ministry of Justice five-year NZCVS analysis found 4 percent of New Zealanders are highly victimised and that Māori make up 30 percent of that group, twice their share of the wider population.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Justice five-year analysis of the New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey (released May 2024); true if it reports ~4% highly victimised and Māori at ~30% of that group at roughly double the rest-of-population rate, false if the figures materially differ.

veracity.statement: The analysis shows that a small group of New Zealanders are experiencing the most crime: 137,000 people are considered to be highly victimised every year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the NZCVS five-year analysis puts the number of highly victimised New Zealanders (four or more offences in 12 months) at 137,000 a year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Justice NZCVS five-year analysis; true if it states approximately 137,000 highly victimised people annually, false if the published figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: We are prioritising the 35,000 extra Māori who ended up on a benefit over the last six years, and the 60 percent of Māori tamariki who didn’t make it to school as a result of the Labour education approach, and also the 1,700 Māori households who are currently living in emergency housing up and down the country in places like Fenton Steet, Rotorua, and Ulster Steet, Hamilton West, and making sure that we address the needs of Māori and all New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Three factual assertions: 35,000 additional Māori on a benefit over six years; 60 percent of Māori children not attending school; 1,700 Māori households in emergency housing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit statistics for Māori main-benefit recipients 2017–2023 (true if the increase is ~35,000); Ministry of Education regular attendance data for Māori students (true if ~60% are not regularly attending); HUD emergency housing special needs grant data by ethnicity (true if ~1,700 Māori households). False if any figure is materially off.

veracity.statement: I’m very proud to be part of a party that started the historic Treaty settlements process over 30 years ago. I stand with my esteemed colleague the Hon Paul Goldsmith, who has continued in the vein of Christopher Finlayson and Doug Graham.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that his party (National) initiated the Treaty settlements process more than 30 years ago.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Historical record of Treaty settlement legislation and the Waitangi Tribunal's jurisdiction — true if the modern settlement process (e.g. the 1992 fisheries settlement, 1995 Waikato-Tainui settlement, Office of Treaty Settlements) was begun under a National government; false if the initiating steps (e.g. the Treaty of Waitangi Amendment Act 1985 extending claims back to 1840) are properly credited to another party.

veracity.statement: This strategy focused on climate minerals, otherwise known as green minerals, and as the International Energy Agency has articulated, the world, in order to reach net zero by 2050, will need six times more minerals for low-emissions technology.
veracity.explanation: Relays an IEA finding that reaching net zero by 2050 requires six times more minerals for low-emissions technology.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: IEA publications on critical minerals (e.g. 'The Role of Critical Minerals in Clean Energy Transitions', Net Zero by 2050 scenarios); true if the IEA states a roughly sixfold increase in mineral demand under a net-zero pathway, false if the IEA's stated multiple is materially different.

specificity.statement: It identified that of the 4 percent of New Zealanders who are highly victimised, Māori are disproportionately represented, comprising 30 percent of that group. This is twice the rate of the rest of the population.
specificity.explanation: Named source, two percentages and an explicit comparison ratio — directly checkable against the published analysis.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve already introduced legislation to give police extra tools to deal with gangs, we’ve taken the first steps to ensure that prisoners on remand can get rehabilitation programmes, and we’re progressing well with strengthening the sentencing regime in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Three named workstreams (gang legislation, remand rehabilitation, sentencing reform) but no bill names, numbers, funding or timeframes; 'progressing well' carries no checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are prioritising the 35,000 extra Māori who ended up on a benefit over the last six years, and the 60 percent of Māori tamariki who didn’t make it to school as a result of the Labour education approach, and also the 1,700 Māori households who are currently living in emergency housing up and down the country in places like Fenton Steet, Rotorua, and Ulster Steet, Hamilton West, and making sure that we address the needs of Māori and all New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Three separate figures, a time span, and named streets and towns for the emergency housing claim — all checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Talofa lava. One more sleep to go, heigh-ho-hippy-ho, and we hope to see tax relief for many Māori and all New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Asked about cuts to Māori initiatives, offers only an undefined hope of 'tax relief' — no amount, no threshold, no mechanism, no named programme.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will he commit to no new coal mines on public conservation land; if not, why not?
specificity.explanation: A precisely bounded ask — a named activity (new coal mines) on a named land category (public conservation land) — such that any answer could be checked against subsequent consenting decisions.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Do Māori stand to gain from a Budget that delivers responsible economic management?
specificity.explanation: No figure, measure, Budget line or timeframe; 'responsible economic management' is a slogan, and the question commits to nothing that could be checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s why Māori are more likely to benefit from the measures of our Government to reduce crime.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion is drawn straight from victimisation statistics, but it requires an unstated and unsupported premise — that the Government's crime measures actually reduce the victimisation of this group. Higher exposure to crime does not by itself entail benefit from a given policy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Firstly, we won’t continue the falsehood of importing minerals from countries that have abysmal environmental standards, abysmal child work safety practices—but, no, sir, this vision, which I’ve articulated on behalf of the Government, will boost not only regional productivity, resilience, and although it may be modest in size, in order to save the climate, we must mine our way to the future.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy plus a leap: the premise that some overseas suppliers have poor environmental and labour standards does not establish that domestic mining is the alternative, and 'in order to save the climate, we must mine our way to the future' asserts a necessity that nothing offered here supports.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Before I resume my seat, my acknowledgment to our Matua Willie Jackson for returning from the Oxford debate successfully. I understand your colleagues have been very happy in your absence.
civility.explanation: Opens with a genuine acknowledgment, then turns it into a jibe at a named member — the suggestion that his own colleagues preferred him away is mockery aimed at the person rather than at any argument, though it is light-handed rather than contemptuous.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, Mr Speaker, I wanted to—with respect—get a position from the Minister in terms of what basically sums up the Government’s Māori and Treaty policy, and that’s why I’m giving the examples of David Seymour, the Hon Winston Peters, and the last person I want to give as an example was the Prime Minister, whose view on Māori policy and Treaty policy is that Māori can only protest on the weekend, when it is convenient to him.
civility.explanation: Characterises the Prime Minister's position as wanting protest only 'when it is convenient to him' — an imputation of self-serving motive to a named individual, short of a direct insult but no longer purely about the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can he stand by his statement when all that Māori see are cuts to Māori initiatives and the continued undermining of the Treaty of Waitangi?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny directed at government policy rather than at the other party's character, but no specific cut, programme or figure is named — the policy content stays at the level of general direction.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, Mr Speaker, I wanted to—with respect—get a position from the Minister in terms of what basically sums up the Government’s Māori and Treaty policy, and that’s why I’m giving the examples of David Seymour, the Hon Winston Peters, and the last person I want to give as an example was the Prime Minister, whose view on Māori policy and Treaty policy is that Māori can only protest on the weekend, when it is convenient to him.
focus.explanation: Frames a policy question entirely through the personalities of three coalition figures rather than through any measure, mechanism or outcome; the only substantive content is the characterisation of what each individual is like on the Treaty.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m very proud to be part of a party that started the historic Treaty settlements process over 30 years ago. I stand with my esteemed colleague the Hon Paul Goldsmith, who has continued in the vein of Christopher Finlayson and Doug Graham.
focus.explanation: Asked what sums up the Government's Treaty policy, the answer offers party pride and a lineage of past ministers; it names a real policy (Treaty settlements) but the weight is party credit rather than the current position asked about.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can the Minister confirm that this debate was settled by Sir Apirana Ngata in a seminal document reflecting his understanding a lot closer to the signatories of the Treaty of Waitangi, and the Treaty of Waitangi is an indivisible, bilingual, bicultural document incapable of being dismembered to suit the fads of the minor party of Parliament?
focus.explanation: A genuine constitutional point about the Treaty's interpretation and Ngata's writing, but it is steered into a swipe at a coalition partner's 'fads', so a real substantive question is carried inside inter-party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I shared that our strategy will actually double the mineral exports value and, with the right direction and settings, jobs will grow regional resilience and we’ll no longer rely on the Congo for our minerals.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the minerals strategy will double the value of New Zealand's mineral exports, on the 2035 horizon named in the question.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / MBIE mineral export value series; true if the annual value of New Zealand mineral exports in 2035 is at least double the 2023/24 baseline (approximately $1.1 billion), false if it falls short.

veracity.statement: The first of those is $250—$250 a fortnight is what Nicola Willis and Christopher Luxon promised the average New Zealand family in tax cuts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that National's pre-Budget/election tax policy promised the average New Zealand family $250 a fortnight.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's published tax plan (2023 'Back Pocket Boost') and Willis/Luxon statements: true if the $250/fortnight figure was presented as the gain for an average family; false if $250 was presented only as a maximum for a specific household type (e.g. a family with young children receiving FamilyBoost/in-work credits) rather than the average family.

veracity.statement: The second number they should keep in mind is $2.9 billion—$2.9 billion is the cost of the tax breaks that the Government has chosen to prioritise for landlords.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the fiscal cost of the Government's restoration of interest deductibility for residential rental property is $2.9 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD costings for the restoration of interest deductibility as published in Budget 2024 or the March 2024 taxation bill's regulatory/fiscal impact material: true if the cost is about $2.9b over the forecast period, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: What are the reasons that inflation is staying higher for longer? They are: (1) increased rents; (2) increased insurance; (3) increased rates.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, attributing it to the Reserve Bank that week, that rents, insurance and council rates are the drivers of persistently high inflation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ May 2024 Monetary Policy Statement and Stats NZ CPI non-tradables breakdown: true if rents, insurance and local authority rates are identified there as leading contributors to persistent inflation; false if the RBNZ attributes persistence chiefly to other components.

veracity.statement: We’ve seen the results of that before in the form of Mycoplasma bovis, among other things—a disease that cost hundreds of millions of dollars for New Zealand to eradicate.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Mycoplasma bovis eradication programme cost New Zealand hundreds of millions of dollars.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI's published Mycoplasma bovis eradication programme cost figures: true if total programme cost (compensation plus response) is in the hundreds of millions, false if it is tens of millions or less.

veracity.statement: The Waitangi Tribunal has called out this Government. It is a breach of Te Tiriti o Waitangi that you will take out Māori wards.
veracity.explanation: Relays a finding attributed to the Waitangi Tribunal that removing the Māori wards provisions breaches Te Tiriti/Treaty principles.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal's 2024 urgent inquiry report on the Māori wards policy: true if the Tribunal found the policy breaches the principles of the Treaty, false if it made no such finding or declined the inquiry.

veracity.statement: Last week, Far North District Council stood, and they provided a motion of tautoko to Local Government New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Far North District Council passed a motion of support to Local Government New Zealand in the week before 29 May 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Far North District Council meeting minutes for May 2024: true if a motion supporting LGNZ (on Māori wards) was passed, false if no such motion appears in the minutes for that period.

specificity.statement: The second number they should keep in mind is $2.9 billion—$2.9 billion is the cost of the tax breaks that the Government has chosen to prioritise for landlords.
specificity.explanation: A named policy with a precise dollar figure that can be checked against Budget documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, we know that they’re going to be hiking up public transport costs, we know that they’re going to be taking away free prescriptions, we know that they’re going to be making cuts to the disability sector, we know that they are going to be halving the value of the school lunches programme—it’s kind of gone from a free and healthy school lunch programme to a slightly less healthy snack programme in schools as a result of the Government’s changes—and, of course, we know that they are going to rob a whole generation of New Zealanders of the dream of homeownership by doing something that none of them said they were going to do before the election, in cutting the first-home buyer grant scheme.
specificity.explanation: Names five specific programmes and the direction of change, but supplies no figures or dates beyond 'halving'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Let’s look at the laws: Te Aka Whai Ora, smoke-free legislation, te reo Māori, threats on the Māori and Pacific admission scheme and also on the Waitangi Tribunal, 7AA, gang laws, the laws around tenancy and also for our whānau in rental accommodation, fast-track legislation, the removal of accountability for Te Mana o te Wai yesterday in this House, the removal of clauses relating to Te Tiriti in corrections, the funding freeze on marine and coastal area takutai moana claims, the full-scale review of Te Tiriti clauses within our legislation, and, of course, the Treaty principles bill.
specificity.explanation: A long list of named, identifiable measures (Te Aka Whai Ora, section 7AA, Te Mana o te Wai, the Treaty principles bill, fast-track legislation) that a reader could go and check, though no figures, dates or mechanisms are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: New Zealanders will want to see that in the Budget tomorrow, because until the Government addresses those three issues—increased rents, increased insurance, and increased rates—interest rates are going to stay higher for longer.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy, but it leans on an appeal to authority ('The Reserve Bank has been very clear about that') and leaves a gap: nothing offered to show that Budget measures could move rents, insurance premiums and council rates, which are largely outside central government's direct control.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Up and down the country, we’re hearing reports from those working in infrastructure and in the building and construction sector where those sectors have had the bottom fall out since this Government was elected because the Government had decided on coming into office that they’d stop all the school rebuild projects and the school upgrade projects, they’d slow down or stop the hospital rebuild projects, they’d grind the transport infrastructure projects to a halt, and they’d stop investment in water infrastructure, among other things, and the thousands of people working in those sectors have suddenly found that their work has dried up.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning resting on anecdote: the evidence offered is 'reports we're hearing', and the collapse in private construction work is attributed wholly to government project decisions with nothing offered to exclude the interest-rate and private-demand cycle.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The cuts that the Government is making to supposedly back-office services highlight just what a farce the notion of the back-office/front-line distinction is. Cutting people who work on child exploitation is a cut to a front-line service. Cutting people who prevent online scams is a cut to a front-line service.
rigor.explanation: A valid counterexample argument: if roles classified as back-office deliver front-line services, the distinction does not hold. The gap is that a few examples show the line is imprecise, not that the whole distinction is a 'farce' — a modest overreach from example to general conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The tūtae, the human excrement, is a representation of the obliteration and the undermining of rangatiratanga of Pākehā on our people in 1845. And, I say to you, this has not changed. We are watching the recolonisation of Aotearoa New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Argument from historical analogy: an 1845 symbolic act is offered as establishing that present-day policy is 'recolonisation', with nothing supplied to connect the two beyond the assertion that 'this has not changed'.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Well, we know that they’re going to be hiking up public transport costs, we know that they’re going to be taking away free prescriptions, we know that they’re going to be making cuts to the disability sector, we know that they are going to be halving the value of the school lunches programme—it’s kind of gone from a free and healthy school lunch programme to a slightly less healthy snack programme in schools as a result of the Government’s changes—and, of course, we know that they are going to rob a whole generation of New Zealanders of the dream of homeownership by doing something that none of them said they were going to do before the election, in cutting the first-home buyer grant scheme.
divination.explanation: Forecasts, the day before Budget 2024, five specific measures the Budget will contain: higher public transport costs, removal of free prescriptions, disability sector cuts, halving the school lunch programme's value, and abolition of the first-home buyer grant.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents (Vote Health, Vote Education, Vote Transport, Vote Social Development) and associated Government announcements: true if each of the five measures appears; partially/wholly false to the extent a measure (in particular the halving of the Ka Ora Ka Ako school lunch funding) is not in Budget 2024.

divination.statement: The $250 a fortnight that they’ve promised to families—will they get it? Probably not, because $2.9 billion in tax breaks for landlords is a higher priority for them.
divination.explanation: Predicts that the Budget delivered the next day will not give families the promised $250 a fortnight.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 personal income tax package as published by Treasury/IRD: false if an average family's fortnightly gain is about $250 or more; true if the typical/average family gain is materially below $250.

civility.statement: So every time Nicola Willis says, “We’ve had to make tough choices.”, “We can’t fund this.”, or “We’ve cut that.”, keep in mind that that is because they prioritised $2.9 billion in tax cuts for landlords.
civility.explanation: Names the Minister but attacks the fiscal choice, not her character or competence; robust and pointed while staying on the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Who wrote this rubbish?
civility.explanation: A heckle that both dismisses the speech as 'rubbish' and insinuates the member did not write her own words — mockery aimed at the person rather than any argument she made.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Let’s talk about Māori wards, Matua Winston. Let’s talk about it.
civility.explanation: Answers a heckle that called her speech 'rubbish' by inviting the interjector onto the substance of a specific policy, addressing him respectfully and returning no personal jibe.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We’ve had 40 percent inflation since 2010 and that has forced people into higher tax brackets, with a result that for people on the median income their average tax rate has gone from 15 percent to 21 percent, and that takes a lot of money out of the pockets of average-income-earning New Zealanders because of inflation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two quantities: cumulative NZ CPI inflation of about 40 percent between 2010 and 2024, and a rise in the average (not marginal) tax rate faced by a median-income earner from 15 percent to 21 percent over that period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI index, June 2010 quarter to March 2024 quarter: true if the cumulative increase is approximately 40 percent, false if materially different. For the tax claim: Treasury/IRD calculation of the average income tax rate on the median full-time wage in 2010 versus 2024; true if it moved from roughly 15 percent to roughly 21 percent, false if the start or end figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: And what we saw over the last six years was an 80 percent increase in spending.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that core government spending rose by about 80 percent over the six years of the previous government (roughly 2017/18 to 2023/24).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Budget Economic and Fiscal Update / Financial Statements of the Government: core Crown expenses for the 2017/18 year compared with 2023/24; true if the nominal increase is approximately 80 percent, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: So it looked like we’re in deficit, but, actually, we’re in a much worse deficit because things like basic pharmaceutical funding hadn’t been funded into the future, and we had to find that extra money.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Pharmac's baseline pharmaceutical funding was not provided for beyond the immediate forecast years by the previous government, so the incoming government had to find additional money in Budget 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2023 and Budget 2024 Vote Health estimates and Treasury forecast tables for the Pharmac Combined Pharmaceutical Budget: true if the pharmaceutical appropriation was time-limited and lapsed within the forecast period, requiring new funding in Budget 2024; false if baseline pharmaceutical funding was already appropriated across the forecast period.

veracity.statement: That Labour Government came in in 2017 and cancelled the former National Government’s commitment to the Woodend Bypass, and it’s brilliant to be part of a coalition Government that will reinstate that commitment and start construction in its first term.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the government elected in 2017 cancelled a pre-existing National government commitment to build the Woodend Bypass.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Transport Agency project records and the 2018 Government Policy Statement on land transport: true if the Woodend Bypass was a funded/committed project before 2017 and was subsequently removed or deferred indefinitely; false if it was never a committed project or remained in the programme.

veracity.statement: The Auditor-General also said he could not identify any value for money for taxpayers out of that funding announcement by that last Labour Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Auditor-General's 2024 report on mental health funding concluded that value for money from the previous government's $1.9 billion mental health package could not be identified.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Office of the Auditor-General's 2024 report on mental health and addiction funding: true if it states it could not determine or demonstrate value for money from the $1.9 billion package; false if it made no such finding or reached a contrary conclusion.

veracity.statement: Our New Zealand search and rescue delivers thousands of lifesaving rescues every year, directly attributable last year to saving 161 lives.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand search and rescue services performed thousands of rescues in the year to 2023/24 and that 161 lives were directly saved.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Search and Rescue Council / Coastguard NZ and Surf Life Saving NZ annual reports for 2023 or 2023/24: true if the reported number of lives saved is 161 and rescue counts run into the thousands; false if the published figures differ materially.

specificity.statement: We’ve had 40 percent inflation since 2010 and that has forced people into higher tax brackets, with a result that for people on the median income their average tax rate has gone from 15 percent to 21 percent, and that takes a lot of money out of the pockets of average-income-earning New Zealanders because of inflation.
specificity.explanation: Carries a date, an inflation figure, a defined income reference point and start and end tax rates — all of which someone could go and check or recompute.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Then with Gumboot Friday, we announced through a coalition agreement in Budget 2024, we’re going to fund I Am Hope Foundation $24 million—$6 million a year over four years—that will deliver much-needed mental health counselling services to young people aged five to 25.
specificity.explanation: Names the recipient organisation, the total and annual amounts, the funding period, the service delivered and the eligible age range — fully checkable and actionable detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It was also a privilege to stand with the Prime Minister and the transport Minister, Simeon Brown, to announce $63 million towards Coastguard and Surf Life Saving—$19 million for Coastguard, $44 million for Surf Life Saving.
specificity.explanation: Gives a total and a breakdown by recipient organisation; precise enough to be verified against the Budget documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We’ve got Willie Jackson even going to Oxford in order to strut around in order to increase his credentials as potential leader of the Labour Party.
civility.explanation: Attributes a named member's overseas engagement to personal vanity and leadership ambition — mockery of the person rather than engagement with anything he said or did in policy terms.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Even the doyen of tax policy over on the Labour side David Parker, who always looks a little bit dishevelled, but David “Piketty” Parker is the guy that sends all the thinking over at the Labour Party about yet more taxes to the solution.
civility.explanation: Includes a jibe at a named member's personal appearance ("always looks a little bit dishevelled") and a mocking nickname — an attack on the person, not on his tax position.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And it’s been made much worse by the fact that the previous guy—Grant Robertson—concealed a lot of the size of the deficit because they refused to actually fund a whole lot of things past one or two years, and so we’re having to deal with that in the Budget.
civility.explanation: Imputes deliberate concealment — bad faith — to a named individual, referred to dismissively as "the previous guy", rather than criticising the budgeting practice itself.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ve got Willie Jackson even going to Oxford in order to strut around in order to increase his credentials as potential leader of the Labour Party.
focus.explanation: Entirely about another party's internal leadership contest and a member's supposed motives; no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Even the doyen of tax policy over on the Labour side David Parker, who always looks a little bit dishevelled, but David “Piketty” Parker is the guy that sends all the thinking over at the Labour Party about yet more taxes to the solution.
focus.explanation: Characterises an opposing member and his party's disposition toward tax; no specific tax measure, rate or proposal is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: On that side of the House, they will fight tooth and nail never—never—to yield a cent of tax revenue, and that’s what we saw from Chris Hipkins; it’s what we’re seeing.
focus.explanation: Tax policy is the topic, but the content is a characterisation of the opposing party's general disposition rather than any named tax measure, threshold or figure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Only that Government could spend that amount of money for waiting times to go up.
focus.explanation: A sneer at the previous government's general competence; it gestures at spending and wait times but names no programme, figure or mechanism, so the weight of the sentence is party framing rather than policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I defy anybody in this country anywhere to be able to point towards an 80 percent improvement in the delivery from the Government over the six years under Labour.
rigor.explanation: Argument from absence of evidence combined with a burden shift: the speaker offers no measure of "delivery" and instead challenges others to disprove him. It also assumes an input increase should map one-to-one onto a proportional output improvement, which does not follow.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But I will just say that when it comes to Oranga Tamariki, the Minister of Finance promised, before the election, that Oranga Tamariki, along with a few other agencies, would be specifically excluded from this fiscal savings initiative.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister of Finance publicly committed, before the 2023 election, that Oranga Tamariki would be exempt from the baseline savings exercise.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's pre-election fiscal plan and Nicola Willis's pre-election statements listing agencies exempted from the back-office savings target; true if Oranga Tamariki is named among the excluded agencies, false if it is not.

veracity.statement: What we have seen in the Minister of Finance’s requirement of the Minister for Children, because of the Minister of Finance’s incompetence to make her plan stack up, is that they have gone through a restructuring proposal, and in that proposal they are proposing to cut 447 jobs from Oranga Tamariki—jobs they believe are back-office jobs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Oranga Tamariki's restructuring proposal proposed cutting 447 roles.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki's 2024 change/restructuring proposal document and contemporaneous reporting; true if the proposal disestablishes approximately 447 roles, false if the proposed figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: The Minister, in answer to written question No. 11262, in 2024, said that the chief executive of Oranga Tamariki is not a front-line role.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of a specific named written parliamentary question answer — that the Minister classified the Oranga Tamariki chief executive as not front line.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of written parliamentary question 11262 (2024) on the Parliament website; true if the Minister's answer excludes the chief executive from front-line roles, false if it does not say that.

veracity.statement: But worse than that, the chief executive of Oranga Tamariki is responsible for the 7,000 children who are in care and protection under the chief executive.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 7,000 children were in the care and protection custody/guardianship of the Oranga Tamariki chief executive at the time.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki quarterly reporting on the number of children in care/custody of the chief executive as at mid-2024; true if approximately 7,000, false if materially different (e.g. nearer 4,000).

veracity.statement: How many of their contracts are going to be cut? How many of those services are going to be impacted because this Government is finding those tax savings and cost cutting here to give $2.9 billion to landlords?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's restoration of interest deductibility for residential rental property is worth $2.9 billion to landlords.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD costings for the restoration of interest deductibility published with Budget 2024 or the enacting legislation; true if the fiscal cost is approximately $2.9 billion over the forecast period, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: A recent report from the University of Canterbury revealed 24 percent of New Zealand’s native vegetation—approximately 2.4 million hectares—is on sheep and beef farms.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific research finding on the share and area of NZ native vegetation located on sheep and beef farmland.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The University of Canterbury / Beef + Lamb NZ study on native vegetation on sheep and beef farms; true if it reports approximately 24 percent and about 2.4 million hectares, false if the reported figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: A Federated Farmers survey last year found over 70 percent of farmers’ mental health and wellbeing was being adversely affected just by doing their job.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 2023 Federated Farmers survey finding that over 70 percent of farmers reported their mental health and wellbeing adversely affected by their work.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Federated Farmers' 2023 survey publications (e.g. Farm Confidence Survey / mental wellbeing survey); true if a reported figure exceeds 70 percent on that measure, false if the survey reports a materially lower figure or no such measure.

veracity.statement: We have Matt Doocey, New Zealand’s first ever Minister for Mental Health, and we’re funding the Gumboot Friday initiative $24 million over four years as part of tomorrow’s Budget.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Budget 2024 funds Gumboot Friday at $24 million over four years and that Matt Doocey is New Zealand's first Minister for Mental Health.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Health documents and the ministerial list; true if the Gumboot Friday appropriation is $24m over four years and Doocey is the first holder of the Mental Health portfolio, false if either figure or claim differs.

civility.statement: What we have seen in the Minister of Finance’s requirement of the Minister for Children, because of the Minister of Finance’s incompetence to make her plan stack up, is that they have gone through a restructuring proposal, and in that proposal they are proposing to cut 447 jobs from Oranga Tamariki—jobs they believe are back-office jobs.
civility.explanation: Attributes the outcome to the Minister of Finance's personal 'incompetence' — an attack on an individual's competence rather than on the savings policy itself.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Minister, in answer to written question No. 11262, in 2024, said that the chief executive of Oranga Tamariki is not a front-line role.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact written question number, the year, and the precise classification claimed — directly checkable by anyone.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A recent report from the University of Canterbury revealed 24 percent of New Zealand’s native vegetation—approximately 2.4 million hectares—is on sheep and beef farms.
specificity.explanation: Gives a named source, a percentage and an absolute hectare figure — someone could locate and check the report.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have Matt Doocey, New Zealand’s first ever Minister for Mental Health, and we’re funding the Gumboot Friday initiative $24 million over four years as part of tomorrow’s Budget.
specificity.explanation: Names the initiative, the amount and the period over which it is funded, and ties it to a specific Budget.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Anyone who thinks that a Government agency can run without a chief executive needs a 101 on how our Government works.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: classifying the chief executive as a back-office rather than front-line role is not a claim that the agency can run without a chief executive, so the conclusion attacks a position nobody advanced.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We can’t fix the weather, but changes to the Resource Management Act mean we don’t have to worry about more red tape slowing us down, about ridiculous rules and compliance costs getting in the way.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur in the drought context: nothing is offered connecting the RMA amendments to the compliance burdens farmers face in a drought, and the conclusion that red tape is no longer a worry is far stronger than the premise supports.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We have seen the cuts to the organisation and those that provide the services to them, but we are going to see tomorrow the cuts to the services and the contracts that are provided to them and those services in the community.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Budget 2024, delivered the following day, will contain cuts to community-provider service contracts for children's services.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Oranga Tamariki documents and subsequent provider contract decisions; true if community service contracts/funding for children's services are reduced or discontinued, false if provider funding is maintained or increased.

focus.statement: They are prioritising landlords over our most vulnerable children.
focus.explanation: A real policy trade-off (interest deductibility versus children's services funding, quantified in the surrounding sentences) but stated here as a bare framing about the other side's priorities rather than a mechanism or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The previous Government spent six years undermining the future of farming with a raft of unnecessary, often conflicting, rules and regulations that were bad for farmers and rural communities.
focus.explanation: Gestures at regulation as the subject but names no rule, cost or measure; the weight of the sentence is a general characterisation of the previous Government's record.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Even in Opposition, they’re attacking farmers. They don’t get farmers, they don’t get rural New Zealand; we do and we’re proving it.
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of what the other side is like; no policy, figure, measure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As the party with the largest Māori mandate and Māori electorates, I feel extremely confident in being able to stand and say that we have heard our people’s call that they have reached the absolute point of intolerance.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that her party holds the largest Māori mandate and the most Māori electorate seats.
veracity.subject: speaker
