divination.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record and division/voice-vote result for the third reading of the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) (Overseas Travel Reporting) Amendment Bill; true if the bill passed third reading on 29 May 2024, false if it was defeated, adjourned or not concluded that day.

specificity.statement: Looking at the actual requirements and the legislative remits of this bill, it would amend the Act to require registered child sex offenders to provide additional information to the police before travelling overseas for more than 48 hours.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (amend the Act), who is affected (registered child sex offenders), what is required (additional information to police) and the threshold (more than 48 hours). Checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So this is part of a suite—this member’s bill—of a National Party programme where we are putting the family, the children at the centre of it.
specificity.explanation: Refers to a 'suite' and a 'programme' without naming a single policy, figure, mechanism or timeframe; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And why wouldn’t we give all the tools that we could to the authorities to protect children as best as we can? As we often say in this House: even if it saves one child, it’s all been worth it.
rigor.explanation: A rhetorical question plus a bare appeal to emotion: no evidence or reasoning is offered that this particular reporting requirement will prevent harm, and 'even if it saves one child' would justify any measure whatever, so it does no work in supporting the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And I hope that the Green Party, whose co-leader was the Minister for the Prevention of Family and Sexual Violence, come around and support this on the third reading.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy anchor — the third reading vote on the bill before the House — but the weight of the sentence is pressure on another party and an implied contrast with a rival's former portfolio, rather than engagement with what the bill does.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And I hope that the Green Party, whose co-leader was the Minister for the Prevention of Family and Sexual Violence, come around and support this on the third reading.
civility.explanation: Pointed: invoking the Green co-leader's former ministerial title implies inconsistency on her part, but it stops short of any attack on her character or competence and stays framed as a hope that the party will support the bill.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That actually surprises a number of us in the House that arrived only in October—and it will surprise some in the public as well—that domestic travel had reporting requirements but international travel didn’t for registered child sex offenders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that, before this amendment, the child sex offender register regime imposed travel reporting obligations for domestic travel but none for international travel.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The reporting obligations in the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) Act 2016 as in force before the 2024 amendment (notably the sections on reportable information and intended absence from New Zealand), and the bill's explanatory note / departmental report. True if the pre-amendment Act imposed no overseas travel reporting duty; false if it already required registrable offenders to report intended travel out of New Zealand (with the amendment merely adding detail such as overseas addresses).

veracity.statement: We have walked into a situation where child poverty stats—according to Stats NZ, released in January this year for the year June to 30 June 2023 had deteriorated—had deteriorated: material hardship was up; key indicators were up.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Stats NZ child poverty statistics for the year ended 30 June 2023, released early in 2024, showed a deterioration, including a rise in the child material hardship rate and in other key measures.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Child Poverty Statistics release for the year ended June 2023 (child poverty related indicators, including the material hardship measure). True if the material hardship rate and other primary measures rose relative to the year ended June 2022 by more than sampling error, and the release date matches roughly the month stated; false if the measures were flat or fell, or the release did not report a deterioration.

veracity.statement: Again, the protection of children—we inherited a Government where 6,500 people were living in emergency housing, nearly half of them were children.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that at the change of government (late 2023) about 6,500 people were in emergency housing and that close to half of them were children.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Social Development emergency housing special needs grant data for the quarter ending December 2023 (households and individuals, adults and children, in emergency housing motels). True if the total number of people is around 6,500 and children make up roughly 45-50%; false if the totals or the child share differ materially.

veracity.statement: That is why we are so proud to stand here as the party with the first ever Minister for the Prevention of Family and Sexual Violence.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Green Party holds/held the first ever ministerial portfolio for the Prevention of Family and Sexual Violence in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial warrant records / DPMC ministerial lists: true if the Prevention of Family and Sexual Violence portfolio was created for the first time and its first holder was a Green Party MP (Marama Davidson, 2020); false if the portfolio pre-dated that appointment or its first holder belonged to another party.

veracity.statement: The way that we came to change our position on this bill is because when the first and second readings of this bill happened and myself and my colleague Kahurangi Carter, who is the spokesperson for children, realised that we were the only party that was not supporting this bill, we had some serious questions and it didn’t make sense to us.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that at the first and second readings of this bill the Green Party was the only party in the House voting against it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard party-vote records for the first and second readings of the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) Amendment Bill: true if the Green Party was the sole party recorded against on both occasions; false if any other party also voted against, or if the Greens supported either reading.

veracity.statement: It’s great that we’ve got unanimity across the House in taking this important step.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that every party in the House now supports the bill at its third reading.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The division/voice-vote record for the third reading of the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) Amendment Bill: true if the bill was agreed to with no party recorded against; false if any party voted against or abstained in opposition.

veracity.statement: So this bill amends the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) Act 2016 to require registered child sex offenders to provide additional information to police before travelling overseas.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the bill does: amends the 2016 Act to impose additional pre-travel information requirements on registered child sex offenders.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) Amendment Bill as passed: true if it amends the 2016 Act to require registered offenders to give police additional information before overseas travel; false if it amends a different Act or imposes no such requirement.

veracity.statement: I think the key thing that we really want to emphasise is that registers by themselves do little in and of themselves to reduce offending.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an empirical claim about the effectiveness of sex offender registers in reducing offending.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Peer-reviewed evaluations and systematic reviews of sex offender registration schemes (and the Ministry of Justice / Attorney-General advice on this bill): true if the weight of the evidence finds no or minimal reduction in reoffending attributable to registration alone; false if the evidence base shows a substantial reduction in offending from registers themselves.

veracity.statement: We also stand by the very important submission made by the Attorney-General on the impact that this bill has on human rights, and the Ministry of Justice, who were at pains to highlight that this legislation is inconsistent with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act (NZBORA) and therefore risks a dangerous precedent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Attorney-General and the Ministry of Justice advised that this legislation is inconsistent with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Attorney-General's report to the House under s7 of NZBORA on this bill and the Ministry of Justice departmental advice/regulatory material: true if either identifies an inconsistency with NZBORA; false if no such inconsistency was reported.

veracity.statement: The Justice Committee’s own report noted the statement of the Attorney-General that evidence is limited as to the effectiveness of sex offender registers in improving public safety.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of the Justice Committee's report on this bill — that it recorded the Attorney-General's view that evidence on register effectiveness is limited.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee report on the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) Amendment Bill: true if it records the Attorney-General as saying evidence of register effectiveness for public safety is limited; false if no such passage appears.

specificity.statement: So this bill amends the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) Act 2016 to require registered child sex offenders to provide additional information to police before travelling overseas.
specificity.explanation: Names the parent Act and year, the class of person affected, the obligation created and its trigger — a checkable description of the measure rather than a general statement of purpose.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, in closing, I repeat: the Greens want a world where all children, here and across the world, live safe lives free from sexual violence and abuse.
specificity.explanation: A statement of aspiration with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named action; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We also stand by the very important submission made by the Attorney-General on the impact that this bill has on human rights, and the Ministry of Justice, who were at pains to highlight that this legislation is inconsistent with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act (NZBORA) and therefore risks a dangerous precedent.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the measure — its rights implications and the official advice on the bill before the House — rather than the other parties.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But that wouldn’t be the first time that we had supported a bill that had some warnings against NZBORA. We do so because we believe in the rights of children to live free from violence.
rigor.explanation: An inference is offered — support the bill despite a NZBORA inconsistency because children's rights outweigh it — but the supporting move is partly an appeal to past practice ('not the first time') and to a value, with no weighing shown against her own earlier premise that registers do little to reduce offending.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Again, Ms Paul actually talked about the kind of horrendous acts of sexual violence against children in New Zealand, and they are some appalling statistics—one in four girls and one in six boys are sexually abused before the age of 18.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a New Zealand prevalence statistic for childhood sexual abuse: one in four girls and one in six boys abused before age 18.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand prevalence research on childhood sexual abuse (e.g. the NZ Family Violence Study / Fanslow et al., Ministry of Justice or Ministry of Social Development published prevalence figures); true if reputable NZ data put lifetime childhood sexual abuse at approximately 25% of girls and approximately 17% of boys before age 18, false if the published NZ figures are materially different.

veracity.statement: Some stats suggest that around 2 million children around the world are victims of sex tourism every year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that published estimates put the global number of child victims of sex tourism at roughly 2 million per year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: UNICEF, ECPAT International or ILO published estimates of children exploited in commercial sexual exploitation / child sex tourism; true if a recognised body publishes an annual figure of approximately 2 million child victims specifically of sex tourism, false if the commonly cited 2 million figure refers to a materially different category (e.g. all commercial sexual exploitation) or if no such estimate exists.

veracity.statement: So, again, in Australia, they have a similar law where each state and territory must report these details of offenders—where they are, and if they travel outside of Australia, permission is needed, and, of course, those people are tracked, similar to our bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Australian law requires each state and territory to report offender details, and that registered child sex offenders need permission to travel outside Australia and are tracked.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Australian state/territory Child Protection (Offender Reporting) Acts and the National Child Offender Register, plus the Commonwealth Passports Amendment (Overseas Travel by Child Sex Offenders) Act 2017; true if reportable offenders must report to a register and are prohibited from, or require authorisation for, overseas travel, false if no such reporting/travel-control regime exists.

veracity.statement: And then, obviously, in the United States, there are different laws, but again, one of them is the international Megan’s Law, which is to prevent child exploitation by, again, requiring notification as people who are sex offenders travel outside the US.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the United States has an 'International Megan's Law' whose mechanism is notification when registered sex offenders travel abroad.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: US Public Law 114-119, the International Megan's Law to Prevent Child Exploitation and Other Sexual Crimes Through Advance Notification of Traveling Sex Offenders (2016); true if that statute exists and requires advance notification to destination countries of travelling registered child sex offenders, false otherwise.

specificity.statement: So, again, in Australia, they have a similar law where each state and territory must report these details of offenders—where they are, and if they travel outside of Australia, permission is needed, and, of course, those people are tracked, similar to our bill.
specificity.explanation: Names a jurisdiction and describes the actual mechanism — per-state reporting of offender location, permission required for overseas travel, tracking — enough that someone could go and check the regime.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I really think that this is a great piece of legislation which does its small but important part to add to our laws that do protect our children.
specificity.explanation: A general endorsement — 'great piece of legislation', 'small but important part' — with no figure, mechanism or timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Also, other countries have already got legislation such as this, so I think it’s important that New Zealand does its piece to actually update our international obligations.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to common practice: the fact that other countries have enacted similar laws is offered as the reason New Zealand should, with no argument that the laws work or that they bear on New Zealand's circumstances. It also slides from 'other countries have laws' to 'our international obligations' without establishing any obligation.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We obviously had an Amendment Paper from Erica Stanford, which has been incorporated, making some useful changes around the inter-agency sharing of data and making sure that that was all linked up.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — names a specific Amendment Paper and what it changes (inter-agency data sharing). No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill proposes amendments to existing legislation which requires registerable offenders to provide additional information to the authorities before they travel overseas for more than 48 hours.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (additional pre-travel information to authorities) and a concrete threshold (48 hours), so the description of the bill can be checked against its text, though no figures on scope or cost.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Tamariki Māori, who make up near 70 percent of those in State care, are also victim to sexual crime and to abuse in care.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise, checkable proportion (near 70 percent) attached to a defined population (tamariki Māori in State care), which someone could verify against agency data.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This bill proposes amendments to existing legislation which requires registerable offenders to provide additional information to the authorities before they travel overseas for more than 48 hours.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the amendment bill requires registered offenders to give additional information before overseas travel exceeding 48 hours.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) (Overseas Travel Reporting) Amendment Bill as reported back in 2024, and the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) Act 2016 it amends; true if the reporting duty is triggered by intended overseas travel of more than 48 hours, false if the threshold or trigger in the enacted text differs.

veracity.statement: Tamariki Māori, who make up near 70 percent of those in State care, are also victim to sexual crime and to abuse in care.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that close to 70 percent of children and young people in State care in New Zealand are Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki published care-population statistics for 2023/24 (children and young people in care by ethnicity); true if the Māori share of those in State care is approximately 65-70%, false if it is materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: The current attempt to remove section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act is yet another example of this.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that at the time of speaking (May 2024) the Government was actively seeking to remove section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliamentary bill record for the Oranga Tamariki (Repeal of Section 7AA) Amendment Bill; true if such a bill repealing section 7AA had been introduced and was before the House as at 29 May 2024, false if no such measure existed or it did not concern section 7AA.

rigor.statement: So it is possible, I believe, that these extra measures provided for in this bill could be the deterrent that they need to finally take responsibility for their actions and take ownership of their life which they have a second chance at.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the reporting requirements will deter reoffending rests only on speculation about what an offender might think in the moment — no evidence, study or mechanism is offered connecting travel-reporting duties to reduced reoffending. An appeal to plausibility rather than an inference from stated premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So how can we provide better care and protection of tamariki overseas and not do the same of our own?
rigor.explanation: An argument from inconsistency: because the House legislates to protect children abroad from travelling offenders, it should equally retain section 7AA domestically. It engages the policy, but the inference has a real gap — it treats two different instruments as interchangeable measures of the same commitment, and assumes without showing it that repealing 7AA removes protection.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So it is possible, I believe, that these extra measures provided for in this bill could be the deterrent that they need to finally take responsibility for their actions and take ownership of their life which they have a second chance at.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the measure before the House and its claimed deterrent effect on registered offenders; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I intend to call out this Government on their inconsistencies when it comes to the care of tamariki. I do this as it is tamariki Māori who disproportionately suffer from this Government’s failings. The current attempt to remove section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act is yet another example of this.
focus.explanation: Names a specific legislative measure (the repeal of section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act) and a specific policy area, which is legitimate scrutiny rather than generalised party attack, though the middle sentence is broad framing about 'this Government's failings'.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: So that’s why it is very important for us to continue to support this bill, and we believe that it will be received very well and we commend it to the House.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the bill will be well received by the House at its third reading — i.e. that it passes with broad or unopposed support rather than facing significant opposition.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Hansard third reading record and division (if any) for the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) (Overseas Travel Reporting) Amendment Bill; true if it passed third reading without a party voting against, false if any party opposed it or the bill did not pass.

civility.statement: Perhaps it is the term “Māori” that Government are desensitised too. Should I say the “indigenous children of this country”? Would it resonate better with this House?
civility.explanation: Sneering and imputing bad faith — that the Government and the House tune out when Māori children are mentioned — rather than engaging the substance of the disagreement. It targets no individual member, which keeps it above a personal attack, but the rhetorical needling is a departure from civil engagement.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And, of course, all my learned colleagues here are invested and committed to Te Aorerekura—the all-Government, prevention-focused, Tiriti-centred, strength-based, community-led, and whole-whānau embedded strategy to eliminate violence over the next couple of generations.
specificity.explanation: Names a real strategy (Te Aorerekura) but describes it entirely with a string of generic adjectives — no measures, figures, targets or timeframes beyond 'the next couple of generations'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Police will now tell Customs when a child sex offender is travelling, and Customs can use the resources and tools at their disposal to alert the other country or to monitor the offender closely. This makes the bill more effective at achieving its intent to reduce harm and prevent the horror of child sex tourism.
specificity.explanation: Describes an actual mechanism — Police-to-Customs notification of a travelling registered offender, and what Customs may then do — but gives no thresholds, numbers or commencement detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Section 21 requires, currently—without the amendments—that registered sex offenders advise the registrar of their travel plans if they are travelling overseas for more than 48 hours, with the dates that they are leaving and returning, but not the name of the country of destination, and section 22 requires that registered sex offenders advise the registrar if the date of their return to New Zealand changes while they’re overseas.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific sections of the principal Act, the 48-hour threshold, and exactly which particulars are and are not currently required — fully checkable against the statute.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Now, before the committee of the whole House, we were informed that member Erica Stanford’s amendment to strengthen the bill and provide clear improvements to the bill were accepted.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an amendment in Erica Stanford's name to the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) (Overseas Travel Reporting) Amendment Bill was accepted at the committee of the whole House stage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard record and Supplementary Order Paper list for the committee of the whole House stage of the named bill (2024); true if an amendment/SOP in Erica Stanford's name was agreed to, false if no such amendment was moved or it was not agreed.

veracity.statement: Section 21 requires, currently—without the amendments—that registered sex offenders advise the registrar of their travel plans if they are travelling overseas for more than 48 hours, with the dates that they are leaving and returning, but not the name of the country of destination, and section 22 requires that registered sex offenders advise the registrar if the date of their return to New Zealand changes while they’re overseas.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of sections 21 and 22 of the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) Act 2016 as they stood before this amendment bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of ss 21 and 22 of the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) Act 2016 as at May 2024 on legislation.govt.nz; true if s 21 requires notice of overseas travel exceeding 48 hours with departure/return dates but not destination country, and s 22 requires notice of a change to the return date; false if the sections say otherwise.

veracity.statement: These arguments have been based around the section 7 report of the Attorney-General to the Justice Committee commenting that this bill appears to be inconsistent with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act on several fronts—namely, these fronts: the right of an offender to benefit from the lesser penalty where penalties change, and the right to freedom from double jeopardy and retrospectivity.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Attorney-General issued a section 7 New Zealand Bill of Rights Act report on this bill identifying inconsistency with the lesser-penalty right and the double jeopardy/retrospectivity rights.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Attorney-General's s 7 BORA report on the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) (Overseas Travel Reporting) Amendment Bill, published on justice.govt.nz/parliament; true if such a report exists and cites ss 25(g)/26 grounds as described, false if no s 7 report was issued or it cited materially different grounds.

veracity.statement: Of the sexual abuse that takes place in New Zealand, 90 percent is perpetrated by people that are known to the victim.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 90 percent of sexual abuse in New Zealand is committed by someone known to the victim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Crime and Victims Survey (Ministry of Justice) and Police/ACC published figures on offender-victim relationship in sexual assault; true if the known-perpetrator share is approximately 90 percent, false if materially lower (e.g. nearer 60-75 percent).

rigor.statement: The Police will now tell Customs when a child sex offender is travelling, and Customs can use the resources and tools at their disposal to alert the other country or to monitor the offender closely. This makes the bill more effective at achieving its intent to reduce harm and prevent the horror of child sex tourism.
rigor.explanation: The inference runs from a real mechanism (information sharing) to the conclusion that the bill will be more effective at reducing harm; the step is plausible but the effectiveness claim is asserted rather than supported — a gap between what was shown (a notification pathway) and what was concluded (reduced offending abroad).
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So, in these various stages, we’ve heard the cry of some that oppose this bill because it, apparently, infringes on the human rights of registered sex offenders, of sex predators.
civility.explanation: No individual is attacked, but 'the cry of some' plus 'apparently' is a dismissive, faintly sneering characterisation of opponents' motives rather than an engagement with their argument; short of a personal attack but no longer fully civil.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But I do want to just touch on the human rights aspect, because I do think this House should absolutely pause when the Attorney-General says, “The proposed measure, in my independent and considered opinion, is not a justified limitation on human rights.”, and it should be only with the utmost gravity that this House puts that to one side and adopts that measure anyway.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the measure before the House — the Attorney-General's section 7 BORA advice on the bill — with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Additional information—when offenders intending to return to New Zealand leave the country, they must report where they’re going, where they will be living, and when they will be coming back or departing from the country that they are headed to. Offenders must also provide information if they do not intend to return to New Zealand, where they will be staying.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of the measure before the House; no reference to any party.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But I do want to just touch on the human rights aspect, because I do think this House should absolutely pause when the Attorney-General says, “The proposed measure, in my independent and considered opinion, is not a justified limitation on human rights.”, and it should be only with the utmost gravity that this House puts that to one side and adopts that measure anyway.
specificity.explanation: Names and directly quotes the Attorney-General's conclusion on the measure, which is checkable, but the statement itself supplies no figures, mechanism or clause detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Additional information—when offenders intending to return to New Zealand leave the country, they must report where they’re going, where they will be living, and when they will be coming back or departing from the country that they are headed to. Offenders must also provide information if they do not intend to return to New Zealand, where they will be staying.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the actual reporting obligations the bill creates — destination, residence, and dates of travel — in enough detail that a reader could check them against the bill's clauses. No dates or costs, which keeps it short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I would love to see, in the Budget tomorrow, some money go into making our net safer for our children, and stopping a lot of the stuff that comes into New Zealand by putting money into the safety of our net—and let’s see whether it happens; it’s the kind of thing that should be cross-party.
specificity.explanation: Points at a real fiscal event with a timeframe (tomorrow's Budget) and a broad area of spending, but names no amount, no programme and no mechanism — 'some money' into 'the safety of our net' is not something anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: One of the observations or one of the statements or reasons of the Attorney-General in the report was that there is actually modest evidence of a strong link between prevention of child sex offending and this register, and I think that’s a gap that we need to fill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Attorney-General's report on this bill stated the evidence linking the child sex offender register to prevention of offending is modest.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Attorney-General's section 7 New Zealand Bill of Rights Act report on the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) (Overseas Travel Reporting) Amendment Bill, presented to the House; true if the report characterises the evidence of a link between the register and prevention of child sex offending as modest/limited, false if it makes no such characterisation or asserts strong evidence.

veracity.statement: The Supreme Court did find in, I think it’s, “D” v Attorney-General, that the child sex offender is part of a punishment or a penal regime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a New Zealand Supreme Court decision held the child sex offender register to be part of a punitive or penal regime. Note the speaker hedges on the case name.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Supreme Court judgments on the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) Act 2016 — in particular D (SC 31/2019) v New Zealand Police [2021] NZSC 2; true if the Court held registration constitutes a penalty/punishment (e.g. for s 26(2) NZBORA purposes), false if it held registration is not punitive.

veracity.statement: With the awareness that this law change could impinge on human rights of registered sex offenders in terms of exposing them to more punishment, there have been steps proposed and accepted by the Justice Committee to ensure that all registered offenders are aware that this bill is going to happen. So there will be a delayed commencement time to allow police to fully inform everyone affected by this change.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Justice Committee recommended, and the bill as reported back contains, a delayed commencement date so police can notify all existing registrants of the new obligations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's report on the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) (Overseas Travel Reporting) Amendment Bill and the bill as reported back; true if the committee recommended and the bill provides for a deferred commencement to permit police notification of registered offenders, false if the bill commences immediately on assent or contains no such deferral.

veracity.statement: I thank the Greens for coming around on this bill and supporting it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Green Party changed its position on this bill, having not supported it at an earlier stage and supporting it at this one.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard party-vote records for the first, second and third readings of the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) (Overseas Travel Reporting) Amendment Bill; true if the Green Party voted against (or abstained) at an earlier reading and voted in favour at this stage, false if the Greens supported it throughout or did not support it here.

rigor.statement: Certainly the purpose of this register is not punitive; whatever the court sentenced, that has happened. This is to protect children from people, and that’s the primary objective, but also to put a framework around offenders and their behaviour—in a sense, protect them from themselves.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure, but it moves from the register's stated purpose to the conclusion that it is not punitive, which does not follow — the Supreme Court finding he has just cited turned on the regime's effect on the offender, not its declared intent. The gap between purpose and effect is left unbridged.

veracity.statement: Most beers are around the 5 percent mark.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Alcohol content data for beers sold in New Zealand (e.g. Brewers Association / Health Promotion Agency standard-drink guidance, major brewery product labels); true if the typical/median ABV of beer on the NZ market sits at roughly 4–5.5 percent, false if the central tendency is materially outside that band.

veracity.statement: The Brewers Guild, who represent brewers in New Zealand, including small artisan brewers, were really quite keen for this to be included.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The Brewers Guild of New Zealand's written or oral submission to the Justice Committee on the Sale and Supply of Alcohol (Cellar Door Tasting) Amendment Bill; true if the submission asks for breweries to be included in the tasting regime, false if it is silent on or opposed to inclusion.

veracity.statement: So while we’re on the subject of teaspoons—so we’re talking a maximum of 7 teaspoons for a wine tasting, we’re talking 23 teaspoons for a beer tasting. Actually, if you look on the Garage Project website, you can find several beers at 12 percent alcohol, which is what a lot of wines are at. So you’ve an immediate anomaly there.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Garage Project's product listings as at May 2024 (or the Wayback Machine capture); true if more than one beer is listed at or near 12 percent ABV, false if the range tops out materially below that.

veracity.statement: But the definition of a “craft brewery”—well, there isn’t one. Nothing in the law, anyway, or the standards that I’m aware of.

divination.statement: If someone wants to bring a bill along that line—and I’m expecting to see Dr Webb’s name on one of those bills in the ballot, very shortly—that would be where they would go through all those potential fish-hooks that could be ironed out.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Duncan Webb will lodge a member's bill on brewery/beer tasting into the members' bills ballot in the near future.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Clerk's published list of members' bills in the ballot; true if a bill in Duncan Webb's name dealing with brewery or beer cellar-door tastings is lodged in the ballot by the resolve-by date, false if no such bill appears.

veracity.statement: So prior to this Parliament, 12 submissions were received in the previous select committee, and in this parliamentary term, the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee reopened for submissions, and we heard from eight interested groups and individuals, and then we heard from four orally.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee report and submissions list on bills.parliament.nz for the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill; true if the earlier committee received 12 submissions and the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee received 8 submissions with 4 heard orally, false if the recorded counts differ materially.

veracity.statement: In 2016, they launched a gift card campaign and then, in 2022, they did a review of 61 gift cards. veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Consumer NZ's 2022 gift card review (and its submission to the committee); true if the review covered 61 cards with the expiry breakdown given (14 at 12 months, 1 at 18 months, 19 at two years, 6 at three years, 1 at four years, 6 at five years, 14 with no expiry), false if the sample size or breakdown differs materially.

specificity.statement: We decided that it should be an infringement offence to contravene the new sections of the Act and that fines not exceeding $10,000 should apply for an individual, or $30,000 for an organisation.

specificity.statement: In 2016, they launched a gift card campaign and then, in 2022, they did a review of 61 gift cards. rigor.statement: Having it as an infringement notice means that each instance of a breach could be considered and its own penalties apply. We think that that would therefore provide a very stiff incentive to comply with the law.

rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is a win for consumers in New Zealand and this is another way that this Government is getting this country back on track.

focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The issue was that the member in charge, Stuart Smith, and the committee were weary of putting overly burdensome regulations and requirements in place for wine cellar door operators whereby they may have to go and get commercial kitchen - grade food licences if they were to have to provide full host responsibility requirements, where they may well be settled with thousands of dollars of compliance and costs, all for the sake of making a bit of money back on the cost recovery for their sample sizes.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the clause before the committee — why a food-provision requirement risked imposing commercial kitchen licensing costs on cellar door operators. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We had colleagues from the other side of the House heckling, saying, “New material, new material.” Well, here’s some new material and wake up, because one of the aspects included here is around the provision of water, which we actually haven’t had any discussion or contribution or just debate on.

focus.statement: The first one of them is that the idea of having a 10-kilometre radius seems, to me, to be very arbitrary. rigor.statement: The advice came back that the cost would be in the vicinity of $200 to $300 over two or three years—I can’t quite recall what it was. rigor.statement: Well, I thank the member, but I think he answered his own question. He had a glass of water there, and that is why you have water there. If you’ve got alcohol available, you should always have a non-alcohol option, and that is water, in this case, and they’ll have to provide it.

rigor.statement: So we don’t have that, but I wonder if any thought was given—and I look both across the aisle there, but also to you, Stuart Smith—about making it just simply “alcoholic beverages”, because we get ourselves into the situation of trying to micromanage these things to say that that one’s in and that one’s out. veracity.statement: The advice came back that the cost would be in the vicinity of $200 to $300 over two or three years—I can’t quite recall what it was. veracity.statement: Ironically, if you’re giving samples away for free, you don’t have to provide food. Under this bill, they’ll be able to charge for samples, but they’ll have to provide food.

veracity.statement: Originally, it was tried to be added to the bill, but it was ruled to be likely to be out of scope.

civility.statement: The member Dr Duncan Webb has brought it in legitimately through Amendment Paper 31, and it is legitimately here for the vote, but the reality is that the work hasn’t been done on it. divination.statement: I’d like to extend, first of all, my congratulations to Melissa Lee, assuming that this will go through.

divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary records for the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill; true if the bill passed the reading being debated on 2024-05-29 and continued its passage, false if it was voted down at that reading.

civility.statement: It is interesting that that’s where the line is for a party like ACT, because this is, in a way, all about freedom, and it’s about consumer rights. I would have thought there was some common ground there, and I’m disappointed that we aren’t in a unanimous position on a bill like this.
civility.explanation: Disagrees with another party's stance on a contested bill without any personal attack, imputation of bad faith or mockery.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is interesting that that’s where the line is for a party like ACT, because this is, in a way, all about freedom, and it’s about consumer rights. I would have thought there was some common ground there, and I’m disappointed that we aren’t in a unanimous position on a bill like this.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point (the bill concerns consumer rights and freedom) but framed principally around what another party's position reveals about that party rather than the mechanism of the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’d ask the people here tonight who are from ACT to think: in that situation, how does that work for the grandma who has paid the money for the present card? How does it work for the person who has the petrol voucher? How is the balance struck in this situation, if this is what we do?
focus.explanation: Directly interrogates the substance of the opposing party's stated position on the bill — who bears the cost of unregulated expiry dates — rather than attacking the party in general terms.

veracity.statement: Consumer New Zealand had done research in 2022, and they’d found that there were a lot of losses to real-life people, and, right now, those are real-life losses.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Consumer New Zealand conducted research in 2022 that found substantial consumer losses from gift card expiry.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Consumer NZ publications/research from 2022 on gift cards and vouchers; true if a 2022 Consumer NZ study documenting consumer losses from gift card expiry exists, false if no such 2022 research exists or it found no material losses.

veracity.statement: And we’ve got a penalty in which was the original penalty that had been drafted in, and it was $10,000 for a person and $30,000 for a company that exploits this, because people do, unfortunately, exploit these things, and we need to make sure that these fines are real for people.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill as reported back carries penalties of $10,000 for an individual and $30,000 for a body corporate, and that these were the originally drafted figures.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill as introduced and as reported back by the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee; true if the penalty provisions state $10,000 (individual) and $30,000 (body corporate), false if the amounts differ.

veracity.statement: It costs this country so much more, not tenfold, hundredfold more, than benefit fraud—white-collar fraud.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that white-collar fraud costs New Zealand roughly one hundred times more than benefit fraud.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published NZ estimates of white-collar/occupational fraud losses (e.g. Serious Fraud Office, Deloitte/KPMG NZ fraud surveys) versus MSD benefit fraud figures for a comparable period; true if the ratio is around 100:1 or greater, false if the ratio is materially smaller (e.g. of the order of ten times or less).

rigor.statement: I never got to use the voucher, I never got the experience, and there was no comeback on that company because there were expiries involved. And, actually, it’s not a very long time for a large amount of money like that.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single personal anecdote (her own unused balloon voucher) to a conclusion about the adequacy of the statutory expiry period — an appeal to anecdote, though it does illustrate the mechanism at issue.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And we’ve got a penalty in which was the original penalty that had been drafted in, and it was $10,000 for a person and $30,000 for a company that exploits this, because people do, unfortunately, exploit these things, and we need to make sure that these fines are real for people.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact penalty figures in the bill for individuals and companies and the drafting history — precise and checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need to set aside some of the ideologies that we have and think—absolutely with common sense—about what will matter to our thriving businesses and what will matter to our people in New Zealand, what will matter to their wellbeing.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic appeals — common sense, thriving businesses, wellbeing — with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named provision to check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.explanation: Asserts three figures sourced to Consumer New Zealand: >$250m of gift card value outstanding, $10m a year lost, and one in five New Zealanders holding an expired gift card.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Consumer New Zealand's published gift card research/campaign material and its submission to the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee on the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill; true if those figures ($250m outstanding, $10m/year lost, 1 in 5 with an expired card) appear substantially as stated, false if the published figures are materially different.

veracity.statement: This is a bill that affects a majority of people—77 percent of New Zealanders regularly receive gift cards.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 77 percent of New Zealanders regularly receive gift cards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Consumer New Zealand (or comparable) survey data cited in submissions on the bill; true if a survey reports ~77% of New Zealanders regularly receiving gift cards, false if the published figure is materially different or no such figure exists.

specificity.statement: We’ve heard the stats from Consumer New Zealand: there’s over $250 million floating around of gift cards; $10 million a year of value of gift cards is lost—that’s immense—and one in five New Zealanders is stuck with an expired gift card.
specificity.explanation: Three named, checkable figures with an identified source, tied directly to the problem the bill addresses.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Again, the other point they made was this: that there should be a transition time of 12 months so that the retailers get enough time to transition to the expiry date which will be set by this bill—that is, of three years.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism and two figures — a 12-month transition period before a three-year minimum expiry takes effect — which someone could check against the submission or act on in drafting.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, essentially, none actually ended up changing their mind. That shows how important regulation actually is in addressing market failures, because, essentially, when consumers don’t end up being able to spend their gift cards, that’s a massive market failure.
rigor.explanation: Infers from an observed failure of voluntary change (companies approached did not alter expiry policies) that regulation is needed to correct a market failure. The inference tracks the evidence offered, but generalises from a single small sample of 14 firms and slightly overstates it (one firm did change before reverting), leaving a modest gap between evidence and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, in fact, when members in ACT are concerned about business not being aligned, well, when Retail New Zealand and the booksellers association, in consultation with their members, have said that they would support the aims of the bill, then it’s something to perhaps think about.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts a concern about business opposition by pointing to two industry bodies supporting the bill's aims — an appeal to representative authority that does not establish that businesses generally are content, and supporting broad 'aims' is weaker than supporting the measure.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: No matter what length of time is given, there will always be some consumers who will not be able to redeem that gift card. There is no guarantee that if there is a longer expiry date, all of the consumers—those who receive gift cards—will be able to redeem that gift card.
rigor.explanation: Perfect-solution (nirvana) fallacy: because a three-year minimum will not rescue every unredeemed card, the measure is treated as unjustified. Nothing offered addresses whether it would reduce the number of consumers who miss out, which is the actual claim in issue.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Here, to imply that somehow businesses are not doing the right thing by giving an expiry date of six months or 12 months, I reject that notion. That is not the case, because businesses know how they operate; businesses know what their marketing strategy should be.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: that businesses understand their own operations and marketing does not establish that their expiry settings are fair to consumers — the premise is about firms' self-knowledge, the conclusion about the interests of a different party. It also rebuts an imputation ('businesses are not doing the right thing') that overstates the case actually made for the bill.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So, in fact, when members in ACT are concerned about business not being aligned, well, when Retail New Zealand and the booksellers association, in consultation with their members, have said that they would support the aims of the bill, then it’s something to perhaps think about.
focus.explanation: Names another party's position but immediately answers it with specific submitter evidence on the measure before the House, so the weight is on the policy rather than on ACT itself.

focus.statement: No matter what length of time is given, there will always be some consumers who will not be able to redeem that gift card. There is no guarantee that if there is a longer expiry date, all of the consumers—those who receive gift cards—will be able to redeem that gift card.

specificity.statement: The latest figures show annual Consumers Price Index inflation falling from 4 percent in the March quarter to 3.3 percent in the June quarter, and quarterly inflation easing from 0.6 percent to 0.4 percent. At 3.3 percent, annual inflation is the lowest it has been for three years, far lower than under the previous Government.
specificity.explanation: Four precise, sourced figures with named quarters and a named series; anyone could check it against the Stats NZ release.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Health New Zealand’s overly centralised operating model and poor financial controls have plagued the organisation since its creation by the previous Government. We’re taking decisive action to fix those problems by installing commissioners and giving them a mandate to deliver New Zealanders the healthcare that they deserve.
specificity.explanation: A named mechanism (installing commissioners) but no numbers, milestones or dates attached to the fix.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s why we’re very proud to see smoking go from 8.6 percent to 6.8 percent in the last 12 months, and we’re going to continue that march.
specificity.explanation: Two exact percentages and a stated period; checkable against the published survey.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Heated tobacco products—if we can halve excise tax, we’ll do a 12-month trial, see how it goes.
specificity.explanation: A named mechanism (halving excise on a named product class) and a stated duration, but no target, threshold or criteria for judging the trial.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Did the Ministry of Health advise the Government that heated tobacco products would likely compound existing concerns about youth uptake in addition to nicotine products, and that addiction rates for snus can be higher than for smoked tobacco products, and that snus can increase the risk of certain types of cancer?
specificity.explanation: Three named, checkable propositions attributed to a named source — youth uptake, comparative addiction rates for snus, and cancer risk. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The latest figures show annual Consumers Price Index inflation falling from 4 percent in the March quarter to 3.3 percent in the June quarter, and quarterly inflation easing from 0.6 percent to 0.4 percent. At 3.3 percent, annual inflation is the lowest it has been for three years, far lower than under the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Stats NZ's June 2024 quarter CPI showed annual inflation of 3.3% (down from 4.0% in March), quarterly inflation of 0.4% (down from 0.6%), and that 3.3% is a three-year low.
