veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents (Treasury Budget Economic and Fiscal Update / Taxation (Budget Measures) Bill 2024 costings) for the total four-year cost of the personal income tax package; true if the package totals approximately $14 billion, false if materially different (e.g. under $10b or over $20b).

veracity.statement: I’m not sure whether or not that was who the general public were screaming out for to get support, but they decided that $2.9 billion worth of tax breaks to landlords was the priority.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Budget/Government's restoration of interest deductibility for residential landlords is worth $2.9 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury / IRD costings for the phased restoration of interest deductibility for residential rental property over the forecast period; true if approximately $2.9 billion, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: They were 9,000 beneficiaries on whom she said she didn’t get any advice with regard to their losing anything with the changes to the tax system, and yet it was in the regulatory impact statement—the regulatory impact statement that went with the bill, that went to Cabinet, and that she should have read, but, clearly, she did not read it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the regulatory impact statement accompanying the tax bill disclosed that around 9,000 beneficiaries would be worse off, contrary to the Minister's statement that she received no such advice.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement accompanying the Taxation (Budget Measures) Bill 2024; true if it identifies approximately 9,000 benefit recipients as losing from the tax changes, false if no such figure or group appears in it.

veracity.statement: Certainly not with the poorest New Zealanders, and we should be concerned about them because in the last eight, nine months since that Government took office, we’ve seen 20,000 more New Zealanders on benefit, with the backdrop to that being that, apparently, there is a public sector target in place that we’re going to see a 50,000 reduction in beneficiaries in the welfare system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts benefit numbers rose by about 20,000 in the roughly eight to nine months after the Government took office in late 2023, and that a public sector target exists for a 50,000 reduction.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets for main benefit recipients, December 2023 quarter versus June 2024 quarter; true if the increase is approximately 20,000. The target is checkable against the nine Government targets announced in April 2024; true if one is a 50,000 reduction in people on Jobseeker Support.

veracity.statement: Forty-four of our budgeting services across the country are closing down as a direct result of that Government ignoring them and choosing not to invest in their very important service.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 44 budgeting services nationally are closing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD building financial capability contract/provider records or contemporaneous reporting on budgeting service closures in 2024; true if approximately 44 services closed or announced closure, false if the number is materially smaller.

veracity.statement: Now, to their credit, very quietly, that Government has injected, or found, an additional $6 million to support those social services up until Christmas, but that’s not a plan.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Government provided an additional $6 million to food banks and social service providers running to Christmas 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial announcements and MSD funding records for food security / food bank support in mid-2024; true if approximately $6 million was allocated with funding running to December 2024, false if the amount or period differs materially.

veracity.statement: We’re not seeing the investment that we need in terms of their overall expenses; in fact, we’ve seen that taken away with the end to free prescriptions and free and half-price public transport.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Government ended free prescriptions and ended free and half-price public transport concessions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 decisions and Ministry of Health / Ministry of Transport policy records; true if the $5 prescription co-payment was reinstated for the general population and the half-price fare and free under-13 fare schemes were discontinued in 2024, false if either scheme continued.

specificity.statement: I’m not sure whether or not that was who the general public were screaming out for to get support, but they decided that $2.9 billion worth of tax breaks to landlords was the priority.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific beneficiary group and a specific dollar figure attached to a specific tax change — checkable content, though it stops short of naming the mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Certainly not with the poorest New Zealanders, and we should be concerned about them because in the last eight, nine months since that Government took office, we’ve seen 20,000 more New Zealanders on benefit, with the backdrop to that being that, apparently, there is a public sector target in place that we’re going to see a 50,000 reduction in beneficiaries in the welfare system.
focus.explanation: Names a specific outcome (benefit numbers) and a specific named government target, and sets the two against each other. This is accountability on a named commitment, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I haven’t even seen any evidence to support that that works, but, again, all it is is rhetoric and trying to make the numbers look good for the sake of saying, perhaps, that they’ve got more New Zealanders in case management, and yet all they’re doing is giving them a phone call.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages a named operational policy (phone-based case management) and what it delivers, rather than the other party in general, even though the inference offered is weak.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We have seen so much taken away from the poorest New Zealanders in the most recent Budget that that side of the House should, quite frankly, just be ashamed of themselves.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy claim about the Budget's effect on low-income New Zealanders, but it carries no named measure or figure and the weight of the sentence falls on condemning the other side rather than on the substance.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Forty-four of our budgeting services across the country are closing down as a direct result of that Government ignoring them and choosing not to invest in their very important service.
rigor.explanation: Offers a plausible causal chain (services sought funding, received none, are closing) but asserts closure is a 'direct result' of the Budget without ruling out other causes — a gap between the evidence offered and the causal conclusion drawn.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: New Zealanders are interwoven; we are self-reliant. When New Zealanders lose jobs, then everyone suffers—be that local businesses, be that the whole economy—and that’s exactly what we’re seeing now. Now we’re seeing more New Zealanders on benefit as a result of that.
rigor.explanation: The mechanism from public sector redundancies to wider economic harm is plausible, but the conclusion that the rise in benefit numbers is 'a result of that' is asserted rather than shown — no figure links the redundancies to the benefit increase, so the causal step outruns the premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I was saying to one of our social service providers how would those guys on that side of the House like it if every single one of the people who was denied emergency housing in a motel showed up on their street, sleeping outside their houses, with their children, and with the sicknesses that they have, their disabilities, and their mental health issues? How would that side of the House feel? Well, that is what that type of policy decision leads to, and the sad reality is that we have not had the answers from that Minister or from many of the other Ministers with regard to the implications of some of their policy decisions.
rigor.explanation: A bare appeal to emotion: an imagined scenario about how MPs would feel is offered as the support for the conclusion about what the policy 'leads to'. Nothing evidential connects the target to the outcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I haven’t even seen any evidence to support that that works, but, again, all it is is rhetoric and trying to make the numbers look good for the sake of saying, perhaps, that they’ve got more New Zealanders in case management, and yet all they’re doing is giving them a phone call.
rigor.explanation: Argument from absence of evidence — the speaker's own not having seen evidence is treated as showing phone-based case management does not work — compounded by an assumed motive rather than a demonstrated one.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It was a $7 million investment that the previous Labour Government had put into Fire and Emergency New Zealand, and we funded $51.3 million for the replacement, refurbishment, and upgrade of fire stations across the country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two funding figures: $7m for the Kaikōura fire station and $51.3m for a national fire station replacement/upgrade programme under the previous Labour Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget/NZ Upgrade Programme appropriations and FENZ announcements 2020-2023; true if a ~$7m Kaikōura station build and a $51.3m national fire station replacement/refurbishment package are recorded, false if the figures or the programme differ materially.

veracity.statement: He did talk about the large-scale asset purchase programme, but one of the biggest reasons why New Zealand’s inflation went up, similar to other countries in the world, was because of tradeable supply shocks across the world. Members will recall that during COVID, borders were closed across the world, supply chains were restricted, and New Zealand, being at the bottom of the world, found itself in a position where our tradeable inflation was high.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that global tradeable supply shocks were one of the biggest drivers of New Zealand's inflation and that tradeable inflation was high during the COVID period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI decomposition into tradeable and non-tradeable inflation, 2021-2023, and RBNZ Monetary Policy Statements attributing the inflation surge; true if tradeable inflation peaked at or above non-tradeable and official analysis names global supply shocks as a leading cause, false if tradeables contributed only marginally.

veracity.statement: But, as I showed the House today, when adjusted for inflation, there is an increase in operating expenses in Vote Health of only 0.4 percent—0.4 percent—and how do I know this? Because it’s in this document, the Budget Economic and Fiscal Update.
veracity.explanation: Claims Vote Health operating expenditure rises only 0.4 percent in real terms in Budget 2024, sourced to the Budget Economic and Fiscal Update.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Health appropriations in the BEFU/Estimates deflated by the BEFU CPI forecast; true if the real increase is approximately 0.4%, false if the inflation-adjusted change differs materially from that figure.

veracity.statement: Net core Crown debt is higher by $17.1 billion by the 2027-28 fiscal year relative to the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update. There is also an increase of $12 billion in the bond programme over that forecast period.
veracity.explanation: Two comparative fiscal claims: net core Crown debt in 2027-28 is $17.1bn higher in BEFU 2024 than in HYEFU 2023, and the bond programme rises by $12bn over the forecast period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare net core Crown debt track for 2027-28 and the NZDM bond programme totals in BEFU 2024 against HYEFU 2023; true if the differences are approximately $17.1bn and $12bn, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: But outside of the worst year of COVID—2020—a deficit from this Government in this year’s Budget of 3.1 percent of GDP is higher than any other that the Labour Government ran.
veracity.explanation: Claims the forecast 2024-25 OBEGAL deficit of 3.1% of GDP exceeds every Labour-era deficit except the worst COVID year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OBEGAL as a percentage of GDP in the Crown Financial Statements for 2017-18 through 2022-23 compared with the BEFU 2024 forecast for 2024-25; true if only the 2019-20 (or 2020-21) COVID deficit exceeds 3.1%, false if any other Labour-era year also exceeded it.

veracity.statement: Again, our communities are suffering because even though those members promised $250 in tax cuts, what do our poorest New Zealanders get? Those on the minimum wage, basically, get $12.50.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the advertised tax cut was $250 and that a minimum-wage earner receives $12.50 under Budget 2024's tax changes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 tax plan headline figure and the Budget 2024 personal income tax threshold changes applied to a full-time minimum-wage income; true if the headline was $250 a fortnight and the minimum-wage gain is about $12.50 a fortnight, false if either figure is materially different or the periods are not comparable.

veracity.statement: A lot of pensioners still own their homes and their rates have gone up by 19 percent in the last quarter, and they also have to insure those homes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts local authority rates rose 19 percent in the most recent quarter before July 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI local authority rates and payments subgroup for the quarter preceding July 2024; true if the recorded rise is about 19%, false if the quarterly (or annual) increase is materially lower.

specificity.statement: It was a $7 million investment that the previous Labour Government had put into Fire and Emergency New Zealand, and we funded $51.3 million for the replacement, refurbishment, and upgrade of fire stations across the country.
specificity.explanation: Two precise dollar figures attached to a named agency and a named programme; directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But, as I showed the House today, when adjusted for inflation, there is an increase in operating expenses in Vote Health of only 0.4 percent—0.4 percent—and how do I know this? Because it’s in this document, the Budget Economic and Fiscal Update.
specificity.explanation: A single precise, inflation-adjusted percentage tied to a named vote and a named source document.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Net core Crown debt is higher by $17.1 billion by the 2027-28 fiscal year relative to the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update. There is also an increase of $12 billion in the bond programme over that forecast period.
specificity.explanation: Named fiscal aggregates, exact dollar amounts, a named fiscal year and a named baseline document.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It sends out a warning to New Zealanders that in the allowances for health capital spending, there’s a risk to Nelson Hospital, there’s a risk to Dunedin Hospital, there’s a risk to Whangārei Hospital, and guess how much this Government has put aside as a contingency just in case those hospital builds are too expensive!
specificity.explanation: Names three specific hospital projects and the budget line at issue, though the risk itself is not quantified in this sentence.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Again, our communities are suffering because even though those members promised $250 in tax cuts, what do our poorest New Zealanders get? Those on the minimum wage, basically, get $12.50.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete dollar figures tied to a named policy and an identified group of earners.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Was it wasteful spending to spend $7 million on his local Kaikōura Fire Station? That was not what he was saying when he was helping me cut the ribbon at the Kaikōura Fire Station, and there are 26 fire stations across the country that were upgraded because of the Labour Government’s spending on infrastructure.
civility.explanation: Points at a named member's inconsistency, which edges toward the person, but the charge is anchored to his own words and a specific project rather than to his character.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, I know that some members on the other side of the House don’t like to read, so, please, indulge me so that I can help summarise some of the numbers that are in this Budget Economic and Fiscal Update.
civility.explanation: Condescending jibe at the literacy and diligence of other members; attacks their competence rather than any argument.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Was it wasteful spending to spend $7 million on his local Kaikōura Fire Station? That was not what he was saying when he was helping me cut the ribbon at the Kaikōura Fire Station, and there are 26 fire stations across the country that were upgraded because of the Labour Government’s spending on infrastructure.
focus.explanation: Names a specific project, a specific dollar figure and a count of upgraded stations; this is accountability for a spending characterisation, not content-free party-bashing.

focus.statement: Now, I know that some members on the other side of the House don’t like to read, so, please, indulge me so that I can help summarise some of the numbers that are in this Budget Economic and Fiscal Update.
focus.explanation: The sentence's content is entirely a characterisation of the other side; no policy, figure or measure is engaged within it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What is the driver of these larger amounts of debt—again, more than Labour borrowed? More debt. What is the cause of it? It’s because this Government doesn’t have enough money to keep the lights on. That is why this Government has had to borrow for tax cuts as well, because if you look at the income tax component—tax cuts—it is just under $10 billion.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the Budget's borrowing and tax package, with figures, rather than on the other party's character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It sends out a warning to New Zealanders that in the allowances for health capital spending, there’s a risk to Nelson Hospital, there’s a risk to Dunedin Hospital, there’s a risk to Whangārei Hospital, and guess how much this Government has put aside as a contingency just in case those hospital builds are too expensive!
focus.explanation: Engages the health capital allowance and named projects — scrutiny of a specific budget decision.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: He did talk about the large-scale asset purchase programme, but one of the biggest reasons why New Zealand’s inflation went up, similar to other countries in the world, was because of tradeable supply shocks across the world. Members will recall that during COVID, borders were closed across the world, supply chains were restricted, and New Zealand, being at the bottom of the world, found itself in a position where our tradeable inflation was high.
rigor.explanation: A causal argument with stated mechanism (closed borders, restricted supply chains, distance) supporting the conclusion that tradeables drove inflation; the inference is coherent though it asserts rather than weighs the relative contribution against the monetary explanation raised by the other member.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What is the driver of these larger amounts of debt—again, more than Labour borrowed? More debt. What is the cause of it? It’s because this Government doesn’t have enough money to keep the lights on. That is why this Government has had to borrow for tax cuts as well, because if you look at the income tax component—tax cuts—it is just under $10 billion.
rigor.explanation: Infers a specific causal attribution — that the extra borrowing is for the tax cuts — from the co-existence of higher debt and a ~$10bn tax package; this is a post hoc attribution, since a higher bond programme does not by itself identify which spending it funds.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: The Budget Economic and Fiscal Update shows unemployment is increasing. Poverty will increase. Child poverty will increase.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that poverty and specifically child poverty will rise following Budget 2024.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Child Poverty Statistics releases for the years ended June 2025 and June 2026; true if the material hardship rate or a primary child poverty measure rises outside sampling error relative to the year ended June 2024, false if the measures are flat or fall.

veracity.statement: We’ve had good news just recently with the inflation rate coming in under expectation, at 3.3 percent, and while our tradable inflation is down significantly, non-tradable inflation is pretty sticky.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the most recent annual CPI inflation print was 3.3 percent, below market expectation, with tradables inflation falling sharply and non-tradables inflation remaining elevated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index release for the June 2024 quarter: true if annual CPI inflation is 3.3% and the tradables component fell materially more than the non-tradables component; false if the annual rate differs materially or the tradables/non-tradables split runs the other way.

veracity.statement: Those two things cancelled one another out, if the OCR rise did, in fact, cancel it out at all, but it may not have, and when we’ve asked the Reserve Bank Governor why he continued to do that, rather than to shut it off—as most logical people would do—he said that he had a moral obligation to the banks.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Reserve Bank Governor, questioned in select committee about keeping the Funding for Lending Programme open while raising the OCR, answered that he had a moral obligation to the banks.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Transcript/Hansard record of Finance and Expenditure Committee hearings with the Reserve Bank Governor (2022–2024): true if he gave an answer to that effect about an obligation or commitment to the banks regarding the Funding for Lending Programme; false if no such evidence exists or his stated reason was materially different.

veracity.statement: In fact, a full-time worker now pays 5 percent more than they did 10 years ago, which is a huge amount of extra tax, and that wasteful spending is a really good place where the Minister of Finance and Cabinet members went through an exercise of finding savings.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that fiscal drag has raised a full-time worker's tax burden by 5 percent (apparently 5 percentage points of effective tax rate) over the decade to 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD fiscal drag analysis of the average effective tax rate on the average full-time wage, 2014 compared with 2024: true if the increase is about 5 percentage points (or 5% of income); false if materially smaller or larger.

veracity.statement: They’ve found 240 savings initiatives and have driven down the expenditure in Government departments.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Budget 2024 savings exercise identified 240 distinct savings initiatives and reduced departmental expenditure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents (Treasury savings summary / Minister of Finance Budget speech and annexes): true if the published count of savings initiatives is 240 and departmental baselines were reduced; false if the published count differs materially.

veracity.statement: The part that failed was overdue for replacement by months.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the component whose failure disabled the Kaitaki in Cook Strait in January 2023 was past its scheduled replacement date by a matter of months.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: TAIC (Transport Accident Investigation Commission) / Maritime NZ report into the Kaitaki propulsion failure of 28 January 2023: true if the report finds the failed component was past its scheduled maintenance or replacement interval by months; false if it was within its interval or the overrun was not of that order.

veracity.statement: That’s not true. That is absolutely not true, because even if it had gone ahead, those ships—the new ones—wouldn’t have been delivered until 2026, and they wouldn’t have been able to berth and operate, because that landside work wouldn’t have been completed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the iReX project the new ferries were not scheduled for delivery until 2026, and that the associated landside/terminal infrastructure would not have been complete by then.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: KiwiRail/Treasury iReX project documentation and the Ministerial Advisory Group material on ferry replacement: true if contracted delivery of the new vessels was scheduled for 2026 with landside works scheduled to complete later; false if delivery was scheduled earlier or the terminals were due to be ready on arrival.

veracity.statement: That is just poor management—out-and-out poor management—and I would point out that the average age of those KiwiRail ships is between 26 and 29 years old, and we’ve just retired the Hercules, which were 60 years old. So it’s completely untrue that those ships are too old and not fit for purpose.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the KiwiRail Interislander vessels average between 26 and 29 years of age, and that the recently retired RNZAF Hercules were 60 years old.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Build years of the Interislander fleet (Kaitaki, Aratere, Kaiarahi) against 2024, and the 1965 in-service date of the RNZAF C-130H fleet retired in 2024: true if the vessel ages fall in the 26–29 range and the Hercules were about 60 years old; false if either is materially off.

veracity.statement: There’s a significant lack of snow in the back country, which is something we all should be concerned about because that feeds into the hydro lakes, and we already know that just recently, Meridian Energy has asked Tīwai Point to reduce their electricity take because of the lower lake levels.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Meridian Energy recently requested the Tiwai Point aluminium smelter to reduce its electricity consumption owing to low hydro lake storage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Meridian Energy and NZAS market announcements / media reports from mid-2024: true if Meridian invoked demand response at Tiwai Point citing low hydro storage in the period before 23 July 2024; false if no such request was made.

rigor.statement: Now, COVID absolutely needed a response, and I don’t think anyone disagrees with that, but having that money go out the door in the way it did and not looking for value for money actually drove inflation much higher than it needed to be.
rigor.explanation: The cited premise is an Auditor-General report on the speed of infrastructure investment decisions and weak value-for-money testing; the conclusion drawn is a quantitative causal one about the inflation rate. Nothing offered bridges process criticism to inflation magnitude, and no counterfactual or monetary channel is specified — a real gap between evidence and conclusion, though the inference direction is not absurd.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, we have been criticised for that, but I’ve been out and about amongst my constituents—as I’m sure other members have during the recess—and I can tell you that businesses are driving costs down themselves and having to let staff go, because they are under pressure. That’s what you do when you take undertake responsible budgeting, and that is what our Government has done.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote (conversations with constituents) combined with a false analogy: that private firms cut costs under commercial pressure does not establish that the same response is correct or 'responsible' for a government, whose fiscal position and counter-cyclical role differ. The conclusion rests entirely on the analogy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s not true. That is absolutely not true, because even if it had gone ahead, those ships—the new ones—wouldn’t have been delivered until 2026, and they wouldn’t have been able to berth and operate, because that landside work wouldn’t have been completed.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts the claim that cancelling iReX caused the current ferry failures by showing the replacement ships could not have been in service yet — a valid counterfactual: a project whose assets arrive after the failures cannot have prevented them. Conclusion follows from the timeline premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is just poor management—out-and-out poor management—and I would point out that the average age of those KiwiRail ships is between 26 and 29 years old, and we’ve just retired the Hercules, which were 60 years old. So it’s completely untrue that those ships are too old and not fit for purpose.
rigor.explanation: Faulty analogy: that RNZAF C-130 aircraft remained in service at 60 years does not establish that 26–29-year-old roll-on/roll-off ferries in Cook Strait service are fit for purpose — different asset classes, duty cycles and maintenance regimes. The conclusion is also in tension with his own concession in the following sentence that the ships need replacing.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, COVID absolutely needed a response, and I don’t think anyone disagrees with that, but having that money go out the door in the way it did and not looking for value for money actually drove inflation much higher than it needed to be.
focus.explanation: Engages fiscal policy directly — COVID spending, value-for-money testing, and the inflation consequence — rather than characterising the opposing party. A named report and a named mechanism are at issue.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, what about his moral obligation to the taxpayer, because when you’re paying your mortgage rate every month, just spare a moment to take a thought about the Reserve Bank Governor actually having a moral obligation to the banks, which, in his view, was higher than the moral obligation to the taxpayer.
civility.explanation: Criticism of a named individual's decision that shades into imputing misplaced moral priorities — that he valued banks above taxpayers — and invites the public to resent him personally while paying their mortgage. Pointed and edging onto the person rather than confined to the policy choice, but short of an insult.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, we have been criticised for that, but I’ve been out and about amongst my constituents—as I’m sure other members have during the recess—and I can tell you that businesses are driving costs down themselves and having to let staff go, because they are under pressure. That’s what you do when you take undertake responsible budgeting, and that is what our Government has done.
specificity.explanation: Defends the savings programme with no figure, no named saving and no measure of the business conditions described — 'driving costs down', 'under pressure', 'responsible budgeting' are unquantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That is just poor management—out-and-out poor management—and I would point out that the average age of those KiwiRail ships is between 26 and 29 years old, and we’ve just retired the Hercules, which were 60 years old. So it’s completely untrue that those ships are too old and not fit for purpose.
specificity.explanation: Carries checkable detail — fleet ages given as a range, a named comparator asset and its age — enough for someone to verify or rebut, though no maintenance figures or costs are supplied.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We will be looking into the primary production side of it as well—rural lending—and it will be something that will tie in nicely with the final draft of the Commerce Commission’s market study which will be released soon.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Commerce Commission will release the final report of its banking market study in the near future.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Commerce Commission publications: true if the final report of the personal banking services market study is published within roughly six months of 23 July 2024; false if publication slips beyond that.

specificity.statement: Amongst a slash-and-burn Budget, where almost every other facet of our public services has been cut, there’s one area that has gotten a massive amount of investment, and that’s the Budget line that has $1.9 billion going into increasing Vote Corrections, with a large chunk of money going towards a mega-prison at Waikeria.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific Budget vote, a dollar figure and a named capital project (Waikeria); someone could go and check the appropriation.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If we look at the areas that the Government has made cuts to within this Budget, we can see that there’s $1.81 billion worth of cuts within the housing space, including scrapping the Homelessness Action Plan, making it easier to evict people from emergency housing and from public housing, and reducing the funding for rangatahi transitional housing.
specificity.explanation: Gives a total figure and itemises named programmes affected, so the claim is checkable against the Budget documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I ask that we be a bit more creative in our response to the harm that is created in our communities and that we invest in those things that we know are the drivers of crime, instead of continually focusing on bottom-of-the-cliff approaches.
specificity.explanation: A direction of travel with no named programme, mechanism, amount or timeframe; 'be more creative' and 'invest in the drivers' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Cuts to Vote Environment have totalled $617 million over the next four years, and these are across significant programmes of work like cutting $20 million from the indigenous biodiversity fund or cutting $47 million from the Freshwater Improvement Fund.
specificity.explanation: A four-year total plus two itemised, named fund reductions with figures — fully checkable against the Budget.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Amongst a slash-and-burn Budget, where almost every other facet of our public services has been cut, there’s one area that has gotten a massive amount of investment, and that’s the Budget line that has $1.9 billion going into increasing Vote Corrections, with a large chunk of money going towards a mega-prison at Waikeria.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Budget 2024 allocated $1.9 billion of new funding to Vote Corrections, a large part of it for expansion of Waikeria prison.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Corrections appropriations and the Corrections Budget 2024 package summary; true if new Corrections funding of approximately $1.9b is recorded with a substantial capital tranche for Waikeria expansion, false if the figure or the Waikeria allocation is materially different.

veracity.statement: We have a Government that says that they care about victims, but if they did, they would not have cut $25 million tagged for improving outcomes for the victims of crime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Budget 2024 cut $25 million of funding tagged for improving outcomes for victims of crime.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Justice / Vote Courts appropriations and the Ministry of Justice Budget documents for victims-of-crime initiatives; true if an approximately $25m reduction to victim-tagged funding is recorded, false if no such reduction appears or the amount is materially different.

veracity.statement: If we look at the areas that the Government has made cuts to within this Budget, we can see that there’s $1.81 billion worth of cuts within the housing space, including scrapping the Homelessness Action Plan, making it easier to evict people from emergency housing and from public housing, and reducing the funding for rangatahi transitional housing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts $1.81 billion of housing-related cuts in Budget 2024, including the ending of the Homelessness Action Plan and reduced rangatahi transitional housing funding.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Housing and Urban Development appropriations and savings tables; true if reductions summing to approximately $1.81b across housing appropriations (including the Homelessness Action Plan and rangatahi transitional housing lines) are recorded, false if the total or the named programme changes are materially different.

veracity.statement: We’re building jails and building prisons at a rate that matches the United States; in fact, Aotearoa now has one of the highest rates of imprisonment in the world.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's imprisonment rate is among the highest internationally and that its rate of prison building matches that of the United States.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: World Prison Brief / Institute for Crime & Justice Policy Research imprisonment rates per 100,000 for 2024; true if New Zealand ranks in the top decile of countries, false if it sits near or below the middle of the international distribution (note the US rate is roughly 3-4x New Zealand's).

veracity.statement: I knew that the environment wasn’t really a priority for this Government when they left all the environment Ministers out of Cabinet and scrapped really early on the Natural and Built Environment Act and the Spatial Planning Act.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that every environment-related Minister was excluded from Cabinet on the Government's formation, and that the Natural and Built Environment Act and Spatial Planning Act were repealed early in the term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Cabinet and ministerial list published in November 2023 (whether the Minister for the Environment and Minister of Conservation held Cabinet rank) and the enactment record for the Natural and Built Environment Act Repeal and Interim Fast-track Consenting Act; true if no environment portfolio holder sat in Cabinet and both Acts were repealed, false if any environment Minister was inside Cabinet.

veracity.statement: Cuts to Vote Environment have totalled $617 million over the next four years, and these are across significant programmes of work like cutting $20 million from the indigenous biodiversity fund or cutting $47 million from the Freshwater Improvement Fund.
veracity.explanation: Asserts $617m of savings taken from Vote Environment over the forecast period, including $20m from the indigenous biodiversity fund and $47m from the Freshwater Improvement Fund.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Environment estimates and the savings/reprioritisation tables; true if the four-year reductions total approximately $617m and the two named funds show reductions of about $20m and $47m, false if the totals or the named lines are materially different.

veracity.statement: First of all, the Ministry for the Environment has suffered a funding cut of $65 million, and that’s a crippling 39 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $65 million reduction to the Ministry for the Environment's funding, amounting to 39 percent of the relevant baseline.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Environment departmental output appropriations for the Ministry for the Environment compared with 2023/24 baselines; true if the reduction is approximately $65m and equals about 39 percent of the stated baseline, false if either figure is materially different or the percentage is computed off a baseline that does not support it.

veracity.statement: They manage a third of the country on a meagre, shoestring budget and they’ve been awarded in this Budget a $48 million cut, which will have very real implications for their ability to carry out their role.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Department of Conservation administers about a third of New Zealand's land area and received a $48 million funding reduction in Budget 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DOC's published estimate of public conservation land as a share of New Zealand's land area, and Budget 2024 Vote Conservation savings; true if DOC-administered land is around one third of the country and Vote Conservation savings total approximately $48m, false if either is materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, we got to ask the Minister that during scrutiny, and she believes that the balance had swung too far towards the environment, and what was really concerning about that was that she couldn’t point to any evidence within her own ministry that actually informed her of that view.
veracity.explanation: Reports what the Minister said at a Budget scrutiny hearing — that the balance had swung too far towards the environment — and that she cited no ministry evidence for that view when asked.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The transcript or recording of the 2024 Budget scrutiny week hearing of the Environment Committee with the Minister for the Environment; true if the Minister expressed that view and did not identify supporting ministry evidence when questioned, false if she did not say it or did cite ministry advice.

focus.statement: But this Government and its Budget isn’t motivated by reducing harm in communities; they’re motivated by looking like they’re doing something.
focus.explanation: Characterises the Government's motives rather than engaging any mechanism, cost or outcome; strip out the claim about what the other side is 'really' after and no policy content remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s a real privilege to be able to rise tonight to speak to the very real implications of this Budget, because here’s the thing: the Government members purport to be so laser-focused on their outdated, very narrow view of the economy that they fail to see te ngahere for te rākau, or the wood for the trees.
focus.explanation: Frames the debate around what Government members are like and how they see the world rather than naming a measure, figure or outcome; the policy content arrives only in later passages.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We have a Government that says that they care about victims, but if they did, they would not have cut $25 million tagged for improving outcomes for the victims of crime.
rigor.explanation: A real inference from a named funding decision to a claimed inconsistency, but it treats one appropriation line as decisive on the whole question of concern for victims — a genuine gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If prisons worked, this Government wouldn’t be increasing the budget for prisons by $2 billion, and if prisons worked, their populations wouldn’t keep rising year on year.
rigor.explanation: Denying the antecedent / affirming the consequent: rising spending and rising muster are consistent with several explanations (crime rates, sentencing law, policy choice) and do not on their own establish that imprisonment fails to achieve its objectives.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, those are valid needs, but you don’t need to scrap our entire environmental framework in order to achieve them.
rigor.explanation: Rejects a trade-off between housing/infrastructure and environmental protection by bare assertion, and does so against an overstated version of the Government's position ('scrap our entire environmental framework') — nothing is offered to show the two goals are compatible at the scale claimed.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As of last year, we have to fix up our ransacked and damaged home, and I’m proud of the fact that there’s a massive focus in our first Budget as a Government—and an awesome one, if I may add—and I’d like to highlight a few focuses that really resonate with my neighbours in Takanini South and East Auckland: tax relief, education, health, infrastructure, and law and order.
focus.explanation: Names five genuine policy areas of the Budget, but the weight of the sentence is the 'ransacked home' framing of the previous government rather than any mechanism, figure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Finally, after being promised twice by the former Government that Mill Road will be built and its reneging on that promise, we are getting back to work on Mill Road.
focus.explanation: Names a specific project (Mill Road) and a specific outcome (promised, then cancelled, now restarted) — accountability on a named policy rather than party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That’s the reality that we face in South Auckland, and it angers me, actually, when other people make out as if our Government is just trying to please some type of vague group. No, we’re addressing issues that are the reality in South Auckland.
focus.explanation: A real policy point about the justification for the law-and-order investment, but framed as a rebuttal to unnamed critics' characterisation of the Government rather than to a named policy or figure.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In eight days—yes, that’s right; eight days—on 31 July, 3.5 million New Zealanders are set to receive tax relief for the first time in years.
specificity.explanation: Carries a date (31 July), a beneficiary count (3.5 million) and a named policy change; fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re extending the eligibility for the independent earner tax credit, we’re increasing the in-work tax credit, we’re lifting the minimum family tax credit, and we’re introducing the FamilyBoost payment.
specificity.explanation: Four named, identifiable mechanisms, but no amounts, thresholds or dates attached to any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re committing, despite the ransacked home that we have to fix up, $2.9 billion to the education sector over the next four years.
specificity.explanation: A named sum and a stated period for a named sector.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s going to cater for 600 students from years 1 to 6, and construction starts later this year.
specificity.explanation: Roll size, year levels and a construction start window for a specific announced school.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Despite the ransacked home, our health sector will also get a significant boost of more than $16 billion allocated to health across the next three Budgets.
specificity.explanation: Gives a figure and a horizon, but 'across the next three Budgets' leaves the annual profile and destination unstated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As part of our commitment to restoring safety, we’re going to be investing $651 million over the next four years in critical support for our amazing, exceptional police force.
specificity.explanation: A named sum over a stated period directed at a named agency.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In eight days—yes, that’s right; eight days—on 31 July, 3.5 million New Zealanders are set to receive tax relief for the first time in years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's tax package takes effect on 31 July 2024 and that approximately 3.5 million New Zealanders receive relief from it, and that no comparable relief has occurred for years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 / Inland Revenue documentation on the personal income tax threshold changes: true if the changes commenced 31 July 2024 and official costings state roughly 3.5 million taxpayers benefit; false if the commencement date differs materially or the official beneficiary figure is materially different from 3.5 million.

veracity.statement: We’re committing, despite the ransacked home that we have to fix up, $2.9 billion to the education sector over the next four years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Budget 2024 allocates $2.9 billion to education over the following four years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Education summary / Treasury Budget-at-a-glance: true if the announced education package is approximately $2.9 billion over four years; false if the headline operating and capital figure for education differs materially.

veracity.statement: Despite the ransacked home, our health sector will also get a significant boost of more than $16 billion allocated to health across the next three Budgets.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that health is allocated more than $16 billion spread over three Budget cycles from Budget 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Health documents and the Government's announced three-year health funding uplift: true if the stated allocation exceeds $16 billion across three Budgets; false if the official figure is materially below that.

veracity.statement: Despite the broken, ransacked home, $2.68 billion will be invested into our roads, rail, and public transport.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Budget 2024 provides $2.68 billion for roads, rail and public transport.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Transport / transport package announcement: true if the headline transport investment figure is approximately $2.68 billion; false if the official figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Finally, after being promised twice by the former Government that Mill Road will be built and its reneging on that promise, we are getting back to work on Mill Road.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Labour-led Government committed to building Mill Road on two occasions and subsequently withdrew that commitment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Upgrade Programme announcements (2020) and subsequent Waka Kotahi/Government decisions on Mill Road up to 2023: true if there are two distinct government commitments to build Mill Road followed by cancellation or indefinite deferral; false if there was only one commitment, or if it was never withdrawn.

veracity.statement: As part of our commitment to restoring safety, we’re going to be investing $651 million over the next four years in critical support for our amazing, exceptional police force.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Budget 2024 allocates $651 million over four years to police.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Police documents: true if the announced police package is approximately $651 million over four years; false if the official figure is materially different.

rigor.statement: That’s the reality that we face in South Auckland, and it angers me, actually, when other people make out as if our Government is just trying to please some type of vague group. No, we’re addressing issues that are the reality in South Auckland.
rigor.explanation: The support offered for the conclusion that the law-and-order spending addresses a real problem is two individual retail crime anecdotes — an appeal to anecdote, with no aggregate evidence connecting them to the scale of the problem or the effectiveness of the spend.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We have the highest rental prices in New Zealand, and that is crazy for a city of 160,000 people that we have the highest rental prices.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Tauranga has the highest rental prices of anywhere in New Zealand as at mid-2024, and that its population is about 160,000.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tenancy Services (MBIE) bond-lodgement median weekly rent, and/or Trade Me Rental Price Index, by main urban area for mid-2024: true if Tauranga records the highest median weekly rent of NZ urban areas; false if another centre (e.g. Queenstown, Auckland, Wellington) is higher.

veracity.statement: We need to get housing right, and we look at where the previous Government was, where we saw homelessness up by 400 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that homelessness rose by 400 percent (a fivefold increase, or fourfold as he restates it) under the 2017–2023 Labour government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ severe housing deprivation estimates and/or MSD emergency housing and transitional housing placement data for 2017 vs 2023: true if the measure cited rose by approximately 400 percent over that period; false if the increase is materially smaller on the standard homelessness measures.

veracity.statement: We saw rents increase by $170 a week.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that weekly rents rose by $170 over the term of the previous government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE bond-lodgement national median weekly rent, comparing late 2017 with late 2023: true if the increase is approximately $170 per week; false if materially different.

veracity.statement: We export, and it was 44 percent of New Zealand’s goods that were leaving out of the Port of Tauranga, if I’m correct on that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 44 percent of New Zealand's exported goods leave through the Port of Tauranga.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Port of Tauranga annual report and Stats NZ / Ministry of Transport freight statistics on export volumes by port: true if Tauranga's share of New Zealand export cargo is approximately 44 percent; false if materially different on the standard volume or TEU measure.

veracity.statement: Then they could be $75 a week better off as part of our FamilyBoost policy.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the FamilyBoost childcare payment is worth up to $75 a week to a family.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IRD FamilyBoost scheme rules as legislated in 2024: true if the maximum rebate is $75 per week (25 percent of childcare costs up to a $300 weekly cap); false if the maximum differs.

veracity.statement: This is a happy Budget, this is a good Budget, and when they get their tax cut and they go and spend it on their food, they will see that food prices have only gone up—wait for it—0.2 percent in the last year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that food prices rose 0.2 percent in the year to the most recent release before 23 July 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Food Price Index, annual percentage change for the month most recently released as at July 2024 (June 2024): true if the annual increase is 0.2 percent; false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Inflation is down to 3.3 percent. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand predicted 3.6 percent, and we’ve got it at 3.3 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that annual CPI inflation for the June 2024 quarter was 3.3 percent and that the Reserve Bank had forecast 3.6 percent for that quarter.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI release for the June 2024 quarter (annual rate) and the RBNZ May 2024 Monetary Policy Statement forecast track for June 2024 annual CPI: true if the outturn is 3.3 percent and the RBNZ forecast was 3.6 percent; false if either figure differs materially.

civility.statement: That is unbelievable from a Government that talked about how much they care for the poor and vulnerable. Homelessness increased four-fold—shameful, very shameful.
civility.explanation: Harsh condemnation of a previous government's record, with a hint of imputed hypocrisy, but aimed at a government rather than any individual member; no personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is unbelievable from a Government that talked about how much they care for the poor and vulnerable. Homelessness increased four-fold—shameful, very shameful.
focus.explanation: Names a specific outcome (homelessness levels) under a named government — legitimate scrutiny of a record rather than content-free party-bashing, though the 'they said they cared' framing adds some party colouring.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We saw a Government that ignored the advice of Treasury around what to do with interest rate deductions. Where did that go? They said it would increase rental prices; that’s exactly what it did.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages a named policy (removal of interest deductibility for landlords), the official advice on it, and its claimed effect on rents.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We saw a Government that ignored the advice of Treasury around what to do with interest rate deductions. Where did that go? They said it would increase rental prices; that’s exactly what it did.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: rents rose after the policy, so the policy caused the rise. No attempt to separate the deductibility change from interest rates, migration or supply, which were operating on rents over the same period.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I mean, to put it the other way around, it might be like me going to the Governor-General in a couple of years’ time and saying, “The previous lot was so bad, let’s not give democracy to the Kiwis. Let’s make sure we keep National in power.” That would be completely unacceptable and that was unacceptable, and Tauranga has democracy, so that is fantastic.
rigor.explanation: A reductio by analogy against the proposed hybrid governance model for Tauranga. The analogy is strained — appointed commissioners after a council failure is not equivalent to a governing party cancelling a general election to retain power — so the conclusion outruns what the comparison establishes.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We drove over the Kaimais and I was looking for potholes and I couldn’t spot one, and maybe that’s because our Government is taking roads seriously because we believe they are the best way to deliver people and goods efficiently and safely around the country and around the Bay of Plenty and around Tauranga.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote: one drive with no potholes observed is offered as evidence that the government's roading approach is working. A single observation over one stretch of highway supports nothing about national road condition, and no data is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re going to ask councils, such as the newly elected council in Tauranga, to deliver 30 years’ worth of houses. They can go out, they can go up; they need to make it happen.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete requirement (30 years of housing capacity) and who it falls on, but gives no mechanism, no enforcement, no numbers of dwellings and no timeframe for the requirement taking effect.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There were good announcements recently from Minister Chris Penk around building and construction, allowing competition in building materials, and looking at things that are adding $20,000 to $50,000 worth of cost and asking questions as to whether that is necessary.
specificity.explanation: Names the responsible Minister, the mechanism (opening up building-materials competition) and a dollar range for the cost at issue, though the announcements themselves and the timing are not identified.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Good news too, because in a few days’ time, they are going to find out that the average household in New Zealand and in Tauranga is $102 a fortnight better off—how good?
divination.explanation: Forecasts that when the Budget 2024 personal income tax changes take effect at the end of July 2024, the average New Zealand household will be $102 a fortnight better off.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD Budget 2024 tax package distributional analysis of the tax changes effective 31 July 2024: true if the average household gain is approximately $102 per fortnight; false if the average household gain is materially below that (for example if $102 applies only to households with children on average incomes).

civility.statement: What a sad, sad speech—what a sad, sad speech.
civility.explanation: Opens by dismissing the previous member's contribution with mocking repetition rather than engaging anything in it — sneering, though stopping short of a direct personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We saw Minister Goldsmith today filling in for the Māori development Minister, and, as we know, he’s a little bit confused too about whether he’s a Māori or a Pākehā—and we’ve seen that released by the National Party in the past.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe about another member's identity and self-understanding; it addresses nothing about the Budget and targets the man rather than any argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We’ve got a Minister over there who knows nothing about things Māori and, sadly, we’ve got a Minister for Māori Development having to listen to people like him.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on another member's competence and knowledge, plus the dismissive 'people like him'; nothing in it engages a policy argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think this is a shameful Budget. The Minister for Children should be ashamed.
civility.explanation: Moves from condemning the Budget — which would be fully civil — to a moral judgement on the Minister personally ('should be ashamed'), which lands on the person rather than the decision.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s a little bit delusional, this Government because they waffle on about how much they have done for Māori.
focus.explanation: Characterises the governing parties in general ('delusional', 'waffle on') rather than naming a measure, figure or outcome; the only policy anchor is a vague gesture at claims about Māori.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government has chosen to prioritise tax breaks for landlords over our most vulnerable children and their families.
focus.explanation: Names an identifiable policy choice (landlord tax changes set against child-focused spending), so it is more than party-bashing, but the weight is on framing rather than mechanism, cost or affected group.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s a shocking Budget because we’re talking about a $96.7 million cut in terms of Māori development.
specificity.explanation: Names a single precise figure attached to a named area of spending, which anyone could look up in the Budget documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That has resulted in 419 jobs being cut from Oranga Tamariki. That is about 9 percent of the organisation, but that is 25 to 30 percent of the back office.
specificity.explanation: An exact headcount plus two proportions tied to a named agency and a named restructure — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They are investing over $5 million into a pilot programme for 10 young people to send them to a boot camp experiment which evidence shows has failed in the past.
specificity.explanation: Gives a spend figure and a participant count for a named programme, though the 'evidence shows' half carries no citation.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s a shocking Budget because we’re talking about a $96.7 million cut in terms of Māori development.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Budget 2024 reduced Māori development spending by $96.7 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Māori Development / Estimates of Appropriations and the associated savings schedule; true if the total identified reductions to Māori development appropriations total approximately $96.7 million, false if the figure is materially different or does not correspond to any published savings total.

veracity.statement: We put $130 million into Māori broadcasting in the previous three years—$130 million.
veracity.explanation: Claims the previous Labour government appropriated $130 million to Māori broadcasting over its final three years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Vote Māori Development / Vote Arts, Culture and Heritage appropriations for Whakaata Māori and Te Māngai Pāho, Budgets 2020–2023; true if new or additional Māori broadcasting funding over those years sums to approximately $130 million, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: In the last four years, we delivered a billion dollars a year back in terms of Māori—a billion dollars right across the spectrum—in terms of employment and in terms of Māori health.
veracity.explanation: Claims the previous government delivered about $1 billion per year in Māori-directed spending across employment, health and other areas over four years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2020–2023 Māori-specific packages as totalled in Treasury Budget documents and Te Puni Kōkiri reporting; true if annual Māori-targeted new spending averaged roughly $1 billion, false if the total across the four years is materially below $4 billion.

veracity.statement: It is a shocking Budget for Māori, so much so now that in Māori broadcasting, we’ve got Māori Television, or Whakaata Māori, announcing that they are going to be in deficit for the next two years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Whakaata Māori has publicly announced it will run a deficit for the next two financial years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Whakaata Māori public statements and annual report / statement of performance expectations for 2024/25 and 2025/26; true if the broadcaster announced forecast deficits for two consecutive years around July 2024, false if no such announcement was made.

veracity.statement: That has resulted in 419 jobs being cut from Oranga Tamariki. That is about 9 percent of the organisation, but that is 25 to 30 percent of the back office.
veracity.explanation: Asserts 419 roles were cut at Oranga Tamariki, equal to about 9 percent of all staff and 25–30 percent of back-office staff.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki restructure decision documents and 2024 annual report staffing figures; true if the confirmed reduction is approximately 419 positions and the proportions match total and corporate headcount, false if the confirmed number or proportions differ materially.

veracity.statement: Now, in scrutiny week, it was very clear: they said that this would be sorted by 1 July. Well, it is 23 July and this has still not been sorted.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Oranga Tamariki told a select committee during scrutiny week that community provider contracts would be resolved by 1 July, and that as at 23 July 2024 they had not been.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Social Services and Community Committee scrutiny week transcript/evidence for Oranga Tamariki 2024, plus contemporaneous reporting on unresolved provider contracts in late July 2024; true if the 1 July commitment was given and contracts remained unconfirmed at 23 July, false if no such commitment was made or contracts had been settled.

veracity.statement: They are investing over $5 million into a pilot programme for 10 young people to send them to a boot camp experiment which evidence shows has failed in the past.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the military-style academy pilot costs over $5 million and covers 10 participants.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 youth justice appropriation documents and Oranga Tamariki material on the military-style academy pilot; true if the pilot's funding exceeds $5 million and the initial cohort is 10 young people, false if the funded amount or cohort size is materially different.

rigor.statement: He has failed us and this Government has failed us, because there’s two types of strategies necessary for Māori. You, obviously, have to have a universal one, but you must also have a by Māori, for Māori one, and now we’ve got a Minister who has actually delivered us a Māori budget that is in absolute deficit.
rigor.explanation: A real inference — a stated premise (two strategies are required) plus evidence of cuts earlier in the speech — but the leap from 'the by-Māori stream was cut' to 'the Minister has failed us' is asserted rather than shown, and 'absolute deficit' does the work a comparison should.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is an expensive experiment, and that money could be better spent in providers that I visited during the recess like Kirikiriroa Family Services Trust or Ko Wai Au in Te Awamutu, who said that they could do better work with our rangatahi and get better outcomes than a boot camp experiment that this Government is hell-bent on starting on Monday.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the money would be better spent elsewhere rests on an appeal to anecdote — two providers' own assurances about their own effectiveness, offered without outcome data.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It is an expensive experiment, and that money could be better spent in providers that I visited during the recess like Kirikiriroa Family Services Trust or Ko Wai Au in Te Awamutu, who said that they could do better work with our rangatahi and get better outcomes than a boot camp experiment that this Government is hell-bent on starting on Monday.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Government's military-style academy (boot camp) pilot will begin on the Monday following 23 July 2024.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki / Ministerial announcements and news reporting on the military-style academy pilot start date; true if the pilot commenced on or about 29 July 2024, false if it began later or was deferred.

veracity.statement: Police got $107.7 million less than they did in the previous Budget.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Budget 2024's police appropriation was $107.7 million lower than the previous Budget's.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare Vote Police appropriations in Budget 2024 Estimates with the 2023 Budget/Supplementary Estimates; true if the stated year-on-year reduction is approximately $107.7 million on a comparable basis, false if the appropriation rose or the gap is materially different.

veracity.statement: Most scary to me is the fact that police have now advised the Minister of Police that they are so stretched on resources that they will no longer be attending family violence call-outs, even though partner agencies are not prepared to take up that slack and that there is a risk associated with this change in direction that may result in loss of life if risk isn’t adequately calculated.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that NZ Police have formally advised the Minister they will cease attending family violence call-outs because of resourcing, and that partner agencies will not absorb the work.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police briefings/advice to the Minister of Police (and Police public statements) from 2024 on attendance at family harm call-outs; true if Police advised a withdrawal from attending family violence call-outs on resourcing grounds, false if the advice concerned a different call-out category or no such withdrawal was advised.

veracity.statement: My concern is that with 124 fewer police since this Government came into power, all that is happening is taking police from one area to another to make the shop front look good, but the reality is that behind the scenes it’s an utter shambles.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a net decrease of 124 sworn police officers between the November 2023 change of government and July 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police monthly constabulary strength (FTE) figures for November 2023 and June/July 2024; true if the net change is a decrease of about 124, false if numbers rose or the decrease is materially different.

veracity.statement: Not enough to keep police here in New Zealand: 322 police officers have left to go to Australia.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 322 New Zealand police officers have departed for Australia (implicitly, recruitment by Australian forces over the recent period).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police attrition data / Official Information Act responses on officers resigning to join Australian police services in the period to mid-2024; true if the count is approximately 322, false if materially lower or if the figure covers a different destination or category.

veracity.statement: We know that every dollar spent on insulation brings at least $6 in benefits, according to a review of 45,000 Warmer Kiwi Homes whare. That’s through analysis done by the Motu economics institute.
veracity.explanation: Attributes to Motu, on a review of 45,000 Warmer Kiwi Homes retrofits, a finding of at least $6 of benefit per $1 of insulation spending.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Motu Research evaluation of the Warmer Kiwi Homes programme; true if it reports a benefit-cost ratio of at least 6:1 over a sample of about 45,000 homes, false if the reported ratio or sample size is materially different.

veracity.statement: A warm, cosy home safe from the elements is a basic human right, and as a country, we can ensure everyone has access to healthy, sustainable homes in caring communities, but this Government has cut $178.5 million of funding to the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority, and that will ensure that more children, more elderly, more whānau will suffer energy poverty.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $178.5 million reduction in funding to the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority in Budget 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Estimates for Vote Energy / EECA appropriations compared with the previous year; true if reductions totalling about $178.5 million to EECA are identifiable, false if the reduction is materially smaller or applies to a different agency or period.

veracity.statement: Another recommendation is multi-disciplinarity to address what are complex social situations, but instead we see $2.9 billion going to give landlords a tax break.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government is providing $2.9 billion to landlords via a tax change (the restoration of interest deductibility on rental property).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD costings published with Budget 2024 for the restoration of interest deductibility for residential rental property; true if the forecast fiscal cost is about $2.9 billion over the forecast period, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: And that’s not all: this Government has also gutted the Community Energy Fund, taking $30 million for tax cuts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that $30 million was removed from the Community (Renewable) Energy Fund and redirected to fund tax cuts.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 savings schedules and Vote Energy appropriations for the Community Renewable Energy Fund; true if about $30 million was returned to the centre as a savings initiative contributing to the tax package, false if the fund retained its appropriation or the amount is materially different.

specificity.statement: Police got $107.7 million less than they did in the previous Budget.
specificity.explanation: A single precise, checkable dollar figure attached to a named comparison (this Budget vs the previous one).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What they did get was less money in crime prevention; less money in youth services; job cuts to all those who support police—200 job cuts; critical IT projects to enable the front line have been put on ice; and all of that, on top of that, police are so stretched in their resources they are stepping away from attending family violence call-outs.
specificity.explanation: Names four concrete budget lines and one numeric figure (200 job cuts), but gives no amounts or dates for the crime prevention, youth services or IT items.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The additional police officers put into the Auckland CBD came from Counties Manukau and they came from North Shore—they were taken off other duties to go on foot patrols.
specificity.explanation: Names the receiving location, the two source districts and the mechanism (redeployment off other duties); checkable against Police deployment records.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We know that every dollar spent on insulation brings at least $6 in benefits, according to a review of 45,000 Warmer Kiwi Homes whare. That’s through analysis done by the Motu economics institute.
specificity.explanation: A named ratio, a named sample size and a named source institution — someone could go and check the study.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: When the Minister of Police was asked about ReFrame at the scrutiny week, his response was that it’s “airy-fairy”. Well, I doubt that he even actually comprehends the benefits that a project like ReFrame could actually deliver for front-line effectiveness and good services for Kiwis.
civility.explanation: Moves from the Minister's quoted remark to a direct attack on his personal comprehension — questioning the individual's grasp rather than the merits of the ReFrame decision.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Do you expect that would happen when the Prime Minister himself doesn’t even know what a front-line new police officer earns? I’ll give you a hint: it’s not $90,000 a year.
civility.explanation: Mocking the Prime Minister's personal ignorance of a figure, complete with 'I'll give you a hint' — the jab lands on the individual rather than on the pay settlement itself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: When the Prime Minister can spend $95,000 renovating Government House, a house that the Prime Minister prefers not to live in but only to hold family Christmas gatherings in, we can recognise the signs of privilege rather than care for those most vulnerable in our communities.
