civility.explanation: Turns from the Budget to the Prime Minister's personal living arrangements and family gatherings, imputing privilege and indifference to him as a person rather than contesting a decision.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My concern is that with 124 fewer police since this Government came into power, all that is happening is taking police from one area to another to make the shop front look good, but the reality is that behind the scenes it’s an utter shambles.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named outcome — a specific change in constabulary numbers and a specific deployment practice — rather than generalised party-bashing, though the closing 'shop front'/'shambles' framing is rhetorical.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Mr Speaker, thank you. Ned Stark warned us several years ago that “Winter is coming”, but with this coalition Government, we know it’s well and truly here, and it’s not good. Budget 2024 showed us this Government’s heart is made of ice.
focus.explanation: Names Budget 2024 but carries no policy content — an extended characterisation of the coalition's character rather than of any measure, figure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So that’s what makes this so outrageous: to not only cut the Warmer Kiwi Homes funding but also to cut the new programmes which were going to deal with those complex issues—the programmes that were going to ensure that people could afford to heat their homes, programmes that would ensure that people could afford to have hot water, programmes that would reach those who distrust the State, who have been subject to abuse in State care and need special social support.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: a named programme, the specific extensions cut, and the groups those extensions were designed to reach.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In the long term, those who are going to pay for this are the victims of crime in New Zealand—and having communities that are less safe. We know that because the latest poll from TV ONE shows that there are a whole lot of New Zealanders feeling less safe than they used do under this Government.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (communities will actually be less safe and more people victimised) is supported only by a poll of how people feel — an appeal to popularity, and a measure of perception offered as evidence of an objective outcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: So when you set up a gang unit and it’s meant to be operating by 1 July and it’s not, and it’s only got five staff in it—not even necessarily police officers—that’s because the 500 promised to New Zealanders will not be delivered in two years. There is no way that that is going to happen.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Government will fail to deliver its promised 500 additional police officers within its two-year commitment window.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NZ Police constabulary strength reporting against the coalition's commitment to 500 additional officers by late November 2025; true (prediction correct) if fewer than 500 additional officers were on the front line by that deadline, false if the 500 target was met on time.

veracity.statement: The Minister of Health has appointed this week a commissioner for the health sector.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in the week of 23 July 2024 the Minister of Health appointed a commissioner over the health sector (Health New Zealand / Te Whatu Ora).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial announcements and Health NZ / Te Whatu Ora records for July 2024; true if a commissioner was appointed to the health entity in that week, false if no such appointment occurred at that time.

veracity.statement: And, like I say, 80 percent of what happens in the health system is actually—you can find the cause of that outside of the health system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a quantified claim that roughly 80 percent of health outcomes are caused by factors outside the health system (social and economic determinants) rather than by clinical care.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published health-determinants literature (e.g. County Health Rankings model, WHO social determinants reviews) on the share of health outcomes attributable to non-clinical factors; true if mainstream estimates put non-healthcare determinants at approximately 80 percent, false if the accepted estimates are materially different.

veracity.statement: This Budget is about choices, and the Government chose to give tax cuts, big tax breaks to landlords and to those with high incomes, and to throw a few pennies—$2.50 a week—to people on superannuation; about $12 to people on low incomes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific weekly gains from the Budget 2024 personal tax changes: about $2.50 a week for superannuitants and about $12 a week for people on low incomes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury / IRD Budget 2024 tax package distributional tables; true if the published weekly gain for a superannuitant is about $2.50 and for a low-income earner about $12, false if the official figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: Well, let’s have a look: $12 billion is being borrowed and $10 billion is going out in tax cuts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two Budget 2024 figures — approximately $12 billion of new borrowing and approximately $10 billion going out in tax cuts — implying the tax package is debt-funded.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Fiscal Strategy Report and the tax package costings; true if the new borrowing figure is about $12 billion and the tax package about $10 billion on a comparable basis, false if either figure is materially different from the official numbers.

veracity.statement: Well, we support that in Opposition; in fact, we had strong growth, even through COVID, of our export earnings in this country, through a really tricky time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's export earnings grew strongly during the COVID period under the previous Labour government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ overseas merchandise trade and total exports of goods and services series, 2019-2023; true if total export earnings rose materially across that period, false if they were flat or fell.

veracity.statement: He’s not apologised, and he should in my view.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at 23 July 2024 the Prime Minister had not apologised for his remarks about the calibre of people on previous trade missions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: News and Hansard record up to 23 July 2024; true if no apology or retraction by the Prime Minister for those remarks is on record, false if one is.

veracity.statement: No more money for Trade and Enterprise—in fact, cuts to the budget for New Zealand Trade and Enterprise.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Budget 2024 provided no new funding for New Zealand Trade and Enterprise and in fact reduced its appropriation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Business, Science and Innovation estimates for the NZTE appropriations compared with the previous year; true if the appropriation falls with no new initiative funding, false if new funding was appropriated or the baseline rose.

civility.statement: That was actually one of the key themes that came through the report into the health system that the health reforms were sort of quasi based upon—a report that most of the recommendations in some ways were torn up and thrown away by a Minister of Health who’d been in place for less than five months when he decided that he knew better and it would be better to have, instead of a slow transition and a process that should take between five and 10 years to implement, they would do it in the space of one year.
civility.explanation: Engages a real decision (the pace of the health reforms versus the review's recommended transition), but the phrase 'he decided that he knew better' imputes arrogance and bad judgement to the individual former Minister rather than staying on the decision itself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There were days when people would trust what a doctor told you. Well, you certainly can’t trust what that doctor, Dr Vanessa Weenink, tells us. She should be ashamed, because, as a doctor, she knows that the imposition once again of prescription fees and the removal of the obligation to make homes drier and warmer will be an impost on many of the people that come to doctors up and down this country to look after their children.
civility.explanation: Names an individual member and attacks her honesty and professional integrity directly — she cannot be trusted and should be ashamed — rather than confining the attack to the prescription-fee and healthy-homes policies he goes on to cite.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And I want to thank all those people involved in exporting—thank the A-listers and the C-listers, the people who were insulted by a Prime Minister who once again put his foot in his mouth.
civility.explanation: Criticism of remarks the Prime Minister actually made, but 'once again put his foot in his mouth' generalises to a pattern of personal ineptitude rather than staying on the remark itself.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That was actually one of the key themes that came through the report into the health system that the health reforms were sort of quasi based upon—a report that most of the recommendations in some ways were torn up and thrown away by a Minister of Health who’d been in place for less than five months when he decided that he knew better and it would be better to have, instead of a slow transition and a process that should take between five and 10 years to implement, they would do it in the space of one year.
focus.explanation: Squarely on policy: names the underlying health system review, the recommended five-to-ten year transition, and the one-year implementation actually chosen. Specific policy content, not party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is an immoral Budget from a coalition Government that just cares about the people at the top and still believes in the trickle-down theory.
focus.explanation: Refers to the Budget but names no measure, figure or outcome; the weight is a characterisation of what the other side is 'really like' and what it believes, rather than engagement with any specific appropriation.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So instead of having 20 district health boards, we had one Te Whatu Ora (TWO), plus we had the regions, but then we had, on top of that, districts underneath them.
specificity.explanation: Names the entities and gives a count for the prior structure, and describes the replacement's layers (national body, regions, districts); still lacks figures for the new structure's size or cost.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s about caring, it’s about the way that we do things, not about the size of the money that we’re putting in.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues offered as the account of the Budget's health effect; no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named measure that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Some of the things that people also wouldn’t think of as being a health improvement function would be tax cuts, but actually improving people’s incomes and the money that they have in their hands is directly related to their health outcomes.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy — income is linked to health outcomes, therefore tax cuts are a health measure — but it moves from a population-level correlation to a particular policy without addressing who receives the cuts or their size, so the conclusion outruns the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There were days when people would trust what a doctor told you. Well, you certainly can’t trust what that doctor, Dr Vanessa Weenink, tells us. She should be ashamed, because, as a doctor, she knows that the imposition once again of prescription fees and the removal of the obligation to make homes drier and warmer will be an impost on many of the people that come to doctors up and down this country to look after their children.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur resting on the personal attack: that a member supports policies the speaker considers harmful does not establish that what she tells the House cannot be trusted. The policy premises are stated but do not support the conclusion drawn about her trustworthiness.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It has simply transferred wealth from poorer people to more wealthy people, and the disparities in this country are growing, the division in this country is growing, and that is because of choices that have been made by the coalition Government, not because of inflation, not because of anything else, but because this Government has chosen to look after its wealthy mates instead of looking after the people in this country who need assistance.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy plus bare assertion of causation: growing disparity is attributed wholly to Budget choices with 'not because of inflation, not because of anything else' ruling out every alternative cause without offering any evidence or mechanism to do so.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Irresponsible fiscal management by a National coalition Government, to ensure that child poverty will go up, unemployment will go up.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that following Budget 2024 both child poverty and unemployment in New Zealand will rise.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ child poverty statistics (material hardship and after-housing-costs measures) and the HLFS unemployment rate; true if both series are higher in the years following Budget 2024 than at the time of the statement, false if either fails to rise.

veracity.statement: What we see instead is $1.1 billion over 5 years, which will just about keep the lights on, as it stands.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Budget 2024's disability support allocation was $1.1 billion spread over five years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents (Vote Social Development / Whaikaha disability support services appropriations); true if the Budget 2024 disability support package is $1.1b over five years, false if the headline figure or period differs materially.

veracity.statement: And yet it is that very flexibility that was removed, with no heads-up, on 18 March and not returned through Budget 2024.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that flexible-funding rules for disability support were changed on 18 March 2024 without prior notice, and that Budget 2024 did not reinstate them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Whaikaha–Ministry of Disabled People announcements and media reporting dated 18 March 2024, plus Budget 2024 disability appropriations; true if the flexibility change was announced on that date without consultation and no reinstatement appears in Budget 2024, false if the date, the lack of notice, or the non-reinstatement is contradicted.

veracity.statement: It’s about 900 disabled people who will be paid about $2 as a result of this.
veracity.explanation: Asserts roughly 900 disabled people are employed under minimum wage exemption permits at around $2 per hour.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE minimum wage exemption permit data for 2023/24; true if the number of active permit holders is near 900 and typical permit rates are around $2/hour, false if the permit count or rates differ materially.

veracity.statement: Why didn’t this Minister push back on the 6.5 percent cuts to DOC funding, for a department that is already so stretched?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Budget 2024 imposed a 6.5 percent funding cut on the Department of Conservation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Conservation appropriations and DOC's published savings target; true if DOC's baseline savings/cut is approximately 6.5 percent, false if the figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: The Jobs for Nature programme, alone, in 2023, provided jobs for 11,000 people while protecting the environment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Jobs for Nature programme supported 11,000 jobs in 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DOC/MfE Jobs for Nature programme reporting on employment numbers for 2023; true if reported jobs supported are around 11,000, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: There are 141 people on the social housing wait-list, up from 105 in 2021.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Timaru/South Canterbury social housing register stood at 141 applicants, having risen from 105 in 2021.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD Housing Register quarterly data for the Timaru/South Canterbury area; true if the register figure is about 141 at the relevant quarter and about 105 in 2021, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: I want to talk about the broken promise, the broken promise on the campaign trail from that side of the House that families were going to be getting an extra $250 a week.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the National campaign promised families an extra $250 per week.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 'Back Pocket Boost' tax plan documents and campaign advertising; true if the headline figure was up to $250 a week, false if the promise was expressed as up to $250 a fortnight or another amount/period.

veracity.statement: What they didn’t campaign on was that parents were going to have to collect receipts for it, then they were going to have to lodge it with IRD—it was going to be a big process.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the FamilyBoost ECE rebate requires parents to collect ECE receipts and submit them to Inland Revenue to claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue's published FamilyBoost application requirements as at 2024; true if claimants must supply ECE invoices/receipts to IRD, false if the rebate is paid automatically or via providers without receipt submission.

specificity.statement: Why didn’t this Minister push back on the 6.5 percent cuts to DOC funding, for a department that is already so stretched?
specificity.explanation: Names the department, a precise percentage cut and the accountable Minister — a checkable, actionable question rather than a general complaint.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are 141 people on the social housing wait-list, up from 105 in 2021.
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures with a baseline year for the named locality's housing register; directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So much under the knife by a Minister who has no ambition for the environment and has clearly said that he’s fine with species extinction and that 30 percent marine conservation protection by 2030 is just “an aspiration”.
civility.explanation: Moves from the Budget to the Minister personally — attributing to him an absence of ambition and a willingness to accept species extinction, which imputes bad faith rather than contesting the decision.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I would not be surprised if this ends up being a one-term Government.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the National-led coalition formed after the 2023 election will not be returned to government at the following general election.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The official result of the next New Zealand general election and subsequent government formation; true if the National-led coalition parties do not form the government after that election, false if they return to government.

focus.statement: I don’t think they realised what they voted for is quite what they were going to get, but, thankfully, I think Kiwis out there are beginning to see exactly what this Government stands for, which is not much.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the other side is 'really like' and how voters perceive them; no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If this was a Government that had a laser-sharp focus on the cost of living, they would not have brought back 90-day trials, they would not have got rid of fair pay agreements, and they would not force thousands of people to lose their jobs—absolutely irresponsible and heartless from this Government.
focus.explanation: Names three specific policy decisions (90-day trials, fair pay agreements, public sector job losses) and ties them to a stated government priority.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, how can that possibly be the case when we are seeing Kāinga Ora housing projects right across the country being paused and put on hold?
focus.explanation: Tests a government claim about improving housing access against a named programme's paused developments — scrutiny directed at a specific policy outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If this was a Government that had a laser-sharp focus on the cost of living, they would not have brought back 90-day trials, they would not have got rid of fair pay agreements, and they would not force thousands of people to lose their jobs—absolutely irresponsible and heartless from this Government.
rigor.explanation: The conditional assumes without argument that the named employment-law changes necessarily worsen the cost of living, so the conclusion that the priority is not genuine rests on an unstated and unsupported link; a real inference about real policies, but a weak one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, I can tell you, the local chemist that I’ve spoken to in Ashburton has expressed real concerns about the removal of the free prescriptions, because that has been something that ensured that people would come and pick up their prescriptions. What this will do is simply benefit the likes of Chemist Warehouse.
rigor.explanation: Argument from a single anecdote (one pharmacist's view), and the conclusion that the change will 'simply benefit' a large discount chain is a non sequitur — nothing offered connects the co-payment change to that market outcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Why? Because the country was in the wrong direction. Why? Because New Zealanders had voted on 14 October 2023 to make sure that we are turning the country and bringing it back on track.
civility.explanation: Criticises the previous government's overall direction without naming, mocking or impugning any individual. Entirely impersonal.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why? Because the country was in the wrong direction. Why? Because New Zealanders had voted on 14 October 2023 to make sure that we are turning the country and bringing it back on track.
focus.explanation: In a Budget debate, this names no measure, figure or outcome — it is generalised 'wrong direction / back on track' framing about the previous government and the election result.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The other reason why we are doing it online for every quarter is when you have a blanket policy—like the 20 hours or the 30 hours that the Labour Party campaigned on during the last election—when you have, basically, a blanket policy out there for anyone to just get it for free, you have also provided financial assistance to families who don’t necessarily need it, but it is their right to have it.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the design of FamilyBoost against a named alternative policy (free ECE hours), addressing who receives support and how it is delivered.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The other reason why we are doing it online for every quarter is when you have a blanket policy—like the 20 hours or the 30 hours that the Labour Party campaigned on during the last election—when you have, basically, a blanket policy out there for anyone to just get it for free, you have also provided financial assistance to families who don’t necessarily need it, but it is their right to have it.
rigor.explanation: The premise (universal entitlements also pay households that don't need the money) does support a case for targeting, but the conclusion being defended is the quarterly online invoice-upload mechanism. Targeting does not entail that particular claiming process — there is a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Guess what! When you need support, you will do the extra mile to get the support that you really need.
rigor.explanation: Answers an objection about the compliance burden of collecting invoices and filing them with IRD by simply asserting that needy families will overcome it. The conclusion (the burden is not a barrier) is assumed rather than supported — nothing is offered about uptake, capability or cost of compliance.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The other reason why we are doing it online for every quarter is when you have a blanket policy—like the 20 hours or the 30 hours that the Labour Party campaigned on during the last election—when you have, basically, a blanket policy out there for anyone to just get it for free, you have also provided financial assistance to families who don’t necessarily need it, but it is their right to have it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Labour Party campaigned at the 2023 general election on a blanket free ECE entitlement of 20 or 30 hours.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Labour Party 2023 general election ECE policy as published in its manifesto and policy announcements; true if Labour campaigned on a universal free ECE hours entitlement of 20 or 30 hours as described, false if no such free-hours extension formed part of its 2023 campaign.

veracity.statement: So I ran in 2020; didn’t make it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that she stood as a candidate at the 2020 New Zealand general election and was not elected.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission official candidate lists and results for the 2020 New Zealand general election; true if Nancy Lu appears as a candidate (electorate or list) and was not returned, false if she did not stand in 2020.

specificity.statement: There is so much that we are doing as a Government. We are doing the extra sitting hours. We are doing urgency. We are doing law and order because law and order also matters for New Zealand as a whole.
specificity.explanation: Offered as an account of what the Government is delivering, but carries no measure, figure, timeframe or mechanism — 'doing urgency' and 'doing law and order' name no policy anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: While we have the onus to sit here and reflect about the measly tax cuts that you are giving to disguise the all-out war that you’re waging on tangata whenua and, indeed, the poor, this Budget removes half-price transport and $5 prescription fees.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific Budget 2024 decisions: the removal of half-price public transport concessions and the removal of the free-prescription policy (i.e. reinstatement of the $5 prescription co-payment).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents / Vote Health and Vote Transport appropriations and Government announcements for 2024: true if Budget 2024 discontinued the half-price public transport fare subsidy and reinstated the $5 prescription charge; false if either policy was retained.

veracity.statement: They have cut minimum wage, benefit increases, support for disabled communities, while putting $1.9 million into what?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government cut the minimum wage, cut benefit increases and cut disability support, while allocating $1.9 million to prisons.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The April 2024 minimum wage order (was the statutory minimum wage rate reduced, or increased?); the Budget 2024 change to benefit indexation (wage-indexation to CPI) and whether that reduced scheduled increases; Whaikaha disability support funding decisions of March–May 2024; and the Budget 2024 Vote Corrections appropriation for prison capacity, checked against the $1.9 million figure stated. True if each element matches the record including the order of magnitude of the corrections figure; false where it does not.

veracity.statement: The only thing that can be remembered is the tens of thousands of Māori, tangata Tiriti, tangata Pasifika who got up and showed you exactly what they thought of your Budget.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that tens of thousands of people took part in the Budget-day protest activations against Budget 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous police and media crowd estimates for the Te Pāti Māori / Toitū te Tiriti Budget-day (30 May 2024) national day of action, aggregated across locations: true if total participation is credibly reported at 20,000 or more, false if reported totals are in the low thousands.

focus.statement: While we have the onus to sit here and reflect about the measly tax cuts that you are giving to disguise the all-out war that you’re waging on tangata whenua and, indeed, the poor, this Budget removes half-price transport and $5 prescription fees.
focus.explanation: Names two specific Budget measures and their effect, which is legitimate scrutiny, but the policy content is wrapped in a broad 'all-out war you're waging' framing of the other side.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government and its coalition will be remembered for being the meanest-spirited Government ever.
focus.explanation: A characterisation of the other side in general terms during a Budget debate; no measure, figure, mechanism or named outcome is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They have cut minimum wage, benefit increases, support for disabled communities, while putting $1.9 million into what?
specificity.explanation: Names four concrete areas of spending change and attaches a dollar figure, so the claim is checkable against Budget documents, even though the figure's magnitude is questionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: This was the signing of a licence—the signing of a licence that proves that this will only ever be a one-term—thankfully—coalition Government.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the National–ACT–NZ First coalition will serve only one parliamentary term and will not be returned to government at the following general election.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The official Electoral Commission result of the next general election and the government formed after it: true if the National–ACT–NZ First coalition parties do not together form the government; false if they are returned to office.

civility.statement: Today we have seen—and yesterday we have seen—the behaviour of political leaders who lack the decorum and indeed the relevance and relatability to our people, who, instead of using their sphere of influence to make life easier and better and relatable for those struggling, in fact get to resort to name-calling; get to use words that we have absolutely fought our lives against hearing our disabled communities have to hear in this place.
civility.explanation: Criticises unnamed members' conduct in the House, which is legitimate, but goes beyond the conduct to judge them as lacking decorum, relevance and relatability — a personal characterisation rather than an argument about what was said.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is the most anti-Māori Budget in a generation: attacks on Māori ward representation; demolishing the Māori Health Authority; removing section 7AA provisions at Oranga Tamariki; rushing through the fast-track approvals bill; a 45 percent cut from Matariki funding; erasing te reo Māori from the Public Service; $40 million cut for supply and capability of Māori housing; $2 million cut for Aotearoa Reorua Bilingual Towns and Cities; a $6 million cut for the Mana Ōrite agreement between the Justice Sector Leadership Board and Ināia Tonu Nei to help transform the justice sector; a $96.7 million cut to Māori Development, including Te Tumu Paeroa; trying to remove the Treaty from legislation; $21.9 million cut for mātauranga and iwi-focused qualifications; a $4 million cut pertaining to strengthening Māori education; $37 million cut from backing mātauranga Māori to reduce emissions; $35.5 million cut, disestablishing the Māori Health Authority; a $9.5 million cut to claimant funding for historical Treaty claimants; and a $25 million on-hold for iwi and community-led rangatahi district courts.
specificity.explanation: A long enumeration of named programmes, agencies and dollar figures, each individually checkable against Budget 2024 vote documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is the most anti-Māori Budget in a generation: attacks on Māori ward representation; demolishing the Māori Health Authority; removing section 7AA provisions at Oranga Tamariki; rushing through the fast-track approvals bill; a 45 percent cut from Matariki funding; erasing te reo Māori from the Public Service; $40 million cut for supply and capability of Māori housing; $2 million cut for Aotearoa Reorua Bilingual Towns and Cities; a $6 million cut for the Mana Ōrite agreement between the Justice Sector Leadership Board and Ināia Tonu Nei to help transform the justice sector; a $96.7 million cut to Māori Development, including Te Tumu Paeroa; trying to remove the Treaty from legislation; $21.9 million cut for mātauranga and iwi-focused qualifications; a $4 million cut pertaining to strengthening Māori education; $37 million cut from backing mātauranga Māori to reduce emissions; $35.5 million cut, disestablishing the Māori Health Authority; a $9.5 million cut to claimant funding for historical Treaty claimants; and a $25 million on-hold for iwi and community-led rangatahi district courts.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named Budget against named line items and amounts; entirely about policy content rather than the other party's character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If Māori make up 20 percent of this country’s population, a “by Māori, for Māori, to Māori” approach means that Māori should get 20 percent of the total Budget.
focus.explanation: Squarely a policy proposition about how the Budget should be allocated, with a stated share; no party-bashing content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is not surprising that this request to continue wasn’t supported, because—the truth be known—my esteemed co-leader Rawiri Waititi was giving facts, and the ecosystems of colonisation are really hard to swallow from those who are the absolute emboldeners; the absolute empowerers of that type of situation.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the motives and character of the other side over a procedural refusal; no policy, measure or figure is named.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Māori are not mentioned once in the priority areas of this Budget.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the stated priority areas of Budget 2024 contain no mention of Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Budget 2024 'Budget at a Glance' / summary document's stated priority areas; true if the word 'Māori' does not appear in that priority-areas section, false if it appears there.

veracity.statement: But we are sick and tired of Pākehā Governments continuing to fund themselves on the dysfunction it has created amongst Māori: 50 percent of the male prison population is Māori; 64 percent of the female prison population is Māori; 80 percent of Oranga Tamariki is Māori.
veracity.explanation: Three statistical claims: Māori share of the male prison muster, of the female prison muster, and of children in Oranga Tamariki care.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections prison population statistics by ethnicity and gender for 2024, and Oranga Tamariki quarterly care statistics by ethnicity; true if each figure matches within a couple of percentage points, false if any is materially off.

veracity.statement: You’ve got an Associate Minister for Health advising Pharmac to ignore any of its obligations to Te Tiriti o Waitangi, when there are huge health inequities that Māori have when it comes to accessing medication.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Associate Minister of Health directed or advised Pharmac to disregard Treaty of Waitangi obligations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2024 Associate Minister of Health letter of expectations to Pharmac and Pharmac's published response; true if it instructs Pharmac to drop or not act on Te Tiriti obligations, false if it retains or is silent on them.

veracity.statement: We’re dying seven to 10 years earlier than anybody else.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a Māori life-expectancy gap of seven to ten years relative to other New Zealanders.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ period life tables for Māori and non-Māori around 2022-2024; true if the gap falls in the 7-10 year range, false if materially outside it.

veracity.statement: Tonight, we look at housing: 100,000 people in Aotearoa will be sleeping rough on the streets, in tents, in cars, in garages, and unlivable houses—things that the super-wealthy could never truly ever understand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 100,000 people in New Zealand are without adequate housing — rough sleeping, temporary or uninhabitable accommodation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / University of Otago severe housing deprivation (homelessness) estimates from the most recent census; true if the estimate is around 100,000, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: Māori currently make up 50 percent of the social housing wait-list, and by no doubt they will be some of this one over here’s whanaunga. Therefore, they should be given 50 percent of the social housing Budget, but no—no.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori are 50 percent of applicants on the social housing register.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Housing and Urban Development Housing Register quarterly data by ethnicity for 2024; true if the Māori share is approximately 50 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: They’ve also cut Māori housing by $40 million and action to address rangatahi homelessness by $20 million.
veracity.explanation: Two specific Budget 2024 savings claims: $40 million from Māori housing and $20 million from rangatahi homelessness measures.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Māori Development / Vote Housing and Urban Development savings tables; true if reductions of approximately $40m and $20m appear against those lines, false if the amounts or lines do not exist.

veracity.statement: In the meantime, they’re giving $3 billion to who? The landlords. That’s it. More than the sum total of Tiriti settlements combined.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the restoration of interest deductibility for landlords is worth about $3 billion, and that this exceeds the total value of all Treaty of Waitangi settlements combined.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury costing of the interest deductibility change in the Budget 2024 fiscal forecasts, compared with the Office for Māori Crown Relations total of Treaty settlement redress to date; true if the former exceeds the latter, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: In 1889, King Tāwhiao funded Te Peeke o Aotearoa, the first Māori bank with our Māori currency.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Peeke o Aotearoa, the first Māori bank issuing its own currency, was founded by King Tāwhiao in 1889.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Ara / Waikato-Tainui and Reserve Bank historical accounts of Te Peeke o Aotearoa's founding date; true if established in 1889, false if the accepted founding date is a different year.

rigor.statement: If Māori make up 20 percent of this country’s population, a “by Māori, for Māori, to Māori” approach means that Māori should get 20 percent of the total Budget.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: a population share does not by itself entail a proportional share of total appropriations, and nothing in the premise about a 'by Māori, for Māori' delivery model supplies the missing step from demographic share to budget allocation.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Māori currently make up 50 percent of the social housing wait-list, and by no doubt they will be some of this one over here’s whanaunga. Therefore, they should be given 50 percent of the social housing Budget, but no—no.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion does not follow from the premise: a share of the waiting list does not by itself establish an entitlement to the same share of the housing budget, since need per applicant and programme design are not addressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is not surprising that this request to continue wasn’t supported, because—the truth be known—my esteemed co-leader Rawiri Waititi was giving facts, and the ecosystems of colonisation are really hard to swallow from those who are the absolute emboldeners; the absolute empowerers of that type of situation.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to members opposite — that they refused leave because they could not bear the truth and are 'emboldeners' of colonisation. Short of a direct personal insult, but sneering rather than engaging substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We have people here for the first time discovering that they may have a new idea—and, in fact, teaching rangatahi how to iron may be a way to actually sit themselves and navigate through justice.
civility.explanation: Mockery directed at members opposite — ridiculing them for 'discovering' an idea rather than engaging the youth justice policy itself.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Imagine if we were to create a Māori bank today while the Māori economy sits at $70 billion and is projected to reach $100 billion in the next five years.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Māori economy (asset base) will reach $100 billion within five years of July 2024.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: A published Māori economy valuation (e.g. BERL/Reserve Bank Te Ōhanga Māori series) dated on or before mid-2029; true if the Māori asset base is assessed at $100 billion or more, false if below.

focus.statement: I am excited—well, no, I’m not excited about this, because it’s been quite disappointing to listen to the vacuous speeches of the other side who can’t really tell us what they are doing with the Estimates.
focus.explanation: A characterisation of the other side's speeches as 'vacuous' with only a gesture at the Estimates; no policy, figure or measure is named. Mostly about the other team rather than the substance.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Te Ao Mārama, the initiatives of the court which are working, which are taking young people at the earliest opportunity and shifting them away from the conveyor belt of court, trial, prison, and return again—now, those programmes that the courts have been initiating have been put on hold by this Government cutting the budget for them while they have a think about it.
focus.explanation: Names a specific court initiative, what it does, and the specific budget decision said to have stopped it. Scrutiny of a named programme against a named outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Like my colleague Dr Duncan Webb, I have to say the only good thing I have heard from the Government benches about this Budget is the engagement of Tom Rutherford—congratulations for that.
focus.explanation: A quip about the Government benches generally, with no policy, appropriation or measure named; the only content is a jibe at the other side's contributions.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Budget explicitly stops advocacy for the environment, and we see that with the Environmental Legal Assistance Fund—that’s cut, gone.
focus.explanation: Names a specific fund and a specific Budget decision affecting it — scrutiny of a named appropriation rather than party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I mean, really, this Government has TikTok policies for justice, because you only have to go—and I do go online and look at the members and the Ministers in the justice sector and see what they’re saying, and they’re full of three-line slogans, but no policy and no real evidence.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the Government has 'no policy and no real evidence' is inferred entirely from the style of Ministers' social media posts — a non sequitur, since the medium's brevity says nothing about the underlying policy work.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The true irony of announcing boot camps in a week when we’re getting a report on abuse in State care—I cannot believe that they haven’t joined the dots and realised that an authoritarian and oppressive disciplinary regime in respect of young people leads to trauma and harm.
rigor.explanation: Argues from the abuse-in-State-care inquiry to the harms of military-style academies by treating the two regimes as equivalent. There is a real inferential link offered (institutional discipline of young people → trauma), but the equivalence is asserted rather than established — a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because if you put enough people in jail, well, eventually all the bad ones will be in jail and there’ll be no crime—another failed policy.
rigor.explanation: A strawman: it attributes to the Government an absurd 'incapacitate everyone' theory that no one advanced, then rejects that version rather than the actual policy.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The true irony of announcing boot camps in a week when we’re getting a report on abuse in State care—I cannot believe that they haven’t joined the dots and realised that an authoritarian and oppressive disciplinary regime in respect of young people leads to trauma and harm.
civility.explanation: Fierce criticism of the boot camps policy and of the Government's judgement collectively; no individual is attacked.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The bill says we will facilitate development that three Ministers want to have for pet projects—pet projects that will benefit our mates.
civility.explanation: Goes beyond criticising the decision-making mechanism to impute corrupt motive — that the three Ministers will use the power to benefit 'our mates'. Bad faith attributed to identifiable office-holders, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We know the military want nothing to do with it, and good on them as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the New Zealand Defence Force declined to be involved in the Government's military-style academies / boot camps.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZDF and Minister of Defence public statements or OIA responses on NZDF involvement in the 2024 military-style academy pilot; true if NZDF declined or ruled out delivering the academies, false if NZDF was a delivery partner or publicly agreed to participate.

veracity.statement: Three strikes; another failed policy which will cost—and I’ve asked and been told by the Minister—tens of millions of dollars.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister told him the reinstated three-strikes regime will cost tens of millions of dollars.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement / Budget or Corrections costings for the Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Bill, and the Minister's written or oral answers to Webb; true if the official costing is in the tens of millions, false if materially lower or higher (e.g. under $10m or in the hundreds of millions).

veracity.statement: Now, on Q+A recently, the Minister actually was quite clear that he wasn’t doing this to deter criminals; he just wanted to put more people inside.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister of Justice said on TVNZ's Q+A that the sentencing policy was not intended as a deterrent but to increase the prison population.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The TVNZ Q+A transcript/recording of the Minister's interview in the weeks before 23 July 2024; true if the Minister disclaimed deterrence and stated the aim was more people in prison, false if he advanced deterrence as a rationale or made no such statement.

veracity.statement: We know that broken families cause crime, that families with a person in jail are more likely for a child to grow up and be in jail, and that the educational outcomes, the financial outcomes for those families, they will be adverse and be more likely to result in criminal offending.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an intergenerational effect of imprisonment: children of prisoners are more likely to be imprisoned themselves and have worse educational and financial outcomes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections / Ministry of Justice research and peer-reviewed criminological literature on children of incarcerated parents in New Zealand; true if studies show materially elevated rates of later imprisonment and worse educational/financial outcomes for this group, false if the literature finds no such association.

veracity.statement: Te Ao Mārama, the initiatives of the court which are working, which are taking young people at the earliest opportunity and shifting them away from the conveyor belt of court, trial, prison, and return again—now, those programmes that the courts have been initiating have been put on hold by this Government cutting the budget for them while they have a think about it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that funding for the Te Ao Mārama court initiative was cut in Budget 2024 and that the roll-out has been paused as a result.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Courts appropriations and Ministry of Justice statements on Te Ao Mārama funding and roll-out; true if funding was reduced/not continued and expansion paused, false if funding continued at or above prior levels and roll-out proceeded.

veracity.statement: Circuit-breaker, the initiative that we put in place, has not been extended as planned.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Circuit Breaker youth-offending programme established under the previous government was not extended as had been planned.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 appropriations and Ministry of Justice/Oranga Tamariki statements on the Circuit Breaker programme; true if the planned extension did not proceed, false if the programme was extended as originally planned.

veracity.statement: Pine trees are no good when they are wilding pines and they need to be controlled, and of course that’s been cut.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that funding for wilding conifer control was cut in Budget 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Biosecurity / Vote Conservation appropriations for the National Wilding Conifer Control Programme; true if the appropriation was reduced relative to the prior year, false if maintained or increased.

veracity.statement: We have a Minister whose title is Minister for the Environment, who says that the balance has swung too far in favour of the environment with environmental regulation.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim about what the Minister for the Environment has said — that environmental regulation has swung the balance too far in favour of the environment.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, interviews or Hansard/select committee records of the Minister for the Environment before 23 July 2024; true if she stated the regulatory balance had swung too far toward the environment, false if no such statement exists or she said the opposite.

veracity.statement: We heard that in the Prime Minister’s answers to questions today, which were, frankly, outrageous, when he said that the Greens should support the fast-track bill because it will do more for renewable energy.
veracity.explanation: Relays what the Prime Minister said in question time that day: that the Greens should support the Fast-track Approvals Bill on renewable-energy grounds.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard oral questions for 23 July 2024; true if the Prime Minister made that argument to the Green Party, false if no such exchange occurred.

veracity.statement: There is no Treaty clause in that piece of legislation; there is nothing for any group of Māori that is not a settled iwi.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Fast-track Approvals Bill as before the House contained no Treaty of Waitangi clause and provided nothing for Māori groups without a completed Treaty settlement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Fast-track Approvals Bill as introduced in March 2024; true if it contains no Treaty of Waitangi clause and its Māori-related provisions are confined to Treaty settlement obligations, false if a general Treaty clause or non-settlement Māori provisions appear.

veracity.statement: There is absolutely no plan for 30 percent protected marine areas by 2030.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government has no plan to achieve 30 percent marine protection by 2030.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Conservation / Ministry for Primary Industries published marine protection work programme as at mid-2024, and Budget 2024 appropriations; true if no published plan or pathway to 30 percent by 2030 existed, false if a government plan with that target was in place.

veracity.statement: The Budget explicitly stops advocacy for the environment, and we see that with the Environmental Legal Assistance Fund—that’s cut, gone.

civility.explanation: Attributes deliberate bad faith to the Minister's consultation process — rigging the audience to manufacture a predetermined answer — and closes with a sneering aside rather than an argument about the process itself.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They tried to blame their underfunding and their incompetence on the previous Government, and Kiwis aren’t having it. They aren’t dumb; they can see a spin job when they face one, and they saw one this week.
focus.explanation: Almost entirely about the other side's public-relations conduct and how voters perceive them; no specific policy, figure or programme is named once the party framing is removed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: People have the right to be suspicious when the fox takes a sudden interest in the workings of the hen house.
focus.explanation: A metaphor about the other party's motives and character with no policy, measure or outcome named.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Next week, 83 percent of hard-working New Zealanders will receive tax relief for the first time in 14 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 83% of New Zealanders receive tax relief from the Budget 2024 package taking effect the following week, and that no income tax relief has been delivered for 14 years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD Budget 2024 tax package documentation: true if official material states approximately 83% of New Zealanders (or of taxpayers/households as she frames it) benefit from the 31 July 2024 threshold changes, and if the previous personal income tax threshold change took effect in 2010; false if the coverage figure is materially different or if thresholds/rates were changed more recently than 14 years prior.

veracity.statement: We’re already starting to see some positive news: 3.3 percent inflation, this is the lowest inflation we’ve seen in the last few years, and this is promising news for people who are struggling with their mortgage, struggling to pay those grocery bills, struggling to pay those electricity bills.
veracity.explanation: Asserts annual CPI inflation is 3.3 percent at the time of speaking and that this is the lowest rate in several years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index, annual inflation for the June 2024 quarter (released 17 July 2024): true if the annual rate is 3.3% and no quarter in the preceding ~3 years printed lower; false if the rate differs materially or a more recent quarter was lower.

veracity.statement: Our FamilyBoost tax rebate of up to $150 a fortnight has been incredibly well received by parents and early childhood teachers, because early childhood is very, very expensive and it’s really taking its toll on a lot of hard-working families out there.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the FamilyBoost rebate is worth up to $150 a fortnight.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 / IRD FamilyBoost policy documents: true if the maximum payment is $150 per fortnight (25% of weekly ECE fees up to a $150 fortnightly cap); false if the stated maximum differs.

veracity.statement: I’m also really excited in this Budget about our commitment to infrastructure—$68 billion in infrastructure over the next five years to fix the infrastructure deficit in this country; getting things built; actually investing in roading, 17 roads of national significance have been committed to by our Government, and a four-lane expressway for Hawke’s Bay is one of those roads of national significance.
veracity.explanation: Two checkable assertions: a $68 billion infrastructure investment over five years in Budget 2024, and a commitment to 17 Roads of National Significance including a four-lane Hawke's Bay expressway.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents / National Infrastructure Pipeline for the $68b five-year figure, and the final Government Policy Statement on land transport 2024 for the count of Roads of National Significance: true if the Budget states approximately $68b over five years and the GPS lists 17 RoNS including a Hawke's Bay expressway; false if the figures or count differ materially.

veracity.statement: Rents went up $180 per week in the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts weekly rents rose by $180 over the term of the 2017-2023 Labour government.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE tenancy bond data, national median weekly rent, comparing roughly October 2017 with October 2023: true if the increase is about $180/week; false if materially different.

veracity.statement: That is why it is so good to see $57 million in this Budget to roll out structured literacy across all of our schools across New Zealand, because that is what’s going to lift performance in education.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Budget 2024 allocated $57 million to rolling out structured literacy across all New Zealand schools.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Education documents and the Education Minister's structured literacy announcements: true if the allocation for structured literacy rollout is approximately $57 million; false if the figure is materially different or covers a different programme.

veracity.statement: In Hawke’s Bay, we actually have one of the largest gang populations in this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Hawke's Bay ranks among the regions with the largest gang membership in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police National Gang List membership by police district (Eastern district covers Hawke's Bay), around 2023-2024: true if Eastern district is among the highest districts by gang members per capita or in total; false if it sits mid-range or lower on both measures.

veracity.statement: So we’ve made a big investment—$1.94 billion in the Budget—into front-line Corrections, more support for offenders to turn their lives around as well, and more rehabilitation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Budget 2024 allocated $1.94 billion to front-line Corrections including rehabilitation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Corrections appropriations and the Corrections Minister's Budget release: true if the announced package is approximately $1.94 billion (over the forecast period); false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Two-thirds of this Budget is going towards health, education, and law and order.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that two-thirds of Budget 2024 spending goes to health, education and law and order.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Fiscal Strategy Report / Budget at a Glance: true if roughly two-thirds of the new operating allowance (the measure the Government used) went to those three areas; false if the share is materially lower, or if the claim cannot be sustained on either total-spend or new-spend measures.

specificity.statement: Next week, 83 percent of hard-working New Zealanders will receive tax relief for the first time in 14 years.
specificity.explanation: Carries a percentage, a timeframe ('next week'), and a comparison period — checkable and precise.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m also really excited in this Budget about our commitment to infrastructure—$68 billion in infrastructure over the next five years to fix the infrastructure deficit in this country; getting things built; actually investing in roading, 17 roads of national significance have been committed to by our Government, and a four-lane expressway for Hawke’s Bay is one of those roads of national significance.
specificity.explanation: Dollar figure, timeframe, a counted programme and a named local project — all checkable, though no per-project costings.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So we’ve made a big investment—$1.94 billion in the Budget—into front-line Corrections, more support for offenders to turn their lives around as well, and more rehabilitation.
specificity.explanation: A precise dollar figure attached to a named vote, with the broad purposes identified, though no breakdown or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are being fiscally responsible and we are restoring care and discipline and fiscal management.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — no figure, mechanism, target or timeframe that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Interest rates are forecast to come down, and that is a result of the work that this Government is doing to get on top of spending and get on top of inflation.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that interest rates will fall.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: RBNZ Official Cash Rate decisions and RBNZ published mortgage/retail interest rate series in the 12 months following the statement: true if the OCR and average new-lending mortgage rates are lower on 23 July 2025 than on 23 July 2024; false if they are level or higher.

rigor.statement: Interest rates are forecast to come down, and that is a result of the work that this Government is doing to get on top of spending and get on top of inflation.
rigor.explanation: The causal half of the claim does not follow from anything offered: forecast rate falls are attributed to the Government's spending restraint with no mechanism or evidence linking the two, and monetary policy is set independently by the Reserve Bank. Post hoc reasoning.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We are reducing the number of unnecessary road cones, which are costing the taxpayers and just epitomises the wasteful spending by the previous Government over the last six years.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that road cones 'epitomise' six years of wasteful spending — is asserted rather than supported; no cost figure or comparison is offered, and the support that follows is anecdotal (photos sent by motorists). Hasty generalisation from anecdote.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is why it is so good to see $57 million in this Budget to roll out structured literacy across all of our schools across New Zealand, because that is what’s going to lift performance in education.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the rollout will lift national education performance rests on a family anecdote about a six-year-old's reading plus one rural school's enthusiasm — appeal to anecdote, with no evidence base cited.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We need to build things faster and get things done, and that’s why our fast-track bill and the amendments to the Resource Management Act are going to make a huge difference to New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single anecdote about one Havelock North supermarket's consenting delay to a national conclusion about two pieces of legislation; nothing connects the named reforms to the delay described. Appeal to anecdote.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We are reducing the number of unnecessary road cones, which are costing the taxpayers and just epitomises the wasteful spending by the previous Government over the last six years.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point (traffic management cost and road cone use) but it is wrapped in a generalised charge about the previous Government's six-year record rather than a named measure or figure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Away with the wasteful, ideological projects like Auckland light rail and cycleways across the harbour bridge; it’s time to get real and invest in what really makes a difference, and that is good roads and good infrastructure in this country.
focus.explanation: Names two specific projects being cancelled and the alternative spending priority, though the closing half slides into general framing rather than mechanism or cost.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Away with the wasteful, ideological projects like Auckland light rail and cycleways across the harbour bridge; it’s time to get real and invest in what really makes a difference, and that is good roads and good infrastructure in this country.
civility.explanation: Harsh about two named projects and nobody at all; the criticism lands entirely on the policy choices.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Look, this is a great Budget in terms of delivering tax relief for the squeezed middle, giving average-income households up to $102 a fortnight.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Budget 2024's tax package delivers up to $102 a fortnight to average-income households.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD Budget 2024 tax relief tables and the Government's published examples; true if the stated maximum fortnightly gain for an average-income household from the 31 July 2024 threshold changes is $102 (or close to it), false if the published maximum is materially different.

veracity.statement: We’ve also got $3.4 billion for hospital and specialty services, $2.2 billion for primary care and public health, $1.7 billion for Pharmac—even more than that—which is fantastic, and $24 million for Gumboot Friday, which I have had a huge amount of response about.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific Budget 2024 health appropriations: $3.4b hospital and specialist services, $2.2b primary care and public health, $1.7b Pharmac, $24m Gumboot Friday.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Health estimates and the Government's Budget 2024 health package announcements; true if each of the four figures matches the published appropriation (allowing for the stated four-year aggregation), false if any is materially misstated.

veracity.statement: We have police on the beat and we are also investing $651 million over four years to deliver 500 extra police officers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a Budget 2024 appropriation of $651 million over four years for 500 additional police officers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Police estimates and the Police Minister's Budget announcement; true if the announced figure is $651m over four years tied to 500 extra officers, false if the amount or officer number differs materially.

veracity.statement: The Budget provides—which is also important in my electorate—$140 million to fund 1,500 new social housing places delivered by community housing providers, and that’s outstanding.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Budget 2024 funds 1,500 new social housing places through community housing providers at a cost of $140 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Housing and Urban Development estimates and the Housing Minister's Budget 2024 release; true if $140m is appropriated for 1,500 CHP-delivered social housing places, false if the figure or the number of places is materially different.

veracity.statement: And the numbers tell you—in the year ended June 2023, export receipts from our agricultural exports were $57 billion. This year it dropped to $54 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts agricultural/primary export receipts fell from $57 billion in the year to June 2023 to $54 billion in the year to June 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries (June 2024) food and fibre export revenue series, cross-checked against Stats NZ merchandise trade; true if the June 2023 figure is about $57b and the June 2024 figure about $54b, false if either departs materially from the published series.

specificity.statement: We’ve also got $3.4 billion for hospital and specialty services, $2.2 billion for primary care and public health, $1.7 billion for Pharmac—even more than that—which is fantastic, and $24 million for Gumboot Friday, which I have had a huge amount of response about.
specificity.explanation: Four named funding lines each with a dollar figure attached to a named service area; entirely checkable against the Budget documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We set out and achieved what we said we were going to do: focusing on growing the economy, restoring law and order, and delivering better public services.
specificity.explanation: A claim of achievement expressed entirely in generic objectives — no target, figure, timeframe or measurable outcome that anyone could check the 'achieved' against.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: A retired couple on superannuation will get an extra $9 a fortnight, rising up to around $26 a fortnight by 2026.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the fortnightly gain for a superannuitant couple from the tax package grows from $9 now to roughly $26 a fortnight by 2026 as superannuation is indexed to after-tax wages.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NZ Superannuation payment rates published by MSD for the April 2026 adjustment compared with the counterfactual rates absent the 2024 threshold changes, plus Treasury's published projections; true if the additional after-tax amount for a qualifying couple is around $26 a fortnight, false if materially below or above.

rigor.statement: I’ve been out and about in my electorate in the recess and I’ve enjoyed talking to people and they are very excited about this. It makes a real difference.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the package 'makes a real difference' rests entirely on anecdotal enthusiasm from people the speaker happened to meet — an appeal to anecdote, with no evidence connecting reported excitement to actual effect.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is worth investing in them now so that we don’t have to pay in the future for the legal fees and prison costs.
rigor.explanation: A genuine cost-offset inference about social investment, but the conclusion that early spending avoids later justice costs is asserted rather than supported — no evidence, modelling or magnitude is offered to bridge the premise and the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We have massively blown the Budget over the last six years, so Nicola Willis and her team went through line by line to stop spending.
focus.explanation: There is a real fiscal-policy point here — a line-by-line spending review — but it is carried mostly by a generalised charge about the previous six years, with no specific programme, saving or figure named.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, if that was the future ticket of the once-great Labour Party, this country really is in trouble. What a sad, sad day for the once-great party of the workers; the great socialist party who fought for decades and decades for workers’ rights and are about to vote against tax relief for working New Zealanders for the first time in 14 years.
civility.explanation: Sneers at a party ("once-great", "sad, sad day") but names and attacks no individual; the barb lands on Labour's collective position, not on a person's character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I know what Chris Hipkins is getting for Christmas: he’s getting that dodo ticket because after they vote against this Budget—after they vote against tax cuts for working New Zealanders—his leadership will be dead as a dodo, as will the Labour Party.
civility.explanation: Mockery directed at a named individual — jeering at Chris Hipkins personally with a Christmas-present gag about his leadership being "dead as a dodo" rather than engaging his argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Maybe he needs to whirl up his own fact-check machine, but I don’t think there’s enough solar-powered panels in the world to actually power that machine, given what come across the aisle.
civility.explanation: A sneer at a named member — the joke is about how much nonsense Kieran McAnulty personally produces, not about any claim he made.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, if that was the future ticket of the once-great Labour Party, this country really is in trouble. What a sad, sad day for the once-great party of the workers; the great socialist party who fought for decades and decades for workers’ rights and are about to vote against tax relief for working New Zealanders for the first time in 14 years.
focus.explanation: Does point to a specific thing — Labour's vote on the Budget's tax relief — but the bulk of the passage is generic framing about what Labour used to be, so it is a real policy point wrapped in party rhetoric.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I point to one in my electorate, at Ashburton College: underfunded for their rebuild by $23 million; promised a three-stage rebuild, cut off at the knees in November—just after the election, actually.
focus.explanation: Names a specific project, a specific dollar shortfall and a specific decision date — accountability for a named commitment rather than generalised party criticism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Members opposite have been asking where they are going to recruit these police from. What are we going to do? Well, in 2026, I can see a few job vacancies up for grabs on the other side of the road, so get your applications in.
focus.explanation: A real question about police recruitment is answered with a joke about Opposition MPs losing their seats at the next election; no mechanism, number or timeframe for recruitment is offered.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Well, I know what Chris Hipkins is getting for Christmas: he’s getting that dodo ticket because after they vote against this Budget—after they vote against tax cuts for working New Zealanders—his leadership will be dead as a dodo, as will the Labour Party.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Hipkins's leadership of Labour will end as a consequence of Labour voting against the Budget.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Whether Chris Hipkins ceases to be leader of the Labour Party following the Budget 2024 votes; true if he is replaced as Labour leader (party leadership records/news reporting) before the resolve-by date, false if he remains leader.

veracity.statement: Because, finally, after 14 years, the people of this country—working New Zealanders—are getting tax relief under a Budget which will pass imminently with support of this coalition Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Budget 2024's tax changes are the first tax relief for working New Zealanders in 14 years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Whether any reduction in personal income tax rates or shift in tax thresholds took effect between October 2010 and Budget 2024 (IRD/Treasury records of personal income tax rates and thresholds); true if Budget 2024 is the first such reduction in 14 years, false if an intervening change delivered personal income tax relief.

veracity.statement: If I talk about those great constituents in Rangitata and share with you a few home truths, because, of course, one-fifth of those working in Rangitata list their occupation as a labourer; 16 percent work in the manufacturing sector; and then we’ve got the hundreds and hundreds—if not thousands—of people who work in our agricultural sector, who work tirelessly every day to serve our community, serve our economy, serve our regions, and keep this economy going.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific workforce composition figures for the speaker's electorate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census occupation and industry data for the Rangitata electorate; true if roughly 20% of employed residents give their occupation as labourer and about 16% work in manufacturing, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Because the other one you might not know is that we are ranked number one in the country for share of workers who work between 50 and 59 hours a week—50 and 59 hours a week, they are ranked number one.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Rangitata ranks first among New Zealand electorates for the share of workers working 50–59 hours a week.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Census hours-worked data broken down by general electorate; true if Rangitata has the highest share of employed people working 50–59 hours per week of any electorate, false if another electorate ranks higher.

veracity.statement: I point to one in my electorate, at Ashburton College: underfunded for their rebuild by $23 million; promised a three-stage rebuild, cut off at the knees in November—just after the election, actually.
