veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific funding shortfall and a specific timing for the curtailment of the Ashburton College rebuild.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education records and correspondence on the Ashburton College rebuild; true if the project was short of its cost by about $23 million and a promised three-stage rebuild was curtailed in November 2023, false if the shortfall figure or the November decision is materially different.

veracity.statement: I want to point out to Mr McAnulty, who talked about funding for flood resiliency and stopbanks. Well, actually, Mr McAnulty, there was $200 million set aside in the Budget under the Regional Infrastructure Fund.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $200 million Budget 2024 allocation for flood resilience under the Regional Infrastructure Fund.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents for the Regional Infrastructure Fund; true if $200 million was allocated within the fund for flood resilience/water storage works, false if no such allocation of that size exists.

veracity.statement: In this Budget, we also see that local catchment groups will be receiving funding—additional funding—and I’m very proud to see that in Budget 2024, $950,000 is going to be given over four years to the Ōtūwharekai Ashburton Lakes catchment group.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a named Budget 2024 allocation of a specific amount over a specific period to a named catchment group.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Environment / Ministry for the Environment funding documents; true if $950,000 over four years is allocated to the Ōtūwharekai Ashburton Lakes catchment group, false if the amount or term differs materially.

veracity.statement: Of course, we’ve got a 51 percent increase in funding for State highway pothole prevention and an extra $186 million for pothole prevention in Canterbury.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a percentage increase in national State highway pothole prevention funding and a dollar figure for Canterbury.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA National Land Transport Programme 2024–27 and the Government Policy Statement on land transport; true if State highway pothole prevention funding rises by about 51% and Canterbury receives about $186 million additional pothole prevention funding, false if either figure is materially different.

specificity.statement: If I talk about those great constituents in Rangitata and share with you a few home truths, because, of course, one-fifth of those working in Rangitata list their occupation as a labourer; 16 percent work in the manufacturing sector; and then we’ve got the hundreds and hundreds—if not thousands—of people who work in our agricultural sector, who work tirelessly every day to serve our community, serve our economy, serve our regions, and keep this economy going.
specificity.explanation: Carries two checkable proportions tied to a named electorate, though the agricultural figure trails off into "hundreds and hundreds—if not thousands".
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In this Budget, we also see that local catchment groups will be receiving funding—additional funding—and I’m very proud to see that in Budget 2024, $950,000 is going to be given over four years to the Ōtūwharekai Ashburton Lakes catchment group.
specificity.explanation: Names the recipient organisation, the exact amount and the period over which it is paid.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are committed to restoring law and order in this country, we are committed to keeping New Zealanders safe, and we are committed to investing not only to prevent crime from happening now but to prevent it from happening in 15 years’ time.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic commitments — no figures, named programmes or mechanisms, and "15 years' time" is rhetorical rather than a deliverable timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m incredibly proud of this Budget. I’m incredibly proud of our Minister of Finance and our Prime Minister. It is a fiscally responsible Budget, the first one in seven years, I have to say. It’s a Budget for all New Zealanders, a Budget for everyday Kiwis, including those that live in the mighty Rangitīkei—my fantastic electorate, 12,500 square kilometres of greatness.
specificity.explanation: Praise and slogans about the Budget with no spending figure, mechanism or named initiative; the only concrete number is the geographic size of her electorate.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They are the hardest-working, by definition, people in this country and it is about time they get the tax relief that they deserve.
rigor.explanation: Equivocation: a top ranking on one narrow hours band (50–59) is treated as establishing "hardest-working ... by definition", which neither follows from the statistic (people working 60+ hours sit outside that band) nor from any definition offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill strengthens our local democracy by reinstating polls on Māori wards and Māori constituencies. It requires councils to hold a binding poll at the 2025 local elections if they did not hold a poll when establishing Māori wards, and it adjusts the statutory time frames for local elections to give more time for the postal delivery of voting papers.
specificity.explanation: Names the measure, the mechanism (binding poll), the trigger condition (councils that established wards without a poll), the occasion (2025 local elections) and a second concrete change to statutory timeframes. Someone could check each against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Amendment Paper will require councils either to resolve to reverse their previous decision to establish Māori wards or to resolve to hold a poll at the 2025 local elections by 6 September 2024.
specificity.explanation: A precise procedural requirement: the two permitted resolutions, who must make them, and a hard calendar deadline of 6 September 2024. Fully actionable by a council reading it.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I hear members opposite already discounting individuals and views and organisations, and they’ll have their turn soon to be able to have their say on this particular piece of legislation.
civility.explanation: Pointed — it imputes dismissiveness to members opposite in response to an interjection — but it lands on their conduct in the debate rather than on any person's character or competence, and it concedes them their turn to speak.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: On the other side, they are anti-democratic—anti-democratic—and we are actually upholding the principles of democracy.
civility.explanation: A blunt charge levelled at a bloc of the House rather than at any named individual; no person's character, competence or worth is attacked, so it passes Civility despite its force. The tribalism is a Focus problem, not a Civility one.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I hear members opposite already discounting individuals and views and organisations, and they’ll have their turn soon to be able to have their say on this particular piece of legislation.
focus.explanation: Prompted by a policy debate but the content is entirely about how the other side is behaving toward submitters; no provision, figure or outcome of the bill is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: On the other side, they are anti-democratic—anti-democratic—and we are actually upholding the principles of democracy.
focus.explanation: Pure party characterisation. No clause, cost, timeframe, figure or named outcome appears; remove the labels 'anti-democratic' and 'upholding democracy' and nothing about the bill remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Amendment Paper will require councils either to resolve to reverse their previous decision to establish Māori wards or to resolve to hold a poll at the 2025 local elections by 6 September 2024.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the measure before the House — what councils must decide and by when. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, I would make the point that there are lots of people on the other side of the House, and there were a number of submitters who came through, who talk a lot about localism, but what they then reject is giving local people the opportunity to have their say.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy — that opposing binding polls is inconsistent with professed localism — but it rests on an equivocation on 'localism': decisions taken by a democratically elected local council are also local decision-making, so rejecting a referendum is not by itself rejecting local say. The inconsistency only follows if localism is defined as direct referendum, which is assumed rather than argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: If a local community decides, such as what Wairoa did, where they had a referendum and they voted to have a Māori ward and they have that Māori ward, we will respect that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the Wairoa district held a referendum/poll on establishing a Māori ward and that the vote was in favour, with the ward subsequently in place.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Wairoa District Council and Local Government NZ records of the binding poll on a Māori ward held with the 2022 local elections: true if a poll was held and a majority voted in favour, with a Māori ward established for Wairoa; false if no poll was held, if the poll was lost, or if no Māori ward resulted.

veracity.statement: These rights were hastily taken away by the previous Government, and now it is the time to do the right thing and give local communities their voice once again.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous (Labour) Government removed electors' rights to demand a binding poll on Māori wards, and that it did so hastily — i.e. with abbreviated parliamentary process.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2021 and its Hansard passage record: true if that Act repealed the poll/petition provisions of the Local Electoral Act 2001 and was passed under urgency or without full select committee scrutiny; false if the poll provisions survived or if the bill went through the ordinary select committee process with standard timeframes.

specificity.statement: When New Zealanders look back at New Zealand, the passing of this Budget will mark a turning point. It will mark a return to responsible economic management, a return to showing respect for taxpayers in the way we invest their money, a return to driving value for the dollars that the Crown uses on behalf of everyday people.
specificity.explanation: Opening framing of the Budget carries no figures, mechanisms, timeframes or named measures — a string of generic virtues ('responsible economic management', 'respect for taxpayers', 'driving value'). She was presenting a Budget with abundant concrete content available, so a far more specific opening was possible.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m proud that in this Budget, we are investing in structured literacy, we are investing in training teachers for the front line, we are investing in better classrooms, we are investing in special schools for children whose needs are complex.
specificity.explanation: Four named and identifiable spending lines — structured literacy, teacher training, classrooms, special schools — so there is real direction here, but no amounts, no timeframes and no targets attached to any of them, in a speech where Budget figures were available.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In just a week, we will deliver 3.5 million New Zealanders the overdue tax reduction they are owed.
specificity.explanation: Names the number of people affected (3.5 million), the measure (the personal income tax reduction) and a timeframe of one week, all of which are checkable. Falls short of 1.0 only because no dollar amount or threshold change is stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Well, there are the plans for light rail, which graced the front pages of the New Zealand Herald probably dozens of times, but never was a metre of track laid.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous government's Auckland light rail programme produced no constructed track at all despite heavy publicity.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Light Rail Ltd / Ministry of Transport project records and Auditor-General reporting up to July 2024: true if no rail track was physically laid for the project, false if any track construction occurred.

veracity.statement: There was $1.2 billion that was invested in the entirely wrongheaded three waters proposal.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure — $1.2 billion — spent on the Three Waters reform programme by the previous government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Internal Affairs / Treasury appropriations and reported expenditure on the Three Waters (Affordable Water) reform programme to 2023-24: true if total spend was approximately $1.2b, false if materially different (e.g. under $1b or over $1.5b).

veracity.statement: That was a legacy of a Government who chose, at a time of extraordinary inflationary pressure, not to take their foot off the spending gas but, instead, to throw spending fuel on the inflation fire, who embarked on an extraordinary programme of spending expansion at a time of extraordinary inflation. The result of that is that inflation in New Zealand has been both higher and has persisted longer than it needed to, than it should have, than it did in other parts of the world.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's inflation was both higher in level and longer in duration than inflation in other parts of the world.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI versus OECD/IMF CPI series for 2021-2024: true if NZ's peak annual inflation exceeded the OECD average and NZ returned to target later than comparable economies; false if NZ's peak was at or below the OECD average and its disinflation broadly matched peers.

veracity.statement: It should be to the shame of the members opposite that they were part of a Government that despite spending millions on education oversaw a decline in achievement not just by the average student but, most importantly, by those who had the least to begin with.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that educational achievement declined under the previous government, both on average and specifically for the most disadvantaged students.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: PISA 2018 vs 2022 NZ results, NMSSA and NCEA attainment series across 2017-2023, disaggregated by decile/equity index: true if both the overall and the lowest-socioeconomic measures declined, false if either held steady or improved.

veracity.statement: In this Budget, we haven’t just set out a framework that forecasts lower inflation—3.3 percent, by the latest number; lower than it was forecast to be, on track to allow Mr Orr to do his magic with those interest rates.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an inflation number of 3.3 percent as 'the latest', and that it is lower than had previously been forecast.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual increase for the June 2024 quarter and the Budget 2024 (BEFU) CPI track against the previous (HYEFU 2023) forecast: true if the latest print is 3.3% and it undershoots the earlier forecast for that period, false if the figure or the direction of revision differs.

rigor.statement: That was a legacy of a Government who chose, at a time of extraordinary inflationary pressure, not to take their foot off the spending gas but, instead, to throw spending fuel on the inflation fire, who embarked on an extraordinary programme of spending expansion at a time of extraordinary inflation. The result of that is that inflation in New Zealand has been both higher and has persisted longer than it needed to, than it should have, than it did in other parts of the world.
rigor.explanation: A genuine causal argument about fiscal policy: spending expansion during an inflationary period raised and prolonged inflation. The mechanism is stated and the conclusion tracks the premise, but the counterfactual ('longer than it needed to') is asserted rather than supported, and no evidence is offered to separate fiscal impulse from the supply and monetary factors — a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’ve done away with the pipe dream that was the previous Government’s position, that if they just stopped building prisons, everything would get better—if they just stopped building prisons, magically things would solve themselves. Well, that little experiment failed, and so, in this Budget, we have provided for new prison places.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the opponent's position is restated as a belief that halting prison construction would 'magically' fix things, a formulation nobody advanced, and the conclusion that new prison places are needed is drawn from the failure of that caricature. 'That little experiment failed' is also asserted with no measure of failure offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because there is an opportunity cost for every dollar wasted on a bureaucrat that isn’t delivering on a project that doesn’t get finished, on an idea that is never realised. That opportunity cost is more hip operations and better education standards.
rigor.explanation: A sound opportunity-cost inference: within a fixed appropriation, spending that yields no output forgoes alternative outputs, so the conclusion follows from the premise. It leans on the unargued assumption that the spending in question genuinely delivers nothing, which is the remaining gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It should be to the shame of the members opposite that they were part of a Government that despite spending millions on education oversaw a decline in achievement not just by the average student but, most importantly, by those who had the least to begin with.
civility.explanation: The substance — spending versus achievement outcomes — is legitimate, but 'it should be to the shame of the members opposite' directs moral reproach at named opposing members personally rather than staying on the record itself. Pointed and shaming, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And, no, we haven’t chosen to prioritise new bureaucracy, new layers of management and administration as the other side of the House would have us do; we’ve chosen to prioritise funding for nurses, for doctors, for Gumboot Friday mental health services.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point here — the allocation of health funding between administration and front-line staffing, with a named service (Gumboot Friday). But half the sentence's weight is a characterisation of what 'the other side of the House would have us do' rather than the measure itself, so the policy content comes wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ve done away with the pipe dream that was the previous Government’s position, that if they just stopped building prisons, everything would get better—if they just stopped building prisons, magically things would solve themselves. Well, that little experiment failed, and so, in this Budget, we have provided for new prison places.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a policy question before the House — prison capacity funding in the Budget — and it names the concrete outcome (new prison places), but the argument is routed through a characterisation of the previous government's mindset rather than the corrections data.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: In this Budget, we haven’t just set out a framework that forecasts lower inflation—3.3 percent, by the latest number; lower than it was forecast to be, on track to allow Mr Orr to do his magic with those interest rates.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that falling inflation puts the Reserve Bank in a position to reduce interest rates — a prediction about an outcome outside the speaker's own control.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: RBNZ Monetary Policy Committee decisions: true if the Official Cash Rate is reduced at least once within twelve months of this statement, false if the OCR is held or raised throughout that period.

civility.statement: We oppose the legislation introduced by the former Minister for Local Government the Hon Nanaia Mahuta on the basis that it was an aberration to our democracy.
civility.explanation: Hard criticism aimed at the legislation itself; the former Minister is named only as its author, with no attack on her character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, I don’t know if MP Shanan Halbert is interested in improving the environment and engaging with mana whenua groups and Māori in the communities where infrastructure’s being delivered—all I hear from that side of the House is a racket.
civility.explanation: Turns on a named member, casting doubt on whether he cares about the environment or about engaging with Māori, and dismisses him as noise — bad-faith imputation rather than engagement with anything he argued.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The departmental comment: the process for creating Māori wards in the Local Electoral Act by local council resolution was—until it was changed by Labour in 2021—subject to a petition of 5 percent of the electors in a binding poll, the same as it is for changing electoral systems.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that before the 2021 amendment, a council resolution to create a Māori ward could be overturned by a binding poll demanded by a petition of 5 percent of electors, and that the same 5 percent threshold applied to changing the electoral system.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Text of the Local Electoral Act 2001 (ss 19Z–19ZH and s 27) as it stood immediately before the Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2021; true if the pre-2021 provisions required a poll on a petition of 5% of electors for Māori ward resolutions and the same 5% threshold applied to electoral system change, false if the thresholds or mechanism differed.

veracity.statement: The bill was passed by a supermajority of Labour and its willing and able enablers in the Green Party, and received Royal assent less than a month after it was introduced on 1 March 2021.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the 2021 Māori wards amendment passed with Labour and Green votes and received Royal assent less than a month after its introduction (the speaker's word order garbles which date is 1 March).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: legislation.govt.nz record for the Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2021 — introduction date and Royal assent date — plus the Hansard division records for its readings; true if assent came under one month after introduction and Labour and the Greens voted in favour, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: Like it or not, this is the three coalition parties doing exactly what we campaigned on, delivering on our promises to New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that restoring binding polls on Māori wards was something all three governing parties campaigned on and promised.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2023 election policy documents of National, ACT and NZ First and the two coalition agreements signed November 2023; true if a commitment to restore local referendums on Māori wards appears in the coalition agreements and in the parties' campaign material, false if the commitment is absent from any of them or was added only post-election.

specificity.statement: The departmental comment: the process for creating Māori wards in the Local Electoral Act by local council resolution was—until it was changed by Labour in 2021—subject to a petition of 5 percent of the electors in a binding poll, the same as it is for changing electoral systems.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute, the mechanism, the exact petition threshold and the year of change — anyone could look it up.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We want to give local communities the right to choose their representation arrangements.
specificity.explanation: States a direction but supplies no mechanism, threshold or timeframe for how communities would exercise that choice; the detail he gave earlier (the 5 percent poll) is not carried into this commitment.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is the legacy that Te Pāti Māori seek to perpetuate in their absolutely callous seeking of votes from people who are uninformed about our democracy.
focus.explanation: No policy, figure or mechanism is engaged; the whole content is an account of another party's motives and the supposed ignorance of its voters.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, the ACT Party’s not obsessed with race, unlike the members of the Opposition.
focus.explanation: Pure party contrast — a characterisation of what the other side is 'really like', naming no measure, cost, or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We want to give local communities the right to choose their representation arrangements.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance of the bill before the House — who decides local representation arrangements — with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is the parties now in Opposition who led this divisive conversation in 2021, and it is the parties in Opposition that now sit in Opposition largely because they insisted on dividing New Zealanders by race, assigning different rights in our democracy to different groups, when what New Zealanders really, really are asking for is an opportunity for better infrastructure, and enabling more affordable housing, making it easier to get around, and a cleaner environment we can all enjoy.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc causal inference: because the 2021 law preceded the election loss, the loss is attributed to it, with nothing offered (polling, vote shifts, survey evidence) to link the two; the closing list of what New Zealanders 'really' want is asserted, not evidenced.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That side of the House are bringing in different provisions for wards established for Māori than what exist for any other ward.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill before the House imposes requirements (a poll/referendum) on Māori wards that do not apply to the establishment of general, urban or rural wards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The enacted text of the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill 2024 and the Local Electoral Act 2001: true if the bill imposes poll/disestablishment requirements that apply only to Māori wards and constituencies and not to other ward types; false if the same requirements apply across all wards.

veracity.statement: So the Labour Government fixed it. They brought the provisions to establish Māori wards in exactly the same as any other ward, as it should be, and they left that decision up to local councils, as it should be.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Labour Government's amendment removed the binding-poll mechanism that applied only to Māori wards, putting them on the same footing as other wards and leaving the decision to councils.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2021: true if it repealed the poll/petition provisions applying only to Māori wards, leaving establishment to council resolution as for other wards; false if differential provisions remained.

veracity.statement: With over 10,000 submissions presented to the Justice Committee within a five-day period—only five days, that’s the lack of respect that this Government has to the people of New Zealand; 10,000 people and more put in submissions to the select committee so their voice could be heard, 10,000-plus.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two facts: that the Justice Committee received more than 10,000 submissions on the bill, and that the submission window was five days.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's report on the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill and the committee's published call for submissions: true if the report records more than 10,000 submissions and the submission period was about five days; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: The Waitangi Tribunal has found that this legislation breaches Te Tiriti.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Waitangi Tribunal, in its urgent inquiry, found this bill to be in breach of the Treaty of Waitangi.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal's 2024 urgent inquiry report into the Māori wards legislation: true if the Tribunal found the bill breaches Treaty principles; false if it made no such finding or declined the urgency.

veracity.statement: Whangārei District Council actually said that this legislation could drive a wedge in our communities, that it could be divisive and could actually undermine the important relationship that council has with hapū in their district.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of Whangārei District Council's submission to the select committee — that the bill risks division and damage to the council's relationship with hapū.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Whangārei District Council's written or oral submission to the Justice Committee on the bill: true if it warns of divisiveness and harm to the council–hapū relationship; false if its submission makes no such statement or takes a contrary position.

focus.statement: That side of the House are bringing in different provisions for wards established for Māori than what exist for any other ward.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the measure before the House — the differential provisions it creates — rather than on the other party in general.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I don’t believe that individually they are racist, but what I do believe they are is spineless and gutless because they have given in to the whims of their coalition partners just to get into power.
focus.explanation: Strip out the characterisation of the other side's motives and the coalition deal and no policy content remains — no mechanism, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Remembering, e te whānau, this is one man, one vote. Māori only get one vote. If you’re on the Māori electoral roll, you only get to vote in the Māori ward. It’s no special treatment. It’s just like our Māori electorates that we have in this Whare.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual mechanism of Māori wards and the electoral roll rather than the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They can signal to me to be quiet all they like; bugger them. I’m not going to be quiet, because this is a disgrace. This is an absolute disgrace.
civility.explanation: 'Bugger them' is aimed at the members opposite rather than at any argument — dismissive of colleagues rather than engaging them, though short of a personal insult. The 'disgrace' half is directed at the bill and costs nothing.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I don’t believe that individually they are racist, but what I do believe they are is spineless and gutless because they have given in to the whims of their coalition partners just to get into power.
civility.explanation: 'Spineless and gutless' is a direct attack on the character of the members opposite, not on their argument. The disclaimer about individual racism does not offset a fresh characterological insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s a disgrace, and you, sir, should be ashamed of yourself. You won’t, because you’re sitting there smug, but you should be.
civility.explanation: A sustained personal address to a named member — telling him to be ashamed and characterising him as smug. The target is the individual, not the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: May I translate: I feel very special because Māori are once again being singled out. We’re being singled out by this legislation. The Green Party have already shared that it’s racist to te iwi Māori.
civility.explanation: Very hard criticism — calling the legislation racist — but it is directed at the measure, not at any member. The sarcasm of 'I feel very special' lands on the bill's effect rather than on a person.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Let’s look at this bill. Does this bill bring in provisions just for Māori? Yes. Is that discrimination? Yes. Is this institution—Government—targeting people because of their race? Yes. In any other sphere, an act that can be described like that and fit that definition would be racism, because that is the definition of racism.
rigor.explanation: A structured subsumption argument: a definition is stated, then the bill is tested against each element. The inference is orderly, but the second step equivocates — it moves from 'provisions just for Māori' to 'discrimination' without argument, which is the contested premise the whole conclusion rests on.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They certainly didn’t listen to councils, because there are more councils that oppose this bill than support their water bill.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that the Government did not listen to councils on this bill — is supported by a comparison against council support for an unrelated water bill. The comparison class is irrelevant to the inference; council opposition to this bill would need to be measured against this bill's treatment of it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: A couple of years later, they brought in Māori wards—there was not even a peep, because those who were concerned about it realised that those concerns weren’t founded and they had nothing to worry about.
rigor.explanation: Infers a general proposition — that opposition to Māori wards dissolves once concerns prove unfounded — from a single local anecdote, and attributes a specific change of mind to opponents from the mere absence of protest. Appeal to anecdote plus an argument from silence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Remembering, e te whānau, this is one man, one vote. Māori only get one vote. If you’re on the Māori electoral roll, you only get to vote in the Māori ward. It’s no special treatment. It’s just like our Māori electorates that we have in this Whare.
rigor.explanation: A valid rebuttal of the 'special treatment' objection: if roll enrolment is exclusive, a Māori ward vote substitutes for a general ward vote rather than adding to it, so no elector gets extra voting power. The analogy to Māori electorates is apt rather than decorative.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I guarantee, in the future, they will look back on this moment, because inevitably it will pass because they have the numbers, and when they’re old, they’ll look back on their career, and none of them will highlight this as a highlight in their career.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the bill will pass the House on Government numbers (the checkable core of the claim; the further prediction about how members will regard their careers in old age is not operationalisable).
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The division record for the third reading of the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill: true if the bill passed on Government party votes; false if it was defeated, withdrawn or lapsed.

specificity.statement: Now, they do it all the time. They’ve done it in the Budget. They’ve stripped funding. They’ve made it harder.
specificity.explanation: Attempts to convey substance about Budget decisions but names no programme, no appropriation and no figure; 'stripped funding' and 'made it harder' are not checkable or actionable as stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: With over 10,000 submissions presented to the Justice Committee within a five-day period—only five days, that’s the lack of respect that this Government has to the people of New Zealand; 10,000 people and more put in submissions to the select committee so their voice could be heard, 10,000-plus.
specificity.explanation: Carries a submission count and a submission-window length, both attributed to a named committee — checkable against the committee record.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This has taken us two months to get to this point. It took Labour just two weeks to get through the entire process last time round.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the current bill's process has run two months, versus about two weeks for the 2021 Labour-led Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary records for the 2021 Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill (introduction date to Royal assent, passed under urgency) and for the 2024 Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill; true if the 2021 bill completed all stages in roughly two weeks and the 2024 bill has taken roughly two months, false if either elapsed time is materially different.

veracity.statement: These are the actual numbers: between 3,123 and 4,277 first preference votes in the general ward. In the Māori ward, Te Whanganui-a-Tara ward, it was 888.
veracity.explanation: Asserts first-iteration STV first-preference vote totals for successful candidates in Wellington's general wards (3,123–4,277) versus the Te Whanganui-a-Tara Māori ward (888) at the 2022 local election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Wellington City Council official 2022 local election STV results; true if the successful general-ward candidates' first-iteration first preferences fall in the 3,123–4,277 range and the Te Whanganui-a-Tara Māori ward figure is about 888, false if the published figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: I thought that this exciting new innovation, it might encourage more people to vote. Actually, it didn’t. It did exactly the reverse. The turnout in the Māori ward was very, very low.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that turnout in Wellington's Te Whanganui-a-Tara Māori ward at the 2022 local election was very low, and by implication lower than under the prior arrangement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Wellington City Council / LGNZ published 2022 local election turnout percentages by ward; true if Māori ward turnout was materially below the general-ward and citywide turnout, false if it was comparable or higher.

veracity.statement: There’s nothing in that section that says Māori wards are exempt from that requirement, and there’s also nothing in section 19Z which sets the framework for establishing Māori wards or constituencies.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that neither section 19V nor section 19Z of the Local Electoral Act 2001 contains an exemption for Māori wards from the fair-representation (±10 percent) requirement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Text of sections 19V and 19Z of the Local Electoral Act 2001 on legislation.govt.nz; true if neither section contains a Māori ward exemption from the ±10 percent rule, false if either section (or a cross-reference within them) provides one.

veracity.statement: In fact, the law says plus or minus not 10 percent but 5 percent, and that’s general and Māori wards.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the statutory population tolerance for parliamentary electorate boundaries is ±5 percent, applying to both general and Māori electorates.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Act 1993 provisions governing the Representation Commission's electoral population quota tolerance (s 269 and related); true if the permitted variation is ±5 percent for both general and Māori electorates, false if a different tolerance applies or it differs between the two.

veracity.statement: To achieve that in the last electoral review in 2019, what happened? An extra seat was created and 22 seats—22 seats—had their boundaries changed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the most recent Representation Commission review created one additional electorate and altered the boundaries of 22 electorates.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Representation Commission final report for the 2019/2020 boundary review; true if one new general electorate was created and 22 electorates had boundary changes, false if the counts differ materially.

civility.statement: The second point I want to make—and this might be educational for people on the other side—is that there were some consequences of rushing this process.
civility.explanation: Condescension toward opposing members — the aside implies they need educating — though it stops well short of a personal insult and the substance is about the process.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: These are the actual numbers: between 3,123 and 4,277 first preference votes in the general ward. In the Māori ward, Te Whanganui-a-Tara ward, it was 888.
specificity.explanation: Exact first-preference vote counts for named wards in a named election system; directly checkable against the published results.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: By having dedicated Māori representation in councils, we can grow Māori participation in local elections and actually legitimise the actions of councils.
specificity.explanation: Names a mechanism and two intended outcomes but supplies no figures, timeframe or evidence for either.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It means that every prospective voter—and I say “prospective voter”—in the Māori ward is worth 1.67 prospective voters in the average general ward.
rigor.explanation: The inference tracks the arithmetic he laid out: an entitlement calculated at 0.609 councillors rounded up to one implies a vote-weight ratio of roughly 1/0.609 ≈ 1.64–1.67. The conclusion follows from the stated premise, with a minor slide between enrolled-population entitlement and individual voter weight.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I thought that this exciting new innovation, it might encourage more people to vote. Actually, it didn’t. It did exactly the reverse. The turnout in the Māori ward was very, very low.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts a general claim (Māori wards raise turnout) with a single jurisdiction's result — a hasty generalisation from one case — and infers causation ('did exactly the reverse') from one low turnout figure without a counterfactual.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This Government goes on about democracy, but how democratic can a system actually be if no one is paying any attention to it?
rigor.explanation: A rhetorical question offered in place of an argument: it equates low attention with a lack of democratic legitimacy without establishing either the premise or the link, and leans on the contrast with the Government's rhetoric rather than on evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: By having dedicated Māori representation in councils, we can grow Māori participation in local elections and actually legitimise the actions of councils.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — the mechanism of dedicated Māori representation and its claimed effect on participation and legitimacy — with no party-directed content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government goes on about democracy, but how democratic can a system actually be if no one is paying any attention to it?
focus.explanation: Contains a real point about democratic legitimacy and engagement, but it is framed as a swipe at what the Government 'goes on about' rather than at any named provision or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, every single one of them is very clear that their council and their people and their communities are better off because they’re there. Why? Because they know they are their own walking, talking, Māori solution.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the effect of Māori ward councillors in Tai Tokerau councils — a named policy and its outcome, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill forces binding referenda on one issue. Why not have a referendum on three waters? Why not have a referendum on cycleways? Why not have a referendum on the number of councillors a council has. They’re all things that you could have a referendum on, but you’ve just chosen a Māori ward or not a Māori ward. That is incredibly selective, it’s illogical, it’s inconsistent to say one decision is subject to a poll.
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism of the bill itself — which council decisions are made subject to a binding poll — and tests it against comparable decisions. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I will not be lectured by a party who in 108 years of their history has not had a single Māori leader.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's internal history. No policy, measure, figure or outcome connected to the bill before the House is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And that goes to the root of this bill, because this bill restores the situation to what it was in the early 2000s, when it was first introduced by Helen Clark, by the Labour Government, and sustained all the way through to 2021. We are doing nothing more than restoring it to the status quo.
focus.explanation: Engages what the bill actually does — reinstating the poll provisions that existed in law between the early 2000s and 2021.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, every single one of them is very clear that their council and their people and their communities are better off because they’re there. Why? Because they know they are their own walking, talking, Māori solution.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that communities are better off rests entirely on the self-report of the councillors themselves plus an assertion about what they represent — appeal to anecdote and self-assessment, with no independent evidence connecting the premise to the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This bill forces binding referenda on one issue. Why not have a referendum on three waters? Why not have a referendum on cycleways? Why not have a referendum on the number of councillors a council has. They’re all things that you could have a referendum on, but you’ve just chosen a Māori ward or not a Māori ward. That is incredibly selective, it’s illogical, it’s inconsistent to say one decision is subject to a poll.
rigor.explanation: A genuine consistency argument: if binding polls are appropriate for contested local decisions, singling out one decision needs a justification. It stops short of showing that no relevant difference exists, so the charge of illogicality is asserted rather than established.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: He called you a Nazi, James, and you had feelings.
civility.explanation: An interjection aimed at a named member personally, mocking him for taking offence at being compared to a Nazi. It engages no argument; the target is the man.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In fact, I suspect some of them would quite like to go back to before 1893 and it would be one man, one vote.
civility.explanation: Imputes a desire to disenfranchise women to the people who submitted in support of the bill. Not a direct insult to a named member, but a sneering attribution of bad faith rather than engagement with their argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: No wonder he doesn’t understand transgender.
civility.explanation: A jibe at a named member's personal understanding, prompted by his interjection. Attacks the man, not any argument he made.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: My first thankyou goes to the white saviours on the other side of the House: Kieran McAnulty and Celia Wade-Brown. Thank you for saving us poor, helpless Māori from our own ill will!
civility.explanation: Names two members and derides their motives through sustained sarcasm — a personal characterisation of them as condescending 'white saviours' rather than any engagement with what they argued.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Oh, Mr Speaker, I don’t take offence to the member’s comments. Much of what she says does not make any sense, and that’s another one of them.
civility.explanation: Dismisses a named member's contributions as generally incoherent — an attack on her competence rather than on anything she argued.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I did want to thank, also, members of the committee for the generally collegial way in which they approached the work, although we did have Willie Jackson sitting on our subcommittee and, in between terrorising Don Brash and popping out to have a go at the Taxpayers’ Union, he did make some very disparaging remarks about Helen Clark, which I thought were very unfair.
civility.explanation: Singles out a named member and characterises his conduct in committee mockingly ('terrorising', 'popping out to have a go'). Pointed at the person's behaviour rather than at any argument, though it stops short of abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Since the referendum option was removed in 2021, there has been an explosion of Māori wards.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that removing the binding-poll mechanism in 2021 was followed by a large increase in the number of councils establishing Māori wards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Count of territorial and regional authorities with Māori wards or constituencies before the 2021 amendment to the Local Electoral Act versus after (Local Government NZ / DIA records for the 2022 local elections); true if the number rose sharply (e.g. from a handful to dozens), false if the number was broadly unchanged.

veracity.statement: Representation is so critical to our system of local government, and I’m really disturbed that less than a third of eligible voters voted in the Tauranga election last weekend.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that turnout in the Tauranga local election of the preceding weekend was under one-third of eligible voters.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official turnout figure for the Tauranga City Council election held 20 July 2024 (Tauranga City Council / DIA declaration of result); true if turnout was below 33.3% of enrolled electors, false if it was at or above that.

veracity.statement: I will not be lectured by a party who in 108 years of their history has not had a single Māori leader.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in 108 years the Labour Party has never had a Māori party leader.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The list of Labour Party leaders since the party's founding in 1916 (Parliamentary/party records); true if none identified as Māori, false if any leader was Māori. The '108 years' span is also checkable against the 1916 founding date.

veracity.statement: I will not be lectured by a party who had a deputy leader and for three years with a majority Government refused to make him the Deputy Prime Minister of this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that during the 2020–2023 majority Labour Government the party's deputy leader was not made Deputy Prime Minister.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial list for the 2020–2023 Labour Government and Labour's deputy leadership over that period; true if Labour's deputy leader (Kelvin Davis) was not appointed Deputy Prime Minister while Labour governed alone, false if he held that office.

veracity.statement: If members care to actually read their papers and consider the departmental report, they will see that those written submissions were two-thirds opposed to the bill and one-third in favour.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a roughly 2:1 opposed-to-supportive split among the written submissions analysed in the departmental report.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's departmental report on the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Constituencies) Amendment Bill; true if the tally of written submissions received via the online portal was approximately two-thirds opposed and one-third in support, false if the split materially differs.

veracity.statement: And that goes to the root of this bill, because this bill restores the situation to what it was in the early 2000s, when it was first introduced by Helen Clark, by the Labour Government, and sustained all the way through to 2021. We are doing nothing more than restoring it to the status quo.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the referendum/poll provision this bill reinstates was introduced by the Clark Labour Government in the early 2000s and remained law until 2021.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Local Electoral Act 2001/2002 amendments introducing binding polls on Māori wards, and the Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2021 that removed them; true if the poll mechanism was enacted under the Clark Government in the early 2000s and remained in force until 2021, false if it originated elsewhere or lapsed earlier.

specificity.statement: But let it be clear: a Māori ward provides for people on the Māori roll to vote for candidates standing in that ward. It is not an extra vote.
specificity.explanation: States the actual mechanism — who votes, in which ward, and that it substitutes for rather than adds to a general-ward vote. Concrete enough to check against the Local Electoral Act, though it carries no figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If members care to actually read their papers and consider the departmental report, they will see that those written submissions were two-thirds opposed to the bill and one-third in favour.
specificity.explanation: Names the source (the departmental report) and gives a precise split of written submissions — anyone can go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I also accept the kōrero that the individual members on the other side are not particularly racist at all. I accept that kōrero. But this policy is absolutely racist.
civility.explanation: An extremely hard charge levelled at the policy while explicitly exempting the individual members opposite from it. The attack lands entirely on the measure, not on any person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Mr Meager, when you accuse others of not doing their job, you’re not doing your job as one of our young Māori aspirant leaders, and one day you’re going to have to face Māori properly, Mr Meager, rather than sit around with your mates in the National Party.
civility.explanation: A direct, sustained personal attack on a named member — impugning his performance of his role and his standing with his own people, following the earlier description of him as 'the sell-out'.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That’s what drove this legislation, and the Opposition can’t get it through their stupid thick heads that this is what Māoridom wanted.
civility.explanation: Abuse ('stupid thick heads') aimed at opponents collectively rather than at a named individual — short of a personal insult but well past civil engagement.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s interesting that we listened to Willie Jackson last night—he suffers from acute amnesia, because he was part of The Alliance and part of the 46th Parliament that passed the provisions for Māori seats and the community’s right to petition for a referendum back in 2002, with the Local Electoral Amendment Act 2002.
civility.explanation: 'Suffers from acute amnesia' is mockery of a named member's faculties rather than of his argument — short of a direct insult, but sneering at the person.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That’s what drove this legislation, and the Opposition can’t get it through their stupid thick heads that this is what Māoridom wanted.
focus.explanation: Despite the framing, the sentence makes a substantive claim about the motivation for the Māori wards legislation and what Māori communities sought from it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Do you think Rawiri Waititi, for one second, could get on to a council? Do you think Willie Jackson for one second could get on to a council? There is absolutely no chance for anyone with a pro-Māori agenda; there is no chance, there is no opportunity in getting on a council.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy question at issue: whether Māori candidates can win election to councils without Māori wards. No party-bashing content, weak inference notwithstanding.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The barrier’s not going to be put in the way of property owners having multiple votes in multiple districts. No, it is only Māori wards and their voters that must be approved by a district-wide vote.
focus.explanation: Engages the specific mechanism of the bill before the House — which ward types the poll requirement attaches to — with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The bill really only seeks to restore the policy settings for Māori wards, which were in place, as Mr Brewer has pointed out, for 19 years before the previous Government changed it, effectively denying the democratic voting rights of local communities to choose and to have a say about their own governance.
focus.explanation: Describes what the bill does and the settings it restores, naming the timeframe and the prior regime — entirely on the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Do you think Rawiri Waititi, for one second, could get on to a council? Do you think Willie Jackson for one second could get on to a council? There is absolutely no chance for anyone with a pro-Māori agenda; there is no chance, there is no opportunity in getting on a council.
rigor.explanation: A universal conclusion ('absolutely no chance for anyone with a pro-Māori agenda') drawn from rhetorical questions about two or three named individuals — an argument from anecdote, and one undercut by the counter-examples the speaker himself supplies moments later (Derek Fox as mayor).
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So the ACT Party does a deal with the National Party in Epsom. They do a deal so that their leader can win the seat in Epsom, but then they say, “Oh, that’s got nothing to do with tweaking democracy.” Democracy has been tweaked many times, and the Treaty is an important and an implicit part of that model.
rigor.explanation: A tu quoque: the opponents' acceptance of an electorate accommodation is offered as grounds for accepting Treaty-based representation. Even granting the Epsom premise, nothing connects an electoral arrangement between parties to the constitutional status of the Treaty in local government — the conclusion outruns the analogy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So in 2010, with no Māori wards in Auckland Council, we got 20 percent Māori. We did it then and we’ll do it again.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from four named winners in a single 2010 election to the claim that Māori representation is secure without Māori wards — an argument from selected anecdote that does not address whether those candidates campaigned on, or were elected because of, Māori representation.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Derek became a mayor, but over 50 percent of his voter base are Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Derek Fox was elected mayor in a district whose electorate is majority Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Local authority election records confirming Derek Fox's mayoralty (Wairoa District), plus Stats NZ census/electoral-roll data for that district; true if Māori are more than 50% of the district's population/electors at the time of his election, false if materially below 50%.

veracity.statement: If you’re a multiple property owner, you can vote two, three, four times.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under New Zealand local electoral law a person owning property in several districts may cast a vote in each.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Local Electoral Act 2001 and Electoral Commission/DIA guidance on the ratepayer elector roll; true if non-resident ratepayers may enrol and vote in each district where they own qualifying property, false if a person is limited to a single local-authority vote.

veracity.statement: The barrier’s not going to be put in the way of property owners having multiple votes in multiple districts. No, it is only Māori wards and their voters that must be approved by a district-wide vote.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill imposes a binding district-wide poll requirement on Māori wards alone and on no other ward type.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill as introduced; true if the poll/referendum requirement applies only to Māori wards and constituencies, false if general, rural or other ward arrangements are subject to the same requirement.

veracity.statement: It’s interesting that we listened to Willie Jackson last night—he suffers from acute amnesia, because he was part of The Alliance and part of the 46th Parliament that passed the provisions for Māori seats and the community’s right to petition for a referendum back in 2002, with the Local Electoral Amendment Act 2002.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Willie Jackson was an Alliance MP in the 46th Parliament and that the Local Electoral Amendment Act 2002, passed by it, created both Māori wards and a community right to demand a referendum on them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary membership records for the 46th Parliament (1999–2002) and the text of the Local Electoral Amendment Act 2002; true if Jackson was an Alliance list MP in that Parliament and the Act contains both the Māori ward provisions and the poll-demand mechanism, false on either count.

veracity.statement: Submissions were open for two days under Minister Mahuta.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2021 legislation removing the Māori ward poll provisions allowed only a two-day window for public submissions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's record for the Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill 2021 — whether it went to select committee and, if so, the published submission period; true if submissions were open for about two days, false if the period was materially longer or if the bill was passed under urgency with no submission process at all.

veracity.statement: So in 2010, with no Māori wards in Auckland Council, we got 20 percent Māori. We did it then and we’ll do it again.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 20 percent of those elected to the inaugural Auckland Council in 2010 were of Māori descent, without any Māori ward.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The list of the 20 councillors elected to Auckland Council in October 2010 and their published iwi/Māori descent affiliations; true if four (20%) were of Māori descent, false if materially fewer.

veracity.statement: The bill really only seeks to restore the policy settings for Māori wards, which were in place, as Mr Brewer has pointed out, for 19 years before the previous Government changed it, effectively denying the democratic voting rights of local communities to choose and to have a say about their own governance.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the poll-based Māori ward settings the bill restores were in force for 19 years before being repealed by the previous Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Commencement of the Local Electoral Amendment Act 2002 and the date of the 2021 amendment removing the poll provisions; true if the interval is about 19 years and the restored settings match the pre-2021 regime, false if the interval is materially different or the bill does not restore the same settings.

specificity.statement: This Government is determined to stop the division of New Zealanders where in-group rights and collective identity is used, when we should be celebrating the common humanity that unites us all.
specificity.explanation: A statement of general sentiment offered as the rationale for the bill: no mechanism, no figure, no named provision, and nothing here that could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And there it is—the arrogance and the ignorance of the National Party and this Government. This Government is taking New Zealand race relations backwards—backwards by decades, by centuries.
focus.explanation: Characterises the other party's general disposition ('arrogance and ignorance') and makes a sweeping claim about race relations; no measure, mechanism, figure or named outcome is engaged, even though a bill is before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill, essentially, breaks the promise of this Government to give local bodies more control.
focus.explanation: Holds the Government to a named commitment (devolving control to local bodies) against the specific measure before the House — accountability tied to a policy, not party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But this Government is determined, driven by the extreme views of its coalition partners, to take a one-size-fits-all approach. It’s shameful.
focus.explanation: Gestures at a policy stance ('one-size-fits-all approach') but the weight is on the other side's coalition politics and motives rather than on any mechanism, cost or effect of the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Yet across the room, I see Cameron Brewer with his chest out talking about taking this country backwards.
civility.explanation: Mockery of a named member's bearing ('with his chest out') rather than engagement with what he argued; short of a direct insult but sneering at the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In fact, today I’m calling out the Minister. He’s National’s version of David Seymour, because under his leadership and this Government’s leadership, we have seen some of the most racist legislation come through this House in a mere six months.
civility.explanation: A direct personal attack on the Minister — naming him as the party's version of another member and attributing racist legislation to his personal leadership, rather than criticising the bill's contents.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think of the utu politics of this Minister and his intention to quickly change the names back of Waka Kotahi, to change back road signs that listed Māori names within our communities.
civility.explanation: Imputes a personal motive of revenge ('utu politics') to the Minister; the criticism lands on his character rather than on the merits of the naming decisions.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We heard Cameron Brewer do politics by anecdote as he ran through electors, people of Māori descent who had been elected in Auckland’s elections.
civility.explanation: Pointed characterisation of a named member's method ('politics by anecdote'); it targets how he argued rather than insulting him, but edges toward the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There was never a situation where Māori had more than one vote under the Māori ward system; they only ever had one vote, and that was for the ward that they chose to vote in. To say otherwise is pernicious and quite misleading.
civility.explanation: 'Pernicious' imputes bad faith to those making the opposing claim, going beyond calling the claim wrong, though no individual is named.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There we had it last night, with James Meager calling my colleague Kieran McAnulty and one of the Green colleagues “white saviours”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that James Meager used the phrase 'white saviours' of Kieran McAnulty and a Green MP in the House on the preceding sitting day.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard transcript for the Local Government (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill debate of 22–23 July 2024; true if Meager's speech contains the phrase applied to those members, false if it does not appear.

veracity.statement: Many, many councils told them that they do not support this legislation that is going through the House today.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a large number of territorial and regional councils formally opposed the Māori wards bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Submissions and the Justice/Governance select committee report on the Local Government (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill 2024; true if numerous council submissions opposed the bill, false if council submissions were predominantly supportive or absent.

veracity.statement: In a nutshell, the Attorney-General agrees that this bill takes Māori backwards.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Attorney-General's report on the bill concluded it disadvantages Māori representation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Attorney-General's report to Parliament on the Local Government (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill 2024; true if it states the bill is likely to reduce Māori representation or disadvantage Māori-roll electors, false if it reaches no such conclusion.

veracity.statement: But have a look at the select committee report. Between 2002 and 2019, only two councils managed to establish Māori wards. The facts of it were clear. Even if you go through all of the elected members, it was a recognised problem that Māori were not getting a seat around the table on a consistent basis, because they simply weren’t getting voted in. So there was a problem to be addressed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that only two councils established Māori wards in the period 2002–2019.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Local Government Commission / select committee report records of Māori ward establishment under the Local Electoral Act 2001; true if exactly two councils had wards established over 2002–2019, false if the count is materially different.

veracity.statement: There was never a situation where Māori had more than one vote under the Māori ward system; they only ever had one vote, and that was for the ward that they chose to vote in. To say otherwise is pernicious and quite misleading.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that electors under the Māori ward system held only one vote, cast in the ward of their chosen roll, and never an additional vote.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Local Electoral Act 2001 provisions on Māori roll electors and council voting entitlements; true if Māori-roll electors vote only in the Māori ward, false if they were entitled to vote in both a general and a Māori ward.

specificity.statement: I think of the utu politics of this Minister and his intention to quickly change the names back of Waka Kotahi, to change back road signs that listed Māori names within our communities.
specificity.explanation: Names two concrete, checkable actions — reverting the Waka Kotahi agency name and reversing te reo Māori road signage — though with no dates, costs or mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But here’s the real kicker: local bodies with Māori wards with effective and meaningful and consistent Māori representation around the table, representing Māori communities, are more effective. They do a better job. They run into problems less frequently. They find themselves being hauled through the Environment Court less frequently. They have a breakdown of relationship with iwi and hapū less frequently.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete indicator (Environment Court proceedings) but supplies no figures, no comparison set and no timeframe; 'do a better job' and 'less frequently' commit to nothing measurable.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But have a look at the select committee report. Between 2002 and 2019, only two councils managed to establish Māori wards. The facts of it were clear. Even if you go through all of the elected members, it was a recognised problem that Māori were not getting a seat around the table on a consistent basis, because they simply weren’t getting voted in. So there was a problem to be addressed.
rigor.explanation: Offers a documented datum (two councils over seventeen years) and draws the limited conclusion that a representation problem existed; the inference tracks the evidence, with a modest gap in that low ward uptake and low election of Māori members are treated as one fact.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But here’s the real kicker: local bodies with Māori wards with effective and meaningful and consistent Māori representation around the table, representing Māori communities, are more effective. They do a better job. They run into problems less frequently. They find themselves being hauled through the Environment Court less frequently. They have a breakdown of relationship with iwi and hapū less frequently.
rigor.explanation: A chain of comparative performance claims offered with nothing but the speaker's own impression of select committee testimony — an appeal to anecdote, with no data connecting ward representation to fewer Environment Court appearances.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We’re going to force you to go to a referendum; a referendum that we know will be much harder to succeed in than the local bodies would otherwise want.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the binding polls the bill mandates will mostly fail to retain the Māori wards that councils had chosen to establish.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Official results of the Māori ward polls held with the 2025 local body elections; true if a majority of the councils polled voted to disestablish their Māori ward, false if most polls returned a vote to retain.

specificity.statement: I want it to be crystal clear: this bill will restore the ability for communities to have a direct influence on the establishment of Māori wards and Māori constituencies by restoring the ability of 5 percent of council’s electors to call for a binding poll on Māori ward establishment decisions.
specificity.explanation: Names the measure and the operative mechanism with a threshold (5 percent of electors triggering a binding poll) — checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The ultimate goal is to provide Kiwis with greater choice: choice about who you bank with and who you get your electricity from; choice about how you manage your finances and what technology plan you sign up for. Choice is freedom, and when customers have choice, businesses have to compete.
specificity.explanation: A statement of aims in slogan form — no figures, thresholds, timeframes or mechanisms, in a speech that elsewhere supplies them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The data-sharing framework is entirely opt-in, meaning that customers must first give their explicit consent for their data to be shared.
specificity.explanation: States a concrete design feature of the regime — explicit customer consent as a precondition for any data sharing — that can be checked against the bill's clauses.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I want it to be crystal clear: this bill will restore the ability for communities to have a direct influence on the establishment of Māori wards and Māori constituencies by restoring the ability of 5 percent of council’s electors to call for a binding poll on Māori ward establishment decisions.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of the bill before the House; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Māori New Zealanders, let’s be clear, have successfully been elected as councillors and mayors without the need for Māori wards. Councils have responsibilities to consult with mana whenua on issues that affect them. Changes to Māori wards do not affect these responsibilities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori candidates have been elected to councils and mayoralties in general (non-Māori) wards, and that statutory consultation duties with mana whenua are unaffected by the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Local Government NZ / council election records showing Māori candidates elected as councillors and mayors in territorial authorities without Māori wards (true if such elections exist), plus the Local Government Act 2002 consultation and Māori-participation provisions being untouched by the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill (false if the bill amends those duties).

veracity.statement: There was a submission from three Western Bay of Plenty District councillors that considered that the consultation processes involved in establishing a Māori ward were not an adequate substitute for a referendum in which all ratepayers would have the right to express their opinion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a submission from three named-in-kind Western Bay of Plenty District councillors was made to the Justice Committee arguing consultation is not an adequate substitute for a referendum.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published submissions to the Justice Committee on the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill; true if a submission from three Western Bay of Plenty District councillors makes that argument, false if no such submission exists.

veracity.statement: New Zealand has some of the world’s most profitable banks. Our four big banks are Australian-owned and the fact that they make bigger profits in New Zealand than at home speaks to the lack of competition.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that NZ's four largest banks are Australian-owned, and that those banks earn higher profits (profitability) in New Zealand than in Australia.
veracity.subject: speaker
