veracity.falsification_criterion: Commerce Commission market study into personal banking services (2024) and RBNZ bank disclosure data, plus the Australian parents' segment reporting; true if ANZ, ASB, BNZ and Westpac are Australian-owned and their NZ returns on equity/assets exceed their Australian group figures, false if NZ profitability is at or below the Australian figures.

veracity.statement: For example, many of the big Australian banks offer 10-minute online home loans to the Australian customers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that several major Australian banks provide home loan approval through an online process taking about ten minutes for Australian customers, as at mid-2024.
veracity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The bill is supported by the Privacy Commissioner and complements existing protections in the Privacy Act.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Privacy Commissioner's public statements and submission on the Customer and Product Data Bill; true if the Commissioner expressed support, false if the Commissioner opposed it or expressed no position.

veracity.statement: Just a few weeks ago, the OECD recommended that New Zealand introduce a consumer data right regime.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The OECD Economic Survey of New Zealand 2024 (and any OECD report published in mid-2024 on NZ); true if it contains a recommendation to introduce a consumer data right / open banking regime, false if no such recommendation appears.

rigor.statement: Māori New Zealanders, let’s be clear, have successfully been elected as councillors and mayors without the need for Māori wards. Councils have responsibilities to consult with mana whenua on issues that affect them. Changes to Māori wards do not affect these responsibilities.

rigor.statement: New Zealand has some of the world’s most profitable banks. Our four big banks are Australian-owned and the fact that they make bigger profits in New Zealand than at home speaks to the lack of competition.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable but with a real gap: higher profitability is consistent with weak competition, but it is offered as if it settles the matter, with no ruling out of cost, scale or risk-weighting differences between the two markets.

civility.statement: Māori New Zealanders, let’s be clear, have successfully been elected as councillors and mayors without the need for Māori wards. Councils have responsibilities to consult with mana whenua on issues that affect them. Changes to Māori wards do not affect these responsibilities.

divination.statement: Even our colleagues across the aisle support it, and I’d just like to acknowledge previous commerce and consumer affairs Ministers who have worked on this bill.

divination.falsification_criterion: The division records for the Customer and Product Data Bill's first and subsequent readings; true if Labour voted in favour at each reading, false if Labour voted against at any reading.

veracity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But this gives me an opportunity to speak about the more competitive space in the banking system. They made $7.2 billion last year, just in 2023.

focus.statement: That’s why successive Labour Ministers have shepherded through this work, and it’s great to see that the Minister has picked this up and prioritised it on his work programme.

specificity.statement: But this gives me an opportunity to speak about the more competitive space in the banking system. They made $7.2 billion last year, just in 2023.

veracity.statement: MBIE is one of the largest regulatory agencies and is responsible for more than 100 pieces of legislation across a wide range of subjects.

specificity.statement: The Regulatory Systems (Economic Development) Amendment Bill amends 24 Acts and associated regulations across five portfolios, including Commerce and Consumer Affairs, Science, Innovation and Technology, Media and Communications, Justice, and Energy.

specificity.statement: Our Government is a pro-growth Government. We believe in a better economic outcome for all New Zealand.

rigor.statement: Many of these changes are small in nature, but together they add up to countless hours no longer wasted on paperwork and barriers to success in our economy.

focus.statement: Our Government is a pro-growth Government. We believe in a better economic outcome for all New Zealand.

rigor.statement: There’s some elements of this bill, although I’ll be supporting it, that look slightly upside down, that turn people into units. You see that even in the shift of naming from what the similar bill we had was, and was called, through to what it’s called now.

rigor.explanation: The support offered for the bill is a single personal experience plus an assumed universal reaction — an appeal to anecdote and to popularity, with nothing connecting the bill's provisions to the difficulty described.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Information asymmetry creates market power and anti-competitive behaviour and it’s in that vein that this bill seeks to address these key issues in some of our biggest and most important sectors in the domestic economy in New Zealand.

rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In terms of the banks and the 10-minute loans that are available overseas, as the Hon Andrew Bayly mentioned in his speech, as well as other innovations in the banking sector, we do not have the same access to those things as the countries that we like to compare ourselves do, so it is time we made those changes.

veracity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I also want to look at where this bill came from, and the genesis of this bill was from the work of former Ministers of Commerce and Consumer Affairs David Clark and Duncan Webb, so I wanted to acknowledge their work in getting the ball rolling for this bill.

veracity.statement: This bill came through with strong intellectual vigour that was given to it by David Clark and then given to it by Duncan Webb, and it’s come through with the full support of the House, as I understand it, today.

focus.statement: There’s some elements of this bill, although I’ll be supporting it, that look slightly upside down, that turn people into units. You see that even in the shift of naming from what the similar bill we had was, and was called, through to what it’s called now.

focus.statement: I’ve certainly, over the most recent recess, had the opportunity to speak to a lot of people in my community and around New Zealand who didn’t vote for a lot of the things that they are seeing being moved through this Government at the moment.
focus.explanation: Departs from the bill entirely to make a general point about the Government's mandate; no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There’s a risk that this bill in its current form has morphed into something that is just there to back business.

specificity.statement: We need more competition. We need to strengthen the economy. This is one of the ways that we’re doing that. We’re simplifying processes, we’re making it easier for businesses to get things done, we’re making it easier for consumers to make decisions.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic aims — more competition, simpler processes, easier decisions — with no figures, timeframes or named mechanisms from the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I’m sure it’s so well done that we will just pass it all the way through, and I’m looking forward to that process.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Customer and Product Data Bill will proceed through the remaining parliamentary stages and be enacted.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The parliamentary record for the Customer and Product Data Bill: true if the bill is reported back and passes its third reading into law; false if it is defeated, withdrawn, or still not passed by the end of the parliamentary term.

divination.statement: I will be on that select committee and I’ll be zealously guarding the needs of the ordinary New Zealanders when we look at the detail, because we, sure as eggs, will have people lobby us on that committee to try and water it down, to try and say it’s too hard.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that industry interests will make submissions to the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee seeking to narrow or weaken the bill on grounds of difficulty or cost.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Published submissions to the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee on the Customer and Product Data Bill: true if bank, telco or electricity industry submitters sought narrowed scope, delayed commencement or reduced obligations citing implementation difficulty or cost; false if no such submissions were made.

focus.statement: The doubling exports in 10 years—let’s be aspirational, but let’s actually have a plan and let’s actually have investment to make sure that happens.
focus.explanation: Engages a named government commitment (doubling exports in 10 years) and asks for the plan and investment behind it — legitimate scrutiny of a specific target rather than party-bashing.

focus.statement: I guess it is worth noting the political tensions raised by the Minister for Economic Development around this belief that sensible regulation can be really good for the wellbeing of the country, while at the same time there is a political drive to slash regulations that actually often protect, for example, the safety of workers in the workplace or allow them to stay well.
focus.explanation: A genuine regulatory-policy point, but the weight of it is about the Government's general political direction rather than any provision of the bills before the House.

civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The doubling exports in 10 years—let’s be aspirational, but let’s actually have a plan and let’s actually have investment to make sure that happens.
specificity.explanation: Names the export target but supplies no figures, mechanism or timeframe of his own — the call for 'a plan' and 'investment' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But they make amendments to things like the Electricity Act 1992, to the Employment Relations Act 2000, the Gas Act 1992, the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015, the Immigration Advisers Licensing Act 2007, as well as the Mines Rescue Act 2013 and the Parental Leave and Employment Protection Act 1987.
specificity.explanation: Names seven specific Acts amended by the bill, each with its year — precisely checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As an immigration spokesperson, having worked with people who have been failed by immigration advisers, I think it’s important that we have robust systems in place to make sure that that workforce, which does really important work in supporting our migrant workers, actually has clear guidelines around, for example, what, how, and when their licence will be struck or suspended if they don’t act accordingly.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act and the mechanism (guidelines for when a licence is struck or suspended) but offers no proposed wording, threshold or figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill will be improving four pieces of workplace relations and safety legislation that I’m responsible for: the Employment Relations Act 2000, the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015, the Mines Rescue Act 2013, and the Parental Leave and Employment Protection Act 1987.
specificity.explanation: States a count and names each of the four Acts affected within her portfolio — directly checkable against the bill.

specificity.statement: It does this now by only requiring that the regulator make reasonable efforts to establish whether a relevant regulator or regulatory agency is taking action, or intends to act, regarding a situation, rather than having to contact over 100 entities, which it currently does, and it will assist in reducing the number of invoices for ACC CoverPlus Extra customers.

rigor.statement: I’ve been travelling the country over our recess, meeting with businesses and economic development agencies and sort of hearing about the challenges and things. One of the things, and with this legislation, is about how clunky much of what Government does is, how clunky the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment system is.
rigor.explanation: A general conclusion about MBIE's systems being 'clunky' rests solely on anecdotal conversations during a recess tour — an appeal to anecdote, with no data or example offered to connect the visits to the conclusion.

rigor.statement: I guess it is worth noting the political tensions raised by the Minister for Economic Development around this belief that sensible regulation can be really good for the wellbeing of the country, while at the same time there is a political drive to slash regulations that actually often protect, for example, the safety of workers in the workplace or allow them to stay well.

veracity.statement: The amazing thing about this legislation is it is so interesting because that piece of legislation in the Regulatory Systems (Economic Development) Amendment Bill does something really important: it replaces “by the Customs” with “Customs”.

rigor.statement: That’s what this side of the House is about, because it’s only through economic growth that we can afford the healthcare and social services and the education that we all want our kids and mokopuna to access.

civility.statement: However, we have had recent situations where the Minister has departed from the general bipartisan approach of talking to business associations, unions, the wider community—having open consultation.

rigor.statement: In fact, it actually works across 24 pieces of legislation, and 24 is a large number, so it is a good use of our time in this House.

veracity.statement: In fact, it actually works across 24 pieces of legislation, and 24 is a large number, so it is a good use of our time in this House.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Regulatory Systems (Economic Development) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Immigration and Workforce) Amendment Bill as introduced in 2024, on legislation.govt.nz/bills.parliament.nz; true if the number of principal Acts amended across the two bills is 24, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Secondly, to those who might choose to stop work—a number of parents obviously want to return but some, shortly after birth, might choose to stop; but they don’t lose that entitlement, thanks to these changes, to still get that paid parental leave that they had earned by working leading up to that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill's amendments to the Parental Leave and Employment Protection Act 1987 preserve paid parental leave entitlement for parents who do not return to work after the birth.
veracity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I just wonder: is this as ambitious as we get from this Government?

specificity.statement: One, starting around clause 45, is the protections that were sort of touched on briefly before, for pre-term babies.

focus.statement: This is an important bill—more important, the Government would say, than their last bill which they tried to introduce to this House but could not because the Minister was not ready to take the call.

rigor.statement: This bill unlocks the growth potential there, but it does nothing to guarantee to those investors who are interested in those assets that the Government will back aquaculture and will back the primary industry growth in that area.

specificity.statement: The region has no certainty that the Government won’t put 3,000 more trucks on their regional roads and make the ratepayers there pay for the damage that those trucks will do to support the aquaculture industry.

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It provides rangatiratanga, it improves the governance arrangements, it empowers the MIOs, the mandated iwi organisations, to have more direct control over moana and Aotearoa Fisheries Ltd by removing those intermediary decision-making bodies.

veracity.statement: Or will this Government go back to the days where there was no certainty in investment in the ferries and no certainty in the rail industry in Marlborough and house prices in Picton plummeted—where, for a decade, no one could sell their Picton homes because there was no certainty of jobs, because their construction industry was bottomed out, because their builders and tradies could not rely on any work, and so investment from that region fled?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in an earlier period of ferry/rail investment uncertainty, Picton house prices fell sharply and homes were effectively unsaleable for a decade.

veracity.falsification_criterion: REINZ/QV median house price and days-to-sell series for Picton/Marlborough over the decade referenced; true if median prices fell materially and sales volumes/days-to-sell show a sustained decade-long collapse, false if prices were flat or rising and homes continued to sell over that period.

veracity.statement: I’m really interested in the way that it has progressed, because it has been something that has garnered bipartisan support, where there was not bipartisan support in the select committee stage.

veracity.statement: It’s been 32 years since the signing of the fishery settlement, and Te Ohu Kai Moana and the iwi mandated authorities have been working hard to manage this fishery on behalf of te iwi Māori.

veracity.statement: Collectively, te iwi Māori own 40 percent of commercial fisheries quota and related commercial fisheries assets.

specificity.statement: This legislation will afford Māoridom greater autonomy—which it deserves—better investment, surety, and opportunity, and an industry which is worth billions will only grow out of the back of that, certainly helping Māori communities in doing so.

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s made a number of changes to update and modernise the governance framework to give iwi more authority over the entity that looks after Māori fisheries assets, Te Ohu Kai Moana and Aotearoa Fisheries Ltd, and making sure that iwi have greater authority to appoint and remove directors.

rigor.statement: As we know, it’s by the appointment and removal of directors that organisations can have the authority to change the direction of an organisation.

rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: On this side of the House—I’m sure actually on that side too; to a lesser degree perhaps—we believe in the power of economic development in transforming communities, the power of driving economic development to lift people up out of poverty, to lift Māori communities to a better place in life.

focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We are at the third stage, so this will become law if it goes through today, which I suspect it may very well do, from what I’m hearing from various parts of the House.

divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Hansard third-reading record for the Māori Fisheries Amendment Bill; true if the bill passed its third reading on 23 July 2024, false if the reading was not completed that day or the bill was defeated.

focus.statement: So this bill grants greater rangatiratanga and mana motuhake over decision making when it comes to the fishing interests of those particular iwi and Māori organisations.

focus.explanation: A genuine point about the bill and Te Tiriti obligations, but the weight rests on an unnamed 'everything else that is going on' by the Government rather than on any identified policy or measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But yes, since Ōpōtiki was referenced, we were able to visit there, and we heard loud and clear that they also were hoping to gain certainty and had faith in our fast-track bill—that this would go a long way towards helping that region over there get certainty around the Ōpōtiki Harbour development.
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure (the fast-track bill) and a specific outcome (certainty for the Ōpōtiki Harbour development) rather than characterising opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So the offshore stuff, in terms of population, where Ngāpuhi had a huge population—the modelling, to me, I think needed a greater balance in terms of the distribution.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the allocation model: because a small-population iwi may hold a long coastline, population-weighted offshore allocation is unbalanced. The premises are offered but the link between coastline interest and entitlement is asserted rather than shown, leaving a gap between evidence and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When Te Tiriti is honoured, our migrant communities are better able to flourish, are better able to find a sense of purpose and belonging in this land, because we’re connected to the history of this land.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that migrant communities flourish when Te Tiriti is honoured rests on an appeal to sentiment and a bare assertion of connection to history; no mechanism or evidence links the premise to the claimed effect.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But yes, since Ōpōtiki was referenced, we were able to visit there, and we heard loud and clear that they also were hoping to gain certainty and had faith in our fast-track bill—that this would go a long way towards helping that region over there get certainty around the Ōpōtiki Harbour development.
rigor.explanation: Support for the fast-track legislation is inferred from what the speaker personally heard on a select committee visit — an appeal to anecdote, with no data or analysis offered about whether the bill delivers the certainty claimed.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m glad that this particular legislation is able to deal with those particular issues, because we’re talking 20, 30 years of iwi not being able to draw down on it, because there were iwi conflicts between our interpretation of mana, where mana sat in hapū and not in iwi organisations.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete problem (drawdown blocked by the registered/mandated iwi organisation structure) and a rough timeframe of 20-30 years, but carries no figures, clauses or mechanism for how the bill fixes it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I think we should be careful, or the Government should be careful, of claiming that they are honouring the Crown’s Te Tiriti obligations with just the passing of this bill, in the context of everything else that is going on that is, effectively, trampling over Te Tiriti.
specificity.explanation: The alleged breaches are left entirely unspecified — no policy, bill or action is named, so there is nothing a listener could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So that was to grant that more straight governance control, and then to redistribute the shares of Te Ohu Kai Moana and Aotearoa Fisheries Ltd, which, as is noted, own 60 percent of the shares in Sealord.
specificity.explanation: Names the entities, the mechanism (removing intermediary bodies, redistributing shares) and a percentage shareholding — concrete enough to check.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In essence, the changes, the amendments, that will be made through this bill will ensure that iwi have more control and input against the backdrop of rangatiratanga over their fisheries assets, all the while improving the benefits for Māori and also reducing costs.
specificity.explanation: A summary of intended effects — more control, more benefit, lower cost — with no figures, no named governance change and no timeframe attached to any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think we should be careful, or the Government should be careful, of claiming that they are honouring the Crown’s Te Tiriti obligations with just the passing of this bill, in the context of everything else that is going on that is, effectively, trampling over Te Tiriti.
civility.explanation: Contested territory and a pointed criticism, but aimed at the Government's claim and conduct, not at any individual; no person is impugned.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So that was to grant that more straight governance control, and then to redistribute the shares of Te Ohu Kai Moana and Aotearoa Fisheries Ltd, which, as is noted, own 60 percent of the shares in Sealord.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Māori fisheries settlement entities (Te Ohu Kai Moana / Aotearoa Fisheries Ltd, trading as Moana New Zealand) hold a 60 percent shareholding in Sealord Group.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Sealord Group ownership records — NZ Companies Office shareholding register and Moana New Zealand / Te Ohu Kai Moana annual reports for 2024; true if the Māori-owned entity's stake is 60 percent, false if it is materially different (e.g. 50 percent, with Nippon Suisan holding the remainder).

specificity.statement: So, to achieve this objective—and I’m going to get a bit technical, but that’s OK because we’re hearing beautiful submissions from around the House, so I’ll delve into the technical side of it—the Māori Fisheries Act established several statutory entities, including Te Ohu Kai Moana Trust; Te Ohu Kai Moana Trustee Ltd, to act as a corporate trustee company in which iwi are shareholders; Te Pūtea Whakatupu Trustee Ltd, to represent urban Māori interests, which was raised earlier as well; and Te Wai Māori Trustee Ltd, to advance Māori freshwater fisheries interests.
specificity.explanation: Names each statutory entity created by the principal Act and states the function of each; a listener could check the structure against the Act.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s only through a strong economy that we can solve the cost of living crisis, lift incomes, and afford the public services we all deserve.
specificity.explanation: A general slogan about economic strength — no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named measure that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Act also required an independent review, and that independent review was completed in March 2015, and it recommended substantive changes to the governance structure of the settlement entities, and it essentially simplified processes for trading assets.

veracity.statement: I personally—as someone that’s not Māori but I love Māori friends and people I consider family that I do know—am proud of the fact that the Māori economy is about $70 billion and that fisheries makes the muscle and titan part of this.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published estimates of the Māori economy/asset base (BERL 'Te Ōhanga Māori' reports, Reserve Bank/Treasury summaries) current at July 2024: true if the accepted estimate is around $70 billion, false if the accepted figure is materially different (e.g. substantially above or below that order).

veracity.statement: If you read through their annual reports and you read through their vision statements and their mission statements in the annual plans, you will see a clear play for protecting and restoring the health and wellbeing of the moana.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Ohu Kaimoana annual reports and annual plans (vision/mission statements) up to 2024: true if they state objectives of protecting or restoring the health and wellbeing of the marine environment, false if those documents contain no such stated objective.

focus.statement: Mr Speaker, if you don’t mind, I’d also like to just reiterate, if I can, and perhaps sum up that National supports this bill, that getting our primary industries and fishing sector back on track is all part of the Government’s plan to rebuild the economy and get it working for all Kiwis.

focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: As we look towards the future and what that means, I’m excited that Te Ohu Kai Moana is going to go around again and engage with iwi on a roadshow, starting in August.

divination.falsification_criterion: Te Ohu Kaimoana's own website/news and hui notices: true if iwi roadshow/engagement hui were held commencing in August 2024, false if no such hui series ran or it began materially later.

rigor.statement: But, more importantly, if you restore the kelp into the moana, it brings back so many more species; it means that the ocean is healthy.
rigor.explanation: A causal chain is offered (kelp restoration → more species → ocean health) and the steps are connected, but the leap from species return to 'the ocean is healthy' is asserted rather than supported, and no evidence is given for the mechanism.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But it would be folly for this House to think that the aspirations of Te Aupōuri are the same as the aspirations of Ngāi Tahu, at the other end of the country, which is why these iwi hui are important.

rigor.statement: I think that actually shows the importance of that broader level of engagement with stakeholders, particularly with iwi and others as well.

civility.statement: There were some other suggestions that were floated, as part of this process, by the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries, and I am pleased that those changes have not flowed through to the final stage of this bill.

focus.statement: We need to support our fisheries industries with less red tape, less regulation, and actually get the wheels moving.

veracity.statement: The Māori economy, as we know, is estimated at nearly $70 billion, and fisheries make up a huge proportion of this.

specificity.statement: So seafood export revenue is expected to increase 5 percent to reach $2.2 billion in the year 30 June 2024, and is expected to continue to grow, because it’s a growth export market.

specificity.statement: We need to support our fisheries industries with less red tape, less regulation, and actually get the wheels moving.

specificity.statement: The electoral college system will be removed and, instead, MIOs, recognised iwi organisations, and representative Māori organisations will vote to appoint directors of the entity.

specificity.statement: It’s only through a strong economy, we know, that we can solve the cost of living crisis, that we can deliver future prosperity across much different communities and across our country, lift incomes, and then afford the public services that we all deserve.

rigor.statement: That is why it was important that these governance requirements were reviewed, that there was good consultation, that the select committee engaged very thoroughly with everybody who made submissions, that the Ministers were engaged and that those Ministers had gone across this House.

The inference is sound in direction but the step from 'diverse beneficiaries' to 'this particular consultation process was the right one' is asserted rather than shown.

veracity.statement: Last week, Police announced changes to their eligibility criteria, with individuals on their restricted driver’s licence and those holding a residence visa now allowed to start the recruitment process.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in the week before 24 July 2024 NZ Police changed recruitment eligibility so that restricted-licence holders and residence-visa holders can begin the recruitment process.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police recruitment eligibility criteria and Police media releases dated mid-July 2024; true if both the restricted-licence and residence-visa changes were announced in that week, false if no such change was made or the criteria differ materially.

veracity.statement: Although it’s too early to claim victory, I can advise that over the last week, Police received 630 applications.
veracity.explanation: Asserts NZ Police received 630 recruitment applications in the week preceding 24 July 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police weekly recruitment application figures (or an OIA/ministerial release of them) for the week ending ~21 July 2024; true if the count is 630 or within rounding, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: In terms of applicant numbers, I’m advised that in the first six months of 2024, Police have received an average of 526 applications per month. This is 53 percent higher than the monthly average over 2023.
veracity.explanation: Two linked data claims: a monthly average of 526 police applications for Jan–Jun 2024, and that this is 53 percent above the 2023 monthly average.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police recruitment application statistics for January–June 2024 and for calendar 2023; true if the 2024 monthly mean is ~526 and exceeds the 2023 monthly mean by ~53%, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Police numbers have dropped since November 2023, but this was expected, with no recruit wings commencing at RNZPC between October 2023 and January 2024 due to the Christmas closedown period and the transition.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no recruit wings commenced at the Royal New Zealand Police College between October 2023 and January 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RNZPC wing commencement records / Police responses to written questions for Oct 2023–Jan 2024; true if no wing began in that window, false if any wing commenced.

veracity.statement: Why isn’t the Government doing more to retain the police officers we currently have, given there are 124 fewer police officers since her Government took office?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that sworn police officer numbers are 124 lower than when the current Government took office in late November 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police monthly sworn-staff (FTE) figures for November 2023 versus June/July 2024; true if the decline is ~124, false if materially different or if numbers rose.

veracity.statement: I am happy to tell members that the number of people using the tax calculator has recently reached half a million—to be precise, 513,000 people have used the calculator to see what they will be getting in long overdue tax relief that the other side of the House voted against.
veracity.explanation: Asserts 513,000 uses of the Budget 2024 tax calculator as at 24 July 2024, and additionally that the Opposition parties voted against the tax relief package.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/Budget website usage statistics for the Budget 2024 tax calculator as at late July 2024 (true if ~513,000, false if materially different); the Hansard division record for the Taxation (Budget Measures) Act 2024 settles the second limb.

veracity.statement: From next Wednesday, personal income tax thresholds will rise from $14,000 to $15,600, from $48,000 to $53,500, and from $70,000 to $78,100.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the precise new personal income tax thresholds taking effect on 31 July 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Taxation (Budget Measures) Act 2024 / Inland Revenue published income tax thresholds effective 31 July 2024; true if the three threshold pairs match, false if any differ.

veracity.statement: And I’m proud that this Government will do exactly that on Wednesday next week, when tax brackets are adjusted for the first time in 14 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no adjustment to personal income tax brackets had occurred in the 14 years before 31 July 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue history of personal income tax thresholds; true if the last threshold change took effect in 2010, false if any threshold was altered between 2010 and 2024 (the 2021 addition of a new 39% top rate would need to be assessed as an 'adjustment').

veracity.statement: It has increased, and it’s happened because the previous Government increased Government spending by 84 percent. It drove up domestic inflation. When that happens, it raises interest rates. That slowed the economy, and it’s risen to high levels of unemployment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government increased Government spending by 84 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenses series for the 2017/18 to 2022/23 fiscal years; true if the increase is ~84% on a like-for-like measure, false if materially lower or if no comparable measure supports it.

veracity.statement: This Government’s determined to kill inflation to get it under control. It’s great to see last week it’s at 3.3 percent.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index release for the June 2024 quarter (published 17 July 2024); true if annual CPI inflation was 3.3%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, can he confirm that his Government’s decision to increase the cost of car registration, reintroduce prescription fees, scrap public transport subsidies for young people, scrap affordable water reforms and other changes that increase costs for Kiwis has actually added half a percent to inflation in the last quarter, meaning we would already be within the 1 to 3 percent target inflation range now if they hadn’t done those things?

specificity.statement: Well, can he confirm that his Government’s decision to increase the cost of car registration, reintroduce prescription fees, scrap public transport subsidies for young people, scrap affordable water reforms and other changes that increase costs for Kiwis has actually added half a percent to inflation in the last quarter, meaning we would already be within the 1 to 3 percent target inflation range now if they hadn’t done those things?

rigor.statement: Police numbers have dropped since November 2023, but this was expected, with no recruit wings commencing at RNZPC between October 2023 and January 2024 due to the Christmas closedown period and the transition.
rigor.explanation: A genuine causal explanation: the conclusion (the drop was expected) follows from the stated gap in recruit wings, since attrition without intake reduces headcount. The gap is that a training pause explains a pause in additions but not the retention side, so there is a modest gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It has increased, and it’s happened because the previous Government increased Government spending by 84 percent. It drove up domestic inflation. When that happens, it raises interest rates. That slowed the economy, and it’s risen to high levels of unemployment.
rigor.explanation: A stated causal chain (spending → domestic inflation → interest rates → slower economy → unemployment) that is internally coherent, but presents a single cause as the whole explanation and offers nothing to exclude global inflation, monetary settings or COVID-era effects — a single-cause fallacy sitting on an otherwise valid chain.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, can he confirm that his Government’s decision to increase the cost of car registration, reintroduce prescription fees, scrap public transport subsidies for young people, scrap affordable water reforms and other changes that increase costs for Kiwis has actually added half a percent to inflation in the last quarter, meaning we would already be within the 1 to 3 percent target inflation range now if they hadn’t done those things?
rigor.explanation: The arithmetic inference is sound on its own premises — removing 0.5 points from a 3.3 percent rate puts inflation inside the band — though it assumes the removed measures had no offsetting effects elsewhere.

divination.statement: Wing 376 will graduate next week on 1 August and a further wing will graduate every five weeks from then on.

divination.falsification_criterion: NZ Police graduation records and media releases; true if Wing 376 graduated on 1 August 2024 and successive wings graduated at roughly five-week intervals through the following year, false if the graduation slipped or the cadence was not maintained.

divination.statement: We expect interest rates to come down when we get it back in the band.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that interest rates will fall once annual CPI inflation returns to the 1–3 percent target band.

rigor.statement: What that Government had budgeted for was to grossly increase costs on landlords, which, I believe, would have been passed on to tenants in the rents that were charged.

rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the policy — if the private return is that favourable, a mandate is redundant — but it presents a false dichotomy between incentives and regulation, ignoring the split-incentive and information-failure reasons building codes exist.

rigor.statement: The point there, that’s a very astute one on behalf of His Worship, is that we have a blunt instrument at the moment, such that the settings in Northland are exactly the same as they are in Southland.
rigor.explanation: The inference is valid on its own terms: if one national setting applies identically across very different climates, calling it a blunt instrument follows. Whether the premise about identical settings holds is a separate question.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And I’ll tell you what we’re not doing: we’re not going around New Zealand promising people we’ll build 100,000 KiwiBuild homes.
focus.explanation: Names a specific past policy (KiwiBuild's 100,000 homes) but only as a contrastive jibe at the other party; it advances no mechanism, cost or outcome of her own government's approach.

focus.statement: And I’m glad that I’ve made a decision rather than waiting another nine months to make a decision.
focus.explanation: Attached to a real decision, but the sentence itself carries no policy content — its weight is a contrast with the previous government's alleged delay.

veracity.statement: I would also point her to market analysts who agree that inflation is now lower than it had been forecast to be at this point in the cycle.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare Stats NZ CPI annual inflation for the June 2024 quarter against the RBNZ Monetary Policy Statement / Treasury Budget 2024 forecasts for that quarter, plus contemporaneous bank economist commentary; true if the actual print is below the earlier forecast track, false if at or above it.

veracity.statement: So too is the Mayor of the Far North, Mr Moko Tepania, who said he would like the H1 changes reversed—again, listening to his constituents—because in his view, these are contributing to the critical shortage of affordable housing that they so desperately need.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Media reports or council statements from Moko Tepania in July 2024; true if he is recorded calling for the H1 changes to be reversed/paused on affordability grounds, false if no such statement exists or he took the contrary position.

veracity.statement: The point there, that’s a very astute one on behalf of His Worship, is that we have a blunt instrument at the moment, such that the settings in Northland are exactly the same as they are in Southland.

veracity.statement: Is the Minister comfortable committing more families to cold and unhealthy under-insulated housing when almost one in five hospital admissions of young children with acute respiratory infections could be prevented if their homes were free from damp and cold?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that close to 20 percent of young-children hospitalisations for acute respiratory infection are attributable to, and preventable by removing, damp and cold housing conditions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ housing-and-health research (e.g. He Kāinga Oranga/University of Otago population attributable fraction estimates, Ministry of Health hospitalisation data); true if a published estimate puts the preventable fraction at roughly one in five, false if the published attributable fraction is materially lower.

veracity.statement: The funding has provided a $25 million funding boost to conservation, including $5 million for Cathedral Cove, Mautohe, and $6 million for enhancing tracks and expanding Department of Conservation’s (DOC’s) network of short walks and day hikes.

focus.explanation: Tests a named policy (restoration of interest deductibility) against its stated purpose and a measured outcome — accountability for a specific commitment, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Well, what I can tell that member is, in the previous administration, rents went up $175 a week. What we are doing is making sure that we increase the supply of houses being built, the supply of rental properties being available, and the supply of social housing being available. If we can do that, we can put downward pressure on rents. We can make sure that people get affordable housing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that weekly rents rose by $175 over the term of the previous Labour Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE tenancy bond lodgement data (national median weekly rent) between October 2017 and October/November 2023; true if the increase is approximately $175 per week, false if materially different (e.g. under $140 or over $210).

veracity.statement: What I’d say to you is that we are going to double the amount of renewable energy in this country. It is unacceptable to take eight years to consent a wind farm and then two years to build it. I would encourage that member and the Labour Party to actually support that legislation so we can get renewable projects consented in one year and built much quicker.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that consenting a wind farm in New Zealand takes eight years and building it a further two.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Consenting timelines for recent New Zealand wind farms (e.g. resource consent lodgement-to-grant dates recorded by MfE/EPA or councils for projects such as Mt Cass, Kaiwaikawe, Harapaki); true if typical or cited cases show roughly eight years from application to consent plus about two years' construction, false if typical timelines are materially shorter.

veracity.statement: How does the Prime Minister feel knowing that his Government’s decision under even just the emissions reduction plan alone has taken us off track to meet our climate goals and will increase inequality?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's decisions in the emissions reduction plan have moved New Zealand off track to meet its climate goals.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry for the Environment emissions projections published alongside the 2024 draft emissions reduction plan, and the Climate Change Commission's assessment of it; true if those assessments show projected emissions exceeding emissions budgets 1–3 or the 2050 target pathway, false if they show the budgets being met.

veracity.statement: Well, we remain on track to deliver the emissions reductions budget one and emissions reduction budget two.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's projected emissions remain within emissions budgets one (2022–25) and two (2026–30) as at the time of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry for the Environment emissions projections current in mid-2024 and the subsequent Climate Change Commission monitoring reports; true if projected net emissions sit within EB1 and EB2, false if projections show either budget being exceeded.

veracity.statement: Planning for a replacement to the Brynderwyns was abruptly stopped by the last Government and it’s left Northland far too often in a vulnerable disruption.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government halted planning work on a replacement route for the Brynderwyn Hills section of SH1.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA Waka Kotahi project records and Government Policy Statement / funding decisions 2018–2023 on a Brynderwyns alternative route; true if planning or investigation work was discontinued or defunded under that Government, false if the work continued or was never commenced under the prior National Government either.

veracity.statement: Last year, a report by the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research found that the Warkworth to Wellsford section of the expressway alone would increase New Zealand’s annual GDP by $497 million including benefits for Northland. The AA has said, following this announcement, that this would be a “game changer” for Northland.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a 2023 NZIER report put the annual GDP gain from the Warkworth to Wellsford section at $497 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZIER report on the Northland/Warkworth–Wellsford expressway published in 2023; true if it states an annual GDP effect of approximately $497 million for that section, false if it gives a materially different figure or covers a different scope.

veracity.statement: The last Government cancelled the Roads of National Significance programmes—one of the worst decisions they made.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government cancelled the Roads of National Significance programme.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2018 Government Policy Statement on land transport and subsequent NZTA funding decisions; true if the RoNS programme as a whole was discontinued or its projects cancelled/deferred, false if the programme continued to be funded under that Government.

veracity.statement: What specific initiative, if any, can she point to in Budget 2024 that will reduce insurance that is up 14 percent, with some families paying an additional $2,000 per year or $45 per week extra?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that insurance costs have risen 14 percent, and that this amounts to about $2,000 a year or $45 a week for some households.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index dwelling/contents insurance subgroup, annual change to the June 2024 quarter; true if the annual increase is approximately 14 percent and the dollar figures are consistent with typical premium levels, false if materially different.

rigor.statement: Well, what I can tell that member is, in the previous administration, rents went up $175 a week. What we are doing is making sure that we increase the supply of houses being built, the supply of rental properties being available, and the supply of social housing being available. If we can do that, we can put downward pressure on rents. We can make sure that people get affordable housing.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference offered conditionally: increasing the supply of housing, rentals and social housing puts downward pressure on rents. The supply-price link is a standard and supported step, and the conditional framing ('if we can do that') does not overreach; the gap is that no reason is given to think the supply increase will be delivered at a scale that moves rents.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So it was absolutely fantastic news yesterday that this Government is accelerating work on a four-lane expressway from Auckland to Whangārei as part of our hugely successful roads of national significance. We know the difference that roads like Waikato expressway and the Kāpiti expressway have made for the regions, and now we’re bringing that to Northland.
rigor.explanation: The inference is an argument from analogy — Waikato and Kāpiti expressways made a difference, therefore Northland's will — with nothing offered to establish that the Northland case shares the relevant features (traffic volumes, geography, cost-benefit).
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I can point to the fact that this is a Government that is spending wisely and that, therefore, the overall impact of our Budget is to reduce pressure on inflation.
rigor.explanation: Close to circular: the premise ('spending wisely') is simply a favourable restatement of the conclusion ('reduces inflation pressure'), with no independent support offered for either.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: A specific initiative in Budget 2024 is the establishment of the Regional Infrastructure Fund. And the first set of projects that that fund will support are flood-mitigation projects, including stop banks across our regions, which is intended to reduce the risk of major climatic events, which, in turn, will help the context in which insurance rates are set.
rigor.explanation: The causal chain is offered but has a real gap: stop banks do not 'reduce the risk of major climatic events', only the damage from them, and the further step from mitigation works to lower insurance premiums is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In answer to the question specifically about rents, I can tell you this: increasing costs on landlords through removing their interest deductibility increased pressure on rents. And so the corollary is this: in an environment where interest deductibility was not restored, I guarantee rents would have increased faster.
rigor.explanation: The cost pass-through premise is plausible, but the conclusion is an unobservable counterfactual asserted with a guarantee and no modelling, evidence or estimate of the pass-through rate offered to support it.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Again, it is rich taking a lecture from that member on outcomes—this was a Government that spent more money, hired more people, delivered worse outcomes completely. You can’t hide from that record. We’re determined; we publish it every quarter. We’re very transparent with the New Zealand people. We have a quarterly plan. We actually announce our scorecards. We announce our progress against our targets. We’re going to keep doing it.
specificity.explanation: Names a real mechanism — quarterly plan, published quarterly progress against targets — but supplies no target, no figure and no result, and the characterisation of the previous government carries no measure at all.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So it was absolutely fantastic news yesterday that this Government is accelerating work on a four-lane expressway from Auckland to Whangārei as part of our hugely successful roads of national significance. We know the difference that roads like Waikato expressway and the Kāpiti expressway have made for the regions, and now we’re bringing that to Northland.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific project (four-lane Auckland–Whangārei expressway) and comparator projects, but gives no cost, no route staging, no start or completion date.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Can the Prime Minister name just one policy in the Government’s draft emissions reduction plan that will “make it cheaper for households to reduce net emissions”?
specificity.explanation: Identifies the exact document and the exact claimed benefit being tested, so the answer required is checkable; it stops short of naming a figure or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What I’d say to you is that we are going to double the amount of renewable energy in this country. It is unacceptable to take eight years to consent a wind farm and then two years to build it. I would encourage that member and the Labour Party to actually support that legislation so we can get renewable projects consented in one year and built much quicker.
specificity.explanation: Carries concrete numbers — doubling renewable generation, eight years to consent, one year as the target — but attaches no date to the doubling and no mechanism beyond 'that legislation'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As part of our Roads of National Significance programme, we have agreed to an accelerated delivery model to deliver this project faster and more efficiently. Our accelerated delivery strategy includes a progressive public-private partnership model that will achieve efficiencies and innovation in planning, procurement, design, and construction across the entire roading corridor between Auckland and Whangārei. It will do this by treating the three roads of national significance as three stages of the same project and incentivising the partner to deliver excellence in design, construction, finance, maintenance, and operation for each phase of the expressway. This Government is focused on getting infrastructure built.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete delivery mechanism (progressive PPP, three RoNS bundled as three stages of one project, single partner across design through operation) but supplies no cost, no procurement date and no completion timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Last year, a report by the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research found that the Warkworth to Wellsford section of the expressway alone would increase New Zealand’s annual GDP by $497 million including benefits for Northland. The AA has said, following this announcement, that this would be a “game changer” for Northland.
specificity.explanation: A named source, a named section of the project, a dated report and a precise dollar figure — directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What specific initiative, if any, can she point to in Budget 2024 that will reduce rates that are up an average of 9.6 percent?
specificity.explanation: Names the Budget, names the cost being tested (council rates), and supplies a precise figure for the increase, so the question is checkable and the answer it demands is a named initiative.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I can point to the fact that this is a Government that is spending wisely and that, therefore, the overall impact of our Budget is to reduce pressure on inflation.
specificity.explanation: Asked to name an initiative, the answer names none; 'spending wisely' is a characterisation with no mechanism, figure or timeframe attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What specific initiative, if any, can she point to in Budget 2024 that will reduce insurance that is up 14 percent, with some families paying an additional $2,000 per year or $45 per week extra?
specificity.explanation: A percentage, an annual dollar figure and a weekly equivalent, tied to a named Budget — precise enough for anyone to check or to answer directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A specific initiative in Budget 2024 is the establishment of the Regional Infrastructure Fund. And the first set of projects that that fund will support are flood-mitigation projects, including stop banks across our regions, which is intended to reduce the risk of major climatic events, which, in turn, will help the context in which insurance rates are set.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific Budget initiative (the Regional Infrastructure Fund) and a specific first category of projects (flood mitigation, stop banks), though with no funding figure, no project list and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why have rents increased by 4.8 percent when she said her $2.9 billion tax break for landlords would put “downward pressure on rents”?
specificity.explanation: Pairs a precise rent movement with a precise fiscal cost and the Minister's own quoted claim, so every element of the question can be checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My vision for conservation is to encourage more visits by tourists and New Zealanders to our iconic landscapes, activate commercial opportunities of public conservation land, and, ultimately, to enhance biodiversity across our country within the fiscal responsibility championed by our Government and manu pūtea, Minister Willis.
specificity.explanation: A string of directional aspirations — more visits, commercial opportunities, enhanced biodiversity — with no figures, mechanisms, named programmes or timeframes. The surrounding sentences add only one named site, not detail on how any of this is done.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Just last week, we announced that an additional four thousand 18- to 24-year-olds will be case-managed over the phone.
specificity.explanation: Gives a number (4,000), an age band (18-24), a delivery mechanism (phone case management) and a timeframe (last week) — all checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s why we have work obligations. They’re quite simple: have a CV, turn up to a job interview, take a job that’s offered, meet with MSD on a regular basis.
specificity.explanation: Names four concrete obligations a jobseeker must meet, which someone could act on or check against MSD rules, but gives no detail on frequency, enforcement or consequences.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is she concerned that only 297 jobseeker support recipients exited into work, as reported in the most recently published weekly update—a worse result than even at the height of COVID?
specificity.explanation: Cites an exact figure (297), the measure (exits into work), and the named source (the most recently published weekly update), so the claim can be looked up directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government is progressing work to require building consent authorities to use remote visual inspections as the default approach, so building a home in New Zealand can be easier and more affordable.
specificity.explanation: Names the actor (building consent authorities), the mechanism (remote visual inspections as the default) and the intended effect, but carries no cost figures, savings estimate or timeframe for the change.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yesterday, I announced that fund-raising lotteries run by not-for-profits such as the Heart Foundation, the Coastguard, the Auckland Rescue Helicopter Trust, and many more throughout New Zealand will be able to operate online permanently.
specificity.explanation: A named decision with named beneficiary organisations and a stated permanence, though no regulatory instrument, date of effect or financial figures are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What we have done in the past budget is increase our uplift, our cost pressure uplift, by the greatest amount ever over three budgets, $16.67 billion, to take into account and to make sure that we are appropriately staffed across our hospital sector.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise total ($16.67 billion), the funding type (cost pressure uplift) and the period (three budgets), though it does not say how any of it translates into ward staffing levels.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The community allocation in the last budget was around $531 million, increasing in each of the following three budgets.
specificity.explanation: Supplies a figure and a trajectory, but leaves the share going to general practice — the actual subject of the question — unquantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I hope members of the Opposition will spend more valuable time on our DOC estate rather than beavering away in their little chains.
civility.explanation: A belittling jibe at named colleagues ('beavering away in their little chains') that mocks opposition members personally rather than engaging any argument they have made. Short of sustained abuse, but clearly condescending.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m really thrilled that that member is finally interested in benefit numbers, given the six years she was in office, there was a 51 percent increase in the number on jobseeker benefit.
civility.explanation: Opens with sarcasm aimed at the questioner personally ('really thrilled that that member is finally interested'), implying indifference on her part rather than addressing the point. The record claim that follows is legitimate; the sneer is not.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is it the Minister’s plan to achieve her target of 50,000 people off the jobseeker benefit by simply sanctioning them until they leave?
civility.explanation: Frames the question so that the Minister's motive is punitive ('simply sanctioning them until they leave'), imputing bad faith rather than asking what the mechanism is. Pointed at the person's intent, not just the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I hope members of the Opposition will spend more valuable time on our DOC estate rather than beavering away in their little chains.
focus.explanation: Appended to a conservation-policy answer, this sentence names no policy, figure or outcome — it is entirely a characterisation of the other side's behaviour.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can she claim that she’s focused on getting beneficiaries into work when there are over 20,000 more people on benefits since she took office?
focus.explanation: Direct scrutiny of the Minister's stated objective against a specific named outcome (the change in benefit numbers since she took office) — accountability on a measurable figure, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why did she ignore advice from the Ministry of Social Development when she picked a 50,000 reduction target for jobseeker beneficiaries rather than an exit into work target as was recommended by officials to her?
focus.explanation: Engages the design of a named policy target and the official advice behind it — the mechanism and the evidence, not the other party in general.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When agreeing to the amount of cost pressure funding that would be allocated to Health New Zealand, did the Minister become aware of any other plans for cost pressure funding that had been set by, for example, other political parties, and, if so, were those more or less than the amount the Government agreed to?
focus.explanation: Nominally about health cost-pressure funding, but the question's purpose is to elicit a comparison with other parties' funding intentions rather than to probe any mechanism, figure or outcome of the funding itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If his view that the health system is funded adequately is correct, when will hiring restrictions in public hospitals end and when will general practice get the funding it needs to stop the public paying more for having to go to the doctor?
focus.explanation: Ties the Minister's own position on funding adequacy to two specific, testable consequences — the end of hospital hiring restrictions and general practice funding affecting patient fees. Scrutiny anchored in named outcomes.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Just last week, we announced that an additional four thousand 18- to 24-year-olds will be case-managed over the phone.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in the week before 24 July 2024 the Government announced phone-based case management for an additional 4,000 jobseekers aged 18-24.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD/ministerial press releases from mid-July 2024: true if an announcement in that week specifies approximately 4,000 additional 18-24 year olds receiving phone-based case management; false if no such announcement exists or the cohort size/age band differs materially.

veracity.statement: The Budget Economic and Fiscal Update always forecast benefit numbers to rise until January 2025, and we acknowledge the current numbers are tracking slightly ahead of these forecasts.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that Budget 2024's BEFU forecast benefit numbers rising until January 2025, and that actual numbers as at July 2024 exceeded that forecast track.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Budget Economic and Fiscal Update 2024 benefit-recipient forecasts compared with MSD benefit statistics for June/July 2024: true if BEFU shows the recipient count peaking around January 2025 and actuals were above forecast at the date of the statement; false if BEFU shows a different peak timing or actuals were at/below forecast.

veracity.statement: I’m really thrilled that that member is finally interested in benefit numbers, given the six years she was in office, there was a 51 percent increase in the number on jobseeker benefit.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the number of people on jobseeker support rose 51 percent over the six years of the previous Labour-led government in which Sepuloni was a minister.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets for the jobseeker support recipient count at roughly October 2017 and November 2023: true if the increase is about 51 percent, false if materially different from that figure.

veracity.statement: How can she claim that she’s focused on getting beneficiaries into work when there are over 20,000 more people on benefits since she took office?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the number of people receiving benefits increased by more than 20,000 between the Minister taking office (late November 2023) and July 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD main benefit recipient counts for the quarters ending December 2023 and June 2024: true if the increase exceeds 20,000, false if it is materially smaller.

veracity.statement: Is she concerned that only 297 jobseeker support recipients exited into work, as reported in the most recently published weekly update—a worse result than even at the height of COVID?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that MSD's most recent weekly benefit update recorded 297 jobseeker support recipients exiting into work, and that this is lower than the equivalent weekly figure during the peak of the COVID-19 period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD weekly benefit updates for July 2024 and for the 2020 COVID-19 lockdown period: true if the July 2024 week shows 297 exits into work and no COVID-peak week is lower; false if the figure differs or a COVID-peak week was lower.

veracity.statement: Why did she ignore advice from the Ministry of Social Development when she picked a 50,000 reduction target for jobseeker beneficiaries rather than an exit into work target as was recommended by officials to her?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that MSD officials recommended an exit-into-work target and that the Minister chose a 50,000 caseload-reduction target instead of that advice.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD briefing papers on welfare target-setting released under the OIA or proactively in 2024: true if officials recommended an exits-into-work measure and the Minister adopted a different caseload target; false if officials recommended the caseload target or made no such recommendation.

veracity.statement: During 2020, a temporary exemption was granted but only until October of this year, after which charities would be required to return to selling tickets via the post or in person.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a temporary exemption allowing charitable lotteries to operate online was granted in 2020 and was due to expire in October 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Gambling Act class 3 lottery exemption notices/regulations made in 2020 and their stated expiry: true if a 2020 temporary online-sales exemption expires in October 2024; false if the year granted or the expiry date differs.

veracity.statement: Yes, and I also agree with his comment that a $1.4 billion deficit was entirely unacceptable, because never before has there been so much money invested into healthcare.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that health funding at the time was the highest ever invested in New Zealand healthcare.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Vote Health appropriations across Budgets (Treasury estimates): true if the 2024/25 health appropriation is the largest on record in the terms the Minister uses (nominal total), false if an earlier year was higher on that basis.

veracity.statement: To the second arm of the question, up to March 2024 I was advised that Health New Zealand was tracking towards a forecast surplus of $583 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that advice received by the Minister up to March 2024 forecast a Health New Zealand surplus of $583 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand financial reporting and ministerial briefings from late 2023 to March 2024: true if a forecast surplus of about $583 million was reported to the Minister; false if the advice showed a deficit or a materially different figure.

veracity.statement: What we have done in the past budget is increase our uplift, our cost pressure uplift, by the greatest amount ever over three budgets, $16.67 billion, to take into account and to make sure that we are appropriately staffed across our hospital sector.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Budget 2024 provided a health cost-pressure uplift of $16.67 billion across three budgets, and that this is the largest such uplift ever.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Health documents: true if the cost-pressure funding totals about $16.67 billion over the three-year period and exceeds any prior equivalent uplift; false if the figure or the 'greatest ever' comparison does not hold on that basis.

veracity.statement: I am encouraged by the increasing health workforce that we have had every single month, despite that member claiming that there’s been a hiring freeze.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the health workforce has grown in every single month over the relevant period, contrary to claims of a hiring freeze.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand monthly workforce/FTE reporting for the months preceding July 2024: true if headcount or FTE rose in every month in that series; false if any month shows a decline or flat result.

rigor.statement: The economy has been weak for two years, which inevitably means there are fewer job vacancies for those on welfare to move into.
rigor.explanation: A real causal inference about the labour market: weak economy to fewer vacancies is a supported step, but 'inevitably' overstates a relationship that is empirical rather than necessary, and nothing (e.g. vacancy data) is offered to connect the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yes, and I also agree with his comment that a $1.4 billion deficit was entirely unacceptable, because never before has there been so much money invested into healthcare.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (the deficit is unacceptable) is made to rest on record total funding, which does not bear on whether the deficit was avoidable given cost growth and demand — a non sequitur that treats the size of an input as settling a question about adequacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We have to recognise the economic conditions we are in today, and the forecasts show, unfortunately, those numbers are due to get worse before they get better.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that jobseeker/benefit recipient numbers will continue rising for a period and will then fall.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MSD quarterly benefit statistics from July 2024 onward: true if the jobseeker support recipient count peaks and then shows a sustained decline by mid-2026; false if the count is still rising, or higher than its 2024 level, at that point.

specificity.statement: As part of the reset, we will be returning to a degree of regionalisation that will encourage regions to be able to recruit to their needs, and have the ability, the commissioning, and the budget to recruit to their needs. This will then mean that we’ll be able to flex our health workforce much closer to the health needs, closer to the front line, and that will deliver better patient outcomes.
specificity.explanation: Names a direction (regionalised commissioning and recruitment budgets) but supplies no figures, no timeframe, no named regions and no mechanism for how budgets would be devolved.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We know 727,000 households are projected to receive a minimum of $75 per fortnight from 31 July; 187,000 households will be benefiting by at least $100 a fortnight by 31 July.
specificity.explanation: Two household counts, two dollar amounts, a per-fortnight unit and a start date — fully checkable against the Budget 2024 tax package costings.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The New Zealand people can see what they hear in the news every day from front-line workers about the cuts that are already happening on the front line: nurses being told that vacancies they have can no longer be filled; vacancies that are on the Te Whatu Ora website just being removed; people finding out that their maternity leave can no longer be filled; Whangārei Hospital saying the emergency department is routinely overwhelmed; nurses going on the record saying it’s routinely in code black; nurses and graduates not being able to get work in our public hospital system because they cannot find the budget to employ them anymore.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific hospital, a specific mechanism (vacancies removed from the Te Whatu Ora website, unfilled maternity cover) and a specific escalation status (code black), but carries no counts, dates or dollar figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As part of the reset, we will be returning to a degree of regionalisation that will encourage regions to be able to recruit to their needs, and have the ability, the commissioning, and the budget to recruit to their needs. This will then mean that we’ll be able to flex our health workforce much closer to the health needs, closer to the front line, and that will deliver better patient outcomes.
rigor.explanation: A real inference chain about the policy — devolved recruitment budgets will let the workforce flex to local need, which will improve patient outcomes — but each link is asserted rather than supported, leaving a gap between the structural change and the clinical outcome claimed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We know, by travelling up and down this country over the last three-week recess and talking to real New Zealanders, that the cost of living is the number one issue facing New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote: the conclusion about the country's top issue rests solely on the speaker's own conversations during recess, with no polling or survey evidence offered to support a national claim.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: On this side of the House, we’re the party of workers because they voted against it; they keep voting against tax relief.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: that an opposing party voted against one tax measure does not establish that the speaker's party represents workers. The conclusion is far broader than the single premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Saying changes in back-office staff that happened over six years could cause a budget blowout in March of this year is totally ridiculous.
