rigor.explanation: There is a genuine timing argument implied — a gradual six-year trend is an odd explanation for a sudden in-year blowout — but it is asserted as absurd rather than demonstrated, and it ignores the possibility of cumulative cost growth reaching a threshold, so the conclusion outruns what is shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Mr Speaker, it’s only one week to go until New Zealanders will, for the first time in 14 years, get tax relief in this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no tax relief has been delivered to New Zealanders in the 14 years before July 2024 — i.e. that the last such change was in 2010.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IRD/Treasury record of personal income tax rate and threshold changes between 2010 and July 2024, plus the Taxation (Budget Measures) Family Incomes Package Act 2017. True if no personal income tax threshold/rate reduction took effect for taxpayers in that period; false if any such change (including the 2017 package, had it not been repealed, or the independent earner/Working for Families adjustments that did take effect) delivered tax relief in that window.

veracity.statement: We know 727,000 households are projected to receive a minimum of $75 per fortnight from 31 July; 187,000 households will be benefiting by at least $100 a fortnight by 31 July.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific household counts benefiting by at least $75 and at least $100 a fortnight from the 31 July 2024 tax changes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD Budget 2024 personal income tax package distributional analysis. True if the published modelling shows ~727,000 households gaining at least $75 a fortnight and ~187,000 gaining at least $100 a fortnight from 31 July 2024; false if the official figures differ materially or apply to a different measure (e.g. families rather than households).

veracity.statement: We remember, seven years ago when National last put tax relief in place, what did Labour do? They cancelled it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that tax relief legislated by National in 2017 was cancelled by the incoming Labour-led government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Legislative record for the Taxation (Budget Measures) Family Incomes Package Act 2017 and the Families Package (Income Tax and Benefits) Act 2017. True if the 2017 threshold changes were repealed before taking effect in April 2018; false if they took effect or were left in place.

veracity.statement: On 1 March this year, those of us diligently sitting in the Health Committee heard from Te Whatu Ora about their budget troubles.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Whatu Ora told the Health Committee about its budget difficulties at a hearing on 1 March 2024, before Budget 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health Committee Hansard/transcript and minutes for 1 March 2024. True if Te Whatu Ora appeared that day and raised budget pressures; false if no such hearing occurred on that date or budget difficulties were not raised.

civility.statement: Well, Chris Hipkins, he’s been to that foreign land of Auckland.
civility.explanation: Sneering mockery aimed at a named member personally — casting Hipkins as a stranger to Auckland — rather than engaging anything he has said or done in policy terms.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It had all the hallmarks of a conspiracy: a crisis manufactured from a growing deficit, a Prime Minister and health Minister at the podium speaking to a slanderous Cabinet paper, a long cast of alleged villains, but 24 hours later the Government’s efforts at spin have not stood up to basic scrutiny.
civility.explanation: Imputes deliberate bad faith to named office-holders — the Prime Minister and health Minister knowingly fronting a 'slanderous' paper and a 'manufactured' crisis — which goes past criticising the decision to alleging dishonesty.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: As we traversed in the House yesterday, Dr Reti blamed growing middle management over the last six years for overspends in Te Whatu Ora. Well, that’s farcical. It shows how financially illiterate he must be.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on a named Minister's competence — calling him financially illiterate — rather than on the reasoning of the claim she is disputing.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We all remember KiwiBuild, don’t we, and what a useless mess that was.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy (KiwiBuild), which keeps it above pure tribalism, but supplies no target, figure or outcome — the content is derision about the other party's record rather than scrutiny of it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Of course, what they think the best way to do that is to sit behind a desk in an office. That’s how you find out what Aucklanders think. You’ve got to have an office, you’ve got to have a desk, you’ve got to sit behind it. That’s how they think they’re going to win the next election.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's electioneering and supposed remoteness; no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named anywhere in the passage.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Aucklanders will continue to reject the Labour Party.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Labour will again fare badly with Auckland voters at the next general election, continuing its 2023 result.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission official results for the next general election: true if Labour's Auckland party vote share is at or below its 2023 Auckland share and it wins fewer Auckland general electorates than National; false if Labour's Auckland party vote share rises materially and it wins a majority of Auckland general electorates.

veracity.statement: Well, during the recess, something very exciting happened—something very, very exciting happened—and that was that the University of Otago, my old university, now led by a former member of this House, the Hon Grant Robertson, released its free speech policy on 10 July.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable facts: that Grant Robertson now heads the University of Otago, and that the university released a free speech policy on 10 July 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: University of Otago official announcements and its published free speech/freedom of expression policy: true if the policy was released on 10 July 2024 and Grant Robertson was by then the university's Vice-Chancellor; false if the release date differs materially or Robertson did not hold that role.

veracity.statement: It does remind me of some of the members on the other side of the House when they did actually try to bring in hate speech laws, which, again, this Government got rid of, which would have actually severely undermined the rights of Kiwis to have a free and open debate.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that opposition members attempted to introduce hate speech legislation and that the current Government removed or cancelled it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Legislative record: the Labour government's proposed incitement/hate speech law changes (2021-22 consultation and the Crimes Amendment / religious-hate provisions), and whether the National-led coalition formally dropped or withdrew them after October 2023. True if a hate speech measure was advanced by the previous government and discontinued by the current one; false if no such measure was advanced or it was abandoned before the change of government.

veracity.statement: In terms of our carbon emissions, some 20 percent of New Zealand’s carbon emissions are directly involved in the construction and in the use of buildings.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that around 20 percent of New Zealand's carbon emissions arise from the construction and use of buildings.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE Building for Climate Change / Ministry for the Environment emissions accounting for the built environment: true if construction plus building operation accounts for approximately 20% of national emissions, false if the published figure is materially different (e.g. under 12% or over 30%).

veracity.statement: He is the only member of this House who is actually a licensed building practitioner.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Cameron Luxton is the sole sitting MP holding a Licensed Building Practitioner registration.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The MBIE Licensed Building Practitioners public register cross-checked against the roster of MPs in the 54th Parliament: true if Luxton is listed and no other sitting MP is, false if another MP also holds an LBP licence or Luxton does not.

focus.statement: It does remind me of some of the members on the other side of the House when they did actually try to bring in hate speech laws, which, again, this Government got rid of, which would have actually severely undermined the rights of Kiwis to have a free and open debate.
focus.explanation: Names a specific legislative measure (hate speech laws) and a specific government action on it, though framed around 'members on the other side' rather than the content of the law.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Time and time again, I think we’ve seen too many universities actually try to censor free speech and not let there be a free and open debate of ideas.
specificity.explanation: A general assertion about repeated censorship with no named university, no incident, no date and no figure — nothing a listener could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As a percentage of GDP, it might be as much as 6 to 10 percent on some measurements, with ripple effects out to the rest of the economy, of course. One in 10 workers is directly employed in the management of the built environment.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the sector's economic weight with a GDP share range and a workforce proportion; checkable figures, though the GDP range is hedged with 'on some measurements'.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As it happens, it is a false choice to say we can either have quality versus affordability, or sustainability versus affordability. The better way to look at it is to say that if we can have much better productivity, then the people who know what they’re doing in this country can be enabled by the Government to get on and do it.
rigor.explanation: Correctly identifies a false dichotomy and offers productivity as the resolving mechanism, but the claim that productivity gains are sufficient to dissolve the quality/affordability trade-off is asserted rather than supported — a real gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They are the ones who are engaged in the work. They know what is needed and our role in this House should be to support them to do that work well, not to get in their way.
rigor.explanation: An appeal to authority/experience: practical involvement in building is taken to establish that practitioners know what policy settings are needed, with nothing offered to bridge hands-on expertise and correct regulatory design.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s time to expose this terrible Government—particularly what they’re trying to do in terms of passing the Treaty principles bill by stealth.
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure (the Treaty principles bill) and a specific alleged practice (introducing it by stealth), but the weight of the sentence is a general denunciation of 'this terrible Government' rather than the bill's content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, almost 40 years later, we have reactionary, angry ACT supporters wanting to dump all that and remove all the obligations for the State to work with Māori.
focus.explanation: There is a policy kernel (removing statutory obligations on the State to work with Māori), but the sentence is framed as a character description of another party's supporters rather than an engagement with the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Labour want to work with Māori; ACT wants to work against them.
focus.explanation: Pure party-versus-party framing: no policy, mechanism, figure or outcome is named on either side of the contrast.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But in Hokianga we have our kaumātua, we have our whānau, and we have our mokopuna in tents, in their vehicles, in shacks—kāinga kore in their own tūpuna whenua.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the housing question and the population affected in a named place; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We have funded initiatives through the last Government and this current Government whether it be Kāinga Ora, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development, also the Homelessness Action Plan where we have Te Hau Ora ō Ngāpuhi and also He Korowai Trust trying to deliver support to whānau.
focus.explanation: Engages the delivery mechanism for housing in the region and credits both the previous and current Governments — accountability without party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Although National are only supporting it to select committee, it’s already causing considerable damage, which they need to take responsibility for.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the National Party's support for the Treaty Principles Bill extends only as far as select committee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National–ACT coalition agreement (November 2023) and National's public statements on the Treaty Principles Bill: true if National committed to supporting the bill only to select committee/first reading and stated it would not support it further; false if National committed to supporting it beyond that stage.

veracity.statement: With no Treaty principles legislation in place, he and this Government have arrogantly told Government departments to use their English names more prominently than Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government has instructed public service departments to give their English names primacy over their Māori names.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cabinet/Public Service Commission directives and the NZ First–National coalition agreement: true if a government instruction requiring departments to use their English names as the primary name exists; false if no such directive was issued.

veracity.statement: They told Corrections to no longer have Treaty provisions in their legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government directed the removal of Treaty of Waitangi provisions from the Corrections legislation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Corrections Amendment Bill / Corrections Act 1994 section 8(2)(h) and associated Cabinet papers: true if the Government moved to repeal the Treaty clause in the Corrections Act; false if no such repeal was proposed or directed.

veracity.statement: And the most recent nonsense: directing Pharmac to stop wasting time on the Treaty.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government has directed Pharmac to cease its Treaty of Waitangi work.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Minister's letter of expectations to Pharmac and Pharmac's published response: true if the Government instructed Pharmac to remove or stop Treaty-related work; false if no such instruction was given.

veracity.statement: Former National Treaty Minister Doug Graham said he couldn’t see any sense in the proposal.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that former Treaty Negotiations Minister Doug Graham publicly criticised the Treaty Principles Bill proposal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published interviews or reported remarks by Sir Douglas Graham on the Treaty Principles Bill before 24 July 2024: true if he is on record dismissing the proposal; false if no such statement exists or he supported it.

veracity.statement: Not even the secretary of Justice, Andrew Kibblewhite, supports the Treaty principles Bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Secretary for Justice, named as Andrew Kibblewhite, does not support the Treaty Principles Bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice departmental advice and regulatory impact material on the Treaty Principles Bill released under the Official Information Act: true if the Secretary for Justice / Ministry advised against the bill in the terms quoted; false if the Ministry's advice was supportive or Kibblewhite was not Secretary for Justice.

civility.statement: For example, just look at the disgraceful behaviour of David Seymour in this Government already.
civility.explanation: Moves from the policy to a named individual, characterising him personally as behaving disgracefully rather than criticising the decisions themselves.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Can someone tell Mr “Know-it-all” Seymour that the Treaty is part of our constitution and he and his stupid party are wrong?
civility.explanation: A mocking nickname aimed at a named member plus the epithet 'stupid' — the attack lands on the person rather than on the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, Mr Seymour, if you’re right, then everyone else is wrong.
rigor.explanation: The inference rests on an appeal to authority and to numbers — that because a list of former ministers, lawyers and officials disagree with him, the bill's author must be wrong. Nothing about the bill's own content is offered to bridge the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have funded initiatives through the last Government and this current Government whether it be Kāinga Ora, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development, also the Homelessness Action Plan where we have Te Hau Ora ō Ngāpuhi and also He Korowai Trust trying to deliver support to whānau.
specificity.explanation: Names actual agencies, a named plan and named delivery organisations, but gives no funding amounts, volumes or timeframes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: These are all initiatives that are trying their best, but it doesn’t take away from the fact that Hokianga needs help now and into the future that is sustainable for our kaumātua, is sustainable for our mokopuna, that they may wash in their rivers, that they may sustain themselves on their whenua tūpuna, and, like you, ngā mōrehu, stand proud with your whakapapa now and for ever.
specificity.explanation: A call for unspecified 'help' expressed through generic aspirations — no mechanism, quantum, agency or timeframe that anyone could act on or check.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It was small compensation for Onehunga’s loss of its waterfront when State Highway 20 was set up in the 1970s.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Onehunga lagoon was created in the 1970s as compensation for waterfront lost to the State Highway 20 motorway works.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council / NZTA historical records and Onehunga Bay Reserve heritage documentation on the origin of the Onehunga lagoon; true if the lagoon/foreshore reserve was created in connection with SH20 reclamation works in the 1970s as compensation for lost waterfront access, false if it predates SH20 or was unconnected to the motorway.

veracity.statement: Our current bridge was badly damaged in 2011. It’s only had a temporary repair since.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Pages Road Bridge in New Brighton was badly damaged in the 2011 Christchurch earthquake and has since received only a temporary repair rather than a permanent replacement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Christchurch City Council / NZTA engineering and asset records for the Pages Road Bridge; true if the bridge sustained significant earthquake damage in 2011 and has since had only temporary/interim remedial works, false if it was undamaged or has had a permanent rebuild or full strengthening.

specificity.statement: So I say, please, to Auckland City Council, prioritise that, dredge it, and make it once again a beautiful asset for the people of Maungakiekie.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete action (dredging), a specific site (the Onehunga lagoon, named in the surrounding sentences) and the responsible body, but supplies no cost, funding source or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Minister Simeon Brown is missing in action.
civility.explanation: Moves off the transport policy and onto the named Minister personally, characterising him as absent and neglectful rather than criticising a decision or a document.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does the Minister even know what that means? Not when it comes to New Brighton and the Pages Road Bridge, he doesn’t. He either doesn’t know or he simply does not care.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the Minister's personal competence and on his motives — either ignorant or indifferent — rather than on the content of the policy statement.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: At the start of this month, we hosted our annual fireworks display in New Brighton. It’s a massive night: 1980s bangers and 10 minutes of fireworks. But at the end, when everybody goes to get home, it takes over an hour to get across that bridge. If there’s a tsunami coming, we will not have an hour.
rigor.explanation: Argues from a single observed case (post-fireworks congestion) to evacuation capacity in a tsunami; the analogy is apt and the premise is offered, but it generalises from one anecdote and assumes evacuation traffic behaves like event traffic, so there is a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: At the heart of this report are the stories of 2,400 survivors—many of whom are here today.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Royal Commission's final report is built on the accounts of 2,400 survivors who took part in the inquiry.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The final report of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care (Whanaketia, July 2024) and its accompanying statistics on survivor participation; true if the number of survivors who gave evidence/accounts is approximately 2,400, false if materially different (e.g. under 2,000 or over 3,000).

veracity.statement: Māori, Pacific, deaf, and disabled people disproportionately bore the brunt of a lot of what had occurred, and not only did this have a devastating impact on your life but also on your families and your communities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori, Pacific, deaf and disabled people were over-represented among those abused in State and faith-based care.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission's final report findings on the demographic profile of survivors; true if it finds Māori, Pacific, deaf and disabled people were over-represented relative to their share of the population in care, false if it finds no such disproportionality.

veracity.statement: Patients at Lake Alice were given electric shocks without anaesthetic, as well as painful and immobilising paraldehyde injections.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact the specific practices used on child and adolescent patients at the Lake Alice Child and Adolescent Unit: unmodified (un-anaesthetised) ECT and paraldehyde injections.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission's Lake Alice report, the UN Committee against Torture decisions in Zentveld and Richards, and the NZ Police/Crown records; true if those sources document unmodified electroconvulsive treatment without anaesthetic and paraldehyde injections at Lake Alice, false if the documented record shows anaesthetic was used or paraldehyde was not administered in that way.

veracity.statement: I want to acknowledge both of them because they took cases against New Zealand to the United Nations Committee against Torture.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Paul Zentveld and Malcolm Richards each brought complaints against New Zealand before the UN Committee against Torture.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The UN Committee against Torture's published communications/decisions; true if both Zentveld and Richards appear as complainants in decisions against New Zealand, false if either did not bring such a case.

veracity.statement: The report has taken six years to write, and it is almost 3,000 pages long, comprising 16 volumes. Because of this, the content needs to be considered with respect and with care, it cannot be rushed, and the findings in this report need to be widely understood.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three checkable properties of the final report: roughly six years in preparation, close to 3,000 pages, and 16 volumes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published final report of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care; true if the volume count is 16, the page total is near 3,000, and the inquiry ran roughly six years from its 2018 establishment; false if the volume count, page count or duration differ materially.

rigor.statement: The report has taken six years to write, and it is almost 3,000 pages long, comprising 16 volumes. Because of this, the content needs to be considered with respect and with care, it cannot be rushed, and the findings in this report need to be widely understood.
rigor.explanation: A modest but valid inference: from the report's stated length, volume count and time taken, he concludes it should not be rushed and needs to be widely understood. The premises (scale and complexity) do support the conclusion about careful consideration; the further step to 'needs to be widely understood' is asserted rather than derived.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Erica Stanford will lead a ministerial group to respond to the report’s findings and the 138 recommendations. The first step is a formal apology, which will take place on 12 November.
specificity.explanation: Names the responsible Minister, the mechanism (a ministerial group), the exact number of recommendations to be responded to, and a firm date for the first step. Concrete and checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I know survivors have been waiting a long time for changes to how the State and churches provide redress, and I want to assure you that we understand the urgency and the importance of that work, and we will provide clarity before the end of the year.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the subject (redress arrangements) and gives a loose deadline ('before the end of the year'), but supplies no mechanism, no design of the redress scheme and no amounts — only a promise of future 'clarity'.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Another highlight was sharing with my neighbours in Takanini and beyond the excellent news that Mill Road is on the list of seven roads of national significance, and work will begin in three years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Mill Road project has been included on the Government's roads of national significance list, and characterises that list as comprising seven roads.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government/NZTA Roads of National Significance list as set out in the Government Policy Statement on land transport 2024 and associated NZTA announcements: true if Mill Road appears on that list and the relevant list named at the time contained seven roads; false if Mill Road is absent or the list count is materially different.

veracity.statement: This is part of our Government’s Budget 2024—a $466 million investment for school property growth.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Budget 2024 contained a $466 million allocation specifically for school property growth.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents (Vote Education, Budget at a Glance) and the Minister of Education's Budget 2024 education package release: true if a school property growth line of approximately $466 million appears, false if the figure or its purpose is materially different.

veracity.statement: That area of Takanini is in fact the second-fastest growing area in the country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Flat Bush/Takanini area ranked second nationally for population growth at the time of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates / statistical area growth rankings for the years immediately preceding July 2024: true if the named area ranks second by population growth on a standard Stats NZ measure, false if it ranks materially lower or no such ranking supports it.

veracity.statement: This Government is committed to replacing the Resource Management Act, though, by July 2026.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an existing government commitment to a specific deadline — RMA replacement by July 2026.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government RMA reform announcements and the coalition agreements / Minister for RMA Reform statements current in July 2024: true if a July 2026 (or mid-2026) deadline for replacement legislation was publicly committed, false if the stated commitment carried a different date or no date.

veracity.statement: It would be fair to say that when I heard a decision a week or so ago that commissioners had declined to consent a port in Northland and that that was going to be a constraint on the economic development of that region, it’s very disappointing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that consenting commissioners declined consent for a Northland port project in roughly mid-July 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The relevant consent decision record (Northland Regional Council / independent commissioners' decision on the Northland port application) around July 2024: true if a decision declining consent for a Northland port project was issued in that period, false if no such decision exists or consent was granted.

divination.statement: Another highlight was sharing with my neighbours in Takanini and beyond the excellent news that Mill Road is on the list of seven roads of national significance, and work will begin in three years.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that physical work on Mill Road will begin about three years from July 2024.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NZTA Waka Kotahi project pages and construction-start announcements for Mill Road: true if construction is recorded as starting on or before mid-2027, false if the start date has slipped beyond that or the project has been deferred/cancelled.

divination.statement: The school is going to cater for 600 children from years 1 to 6, and the intended building will be complete by 2026. Construction will begin later this year.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the new Flat Bush primary school building will be completed by 2026.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education school property announcements and the school's opening record: true if the new primary school at 121 Murphys Road, Flat Bush is completed during or before 2026, false if completion slips into 2027 or later.

specificity.statement: The school is going to cater for 600 children from years 1 to 6, and the intended building will be complete by 2026. Construction will begin later this year.
specificity.explanation: Gives roll size, year levels, a completion year and a construction start timeframe for a named project — concrete and checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re going to start work on the first of three stages of that road. The Warkworth to Te Hana stage: we’re going to get going on that so that the people of the North, their local government, all of those private sector investors can put their own money on the table, with confidence, and get on with making their own investments to support development in Northland.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific stage (Warkworth to Te Hana) of a staged project, but supplies no dates, costs or delivery milestones.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Sitting next to me is my colleague Mark Cameron, a dairy farmer from Ruawai, who tells me regularly how much more efficient and productive Northland could be if it had better roading connectivity. The Northland roads of national significance are going to deliver that to the region, so is the work we’re doing to fund and finance it for our PPP programme and replacing the Resource Management Act with a system based on property rights.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the roads programme will deliver efficiency and productivity gains rests on a single colleague's repeated testimony — an appeal to anecdote, with no data, modelling or cost-benefit evidence connecting the roading investment to the claimed regional gains.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: According to the definition outlined by the Solicitor-General, the children who were sent to Lake Alice went through torture.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Solicitor-General's stated definition of torture was met by the treatment of children at Lake Alice Child and Adolescent Unit.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Solicitor-General's published advice/opinion on whether conduct at Lake Alice met the legal definition of torture, and the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care's Lake Alice findings; true if the Solicitor-General's definition was applied to Lake Alice and found to be met, false if no such determination exists or it concluded otherwise.

veracity.statement: Time and time again, the report points out Māori being disproportionately affected, being massively overrepresented in numbers of children and young people taken from their homes and put into State care.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Royal Commission's report repeatedly documents Māori overrepresentation among children taken into State care.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care final report (Whanaketia, July 2024); true if it repeatedly records Māori disproportionality/overrepresentation among children placed in State care, false if the report contains no such finding.

specificity.statement: I have made my expectations crystal clear that the children’s system as a whole needs to work to recognise harm and stop it from happening. We are making changes to address the issues in care and protection system, but there is way more to do and it is far from perfect.
specificity.explanation: As the responsible Minister she refers to 'changes' to the care and protection system without naming a single measure, mechanism, figure or timeframe; the content is an expectation and a direction only.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The unchecked power that people had over children in far too many facilities across this nation, combined with access to isolated physical environments away from families and support networks, led to the ideal environment for abusers to do whatever they wanted, with little to no consequences.
rigor.explanation: A causal inference with stated premises — unchecked authority plus physical isolation from family and oversight — and a conclusion (conditions favourable to abuse without consequence) that follows reasonably from them. No fallacy; the gap is only that the mechanism is asserted rather than evidenced.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Our Government set up this inquiry and we’d made some changes. We changed the redress rules on an interim basis and we did set up the Survivor Experiences Board.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three specific actions by the previous Labour government: establishing the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care, making interim changes to redress rules, and establishing a survivor experiences body.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official record of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care's establishment (Order in Council / terms of reference, and which government issued them), Cabinet papers or ministerial announcements on interim changes to Crown redress settings, and the establishing documents for the Survivor Experiences Service/Board; true if the Labour-led government established the inquiry, made interim redress changes and set up that body, false if any of the three was not done by that government.

veracity.statement: They are a ruler that we should measure our actions today against because the abuse in State care is not over.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as present fact that abuse of people in State care is still occurring, not merely a historical phenomenon confined to the inquiry period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki and Ministry of Social Development reports-of-concern and substantiated harm-in-care data for the most recent reporting years, plus the Royal Commission's finding on whether contributing factors persist; true if there are substantiated findings of abuse of people in State care after the inquiry period, false if no such substantiated findings exist.

veracity.statement: The State and its institutions not only allowed this abuse to happen; it then denied you your voice and, worse, covered up the extent of the atrocities that took place.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that State institutions not only permitted abuse in care but actively suppressed survivors' complaints and concealed its scale.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care's final report (Whanaketia) findings on institutional responses to complaints and concealment; true if the report finds State agencies suppressed or disbelieved complaints and concealed the extent of abuse, false if the report finds no such suppression or concealment.

specificity.statement: Our Government set up this inquiry and we’d made some changes. We changed the redress rules on an interim basis and we did set up the Survivor Experiences Board.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete actions — the inquiry, an interim change to redress rules, a named body — but supplies no figures, dates or detail on what the redress change actually was.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We must remember that. We must acknowledge that the shameful history of abuse in State care has led to prisons overflowing with some of the survivors of that abuse. Gangs contain survivors of that abuse.
rigor.explanation: The causal conclusion about the prison and gang populations rests on the single survivor account just quoted (one man recognising 45 of 50 men in a prison yard) — an argument from anecdote, offered without the population-level evidence that would support the inference, though the conclusion is hedged with 'some'.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I have been part of the ministerial group that was established by Cabinet to guide the Government’s response to the royal commission’s recommendations.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Cabinet established a ministerial group on the royal commission response and that Costello was a member of it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cabinet papers / official Beehive announcements listing the membership of the ministerial group on the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care response as at July 2024; true if Casey Costello is named as a member of a Cabinet-established group, false if no such group existed or she was not a member.

veracity.statement: I would also acknowledge the nearly 3,000 survivors who shared their experiences of abuse and neglect with the commission.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the number of survivors who gave their accounts to the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care was close to 3,000.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission's final report (Whanaketia, July 2024) figures for survivors engaged with via private sessions, written accounts and interviews; true if the total is in the ~2,700–3,000 range, false if materially lower (e.g. around 2,300) or higher.

veracity.statement: This report was six years in the making.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Royal Commission's inquiry ran for approximately six years before delivering its final report.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Date the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care was formally established (Order in Council / terms of reference) compared with the final report's presentation date of 24 July 2024; true if the interval is approximately six years, false if materially shorter or longer.

specificity.statement: We are not yet at a destination. The Government is continuing to digest the commission’s final report.
specificity.explanation: Describes the state of the Government's response but supplies no mechanism, no named recommendation, no process step and no timeframe — a statement of position with nothing checkable or actionable in it.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Our State care system had 655,000 children, rangatahi and pāhake go through it. Over 200,000 were abused that we know of—that we know of.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two figures drawn from the Royal Commission's Whanaketia report: the total number of people who passed through State (and faith-based) care, and the number abused.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care final report (Whanaketia, July 2024) headline estimates; true if the report puts the number who went through care at approximately 655,000 and the number abused at approximately 200,000, false if the report's figures differ materially from those numbers.

veracity.statement: Yet here we are, in the Government—they’re saying how sorry it is, but it continues to create mega-prisons, removes section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act, and experiments with our rangatahi and justice in boot camps.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government was, as at July 2024, expanding prison capacity, repealing section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989, and running boot camps for young offenders.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government announcements and legislation as at July 2024: true if (a) the Oranga Tamariki (Repeal of Section 7AA) Amendment Bill was before the House or enacted, (b) a military-style academy/boot camp pilot for young offenders had been announced or begun, and (c) additional prison capacity had been funded or announced; false if any of these were not government policy at that date.

veracity.statement: At the boot camps on Great Barrier, boys were forced to dig their own graves. They were made to lie face down in those holes while they were being shot at.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact a specific practice at the Great Barrier Island youth programme covered by the inquiry — boys digging graves and being shot at while lying in them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Survivor testimony and findings recorded in the Royal Commission's Whanaketia report concerning the Whakapakari youth programme on Aotea/Great Barrier Island; true if the report records accounts of boys being made to dig graves and lie in them while firearms were discharged, false if no such accounts appear in the inquiry record.

veracity.statement: Young boys in Oranga Tamariki care who are fighting each other in mixed martial arts - style fights and being filmed by the staff; the staff who were not vetted, who were not trained, who were not trained in care and protection—these stories may well have been in these reports, but they’re happening now.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that staged fights between children in current Oranga Tamariki residences, filmed by staff, were occurring at the time of speaking — not merely historically.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki, Independent Children's Monitor or Police findings/reports from 2023-2024 into staged 'fight club' incidents at an Oranga Tamariki youth justice residence; true if such incidents involving staff filming were substantiated in that period, false if no contemporaneous substantiated case exists.

specificity.statement: Our State care system had 655,000 children, rangatahi and pāhake go through it. Over 200,000 were abused that we know of—that we know of.
specificity.explanation: Two precise, checkable population figures rather than a general assertion that abuse was widespread; anyone could verify them against the report.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Today is historic as we table the royal commission report with an apology to follow on 12 November and we will work alongside, and we are working alongside, survivors to design how and where that apology takes place.
specificity.explanation: Gives a named action and a firm date (the formal apology on 12 November) plus the mechanism of co-design with survivors, but no detail on form, venue or what the apology will contain.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This is the place where you lay your mamae and you leave it here. You leave it here with those with a forked tongue.
civility.explanation: 'Those with a forked tongue' imputes deliberate dishonesty to others present in the House. It names no individual and is not direct abuse, but it attributes bad faith to people rather than criticising a policy — a real civility failure under the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yet here we are, in the Government—they’re saying how sorry it is, but it continues to create mega-prisons, removes section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act, and experiments with our rangatahi and justice in boot camps.
focus.explanation: Names three specific measures — prison expansion, the repeal of section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act, and the boot camp programme — and holds the Government to account against the report's findings. This is scrutiny with named policy content, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yet here we are, in the Government—they’re saying how sorry it is, but it continues to create mega-prisons, removes section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act, and experiments with our rangatahi and justice in boot camps.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: contrition is contradicted by contemporaneous policy. The three named policies do bear on the report's findings, so the argument is not empty, but the conclusion drawn nearby ('nothing learnt', 'everything you have told us has been ignored') is a sweeping generalisation from three instances, leaving a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There are 138 recommendations.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a countable fact about the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care's final report: that it contains 138 recommendations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The final report of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care in State and Faith-based Institutions (Whanaketia, tabled July 2024); true if the report's recommendation list numbers 138, false if it is a materially different count.

specificity.statement: When I look at recommendations, I see that our current system is so out of step with what is recommended that there is a huge job for us to do.
specificity.explanation: Trying to convey substance about the gap between the recommendations and the current system, but names no recommendation, no part of the system and no measure of the gap — 'a huge job' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Green Party is unified in its cross-partisan support to accept and implement, in full, all recommendations and implores the Government to join us.
specificity.explanation: Names a definite object — full acceptance and implementation of all of the inquiry's recommendations — which is checkable as a position, but supplies no mechanism, sequencing, cost or timeframe for implementation.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We welcome the apology that will be offered by the Prime Minister on behalf of the State.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Prime Minister will deliver a formal apology to survivors on behalf of the State following the report.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Hansard and official records of a formal Crown apology delivered in the House by the Prime Minister to survivors of abuse in care; true if such an apology is delivered, false if none is given by the resolve-by date.

rigor.statement: I want to be clear that people on this side with the Government have not apologised today because we believe it is so important that we make sure that this report and its recommendations are properly considered and the form of apology and anything else that goes with it is not done to those survivors but actually created with them, so that it is genuine.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: the premise that an apology must be co-designed with survivors to be sincere supports the conclusion that the Government withheld an apology today. The gap is that nothing is offered to show a same-day apology would preclude later co-designed redress, so the conclusion is supported but not tightly.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Everyone who’s ever done PSYC 101 has heard of the Milgram experiment and the Stanford prison experiments. We can hardly claim ignorance as an excuse.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that ignorance is no excuse rests on an appeal to two famous studies and a sweeping generalisation about who has heard of them; the studies concern obedience and role-assignment in short-term settings and nothing is offered to bridge them to the institutional care failures being discussed.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I want to be clear that people on this side with the Government have not apologised today because we believe it is so important that we make sure that this report and its recommendations are properly considered and the form of apology and anything else that goes with it is not done to those survivors but actually created with them, so that it is genuine.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Government members did not offer an apology during this 24 July 2024 debate on the royal commission's final report.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of the 24 July 2024 debate on the Abuse in Care Royal Commission final report; true if no Government (National/ACT/NZ First) speaker offered an apology on the day, false if a Government speaker apologised in that debate.

specificity.statement: The second thing that the State failed to do was to have the accountability and the oversight and the protection, given that very obvious danger in any kind of residential facility or institution, not only in its own facilities but in facilities run by faith-based and other organisations.
specificity.explanation: Names a definite category of failure (oversight and accountability, extending to faith-based providers) but supplies no figures, mechanisms or named agencies, so it conveys a direction rather than checkable detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A great many of those children and young people who were already abused and traumatised were placed in institutions like Templeton, Lake Alice, Tokanui, Sunnyside, and countless others whose names have acquired an unpleasant aura.
specificity.explanation: Names four specific institutions, which makes the claim locatable in the report, but quantifies nothing ('a great many', 'countless others') and gives no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Today, I say to the Pākehā State: you must answer to your crimes against all tamariki who you have made and watched suffer—the bare minimum response, financial compensation, and enacting all 138 recommendations in this report.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care report released in July 2024 contains 138 recommendations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The recommendations count in the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care final report (Whanaketia, July 2024); true if the report contains 138 recommendations, false if the count is materially different.

veracity.statement: Our tamariki Māori currently make up 70 percent of those in State custody, and further, they make up 80 percent of the currently abused by the State.
veracity.explanation: Two statistical claims: that Māori children are 70% of children in State custody and 80% of those currently abused in State care.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki care-population statistics for 2024 for the Māori share of children in State custody, and Oranga Tamariki/Royal Commission data on the ethnicity of children recorded as abused in State care; true if both figures are within a few percentage points, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Part 1 amends the Local Electoral Act 2001. It puts the poll provisions back in in relation to Māori wards. These are the same provisions that were in place prior to the last Government’s change.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the poll/referendum provisions reinstated by this bill are the same as those in the Local Electoral Act 2001 before the previous Government repealed them in 2021.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the poll provisions in the bill as tabled with the Local Electoral Act 2001 sections repealed by the Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2021; true if materially the same provisions are restored, false if the restored provisions differ in substance.

specificity.statement: Today, I say to the Pākehā State: you must answer to your crimes against all tamariki who you have made and watched suffer—the bare minimum response, financial compensation, and enacting all 138 recommendations in this report.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete demand (financial compensation) and a checkable benchmark (all 138 recommendations), though without amounts or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our tamariki Māori currently make up 70 percent of those in State custody, and further, they make up 80 percent of the currently abused by the State.
specificity.explanation: Two precise, checkable percentages tied to a named population.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Relevant communities, including iwi, hapū, and whānau must be resourced to shape the destinies of their own babies. For us, for Te Pāti Māori, this looks like the Mokopuna Māori Authority, which will prioritise indigenous care models and empower communities.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific proposed body and its broad purpose, but supplies no funding, mechanism, powers or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Part 1 amends the Local Electoral Act 2001. It puts the poll provisions back in in relation to Māori wards. These are the same provisions that were in place prior to the last Government’s change.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act amended, the part of the bill, and the specific mechanism restored.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There’s also two tabled amendments from me. Firstly, there’s one which is more substantive, and that is in relation to requiring councils to make a choice as to whether they will rescind, disestablish, or have a referendum. So that is requiring councils by 6 December to make that decision.
specificity.explanation: States the number of amendments, the exact options councils must choose between, and a hard date for the decision.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Relevant communities, including iwi, hapū, and whānau must be resourced to shape the destinies of their own babies. For us, for Te Pāti Māori, this looks like the Mokopuna Māori Authority, which will prioritise indigenous care models and empower communities.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy question — who should hold responsibility for the care of Māori children — and offers her party's alternative rather than attacking opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No, the Government is not willing to accept that amendment. This bill is in relation to Māori wards, wards based on race, ethnicity, rather than geography.
focus.explanation: Answers the policy question directly and gives the substantive ground for the bill's scope; no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Would the Minister consider an amendment to include all wards of local body areas, all wards under local councils, not just Māori wards—that they be treated the same under the proposals within this bill?
focus.explanation: A direct question on the mechanism of the bill before the committee, naming the specific change sought; no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If a local council wants to establish Māori wards, the Minister is asking us to vote for a bill that would make that process harder.
focus.explanation: States precisely what the measure before the House does and its practical effect on councils — accountability on the substance, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The difference is that it divides the people in that community based on which roll they’re on. An urban ward or a rural ward does not divide the people in those wards based on what roll they’re on.
rigor.explanation: Offers a real distinction (roll-based versus geography-based electorates) as the ground for treating Māori wards differently, but the inference leaves a gap: no reason is given why a roll-based division specifically requires a public poll when other ward boundaries, which also determine who votes for whom, do not.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So there we have it right off the bat. The Government is treating the consideration of the establishment of Māori wards differently to all other wards—probably the most upfront thing the Minister has said in this House, and we got it right from the get-go, which I appreciate and thank him for.
civility.explanation: The thanks are wrapped around a sneer at the Minister personally — the implication that he is usually not upfront imputes habitual evasiveness to the person rather than criticising the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: My next question is: does the Minister know what institutional racism is?
civility.explanation: A loaded rhetorical question aimed at the Minister's understanding and motives rather than at the provisions of the bill; pointed and condescending without being a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Well, the Far North District Mayor and that council presented to the select committee on this particular bill and made it very clear that, actually, what’s happening in Te Tai Tokerau is already working really well with Māori wards and the members who are on that council.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Far North District Mayor and council made a submission to the select committee on this bill, and that their submission said the existing Māori ward arrangements in Te Tai Tokerau are working well.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee submissions record for the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Constituencies) Amendment Bill 2024; true if a Far North District Council submission/oral presentation exists and supports retaining Māori wards as working well, false if no such submission exists or it took a contrary position.

veracity.statement: The other challenge with that too, if I think about the great city that the Minister and I live in, he might recall the recent referendum that was done on Māori wards at the beginning of this year in Tāmaki Makaurau, and he’ll understand just exactly how hard it was to engage right across such a big city.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a referendum on Māori wards was held in Auckland at the beginning of 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council decision and election records for late 2023 / early 2024; true if a public poll or referendum on establishing Māori wards was actually conducted in Auckland in that period, false if the matter was resolved by a council decision with no public vote.

veracity.statement: Of course there’s obligations within the Local Government Act for local government to engage with Māori; that is in the Local Government Act. That principle remains; that’s not being changed by this legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that the Local Government Act 2002 imposes obligations on councils to engage with Māori, and that this bill leaves those obligations untouched.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Local Government Act 2002 (e.g. ss 4, 14(1)(d), 81) together with the text of the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Constituencies) Amendment Bill; true if those engagement provisions exist and the bill does not amend or repeal them, false if the bill alters them.

veracity.statement: In terms of Auckland, there wasn’t a referendum early in the year. The council did make a decision not to proceed with establishing a Māori ward.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no Auckland referendum on Māori wards occurred in early 2024 and that Auckland Council instead resolved not to establish a Māori ward.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council governing body minutes and any electoral poll records for 2023–2024; true if the council resolved not to establish a Māori ward and no public referendum was held in early 2024, false if a referendum was held.

veracity.statement: Prior to the 2022 election, we had one mayor, elected through first past the post, and we had 12 councillors elected at large, also through first past the post. There was a representation review undertaken through the council, and the change was made to have the mayor elected through single transferrable vote, or STV, and for those 12 positions to be broken up into geographic wards, of which there are two, and a general ward and a Māori ward.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the detail of Nelson City Council's representation review: pre-2022 one mayor and 12 at-large councillors under FPP, and a post-review move to STV plus two geographic wards, a general ward and a Māori ward.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Nelson City Council's representation review determination applying to the 2022 local election and Local Government Commission records; true if the pre- and post-review arrangements match the numbers and voting systems stated, false if they differ materially.

veracity.statement: On that note, for the first time in its entire history under a Māori ward—125 years, I think, of Nelson City Council—we’ve had a Māori councillor; after 125 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the councillor elected to Nelson City Council's Māori ward in 2022 is the first Māori councillor in the council's roughly 125-year history.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Nelson City Council historical councillor records and local-history/iwi sources on the ethnicity of past councillors, plus the council's founding date; true if no earlier Māori councillor is recorded and the council is about 125 years old, false if an earlier Māori councillor is documented.

focus.statement: I wonder—and this is an offer to the Minister, while he might be hell bent on getting rid of Māori wards—if in his exchange and his commitment to engagement with the community, he might look towards whether or not notifications in te reo Māori might be accepted; notifications that engage with the community that this directly affects—whether or not there is any indication, because I don’t see it in this particular bill, to actually reach those who this is impacting the most, and that is the Māori community.
focus.explanation: Engages directly with the bill's notification provisions and proposes a concrete change (te reo Māori notification), rather than attacking the governing parties generally.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We have a situation where people are campaigning, outlaying money, and putting their lives on hold in order to run for an elected position, which they subsequently win, but at the same time, through that referendum, the voting public vote to disestablish that Māori ward.
focus.explanation: Poses a concrete operational consequence of the bill's referendum timing for candidates in a Māori ward election; entirely about the measure's mechanism, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I wonder—and this is an offer to the Minister, while he might be hell bent on getting rid of Māori wards—if in his exchange and his commitment to engagement with the community, he might look towards whether or not notifications in te reo Māori might be accepted; notifications that engage with the community that this directly affects—whether or not there is any indication, because I don’t see it in this particular bill, to actually reach those who this is impacting the most, and that is the Māori community.
civility.explanation: Pointed characterisation of the Minister as 'hell bent' attributes personal zeal rather than engaging only the policy, but stops short of insult and is paired with a constructive offer.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In terms of Auckland, there wasn’t a referendum early in the year. The council did make a decision not to proceed with establishing a Māori ward.
civility.explanation: Corrects an opposition member's factual error squarely on the substance, with no jibe about the member who made it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There are words I know that I can’t use in this House. If I could, I would.
civility.explanation: Signals unparliamentary language she would use about the singling out of Māori wards; robust and faintly sneering in implication, but no person is named or attacked.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So there’s specific provisions in relation to Tauranga there, and the decision was made by Cabinet to hold the referendums at the same time as the next local election to ensure that the costs were reduced for local councils. That means they could hold them at the same time and the implementation, therefore, comes into effect from 2028.
specificity.explanation: Names the decision-maker (Cabinet), the mechanism (referendums run with the next local election), the rationale (reduced cost) and the implementation year (2028).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Prior to the 2022 election, we had one mayor, elected through first past the post, and we had 12 councillors elected at large, also through first past the post. There was a representation review undertaken through the council, and the change was made to have the mayor elected through single transferrable vote, or STV, and for those 12 positions to be broken up into geographic wards, of which there are two, and a general ward and a Māori ward.
specificity.explanation: Names the council, the election year, the number of councillors, the voting systems before and after, and the exact ward structure created.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So there’s specific provisions in relation to Tauranga there, and the decision was made by Cabinet to hold the referendums at the same time as the next local election to ensure that the costs were reduced for local councils. That means they could hold them at the same time and the implementation, therefore, comes into effect from 2028.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (align referendums with the local election, implementation from 2028) follows from the premises offered about Tauranga's off-cycle election and shared election costs; no fallacy, though the cost saving is asserted rather than quantified.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Why is there such inconsistency in the application of a referendum based on this idea of democracy that the Minister has put forward, which we all uphold? If you’re going to apply it, apply it to all decisions that sit under the representation review.
rigor.explanation: A valid consistency argument: if the stated principle is that voters should decide representation arrangements, it should apply to every element of the same representation review, not only the Māori ward. The inference follows from the premise she attributes to the Minister; no fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I appreciate the response from the Minister, but it was unnecessary, because we know what the motivations of the Government are.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the Minister's answer as 'unnecessary' and asserts knowledge of concealed Government motives — an imputation of bad faith rather than engagement with what was said. Short of a personal insult, but past the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And in the cruellest of cruel ironies, here we are, the very first item immediately after on the Order Paper, and the Minister is asking us to vote for a bill that treats Māori people differently, creates an unfair advantage for non-Māori, and creates a pathway for communities that have already made their decisions more difficult and more likely to be reversed.
civility.explanation: Very hard criticism, but every charge lands on the bill and its effects rather than on the Minister as a person. Fierce policy attack is the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I have to say I hope that the Minister of Local Government will reflect on that—hopefully—unthought-through little bit of heckling yesterday.
civility.explanation: 'Unthought-through little bit of heckling' is condescending toward a colleague's conduct and character of thought rather than engaging an argument, though it stops well short of direct abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And the cute argument about, “Well, some people are on different rolls; therefore, we want everyone on the same roll” doesn’t wash because we’re talking about the establishment of a ward, the recognition of a decision of a council.
rigor.explanation: A genuine rebuttal that tries to distinguish the roll question from the ward-establishment question, but the distinction is asserted rather than shown — no reason is given why the roll composition is irrelevant to how a ward is established. A real inference, weakly supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, I think the committee should reflect on that in the few moments that we have before the dinner break, because I am very interested to hear the Minister’s view as to how what he is proposing in this bill—that would treat Māori differently to everybody else in the country—does not fit the definition that I’ve just read out.
rigor.explanation: Reads out a definition and applies it to the bill — a structured argument. But the key premise (that the bill 'would treat Māori differently to everybody else') is assumed rather than established against the Minister's contrary characterisation, so the syllogism rests on the contested step.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And, of course, as I’ve outlined in my speeches on this issue, that side of the House talks about localism, but the localism stops at the council table. We’ve actually said localism should flow through to the voters, the electors, the people who the councillors and the mayor are meant to represent.
rigor.explanation: A real inference answering the localism objection: if localism means devolving decisions to the local level, extending it past the council to the electors is a coherent extension. The gap is that it is asserted rather than argued why an electoral-system decision made by elected representatives is not itself local.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.explanation: One concrete action is named (personal visits to the facilities, more than once), but 'changes have been made' is left entirely unspecified — no change, timeframe or verification mechanism is identified.
