specificity.statement: This morning, I announced alongside the Hon Nicola Willis and the Hon Chris Bishop that the coalition Government is investing into the Wairarapa and Manawatū commuter rail lines, which will deliver a fleet of 18 new trains as part of a funding agreement between the Government and the Greater Wellington and Horizons regional councils.
specificity.explanation: Names the lines, the number of trains (18), and the counterparties to the funding agreement, though no dollar figure or delivery date is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Speeds on the Wairarapa line will be increased from 90 kilometres per hour to 110 kilometres per hour on the train line with these upgrades, resulting in significant travel-time savings of 15 minutes for passengers travelling between Wellington and Masterton.
specificity.explanation: Before-and-after line speeds, a named route, and a quantified time saving — precise enough for anyone to check against the project documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But, in summary, I can tell the member that an estimated 727,000 households will benefit by at least $75 a fortnight; 187,000 will benefit by at least $100 a fortnight. On average, households will benefit by $60 a fortnight, and households with children by $78 a fortnight.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific Budget 2024 tax package distributional figures: 727,000 households at least $75 a fortnight better off, 187,000 at least $100, averages of $60 and $78.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 tax package documents (Treasury/IRD distributional analysis, budget.govt.nz). True if those documents give 727,000 households at $75+/fortnight, 187,000 at $100+/fortnight, and averages of $60 and $78; false if the published figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: And what you did was vote against every dollar of tax relief.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Labour opposition voted against the Government's tax relief measures in their entirety.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Division records for the Taxation (Budget Measures) (Tax Relief) Bill 2024 and the Budget 2024 appropriation votes. True if Labour voted against at every stage of the tax relief legislation; false if Labour supported any stage or any component of it.

veracity.statement: My reflection would be that New Zealanders are very interested in tax relief, because they haven’t seen it for 14 long years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no personal income tax relief has been delivered in New Zealand for 14 years prior to July 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue record of changes to personal income tax rates and thresholds since 2010. True if the last change to personal income tax thresholds/rates took effect in 2010; false if any personal income tax rate or threshold reduction occurred between 2011 and 2024 (noting the 2021 addition of the 39% top rate is an increase, not relief).

veracity.statement: What are specific examples of how the boot camps will incorporate a te ao Māori approach when nine out of 10 of the young people participating are Māori?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that nine of the ten young people in the military-style academy pilot are Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki figures on the ethnicity of the ten participants in the July 2024 military-style academy pilot (OIA responses, Ministerial statements, or select committee evidence). True if 9 of 10 identified as Māori; false if the figure differs.

veracity.statement: This morning, I announced alongside the Hon Nicola Willis and the Hon Chris Bishop that the coalition Government is investing into the Wairarapa and Manawatū commuter rail lines, which will deliver a fleet of 18 new trains as part of a funding agreement between the Government and the Greater Wellington and Horizons regional councils.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a funding agreement between the Government and the Greater Wellington and Horizons regional councils will deliver 18 new trains for the Wairarapa and Manawatū lines.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 25 July 2024 Government announcement and the associated funding agreement documents. True if the agreement provides for 18 new trains with those two councils as parties; false if the train count or the parties differ.

veracity.statement: Is she concerned that police have investigated approximately 3,000 fewer family violence incidents since December 2023 and that this will further decrease the current reporting rate of family violence; if not, why not?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand Police have investigated approximately 3,000 fewer family violence incidents in the period since December 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Police family harm / family violence investigation statistics for the period December 2023 to mid-2024 compared with the equivalent prior period (Police data releases or OIA responses). True if the reduction is of the order of 3,000 investigations; false if the data show no material reduction or a materially different magnitude.

veracity.statement: When was she informed that police are stepping back from attending family violence call-outs now, that this is being done—quote, from police—“regardless of the readiness of partner agencies”, and they have warned that this may result “in poor safety outcomes or a threat to life”?
veracity.explanation: Relays two direct quotations attributed to Police — that the withdrawal from family violence call-outs is proceeding 'regardless of the readiness of partner agencies' and that it may result 'in poor safety outcomes or a threat to life'.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Police internal advice or briefing documents on the family harm call-out change (released under the OIA or tabled in the House). True if those documents contain the quoted phrases in substantially that context; false if no such Police document contains them.

focus.statement: What are specific examples of how the boot camps will incorporate a te ao Māori approach when nine out of 10 of the young people participating are Māori?
focus.explanation: Names the specific programme (the military-style academy pilot), cites the cohort composition, and asks for the operational detail of a stated policy commitment. Textbook scrutiny of a named policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What are specific examples of the day-to-day military-style activities that young offenders will participate in, in the boot camps that she launched last week?
focus.explanation: Directed entirely at the operational content of a named, just-launched policy; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, on this side of the House, we actually deliver. On that side of the House, they just talk.
focus.explanation: Pure team-versus-team framing. No policy, figure, measure or outcome is named — asked about rail infrastructure, the answer is entirely a characterisation of the two sides of the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: OK. Well, all I’d say to the member opposite is, as I said earlier, this Government is about delivery; that Government was simply about announcements, and that’s why they got voted out on 14 October last year.
focus.explanation: Asked a specific question about whether the funding was reannounced from a previous Budget, the reply names no funding line, Budget or figure and consists of a general characterisation of the previous Government plus the election result.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is the Government so desperate to announce something that is not a cut that they are now resorting to reannouncing previous Governments’ announcements?
focus.explanation: There is a genuine accountability point buried here — that today's rail funding was already announced under the previous Budget — but it is carried entirely by party framing ('so desperate') rather than by naming the appropriation, figure or prior announcement.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is she concerned that police have investigated approximately 3,000 fewer family violence incidents since December 2023 and that this will further decrease the current reporting rate of family violence; if not, why not?
focus.explanation: Names a specific measurable outcome (a fall of about 3,000 investigated family violence incidents since a stated date) and asks the responsible Minister to account for it. Scrutiny of a named outcome, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: To the first part of the question, yes, I would assume that they have had care and protection before, because they are in a place that has care and protection under Oranga Tamariki.
rigor.explanation: The question asked about a prior history of care and protection; the inference offered is that they must have such a history because they are currently in an Oranga Tamariki setting. That conflates present custody with prior care and protection involvement — the conclusion does not follow from the premise, and the reasoning is close to circular.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because the police are not investigating certain things does not mean other agencies are not stepping in when it is their job to be dealing with that particular issue.
rigor.explanation: The logical point is sound — a fall in police investigations does not by itself entail that no agency responded — so the rebuttal is valid as far as it goes. But it is offered as a reassurance without any evidence that other agencies are in fact absorbing the cases, which is the gap between what was shown and what was implied.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, on this side of the House, we actually deliver. On that side of the House, they just talk.
civility.explanation: Dismissive and sneering in tone, but aimed at the opposite side of the House collectively rather than at any individual member; no personal attribute is attacked.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: How can she stand by her statement that she expects people to be able to access the right response to their needs when she has made no Budget bids for the prevention of family violence, this Government is gutting agencies who support the victims of family violence, and now police are stepping back from the lead partner in family violence with no services in place to take up that gap?
veracity.explanation: Asserts three factual premises: that the Minister made no Budget 2024 bids for family violence prevention, that agencies supporting family violence victims are being cut, and that police are withdrawing from their lead-partner role in family violence without replacement services.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Social Development / Te Puna Aonui budget-bid documents and Minister Chhour's portfolio bid disclosures (true if no prevention bid was lodged, false if one was); NZ Police public statements and the mid-2024 police 'demand and capability' review on withdrawing from family-harm callouts.

veracity.statement: Almost a billion dollars has been invested into family violence and sexual violence in the period from 2018 to 2023.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that close to $1 billion of government funding went into family violence and sexual violence services across the 2018–2023 period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Puna Aonui / Budget appropriations for family violence and sexual violence services, Budgets 2018–2023 summed; true if the total is near $1b, false if materially below or above.

veracity.statement: The actual number of children living in material hardship increased by 23,400 in 2022-23.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific year-on-year increase of 23,400 in the number of children in material hardship for the 2022/23 year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Child Poverty Statistics, material hardship measure (DEP-17), year ended June 2023 versus June 2022; true if the increase in the estimated number of children is ~23,400, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: How many kids could she have lifted out of poverty if the Government chose to spend $2.9 billion on benefit increases instead of tax cuts on landlords?
veracity.explanation: Embeds the factual premise that the Government's restoration of interest deductibility for residential landlords costs about $2.9 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 / Treasury fiscal costings for restoring interest deductibility on residential rental property over the forecast period; true if the figure is approximately $2.9b, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: There’s no cuts to benefit increases.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government has not cut benefit increases, in response to a claim that Budget 2024 reduced them; the surrounding sentence clarifies she means the method of future indexation changed rather than rates being reduced.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 welfare decisions and the Social Security Act indexation provisions; true if main benefit rates were not reduced and future annual adjustments were unchanged, false if the indexation basis was switched (e.g. from average wage growth to CPI) so that scheduled increases are lower than under the previous settings.

veracity.statement: Is she ashamed of her weak child poverty targets, and, if not, why did she fail to engage with stakeholder organisations about them and neglect to announce them with a press release?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister did not consult stakeholder organisations on the intermediate child poverty targets and did not announce them by press release.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: beehive.govt.nz press-release record for the 2024 intermediate child poverty targets around the Budget 2024 period, plus MSD/DPMC consultation records; true if no release was issued and no stakeholder consultation occurred, false if either is documented.

veracity.statement: We are also helping 4,000 more job seekers aged 18 to 24 by providing them with case management over the phone because the number of 18- to 24-year-olds who shifted on to the jobseeker benefit, unfortunately, increased by 58 percent under the last Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the number of 18- to 24-year-olds moving onto jobseeker support rose by 58 percent during the previous Government's term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit statistics for jobseeker support recipients aged 18–24, comparing the 2017 and 2023 quarters; true if the increase is about 58 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: While 60,000 people have a case manager, this leaves 135,000 job seekers without one, so we’ve established two new check-ins to create more opportunities to provide job seekers the support they need, to check they are fulfilling their obligations to become work ready, and, of course, to find a job.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 60,000 beneficiaries currently have a case manager and about 135,000 jobseekers do not.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD case management and jobseeker support caseload figures for mid-2024; true if approximately 60,000 are case-managed out of a jobseeker population leaving ~135,000 unmanaged, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Because, for young people on a benefit, they are estimated to spend in future years, on average, 21.3 years throughout their lifetime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an actuarial estimate that young people going onto a benefit will spend an average of 21.3 years of their remaining lifetime on a benefit.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD's benefit system actuarial valuation (Taylor Fry) estimate of average future years on benefit for the 18–24 cohort; true if the figure is about 21.3 years, false if materially different.

focus.statement: How can she stand by her statement that she expects people to be able to access the right response to their needs when she has made no Budget bids for the prevention of family violence, this Government is gutting agencies who support the victims of family violence, and now police are stepping back from the lead partner in family violence with no services in place to take up that gap?
focus.explanation: Names a specific portfolio commitment, the Budget bid process, and the police change of role — concrete scrutiny of government policy rather than party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Has she set weaker child poverty reduction targets because she will plunge more children into material hardship with her choice to cut benefit increases and to inflict more punitive sanctions on beneficiaries?
focus.explanation: Names identifiable policy decisions (benefit indexation changes, welfare sanctions) and links them to a named target, so it is substantive scrutiny rather than party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We are resetting the welfare system because too many people were on the jobseeker benefit when we came into Government, and the economic mess we inherited meant those numbers were always going to get worse before they got better.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point about jobseeker numbers and the welfare reset, but a substantial part of the weight is carried by the 'economic mess we inherited' framing of the predecessor rather than by the policy itself.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Almost a billion dollars has been invested into family violence and sexual violence in the period from 2018 to 2023.
specificity.explanation: Gives a dollar magnitude and a defined period, though not broken down by programme or year.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The actual number of children living in material hardship increased by 23,400 in 2022-23.
specificity.explanation: A precise figure attached to a named measure and a named year — directly checkable against the official series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How many kids could she have lifted out of poverty if the Government chose to spend $2.9 billion on benefit increases instead of tax cuts on landlords?
specificity.explanation: Poses a precise counterfactual with a named dollar amount and two named uses of it; a question can be as specific as an answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are also helping 4,000 more job seekers aged 18 to 24 by providing them with case management over the phone because the number of 18- to 24-year-olds who shifted on to the jobseeker benefit, unfortunately, increased by 58 percent under the last Government.
specificity.explanation: Names the cohort, the number receiving the new service, the delivery mechanism and a percentage change — all checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: While 60,000 people have a case manager, this leaves 135,000 job seekers without one, so we’ve established two new check-ins to create more opportunities to provide job seekers the support they need, to check they are fulfilling their obligations to become work ready, and, of course, to find a job.
specificity.explanation: Two caseload figures plus a named mechanism (two new check-ins) and its stated purpose.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because actual child poverty rates worsened under the last Government in the 2023 year, which means the new intermediate targets have to account for the fact that progress in reducing child poverty is miles behind what was forecast when the last Government originally established the targets.
rigor.explanation: The inference — a worse starting baseline requires resetting intermediate targets — follows reasonably from the premise, but nothing offered connects the baseline shift to the particular size of the weaker target, so there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The economy has been weak for the last two years, which, inevitably, means there are fewer job vacancies.
rigor.explanation: The link from a weak economy to fewer vacancies is a sound and standard inference; 'inevitably' overstates a relationship that is strong but contingent, which is the only real gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: According to the after housing cost measure, which is most closely connected to material hardship, Budget 2024 is forecast to see 17,000 fewer children in poverty.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Budget 2024 package will reduce the number of children in poverty on the after-housing-cost measure by 17,000.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Child Poverty Statistics, AHC 50% of median measure, for the years following Budget 2024; true if the number of children below the AHC line falls by about 17,000 relative to the pre-Budget baseline, false if it falls materially less or rises.

divination.statement: It is forecast that job seeker numbers will continue to increase until January 2025.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the jobseeker support caseload will keep rising and turn around from about January 2025.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MSD monthly/quarterly benefit statistics for jobseeker support; true if the caseload peaks around January 2025 and declines thereafter, false if numbers continue rising materially beyond that date.

civility.statement: Has she set weaker child poverty reduction targets because she will plunge more children into material hardship with her choice to cut benefit increases and to inflict more punitive sanctions on beneficiaries?
civility.explanation: Frames the Minister as personally choosing to 'plunge' children into hardship and to 'inflict' punishment — imputes bad faith to her rather than confining the attack to the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The member hasn’t realised the point is we have to set a target based on what the reality is today.
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed at the questioner's comprehension rather than at his argument; short of an insult but no longer purely on the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is she ashamed of her weak child poverty targets, and, if not, why did she fail to engage with stakeholder organisations about them and neglect to announce them with a press release?
civility.explanation: 'Is she ashamed' targets the Minister personally rather than the target-setting itself — a sneer wrapped around the procedural question.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I’m thrilled that the Customer and Product Data Bill passed with unanimous support yesterday at its first reading.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Customer and Product Data Bill passed its first reading the previous sitting day without any party opposing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard record of the first reading of the Customer and Product Data Bill (July 2024); true if the first reading was agreed with no party voting against, false if any party voted against or if the reading occurred on a different occasion.

veracity.statement: Recently, the OECD ranked New Zealand dead last when it came to digital regulation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a recent OECD ranking placed New Zealand bottom of the member countries on digital regulation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD digital-regulation indicators (e.g. the OECD Digital Government Index / OECD product market regulation digital measures) published before July 2024; true if New Zealand is ranked last among OECD members on a digital regulation measure, false if it is ranked anywhere above last or no such OECD ranking exists.

veracity.statement: Finally, it’s worth noting that the Privacy Commissioner supports this bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Office of the Privacy Commissioner's position on the Customer and Product Data Bill is one of support.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Privacy Commissioner's public statements or submission on the Customer and Product Data Bill; true if the Commissioner expressed support for the bill, false if the Commissioner opposed it or took no supportive position.

veracity.statement: One of the reasons why banks support these proposals is, for instance, in Australia, you can change your mortgage provider within 10 minutes by completing an online application.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Australia's open banking regime allows a consumer to switch mortgage provider in about ten minutes via an online application.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Australian Consumer Data Right / open banking documentation and lender evidence on mortgage switching times; true if mortgage provider switching can be completed via online application in roughly ten minutes, false if the process materially exceeds that (e.g. days for approval and settlement).

rigor.statement: We are behind the eight ball. Recently, the OECD ranked New Zealand dead last when it came to digital regulation. This bill will pave the way for greater competition; in turn, boosting productivity.
rigor.explanation: A poor digital-regulation ranking is offered as evidence that this particular bill will raise competition and hence productivity; the ranking supports 'something needs fixing' but nothing is offered to link this bill's mechanism to the productivity conclusion. A real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Choice and competition are good things as they ultimately lead to lower prices and greater choice.
rigor.explanation: Circular: choice is justified on the ground that it produces choice. The price half is asserted without support.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government is making changes to make sure that data exchange is entirely opt-in. You have to give your express permission to access the data. Second, businesses that you authorise to use the data will need to be accredited. Third, there will be also a customer verification process which will require the entity that holds the data, such as a bank or telco, to verify that it is you making the request and not a scammer.
specificity.explanation: Names three distinct, checkable mechanisms in the regime — express opt-in consent, accreditation of recipients, and a holder-side customer verification step — though without figures or dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How, then, does she reconcile the repeal of section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act with the recommendations of this report—for example, recommendation 39, on the need to empower whānau, hapū, iwi, and Māori to care for our tamariki in accordance with our tikanga, or recommendation 126, which calls on the State to give effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi by allowing tangata whenua to design our own solutions in State care?
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact statutory provision (s 7AA, Oranga Tamariki Act) and two numbered recommendations with their content — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m happy to answer the second question the member put, around the Treaty of Waitangi, and the answer to that question is that we will be considering all of the recommendations in the report in due course, in the context of the entire report, which I have read, and many of my other Ministers have read.
specificity.explanation: Commits to no mechanism, no timeframe ('in due course') and no position on any particular recommendation; the only concrete content is that the report has been read.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: In time, the consumer data framework will likely be extended to other industries such as the telecommunications and insurance sectors.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the consumer data right regime will be designated beyond banking and electricity to cover telecommunications and/or insurance.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Regulations made under the Customer and Product Data Act designating sectors; true if telecommunications or insurance is designated by the resolve-by date, false if only banking (and/or electricity) remains designated.

focus.statement: How, then, does she reconcile the repeal of section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act with the recommendations of this report—for example, recommendation 39, on the need to empower whānau, hapū, iwi, and Māori to care for our tamariki in accordance with our tikanga, or recommendation 126, which calls on the State to give effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi by allowing tangata whenua to design our own solutions in State care?
focus.explanation: Squarely on policy: names a specific legislative repeal and two numbered recommendations of the royal commission report, and asks how they are reconciled. Legitimate scrutiny, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Does the Minister disagree with Fletcher Building’s Residential and Development Chief Executive Steve Evans, who was reported by RNZ as saying, “The insulation standards were going well, particularly that wall insulation and other improvements required were providing significant benefits to people by keeping out cold and damp.”?
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim attributed to Fletcher Building's residential chief executive Steve Evans, as reported by RNZ, that the H1 insulation standards were working well and delivering significant benefits.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: RNZ's published reporting from July 2024 on the H1 insulation standards review; true if RNZ quoted Steve Evans of Fletcher Building to substantially this effect, false if no such reported statement exists or he said the opposite.

veracity.statement: Well, when he says that the building sector has a range of different views, does anyone disagree with the Master Builders Association and the Certified Builders Association when they endorsed the insulation standards?
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that both the Registered Master Builders Association and the New Zealand Certified Builders Association endorsed the existing H1 insulation standards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, media releases or MBIE submissions from Registered Master Builders and NZ Certified Builders around mid-2024; true if both organisations publicly supported retaining the H1 insulation standards, false if either opposed them or took no position.

veracity.statement: Since 1978, we have required at least some insulation in New Zealand houses. Prior to that, which accounts for half of the housing stock in this country, there was no requirement.
veracity.explanation: Two factual claims: that New Zealand has mandated some level of house insulation since 1978, and that dwellings built before that date make up about half the current housing stock.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The history of insulation requirements in NZ building bylaws/NZS 4218 (true if a mandatory minimum dates from 1978), and Stats NZ/BRANZ house-age data (true if roughly half of occupied dwellings predate 1978, false if materially below that share).

veracity.statement: Now, one could argue that it has been addressed, but it’s my view—and I would wager the view of this side of the House—that simply having a Minister in the committee stage standing up and saying, “We won the election; therefore, we have a mandate.” isn’t actually answering a question, which is what is required of the Minister at this point, especially when there is an Amendment Paper that is actually larger than the original bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Amendment Paper before the committee is larger than the bill it amends.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the tabled Amendment Paper with the bill as introduced on legislation.govt.nz/parliament.nz; true if the Amendment Paper exceeds the bill in page or clause count, false if it is smaller.

veracity.statement: But given the cost that is being imposed on councils through these referenda, and given that it actually—in the words of the 52 local councils that signed the letter opposing what the Government is putting forward—is an example of an overreach, that this is undermining their decisions, and is actually counter to the rhetoric that the Government said they were going to do in regards to local government, I think the Minister owes the committee an answer to a very simple question: what councils asked for this?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 52 local councils signed a letter opposing the Government's measure and characterised it as an overreach that undermines council decisions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The joint letter from councils/mayors to the Government on the Māori wards referendum policy in 2024; true if 52 councils were signatories and the letter used overreach/undermining language, false if the signatory count or characterisation is materially different.

focus.statement: Is the Minister telling the House that his proposal to reduce insulation requirements will not result in any homes being colder and damper?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the named policy — the proposed change to H1 insulation requirements — and its concrete consequence for housing warmth and dampness. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, I don’t suggest that those who are making a particular argument in terms of the current settings are ill-motivated, but I would say it’s important that we listen to a range of voices and a range of different interests who have a view about the complexity, the practicality, and the affordability of the changes as they have currently been made.
civility.explanation: Having just read out a submission that called the H1 changes the 'fanciful ideas of environmentalists and greedy suppliers', he explicitly declines to impute bad motives to anyone and frames the disagreement as one about complexity, practicality and cost.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If she were to listen to some people who are engaged in the building sector who have different views from those she’s already expressed and chooses to listen to, she will learn a thing or two.
civility.explanation: Turns from the policy to the questioner: tells her she would 'learn a thing or two' and implies she selectively chooses whom to listen to. Condescension plus an imputation about her motives, not a criticism of an argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, one could argue that it has been addressed, but it’s my view—and I would wager the view of this side of the House—that simply having a Minister in the committee stage standing up and saying, “We won the election; therefore, we have a mandate.” isn’t actually answering a question, which is what is required of the Minister at this point, especially when there is an Amendment Paper that is actually larger than the original bill.
civility.explanation: Criticises the adequacy of the Minister's answers in the committee stage rather than the Minister himself, and quotes what was said rather than characterising his character. Pointed about conduct in the House, but it lands on the answer, not the man.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, for example, I’d invite the member to look into the detail, for example, of whether the schedule method in clause H1 of the building code is more effective than the modelling method whereby you have a relatively blunt instrument that applied in different parts of the country that is proving impracticable and expensive.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific provision (clause H1) and contrasts two identifiable compliance pathways (schedule versus modelling method), but supplies no figures, no regional detail and no timeframe for any change.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I haven’t suggested that for a moment. I’ve suggested that we have a set of requirements in relation to insulation that actually achieve the aim without reducing housing affordability.

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, what’s unusual is that, as it’s proposed, they don’t go through the same process as other councils because, of course, if there isn’t 5 percent—and I believe that threshold should be higher, but none the less, if there is 5 percent of people that sign a petition to start a referendum, they’ll be able to do that.

rigor.statement: My submission to the Minister here for his consideration is whether or not he would consider pausing this to allow the important work of the select committee to continue in order to make sure that as this particular amendment, as proposed by the Government, moves forward—and we accept that they do have the numbers—whether or not we can pause it to ensure that the Electoral Commission and all the institutions that support the amendments that are being proposed here will be better executed in the future.

veracity.statement: I’d like to acknowledge that I think it was a National-led Government that brought in the 30-year infrastructure planning, which was a great step forward.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The amending statute that introduced the 30-year infrastructure strategy requirement into the Local Government Act 2002 (Local Government Act 2002 Amendment Act 2014, s101B) and which government was in office when it was enacted; true if enacted under a National-led government, false if enacted under a Labour-led government or if no such requirement was introduced then.

veracity.statement: When a council creates a long-term plan, they do that every six years, but they can change it every three years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a six-yearly cycle for adopting a council long-term plan, with amendment possible every three years.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Local Government Act 2002, s93 — the statutory frequency at which a territorial authority must adopt a long-term plan; true if the Act requires adoption every six years, false if it requires adoption every three years (covering a ten-year period).

veracity.statement: The poll outcomes will apply for six years, as was the case before 2021.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that, prior to the 2021 amendment, a binding local poll on Māori wards applied for six years (two triennial elections).

veracity.falsification_criterion: The Local Electoral Act 2001 as it stood before the Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2021 — the provisions on the duration for which a poll result on Māori wards was binding; true if the result bound the council for two triennial general elections (six years), false if a different period applied.

veracity.statement: There are, by my count, 32 group 1 local authorities and 13 group 2 local authorities, so about 45 local authorities all up.

veracity.statement: I would love to see our Māori Affairs Committee members make a contribution to this and ask some questions of the Minister themselves, simply because, in the establishment of the original legislation here, the select committee process did go through the Māori Affairs Committee.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the legislation this bill reverses was itself considered by the Māori Affairs Committee rather than another select committee.

veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Parliament bill records for the legislation that established the current Māori wards regime (the Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill 2021, and if relevant the Local Electoral Amendment Act 2002 that first created Māori wards) — which select committee, if any, the bill was referred to; true if referred to the Māori Affairs Committee, false if referred elsewhere or passed without select committee consideration.

civility.statement: At the same time, I’m encouraged by the keenness of members on the other side of the Chamber to stand up with what I hope are questions but which is, I think, actually an attempt to shut this debate down through closure motions.

veracity.statement: In the Electoral Act, we have a requirement, which the Representation Commission deals with, of each electorate being within plus or minus 5 percent of the other—so the populations are within plus or minus 5 percent. But if you only have one Māori ward—and this is in Schedule 1A—it can be plus or minus 50 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three statutory population-tolerance figures: ±5% for parliamentary electorates under the Electoral Act, ±10% for general wards and for multiple Māori wards under the Local Electoral Act, and up to ±50% where a council has a single Māori ward under Schedule 1A.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Act 1993 s 35(3)(a) (electorate quota tolerance) and Local Electoral Act 2001 Schedule 1A (fair representation / population tolerance for general and Māori wards); true if the statute sets ±5%, ±10% and a single-Māori-ward tolerance of ±50%, false if any of those figures differs materially.

veracity.statement: The tribunal also said the Government’s prioritising of its political agenda over the desires of Māori for dedicated political representation at a local level breached the Crown’s duty to actively protect the rights and interests of Māori.

veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal's 2024 urgent inquiry report into the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill; true if the report contains a finding in those terms, false if no such finding appears.

veracity.statement: So, I guess, around not being offensive to local councils, not being offensive to local communities—I mean, thousands of people have spoken against this.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's report on the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill and its submission tallies; true if submissions opposing the bill numbered in the thousands or more, false if the opposing total was in the hundreds or fewer.
