veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: (a) Recordings/transcripts of Luxon's pre-election remarks; true if the quoted words are substantially as spoken, false if not attributable to him. (b) The terms of reference/appointment notice for the Ministerial Advisory Group on Victims of Retail Crime chaired by Sunny Kaushal; true if it is required to report back only after two years, false if it is required to provide advice sooner.

veracity.statement: The Tertiary Education Commission (TEC) has recently exercised its statutory intervention power to require Te Pūkenga to obtain specialist external help to conduct the necessary cost-out work, to develop clear pathways to re-establishing an Institutes of Technology and Polytechnics of New Zealand (ITP) network and to implement this work.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that TEC used its statutory intervention power over Te Pūkenga to require external specialist help for cost reduction and ITP network re-establishment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: TEC's published intervention notice/correspondence for Te Pūkenga in 2024 (Education and Training Act statutory intervention powers); true if such an intervention was issued with those requirements, false if no intervention was exercised or its content differs.

veracity.statement: The previous Government reduced funding rates for front-line education delivery by polytechnics and other providers, diverting funding into central projects. This has also driven the increase in their deficits.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government cut per-student funding rates for front-line delivery at polytechnics and other providers, redirecting the money to central projects.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: TEC published funding rate schedules and Vote Tertiary Education appropriations for 2018-2023; true if front-line delivery rates for ITPs/other providers were reduced in that period with funding moved to centralised projects, false if rates were held or increased.

veracity.statement: Did Te Pūkenga advise her that her directive to cease restructuring ahead of her promised plan would result in additional costs of $53 million in 2024?
veracity.explanation: Presupposes that Te Pūkenga advised the Minister her directive to halt restructuring would add $53 million of cost in 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga/TEC advice or correspondence to the Minister released under the OIA; true if advice quantifying an additional ~$53m cost in 2024 from the pause on restructuring was provided to her, false if no such advice exists or the figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: Good news too: from tomorrow, 31 July, 11 pages of overly prescriptive affordability regulations will no longer be part of the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act—commonly referred to as the CCCFA.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 11 pages of affordability regulations under the CCCFA were revoked with effect from 31 July 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Amendment Regulations 2024 as gazetted and their commencement date; true if the affordability regulations of that extent were revoked effective 31 July 2024, false if the date or scope differs.

veracity.statement: Borrowers were required to explain why they did things like buy an occasional coffee, join a gym, or treated the family to fish and chips every now and again—even when they clearly could afford to.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the CCCFA affordability regulations required borrowers to justify individual discretionary purchases such as coffees, gym memberships and takeaways, even where affordability was clear.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the CCCFA affordability regulations (2021) and the Responsible Lending Code as they stood before 31 July 2024, plus Commerce Commission guidance; true if lenders were obliged to obtain borrower explanations for itemised discretionary spending irrespective of evident affordability, false if the regulations required only estimation/verification of relevant expenses with discretion about clearly affordable applications.

veracity.statement: Overall, it showed a weakening of farmer confidence with a net 66 percent of farmers pointing out that current economic conditions are very challenging and that profit margins for many are squeezed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Federated Farmers' 31st farm confidence survey found a net 66 percent of farmers describing current economic conditions as very challenging, and showed confidence weakening.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Federated Farmers Farm Confidence Survey published July 2024; true if the net negative reading on current economic conditions is approximately 66 percent and the survey records a fall from the prior wave, false if the figure or direction differs materially.

rigor.statement: The previous Government reduced funding rates for front-line education delivery by polytechnics and other providers, diverting funding into central projects. This has also driven the increase in their deficits.
rigor.explanation: A causal conclusion ('has driven the increase in deficits') is asserted from a single antecedent with nothing offered to connect them — post hoc reasoning; no share of the deficit is attributed or evidenced.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: These results underscore the importance of our efforts to get Government spending under control and to put downward pressure on inflation, do the rural banking inquiry through the Primary Production Committee, and for improving the regulatory environment for farmers.
rigor.explanation: A non sequitur: a sentiment survey showing squeezed margins is treated as establishing that this particular set of policies is the right response, with no link drawn between the reported causes of low confidence and the listed measures.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is the Minister saying that she has no recollection of any correspondence that clearly sets out, addressed to her, her decisions costing Te Pūkenga $53 million; and how could she possibly forget a sum of $53 million?
civility.explanation: The first half is legitimate pressing; the tail ('how could she possibly forget') turns from the decision to the Minister herself, using incredulity at her memory rather than the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Firstly, it restores the rights of communities to determine whether to introduce Māori wards, by reinstating binding polls for Māori wards and constituencies, a policy that was put in place by the Helen Clark Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the binding-poll mechanism for Māori wards and constituencies was originally created under the Helen Clark-led Labour government, and that this bill reinstates it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Local Electoral Act 2002 and its amendments (enacted under the 1999-2008 Labour government) as against the text of the 2024 Amendment Bill: true if the poll/petition provisions for Māori wards were introduced by legislation passed under the Clark government and the 2024 bill restores a binding-poll requirement; false if the poll provisions originate from a different government or the bill does not reinstate binding polls.

veracity.statement: As part of National’s coalition agreement with New Zealand First and the ACT Party, we are restoring the right for local referendums on the establishment and ongoing use of Māori wards.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that restoring local referendums on the establishment and ongoing use of Māori wards is a commitment contained in the coalition agreements between National and both New Zealand First and ACT.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published National-NZ First and National-ACT coalition agreements (Nov 2023): true if a commitment to restore local referendums on Māori wards appears in the agreement(s) as described; false if no such commitment appears, or if it appears in only one agreement contrary to the attribution to both.

veracity.statement: They put this bill through when they were in Government with only two days for public submissions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous government's 2021 Māori wards legislation allowed the public only two days to make submissions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliament record for the Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill 2021 — first reading date, whether it was referred to a select committee, and the advertised submission window: true if the public submission period was approximately two days; false if it was materially longer, or if there was no select committee submission process at all (the bill having passed under urgency).

specificity.statement: Firstly, it restores the rights of communities to determine whether to introduce Māori wards, by reinstating binding polls for Māori wards and constituencies, a policy that was put in place by the Helen Clark Government.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific mechanism being reinstated (binding polls for Māori wards and constituencies) and attributes its origin to a named government; checkable against the statute.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For those councils which have gone and put in place Māori wards since 2021, this bill requires them by 6 September to either rescind or disestablish that ward or go to the people in their community and let the people in their community have their say.
specificity.explanation: States precisely which councils are captured, the statutory deadline (6 September) and the binary choice the bill imposes on them; directly checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill also makes some important changes in terms of the time frame for local elections by extending the time frame for postal services, to ensure that the next local elections in 2025 can have enough time for the post to be able to deliver.
specificity.explanation: Names the area changed (postal timeframes for the 2025 local elections) but gives no length of extension, no dates and no mechanism — a direction with partial detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Divisive changes were introduced by the previous Government which denied—denied—local communities the ability to determine whether to establish local Māori wards in their communities.
focus.explanation: Directed at a specific legislative change (the 2021 removal of the Māori ward poll mechanism) and its concrete effect, rather than at Labour's general character; party framing ('divisive') is present but the policy is identifiable.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When it comes to localism, they want to leave it with the mayor and the council. We believe that, actually, voters should be able to have their say and actually make decisions in terms of what goes down in their local communities.

focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Hon Willie Jackson hasn’t learned a single thing from what happened on 14 October. He still thinks democracy has changed. He thinks that we should be taking the power away from local people.
focus.explanation: Almost entirely about the opposing member and the election result; the only policy trace is the generic 'taking the power away from local people', with no measure, figure or mechanism named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They rammed it through to get rid of democracy because that’s what that side of the House does. They don’t believe in democracy, and we do.
focus.explanation: Content-free characterisation of the opposing party's beliefs and habits; no policy, process detail or outcome is named once the party framing is removed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That should not be a point that is being debated in this House this afternoon, but it’s a point which the Labour Party, the Green Party, and the Māori Party have walked far, far, far away from in their most recent policies and their most recent statements.
focus.explanation: A sweeping claim about three opposing parties' general direction; gestures at 'recent policies and statements' without naming a single policy, measure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When it comes to localism, they want to leave it with the mayor and the council. We believe that, actually, voters should be able to have their say and actually make decisions in terms of what goes down in their local communities.
rigor.explanation: The contrast is asserted rather than argued: it defines 'localism' as direct voter decision by stipulation and does not address why a decision by democratically elected councillors would not also count. A definitional assertion doing the work of a premise, though the inference from that premise to the bill is coherent.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, the people of New Zealand rejected your form of democracy, Willie Jackson. They rejected it on 14 October, and they voted in the coalition Government to restore local democracy in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Infers a specific mandate on Māori ward polls from a general election result — an appeal to popularity, with nothing offered to connect the vote to this particular measure.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Hon Willie Jackson hasn’t learned a single thing from what happened on 14 October. He still thinks democracy has changed. He thinks that we should be taking the power away from local people.
civility.explanation: Turns from the bill to a named member, asserting he has 'learned' nothing — a jibe at the individual's judgement rather than at his argument.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Sadly, I suspect today is going to be another one of those days.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the House will, on this sitting day, pass the Māori wards legislation he characterises as discriminatory — i.e. that the bill completes its passage today.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Hansard third-reading division record for the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Constituencies) Amendment Bill: true if the bill was read a third time and passed on 30 July 2024, false if it did not pass that day.

specificity.statement: The representation review will look at the establishment of or whether we should continue with community boards or ward committees; the number of ward councillors there should be; the number of at-large councillors there should be; and, yes, whether or not to have, or to continue having, a Māori ward.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific council process and itemises the concrete decisions within it (community boards/ward committees, ward councillor numbers, at-large councillor numbers, Māori ward), so the comparison he goes on to draw is checkable. No figures or dates, hence not top of scale.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: None of those things is subject to a referendum. The only thing that is subject to a referendum is whether there should be a Māori ward or not. That is discrimination. That is absolutely discrimination.
rigor.explanation: A valid differential-treatment inference: if a poll is mandated for one category of ward and for no other, the category is being treated differently. The only gap is that 'discrimination' is asserted rather than distinguished from justified differentiation; no fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They still get the number of votes that every other person gets. Having Māori wards is absolutely consistent with the principle of “one person, one vote”. It’s absolutely consistent with that.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows directly from the stated premise: if Māori-roll voters cast the same number of votes as everyone else, the arrangement does not breach one-person-one-vote. Valid given its assumption; repetition adds emphasis, not inference.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: None of those things is subject to a referendum. The only thing that is subject to a referendum is whether there should be a Māori ward or not. That is discrimination. That is absolutely discrimination.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of the measure before the House — which decisions the bill subjects to a poll and which it does not. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is a Government that is determined to “other” Māori within their own country. They see Māori as a people to be put back in their place.
focus.explanation: Characterises the Government's motives and intent rather than any mechanism, cost or outcome of the bill; no policy, figure or named measure is engaged in these sentences.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m not surprised the members opposite are so quiet now during this debate after all the shouting of the last contribution has disappeared, because they’ve got their heads down because they know that what I’m saying is true.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the demeanour and silence of the other side; strip that out and no policy content, figure or outcome remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I stand on behalf of the Green Party and share with this Whare that te iwi Māori are sick of the attacks of this coalition Government on our people: te reo Māori, Te Aka Whai Ora, 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act, the mega-prison, boot camps, killing our people with tobacco, reviewing all Treaty clauses within legislation and ripping them out, the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act—you dare attack our takutai moana, touch it, watch te iwi Māori respond.
focus.explanation: Names real measures (Te Aka Whai Ora, 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act, boot camps, Treaty clause review, the Takutai Moana Act), so it is not content-free party-bashing; but it is a litany of grievance about the Government's record rather than engagement with the Māori wards bill before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s also important to note that having a separate Māori ward confers no additional rights on Māori compared to non-Māori. Māori still only get the same number of votes as non-Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the Local Electoral Act a voter on the Māori roll votes in the Māori ward instead of, not in addition to, a general ward, so a Māori ward grants no extra votes or rights.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Local Electoral Act 2001 provisions on Māori wards and roll-based ward allocation: true if Māori-roll electors vote in one ward only (the Māori ward) and cast the same number of councillor votes as general-roll electors; false if the Act gives Māori-roll electors an additional or extra ward vote.

veracity.statement: If we’re actually talking about “one person, one vote”, why is it that wealthy property owners can have multiple votes but Māori aren’t allowed Māori wards?
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that property owners can vote in more than one local authority election in New Zealand (the non-resident ratepayer elector entitlement).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Local Electoral Act 2001 ratepayer-elector provisions and Electoral Commission/DIA guidance: true if a person owning rateable property in a district where they do not reside may enrol and vote there in addition to voting in their home district, false if no such multiple-district entitlement exists.

veracity.statement: I want to quote from the mayors themselves, who wrote to the Government and said that they did not want this legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that mayors (he later specifies 52 mayors and chairs) wrote to the Government opposing this Māori wards poll legislation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2024 open letter from mayors/regional council chairs to Ministers on mandatory Māori ward polls, as reported by Local Government New Zealand and contemporaneous media: true if such a letter exists and states opposition to the mandated polls, false if no such letter exists or it did not oppose the legislation.

civility.statement: I’m not surprised the members opposite are so quiet now during this debate after all the shouting of the last contribution has disappeared, because they’ve got their heads down because they know that what I’m saying is true.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to members opposite — claiming they are silent because they privately know he is right — which is sneering about their conduct in the Chamber rather than engaging their arguments. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: These 50 mayors that are complaining that they want to have a say—they have a say. They can either choose to disestablish a Māori ward if it was created without the consent of a binding referendum from their people, or they can go to a referendum.
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism the bill actually creates — the disestablish-or-poll choice councils face — rather than characterising the other side.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Minister of Local Government at the time, under the Labour Party Government, took away the ability of people who had gone out, done the hard work in collecting signatures, and had their say—to just be wiped over.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a specific past legislative decision and its named local consequence, not generalised party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: These 50 mayors that are complaining that they want to have a say—they have a say. They can either choose to disestablish a Māori ward if it was created without the consent of a binding referendum from their people, or they can go to a referendum.
rigor.explanation: Real inference about the measure, but a constrained choice between two outcomes imposed by statute is offered as equivalent to 'having a say'; the conclusion outruns the premise and the options presented are framed as exhaustive.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The problem, though, in the Local Electoral Act is that in Schedule 1A of the Act—and you might want to have a look at it—what it does is it allows a Māori ward to be established, potentially, on 50 percent of the size of the population of a general ward. So, effectively, that means that in that situation, a vote in a Māori ward is still one vote, but it has twice the weight of a vote in a general ward.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion about relative vote weight follows arithmetically from the stated premise about permitted ward population ratios; the inference is stated and tracked.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There are local communities who have established Māori wards: 45 councils have established a Māori ward without a binding poll, but four have established a Māori ward which will not be affected by this legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific split of councils with Māori wards into those established without a binding poll (45) and those exempt from the bill (4).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Internal Affairs / Local Government Commission record of councils with Māori wards or Māori constituencies as at July 2024, and the bill's exemption for wards established following a poll; true if 45 councils established one without a binding poll and 4 are unaffected by the legislation, false if the counts differ materially.

veracity.statement: Post-settlement governance entities represent 81.2 percent of Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific coverage figure for post-settlement governance entities across the Māori population.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Arawhiti / Office for Māori Crown Relations figures on the proportion of Māori affiliated to iwi with completed Treaty settlements and post-settlement governance entities; true if approximately 81.2%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The Minister of Local Government at the time, under the Labour Party Government, took away the ability of people who had gone out, done the hard work in collecting signatures, and had their say—to just be wiped over.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the then Labour Minister of Local Government removed the petition-triggered poll right after Tauranga electors had collected the required signatures.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2021 and contemporaneous records of poll-demand petitions in Tauranga; true if the 2021 amendment removed the poll/petition mechanism and nullified a petition or poll process under way in Tauranga, false if no such petition existed or the mechanism was not removed.

veracity.statement: Across the board, the general wards’ turnout is 47 percent and the Māori wards’ turnout is 28 percent, so it’s significantly lower, and what that means under STV is that at the first iteration, on average, you require three times as many votes to be elected—three times as many votes to be elected—in a general ward than you do in a Māori ward.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific average turnout percentages for general wards versus Māori wards, and a resulting three-to-one ratio in votes required for election at the first STV iteration.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Internal Affairs local authority election statistics for the 2022 local elections; true if average general-ward turnout is approximately 47% and average Māori-ward turnout approximately 28%, false if materially different.

specificity.statement: There are local communities who have established Māori wards: 45 councils have established a Māori ward without a binding poll, but four have established a Māori ward which will not be affected by this legislation.
specificity.explanation: Two precise counts tied to a named legislative effect; directly checkable against the council record.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Post-settlement governance entities represent 81.2 percent of Māori.
specificity.explanation: A precise percentage attached to a named class of entity; someone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For example, take again the Tauranga City Council. We have the tangata whenua and council committee, which is a standing committee; we have the Rangapū Mana Whenua o Tauranga Moana Partnership, which implements initiatives as well as advances and protects the interests of tangata whenua; and we have the Kāhui Kaumātua, which is the kaumātua forum in which any kaumātua in and around Tauranga can raise concerns and issues with the mayor, the chief executive, and the staff.
specificity.explanation: Three named council bodies with their function and who may participate; concrete enough to verify against Tauranga City Council's governance structure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This change is not an attack on Māori. It is a defence of the liberal value that all human beings have equal moral worth, and our political rights flow from that fundamental principle.
specificity.explanation: An abstract statement of principle about the bill; no figure, mechanism, timeframe or provision that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The problem, though, in the Local Electoral Act is that in Schedule 1A of the Act—and you might want to have a look at it—what it does is it allows a Māori ward to be established, potentially, on 50 percent of the size of the population of a general ward. So, effectively, that means that in that situation, a vote in a Māori ward is still one vote, but it has twice the weight of a vote in a general ward.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute, the schedule and the numeric threshold, and spells out the consequence; directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Across the board, the general wards’ turnout is 47 percent and the Māori wards’ turnout is 28 percent, so it’s significantly lower, and what that means under STV is that at the first iteration, on average, you require three times as many votes to be elected—three times as many votes to be elected—in a general ward than you do in a Māori ward.
specificity.explanation: Two turnout figures, the electoral system they apply to, and a quantified consequence at a named stage of the count.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That is a form of consultation that I think—if the members on the other side of the House would listen carefully—takes into account the feelings and the issues that are affecting mana whenua in their regions and brings that to the community and to the council without having to have a race-based ward.
civility.explanation: Substantive point about consultation mechanisms, but carries a mild condescension toward opposing members' willingness to listen; edges toward the people without landing an attack.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Chris Hipkins said that Māori wards are one person, one vote, and that it doesn’t give Māori extra votes, and he’s correct on that. But what he has failed to see is that there is a major flaw in the Local Electoral Act.
civility.explanation: Explicitly concedes an opponent's point and disagrees only about a statutory provision; attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’ll explain to you, Willow-Jean Prime, if you wanted to listen.
civility.explanation: Names a member and implies she is unwilling to listen — condescension aimed at the person rather than her argument, though short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I know numbers confuse you, Willie. I know numbers confuse you, but they are important and electoral integrity is important.
civility.explanation: A direct jibe at another member's numeracy, naming him ('Willie'). The attack lands on the person's competence rather than on any argument he made.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I had a number of words written in preparation for this third reading speech tonight, but I’m not sure whether it’s worth it, because, clearly, many of the members opposite haven’t actually read the bill, don’t understand what the bill does, and don’t actually acknowledge any part of the bill.
civility.explanation: Imputes to named colleagues opposite that they have not read the bill and cannot understand it — an attack on the members' diligence and comprehension rather than on anything they argued, though it stops short of direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Just in conclusion, Labour’s legislation was rushed through in less than one eighth—I’ll use another number—of the time that this bill has taken to get through.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2021 Labour legislation on Māori wards took less than one eighth of the elapsed parliamentary time that the current bill took to pass.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary records for the Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2021 (introduction to third reading, passed under urgency) compared with the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill 2024 (introduction to third reading, 30 July 2024); true if the 2021 elapsed time is under one eighth of the 2024 elapsed time, false if greater.

veracity.statement: Māori wards are generally far smaller than general wards in terms of population represented per person. Half the people with Māori whakapapa choose not to enrol in the Māori electorates or rolls, but choose the general ones, and the turnout in those wards is between a third and a half of what it is in the general wards. So there is a fundamental problem and, in my view, the Act—regardless of this bill—remains fundamentally flawed.
veracity.explanation: Two checkable claims: that about half of people of Māori descent choose the general roll rather than the Māori roll, and that turnout in Māori wards is between one third and one half of turnout in general wards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission enrolment statistics on the proportion of enrolled voters of Māori descent choosing the Māori roll, and Local Government NZ / Department of Internal Affairs local election turnout figures for Māori wards versus general wards at the 2022 local elections; true if roughly half opt for the general roll AND Māori ward turnout is 33–50% of general ward turnout, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: The greatest unspoken majority in the current structure of our local democracy is the ratepayer—the ratepayer who has multiple votes, potentially.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a ratepayer can potentially cast more than one vote in New Zealand local government elections.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Local Electoral Act 2001 ratepayer-elector provisions and Department of Internal Affairs guidance on the non-resident ratepayer roll; true if a person can be enrolled and vote both as a residential elector in one district and as a ratepayer elector in another, false if each person is limited to a single local vote.

veracity.statement: Over the course of the submissions process, I sat and listened to council after council plead with the select committee, asking for retention of Māori wards but clearly that fell on deaf ears.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that multiple territorial authorities made submissions to the select committee seeking retention of Māori wards, and that the committee did not act on them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published submissions and select committee report on the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill; true if numerous councils submitted in favour of retaining Māori wards and the reported bill did not adopt that position, false if few or no councils so submitted or the committee amended the bill accordingly.

veracity.statement: The bill doesn’t remove Māori wards. The bill doesn’t remove constituencies. The bill reverts the law back to where it was in 2021 under Jacinda Ardern.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill neither abolishes Māori wards nor constituencies, and that it restores the legal position that existed prior to the 2021 amendment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill as passed, compared with the Local Electoral Act 2001 as it stood before and after the Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2021; true if the bill only reinstates the poll mechanism and abolishes no ward, false if it disestablishes wards or imposes requirements (e.g. compulsory 2025 polls or disestablishment) that did not exist pre-2021.

rigor.statement: Māori wards are generally far smaller than general wards in terms of population represented per person. Half the people with Māori whakapapa choose not to enrol in the Māori electorates or rolls, but choose the general ones, and the turnout in those wards is between a third and a half of what it is in the general wards. So there is a fundamental problem and, in my view, the Act—regardless of this bill—remains fundamentally flawed.
rigor.explanation: The premises (smaller ward populations, split enrolment, lower turnout) are offered to support the conclusion that the Act is 'fundamentally flawed', but no link is supplied between low voluntary turnout and legislative flaw — a non sequitur, since low turnout in a ward does not by itself impugn the statute that created it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Why do we have a bill of rights? We have a bill of rights because it has been well understood for centuries in the formulations of democracies across the world that there was a very evident problem with democracy: the tyranny of the majority—the tyranny of the majority. It is impossible by a purely majority rule to protect minority interests, and, indeed, persecution of minorities becomes nearly inevitable if you allow that tyranny. Therefore, all functional democracies have a bill of rights to guard against the tyranny of the majority.
rigor.explanation: A genuine argument with premise and conclusion, and the structure holds: if majority rule cannot protect minority interests, a rights instrument is a coherent remedy. Marked down for the overreaching step that persecution becomes 'nearly inevitable' and the universal 'all functional democracies', neither of which is supported by what was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The removal of Māori wards is merely another open invite to racists across this whenua to the open season against te iwi Māori.
rigor.explanation: Engages the measure itself but the inference is a non sequitur: nothing is offered connecting a change to the poll requirements for Māori wards to an increase in racist conduct, and 'open invite' asserts the causal link rather than establishing it.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s quite clear that the Opposition either doesn’t understand or doesn’t want to listen, but this is a fundamental problem for the democratic structure of this bill.
focus.explanation: Most of the weight is a characterisation of the Opposition's comprehension and willingness to listen; the policy content is a bare assertion of a 'fundamental problem' with no mechanism, figure or clause named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is the poisonous untruth that permeates the programme of this anti-Māori Government: that by nullifying Māori rights, we make us all the better; we make us somehow more equal.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point underneath — a challenge to the equality rationale for the measure — but it is delivered as a characterisation of the Government's whole programme as 'anti-Māori', with no specific provision, cost or outcome named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: All the bills, amendments, removals, and disestablishments to date are this Government’s attempt to normalise racism in the face of our nation so that no one, including their own, will speak up to fight for us when it reaches to that point; that today it may seem so unbelievable, but tomorrow it’s a reality.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the Government's supposed motives and character across an unspecified set of 'all the bills'; no particular measure, clause or outcome is named for the House to engage with.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I thought I would make a contribution, because one of the themes that comes across from the members opposite is that they believe that they have the single dictate, that they have the one true idea in the world on what it is to be Māori, on what it is to count as a Māori, and what it is to have your view count as being one that is of Māori world view.
focus.explanation: Wholly about what the members opposite supposedly believe and who they think counts; no provision, cost, timeframe or outcome of the bill is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill does one very simple thing: it restores the rights for local communities to have a say on the creation of Māori wards—a special ward created by statute. It is only right that locals have a say on the creation of those wards.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: what the bill does mechanically (restores a local say on the creation of Māori wards) and why the speaker supports it.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: So now we have the opportunity for those mayors and councillors to go out to the public and get a mandate to support what has been so effective for them, and I’m sure many will get across the line and retain their Māori wards.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that many councils holding the binding Māori ward referendums required by this bill will vote to retain their Māori wards.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Official results of the Māori ward polls held alongside the 2025 local body elections (Local Government NZ / council declarations); true if a substantial share — say a majority — of the councils polling vote to retain their Māori ward, false if the large majority vote to abolish.

veracity.statement: Māori can still get elected, and they do in huge numbers: 35 percent of our Cabinet.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 35 percent of the current Cabinet identify as Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Composition of the Cabinet as at July 2024 against ministers' publicly stated iwi/Māori affiliation; true if roughly 35% (about 7 of 20) identify as Māori, false if materially fewer.

veracity.statement: As I said in the second reading, 20 percent of Auckland councillors in that inaugural Auckland Council election were Māori and they’ve all stood in general wards.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 20 percent of the councillors elected at the first Auckland Council election (2010) were Māori and that all of them stood in general wards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The declared results of the 2010 Auckland Council election and the elected councillors' publicly recorded Māori affiliation; true if about 4 of the 20 councillors were Māori and none held a designated Māori seat, false if materially fewer.

veracity.statement: The Government members say, “But the Labour Government put this in place” Well, that was back in the 1990s, and under the last Government we took away this barrier that disabled Māori from having better representation, because we recognised that it was only a barrier that was put in place for Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the poll provision for Māori wards was enacted by a Labour Government in the 1990s, and that it was repealed under the 2017–2023 Labour Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative record: which statute first created the Māori ward poll/petition mechanism and in what year (Local Electoral Act 2001/2002 vs any 1990s Act), and the Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2021 repeal; true if the mechanism dates from the 1990s, false if it was enacted in 2001–02.

veracity.statement: I end my contribution for today that this started when the Minister made a decision not to put this through the Māori Affairs Committee—not to include Māori and to obstruct them from this discussion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill was deliberately referred away from the Māori Affairs Committee by the Minister.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard and the Order Paper for the bill's first reading: which select committee the bill was referred to and whether the referral motion moved by the Minister nominated the Justice Committee rather than the Māori Affairs Committee; true if the Minister's motion sent it to Justice, false if the committee was chosen by another mechanism.

veracity.statement: The first councillor of Filipino descent was elected in Ashburton in 2017, and it was a big surprise to all of us.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's first councillor of Filipino descent was elected to Ashburton District Council in 2017.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ashburton District Council election/by-election records for 2017 and contemporaneous reporting on the first Filipino-descent local body councillor in New Zealand; true if such a councillor was elected there that year and was the first, false if the date, council or 'first' claim is wrong.

veracity.statement: Ko te take i tīni ai te ture kia whai tūru Māori ki runga i ngā kaunihera, koirā te take nā te mea mai i tērā ture tawhito o te tau 2002 tae noa ki te tau 2019, kotahi anake te kaunihera i eke.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the previous law, between 2002 and 2019 only one council succeeded in establishing Māori seats.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Internal Affairs / Local Government NZ records of Māori ward and constituency establishment 2002–2019, including poll outcomes; true if only one council successfully established Māori seats in that period, false if others (e.g. Waikato Regional Council, Wairoa District Council, Bay of Plenty Regional Council) did so.

veracity.statement: Rima tekau ngā kaunihera whai tūru Māori ināianei.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that fifty councils currently have Māori seats (wards or constituencies).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Internal Affairs / Local Government NZ count of councils with Māori wards or Māori constituencies as at mid-2024; true if approximately 50, false if materially different (e.g. around 45).

specificity.statement: As I said in the second reading, 20 percent of Auckland councillors in that inaugural Auckland Council election were Māori and they’ve all stood in general wards.
specificity.explanation: Carries a percentage, a named election and a named ward type — someone could go and check it against the 2010 results.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But we in this Government are determined to celebrate the humanity that unites all of us and not to focus on division by using in-group rights and collective identity as a supervening fact over the equality of all of us.
specificity.explanation: A statement of general values — unity, equality, no division — with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named provision of the bill attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No, it is only Māori wards and their voters that must be approved through a district-wide vote.
focus.explanation: Names the specific mechanism in the bill before the House — the district-wide poll requirement — and who it applies to. Squarely on the measure, not on the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The amendment bill seeks only to bring back to local communities their opportunity to have a say in their own governance.
focus.explanation: Describes what the bill before the House does, in terms of the decision it returns to communities. On the measure rather than on the other party, though without detail.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: He tino hōhā—hōhā—te noho ki roto i te Whare i tēnei ahiahi ki te whakarongo ki te kōrero a tērā taha.
focus.explanation: Entirely about how irritating the other side's speeches are; no provision, figure or outcome of the bill is engaged in this sentence.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This barrier is not going to be put in the way of property owners having multiple votes in multiple districts where they own property, just like our Prime Minister.
civility.explanation: The substantive point is about the ratepayer-elector rule, but the closing clause turns it onto the Prime Minister's personal property holdings to imply self-interest. Pointed, edging onto the person without a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And the fact that the Minister and Government members are so boastful—so whakahīhī—about what they are doing today is simply disgraceful.
civility.explanation: Moves off the measure and onto the character and demeanour of the Minister and Government members — characterising them as boastful and their conduct as disgraceful rather than engaging the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I end my contribution for today that this started when the Minister made a decision not to put this through the Māori Affairs Committee—not to include Māori and to obstruct them from this discussion.
civility.explanation: Imputes a deliberate intention to exclude and obstruct Māori to the Minister personally — bad faith attributed to an individual rather than criticism of the referral decision itself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Mōhio ana rātou, nō reira kahore ahau, kei tēnei taha, e tautoko ana i tā rātou mahi kaikiri nei.
civility.explanation: Goes beyond calling the policy racist to asserting that members opposite know it is racist and are doing it anyway — an imputation of knowing bad faith to the people, not just criticism of the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If I am not mistaken, Māori, Filipinos, Chinese, Indians, Pākehā form part of the local communities, so when we want to specify a specific treatment to a specific group—in the words of leader of the Labour Party who spoke earlier—when a specific group is treated differently, that is discrimination.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion does not follow from the premise offered: that several ethnicities make up local communities does not establish that a designated ward is discriminatory. It leans on an opponent's quoted formula applied in a different context (appeal to authority plus equivocation on 'treated differently').
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Ko te take i tīni ai te ture kia whai tūru Māori ki runga i ngā kaunihera, koirā te take nā te mea mai i tērā ture tawhito o te tau 2002 tae noa ki te tau 2019, kotahi anake te kaunihera i eke.
rigor.explanation: A properly structured causal argument: the old poll mechanism produced almost no Māori seats over seventeen years, which is offered as the reason the law was changed. The conclusion tracks the evidence given.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I want to say to that previous speaker, James Meager, I find that type of kōrero sad because nobody on this side questions that member’s whakapapa at all—at all. What we question, Mr Meager, is your commitment to kaupapa Māori.
civility.explanation: Contested exchange with a named member, so a real chance to be uncivil. Jackson explicitly affirms Meager's whakapapa and directs the disagreement at his policy commitment rather than his character; 'I find that type of kōrero sad' is pointed but lands on the argument, not the man.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This lot are allowing their arguments of standing up for democracy to mask the petty bigotry that they are really peddling.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith and bigotry as the real motive behind the other side's stated position — a sneer at motive rather than engagement with the democracy argument. No individual is named, so it stops short of a direct personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think, in terms of this, it’s an insult for right-wing politicians to claim they want to decentralise power when they’re robbing councils of their right to have a Māori ward.
rigor.explanation: A genuine consistency argument: a stated principle (decentralisation) is set against a measure said to override council decisions. The inference holds only if removing the Māori-ward decision from councils is centralisation, which is assumed rather than shown — the conclusion partly builds in its premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’re getting lectured on the sanctity of one person, one vote when so many of the National Party and ACT Party colleagues and friends can vote multiple times in multiple elections if they own multiple properties.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque: the alleged inconsistency of opponents' own voting entitlements is offered as the reason the one-person-one-vote objection fails, but the entitlement of ratepayer electors does not bear on whether Māori wards satisfy that principle.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Hilda Harawira, for example, is a wonderful candidate in the north who would not have got through on general wards.
rigor.explanation: Argument from anecdote plus an unsupported counterfactual: a single named candidate's assumed failure on a general ward is offered as evidence that Māori wards are necessary for Māori representation, with nothing supplied to establish the counterfactual.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’ve just heard that the only way to get this opportunity is through the provision of Māori wards. Well, can I mention a few names as to other ways that one can get elected?
rigor.explanation: Strawman plus a category shift: Jackson's claim concerned participation and local representation, and the rebuttal answers it with a list of MPs elected to Parliament via general electorates and party lists, which says nothing about local-government ward arrangements.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I support this because we have a mandate from the New Zealand public. We have a mandate—a strong mandate; a strong mandate.
rigor.explanation: The reason offered for supporting the bill is an appeal to mandate, asserted and then repeated rather than evidenced at this point; the coalition agreements cited immediately afterwards give it some support, but repetition is doing much of the work here.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We’re getting lectured on the sanctity of one person, one vote when so many of the National Party and ACT Party colleagues and friends can vote multiple times in multiple elections if they own multiple properties.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that people who own property in more than one local authority area can cast votes in more than one local election under existing NZ local electoral law.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Local Electoral Act 2001 ratepayer-elector provisions and DIA/Electoral Commission guidance on local elections; true if a person owning rateable property in more than one territorial authority district may be enrolled and vote in each of those local elections, false if the law permits only a single local-election vote per person.

veracity.statement: When we were a Government, we were a Government with 37 percent of the vote.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Labour-led government Jackson served in was formed on roughly a 37 percent party vote.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission official party-vote results for the general election that produced the Labour-led government referred to (2017); true if Labour's party vote was approximately 37 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Then, last Friday, we had the shocking revelation that, again, the Government is attacking Māori in terms of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 and overturning the Court of Appeal decision—overturning a Court of Appeal decision.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in the week before 30 July 2024 the Government announced it would legislate to overturn a Court of Appeal decision on the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government announcements in late July 2024 and the subsequent Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) amendment legislation; true if the Government announced it would legislate to reverse the Court of Appeal's customary marine title test in Re Edwards, false if no such announcement or no reversal of that decision was proposed.

veracity.statement: None of them were elected through Māori wards or through Māori seats.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the named ministers (Peters, Seymour, Jones, Costello, Reti, Potaka, McKee, Chhour) all entered Parliament without a Māori electorate seat or a Māori ward.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission records of how each named MP entered Parliament; true if none was elected in a Māori electorate (Māori wards being a local-government mechanism only), false if any of them held a Māori seat.

veracity.statement: We have now got a Cabinet of 35 percent Māori, something that a majority Labour Government didn’t achieve in the last term.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori make up 35 percent of the current Cabinet and that this exceeds the proportion in the 2020–2023 Labour Cabinet.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The official Cabinet list as at 2024 and the 2020–2023 Labour Cabinet list, with ministers' Māori descent; true if roughly 35 percent of current Cabinet ministers are Māori and that share is higher than Labour's, false if the current share is materially lower or Labour's was equal or higher.

veracity.statement: In fact, it’s been well signalled since February 2021, when Labour rushed, without warning—rushed—the process through. Two days for submissions, am I right, Mr Chair of the Justice Committee? Two days for submissions, and two weeks from go to whoa.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Labour's February 2021 Māori wards legislation had a two-day public submission window and passed within about two weeks of introduction.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary records for the Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill 2021 — the select committee submission period and the elapsed time from introduction to third reading; true if submissions were open about two days and the bill passed within about two weeks, false if materially longer.

veracity.statement: Sixty-eight percent were against, in the public.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 68 percent of the 12,000-plus public submissions to Auckland Council's 2023 Māori wards consultation opposed establishing Māori wards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council's published analysis of its 2023 Māori wards consultation; true if approximately 68 percent of submissions opposed, false if the reported opposition share is materially different.

focus.statement: There’s no better example of that than this rotten Government.
focus.explanation: A policy debate is live (Māori wards, majoritarianism), but this sentence names no measure, figure or outcome — it is a characterisation of the other side's government as a whole.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What’s wrong with giving locals a say with how their local representatives are elected? Locals deserve to have a say on their governance representation arrangements.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — who decides local representation arrangements — with no party framing or characterisation of opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have now got a Cabinet of 35 percent Māori, something that a majority Labour Government didn’t achieve in the last term.
specificity.explanation: A precise percentage attached to a named body and an explicit comparison to a named previous administration — someone could go and count it.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: To those councils that installed Māori wards without referendum, they will now have their decision tested at the 2025 local government elections.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that councils which established Māori wards without a poll will face binding public polls on those wards at the 2025 local body elections.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Local government election results for October 2025; true if the affected councils held binding Māori ward polls alongside those elections, false if the poll requirement was repealed, deferred, or not in fact held.

specificity.statement: I remind the House that this bill enables every single owner of a marine-farming permit at the moment to enjoy confidence and greater certainty because their permits will be extended until 2050.
