rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So why is it that this Government is so obsessed with getting references to this hierarchy out of legislation—legislation that is not even mentioned in the first place? That can only be because they want more pollution, and that will lead to dirtier water that people will drink.
rigor.explanation: False dilemma: 'that can only be because they want more pollution' treats one imputed motive as the sole possible explanation for the drafting choice, with nothing offered to exclude alternatives (e.g. removing legal uncertainty for the regulator). The causal chain to 'dirtier water' is asserted, not argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Another curious thing about this bill is that they insert a new section 138A, and that is a “King Henry VIII” clause so that, if this national policy statement on fresh water is amended, the insertion I’ve just been talking about can be repealed.
specificity.explanation: Names the precise provision (new section 138A), classifies the drafting device, and states the exact trigger and effect. Anyone could go to the bill and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, for example, where I live in the Waikato and Hamilton City Council, there were 24 entities or 24 councils that would make up Entity B, even though Hamilton City Council’s water assets are around $2 billion.
specificity.explanation: Carries a council count, a named entity, and a dollar valuation — precise enough for someone to go and verify or dispute.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So why is it that this Government is so obsessed with getting references to this hierarchy out of legislation—legislation that is not even mentioned in the first place? That can only be because they want more pollution, and that will lead to dirtier water that people will drink.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages a named provision of the bill and the specific clause of the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management it disapplies; the party framing is a wrapper on genuine policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill enables councils to do what they can already do, in terms of having council-controlled organisations.
focus.explanation: A direct claim about what the measure before the House actually does, comparing it to existing council powers. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They came up with four names: the first one was called Entity A; the second one was called Entity B. It was ludicrous.
focus.explanation: Mockery of the previous Government's naming convention. No mechanism, cost, effect or outcome is named — strip out the jibe at the other side and no policy content remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No localism, no control, no certainty; central government knows best and we’re in here to clean up the mess.
focus.explanation: Gestures at a real policy theme (centralisation under the previous reforms) but names no measure, figure or outcome; the weight of the line is 'we are cleaning up their mess' party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The former speaker, the Hon Rachel Brooking, was entertaining, albeit a little bit incorrect, because whilst council-controlled organisations (CCOs) do exist and can and, in fact, are encouraged under this bill, what this does is this is only bill two out of three, so I can tell you the trilogy is not yet complete; wait for bill three.
civility.explanation: Calling the previous speaker 'entertaining, albeit a little bit incorrect' is faintly patronising and edges toward the person, but he immediately engages her substantive claim about CCOs rather than her character.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This is a response to gang membership increasing by 51 percent over the past five years, alongside violent crimes increasing by 33 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two statistical facts about the five years to 2024: that gang membership rose 51% and that violent crime rose 33%.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police National Gang List membership figures for the five years to mid-2024 (true if the increase is ~51%, false if materially different) and NZ Police recorded violent offence/victimisation statistics over the same period (true if ~33% increase, false if materially different).

veracity.statement: There were 11 gangs that were removed from the list as they were now considered defunct, and there were also some gangs that were added to the list.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Justice Committee's recommended changes to the schedule of identified gangs removed exactly 11 gangs as defunct and added others.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's report on the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill (July 2024) and the schedule as reported back; true if 11 gangs were recommended for removal as defunct, false if the number differs.

civility.statement: Over the past week or so, we’ve heard many harrowing stories from the royal commission into abuse in care, including on people who went on to join gangs. No abuse in care is ever acceptable. At the same time, no society can function safely if people are not held to account and held responsible for things they do today.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested point — whether abuse-in-care histories mitigate gang offending — handled without disparaging survivors, gang members' character, or any opponent. Engages the substance only.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Insignia such as gang patches cause fear and intimidation to some members of the public. They’re also status symbols the gangs use to market themselves to potential prospects and future recruits. They also have the potential to exacerbate inter-gang rivalries, leading to violence. This ban on gang insignia in public will reduce the negative effects on communities.
rigor.explanation: Premises (intimidation, recruitment signalling, rivalry escalation) are offered and the conclusion tracks them in direction, but the step from 'patches have these effects' to 'banning them in public will reduce the harms' is asserted rather than argued — no mechanism is given for why displacement or substitution would not occur, so there is a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Insignia such as gang patches cause fear and intimidation to some members of the public. They’re also status symbols the gangs use to market themselves to potential prospects and future recruits. They also have the potential to exacerbate inter-gang rivalries, leading to violence. This ban on gang insignia in public will reduce the negative effects on communities.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific measure (a public ban on gang insignia) and identifies three concrete harm channels, but supplies no figures, no evidence base and no measure of the expected reduction.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill creates a new dispersal power to stop gang members from gathering in public and, once issued, it will prevent them from associating in public for seven days.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (dispersal notice), who it binds, what it prohibits and the exact duration (seven days) — fully checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I am putting gangs on notice and letting them know that this Government is indeed committed to law and order.
specificity.explanation: A slogan restating a general commitment to 'law and order'; no figure, mechanism, date or named action, and nothing here that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It will stop the violence and prevent the antisocial behaviour of gangs becoming normalised in New Zealand.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the enacted gangs legislation will halt gang violence and prevent gang antisocial behaviour becoming normalised — an outcome in the world, not merely a promise to legislate.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NZ Police recorded violent offence and gang-related offending statistics for the 12 months after the Act's commencement on 21 November 2024, compared with the preceding 12 months; true if gang-related violent offending falls substantially, false if it is flat or rises.

focus.statement: Banning gang patches typifies the approach that this Government takes to law and order: it is cosmetic and ornamental.
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure (the gang patch ban) and characterises it as cosmetic, but much of the weight is a general characterisation of the Government's approach rather than the mechanism itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But what I would like to know is what this bill does to stop young people growing up in homes where they see and experience family violence on a daily basis.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the bill before the House and what outcome it is expected to produce; no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It merely ticks a box that serves a purpose in a focus group to give a couple of extra points to the National Party or to ACT or to New Zealand First to show that they’re delivering and getting tough and they’re going to show who’s who and what’s going to happen, but, in reality, there are no real answers, and that is the sad part.
focus.explanation: Shifts from the measure to the electoral motives of the three governing parties; no policy mechanism, figure or outcome is named, only an imputation about polling gains.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Dispersal notices will be provided to gang members by asking them to provide their email address, and if they don’t have one, they are then required to accompany an officer to the station to get a printed copy.
specificity.explanation: Describes a concrete statutory mechanism — mode of service, the email step, and the fallback of accompanying an officer — which someone could check against the bill's text.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Dispersal notices will be provided to gang members by asking them to provide their email address, and if they don’t have one, they are then required to accompany an officer to the station to get a printed copy.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill's dispersal-notice service provisions work by obtaining an email address, with attendance at a police station as the fallback where the person has no email.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The service-of-notice clauses of the Gangs Bill as reported back from the Justice Committee (July 2024); true if the bill provides for notices to be given by email and requires the recipient to accompany an officer to a station for a printed copy where no email address is available, false if the bill provides other ordinary means of written service without such a requirement.

veracity.statement: There is no other law in New Zealand, or even overseas, that we can find where someone who doesn’t even get a written notice delivered to them is up for a five-year imprisonment penalty.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no comparable statute, domestic or foreign, attaches a five-year maximum imprisonment penalty to breach of a notice that was not delivered in writing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Statutory search of NZ legislation and comparable jurisdictions (Australia, UK, Canada) for offences carrying a maximum of five years' imprisonment for breaching an order or notice that may be imposed without written service; false if any such provision is identified, true if none is.

veracity.statement: We know that for sure because Vote Police received a $107 million less in this Budget compared to the last Budget.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that total appropriations for Vote Police in Budget 2024 were $107 million lower than in Budget 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Estimates of Appropriations for Vote Police, Budget 2024 versus Budget 2023 (Treasury); true if the year-on-year difference in total Vote Police appropriation is a reduction of approximately $107 million, false if the appropriation rose or the reduction is materially different.

veracity.statement: The Police Association themselves have said that the risk of this bill is it threatens to undermine the credibility of police when there are some parts of New Zealand where it just won’t be able to be enforced, and that is of real concern.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim that the Police Association warned the bill risks undermining police credibility because it will be unenforceable in some parts of the country.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZ Police Association's written or oral submission to the Justice Committee on the Gangs Bill (2024); true if it raises unenforceability in some areas and consequent damage to police credibility, false if no such concern appears.

veracity.statement: There were 3,000 fewer family violence investigations since December this year. In addition to that, there was a 29 percent reduction where the victim has known the offender.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fall of about 3,000 in police family violence investigations over the period since December, and a 29 percent reduction in investigations where the victim knew the offender.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police family harm investigation statistics for the months from December 2023 to mid-2024 compared with the equivalent prior period; true if investigations fell by approximately 3,000 and known-offender cases fell by about 29 percent, false if the counts are materially different or rose.

rigor.statement: The police have got $107 million less in the Budget and they’ve been required to be more visible. Well, something’s got to give, and it has—it’s called family violence.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc causal inference: a budget figure and a ministerial directive are offered, and a fall in family violence investigations is attributed to them without evidence linking the two; alternative causes (recorded-crime trends, changed reporting or triage practice) are not addressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: There are parts of New Zealand where there are insufficient police and insufficient resources to be able to enforce this law, so it might work in urban areas, but it definitely won’t work in parts of rural New Zealand.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the gang patch ban and dispersal notice regime will prove unenforceable in rural parts of New Zealand once in force, while functioning in urban areas.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Police enforcement data and reporting on gang insignia offences and dispersal notices after the Act's commencement; true if rural districts record negligible enforcement alongside substantive urban enforcement, or police/Police Association publicly report inability to enforce in rural areas; false if enforcement activity occurs across rural districts at broadly comparable rates.

civility.statement: This is a cosmetic solution that looks good on the telly, that gives you a sound bite, and that might even get a TikTok video if you’re Paul Goldsmith, but it does absolutely nothing to make our communities any safer, and I think that the police will struggle to be able to actually enforce this law in some parts.
civility.explanation: Mostly criticism of the policy, but the aside naming Paul Goldsmith mocks him personally as chasing social media publicity — sneering at the individual rather than his argument.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The second reason is because the surveillance-and-suppression approach is ideologically driven and isn’t informed by evidence; instead, it is driven by political expediency, and it has been completely designed to win votes, as opposed to making our community safer.
focus.explanation: A real policy point — the evidential basis of the suppression approach — but the weight of the sentence is an attribution of electoral motive to the Government rather than engagement with the mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Nothing was done under the previous Government, so we are bringing in a different approach where we are actually tackling head-on the issue of gangs and a number of other criminal justice issues.
focus.explanation: The substance is a blanket characterisation of the previous Government's record with no named measure or outcome; the only policy content is the generic claim to be 'tackling head-on' gangs and unspecified criminal justice issues.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: These tools—the non-consorting orders, the dispersal notices, and adding being a gang member to the aggravating factors within sentencing—will disproportionately impact Māori, as we have seen in other jurisdictions around the world where indigenous people bear the brunt of tools like this.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the three named tools in the bill, once in force, will fall disproportionately on Māori.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NZ Police / Ministry of Justice data on the ethnicity of people issued dispersal notices, non-consorting orders, or sentenced with gang membership as an aggravating factor after the Act commenced; true if the Māori share materially exceeds the Māori share of the general population, false if it is at or below population share.

specificity.statement: These tools—the non-consorting orders, the dispersal notices, and adding being a gang member to the aggravating factors within sentencing—will disproportionately impact Māori, as we have seen in other jurisdictions around the world where indigenous people bear the brunt of tools like this.
specificity.explanation: Names the three specific mechanisms in the bill and the affected population, but carries no figures or estimated magnitude.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I spoke to Senator David Shoebridge over in New South Wales, who sent me this report, which is about the use of non-consorting orders in Sydney, and despite the fact that indigenous people only make up 2 percent of the general population there, the non-consorting orders have been used between 50 and 75 percent in all of their jurisdictions within New South Wales.
specificity.explanation: Named source, named jurisdiction, named instrument and two quantified proportions — someone could go to the report and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Over the past five years, gangs have recruited more than 3,000 members—that’s a 51 percent increase—and we’ve seen a significant escalation in gang violence, crime, public intimidation, and shootings.
specificity.explanation: Gives a count, a percentage and a time window — directly checkable against the police gang list.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ll be putting a cap on the discounts around sentences, we’ll also be doing some things to ensure that the victims of crime are prioritised, and—importantly—we are actually delivering 500 more front-line police by the end of 2025.
specificity.explanation: One precise commitment with a number and a date (500 front-line police by end of 2025) sitting alongside undefined items — an uncapped 'cap' on sentence discounts and 'some things' for victims.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Last week, we had the release of the report of the royal commission of inquiry into abuse in State care, detailing the abuse of 200,000 children by the State and faith-based institutions between 1950 and 1999, and this was the person who was on the cover when that dropped last week.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care's final report documents the abuse of 200,000 children in State and faith-based care between 1950 and 1999.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission's final report 'Whanaketia' (July 2024): true if it estimates approximately 200,000 people abused in care over the 1950–1999 inquiry period, false if its estimate differs materially or covers a different period.

veracity.statement: I want to make it really clear that not every person that was abused in State care became a gang member, but we know that almost every gang member has been traumatised, abused, raped, or tormented within State care, which sows the seeds for a lifetime of shame, violence, addiction, and fear.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that almost every gang member in New Zealand suffered trauma or abuse while in State care.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published research linking the National Gang List to care histories (e.g. Ministry of Social Development / Oranga Tamariki or Department of Corrections analyses of gang members' State care involvement); true if the large majority of gang members are recorded as having been abused or traumatised in State care, false if the recorded proportion is well short of 'almost every'.

veracity.statement: This bill is actually quite useless, because all of the powers that are in the bill already exist.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that every power created by the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill already exists in New Zealand law.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Gangs Act 2024 / Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill as reported back, compared with the Summary Offences Act 1981, the Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Act 2013 and the Sentencing Act 2002; false if the bill creates powers with no existing statutory equivalent (e.g. dispersal notices or non-consorting orders), true if every power is already available.

veracity.statement: I spoke to Senator David Shoebridge over in New South Wales, who sent me this report, which is about the use of non-consorting orders in Sydney, and despite the fact that indigenous people only make up 2 percent of the general population there, the non-consorting orders have been used between 50 and 75 percent in all of their jurisdictions within New South Wales.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Aboriginal people are about 2 percent of the NSW population yet account for between 50 and 75 percent of consorting-law uses across NSW jurisdictions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NSW Ombudsman's statutory review of the consorting provisions (and NSW Police consorting data) plus ABS population figures; true if Aboriginal people are recorded at 50–75 percent of consorting warnings across NSW areas at roughly 2–3 percent of population, false if the recorded Aboriginal share is materially lower or the figure applies only to selected localities.

veracity.statement: There was some refusal from Ministers, like Minister Mitchell, who refused to meet with gang members, but I think he’s coming around to the idea that if you want to influence communities that are already hard to reach, you need to go and talk to the leaders of those communities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Police Minister Mark Mitchell declined to meet with gang members.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Mitchell's public statements and contemporaneous media reporting up to July 2024; true if he is on record declining to meet gang members or gang leaders, false if no such refusal is recorded or he is recorded as having met them.

veracity.statement: Over the past five years, gangs have recruited more than 3,000 members—that’s a 51 percent increase—and we’ve seen a significant escalation in gang violence, crime, public intimidation, and shootings.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the National Gang List grew by more than 3,000 members, a 51 percent increase, over the five years to 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police National Gang List figures for 2019 and 2024; true if the roll grew by more than 3,000 and by about 51 percent over that period, false if the growth figure or percentage differs materially.

veracity.statement: Nothing was done under the previous Government, so we are bringing in a different approach where we are actually tackling head-on the issue of gangs and a number of other criminal justice issues.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2017–2023 Government took no action on gangs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Legislation and operational measures enacted 2017–2023 touching gangs (e.g. the Firearms Prohibition Orders Legislation Act 2022, Operation Cobalt, gang-focused Police funding); false if any such measure was enacted or funded, true if none can be identified.

veracity.statement: Actually, all of the amendments that the Minister spoke to and accepted were passed unanimously by members of the Justice Committee.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Justice Committee's recommended amendments to the bill were agreed unanimously by committee members from all parties.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's report on the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill, including any differing or minority views; true if the recommended amendments are recorded as unanimous, false if the report records dissent on any of them.

rigor.statement: There are no patches worn in prison, so eliminating their visual presence in some communities is not going to reduce their membership, at all.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the bill's mechanism, but it over-generalises from one setting to another: that recruitment happens in prisons without patches does not establish that patch visibility has no recruitment effect in the community, and the absolute 'at all' outruns the evidence offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This bill is actually quite useless, because all of the powers that are in the bill already exist.
rigor.explanation: Valid given its premise — if a bill confers only powers that already exist it adds nothing — so the reasoning tracks, independent of whether the premise holds.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They couldn’t afford counselling or therapy and they couldn’t trust the institutions set up to support them; they could only turn to each other, and that—right there—is where gangs come from.
rigor.explanation: A plausible causal narrative pushed to a single-cause conclusion: the premises about isolation and distrust support a contributing factor, not the claim that this is where gangs come from, and the support offered is individual testimony rather than evidence about gang formation generally.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We all know that, and to hear Opposition members continuously get up in this House and through the select committee to support gangs and their way of life—which, as we know, is around organised crime—is, to me, extremely disappointing.
focus.explanation: Characterises Opposition members as supporters of gangs and organised crime. No mechanism, clause, figure or outcome of the bill is engaged — the content is entirely about what the other side is like.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill is trying to achieve some fresh signals from this Government towards raising the issue of prohibiting gang insignia in public places, enabling police to issue dispersal notices, and empowering the courts to issue consorting prohibition notices, which all signal to gangs that the game is up.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: what the bill does, clause by clause in substance.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Gang members that ruin so many people’s lives are now facing consequences for their behaviour—and the Opposition members continuously shout out in this House in support of gangs, probably because they were the only ones that voted for them at election time.
focus.explanation: The second half is a claim about who voted for the Opposition, with no policy, mechanism or outcome attached. It is about the other side's supporters rather than about the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, apparently, nothing, because it’s clearly understood that when this law was last in place, it did nothing to reduce offending.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure itself by pointing to the evidence on how a comparable prohibition performed previously — scrutiny of the policy, not of the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Since 2017—and this is the biggest part of this—there have been 5,343 registered gang members. By 2024, going by what the Minister of Police said in his press release recently this year, there were 8,607 registered gang members.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific National Gang List counts: 5,343 registered gang members in 2017 and 8,607 in 2024, the latter sourced to a Police Minister press release.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police National Gang List membership figures for 2017 and 2024, and the 2024 Minister of Police press release cited; true if the list stood at approximately 5,343 in 2017 and approximately 8,607 in 2024, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: That was a 61 percent increase in gang members under the Government of members on that side of the House, who were soft on gangs, and their way of fixing it was to give millions of dollars to gangs and to hand out money.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that gang membership rose 61 percent under the 2017–2023 Labour-led government, and that that government gave millions of dollars to gangs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: (a) Arithmetic on the National Gang List figures — 5,343 to 8,607 is a rise of about 61 percent; true if the underlying counts support that percentage. (b) Proceeds of Crime Fund / Crown funding records for 2017–2023; true if millions of dollars were allocated to gang-affiliated organisations or programmes, false if no such allocations exist.

veracity.statement: That has been updated and it can continue to be updated, and clause 30 of the bill gives the Governor-General, by Order in Council, the ability to update that list as it is required to be.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that clause 30 of the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill confers power on the Governor-General, by Order in Council, to update the list of identified gangs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of clause 30 of the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill as reported back by the Justice Committee; true if it empowers the Governor-General by Order in Council to amend the schedule of identified gangs, false if that power sits in a different clause or with a different decision-maker.

veracity.statement: New Zealand First had committed to this in our manifesto, and now we are delivering what was set out in our coalition agreement into legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the anti-gang measures in the bill appeared in the New Zealand First 2023 manifesto and in the National–New Zealand First coalition agreement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand First 2023 election manifesto and the published National–New Zealand First coalition agreement (Nov 2023); true if both contain commitments matching this bill's measures (gang insignia ban, gang membership as an aggravating factor at sentencing), false if either is silent on them.

veracity.statement: Over a 30-year period, he led three investigations into New Zealand’s justice system and increasingly found structural racism, systemic racism, and racist attitudes that permeated the entire justice system and that consistently produced more negative outcomes for Māori than any other group in Aotearoa.
veracity.explanation: Relays the record of Moana Jackson's work: that he led three inquiries into the justice system across roughly thirty years and that each found systemic and structural racism producing worse outcomes for Māori.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published reports Moana Jackson led or co-led (He Whaipaanga Hou, 1987–88; and subsequent justice-system inquiries up to Ināia Tonu Nei, 2019); true if three such inquiries spanning about 30 years exist and each records findings of systemic/structural racism, false if the count or the findings differ materially.

veracity.statement: Well, apparently, nothing, because it’s clearly understood that when this law was last in place, it did nothing to reduce offending.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous gang-insignia prohibition produced no reduction in offending.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published evaluations of the Wanganui District Council (Prohibition of Gang Insignia) Act 2009 and the Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Act 2013 — e.g. Ministry of Justice or police reviews; true if evaluations found no measurable reduction in offending, false if a reduction attributable to the prohibition is documented.

veracity.statement: It’s clearly understood that the bill is in breach of human rights and that it breaches Te Tiriti o Waitangi, yet it continues.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two findings about the bill: that it breaches human rights, and that it breaches Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Attorney-General's section 7 report on the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill under the NZ Bill of Rights Act, and any Waitangi Tribunal report or Crown Treaty-impact advice on the bill; true if the Attorney-General reported an unjustified inconsistency with the Bill of Rights and a Tribunal/Crown assessment found a Treaty breach, false if neither exists.

veracity.statement: We pretty much received submissions from all of the national legal bodies—the Law Society, law associations, Te Hunga Rōia Māori o Aotearoa, and many others—and they unequivocally, in unison, said that the bill was rubbish, that the bill should not have made it this far, that the bill should be thrown out, and that the Government should start again from a more restorative starting point.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the national legal bodies which submitted on the bill were unanimous in opposing it and in recommending it be discarded and restarted.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's published submissions on the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill from the NZ Law Society, district law associations and Te Hunga Rōia Māori o Aotearoa; true if each opposed the bill and recommended it not proceed, false if any supported it or recommended only amendment.

specificity.statement: Since 2017—and this is the biggest part of this—there have been 5,343 registered gang members. By 2024, going by what the Minister of Police said in his press release recently this year, there were 8,607 registered gang members.
specificity.explanation: Two exact figures, both dated, with a named source for the later one. Directly checkable against the gang list.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill is trying to achieve some fresh signals from this Government towards raising the issue of prohibiting gang insignia in public places, enabling police to issue dispersal notices, and empowering the courts to issue consorting prohibition notices, which all signal to gangs that the game is up.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete mechanisms in the bill — the insignia prohibition, dispersal notices and consorting prohibition notices — though without thresholds, penalties or timeframes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That has been updated and it can continue to be updated, and clause 30 of the bill gives the Governor-General, by Order in Council, the ability to update that list as it is required to be.
specificity.explanation: Cites a numbered clause and the exact legal instrument and decision-maker involved.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We pretty much received submissions from all of the national legal bodies—the Law Society, law associations, Te Hunga Rōia Māori o Aotearoa, and many others—and they unequivocally, in unison, said that the bill was rubbish, that the bill should not have made it this far, that the bill should be thrown out, and that the Government should start again from a more restorative starting point.
specificity.explanation: Names the submitting organisations and summarises their recommendation, but carries no submission counts, quotations or dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The bill seeks to reduce the behaviour engaged in by gangs and to disincentivise gang membership, because as it seeks to deal with the elements that make gang membership exciting, probably, and alluring to many, they will be dampened down.

rigor.statement: Again, it’s relatively frustrating and really annoying that at this time of night, having heard no really substantive contributions from the Government—I mean, we’ve heard contributions that talk around the edges, that talked about the technicalities, and that talked about fairly innocuous or fairly mundane aspects of the process, but we haven’t heard anybody really come out and sell this bill tonight. specificity.statement: In addition to the new offence of wearing gang patches and displaying insignia, with also the gathering together, there will be the opportunity for the police to ask the courts to issue non-consorting orders to prevent the long-term association of people who are clearly of a menacing and dangerous association.

veracity.statement: In 2022 we’re seeing that only 32.9 percent of all Māori school leavers have attained NCEA level 3, which is a decrease of 44 percent from 2021.

specificity.statement: In 2022 we’re seeing that only 32.9 percent of all Māori school leavers have attained NCEA level 3, which is a decrease of 44 percent from 2021.

specificity.statement: They have a proud heritage, but it is nevertheless a small omnibus, and I just think it’s curious that sometimes we have bills on issues of this scale when there are much, much larger things which don’t require legislation at all.

rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So, you know, when we’re talking about whether it’s gang patches, when we’re talking about Māori wards, you know, I would like to see those students as part of this bill—when it talks about recognising the emblem that is associated with the 28th Māori Battalion, I would like to see those students who are able to wear those emblems to be able to wear them proudly down the street without having to be concerned about the fact they might be mistaken for gang patches.

veracity.statement: It was with dismay that when this bill was first introduced, those opposite who now have swapped benches with us were opposed to it.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard first reading record and division for the Regulatory Systems (Education) Amendment Bill; true if National/ACT/NZ First voted against at first reading, false if they supported it.

veracity.statement: I could talk about the fact that the school builds have all stalled, except perhaps I won’t be the same as those colleagues on the other side and not support what is, I think, universally seen around the House as a good piece of legislation that takes forward a few small but very significant changes.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education school property programme records and 2024 announcements on paused/cancelled school builds; true if effectively all school build projects were halted, false if projects were continuing and only a subset were paused or reviewed.

veracity.statement: I think one particular point I would like to make in relation to this bill is the interesting context that we have with this bill coming through the House today: tomorrow we are seeing a tax relief after 14 long years, and in this bill we’re seeing the inflation adjustment of the expenditure amounts from 1972 to today of $500 to $10,000—important context if you think about the timing when we are shepherding that tax relief through the House tomorrow.

veracity.falsification_criterion: For the tax claim, the record of personal income tax threshold changes since 2010 (Taxation (Annual Rates...) legislation); true if the last threshold adjustment was 14 years earlier, false if thresholds were adjusted more recently. For the bill figure, the text of the Regulatory Systems (Education) Amendment Bill amending the Pacific Education Foundation Act 1972; true if the amount moves from $500 to $10,000.

specificity.statement: Ngarimu scholarships in 2024 included one doctoral, four masters, four undergraduate, and two vocational education and training awards.
specificity.explanation: Exact counts broken down by award category for a named year and named scholarship — directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I mean, there are things that I could talk about in education which I would like this Government to address—for example, the terrible charter school legislation that it’s brought in, while, at the same time, creating a whole, entire other bureaucracy of new charter schools.
specificity.explanation: Names a policy and one alleged effect (a new bureaucracy) but supplies no figures, cost, mechanism or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I think one particular point I would like to make in relation to this bill is the interesting context that we have with this bill coming through the House today: tomorrow we are seeing a tax relief after 14 long years, and in this bill we’re seeing the inflation adjustment of the expenditure amounts from 1972 to today of $500 to $10,000—important context if you think about the timing when we are shepherding that tax relief through the House tomorrow.
specificity.explanation: Gives the named statutory amounts ($500 to $10,000), the originating year (1972) and a dated legislative event — all checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, as a Māori, she was confused as to why she was asked to speak to these students. Well, there were no Pacific students to ask to speak to them, in structural engineering at Auckland Uni. So this bill really is so wonderful because it gives us the opportunity to encourage Pacific students to take up tertiary education.
rigor.explanation: Argument from a single family anecdote: one course at one university having no Pacific students is offered as the ground for concluding the bill is the remedy. Appeal to anecdote, with no link shown between the bill's mechanism and the enrolment gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I don’t think we need a hierarchy of things that are important, but maybe this is a prescient lesson for those who sit around this House to not undermine the importance of some of these smaller pieces of legislation just because they happened to be introduced by a party of which you are not a part.
civility.explanation: Imputes a partisan bad-faith motive to members opposite and delivers it as a lesson to them — condescending, though it stops short of naming or insulting any individual.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I mean, there are things that I could talk about in education which I would like this Government to address—for example, the terrible charter school legislation that it’s brought in, while, at the same time, creating a whole, entire other bureaucracy of new charter schools.
civility.explanation: Harsh about a named policy (the charter school legislation) and about no person; criticism stays entirely on the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why has Health New Zealand frozen relocation costs for overseas doctors, driving many to abandon job applications, when we’ve got understaffed hospitals, like Dargaville, that can’t find a doctor at all?
focus.explanation: Names a specific decision (Health NZ freezing relocation costs for overseas doctors), a consequence (abandoned applications) and a named hospital. This is scrutiny of a specific policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As I have said to that member, we have worked and will continue to work on making sure we get workforce into the New Zealand healthcare system. We are growing our home-grown doctors. We have got open immigration settings to bring doctors from overseas here. We have made good progress. There are 2,900 extra nurses in the system than there were 12 months ago. We know it’s challenging getting workforce into rural settings, but we’ll continue to work hard at it.
focus.explanation: Stays on the health workforce topic throughout — training, immigration settings, nurse numbers, rural recruitment — with no detour into the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How many doctors’ salaries could the Government fund for the over $200 million in tax breaks they have just given to tobacco companies?
focus.explanation: Names a specific fiscal measure and a specific sum and contrasts it with a named spending alternative; party framing is present in 'tax breaks for tobacco companies' but a real policy decision is at issue.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Again, I would just say that it is very rich from that member who actually created a situation and is now criticising us for trying to solve the problem.
focus.explanation: Answers a question about tobacco excise and doctors' salaries entirely by characterising the questioner's record; no policy, figure or mechanism is named in this sentence.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Thank you. Look, the Government’s amending the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act to clarify the test for customary marine title. We are very proud of the legislation that—a National-led Government passed in 2011—actually legitimately recognises Māori customary title and also balances the legitimate use of coastal areas for all New Zealanders. Unfortunately, under the court action, that threshold has been lowered. All we are doing is restoring it back to what was intended by this Parliament in 2011.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure directly: the named Act, the specific element being amended (the customary marine title test), and the stated purpose of the amendment.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why, then, is he amending the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act to make it possible for the courts to recognise Māori rights over their foreshore and seabed as guaranteed under Te Tiriti o Waitangi?

focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: By over-ruling the Court of Appeal judgment that “Far from recognising and promoting customary interests, [the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act] would in many cases extinguish those interests.”, is this Government seeking to extinguish Māori rights and interests over our foreshore and seabed?
focus.explanation: Cites a specific judicial finding about the named Act and asks about the effect of the specific amendment — substantive scrutiny of a measure, not party attack.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.explanation: There is a genuine interpretive question about article 2 underneath, but the question is framed almost entirely as a contrast between a revered figure and 'the Te Pāti Māori radicals' — party labelling carries most of the weight.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, I think there has been a lot of misunderstandings. Let me be clear, we are not touching the Treaty. The Government has no plans, has never had any plans, to rewrite the Treaty of Waitangi. We’re going to continue to honour the Treaty and honour all Treaty settlements.

focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Unfortunately, under the court action, that threshold has been lowered.

veracity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: By over-ruling the Court of Appeal judgment that “Far from recognising and promoting customary interests, [the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act] would in many cases extinguish those interests.”, is this Government seeking to extinguish Māori rights and interests over our foreshore and seabed?

veracity.statement: What is his response to the more than 150 signatories of the open letter by ActionStation Aotearoa to “stop the Treaty Principles Bill and ensure it is withdrawn prior to the select committee process”?

specificity.statement: Thank you. Look, the Government’s amending the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act to clarify the test for customary marine title. We are very proud of the legislation that—a National-led Government passed in 2011—actually legitimately recognises Māori customary title and also balances the legitimate use of coastal areas for all New Zealanders. Unfortunately, under the court action, that threshold has been lowered. All we are doing is restoring it back to what was intended by this Parliament in 2011.

civility.statement: Again, I would just say that it is very rich from that member who actually created a situation and is now criticising us for trying to solve the problem.

rigor.statement: I’m asking the Prime Minister, does he agree with that brilliant legal and Māori scholar Sir Apirana Ngata’s version of article 2 of the Treaty of Waitangi or the Te Pāti Māori radicals’ version of article 2 of the Treaty of Waitangi?

civility.statement: I seek leave to table a series of documents, being correspondence between yourself and the ACT Party whip, dated from 25 July—last Thursday—to today, in which you appear to give a green light to racial harassment in this Parliament.

civility.statement: Now, with the greatest respect, I think he should get a better fix on Standing Orders before he so prematurely gets to his feet.

civility.statement: If you are seriously saying that you’re not going to let people ask and answer questions in this House because they’re wearing a pin—as they’ve been allowed to for year after year—I think more and more people are going to ask what your priorities actually are.
civility.explanation: Casts doubt on the Speaker's priorities personally and invokes public opinion against him, rather than confining the challenge to the ruling itself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’d just say, if he keeps saying sensible things like that, he could join the National Party and finally let Kieran McAnulty have his time in the sun!
civility.explanation: Mockery aimed at the Leader of the Opposition personally — the joke is that he should be replaced as leader. Light in tone, but it is about the man, not the tax question.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I’d just say, it is ironic—it is ironic—after six years, that member has the audacity to ask about a question about the healthcare system that he presided over and ran into the ground.
civility.explanation: 'Has the audacity' is a sneer at the questioner personally, framing the asking of a legitimate question as effrontery rather than engaging what was asked.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: And it’s a senior Government Minister, who will shortly be deputy Prime Minister, who’s doing it; it’s utterly unacceptable.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that David Seymour will take up the office of Deputy Prime Minister in the near future.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The official record of ministerial appointments (DPMC / Governor-General's warrant list): true if David Seymour is sworn in as Deputy Prime Minister of New Zealand; false if the handover does not occur and someone else holds the office through the parliamentary term.

veracity.statement: Mr Mallard clearly ruled that pins were exempt from that ruling in 2018.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Speaker Trevor Mallard issued a ruling in 2018 that lapel pins were exempt from the restriction on displays or badges in the debating chamber.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Speakers' rulings and Hansard for 2018: true if a ruling by Speaker Mallard exempting pins/badges from the dress-and-display rules is on the record for that year; false if no such ruling exists or if the ruling in fact restricted pins.

veracity.statement: The report goes on to say, “Overall, 83 percent of Kiwis—94 percent of households—will benefit from the tax package”, which comes into effect today.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 83 percent of New Zealanders and 94 percent of households will benefit from the coalition Government's tax package taking effect on 31 July 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury / Budget 2024 distributional analysis of the personal income tax threshold changes and FamilyBoost: true if the published modelling gives approximately 83% of individuals and 94% of households receiving a positive net benefit; false if the official figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: I received an update this morning from the Treasury, which shows the tax calculator has hit a new high of 591,414 visits, as Kiwis find out how much they will be getting in long-overdue tax relief.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific Treasury-reported visit count for the online tax calculator as at the morning of 31 July 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's reported analytics for the Budget 2024 tax calculator: true if the cumulative visit count as at 31 July 2024 was approximately 591,414; false if the published/OIA-released figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: That supportive comment was made this morning on Breakfast TV by none other than the Leader of the Opposition, Chris Hipkins.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Chris Hipkins said on Breakfast on the morning of 31 July 2024 that bracket adjustment is a legitimate and sensible thing to do.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The TVNZ Breakfast broadcast/transcript of 31 July 2024: true if Hipkins made a comment to that effect on that programme that morning; false if he did not appear or did not say it.

veracity.statement: So I want to be really clear: there are way too many layers of management, there are 2,500 management back-office function people that are there, and there’s a big division between the front line and the decision makers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Health New Zealand carries 2,500 management and back-office staff of the kind he characterises as surplus layers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand / Te Whatu Ora workforce data and the Health Select Committee or OIA breakdowns of administrative and managerial FTE: true if roughly 2,500 management/back-office positions are identified on the agency's own classification; false if the agency's figures for that category differ materially.

veracity.statement: It’s because the previous Government did not actually merge into one entity the 21 district health boards, and just whacked 2,500 people over the top of it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government's health reforms did not actually amalgamate the 21 district health boards into a single organisation, but added a layer of 2,500 staff above them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 and Health NZ establishment documents: true if the 21 DHBs continued as separate legal entities after 1 July 2022; false if the Act disestablished them and transferred their functions into a single entity, Health New Zealand.

veracity.statement: You would remember that there was an annual report before this Government came to power, in October, saying that there was a potential deficit in health.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an annual report published in October 2023, before the change of government, flagged a potential deficit in the health system.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Whatu Ora / Health New Zealand annual report for 2022/23 as tabled in late 2023: true if it records or forecasts a deficit position; false if it reports no such deficit or was not published before the new Government took office.

veracity.statement: Why did his Government remove the financial sustainability priority in the Government’s health policy statement?
veracity.explanation: Asserts, by presupposition, that the current Government's Government Policy Statement on Health removed a financial sustainability priority that had previously been included.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the Government Policy Statement on Health 2024–27 with its predecessor: true if a financial sustainability priority present in the earlier statement is absent from the 2024 one; false if the priority is retained in the current statement.

veracity.statement: Well, in light of his last answer, why did he say that he first became aware of financial problems at Health New Zealand in October 2023, when his health Minister said that he first became aware five months later, in March 2024, a claim that he has now just repeated?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a documented inconsistency: that Luxon publicly dated his awareness of Health NZ's financial problems to October 2023 while Shane Reti dated his own awareness to March 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, interviews and Hansard from July 2024: true if Luxon is on record citing October 2023 and Reti on record citing March 2024 for first awareness of the financial problems; false if either attribution is not supported by the record.

veracity.statement: Why has the Government frozen relocation costs for overseas doctors, driving many to abandon their job applications, when we’ve got understaffed hospitals, like Dargaville, who can’t find doctors at all?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government has stopped paying relocation costs for internationally recruited doctors and that this has caused applicants to withdraw, while hospitals such as Dargaville remain unable to recruit.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand recruitment policy documents and OIA releases from mid-2024 on international relocation support: true if relocation payments were suspended or withdrawn in that period and recruitment records show withdrawn applications; false if relocation support continued unchanged.

specificity.statement: The report goes on to say, “Overall, 83 percent of Kiwis—94 percent of households—will benefit from the tax package”, which comes into effect today.
specificity.explanation: Two precise percentages, a named package and a commencement date — directly checkable against the published modelling.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I received an update this morning from the Treasury, which shows the tax calculator has hit a new high of 591,414 visits, as Kiwis find out how much they will be getting in long-overdue tax relief.
specificity.explanation: A named source, an exact figure and a time reference. Someone could request the underlying number and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I want to be really clear: there are way too many layers of management, there are 2,500 management back-office function people that are there, and there’s a big division between the front line and the decision makers.
specificity.explanation: Carries one concrete, checkable headcount figure, but the surrounding claims ('way too many layers', 'a big division') supply no measure of what the right number would be or what will change.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, in light of his last answer, why did he say that he first became aware of financial problems at Health New Zealand in October 2023, when his health Minister said that he first became aware five months later, in March 2024, a claim that he has now just repeated?
specificity.explanation: Names both officeholders, two precise dates and the gap between them. The question can be checked against the public record without further clarification.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It goes on to quote a man as saying, “I see it was targeted at the right people.” These people are right. Responsibly funded tax relief is needed, and it is targeted at low and middle income workers.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the package is well targeted rests on three vox-pop remarks from members of the public quoted in a radio item — an appeal to anecdote. Nothing about the distribution of the relief itself is offered to support the inference.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If you look at the letter that the Minister of Finance released, as of, I think, 20 March or somewhere around that window of time, they were forecasting a slightly smaller surplus, but then they projected a deficit going forward, in one month.
rigor.explanation: A real inference with documentary support: a forecast that flipped from surplus to deficit inside a month is offered as evidence of unreliable reporting, and the conclusion tracks the evidence. It is weakened by resting on a single swing, which could equally reflect a genuine change in conditions rather than reporting quality.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It goes on to quote a man as saying, “I see it was targeted at the right people.” These people are right. Responsibly funded tax relief is needed, and it is targeted at low and middle income workers.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the tax package and its incidence, not about the other party. The argument is weak, but the subject matter is the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’d just say, if he keeps saying sensible things like that, he could join the National Party and finally let Kieran McAnulty have his time in the sun!
focus.explanation: Pure party-and-personality banter inserted into an answer about tax relief. No policy content in this passage: no mechanism, figure, cost or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, I’d just say, it is ironic—it is ironic—after six years, that member has the audacity to ask about a question about the healthcare system that he presided over and ran into the ground.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the previous Government's record in general terms — 'ran into the ground' — with no named policy, figure or outcome. This is party framing standing in for an answer.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s because the previous administration had a botched restructure, didn’t know how to run anything—we saw it with Te Pūkenga, we’ve seen it now with Health New Zealand, we’ve seen it with disability services.
focus.explanation: Three specific agencies are named, which is genuine content, but the weight of the sentence is a sweeping characterisation of the other party — 'didn't know how to run anything' — rather than an account of what went wrong in any of them.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, in light of his last answer, why did he say that he first became aware of financial problems at Health New Zealand in October 2023, when his health Minister said that he first became aware five months later, in March 2024, a claim that he has now just repeated?
focus.explanation: Direct scrutiny of a named decision-making timeline on a specific policy failure, with dates attached. This is accountability on the substance, not party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why has the Government frozen relocation costs for overseas doctors, driving many to abandon their job applications, when we’ve got understaffed hospitals, like Dargaville, who can’t find doctors at all?
focus.explanation: Names a specific spending decision, its claimed effect on recruitment, and a named hospital affected. Concrete policy scrutiny rather than generalised attack.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We took action by appointing a Crown observer, a board member with financial expertise, a new chair was appointed, and, finally, appointing a commissioner.
specificity.explanation: Names four concrete governance actions taken at Health New Zealand, though without dates or names.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Gang membership has increased by 51 percent in the previous six years, and in the same time, violent crime has gone up by 33 percent and retail crime by 110 percent.
specificity.explanation: Three precise percentage figures over a stated six-year period; directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill does four things: it creates a criminal offence for displaying gang insignia in public, which often causes fear and intimidation; it gives the police the power to stop gang members gathering in public; it creates a non-consorting order that can be imposed by the court; and it gives greater weight to gang membership in sentencing.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates four named operative provisions of the named bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On behalf of the Minister, the Government has been clear that we are protecting front-line services, and we are also clear about the requirement to support families in need.
specificity.explanation: General assurances about protecting front-line services with no figures, services named or mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On behalf of the Minister, I understand that it is challenging for organisations that are in a period of time waiting for confirmation of contracts, but our Government is committed to ensuring that the tax that is paid by hard-working New Zealanders goes to services that are getting the outcomes that we expect and need for New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Acknowledges the contract uncertainty but supplies no timeframe, criteria or numbers — a statement of commitment only.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What does she say to the 400 front-line Oranga Tamariki service providers, including early years and teen parent services, counselling, and family and sexual violence services, whose contracts have ended on 30 June and have not had clear direction on when or if their contracts will be renewed?
specificity.explanation: Names a count of providers, the service types affected and the date their contracts ended.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yes, I do, but I did look back, as I gave an undertaking to, and I can confirm that on 8 December 2023, I received advice from the Tertiary Education Commission (TEC)—which is a different entity to Te Pūkenga—which noted that certain financial risk may result in Te Pūkenga achieving a worse deficit than the $93 million forecast for 2024.
specificity.explanation: Gives a date, the source of the advice and the forecast deficit figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is the Minister asserting that the letter that was sent to her on 8 December 2023 by Te Pūkenga does not include an amount of $53 million that she has directly cost them and the taxpayer?
specificity.explanation: Pins the question to a dated letter, a named entity and a specific dollar figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is she aware that giving direct instructions to the chair and the chief executive of a Crown entity is a breach of the Crown Entities Act and the Cabinet Manual?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific instruments said to be breached and the conduct alleged to breach them.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We took action by appointing a Crown observer, a board member with financial expertise, a new chair was appointed, and, finally, appointing a commissioner.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government appointed, in sequence, a Crown observer, a board member with financial expertise, a new chair and a commissioner to Health New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial announcements and Health New Zealand board records for 2024; true if all four appointments (Crown observer, finance-skilled board member, new chair, commissioner) were made by this Government, false if any did not occur.

veracity.statement: Gang membership has increased by 51 percent in the previous six years, and in the same time, violent crime has gone up by 33 percent and retail crime by 110 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 51% rise in gang membership, a 33% rise in violent crime and a 110% rise in retail crime over the six years to 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Police National Gang List figures and NZ Police / NZ Crime and Victims Survey victimisation data for the six years to mid-2024; true if each of the three figures is within rounding of the official series, false if any is materially different.

veracity.statement: The Justice Committee recommended the commencement date of 21 November, and the impact of this will be felt well before Christmas.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Justice Committee recommended 21 November as the commencement date for the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's report on the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill; true if the reported bill's commencement clause recommends 21 November 2024, false if it recommends another date.

veracity.statement: What does she say to the 400 front-line Oranga Tamariki service providers, including early years and teen parent services, counselling, and family and sexual violence services, whose contracts have ended on 30 June and have not had clear direction on when or if their contracts will be renewed?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that about 400 Oranga Tamariki-contracted front-line providers had contracts expire on 30 June 2024 without confirmation of renewal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki contracting records / OIA responses on provider contracts expiring 30 June 2024; true if roughly 400 provider contracts lapsed that date pending renewal decisions, false if the number is materially smaller or renewals had been confirmed.

veracity.statement: Does she stand by her statement that “It is important that we act decisively and honour the courage of these victims and survivors by making sure that something like this never happens again.”, and, if so, why is she implementing a $120 million cut in funding for service providers, which will significantly impact front-line care and prevention for children at risk?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister is implementing a $120 million cut to funding for Oranga Tamariki service providers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Oranga Tamariki appropriations and Oranga Tamariki savings documentation; true if roughly $120m of provider/community services funding was cut, false if the figure or its target is materially different.

veracity.statement: Yes, I do, but I did look back, as I gave an undertaking to, and I can confirm that on 8 December 2023, I received advice from the Tertiary Education Commission (TEC)—which is a different entity to Te Pūkenga—which noted that certain financial risk may result in Te Pūkenga achieving a worse deficit than the $93 million forecast for 2024.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that TEC advice dated 8 December 2023 warned of risks to a $93 million forecast 2024 deficit for Te Pūkenga.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 8 December 2023 TEC briefing to the Minister for Tertiary Education and Skills (releasable under the OIA); true if it is from TEC and cites a $93m 2024 forecast deficit at risk, false if no such briefing exists or the figures differ.

veracity.statement: It is a matter of fact that that has not occurred and that the actions that this Government has taken have improved the financial situation of Te Pūkenga considerably.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Pūkenga's financial position improved considerably rather than deteriorating as the warned risk suggested.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga's 2024 annual report / TEC monitoring reports; true if the 2024 deficit came in materially better than the $93m forecast, false if it was equal to or worse than forecast.

veracity.statement: Is she aware that giving direct instructions to the chair and the chief executive of a Crown entity is a breach of the Crown Entities Act and the Cabinet Manual?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a Minister giving direct instructions to a Crown entity's chair and chief executive breaches the Crown Entities Act 2004 and the Cabinet Manual.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Crown Entities Act 2004 (esp. ss 103-115 on ministerial powers of direction) and the Cabinet Manual's provisions on ministers and Crown entities; true if directing a chair/CE on operational matters outside the statutory direction process is prohibited by those instruments, false if such instructions are permitted.

focus.statement: I stand by the decision to appoint a commissioner to address the terrible financial situation that that previous party left.
focus.explanation: Names a specific decision (appointing a commissioner) but frames the reason as the other party's legacy rather than the substance of the financial position.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And to our police, who put their lives on the line to protect our communities, that comment must feel like a kick in the guts.
focus.explanation: An emotive response to another party's remark; no element of the gangs legislation or any policy mechanism is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No, I do not. And the very suggestion is repugnant. And apparently, the Green Party aren’t sure.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the Green Party supposedly thinks; no policy, figure or measure is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill does four things: it creates a criminal offence for displaying gang insignia in public, which often causes fear and intimidation; it gives the police the power to stop gang members gathering in public; it creates a non-consorting order that can be imposed by the court; and it gives greater weight to gang membership in sentencing.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Why won’t he give a direct answer to questions about the lead-up to an important decision he took when he is busy accusing others of a lack of transparency?
civility.explanation: Imputes evasiveness and hypocrisy to the Minister personally rather than contesting the substance of his answers.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: However, I’m pleased to advise the Speaker that my letter of expectation on 5 December 2023 and clarification on 20 May 2024 reinforcing the need to progress financial sustainability initiatives has ensured that the deficit to date is tracking considerably better than the deficit forecast, not worse.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: the improved deficit is attributed causally to her two letters with nothing offered to link them beyond sequence.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yes, and especially our efforts to abolish the Auckland regional fuel tax. I was so pleased to see reporting yesterday confirming that the Auckland regional fuel tax has been fully passed on to motorists. The previous Government didn’t care about working New Zealanders, frankly, who were trying to drive to school or drop their kids off to school. And that’s why they were so happy to soak them up with taxes to pay for speed bumps and cycleways. We axed the tax. We’re getting Government focused and back on the basics.
focus.explanation: A real policy is named (the Auckland regional fuel tax, its abolition and its pass-through), but half the answer is generalised characterisation of the previous Government's motives — 'didn't care', 'happy to soak them up' — rather than policy content. A genuine policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can he justify his Government’s failure to impose sanctions on Israel for its illegal occupation of Palestine while supporting sanctions against Russia for its illegal invasion of Ukraine, and is this not just a double standard regarding whose rights Aotearoa New Zealand is willing to uphold under his Government?
focus.explanation: Squarely on a specific instrument of policy — the use of autonomous sanctions — and contrasts two named, concrete applications of it. Legitimate scrutiny of a government decision, not party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Of course, the previous Government had a different plan to what this Government has. The previous Government was intent upon spending on corporate welfare. This Government is spending $2.6 billion on various climate initiatives.
focus.explanation: Asked what replacement policies would cover industrial decarbonisation, the answer spends two of three sentences characterising the previous Government's approach and offers a single unallocated dollar figure. No replacement policy is named.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I was so pleased to see reporting yesterday confirming that the Auckland regional fuel tax has been fully passed on to motorists.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that reporting published on or about 30 July 2024 confirmed the removal of the 11.5c/litre Auckland regional fuel tax was passed through in full to pump prices (the literal word order is a spoken slip — the intended claim is that the saving from scrapping the tax reached motorists).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Fuel price monitoring for Auckland (MBIE weekly petrol price series, AA or Gaspy comparisons of Auckland vs rest-of-country pump prices before and after 30 June 2024) reported in late July 2024; true if the Auckland price fell by the full ~11.5c/litre (incl. GST) relative to the rest of the country, false if only part of the reduction appeared at the pump.

veracity.statement: We’ve put $17 million of humanitarian aid in, and we continue to call for the two-State solution.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand had contributed $17 million in humanitarian aid in response to the Gaza conflict as at 31 July 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MFAT humanitarian funding announcements and Beehive releases tallying New Zealand's Gaza/Palestinian humanitarian contributions from October 2023 to 31 July 2024; true if the cumulative total is $17 million (±rounding), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: For example, Labour said yes to a special visa for the Ukraine, but said no to a special visa for Sudan.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Labour Government created a special visa category for Ukrainians and declined to create one for Sudanese nationals.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Immigration New Zealand visa category records and Cabinet/ministerial announcements; true if the 2022 Special Ukraine Policy visa exists and no equivalent Sudan-specific special visa was created following the April 2023 Sudan conflict, false if either element is wrong.
