veracity.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that every New Zealander in Gaza, contrary to what the questioner said, has been assisted out of Gaza by Foreign Affairs and other embassy work around the world in this country’s interests?
veracity.explanation: The question asserts that every New Zealander who was in Gaza had been assisted out by MFAT and its embassies as at 31 July 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MFAT consular statements and media reporting on New Zealand citizens and residents in Gaza between October 2023 and July 2024; true if MFAT records show all New Zealanders in Gaza were evacuated, false if any New Zealand citizen or resident remained in Gaza at that date.

veracity.statement: Does he agree with the Minister of Immigration, who said, regarding this country’s failure to grant visas for families of New Zealanders currently in Gaza, “It is not a visa issue; it is a border issue.”, and, if so, is he aware that the Palestinian Embassy in Cairo estimates that since October over 100,000 Gazans have crossed into Egypt?
veracity.explanation: Relays an estimate attributed to the Palestinian Embassy in Cairo that more than 100,000 Gazans had crossed into Egypt between October 2023 and July 2024.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Statements by the Palestinian Embassy in Cairo, and Egyptian/UN figures on Rafah crossings, reported between October 2023 and July 2024; true if such an estimate of over 100,000 crossings exists and is broadly corroborated, false if the embassy gave no such figure or the crossings were materially fewer.

veracity.statement: This Government is spending $2.6 billion on various climate initiatives.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the current Government's climate-related spending totals $2.6 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents and Treasury/Ministry for the Environment summaries of climate-related appropriations (including ETS-proceeds-funded initiatives) over the forecast period; true if the identifiable total is approximately $2.6 billion, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: What replacement policies will his Government put in place for industrial decarbonisation to put us back on track to meeting emissions targets, given the now scrapped Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry Fund is expected to deliver projects that would account for 17 percent of total emissions reductions in the first budget and 35 percent of emissions reductions planned in the second emissions budget?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that GIDI-funded projects were expected to deliver 17 percent of total emissions reductions in the first emissions budget and 35 percent of planned reductions in the second.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: EECA/MBIE GIDI programme documentation and the Climate Change Commission's 2024 monitoring report; true if the 17% and 35% shares of budgeted emissions reductions are stated there, false if the documented shares are materially different.

veracity.statement: Is he concerned that the Climate Commission’s analysis shows that the scrapping of the Clean Car Discount and agricultural emissions pricing have elevated the risk of not meeting the first emissions budget, which, under the previous Government, we were on track to meet?
veracity.explanation: Relays a finding attributed to the Climate Change Commission — that removing the Clean Car Discount and agricultural emissions pricing has raised the risk of missing emissions budget 1, which was previously on track to be met.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Climate Change Commission's July 2024 monitoring report on the Government's emissions reduction plan; true if it identifies those two policy reversals as increasing the risk to emissions budget 1 and records that the budget had previously been on track, false if it does not.

veracity.statement: For example, in 2015 in the Auckland market, the balcony size requirements increased the cost of an apartment by $40,000 to $70,000 per unit.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a quantified 2015 cost impact of Auckland's balcony size requirements of $40,000–$70,000 per apartment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2015 Auckland apartment cost analysis relied on (Auckland Council / MBIE / consultant economic evidence on the Unitary Plan's balcony and minimum-size rules); true if it estimates an added cost in the $40,000–$70,000 per-unit range, false if the estimate is materially different or no such analysis exists.

specificity.statement: Yes, I do stand by those statements and I’m proud of the work that we’ve done with the two Prime Ministers to generate now what is three joint statements. What we have been doing is we’ve been calling for a ceasefire since this conflict started. We’re asking for Hamas to release the hostages; we definitely need to see that. We’re asking Israel to meet all of its obligations. We’ve actually supported the UN remit to actually broaden the participation of Palestine within the UN. We’ve put $17 million of humanitarian aid in, and we continue to call for the two-State solution.
specificity.explanation: Carries checkable content — a named count of joint statements, a named UN vote, a dollar figure for aid — though the actions listed ('calling for', 'asking') have no mechanism or timeframe attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What I’d say to you is they’re different situations and we respect the ICJ rulings and we’ll continue to do so.
specificity.explanation: Asked why New Zealand joined one ICJ case and not the other, the reply asserts a difference without naming a single distinguishing feature, threshold or criterion. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he think that the genocide convention is a crucial instrument for the prevention and punishment of genocide, and, if so, why has New Zealand, under his Government, neglected to join South Africa’s International Court of Justice (ICJ) case against Israel despite how he joined Ukraine’s case against Russia in 2022?
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument (Genocide Convention), the two specific ICJ proceedings and the year of the earlier intervention. A precise, checkable question that pins the Minister to an identifiable decision.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What replacement policies will his Government put in place for industrial decarbonisation to put us back on track to meeting emissions targets, given the now scrapped Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry Fund is expected to deliver projects that would account for 17 percent of total emissions reductions in the first budget and 35 percent of emissions reductions planned in the second emissions budget?
specificity.explanation: Names the scrapped programme (GIDI) and attaches two precise shares of planned reductions to two named emissions budgets. Fully checkable, and it pins the Minister to a specific gap.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I announced earlier this month six changes we’ll be making as part of pillar one of this plan. Firstly, the establishment of housing growth targets for tier 1 and 2 councils. Secondly, new rules requiring cities to be allowed to expand outwards at the urban fringe. Thirdly, a strengthening of the intensification provisions of the National Policy Statement on Urban Development. Fourthly, new rules requiring councils to enable mixed-use development in our cities. Fifthly, the abolition of minimum floor area and balcony requirements. And, sixthly, new provisions making the medium-density residential standards rules optional for councils.
specificity.explanation: Six enumerated, named mechanisms, each identifying the instrument being changed and who it binds. Missing only commencement dates and quantities.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, what I’d say to the member is that Immigration is prioritising individual visa applications. Successive Governments—previous Governments and our Government—look at each conflict on its merits. For example, Labour said yes to a special visa for the Ukraine, but said no to a special visa for Sudan. So what we’ve done is we’re looking at the situation in Gaza. It is different. There are real challenges around documentation, there is limited consular support, the borders have been, effectively, closed, and we will continue to access each individual case and process it on its merits.
rigor.explanation: A real inference with a precedent premise (governments assess each conflict on its merits, illustrated by Ukraine vs Sudan) and three stated features of Gaza. The gap: the features offered — poor documentation, no consular support, closed borders — are reasons a special visa category would be hard to administer, not reasons it should not exist, so the conclusion is under-supported rather than invalid.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yes, I agree with the Prime Minister. We welcome the commission’s advice but note it is based on older data and does not take into account the Government’s draft emissions reduction plan No. 2.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: the commission's conclusions can be discounted because its data pre-dates the second emissions reduction plan. But the plan is only a draft with no quantified reductions offered here, so the step from 'newer plan exists' to 'the commission's conclusion is superseded' has a real gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Government is on track to deliver the first two emissions budgets. We are investing in electric vehicle chargers and we are investing in low-emissions public transport. The commissioner’s report did not have this data available.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion ('on track') rests on two unquantified investments plus an argument from absence of evidence — that the commission's contrary finding can be set aside because it lacked this data. Nothing is offered showing the omitted measures close the gap the commission identified.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We are on track to deliver the second emissions budget, which takes into account reversing the oil and gas ban. As we know, gas is a transitional fuel. We are not going to let the lights go out in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Closes on a false dichotomy — that the alternative to reversing the exploration ban is the lights going out — and the 'gas is a transitional fuel' premise is asserted as common knowledge rather than supported. No evidence connects the reversal to meeting the budget it is said to be consistent with.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Many, including the coalition Government’s granny flat policy; but specifically, earlier this month, proud to announce the Government’s Going for Housing Growth policy, or at least the first stages of it, allowing our cities to grow both up and out. Housing in this country is too expensive because we’ve made it difficult for our cities to grow. Fixing our housing crisis will improve our economy, improve intergenerational equity, decrease material hardship, and it will help the Government get the books back in order. We will be setting housing growth targets through this plan, making councils make more land available for development. We’re going to improve infrastructure funding and financing and incentivise councils to grow.
rigor.explanation: The causal premise (prices are high because growth is constrained) is stated as the single cause with nothing offered in support, and the chain of four downstream benefits — economy, intergenerational equity, material hardship, the fiscal books — is asserted rather than argued. The supply-to-price step is coherent; the leap to the wider benefits is not carried.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, there are some people in the media who’ve expressed concern about “shoebox apartments” or “slums”. And I say to them this: it is true that smaller dwellings won’t be the right solution for everyone, but one thing is definitely true: something that is smaller than a so-called “shoebox apartment” is a car or a tent or an emergency housing motel room. And this Government is focused on fixing the mess we inherited from the last Government.
rigor.explanation: A false dichotomy: the objection is that removing minimum sizes produces poor-quality apartments, and the reply treats the only alternative to a small apartment as a car, a tent or a motel room. Nothing is offered to show those are the actual counterfactuals for the people who would occupy the smaller dwellings.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: The Government is on track to deliver the first two emissions budgets.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that New Zealand's actual net emissions will fall within both the first emissions budget (2022–2025) and the second (2026–2030).
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand's Greenhouse Gas Inventory and the Climate Change Commission's final accounting against emissions budget 1 (2022–2025) and budget 2 (2026–2030); true if net emissions fall within both budgets, false if either is exceeded.

veracity.statement: I cannot and I did not direct Te Pūkenga to take action.
veracity.explanation: Simmonds asserts that she gave Te Pūkenga no direction to act, only expressed views and conveyed Government policy.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial correspondence and Te Pūkenga board papers released under the OIA, plus any Public Service Commission / Ombudsman findings on the Minister's dealings with Te Pūkenga: true if no formal ministerial direction was issued, false if a direction (or an instruction functioning as one) to Te Pūkenga is on record.

veracity.statement: I’m advised that since the details went up on the Government procurement website, there have been over 300 inquiries—and some of them from Australia—from interested providers within the mental health and addiction sector, all with innovative ideas on how to lift the performance of the mental health and addiction system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a count of more than 300 inquiries received about the innovation fund since it was listed on GETS, including some from Australia.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Health NZ records of inquiries logged against the Mental Health and Addiction Community Sector Innovation Fund GETS listing as at 31 July 2024: true if the logged inquiry count exceeds 300, false if materially fewer.

veracity.statement: Here’s the party that allowed the shutdown of Marsden Point, allowed the Ned Kellys to commit economic sabotage by drilling holes in the pipes and filling them with concrete, and abandoned our greatest and the most essential strategic assets our country had.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that during the Marsden Point refinery's closure, pipework was deliberately drilled and filled with concrete, and that this occurred under the previous government's watch.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Channel Infrastructure / Refining NZ decommissioning documentation and contemporaneous reporting on the 2022 refinery conversion: true if refinery pipework was in fact drilled and concrete-filled during decommissioning, false if the plant was mothballed or dismantled without such works.

veracity.statement: What Miss Williams doesn’t mention in her article is the fact that in 2020, when yours truly was the Minister in charge, we ensured a cost of no more than $400 million was set for replacement ferries—no more than $400 million for two ferries.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a $400 million cap for two replacement Cook Strait ferries was set in 2020 while Peters was the responsible Minister.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: 2020 Cabinet papers and KiwiRail/NZ Rail investment decisions on ferry replacement: true if a ceiling of about $400 million for two ferries was set in 2020, false if the approved figure or scope differed materially or no such cap was set.

veracity.statement: Once Labour took over, they allowed the project to bloom to guess how much? To $3.2 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Cook Strait ferry replacement project's cost grew to $3.2 billion under the previous Labour government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: KiwiRail and Treasury iReX project cost estimates as reported to Ministers in 2023: true if the total project cost estimate reached approximately $3.2 billion, false if the peak estimate was materially different.

civility.statement: When is she going to ask the Prime Minister the $53 million question—to put her out of her misery and fire her?
civility.explanation: Frames the demand as a personal humiliation of the Minister ('put her out of her misery'), sneering at her rather than engaging the $53 million decision itself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But, first, let’s have a look at this pointless, ill-informed, nonsense article that Arena Williams, Labour MP, had published in the New Zealand Herald today about the Cook Strait ferries.
civility.explanation: Dismissive of a named member's article in terms ('ill-informed', 'nonsense') that edge from the argument toward the author's competence, but stops short of a direct personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The headline should read—but in her shouting over there, she knows enough to think she is right, but doesn’t know enough to know she’s wrong.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on a named member's grasp and judgement, plus a jibe at her 'shouting' — aimed at the person, not the claim.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: You’ve got it in the article, honey, don’t worry about it.
civility.explanation: Addresses a female member as 'honey' and tells her not to worry — belittling and condescending to the person rather than answering the interjection.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But over there now they wouldn’t know what a worker looked like if they fell over one. And you can see the way they lie and sit down there—ask them to turn their hands down; there are no veins showing. You know why? Never done any physical work. That’s their problem, and it shows.
civility.explanation: Sneering commentary on opposing members' bodies and life histories — mockery of the people themselves, not of any argument they made.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Oh no—look, Mr Waititi, you wouldn’t know what work looked like, either. We all know about your background. You’re all talk, mate.
civility.explanation: A sustained personal attack on a named member's character and background.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Hey, sunshine, I’m not going to have a duel of wits—I’m not having a duel of wits with an unarmed opponent. What a waste of my time.
civility.explanation: Belittling form of address plus a direct jibe at another member's intelligence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: You wouldn’t know what work is—you’ve been in here for so long.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe at another member's working life rather than at anything he argued.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Today, I announced that applications will open for the Government’s new $10 million Mental Health and Addiction Community Sector Innovation Fund.
specificity.explanation: Named fund, named dollar figure and a stated timing for applications opening — checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: To be eligible for funding through the innovation fund, providers will need to demonstrate that their initiative is scalable, increases access to mental health and addiction support, delivers a positive social return on investment, and uses a workforce outside the publicly funded mental health workforce.
specificity.explanation: Sets out four concrete eligibility criteria applicants could act on, though without thresholds for how each is measured.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The request for proposals for the first round of funding will open today on the Government procurement website gets.govt.nz. I expect the first contracts with providers to be in place by early November.
specificity.explanation: Names the process, the channel and a dated milestone for contracts.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government is committed to getting money out of Wellington, out of the bureaucracy, and investing in our hard-working NGO and community mental health providers who are already delivering.
specificity.explanation: A direction of travel expressed in slogan form — no amounts, mechanisms or timeframes in this sentence.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No doubt today we’re going to hear speeches from the Labour Party, the Greens, and “Te Pāti of radicals” about how they think our Government is racist colonisers and anti-Māori because we’ve restored democracy to local ratepayers.
focus.explanation: Almost entirely a characterisation of what other parties will say; the only policy referent (Māori wards / local ratepayer votes) is a passing slogan with no measure, cost or effect named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But over there now they wouldn’t know what a worker looked like if they fell over one. And you can see the way they lie and sit down there—ask them to turn their hands down; there are no veins showing. You know why? Never done any physical work. That’s their problem, and it shows.
focus.explanation: No policy, measure or figure at all; entirely a characterisation of what the other party's MPs are 'really like'.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: You know, the Labour Party’s entire election strategy—and I’ve found out from inside information—is the sort of jilted boyfriend or girlfriend or the divorced person who says, standing back after the divorce, “Don’t you miss me yet?” That’s their whole plan for next year.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the opposing party's internal electoral posture; no policy, measure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What Miss Williams is saying is that they may as well have made it $10 billion and let us sign the contract.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: nothing quoted from the article supports the claim that its author would accept any price; the conclusion is attributed to her rather than derived from what she argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Today is a great day for Kiwis—31 July—because for the first time in 14 years New Zealanders are getting tax relief.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the personal income tax changes taking effect on 31 July 2024 are the first tax relief delivered to New Zealanders in 14 years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IRD/Treasury record of changes to personal income tax rates and thresholds: true if the last reduction in personal income tax rates/thresholds before 31 July 2024 occurred in or around 2010; false if any comparable personal income tax reduction took effect between 2011 and 2024.

veracity.statement: It’s a great day for Kiwis—83 percent of Kiwis will be better off; 94 percent of households will benefit.
veracity.explanation: Two distributional claims about the July 2024 tax package: 83 percent of New Zealanders better off, 94 percent of households benefiting.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD distributional analysis published with Budget 2024 for the personal income tax changes: true if the official modelling shows ~83% of individuals better off and ~94% of households receiving a benefit, false if the published figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: Well, that’s sort of OK up to a point, until we worked out dead people got it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2022 cost of living payment was paid to deceased people.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IRD statements and Official Information Act releases on cost of living payment eligibility errors: true if IRD confirms payments were made to deceased recipients, false if no such payments occurred.

veracity.statement: Then we had all the rinky-dink fuel tax cuts that were temporary, except they weren’t actually temporary—they kept on going.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the 2022 fuel excise duty reduction, announced as temporary, was repeatedly extended beyond its announced end date.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Gazette/Government announcements on the fuel excise duty cut from March 2022: true if the initially announced end date was extended one or more times, false if the cut ended as first announced.

veracity.statement: In February, the Government was warned that up to 13,000 more children will be pushed into poverty as a result of benefit changes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official advice in February 2024 estimated up to 13,000 additional children in poverty as a result of the benefit indexation change.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD/Treasury regulatory impact statement or Budget advice from February 2024 on changing benefit indexation from wages to CPI: true if it estimates up to ~13,000 more children in poverty, false if the advice contains no such estimate or a materially different figure.

veracity.statement: And when I asked Louise Upston, Minister for Social Development and Employment, about cuts to benefit increases, she said it’s not a cut.
veracity.explanation: Relays what the Minister said in answer to a question — that the change to benefit increases is not a cut.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard record of oral/written questions to the Minister for Social Development and Employment in 2024 on benefit indexation: true if she characterised the change as not a cut, false if no such answer appears.

veracity.statement: The Government quietly shrank its own child poverty reduction targets, which will see over 20,000 more children experiencing material hardship—a definition that means children will be struggling to actually meet their essential needs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Government revised its intermediate child poverty reduction targets downward in July 2024, with the effect that over 20,000 more children would be in material hardship than under the previous targets.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The intermediate child poverty reduction targets gazetted/announced in 2024 compared with the previous set under the Child Poverty Reduction Act: true if the material hardship target was weakened and the implied difference exceeds 20,000 children, false if the targets were unchanged or tightened, or the implied gap is materially smaller.

veracity.statement: And yet at the same time, this Government wants us to believe that we should join in celebrating tax cuts that will actually benefit those families the least while benefiting the richest New Zealanders the most.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the July 2024 tax package delivers the smallest benefit to low-income families and the largest to the highest earners.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD distributional analysis of the 31 July 2024 personal income tax changes by household income decile: true if dollar gains rise with income and the lowest-income families with children receive the smallest gains, false if the published distribution shows the largest gains going to lower-income families.

veracity.statement: So while they talk about inflation going down, they ignore the fact that rents continue to be the driving force behind inflation, behind the cost of living, the cost of inequality crisis that we have in this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that rents are the leading contributor to inflation in New Zealand at the time of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI contribution breakdown for the June 2024 quarter and annual CPI: true if rent is among the largest single contributors to the annual CPI increase and rent inflation exceeds headline CPI, false if rent's contribution is minor relative to other components.

specificity.statement: It’s a great day for Kiwis—83 percent of Kiwis will be better off; 94 percent of households will benefit.
specificity.explanation: Two precise percentages attached to a named, dated policy change; a reader could go and check them against the Budget modelling.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In February, the Government was warned that up to 13,000 more children will be pushed into poverty as a result of benefit changes.
specificity.explanation: Dated, sourced and numbered: a named month, a named policy change, and a specific figure that can be checked against the published advice.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Greens campaigned to end child poverty once and for all, because we know that it is not impossible, that if we put forward policies that will see the wealthiest few paying their share, we can absolutely eliminate poverty in this country.
specificity.explanation: Direction only: 'policies that will see the wealthiest few paying their share' names no tax, rate, threshold, cost or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The response from members opposite, on the Labour benches and beyond, has been to come up with a series of rinky-dink, dumb policies, all of which have been based upon the idea that the Government can spend money better than individuals.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy contrast buried here (state spending versus individual spending), but the sentence names no measure, figure or outcome and its weight is a characterisation of the other side's policies as a class.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is why we have put a stop to stupid Labour programmes like Lake Onslow, like industry transformation plans; these massive doorstops that once we abolish, no one even knew we’d gotten rid of them because no one bothered to read them, other than an army of public servants creating them.
focus.explanation: Names two specific programmes (Lake Onslow, industry transformation plans) and a specific action taken, but the point is wrapped in party framing and a swipe at officials rather than engaging what the programmes did or cost.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Government has made it so clear whose side they’re on, and it’s not on the side of children living in poverty, renters, or workers who struggle to make ends meet. It’s on the side of mega landlords, of mining CEOs, and those already raking in millions.
focus.explanation: A claim about whose side the other side is on, with no policy, measure, figure or outcome named; the substance arrives only in later passages.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Again, I see the members sitting to the opposite of me just looking confused and looking angry. They seem to be angry at the facts that are being presented to them, the facts that they have probably read and just ignore because they don’t care.
focus.explanation: Entirely about how the other side is behaving and what they supposedly feel; no policy, measure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is why we have put a stop to stupid Labour programmes like Lake Onslow, like industry transformation plans; these massive doorstops that once we abolish, no one even knew we’d gotten rid of them because no one bothered to read them, other than an army of public servants creating them.
rigor.explanation: The inference is that the programmes were worthless because nobody noticed their abolition — an argument from absence of public reaction, which does not establish the programmes' merit or lack of it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Greens campaigned to end child poverty once and for all, because we know that it is not impossible, that if we put forward policies that will see the wealthiest few paying their share, we can absolutely eliminate poverty in this country.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — poverty can be eliminated absolutely — is asserted from the premise that the wealthy could pay more, with no mechanism, quantum or link offered between the two; the supporting reason ('we know that it is not impossible') is a restatement of the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It seems like Sam Uffindell needs to read his own Government’s advice and realise the facts.
civility.explanation: Directed at a named member and condescending — suggesting he has not read and does not grasp the material — rather than engaging the point he interjected.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Again, I see the members sitting to the opposite of me just looking confused and looking angry. They seem to be angry at the facts that are being presented to them, the facts that they have probably read and just ignore because they don’t care.
civility.explanation: Mocks members' appearance and demeanour and imputes deliberate indifference — bad faith attributed to individuals present, well short of engaging the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Today was an utter, utter shambles of a demonstration of a Government. If members on the other side are looking for a new job, they might want to try being a bus driver, because, time and time again today, we saw the bus driving and them throwing each other under the bus.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side's internal blame-shifting and general character as a Government. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named. Nobody is personally insulted, so this is a Focus failure rather than a Civility one.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government is a shambles. It is 14 layers of a shambles of a Government. Shame on you.
focus.explanation: Pure party-directed characterisation with no policy, figure or outcome named. No individual is insulted, so Civility is untouched; this is exactly the tribalism Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But are they $250? Go and have a chat to the pensioners who now only get $2.50 a week, to the minimum-wage earners, who get $12.50 a week.
specificity.explanation: Names two identified groups and gives precise weekly dollar amounts against the headline figure; anyone could check the per-group gain from the tax package.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A lot of people are actually very excited to get their tax cuts: 83 percent of New Zealanders are getting a tax cut today and 94 percent of households are getting a tax cut today, and that really is making a difference.
specificity.explanation: Two precise percentages tied to a dated policy change; directly checkable against the Government's own tax package documentation.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) has put forward $20,000 of funding for the New Zealand Veterinary Association, to go towards animal welfare work in the Hurunui area.
specificity.explanation: Named agency, named recipient, exact dollar figure, named region and stated purpose.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But are they $250? Go and have a chat to the pensioners who now only get $2.50 a week, to the minimum-wage earners, who get $12.50 a week.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the per-week value of the 31 July 2024 tax threshold changes for pensioners ($2.50) and minimum-wage earners ($12.50).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IRD/Treasury tax-package tables for the 31 July 2024 personal income tax threshold changes: true if a superannuitant's weekly after-tax gain is about $2.50 and a full-time minimum-wage earner's is about $12.50; false if either figure is materially different (e.g. superannuitant gain of $4-5/week).

veracity.statement: In the last quarter, rates are up 9.6 percent, because of the choices this Government made to unwind affordable water reforms.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 9.6 percent increase in council rates in the most recent quarter's data.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI local authority rates and payments subgroup for the June 2024 quarter/year: true if the increase is about 9.6 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Again, insurance—another area that has gone up by 14 percent because of the choices made by this Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts insurance prices have risen 14 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI insurance group, annual movement to the June 2024 quarter: true if about 14 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: And, just in the last 24 hours, the monitoring report for emissions reductions was released and basically said that this Government is lumping the future generations of New Zealand with at least a $240 billion bill, coming to 2030.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a just-released emissions monitoring report puts the liability being passed to future generations at at least $240 billion by 2030.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The emissions reduction monitoring report published in late July 2024 (Climate Change Commission): true if it states a cost to future generations of at least $240 billion to 2030, false if it contains no such figure or a materially smaller one.

veracity.statement: They removed $6 billion from the National Resilience Plan so it can go and pay for a measly tax cut that won’t matter to anybody.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Budget 2024 stripped $6 billion from the National Resilience Plan.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents (Treasury Budget Economic and Fiscal Update / Budget at a Glance) on the National Resilience Plan: true if approximately $6 billion of the multi-year capital allowance for that plan was removed or reallocated, false if no such removal occurred or the amount is materially different.

veracity.statement: A lot of people are actually very excited to get their tax cuts: 83 percent of New Zealanders are getting a tax cut today and 94 percent of households are getting a tax cut today, and that really is making a difference.
veracity.explanation: Asserts coverage rates of the 31 July 2024 tax cuts: 83 percent of New Zealanders and 94 percent of households.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD distributional analysis of the 31 July 2024 personal income tax changes: true if roughly 83 percent of individuals and 94 percent of households receive a tax reduction, false if either share is materially lower.

veracity.statement: Today is also the day that the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act has been—well, what is it: 11 pages. It has been scrapped in the last 24 hours.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an 11-page piece of CCCFA regulation was removed effective the day of the speech.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Gazette / Legislation website for the CCCFA affordability and suitability regulations: true if an 11-page set of CCCFA regulations was revoked effective 31 July 2024, false if the revocation was of a different length, a different date, or if the Act itself remains in force in a way that makes 'scrapped' inaccurate.

veracity.statement: The Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) has put forward $20,000 of funding for the New Zealand Veterinary Association, to go towards animal welfare work in the Hurunui area.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific MPI grant of $20,000 to the NZVA for Hurunui animal welfare work.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI announcements/drought support funding records for mid-2024: true if MPI allocated $20,000 to the New Zealand Veterinary Association for animal welfare work in Hurunui, false if no such allocation exists or the amount/recipient differs.

civility.statement: Well, how about Charmaine from Wakapuaka, which is in the South Island, which I understand Simeon Brown is still trying to find.
civility.explanation: A jibe at a named individual's competence/geographical ignorance rather than at any policy he is responsible for.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In the last quarter, rates are up 9.6 percent, because of the choices this Government made to unwind affordable water reforms.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc ergo propter hoc: a rates rise measured in the immediately preceding quarter is attributed causally to the repeal of the water reforms, with no mechanism or counterfactual offered to link a very recent legislative change to already-set rates.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I had a person in my office who was very upset about the intrusive nature of the questions that were asked by banks when that person was going for a loan. She told me that she felt very embarrassed and ashamed by the questions that were being asked, and I think it was an absolutely appalling piece of legislation.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote: a single constituent's experience is offered as the basis for a general verdict on the legislation. He does later add a mechanism (scrutiny of bank payment records), which lifts it above a bare appeal, but the conclusion still rests mainly on the one case.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, that may have changed in the last 24 hours, but we all should be concerned about that because that drives the lake levels that secure having the lights remaining on in New Zealand, and given that pernicious ban of oil and gas exploration, we now are very much short of gas to secure our electricity supplies.
rigor.explanation: A causal chain is asserted (low snowpack to low lake levels to reliance on gas) but the final link attributes the current gas shortage to the exploration ban without addressing that the ban did not affect existing permits or fields whose output determines present supply. The conclusion outruns what is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Labour Government’s—that has just been unceremoniously turfed out—anti-car approach led to an imposition on the life of road users and took their eye off the important job of maintenance on our roads.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point buried here (road maintenance was neglected in favour of speed-reduction measures), but the sentence is framed around characterising the previous party's general 'approach' and its electoral defeat rather than naming a measure, figure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Labour’s anti-car, safety-ism approach led to wire barriers spreading over the country like the roots of a noxious weed.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy referent (median wire rope barriers) wrapped mostly in party characterisation and metaphor; no figures, locations or programme detail in the sentence itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is almost as though the last Labour Government forgot that people lived along these roads.
focus.explanation: Content-free characterisation of the previous government's attitude; strips out the party framing and no policy detail, figure or outcome remains in the sentence.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: God forbid, if a tsunami was to strike the Western Bay of Plenty, there would be a barrier stopping people from quickly escaping to the hills.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the consequences of a specific piece of infrastructure for a named community — on-policy, whatever the quality of the inference.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The previous Government wanted to tax, tax, tax—that’s how they thought they would get our economy back on track—and spend, spend, spend.
focus.explanation: Pure characterisation of the other party's disposition — no tax, no programme, no figure and no outcome is named, so nothing remains once the party framing is removed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Our regions have been neglected in the past six years.
focus.explanation: A blanket verdict on the previous government's six years with no policy, programme, funding line or measurable outcome attached to anchor it.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Earlier this year, the Transport and Infrastructure Committee conducted an investigation, after it was suggested that we examine the extreme costs of building a single raised speed table in Auckland—Williamson Ave, to be specific; $490,000.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a select committee investigated, and that a single raised speed table on Williamson Ave, Auckland cost $490,000 to build.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Transport and Infrastructure Committee records for 2024 and Auckland Transport's published cost breakdown for the Williamson Ave raised speed table; true if the recorded cost is approximately $490,000 and a committee briefing/inquiry on it occurred in 2024, false if the cost is materially different or no such committee work took place.

veracity.statement: A large proportion of the cost was spent on complying with ridiculous traffic management plans.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that traffic management compliance made up a large share of the $490,000 Williamson Ave speed table cost.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Transport's itemised cost breakdown for the Williamson Ave raised speed table (as supplied to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee); true if temporary traffic management is a substantial share (say, a quarter or more) of the total, false if it is a minor line item.

veracity.statement: Last week, along with the local member Scott Simpson, I attended a meeting of over 350 concerned residents who live on State Highway 2 between Ōmokoroa and Katikati.
veracity.explanation: Asserts attendance at a public meeting of more than 350 residents concerning SH2 between Ōmokoroa and Katikati, in the week before 31 July 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Local media reporting (e.g. Bay of Plenty Times, SunLive) and organiser accounts of the Katikati public meeting held in late July 2024; true if a meeting with roughly 350 or more attendees is reported, false if no such meeting occurred or attendance was materially smaller.

veracity.statement: The reason these residents got together was because the New Zealand Transport Agency (NZTA), under the direction of the last Government’s Road to Zero programme, decided to put wire barriers down the centre of their road.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that NZTA, acting under the Road to Zero programme, had decided to install median wire rope barriers on the two-lane SH2 section between Ōmokoroa and Katikati.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA project documentation for the SH2 Ōmokoroa–Katikati safety improvements and the Road to Zero speed and infrastructure programme; true if median barriers on that section were a confirmed NZTA decision under that programme, false if no median barrier was planned there or it sat under a different programme.

veracity.statement: Today, after 14 years, those bus drivers and the hard-working New Zealanders are getting tax relief—yes, tax relief.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the personal income tax relief taking effect on 31 July 2024 was the first in 14 years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IRD/Treasury record of personal income tax threshold changes; true if the previous adjustment to personal income tax rates or thresholds took effect in 2010, false if any intervening change (e.g. the Independent Earner Tax Credit or threshold shifts) reduced income tax in the interim.

veracity.statement: In fact, 83 percent of New Zealanders will from today be paying less tax, because, on this side of the House, we respect hard-working New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 83 percent of New Zealanders pay less income tax from 31 July 2024 under the Budget 2024 threshold changes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD distributional analysis of the Budget 2024 personal income tax threshold changes; true if approximately 83% of New Zealanders (or of taxpayers, on the government's stated basis) receive a reduction, false if the published share is materially different.

veracity.statement: Kiwis earn their money and they should be able to keep more of what they earn and not have it wastefully spent by ideological projects—$1.2 billion on three waters, Te Pūkenga, all sorts of wasteful spending that doesn’t get delivery, doesn’t get results; just wasting taxpayers’ money.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that $1.2 billion was spent on the Three Waters reform programme.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Internal Affairs and Treasury reporting on total appropriations and actual spend on the Three Waters/Affordable Water reform programme to 2024; true if cumulative spend is around $1.2 billion, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: In fact, the average household in New Zealand will be getting $102 more a fortnight.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the average New Zealand household gains $102 per fortnight from the 31 July 2024 tax package.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's Budget 2024 tax package household impact tables; true if the average household figure is about $102 a fortnight, false if $102 applies only to a narrower group (e.g. average-income households with children) or the average household figure is materially lower.

veracity.statement: We’re already seeing some green shoots: 3.3 percent inflation recently announced, the lowest that we’ve seen in the last couple of years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the most recently announced annual inflation rate was 3.3 percent and that this was the lowest figure in roughly two years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index release for the June 2024 quarter; true if annual CPI inflation was 3.3% and no lower quarterly annual print occurred in the preceding two years, false if either part differs.

specificity.statement: Earlier this year, the Transport and Infrastructure Committee conducted an investigation, after it was suggested that we examine the extreme costs of building a single raised speed table in Auckland—Williamson Ave, to be specific; $490,000.
specificity.explanation: Names the committee, the street, the city, the type of infrastructure and an exact dollar figure — fully checkable and actionable detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The ACT Party is here to advance the removal of barriers, freeing our citizens and our businesses, to grow and achieve for the betterment of all New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: A party slogan trading on a pun between physical road barriers and regulatory ones; no measure, mechanism, quantity or timeframe that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In fact, 83 percent of New Zealanders will from today be paying less tax, because, on this side of the House, we respect hard-working New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Carries a precise percentage and a commencement date tied to a named change, so the coverage claim can be checked directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In fact, the average household in New Zealand will be getting $102 more a fortnight.
specificity.explanation: A precise dollar amount attached to a named unit (the average household) and a stated frequency — directly checkable against Treasury's package tables.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our regions have been neglected in the past six years.
specificity.explanation: 'Neglected' is not operationalised — no spending figure, project, or service level is given that would let anyone check or act on the claim.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: God forbid, if a tsunami was to strike the Western Bay of Plenty, there would be a barrier stopping people from quickly escaping to the hills.
rigor.explanation: An appeal to a vivid worst-case scenario: the conclusion that median barriers would trap people in a tsunami is asserted without any evacuation modelling, and without addressing designed gaps or emergency access in the barrier layout.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: While it is difficult to say exactly what pushed NZTA to make this announcement, it is clear that fierce advocacy and protests from the locals has been effective.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning — the announcement followed the campaign, therefore the campaign caused it — though the speaker does hedge by conceding the cause is hard to establish, which is why this is a gap rather than a bare fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Getting rid of the Auckland regional fuel tax, restoring interest deductibility so we can see our rents go down and more housing supply, getting things built in this country—all about delivery.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that restoring mortgage interest deductibility for landlords will lead to falling rents and increased housing supply.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ rental price index (flow and/or stock measures) and consent/dwelling completion data; true if national rents decline in nominal terms over the two years following the statement, false if rents continue to rise.

focus.statement: Fourteen layers of dysfunction fully on display on the other side here today. In fact, I think we could probably even find more layers of dysfunction over there, especially after the member Catherine Wedd, who has just taken her seat, has had the floor.
focus.explanation: No policy, measure or outcome is named — the content is entirely a characterisation of the other side of the House and of a named member's contribution.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They’ve got one Minister that comes into the House and can’t answer the most basic of questions that are put on notice, and we’ve got another Minister that is more interested in wearing the insignia of her gang than defending her Government or her ministerial record.
focus.explanation: It is scrutiny of ministerial performance in question time, but no specific policy, figure or outcome is named — the weight is on how ministers are behaving and dressing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are problems, and we are firing up the popcorn machine for the day that David Seymour becomes Deputy Prime Minister. That’s going to be an interesting episode for us to watch.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the coalition partners' internal dynamics and a future leadership handover; no policy content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What they’ve got rid of, in the Decarbonising Industry Fund, is something that was accounting for 17 and 35 percent of the emissions reductions that we needed to achieve.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named government decision and its measured consequence — textbook scrutiny of a specific policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The attack on Māori wards—punch. Demolishing of the Māori Health Authority—punch. Removing section 7AA—punch. Rushing through the Fast-track Approvals Bill—punch. Cutting Matariki funding—punch. Erasing te reo Māori from public service—punch. Cutting supply and capability of Māori housing—punch. The establishment of youth bootcamps—punch. Gang legislation that will disproportionately target Māori—punch. Ignoring tribunal and High Court rulings—punch. And, yet to come, the Treaty principles bill—punch.
focus.explanation: Every item names a specific measure or decision — Māori wards, the Māori Health Authority, section 7AA, the Fast-track Approvals Bill, the Treaty principles bill. This is itemised scrutiny of the government's programme, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Fourteen layers of dysfunction fully on display on the other side here today. In fact, I think we could probably even find more layers of dysfunction over there, especially after the member Catherine Wedd, who has just taken her seat, has had the floor.
civility.explanation: Beyond attacking the government generally, it singles out Catherine Wedd by name and implies her speech added to the 'dysfunction' — sneering at a person rather than her argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They’ve got one Minister that comes into the House and can’t answer the most basic of questions that are put on notice, and we’ve got another Minister that is more interested in wearing the insignia of her gang than defending her Government or her ministerial record.
civility.explanation: Imputes vanity and bad faith to an individual Minister ('the insignia of her gang', more interested in jewellery than her job) rather than engaging what she said.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We are punch drunk from the racist agenda this anti-Māori Government lead and have been led by the “dark triad”. The dark triad are leading an anti-Māori agenda in this House.
civility.explanation: 'Dark triad' is a clinical label for narcissism, Machiavellianism and psychopathy applied to the three coalition leaders — an attack on the character of identifiable individuals rather than on their policies.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The dark triad, like any abuser, is grooming us. In actual fact, this Government and successive Governments have been grooming us for the past 180-odd years through colonialist tools like divide and conquer.
civility.explanation: Casts identifiable individual leaders as abusers and groomers — an attack on their character, not on the substance of what they have done.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Specifically, I want to talk about the $3 billion that was cut from climate initiatives to fund tax cuts, interest deductibility for landlords.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that $3 billion was removed from climate programmes and used to fund the 2024 tax package including restored interest deductibility.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents and Treasury's Climate Emergency Response Fund reprioritisation tables; true if the total reprioritised away from climate initiatives to the tax package is approximately $3 billion, false if materially lower or not directed to the tax package.

veracity.statement: I want that member to go back to rural New Zealand, to Hawke’s Bay, and tell her constituents that the Climate Change Commission has said that the result of this Government’s inaction in transport and agriculture climate initiatives means that $300 a tonne emissions pricing is coming.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Climate Change Commission has stated that weaker transport and agriculture policy implies emissions pricing reaching $300 a tonne.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Climate Change Commission 2024 advice on the second emissions reduction plan / NZ ETS settings; true if the Commission's published modelling states an NZU price of around $300 per tonne as a consequence of reduced complementary transport and agriculture policy, false if no such figure or consequence appears in its advice.

veracity.statement: Now, at only $200 a tonne that means an extra 40c on the cost of a litre of petrol.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the ETS pass-through to pump prices: a carbon price of $200 per tonne adds about 40 cents per litre of petrol.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Standard ETS pass-through arithmetic (approximately 2.3–2.4 kg CO2 per litre of petrol) and MBIE/Treasury published price-impact estimates; true if $200/tonne implies roughly 40c per litre, false if the implied figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: What they’ve got rid of, in the Decarbonising Industry Fund, is something that was accounting for 17 and 35 percent of the emissions reductions that we needed to achieve.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry (GIDI) fund accounted for between 17 and 35 percent of New Zealand's required emissions reductions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE/EECA published abatement estimates for the GIDI fund against the emissions budget shortfall in the relevant emissions reduction plan; true if the fund's contribution falls in the 17–35 percent range, false if materially outside it.

veracity.statement: Treasury has told us New Zealanders are facing a bill of $24 billion because of climate inaction, and that is on this Government and their inaction.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific Treasury estimate of $24 billion in cost arising from failure to act on climate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's published estimates of the cost of meeting New Zealand's first Nationally Determined Contribution / offshore mitigation; true if a Treasury figure of approximately $24 billion exists, false if Treasury's published range does not reach that figure.

veracity.statement: Māori only have less than 5 percent—95 percent of the land is out of Māori ownership.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that less than 5 percent of land in New Zealand remains in Māori ownership.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Puni Kōkiri / Māori Land Court data on the area of Māori freehold land as a share of New Zealand's total land area; true if under 5 percent, false if materially higher.

veracity.statement: No, we didn’t. The majority was confiscated.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the majority of Māori land that passed out of Māori ownership was confiscated rather than sold.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal and historical land-alienation records comparing area lost through raupatu (confiscation under the New Zealand Settlements Act) with area alienated by Crown purchase and Native Land Court sale; true if confiscation accounts for more than half the total, false if purchase/Native Land Court alienation accounts for the majority.

specificity.statement: What they’ve got rid of, in the Decarbonising Industry Fund, is something that was accounting for 17 and 35 percent of the emissions reductions that we needed to achieve.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific fund abolished and attaches a quantified share of required emissions reductions; someone could go and check the figure against the fund's published abatement estimates.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The attack on Māori wards—punch. Demolishing of the Māori Health Authority—punch. Removing section 7AA—punch. Rushing through the Fast-track Approvals Bill—punch. Cutting Matariki funding—punch. Erasing te reo Māori from public service—punch. Cutting supply and capability of Māori housing—punch. The establishment of youth bootcamps—punch. Gang legislation that will disproportionately target Māori—punch. Ignoring tribunal and High Court rulings—punch. And, yet to come, the Treaty principles bill—punch.
specificity.explanation: Eleven named policies and bills, each individually checkable, but no figures, dates or mechanisms attached to any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Have we heard one alternative from this Government of what they’re going to do? No. We have a Government that is hell-bent on increasing emissions in this country.
rigor.explanation: Argument from absence of evidence plus a non sequitur: not having heard an alternative announced does not support the conclusion that the government intends to increase emissions.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I spoke to one of our iwi leaders today, and they said they went to an iwi hui where Ministers were promising all this money, and our leaders were drunk like alcoholics on the Government’s money. These are the tactics that the Government constantly uses: divide and conquer.
rigor.explanation: A single second-hand anecdote about one hui is generalised into a claim about what the Government 'constantly' does — hasty generalisation from anecdote.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: He hīkoi nui kei te haere. He whawhai nui kei te haere.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that a major march (hīkoi) and a major fight are coming in response to the government's agenda.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: News and police/organiser crowd reporting on national Māori protest marches in the period following the statement; true if a large-scale national hīkoi on Treaty/Māori rights takes place, false if no significant national march eventuates.

specificity.statement: I’m not going to give financial advice, but if we were to take the $20 for those who say it’s not enough—and some in the Opposition might like to follow this advice; at your own risk, of course—and put it into an investment fund, like a KiwiSaver but not one that locks it up for retirement, and you did that every week for 10 years at 8 percent, you would have a total of $15,654.55, where about $5,000 of that would be pure interest.
specificity.explanation: Carries an exact contribution amount, a time horizon, an assumed rate of return and a precise total with an interest breakdown — anyone could reproduce the calculation.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The changes will provide enduring social, environmental, and economic dividends to the people of New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic benefit categories with no named change, no quantum, no mechanism and no timeframe — nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: At its core, the bill changes the purposes in the trust deed by confirming that any woman and child can be assisted by the trust, making it more accessible, and by removing any suggestion that the previous wording had that women had to be of particular standing or from a particular social class.
specificity.explanation: Names the precise legal mechanism (amendment of the purposes in the trust deed) and the two concrete effects — universal eligibility and removal of the social-class qualifier — rather than describing the bill in general terms.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill now speaks of a little tweak, which has to do with the provision of the will which referred to women and their children in Canterbury now applying to women who are from Canterbury and who may be transitioning elsewhere for various reasons, possibly including family violence or having to relocate their children or themselves away from Canterbury.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the particular provision being altered and the precise change in its scope — from women located in Canterbury to women from Canterbury who may move away — though it gives no clause reference or numbers.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’m not going to give financial advice, but if we were to take the $20 for those who say it’s not enough—and some in the Opposition might like to follow this advice; at your own risk, of course—and put it into an investment fund, like a KiwiSaver but not one that locks it up for retirement, and you did that every week for 10 years at 8 percent, you would have a total of $15,654.55, where about $5,000 of that would be pure interest.
rigor.explanation: The arithmetic illustration does support the stated conclusion that small weekly amounts compound, but the inference leans entirely on an unstated-as-assumption 8 percent return with no allowance for fees, tax or inflation, leaving a gap between the modelled figure and the real-world claim.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Or how about Darryl in Te Rapa, who couldn’t afford a coffee for a while, and now, on smoko break, as the sun pops out through the dark, foggy Waikato mornings, and the sun warms his face, he can go and sip his flat white, with his extra $3.50 a day.
rigor.explanation: A single illustrative anecdote is offered as the support for the claim that the tax relief is materially worthwhile — an appeal to anecdote, with nothing connecting the one case to the general effect.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I’m not going to give financial advice, but if we were to take the $20 for those who say it’s not enough—and some in the Opposition might like to follow this advice; at your own risk, of course—and put it into an investment fund, like a KiwiSaver but not one that locks it up for retirement, and you did that every week for 10 years at 8 percent, you would have a total of $15,654.55, where about $5,000 of that would be pure interest.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that $20 invested weekly for 10 years at 8 percent yields $15,654.55, of which about $5,000 is interest.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Standard future-value-of-an-annuity calculation for $20 weekly contributions over 520 weeks at 8% p.a.; true if the total is approximately $15,654.55 and total contributions ($10,400) leave roughly $5,000 in interest, false if the figure is materially different from that arithmetic.

veracity.statement: The McLean Institute is a charitable institute, established in Christchurch in accordance with the will of Allan McLean, who actually passed away in 1907.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the McLean Institute was founded in Christchurch under Allan McLean's will and that McLean died in 1907.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Charities Register entry for the McLean Institute plus New Zealand probate/death records and the bill's explanatory note; true if the institute was established in Christchurch under McLean's will and McLean's death is recorded in 1907, false if the founding location, instrument or death year differ.

veracity.statement: The McLean Institute is a charitable institute established pursuant to the will of Allan McLean, who passed away on 12 November 1907, 120 years ago.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific death date of 12 November 1907 for Allan McLean and that this was 120 years before the date of the speech (2024).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand death/probate records for Allan McLean; true if the death date is 12 November 1907 and the interval to the statement date is approximately 120 years, false if the date differs or the stated interval is materially wrong (1907 to 2024 is 117 years).

veracity.statement: The institute was established by will in 1904 and by a codicil, an addition to the will, in 1906.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the founding will dates from 1904 and was supplemented by a codicil in 1906.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The McLean Institute trust deed / probate documents and the bill's explanatory note; true if the will is dated 1904 and a codicil 1906, false if either instrument bears a different year.

focus.statement: Or how about Darryl in Te Rapa, who couldn’t afford a coffee for a while, and now, on smoko break, as the sun pops out through the dark, foggy Waikato mornings, and the sun warms his face, he can go and sip his flat white, with his extra $3.50 a day.
focus.explanation: It is directed at the Budget's tax relief and attaches a per-day figure to it, but the substance is a colour vignette rather than the mechanism, cost or coverage of the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So the average cost of housing for New Zealanders has gone up 14.5 percent. That includes 4 percent increase in rents, 27.5 percent increase in mortgages, 5.9 percent increase in property rates, 14.1 percent increase in building-related insurance costs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Stats NZ figures for the year ended June 2023: total housing costs up 14.5%, with rents +4%, mortgage payments +27.5%, rates +5.9%, building insurance +14.1%.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Living-costs Price Indexes, year ended June 2023 quarter, housing and household utilities subgroups; true if the overall housing figure is 14.5% (± rounding) and the four component figures match, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: In the year ended June 2023, 8.5 percent of New Zealand’s population were in material hardship. That is another 1.1 percent increase than the previous 12 months, and also 0.9 percent increase in New Zealand’s population in severe material hardship.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a material hardship rate of 8.5% of the population for the year to June 2023, up 1.1 percentage points, with severe material hardship up 0.9 points.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Economic Survey child poverty / material hardship statistics for the year ended June 2023; true if the population material hardship rate is 8.5% and the year-on-year changes are 1.1 and 0.9 points, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: We had a record low of 3.3 percent inflation under the National Government for the last 12 months.
veracity.explanation: Asserts annual CPI inflation of 3.3%, characterises it as a record low, and attributes the 12-month period to the National Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation for the June 2024 quarter, and the historical CPI series; true if annual inflation was 3.3% and no lower annual rate appears in the series, false if lower annual rates exist (which would make 'record low' wrong) or if the rate was not 3.3%. The attribution is checkable against the date the National-led government took office (November 2023).

veracity.statement: I must emphasise: 83 percent of the New Zealanders—and that is 83 percent of people who are listening in and tuning in on TV—83 percent of you will have some support and some benefits from the tax relief that will be effective from today.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 83 percent of New Zealanders receive some benefit from the tax package taking effect on 31 July 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 / Treasury and IRD documentation on the personal income tax threshold changes; true if official costings state approximately 83% of New Zealanders (on the stated population base) receive a tax reduction, false if the official figure is materially different or applies to a different base.

veracity.statement: Over the same four years, tax cuts will cost $14.7 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the four-year fiscal cost of the Budget 2024 personal tax package is $14.7 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents (Treasury costing of the personal income tax package over the forecast period); true if the stated four-year cost is approximately $14.7 billion, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Under Labour: 11 surpluses and four deficits. Under National, while I’ve been here: two surpluses and seven deficits.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a surplus/deficit tally across his 22 years in Parliament: 11 surpluses and 4 deficits under Labour, 2 surpluses and 7 deficits under National.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Financial Statements of the Government of New Zealand, OBEGAL result for each financial year from 2002/03 to 2023/24, allocated to the government of the day; true if the counts match, false if they do not (note the stated Labour years total 15 against 13 years of Labour government).

veracity.statement: They complained about a lack of nurses and now they’ve put a ban on employing more nurses.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government has imposed a ban on hiring additional nurses, having previously criticised nurse shortages.
veracity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One of the key ones that is being made here is the change not just to recital (10A) in the preamble, which sort of highlights it, but it’s perhaps better captured—in view of the time—in clause 6, where it talks about the fact that although the McLean Institute was incorporated in this Act of Parliament in 1909, from that point on, Part 3 of the Charitable Trusts Act 1957 applied to the institute and the fund.

rigor.statement: I guess the point that I would make as I reflect on this is to ask what’s most important to us. Is it to set broad objects and broad beneficiaries, and then to pick good trustees and to trust them to do the job? You don’t want to have them hamstrung at every corner.
