specificity.statement: As many people have said, it allows it to be updated so that it’s relevant so that the types of circumstances that people may find themselves in reflect the environment of the more modern world, and, therefore, it’s allowed to focus on its core intentions, which was to provide that emergency transitional housing and all of the other social support to allow people to live independently and to allow them to live with dignity.
specificity.explanation: Trying to convey the bill's substance, but carries almost no checkable detail: 'updated so that it's relevant' and 'the environment of the more modern world' are generalities. The single concrete element is 'emergency transitional housing'; no clause, mechanism, figure or beneficiary count is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We look also—today, as we reflect on Allan McLean and his enduring gift to this country—to the late Josie and Julian Robertson, who bequeathed 15 masterpieces to Auckland Art Gallery, worth $178 million—masterpieces including from Pablo Picasso, including from Monet.
specificity.explanation: Carries a count (15 works), a named recipient institution, a dollar valuation and named artists — precise enough that a reader could go and check each element.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Wine is our sixth-largest goods export by value, earning the country over $2 billion in export revenue annually—$2 billion, Mr Rutherford, how’s that?
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable facts about 2024: that wine ranks sixth among New Zealand's goods exports by value, and that it earns over NZ$2 billion in export revenue a year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ merchandise trade statistics and NZ Winegrowers annual report for the year to mid-2024: true if wine exports exceed NZ$2bn and wine sits sixth in the ranking of goods exports by value; false if the value is materially below $2bn or the rank is materially different (e.g. outside fifth-to-seventh).

veracity.statement: Now, wine tourism also plays a vital role in our broader tourism industry, which happens to be our second-largest export earner.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that tourism was New Zealand's second-largest export earner at the time of speaking (July 2024).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / MBIE export earnings data for the year ending 2024, ranking tourism against goods export categories: true if tourism ranks second (behind dairy); false if it ranks lower than second.

veracity.statement: We received approximately 72 submissions from a diverse range of stakeholders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the number of written submissions the Justice Committee received on the Sale and Supply of Alcohol (Winery Cellar Door Tasting) Amendment Bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's report on the bill and the submissions listed on parliament.nz: true if the submission count is about 72; false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Just to summarise, those major amendments that we made did include tightening that definition of “winery” and “cellar door”, adjusting the maximum sample size from 40 millilitres back down to 35 millilitres, adding those requirements of water and snack food, and clarifying the bill’s applicability to remote cellar door operations to cover those operations where the vineyard was not necessarily on the same block or the same site as the cellar door.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the Justice Committee actually changed in the bill, including that the sample cap was reduced from 40ml to 35ml.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill as reported back by the Justice Committee compared against the bill as introduced: true if the reported-back version reduces the sample cap from 40ml to 35ml, tightens the winery/cellar door definitions, adds water and food requirements, and addresses remote cellar doors; false if these amendments are absent or differ materially.

rigor.statement: The maximum sample size, as outlined by Mr Smith, is set at just 35 millilitres—that’s 7 teaspoons of wine; about a fifth of a standard glass of wine. So no business could viably operate by selling such tiny samples as their primary offering.
rigor.explanation: An economic-viability inference from a stated premise: because the statutory sample cap is tiny, a quasi-bar could not run on samples alone. The conclusion broadly tracks the premise, but 'no business could viably operate' is stronger than what the sample cap alone establishes — repeat sales of multiple samples are not excluded, so there is a real gap between the evidence and the absolute conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In many ways, this legislation actually enhances safety and responsibility, compared with the status quo; where, today, wineries can, if they wanted to, pour unlimited free samples with fewer controls.
rigor.explanation: A comparative inference: the bill adds sample-size caps, water and food requirements, so relative to an unregulated status quo it improves harm controls. The conclusion follows from the stated premises, though it leans on the assumption that paid, capped samples do not increase consumption overall — an untested step.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The maximum sample size, as outlined by Mr Smith, is set at just 35 millilitres—that’s 7 teaspoons of wine; about a fifth of a standard glass of wine. So no business could viably operate by selling such tiny samples as their primary offering.
specificity.explanation: Gives an exact statutory figure (35 millilitres) with two concrete equivalences; anyone could check it against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Just to summarise, those major amendments that we made did include tightening that definition of “winery” and “cellar door”, adjusting the maximum sample size from 40 millilitres back down to 35 millilitres, adding those requirements of water and snack food, and clarifying the bill’s applicability to remote cellar door operations to cover those operations where the vineyard was not necessarily on the same block or the same site as the cellar door.

specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The committee’s view was that this is a specific bill targeted towards fixing the anomaly for wine cellar door operators, and that if members thought it would be appropriate to expand the bill to other industries, they would be welcome to bring a member’s bill themselves.

focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, I know there’ll be members opposite who will argue that this is too ambiguous, but we think it’s pretty clear.
civility.explanation: Anticipates and disagrees with an opposing argument about the bill's drafting without imputing bad faith or disparaging anyone. Contested ground, handled entirely on the substance.

divination.statement: I think the fears of these speakeasys popping up around the place are misplaced.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the new cellar-door tasting provision will not in practice be exploited by retailers or bars to operate as de facto drinking establishments.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Media reporting, District Licensing Committee / Alcohol Regulatory and Licensing Authority decisions, and any amending legislation in the three years after enactment: true if no documented instances of non-winery businesses using the cellar-door tasting provision to operate as de facto bars; false if such cases are documented or the provision is tightened in response to that behaviour.

civility.statement: To be perfectly honest, I did my best to assist the member in tidying those things up, but Stuart Smith has the uncanny ability that every time he speaks, fewer and fewer people want to support this bill. It’s truly quite extraordinary.
civility.explanation: A jibe at a named member's persuasive ability rather than at the bill's content — it targets how Stuart Smith performs personally, not the substance of what he argued. Short of sustained abuse, but clearly landing on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But Mr Smith said, “No, this is just for wine. I like my wine. I like my vineyard mates, and we’re not interested in expanding this to other industries.” And there was no rational reason for that.
civility.explanation: An invented quotation put in a named member's mouth that imputes self-interest and cronyism ('my vineyard mates') as his motive for rejecting amendments. This is a personal attack on motive rather than an engagement with his reasons.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But, once again, the member simply wasn’t interested in entertaining sensible amendments that would actually improve the bill and further its actual objectives, and he just dismissed it out of hand.
civility.explanation: Criticism of the member's handling of the bill edges into imputing closed-mindedness ('simply wasn't interested', 'dismissed it out of hand') rather than addressing the reasons given. Pointed and sneering about the person's conduct, though tied to a real procedural complaint.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, I mean, one of the things that I find stuck in my craw a little is this quite elitist notion that wine is special, and the beer drinkers amongst us need to understand that the association with the land is so important, and if you want to go and taste a beer, then go and swill it down at some bar, because it doesn’t deserve this kind of protection.
rigor.explanation: Argues against a caricature: the bill's stated rationale is a terroir/cellar-door tourism argument, not a claim that beer drinkers are lesser. Recasting it as snobbery ('go and swill it down at some bar') is a strawman — the conclusion that the distinction is elitist does not follow from the premise the bill actually offers.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But charging for it, making food available, water available, and that whole host responsibility, I believe will reduce that effect.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure — that paid tastings plus food, water and host responsibility will cut alcohol harm — but nothing is offered to connect the mechanism to the outcome beyond 'I believe'. A bare assertion standing in for evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In the same way we’re removing these restrictions and barriers around cellar door tasting, it would be a great thing to have support across this House to remove the restrictions on businesses who are employers and drivers of the local community, when it comes to Easter restrictions on those trading hours.
rigor.explanation: Argument by analogy that does not carry: the cellar-door change is justified in the debate by the terroir/tourism link and host-responsibility safeguards, none of which apply to Easter trading hours, which rest on separate public-holiday and worker-protection grounds. rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Companies Office / business directory and licensing records plus the venue's own trading information for a Christchurch establishment trading as 'Cellar Door' around July 2024; true if such a business existed in Christchurch and sold wine in tasting-sized volumes, false if no such business existed or it did not sell by tasting volume.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Business/licensing registers and trade listings for mead producers in southern Wellington suburbs as at mid-2024; true if at least one commercial meadery was operating there, false if none existed.

specificity.statement: I do support this bill, but I would agree with my colleague who says that it doesn’t go far enough. specificity.explanation: A direction with a named actor to talk to, but 'a wider approach' and 'more comprehensive approach' carry no mechanism, scope or timeframe — nothing here could be checked or acted on.

specificity.statement: Well, I think we have done a lot as a Government to remove barriers, and I’m proud to be supporting a member’s bill that would do the same.

specificity.statement: New Zealand First looks at this type of legislation, this bill, as common sense. We are a common-sense party. This bill, again, is common sense.

specificity.statement: The sample sizes, as well, from that 30-millilitre pour is the standard, but the bill gives you the ability to be able to pour up to 35.

rigor.statement: We heard from Mr Webb, asking why we couldn’t add those to this bill; well, quite simply, those tastings or offerings would (1) be different; and (2) we didn’t hear submissions from those people. rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the bill's scope with two stated reasons — product difference and absence of submissions from those sectors. The second reason is essentially an argument from absence of consultation rather than from the merits of inclusion, and the first is asserted rather than shown, so the conclusion is supported but loosely.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The whole idea that you actually have to take some time to make a transaction, you have to have some money available in order to actually pay for the sample, those kinds of things are actually the small things that can stop a person from potentially engaging in alcohol harm.

rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We heard from Mr Webb, asking why we couldn’t add those to this bill; well, quite simply, those tastings or offerings would (1) be different; and (2) we didn’t hear submissions from those people. focus.statement: The issue I have with this bill, which I would like to make a contribution on, is the specific distinction around on-licence and off-licence, which is a structural element of the licensing system.

focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The main reason that I am against this bill is that I asked that the definitions would be very clear, that the host’s responsibility would be also very clear—that, when the bill does pass tonight, there is a real understanding of who will come and access those services being offered in different places around the motu because they’re allowed to, because they have the option of going into a winery, tasting the samples—but there are still important measures that the host has a responsibility to partake in, in terms of offering that service and that product.
focus.explanation: States her reason for opposing in terms of the bill's own provisions — the clarity of its definitions and of host responsibility. No content about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It also allows cellar doors to share the same licence as a cafe or a restaurant without burdening them with those extra costs that, at this stage, they do have if they just want to serve some of their wines.
focus.explanation: Describes a specific effect of the bill — licence sharing between a cellar door and an attached cafe or restaurant — with no party content.

specificity.statement: The issue I have with this bill, which I would like to make a contribution on, is the specific distinction around on-licence and off-licence, which is a structural element of the licensing system.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a named mechanism (the on-licence/off-licence distinction) but does not say what the problem with it is, what change she wants, or what effect it would have.

specificity.statement: But this is an industry that—as we’ve read, and Radio New Zealand have reported on—is a $2.3 billion industry as far as the value of wine exports per annum.

specificity.statement: They’re operating in Queenstown this summer season—I understand at Queenstown International Airport at 120 percent, but the rest of Australian tourism coming inbound is operating at about 75 percent.

specificity.statement: It also allows cellar doors to share the same licence as a cafe or a restaurant without burdening them with those extra costs that, at this stage, they do have if they just want to serve some of their wines.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (sharing one licence with a cafe or restaurant) and the problem it removes, but quantifies neither the current cost nor the saving.

divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Sale and Supply of Alcohol (Winery Cellar Door Tasting) Amendment Bill will complete its third reading and pass on the evening of 31 July 2024.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Hansard record / division result for the third reading of the Sale and Supply of Alcohol (Winery Cellar Door Tasting) Amendment Bill; true if the bill passed its third reading on 31 July 2024, false if it was not passed that sitting.

veracity.statement: According to a Consumer New Zealand campaign to end unfair gift card expiry dates, evidence was shown that one in five gift card holders have actually been stuck with an expired gift card.
veracity.explanation: Relays a Consumer NZ survey statistic that 20% of gift card holders have been stuck with an expired card.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Consumer NZ's published gift card expiry campaign material/survey; true if it reports approximately one in five (≈20%) gift card holders having been left with an expired card, false if the published figure is materially different or no such finding exists.

veracity.statement: Now, the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill seeks to prohibit the sale of gift cards with an expiry date of less than three years after the initial sale date.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the bill's operative effect: a minimum three-year expiry measured from initial sale.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill as reported back from select committee (new section 24A); true if it prohibits supplying gift cards with an expiry date earlier than three years after the date of sale, false if the period or the mechanism differs.

veracity.statement: It’s a good day for New Zealand with the announcement of the tax relief package that comes into effect.
veracity.explanation: Embedded factual claim that the Government's tax relief package came into effect on the day of the debate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue / Budget 2024 personal income tax threshold changes; true if the Government's personal income tax relief package took legal effect on 31 July 2024, false if it took effect on a different date or had not commenced.

veracity.statement: My colleague Tanya Unkovich mentioned that, actually, about one out of every five gift cards in this country expire.
veracity.explanation: Relays a colleague's statistic, restating it as a proportion of cards rather than of cardholders.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare against what Unkovich actually said earlier in this debate and the underlying Consumer NZ figure; true if roughly 20% of gift cards sold in NZ expire unredeemed, false if the underlying finding is about the share of gift card *holders* who have had a card expire rather than the share of cards.

veracity.statement: What this bill, essentially, does is change the Fair Trading Act to require that gift cards have an expiry date of three years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the bill mandates a three-year expiry date, where the operative clause described elsewhere in the debate prohibits expiry dates of less than three years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Text of the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill; true if the bill requires gift cards to carry a three-year expiry date, false if it instead sets a three-year *minimum* (leaving longer or no expiry permitted).

specificity.statement: Now, the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill seeks to prohibit the sale of gift cards with an expiry date of less than three years after the initial sale date.
specificity.explanation: Names the bill, the prohibited conduct, the three-year threshold and the date it runs from — fully checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The reason being is that revenue recognition is often very different for gift cards. While someone might go in and buy a card, they exchange money, the sale is up front but it doesn’t actually qualify for revenue recognition because no goods or services have actually been exchanged yet. So it sits on the balance sheet as a liability for the business owner.
specificity.explanation: Describes a concrete mechanism (revenue recognition timing, liability on the balance sheet, recognition at redemption), though without figures or the compliance cost.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For example, Mr Speaker, if you’re selling a gift card for charitable purposes, that’s not included in this bill. If you receive a gift card for substitution for returned goods—for example, you take your clothes that you got from your birthday back in and you get a gift card voucher—that is not under the definition of this bill.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete categories excluded from the bill's definition of a gift card (charitable sales, refund substitution vouchers), which can be checked directly against the clause; no section numbers or thresholds given.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reason being is that revenue recognition is often very different for gift cards. While someone might go in and buy a card, they exchange money, the sale is up front but it doesn’t actually qualify for revenue recognition because no goods or services have actually been exchanged yet. So it sits on the balance sheet as a liability for the business owner.
rigor.explanation: A genuine supporting inference for why a transition period is needed: the accounting premise (unredeemed cards sit as a liability, revenue recognised only on redemption) does support the conclusion that businesses need lead time to adjust processes. No fallacy; the step from accounting complexity to adjustment time is modest but tracks.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So we have put in a transition time of 18 months, which we think is fair and reasonable for businesses to respond to this piece of legislation.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism and figure — an 18-month transition period in the bill — which anyone could check against the legislation and act on. Lacks only detail of how the period is phased.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What we do know is that 54 percent of New Zealanders have received a gift card in the last two years, and 24 percent of New Zealanders are left with gift cards they can never redeem because they are expired or the business has closed.
specificity.explanation: Two precise, checkable percentages tied to a defined population and timeframe, supporting the case for the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Booksellers Aotearoa New Zealand noted that where we were heading would align us with the Australian model—a three-year expiry date—and that currently they’re selling, usually, with a two-year expiry, although they had extended this during COVID.
specificity.explanation: Names the submitter, the comparator jurisdiction and the exact expiry periods at issue (three years versus the current two), all of which can be checked against the submission.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It is very encouraging to see that almost all parties have signalled that they’re supporting this bill through the House. The only party that’s not is the ACT Party.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that at the second reading of this bill every party in the House except ACT had signalled support, and that ACT alone was opposed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard record of the second reading of the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill (31 July 2024) and the select committee report: true if every party except ACT indicated support at second reading and ACT was the sole dissenting party; false if any other party also opposed, or if ACT did not oppose.

veracity.statement: I think today is probably a day that most New Zealanders know exactly that feeling because they’ve been promised $250 and they discover it’s $2.15.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the tax changes taking effect on 31 July 2024 were promised as $250 but delivered $2.15 to most New Zealanders.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD Budget 2024 personal income tax threshold change tables and the National Party's 2023 tax plan: true if the advertised figure was $250 (per fortnight) and the gain actually received by most New Zealanders was around $2.15; false if $250 was only ever the maximum for a specific household type and typical gains were materially above $2.15.

veracity.statement: What we do know is that 54 percent of New Zealanders have received a gift card in the last two years, and 24 percent of New Zealanders are left with gift cards they can never redeem because they are expired or the business has closed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two survey statistics about New Zealanders' receipt and non-redemption of gift cards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The survey source behind these figures (Consumer NZ / the bill's regulatory impact or select committee evidence on gift card use in New Zealand): true if that evidence reports approximately 54% receiving a gift card in the previous two years and approximately 24% left with unredeemable cards; false if the published figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: It’s worth $267 million dollars in unspent gift cards. That’s only one-tenth the value of the gift card that landlords are getting, but it’s still a lot of money.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that unspent gift cards in New Zealand amount to $267 million, and compares that to the value of the Government's restoration of interest deductibility for landlords.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Select committee evidence or Consumer NZ estimates of the value of unredeemed gift cards in New Zealand: true if a published estimate is around $267 million; false if the published estimate differs materially or no such estimate exists.

civility.statement: Now, most of you—this House, Mr Speaker—doesn’t have necessarily the best grasp of economics, but one of the biggest things you learn in economics is that free markets require the power of information and perfect information.
civility.explanation: Condescension directed at fellow members' competence — telling most of the House they do not understand economics before lecturing them. Short of a direct insult at an individual, but it disparages members rather than the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If I think of the great architects of the ACT Party, the Roger Douglases, the Derek Quigleys, the Richard Prebbles, they would really want to support pieces of legislation that empower the consumer.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority and to tradition: the conclusion that ACT should back the bill rests entirely on what the party's founders would supposedly have wanted, with nothing offered about the bill's actual effects to bridge the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Actually, businesses support this piece of legislation. They support it because it actually helps manage their financial liability. It creates a lower and upper bound on their financial liability for their accounts.
rigor.explanation: A real inference with a stated mechanism — the bill bounds liability, therefore businesses benefit and support it — but it generalises from unnamed submitters to 'businesses' as a class without evidence of how broadly that support runs.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think today is probably a day that most New Zealanders know exactly that feeling because they’ve been promised $250 and they discover it’s $2.15.
focus.explanation: Uses the bill's subject as a hook for a point about the Government's tax package; there is a named policy and figures, but the weight of the remark is partisan framing rather than the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s worth $267 million dollars in unspent gift cards. That’s only one-tenth the value of the gift card that landlords are getting, but it’s still a lot of money.
focus.explanation: Carries a genuine figure about the policy problem the bill addresses, but half the remark is a partisan aside about landlord tax settings unrelated to the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And whilst our ACT Party colleagues may have pinned their hopes on something else, we’re yet to see what that is.
focus.explanation: A remark entirely about another party's unstated position, naming no policy, figure or alternative mechanism; there is nothing for the House to engage with on the substance of the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As we’ve already heard tonight, one in four gift cards is expired, and 54 percent of people have used gift cards in the past two years, so we would definitely see a lot of expired gift cards.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two survey figures: that a quarter of gift cards go unredeemed/expire, and that 54% of people used a gift card in the past two years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Consumer New Zealand gift card survey (and any departmental/MBIE regulatory impact statement for the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill) cited in the 2024 debate; true if those sources report approximately one in four gift cards expiring unused and approximately 54% usage in the last two years, false if the figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: Research has actually found—I’ve read in some of these documents here—that we could be losing $10 million a year on cards before they are redeemed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that research puts the annual value of unredeemed New Zealand gift cards at about $10 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The research relied on in the bill's select committee report / MBIE regulatory impact statement or Consumer NZ analysis; true if a cited study estimates roughly $10 million a year in unredeemed gift card value in NZ, false if no such estimate exists or the published figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: I mean, if we take a little bit of information from internationally, some of the other countries around the world: in Canada, expiry dates are banned, and in the USA, a five-year expiry date is required—five years.
veracity.explanation: Two comparative legal claims: that Canada prohibits gift card expiry dates, and that United States law mandates a minimum five-year expiry.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Canadian provincial consumer protection statutes (e.g. Ontario Consumer Protection Act gift card regulations) and the US Credit CARD Act 2009 gift certificate provisions; true if Canadian jurisdictions generally prohibit expiry on gift cards and US federal law sets a five-year minimum before funds expire, false if either regime does not work that way.

veracity.statement: Actually, I mean, I would say it is a great day for consumers here in New Zealand, an amazing day today because historically, in the past 14 years, New Zealanders have not had tax relief.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no tax relief has been delivered to New Zealanders in the 14 years before 31 July 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue / Treasury record of personal income tax changes between 2010 and 2024; true if no reduction in personal income tax rates or thresholds took effect in that period, false if any personal tax relief measure (rate cut, threshold shift, or a tax credit such as the Independent Earner Tax Credit) took effect.

veracity.statement: I sit on the Finance and Expenditure Committee—as well as the Primary Production Committee, actually—and we are having a banking inquiry at the moment, which is also going to be, you know, very valuable for our consumers out there because we have one of the most uncompetitive banking sectors in the world.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's banking sector ranks among the least competitive internationally.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cross-country competition measures — Commerce Commission personal banking market study (2024), RBNZ and OECD/IMF comparisons of bank concentration, net interest margins and return on equity; true if NZ sits at the extreme low-competition end of comparable economies on those measures, false if NZ is broadly comparable to peer countries such as Australia and Canada.

specificity.statement: As we’ve already heard tonight, one in four gift cards is expired, and 54 percent of people have used gift cards in the past two years, so we would definitely see a lot of expired gift cards.
specificity.explanation: Carries two precise, checkable proportions attached to a named consumer problem.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As we’ve already talked about, the transition period will be over an 18-month period of time, which I think is very, very fair and reasonable.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete feature of the bill with a定 timeframe (an 18-month transition), though it gives no detail on what the transition requires of retailers.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This bill is all about the consumer and being pro the consumer, which is good for business and good for the economy, because we want to support consumers.
rigor.explanation: Circular: the conclusion that a pro-consumer bill is good for business and the economy is supported only by restating that we want to support consumers. No mechanism linking consumer protection to business or economic benefit is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I must say, if you think about kids and they’ve got this gift card and they think they’re going to go and spend it, only to arrive at the shop and discover it’s expired, just the look on the children’s faces; they’re just absolutely devastated that their gift card is expired.
rigor.explanation: Bare appeal to emotion offered as the support for the bill — a vignette of disappointed children stands in place of any argument about why a three-year statutory minimum is the right remedy.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We need to foster consumer confidence in our economy, which is what we’re all about on this side of the House—you know, strengthening our economy and making sure that we are supporting our hard-working consumers out there.
focus.explanation: A general-purpose claim about what her own side of the House stands for, with no policy, mechanism or measure named; the gift card bill under debate drops out entirely in favour of party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And of course, as my colleague has already said, the card cannot be the ones that are used for public transport and utilities and those types of cards and vouchers are not able to be included in this bill and have the three-year limit, which, again, seems quite fair.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual scope of the measure before the House — which categories of card are carved out of the three-year expiry rule — with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Now, expiry dates on gift cards have been given the boot in other countries. For instance—and this has been spoken about by other MPs—in most of Canada, they have banned expiry dates on gift cards. In the US and Ireland, they are required to have expiry dates of about five years. In Australia—our neighbouring country—in 2019, they strengthened their laws, requiring gift cards to be valid for a period of three years, and I believe that this is one of the things that we’re trying to do with this bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three comparative legal facts: that most Canadian jurisdictions ban gift-card expiry dates; that the US and Ireland require a minimum validity of about five years; and that Australia legislated a three-year minimum in 2019.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Statutes and regulators: Canadian provincial consumer protection legislation on gift card expiry (e.g. Ontario Consumer Protection Act regs); the US Credit CARD Act 2009 gift certificate provisions; Ireland's Consumer Protection (Gift Vouchers) Act 2019; and the Australian Treasury Laws Amendment (Gift Cards) Act 2018/2019 ACCC guidance. True if each jurisdiction's stated minimum period and ban match; false if any of the three periods or the 2019 Australian date is materially wrong.

veracity.statement: We know from research that New Zealanders are leaving millions and millions of dollars on gift cards unspent. They found that more than a third of New Zealanders have at least one unused gift card, and they’ve put the cumulative value to around about $267 million, which is a staggering amount.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a research finding that more than one third of New Zealanders hold at least one unused gift card and that the cumulative unspent value is approximately $267 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The underlying survey (Consumer NZ / research cited in the bill's select committee report or first reading speeches). True if a published survey reports both a >33% incidence of unused gift cards among New Zealanders and an aggregate unspent value of about $267 million; false if the published figures differ materially or no such study exists.

veracity.statement: When Consumer New Zealand came to make a submission on this bill—and I was one of the substitute MPs that sat in on this particular day at the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee—they told us that they have received many complaints from consumers about expired gift cards. They actually urged the select committee to consider extending it from three years to a period of five years, and they argued that this would be in order to ensure that consumers do not miss out on what is rightfully theirs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Consumer NZ submitted to the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee on this bill and recommended lengthening the minimum expiry period from three years to five.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Consumer NZ's written submission and the committee's report on the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill. True if the submission recommends a five-year rather than three-year minimum; false if it made no such recommendation or supported a different period.

veracity.statement: In this context, we are doing what is right for consumers, and I’d like to actually say that I agree with the author of this bill, Dan Bidois, when he said earlier on that the ACT Party, which is the only party in this House who does not agree with this bill—I find it really interesting because “Consumers” is actually part of their name. ACT stands for the Association of Consumers and Taxpayers, so why is it that on this occasion, ACT is not advocating for and not standing up for consumers of gift cards?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that ACT is the only party in the House opposing the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The party-vote record for the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill's readings in Hansard. True if ACT is recorded as the sole party voting against; false if any other party also opposed or if ACT supported it.

veracity.statement: First of all, I’d like to say a huge congratulations to the National Minister Melissa Lee, and senior MP, for actually putting her name on this and being drawn from the biscuit tin, from the ballot, and also taking it through the first reading. Now it is transferred to the name of Dan Bidois, MP, my really good friend and a really good MP.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the bill was drawn from the members' ballot in Melissa Lee's name, that she took it through its first reading, and that it has since been transferred to Dan Bidois.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bill record for the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill (ballot draw notice, first reading Hansard, and the transfer-of-bill notice). True if Lee is the original member in charge and moved the first reading with a subsequent transfer to Bidois; false if a different member introduced it or no transfer occurred.

specificity.statement: Now, expiry dates on gift cards have been given the boot in other countries. For instance—and this has been spoken about by other MPs—in most of Canada, they have banned expiry dates on gift cards. In the US and Ireland, they are required to have expiry dates of about five years. In Australia—our neighbouring country—in 2019, they strengthened their laws, requiring gift cards to be valid for a period of three years, and I believe that this is one of the things that we’re trying to do with this bill.
specificity.explanation: Names four jurisdictions, the rule in each, a specific number of years, and a year for the Australian change — all directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We know from research that New Zealanders are leaving millions and millions of dollars on gift cards unspent. They found that more than a third of New Zealanders have at least one unused gift card, and they’ve put the cumulative value to around about $267 million, which is a staggering amount.
specificity.explanation: Gives a proportion and a dollar total that could be traced to a source, though the research itself is not named.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When Consumer New Zealand came to make a submission on this bill—and I was one of the substitute MPs that sat in on this particular day at the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee—they told us that they have received many complaints from consumers about expired gift cards. They actually urged the select committee to consider extending it from three years to a period of five years, and they argued that this would be in order to ensure that consumers do not miss out on what is rightfully theirs.
specificity.explanation: Names the submitter, the select committee, and the precise change sought (three years to five years).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill is very helpful for many of our Kiwis and New Zealanders, because it extends the time to at least three years for the gift voucher, gift card, and electronic vouchers, but, also, it allows, actually, consumers to have more time to go through a thorough process—especially now with our cost of living pressure in New Zealand—to really go through and find the item that they really need for their family or for themselves as individuals.
specificity.explanation: Names the minimum period and the instruments covered, but the benefit claimed is left general with no figures or evidence.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In this context, we are doing what is right for consumers, and I’d like to actually say that I agree with the author of this bill, Dan Bidois, when he said earlier on that the ACT Party, which is the only party in this House who does not agree with this bill—I find it really interesting because “Consumers” is actually part of their name. ACT stands for the Association of Consumers and Taxpayers, so why is it that on this occasion, ACT is not advocating for and not standing up for consumers of gift cards?
civility.explanation: Pointed and a little needling toward a party, but no individual is attacked and no bad faith is imputed to a person.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In this context, we are doing what is right for consumers, and I’d like to actually say that I agree with the author of this bill, Dan Bidois, when he said earlier on that the ACT Party, which is the only party in this House who does not agree with this bill—I find it really interesting because “Consumers” is actually part of their name. ACT stands for the Association of Consumers and Taxpayers, so why is it that on this occasion, ACT is not advocating for and not standing up for consumers of gift cards?
focus.explanation: A real point about a party's position on the measure before the House, but the weight of it is party framing (what ACT's name stands for) rather than the substance of expiry periods.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill is very helpful for many of our Kiwis and New Zealanders, because it extends the time to at least three years for the gift voucher, gift card, and electronic vouchers, but, also, it allows, actually, consumers to have more time to go through a thorough process—especially now with our cost of living pressure in New Zealand—to really go through and find the item that they really need for their family or for themselves as individuals.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: the mechanism (a minimum three-year period), what it covers, and who it affects.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In this context, we are doing what is right for consumers, and I’d like to actually say that I agree with the author of this bill, Dan Bidois, when he said earlier on that the ACT Party, which is the only party in this House who does not agree with this bill—I find it really interesting because “Consumers” is actually part of their name. ACT stands for the Association of Consumers and Taxpayers, so why is it that on this occasion, ACT is not advocating for and not standing up for consumers of gift cards?
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur / argument from a party's name: that 'Consumers' appears in ACT's acronym gives no reason why a three-year minimum expiry period must be good consumer policy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, as a young mother who is still experiencing the six years of my baby brain, I really think that extending the expiry date for gift cards will be beneficial for many people, including the new mums out there in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single personal anecdote to a benefit for a broad class of people — an appeal to anecdote, with nothing offered to show her experience is representative.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The ACT Party have opposed this bill that we are talking about tonight for exactly the same reasons they opposed those reforms when Labour was in Government, because having a swing at big business is not the end of town that they will be going for.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that ACT voted against/opposed the gift card expiry bill, and that ACT also opposed Labour's supermarket-duopoly reforms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard division record for the third reading of the Gift Cards (Expiry of Gift Cards) Amendment Bill on 31 July 2024, plus the division record for the Grocery Industry Competition Act 2023: true if ACT is recorded voting against both, false if ACT supported either.

veracity.statement: The idea that a Government can advance a pro-consumer agenda while, at the same time, growing the economy is absolutely the approach that advanced economies around the world at the moment are taking. We’ve seen the Biden administration working through a huge, huge piece of legislation called the Inflation Reduction Act, which has a number of these initiatives which are about making things easier for consumers, making it harder for the large corporates that exercise a huge amount of market power in their market to be able to take advantage of ordinary people.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the US Inflation Reduction Act contains a number of measures aimed at helping consumers and curbing the market power of large corporates.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The enacted text and official summaries of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (e.g. Medicare drug price negotiation, consumer energy rebates): true if the Act contains multiple provisions directed at consumer costs and corporate pricing power, false if its provisions are confined to matters unrelated to consumer protection or corporate market power.

veracity.statement: That’s why jurisdictions around the world, as my colleague the Hon Jenny Salesa has said, have set their expiry dates up to five years—in some cases, seven; in some cases, there are no expiries at all—and that would be an appropriate thing for, I think, New Zealand to move to in future, where we can be sure that consumers are always going to be able to get the goods and services that they think they have paid for from these businesses.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that comparable overseas jurisdictions set gift card minimum expiry periods of up to five or seven years, and that some prohibit expiry entirely.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Statutory gift card expiry rules in comparable jurisdictions (e.g. Australian Competition and Consumer Act minimum period, Canadian provincial rules, US state gift card statutes): true if at least one jurisdiction mandates a minimum of around five years or more and at least one prohibits expiry, false if the longest mandated minimums are materially shorter and no jurisdiction bars expiry.

veracity.statement: It’s interesting, one in five recipients lose out when they don’t redeem before expiry, which is costing—as has been mentioned—approximately $10 million a year, which would be for our everyday Kiwis.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that one in five gift card recipients fail to redeem before expiry and that the resulting loss to consumers is about $10 million a year in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE advice / the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee report on the Gift Cards (Expiry of Gift Cards) Amendment Bill: true if those documents give a non-redemption rate of about 20% and an annual consumer loss of about $10 million, false if the cited figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: It’s a good day for all New Zealanders, with tax relief, being 31 July.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's personal income tax relief took effect on 31 July 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Taxation (Budget Measures) Act 2024 commencement provisions and IRD guidance on the new personal income tax thresholds: true if the threshold changes applied from 31 July 2024, false if they commenced on a different date.

focus.statement: The ACT Party have opposed this bill that we are talking about tonight for exactly the same reasons they opposed those reforms when Labour was in Government, because having a swing at big business is not the end of town that they will be going for.
focus.explanation: Names a specific bill and a specific party position (legitimate policy content), but the weight of the sentence is an imputation about which 'end of town' ACT serves rather than the measure itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think there is more that we could be doing here on things like junk fees. Consumers across New Zealand’s market are paying extra, more than the ticket price, when they’re buying things like airline fees, when they’re paying for things like concert tickets, and that is incredibly frustrating for consumers in exactly the same way that having an expired gift card is.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a consumer-policy question — add-on fees beyond the advertised price — with concrete sectors named and no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’d love the Government to continue that work, and not for it to be something that is relegated to members’ bills only, not for it to be something that is popular to do—because a pro-consumer agenda is popular when they are in Opposition—but something that they are focused on in Government.
focus.explanation: A real policy ask (carry on the pricing-transparency work rather than leaving it to members' bills) wrapped in a claim about the governing parties' opportunism.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The idea that a Government can advance a pro-consumer agenda while, at the same time, growing the economy is absolutely the approach that advanced economies around the world at the moment are taking. We’ve seen the Biden administration working through a huge, huge piece of legislation called the Inflation Reduction Act, which has a number of these initiatives which are about making things easier for consumers, making it harder for the large corporates that exercise a huge amount of market power in their market to be able to take advantage of ordinary people.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that this is the right approach rests on an appeal to what other 'advanced economies' are doing, with a single illustrative example offered; nothing connects the cited legislation's effects to the claim that pro-consumer rules and economic growth go together.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I think there is more that we could be doing here on things like junk fees. Consumers across New Zealand’s market are paying extra, more than the ticket price, when they’re buying things like airline fees, when they’re paying for things like concert tickets, and that is incredibly frustrating for consumers in exactly the same way that having an expired gift card is.
specificity.explanation: Names the problem and two example markets (airlines, concert tickets) but gives no figures, no mechanism and no timeframe for any remedy.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s interesting, one in five recipients lose out when they don’t redeem before expiry, which is costing—as has been mentioned—approximately $10 million a year, which would be for our everyday Kiwis.
specificity.explanation: Carries a proportion and a dollar figure tied to a defined harm; both are checkable against the select committee material.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I feel for Mr Jackson over there. He’s been looking a bit sad and grumpy lately, and I thought, actually, for Father’s Day, we could all chip in and get him a Prezzy Card and cheer him up, because I’m really feeling for him and I want to encourage him because I really like him.
civility.explanation: Remarks on another member's demeanour ('sad and grumpy') and makes him the butt of a joke, which lands on the person rather than any argument, though it is softened by explicit goodwill.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But as has been mentioned, in other countries like Canada, expiry dates are banned—they don’t even have expiry dates.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Canada prohibits expiry dates on gift cards outright.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Canadian provincial consumer protection legislation (e.g. Ontario Consumer Protection Act gift card regulations, BC, Alberta, Quebec) and federal guidance as at July 2024; true if gift card expiry dates are prohibited for general-purpose retail gift cards across Canadian jurisdictions, false if expiry dates remain lawful generally or the ban is limited to a minority of provinces or card types.

veracity.statement: And the US has a five-year expiry.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that United States law sets a five-year expiry rule for gift cards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The US Credit CARD Act 2009 gift certificate provisions and Federal Reserve Regulation E subpart B; true if federal law requires gift card funds to remain valid for at least five years from issue/last load, false if the federal minimum is a different period or no such rule exists.

veracity.statement: Of the few retailers who publish non-redemption information, they calculate non-redemption rates between 5 and 10 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that retailers which disclose breakage report non-redemption rates in the 5–10 percent range.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Consumer NZ's published gift card research and the breakage/unredeemed-balance disclosures in the annual reports of retailers that publish them; true if disclosed non-redemption rates fall in the 5–10% band, false if the published figures sit materially outside that range.

veracity.statement: As has been mentioned, approximately $267 million of gift cards throughout New Zealand have been unused.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a national total of roughly $267 million in unredeemed gift card value in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Consumer NZ gift card research, the bill's regulatory impact statement / departmental advice on the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill; true if a figure of about $267m in unused New Zealand gift card value is documented there, false if the sourced estimate is materially different or no such estimate exists.

veracity.statement: In the fiscal year 2021—talking about the market, Mr Luxton—Starbucks reportedly claimed a staggering $181 million in revenue from unused gift cards and loyalty accounts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Starbucks recognised about US$181 million of breakage revenue from unredeemed gift cards and loyalty balances in its 2021 financial year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Starbucks Corporation FY2021 Form 10-K, stored value card liability / breakage revenue disclosure; true if the recognised breakage figure is approximately $181m, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Once upon a time—actually, last year—in the bustling, fastest-growing city in New Zealand called Hamilton, or Kirikiriroa, there lived a young woman named Lauren.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, inside an illustrative story, that Hamilton is New Zealand's fastest-growing city.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates for the year to June 2023/2024; true if Hamilton city records the highest percentage population growth of New Zealand cities, false if another territorial authority classed as a city (e.g. Tauranga, Queenstown-Lakes, Auckland) grew faster in percentage terms.

rigor.statement: Cash or money doesn’t expire, so why do we put these artificial, constructed rules on these Prezzy Cards?
rigor.explanation: An argument from analogy: gift cards are treated as equivalent to cash, so expiry rules are inferred to be arbitrary. The analogy is asserted rather than defended — a gift card is a prepaid contractual claim on one retailer, not legal tender, and the differences (unclaimed liability accounting, business closure, redemption administration) are precisely what would justify or refute expiry. The conclusion leans on the unargued equivalence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You can appreciate it’s the net income, because they’ve got no cost against the Prezzy Card—it’s pure profit.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: because unredeemed card balances carry no cost of goods sold, breakage revenue drops largely to the bottom line, which explains why it is a larger share of net income than of total sales. The reasoning tracks — it overlooks card issuance and administration costs, so 'pure profit' overshoots slightly, but the conclusion broadly follows from the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Of the few retailers who publish non-redemption information, they calculate non-redemption rates between 5 and 10 percent.
specificity.explanation: Gives a quantified range (5–10 percent) tied to a named class of evidence (retailers who publish non-redemption information), so the claim can be checked against disclosures.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As has been mentioned, approximately $267 million of gift cards throughout New Zealand have been unused.
specificity.explanation: A single precise dollar figure for a named national quantity — checkable against the source, though the period it covers is not stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the fiscal year 2021—talking about the market, Mr Luxton—Starbucks reportedly claimed a staggering $181 million in revenue from unused gift cards and loyalty accounts.
specificity.explanation: Names the company, the fiscal year and an exact dollar amount, with the source of the revenue identified — directly verifiable against the filing.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Unfortunately, this one, we have 3.25 million New Zealanders that are KiwiSaver members—$93.7 billion invested.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two figures about KiwiSaver as at the time of speaking: total membership of 3.25 million and total funds invested of $93.7 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: FMA KiwiSaver Annual Report / IRD KiwiSaver statistics for the year to 31 March 2023 or 2024: true if membership is ~3.25m and total funds under management ~$93.7bn (within rounding), false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: In 2008, the National Government amended the KiwiSaver Act 2006 to clarify that whilst compulsory employer contributions must be paid in addition to an employee’s gross salary or wages, employers and employees can contract out of the requirement through good-faith bargaining.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a 2008 amendment made by a National government to the KiwiSaver Act 2006 allowed parties to contract out of the requirement that compulsory employer contributions be paid on top of gross salary, via good-faith bargaining.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative history of the KiwiSaver Act 2006 (amendments passed in 2008, e.g. the Taxation (Urgent Measures and Annual Rates) Act 2008) and the resulting 'total remuneration' contracting-out provision: true if a 2008 amendment under the National government inserted that contracting-out-by-good-faith-bargaining provision, false if the provision dates from a different year or government.

veracity.statement: The select committee process—unfortunately, ACT and National and New Zealand First in the Finance and Expenditure Committee report back had quite significant concerns with it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the National, ACT and NZ First members of the Finance and Expenditure Committee recorded significant concerns with the bill in the committee's report back to the House.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Finance and Expenditure Committee report on the Employment Relations (Protection for KiwiSaver Members) Amendment Bill: true if the report (or a minority view within it) records National, ACT and NZ First members opposing or raising significant concerns, false if no such view is recorded.

specificity.statement: In 2008, the National Government amended the KiwiSaver Act 2006 to clarify that whilst compulsory employer contributions must be paid in addition to an employee’s gross salary or wages, employers and employees can contract out of the requirement through good-faith bargaining.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act, the year, the amending government and the precise legal mechanism (contributions on top of gross pay, contract-out via good-faith bargaining) — directly checkable against the statute.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Unfortunately, this is more of an ideological bill, because what it says is that the relationship and the discussion and contract between employees and employers is broken.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the conclusion that the bill is 'ideological' rests on attributing to it a premise it does not state — that employer/employee bargaining is broken in general. A bill creating a narrow protection does not entail that claim, so the inference does not follow.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Actually, it has the real risk, if it was to pass, that cases that do need the attention of the Employment Tribunal would be blocked up with something, like this, that actually has no place to be there, because we believe it is important that an employer and an employee have the ability to bargain in good faith.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur in the stated reason: the belief that parties should bargain in good faith does not support the empirical conclusion that the tribunal would be clogged. No caseload evidence or volume estimate is offered to connect the new personal-grievance ground to congestion.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Unfortunately, this is more of an ideological bill, because what it says is that the relationship and the discussion and contract between employees and employers is broken.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the measure before the House and what it would do, rather than about the other party's record or character — high focus even though the inference is weak.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s like a problem-searching missile that’s just kind of cruising around, trying to land, and hasn’t quite landed it.
civility.explanation: Mocking, but the mockery lands on the bill rather than on Dr McLellan; the sneering tone about the bill's purpose edges toward the sponsor's motives without attacking her.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That context was a botched merger of district health boards (DHBs) where national planning and budgeting was disconnected from local management, where financial reporting was ineffective, where data systems were fragmented, and where, in consequence, there was limited oversight of financial performance.
civility.explanation: Harsh language ('botched') is aimed entirely at the structural reform and its systems, not at any individual. Under the re-anchored scale, brutal criticism of a policy is the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Should, then, directors working for her Government be aware that their reputations can be defamed without due process if it is politically convenient for the Government?
civility.explanation: Goes beyond the substance of the decision to impute bad faith — that the Minister defames appointees when it is 'politically convenient'. That is an attribution of motive, not an argument about the merits.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I reject the characterisation that the member has made, and that’s for this reason: I would agree that each of the individuals who served on the Health New Zealand board are capable individuals, and I believe that every one of them was on that board because they wanted to do better for New Zealanders in the health system.
civility.explanation: Faced with a hostile question, she rejects the framing while explicitly crediting the board members' capability and good intentions; the criticism is redirected to the system, attacking no person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m asking the Minister: given that the National Party brought in kura kaupapa Māori, why is he now being lectured on it?
civility.explanation: 'Being lectured on it' dismisses the questioner's standing to ask rather than engaging what was asked; condescending toward the member without landing a direct personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The aim is to change the culture inside the public sector after years of opaque, inefficient, and wasteful spending.
civility.explanation: A severe judgement — 'opaque, inefficient, and wasteful' — directed at spending practice and institutional culture, naming and disparaging no individual.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That context was a botched merger of district health boards (DHBs) where national planning and budgeting was disconnected from local management, where financial reporting was ineffective, where data systems were fragmented, and where, in consequence, there was limited oversight of financial performance.
specificity.explanation: Names the reform (DHB merger) and lists four concrete deficiencies (planning/budgeting disconnect, reporting, data systems, oversight), but supplies no figures, dates or documents that would let someone check the characterisation.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When did the Minister of Health communicate to her that the Te Whatu Ora board rejected her allegations about their performance, and did she seek a meeting with them in light of their letter to the Minister of Health dated 22 March?
specificity.explanation: Pins the question to a named body, a named document and an exact date (22 March letter), so the answer is checkable rather than open-ended.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Given her concerns, why does she feel more qualified than board members whose experience includes overseeing the largest Government IT project that was on time and under budget, the executive of Air New Zealand and NZX50 companies, and a former National Party finance spokesperson?
specificity.explanation: Itemises four concrete credentials (a named-scale IT programme delivered on time and under budget, Air New Zealand executive, NZX50 directorships, a former National finance spokesperson), each identifiable and checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have set ambitious targets for education and committed to excellent outcomes, including attendance and achievement, and with tools such as structured literacy.
specificity.explanation: Names one identifiable instrument (structured literacy) and two domains, but no target figures, no baselines and no dates, so 'ambitious targets' and 'excellent outcomes' carry no checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Hei waha kōrero mō te Minita Mātauranga [On behalf of the Minister of Education], the Minister is currently progressing a number of matters in relation to this report, but particularly asking for advice on the report, and when that advice is received back from officials, she will give it due consideration.
specificity.explanation: Asked what actions will be taken, the answer names no action, no timeframe and no mechanism — 'a number of matters', 'asking for advice' and 'due consideration' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Given the report cited the very poor state of buildings and infrastructure of several of the kura shown to them, will she commit to reinstating the building programmes of the 15 kura Māori that have had their building programme stopped as a result of the Government’s cost-saving measures; if not, why not?
specificity.explanation: Names a precise number of affected kura (15), the specific programmes halted, the stated cause, and the exact remedy sought — reinstatement — so the answer can be checked against the record.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: However, I will note that in Budget 2024, 19 kura have been supported for renovation.
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable figure tied to a named Budget — 19 kura funded for renovation — though no dollar amount or schedule is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are 137 investments in planning, with an estimated value of $93.7 billion, and 171 investments in delivery, with a combined approved budget of $79.4 billion.
specificity.explanation: Four exact figures — counts and dollar values for both the planning and delivery pipelines — all traceable to a named published report.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In June alone, Health New Zealand has advised that over 883 people were hired, including 124 doctors, 243 nurses, 30 midwives, and 140 allied health professionals. That doesn’t sound like a hiring freeze to me.
specificity.explanation: A named month, a total and a four-way breakdown by occupational group, sourced to the agency that supplied the figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: He was talking about cash-flow analysis and said, “To even get an understanding of cash flow from the system has been incredibly difficult.”, and that is exactly what I’ve just been saying.
veracity.explanation: Willis relays a direct quotation attributed to the Prime Minister and asserts its subject matter was cash-flow analysis rather than the broader claim put to her.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Prime Minister's public remarks on Health New Zealand finances in the days preceding 1 August 2024 (transcripts, press-conference recordings or media reports); true if he used words materially identical to 'To even get an understanding of cash flow from the system has been incredibly difficult' in a discussion of cash flow, false if no such statement exists or the quotation misrepresents what he said.

veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Health New Zealand board members' experience included overseeing the largest Government IT project delivered on time and under budget, Air New Zealand executive office, NZX50 company directorships, and a former National Party finance spokesperson.

veracity.statement: What that has shown, in due course, is that actually the financial position was a lot worse than was made clear at the time.

veracity.statement: Given that the Waitangi Tribunal described kura kaupapa Māori as “a proven model” where “success has been achieved”, what actions will she take to expedite the development and expansion of kaupapa Māori education as a means of closing the Māori educational achievement gap?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Waitangi Tribunal's report described kura kaupapa Māori as 'a proven model' in which 'success has been achieved'.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Waitangi Tribunal report Kei Ahotea Te Aho Matua (Wai 3310); true if the quoted phrases appear and carry that meaning about kura kaupapa Māori, false if the phrases are absent or used in a materially different sense.

veracity.statement: Given the report cited the very poor state of buildings and infrastructure of several of the kura shown to them, will she commit to reinstating the building programmes of the 15 kura Māori that have had their building programme stopped as a result of the Government’s cost-saving measures; if not, why not?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the building programmes of 15 Māori-medium schools were stopped as a result of the Government's cost-saving measures.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education school property programme records and Budget 2024 capital decisions for Māori-medium schools; true if approximately 15 kura had approved building programmes halted or deferred on cost-saving grounds, false if the number is materially different or the stoppages are not attributable to savings decisions.

veracity.statement: I’m asking the Minister: given that the National Party brought in kura kaupapa Māori, why is he now being lectured on it?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the National Party established or introduced kura kaupapa Māori.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative and administrative record for the formal recognition and state funding of kura kaupapa Māori — principally the Education Act 1989 (s155) and the ministerial decisions preceding it — and which party held government at that time; true if kura kaupapa Māori were brought into the state system under a National government, false if under Labour.

veracity.statement: However, I will note that in Budget 2024, 19 kura have been supported for renovation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Budget 2024 provided support for the renovation of 19 kura.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 education capital allocations and Ministry of Education announcements on Māori-medium school property; true if 19 kura were funded for renovation under Budget 2024, false if the number is materially different or no such allocation exists.

veracity.statement: There are 137 investments in planning, with an estimated value of $93.7 billion, and 171 investments in delivery, with a combined approved budget of $79.4 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific pipeline counts and values from the Quarterly Investment Report for the quarter ending March 2024.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's Quarterly Investment Report for the quarter ending March 2024; true if it records 137 investments in planning valued at about $93.7 billion and 171 in delivery with an approved budget of about $79.4 billion, false if the published figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: In June alone, Health New Zealand has advised that over 883 people were hired, including 124 doctors, 243 nurses, 30 midwives, and 140 allied health professionals. That doesn’t sound like a hiring freeze to me.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand recruitment/commencement data for June 2024 (as released to the Minister, in OIA responses, or in select committee evidence); true if total hires exceeded 883 with roughly those occupational splits, false if the totals or categories differ materially.

focus.statement: When did the Minister of Health communicate to her that the Te Whatu Ora board rejected her allegations about their performance, and did she seek a meeting with them in light of their letter to the Minister of Health dated 22 March?

veracity.statement: This Government is implementing a more proactive welfare system to support New Zealanders into work, because in the six years before we came to office the number of people receiving the jobseeker benefit increased by 70,000, or 57 percent.

veracity.explanation: Asserts that Treasury advice dated 23 February 2024 stated 9,000 beneficiaries would be worse off as a result of the tax changes.
