veracity.statement: Is cutting $120 million in community prevention services, like Family Start, the change that community organisations have called for when Social Service Providers Aotearoa chief executive Belinda Himiona is saying that providers are very worried that child safety and that whānau wellbeing is going to be impacted by these reductions?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that $120 million has been cut from community prevention services including Family Start, and that the named sector chief executive has publicly expressed those concerns.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Oranga Tamariki / Vote Social Development appropriations and Oranga Tamariki savings announcements for 2024: true if reductions to community prevention/early intervention contracts (including Family Start) total approximately $120m, false if the documented figure is materially different; plus a contemporaneous public statement by Belinda Himiona of Social Service Providers Aotearoa in those terms.

veracity.statement: What I would say is that since I’ve started as the children’s Minister, I have always made it very clear that the best interests and the safety of the children should be at the forefront of every decision made, whether you’re Māori, non-Māori, or any ethnicity in this country, because I’m sick to death of us accepting the fact that we lose one baby every five weeks in this country to the hands of somebody who is supposed to care about them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on average one infant is killed in New Zealand every five weeks by a caregiver — roughly ten child deaths a year at the hands of someone responsible for their care.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police homicide victim statistics and Family Violence Death Review Committee reports on child homicide: true if child/infant homicides by a caregiver average approximately 10 per year (one per five weeks), false if the recorded rate is materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: The maths achievement data released on the weekend was deeply concerning, especially for the just 12 percent of young Māori who are not at curriculum in maths at year 8, according to the data from last year. Shockingly, 76 percent were more than a year behind.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 76 percent of Māori year 8 students were more than a year behind the maths curriculum in the 2023 achievement data (the '12 percent' clause is a spoken word-order slip for 12 percent being AT curriculum level).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Education Curriculum Insights and Progress Study (maths, year 8, 2023) released in August 2024: true if the reported share of Māori year 8 students more than a year behind curriculum expectation is approximately 76 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: I’d just like to say, police will always play a role when it comes to responding to violence, including family violence or where there has been a crime where someone is in immediate danger. But I would also like to remind them that it’s important to note that the six-month proof of concept trial for this was trialled by the previous Government before we even began this. So this is something that the previous Government was on board with and I would expect they still will be.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the six-month proof-of-concept trial of the police family-violence call triage approach was begun under the previous (Labour) Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police announcements and Police/Ministerial records on the start date of the family violence call triage proof-of-concept trial: true if the six-month trial commenced before the change of Government in November 2023, false if it began under the current Government.

veracity.statement: Does she agree with Mark Mitchell regarding the 3,000 fewer family violence investigations since December 2023, “Those calls are being triaged and the number has come down”; if not, why not?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that there have been approximately 3,000 fewer police family violence investigations since December 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police family violence investigation counts (monthly Police data / responses to written questions) comparing the period from December 2023 with the equivalent prior period: true if the decline is approximately 3,000 investigations, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Why, then, has there been a reduction in victimisations where the offender is known to the victim, by 24 percent since December last year?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 24 percent fall in recorded victimisations where the offender was known to the victim since December 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police victimisation time-series data (offender known to victim category) for December 2023 to mid-2024: true if the recorded reduction is approximately 24 percent, false if materially different.

rigor.statement: It’s commonplace in outlawed motorcycle gangs to wear sort of silver jewellery with motifs on it which fit the description of gang insignia. They signify some kind of association with a gang, but, of course, if you’re walking down the road and someone is wearing a silver ring, you’re not going to even notice that it’s a gang insignia. However, that could be used as a reason for the police to detain and remove that ring, and so on and so forth, in a way which is actually at odds with the purpose of the bill, because it wasn’t intimidating at all.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the committee: premise that the bill's stated purpose is preventing intimidation, premise that a ring bearing gang motifs is not noticeable, conclusion that seizing it would not serve that purpose. The conclusion tracks the premises; the only gap is the unstated assumption that the definition in the bill actually captures jewellery.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Really, by having dispersal notices, banning gang patches, and having the impact of those, there is some quite good research that demonstrates that that just entrenches those whānau within those communities.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on a bare appeal to unnamed authority — 'some quite good research' — with no study, finding or mechanism identified, so nothing is offered that connects dispersal notices and patch bans to entrenchment.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would propose to the Minister that the introduction of this legislation alongside this Government’s proposal to remove section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act would make Māori tamariki and rangatahi even more susceptible to mismanagement by the State, if they have a primary caregiver who is no longer able to take up that role, as a result of incarceration.
rigor.explanation: A coherent conditional chain — incarceration of caregivers, loss of the section 7AA protections, greater State-care exposure — but the step from this bill to increased incarceration of caregivers is asserted rather than shown, leaving a real gap between what is offered and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And yet children, presumably, are subject to this quasi-criminal regime, and it strikes me that there hasn’t been a lot of thinking done around how this bill will fit with the wider framework around the behaviour of young people and the response of not only police courts but also Oranga Tamariki and other agencies to those behaviours.
rigor.explanation: Argument from absence of evidence plus personal impression ('it strikes me'): the conclusion that insufficient analysis was done is inferred from the speaker not having seen it, and the premise that children are covered is itself hedged with 'presumably'.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s commonplace in outlawed motorcycle gangs to wear sort of silver jewellery with motifs on it which fit the description of gang insignia. They signify some kind of association with a gang, but, of course, if you’re walking down the road and someone is wearing a silver ring, you’re not going to even notice that it’s a gang insignia. However, that could be used as a reason for the police to detain and remove that ring, and so on and so forth, in a way which is actually at odds with the purpose of the bill, because it wasn’t intimidating at all.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the mechanism of the bill — the definition of gang insignia and the police power it would trigger — with a concrete worked example. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Really, by having dispersal notices, banning gang patches, and having the impact of those, there is some quite good research that demonstrates that that just entrenches those whānau within those communities.
focus.explanation: Engages the named instruments in the bill (dispersal notices, the patch ban) and their claimed downstream effect on families. Weak as an argument, but entirely about the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And yet children, presumably, are subject to this quasi-criminal regime, and it strikes me that there hasn’t been a lot of thinking done around how this bill will fit with the wider framework around the behaviour of young people and the response of not only police courts but also Oranga Tamariki and other agencies to those behaviours.
focus.explanation: Directed at how the bill's dispersal and infringement regime interacts with the youth justice and Oranga Tamariki framework — a concrete gap in the measure before the committee, with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So the amendment, which has got a “w” on it—marked “w”—suggests that in the definition of “gang insignia”, a further paragraph is added: “(c) but does not include any insignia or item that is not readily visible and identifiable as gang insignia from a reasonable distance, such as jewellery”.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the Amendment Paper, the defined term it alters, the paragraph it inserts, and quotes the proposed drafting in full. Anyone could check or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’d just point out for the benefit of the member that the purpose of the bill is indeed to deal with intimidation by gangs, but that’s not the only purpose. The purpose is to reduce the ability of gangs to operate; secondly, to cause fear; thirdly, to cause intimidation; and, fourthly, to cause disruption to the public. So there are a number of purposes.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates four named purposes drawn from the bill rather than a generality, but cites no clause number and gives no figures, thresholds or mechanisms.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As reflected in the research and also as laid out in the regulatory impact statement that’s been tabled, gang members are disproportionately young male Māori and live in more deprived communities in New Zealand. So the overview of that is that about three-quarters of those on the National Gang List are Māori.
specificity.explanation: Names the source (the tabled regulatory impact statement), the dataset (the National Gang List) and a quantified share, all checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I would propose to the Minister that the introduction of this legislation alongside this Government’s proposal to remove section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act would make Māori tamariki and rangatahi even more susceptible to mismanagement by the State, if they have a primary caregiver who is no longer able to take up that role, as a result of incarceration.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific statutory provision (section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act) and a specific interaction with the bill, but supplies no numbers, thresholds or estimate of the effect.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We don’t agree with much of this bill, but stopping intimidation is a proper purpose and it’s a proper thing to pursue, but just cracking down on gang insignia for the sake of it clearly isn’t.
civility.explanation: A contested committee-stage debate where an attack on the Minister was readily available. The disagreement is aimed entirely at the bill's purpose, with no imputation of bad faith or any remark about the Minister personally.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’d just point out for the benefit of the member that the purpose of the bill is indeed to deal with intimidation by gangs, but that’s not the only purpose. The purpose is to reduce the ability of gangs to operate; secondly, to cause fear; thirdly, to cause intimidation; and, fourthly, to cause disruption to the public. So there are a number of purposes.
civility.explanation: Answers on the substance of the bill's purpose clause, but the framing 'for the benefit of the member' carries a mild note of condescension — pointed, edging toward the person without landing on them.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I’d just point out for the benefit of the member that the purpose of the bill is indeed to deal with intimidation by gangs, but that’s not the only purpose. The purpose is to reduce the ability of gangs to operate; secondly, to cause fear; thirdly, to cause intimidation; and, fourthly, to cause disruption to the public. So there are a number of purposes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the bill's purpose provision contains: that it names four objects — reducing gangs' ability to operate, to cause fear, to cause intimidation, and to cause disruption to the public — rather than intimidation alone. (The clipped phrasing of the second to fourth limbs is plainly elliptical for 'reduce the ability of gangs to ...'.)
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The purpose clause of the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill as it stood at committee of the whole House on 6 August 2024 (legislation.govt.nz / the bill as reported back): true if the clause lists those four objects, false if the stated purpose is confined to intimidation or differs materially in its listed limbs.

veracity.statement: As reflected in the research and also as laid out in the regulatory impact statement that’s been tabled, gang members are disproportionately young male Māori and live in more deprived communities in New Zealand. So the overview of that is that about three-quarters of those on the National Gang List are Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific composition figure: approximately 75 percent of people recorded on the Police National Gang List identify as Māori, and that gang members are disproportionately young, male and from deprived areas.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police National Gang List ethnicity breakdown as at 2024, and the regulatory impact statement accompanying the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill: true if the Māori share is approximately three-quarters (roughly 72–78%), false if it is materially different (e.g. around or below two-thirds).

focus.statement: I was just wondering, in terms of the interests of transparency and also the public interest of New Zealanders, who, I’m sure, are very curious as to how this legislation will play out in practice, whether he wants to enlighten us as to what paragraph 118 of the regulatory impact statement actually says.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: she names a specific document (the regulatory impact statement) and a specific paragraph, and asks the Minister about its content. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is a real concern, because what that pretty much says is that this Government is prepared to want to look tough so much that they’re prepared to risk the actual credibility of our police service, who do an amazing job, to actually risk that credibility of being able to enforce the law in order to demonstrate on the tally that they’re looking tough and they’re doing something.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point underneath (enforceability and its effect on police credibility), but the weight of the sentence is a characterisation of the Government's motives rather than the mechanism of the law.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We do know that, since coming into office, this Government has fewer police officers on the front line than it did when it came in. I think that number is currently sitting at around 124, and as we see a new wing graduate, the new wings now have around about—used to have about 90-plus; they’re now looking at, sort of, high 60s for a wing.
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete figure (a shortfall of about 124 front-line officers) and a comparison of wing graduation sizes (90-plus down to high 60s), which someone could check; marked down because the numbers are hedged with 'around' and 'sort of'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, in response to the observations by our member from the Māori party, Mr Ferris, what I would point out is that if our only response to the increase in violent crime that people have seen in our community and the rise of gang activity—if the only response from this Government was this legislation, he might have a point. But that is not the only response of this Government: we continue to invest widely in many innovations such as Te Ao Mārama, court system, and many aspects of our justice system which are designed very much to work with specific needs and requirements of Māori in relation to crime, and we work very closely with many iwi groups right up and down the country.
specificity.explanation: Names one concrete initiative (Te Ao Mārama in the court system), but the rest is 'many innovations', 'many aspects', 'many iwi groups' — no amounts, timeframes or measurable outputs.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It seems quite clear that an “immediate family” means “family, whānau, or other culturally recognised groups” and then, in (b), “to avoid doubt, [that] includes—” a list of six people.
specificity.explanation: Quotes the operative definition from the bill, identifies the subclause and the number of listed categories — precise enough for anyone to check against the text; short of 1.0 only because he does not enumerate the six.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We do know that, since coming into office, this Government has fewer police officers on the front line than it did when it came in. I think that number is currently sitting at around 124, and as we see a new wing graduate, the new wings now have around about—used to have about 90-plus; they’re now looking at, sort of, high 60s for a wing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the number of front-line police officers as at August 2024 is lower than when the Government took office in late 2023, by roughly 124, and that recruit wings have shrunk from 90-plus to the high 60s.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police constabulary/front-line officer headcount published by NZ Police (workforce data, or answers to written parliamentary questions) comparing November 2023 with mid-2024: true if front-line numbers are lower by approximately 124, false if numbers rose or the gap is materially different; wing sizes checkable against NZ Police recruit wing graduation releases for 2024.

veracity.statement: There also is the concern that has been raised, quite rightly, by the Police Association that having a law that is not operationally able to be implemented risks undermining the confidence that the New Zealand public have in the New Zealand Police, and that is a real concern.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim attributed to the Police Association: that it has publicly warned an unenforceable gang-insignia law risks undermining public confidence in police. The checkable element is whether the Association said this.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, media interviews or select committee submissions by the New Zealand Police Association (or its president) on the Gangs Bill during 2024: true if the Association raised enforceability concerns framed around public confidence in police, false if no such statement exists.

veracity.statement: Look, I just want to probe a bit at some of the underlying things I believe are missing, and it’s based, really, on the fact that, given what we know and understand around things like Māori incarceration as a country, around things like poverty that Māori endure and have endured for centuries as a country, the things that we already know—Māori are overrepresented in incarceration figures, as we know.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori are overrepresented in New Zealand's prison population relative to their share of the general population.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections prison population statistics compared with Stats NZ census population shares: true if the Māori share of the prison population materially exceeds the Māori share of the national population, false if the shares are comparable.

veracity.statement: We recognise that Māori are more likely to be victims of crime than other New Zealanders, and that is why we’re very focused on this legislation reducing the negative impact of gangs on young Māori growing up throughout the country and getting drawn into a very negative way of life.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori experience a higher rate of criminal victimisation than other New Zealanders.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey victimisation rates by ethnicity: true if the Māori victimisation rate is significantly higher than the national or non-Māori rate, false if it is comparable or lower.

rigor.statement: With the number of police who are retiring or choosing to take on other work, that number of police coming in is not sufficient to meet attrition currently, and that is why the numbers of front-line serving police have decreased under this Government.
rigor.explanation: A clean inference: if recruitment intake is below attrition, the total falls. The conclusion follows directly from the premise offered, whatever the accuracy of the underlying numbers.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is a real concern, because what that pretty much says is that this Government is prepared to want to look tough so much that they’re prepared to risk the actual credibility of our police service, who do an amazing job, to actually risk that credibility of being able to enforce the law in order to demonstrate on the tally that they’re looking tough and they’re doing something.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur about motive: from a stakeholder's operational concern about enforceability she concludes the Government is knowingly willing to sacrifice police credibility for appearances. Nothing offered connects the enforcement concern to that intent.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, in response to the observations by our member from the Māori party, Mr Ferris, what I would point out is that if our only response to the increase in violent crime that people have seen in our community and the rise of gang activity—if the only response from this Government was this legislation, he might have a point. But that is not the only response of this Government: we continue to invest widely in many innovations such as Te Ao Mārama, court system, and many aspects of our justice system which are designed very much to work with specific needs and requirements of Māori in relation to crime, and we work very closely with many iwi groups right up and down the country.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: Ferris argued that historical dispossession underlies Māori offending, not that this bill was the Government's sole response. Goldsmith rebuts the claim of sole response, which was not made, so the conclusion does not answer the argument actually advanced.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There’s a number of specific questions, particularly around immediate family members. I’m struggling to understand the member’s confusion.
civility.explanation: Pointed and mildly condescending — it locates the problem in the member's comprehension rather than the drafting — but it stops short of an attack on the person and he goes straight on to answer the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But it beggars belief that the Minister has had months and months to dwell on his gang patch ban, and then, at the last moment, when there is no real ability to scrutinise this proposed offence, he slips it in in the dark of night.
civility.explanation: The procedural complaint is legitimate, but 'slips it in in the dark of night' imputes deliberate bad faith to the Minister personally rather than criticising the amendment itself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In relation to the member’s last commentary around knowingly, and the mens rea and actus reus around the commission of an offence, this bill doesn’t seek to undo the justice process; therefore, the commentary around not knowing and acting, I’m a little bit confused, but I can assure the member that the clause 7(1) states: “A person commits an offence if the person knowingly, and without reasonable excuse, displays gang insignia”, and I think that’s relatively straightforward.
civility.explanation: Replies to a direct and hostile line of attack by engaging the clause and the member's question; the only edge is 'I'm a little bit confused', which criticises the argument, not the member.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But the idea that someone who has been in trouble for having gang patches, all of a sudden because they’ve got their dad’s jacket hanging in the spare wardrobe, can go to jail for a year, that is utterly disproportionate, inconsistent with the purposes of this bill, and the procedure is utterly woeful.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance of new clause 8A — the conduct captured, the penalty, and the fit with the bill's stated purpose. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So the two questions are whether the actus reus and mens rea under clause 7(1) need to happen concurrently. The second part is: has there been any consideration given to the burden of proof that will be placed on the Crown prosecutor in the event that something like this would then need to go to trial?
focus.explanation: Entirely directed at the drafting of the measure before the committee; no reference to any party or opponent.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In a potential scenario, if you had a person with an FPO—maybe they’re before the courts—and simultaneously police request for this person to receive a prohibition for owning any gang insignia and also a firearm prohibition order upon them as well, am I correct in understanding that police would then be within their powers to go around to this person’s house any time they wanted, endlessly, to check for weapons?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny of how the clause before the committee would operate alongside a named existing regime; no party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But the idea that someone who has been in trouble for having gang patches, all of a sudden because they’ve got their dad’s jacket hanging in the spare wardrobe, can go to jail for a year, that is utterly disproportionate, inconsistent with the purposes of this bill, and the procedure is utterly woeful.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: the clause's penalty is set against an illustrative instance of the conduct it captures to argue disproportionality. The hypothetical is doing a lot of work and the 'purposes of this bill' premise is asserted rather than shown, but the conclusion broadly tracks the premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’ll highlight that this is relating to a court prohibition order, so this isn’t a power set upon the police; it’s the court applying a prohibition order.
rigor.explanation: Valid as far as it goes: if the trigger is a court-issued prohibition order, it follows that the decision to impose it is not a police power. It does not reach the objection about what police may then do to enforce it, but the inference stated is sound.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In relation to the member’s last commentary around knowingly, and the mens rea and actus reus around the commission of an offence, this bill doesn’t seek to undo the justice process; therefore, the commentary around not knowing and acting, I’m a little bit confused, but I can assure the member that the clause 7(1) states: “A person commits an offence if the person knowingly, and without reasonable excuse, displays gang insignia”, and I think that’s relatively straightforward.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: that the bill 'doesn't seek to undo the justice process' does not establish that the concurrence requirement is satisfied, and re-quoting the clause restates rather than supports the conclusion that the point is 'relatively straightforward'.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So it is unlikely that a former gang member who is doing art will be subject to a prohibition order given that the member has just referred to them as being a former gang member who’s now doing art.
rigor.explanation: Circular: the reason offered is simply the way the questioner described the hypothetical person. Whether someone described as a 'former gang member doing art' would in fact be subject to a prohibition order is the very question asked, and nothing beyond the label is advanced to answer it.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It creates an offence punishable by a year in jail. There’s not even provision for an alternative sentence.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the new clause 8A added by the Amendment Paper sets a maximum penalty of one year's imprisonment with no alternative (non-custodial or fine) penalty provided in the clause.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of new clause 8A in the Amendment Paper to the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill (as enacted in the Gangs Act 2024, breach of a gang insignia prohibition order): true if the stated maximum penalty is imprisonment of up to 12 months and the provision specifies no fine or alternative penalty; false if the maximum term differs or a fine/alternative is provided.

veracity.statement: Not one citizen gets a chance to have a say about this because it was slipped in after the select committee process.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the new offence in clause 8A was introduced by Amendment Paper after the Justice Committee reported the bill back, so no member of the public was able to make a submission on it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's Parliament page history: the date the Justice Committee reported the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill back versus the date the Amendment Paper containing new clause 8A was tabled. True if the Amendment Paper post-dates the select committee report and the offence appears in no version open for submissions; false if the offence was in the bill as introduced or was before the committee.

veracity.statement: In response to the member’s earlier commentary around new clause 8A, this clause was added to address police concerns about the ability to enforce the gang insignia prohibition.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the origin of new clause 8A was police-raised concerns about the enforceability of the gang insignia prohibition.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The departmental disclosure statement / regulatory impact material for the Amendment Paper and any NZ Police advice or submission on the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill: true if police enforceability concerns are recorded as the stated reason for the added clause; false if the official advice records a different origin or no such police concern.

veracity.statement: I’m really interested to know from the Minister how this interacts with the new firearm prohibition orders (FPO) regime, which effectively enables or gives police the broad powers of searching without a warrant or without even a cause.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the firearms prohibition order regime permits police to search an FPO subject without a warrant and without needing cause or suspicion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The compliance-search provisions of the Arms Act 1983 as amended by the Arms (Firearms Prohibition Orders) Amendment Act 2022: true if police may conduct warrantless searches of an FPO subject's home or vehicle for compliance purposes without requiring reasonable grounds to suspect an offence; false if a warrant, or grounds for suspicion, is required.

specificity.statement: So the two questions are whether the actus reus and mens rea under clause 7(1) need to happen concurrently. The second part is: has there been any consideration given to the burden of proof that will be placed on the Crown prosecutor in the event that something like this would then need to go to trial?
specificity.explanation: Names the clause (7(1)), the precise legal doctrine at issue (concurrence of actus reus and mens rea) and a concrete operational consequence (burden of proof on the Crown prosecutor). Someone could answer or check each.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In a potential scenario, if you had a person with an FPO—maybe they’re before the courts—and simultaneously police request for this person to receive a prohibition for owning any gang insignia and also a firearm prohibition order upon them as well, am I correct in understanding that police would then be within their powers to go around to this person’s house any time they wanted, endlessly, to check for weapons?
specificity.explanation: Sets out a concrete, checkable scenario — two named order types applied to the same person, a warrantless compliance search, and the resulting one-year imprisonment exposure — though it leaves the statutory search power itself unquantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This is the dog’s breakfast that we’ve got here, right?
civility.explanation: Blunt, dismissive language aimed entirely at the bill; no person is attacked or impugned. Harsh criticism of a measure is the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, in the spirit of bipartisanship, we have looked at the tabled amendment put forward and decided that there is some merit in what the member has to say.
civility.explanation: In a contested committee exchange where the opponent had just called the bill a dog's breakfast, he engages the substance of the amendment and credits the member. Nothing directed at the person.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Not only is it poorly thought-out in the detail—“We didn’t think about headstones.”, I get that; it’s always going to happen—but it’s poorly thought-out conceptually because we’re banning all gang insignia regardless of purpose, regardless of whether they’re used in a particular way, regardless of whether they intimidate or not.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: the ban is drafted without reference to intimidatory purpose or effect, therefore it captures cases (gravestones) that do not serve the bill's stated purpose. The conclusion tracks the premise about how the prohibition is framed; the gap is that he asserts rather than shows the bill has no purposive limb.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But the challenge is that you’ve got these headstones out there, and on the bill, as it was presented to this committee, would either criminalise local bodies or it would require kind of the painting over—essentially, the desecration—of the headstones.
rigor.explanation: Presents only two consequences — prosecution of councils or defacement of headstones — as though they exhausted the options; a false dichotomy that omits prosecutorial discretion, non-enforcement or existing exemptions. The underlying point about coverage is nonetheless connected to the drafting.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Just in relation to that in terms of consultation, of course we’ve just had a very lengthy select committee process, where there have been more than a hundred people making submissions on the bill, and I can assure the member that the Ministry of Justice, through its many liaison committees with Māori iwi and hapū, will have had many conversations.
rigor.explanation: Asked whether named former gang members were consulted, he infers that consultation happened from the mere existence of a submissions process and of ministry liaison committees — 'will have had many conversations' is a presumption, not evidence. The conclusion does not follow from the institutional machinery cited.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It might be a little bit extreme to think that the police would breach that line, but we need some assurances, given the amount of ex - gang members now who are making a real effort and are turning around people’s lives.
rigor.explanation: Concedes the feared police conduct is unlikely, then concludes assurances are needed anyway on the strength of anecdote about reforming ex-members. The reason offered (people are turning their lives around) does not establish that the clauses create the risk; it leans on sympathetic anecdote rather than on the drafting.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Not only is it poorly thought-out in the detail—“We didn’t think about headstones.”, I get that; it’s always going to happen—but it’s poorly thought-out conceptually because we’re banning all gang insignia regardless of purpose, regardless of whether they’re used in a particular way, regardless of whether they intimidate or not.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the drafting of the measure before the committee — its scope and the absence of an intimidation test. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I don’t know if he is ex or current, but Denis O’Reilly, another long-time veteran gang member, is worried, again, about the implications of this bill, particularly these clauses 7 and 8, where we’re talking about the display of gang insignia, and particularly when they’ve got them stored away in their houses.
focus.explanation: Directed at named clauses of the measure before the committee and their effect on a specific group; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: You’ll see that I do have a tabled amendment marked “R” which was put in earlier in the last session, last week, which would exclude a permanent memorial, grave mark, or headstone erected prior to the assent of this bill.
specificity.explanation: Names the tabled amendment, when it was lodged, and the precise carve-out it would create (memorials erected before assent). Someone could look it up and act on it; no figures or cost, so short of full marks.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I have put in an Amendment Paper under my name which achieves half of what he set out to achieve, which is to say, including “a headstone or grave marker erected before the commencement of this Act”, so as to achieve part of the purpose.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument (an Amendment Paper in his own name) and quotes the operative wording it inserts. Checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our broader approach extends into matters of dealing with addictions, dealing with emergency housing accommodation, and dealing with a whole range of issues which are equally important, as well as the broader effort through the Te Ao Mārama courts and many other engagements across the justice sector.
specificity.explanation: Gestures at policy areas and names the Te Ao Mārama courts, but supplies no mechanism, funding figure or timeframe; 'a whole range of issues' and 'many other engagements' carry no checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I don’t know if he is ex or current, but Denis O’Reilly, another long-time veteran gang member, is worried, again, about the implications of this bill, particularly these clauses 7 and 8, where we’re talking about the display of gang insignia, and particularly when they’ve got them stored away in their houses.
specificity.explanation: Names the clauses at issue (7 and 8), the named individual raising the concern, and the precise scenario — insignia stored in a private house. No figures, and the concern itself is reported rather than evidenced.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But a quick search shows up numerous gravestones with gang insignia on them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that publicly findable records show multiple New Zealand gravestones bearing gang insignia.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Publicly searchable images, cemetery records or news reports of NZ graves bearing gang insignia; true if several distinct such headstones can be identified, false if effectively none can be found beyond an isolated case.

veracity.statement: So I have put in an Amendment Paper under my name which achieves half of what he set out to achieve, which is to say, including “a headstone or grave marker erected before the commencement of this Act”, so as to achieve part of the purpose.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an Amendment Paper lodged in Goldsmith's name exempts a headstone or grave marker erected before the commencement of the Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Amendment Papers recorded against the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill 2024 on Parliament's website; true if one in Goldsmith's name contains an exclusion for a headstone or grave marker erected before commencement, false if no such paper exists.

veracity.statement: Just in relation to that in terms of consultation, of course we’ve just had a very lengthy select committee process, where there have been more than a hundred people making submissions on the bill, and I can assure the member that the Ministry of Justice, through its many liaison committees with Māori iwi and hapū, will have had many conversations.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than one hundred people made submissions on the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill at select committee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's report on the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill 2024 and Parliament's submissions listing; true if the recorded number of submitters exceeds 100, false if materially fewer.

specificity.statement: I know there was some talk by, I believe, the Minister of Police, the Hon Mark Mitchell, around some of the work that they’ve been doing in Australia in banning gang patches, and I’m interested to know whether that has had any positive public safety improvements in those areas and what the consequences of those provisions have been, particularly reflecting on the Prime Minister’s Chief Science Advisor’s report that is all about minimising gang harm and addresses the drivers of gang membership, where it says, “A stronger focus on prevention and early intervention will slow the flow of young people into gangs and alleviate pressure on multiple systems (justice, health, corrections) in the long‐term.”, and whether he has considered the Chief Science Advisor’s strong advice that we can’t arrest our way out of the gang problem.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific source (the Prime Minister's Chief Science Advisor's report on minimising gang harm), quotes it directly, and points to a named comparator jurisdiction's patch bans. A listener could go and check the document and the claim it is said to support.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is a Government that has been really strong on giving very strong messages to a number of our NGOs who work in a variety of social services—that there is a clear expectation that has been delivered by this Government that they’re required to demonstrate their return on investment by going through an organisation such as ImpactLab and having their spend assessed, through looking at what each dollar provided will give in return.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (return-on-investment assessment, dollar-for-dollar) and a named organisation carrying it out, but gives no figures, contracts or dates, so it is a detailed direction rather than a fully checkable particular.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: All this does appear to be, to many New Zealanders, is a cosmetic and superficial way of looking like more resources are being put into restoring law and order when in reality, in the last Budget, Police received $107 million less than in the previous Budget.
specificity.explanation: Carries one precise, checkable number tied to a named comparison (last Budget versus the previous Budget for Police), though it is embedded in otherwise general framing and does not identify which appropriation is being compared.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I know there was some talk by, I believe, the Minister of Police, the Hon Mark Mitchell, around some of the work that they’ve been doing in Australia in banning gang patches, and I’m interested to know whether that has had any positive public safety improvements in those areas and what the consequences of those provisions have been, particularly reflecting on the Prime Minister’s Chief Science Advisor’s report that is all about minimising gang harm and addresses the drivers of gang membership, where it says, “A stronger focus on prevention and early intervention will slow the flow of young people into gangs and alleviate pressure on multiple systems (justice, health, corrections) in the long‐term.”, and whether he has considered the Chief Science Advisor’s strong advice that we can’t arrest our way out of the gang problem.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Prime Minister's Chief Science Advisor produced a report on minimising gang harm containing the quoted sentence, and that its advice is that enforcement alone cannot solve gang membership.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Prime Minister's Chief Science Advisor's 2024 report on gang harm: true if such a report exists, contains the quoted sentence about prevention and early intervention, and advises a prevention-led rather than arrest-led approach; false if no such report exists or the quoted wording and advice are not in it.

veracity.statement: Particularly because we currently do have legislation in place that prohibits gang places in public places—that Act has been around since 2013 and yet, as the Minister of Justice continues to quote, the membership of gangs continues to rise. If that legislation in itself has not been effective at driving down membership, why does he believe that this iteration of banning insignia would be any more successful?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a gang-insignia prohibition has been law since 2013 and that gang membership has continued to rise since then.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Act 2013 (enactment/commencement date) and NZ Police National Gang List membership counts from 2013 to mid-2024: true if the Act dates from 2013 and the gang list has grown over that period; false if the Act is from another year or gang list numbers have not risen.

veracity.statement: The member also referred to a ban currently being in place. Yes, there is a ban on gang insignia in public buildings—and that is hospitals and schools and courts. So that has been in place and has been largely successful.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both the scope of the existing insignia ban (hospitals, schools, courts) and that it has been largely successful in operation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Act 2013 and the premises prescribed under it, plus any official review, Police enforcement or prosecution data on its operation: true if the Act covers the premises named and the available evidence shows effective compliance/enforcement; false if those premises are not covered or reviews and prosecution data show it has had little effect.

veracity.statement: This is a Government that has been really strong on giving very strong messages to a number of our NGOs who work in a variety of social services—that there is a clear expectation that has been delivered by this Government that they’re required to demonstrate their return on investment by going through an organisation such as ImpactLab and having their spend assessed, through looking at what each dollar provided will give in return.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government has set a clear expectation that social service NGOs demonstrate return on investment, including via assessment by an organisation such as ImpactLab.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government social-investment and social-services contracting requirements in 2024 (Social Investment Agency / Ministry of Social Development guidance, ministerial statements) and ImpactLab's engagements with funded NGOs: true if NGOs were required or expected to evidence return on investment through such assessment; false if no such expectation was set.

veracity.statement: All this does appear to be, to many New Zealanders, is a cosmetic and superficial way of looking like more resources are being put into restoring law and order when in reality, in the last Budget, Police received $107 million less than in the previous Budget.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Police funding in the most recent Budget was $107 million lower than in the preceding Budget.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Vote Police appropriations in the Budget 2024 Estimates compared with Budget 2023: true if the relevant total Police appropriation is about $107 million lower in 2024; false if it is equal to or higher than the previous year on the comparable measure.

focus.statement: Particularly because we currently do have legislation in place that prohibits gang places in public places—that Act has been around since 2013 and yet, as the Minister of Justice continues to quote, the membership of gangs continues to rise. If that legislation in itself has not been effective at driving down membership, why does he believe that this iteration of banning insignia would be any more successful?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: names the existing statute, its date, the stated outcome measure (gang membership) and asks why extending the same mechanism would work differently. Legitimate scrutiny of a named policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m surprised to see that my colleagues in the “Freedom of Speech” Party have not made any strong statements about freedom of expression and what people are allowed to wear—but anyway.
focus.explanation: The point is the other party's inconsistency with its own branding rather than the clause at issue; the freedom-of-expression reference is a hook for the party jibe, and no provision, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So, given that this expectation has been provided to NGOs and those working in various social service provisions, what work has the Government done on itself to be able to evidence what the cost of this is in terms of the taxpayer and in terms of law enforcement—the type of resources that Police will need to be putting into this?
focus.explanation: Directly on the measure: asks for the fiscal and enforcement cost of the policy and the safety benefit it buys, applying the Government's own stated funding test to its own bill.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Particularly because we currently do have legislation in place that prohibits gang places in public places—that Act has been around since 2013 and yet, as the Minister of Justice continues to quote, the membership of gangs continues to rise. If that legislation in itself has not been effective at driving down membership, why does he believe that this iteration of banning insignia would be any more successful?
rigor.explanation: A real inference — prior insignia ban plus rising membership, therefore doubt about a wider ban — but it treats the two bans as equivalent in scope (the existing one covers government premises only, not all public places) and assumes membership trends measure that ban's effect, so there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We know this because when Eugene Ryder came and spoke to us at the Justice Committee, he wore a number of different T-shirts and asked which one was the Black Power T-shirt. It turned out that all three of them were completely irrelevant to gang insignia, but it shows that some of the symbolism that gangs use are prominent in other ways.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single committee anecdote to a claim about enforcement difficulty. The anecdote is genuinely on point for the identification problem it illustrates, but one demonstration is thin support for the broader conclusion about symbols in general — an argument from anecdote.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, I suppose the question is: why don’t they wear red? Ultimately, it is because of fear of doing so, that there is a chance that if one does, one gets confused and gets beaten up or is subject to some threat of violence.
rigor.explanation: Supplies a causal explanation (fear of violence) for the observed avoidance of a colour with nothing offered to establish it, and then uses that assumed cause to justify a patch ban — which does not address colour-based intimidation at all. The inference has a real gap between premise and remedy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, ultimately, Parliament and New Zealanders have to decide—there are balancing and competing rights. Of course the rights of people to be able to go about their normal life without fear of being intimidated or preyed upon by organised crime is also a freedom that we stand up for. So, in many instances, we have to weigh up those freedoms. On this occasion, we believe that the impact on freedom of expression by banning gangs and gang patches in public places is justified in order to deal with what is a real issue confronting our many communities.
rigor.explanation: A coherent proportionality argument that concedes the rights impingement and weighs it against a competing interest. The weakness is that the conclusion assumes the ban will deliver the countervailing benefit; no evidence of effectiveness is offered to complete the balance.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, given that this expectation has been provided to NGOs and those working in various social service provisions, what work has the Government done on itself to be able to evidence what the cost of this is in terms of the taxpayer and in terms of law enforcement—the type of resources that Police will need to be putting into this?
rigor.explanation: A consistency argument: if a return-on-investment standard is imposed on funded providers, the same standard should apply to this spend. The inference holds, though it assumes the two kinds of spending are comparable enough for the same test.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We only need to look back in history to when anything is made illegal, whether that be a drug, whether that be alcohol; ways of subverting and driving that underground typically start to take shape.
rigor.explanation: An argument from loose historical analogy: prohibition of drugs and alcohol is offered as showing what a patch ban will do, with nothing to establish that displaying insignia behaves like a prohibited commodity market. The analogy carries the whole conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I guess what I’m getting at is whether this is a wise investment of that Police resource, because what it does appear to quite a few people out there—and I’ve received a few emails on this one—is that it’s a cosmetic approach to addressing what is quite a deep-rooted problem within our community.
rigor.explanation: The support offered for the conclusion is that it is how it appears to 'quite a few people' and a few emails she received — an appeal to popularity plus anecdote, with no evidence bearing on whether the approach is in fact cosmetic.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I think that the member Tamatha Paul’s speech made the point very well for us around fear and intimidation when she referred to some towns—I think Tokoroa was the one she referred to—where people just don’t wear red.
civility.explanation: A contested rebuttal that engages what the member actually said and turns it against her case without any slight to her character or competence. Pointed, but entirely on the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I think the member the Hon Ginny Andersen is a little bit confused on a couple of matters.
civility.explanation: Mild condescension aimed at the person rather than her argument — characterising the member as 'confused' rather than saying why her point is mistaken. Short of an insult, but it edges past engaging the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: You’re probably drafting a way to try to usurp my Amendment Paper as we speak.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the Minister personally — scheming to undercut a colleague's amendment — rather than engaging the amendment's merits. Jocular in tone, but it lands on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So I’d like a really good answer as to why there is this going on if he does not agree with the suggestion that this is, in fact, just sort of a signifier, it is just an attempt to placate a public by pulling the wool over their eyes.
civility.explanation: Imputes deliberate deception to the Minister — 'pulling the wool over their eyes' — which is a bad-faith attribution to the person rather than a criticism of the measure's design.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In relation to taking away resources from other things that the Police might be doing to deal with organised crime, of course, nothing in this legislation changes the absolute independence of Police in deciding what the priorities are, in an operational sense of how to enforce the law. The Police are able to make those judgments, and in any circumstance, where they put the resources in any given moment in relation to crime in a particular community, that will be for the Police Commissioner ultimately to decide.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the mechanism of the bill and the operational question raised about police resourcing; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: You could think of any number of situations where you’ve got a publication of some sort, and it’s not being used for educational purposes. It’s not media, and it’s not art. It’s just a book. It’s just a magazine, and it doesn’t fall within the exceptions.
focus.explanation: Engages the drafting of the bill directly — the scope of the offence and the exceptions clause — with a concrete class of cases.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In relation to taking away resources from other things that the Police might be doing to deal with organised crime, of course, nothing in this legislation changes the absolute independence of Police in deciding what the priorities are, in an operational sense of how to enforce the law. The Police are able to make those judgments, and in any circumstance, where they put the resources in any given moment in relation to crime in a particular community, that will be for the Police Commissioner ultimately to decide.
rigor.explanation: Partial non sequitur: the objection was that new powers divert finite police effort from organised crime, and the answer that police retain operational independence over priorities does not address whether resources are diverted — independence in choosing priorities is compatible with the diversion alleged.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You could think of any number of situations where you’ve got a publication of some sort, and it’s not being used for educational purposes. It’s not media, and it’s not art. It’s just a book. It’s just a magazine, and it doesn’t fall within the exceptions.
rigor.explanation: A reductio worked from the bill's own structure: if the prohibition is general and the exceptions are enumerated, cases outside the enumerated purposes are caught. The inference tracks the premise, though it assumes without argument that 'display' extends to incidental cover images.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But this, now is Fahrenheit 451 stuff. This becomes a prohibited publication. Let’s burn the books.
rigor.explanation: Slippery slope plus appeal to emotion: even granting that a publication could be caught by the display offence, nothing offered connects that to state destruction of books, which is what the Fahrenheit 451 analogy asserts.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If it is somebody walking past a window, that’s not actually what’s frightening the New Zealand public. What is frightening the New Zealand public is quite different, and it’s already covered by an Act.
rigor.explanation: The argument — active displays already covered by the Insignia Act, so the marginal extension to passive display adds nothing that addresses public fear — is structurally sound, but the key premise about what actually frightens the public is asserted rather than evidenced.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are a number of things that this legislation does, but it fits within a much broader response across Government, dealing with long-term social issues, dealing with housing, dealing with education—all these other things that continue apace.
specificity.explanation: A list of policy domains with no named programme, figure, mechanism or timeframe; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But I want to draw people’s attention also to the regulatory impact statement on page 30 where Option Three that was suggested, which is what we are doing right now, specifically says, “Reducing”—and it’s got a plus-plus next to it—“displays of gang insignia may make communities feel safer.”—“feel” being the keyword, not necessarily safer.
specificity.explanation: Names the document, the page, the option number, the rating symbol and quotes the wording — a reader could open the RIS and verify it directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, coming back to the question that I was going to ask, because those are just clarifications based on what the Minister has already mentioned just now, my question’s around clause 7(2), which is around “a term of imprisonment not exceeding 6 months or a fine not exceeding $5,000.” I couldn’t see it in the regulatory impact statement, but I want to know from the Minister: what was the balancing and proportionality test that was undertaken to determine that imprisonment length and also that fine amount, and what other examples were used as part of that?
specificity.explanation: Cites the clause number, quotes the exact penalty ceilings, and asks a precise, answerable question about the test used to set them. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It says the extension here is that it will now cover “passive displays of insignia in private places viewable by the public”—so the window of a house or on social media.
specificity.explanation: Quotes the operative wording from the advice and translates it into two concrete cases the new offence would reach; precise enough to be checked against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But I want to draw people’s attention also to the regulatory impact statement on page 30 where Option Three that was suggested, which is what we are doing right now, specifically says, “Reducing”—and it’s got a plus-plus next to it—“displays of gang insignia may make communities feel safer.”—“feel” being the keyword, not necessarily safer.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that page 30 of the Ministry of Justice regulatory impact statement on the gang insignia bill describes Option Three as one that may make communities 'feel safer', with a '++' rating.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published Ministry of Justice Regulatory Impact Statement for the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill (2024): true if the options table at or about page 30 rates the insignia-ban option with the wording 'displays of gang insignia may make communities feel safer' and a ++ marker; false if the text or rating differs materially.

veracity.statement: This is paragraph 138 on page 31 of the regulatory impact statement, it says, “The Ministry of Justice’s preferred option is option one”, which is the “status quo”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Ministry of Justice's regulatory impact statement states, at paragraph 138 on page 31, that the ministry's preferred option is option one, the status quo.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published Regulatory Impact Statement for the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill: true if paragraph 138 (or its equivalent) states the Ministry of Justice's preferred option is option one / the status quo; false if the RIS names a different preferred option.

veracity.statement: Of course, this regulatory impact statement was made and delivered prior to a number of Cabinet decisions, and one of the Cabinet decisions we made was not to include the ban on private property visible from the outside, which is what this part of the regulatory impact statement is referring to.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Cabinet decided, after the regulatory impact statement was written, not to include a prohibition on gang insignia displayed on private property that is visible from outside.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill as reported back / enacted and the associated Cabinet papers on prohibiting gang insignia; true if the prohibition is confined to public places and excludes display on private property visible from outside, false if the enacted provision captures insignia on private property visible from a public place.

veracity.statement: We keep a close eye on that one because we know that gang membership increased particularly since the 501s came back from Australia and added a layer of complexity that New Zealand had not seen before in criminal organisations.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that recorded gang membership in New Zealand rose notably following the return of 501 deportees from Australia.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police National Gang List membership figures over 2015–2024 alongside published counts of section 501 deportees and Police/Ministry of Justice analysis linking them; true if gang list numbers rose materially over the period of 501 returns and officials attribute part of that rise to deportees, false if the list was flat or falling over that period.

civility.statement: I’d encourage her to keep up to date as to what’s actually happened since the regulatory impact statement was drawn up.
civility.explanation: A pointed put-down implying the member has not done her homework — it edges onto the member rather than the argument, though it stops well short of an insult.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But we weren’t going to follow it, because we had made commitments to the people of New Zealand and we are keen to carry on.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (reject the Ministry of Justice's advice) rests entirely on an electoral-mandate premise; it is an appeal to popularity/mandate that does not engage the substance of the advice, though the democratic-legitimacy premise is at least relevant.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So it is a Te Tiriti issue because we have had the gross breach of the right to protection, the gross breach of care for these young people, these whaikaha, these tamaiti, and these adults who were placed into the care of the State or faith-based institutions, and then, huri rawa ake, [when it finally comes around] they come out and join gangs.
rigor.explanation: Offers a real chain — State care failures, disproportionately of Māori, feed gang membership — supported by the quoted regulatory impact statement, but the step from that correlation to 'therefore this bill is a Te Tiriti article 2 issue' is asserted rather than shown; a genuine gap between evidence and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, some of these gangs are doing quite positive things within our community, so I do worry about this part whereby it will prohibit their ability to congregate.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific provision of the bill before the committee (the restriction on gang members congregating) and its likely effect, rather than the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So the problem is that they came and they campaigned on stuff, and said, “We’re going to do some stuff.”, and irrespective of there actually being a problem, this is where we land now.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point here — the regulatory impact statement's problem definition is a coalition commitment rather than an identified harm — but it is delivered mostly as generalised framing about what 'they' campaigned on.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If the overarching objective of this legislation is to reduce gang harm, how does taking off gang patches reduce gang harm?
focus.explanation: A direct question about the causal mechanism of the measure before the committee — squarely on the policy, with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So the options that are laid out here, in terms of the criteria used to compare different options to the status quo—the criteria they’ve developed are improving public confidence, reducing gang membership, reducing rates of offending, and also compliance with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act—so we’ll rule out the last one now!
specificity.explanation: Names the four assessment criteria from the regulatory impact statement precisely enough that someone could check them against the document and later measure the legislation against them.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I actually think that the legislation we’re debating right now will do the complete antithesis of what the criteria say. It is going to increase reoffending, particularly for gang members, to the point where you’re seeing those numbers go.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the gang insignia legislation will increase reoffending, particularly among gang members, rather than reduce it as the regulatory impact statement's criteria intend.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / Department of Corrections reoffending statistics and prosecution data for gang insignia offences in the period after the Act commenced (21 November 2024); true if reoffending rates among gang members rise relative to the pre-commencement baseline, false if they are flat or fall.

veracity.statement: We talked a great length about the 50 percent increase in gang membership over the past six years under the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that recorded gang membership rose by 50 percent over the six years of the previous Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police National Gang List membership totals for 2017 and 2023; true if the increase over that period is approximately 50 percent or more, false if materially smaller.

veracity.statement: And, look, I’ve dealt with this and I’m just conscious of the fact that this is probably the 15th time that I’ve responded to questions in relation to its impact on Māori, and I’ve made the same point many times, which is to say that Māori are more likely to be the victims of crime in this country as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori have a higher rate of criminal victimisation than other New Zealanders.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Crime and Victims Survey victimisation rates by ethnicity; true if the Māori victimisation rate is significantly above the national/non-Māori rate, false if it is at or below it.

veracity.statement: Because we know that a majority of people who are in gangs are Māori and we know that for wearing a patch, they could end up with a $5,000 fine or they could end up in prison—even though they might not even commit a crime while wearing that patch.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that Māori form a majority of gang members, and that the bill exposes a patch-wearer to a $5,000 fine or imprisonment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police National Gang List ethnicity breakdown (true if Māori are over 50 percent of listed members) and the penalty provision in clause 7 of the Gangs Bill as introduced (true if the maximum is a $5,000 fine, false if the stated penalties differ, particularly the availability of imprisonment for a first insignia offence).

veracity.statement: We know that Māori are more likely to be imprisoned, and we know that we are over-represented in our prisons and we’re more likely to receive harsher punishments and to be the subject of surveillance more than our non-Māori counterparts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Māori over-representation in the prison population and, separately, that Māori receive harsher sentencing outcomes than non-Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections prison population statistics by ethnicity (true if the Māori share of prisoners far exceeds their population share) and Ministry of Justice / published sentencing research on ethnic disparity in sentencing outcomes controlling for offence and history; false if no disparity is found.

focus.statement: Sometimes they were against them, and sometimes they wanted to give them money to do certain things and run drug rehabilitation courses, and so it was a mixed message.
focus.explanation: Characterises the previous Government's overall posture toward gangs, but anchors it to a named concrete policy (funding gang-run drug rehabilitation), so it is partly scrutiny of a real decision rather than pure party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I really want to understand from the Minister: what advice did he receive around Te Tiriti considerations and the impact on Māori that this particular part would create in terms of prohibiting gang insignia within those public places?
focus.explanation: Directly interrogates a named part of the bill before the committee and the advice underpinning it; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My proposed amendment simply adds the words “in a manner which would be threatening or intimidating to a reasonable person”, because that is the whole purpose of this legislation.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the drafting of clause 7(1) and the fit between the offence and the bill's stated purpose.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is that person the funeral director? Is that person the person carrying out the funeral? Is that person the executor of the estate?
focus.explanation: Probes the operation of the definition of 'person' in Part 2 in a concrete scenario; no party content whatsoever.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Reference was made to the science advisors, and it’s not a binary choice. You don’t choose between, on the one hand, only dealing with the long-term causes and drivers of crime and dealing with what we have here today and ensuring that people are caught and held to account for actions that they are responsible for today. You have to do both.
rigor.explanation: A valid rebuttal of a false dichotomy: he identifies that the two approaches are not mutually exclusive and concludes both are required. The conclusion follows, though he offers nothing to show the enforcement limb actually works alongside the other.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I have to say I’m a little confused, because that member has stood up before and said—I think it was that member—that in Tokoroa, everybody understands that you can’t wear red because that’s not the local colour, and I would have thought an understanding around self-determination to be about what one can or can’t wear is relevant in that context.
rigor.explanation: Turns the opponent's own example against her: if gang presence already dictates what residents may wear, an appeal to self-determination over clothing cuts against gangs too. The inference is real but leans on a tu quoque, and does not establish that the ban restores that freedom.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Self-determination means that you can wake up in the morning and choose the things that you want to do—you are determining for yourself—and that includes what you choose to wear every single day.
rigor.explanation: Equivocation: slides from tino rangatiratanga under article 2, a collective constitutional guarantee, to an individual's daily clothing choice, and treats the second as established by the first. The conclusion about gang patches does not follow from the Treaty premise as stated.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Because we know that a majority of people who are in gangs are Māori and we know that for wearing a patch, they could end up with a $5,000 fine or they could end up in prison—even though they might not even commit a crime while wearing that patch.
specificity.explanation: Names the penalty amount, the conduct it attaches to and the affected population — all checkable against the bill and police data.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My proposed amendment simply adds the words “in a manner which would be threatening or intimidating to a reasonable person”, because that is the whole purpose of this legislation.
specificity.explanation: Quotes the exact wording of the amendment and identifies the clause it attaches to; anyone could check or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is that person the funeral director? Is that person the person carrying out the funeral? Is that person the executor of the estate?
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete candidate defendants for liability under the part, so the Minister could answer each in turn; stops short of citing the provision itself.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But this is obviously not a concern for the Minister. Does the Minister even care that this piece of legislation and particularly that this part will lead to more Māori being imprisoned simply for what they’re wearing?
civility.explanation: Moves from the policy to the Minister's personal indifference, imputing that he does not care about Māori imprisonment rather than arguing the effect of the clause.
civility.subject: speaker
