specificity.statement: My tabled amendment, which is marked “v”, addresses the problem in clause 6, because the only punishment given in clause 6 for someone who breaches this order is imprisonment not exceeding one year.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific amendment, the specific clause, and the exact penalty it imposes — all directly checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: My tabled amendment, which is marked “v”, addresses the problem in clause 6, because the only punishment given in clause 6 for someone who breaches this order is imprisonment not exceeding one year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that clause 6 of the bill provides only imprisonment of up to one year, with no fine alternative, as the penalty for breaching a gang insignia prohibition order.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of clause 6 of the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill as reported back / as enacted in the Gangs Act 2024: true if the penalty for breach of the order is imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year with no fine specified; false if the clause carries a fine, a different maximum term, or a different penalty structure.

veracity.statement: Now, in every other offence clause that we look at, there’s a fine alternative.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that all the other offence-creating provisions in the bill before the committee provide a fine as an available penalty, unlike clause 6.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare every offence provision in the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill (e.g. the clause 7 public display offence and the other insignia offences): true if each of them specifies a fine as a penalty or alternative, false if any other offence clause is imprisonment-only.

rigor.statement: But, certainly, a fine should be an alternative because, you know, an offence for your kid having grandad’s gang patch jacket in the spare wardrobe clearly doesn’t warrant any imprisonment.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (a fine must be available) rests on a single sympathetic hypothetical rather than on the clause's actual elements; it is an appeal to an extreme anecdotal case, and it is not established that the imagined scenario would even be caught by the clause.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: My point is this: despicable as this whole clause is, you simply don’t need (c), because the person, if it’s in that boarding house situation or in a gang house situation, can’t have possession of the gang insignia and they can’t have control of the gang insignia.
rigor.explanation: A clean inference: having set up the communal-living case, he shows the trigger in (c) can be met where the possession and control limbs cannot, so (c) extends the order to conduct the person does not command. The conclusion tracks the premises offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is almost kind of creating a thought crime in the sense that you’re not allowed to have, in your own bedroom, a symbol on the wall which represents a gang affiliation.
rigor.explanation: Slides from a restriction on private possession of a physical object to 'thought crime' — the conclusion is a category jump; prohibiting display of an item is not a prohibition on holding a belief, and nothing is offered to bridge the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It puts a harder burden on the individual police officer or the person who is watching and reporting on this to prove that the individual actually knew, because they could be at the laundromat and they could be just drying their clothes.
rigor.explanation: Reasons from the 'knowingly' element in clause 7(1) to a real evidential burden on prosecutors, illustrated by a case where knowledge would plainly be hard to prove. Sound as far as it goes, though it leans on the illustration rather than on any authority about how the mental element would be applied.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But, certainly, a fine should be an alternative because, you know, an offence for your kid having grandad’s gang patch jacket in the spare wardrobe clearly doesn’t warrant any imprisonment.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the penalty structure of a named clause in the bill; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is almost kind of creating a thought crime in the sense that you’re not allowed to have, in your own bedroom, a symbol on the wall which represents a gang affiliation.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual reach of the proposed clause into private space; the argument is about the measure, not about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It puts a harder burden on the individual police officer or the person who is watching and reporting on this to prove that the individual actually knew, because they could be at the laundromat and they could be just drying their clothes.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the operation of a named clause — the mental element and how it would be proved. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because if you’re in the supermarket, if you’re at the cemetery, and if you’re going about your daily business and you didn’t realise that you were in a public place, like the playground, with your tamariki—how are the police going to prosecute a mother with her children, who is just strolling along to the playground locally, just down the road, and she just happens to be wearing a bandana and a “Mangu Kaha” T-shirt?
focus.explanation: Presses the enforcement question raised by the bill's 'public place' and 'insignia' definitions with concrete scenarios; the weight is on how the measure would work, not on the Government as a party.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: My point is this: despicable as this whole clause is, you simply don’t need (c), because the person, if it’s in that boarding house situation or in a gang house situation, can’t have possession of the gang insignia and they can’t have control of the gang insignia.
civility.explanation: Calls the clause 'despicable' — brutal about the drafting, but the target is the provision, not the Minister or any member.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, Minister, you’re not exactly leaping to your feet in response to my question, so I might, if I may, go on to a further tabled amendment on that same clause—the clause that you’ve slipped in by stealth, thinking that perhaps we’re going to debate it, but this is the only chance we’ll get—and that is why I want to talk about the clause 8A(1), which starts off, “A court must make a gang insignia prohibition order”.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the Minister personally — that he 'slipped in' the clause 'by stealth' to evade debate — and needles him for not rising. Short of a direct insult, but it is an attack on motive rather than on the provision.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Because if you’re in the supermarket, if you’re at the cemetery, and if you’re going about your daily business and you didn’t realise that you were in a public place, like the playground, with your tamariki—how are the police going to prosecute a mother with her children, who is just strolling along to the playground locally, just down the road, and she just happens to be wearing a bandana and a “Mangu Kaha” T-shirt?
civility.explanation: A hostile challenge to the bill in a genuinely contested committee debate, put entirely as a question about the provision's operation; nobody is attacked.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of the Amendment Papers around someone being convicted three times for flouting the gang patch ban, there is a series of consequences that flow, so as to give the judicial system greater ability to deal with recidivist offenders in this way, and we think that’s appropriate.
specificity.explanation: Names the Amendment Papers and the three-conviction trigger, but the 'series of consequences' is never enumerated — a direction with detail missing on the how.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I have three questions for the Minister in terms of clause 7(2). What happens if the gang member is under 18? Is there going to be any modelling done around eligibility or resources that will be required for home detention if they have been sentenced? And have any considerations been given in terms of the proportionality around six months or the fine of $5,000?
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the penalty figures ($5,000, six months), the age threshold and the specific mechanism (home detention eligibility) — precise enough to be answered or checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There should be a harsh punishment for parents or for immediate family members who are dressing young people in their control in gang insignia, and there should be a harsh punishment for people who wish to recruit young people to gangs and have them wearing gang insignia.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the target group clearly but 'harsh punishment' carries no penalty level, mechanism or drafting — the direction is clear, the content is not.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Many people have suffered the violent consequences for wearing the wrong thing in the wrong place, and the only reason why it would be an unwritten rule that we don’t wear red in Whangārei is because of precisely the matters that we’re trying to deal with in this legislation.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the rationale for the legislation — the harm it is said to address.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I would like to just clarify to the Minister that it is not greater authority. The principle of comity states that it is already the rights of courts to be independent and for the judiciary and for the legislature not to impede on the independence of the judiciary.
focus.explanation: Directly engages clause 8(a) and the mechanism it uses — whether it confers new authority on the District Court.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I have three questions for the Minister in terms of clause 7(2). What happens if the gang member is under 18? Is there going to be any modelling done around eligibility or resources that will be required for home detention if they have been sentenced? And have any considerations been given in terms of the proportionality around six months or the fine of $5,000?
focus.explanation: Entirely about the operation of a named clause; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When courts or police are asked to come back to what the intention of Parliament was when this bill was passed, I want to be clear as a Parliament that the Minister has not answered my question, and so they must conclude that it is the intention of Parliament that undertakers, that people who carry on the business of funeral direction, that hospitals, and that people who conduct the affairs of the marae as the legal owners of the marae are not intended to be considered as persons under his provision at Part 2, clause 7(1).
focus.explanation: Engages a named provision (Part 2, clause 7(1)) and who it captures — substantive scrutiny of the measure, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Many people have suffered the violent consequences for wearing the wrong thing in the wrong place, and the only reason why it would be an unwritten rule that we don’t wear red in Whangārei is because of precisely the matters that we’re trying to deal with in this legislation.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a sole cause ('the only reason') from an anecdotal unwritten rule, and jumps from the existence of intimidation to this bill being the answer — a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would like to just clarify to the Minister that it is not greater authority. The principle of comity states that it is already the rights of courts to be independent and for the judiciary and for the legislature not to impede on the independence of the judiciary.
rigor.explanation: A real inference from a named legal principle, but there is a gap: that courts are already independent does not itself establish that a statutory direction confers no additional authority.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When courts or police are asked to come back to what the intention of Parliament was when this bill was passed, I want to be clear as a Parliament that the Minister has not answered my question, and so they must conclude that it is the intention of Parliament that undertakers, that people who carry on the business of funeral direction, that hospitals, and that people who conduct the affairs of the marae as the legal owners of the marae are not intended to be considered as persons under his provision at Part 2, clause 7(1).
rigor.explanation: Argument from silence: the Minister's failure to answer is treated as establishing a positive parliamentary intention that named parties fall outside clause 7(1). The conclusion does not follow from the absence of a reply.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I just wanted to respond to one of the questions that the previous speaker, Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan, raised in relation to the three-strikes legislation—and I’m sure that he’s fully aware of this: that three-strikes legislation has particular offences that are included in strike offences, which does not include the gang patch one.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the schedule of qualifying strike offences under the three-strikes regime does not include the gang insignia offence created by this bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The schedule of strike offences in the three-strikes legislation before Parliament in 2024 (Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Bill / Sentencing Act 2002 as amended); true if the gang insignia display offence is absent from that list, false if it appears.

veracity.statement: Of course, it also has 24 months’ imprisonment as a threshold as well, which is obviously more than six months.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the three-strikes regime has a 24-month imprisonment sentencing threshold for an offence to count as a strike.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the three-strikes legislation before Parliament in 2024; true if a qualifying strike requires a sentence of 24 months' imprisonment or more, false if the threshold is a different figure or absent.

veracity.statement: But when the discussion has gone on in this committee stage, we have talked about proposed clause 8A, which actually talks about insignia inside of the home and a prohibition occurring there.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that proposed clause 8A of the bill extends a prohibition on gang insignia to inside a private home, contrary to an earlier assurance that the bill applied only to public places.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of proposed clause 8A as introduced by the Amendment Paper to the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill; true if it permits prohibition of insignia display within a private dwelling, false if its application is confined to public places.

civility.statement: The reason this contribution isn’t repetitive, for the benefit of the member—I think the member from Northland—is that the Minister hasn’t considered this.
civility.explanation: Answers an interjection pointedly, with a mild dig at not knowing the interjector's name, but stops short of landing on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In terms of workability, it’s an absolute dog’s breakfast and it’s a horrendous piece of legislation.
civility.explanation: Brutal about the bill itself; no person is attacked, no bad faith imputed. Under the re-anchored scale, fierce criticism of a measure is the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So I’m hopeful that when we come to talk about those further Amendment Papers, he will at least have the decency to mention the paper and mention his position on it, and perhaps he can find it in his heart to give a reason why he takes the position he does.
civility.explanation: Sarcasm directed at the Minister personally — 'have the decency', 'find it in his heart' impute discourtesy and indifference rather than engaging the substance of his position.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of the residence question, the point is that this is a truly extraordinary intrusion into someone’s personal life in that you’re not only prohibiting them from having gang insignia in their possession or in their room; you’re prohibiting their flatmates from having gang insignias—if they know about it—in another room.
specificity.explanation: Describes the concrete reach of the clause — possession in one's own room versus a flatmate's room, conditioned on knowledge. Checkable against the clause text, though no figures or dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So my question to the Minister is: how does the dispersal notice get issued if a person doesn’t provide their email and doesn’t choose to accompany a constable or a police officer to a police station to receive such a notice?
specificity.explanation: Names the exact operational gap — the two service routes she has identified and the case where both fail. A precise question the Minister could answer concretely.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My question to the Minister is: is it necessary for the news to show the full image of gang insignia, or would it be more appropriate for gang insignia to either be blurred or to be used in a way which does not show the full picture?
specificity.explanation: Attaches to a named exception in clause 8 and proposes a concrete alternative (blurring / partial display), but offers no drafting, threshold or test for when it would apply.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s pretty well established that there are not the police resources in many modest towns and provincial centres to break up a big motorcade, and once that motorcade has come and gone, the whole purpose of a dispersal order is expired, so you’ve got a strange situation where you can’t do it when it’s happening because you haven’t got the resources, and then once it’s occurred, it doesn’t matter anymore anyway because it’s of historical significance only.
rigor.explanation: A genuine dilemma argument: given the resourcing premise and the in-the-moment purpose of a dispersal order, the conclusion that the power is unusable either way follows. Marked down because the key premise is carried entirely by 'it's pretty well established' — an appeal to common knowledge with nothing offered to support it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So it feels like there’s an awful lot of cooperation involved in a process that by its very nature is a dispersal notice and therefore is probably not likely, necessarily, to come with that requisite cooperation from those parties.
rigor.explanation: Valid inference from the service mechanism she has just described: the procedure depends on cooperation from people who are by definition being ordered to disperse. Hedged rather than fallacious; loses some credit because the cooperation premise is asserted from impression ('so we're certainly led to believe').
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So my question to the Minister is: how does the dispersal notice get issued if a person doesn’t provide their email and doesn’t choose to accompany a constable or a police officer to a police station to receive such a notice?
focus.explanation: Entirely on the mechanism of the measure before the committee; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So my question is around why the Minister chose to ignore advice from justice officials around enforcing this ban on gangs gathering in a public place and how it is likely to undercut “efforts to cultivate pro-social activities within gang communities, for those groups that have moved towards adopting such behaviours”.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named provision against the official advice on it — the archetype of on-policy opposition questioning.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So my question is around why the Minister chose to ignore advice from justice officials around enforcing this ban on gangs gathering in a public place and how it is likely to undercut “efforts to cultivate pro-social activities within gang communities, for those groups that have moved towards adopting such behaviours”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that officials from the justice sector gave written advice warning that the public-place gathering ban would undercut efforts to cultivate pro-social activity in gang communities, and that this advice was not followed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice departmental report / Regulatory Impact Statement and released advice on the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill (2024): true if official advice contains the quoted or materially equivalent warning about undercutting pro-social activity within gang communities and the gathering-ban provision proceeded unchanged; false if no such advice exists in the released documents.

veracity.statement: We know that Mark Pitman, leader of Black Power, was instrumental in getting vaccinations into the Black Power community.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a named Black Power leader, Mark Pitman, played a leading role in driving COVID-19 vaccination uptake within the Black Power community.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous NZ news reporting and Ministry of Health / Whānau Ora vaccination-outreach records from 2021: true if Mark Pitman is identified as a Black Power leader who led or fronted vaccination efforts in that community; false if no such person or role is documented, or the individual is misidentified.

veracity.statement: We know that Harry Tam, as well, who is a lifetime affiliate of the Mongrel Mob, was also involved in encouraging his community to get vaccinated.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Harry Tam, a lifetime Mongrel Mob affiliate, was involved in encouraging COVID-19 vaccination within his community.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ news reporting from 2021 and public records of gang-community vaccination outreach: true if Harry Tam is documented as a Mongrel Mob affiliate involved in promoting vaccination uptake; false if no such involvement is recorded.

civility.statement: I’m just giving some examples because, before the dinner break, it seemed the Minister wasn’t aware of some of these pro-social activities.
civility.explanation: Pointed — it implies the Minister was uninformed — but the remark stays on what was and wasn't covered in debate rather than on his character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But with respect, the member is mistaken when she’s suggesting for a moment that the so-called pro-social activities of gangs will be stopped by this process, because police need to reasonably believe that the dispersal notice is necessary to avoid the gang unreasonably disrupting the activities of other members of the public.
civility.explanation: Contradicts the member directly and the 'so-called' is mildly dismissive, but the disagreement is about her reading of the clause, not about her.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is providing a positive social outcome for that community, which would not be possible had these laws been in place, because these laws would be used against them.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: what the dispersal-notice provisions would do to specific community gatherings. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But what this bill does is it puts a huge amount of responsibility on the person issuing the dispersal notice to, first of all, determine whether that person is a gang member and then it also asks them to look at whether it’s an unreasonable disruption, and that isn’t connected to their gang activity.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of clause 9 — the two judgements the issuing officer must make and the missing link between them. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is providing a positive social outcome for that community, which would not be possible had these laws been in place, because these laws would be used against them.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on a bare assertion of the contested premise — 'these laws would be used against them' is exactly what is in dispute, and nothing in the clause or in practice is offered to connect the notice power to these gatherings. Begging the question.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Our clear understanding is that, on balance, they do more harmful things for the community, and that’s why we have this piece of legislation that is giving the police extra powers to deal with gang activity.
rigor.explanation: The load-bearing premise — that gangs are on balance net harmful — is supported only by an appeal to the Government's own 'clear understanding'. No evidence, advice or data is offered, so the justification for the extra powers rests on unsupported authority.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But with respect, the member is mistaken when she’s suggesting for a moment that the so-called pro-social activities of gangs will be stopped by this process, because police need to reasonably believe that the dispersal notice is necessary to avoid the gang unreasonably disrupting the activities of other members of the public.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference from the statutory test: if the threshold requires reasonable belief of unreasonable disruption, gatherings that cause none fall outside it. The gap is that it assumes the test will be applied as drafted rather than at police discretion, which he elsewhere emphasises is broad.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But what this bill does is it puts a huge amount of responsibility on the person issuing the dispersal notice to, first of all, determine whether that person is a gang member and then it also asks them to look at whether it’s an unreasonable disruption, and that isn’t connected to their gang activity.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the text she has quoted: if the threshold test does not require the disruption to be gang-related, an officer's judgement is doing the work. The inference is sound, though it treats the drafting gap as necessarily producing the wide use she fears without showing that.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But we also know that there are many gangs that provide really important family violence prevention services and addiction-based health groups, such as the Kahukura marae-based programme run by the Mongrel Mob that helped its members and its community to move away from methamphetamine use.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a marae-based methamphetamine programme called Kahukura was run by the Mongrel Mob and assisted members and their community away from meth use.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public records of the Kahukura / Hard to Reach programme (Proceeds of Crime fund allocation, Ministry of Health and Te Puni Kōkiri reporting, and the independent Massey/Kupenga evaluation): true if a Mongrel Mob-affiliated marae-based methamphetamine programme of that name existed and evaluation reported reduced use among participants; false if no such programme is recorded or it was not gang-run.

veracity.statement: Because this is providing the police with one extra tool in order to help them deal with the disruptive activities of gangs in the public sphere following a 50 percent increase in gang membership over the past six years, and widespread public concern.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that gang membership in New Zealand rose by 50 percent over the six years preceding August 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Police National Gang List membership figures for 2018 and 2024 (as released by NZ Police / in answers to written questions): true if the recorded membership grew by approximately 50 percent or more across that span, false if the growth was materially below 50 percent.

specificity.statement: But we also know that there are many gangs that provide really important family violence prevention services and addiction-based health groups, such as the Kahukura marae-based programme run by the Mongrel Mob that helped its members and its community to move away from methamphetamine use.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific programme, its setting, the gang running it and the harm it addressed — checkable — though no figures on participants or outcomes are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Or if they didn’t have an email, which has been raised if someone didn’t offer up an email address, then the police have the power to take them to the station to provide a printed-off copy if that is what is required.
specificity.explanation: Sets out a concrete operational mechanism — the fallback service method and the power to take a person to a station to effect it — which can be checked against the bill and acted on by police.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Because this is providing the police with one extra tool in order to help them deal with the disruptive activities of gangs in the public sphere following a 50 percent increase in gang membership over the past six years, and widespread public concern.
specificity.explanation: Gives a quantified justification — a named magnitude and a stated period — alongside the function of the power, all checkable; 'widespread public concern' is the only vague element.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It specifies here that a person commits an offence if they’ve been served with a dispersal notice and then knowingly, without any reasonable excuse, associate with a named person in a public place during a period of time in which the notice is in effect.
veracity.explanation: Andersen characterises what clause 17 of Part 3 of the gangs bill provides — that breach of a dispersal notice consists of knowingly associating, without reasonable excuse, with a named person in a public place while the notice is in force.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of clause 17 of the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill as reported back from the Justice Committee (2024); true if the offence provision is framed as knowing association, without reasonable excuse, with a person named in the notice in a public place during the notice period; false if the clause's elements differ materially (e.g. no knowledge element, or not limited to public places).

veracity.statement: Māori, being the most impacted people by this legislation, have not been consulted or engaged with.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two things: that Māori are the group most affected by the gangs legislation, and that no consultation or engagement with Māori was undertaken on the bill's proposal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Justice regulatory impact statement and departmental disclosure statement for the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill (2024), plus the Justice Committee report; true if those documents record that no targeted consultation or engagement with Māori or iwi was carried out on the proposal, and that Māori are disproportionately represented among those the measures apply to; false if a Māori/iwi consultation process is documented.

veracity.statement: Sorry, just in relation to the concerns that the member has raised about whānau and important relationships, it’s worth noting that both the dispersal notices are for seven days or the non-consorting orders do have exemptions for immediate family members and for those engaging in activities like work or education or healthcare, so you’re not going to be stopped from consorting with your family members and your co-workers if you happen to have a job, and exemptions can be applied for lawful attendance at tangi, for example.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that dispersal notices run for seven days and that both dispersal notices and non-consorting orders carry exemptions covering immediate family members and employment, education and healthcare activities, with further exemptions available on application.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill as reported back (Part 3, dispersal notice and non-consorting order provisions); true if the notice duration is seven days and the exemption clauses list immediate family, employment, education and health services with an application mechanism for other lawful purposes; false if any of those exemptions are absent or the duration differs.

veracity.statement: In terms of the consultation, I will remind the member that the bill has been before a select committee with the opportunity for anybody to engage and have their views on this legislation over the past four months, which is how the process normally works, and people get an opportunity to have their say.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill had been before a select committee, open to submissions from anyone, for the preceding four months.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bill page for the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill: first reading/referral date, submission opening and closing dates, and the Justice Committee report-back date; true if the period between referral and this August 2024 debate is about four months with a public call for submissions; false if the period is materially shorter or submissions were not publicly open.

focus.statement: Say those five gang members from the main street have all been issued with a dispersal notice and are subsequently at another house where they’re not doing illegal activity but they are together and a police officer comes across them, then how will the police officer prove, how will the prosecution prove, that in fact they are the same two members who should not be associating together, who have breached that dispersal notice and are therefore liable for a six-month imprisonment period or a fine of up to $5,000?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanics of the measure before the committee: the evidential burden for proving a breach of a dispersal notice, and the penalty attached. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Further, in terms of the prohibition orders of five years, that’s quite taimaha, that’s quite a heavy burden, again, for the individual, for over a five-year period not to associate with their whanaunga with gang affiliations.
focus.explanation: Engages a named feature of the bill — the five-year duration of prohibition/non-consorting orders — and who it affects. No content about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Say those five gang members from the main street have all been issued with a dispersal notice and are subsequently at another house where they’re not doing illegal activity but they are together and a police officer comes across them, then how will the police officer prove, how will the prosecution prove, that in fact they are the same two members who should not be associating together, who have breached that dispersal notice and are therefore liable for a six-month imprisonment period or a fine of up to $5,000?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific enforcement scenario, the identification problem, and the exact penalty (six months' imprisonment or a $5,000 fine); a minister could act on or answer it directly. Missing only a statutory reference.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Further, in terms of the prohibition orders of five years, that’s quite taimaha, that’s quite a heavy burden, again, for the individual, for over a five-year period not to associate with their whanaunga with gang affiliations.
specificity.explanation: Names the order type and its five-year duration and identifies the affected relationship (whanaunga with gang affiliations), but offers no figures, threshold or alternative mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Sorry, just in relation to the concerns that the member has raised about whānau and important relationships, it’s worth noting that both the dispersal notices are for seven days or the non-consorting orders do have exemptions for immediate family members and for those engaging in activities like work or education or healthcare, so you’re not going to be stopped from consorting with your family members and your co-workers if you happen to have a job, and exemptions can be applied for lawful attendance at tangi, for example.
specificity.explanation: Gives the duration of a dispersal notice (seven days) and enumerates the specific statutory exemptions relied on — immediate family, work, education, healthcare, and applied-for exemptions such as tangi.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In terms of the consultation, I will remind the member that the bill has been before a select committee with the opportunity for anybody to engage and have their views on this legislation over the past four months, which is how the process normally works, and people get an opportunity to have their say.
rigor.explanation: Answers an objection about the Crown's specific Te Tiriti consultation obligations by pointing to the general open-submission select committee process. The conclusion — that consultation was adequate — does not follow from the premise that anyone could submit; it substitutes a different standard for the one raised (an appeal to normal process).
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In terms of the consultation, I will remind the member that the bill has been before a select committee with the opportunity for anybody to engage and have their views on this legislation over the past four months, which is how the process normally works, and people get an opportunity to have their say.
civility.explanation: Rebuts a serious charge — that the Crown failed its Treaty obligations — entirely on process grounds, without any dig at the member who made it.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s why I’ve put in Amendment Paper D, which suggests deleting the words “or were gathered”, so when you serve the notice, you can serve it on someone at a gathering or who are gathered.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact amendment paper and the precise words to be deleted from the clause; someone could act on or check this directly. Falls short of 1.0 only in not citing the clause number.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One of the issues that I have is in Part 3, clause 9 when it talks about “a gang member;” or “3 or more gang members”, and I know when I go to the definition that that includes prospecting gang members.
specificity.explanation: Cites the part and clause, quotes the operative words, and identifies the definitional consequence she is probing. Concrete enough that anyone could open the bill and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The “were gathered” makes no sense, because to pop round their house the next day utterly undermines the very purpose of this bill, which is to disperse. They have dispersed, and so to issue a dispersal notice after the dispersal is an absolute nonsense.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: if the sole purpose of the notice is immediate dispersal, serving it after dispersal is self-defeating. Valid given that premise, but it rests on a narrowed account of the purpose (it excludes prevention of re-gathering), so there is a gap between what is shown and the flat conclusion of 'absolute nonsense'.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I do think the member is somewhat lacking in imagination, because it is quite possible that certain gang members might be in the habit of gathering regularly every day for a week in a manner that unreasonably disrupts the activities of the members of the public, and so the purpose of having served the dispersal notice would be to stop the re-gathering in that particular circumstance.
rigor.explanation: The insult is decorative, not load-bearing: the argument is a counterexample that directly rebuts the claim that a post-dispersal notice is purposeless, by identifying a case (habitual re-gathering) where it has a purpose. The conclusion follows from the example offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We already know from experience that we are over-profiled, and it shows where 50 percent of the male population in jail and 65 percent of female are of Māori descent.
rigor.explanation: The inference runs from incarceration shares to the conclusion that Māori are 'over-profiled' by police. Imprisonment composition is downstream of many stages (offending, charging, sentencing) and does not by itself establish profiling at the point of police suspicion — a real gap between evidence and conclusion, reinforced by an appeal to personal experience.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I do think the member is somewhat lacking in imagination, because it is quite possible that certain gang members might be in the habit of gathering regularly every day for a week in a manner that unreasonably disrupts the activities of the members of the public, and so the purpose of having served the dispersal notice would be to stop the re-gathering in that particular circumstance.
civility.explanation: Opens by characterising the member himself as 'lacking in imagination' — condescension aimed at the person rather than the argument. Mild as insults go, but it is a remark about the member, not about what he said.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There’s a lot of devil in the detail on this and it feels completely unworkable to us. I think the more the Minister can clarify in these scenarios exactly what will happen, the more confidence, particularly the police will have, that this terrible piece of legislation could actually have some validity. Otherwise, it really does seem like a terrible piece of lawmaking.
civility.explanation: Extremely harsh about the legislation — 'terrible piece of lawmaking', 'completely unworkable' — but attacks no person, imputes no bad faith, and invites the Minister to clarify. Fierce criticism of a measure is the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That is so dangerous, because, in my eyes and within our experiences, that is stereotyping 101, and I circle the definition of what is “reasonable grounds”, and to use the word “suspect” is very, very dangerous, because we know, and the data shows, that we are over-profiled.
civility.explanation: Strong condemnation of the drafting ('reasonable grounds', 'suspect') and its likely effect. No member is attacked and no bad faith is imputed to anyone.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We already know from experience that we are over-profiled, and it shows where 50 percent of the male population in jail and 65 percent of female are of Māori descent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori make up 50 percent of the male prison population and 65 percent of the female prison population in New Zealand at the time of speaking (August 2024).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections prison population statistics (Prison facts and statistics / quarterly population table) for 2024, broken down by sex and ethnicity: true if the Māori share of male prisoners is approximately 50% and of female prisoners approximately 65%; false if either figure is materially different (more than a few percentage points off).

focus.statement: We already know from experience that we are over-profiled, and it shows where 50 percent of the male population in jail and 65 percent of female are of Māori descent.
focus.explanation: Squarely engaged with the operative test in the bill — whether a constable may 'suspect' someone is a gang member — and the group-level consequence of that test. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Will this happen in our communities? And we know it will.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the dispersal-notice power in the bill will in practice be used against Māori in communities like hers — i.e. that the profiling scenario she has just described will occur once the power is in force.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NZ Police reporting or OIA-released data on dispersal notices issued under the Gangs Act 2024 after commencement (21 November 2024), broken down by ethnicity: true if dispersal notices are issued to Māori and disproportionately so relative to population share; false if no notices are issued, or if Māori are not over-represented among recipients.

veracity.statement: There is, obviously, a degree of operational discretion in place there when they’re making those determinations, but I would really like some reassurance from the Minister that while revocations must be determined by the commissioner within 72 hours—we know that, but there’s not really any further detail about how that might operate.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill requires the Commissioner of Police to determine a revocation of a dispersal notice within 72 hours. The Minister in the same debate states the period is 48 hours, so the bill text settles which figure is right.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the gangs/dispersal-notice bill before the committee of the whole House on 6 August 2024 (Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill), clause governing revocation of a dispersal notice: true if it specifies 72 hours for the Commissioner's determination, false if it specifies a different period (e.g. 48 hours).

veracity.statement: The second point I’ll make in this call is that, in this analysis here, there are three options, and the preferred option to progress, from officials, who did all of this work, is to stick with the status quo.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the regulatory impact statement for this bill canvassed three options and that officials' recommended/preferred option was retaining the status quo.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published regulatory impact statement for the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill dispersal-notice provisions: true if it sets out three options and identifies the status quo as officials' preferred option, false if it lists a different number of options or recommends one of the legislative options.

veracity.statement: If somebody feels that they have been issued with a dispersal notice and they shouldn’t have been, the process is to apply to the Commissioner of Police, and the Commissioner of Police has to reply within 48 hours.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill's revocation route is an application to the Commissioner of Police, who must respond within 48 hours.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill as before the committee on 6 August 2024, clause on revocation of dispersal notices: true if it requires the Commissioner to determine and communicate the outcome within 48 hours, false if the period or the decision-maker differs.

veracity.statement: There have been reports—and I’m sure you’ve done your due diligence and read those reports, because there’s racial profiling within the police.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that published reports establish that racial profiling occurs within the New Zealand Police.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official reviews of NZ Police — e.g. the Understanding Policing Delivery research programme, IPCA reports, and the 2022 Police/Te Puni Kōkiri work on bias: true if one or more such reports find evidence of racial profiling or ethnic bias in NZ Police practice, false if no such report makes that finding.

rigor.statement: The current approach with the transnational organised crime strategy and also resilience to organised crime in our communities—that long-term way of reducing organised crime—will have a long-term effect on reducing gang membership in a far more effective way than dispersing people and driving them underground and, effectively, just doing this cosmetic stuff.
rigor.explanation: The comparative conclusion — that the existing strategy will reduce gang membership 'far more effective[ly]' than dispersal notices — is asserted rather than supported; the only backing offered is that officials prefer it (appeal to authority), with no mechanism or evidence linking the strategy to reduced membership.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Inviting people to a protest for Toitū Te Tiriti could be a cause that if any gang member or group of gang members decided to put that sign up and say, “That was the reason we’re gathering”, then surely no dispersal notice could ever be granted.
rigor.explanation: Reasons from the text of clause 9(3) to a workability problem, but leaps to the absolute conclusion that 'no dispersal notice could ever be granted' — an overgeneralisation from one hypothetical that ignores the other statutory tests she herself cites elsewhere.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The current approach with the transnational organised crime strategy and also resilience to organised crime in our communities—that long-term way of reducing organised crime—will have a long-term effect on reducing gang membership in a far more effective way than dispersing people and driving them underground and, effectively, just doing this cosmetic stuff.

civility.statement: It’s not a way I would describe Dr Webb, and I wanted to perhaps draw the Minister’s attention and utilise his imagination.

civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s a privilege to take the first call on this particular silly bill.

specificity.statement: If somebody feels that they have been issued with a dispersal notice and they shouldn’t have been, the process is to apply to the Commissioner of Police, and the Commissioner of Police has to reply within 48 hours.

specificity.statement: I mean, just to take one example: in clause 10(2), there is an expectation that the constable requests that the person give them their email address or other method of serving electronically, which I imagine is an electronic address, but presumably in the future could include some other forms of address which are not specified in this piece of legislation.
specificity.explanation: Cites a specific subclause and the concrete obligation it places on a constable, and identifies the precise gap (undefined forms of electronic address); a reader could go to clause 10(2) and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Inviting people to a protest for Toitū Te Tiriti could be a cause that if any gang member or group of gang members decided to put that sign up and say, “That was the reason we’re gathering”, then surely no dispersal notice could ever be granted.
focus.explanation: Engages a named subclause of the bill before the committee (clause 9(3)) and works through how it would operate in practice; no party framing at all.

focus.statement: I find this bill really concerning when you’ve got words like “reasonable grounds”. It’s absolutely subjective to suspect that a person is a gang member.
focus.explanation: Targets a specific statutory test in the bill ('reasonable grounds' to suspect gang membership) and the discretion it confers; the objection is to the drafting, not to the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Like my colleague talked about, Hana, 50 percent of the male prison population in Aotearoa are Māori; 65 percent of the female prison population are Māori. That already tells us that we’ve been racially profiled.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific proportions of the NZ prison muster identifying as Māori — 50 percent of male prisoners and 65 percent of female prisoners.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections prison population statistics (Prison facts and statistics / quarterly muster) for 2024: true if the Māori share of the male muster is approximately 50% and of the female muster approximately 65%; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Your Prime Minister agreed that article 2 was to be undisturbed of our property rights—of our taonga, of our moana, of our kāinga.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim that the Prime Minister, in question time in the week before 6 August 2024, accepted that article 2 of the Treaty guaranteed undisturbed possession of Māori property, taonga, waters and homes.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard record of oral questions in the sitting week preceding 6 August 2024: true if the Prime Minister stated or accepted that article 2 guarantees undisturbed possession of Māori property/taonga; false if no such exchange occurred or he declined to accept it.

veracity.statement: I’d like to reassure him that if somebody thought that they were issued with a dispersal notice and they weren’t a gang member, then the process is set out very clearly in clause 18, which is to say they can apply immediately to the Commissioner of Police and the Commissioner of Police has to reply back within 48 hours, and if the individual is not a gang member, then they wouldn’t meet the grounds for the dispersal notice.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Text of clause 18 of the Gangs Bill as reported back from select committee (and the Gangs Act 2024 as enacted): true if it provides for application to the Commissioner of Police with a response required within 48 hours; false if no such review, decision-maker or timeframe appears.

veracity.statement: We’ve got an Electronic Transactions Act that deals with this very problem, and it says that something is delivered only when it enters the information system of the recipient.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's Electronic Transactions Act sets the time of delivery of an electronic communication as the moment it enters the recipient's information system.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electronic Transactions Act 2002 (and its successor provisions in the Contract and Commercial Law Act 2017, ss 213-214): true if the receipt rule is that an electronic communication is received when it enters the recipient's information system; false if the statute sets a different rule or no such provision exists.

veracity.statement: But let’s just be clear about this, and we looked at this in select committee: there is no other situation where you’re given a notice by email and if you don’t comply with it, you can go to jail.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no other New Zealand statute allows a notice to be served by email where non-compliance with that notice is punishable by imprisonment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Search of NZ statutes permitting service of a notice by electronic means where breach of the notice carries a penalty of imprisonment: true if no such provision can be identified, false if any statute is found that both permits email service and makes non-compliance imprisonable.

rigor.statement: Like my colleague talked about, Hana, 50 percent of the male prison population in Aotearoa are Māori; 65 percent of the female prison population are Māori. That already tells us that we’ve been racially profiled.
rigor.explanation: Infers the existence of racial profiling directly from over-representation in the prison muster. The conclusion does not follow from the statistic alone — imprisonment rates have many possible causes, and no step is offered linking the muster to police profiling behaviour.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’ve already got police officers who do a good job. Community policing is the answer, and I already know because we have community policing down there in Whangaparāoa Cape Runaway, where a police officer actually plays rugby with the Mongrel Mob members.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single local anecdote (one officer playing rugby with gang members in one community) to the conclusion that community policing is 'the answer' nationally. Argument from anecdote.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In relation to helping out with vaccination campaigns, again, that is not captured by this legislation, because it would be very hard to describe that as unreasonably disrupting the activities of members of the public.
rigor.explanation: Applies the bill's own statutory test (unreasonable disruption of the activities of members of the public) to the example raised, and the conclusion follows from that premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In terms of racial profiling, I think the only point I’d make there is, you know, it’s very easy to say and very damaging for the many thousands of young men and women in the police force who do their very best every day to keep the community safe.
rigor.explanation: Responds to the allegation of racial profiling by pointing to the harm the allegation causes rather than to whether it is accurate — an appeal to consequences, which leaves the claim itself unaddressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But clause 11A(3) says “A failure to comply with this section does not affect the validity of the dispersal notice.” So you’ve got an obligation to explain, but if you don’t do it, it doesn’t matter.
rigor.explanation: Quotes the savings provision and draws the conclusion that the duty to explain carries no consequence. The inference tracks the text offered — the duty has no remedy attached if breach does not invalidate the notice.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.explanation: Engages the policy question directly by proposing a named alternative approach — community policing — rather than characterising the other party.

focus.statement: But clause 11A(3) says “A failure to comply with this section does not affect the validity of the dispersal notice.” So you’ve got an obligation to explain, but if you don’t do it, it doesn’t matter.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanics of the measure before the committee — a named subclause, its effect, and a proposed amendment; no party framing at all.

civility.statement: In terms of racial profiling, I think the only point I’d make there is, you know, it’s very easy to say and very damaging for the many thousands of young men and women in the police force who do their very best every day to keep the community safe.
civility.explanation: Pushes back on the member's allegation and edges toward suggesting it is cheaply made, but stops short of impugning him personally and stays on the substance of police conduct.
