veracity.falsification_criterion: LGFA lending policy / shareholder announcements and the Government's 8 August 2024 Local Water Done Well announcement; true if LGFA borrowing limits for water CCOs are set at 500% of revenue (versus ~280% for councils), false if a materially different limit or no such facility exists.

veracity.statement: Did the Minister include in his announcement that out of the only 182 submissions who were able to submit as part of the truncated 10-day deadline, only 19 explicitly supported the bill, 18 percent of councils missed out on even having their voice heard, and of those who did, all of them submitted that “the cost and resource implications are both unclear and significant for councils, making it challenging to plan or fund the reforms”?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill received 182 submissions under a 10-day window, that only 19 explicitly supported it, and that 18 percent of councils did not get to submit.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Select committee report and published submissions for the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill; true if the submission total is 182 with 19 in explicit support and the submission period was about 10 days, false if the counts or the window differ materially.

veracity.statement: Can he guarantee that the proposed review of the Māori and Pacific Admission Scheme, which has admitted more than 700 Māori and Pasifika students to medical school in the last 10 years, will not lead to its disestablishment?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that MAPAS has admitted more than 700 Māori and Pasifika students to medical school over the past decade.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: University of Auckland / University of Otago MAPAS admissions data for 2014–2024; true if cumulative admissions exceed 700, false if materially fewer.

veracity.statement: As part of our coalition agreement with ACT, we have agreed to review the Māori and Pacific Admission Scheme (MAPAS). This review is yet to begin, and no decisions about terms of reference have been made.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the National–ACT coalition agreement commits to a MAPAS review and that as at 8 August 2024 the review had not begun and no terms of reference had been decided.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Text of the National–ACT coalition agreement (2023) and Ministry of Health / Ministerial statements on the MAPAS review; true if the agreement contains such a commitment and no review had commenced by 8 August 2024, false if the commitment is absent or the review had already started.

veracity.statement: Can I ask the Minister as to whether his inspiration is a former brilliant Minister of Health—who was a Māori, back over a hundred years ago, called Pōmare—who brought modern medicine to Māori, and is that his intention in 2024, ’25, ’26?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māui Pōmare was a Māori Minister of Health over a hundred years before 2024 who brought modern medicine to Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary and historical records of Sir Māui Pōmare's ministerial appointments; true if he served as Minister of Health (he held the portfolio in the early 1920s) and was Māori, false if he never held the portfolio or the dating is materially wrong.

veracity.statement: Yes. We inherited an economy in recession, a broken health system following a botched merger, and an education system that has been failing too many children for too long.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the economy was in recession at the point the coalition took office in late 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP series for 2023; true if two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth cover the period around the change of government, false if the series shows growth over that period.

veracity.statement: How does stopping the construction of schools, hospitals, and houses, when 6,000 people in the construction industry have lost their jobs, help the economy?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 6,000 people in the construction industry had lost their jobs by August 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey / filled jobs data for the construction industry over the year to mid-2024; true if construction employment fell by approximately 6,000, false if the fall is materially different.

veracity.statement: We inherited an economy that was in recession, interest rates that were at record highs, and inflation was well outside the bounds.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that interest rates were at record highs at the change of government in late 2023, alongside recession and out-of-band inflation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ Official Cash Rate and retail mortgage rate series; true if late-2023 rates were the highest on record, false if earlier periods (e.g. the 8.25% OCR of 2007–08, or 1980s–90s mortgage rates) were higher.

veracity.statement: What we are doing is going through a process to secure their resilience into the future, but, as KiwiRail has made very clear, those ferries are safe to operate until at least 2029.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim attributed to KiwiRail that the existing Interislander vessels are safe to operate until at least 2029.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: KiwiRail public statements, select committee evidence and asset-life advice from 2024; true if KiwiRail stated the current fleet is safe/serviceable to at least 2029, false if KiwiRail's stated end-of-life dates are earlier or no such statement exists.

veracity.statement: What estimates has she received of the cost to New Zealand businesses and the economy of the loss of rail capability on the Interislander ferries, given those ferries currently carry over half a million metres of train freight per year?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Interislander rail-enabled ferries currently carry more than half a million lane metres of rail freight per year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: KiwiRail/Interislander annual reporting of rail freight lane metres carried across Cook Strait; true if the annual figure exceeds 500,000 metres, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: Meitaki ranuinui, Mr Speaker. What steps is the Government taking to address the critical funding shortages faced by Hato Hone St John ambulance service, which have led to the impending national withdrawal of labour of over 2,500 ambulance officers?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than 2,500 Hato Hone St John ambulance officers were about to undertake a national withdrawal of labour over funding shortages.

veracity.falsification_criterion: First Union/ Hato Hone St John strike notices and media reporting from August 2024; true if a national strike notice covering over 2,500 ambulance officers was issued, false if no such action was pending or the number is materially smaller.

veracity.statement: Are they not delivering in health because her Government is leaving clinics like those in Dargaville, Wellsford, Kenepuru, Napier, and Rotorua unstaffed overnight?

veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand service notices and contemporaneous reporting on overnight closures at those five named facilities in 2024; true if each (or substantially all) experienced overnight unstaffed periods, false if the named sites were fully staffed overnight.

veracity.statement: Does she believe that Tākai, which has shut down because of her cuts after 20 years of social service, is a cash cow, and what does she say to the tens of thousands of parents who have benefited from their support?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the parenting support service Tākai closed as a result of the Government's funding cuts, after 20 years of operation.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Tākai/Brainwave and Ministry of Social Development funding announcements in 2024; true if Tākai ceased operating following withdrawal of government funding after roughly two decades, false if it continued operating or closed for unrelated reasons.

veracity.statement: How does giving the tobacco industry a $216 million tax break, leaving less money for health, help the economy?

rigor.statement: Well, on behalf of the health Minister, what I do agree with is the review of MAPAS in line with the coalition agreement. When you think about it, what is wrong with reviewing a programme to ensure it’s meeting its objectives?

civility.statement: On behalf of the Minister of Finance, I’m not sure if she has realised, but the ferries are still operating, providing freight services between the North and South Islands.

focus.statement: If that last Government were still in charge, they’d be spending more, they’d be taxing more, and delivering less.

We know that 77 percent of participants in this programme are Māori.

specificity.statement: We are focused on supporting people off the jobseeker benefit and we want to see fewer children being raised in benefit-dependent households.

veracity.statement: Five hundred places for the community-led programmes will be with a selection of He Poutama Rangatahi which was launched by the previous National Government in 2017 for people aged 18 to 24 who have been on jobseeker support longer than a year. veracity.statement: In the six years before we took over, the number of people receiving the jobseeker benefit increased by 70,000, or 57 percent.

veracity.statement: I can tell that member what this Government won’t do with Pacific unemployment: we will not oversee an increase in six years of 93 percent in Pacific unemployment—that’s outrageous, and that’s your record.

veracity.statement: I’m pleased that that member is finally interested in youth unemployment, because what we saw, unfortunately, was a welfare system stagnating so much that a young person who goes on to benefit under the age of 25 now is forecast to spend two decades on welfare.

veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit system valuation / actuarial report figures for average future years on benefit for entrants aged under 25; true if the forecast is approximately 20 years, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: Does the Minister consider Māori employment rates to be back on track when, under her watch, in just nine months, Māori unemployment has increased from 8.2 percent to 9.1 percent?
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Māori unemployment rate rose from 8.2% to 9.1% over the nine months of the current Government.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey Māori unemployment rate for the September/December 2023 and June 2024 quarters; true if the series moves from ~8.2% to ~9.1%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Can the Minister tell us how she can say youth employment is on track when recent figures show that youth unemployment has increased from 15.1 percent to 20.7 percent just in the last June quarter of 2024?
veracity.explanation: Asserts youth unemployment rose from 15.1% to 20.7% as at the June 2024 quarter.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ HLFS youth (15–24, or the 15–19 sub-series) unemployment rate for the June 2024 quarter and the comparison quarter; true if the rates are ~15.1% and ~20.7% on a consistent age band, false if the figures do not match any published youth series for those periods.

veracity.statement: The bill extends the remediation deadlines for earthquake-prone buildings by four years to give temporary relief to Kiwis while the review is under way.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Building (Earthquake-prone Building Deadlines and Other Matters) Amendment Bill as introduced in 2024; true if it extends remediation deadlines by four years, false if the extension is a different length or of a different kind.

divination.statement: The challenging economic situation we have inherited inevitably means that job seeker numbers were expected to increase until January 2025, before decreasing.

divination.falsification_criterion: MSD monthly/quarterly benefit fact sheets for jobseeker support recipients; true if the recipient count peaks around January 2025 and declines thereafter through 2025, false if numbers continue rising past that point.

rigor.statement: For every New Zealander that loses a job right now, it comes back to the broken economy that we inherited and the damage that that side did.
rigor.explanation: Single-cause attribution: every current job loss is asserted to follow from the inherited economy, with nothing offered to exclude other causes or the Government's own decisions. A sweeping causal leap from a general premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: However, many building owners are currently unable to meet deadlines due to high remediation costs and excessive layering of regulations. This is why we have acted with urgency to bring forward the review to provide certainty and ensure we have a good balance between protecting lives and real-world costs.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (bring the review forward) follows reasonably from the stated premise (owners cannot meet deadlines at current cost), though the premise is asserted rather than evidenced and no link is shown between reviewing and the safety balance claimed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This bill responds to longstanding and widespread concerns by the aquaculture sector about the costs and uncertainty and mahi—that means work—associated with re-consenting processes for existing marine farms under the Resource Management Act. This process of re-consenting is inhibiting aquaculture growth.
rigor.explanation: Answers a proportionality objection ("sledgehammer to crack a nut") by asserting that a problem exists, which establishes a need but does not address whether a blanket 20-year extension is a proportionate remedy — a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m pleased that that member is finally interested in youth unemployment, because what we saw, unfortunately, was a welfare system stagnating so much that a young person who goes on to benefit under the age of 25 now is forecast to spend two decades on welfare.
civility.explanation: "finally interested" is a sneer at the questioner's motives rather than at the argument — short of a direct insult, but it imputes indifference to the member personally.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does the Minister have any plan to get people into work, or is she just planning for the figures to get better once a whole lot of Kiwis move to simple, old Australia?

civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Well, answering both those two questions, the person who first drafted the legislation is the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, namely Simon Upton. This was in 1991.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial press releases / beehive.govt.nz statements by the Minister for Building and Construction dated April 2024; true if an announcement of extended earthquake-prone building deadlines was made in that month, false if no such announcement exists in April 2024.

veracity.statement: We have somewhere between 5,500 and 7,000 buildings listed as earthquake-prone nationally.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the national count of buildings recorded as earthquake-prone as at August 2024 falls in the 5,500–7,000 range.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's national Earthquake-Prone Buildings Register / MBIE reporting on earthquake-prone building numbers as at mid-2024; true if the recorded national total sits within 5,500–7,000, false if materially outside that range.

veracity.statement: Wellington City has some 572 buildings on its earthquake list. For 229 of them, their yellow sticker turns red in 2027—229 of them—and if you include the ones between now and 2027, it’s 305.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three specific counts for Wellington City: 572 buildings on the earthquake-prone list, 229 whose remediation deadline falls in 2027, and 305 with deadlines between August 2024 and 2027 inclusive.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Wellington City Council's earthquake-prone buildings register / MBIE EPB Register entries for Wellington City as at August 2024, and the recorded remediation deadline dates; true if the totals match 572, 229 and 305 within rounding, false if materially different.

rigor.statement: We need to have confidence that it is not being applied differently across the country by different engineering outfits, that there is some trust in a scheme such as that, because, you know, on one end, it can be that 33 to 34 is a requirement to remediate or not, but at the other end, the difference between 66 and 67 percent means that a bank might not lend, therefore you can’t sell your building to someone who’s unable to get a mortgage, and things like that.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (confidence in consistent NBS assessment matters) follows from the premises offered: two named thresholds where a one-point difference flips a legal or financial consequence. The causal chain from rating to lending to saleability is spelled out rather than assumed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We don’t want to have a ratchet effect of councils pushing up compliance, then engineers push up compliance, and then banks push up compliance and we end up over-engineering ourselves out of existence, to the point where, when our civilisation is dead and gone, they can see the expensive buildings that at the time cost a fortune and may have been great for archaeologists of the future to look at, but, actually, was that a good use of our funds on the day?
rigor.explanation: Slippery slope: an escalating chain of three actors ratcheting compliance to the point of civilisational extinction of buildable projects, with nothing offered to show that any link in the chain actually occurs or compounds. The archaeologist image is a rhetorical flourish standing in for evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s not only a stress and a pressure and a financial pressure on the building owners but it’s also a question of the capacity of the market, of the industry, of the experts, to actually be able to do the work that needs to be done in that short period of time. So the extra time is really, really important.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the deadline extension matters follows from the premise established immediately before it — that 305 of Wellington's 572 listed buildings come due within three or four years — via a stated capacity constraint on the strengthening industry.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We don’t want to have a ratchet effect of councils pushing up compliance, then engineers push up compliance, and then banks push up compliance and we end up over-engineering ourselves out of existence, to the point where, when our civilisation is dead and gone, they can see the expensive buildings that at the time cost a fortune and may have been great for archaeologists of the future to look at, but, actually, was that a good use of our funds on the day?
focus.explanation: Squarely about the compliance settings of the building regime — councils, engineers, banks and cost — rather than about another party; the weakness is in the inference, not the subject matter.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But let’s be clear, as we heard from the Hon Julie Anne Genter: this does not fix the problem. There is still a problem; it just gives more time to fix that problem.
focus.explanation: States precisely what the measure before the House does and does not achieve — a deadline extension, not a remediation solution — and concedes the point to an opposition member rather than framing it as a party contest.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I’m sure—the Minister said it’s absolutely fine to hear this as well—we will hear many out-of-scope submissions which are talking about things which are more than just the time table, but they will be valuable.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the select committee process on this bill will attract a substantial number of submissions raising matters beyond the deadline timetable, i.e. outside the bill's scope.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Transport and Infrastructure Committee's submissions and final report on the Building (Earthquake-prone Building Deadlines and Other Matters) Amendment Bill; true if the report or the published submissions record a substantial body of submissions on matters outside the bill's scope (e.g. the wider earthquake-prone building regime, NBS ratings), false if submissions were confined to the timetable provisions or the committee records no out-of-scope material.

focus.statement: All of those questions do not get answered if central government is unable to fulfil the role of holding to the remediation time frames that it sets, and so there is a question there about whether extending the time frames, essentially, rewards procrastination.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — the remediation time frames the bill extends and who they signal to. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We oppose the shortened report-back date. We would like to hear fulsomely from those submitters, particularly in local government, and the homeowners who are affected and the people who have been through these earthquake events before, their reasons about how these deadlines are important to certainty in their areas.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the select committee process for this bill — a named procedural feature of the measure — with no reference to the other party's record or character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It may have been a small number of people—and I agree that that fund hadn’t gone far enough to address the problem and that something needed to be changed there, but, I think, for those people who had already put a lot of time and effort and emotional stress that they were suffering from going through this effort to try and access that fund, to have it taken away like that was unfortunate.
focus.explanation: About a named policy instrument (the assistance fund) and the concrete effect of cancelling it on applicants, rather than about the other party in general.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This legislation just extending the time frames doesn’t address the issue of the compliance cost and of how we actually achieve safer buildings in a sustainable way.
focus.explanation: Directly on what the bill does and does not do — time frames versus compliance cost and building safety — with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: All of those questions do not get answered if central government is unable to fulfil the role of holding to the remediation time frames that it sets, and so there is a question there about whether extending the time frames, essentially, rewards procrastination.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: if deadlines are not enforced, extending them creates an incentive to delay. But the link between extension and 'rewarding procrastination' is asserted rather than shown, and it is hedged into a question rather than argued through.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As has been said by the Minister, we can’t really assess the risk of extending the time frames against a perfect scenario where all of those buildings were remediated by the time frames, because 80 percent of them were not going to be.
rigor.explanation: A sound counterfactual point: the extension should be compared with the realistic baseline rather than with full compliance. The inference follows, though it rests on a figure sourced to the Minister rather than independently supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: All of those questions do not get answered if central government is unable to fulfil the role of holding to the remediation time frames that it sets, and so there is a question there about whether extending the time frames, essentially, rewards procrastination.
civility.explanation: Hard criticism of the Government's approach to deadlines with no attack on any individual; engages the substance of the extension.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It may have been a small number of people—and I agree that that fund hadn’t gone far enough to address the problem and that something needed to be changed there, but, I think, for those people who had already put a lot of time and effort and emotional stress that they were suffering from going through this effort to try and access that fund, to have it taken away like that was unfortunate.
civility.explanation: Criticises a Government funding decision and its effect on applicants while conceding the fund's shortcomings; no individual is impugned and no bad faith is imputed.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We oppose the shortened report-back date. We would like to hear fulsomely from those submitters, particularly in local government, and the homeowners who are affected and the people who have been through these earthquake events before, their reasons about how these deadlines are important to certainty in their areas.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific procedural object of the objection (the report-back date) and the categories of submitters she wants heard, but gives no date, no length of extension and no figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Labour had a solution for this. I won’t go into it as I don’t have time, but solutions around lending to people and requiring them to pay it back only on sale or death might be something here that we need to look to.
specificity.explanation: Describes an actual mechanism — a loan to owners repayable only on sale or death — but supplies no amounts, eligibility criteria or timeframe, and explicitly declines to set out the detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This legislation just extending the time frames doesn’t address the issue of the compliance cost and of how we actually achieve safer buildings in a sustainable way.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the gap (compliance cost, sustainable path to safer buildings) but offers no mechanism, figure or alternative provision.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We have to be mindful that these rules were set up in the wake of the Christchurch earthquake and in the context of things like the Kaikōura earthquake, which represent real tragedies for New Zealand, and we need to make sure that these very real events, which happened in New Zealand and which caused loss of life, huge loss of property, and a huge cost to our national infrastructure, are provided for in our legislation and that we have these settings right.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the current earthquake-prone building rules were created as a response to the Christchurch (Canterbury) earthquake, in the context of events including the Kaikōura earthquake.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative history of the earthquake-prone building regime (Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Act 2016, its explanatory note and the Canterbury Earthquakes Royal Commission recommendations). True if the regime was enacted as a response to the Canterbury earthquakes; false if the regime predates and was unrelated to them.

veracity.statement: But, interestingly, because it was on bedrock in Mount Victoria, it seemed fine over the last 80 years of earthquakes; whereas some modern buildings built on reclaimed land in Wellington that were at 100 percent of NBS didn’t fare so well in the earthquake—in fact, fared quite poorly.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that some modern Wellington buildings rated at 100 percent of the new building standard, built on reclaimed land, performed poorly in an earthquake (in context, the 2016 Kaikōura earthquake).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Post-Kaikōura engineering assessments and MBIE/Wellington City Council reports on Wellington buildings (e.g. Statistics House, 61 Molesworth Street). True if buildings assessed at or near 100% NBS on reclaimed land sustained significant structural damage; false if no such buildings were damaged.

veracity.statement: The Greens have actually long recognised—in our arts, culture, and heritage policy—that the earthquake-strengthening system for heritage buildings is cost-prohibitive and leads to buildings being demolished rather than remediated, which is not always a great outcome.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Green Party's published arts, culture and heritage policy contains a position that earthquake-strengthening requirements for heritage buildings are cost-prohibitive and drive demolition.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Green Party's published arts, culture and heritage policy document. True if it contains a statement to that effect about heritage building earthquake strengthening; false if no such position appears in it.

veracity.statement: She was actually writing on behalf of her mother, who also lives in the Rongotai electorate, who is on a fixed income, on a pension, has owned this apartment, it’s her home, she doesn’t want to give it up, and has found herself in a situation of needing to—alongside the other owners of the building, spent an enormous amount, went through all of the paperwork, finally got through all the hurdles to apply for that assistance fund, and then just as that happened it was announced by this Government that they were cancelling the assistance fund.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the current Government announced the cancellation of the earthquake-strengthening assistance fund for residential apartment owners (the residential earthquake-prone building financial assistance scheme).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents and MBIE announcements on the Residential Earthquake-Prone Building Financial Assistance Scheme. True if the scheme was closed/disestablished by a Government announcement before 8 August 2024; false if it remained open.

veracity.statement: However, 2½ months is a lot better than 10 days, as has been the case for some other legislation we’ve seen earlier this year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that some legislation in 2024 was given a select committee period of about 10 days.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's select committee submission periods for bills referred in the first half of 2024 (Order Paper / committee call-for-submissions records). True if at least one bill had a submission period of around 10 days; false if none were that short.

veracity.statement: As has been said by the Minister, we can’t really assess the risk of extending the time frames against a perfect scenario where all of those buildings were remediated by the time frames, because 80 percent of them were not going to be.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (relaying the Minister) that 80 percent of earthquake-prone buildings were not going to be remediated within the existing statutory time frames.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE analysis / the bill's regulatory impact statement on projected remediation rates under the existing deadlines. True if the estimate of non-compliance is around 80 percent; false if the official estimate is materially different.

veracity.statement: Around 150 buildings have already failed to meet their remediation deadlines, and many more are unlikely to be remediated, due to high costs and other barriers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 150 earthquake-prone buildings were already past their statutory remediation deadline as at August 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's Earthquake-Prone Buildings Register and the Regulatory Impact Statement for the Building (Earthquake-prone Building Deadlines and Other Matters) Amendment Bill; true if the count of buildings past their remediation deadline as at mid-2024 is about 150, false if materially different (e.g. under 100 or over 250).

veracity.statement: In Auckland, interestingly enough, more than 1,700 buildings are registered as being earthquake-prone, which is a big proportion of the over 5,000 earthquake-prone buildings nationwide.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that over 1,700 of the more than 5,000 buildings on the national earthquake-prone buildings register as at August 2024 are in Auckland.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's national Earthquake-Prone Buildings Register (and Auckland Council building consents data) as at August 2024; true if the Auckland count exceeds 1,700 and the national total exceeds 5,000, false if either figure is materially lower.

specificity.statement: The key purpose of this bill is to extend the remediation time frames for earthquake-prone buildings by four years, with a limited power to extend deadlines by an extra two years.
specificity.explanation: Names the measure, the mechanism and the exact durations of both the general extension and the additional discretionary extension; a reader could check it against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In Auckland, interestingly enough, more than 1,700 buildings are registered as being earthquake-prone, which is a big proportion of the over 5,000 earthquake-prone buildings nationwide.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete, checkable counts (Auckland and national) tied to a named register; someone could look both up.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I know and have spoken to people who talk of the financial pressures, the stress, the anxiety, and the constraints on their lifestyle that earthquake strengthening causes, but if we leave people to entirely make their own decisions about the safety of buildings, there is never a good time.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: because the costs of strengthening always bite, voluntary timing will always be deferred, therefore deadlines must be compulsory. The conclusion broadly tracks the premise but rests on anecdote ('people I have spoken to') and generalises 'never a good time' from that, so there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If we don’t strike that balance, we will only see more earthquake-prone buildings rot in our rural towns and our city centres across the country, and if members want to know what that looks like, I invite them to check out the old Molly Malones building on the corner of Courtenay Place and Taranaki Street in central Wellington.
rigor.explanation: The general conclusion — that without the extension buildings nationwide will be left to decay — is supported only by pointing to a single named building. Argument from anecdote; one example does not establish the country-wide trend asserted.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We’ve been nudging people to do the right thing, and the Minister for Building and Construction himself—and I’ve a lot of respect for the work he’s doing—has said that “We encourage people to do this remediation work.”, but on this side of the House, our view is that we can’t just encourage; we’ve got to compel.
civility.explanation: Sharp disagreement with the Minister's chosen approach in a genuinely contested first reading, expressed entirely on the substance (encourage versus compel) and with an explicit acknowledgement of the Minister's work. No attack on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So, for Auckland, where the Mayor of Auckland has said that there’s been no signs of earthquake activity for 100,000 years—well, we know that the Mayor of Auckland sometimes exaggerates and has a turn of phrase.
civility.explanation: Moves off the substance to characterise a named individual's habits — a mild, knowing sneer at the Mayor's tendency to exaggerate rather than an engagement with whether the seismic-risk claim is right. Short of a direct insult but no longer purely civil.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It will result in legislative changes, but then they will go through an exhaustive select committee process and will then be reported back to this House for debate, for further consideration, and, ultimately, for ratification.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the seismic-risk review will produce amending legislation that is introduced, sent to select committee, reported back and passed by the House.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Parliament bills register; true if a Government bill amending the earthquake-prone building provisions of the Building Act arising from the seismic risk review is introduced and referred to select committee by 31 December 2026, false if no such bill has been introduced by that date.

rigor.statement: Extending time frames may save some marae from demolition, but it will not address the core issue, as other members have said across both sides, that many hapū cannot afford to strengthen their marae.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House: the bill changes deadlines, and a deadline change does not change affordability, so the conclusion that the core cost problem remains follows from the premise offered. Mild reliance on 'other members have said' as support, but the reasoning stands on its own.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We have a Minister that is listening, and I think that is what this Government is doing a great job of.
rigor.explanation: The support offered is three selected favourable quotations (two mayors and a government MP), from which a general conclusion about the Minister and the Government is drawn — an appeal to selected testimony; supportive voices were quoted and critical ones were not, so the sample does not carry the general conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’re not supporting the bill, primarily because of a fundamental understanding that if you keep kicking the can down the road, nothing ever gets done.
rigor.explanation: A reason is genuinely offered for the vote, but the premise is a proverb rather than an argument — 'nothing ever gets done' is asserted, not shown, and nothing connects this particular extension to permanent inaction. An appeal to a maxim.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government should fully fund strengthening for marae.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete actor and a concrete action (full Crown funding of marae seismic strengthening), but supplies no cost, mechanism, eligibility rule or timeframe, so it is a direction rather than something that could be checked or costed.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s interesting—I’m pleased to see that we have almost got unanimity within the House to support this bill through to select committee, with the one exception being Labour, which I find rather unusual, given that so far their speeches have pretty much been in support of what the goals of the bill are, to give us more time to do a better job, and yet they’re going to vote against it.
focus.explanation: Anchored to a named measure and a named party's position on it — a real point about the first reading vote — but the weight of the remark is on how odd Labour's stance is rather than on the bill's content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But Labour’s solution in Government was the Residential Earthquake-Prone Building Financial Assistance Scheme, and it has been cancelled by this Government.
focus.explanation: Names a specific scheme and a specific outcome (its cancellation) as the alternative to the bill — squarely on policy, and legitimate scrutiny of a named government decision rather than party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s interesting—I’m pleased to see that we have almost got unanimity within the House to support this bill through to select committee, with the one exception being Labour, which I find rather unusual, given that so far their speeches have pretty much been in support of what the goals of the bill are, to give us more time to do a better job, and yet they’re going to vote against it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that at the first reading of the Building (Earthquake-prone Building Deadlines and Other Matters) Amendment Bill every party except Labour supported it to select committee, and that Labour's own speeches endorsed the bill's goals while Labour intended to vote against.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard first-reading debate and division record for the Building (Earthquake-prone Building Deadlines and Other Matters) Amendment Bill (August 2024); true if Labour was the only party voting against and Labour speakers in that debate expressed support for extending time to review the system, false if another party also opposed or if Labour speakers opposed the bill's goals as well as the bill.

veracity.statement: But Labour’s solution in Government was the Residential Earthquake-Prone Building Financial Assistance Scheme, and it has been cancelled by this Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Residential Earthquake-Prone Building Financial Assistance Scheme was established under the previous Labour Government and has since been discontinued by the current Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE/Treasury records and Budget 2024 documents for the Residential Earthquake-Prone Building Financial Assistance Scheme; true if the scheme was set up under the 2017–2023 Labour Government and formally closed/defunded by the coalition Government, false if the scheme remained open and funded at the time of the statement or was not a Labour-established scheme.

veracity.statement: Whilst nothing could ever have provided any forewarning, and there was no building code that would ever have prevented the CTV Building coming down and taking the life of my friend and workmate, I think it is up to the people who lived through that experience—particularly some of the people who experienced real harm and have dedicated their time since then—to campaign for better regulations and for better safety, particularly with buildings in what can only be described as a very earthquake-prone country that we live in.
veracity.explanation: The factual premise asserted is that no building code could have prevented the collapse of the CTV Building in the 2011 Christchurch earthquake.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Canterbury Earthquakes Royal Commission report on the CTV Building; true if the Commission found the building complied with the code in force at design/consent and that collapse was not attributable to code non-compliance, false if the Commission found the design breached the applicable code or was wrongly consented such that compliance with the existing code would have altered the outcome.

divination.statement: This could potentially be the first of several different extensions, and before we know it we will be no further ahead and we will be regretting that decision.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that this deadline extension will be followed by further extensions of the earthquake-prone building remediation deadlines, leaving the regime no further advanced.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand legislation and MBIE announcements on earthquake-prone building remediation deadlines after the August 2024 bill; true if at least one further statutory extension or deferral of those deadlines is enacted or announced after this bill, false if the deadlines set by this bill stand without further extension.

civility.statement: Whilst the member Grant McCallum, who made the contribution before me, found it somewhat perplexing that we weren’t supporting this particular bill, I likewise find it somewhat perplexing that some things that could have been helpful and could have moved us along in a bit more steady way have been cancelled.
civility.explanation: Directly rebuts a named colleague's point using his own framing, and the criticism lands entirely on a policy decision (a cancelled scheme) rather than on him. No imputation of bad faith or personal jibe.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I think I would respectfully point out to those who are nervous about a shortened select committee report-back period that, first, there has already been considerable consultation and discussion.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure before the House: prior community consultation is offered as a reason a shortened committee stage is acceptable. There is a real gap — informal consultation with councils is not the same function as select committee scrutiny and submissions — so the conclusion is only partly supported by the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Finally, I’d like to point out that the time frame that we are proposing—31 October—for report back will enable us to pass this bill by the end of this calendar year, thereby providing more certainty, more clarity, and less retrospectivity to the question of an extension, whereby for those in the period of time from 2 April until today or such time as this bill comes into effect are in some sort of legal limbo.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the premises: an earlier report-back allows passage within the year, which shortens the window in which the announced extension lacks legal force. The step from 'less retrospectivity' to the shortened committee stage being warranted is asserted rather than weighed against the cost to scrutiny.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I mean, it’s a little ironic to me that we’ve got a bill here which is extending time, kicking the can down the road, and we’re doing it with a truncated process.
rigor.explanation: A rhetorical irony dressed as an argument: that the bill's subject matter is time extension has no logical bearing on how much time the House should take to scrutinise it. The two senses of 'time' are equivocated, so the conclusion does not follow.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think it’s really important in this House that we note that a full select committee process is really, really important so that we have both a good process and a legitimacy around what Parliament is doing, and whilst we know that urgency and shortened processes are useful sometimes, and appropriate—all Governments use them—they certainly have to be very clearly justified.
rigor.explanation: A coherent argument from principle: full committee process confers legitimacy, shortened processes are sometimes legitimate but carry a burden of justification, therefore this one needs justifying. The premise that legitimacy depends on process length is asserted rather than evidenced, but the conclusion follows from it — and he concedes the point against himself (all Governments use urgency).
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But at an individual case level, the principle of equality before the law, as a key aspect of the rule of law, is such that these demographic factors should not be taken into account by the judge when making a decision on these matters at sentencing.
rigor.explanation: Valid given its premise: if equality before the law requires individual rather than group-based treatment, then demographic factors should not enter the individual sentencing decision. The gap is that it does not engage the objection actually raised — that a facially equal rule can produce disproportionate outcomes — so the argument answers a narrower question than the one asked.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We know that Ministers cannot make law merely by announcing, and, certainly in the case of statutory and amendment, we know from the case Fitzgerald v Muldoon and other discussions in our constitutional history that we can’t regard these changes as being effective in law until such time as that law is passed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Fitzgerald v Muldoon stands for the proposition that a ministerial announcement cannot alter the law until legislation is passed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The reported judgment in Fitzgerald v Muldoon [1976] 2 NZLR 615 (NZ Supreme Court): true if the decision held that the Prime Minister's announcement suspending statutory superannuation obligations was unlawful absent legislation (i.e. executive announcement cannot suspend or change statute); false if the case turned on some other point or supports ministerial announcement having legal effect.

veracity.statement: But, pragmatically speaking, some months ago, the Minister issued a press release and let it be known to the community that he was going to take a particular approach and that gave considerable certainty.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister (Chris Penk) publicly announced, by press release some months before 8 August 2024, the approach he intended to take to earthquake-prone building remediation deadlines.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Beehive.govt.nz / Building and Construction ministerial releases between roughly January and July 2024: true if a release under Chris Penk's name announces an intended extension of, or pause to, earthquake-prone building remediation deadlines ahead of legislation; false if no such announcement was made in that period.

specificity.statement: Finally, I’d like to point out that the time frame that we are proposing—31 October—for report back will enable us to pass this bill by the end of this calendar year, thereby providing more certainty, more clarity, and less retrospectivity to the question of an extension, whereby for those in the period of time from 2 April until today or such time as this bill comes into effect are in some sort of legal limbo.
specificity.explanation: Carries a named report-back date (31 October), a passage target (end of the calendar year), and a named start date for the affected period (2 April), plus the mechanism (reducing retrospectivity). Checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I think it’s really important in this House that we note that a full select committee process is really, really important so that we have both a good process and a legitimacy around what Parliament is doing, and whilst we know that urgency and shortened processes are useful sometimes, and appropriate—all Governments use them—they certainly have to be very clearly justified.
specificity.explanation: A direction with almost no detail: no Standing Order cited, no figure for how much scrutiny time is needed, no evidence on the effect of shortened processes. 'Really, really important' and 'clearly justified' carry the weight.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Minister struck a lovely tone, but didn’t actually give us any reason as to why this should be truncated.
civility.explanation: Pointed and faintly sardonic about the Minister's delivery ('lovely tone'), but the criticism lands on the absence of argument rather than on the man; it edges toward the person without attacking him.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But at an individual case level, the principle of equality before the law, as a key aspect of the rule of law, is such that these demographic factors should not be taken into account by the judge when making a decision on these matters at sentencing.

focus.statement: I mean, it’s a little ironic to me that we’ve got a bill here which is extending time, kicking the can down the road, and we’re doing it with a truncated process.

focus.statement: But at an individual case level, the principle of equality before the law, as a key aspect of the rule of law, is such that these demographic factors should not be taken into account by the judge when making a decision on these matters at sentencing.

divination.statement: They’ll be substantive submissions backed by evidence.

divination.falsification_criterion: The submissions published on the Parliament website for the Building (Earthquake-prone Building Deadlines and Other Matters) Amendment Bill: true if the bulk of submissions come from organisations and professionals (engineers, lawyers, councils, property bodies) and cite evidence or technical analysis; false if most are short individual opinion submissions without supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: This is the commencement clause for the change to the Sentencing Act, and, as it’s drafted, it says that “applies only to proceedings commenced on or after the commencement date.” The difficulty with that is that the offence could have been committed two years ago. The New Zealand Bill of Right Act provides that a person is entitled to be charged and sentenced under the law as it stood at the time that the offence was committed, and this actually departs from that. Now, my amendment solves that by replacing “proceedings commenced” with “offences committed”.
rigor.explanation: A clean inference: the commencement clause keys to proceedings rather than the date of the offence; a stated legal principle keys to the date of the offence; therefore the clause departs from that principle, and the stated wording change closes the gap. No fallacy or leap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would point out that while, of course, the NZBORA does have things to say about retrospectivity in relation to criminal matters, we’re not in the serious territory of declaring an act to be a criminal activity or offence that was not at the time that it was perpetrated, but rather a bit of nuance around the extent to which certain factors might be able to be taken into account.
rigor.explanation: A real distinction is drawn — retrospective criminalisation versus retrospective change to sentencing factors — but the conclusion that the second raises no NZBORA concern does not follow from the first; the premise that only criminalisation engages the principle is asserted, not argued, so there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s not the way that crime happens, and we had lots of criminologists and lawyers and people that work in the criminal law space that understand that deterrence theory isn’t accurate and doesn’t work because the people that commit crime and most of the people in prison have got significant mental and cognitive issues.
rigor.explanation: There is a genuine causal argument — deterrence presupposes rational weighing of consequences, and impaired cognition undercuts that — but the support offered is an unnamed appeal to authority ("lots of criminologists and lawyers") and the step from "most prisoners have cognitive issues" to "deterrence doesn't work" generalises well beyond what is shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is the commencement clause for the change to the Sentencing Act, and, as it’s drafted, it says that “applies only to proceedings commenced on or after the commencement date.” The difficulty with that is that the offence could have been committed two years ago. Now, my amendment solves that by replacing “proceedings commenced” with “offences committed”.

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My other amendment is really about the difficulty we have with the aggravating factor simply of being a gang member when it bears no rational relationship to the offending, and my amendment, which has got a “l” on it, adds a subclause there which links it into serious offending so that it’s not shoplifting or, as in Mr Xu-Nan’s example, infecting someone intentionally with a sexually transmitted disease.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the amendment by its letter and states its operative effect (linking the aggravating factor to serious offending) with worked examples of what would be excluded, but gives no statutory threshold or wording.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This is the commencement clause for the change to the Sentencing Act, and, as it’s drafted, it says that “applies only to proceedings commenced on or after the commencement date.” The difficulty with that is that the offence could have been committed two years ago. The New Zealand Bill of Right Act provides that a person is entitled to be charged and sentenced under the law as it stood at the time that the offence was committed, and this actually departs from that. Now, my amendment solves that by replacing “proceedings commenced” with “offences committed”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act entitles a person to be charged and sentenced under the law as it stood when the offence was committed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Text of the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990, ss 25(g) and 26(1), and case law on their application; true if NZBORA confers a right not to be penalised under a law enacted after the offence (including a right to the lesser of available penalties), false if no such entitlement appears in the Act.

veracity.statement: It seems to me that the Attorney-General’s report under section 7 of the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act (NZBORA) did contemplate that question and, indeed, other NZBORA-related matters, and I think it seems to me that the intention isn’t that there be a retrospectivity about the bill and its effects.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Attorney-General's section 7 NZBORA report (or the published Ministry of Justice BORA vet) for the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill 2024; true if such a report exists and discusses the temporal application/retrospectivity of the Sentencing Act amendment, false if no section 7 report was presented or if it does not address that question.

veracity.statement: Today, we had hearings on the three-strikes legislation, which does a similar thing in that it provides more instruction to judges about how they need to sentence and deal with different crimes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that select committee hearings on the three-strikes legislation took place on the day of the debate (8 August 2024).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Justice Committee records and hearing schedule for the Three Strikes Legislation Amendment Bill; true if oral submission hearings were held on 8 August 2024, false if no hearing on that bill occurred that day.

veracity.statement: I’m further concerned that with the un-funding of section 27 reports that our judges aren’t going to have an accurate picture of the person before them to be able to give them an outcome that actually addresses their offending and addresses the needs of the victims, if there are some, in the situation.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / legal aid policy and Budget 2024 decisions on funding for section 27 cultural reports; true if legal aid funding for such reports was withdrawn or capped in 2024, false if funding remained in place unchanged.

veracity.statement: Actually, if you look to the report of the Chief Science Advisor to the Prime Minister about minimising gang harm in Aotearoa, that adviser says in the report that gangs exist because they perform a function within society.

civility.statement: The last time one of my other amendments, the Minister sneakily put an Amendment Paper in as well and usurped me there, so it may be that that’s going to occur.

focus.statement: My other amendment is really about the difficulty we have with the aggravating factor simply of being a gang member when it bears no rational relationship to the offending, and my amendment, which has got a “l” on it, adds a subclause there which links it into serious offending so that it’s not shoplifting or, as in Mr Xu-Nan’s example, infecting someone intentionally with a sexually transmitted disease.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the mechanism of the measure before the committee: which offences the gang-membership aggravating factor should attach to, and the specific subclause proposed to narrow it. No party framing at all.

focus.statement: My question to the Minister is: why doesn’t the Government trust the judiciary to implement the aggravating factor for gang membership that already exists within the legislation, and why is the Government choosing to override the judiciary again?

divination.statement: But what evidence has he seen that longer sentences—which will inevitably come through a bill like this—actually lead to people exiting gangs in the first place?

focus.statement: She alleges that we are overriding the judge’s discretion—indeed, we’re not; we’re actually empowering choices that they make to decide the appropriate weight to place on gang membership in relation to any individual matter before them.

focus.statement: Second, she makes a point around deterrence as though deterrence was the only aim of the criminal justice system. It is not. focus.explanation: Squarely on the purposes of the sentencing regime the bill amends; no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think the appropriate name for the bill would be, probably, “Kick the Māoris in the Guts Again Bill”. I think that’s probably a better title. I’m serious about this, because this is happening every week from the Government, if we think about it.
focus.explanation: Nominally a title amendment, but the content is a general characterisation of what the Government does to Māori 'every week'; no clause, cost, mechanism or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We have to cut to the chase, cut to the root of the problem. Just taking their patches is not going to make communities any safer; it’s got to be a bit more than that.
focus.explanation: Directly on the measure before the committee — what the patch ban will and will not achieve — rather than on the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Second, she makes a point around deterrence as though deterrence was the only aim of the criminal justice system. It is not. There are various others, including prevention, which is by way of saying that if members of the public who have committed violent acts are behind bars for the period of time that they are, society is a bit safer.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: if deterrence is not the sole aim, a measure weak on deterrence may still be justified by prevention. The premise attributed to the other member ('as though deterrence was the only aim') is a mild strawman, and the incapacitation step is asserted rather than evidenced, but the conclusion does follow from the stated premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But Parliament has the ability to provide guidance to judges through the Sentencing Act. rigor.explanation: Partly circular ('that's why we have a Sentencing Act in the first place' restates the premise as its own justification) and closes on a false dichotomy — the objection was to this particular guidance, not to the existence of any sentencing guidelines, so showing that no one opposes guidelines in general does not support the clause at issue.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I want to elaborate, because I’ve had Māori leaders, gang leaders talk to me. I think I know, with respect, probably more gang members than most people in this House.

rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is what Muldoon said, one of the National Party icons and heroes. He said you just can’t leave them to their own devices. People like Muldoon said it’s not just about taking their patches; it’s about providing work.

rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We have to cut to the chase, cut to the root of the problem. Just taking their patches is not going to make communities any safer; it’s got to be a bit more than that.

FALSE if an official evaluation or the crime/victimisation series shows a reduction in gang-related offending or improved perceived community safety attributed to the patch ban; TRUE if no such improvement is identifiable.

specificity.statement: In our school that we set up at my marae at Ngā Whare Waatea, which is open to everyone, 25 percent of our kids had gang fathers.

specificity.statement: During the review period, 1,797 of the 4,257 people who were on the receiving end of a consorting order—so 42 percent—were Aboriginal people.

specificity.statement: It’s the intention that they can be available to advise and assist councils, whereas Crown water services specialists are for when a council fails to submit a plan at all, and mainly when the Minister has lost confidence in a council’s ability to develop a suitable plan or to give effect to the plan.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete distinguishing test — advisory support during plan preparation versus failure to submit or loss of ministerial confidence — though without thresholds or timeframes for when confidence is deemed lost.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You heard Eugene Ryder through the select committee process: you take the patches off, and they’ll just wear colours. It’s just nonsensical legislation.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to a single submitter's authority, and a leap from one asserted workaround to the conclusion that the whole bill is 'nonsensical' — the premise, even if granted, does not carry that conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I know now that, if Mum was alive, she would agree with the new title on this gang legislation.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to emotion and to personal authority: the merits of the proposed title are supported only by a counterfactual claim about what his late mother would have thought.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Having the Government determination as opposed to the local government determination may also add additional financial burden to the local government as well—so that point of clarification as well from the Minister.
rigor.explanation: The inference tracks the figures just offered: if the central framework pays more than the council one and the council bears the cost, a higher burden follows. Appropriately hedged with 'may'; the small gap is that apportionment under clause 21(2)(da) might not fall wholly on the council.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: To give an example based on 2022’s determination, the Government fees framework for someone who is in a position of a chair and scores a score of 24 to 28, is $594 to $1,265. However, for Auckland Council, for the same band of score 24 to 28, it is the cost of $540 to $1,150, which is less.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific daily fee ranges for a chair in band 24–28: $594–$1,265 under the 2022 central government fees framework, and $540–$1,150 under Auckland Council's equivalent schedule.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Cabinet Office Fees Framework (2022 determination) daily fee ranges for chairs scoring 24–28, and Auckland Council's corresponding appointee fee schedule for the same band; true if both figures match as stated (and the council range is the lower), false if either range is materially different or the ordering is reversed.

focus.statement: I’m thinking 8 August 2025 is when we should resume this, because it would fall in line with the strategy that this Government is imploring, which is about attacking Māoris every week.

focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: A question for the Minister: given the ramifications of the Treaty principles bill and this legislation, has the Minister read the Waitangi Tribunal report with regards to colonisation and the effect of gangs?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: names a specific evidential document (the Waitangi Tribunal report on colonisation and gangs) and asks whether the Minister has considered it. Legitimate scrutiny, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If we want this to be an effective law and we want it to be something that, actually, the police and the full system are ready for, why are we rushing to Royal assent instead of giving it a year, instead of really scoping it out?
