specificity.statement: A question for the Minister: given the ramifications of the Treaty principles bill and this legislation, has the Minister read the Waitangi Tribunal report with regards to colonisation and the effect of gangs?
specificity.explanation: Names a specific report and a specific related bill, so the question is checkable and answerable, though it carries no figures, mechanism or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When we have a place like Ōpōtiki, with 2,000 gang members and two police, is Ōpōtiki ready?
specificity.explanation: Names a specific town and gives two concrete figures, making the readiness claim checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, for me, in terms of where we’re at, Royal assent is too quick. Can we look at 18 months to ready the system?
specificity.explanation: Proposes a concrete alternative timeframe (18 months) but does not specify what readiness milestones would need to be met within it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I would refer the member to clause 2 of the bill, which states that the commencement of this bill is from 21 November 2024.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact clause and the exact commencement date, which is directly checkable against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: He wants everyone making a contribution through his rotten select committee process.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic framing of a named member's (Seymour's) handling of the select committee process; it edges past criticism of the process into sneering at him personally, but stops short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m a bit disappointed that that member’s not enjoying my submission, but I hope that he’ll be able to learn something from this kōrero, because I’m talking about the title.
civility.explanation: Responding to a hostile point of order with mild condescension ('be able to learn something') but no insult; pointed rather than personal.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This bill here is hazardous for te iwi Māori.
civility.explanation: A blunt condemnation of the bill itself; no person is attacked and no bad faith is imputed.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So everything that has been commented on is lovely, but it doesn’t correspond to the reality of what the decision is based upon.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the opposing members' contributions as 'lovely' — a condescending brush-off of the speakers rather than a rebuttal of their points.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I thought that was a pretty good suggestion from someone who’s working at the grassroots.
rigor.explanation: The proposed change to the bill's title rests entirely on the endorsement of one individual, credited because he 'works at the grassroots' — an appeal to anecdote and to personal authority, with no evidence connecting the suggestion to the bill's effect.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If we want this to be an effective law and we want it to be something that, actually, the police and the full system are ready for, why are we rushing to Royal assent instead of giving it a year, instead of really scoping it out?
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (delay commencement) follows reasonably from the premises she has laid out about police, court and prison capacity; the gap is that readiness is asserted from examples rather than demonstrated systematically.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We’ve heard from the Hon Ginny Andersen: 500 police short, and yet we’re going to lump this on top of them, in a short period of time.
veracity.explanation: Relays Ginny Andersen's claim that police numbers are 500 short of the relevant target at August 2024.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police / Police Association published constabulary headcount at August 2024 against the coalition commitment of 500 additional officers; true if the shortfall against that target was approximately 500, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: When we have a place like Ōpōtiki, with 2,000 gang members and two police, is Ōpōtiki ready?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Ōpōtiki has about 2,000 gang members and only two police officers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police National Gang List figures for the Ōpōtiki district and NZ Police station staffing returns for Ōpōtiki around 2024; true if gang membership is of the order of 2,000 and sworn staff number about two, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Two week ago, we were giving a beautiful mihi and acknowledging the harm: 90 percent of gang members come from the State harm that’s been inflicted upon them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 90 percent of gang members are products of state care or state-inflicted harm.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care findings and NZ Police / Corrections research on the proportion of gang members with a history of state care; true if the proportion is around 90 percent, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: I would refer the member to clause 2 of the bill, which states that the commencement of this bill is from 21 November 2024.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that clause 2 of the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill sets commencement at 21 November 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of clause 2 of the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill as reported back from select committee; true if it specifies 21 November 2024, false if it specifies another date or mechanism.

veracity.statement: If the member wants to be reminded about the select committee process—which, to the other member’s question, involved a full process in terms of feedback from all related members—those questions were covered in detail and the date is based on feedback and the date requested by the New Zealand Police that aligns with their operational requirements.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 21 November 2024 commencement date was the date requested by New Zealand Police to suit their operational requirements.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The departmental report and NZ Police submission to the Justice Committee on the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill; true if Police sought or endorsed that commencement date on operational grounds, false if Police sought a later date or expressed readiness concerns about it.

veracity.statement: These games were historic for New Zealand, not just for matching our record tally of 20 medals in Tokyo but for clinching the most gold medals New Zealand has ever won and finishing 11th on the medal table, ahead of such sporting powerhouses with far bigger populations, such as Canada, Spain, and Sweden.
veracity.explanation: Asserts four checkable facts about the Paris 2024 Games: that NZ's 20-medal tally matched its Tokyo record, that its gold-medal haul was a national record, that NZ finished 11th on the medal table, and that it placed ahead of Canada, Spain and Sweden.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official IOC/Olympics.com medal table for Paris 2024 and Tokyo 2020: true if NZ's Paris total is 20 medals equalling Tokyo 2020, if the Paris gold count exceeds every previous NZ Games, and if NZ's medal-table rank is 11th with Canada, Spain and Sweden all ranked below; false if any of the rank, totals or comparisons differ.

veracity.statement: One brilliant statistic is that of our team of 204 athletes, 42 of them are coming home with at least one medal around their neck.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the NZ Paris 2024 team numbered 204 athletes and that 42 of them won at least one medal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Olympic Committee Paris 2024 team list and medallist list: true if the team size is 204 and the count of distinct individual medallists is 42; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Dame Lisa Carrington has etched her name in Olympic history with her eighth gold medal.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Lisa Carrington's career Olympic gold-medal total reached eight after Paris 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Olympedia/IOC athlete record for Lisa Carrington: true if her cumulative Olympic golds total eight after Paris 2024, false if the total is any other number.

veracity.statement: Hamish Kerr also made history by becoming the first New Zealand male to win a field event in the Olympic track and field programme.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Hamish Kerr is the first New Zealand man ever to win an Olympic athletics field event.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Historical Olympic athletics results for New Zealand (Olympedia): true if no NZ male won gold in a field event (jumps/throws) before Kerr's 2024 high jump; false if an earlier NZ male field-event champion exists.

veracity.statement: Beijing 2008 silver medallist Sarah Walker from BMX was elected as an independent IOC member.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Sarah Walker, BMX silver medallist at Beijing 2008, was elected an independent member of the International Olympic Committee in 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IOC membership records and the 2024 IOC Session election results: true if Sarah Walker was elected as an individual/independent IOC member in 2024 and held BMX silver from Beijing 2008; false if she was elected in another capacity or not elected.

veracity.statement: I heard what the Prime Minister said about our track and field gold, and I do want to acknowledge, as was mentioned to me by one of my colleagues, Dame Yvette Williams, who was one of our famed Olympians, a gold medallist in the long jump, if I recall correctly, in 1952, I think it was, in Helsinki, who did us all extremely proud.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (with hedging) that Yvette Williams won Olympic gold in the long jump at the 1952 Helsinki Games.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official Olympic results for the 1952 Helsinki Games women's long jump: true if Yvette Williams won gold there; false if the event, year or placing differs.

rigor.statement: If this is just all about being bottom-up, surely there is no need for clauses such as that.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real provision: premise — the Minister describes the regime as 'bottom-up'; conclusion — clause 30's Crown debt recovery from territorial authorities is therefore unnecessary. The gap is unbridged: a bottom-up planning process does not logically exclude a cost-recovery mechanism for ministerial appointees, so the conclusion leans on a false dichotomy between 'bottom-up' and 'any Crown charge'. Engages the clause rather than the other party, so it is scorable here rather than only under Focus.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Then also on Subpart 3, at clause 40A, there’s provision for a levy. The Finance and Expenditure Committee report says, “Well, this is for any Commerce Commission work that might happen.” But what is that work that might be happening and how is that levy good for councils?
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision (clause 40A), the instrument (a levy), the select committee report relied on, and the body whose work the levy would fund. The question is precise enough that a minister could answer it directly and an observer could check the answer against the clause. Falls short of 1.0 only because no amount or timeframe is attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One question we were asked around the expenses and fees framework—I’ve been advised this approach is consistent with what happens in the Local Government Act in relation to other appointees made by the Minister, potentially such as a Crown manager or Crown observer if there are problems with the local authority.
specificity.explanation: Names a statute (the Local Government Act) and two concrete comparator roles (Crown manager, Crown observer) rather than resting on 'standard practice', which gives the answer checkable content. But no section is cited, no figures or process detail are given, and it is hedged with 'potentially', so it stops well short of precise.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Then also on Subpart 3, at clause 40A, there’s provision for a levy. The Finance and Expenditure Committee report says, “Well, this is for any Commerce Commission work that might happen.” But what is that work that might be happening and how is that levy good for councils?
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure before the committee — a named clause, a named funding mechanism and its effect on councils. No party framing at all. Precise scrutiny of a bill's provision is the core of the on-policy end of the scale.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: One question we were asked around the expenses and fees framework—I’ve been advised this approach is consistent with what happens in the Local Government Act in relation to other appointees made by the Minister, potentially such as a Crown manager or Crown observer if there are problems with the local authority.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill's framework for recovering the remuneration and expenses of ministerial appointees from local authorities mirrors the existing treatment of Crown managers and Crown observers under the Local Government Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Local Government Act 2002 provisions on Crown review teams, observers and Crown managers (Part 10 / Schedule, including the cost-recovery provisions) compared with the remuneration-and-expenses clauses of the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill as reported back by the Finance and Expenditure Committee; true if the LGA likewise makes the costs of ministerially appointed officers recoverable from the local authority, false if the LGA places those costs on the Crown with no recovery.

veracity.statement: It was a historic achievement for us, with Aotearoa’s athletes securing 20 medals, as we’ve heard—10 gold, seven silver, and three bronze.
veracity.explanation: Asserts New Zealand's total medal haul at the Paris 2024 Olympics and its breakdown by colour.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official Paris 2024 medal table / NZ Olympic Committee results: true if New Zealand won exactly 20 medals comprising 10 gold, 7 silver and 3 bronze; false if the totals or the breakdown differ.

veracity.statement: But what makes this all the more special is that 14 of these 20 medals were won by our extraordinary women athletes and women’s teams.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 14 of New Zealand's 20 Paris 2024 medals were won by women athletes or women's teams.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Count of New Zealand's Paris 2024 medals awarded in women's events (individual and team) from the official results: true if 14, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: This success comes down to preparation. In October 2018, the then New Zealand Government launched a strategy to address the inequities women and girls experience in sport and recreation, the women and girls in sport initiative. As we can see, the results of this initiative have been massive, and not only in the Olympics.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a New Zealand government strategy on inequities for women and girls in sport and recreation was launched in October 2018.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Sport NZ / Ministerial records for the Women and Girls in Sport and Active Recreation Strategy: true if launched in October 2018, false if launched in a materially different month/year or if no such strategy exists.

veracity.statement: Ellesse Andrews became the second New Zealander to win gold in track cycling, after Sarah Ulmer in 2004. She won gold in the women’s keirin.
veracity.explanation: Two claims: that Andrews is only the second New Zealander to take an Olympic track cycling gold, the first being Sarah Ulmer in 2004; and that Andrews' gold was in the women's keirin.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Olympic track cycling results for New Zealand across all Games: true if Ulmer (Athens 2004) is the only prior NZ track cycling gold medallist and Andrews won the Paris 2024 women's keirin; false if any earlier NZ track cycling gold exists or the event is wrong.

veracity.statement: She leaves Paris having won the same number of gold medals as Usain Bolt.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Lisa Carrington's career Olympic gold medal tally after Paris 2024 equals Usain Bolt's career tally.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Olympic records for career gold medals: true if Carrington's total after Paris 2024 equals Bolt's career total (8); false if the two totals differ.

veracity.statement: We saw the selfless feat of Dylan McCullough falling back during the triathlon to provide much-needed support to his teammate Hayden Wilde, who ended up winning the silver medal.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that McCullough dropped back during the Paris 2024 men's triathlon to assist Wilde, and that Wilde won silver.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Paris 2024 men's triathlon official result and contemporaneous race reports: true if Wilde placed second and McCullough is reported to have paced/assisted him; false if Wilde did not win silver or no such assistance occurred.

veracity.statement: Our Government is absolutely committed to building great roads and Kiwis deserve to be safe when they drive on them, and alcohol and drugs are the number one cause of fatal crashes on New Zealand roads; in fact, around 30 percent of deaths on our roads involve drug-drivers.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that alcohol and drugs are the leading cause of fatal crashes in New Zealand, and that around 30 percent of road deaths involve drug-impaired drivers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport Crash Analysis System / annual road safety statistics: true if alcohol and drugs rank first among recorded contributing factors in fatal crashes and roughly 30% of road deaths involve a driver with impairing drugs detected; false if another factor ranks first or the drug-driver share is materially different from 30%.

veracity.statement: Now, we see inflation is tracking down to 3.3 percent and heading lower, and last week brought more good news for every Kiwi with a mortgage, with the first cut to the official cash rate in 4½ years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts annual CPI inflation is at 3.3 percent and that the Reserve Bank's OCR cut the previous week was the first in four and a half years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI for the June 2024 quarter and the RBNZ OCR decision history: true if annual CPI was 3.3% and the August 2024 cut was the first OCR reduction since roughly March 2020; false if either figure or the interval is materially wrong.

veracity.statement: Does his Government’s Treaty principles bill consider the Waitangi Tribunal’s finding from 10 years ago that “The rangatira who signed Te Tiriti o Waitangi in February 1840 did not cede [their] sovereignty to Britain,” or does he intend to continue to sideline the Waitangi Tribunal?
veracity.explanation: Relays the Waitangi Tribunal's stated finding, and dates it to roughly ten years before August 2024.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal Te Paparahi o Te Raki (Wai 1040) Stage 1 report: true if the report, released around 2014, contains that finding in substantially those words; false if no such finding exists or the date is materially wrong.

veracity.statement: Is it a fact that 102 years ago, in a major thesis, Sir Āpirana Ngata set out the very circumstances of the Treaty and he said that Māori ceded sovereignty—far closer to the action as he was, as were other Māori leaders of that time?
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim about what Āpirana Ngata wrote roughly 102 years before 2024 — that Māori ceded sovereignty under the Treaty.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Āpirana Ngata's published 1922 explanation of the Treaty of Waitangi: true if dated c.1922 and containing a statement that Māori ceded sovereignty/mana to the Crown; false if the text says otherwise or the date is materially wrong.

veracity.statement: We haven’t seen a Treaty principles bill yet.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at 20 August 2024 no Treaty principles bill existed for the Government to have seen.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bills register and Cabinet paper releases as at 20 August 2024: true if no Treaty Principles Bill had been introduced or circulated in draft to Ministers by that date; false if a bill or draft bill was already before Cabinet or the House.

veracity.statement: What responsibility does he take for the fact that since he became Prime Minister, the monthly number of new building consents has dropped 26 percent, 6,000 jobs have gone from the building and construction sector, and 57 percent of construction businesses now report difficulties with Government procurement and work consent conditions, up from 36 percent last year?
veracity.explanation: Three factual assertions about the period since November 2023: monthly new building consents down 26 percent, 6,000 jobs lost in building and construction, and construction businesses reporting procurement/consent difficulties rising from 36 to 57 percent.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ building consents issued (monthly series) and HLFS/filled-jobs data for construction between November 2023 and mid-2024, plus the industry survey Hipkins is citing: true if each figure matches within rounding over that window; false if any of the three is materially different.

rigor.statement: This success comes down to preparation. In October 2018, the then New Zealand Government launched a strategy to address the inequities women and girls experience in sport and recreation, the women and girls in sport initiative. As we can see, the results of this initiative have been massive, and not only in the Olympics.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: a 2018 strategy is followed six years later by a strong medal haul, and the medal haul is offered as evidence that the strategy produced it. No mechanism, counterfactual or intermediate evidence is supplied linking the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We had a plan to fight inflation and we started work on day one: stopping the wasteful spending, removing costs on businesses, and returning the Reserve Bank to a single focus on inflation. Now, we see inflation is tracking down to 3.3 percent and heading lower, and last week brought more good news for every Kiwi with a mortgage, with the first cut to the official cash rate in 4½ years. We know life is tough out there, but there are encouraging early signs that our plan is working to get New Zealand back on track.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc attribution: falling inflation and an OCR cut are offered as evidence the Government's plan is working, with no account of monetary policy lags or other drivers, and no link between the three named actions and the disinflation.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Is it a fact that 102 years ago, in a major thesis, Sir Āpirana Ngata set out the very circumstances of the Treaty and he said that Māori ceded sovereignty—far closer to the action as he was, as were other Māori leaders of that time?
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority, reinforced by an appeal to temporal proximity: one figure's view is offered as settling a contested historical question because he lived nearer the event. Proximity to an event does not establish the correctness of an interpretation of it.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So our Government is taking action, with more funding for roadside tests as part of a package of $1.3 billion for road policing in the next three years.

specificity.statement: We had a plan to fight inflation and we started work on day one: stopping the wasteful spending, removing costs on businesses, and returning the Reserve Bank to a single focus on inflation. veracity.statement: Well, that is a function of bad economic mismanagement and vandalism from the previous administration that created something called inflation, and inflation works because if you have an 84 percent increase in spending—wasteful spending, much of it—you increase debt from $5 billion to $100 billion, and you hire 18,000 more public servants, you get high levels of domestic inflation.
veracity.explanation: Three discrete quantitative claims about the 2017-2023 Labour government: an 84 percent rise in spending, core Crown debt rising from $5 billion to $100 billion, and 18,000 additional public servants.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenses series 2017/18 to 2023/24 (true if the increase is ~84%), Treasury net core Crown debt figures for 2017 and 2023 (true if roughly $5b rising to ~$100b on a consistent measure), and Te Kawa Mataaho Public Service Commission workforce data (true if public service FTEs rose by ~18,000 over the period). False if any figure is materially different on the stated measure.

veracity.statement: Why does the latest Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors’ global monitor survey report that New Zealand’s construction sector is now the most depressed since that survey started and is the most depressed in the world, with more than half of respondents citing as a reason the change in Government in October 2023, which resulted in cuts, delays, and policy change?
veracity.explanation: Asserts three things about the RICS Global Construction Monitor: that New Zealand records the lowest reading since the survey began, that it is the lowest in the world, and that over half of respondents cite the October 2023 change of government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The RICS Global Construction Monitor published in mid-2024; true if New Zealand's activity index is the lowest of all surveyed markets and the lowest in the series' history and more than 50% of NZ respondents attribute the fall to the change of government, false if the report shows otherwise.

veracity.statement: We’ve taken the genius idea from David Parker about fast-track provisions; we’re putting it in and expanding it further.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that fast-track consenting originated with David Parker and that the current government's legislation extends it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The COVID-19 Recovery (Fast-track Consenting) Act 2020 and the Natural and Built Environment fast-track provisions; true if David Parker as the responsible Minister introduced fast-track consenting and the Fast-track Approvals Bill widens its scope, false if fast-track consenting originated elsewhere.

veracity.statement: Well, I’m sure if the member gives a specific question, we can get him a specific answer, but what I would say is that there is $68 billion in this year’s Budget for infrastructure.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $68 billion infrastructure figure attached to Budget 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents and the Treasury capital investment/infrastructure figures; true if Budget 2024 states approximately $68 billion of infrastructure investment on the basis implied, false if the Budget figure is materially different or covers a different period than 'this year's Budget' implies.

veracity.statement: I would also point to the member that having projects with names doesn’t mean they are actually projects, so spending six years on Auckland light rail and spending $250 million to $300 million doesn’t make it happen; it’s just a Post-it note slogan bumper sticker—that’s what that is.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that $250 million to $300 million was spent on Auckland light rail over six years without delivery.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Light Rail Ltd and Ministry of Transport expenditure reporting to the project's cancellation in 2024; true if total spend falls in the $250m-$300m range over roughly six years, false if materially below or above.

veracity.statement: Will he take responsibility for the construction sector business confidence collapsing under his Government’s watch, from one in three businesses having a confident outlook to only one in five now?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fall in construction-sector business confidence from about one in three firms to about one in five.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published construction sector business confidence surveys (e.g. ANZ Business Outlook construction sub-sample or an industry confidence survey) covering the period; true if the share of firms with a confident outlook fell from ~33% to ~20%, false if the series shows no such fall.

veracity.statement: Does he think the 6,000 people who’ve lost their jobs in the building and construction sector and the firms who are closing because they have a shortage of work because of his Government’s decisions think that this is what getting back on track looks like?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 6,000 jobs have been lost in the building and construction sector.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ filled jobs / Household Labour Force Survey construction industry employment for the year to mid-2024; true if construction employment fell by approximately 6,000, false if the fall is materially different.

veracity.statement: Has he got any plans to assign $54 million, for example, for a cycleway over the Auckland Harbour Bridge, and when it’s all over, nothing is done with it?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that $54 million was spent on a proposed Auckland Harbour Bridge cycleway with nothing delivered.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waka Kotahi NZTA expenditure reporting on the Northern Pathway / SkyPath harbour bridge cycleway project to its cancellation; true if spend was approximately $54 million with no structure built, false if the figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: I was delighted to see that last week marked a significant turning point, with the Reserve Bank’s monetary policy committee deciding to cut the official cash rate (OCR) by 25 basis points, to 5.25 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Reserve Bank cut the OCR by 25 basis points to 5.25 percent in the week before 20 August 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ Monetary Policy Statement and OCR decision of 14 August 2024; true if the OCR was cut 25bp to 5.25%, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: During the cost of living crisis, annual Consumers Price Index inflation got to 7.3 percent and was over 7 percent for most of 2022.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 7.3 percent CPI peak and that annual inflation exceeded 7 percent for most of 2022.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation series for the four quarters of 2022; true if the peak print is 7.3% and three or four of the 2022 quarters exceed 7.0%, false if the peak or the run differs materially.

veracity.statement: New Zealanders benefited from long-overdue tax relief, and this tax relief was delivered in a way that was fiscally neutral and did not add to inflationary pressure, with every single dollar accounted for.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Budget 2024 tax package was fiscally neutral — fully funded by offsetting savings and revenue rather than adding to the fiscal impulse.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Economic and Fiscal Update and Treasury commentary on the funding of the tax package; true if the package was fully offset by savings/revenue measures with no net addition to the operating allowance or the fiscal impulse, false if Treasury shows it increased net borrowing or the fiscal impulse.

veracity.statement: Why has Oranga Tamariki ended contracts with 190 front-line social service providers and a further 142 providers have had their funding reduced, or are these contracts wasteful spending, as described by the Prime Minister?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Oranga Tamariki terminated contracts with 190 providers and reduced funding for a further 142.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki contracting data released to the Social Services and Community Committee or under the OIA in 2024; true if approximately 190 provider contracts were ended and 142 reduced, false if the counts are materially different.

veracity.statement: I will make two points: first, overall funding for Oranga Tamariki in the Budget increased; and, second, if that member thinks that the position of a Government should be that every single contract signed up to needs to be stuck in stone and never changed, then she’s delusional.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that overall Oranga Tamariki funding increased in Budget 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Vote Oranga Tamariki appropriations in Budget 2024 compared with the previous year's; true if total appropriation rose, false if it fell on a like-for-like basis.

specificity.statement: Well, that is a function of bad economic mismanagement and vandalism from the previous administration that created something called inflation, and inflation works because if you have an 84 percent increase in spending—wasteful spending, much of it—you increase debt from $5 billion to $100 billion, and you hire 18,000 more public servants, you get high levels of domestic inflation.
specificity.explanation: Carries three checkable figures — a percentage, two debt levels and a headcount — rather than a general assertion of mismanagement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why does the latest Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors’ global monitor survey report that New Zealand’s construction sector is now the most depressed since that survey started and is the most depressed in the world, with more than half of respondents citing as a reason the change in Government in October 2023, which resulted in cuts, delays, and policy change?
specificity.explanation: Names the source survey, the ranking claimed, the proportion of respondents and the dated event they attribute it to — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We think there are five things that we need to grow this country: a world-class education system—we didn’t inherit that from the previous Government—we’ve got to embrace science, technology, and innovation; we need to get rid of the red tape, green tape, and bureaucracy; we need to make sure we’ve got modern, reliable infrastructure; and, importantly, international connections.
specificity.explanation: A list of five generic directions — no figures, mechanisms, named programmes or timeframes; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will he take responsibility for the construction sector business confidence collapsing under his Government’s watch, from one in three businesses having a confident outlook to only one in five now?
specificity.explanation: Names a sector, a measure and before-and-after proportions, so the claim can be checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I was delighted to see that last week marked a significant turning point, with the Reserve Bank’s monetary policy committee deciding to cut the official cash rate (OCR) by 25 basis points, to 5.25 percent.
specificity.explanation: Names the decision-maker, the size of the move, the resulting rate and the timing.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why has Oranga Tamariki ended contracts with 190 front-line social service providers and a further 142 providers have had their funding reduced, or are these contracts wasteful spending, as described by the Prime Minister?
specificity.explanation: Names the agency, two precise provider counts and the distinction between ended and reduced contracts.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is it reasonable, as part of her Budget 2024 baseline savings exercise, for front-line social service providers to provide 100 percent of their contracted Government services with only 70 percent of the Government funding, and is this consistent with the social services commissioning model?
specificity.explanation: Gives the mechanism and a proportion (100 percent of services on 70 percent of funding), though it does not identify which providers or contracts.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, that is a function of bad economic mismanagement and vandalism from the previous administration that created something called inflation, and inflation works because if you have an 84 percent increase in spending—wasteful spending, much of it—you increase debt from $5 billion to $100 billion, and you hire 18,000 more public servants, you get high levels of domestic inflation.
rigor.explanation: A causal chain is offered (spending/debt/headcount → domestic inflation), and the inference from fiscal expansion to domestic inflation is a recognised mechanism, but it is monocausal: it treats the conclusion as following without addressing global price shocks or monetary settings, so there is a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would also point to the member that having projects with names doesn’t mean they are actually projects, so spending six years on Auckland light rail and spending $250 million to $300 million doesn’t make it happen; it’s just a Post-it note slogan bumper sticker—that’s what that is.
rigor.explanation: The inference — money spent over years with nothing built shows the project was not a real project — is supported by the example offered, though it generalises from two cases to a claim about announced projects generally.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s driving inflation down, thankfully—and I would hope the member is joining us in great celebration with the lower interest rates that came through last week—and from that will flow economic growth and, ultimately, more employment opportunities for people.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc attribution: the fall in inflation is credited to the government's spending decisions with nothing offered to separate that from monetary policy or the prior inflation cycle, and economic growth and employment are then asserted to follow.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I will make two points: first, overall funding for Oranga Tamariki in the Budget increased; and, second, if that member thinks that the position of a Government should be that every single contract signed up to needs to be stuck in stone and never changed, then she’s delusional.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the member asked about 190 terminated provider contracts, not about contracts never being changeable; the rebuttal defeats a position nobody advanced, so the conclusion does not answer the premise put.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: When the Prime Minister eventually leaves office, does he anticipate spending his first year out combing the world for statistics to show how badly he buggered the economy?
civility.explanation: Mockery aimed at an individual's post-office conduct and personal responsibility for wrecking the economy; sneering rather than engaging any substance, though short of sustained abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think those 6,000 workers understand that a Government that had six years, mucked around, and actually drove the economy into a hole is a reason why they’re doing it pretty tough.
civility.explanation: Harsh about a previous government's record but aimed at a party in office, not at any individual's character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I will make two points: first, overall funding for Oranga Tamariki in the Budget increased; and, second, if that member thinks that the position of a Government should be that every single contract signed up to needs to be stuck in stone and never changed, then she’s delusional.
civility.explanation: Calls the questioning member 'delusional' — a direct attack on the individual's judgement rather than on her argument.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When the Prime Minister eventually leaves office, does he anticipate spending his first year out combing the world for statistics to show how badly he buggered the economy?
focus.explanation: No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — the whole content is a jibe about what an opponent is supposedly doing with his time.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We think there are five things that we need to grow this country: a world-class education system—we didn’t inherit that from the previous Government—we’ve got to embrace science, technology, and innovation; we need to get rid of the red tape, green tape, and bureaucracy; we need to make sure we’ve got modern, reliable infrastructure; and, importantly, international connections.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the government's economic growth agenda rather than the other party, though it carries one aside about the previous government.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think those 6,000 workers understand that a Government that had six years, mucked around, and actually drove the economy into a hole is a reason why they’re doing it pretty tough.
focus.explanation: Names no policy, measure or figure — the content is a general characterisation of the previous government's six years as mucking around, offered in place of engaging the construction job losses put to him.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he think the 6,000 people who’ve lost their jobs in the building and construction sector and the firms who are closing because they have a shortage of work because of his Government’s decisions think that this is what getting back on track looks like?
focus.explanation: Names a sector, a job-loss figure and holds the government to its own 'back on track' commitment — specific accountability rather than party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is it reasonable, as part of her Budget 2024 baseline savings exercise, for front-line social service providers to provide 100 percent of their contracted Government services with only 70 percent of the Government funding, and is this consistent with the social services commissioning model?
focus.explanation: Engages a named policy — the Budget 2024 baseline savings exercise — its effect on contracted providers, and its consistency with the commissioning model; no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: That’s driving inflation down, thankfully—and I would hope the member is joining us in great celebration with the lower interest rates that came through last week—and from that will flow economic growth and, ultimately, more employment opportunities for people.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that lower inflation and interest rates will produce economic growth and increased employment.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP and Household Labour Force Survey; true if real GDP returns to sustained growth and employment rises (unemployment rate falling) over the following year or so, false if GDP contracts and unemployment continues rising through that period.

divination.statement: What’s more, the bank has set out a forecast track for the official cash rate which shows a steady decline over the next few years, back down to 3 percent in 2027.
divination.explanation: Relays the Reserve Bank's published OCR track, forecasting a steady decline to about 3 percent by 2027.
divination.subject: other
divination.falsification_criterion: RBNZ official cash rate decisions through 2027; true if the OCR declines steadily and sits at approximately 3 percent during 2027, false if it is materially above or below that level by then.

divination.statement: The Reserve Bank’s latest forecast is for inflation in this quarter—that is, the September quarter of 2024—to be well within the target band, at 2.3 percent.
divination.explanation: Relays the Reserve Bank's August 2024 forecast that annual CPI inflation for the September 2024 quarter would be 2.3 percent, inside the 1-3 percent band.
divination.subject: other
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI release for the September 2024 quarter; true if annual inflation printed at approximately 2.3% and within 1-3%, false if materially different or outside the band.

focus.statement: We are particularly conscious that in recent years, social service providers have watched while Wellington grew, the dollars that went into Government agencies expanded, and the number of policy analysts and managers hired grew, and yet those front-line service providers often only saw in return more contracting requirements, more compliance, and, actually, weren’t able to deliver better results. Our Government is focused on ensuring the dollars actually make it to the front line.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance of social service funding — where the money goes, back-office versus front line — with no party attack.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: While those members chuff themselves, I remember they talked a lot about open banking; they didn’t deliver it.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy (open banking) and a specific non-delivery, which is legitimate scrutiny, but the sentence's weight sits on jeering at the other side.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why is she choosing to ignore the research that shows sanctions do not support people into employment and, instead, conflating correlation with causation when it comes to the so-called empirical evidence she quoted?
focus.explanation: Engages the evidentiary basis of the sanctions policy directly, naming the specific methodological defect claimed in the Minister's own figures.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I would like to thank Labour MP Greg O’Connor for his endorsement and for confirming that common sense hasn’t been completely extinguished from the Labour Party.
focus.explanation: Content is entirely about the other party's internal state and supposed lack of common sense; strip the party jab and no policy point about sanctions remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does the Minister stand by her statement that “Our Government remains committed to the Enabling Good Lives approach”, and, if so, how does she reconcile this with her decision to pause Enabling Good Lives?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny tied to a named policy and a named decision — no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does the Minister stand by her statement that “The most critical thing we do is for people who are already accessing and in need of disability support services, that we stabilise the system and give them certainty”; if so, how can she justify uprooting and transferring disability support services from Whaikaha to the Ministry of Social Development, a process for which the cost and time frame is unknown?
focus.explanation: Names the specific machinery-of-government change, the two agencies involved and the missing cost and timeframe information — accountability on the substance.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are particularly conscious that in recent years, social service providers have watched while Wellington grew, the dollars that went into Government agencies expanded, and the number of policy analysts and managers hired grew, and yet those front-line service providers often only saw in return more contracting requirements, more compliance, and, actually, weren’t able to deliver better results. Our Government is focused on ensuring the dollars actually make it to the front line.
specificity.explanation: A direction with no figures, no named programme, no mechanism for shifting dollars to the front line; 'make it to the front line' is close to a slogan.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What does she say to providers like Taeaomanino Trust, Wesley Community Action, Porirua Whānau Centre, Barnardos Aotearoa, Wairere Care Services, North Shore Women’s Centre, WELLfed New Zealand Trust, E Tipu E Rea, and the Salvation Army, who have all had reductions in funding and lost front-line staff as a result of her Budget 2024 baseline savings exercise?
specificity.explanation: Names nine specific providers, a specific consequence (funding reductions and front-line staff losses) and a specific policy instrument (the Budget 2024 baseline savings exercise).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, I’d say to each of those social service providers that the Government values what you do. You play a significant role in helping New Zealanders in need, and our Government wants to work with you to ensure we can make the maximum impact for the people you serve.
specificity.explanation: Generic expressions of value and intent — no figure, no named contract, no mechanism, nothing checkable or actionable in response to a question about specific funding cuts.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We invested every single dollar gained from savings at Oranga Tamariki back into Oranga Tamariki, which, overall, had increased funding in the Budget.
specificity.explanation: Names the agency and makes a precise, checkable claim about the destination of savings and the direction of the Vote's total, though it supplies no dollar figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: At the moment, Kiwibank is only just nipping at the heels of the big Australian-owned banks, with just 5 percent of the market.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete market-share figure for a named institution that anyone could check against the market study.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Possibilities include KiwiSaver funds, New Zealand investment funds, and everyday New Zealanders themselves looking for home-grown places in which to put their money and invest in New Zealand’s future. I will take proposals to Cabinet no later than December this year.
specificity.explanation: Names candidate capital sources and commits to a dated decision point (Cabinet proposals by December), though no amount of capital is specified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: During this time, the number of people on the jobseeker benefit increased by 70,000, or 57 percent, which included periods of prolonged labour shortages. During the same time, the use of sanctions nosedived from 60,588 to 25,329, or a decrease of 58 percent.
specificity.explanation: Exact counts, percentages and a defined period, all traceable to published MSD series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This side of the House is clear that there must be mutual obligations, rights, and responsibilities. Just as the Ministry of Social Development will provide support and assistance, job seekers who fail to hold up their end of the bargain should face some consequences.
specificity.explanation: A statement of principle — 'some consequences', 'support and assistance' — with no sanction levels, thresholds or supports named.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s why last week our Government announced a series of measures to ensure that the increased budget of $2.6 billion is distributed in a fairer, more consistent way, based on need.
specificity.explanation: Gives a dollar total and a timeframe for the announcement, but the 'series of measures' and the allocation method are unnamed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The independent review highlighted dire issues with a disability support service that required urgent action. Our Government is taking that urgent action.
specificity.explanation: Asked to reconcile a stated commitment with pausing Enabling Good Lives, the answer names no measure, no timeframe and no mechanism — 'dire issues' and 'urgent action' carry no checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does the Minister stand by her statement that “Our Government remains committed to the Enabling Good Lives approach”, and, if so, how does she reconcile this with her decision to pause Enabling Good Lives?
specificity.explanation: Quotes the Minister's own words and names the specific decision (pausing Enabling Good Lives) said to contradict them, so the alleged inconsistency is checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: What does she say to providers like Taeaomanino Trust, Wesley Community Action, Porirua Whānau Centre, Barnardos Aotearoa, Wairere Care Services, North Shore Women’s Centre, WELLfed New Zealand Trust, E Tipu E Rea, and the Salvation Army, who have all had reductions in funding and lost front-line staff as a result of her Budget 2024 baseline savings exercise?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that each of the nine named providers suffered funding reductions and lost front-line staff, and that the cause was the Budget 2024 baseline savings exercise.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Funding records/contract variations for the named providers (MSD and Oranga Tamariki contract schedules) plus the providers' own public statements for 2024: true if each named provider recorded a reduction in government contract funding and associated front-line staff losses attributable to Budget 2024 savings; false if the named providers' government funding was unchanged or increased, or the losses trace to another cause.

veracity.statement: We invested every single dollar gained from savings at Oranga Tamariki back into Oranga Tamariki, which, overall, had increased funding in the Budget.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that all savings identified at Oranga Tamariki were reinvested within Oranga Tamariki, and that Vote Oranga Tamariki's total funding rose in Budget 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Oranga Tamariki appropriations and the agency's savings return documented in Budget documents: true if the savings amount identified was matched by reinvestment within the same Vote and the Vote's total appropriation rose year on year; false if any savings were returned to the centre or the Vote's total fell.

veracity.statement: The report makes it clear that our banks are highly profitable compared with international peers, they lack innovation, and do not aggressively compete for market share.
veracity.explanation: Relays what the Commerce Commission's final report into personal banking services found: high profitability relative to international peers, weak innovation, and no aggressive competition for market share.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Commerce Commission's final market study report into personal banking services (released August 2024): true if the report's findings state above-peer profitability, limited innovation and lack of aggressive competition for share; false if the report reaches different or materially qualified conclusions on those points.

veracity.statement: At the moment, Kiwibank is only just nipping at the heels of the big Australian-owned banks, with just 5 percent of the market.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Kiwibank holds about 5 percent of the New Zealand personal banking market.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Commerce Commission personal banking market study and RBNZ bank registered data on shares of home lending/deposits as at 2024: true if Kiwibank's share is approximately 5 percent, false if materially different (e.g. under 3 or over 8 percent).

veracity.statement: During this time, the number of people on the jobseeker benefit increased by 70,000, or 57 percent, which included periods of prolonged labour shortages. During the same time, the use of sanctions nosedived from 60,588 to 25,329, or a decrease of 58 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that between 2017 and 2023 jobseeker recipients rose by 70,000 (57 percent) and that sanctions applied fell from 60,588 to 25,329 (a 58 percent decrease).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets / Statistical Report for the jobseeker support caseload and obligation-failure sanction counts for the years 2017 and 2023: true if the counts match the stated figures within rounding; false if either the caseload change or the sanction counts differ materially.

veracity.statement: I would add that we have seen in July an increase in the number of work exits from a year ago, so I’m confident that what we’re doing is working.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the number of exits from benefit into work in July 2024 was higher than in July 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD monthly benefit statistics for work exits, July 2024 versus July 2023: true if July 2024 work exits exceed July 2023; false if equal or lower.

veracity.statement: Access to disability support services is a postcode lottery based on where someone lives, not their level of need, and Whaikaha - Ministry of Disabled People lacks the capabilities necessary to deliver disability support services effectively, partly due to their rushed establishment under the last Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as findings that access varies by locality rather than need, that Whaikaha lacks delivery capability, and that this is partly attributable to a rushed establishment by the previous government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2024 independent review of disability support services (Wallis/Ministerial review report) and Whaikaha establishment documents: true if the review records regional inconsistency in access and capability deficits, and links them in part to the speed of Whaikaha's establishment; false if the review makes no such findings or attributes the problems to other causes.

veracity.statement: That’s why last week our Government announced a series of measures to ensure that the increased budget of $2.6 billion is distributed in a fairer, more consistent way, based on need.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the disability support budget is $2.6 billion and that it has been increased.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Social Development / Whaikaha appropriations for disability support services: true if the total appropriation is approximately $2.6 billion and exceeds the prior year's; false if the figure or the direction of change is materially different.

civility.statement: Was making funding cuts for Oranga Tamariki providers, who serve our most vulnerable children, worth it to pay for her tax cuts?
civility.explanation: Pointed and loaded — frames the Minister as trading vulnerable children for tax cuts — but the target is the Budget decision rather than the Minister's character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: While those members chuff themselves, I remember they talked a lot about open banking; they didn’t deliver it.
civility.explanation: 'Chuff themselves' is mockery of the members opposite rather than engagement with their position — sneering, though short of a direct personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Why is she choosing to ignore the research that shows sanctions do not support people into employment and, instead, conflating correlation with causation when it comes to the so-called empirical evidence she quoted?
civility.explanation: 'Choosing to ignore' and 'so-called' impute deliberate bad faith to the Minister rather than simply contesting her evidence.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: For sectors like banking, this change will make it easier for consumers to switch providers or for innovative and disruptive new players like fintechs to enter the market and compete.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the consumer data right will lower switching friction in banking and enable new fintech entrants to compete.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Status of the consumer/customer data right regime for banking and MBIE/Commerce Commission reporting: true if the regime is in force for banking with accredited requestors operating and evidence of increased consumer switching or new fintech entrants; false if the regime is not in force for banking, or is in force with no accredited entrants and no measurable switching effect.

rigor.statement: Our Government believes this demonstrates that sanctions are a necessary part of the tools needed, including more proactive support, to motivate people to take the steps needed to shift into work.
rigor.explanation: Infers causation from co-movement: falling sanction use alongside a rising caseload is offered as demonstrating that sanctions are necessary, with no control for the labour market, policy changes or composition — correlation treated as causation.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would add that we have seen in July an increase in the number of work exits from a year ago, so I’m confident that what we’re doing is working.
rigor.explanation: Draws a confident conclusion that the policy 'is working' from a single month's year-on-year movement, with no attribution to the policy and no account of labour-market conditions — a hasty generalisation from one data point.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That was on top of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet stocktake that was undertaken for the previous Government and released before the election, as well as an independent assurance report that also showed poor financial controls.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Section 66 of the Crimes Act 1961 as enacted; true if it is headed 'Parties to offences' and uses the words 'aids', 'abets', 'incites, counsels, or procures', false if section 66 deals with some other subject or uses materially different language.

specificity.statement: Why is seven years the significant period of time we need to have that retrospective power given in terms of those monitoring powers for the Commerce Commission? Why not five years? Why not 10 years?
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision under debate (the seven-year look-back in clause 40) and poses concrete alternatives (five, ten years); the Minister could answer it directly and anyone could check the clause.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Are we talking about innovation in business models, which leads us on to a question which we really see threaded right through many of the clauses in this bill, and we want some certainty from the Minister in the chair around what protections are in place to stop the privatisation of these assets, to ensure that these do stay public assets and that these are things that will continue to be owned by the people that have built them up over many, many, many generations.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a real issue (privatisation safeguards) but points only at 'many of the clauses' rather than a named provision or mechanism, and ends in a generational appeal carrying no checkable detail.

focus.statement: Why is seven years the significant period of time we need to have that retrospective power given in terms of those monitoring powers for the Commerce Commission? Why not five years? Why not 10 years?
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism in the bill before the committee — the retrospective window for Commerce Commission investigation powers. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Are we talking about innovation in business models, which leads us on to a question which we really see threaded right through many of the clauses in this bill, and we want some certainty from the Minister in the chair around what protections are in place to stop the privatisation of these assets, to ensure that these do stay public assets and that these are things that will continue to be owned by the people that have built them up over many, many, many generations.
