focus.statement: I just want to get the specific idea, because we have seen in a previous bill around waste management that once we started charging levies for the work of a commission, we are straddling a very dangerous territory between what is considered a levy and what is considered a tax.
focus.explanation: Engages clause 40A's levy-making power and the cost-recovery mechanism directly; nothing about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I just want to get the specific idea, because we have seen in a previous bill around waste management that once we started charging levies for the work of a commission, we are straddling a very dangerous territory between what is considered a levy and what is considered a tax.
rigor.explanation: An argument from precedent: because a waste-management levy blurred the levy/tax boundary, this levy risks the same. The analogy is offered without establishing that the two levy regimes are structurally alike, so there is a real gap between premise and conclusion — but it is a genuine inference about the clause, not a jibe.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, these are already provided for in the Local Government Act 2002. Nothing in this bill changes those provisions. This bill only relates to local government water service providers. So the Local Government Act provisions apply as a matter of course.
rigor.explanation: A valid chain given its premises: if the anti-privatisation protections sit in the Local Government Act 2002, this bill leaves them untouched, and the bill covers only local government providers, then those protections continue to apply. The conclusion follows; whether the premises hold is a separate question.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As the saying goes, sunlight is the best disinfectant. So information disclosure makes councils act transparently, particularly about the state of the assets, how efficient they are, and their plans to upgrade and replace those assets.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that disclosure will make councils act transparently rests on an aphorism rather than on evidence or a stated mechanism — an appeal to a maxim, with the asserted behavioural effect simply restating the slogan.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’d just caution the member against misrepresenting that particular language, and I would go so far as to say possibly scaremongering.
civility.explanation: Moves from the substance to the member's motives — accusing Dr Russell of misrepresentation and 'scaremongering' imputes bad faith rather than simply disputing the reading of clause 32(2)(c). Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As most members will know, this phrase is a typical safeguard used and found often in the Commerce Act to protect consumers in industries where there is monopoly characteristics.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 'excessive profits' language in clause 32(2)(c) is standard, frequently-used drafting drawn from the Commerce Act 1986's consumer-protection provisions for monopoly industries.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Commerce Act 1986, particularly the Part 4 purpose provision (s 52A) and related regulated-supplier sections: true if wording limiting suppliers' ability to extract excessive profits appears there as an established regulatory safeguard for markets with little or no competition; false if no such phrase or equivalent safeguard exists in the Act.

veracity.statement: Well, these are already provided for in the Local Government Act 2002. Nothing in this bill changes those provisions. This bill only relates to local government water service providers. So the Local Government Act provisions apply as a matter of course.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that protections against privatisation of water assets already exist in the Local Government Act 2002 and that the Local Government (Water Services) legislation does not alter them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Local Government Act 2002 (notably ss 130 and 136–137, requiring councils to retain ownership and control of water services) read against the bill as reported back: true if such protections exist in the LGA 2002 and the bill contains no provision repealing or amending them; false if the LGA 2002 contains no such protection or if the bill amends or overrides those sections.

specificity.statement: I’m asking because under clause 40 of this part, the Minister is introducing new powers for the Commerce Commission to, essentially, investigate situations where it does not have enough information to perform a regulatory role, but those powers are different to the way that it regulates, say, the regulated airports of which it is the infrastructure regulator.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact clause (40), the body concerned, the specific new power (investigating where information is insufficient) and contrasts it with a named existing regulatory regime. Concrete enough for the Minister — or a reader — to check against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, if a determination has been made that information is commercially sensitive and not made available, what is the cause for a local interest group or other group of people who are lobbying to then go to the commission and request for that exemption to be revoked?
specificity.explanation: Identifies a specific statutory mechanism — the commission's power to grant and revoke a commercial-sensitivity exemption — and asks concretely what triggers a revocation request, though it carries no figures or timeframes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As for the question of stormwater and competition asked by the Hon Rachel Brooking, it seems to me that with the exercise of information disclosure, we have the opportunity to have maximum transparency, including for the purpose of ensuring that the efficient systems are in place, which include, you know, therefore, incentivising the innovation and investment in the improving of efficiency of delivery of stormwater services—so competition in a pretty broad sense, I suppose, but nevertheless one that leads inexorably to the most efficient outcome in the way that we understand competition well in some manner of market.
specificity.explanation: Offers a chain of generic virtues — transparency, efficiency, innovation, investment — without naming a mechanism, a threshold or a figure by which competition in stormwater would actually operate.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Under subclause (3), it says that it’s specified that the “entity provides goods or services that are not incidental to or related to delivering water services”. Can the Minister tell me when that would be something that the Commerce Commission would want to do and why they would want to look at that information?
specificity.explanation: Quotes the operative wording of a named subclause and asks a checkable question about when it would be used; carries precise statutory content, though no figures or timeframes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Look, the first one for the Minister is clause 37(3)(a) where, obviously, it says, well, “financial statements”. The obvious question here is: are these audited financial statements?
specificity.explanation: Pinpoints a numbered paragraph of the bill and asks a precisely answerable question about whether the required statements must be audited — actionable as a drafting point.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m asking because under clause 40 of this part, the Minister is introducing new powers for the Commerce Commission to, essentially, investigate situations where it does not have enough information to perform a regulatory role, but those powers are different to the way that it regulates, say, the regulated airports of which it is the infrastructure regulator.
focus.explanation: Entirely directed at the mechanism of the measure before the committee; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So, if a determination has been made that information is commercially sensitive and not made available, what is the cause for a local interest group or other group of people who are lobbying to then go to the commission and request for that exemption to be revoked?
focus.explanation: Squarely on new section 38A and how the exemption power would operate; no content about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In some situations, the Commerce Commission is the regulator of infrastructure providers who have a weighted assets return ratio on their infrastructure, and that’s how they are primarily regulated in their law—say, for example, the three regulated airports which come under the Commerce Commission’s purview.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that three airports are subject to Commerce Commission economic regulation, and that regulated infrastructure providers are regulated primarily by reference to a weighted return on assets.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Part 4 of the Commerce Act 1986 / Airport Authorities Act information-disclosure regime and Commerce Commission airport regulation publications: true if exactly three New Zealand airports (commonly Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch) are subject to Commerce Commission regulation and if that regulation uses a weighted average cost of capital / return-on-investment style measure; false if the number of regulated airports differs or the regulatory basis is materially different.

veracity.statement: When I think back in my own area in the Hutt Valley, you know, significant money was spent on a new event centre and redoing the town hall, and even subsidising a local business owner to build a hotel in the centre of Lower Hutt.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Hutt City Council spent substantial ratepayer money on a new event centre, a town hall refurbishment, and a subsidy to a private developer for a hotel in central Lower Hutt.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hutt City Council long-term plans, annual reports and council-resolution records: true if the council funded a new event centre (e.g. Walter Nash Centre), a Lower Hutt town hall upgrade, and provided financial support to a private hotel development in the Lower Hutt CBD; false if any of those three projects were not council-funded or did not occur.

rigor.statement: As for the question of stormwater and competition asked by the Hon Rachel Brooking, it seems to me that with the exercise of information disclosure, we have the opportunity to have maximum transparency, including for the purpose of ensuring that the efficient systems are in place, which include, you know, therefore, incentivising the innovation and investment in the improving of efficiency of delivery of stormwater services—so competition in a pretty broad sense, I suppose, but nevertheless one that leads inexorably to the most efficient outcome in the way that we understand competition well in some manner of market.
rigor.explanation: Concludes that information disclosure leads 'inexorably' to the most efficient outcome, but offers no mechanism linking transparency to competitive pressure in a sector with no obvious rival suppliers. The step from disclosure to efficiency is asserted, not supported — a non sequitur dressed as necessity.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It wouldn’t be necessarily that the full weight of that dollar amount would be brought to bear against a territorial authority, having not met its obligations. We think that that maximum amount is set at the appropriate level because, of course, the penalties go to conduct.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: because penalties attach to conduct rather than to the nature of the entity, and the maximum need not be imposed in full, the maximum is set appropriately. The premises support the claim that a public entity won't be crushed by the cap, but they do not establish that this particular level is the right one — a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Frankly, if I was writing this piece of legislation, I would just clarify that a little, because in the phrase “quality performance measures”, that adjective “quality” could apply to the “performance measures”.
rigor.explanation: Valid inference from a stated premise: the adjective admits two grammatical attachments, so the drafting is ambiguous, so it should be clarified. The conclusion follows directly from the linguistic observation offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It might be a standard term, but it doesn’t actually answer the substantive issue as to why we’re making profits in this space at all.
rigor.explanation: A valid inference: the Minister's answer established how the phrase is used in the field, which does not bear on the separate question of why profit arises at all. The distinction between terminological and substantive answers is drawn correctly.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because it’s the other way around from what would be expected, there must be a reason for doing it that way.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that 'there must be a reason' rests only on an assumption of deliberate drafting; departure from an expected order is equally consistent with drafting oversight, so the inference overreaches its single premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One efficient mechanism for that is by having people charged for the use of water and, thus, incentivised to notice when there are shortfalls in the pipeline infrastructure and so on.
rigor.explanation: A standard price-incentive inference: charging for a metered input gives users reason to detect losses. It follows, but the link from household charging to detection of network leaks is asserted rather than shown, leaving a gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As to questions around pecuniary penalties and offences, I’m advised—and I’m sure rightly—that this approach is consistent with that taken in the Commerce Act.
rigor.explanation: A bare appeal to authority — the justification is that officials advised it and are 'surely right'; no feature of the penalty regime is offered to support the comparison.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Of course, the effect of not highlighting the costs associated with providing water infrastructure, I think historically has been that many local councils and territorial authorities have probably avoided making such investments, because they’re perhaps not as interesting politically as other types of infrastructure on which a ribbon can be cut and so forth.
rigor.explanation: A causal claim resting on an imputed political motive with no evidence offered; the inference from 'costs are buried in general rates' to 'councils therefore under-invested' is plausible but unsupported, and the ribbon-cutting explanation is asserted by assumption.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We don’t see the principles of establishing a “competitive market” and “benefit to consumers” as being mutually exclusive. Because they’re consistent, we think it’s a moot point as to which would prevail in the event of a conflict, and, therefore, the relative priority is an interesting sort of academic question, but, with all due respect, I don’t think there’s any undermining of either of those priorities or tasks within the legislation.
rigor.explanation: Close to circular: the question asked was what happens if the two principles conflict, and the answer assumes they never conflict in order to declare the question moot. The premise simply restates the conclusion being challenged.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So is that right to shift over from commerce legislation for giant companies—$5 million might be an appropriate penalty, but a council is a public entity; it’s ratepayer money. How is $5 million appropriate for that?
rigor.explanation: A sound transplant objection: a maximum calibrated to large private firms may not transfer to a public body whose penalty falls on ratepayers. The conclusion follows from the premise, though no alternative figure or evidence of disproportionality is supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It might be a standard term, but it doesn’t actually answer the substantive issue as to why we’re making profits in this space at all.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the drafting of the bill's 'excessive profits' provision and the policy question underneath it; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: One of these different words is that it relates to competition of water services. One of the water services is defined as stormwater, so the question is: how does competition relate to stormwater?
focus.explanation: Entirely on the text of clause 32 and the bill's definitions — tests whether a competition principle can coherently apply to a service (stormwater) that has no market. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m interested in what those different classes of water services might be, because my first thought when seeing this discussion around the levy was the concern that some water services entities are much larger than others. Some of them come off a much larger rating base than others. Some of them are going to be in a much better position to pay a levy than others, so I’d like some discussion from the Minister as to how we might set up those different classes of water services entities or what’s going to be taken into account.
specificity.explanation: Anchored to a named provision (clause 40A(2)(d)) and a concrete differentiator — entity size and rating base — but carries no figures, thresholds or proposed formula.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Covering a number of different questions that have been raised by various members around the Chamber, in the committee, I start with, I think, the same member’s question around the levy and observe that different classes of providers could include distinguishing between providers by population size, but that is detail that yet could be provided in the regulation.
specificity.explanation: Names one concrete classing criterion (population size) but expressly defers the design to future regulation, so no thresholds, rates or timing are supplied.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As to the Hon David Parker’s question around what might be described as mixing up the role of regulators, the Resource Management Act will continue to set regulatory standards for waste-water discharges, whereas the economic regulator will consider the quality standards that councils must adhere to when looking at revenue sufficiency and investment choices, so giving them those mechanisms to be able to provide appropriate settings from an economic point of view.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute (Resource Management Act), the regulated subject matter (waste-water discharges) and the economic regulator's distinct remit (revenue sufficiency and investment choices) — a checkable division of functions.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So is that right to shift over from commerce legislation for giant companies—$5 million might be an appropriate penalty, but a council is a public entity; it’s ratepayer money. How is $5 million appropriate for that?
specificity.explanation: Names the penalty figure ($5 million), the source regime (commerce legislation) and the affected entities (councils and council-controlled organisations funded by rates) — precise enough for the Minister to answer directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As to questions around pecuniary penalties and offences, I’m advised—and I’m sure rightly—that this approach is consistent with that taken in the Commerce Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill's pecuniary penalty and offence provisions follow the model used in the Commerce Act 1986.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the penalties/offences subpart of the Local Government (Water Services) Bill with the Commerce Act 1986 pecuniary penalty and offence provisions (ss 79-87); true if the bill mirrors the Commerce Act structure (civil pecuniary penalties sought by the Commission in the High Court, comparable maxima and defences), false if it departs materially in mechanism.

focus.statement: That’s interesting, because that’s a reduction in democratic participation, and we know that a lot of what this Government has talked about has been the need for bottom-up organisation, and it’s been the need for localism—for decisions to be taken at the most local level possible—but this alternative consultation seems to run against that.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the part before the committee — the alternative consultation requirements and their effect on local decision-making — rather than the other party in general.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In fact, a local government entity could overrule what the people in the area that it administers want. They may want more than one round of consultation, but a local government entity could rely on clause 52(2) and say it’s only required to do it once and just leave it at that.
focus.explanation: Entirely directed at the mechanism of a named clause and its effect on councils; no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s interesting, because that’s a reduction in democratic participation, and we know that a lot of what this Government has talked about has been the need for bottom-up organisation, and it’s been the need for localism—for decisions to be taken at the most local level possible—but this alternative consultation seems to run against that.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: the stated government commitment to localism is set against a clause that cuts required consultation, and the tension concluded from it follows. Slight gap in that reduced mandatory consultation is equated with reduced participation without establishing that councils will not consult further.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In fact, a local government entity could overrule what the people in the area that it administers want. They may want more than one round of consultation, but a local government entity could rely on clause 52(2) and say it’s only required to do it once and just leave it at that.
rigor.explanation: Valid reasoning about the difference between a permissive and a mandatory provision: because clause 52(3) only says 'may', the floor set by clause 52(2) is what binds, so the cited rebuttal does not answer the objection. The conclusion tracks the premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Saying that another clause has a “may” doesn’t answer that question as to why reduce the capacity for democratic participation. I would really like the Minister to actually address that issue instead of just brushing it off.
civility.explanation: Robust and pointed — 'brushing it off' characterises the Minister's handling as dismissive, edging toward the person — but it stops short of impugning his character or competence and stays on the question asked.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m asking that question because there are specific references right throughout Part 3 of the Minister’s bill before the committee today on the inserted words “a joint local government arrangement under section 137 of the [Local Government Act 2002]”, and section 137 of the original Act specifically sets out a subsection—it’s subsection (4A)—which says that “An arrangement entered into by a local government organisation is not a joint arrangement [if they are] proposing the use of a levy under the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act 2020 to support the construction of eligible infrastructure:” only for that reason.
specificity.explanation: Names the part of the bill, the cross-referenced section and subsection, the other Act, and quotes the statutory wording — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I’m asking that question because there are specific references right throughout Part 3 of the Minister’s bill before the committee today on the inserted words “a joint local government arrangement under section 137 of the [Local Government Act 2002]”, and section 137 of the original Act specifically sets out a subsection—it’s subsection (4A)—which says that “An arrangement entered into by a local government organisation is not a joint arrangement [if they are] proposing the use of a levy under the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act 2020 to support the construction of eligible infrastructure:” only for that reason.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that section 137(4A) of the Local Government Act 2002 carves arrangements involving an IFF Act 2020 levy out of the definition of a joint arrangement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of section 137(4A) of the Local Government Act 2002 as at August 2024 (legislation.govt.nz); true if it provides that an arrangement is not a joint arrangement where the local government organisation proposes to use an Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act 2020 levy to support eligible infrastructure, false if no such subsection exists or its effect is materially different.

focus.statement: That caught my eye, and I wondered why it requires a statutory declaration for information that is to be disclosed by a water services entity. It seems like quite a high standard of verification, but I’m sure there will be a reason for that.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee — clause 37(5) and the verification standard it imposes on disclosed information. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Particularly, I draw the committee’s attention to the new powers at clause 40(1)(f), where it provides for, in legislation, a requirement that a water services provider would ascertain the expert opinion of a third party, because that acknowledges that the Commerce Commission does not have this kind of advice-giving power in its core remit and would be dependent on infrastructure experts, because that is not what the Commerce Commission currently does.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of a named subclause and which regulator it suits; no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The reason I mention that is because non-financial measures specifically may affect or may be of interest to members of the public. To give a few examples: things like water quality, water security—I’m not an expert on this, but, potentially, stormwater drainage speed.
focus.explanation: Engages the consultation provision and what 'non-financial performance measures' would cover in practice; wholly on the measure, with no reference to other parties.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The purpose of this part is to support councils in terms of setting up water service council-controlled organisations and joint local government arrangements as part of our Local Water Done Well approach. By supporting councils to set up joint organisations between councils, there’s a faster consultation, a streamlined consultation process that’s been put in place. It is about making that process easier and more efficient for local government.
focus.explanation: Explains what the part of the bill does and who it is aimed at; entirely on the measure, with no reference to opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That caught my eye, and I wondered why it requires a statutory declaration for information that is to be disclosed by a water services entity. It seems like quite a high standard of verification, but I’m sure there will be a reason for that.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact mechanism (verification by statutory declaration) attached to a named subclause and identifies who it binds; checkable against the bill text, though it carries no figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Infrastructure Commission itself said, in its recent report about water services, that waste-water, water, and stormwater sectors should be reformed by, including, (a) implementing performance-based economic regulation and water quality regulation to ensure that water providers are incentivised to drive efficiency and deliver excellent customer service; and (b) ensure there is a clear link between the cost of providing water services and the prices that are charged to users.
specificity.explanation: Quotes named, itemised recommendations from an identified source rather than gesturing at 'expert advice'; someone could go and read the report.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I am disappointed that the Minister hasn’t engaged with those points, but I want to ask him whether clause 40 is the clause which is intended to clarify the interface between water services entities and the developer finance water infrastructure provided under the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act, which is an intent which has been stated around giving these extra powers to the Commerce Commission.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the named statute (Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act) and the precise interface she wants confirmed; the question is answerable as put.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The reason I mention that is because non-financial measures specifically may affect or may be of interest to members of the public. To give a few examples: things like water quality, water security—I’m not an expert on this, but, potentially, stormwater drainage speed.
specificity.explanation: Offers concrete illustrative measures (water quality, water security, stormwater drainage speed) attached to a named subclause, but hedges and gives no thresholds or definitions.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, they are quite significant if water services entities fail to supply the information that’s required, and so on. We’re talking up to $5 million.
specificity.explanation: Attaches a concrete maximum penalty figure to a named failure (not supplying required information); checkable against the bill, though the trigger conditions are left loose.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Hon Deborah Russell has been repeating the question around penalties that’s already been addressed. Penalties represent an upper limit.
specificity.explanation: Conveys one real piece of content — that the penalty figures are ceilings, not standard amounts — but supplies no figures, thresholds or criteria for how penalties would be set.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In relation to determinations being secondary legislation, I’m advised this is consistent with the commissioner’s powers in other regulated sectors.
specificity.explanation: Answers with an unnamed 'other regulated sectors' and an unattributed advice source; nothing here can be looked up or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The purpose of this part is to support councils in terms of setting up water service council-controlled organisations and joint local government arrangements as part of our Local Water Done Well approach. By supporting councils to set up joint organisations between councils, there’s a faster consultation, a streamlined consultation process that’s been put in place. It is about making that process easier and more efficient for local government.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy (Local Water Done Well) and the vehicle (water services council-controlled organisations, joint arrangements), but 'faster' and 'streamlined' carry no timeframes, thresholds or description of what the consultation process actually requires.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Infrastructure Commission itself said, in its recent report about water services, that waste-water, water, and stormwater sectors should be reformed by, including, (a) implementing performance-based economic regulation and water quality regulation to ensure that water providers are incentivised to drive efficiency and deliver excellent customer service; and (b) ensure there is a clear link between the cost of providing water services and the prices that are charged to users.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a recent New Zealand Infrastructure Commission (Te Waihanga) report on water services recommended performance-based economic regulation and cost-reflective pricing in the water, waste-water and stormwater sectors.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Te Waihanga report on water services published before 20 August 2024 (e.g. its national infrastructure/water sector advice); true if it contains recommendations to that effect in substantially those terms, false if no such report exists or its recommendations do not include performance-based economic regulation and a cost–price link.

veracity.statement: Now, what we’ve already seen was the way that the Commerce Commission does a lot of work. We’ve just seen with the banking report that’s come out today, that a chunk of it is more or less, I suppose, what we’d call a name and shame strategy.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a Commerce Commission banking report was released on the day of this debate (20 August 2024) and that a substantial part of it works by publicly exposing firms' practices.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Commerce Commission publication record for 20 August 2024; true if a Commerce Commission banking report (e.g. the personal banking services market study final report) was published that day, false if no such report was released on or about that date.

veracity.statement: In relation to the member Arena Williams’ question around the Commerce Commission, the Commerce Commission is well practised in using these tools and the Infrastructure Commission does not have the experience in economic regulation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the New Zealand Infrastructure Commission (Te Waihanga) has no experience in economic regulation, in contrast to the Commerce Commission's established practice with these regulatory tools.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Infrastructure Commission/Te Waihanga Act 2019 functions and Te Waihanga's operational record; true if Te Waihanga has no economic-regulation function and has never made regulatory determinations, false if it has exercised economic regulatory powers. rigor.statement: So it is quite interesting, then, that this particular part of this bill around Watercare Services says that one of the objectives is to share “with consumers the benefits of efficiency gains”, including sharing those benefits “through lower prices”. The premises are offered, but there is a gap — the clause is about sharing efficiency gains relative to the counterfactual, so rising absolute costs do not by themselves contradict it. Not a fallacy, but the conclusion outruns the evidence.

rigor.statement: Theoretically, if you have a community-owned monopoly, you would think the incentives for excessive profit-taking are not as strong as if you have a private sector owner of a monopoly. rigor.explanation: Sets out a premise (public ownership weakens profit-taking incentives but not under-investment incentives), offers observed evidence (sustained under-investment in council water and sewage), and draws the conclusion that regulation of the monopoly is still needed. veracity.statement: Of course, we all know that Northland has a number of councils with very small ratepayer bases that have had huge problems, historically, with water treatment in particular.

veracity.statement: And it’s a very significant part because it concerns the water services for a third of the population of the country and the biggest city in the country.

focus.statement: If he’s going to remind this committee of his commitment to localism, is it then a mistake in clause 62A(1) that it’s the secretary preparing the Watercare charter, and, at clause 62A(2), that it’s consultation with Auckland Council rather than development by Auckland Council?

rigor.statement: If he’s going to remind this committee of his commitment to localism, is it then a mistake in clause 62A(1) that it’s the secretary preparing the Watercare charter, and, at clause 62A(2), that it’s consultation with Auckland Council rather than development by Auckland Council?
rigor.explanation: A clean internal-consistency argument: premise is the Minister's stated commitment to localism, premise is that the clause vests preparation in the secretary with the council merely consulted, conclusion is that the two are in tension. The inference follows from the premises; the only softness is that 'localism' is not defined tightly enough to guarantee the contradiction.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The arrangement set out in Part 4 is mutually beneficial for both Auckland Council and Watercare, and, ultimately, consumers, because it enables them both to borrow independently of each other.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered, but there is a real gap between the premise (independent borrowing capacity) and the conclusion (benefit to consumers); no mechanism is given linking the balance-sheet separation to consumer outcomes, so the consumer limb is asserted rather than derived.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In relation to the issue in clauses 59A and 59B, these clauses are here because, ultimately, Watercare is a monopoly provider and so this is about clarifying that they are a monopoly provider.
rigor.explanation: Close to circular: the justification for the clauses is that Watercare is a monopoly, and the stated effect of the clauses is to say Watercare is a monopoly. specificity.statement: Should clause 62A not read, “Auckland Council to prepare the Watercare charter”, and clause 62A(2)(a) read that Auckland Council, Watercare, and Taumata Arowai would develop, under the commission’s regulation, the draft charter?

specificity.statement: Northland has been left isolated by this treatment for Watercare.
specificity.explanation: Names a region and gestures at a consequence, but supplies no mechanism, no provision, no figure and no account of what 'isolated' means in the bill's terms — a direction of complaint with almost nothing checkable attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Can I just reflect, I just did a document search on the entire legislation for the word “safe”. And the number of times the word “safe” appears in the entire document is zero.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Full-text search of the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill as before the committee on 2024-08-20 for the standalone word "safe"; true if it appears zero times, false if it appears at least once as a standalone word.

veracity.statement: Taumata Arowai doesn’t talk about the Resource Management Act at all or its instruments.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Text search of the Taumata Arowai—the Water Services Regulator Act 2020 and the Water Services Act 2021 for references to the Resource Management Act 1991 or to instruments made under it; true if no such reference exists, false if the Acts reference the RMA or an RMA instrument (e.g. via the s 14 definition of Te Mana o te Wai).

veracity.statement: You cannot make regulations by press releases, and we’ve seen that happen around these national policy statements made under the Resource Management Act, both with freshwater in relation to the Otago Regional Council and also with what Minister Hoggard was trying to do with biodiversity.

rigor.statement: How can that be anything but good for public health, for the health of our society, the health of our communities, and the health of our water? It must be a good thing.

rigor.statement: I think it is really important for us to be very clear that Taumata Arowai will continue to make waste-water standards under the Water Services Act. In terms of “safe” not occurring in it, the legislation isn’t replacing the legislation that sets out drinking-water standards.

civility.statement: It seems very pointed, following from your answer to the last question, Minister, that this legislation makes a real point of removing references to water safety, and makes sure that in consideration of that, the authority responsible for water safety, Taumata Arowai, is told that it must not have regard to the hierarchy of obligations.

veracity.statement: The rural communities were particularly concerned that we were going to have too tough a nutrient attribute, but we didn’t go for a specific dissolved or inorganic nitrogen attribute, and there was considerable flexibility left in the instrument for regional councils to determine how they should, over time, improve the quality of degraded waterways.

veracity.statement: It has been under-invested in for decades, and every single time we have any significant rain event, waste water flows into the creek, and anybody who gets into that creek gets sick.

rigor.statement: I don’t understand what the need is for that revocation of that principle, because my understanding, based on when I was the Minister, was that it wasn’t something that would prevent councils from getting resource consents for what they currently do or want to do in the future.

civility.statement: But there is no regulation that says there wasn’t some flexibility as to how they improve things over time, or some unrealistic standard to which they were being—and I do remember that there were other parties at the time, the Māori Party, with respect, I thought were unrealistic; they thought things should be cleaned up to a drinkable standard, which I thought was an impossible ideal, as much, though, as we would love that.

specificity.statement: I think the Minister might have an opportunity to contextualise, for my benefit, in this jaundiced environment, tino rangatiratanga, giving people self-determination.

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I ask these questions because I wonder whether, firstly, a blanket extension is appropriate for all 1,200 marine farms or whether some form of nuancing might be appropriate, in case, for example, where we do have existing marine farms that do fall short of our regulations of national environmental standards maybe based on their location.

civility.statement: He has told us that this is all about jobs and that these activities are extant. He hasn’t referred to any evidence showing that they are forecast to continue for ever.

civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: To the former Minister for Oceans and Fisheries, one need look no further than the debacle of the salmon company struggling after spending $10 million to seek a resource consent—$10 million down the gurgler of consultants, unelected bureaucrats, and unhelpful scientists, people who are driven to act in a manner inversely related to economic durability in their communities.

civility.statement: They should not be able to drive the outcomes that affect hundreds if not thousands of New Zealand families who do not have university degrees to complicate common-sense things and who do not have access to the deep pockets of those groups who want to weaponise environmental law and hide it behind consultants’ gobbledegook.

civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: And we know, in this case, it will only be ratepayers who could possibly be paying for it, because of the avoidance of section 36 of the Resource Management Act.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Fisheries/aquaculture amendment bill as reported back in August 2024: true if the new review provisions bar a consent authority from charging the permit holder and are not subject to the cost-recovery power in s36 of the Resource Management Act 1991, leaving the regional council (ratepayer-funded) to bear the cost; false if the bill preserves s36 charging or provides another funding source for the review.

veracity.statement: I ask these questions because I wonder whether, firstly, a blanket extension is appropriate for all 1,200 marine farms or whether some form of nuancing might be appropriate, in case, for example, where we do have existing marine farms that do fall short of our regulations of national environmental standards maybe based on their location.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the blanket extension in the bill would apply to roughly 1,200 existing marine farms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry for Primary Industries / regional council aquaculture consent records for 2024: true if the number of consented marine farms in New Zealand is approximately 1,200 (within rounding of the official count), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: To the former Minister for Oceans and Fisheries, one need look no further than the debacle of the salmon company struggling after spending $10 million to seek a resource consent—$10 million down the gurgler of consultants, unelected bureaucrats, and unhelpful scientists, people who are driven to act in a manner inversely related to economic durability in their communities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a salmon company spent $10 million pursuing a resource consent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Company statements, Environment Court/EPA consenting records or contemporaneous reporting on the salmon farming consent application referred to (New Zealand King Salmon): true if the applicant's documented spend on seeking the resource consent was of the order of $10 million, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: The capacity to create additional marine farming enterprises off the coast of Te Tai Tokerau hovers near zero.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that scope for establishing new marine farms in Northland is close to nil — offered as evidence that a regional council has frustrated aquaculture development.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Northland Regional Council coastal permit records and the Northland regional coastal plan for the period preceding August 2024: true if effectively no new marine farming space has been consented or is available for allocation in the region, false if new marine farm consents or allocated aquaculture space exist in material number.

rigor.statement: Why is that needed—in this case, the Director-General for the Ministry for Primary Industries—when regional councils have been doing this work since the beginning of the Resource Management Act and are best placed to assess the adequacy of existing consent conditions and make recommendations according to best practice, if not to the national environmental standards for marine aquaculture?
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that regional councils are 'best placed' rests largely on the fact that they have long done the work — an appeal to incumbency. It is partly shored up by the submissions she cites, but long practice does not by itself establish comparative competence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There is the fiction that amenity and landscape values are of a greater level of significance than jobs and household livelihoods.
rigor.explanation: A strawman built on a false dichotomy: no member argued that amenity ranks above livelihoods, and the framing treats environmental assessment and employment as mutually exclusive rather than as matters to be weighed.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Minister, we had 1,100 submitters—1,000 submitters opposed the bill in its current form.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that of roughly 1,100 submissions on the bill, about 1,000 opposed it in its current form.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee report and published submissions on the Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Bill; true if the total submission count is about 1,100 and roughly 1,000 of them opposed the bill as drafted, false if the totals or the opposed share are materially different.

veracity.statement: This clause requires the permit holder to withdraw the application that they have lodged within a time frame of two months.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the provision under discussion (new subpart 1A, new section 165ZFHD(3)) obliges an existing permit holder who elects to continue under the extant permit to withdraw their live application within two months.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of new section 165ZFHD as it appears in the bill as reported back; true if it imposes a withdrawal obligation on the applicant with a two-month period, false if there is no withdrawal obligation or the period differs.

veracity.statement: I will also, I guess, at this stage like to point out that all regional and unitary councils oppose this bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that every regional council and every unitary authority in New Zealand opposed the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The submissions lodged by regional and unitary councils (and any joint council submission, e.g. via Te Uru Kahika / LGNZ) on the Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Bill; true if all regional and unitary authorities submitted in opposition, false if any supported it or did not oppose.

veracity.statement: When I was talking about evidence, the Minister responded with some examples of where marine farms have not been consented in the first place. But this bill is not about consenting of new marine farms; it is all about extending the consents of existing marine farms.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill's scope is confined to extending existing marine farm coastal permits and does not deal with the consenting of new marine farms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text and explanatory note of the Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Bill; true if its operative provisions apply only to extending or continuing existing coastal permits, false if it also creates or alters a pathway for consenting new marine farms.

focus.statement: I ask the Minister, then, why, aside from the reasons he’s given us, he didn’t seek to give a shorter time frame of the five and 10 years to the sector, for a rollover that would give them certainty and that would give some regional development opportunities for jobs, so that then this would not have been a rushed process and he could have developed a bill that is fit for purpose, that meets all the things that he wanted to do, that gives everyone certainty going forward and looks after the environment, and that ensures proper consultation happens.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: the consent duration, the alternative five/ten-year rollover, and the consultation process. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This clause requires the permit holder to withdraw the application that they have lodged within a time frame of two months.
focus.explanation: Pure clause-level engagement with the bill's text; contains no party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I would like to ask the Minister or the officials whether there has been any sort of modelling around when certain environments or when the agriculture or the consent itself can no longer sustain the same level of jobs or production through a variety of reasons—the degradation of natural resources or the natural environment being one of them.
focus.explanation: Directed entirely at the policy's evidence base — whether the long consent extension is supported by modelling of environmental and production sustainability. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I ask the Minister, then, why, aside from the reasons he’s given us, he didn’t seek to give a shorter time frame of the five and 10 years to the sector, for a rollover that would give them certainty and that would give some regional development opportunities for jobs, so that then this would not have been a rushed process and he could have developed a bill that is fit for purpose, that meets all the things that he wanted to do, that gives everyone certainty going forward and looks after the environment, and that ensures proper consultation happens.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete alternative mechanism (five- and 10-year rollovers instead of the 20-year duration), but the balance of the ask is a list of general goods — 'fit for purpose', 'certainty', 'looks after the environment' — with no figures or process detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This clause requires the permit holder to withdraw the application that they have lodged within a time frame of two months.
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable description of a named clause's operative requirement and its two-month time limit.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I would like to ask the Minister or the officials whether there has been any sort of modelling around when certain environments or when the agriculture or the consent itself can no longer sustain the same level of jobs or production through a variety of reasons—the degradation of natural resources or the natural environment being one of them.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the kind of modelling wanted and one driver (degradation of natural resources), but does not specify a measure, threshold or timeframe that an answer could be checked against.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I put it to you that when we look down at new section 165ZFHK, “Concurrence of Director-General required for review to proceed”, that issue around landscape could be embodied in that so that the director-general will only give concurrence for a review to proceed if the review has nothing to do with amenity or landscape or baches, for instance.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact clause, its heading, and the precise drafting change proposed — a concrete, actionable alternative.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I would like to first thank the Minister for providing me with much-needed entertainment.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic mock-thanks aimed at the Minister personally rather than at his answer's substance — mockery, though brief and not abusive.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The question was about evidence regarding reviews: have regional councils done reviews of existing consented marine farms based on these amenity values that so upset the Minister?
civility.explanation: Pointed — the aside that the amenity values 'so upset the Minister' gently imputes a personal grievance as the policy's driver — but it stops short of attacking him and the question itself is substantive.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It would be really good to get the response from the Minister that if this is really good for regional development—and I really hope that it is; also it did state here in the regulatory impact statement that it does have certainty for industry and consent authorities; this is not my area of specialty—why then would the regional and unitary councils oppose this bill if it’s going to be good for the regions?
rigor.explanation: The inference is that council opposition is evidence the bill is not good for the regions — an appeal to the authority/position of the councils. It is a real argument about the policy and the councils are relevant consenting bodies, but opposition by affected regulators does not establish the regional development claim is false, and no reason for their opposition is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think he may have misheard me because my question was: if amenity is the concern—it’s not ecological things; it’s amenity, it’s landscape—then he should have supported the Natural and Built Environment Act.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur as stated: nothing is offered linking amenity-based review concerns to support for the Natural and Built Environment Act, so the conclusion rests on an unstated premise about what that Act did.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I put it to you that when we look down at new section 165ZFHK, “Concurrence of Director-General required for review to proceed”, that issue around landscape could be embodied in that so that the director-general will only give concurrence for a review to proceed if the review has nothing to do with amenity or landscape or baches, for instance.
rigor.explanation: Valid means-ends reasoning: if the stated mischief is amenity-based reviews, a concurrence test excluding amenity grounds targets that mischief and makes the broader cost carve-out unnecessary. rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When I was talking about evidence, the Minister responded with some examples of where marine farms have not been consented in the first place. But this bill is not about consenting of new marine farms; it is all about extending the consents of existing marine farms.
rigor.explanation: A sound relevance objection: it identifies that the evidence offered concerns a different category (new consents) from the proposition at issue (reviews of existing consents), so it cannot support the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The involvement of the director-general reflects that this Government wants to see the key ministries, such as the Ministry for Primary Industries, driving towards economic development, prosperity, and resilience.
specificity.explanation: Names the agency and the director-general's involvement, but the content is a string of generic goals — economic development, prosperity, resilience — with no mechanism, figure or timeframe attached.

specificity.statement: Instead of a consent authority saying that actually, “No, we’ll recover part of it.”, or whatever it might be, what my Amendment Paper does is effectively sets the maximum so that any costs that would be recoverable would not exceed 50 percent of the total costs incurred.
specificity.explanation: States the exact mechanism of his amendment and the precise cap — 50 percent of total costs incurred — so the proposal can be checked against the Amendment Paper and acted on.

specificity.statement: This bill provides an opportunity for a marine farmer to enjoy the permit they already have extended till 2050, at the latest; or if they’re involved in a process to adjust elements that comprise their entitlements within that defined area, they can’t have two permits at once.

specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If we had a provision like they’ve got here for the regional councils, we would not have that time-wasting, ideological, foreign thinking we’re seeing in Otago.
rigor.explanation: A counterfactual conclusion (the provision would have prevented Otago's conduct) asserted with no mechanism linking the two; the premise is a characterisation of the council's motives rather than evidence, so the conclusion does not follow.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, the Minister has said that he believes that these costs should be borne by the consent authority. That means that those are costs that are to be borne by the ratepayers.
rigor.explanation: A short valid inference: consent authorities are rate-funded councils, so a cost assigned to the authority does land on ratepayers. The step from premise to conclusion holds, with only the minor gap that some council costs are met from other revenue.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reason why the ratepayers and the council will meet the costs of an intervention in the legal, rightful business of a marine farmer is because they will know that it has to be of a particularly egregious nature because they’re going to pay for it themselves.
rigor.explanation: An incentive argument — bearing the cost disciplines the decision — which is coherent, but it is stated circularly (they will only act in egregious cases because they pay, and they pay so they will only act in egregious cases) and offers nothing to show councils actually respond to the cost signal that way.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If we had a provision like they’ve got here for the regional councils, we would not have that time-wasting, ideological, foreign thinking we’re seeing in Otago.

focus.statement: New Zealand is saddled with far too many cases where relatively narrow-minded local government officials are interfering in the rightful business of entrepreneurs and the marine-farming industry.

civility.explanation: Presses the Minister hard on a non-answer and a rushed process while attacking nothing about him personally; the criticism stays entirely on the conduct of the consultation.

civility.statement: New Zealand is saddled with far too many cases where relatively narrow-minded local government officials are interfering in the rightful business of entrepreneurs and the marine-farming industry.
civility.explanation: Does not name an individual, but disparages the character and outlook of a class of officials as 'narrow-minded' rather than criticising their decisions — a sneer at people rather than at conduct or policy.

veracity.statement: For example, I would be interested in hearing the Minister’s thoughts on the expectations as a Te Tiriti partner in so far as this consultation period has gone, and, therefore, the final bill that’s come to the House that we’re debating now and the changes that weren’t made as a result of this very short consultation period—where we’ve had 1,100 submitters, a thousand were opposed, and perhaps not feeling quite listened to.

veracity.statement: This bill provides an opportunity for a marine farmer to enjoy the permit they already have extended till 2050, at the latest; or if they’re involved in a process to adjust elements that comprise their entitlements within that defined area, they can’t have two permits at once.

specificity.statement: So my question to the Minister is, firstly: is subsection (3)(b), in fact, indicating that the limitation of only one review in relation to a coastal permit is for the permit in toto, or is it related to the conditions, and if it is related to the permit in toto, then how is that providing a fair approach to have other conditions, that might be sought to be reviewed effectively, reviewed by the consent authority?

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A council, as we’ve talked about before, can undertake a review, right? They’ve got, in this legislation, up to two years to do that, but they can only do that if the director-general gives them permission to undertake that review.
specificity.explanation: States the mechanism precisely: the review power, the two-year window, and the director-general consent gate that conditions it. No figures beyond the timeframe, but the provision is described exactly enough to check against the bill.

civility.statement: It is not reasonable that people who have spent their life savings, who have got their houses mortgaged to the hilt to create jobs in wee businesses in regional New Zealand, year after year have to put up with the depredations of unelected grandees in these councils, who do not face the costs of their ill-informed, indiscriminate wandering ways, trying to interfere with the lawful business of aquaculture.
civility.explanation: The criticism lands on the people in councils rather than on the consenting regime — 'unelected grandees', 'ill-informed, indiscriminate wandering ways' is sneering at a class of officeholders and imputes carelessness to them personally. Short of a named personal insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They are not going to be allowed to hijack economic development where garden-variety Kiwis are trying to make a living and they fear that their enterprises are going to be hijacked or held hostage by people reading up, or coming up with, the most jaundiced interpretation in respect of the Treaty settlements.

civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Minister, we clearly see your bluster and certainty around the need to trample on your garden-variety Kiwis in the regions who want to have input on what happens in their commons and to make these dictates from on high from the throne of central government.
civility.explanation: Addresses the Minister personally and mocks his manner — 'your bluster', 'dictates from on high from the throne' — rather than engaging the centralising mechanism he objects to. A personal jibe wrapped around a real objection.

veracity.statement: They’ve got permits that go 35 years long, so the fact that I’ve compromised on 2050, I thought, was very modest and reasonable.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that existing aquaculture operators already hold coastal permits with terms of 35 years, offered as the baseline against which the bill's 2050 end-date is said to be modest.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Resource Management Act 1991 s 123 maximum duration for coastal permits, plus regional council coastal permit registers for Marlborough/Tasman aquaculture: true if coastal permits of 35-year duration are legally available and actually held by existing marine farms; false if the statutory maximum or actual granted terms are materially shorter.

veracity.statement: The antibiotics that are put into finfish farms also have an impact on the environment, and the detritus that comes out of a finfish farm can travel for up to 1,000 metres, indiscriminately.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two empirical claims about finfish aquaculture: that antibiotic use has environmental effects, and that waste/detritus from a finfish farm can disperse as far as 1,000 metres from the farm.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Peer-reviewed benthic-dispersal studies and MPI/Cawthron monitoring reports on NZ salmon farms: true if measured deposition footprints or modelled dispersal extend to approximately 1,000 m from cages; false if documented footprints are confined to a substantially smaller radius (e.g. tens to low hundreds of metres).

veracity.statement: Finfish farms make up a tiny percentage of our total farms—around 2 percent of total consents—and so I have a proposed amendment here that would not give this 20-year extension to finfish farms.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that finfish operations account for about 2 percent of total aquaculture consents in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI / Aquaculture New Zealand data on the number of coastal permits authorising aquaculture by species type: true if finfish permits are approximately 2 percent of all aquaculture consents, false if materially different (e.g. well above 5 percent).

veracity.statement: Now, earlier on in the evening, the Minister himself made a point around councils undertaking reviews, and he said, “which are very few”.
veracity.explanation: Relays what the Minister said earlier in the same committee stage — that reviews by councils would be very few — and uses it against his case for a director-general gatekeeping step.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard transcript of the committee stage of this bill on 20 August 2024: true if Shane Jones stated that reviews would be very few in number, false if no such statement appears or he said the opposite.

divination.statement: On the matter of new section 165ZFHI, “Power to undertake review”, when the review is undertaken—and they will be very, very few in number, because this is not really a troublesome industry.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that consent authorities will invoke the new review power in the aquaculture-permit regime only a very small number of times once the Act is in force.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Count of reviews of coastal permit conditions initiated under the new section 165ZFHI (as enacted) reported by MPI / regional councils: true if fewer than roughly five reviews are initiated nationally in the first five years of the provision's operation, false if reviews are initiated routinely (dozens, or a substantial share of extended permits).

focus.statement: But, given the nature of this House, with this current Government being so averse to even the slightest improvement or tweak on an otherwise bad piece of legislation, I wonder if you in your wisdom and experience might consider that there are, in fact, some well-considered amendments that could improve this bill.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine procedural ask at the centre — will the Minister accept amendments to this bill — but most of the weight is a general characterisation of the Government's disposition rather than any named provision, figure or effect.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Finfish farms make up a tiny percentage of our total farms—around 2 percent of total consents—and so I have a proposed amendment here that would not give this 20-year extension to finfish farms.
rigor.explanation: The inference is genuinely supported by what he laid out immediately before: larger and distinct environmental effects justify separate treatment, and the small share of consents means carving them out costs little. The gap is that share-of-consents does not by itself establish low economic cost, but the conclusion tracks the premises offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In actual fact, if councils have to pay, they’re not likely to just go and undertake reviews willy-nilly because of nimbyism and all those other things.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: cost-bearing already disciplines council behaviour, so the director-general safeguard is redundant. Reasonable, but it asserts the deterrent effect rather than evidencing it, and does not address cases where councils face political pressure that outweighs the cost.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair, and thank you to the Minister, the Hon Shane Jones, for addressing a couple of the questions. There is still the issue of the reference to the appeal rights inclusion in the legislation, which the Minister has not addressed, and also I am yet to have a response from the Minister about his view on Amendment Paper 57, which is on the Table and has been available in the public domain for the last couple of weeks.
civility.explanation: Presses the Minister for failing to answer on appeal rights and a named Amendment Paper, but the complaint is entirely about the substance and the process; no imputation of bad faith or personal jibe.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We don’t want this business where these are cafe-sipping people from Ponsonby who can muck around in the Tai Tokerau, wander down to other earthy parts of regional New Zealand and have a say about a highly localised, relatively modest issue. For those reasons, the law clearly states a limited number of people are entitled to be nosy parkers.
civility.explanation: No individual is named, but the argument is carried by sneering caricature — 'cafe-sipping people from Ponsonby', 'nosy parkers' — mocking a class of submitters rather than engaging their case for standing.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What’s not clear in this section, however, is that whilst there might be a time frame for getting the information to the director-general to be able to make a determination on a review, there doesn’t appear to be any time frame for the director-general to make a determination.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific drafting gap in a specific clause of the bill before the committee — the absence of a statutory deadline on the director-general's determination. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We don’t want this business where these are cafe-sipping people from Ponsonby who can muck around in the Tai Tokerau, wander down to other earthy parts of regional New Zealand and have a say about a highly localised, relatively modest issue. For those reasons, the law clearly states a limited number of people are entitled to be nosy parkers.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point here (who should have standing to be heard on a localised consent review), but most of the weight is a geographic/cultural caricature rather than the mechanism or its effects.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, this is an extraordinarily longstanding failure of resource management law. It’s provided an opportunity for people to claim standing. In actual fact, the likelihood of them being impacted by the decision is remote. But then they get involved, they frustrate the local development outcomes of an area, and those types of meddlesome activities are stripped away by this bill—all gone.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy question the clause addresses: who may claim standing under resource management law and what the bill changes about it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No more standing for these self-appointed guardians like Greenpeace lecturing the rest of the world as to how we should live.
focus.explanation: Gestures at a policy outcome (removal of standing) but the content is characterisation of an advocacy organisation's motives rather than any mechanism, threshold or effect.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: What’s not clear in this section, however, is that whilst there might be a time frame for getting the information to the director-general to be able to make a determination on a review, there doesn’t appear to be any time frame for the director-general to make a determination.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the proposed new section (165ZFHK) imposes a time frame for supplying information to the director-general but imposes no time frame within which the director-general must make the determination.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of new section 165ZFHK of the Fisheries Amendment Bill as reported back by the Primary Production Committee: true if it prescribes working-day limits for the provision of information but no limit on the director-general's decision; false if a decision deadline for the director-general appears in that section.

veracity.statement: The Primary Production Committee has changed the wording from “beginning” to “initiating” the review.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the select committee amended the relevant clause (new section 165ZFHM) so that the trigger word reads 'initiating' rather than 'beginning'.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Primary Production Committee's report on the bill, comparing the introduction text with the as-reported text of new section 165ZFHM: true if 'beginning' was replaced with 'initiating', false if the wording is unchanged or was changed differently.

veracity.statement: No one is stripping away the ability of someone to take an appeal in the event statutory authority is exercised.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill as drafted preserves appeal rights against the exercise of the statutory review power, contrary to the concern raised about appeal rights in the legislation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The appeal provisions in the bill as reported back, read with the Fisheries Act: true if a right of appeal against a decision made under the new review power remains available to affected persons, false if the bill excludes or extinguishes appeal in those circumstances.

rigor.statement: Now, this is an extraordinarily longstanding failure of resource management law. It’s provided an opportunity for people to claim standing. In actual fact, the likelihood of them being impacted by the decision is remote. But then they get involved, they frustrate the local development outcomes of an area, and those types of meddlesome activities are stripped away by this bill—all gone.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy — broad standing lets unaffected parties delay development, therefore narrowing standing is justified — but every link is bare assertion: no case, no data, no mechanism showing that objectors are typically unaffected or that their involvement causes the delay. Argument from assertion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You’re not going to exercise statutory authority just because a number of people who have exaggerated the importance of a landscape value to the point that it’s swamping the need of New Zealanders to be in employment. If you’ve got any doubt about that, look at the closure of industries and manufacturing plants today due to the distant corporate ambitions of people who are soon to feel the wrath of our Government.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the evidence offered for restricting objections on landscape grounds is a set of plant closures that he himself attributes to 'distant corporate ambitions', not to landscape objections. The cited fact does not bear on the conclusion it is offered to support.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We do appreciate the florid rhetoric of the Minister, but we also would love to get some solid answers on some quite legitimate questions.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic dig at the Minister's style of speaking rather than a substantive point, but it stops well short of a personal insult and moves straight on to asking for answers.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: A national conversation is most certainly needed, because we have surrendered to a tiny minority of loud, shrill, ill-informed voices who have weaponised not only tikanga Māori but have weaponised the anxieties that people have at a time when New Zealand has very few options other than to engage in trade-off politics and use mother Nature’s bounty—i.e., the iron sands off the coast of Taranaki.
civility.explanation: Characterises opponents personally — 'loud, shrill, ill-informed' and acting in bad faith by 'weaponising' tikanga and public anxiety — rather than engaging their arguments. No individual is named, but the attack is on the people opposing, not the position.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is this not just—for a Minister who talks about getting everything out of Wellington and out into the regions—sucking back decision making to Wellington?
civility.explanation: Pointed charge of inconsistency aimed at the Minister himself rather than the clause, but phrased as a question about his position and stopping short of impugning his character.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It has been fiercely opposed—as the Minister, I’m sure, would know—by the fishing industry for 10 years because it is seen by the commercial wild fisheries industry to be a direct threat to their industry.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the commercial wild-capture fishing industry has opposed seabed (iron sand) mining in the South Taranaki Bight continuously for about a decade, on the grounds that it threatens their fishery.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Records of the Trans-Tasman Resources South Taranaki Bight iron sand applications: EPA marine consent hearing submissions (2013/14 and 2016/17), High Court/Court of Appeal/Supreme Court proceedings, and public statements by fishing-industry bodies (e.g. Talley's, Fisheries Inshore New Zealand, Southern Inshore Fisheries).
