True if those bodies appear as opponents from roughly 2014 onward on threat-to-fishery grounds; false if the fishing industry did not oppose, or opposed only briefly/recently.

veracity.statement: Most recently, another opposition has come in from the offshore wind industry, because they say they will be unable to build their windfarms if the seabed has been so disturbed that it has lost its stability.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that offshore wind developers have recently come out in opposition to seabed mining in the same area, on the stated ground that a destabilised seabed would prevent turbine foundations being built.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public submissions, media statements or regulatory filings from offshore wind developers active in the South Taranaki Bight (e.g. BlueFloat Energy/Elemental, Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, NZ Windfarms consortium) dated 2023–2024. True if at least one such developer has publicly opposed seabed mining citing seabed stability/foundation constraints; false if no such recorded opposition exists.

veracity.statement: Aquaculture allocation—i.e., entitlements—are guided by the New Zealand Coastal Policy Statement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the allocation of aquaculture space/entitlements is governed by the New Zealand Coastal Policy Statement, a central government instrument, rather than solely by regional decision making.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Resource Management Act 1991 and the New Zealand Coastal Policy Statement 2010: true if regional coastal plans and coastal permit decisions for aquaculture must give effect to the NZCPS (RMA s 67(3)(b)/s 104(1)(b)); false if the NZCPS has no bearing on aquaculture allocation decisions.

focus.statement: It has been fiercely opposed—as the Minister, I’m sure, would know—by the fishing industry for 10 years because it is seen by the commercial wild fisheries industry to be a direct threat to their industry.
focus.explanation: Names a specific activity, region and affected industry in support of a question about how the bill balances competing uses of the coastal marine area; entirely on the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is not correct to say this is exclusively an area where local representatives have the ultimate authority. They are guided by guardrails created by central government.
focus.explanation: Answers the allocation-of-the-commons question by reference to the statutory instruments involved; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: A national conversation is most certainly needed, because we have surrendered to a tiny minority of loud, shrill, ill-informed voices who have weaponised not only tikanga Māori but have weaponised the anxieties that people have at a time when New Zealand has very few options other than to engage in trade-off politics and use mother Nature’s bounty—i.e., the iron sands off the coast of Taranaki.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy kernel (a national conversation about extracting iron sands off Taranaki), but most of the sentence's weight is spent characterising the people on the other side of the argument.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why are they excluded from being notified? Why is this not going to be publicly notified, given that they will be the ones footing the bill for this review that has gone through the process of being reviewed?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanics of the bill — the notification list in the new review provision and who bears the cost — with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is this not just—for a Minister who talks about getting everything out of Wellington and out into the regions—sucking back decision making to Wellington?
focus.explanation: A real policy point about centralisation of decision making under the bill, but framed mainly as a contradiction in the Minister's own rhetoric rather than as an argument about the clause.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If we are to impose dictates from on high from central government that override the ability of those regionally elected representatives to make determinations on how to balance these different interests, surely we are in big trouble.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion ('we are in big trouble') is asserted rather than derived — an appeal to consequences with no mechanism offered linking central direction to the harm claimed, and the premise loads the question by characterising the bill as a 'dictate'.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is not correct to say this is exclusively an area where local representatives have the ultimate authority. They are guided by guardrails created by central government.
rigor.explanation: A direct rebuttal that supplies its own support: having established that the NZCPS binds coastal planning, the conclusion that local authority is not exclusive follows from that premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Why are they excluded from being notified? Why is this not going to be publicly notified, given that they will be the ones footing the bill for this review that has gone through the process of being reviewed?
rigor.explanation: Offers a genuine reason (ratepayers fund the review, so ratepayers have an interest) for the conclusion that they should be notified; the step from 'pays for' to 'must be notified' is asserted rather than established, leaving a real gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This adjustment is enabled through a controlled activity status for reconsenting existing marine farms within an aquaculture management area.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact planning mechanism — controlled activity status for reconsenting within a defined aquaculture management area — which someone could check against Marlborough's Variation 1.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The effect of those plans has been to chill, undermine, and freeze economic development in the coastal environment.
specificity.explanation: Three near-synonymous verbs with no figures, no timeframe and no named plan or project; nothing here that could be acted on or measured.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Part 2, in terms of what it proposes to insert, in the sort of number of word count, is quite small, but the implications actually are quite significant because they relate to the entire part of Subpart 1A of this bill.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee — names the Part and the Subpart it interacts with, with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The question is around: are there any provisions under the Resource Management Act Subpart 1A of Part 7A that give the permit holder the opportunity to, at their own volition, shorten a permit if they no longer deem their business to be profitable or they no longer wish to operate under that permit and not replace it with another permit?
focus.explanation: Entirely about the legal mechanism in the bill and the parent Act; no reference to any party or opponent.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m interested to know what evidence there is for saying that there’s never going to be a need to review a consent in that 18 years, or if there’s analysis that other parts of the RMA may be able to override this if their effects are significant.
focus.explanation: Asks for the evidence base and the legal analysis underpinning a specific feature of the bill; pure policy scrutiny with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In the event that someone who enjoys such a permit ends up having the opportunity to extend their permit so it goes beyond 35 years as a consequence of us having a drop-off date of 2050, they’re not going to lose their entitlement.
focus.explanation: A direct substantive answer about what the clause does to existing permit holders; no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We are not going to have a situation where a tiny group, day and night, studying the innards of the Resource Management Act, weaponise every obscure reference to undermine capitalism, to undermine the functioning of the market, after people have made a difficult but admirable decision to invest their own money in creating jobs.
focus.explanation: Strip out the characterisation of opponents' motives and almost nothing about the clause remains; it is about who is asking the questions, not about the permit duration provision.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: My understanding was that Tai Tokerau iwi did not actually support this bill, particularly Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki, who actually had a lot of the marine farms, also did not support the extension.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that iwi in Tai Tokerau, and Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki specifically, opposed the bill and the permit extension. (The speaker partially corrects the Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki geography later in his contribution but maintains the opposition claim.)
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Written and oral submissions to the Primary Production Committee on the Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Bill, plus the committee report's summary of iwi submissions; true if submissions from Tai Tokerau iwi and from Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki oppose the bill/extension, false if they supported it or did not submit.

veracity.statement: That means that there are 18 years’ duration where a consent to discharge cannot be reviewed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that, because review may only commence within 2 years of the subpart's commencement while permits run to 2050, there is an 18-year window in which a discharge consent cannot be reviewed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the bill as reported back by the Primary Production Committee (review-commencement clause) read with the 2050 end date and RMA s128 review powers; true if no review pathway for the extended coastal discharge permits remains available after the 2-year window, false if s128 or other RMA review powers remain available in that period.

specificity.statement: The question is around: are there any provisions under the Resource Management Act Subpart 1A of Part 7A that give the permit holder the opportunity to, at their own volition, shorten a permit if they no longer deem their business to be profitable or they no longer wish to operate under that permit and not replace it with another permit?
specificity.explanation: Names the exact statutory location (Subpart 1A of Part 7A of the RMA) and states precisely the scenario and the power being asked about; a reader could check the sections and answer it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That means that there are 18 years’ duration where a consent to discharge cannot be reviewed.
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable numeric consequence (18 years) attached to a named consent type.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the event that someone who enjoys such a permit ends up having the opportunity to extend their permit so it goes beyond 35 years as a consequence of us having a drop-off date of 2050, they’re not going to lose their entitlement.
specificity.explanation: Gives the concrete mechanism (35-year permits, the 2050 drop-off date, preservation of entitlement), though without naming the affected consents or numbers.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, where there is an egregious case at some ill-defined point in the future, reflective of what the honourable Green member and the former Minister of oceans have referred to through fish farming, and if it did represent a biological threat, there are other pieces of legislation that can be invoked.
specificity.explanation: Answering a question that asked precisely which other legislation applies, he names none — 'other pieces of legislation' at 'some ill-defined point' carries nothing checkable or actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’ve also heard from the Minister that there is an ideological purpose to the bill and he’s told us that he wants to help entrepreneurs. The flip side of that is that it’s allowing pollution—that is what this bill is about.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure, but it leaps from 'the purpose is to help entrepreneurs' to 'that is what this bill is about — allowing pollution' as though the two were the same thing; a false dichotomy between enterprise and environmental control, though she has offered the unreviewable-discharge point elsewhere as partial support.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There may be a few molluscs and rare, obscure snails that go by the way, but I’ll take jobs any day.
rigor.explanation: A false dichotomy about the policy: it presents environmental protection and employment as mutually exclusive and offers nothing to show that the extended permits require the trade-off, or that jobs depend on forgoing review of discharges.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is about allowing pollution, and even if you’re going to make ratepayers pay to try and do some regulation of that pollution—some protection of the environment from that pollution—they can’t do it for 18 years.
civility.explanation: Severe criticism of what the bill does, in a genuinely heated exchange, but aimed wholly at the measure and its cost consequences rather than at the Minister as a person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: On the question of discharges—on the question as to whether or not Part 2, in addressing whether or not there are a small number who have a longer period to run their business without being hassled, undermined, or unnecessarily taxed, in a figurative sense, by these busybodies in regional government, the reality is we’re going backwards.
civility.explanation: Characterises regional council regulators as 'busybodies' who 'hassle' and 'undermine' — sneering at the people administering the regime rather than arguing against the regime itself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We are not going to have a situation where a tiny group, day and night, studying the innards of the Resource Management Act, weaponise every obscure reference to undermine capitalism, to undermine the functioning of the market, after people have made a difficult but admirable decision to invest their own money in creating jobs.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the members questioning him — that their close reading of the Act is a deliberate 'weaponising' aimed at undermining capitalism — rather than engaging what they asked.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: For the Minister to describe this as benign, perhaps he is referring to the word count rather than the actual impact or effect that this might have.
civility.explanation: Pointed and faintly mocking — it suggests the Minister has judged the clause by its length — but the jab stays tethered to the substance of the clause rather than landing on the Minister's character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Again, this is a very reasonable proposition in an otherwise reckless piece of legislation that would make it a little more reasonable, because it recognises that if these worthy businesses, as I’m sure many of them are, are in fact solvent, they should be able to cover the reasonable cost of consent.
civility.explanation: Calls the legislation reckless — hard criticism of the measure — while describing the affected operators as 'worthy businesses'. No person is attacked.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: When are we going to hear an end to these snowflake-prize falsehoods?
civility.explanation: Sneering: labels opponents' arguments as 'snowflake' falsehoods, imputing both bad faith and softness rather than engaging what was claimed. Short of a direct personal insult, but not civil.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does it start at the new proposed section 165ZFHC, which is when it identifies the actual date of conditions, or is it at the point that the coastal permit is updated?
specificity.explanation: Names the exact proposed section and two alternative trigger points, so the Minister could answer it precisely and a reader could check the clause; it lacks figures only because the question is legal-mechanical.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I repeat, again: yes, it is a departure from orthodoxy that the council staff—before they push the go button, before they worsen the prospects of the men and women—hail, sun, rain, shine, are up in the dark early in the morning creating jobs, boosting exports, braving the elements of the Tangaroa and Mother Nature. This bill celebrates their prowess, and the sooner it passes, the better.
specificity.explanation: Offers imagery and generic virtues (creating jobs, boosting exports) with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named provision, despite being a defence of a particular Part of a bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Going back, I did ask—and this is how that 35 year relates—if there is a 20-year extension, the council has two years where they can pay for a review if the director-general applies, but what happens for those other 18 years?
specificity.explanation: Gives the timeframes (35 years, a 20-year extension, a two-year review window, the residual 18 years) and the actor who must trigger a review, so the Minister could answer it directly; the statutory references are left implicit.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Again, this is a very reasonable proposition in an otherwise reckless piece of legislation that would make it a little more reasonable, because it recognises that if these worthy businesses, as I’m sure many of them are, are in fact solvent, they should be able to cover the reasonable cost of consent.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: solvency implies capacity to pay, therefore the cost should sit with the operator rather than the ratepayer. The step from 'can pay' to 'should pay' is asserted rather than argued, and the solvency premise is assumed of the whole sector, so there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I repeat, again: yes, it is a departure from orthodoxy that the council staff—before they push the go button, before they worsen the prospects of the men and women—hail, sun, rain, shine, are up in the dark early in the morning creating jobs, boosting exports, braving the elements of the Tangaroa and Mother Nature. This bill celebrates their prowess, and the sooner it passes, the better.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the bill should pass sooner rests entirely on an evocative portrait of hard-working marine farmers — a bare appeal to emotion. Nothing connects the workers' effort to the specific legal change under debate.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If a council officer is possessed of information requiring him or her to intervene in the legal operations of an enterprise—and these people love their enterprises; they love the environment; they’re not quietly plotting and scheming, at 11 o’clock at night, that they’re going to go tomorrow and release toxic material into the environment. It would destroy the fact that they’re growing food.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the objection raised was that councils would lack power to act on a harmful discharge, not that operators deliberately plot to pollute. The self-interest point ('it would destroy the fact that they're growing food') is a genuine reason but only rebuts intentional harm, leaving accident and negligence — the actual concern — untouched.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s because of the decisions that this Minister and his Government are taking, that’s what is leading to that.
rigor.explanation: A bare causal assertion: job losses are attributed wholly to the Government's decisions with no decision named and no mechanism or evidence offered linking the two. The conclusion does not follow from anything supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When are we going to hear an end to these snowflake-prize falsehoods?
focus.explanation: Characterises the other side's conduct in debate and names no policy, provision, figure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is the catastrophisation that we’ve seen for far too long from that side of politics.
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of the opposing side's general habits of rhetoric; no provision, cost, mechanism or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Going back, I did ask—and this is how that 35 year relates—if there is a 20-year extension, the council has two years where they can pay for a review if the director-general applies, but what happens for those other 18 years?
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the mechanism of the bill — the review window against the length of the extension — and puts a concrete gap to the Minister. Legitimate scrutiny of the measure before the committee.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Ah, the members are happy about this now. This is shameful, and I hope that your voters are listening to it.
focus.explanation: Turns on the demeanour of members opposite and an appeal to their electorates; the 'shameful' judgement carries over from the bill but nothing here names a provision, cost or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Minister is sitting here and is happy to say there should not be environmental protections for 18 years, because of capitalism.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the Minister said in this debate that there should be no environmental protections for the 18 years outside the review window, and that his justification was capitalism. Brooking herself flags uncertainty in the preceding sentences, but this sentence states it flatly.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard transcript of Shane Jones's earlier answers in this committee stage on the Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Bill. True if Jones stated that no environmental protections apply for the remainder of an extension beyond the review window and justified this by reference to enabling commerce/capitalism; false if he made no such statement or expressly said the contrary.

veracity.statement: I’ve not heard one speech on it in this committee stage.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no National MP had spoken in the bill's committee stage, in support of her call for them to state the party's position.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of the committee stage of the Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Bill up to 20 August 2024. True if no National Party member had delivered a speech during that committee stage before this point; false if any National member's contribution is recorded.

civility.statement: Well, Ms Grigg seems to have a lot to say. Perhaps she could take a call on this.
civility.explanation: A pointed dig at a named member for interjecting rather than speaking, but it stops short of insulting her — it needles rather than attacks.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Minister has mentioned a number of things around, you know, the greenies and all of these people, Greenpeace and all of those, but I wondered if this is just a simple case of the fact that the Minister has his head in the sand and this is a bill that is more accurately referred to as the “Resource Management (Head in the Sand) Amendment Bill” or “Tunnel Vision Amendment Bill”.
civility.explanation: Mockery aimed at the Minister personally — 'head in the sand', 'tunnel vision' — characterising him as wilfully blind rather than engaging the provision. Short of direct abuse but not civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We also, earlier in the debates last night, heard about the aberrant councils, and we heard, of course, about the Minister’s disdain, in particular, for the Marlborough council, despite his whip hailing from, or still being a member of, that council. I was suggesting, if this is all being driven because of that particular dislike of that council, it could be the “Resource Management (Punish Aberrant Marlborough Council) Amendment Bill”.
civility.explanation: Imputes a personal motive to the Minister — that he is legislating out of dislike for a particular council — which attributes bad faith to the person rather than contesting the provision.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This bill is a disgrace and should be renamed.
civility.explanation: About as harsh as a verdict on legislation gets, yet it targets the bill alone and insults nobody. Fierce policy criticism sits at the top of this scale.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My question to the Minister is: why is he not prepared to consider in a positive way the introduction of a reference to administrative charges as part of this part—which is entirely in order—given the fact that he has referenced that people are losing their jobs, given the fact that this will be an additional cost that is borne by the ratepayers.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: a named Amendment Paper, the mechanism (administrative charges) and who bears the cost (ratepayers). No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My question to the Minister is: why is he not prepared to consider in a positive way the introduction of a reference to administrative charges as part of this part—which is entirely in order—given the fact that he has referenced that people are losing their jobs, given the fact that this will be an additional cost that is borne by the ratepayers.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (administrative charges in this part of the bill) and an identified cost-bearer, but carries no figures, threshold or drafting detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A maximum of 50 percent could have been borne by the ratepayers in terms of cost recovery—just one aspect, if things were fair and reasonable.
specificity.explanation: Supplies a figure (a 50 percent cap on ratepayer-borne cost recovery) but leaves the instrument, the cost base and how the cap would be imposed unstated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Of course, he already has a mechanism to get over that, because the Director-General of the Ministry for Primary Industries has to agree to any review in the first place.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact statutory gatekeeper (the Director-General of MPI) and the exact step (agreement to any review), which is checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The name of this bill reflects the deep commitment towards giving certainty and confidence to this sector of our economy.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — certainty, confidence, commitment — with no duration, mechanism, figure or named provision that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think one of the things we have heard throughout this entire debate is the fact that the Minister gives very little regard to local government. Indeed, one of the things we did see during the select committee stage is the fact that 90 percent of the submitters were opposed to this bill.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that the Minister disregards local government — is supported only by the share of all submitters opposing the bill, who are not local government. The premise does not reach the conclusion; it is a non sequitur from a general opposition figure to a specific claim about a sector.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think that we’ve reached a point where the public has exhausted its patience listening to these colourful, fanciful suggestions, and we need to return back to the technical language of the bill as reflected in this very sensible, harmless title.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the House should revert to the bill's technical title rests entirely on an asserted state of public patience — an appeal to popularity, with nothing offered to establish the public sentiment invoked or to connect it to the drafting question.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I think one of the things we have heard throughout this entire debate is the fact that the Minister gives very little regard to local government. Indeed, one of the things we did see during the select committee stage is the fact that 90 percent of the submitters were opposed to this bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 90 percent of submitters to the select committee on this bill opposed it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee report and the published submissions on the Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Bill: true if roughly 90% of submissions received were opposed to the bill; false if the opposed share is materially lower.

veracity.statement: Of course, he already has a mechanism to get over that, because the Director-General of the Ministry for Primary Industries has to agree to any review in the first place.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill already contains a Director-General sign-off step controlling which reviews can happen.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Bill as reported back: true if the bill requires the Director-General of the Ministry for Primary Industries to agree before a review of consent conditions may proceed; false if no such approval step exists.

focus.statement: Yes, there are time frames that are already given in terms of the 20 working days for additional information to be provided, but wouldn’t it provide some confidence and certainty—the very things that the Minister wants to provide in this bill—to ensure that the processes that this Government are wishing to set up and put in place can adequately be put in place?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: clause 2 commencement, the existing 20-working-day information timeframe, and whether delaying commencement would let implementation processes be established. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Sadly, that has not been the case, and so I feel that I have to continue with what was proposed there, because, let’s be honest, there is the potential for ongoing degradation of the environment when this Government, effectively, extends permits and the conditions that are currently operating—not about a review but the actual current operation of the permit over a 10-, 15-, 20-year horizon—and beyond.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual operation of the bill — permit duration, conditions carried over, absence of review — and explains why he is persisting with his amendment paper. Policy content throughout.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The other was the “(Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms to Kick the Can Down the Road)”, because this has become symptomatic of this particular Government in terms of their approach to, basically, anything and everything these days.
focus.explanation: Attached to a real amendment paper on the bill's title, but the stated justification is a general characterisation of the Government's approach to 'anything and everything' rather than anything about coastal permits. The weight of the sentence is party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think one of the striking things about this piece of legislation is that it represents a significant overreach of central government, undermining the local authority, the rights of iwi Māori, the essential environmental protections that we have put in place over many years in this country.
focus.explanation: Directed at what the legislation does — the balance of central and local decision-making, iwi rights and environmental standards. It is about the measure, not about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yes, there are time frames that are already given in terms of the 20 working days for additional information to be provided, but wouldn’t it provide some confidence and certainty—the very things that the Minister wants to provide in this bill—to ensure that the processes that this Government are wishing to set up and put in place can adequately be put in place?
rigor.explanation: A real inference: if the director-general and consent authorities need time to stand up processes, a delayed commencement would deliver the certainty the bill claims to seek. The premise that processes are not ready is asserted rather than evidenced, leaving a gap, but the conclusion tracks the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Sadly, that has not been the case, and so I feel that I have to continue with what was proposed there, because, let’s be honest, there is the potential for ongoing degradation of the environment when this Government, effectively, extends permits and the conditions that are currently operating—not about a review but the actual current operation of the permit over a 10-, 15-, 20-year horizon—and beyond.
rigor.explanation: The inference — extending existing permits and their current conditions over a 10-to-20-year horizon without review leaves room for environmental degradation — follows from the stated mechanism. It is weakened by being framed only as 'potential', which makes the conclusion near-unfalsifiable rather than strongly supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yes, there are time frames that are already given in terms of the 20 working days for additional information to be provided, but wouldn’t it provide some confidence and certainty—the very things that the Minister wants to provide in this bill—to ensure that the processes that this Government are wishing to set up and put in place can adequately be put in place?
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, an actual statutory timeframe (20 working days) and an alternative mechanism (commencement six or twelve months post Royal assent), but offers no evidence of what specifically is unready.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I think one of the striking things about this piece of legislation is that it represents a significant overreach of central government, undermining the local authority, the rights of iwi Māori, the essential environmental protections that we have put in place over many years in this country.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the areas affected (local authority, iwi rights, environmental protections) but names no clause, standard, figure or consenting mechanism, so nothing here is directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is a dark day in the relationship between central government and local government, between the Crown and iwi, between the balance that we must strike in providing a living for members of our society and taking care to look after the environment on which all of us rely for generations to come.
specificity.explanation: A closing rhetorical flourish. It commits to no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named provision — nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s, basically, the “King Jones Giveaway Bill”.
civility.explanation: Mockery aimed at the Minister personally: the 'King Jones' label casts a named member as an autocrat handing out public assets, rather than criticising the bill's provisions. Short of a direct insult, but it lands on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I’m very sorry to see the likelihood that this Government will pass this piece of legislation.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Bill will be passed by the House. Not a promise about the speaker's own action — he is predicting the outcome of a vote he opposes.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The parliamentary record for the Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Bill: true if the bill passes its third reading and receives Royal assent; false if it is defeated, withdrawn, or still not passed by the resolve-by date.

focus.statement: It’s unacceptable; we have an unacceptably high amount of prisoners on remand in our corrections system as a result of them trying to get through a court system that’s clogged.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy problem the bill addresses — the remand population and court throughput — with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It completely guts and, quite frankly, ruins large swathes of the intentionality of this bill, and it’s something that we intend to spend a considerable amount of time on, working our way through, because the implications are so profound.
focus.explanation: Directed at a specific change to the bill before the committee — the removal of the Te Tiriti provisions — rather than at the other party's record or character.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill provides for the expanded use of body imaging searches of prisoners. This change will help prevent contraband such as drugs and cellphones from entering our prisons.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (expanded body imaging searches) and the contraband targeted, but gives no figures, thresholds or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As the incoming Minister, my number one priority was around staff safety, and if the staff are safe, then that naturally leads on to a better-run prison with an upside for everyone.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a causal chain (safe staff → better-run prison → 'upside for everyone') with nothing offered to connect the links; the word 'naturally' does the work evidence should. A real inference about the policy, but an unsupported one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: She’s saying that because the Treaty provisions aren’t in the bill, that means that Corrections are not able to actually deliver the services that we all expect of our corrections service, especially in relation to Māori.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the member's argument was that removing the Treaty clause removes the legislative foundation that guided the rest of the bill, not that Corrections is thereby unable to deliver services. Rebutting the weaker restated version does not defeat the argument actually made.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But having the Treaty provisions in there—by the way, the Corrections Act has never had those provisions in there. They’ve never had them and yet Corrections have been extremely effective in the work that they do over successive Governments for many, many years.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to the status quo: that Corrections has operated without a Treaty clause and is judged effective does not establish that adding one would make no difference. The conclusion (the provisions are unnecessary) does not follow from the absence of a counterfactual.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s not just a principle, it’s not just in principle, but everything else that’s in this bill was guided by the legislative foundation that that simple clause in the early stages of the bill guaranteed and supported.
rigor.explanation: Offers a reason for why the removed clause matters — it functioned as the interpretive foundation for the remaining provisions — but the load-bearing claim is asserted rather than demonstrated against any particular clause, leaving a gap between premise and the 'guts the bill' conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Finally, I brought forward an Amendment Paper that makes minor and technical changes to the bill. These changes enhance the workability of the bill and will not change any of the policies in the bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Amendment Paper he lodged to the Corrections Amendment Bill is drafting/technical only and alters no policy in the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Amendment Paper (SOP) lodged by the Minister of Corrections to the Corrections Amendment Bill in August 2024, compared with the bill as reported back: true if every amendment is drafting, consequential or technical; false if any amendment changes a substantive policy setting (e.g. scope of searches, mixing of remand prisoners, disciplinary powers).

veracity.statement: But having the Treaty provisions in there—by the way, the Corrections Act has never had those provisions in there. They’ve never had them and yet Corrections have been extremely effective in the work that they do over successive Governments for many, many years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Corrections Act 2004 has never contained Treaty of Waitangi provisions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Corrections Act 2004 as enacted and as amended up to August 2024 (legislation.govt.nz): true if no section of the Act refers to the Treaty of Waitangi or its principles; false if any operative section or principle in the Act does so.

veracity.statement: The several proposals, the several legs to this bill as was first introduced by the previous Government, have largely been retained.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the substantive proposals in the Corrections Amendment Bill as introduced by the previous Labour government survive largely unchanged in the version before the committee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the Corrections Amendment Bill as introduced with the version reported back from select committee in 2024: true if the main parts (intelligence provisions, disciplinary process, body imaging searches, remand rehabilitation) remain substantively present; false if most were removed or materially rewritten.

civility.statement: She’s saying that because the Treaty provisions aren’t in the bill, that means that Corrections are not able to actually deliver the services that we all expect of our corrections service, especially in relation to Māori.
civility.explanation: Engages the opposing argument directly and courteously; no attack on the member's person, competence or motives, though he recasts her position.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It completely guts and, quite frankly, ruins large swathes of the intentionality of this bill, and it’s something that we intend to spend a considerable amount of time on, working our way through, because the implications are so profound.
civility.explanation: Extremely harsh about the Cabinet decision and the resulting bill, but the attack lands entirely on the measure; no member is impugned.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In your answer just then, Minister, you said that that was not the Department of Corrections’ problem—the overrepresentation of Māori—but it absolutely is.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister, in his immediately preceding committee-stage answer, said Māori overrepresentation was not Corrections' problem. The Minister disputes this characterisation in his reply.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard transcript of Mark Mitchell's answer immediately preceding this call in the committee stage of the Corrections Amendment Bill, 20 August 2024; true if he stated or plainly conveyed that Māori overrepresentation is not Corrections' issue, false if the record shows he made a narrower claim (e.g. that Corrections does not control who enters the system).

veracity.statement: If we want to look at the statistics that back up those claims, we know that the main one is that despite the fact that Māori make up only 17 percent of the general population, they account for 38 percent of people proceeded against by police, 42 percent of adults convicted, and 57 percent of adults sentenced to prison.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Māori are 17% of the population but 38% of those proceeded against by police, 42% of adults convicted and 57% of adults sentenced to imprisonment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ census population share for Māori and Ministry of Justice adult conviction/sentencing and police proceedings data for the most recent year before August 2024; true if each figure matches within rounding, false if any is materially different.

veracity.statement: In the abuse in State care report, which details the abuse endured by people in State care during that time period, one of the harms that was highlighted was the disconnection of children from their culture and whakapapa, which led to the creation of gangs as we know them and the over-incarceration of Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Royal Commission's abuse in State care report identified disconnection from culture and whakapapa as a harm and linked it to gang formation and Māori over-incarceration.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care final report (Whanaketia, July 2024); true if the report identifies cultural/whakapapa disconnection as a harm and draws the link to gang formation and over-incarceration of Māori, false if it makes no such finding.

specificity.statement: The provisions were making access to cultural activities a purpose for which prisoners could be temporarily released or removed from the prison, which is important so that they can attend things like tangi and other cultural activities; ensuring that prisoners have access to cultural activities, regardless of the prison in which they are detained; and were enabling the views of whānau, hapū, and iwi to be taken into account, where appropriate and practicable, in decisions about which prison offenders are accommodated in.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the actual mechanisms of the deleted clauses — temporary release grounds, access regardless of prison, whānau/hapū/iwi input into placement decisions. Concrete enough to be checked against the bill text, though no figures or dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If we want to look at the statistics that back up those claims, we know that the main one is that despite the fact that Māori make up only 17 percent of the general population, they account for 38 percent of people proceeded against by police, 42 percent of adults convicted, and 57 percent of adults sentenced to prison.
specificity.explanation: Four precise percentages against a named population share, each tied to a distinct stage of the justice system — directly checkable against official statistics.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A big focus that I have as Minister of Corrections is also delivering programmes that give them real life skills; that give them the best chance of being able to come into meaningful employment, get some independence, get some pride back, have some options in their lives, and lead them more towards making good decisions instead of bad decisions which put them in that spiral back into our criminal justice system.
specificity.explanation: A direction of travel expressed almost entirely in generic goods — 'real life skills', 'meaningful employment', 'some pride back'. No programme is named, no participant numbers, funding or timeframe given.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We know that there is racism baked in throughout our justice system because researchers have made that clear. Advocates, criminologists—people across our society have made it clear that there is racism baked into our justice system.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to unnamed authority: the conclusion rests entirely on the assertion that researchers, advocates and criminologists have 'made it clear', with no study, finding or mechanism identified. The second sentence restates the first, so the support is close to circular.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’m not saying that having Treaty provisions within this Act will turn those statistics around overnight, but what it does demonstrate is a genuine and sincere commitment from the leadership of Corrections and from the Minister himself to rectify those disparities, which are a disgrace.
rigor.explanation: Explicitly concedes the limits of the claim rather than overreaching, which is sound. But the remaining inference — that statutory provisions demonstrate sincere commitment — is asserted rather than supported, and the converse (that their absence shows a lack of commitment) is assumed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If we know that meeting people’s cultural needs is an important aspect of their willingness to engage with rehabilitation programmes and if we know that people having their cultural needs met is an important aspect for them to have pride in their identity and be able to see themselves differently than the way that they are treated—which is often like animals—then that’s going to be an important step towards rehabilitation.
rigor.explanation: A conditional whose two antecedents are offered as things 'we know' on the basis of a single prison visit, and whose consequent largely restates the first antecedent — near-circular, and the evidential support is anecdotal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I can’t support the Amendment Paper because it would be going against a decision that had already been taken by Cabinet.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority: the reason given is that Cabinet has already decided, which speaks to the constraint on him but offers nothing on the merits of the amendment itself.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We know that we’re grappling as a country with Māori overrepresentation in our criminal justice system—I acknowledge that—but to say that our police and corrections officers and staff are racist: no, I completely reject that. In my experience, our police officers serve without fear or favour and they’re colour-blind.
rigor.explanation: Strawman plus appeal to personal anecdote: the member argued racism is institutionally 'baked in' to the system, not that individual officers are racist, and the rebuttal rests on 'in my experience' rather than any evidence about outcomes.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I guess my question is: why is it that the Government’s coalition agreement is more important than rectifying discrepancies between Māori and non-Māori, and what advice did you receive on the detrimental impact of removing the Treaty provisions from this bill?
civility.explanation: Pointed and imputes a bad ordering of priorities to the Government and, by address, to the Minister, but stops short of attacking him personally; the second half is a straight request for advice.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We know that we’re grappling as a country with Māori overrepresentation in our criminal justice system—I acknowledge that—but to say that our police and corrections officers and staff are racist: no, I completely reject that. In my experience, our police officers serve without fear or favour and they’re colour-blind.
civility.explanation: Faced with an accusation of institutional racism he concedes the overrepresentation, disagrees squarely with the claim, and attacks no one — he defends his staff rather than disparaging the member.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I guess my question is: why is it that the Government’s coalition agreement is more important than rectifying discrepancies between Māori and non-Māori, and what advice did you receive on the detrimental impact of removing the Treaty provisions from this bill?
focus.explanation: Wrapped in a jab at the coalition agreement, but it names the specific measure at issue — the removal of the Treaty provisions from this bill — and asks for the advice behind it.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I see he doesn’t want to answer my question, so I’ll leave that one for him to think about whether in fact he’s actually even read the Waitangi Tribunal’s report on the justice system, which specifically talks about Corrections and the role that Corrections do in fact have as part of the justice system to address the overrepresentation of Māori.
civility.explanation: Insinuates the Minister has not bothered to read the report and is dodging — a jab at his diligence rather than at the substance of his position. Short of a direct insult, but it imputes negligence to the person, so below the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But I completely reject the premise that because the Treaty provisions have been removed at this stage with this bill—by the way, the Treaty provisions have never been a part of the Corrections Act, and it hasn’t stopped those very deep relationships being formed with Māori, hapū, and iwi.
civility.explanation: Flatly rejects the opposing argument and disputes its premise without any reflection on the member personally. Robust disagreement entirely on the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If the Minister had read the regulatory impact statement, he’d have seen, on page 84, section D: improving long-term outcomes for Māori, diagnosing the policy problem, operational changes under way, guided by Hōkai Rangi, that were needed.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific document, a page number, a section heading and a named strategy (Hōkai Rangi). Someone could open the regulatory impact statement and check the passage.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A big part of what this bill is currently about is being able to deliver more programmes to people, especially those on remand, because we have an unacceptably high level of people on remand at the moment.
specificity.explanation: Names the bill's purpose and the affected group (remand prisoners), but supplies no figures, no mechanism for how more programmes will be delivered, and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill before the committee now removes the definition of cultural activities, and that definition simply said, “cultural activities means activities that are integral to establishing and maintaining a person’s connection with their culture”.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a precise change to a named bill and quotes the deleted statutory definition in full, so the claim can be checked directly against the bill as introduced and as reported back.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But if you read your regulatory impact statement and the tribunal’s report, it said what had been happening was insufficient and it needed more done, and the recommendation is to include it in legislation to require it to happen, to give practical effects to the application of those Treaty principles.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: the cited documents found operational action insufficient and recommended a legislative provision, therefore relying on operational action alone is inadequate. The conclusion tracks the cited sources, though it rests on an appeal to the authority of the tribunal and the RIS rather than on independent evidence that legislating would change outcomes.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But I completely reject the premise that because the Treaty provisions have been removed at this stage with this bill—by the way, the Treaty provisions have never been a part of the Corrections Act, and it hasn’t stopped those very deep relationships being formed with Māori, hapū, and iwi.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the policy — relationships with Māori, hapū and iwi have formed without a statutory Treaty provision, therefore the provision is unnecessary. But it argues from absence of a problem to sufficiency: the fact that relationships exist does not address the claim that what exists is insufficient to reduce disparities.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: On the one hand, we are getting rid of reference to cultural activities, but, actually, in the very next breath, the bill refers to cultural, religion-based, te ao Māori activities, which fundamentally are cultural activities.
rigor.explanation: Points to an internal inconsistency in the drafting: the defined term is deleted while the very next provision uses the same concept. The conclusion of incoherence follows directly from the two provisions cited, with no fallacy relied on.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There’s one party who wants the Treaty principles bill—rewrite what all of those might even mean—and there is another party in that coalition agreement who says they will review, repeal, remove, or replace all Treaty references in all legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that one coalition partner's agreement commits to a Treaty Principles Bill and that another (identified in the next sentence as New Zealand First) commits to reviewing and replacing or repealing all references to Treaty principles across legislation.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published National–ACT and National–NZ First coalition agreements (November 2023); true if the ACT agreement commits to a Treaty Principles Bill and the NZ First agreement commits to reviewing all legislation containing references to the principles of the Treaty and replacing or repealing those references; false if either commitment is absent or materially narrower than described (e.g. limited to a subset of statutes).

veracity.statement: But I completely reject the premise that because the Treaty provisions have been removed at this stage with this bill—by the way, the Treaty provisions have never been a part of the Corrections Act, and it hasn’t stopped those very deep relationships being formed with Māori, hapū, and iwi.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of fact that the Corrections Act has never contained Treaty of Waitangi provisions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Corrections Act 2004 and its amendments on legislation.govt.nz, in particular the principles in section 6; true if no section of the Act as enacted or amended has referred to the Treaty of Waitangi or its principles, false if any such reference exists (e.g. in the section 6 principles).

veracity.statement: The Ombudsman said, more in sadness than in anger, that he had seen no real change in the corrections system despite repeated reports where the Department of Corrections said, “Yes, we agree with all of your criticisms about prisoner safety and rehabilitation and lack of resources” but ultimately did nothing.
veracity.explanation: Relays a characterisation of what the Chief Ombudsman told the Justice Committee — that repeated Ombudsman reports on prisoner safety, rehabilitation and resourcing were accepted by Corrections but produced no real change.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Chief Ombudsman's submission and oral evidence to the Justice Committee on the Corrections Amendment Bill (2024), plus his published OPCAT/corrections reports; true if he stated that agreed recommendations had produced no real change in the system, false if his evidence recorded material change or did not make that criticism.

specificity.statement: Well, firstly, the reality is that this Government has made a significant investment—over $70 million—to be able to deliver programmes to prisoners on remand, either remand convicted or remand accused.
specificity.explanation: Names a dollar figure and the specific cohort the spending targets (remand convicted and remand accused), so the commitment is checkable, though no timeframe or per-programme breakdown is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Coming over also to the point that the Minister has mentioned around the presumption of innocence—and particularly I’m looking at the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act (NZBORA), section 25(c), around people who are provided the right to be considered innocent until proven guilty—how does NZBORA then tie into these two categories of remand that have been created as a part of the definition of “accused prisoners”?
specificity.explanation: Names the statute and the exact section (NZBORA s 25(c)) and ties it to a specific definitional provision in the bill, so the Minister could answer it precisely.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In section 6A, in clause 6, if we look at the sections that have been removed, what in this section will not be going ahead as a result of the removal of this section?
specificity.explanation: Identifies the exact clause at issue and asks a concrete, answerable question about its consequences, though it does not itself carry figures or a specified outcome.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Well, firstly, the reality is that this Government has made a significant investment—over $70 million—to be able to deliver programmes to prisoners on remand, either remand convicted or remand accused.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the current Government has allocated over $70 million specifically for delivering programmes to prisoners held on remand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 / Department of Corrections appropriation documents and Vote Corrections: true if a funding allocation of more than $70 million is identifiable for rehabilitation and other programmes for remand prisoners under this Government; false if the figure is materially smaller or is not directed at remand programmes.

veracity.statement: Look, in terms of te reo, or any language that anyone wants to speak inside corrections, absolutely they can; there’s no restrictions on that, they’re very welcome to do that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Corrections places no restriction on prisoners speaking te reo Māori or any other language while in prison.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections policy manual (Prison Operations Manual) and the Corrections Act 2004/Corrections Regulations 2005 on prisoner language use: true if no policy or regulation restricts prisoners speaking te reo Māori or another language; false if any operational policy limits language use (e.g. requiring English in monitored calls or visits).

veracity.statement: The one thing I’d say, and I’d come back to the point that I’ve been making, is that we have never had Treaty provisions inside the Corrections Act ever, and yet the system has been working very well. It’ll continue to work well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Corrections Act has never contained a Treaty of Waitangi provision.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Corrections Act 2004 and its amendments (and the predecessor Penal Institutions Act 1954): true if no provision referring to the Treaty of Waitangi/Te Tiriti o Waitangi or its principles has ever been enacted in the Corrections Act; false if such a provision exists or previously existed.

rigor.statement: The one thing I’d say, and I’d come back to the point that I’ve been making, is that we have never had Treaty provisions inside the Corrections Act ever, and yet the system has been working very well. It’ll continue to work well.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to tradition: the absence of a Treaty clause in the past is offered as evidence that the system works and will keep working, without any measure of how well it works — and it sidesteps the disparity evidence the question was premised on.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Coming over also to the point that the Minister has mentioned around the presumption of innocence—and particularly I’m looking at the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act (NZBORA), section 25(c), around people who are provided the right to be considered innocent until proven guilty—how does NZBORA then tie into these two categories of remand that have been created as a part of the definition of “accused prisoners”?
focus.explanation: Entirely engaged with the mechanism of the measure before the committee — how the bill's definition of accused prisoner interacts with a named rights provision. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In section 6A, in clause 6, if we look at the sections that have been removed, what in this section will not be going ahead as a result of the removal of this section?
focus.explanation: Direct scrutiny of a named clause being deleted by the bill, asking what practical effect the deletion has. Squarely on the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I don’t doubt, on an individual basis, that they do do the best job that they can, but also we’ve heard comments from members around the Chamber, and I think that we must acknowledge that the statistics in relation to Māori are not where they should be and that something needs to be done.
civility.explanation: On a contested clause removal where she could readily have impugned the Minister's motives, she credits corrections staff and confines the criticism to outcomes and the policy. Attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is not colour-blind; in fact, acknowledging Māori, their identity, their whakapapa, and their cultural connections is the very essence of how rehabilitation may well occur.
rigor.explanation: She has just quoted the regulatory impact statement describing Corrections delivering services in a way that recognises whakapapa, and concludes from that evidence that the department is not in fact colour-blind. The inference tracks the cited document; the further step that cultural recognition is 'the very essence' of rehabilitation is asserted rather than evidenced, which is the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You can’t leave it both ways. Either you take it out and it makes a difference to the bill or you leave it in and it stays the same.
rigor.explanation: A dilemma aimed at the Government's justification: either the Treaty clause is doing work (so removal must be defended) or it is not (so removal is pointless). The two branches are close to genuinely exhaustive, so this is not a false dichotomy, though it compresses the possibility that removal has symbolic rather than operational effect.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Just because it hasn’t been done in the past, it doesn’t mean it shouldn’t be done now—now and for the future, because by locking in Te Tiriti o Waitangi into the legislation, it is for strategic purposes, it is for iwi Māori to know that there are protections in there, and it’s above and beyond obligations to a coalition agreement because the original agreement was Te Tiriti o Waitangi, signed in 1840; kia ora tātou.
rigor.explanation: Correctly rejects an appeal to tradition (that it has not been done before is not a reason against doing it) and offers two reasons for statutory Treaty clauses. The closing step — that a 1840 agreement therefore outranks a coalition agreement in the drafting of this bill — is an appeal to precedence asserted rather than argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Just because Waikeria is amazing in what they’re doing to help strengthen our whānau that are incarcerated, it does not mean that it’s consistent across the system.
rigor.explanation: Explicitly declines to generalise from her single site visit to the whole prison system — the opposite of the argument-from-anecdote, and the reasoning that supports her case for a system-wide statutory framework.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m really puzzled by the Minister’s comments that the Department of Corrections should be colour-blind.
civility.explanation: A contested exchange in which she disagrees sharply with the Minister, yet the disagreement lands entirely on the comment made, not on the Minister's character, competence or motives.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In relation to my comment around being colour-blind, if the member had been listening she would have heard that both the Police and Corrections were accused of being racist.
civility.explanation: The substantive clarification is wrapped in a jab at the member's attentiveness — 'if the member had been listening' is condescension aimed at her rather than at her argument. Short of a direct insult, but it has stopped engaging the point and started addressing the person.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I still yet have not heard from the Minister responsible for this legislation why the Treaty references have been taken out of this bill and also why they make the bill better by removing the Treaty references in this bill.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee — the removal of the Treaty provisions from this bill — pressing for the rationale. Legitimate scrutiny of a named change, with no party-directed content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I believe that we need to lock in Te Tiriti o Waitangi to ensure—strategically and operationally—we have firm plans, we have accountability, and monitoring of the system across the board, not by chance.
focus.explanation: Directed at the clause in the bill under debate and what its retention would do, with no party-directed content.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We know that over 50 percent of those incarcerated in our prisons are Māori, and I do not accept that being colour-blind makes any difference or makes it any better.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori make up more than 50 percent of the New Zealand prison population as at August 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections prison population statistics (Ara Poutama Aotearoa quarterly 'Prison facts and statistics') for 2024; true if the Māori share of the total prison population exceeds 50 percent, false if it is 50 percent or below.

veracity.statement: We have, what, 68 percent of wāhine Māori incarcerated, and 53 percent of Māori overall.
veracity.explanation: In context this is the standard spoken compression of the Corrections figures: Māori make up about 68 percent of the women's prison population and about 53 percent of the total prison population. The literal word order is a slip, not the claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections prison population statistics for 2024; true if the Māori share of the female prison population is approximately 68 percent and of the total prison population approximately 53 percent (within a couple of percentage points), false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Because the original intent—and this is what I found; that our officials provided advice and said that Te Tiriti o Waitangi clause which is being removed is the most critical to achieving the original intent of the Treaty provisions, which is to ensure Corrections consistently focuses on improving outcomes for Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that departmental advice to Ministers stated the Treaty of Waitangi clause being repealed was the most critical of the Treaty provisions for ensuring Corrections focuses on improving outcomes for Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement and Department of Corrections advice published for the Corrections Amendment Bill 2024; true if that advice describes the repealed Te Tiriti clause as the most critical to achieving the provisions' intent, false if no such characterisation appears.

specificity.statement: In relation to the question around the removal of the Treaty provisions, again I’d say to the member that, yes, it was a Cabinet decision based on a coalition agreement.
specificity.explanation: Names a decision-making mechanism (a Cabinet decision arising from the coalition agreement), which is checkable in outline, but supplies no clause, no advice, no date and no account of what the decision turned on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have, what, 68 percent of wāhine Māori incarcerated, and 53 percent of Māori overall.
specificity.explanation: Two precise, sourced-style percentages tied to identifiable populations; anyone could go to the Corrections statistics and check them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I believe that we need to lock in Te Tiriti o Waitangi to ensure—strategically and operationally—we have firm plans, we have accountability, and monitoring of the system across the board, not by chance.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic goods — 'firm plans', 'accountability', 'monitoring' — with no named mechanism, reporting requirement, measure or timeframe attached to any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is the Minister still committed to the principles of Hōkai Rangi? I'd like to know that.
focus.explanation: Names a specific government strategy (Hōkai Rangi) and asks the Minister to state whether the commitment to it stands — accountability directed at a named policy, not at the other party in general.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, the law does generally one of three things: it prohibits something, it requires something, or it gives someone a power to do something. My concern with this clause and clauses like it—and there are several through the legislation—is that it does none of those things.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the drafting of the clause before the committee — its legal mechanism and whether it creates any obligation. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Some of the stuff that Kelvin did, I think, was something that should have been bipartisan, could have been supported by a National Government too, as some of the work that Simon Power did in the past was supported by Labour and other people.
rigor.explanation: An argument from precedent/analogy: because Labour supported a National minister's justice work, National should support Labour's. The analogy is asserted rather than established — no reason is given why the two initiatives are relevantly alike — so there is a real gap between premise and conclusion, though the inference is not absurd.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In relation to consultation about the removal of the Treaty provisions, the Treaty provisions have never been part of the Corrections Act. It's very hard to be able to understand what the impacts are when they've never been part of the Corrections Act.
rigor.explanation: Valid conditional inference given its premise: if a provision was never in the Act, there is no removal whose impact could be assessed or consulted on. The conclusion follows from the stated premise; whether the premise holds is a separate question.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, the law does generally one of three things: it prohibits something, it requires something, or it gives someone a power to do something. My concern with this clause and clauses like it—and there are several through the legislation—is that it does none of those things.
rigor.explanation: Sets out an explicit taxonomy of what a legislative provision can do, then shows the clause falls outside all three categories, concluding it has no legal effect. The conclusion tracks the premises; the only soft spot is that the taxonomy is asserted rather than defended.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Simon Power was a National Party Minister; he had gang members coming into Parliament.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Simon Power held office as a National Party Minister and that, in that role, he brought gang members into Parliament for meetings.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary and contemporaneous media records of Simon Power's ministerial term (Minister of Justice 2008–2011): true if he held a National ministerial warrant and there is documented record of gang members/gang leaders being hosted at Parliament in connection with his justice work; false if no such meetings are recorded.

veracity.statement: In relation to consultation about the removal of the Treaty provisions, the Treaty provisions have never been part of the Corrections Act. It's very hard to be able to understand what the impacts are when they've never been part of the Corrections Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the Corrections Act has never contained provisions referring to the Treaty of Waitangi or its principles.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Corrections Act 2004 as enacted and as subsequently amended (legislation.govt.nz), including s 6 principles and s 8: true if no provision of the Act has ever referred to the Treaty of Waitangi or its principles; false if any repealed or current section did so.

veracity.statement: I accept, and the Minister well knows, through exchanges we've had, that Corrections has not met minimum standards, let alone exemplary standards in respect of how it addresses and provides for prisoners in terms of their basic rights.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Department of Corrections has failed to meet minimum standards for prisoners' basic rights.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Chief Ombudsman OPCAT inspection reports on New Zealand prisons and Corrections' own performance reporting for 2022–2024: true if those reports find facilities or practices falling below minimum standards for prisoners' basic rights; false if inspections record minimum standards being met.

civility.statement: It does distress us that the Treaty is being put aside because of a coalition agreement.
civility.explanation: A contested and pointed objection to the Government's policy direction on Treaty provisions, expressed without any attack on a person — engages the decision, not the decision-maker.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This can't be dismissed by saying they do a great job because, I'm sorry, Minister, they don't. We have the words of the Ombudsman on numerous reports and in person to the Justice Committee saying that's not the case.
civility.explanation: Blunt rejection of the department's performance, addressed directly to the Minister but resting on the Ombudsman's findings rather than on any personal characterisation. Hard on the record, civil toward the person.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Coming to the Hon Willie Jackson, yes, I was definitely around in 2019; yes, I definitely support the initiative that Kelvin put in place and acknowledge him for that; yes, we're working with iwi and hapū, as he knows; and, yes, we remain committed to making sure that we continue to develop and deliver the programmes that we think will do the best and move us towards, when people rejoin society, giving them the best possible chance of reintegration and making good decisions in their lives.
specificity.explanation: Confirms the year and the named initiative, but the substance — which programmes, with which iwi and hapū, at what scale or by when — is left as generic commitment language ('the programmes that we think will do the best', 'the best possible chance'). Some checkable anchoring, little actionable detail.
specificity.subject: speaker
