specificity.statement: In this clause, and in other clauses throughout, it says "accused prisoners may,"—so it's not mandatory—"so far as is reasonable"—the first qualifier—"and practicable"—the second qualifier—"in the circumstances within the resources available,"—the third qualifier.
specificity.explanation: Quotes the operative statutory wording and itemises each qualifier individually, so the claim that the duty is diluted can be checked directly against the text of the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Corrections over the last few years have been operating severely under capacity in terms of numbers. We are starting to fix that. For the first time in a long time, we were above the rate of attrition and doing very well with recruitment, training, and deployment of new corrections officers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Corrections was staffed below required numbers for several years and that, as at August 2024, recruitment of corrections officers exceeded attrition.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections annual report / OIA staffing data for 2023-24: true if net frontline corrections officer numbers grew (new recruits deployed exceeding departures) in the period referenced and prior years show vacancy/under-strength figures; false if attrition equalled or exceeded recruitment over that period.

veracity.statement: This is incredibly significant, and this is incredibly significant for the Opposition to hear as well, because this removal took place after the select committee stage, so, in fact, no submitters have been able to comment on this.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Te Tiriti o Waitangi clause was removed from the bill after the select committee process, with the consequence that submitters had no opportunity to comment on the removal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's select committee report and the Amendment Paper/SOP history for the Corrections Amendment Bill: true if the provision was deleted by an amendment introduced at or after the committee-of-the-whole-House stage (i.e. after submissions closed); false if the deletion was recommended in the select committee report on which submitters could and did comment.

veracity.statement: One of the things we know within the prison system, within the correction system, is the disproportionate number of people who are neurodivergent or who have dyslexia.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that neurodivergence and dyslexia are over-represented among the New Zealand prison population relative to the general population.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections prevalence research and peer-reviewed NZ studies on literacy, dyslexia and neurodevelopmental conditions among prisoners: true if measured prevalence in the prison population materially exceeds general-population estimates; false if rates are comparable to or below the general population.

specificity.statement: Corrections over the last few years have been operating severely under capacity in terms of numbers. We are starting to fix that. For the first time in a long time, we were above the rate of attrition and doing very well with recruitment, training, and deployment of new corrections officers.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete measure (recruitment above the rate of attrition) and a trend, but supplies no figures, no baseline vacancy number and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The whole focus of this legislation is to make it safer for both corrections officers and prisoners, and for us to be able to deliver more rehabilitation to those that need it—and that’s exactly what this bill is going to deliver.
specificity.explanation: States generic goals — safer, more rehabilitation — with no mechanism, no quantity of programmes, no timeframe and no named provision, so nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now my second question is on clause 5, which inserts new section 3A, “Transitional, savings, and related provisions”. I want to specifically focus on Schedule 1AA, which is after Schedule 1.
specificity.explanation: Pins the question to a named clause, the new section it inserts, and the specific schedule; the surrounding question adds section 26 of NZBORA and page 31 of the regulatory impact statement, so the Minister and any reader can locate exactly what is asked about.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I can’t give you a very definitive answer on that. The only thing that I would say to you is that Corrections are very sensitive to this. They’ve got very good processes in place. They make sure that the prisons are supported in the best way that they can be.
specificity.explanation: A general assurance — 'very sensitive', 'very good processes', 'best way that they can be' — with no named process, screening tool, programme adaptation or figure that could be checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: To codify it and not give them the flexibility and the ability to be able to recognise the environment that they work in would mean that you could be putting Corrections in a position where they’re breaking the law. And we’re not going to do that.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the drafting choice, but the step from 'codify the requirement' to 'Corrections would be breaking the law' is asserted rather than shown — nothing is offered about which obligation would be breached or why compliance would be impossible, so the conclusion outruns the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The whole focus of this legislation is to make it safer for both corrections officers and prisoners, and for us to be able to deliver more rehabilitation to those that need it—and that’s exactly what this bill is going to deliver.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the measure before the committee and its intended effects; no party framing or reference to opponents at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This is incredibly significant, and this is incredibly significant for the Opposition to hear as well, because this removal took place after the select committee stage, so, in fact, no submitters have been able to comment on this.
civility.explanation: A pointed procedural criticism of how the clause was removed, directed entirely at the process; imputes no bad faith and attacks no member.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, actually, Corrections does have a responsibility and does have some control over who is coming back into the system due to the way that they are being treated.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: premise (in-prison treatment shapes post-release behaviour) to conclusion (Corrections bears responsibility for reoffending). The step is coherent and on point, but the causal premise is asserted rather than evidenced, and the intervening 'treat people like animals' analogy does no argumentative work.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I just want everyone to remember that, actually, they’re looking after people who were taken out of our society because they’re often violent—they’re violent offenders who hurt people or kill people.
rigor.explanation: The supporting material is two anecdotes (a stabbed officer, an assaulted officer) generalised to a conclusion about the prison population, and even granted, the premise that prisoners are violent does not establish the conclusion at issue — that particular restraint weapons are appropriate. Argument from anecdote with a gap to the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It was just quite simply around the fact that you cannot guarantee—anything that you use, you cannot guarantee that there may not be a lethal outcome.
rigor.explanation: A valid rationale for the terminology change: if no tactical option can be guaranteed non-fatal, then 'less-lethal' is the accurate label and 'non-lethal' is not. The conclusion follows directly from the stated premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I was really concerned to see there isn’t even a definition for what “less-lethal” means.
focus.explanation: Names a specific drafting gap in the provision before the committee (the absence of a definition of 'less-lethal' in amended section 85). Squarely on the measure, no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I know the Minister likes to borrow laws from Australia.
civility.explanation: A pointed characterisation of the Minister's personal habit rather than of the policy — it edges toward the man without landing an insult or imputing bad faith. The rest of her contribution stays on the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I did a bit of research and found that New South Wales and South Australia have actually outright banned spit hoods and the use of those spit hoods.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that two named Australian states have enacted outright bans on the use of spit hoods.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NSW and South Australian legislation/police and corrections policy as at August 2024 (e.g. SA's Summary Offences (Prohibition of Spit Hoods) Amendment Act and NSW equivalents); true if both jurisdictions prohibit spit hood use outright, false if either merely restricts their use or has no ban.

veracity.statement: There was one particular incident that was reported on by Guyon Espiner in 2020, which was about an asthmatic woman in Auckland Women’s Prison who had four canisters of gas put under her door and the officers stuffed the door with towels in order to not allow the gas to escape from the cell, and this ended up being taken to court in the Cripps v Attorney-General case.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific 2020 RNZ report by Guyon Espiner about an asthmatic prisoner at Auckland Women's Prison gassed with four canisters while officers blocked the door with towels, and that the incident featured in Cripps v Attorney-General.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RNZ's 2020 reporting by Guyon Espiner on pepper-spray/CS gas use at Auckland Region Women's Corrections Facility and the judgment in Cripps v Attorney-General; true if the report and case describe an asthmatic prisoner, four canisters and towels used to seal the cell door, false if the number of canisters, the prison, the journalist or the case do not match.

veracity.statement: In relation to the changes around tactical options for them, the change from “non-lethal” to “less-lethal” was driven in part by the report that came out from the UN.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a United Nations report was a driver of the legislative change in terminology from 'non-lethal' to 'less-lethal' weapons.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Corrections Amendment Bill's departmental disclosure statement, regulatory impact statement and Corrections advice; true if a UN report (e.g. the UN Subcommittee on Prevention of Torture report on New Zealand or UN human rights guidance on less-lethal weapons) is cited as a reason for the terminology change, false if the officials' documents give no such basis.

veracity.statement: In terms of some of the less lethal options that corrections officers have got, obviously, there are pepper spray and batons.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that pepper spray and batons are among the tactical options available to New Zealand corrections officers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections tactical options / use-of-force policy as at August 2024; true if both pepper spray and batons are authorised equipment for corrections officers, false if either is not issued or authorised.

specificity.statement: There was one particular incident that was reported on by Guyon Espiner in 2020, which was about an asthmatic woman in Auckland Women’s Prison who had four canisters of gas put under her door and the officers stuffed the door with towels in order to not allow the gas to escape from the cell, and this ended up being taken to court in the Cripps v Attorney-General case.
specificity.explanation: Named journalist, named year, named prison, a count of canisters, the physical method, and a named court case — every element is independently checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Minister’s thrown that out and, I guess, I’m asking the Minister—because he said on a number of occasions, “We can still achieve these things; we just don’t need legislation to do it.”—will he be requiring, as Minister, the chief executive to have a strategy, in place of legislation, which focuses on improving outcomes for Māori in the corrections systems?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: the deletion of clause 8 and what will replace the statutory strategy requirement. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So the question is: is this a priority or not, or is this yet another coalition push to delete references to tikanga Māori, to te reo Māori, and to Te Tiriti?
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy question underneath — why clause 19's cultural-activities guarantee was removed — but the weight of the sentence shifts to a general characterisation of the coalition's motives across unrelated measures rather than to this provision's effect.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Minister’s thrown that out and, I guess, I’m asking the Minister—because he said on a number of occasions, “We can still achieve these things; we just don’t need legislation to do it.”—will he be requiring, as Minister, the chief executive to have a strategy, in place of legislation, which focuses on improving outcomes for Māori in the corrections systems?
specificity.explanation: Names the deleted clause, the mechanism removed (a chief executive strategy with monitoring requirements) and asks a precise, answerable question about what will replace it. No timeframe or figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The requirement is that a health professional check daily whether it is still required that they are, essentially, isolated in solitary confinement. Except, subsection (8), once again, says that they don’t have to do it if they don’t think they need to.
specificity.explanation: Pins the criticism to a named provision (new section 61CA, subsection (8)), states the exact obligation (a daily visit by a registered health professional) and the exact exemption. Fully checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In relation to Hōkai Rangi, I’ve been very clear; I’ve said that we’re committed to that. This Government is firmly committed to increasing rehabilitation programmes and access for prisoners to have rehabilitation programmes, and that is contained within the bill.
specificity.explanation: Names one identifiable strategy (Hōkai Rangi) and points to the bill, but 'increasing rehabilitation programmes and access' carries no figure, no mechanism and no timeframe, and no clause of the bill is identified.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Minister has, on repeated occasions, said that he agrees in principle with that as an objective of the corrections system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister of Corrections has said more than once that he agrees in principle with improving outcomes for Māori as an objective of the corrections system.
veracity.subject: other

veracity.statement: I just wanted to follow up on, first of all, the Minister of Corrections’ answers in terms of racism, which were put forward, which I thought were interesting, and the Minister denying that there’s any racism in the police.

veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard transcript of the Minister's answers earlier in this committee-stage debate; true if he denied the existence of racism in the police, false if his answers acknowledged racism or made no such denial.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections prison population statistics by ethnicity for 2024; true if the Māori share of prisoners is approximately 50 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: My short point is a drafting one, and that is that on my reading of section 88 as it currently stands, it doesn’t use the word “non-lethal”, so you can’t replace it with “less lethal”.

civility.statement: This seems to be a kind of excuse to use a device that’s totally unnecessary, and it simply puts a lack of clarity into a section that, because of the seriousness of these devices, needs to be as clear as possible.

civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m really mindful because—with the cultural activities part really not being clear anymore in terms of the compulsion for that to be available and with the knowledge that, often, Māori don’t get the temporary release, because of security concerns—how can we look to bridge that gap?

focus.statement: Look, quite simply the fact of the matter is there are many, many different situations and scenarios, inside a corrections environment, where a passive prisoner, someone that’s refusing to follow instruction, could be putting other people at risk. focus.explanation: Addresses the exact wording at issue in clause 21 and the operational circumstances it is meant to cover; no party content.

focus.statement: This seems to be a kind of excuse to use a device that’s totally unnecessary, and it simply puts a lack of clarity into a section that, because of the seriousness of these devices, needs to be as clear as possible.

specificity.statement: Every month now, I’m going to graduations where they’re recruiting, training, and deploying up to 140 new corrections officers.

specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the section of the principal Act, and the exact words at issue — immediately checkable and actionable by officials.

rigor.explanation: Rebuts a definitional claim by offering concrete counterexamples; if the scenarios described are possible, the conclusion that passive resistance can endanger others follows directly. A valid counterexample argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But I’m a bit perplexed as to why we have, on the end of the sentence, “or any other person”, because passive resistance is, by definition, not threatening any other person.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows only from a stipulated definition of 'passive resistance' that is asserted rather than argued; a definitional premise doing all the work, and it ignores indirect risk. A real inference about the clause, but a leaky one.

focus.statement: Now, Minister, I think we’ve made a mistake here. I don’t think we intend for an employee of a contractor, who is not a sworn officer, to be able to search and surveil a prisoner, because that is an exercise of quite an extraordinary State power.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: the drafting of new section 127F, who the power is conferred on, and the consequence of that. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When I look at new section 127K, inserted by clause 33, which is just a little bit further on from the previous clause that was asked, I do think that the way that’s worded does lend itself to some future sort of misinterpretation.
focus.explanation: Engages a named clause of the bill before the committee and the drafting risk it carries; nothing about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, Minister, I think we’ve made a mistake here. I don’t think we intend for an employee of a contractor, who is not a sworn officer, to be able to search and surveil a prisoner, because that is an exercise of quite an extraordinary State power.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: the statutory definition of 'eligible employee' sweeps in contractors' employees; an extraordinary State surveillance power should rest with officers answerable to the State; therefore the drafting is a slip. The conclusion follows from the premises offered, with a small gap in that the normative premise about who should hold the power is asserted rather than argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Quite simply, why it refers to contractors is, of course, because we have a private prison that’s being run by Serco.
rigor.explanation: A real inference answering the criticism: the definition reaches contractors because a contracted prison operator exists. It is valid as far as it goes, but leaves a gap — it explains why contractors appear in the definition without addressing Webb's actual objection about persons three steps removed from the department.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, Minister, I think we’ve made a mistake here. I don’t think we intend for an employee of a contractor, who is not a sworn officer, to be able to search and surveil a prisoner, because that is an exercise of quite an extraordinary State power.
civility.explanation: Contested committee-stage debate on an invasive power, with an obvious opening to attack the Minister's competence for the drafting; instead the criticism is framed as a shared error in the bill and is directed entirely at the text.

specificity.statement: New section 127F, on page 24 of the bill, says that “(1) The chief executive may authorise an eligible employee to be an authorised intelligence person”.

specificity.statement: Quite simply, why it refers to contractors is, of course, because we have a private prison that’s being run by Serco.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of section 111 of the Corrections Act 2004 as in force in August 2024 (legislation.govt.nz). True if the definition of 'eligible employee' there includes employees of contractors, employees of contracted providers and contracted providers; false if it is confined to employees of the chief executive or otherwise materially differs.

veracity.statement: Quite simply, why it refers to contractors is, of course, because we have a private prison that’s being run by Serco.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections records and the Auckland South Corrections Facility (Kohuora) contract as at August 2024. True if a New Zealand prison was then operated under contract by Serco; false if no Serco-operated prison existed at that date.

focus.statement: My question to the Minister is: as I understand it, the new section actually provides no discretion at all for a visiting justice, who is at the appellate level, to, basically, consider reasons for the failure to present the prisoner, and, if this is so, is he open to make changes in that particular space? It would seem to me that it would be an affront to natural justice if the visiting justice simply was not able to consider an appeal without all of the information.
focus.explanation: Engages the specific mechanism of the clause before the committee — the removal of the visiting justice's appellate discretion — and asks the Minister a direct policy question. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, my experience with visiting justices is that the reasons that are recorded are in the prison’s visiting justice book. Often, it’s a ledger where there are maybe five compartments—date, who the person is, what the penalty is, whether it’s proven, and then a signature or stamp. Is that satisfactory for the purposes of the decision?
focus.explanation: Squarely on clause 40's drafting — what 'must record in writing the decision and reasons for it' will mean in practice. Entirely about the measure, not about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think that the reason why—clearly the reason why the prisoner can’t appeal the fact that he wasn’t there is because he’s refused to actually attend. He can still appeal the actual outcome of the hearing, but he doesn’t have any appeal rights in terms of failing to appear, because he’s been given the opportunity and he’s chosen not to appear.
focus.explanation: Answers on the policy mechanism — which appeal rights survive under the new provision and why — with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The reason I raised those statistics is because it’s clear that the experience of sexual violence is prevalent within our prison population and that things like strip searches and rub-down searches can be retriggering and retraumatising for people who have experienced sexual violence in their lifetime.
focus.explanation: Directly on the bill's body-imaging provisions and the physical-search regime they would displace; argues from evidence about the affected population.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They need to maintain these relationships in order to be able to reflect on their behaviour and their actions and to address that and to change that, but I guess what I’m concerned about is that increased monitoring and surveillance might reduce the ability for prisoners to have that connection, even though that’s a core principle within the bill.
focus.explanation: Engages the bill's monitoring provisions against its own stated guiding principle on family contact — a specific internal tension in the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My question to the Minister is: as I understand it, the new section actually provides no discretion at all for a visiting justice, who is at the appellate level, to, basically, consider reasons for the failure to present the prisoner, and, if this is so, is he open to make changes in that particular space? It would seem to me that it would be an affront to natural justice if the visiting justice simply was not able to consider an appeal without all of the information.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause and the new subsection, identifies the precise legal effect (no discretion at the appellate level over the reasons for non-attendance), and asks a concrete question about amending it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, my experience with visiting justices is that the reasons that are recorded are in the prison’s visiting justice book. Often, it’s a ledger where there are maybe five compartments—date, who the person is, what the penalty is, whether it’s proven, and then a signature or stamp. Is that satisfactory for the purposes of the decision?
specificity.explanation: Describes the actual recording practice in concrete detail (the visiting justice book, the five ledger columns) so the Minister can answer against a definite picture rather than an abstraction.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of whether or not there’s personal mitigating circumstances, that is very operational, but my experience is—and I’m sure it’s the member’s experience too—that Corrections will work around that. They’ll give them every opportunity to appear, and if there’s mitigating circumstances—like a death in the family or, for some reason, they just don’t feel up to it—then Corrections will take that into account and work around it.
specificity.explanation: A general assurance about operational practice — 'Corrections will work around it' — with no named policy, instruction, threshold or process attached, in answer to a question about a specific statutory exclusion.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of the images, the images are kept for 24 hours and then automatically deleted. The only one that sees the image is the person that’s actually operating the scanners at the time.
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable retention period (24 hours), an automatic deletion mechanism, and a stated access restriction — directly answerable detail in response to the privacy question.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: My question to the Minister is: as I understand it, the new section actually provides no discretion at all for a visiting justice, who is at the appellate level, to, basically, consider reasons for the failure to present the prisoner, and, if this is so, is he open to make changes in that particular space? It would seem to me that it would be an affront to natural justice if the visiting justice simply was not able to consider an appeal without all of the information.
rigor.explanation: Premise (the appeal ground is excluded regardless of reason) supports the conclusion (a natural-justice problem), and the earlier passage supplies the connecting reason — that a refusal may stem from circumstances not apparent at the time. The inference tracks what was offered; it is conditional on his reading of the clause, which he flags.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think that the reason why—clearly the reason why the prisoner can’t appeal the fact that he wasn’t there is because he’s refused to actually attend. He can still appeal the actual outcome of the hearing, but he doesn’t have any appeal rights in terms of failing to appear, because he’s been given the opportunity and he’s chosen not to appear.
rigor.explanation: Close to circular on the point at issue: the conclusion assumes the refusal was a free and informed choice, which is precisely what the excluded ground of appeal would have allowed a visiting justice to test. The reason offered ('he's chosen not to appear') restates the premise under challenge rather than supporting it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In terms of whether or not there’s personal mitigating circumstances, that is very operational, but my experience is—and I’m sure it’s the member’s experience too—that Corrections will work around that. They’ll give them every opportunity to appear, and if there’s mitigating circumstances—like a death in the family or, for some reason, they just don’t feel up to it—then Corrections will take that into account and work around it.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal anecdote and assumed shared experience: the conclusion that mitigating circumstances will be accommodated rests on 'my experience is' rather than on any provision, policy or safeguard, which is what the question asked about.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reason I raised those statistics is because it’s clear that the experience of sexual violence is prevalent within our prison population and that things like strip searches and rub-down searches can be retriggering and retraumatising for people who have experienced sexual violence in their lifetime.
rigor.explanation: Cited prevalence figures plus the stated retraumatisation mechanism support the conclusion that searches should be reduced. The retraumatisation link is asserted rather than evidenced, which is the one gap, but the inference otherwise follows from the premises offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They need to maintain these relationships in order to be able to reflect on their behaviour and their actions and to address that and to change that, but I guess what I’m concerned about is that increased monitoring and surveillance might reduce the ability for prisoners to have that connection, even though that’s a core principle within the bill.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (monitoring may undercut the bill's contact principle) is plausible but the causal step — that surveillance reduces prisoners' willingness or ability to maintain contact — is asserted rather than supported; the cited submissions establish that isolation harms wellbeing, not that monitoring produces isolation.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There is also no expectation that that decision would be made available to the prisoner.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Corrections Amendment Bill (No 2) 2024 as reported back, clause 40 and the provisions it inserts, plus the Corrections Act 2004/Corrections Regulations 2005: false if any provision requires the recorded decision and reasons to be given or made available to the prisoner; true if the obligation stops at recording them.

veracity.statement: The other point in terms of—of course the matter has to be recorded by the justice, and of course the prisoner will be informed of the outcome of that hearing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the bill the prisoner will be informed of the outcome of a disciplinary hearing conducted in their absence.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Corrections Amendment Bill (No 2) 2024 as enacted, together with the Corrections Act 2004/Corrections Regulations 2005: true if a provision requires notification of the outcome to the prisoner; false if no such notification requirement exists in statute or regulation.

veracity.statement: In terms of the images, the images are kept for 24 hours and then automatically deleted. The only one that sees the image is the person that’s actually operating the scanners at the time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific operating rule for body-imaging scanners in NZ prisons: images retained 24 hours then auto-deleted, viewable only by the operator at the time of the scan.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections body-imaging technology operating policy / the regulatory impact statement and privacy impact assessment for the Corrections Amendment Bill: true if they specify a 24-hour automatic deletion and single-operator viewing; false if the documented retention period, deletion mechanism or access rules differ materially.

veracity.statement: I also note the statement within the regulatory impact statement for the bill that staff at sites where imaging technology has been deployed report that it is harder to get unauthorised items into prison when body imaging technology is used, compared to strip and rub-down searches.
veracity.explanation: Relays a specific finding said to appear in the bill's regulatory impact statement: staff at deployment sites report imaging technology makes it harder to smuggle unauthorised items than physical searches do.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.subject_name: regulatory impact statement for the Corrections Amendment Bill
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published regulatory impact statement for the Corrections Amendment Bill (No 2) 2024: true if it contains a staff-reported finding to that effect; false if no such statement appears or the RIS reports the opposite.

veracity.statement: These games were historic for New Zealand, not just for matching our record tally of 20 medals in Tokyo but for clinching the most gold medals New Zealand has ever won and finishing 11th on the medal table, ahead of such sporting powerhouses with far bigger populations, such as Canada, Spain, and Sweden.
veracity.explanation: Asserts four checkable facts: NZ's Paris 2024 total equalled its Tokyo 2020 record of 20 medals; the gold tally was an all-time NZ record; NZ finished 11th on the official medal table; and Canada, Spain and Sweden finished below NZ on that table.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official IOC/Olympics.com medal tables for Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024. True if NZ's Paris total is 20 (equal to Tokyo), its gold count is the highest in NZ Olympic history, NZ is ranked 11th on the gold-first medal table, and Canada, Spain and Sweden rank below 11th. False if any of those four does not hold.

veracity.statement: One brilliant statistic is that of our team of 204 athletes, 42 of them are coming home with at least one medal around their neck.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 42 of the 204 New Zealand athletes selected for Paris 2024 won at least one medal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Olympic Committee team list and the Paris 2024 results, counting distinct NZ athletes who received a medal (including team-event members). True if the count is 42 of a 204-strong team; false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Dame Lisa Carrington has etched her name in Olympic history with her eighth gold medal.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Olympic canoe sprint results for London 2012, Rio 2016, Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024. True if Carrington's cumulative gold total is eight after Paris; false if it is a different number.

veracity.statement: To put that feat into the historical context it deserves, eight gold medals is bigger than the haul managed by any of Spain, Sweden, Brazil, or Hungary in Paris.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official Paris 2024 medal table gold counts for Spain, Sweden, Brazil and Hungary. True if all four are below eight; false if any equalled or exceeded eight.

veracity.statement: Hamish Kerr also made history by becoming the first New Zealand male to win a field event in the Olympic track and field programme.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Olympic athletics medal records for New Zealand across all Games. True if no NZ male has previously won an Olympic field event title; false if a prior NZ male field-event winner exists.

veracity.statement: I heard what the Prime Minister said about our track and field gold, and I do want to acknowledge, as was mentioned to me by one of my colleagues, Dame Yvette Williams, who was one of our famed Olympians, a gold medallist in the long jump, if I recall correctly, in 1952, I think it was, in Helsinki, who did us all extremely proud.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Yvette Williams won Olympic gold in the long jump at the 1952 Helsinki Games.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official Olympic records for the 1952 Helsinki Games women's long jump. True if Yvette Williams is listed as the gold medallist; false if the event, year or medal differ.

veracity.statement: We would like today to congratulate our wonderful New Zealand Olympic Games team for their outstanding performance at the Paris Olympics. It was a historic achievement for us, with Aotearoa’s athletes securing 20 medals, as we’ve heard—10 gold, seven silver, and three bronze. But what makes this all the more special is that 14 of these 20 medals were won by our extraordinary women athletes and women’s teams.
veracity.explanation: Asserts New Zealand's Paris 2024 medal tally (20 total: 10 gold, 7 silver, 3 bronze) and that 14 of the 20 were won by women athletes or women's teams.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The official Paris 2024 medal table for New Zealand (IOC / NZ Olympic Committee): true if the tally is 10 gold, 7 silver, 3 bronze, and if a count of NZ medal events won by women or women's teams comes to 14; false if either figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: In October 2018, the then New Zealand Government launched a strategy to address the inequities women and girls experience in sport and recreation, the women and girls in sport initiative.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a government women-and-girls-in-sport strategy was launched in October 2018.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Sport NZ / Ministry for Sport and Recreation records for the Women and Girls in Sport and Active Recreation Strategy: true if launched in October 2018, false if launched in a materially different month or year or if no such strategy exists.

veracity.statement: I wanted to see our athletes, and I was sad to see the muck-up that denied Eisa Mozhdeh and Jemesa Landers a chance to compete, but I think it’s really, really important that we recognise that our athletes, their support staff, their families all experience the blood, sweat, and tears of preparation—years of preparation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an administrative error prevented named New Zealand taekwondo athletes Eisa Mozhdeh and Jemesa Landers from competing at the Paris Olympics.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous reporting and NZ Olympic Committee / Taekwondo NZ statements on the two named athletes' Paris 2024 entry: true if they were excluded from competing owing to an entry or administrative failure, false if they competed or were never entered on selection grounds.

veracity.statement: We know that competing is a costly exercise, so special mention has to go to rower Robbie Manson, who took to posing on an OnlyFans website to raise funds.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand rower Robbie Manson used an OnlyFans account to raise funds for his sporting career.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public reporting and Manson's own statements: true if he ran a paid OnlyFans account and described it as funding his rowing, false if no such account or funding purpose is documented.

veracity.statement: The small coastal town has now hosted the second surfing event at the Olympics, after its introduction at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Olympic surfing debuted at the Tokyo 2020 Games and that Teahupo'o, Tahiti hosted the second Olympic surfing competition.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IOC event records: true if surfing was first contested at Tokyo 2020 and the Paris 2024 surfing competition was held at Teahupo'o, false if surfing appeared at an earlier Games or the Paris venue was elsewhere.

veracity.statement: Ellesse Andrews became the second New Zealander to win gold in track cycling, after Sarah Ulmer in 2004. She won gold in the women’s keirin.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Ellesse Andrews won the women's keirin gold at Paris 2024 and is only the second New Zealander ever to win an Olympic track cycling gold, the first being Sarah Ulmer in 2004.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Olympic results database for track cycling: true if Andrews won keirin gold in 2024 and no New Zealander other than Ulmer (2004) has previously won Olympic track cycling gold; false if any earlier NZ track cycling gold exists or the event/result differs.

veracity.statement: She leaves Paris having won the same number of gold medals as Usain Bolt.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Lisa Carrington's career Olympic gold medal total after Paris 2024 equals Usain Bolt's career total.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Olympic medal records: true if Carrington's cumulative Olympic golds after Paris 2024 equal Bolt's final career total (as recognised by the IOC); false if the two totals differ.

veracity.statement: We saw the selfless feat of Dylan McCullough falling back during the triathlon to provide much-needed support to his teammate Hayden Wilde, who ended up winning the silver medal.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Dylan McCullough dropped back during the Paris 2024 men's triathlon to assist Hayden Wilde, and that Wilde won silver.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Paris 2024 men's triathlon results and race reporting: true if Wilde finished second and McCullough is reported as having paced or assisted him, false if Wilde's placing differs or no such assistance occurred.

veracity.statement: Our Government is absolutely committed to building great roads and Kiwis deserve to be safe when they drive on them, and alcohol and drugs are the number one cause of fatal crashes on New Zealand roads; in fact, around 30 percent of deaths on our roads involve drug-drivers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that alcohol and drugs are the single largest cause of fatal crashes in New Zealand and that roughly 30 percent of road deaths involve drug-impaired drivers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport / NZTA crash analysis system data on contributing factors in fatal crashes: true if alcohol and drugs rank first among identified causes and drug-driver involvement in road deaths is near 30 percent; false if another factor ranks first or the share is materially different from 30 percent.

veracity.statement: Now, we see inflation is tracking down to 3.3 percent and heading lower, and last week brought more good news for every Kiwi with a mortgage, with the first cut to the official cash rate in 4½ years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts annual inflation is at 3.3 percent and that the Reserve Bank's OCR cut in the preceding week was the first in four and a half years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI for the June 2024 quarter and the RBNZ official cash rate decision history: true if annual CPI inflation was 3.3 percent and the August 2024 cut was the first OCR reduction since roughly early 2020; false if either figure or the interval is materially different.

veracity.statement: Does his Government’s Treaty principles bill consider the Waitangi Tribunal’s finding from 10 years ago that “The rangatira who signed Te Tiriti o Waitangi in February 1840 did not cede [their] sovereignty to Britain,” or does he intend to continue to sideline the Waitangi Tribunal?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Waitangi Tribunal made a finding approximately ten years earlier that the rangatira who signed te Tiriti in February 1840 did not cede sovereignty to Britain.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal's He Whakaputanga me te Tiriti / Te Paparahi o Te Raki stage 1 report: true if it contains that finding in substantially those words and was released around 2014, false if the wording or date is materially different or no such finding exists.

veracity.statement: Is it a fact that 102 years ago, in a major thesis, Sir Āpirana Ngata set out the very circumstances of the Treaty and he said that Māori ceded sovereignty—far closer to the action as he was, as were other Māori leaders of that time?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Āpirana Ngata published a major work roughly 102 years before 2024 in which he stated that Māori ceded sovereignty under the Treaty.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ngata's 1922 'The Treaty of Waitangi: an Explanation' (Te Tiriti o Waitangi: He Whakamarama): true if published around 1922 and containing a statement that Māori ceded sovereignty or governing authority to the Crown; false if the date is materially off or the text contains no such statement.

veracity.statement: What responsibility does he take for the fact that since he became Prime Minister, the monthly number of new building consents has dropped 26 percent, 6,000 jobs have gone from the building and construction sector, and 57 percent of construction businesses now report difficulties with Government procurement and work consent conditions, up from 36 percent last year?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 26 percent fall in monthly new building consents, 6,000 jobs lost in construction, and a rise from 36 to 57 percent in construction firms reporting difficulty with government procurement and consent conditions, all since November 2023.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ building consents issued series and HLFS/filled-jobs data for construction between November 2023 and mid-2024, plus the named industry survey (e.g. the construction sector confidence survey) for both years: true if each of the three figures matches within rounding, false if any is materially different.

rigor.statement: As we can see, the results of this initiative have been massive, and not only in the Olympics. Women’s rugby is now thriving, for example, and I hear Grant Robertson is very pleased down in Ōtepoti Dunedin.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: the 2018 strategy is credited with the 2024 medal haul and with women's rugby simply because they followed it, and the supporting evidence offered is an anecdote about one person's pleasure. No causal link is established.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Is it a fact that 102 years ago, in a major thesis, Sir Āpirana Ngata set out the very circumstances of the Treaty and he said that Māori ceded sovereignty—far closer to the action as he was, as were other Māori leaders of that time?
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority and proximity: the conclusion that Māori ceded sovereignty rests on Ngata having been closer in time to the signing, rather than on the evidence Ngata offered. Temporal nearness is not itself a warrant.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So our Government is taking action, with more funding for roadside tests as part of a package of $1.3 billion for road policing in the next three years.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (increased roadside testing), a dollar figure ($1.3 billion) and a timeframe (three years), all checkable against the road policing investment programme.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does his Government’s Treaty principles bill consider the Waitangi Tribunal’s finding from 10 years ago that “The rangatira who signed Te Tiriti o Waitangi in February 1840 did not cede [their] sovereignty to Britain,” or does he intend to continue to sideline the Waitangi Tribunal?
specificity.explanation: Names the measure (the Treaty principles bill), quotes the specific Tribunal finding relied on, and dates it — precise enough for anyone to check and for the Minister to answer directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What responsibility does he take for the fact that since he became Prime Minister, the monthly number of new building consents has dropped 26 percent, 6,000 jobs have gone from the building and construction sector, and 57 percent of construction businesses now report difficulties with Government procurement and work consent conditions, up from 36 percent last year?
specificity.explanation: Three separate checkable figures with a defined baseline period — consent volumes, sector job losses, and a year-on-year survey comparison.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What responsibility does he take for the fact that since he became Prime Minister, the monthly number of new building consents has dropped 26 percent, 6,000 jobs have gone from the building and construction sector, and 57 percent of construction businesses now report difficulties with Government procurement and work consent conditions, up from 36 percent last year?
focus.explanation: Squarely on sector outcomes and named government policy areas (procurement and consenting), holding the Prime Minister to account for measurable results rather than attacking the party in general.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Well, that is a function of bad economic mismanagement and vandalism from the previous administration that created something called inflation, and inflation works because if you have an 84 percent increase in spending—wasteful spending, much of it—you increase debt from $5 billion to $100 billion, and you hire 18,000 more public servants, you get high levels of domestic inflation.
veracity.explanation: Three quantified assertions about the 2017-2023 Labour government: an 84 percent rise in government spending, debt rising from $5 billion to $100 billion, and 18,000 additional public servants.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenses series 2017/18 vs 2023/24 (true if the increase is ~84%); Treasury net core Crown debt series over the same period (true if it moved from about $5b to about $100b on a stated measure); Public Service Commission workforce data (true if public service headcount grew by about 18,000). False if any figure is materially different from the cited source.

veracity.statement: Why does the latest Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors’ global monitor survey report that New Zealand’s construction sector is now the most depressed since that survey started and is the most depressed in the world, with more than half of respondents citing as a reason the change in Government in October 2023, which resulted in cuts, delays, and policy change?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the RICS Global Construction Monitor records New Zealand as the weakest construction market in the world and the weakest in the survey's history, with a majority of respondents attributing it to the change of government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The RICS Global Construction Monitor for the relevant 2024 quarter; true if New Zealand's sentiment index is the lowest of all surveyed markets and the lowest in the series, and if more than half of NZ respondents cite the change in government; false if the report shows otherwise.

veracity.statement: We’ve taken the genius idea from David Parker about fast-track provisions; we’re putting it in and expanding it further.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that fast-track consenting originated with David Parker and that the Government's fast-track legislation extends it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The COVID-19 Recovery (Fast-track Consenting) Act 2020 and its introduction record; true if David Parker as the responsible Minister introduced fast-track consenting legislation that the 2024 Fast-track Approvals Bill builds on, false if the provenance is otherwise.

veracity.statement: Well, I’m sure if the member gives a specific question, we can get him a specific answer, but what I would say is that there is $68 billion in this year’s Budget for infrastructure.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $68 billion infrastructure figure attributable to Budget 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents and the Treasury capital allowance / National Infrastructure Plan figures; true if a $68b infrastructure investment figure appears on a stated basis, false if the Budget contains no such figure.

veracity.statement: I would also point to the member that having projects with names doesn’t mean they are actually projects, so spending six years on Auckland light rail and spending $250 million to $300 million doesn’t make it happen; it’s just a Post-it note slogan bumper sticker—that’s what that is.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly $250-300 million was spent on Auckland light rail over about six years without the project proceeding.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Light Rail Ltd and Ministry of Transport expenditure disclosures to 2023/24; true if total spend falls in the $250m-$300m range over roughly six years, false if materially outside it.

veracity.statement: Will he take responsibility for the construction sector business confidence collapsing under his Government’s watch, from one in three businesses having a confident outlook to only one in five now?
veracity.explanation: Asserts construction-sector business confidence fell from roughly 33 percent to roughly 20 percent of firms holding a positive outlook.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published construction-sector business confidence surveys (e.g. ANZ Business Outlook sector breakdown or an industry survey) for 2023 and mid-2024; true if the confident share moved from about one in three to about one in five, false if the series shows a different movement.

veracity.statement: Does he think the 6,000 people who’ve lost their jobs in the building and construction sector and the firms who are closing because they have a shortage of work because of his Government’s decisions think that this is what getting back on track looks like?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a loss of about 6,000 jobs in building and construction under the current Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ filled jobs / HLFS employment by industry for construction, comparing late 2023 with mid-2024; true if the fall is approximately 6,000, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Has he got any plans to assign $54 million, for example, for a cycleway over the Auckland Harbour Bridge, and when it’s all over, nothing is done with it?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that $54 million was spent on a proposed Auckland Harbour Bridge cycleway that was never built.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA Waka Kotahi disclosures on expenditure for the Northern Pathway / SkyPath Auckland Harbour Bridge cycleway project; true if the sunk cost is about $54 million and the project was cancelled without construction, false if the figure or the outcome differs materially.

veracity.statement: I was delighted to see that last week marked a significant turning point, with the Reserve Bank’s monetary policy committee deciding to cut the official cash rate (OCR) by 25 basis points, to 5.25 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Reserve Bank cut the OCR by 25 basis points to 5.25 percent in the week before 20 August 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ Monetary Policy Statement and OCR decision of 14 August 2024; true if the OCR was reduced by 25bp to 5.25%, false if the size or resulting level differs.

veracity.statement: During the cost of living crisis, annual Consumers Price Index inflation got to 7.3 percent and was over 7 percent for most of 2022.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 7.3 percent peak in annual CPI inflation and that annual inflation exceeded 7 percent through most of 2022.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index annual rates for the 2022 quarters; true if the peak print is 7.3% and the majority of 2022 quarters exceed 7.0%, false if either is materially different.

veracity.statement: The Reserve Bank clearly has confidence that inflation is under control and that the age of extreme price increases is over, after four years where the only way for interest rates was up.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that over the four years preceding August 2024 interest rates moved only upward.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ official cash rate series from August 2020 to August 2024; true if the OCR never fell over that period, false if there was any cut (the OCR was at 0.25% through 2020-21 after the March 2020 reduction).

veracity.statement: Why has Oranga Tamariki ended contracts with 190 front-line social service providers and a further 142 providers have had their funding reduced, or are these contracts wasteful spending, as described by the Prime Minister?
veracity.explanation: Asserts Oranga Tamariki ended contracts with 190 front-line providers and reduced funding for a further 142.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki contract data released under OIA or to select committee in 2024; true if approximately 190 provider contracts were terminated and approximately 142 had funding reduced, false if the counts differ materially.

veracity.statement: I will make two points: first, overall funding for Oranga Tamariki in the Budget increased; and, second, if that member thinks that the position of a Government should be that every single contract signed up to needs to be stuck in stone and never changed, then she’s delusional.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that overall Oranga Tamariki funding increased in Budget 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Oranga Tamariki appropriations compared with the previous year's; true if total appropriations rose, false if they fell.

specificity.statement: Well, that is a function of bad economic mismanagement and vandalism from the previous administration that created something called inflation, and inflation works because if you have an 84 percent increase in spending—wasteful spending, much of it—you increase debt from $5 billion to $100 billion, and you hire 18,000 more public servants, you get high levels of domestic inflation.
specificity.explanation: Carries a percentage, two debt figures and a headcount — all checkable quantities rather than generalities.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why does the latest Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors’ global monitor survey report that New Zealand’s construction sector is now the most depressed since that survey started and is the most depressed in the world, with more than half of respondents citing as a reason the change in Government in October 2023, which resulted in cuts, delays, and policy change?
specificity.explanation: Names the survey, the comparison basis, the date of the event blamed and the share of respondents — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I would also point to the member that having projects with names doesn’t mean they are actually projects, so spending six years on Auckland light rail and spending $250 million to $300 million doesn’t make it happen; it’s just a Post-it note slogan bumper sticker—that’s what that is.
specificity.explanation: Names the project, the period and a dollar range; the closing characterisation is rhetorical but the substance is checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We think there are five things that we need to grow this country: a world-class education system—we didn’t inherit that from the previous Government—we’ve got to embrace science, technology, and innovation; we need to get rid of the red tape, green tape, and bureaucracy; we need to make sure we’ve got modern, reliable infrastructure; and, importantly, international connections.
specificity.explanation: A list of five generic aspirations with no figures, mechanisms, named measures or timeframes; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will he take responsibility for the construction sector business confidence collapsing under his Government’s watch, from one in three businesses having a confident outlook to only one in five now?
specificity.explanation: Gives a before-and-after proportion for a named sector, enough for someone to locate the survey.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he think the 6,000 people who’ve lost their jobs in the building and construction sector and the firms who are closing because they have a shortage of work because of his Government’s decisions think that this is what getting back on track looks like?
specificity.explanation: Names a sector and a job-loss figure that can be checked against official employment data.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Has he got any plans to assign $54 million, for example, for a cycleway over the Auckland Harbour Bridge, and when it’s all over, nothing is done with it?
specificity.explanation: Names a dollar amount and the specific project it relates to.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why has Oranga Tamariki ended contracts with 190 front-line social service providers and a further 142 providers have had their funding reduced, or are these contracts wasteful spending, as described by the Prime Minister?
specificity.explanation: Two precise provider counts tied to a named agency and a named savings exercise.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is it reasonable, as part of her Budget 2024 baseline savings exercise, for front-line social service providers to provide 100 percent of their contracted Government services with only 70 percent of the Government funding, and is this consistent with the social services commissioning model?
specificity.explanation: Puts a concrete ratio — full service delivery on 70 percent of funding — against a named Budget process and a named commissioning model.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That then leads to high levels of interest rates. When interest rates go up, that leads to recession, which is what we’ve been experiencing—thank you to the previous Labour Government!—and, in turn, that leads to rising unemployment.
rigor.explanation: A causal chain (spending → inflation → rates → recession → unemployment) whose individual links are orthodox, but the inference treats domestic fiscal policy as the sole cause of a globally synchronised inflation and tightening cycle; nothing is offered to exclude the alternative causes, so the attribution step does not follow from what was presented.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We have stopped the wasteful spending, we’ve stopped loading costs up on businesses, and we’re getting spending under control. That’s driving inflation down, thankfully—and I would hope the member is joining us in great celebration with the lower interest rates that came through last week—and from that will flow economic growth and, ultimately, more employment opportunities for people.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: the fall in inflation and the OCR cut are attributed to the Government's spending decisions taken months earlier, with no mechanism, lag or counterfactual offered to connect them.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I will make two points: first, overall funding for Oranga Tamariki in the Budget increased; and, second, if that member thinks that the position of a Government should be that every single contract signed up to needs to be stuck in stone and never changed, then she’s delusional.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the question asked why specific contracts were cut, not whether contracts should be permanently fixed; the conclusion is drawn against a position nobody advanced.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why does the latest Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors’ global monitor survey report that New Zealand’s construction sector is now the most depressed since that survey started and is the most depressed in the world, with more than half of respondents citing as a reason the change in Government in October 2023, which resulted in cuts, delays, and policy change?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny built on a named external survey and a named outcome for a specific sector; no party-bashing content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When the Prime Minister eventually leaves office, does he anticipate spending his first year out combing the world for statistics to show how badly he buggered the economy?
focus.explanation: No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — the entire content is a jibe about how an opponent conducts himself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We think there are five things that we need to grow this country: a world-class education system—we didn’t inherit that from the previous Government—we’ve got to embrace science, technology, and innovation; we need to get rid of the red tape, green tape, and bureaucracy; we need to make sure we’ve got modern, reliable infrastructure; and, importantly, international connections.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the Government's own policy programme rather than the other party, even though the content is thin — the classic high-focus, low-specificity case.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think those 6,000 workers understand that a Government that had six years, mucked around, and actually drove the economy into a hole is a reason why they’re doing it pretty tough.
focus.explanation: Answers a question about a specific job-loss figure entirely with a general characterisation of the previous Government's six years; no policy, measure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: When the Prime Minister eventually leaves office, does he anticipate spending his first year out combing the world for statistics to show how badly he buggered the economy?
civility.explanation: Mockery framed as a question, deriding an individual's conduct and record rather than engaging any argument; short of direct abuse but clearly sneering.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I will make two points: first, overall funding for Oranga Tamariki in the Budget increased; and, second, if that member thinks that the position of a Government should be that every single contract signed up to needs to be stuck in stone and never changed, then she’s delusional.
civility.explanation: Calls the questioner "delusional" — a direct attack on the individual's judgement rather than on her argument.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We have stopped the wasteful spending, we’ve stopped loading costs up on businesses, and we’re getting spending under control. That’s driving inflation down, thankfully—and I would hope the member is joining us in great celebration with the lower interest rates that came through last week—and from that will flow economic growth and, ultimately, more employment opportunities for people.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that economic growth and increased employment will follow from lower inflation and interest rates — an outcome in the world, not a promise of the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP and Household Labour Force Survey; true if real GDP growth turns positive and sustained and the unemployment rate falls below its August 2024 level within the following 18 months, false if growth remains negative or flat and unemployment continues to rise over that period.

divination.statement: What’s more, the bank has set out a forecast track for the official cash rate which shows a steady decline over the next few years, back down to 3 percent in 2027.
divination.explanation: Relays the Reserve Bank's published OCR track, forecasting the OCR at around 3 percent in 2027.
divination.subject: other
divination.falsification_criterion: RBNZ official cash rate series during 2027; true if the OCR sits at approximately 3 percent (within about 0.5 percentage points) in that year, false if materially above or below.

divination.statement: Lowering the official cash rate will lead to lower interest rates across the economy; in fact, this process has already started.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that retail borrowing rates across the economy will fall following the OCR cut.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: RBNZ published average mortgage and business lending rates; true if average floating and two-year fixed mortgage rates in August 2025 are below their August 2024 levels, false if they are the same or higher.

divination.statement: The Reserve Bank’s latest forecast is for inflation in this quarter—that is, the September quarter of 2024—to be well within the target band, at 2.3 percent.
divination.explanation: Relays the Reserve Bank's forecast that annual CPI inflation for the September 2024 quarter will be 2.3 percent, inside the 1-3 percent target band.
divination.subject: other
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI release for the September 2024 quarter; true if annual inflation prints at about 2.3% and within the 1-3% band, false if outside the band or materially away from 2.3%.

specificity.statement: Our expectation is that we will drive better results for the taxpayers’ money we invest in social service provision. We are particularly conscious that in recent years, social service providers have watched while Wellington grew, the dollars that went into Government agencies expanded, and the number of policy analysts and managers hired grew, and yet those front-line service providers often only saw in return more contracting requirements, more compliance, and, actually, weren’t able to deliver better results. Our Government is focused on ensuring the dollars actually make it to the front line.
specificity.explanation: A direction of travel (more money to the front line, less to back-office contracting) with no figures, no named appropriations, no mechanism and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What does she say to providers like Taeaomanino Trust, Wesley Community Action, Porirua Whānau Centre, Barnardos Aotearoa, Wairere Care Services, North Shore Women’s Centre, WELLfed New Zealand Trust, E Tipu E Rea, and the Salvation Army, who have all had reductions in funding and lost front-line staff as a result of her Budget 2024 baseline savings exercise?
specificity.explanation: Nine providers named individually and tied to a named fiscal process (the Budget 2024 baseline savings exercise) with a named consequence (funding reductions, front-line staff losses).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, I’d say to each of those social service providers that the Government values what you do. You play a significant role in helping New Zealanders in need, and our Government wants to work with you to ensure we can make the maximum impact for the people you serve.
specificity.explanation: Pure sentiment — 'values what you do', 'maximum impact'. No funding figure, no mechanism, no commitment anyone could check or act on.

focus.statement: What’s the particular need either to shortcut it—because I notice that in clause 52(2) a territorial authority is only required to take consultation once. focus.statement: The fact is that by saying consultation is only done once, it does reduce local participation. rigor.statement: Particularly, I draw the committee’s attention to the new powers at clause 40(1)(f), where it provides for, in legislation, a requirement that a water services provider would ascertain the expert opinion of a third party, because that acknowledges that the Commerce Commission does not have this kind of advice-giving power in its core remit and would be dependent on infrastructure experts, because that is not what the Commerce Commission currently does.

The inference is plausible and grounded in the clause text, but it is a leap from 'the Act permits commissioning expert advice' to 'the Commission is dependent on outside experts' — regulators routinely commission expert input without lacking competence, and the closing clause restates the conclusion as its own premise.

Absence of a provision is legitimate evidence about statutory effect, but the conclusion still leaps from 'not stated in clause 54' to 'no confidence anywhere in the scheme' without canvassing other clauses or general-law duties.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In reply to the Hon Rachel Brooking, she asked if the Local Government Act should be amended for all consultation—well, the scope of this bill is on water services, and councils are looking to be able to move quickly. That’s what this does.
rigor.explanation: The reason given (this bill's scope is water services) establishes why the wider LGA amendment is out of scope for this bill, but is offered as an answer to whether the Government intends to amend the LGA separately — a question scope does not bear on. The conclusion addresses a narrower proposition than the one put.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would like the Minister—if he could, please—just to reconcile those two explanations that he’s given, because they do actually pull against each other slightly and I think we deserve a little better than that.
rigor.explanation: A genuine argument: two different rationales (clarifying unclear LGA requirements vs streamlining the process) were given for the same provision, so at least one is incomplete. The tension is real but weaker than claimed — streamlining and clarifying are not strictly incompatible — so the conclusion somewhat overreaches the premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I wonder whether the Minister has thought about—when it comes to within clause 52(2)—just actually indicating why it can’t just read then that the territorial authority is required to undertake consultation “at least” once? If that was the case, then, actually, it still leaves the next subclause, (3), open to a territorial authority to engage.
focus.explanation: Engages the drafting of a named clause of the bill before the committee and proposes a specific textual alternative; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The legislation is very clear in relation to clarifying that the territorial authority must consult once, but they may decide to undertake further consultation. That is incredibly clear. That is the clarification that councils requested, and that is what is being provided in this legislation.
focus.explanation: Answers squarely on the consultation mechanism in the bill — one mandatory round, further rounds optional — with no reference to the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I find it ironic that the Opposition has become the defender of wanting to maintain ownership, and welcome them to the party, because that is exactly where the Government is at. We thank you that you have finally rejected the position that you’ve taken for the last six years.
focus.explanation: Asked about clause 51 and section 137, the reply is almost entirely about the Opposition's past position and alleged change of heart; the only policy content is the unelaborated phrase "restoring council ownership". No clause, figure or mechanism is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill doesn’t affect what is provided in section 137 of the Local Government Act—that continues, unaffected and unaltered. This is about the consultation requirements, not in relation to the requirements in section 137.

focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The second one is that they are not required to retain control of water pricing, because, if they join up with a buddy down the road, they do not have to be subject to the provisions in section 137, where they must retain public rights to consult on and then be responsible for the pricing of water.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the legal effect of clause 51 on a named statutory protection and the concrete consequence for water pricing accountability.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.explanation: Names clause 52(2) and subclause (3), and specifies the exact wording change sought ("at least" once) and its effect. Actionable and checkable.

That is incredibly clear. That is the clarification that councils requested, and that is what is being provided in this legislation.
specificity.explanation: States the mechanism (must consult once, may consult further) but cites no clause number, no timeframe and no evidence of what councils asked for.

specificity.statement: This bill doesn’t affect what is provided in section 137 of the Local Government Act—that continues, unaffected and unaltered. This is about the consultation requirements, not in relation to the requirements in section 137.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact statutory provision at issue and states precisely what the bill does and does not do to it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The second one is that they are not required to retain control of water pricing, because, if they join up with a buddy down the road, they do not have to be subject to the provisions in section 137, where they must retain public rights to consult on and then be responsible for the pricing of water.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the specific protection (public consultation on and responsibility for water pricing), the statutory source (section 137), and the mechanism by which it is said to be lost.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I wonder whether the Minister has thought about—when it comes to within clause 52(2)—just actually indicating why it can’t just read then that the territorial authority is required to undertake consultation “at least” once? civility.subject: speaker
