civility.statement: I have asked the Minister twice to address questions, to allay the fears of members on this side of the House that his intention here is to make it easier and simpler for councils to privatise their water assets and sell them out of local body ownership without appropriate consultation.
civility.explanation: Goes beyond criticising the bill to ascribe a concealed intention to the Minister personally — an imputation of bad faith — though it stops short of a direct insult and is framed as a fear to be allayed.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Certainly, in my experience around a council table for more than a decade, when it comes to the delivery and provision and access to water services and other key bits of infrastructure, that absolutely would meet the criteria for engagement of a special consultative process.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that water decisions would trigger the special consultative process rests solely on the speaker's personal recollection of council practice — an appeal to personal anecdote/authority rather than to the significance thresholds in the Local Government Act or councils' significance and engagement policies.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The second one is that they are not required to retain control of water pricing, because, if they join up with a buddy down the road, they do not have to be subject to the provisions in section 137, where they must retain public rights to consult on and then be responsible for the pricing of water.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference with stated premises: if a joint arrangement falls outside section 137, the pricing-control duty lapses. The gap is that it assumes without demonstration that the bill disapplies section 137 to such arrangements rather than merely altering consultation.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Certainly, in my experience around a council table for more than a decade, when it comes to the delivery and provision and access to water services and other key bits of infrastructure, that absolutely would meet the criteria for engagement of a special consultative process.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the speaker served on a council for more than a decade, which is offered as the basis for his judgement about special consultative process thresholds.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Palmerston North City Council / NZ local body election records for Tangi Utikere's service as an elected councillor; true if his continuous service exceeded ten years before entering Parliament, false if it was ten years or less.

veracity.statement: The legislation is very clear in relation to clarifying that the territorial authority must consult once, but they may decide to undertake further consultation. That is incredibly clear. That is the clarification that councils requested, and that is what is being provided in this legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that councils themselves requested this particular clarification of the consultation requirement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Select committee submissions and LGNZ/council submissions on the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill; true if councils' submissions sought clarification that only one consultation round is required, false if no such submissions exist or they sought the opposite.

veracity.statement: This bill doesn’t affect what is provided in section 137 of the Local Government Act—that continues, unaffected and unaltered. This is about the consultation requirements, not in relation to the requirements in section 137.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill as introduced/enacted and the current text of section 137 of the Local Government Act 2002; true if the bill contains no amendment to or disapplication of section 137, false if any clause (including clause 51) amends section 137 or exempts joint local government arrangements or water services CCOs from its requirements.

veracity.statement: People back 100 years ago were paying their local council rates to own these water infrastructure assets and there is no requirement under his legislation that they would be retained in council ownership.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill contains no requirement that water infrastructure assets be retained in council ownership.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill together with section 137 of the Local Government Act 2002; true if no provision of the bill or of the law it leaves in force requires retention of water infrastructure assets in council/public ownership for councils forming a joint local government arrangement, false if such a requirement applies.

rigor.statement: That is not referenced when it comes to clause 53(1)(c); it simply states that the council or the authority needs to be “satisfied that it understands its community’s views on the proposal.” So there is an inconsistency here between the two clauses.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the text of the bill: he cites that clause 52(4)(a) invokes section 78(1) of the LGA while clause 53(1)(c) does not, and concludes the two clauses are inconsistent. The conclusion tracks the textual difference he has just laid out; no fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Many of the things that this Government is doing, they’ve signalled that they wish to emulate what is happening in England—like housing, for example, with housing associations. We know that that was a disaster and we know that many of the social houses were sold off in England under that model.
rigor.explanation: Argument by analogy: because an English model produced sell-offs in housing, the water model will too. Nothing is offered to establish that the legal protections are comparable, so the inference from one sector in another jurisdiction to this bill is a weak analogy rather than a supported step.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That is not referenced when it comes to clause 53(1)(c); it simply states that the council or the authority needs to be “satisfied that it understands its community’s views on the proposal.” So there is an inconsistency here between the two clauses.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific clauses (52(4)(a), 53(1)(c)) and the specific statutory provision (s78(1) LGA), and quotes the operative wording — anyone could check the drafting against the claim.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Under the Local Government Act, there are only a few occasions when the special consultative procedure must be used. It is usually up to councils to decide how to consult, using the principles of consultation in section 82 of the Local Government Act 2002.
specificity.explanation: Names the governing statute and the specific section (s82 LGA 2002) carrying the consultation principles, and states the default rule — checkable, though it does not enumerate the occasions on which the special consultative procedure is mandatory.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The answer to the member’s question around privatisation is that there are protections in place in several sections of the Local Government Act that will continue to apply unaffected. This part of the bill, though, that we are debating today here is about consultation and decision making.
specificity.explanation: Asserts protections exist in 'several sections' of the LGA without naming a single section, figure or mechanism; the listener cannot check or act on it without going and finding the provisions themselves.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The purpose of this part is to ensure the financial separation of Watercare and Auckland Council, to enable Watercare to be able to provide water services to Auckland in a financially sustainable way.
specificity.explanation: Names the entities (Watercare, Auckland Council) and the concrete mechanism (financial separation) the part is intended to achieve, but supplies no figures, thresholds or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are two very simple questions to answer, and that is—as the Hon Kieran McAnulty has just referred to—why is clause 59 there and why is this repeal of section 58 needed?
specificity.explanation: Pins the question to two identified provisions (clause 59, the repeal of section 58), which is concrete enough to be answered directly, though it supplies no figures or mechanism of its own.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So my question to the Minister is: why is there an inconsistency between clauses 52 and 53, where section 78(1) of the LGA is engaged in one but it’s not engaged in the other?
focus.explanation: Entirely on the measure before the committee: a named drafting question about two named clauses of the bill, with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If a council-controlled organisation or alternative arrangement is established and they get into financial difficulty, what is stopping them from selling them off?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the bill: what statutory protection prevents an asset sale by a CCO under financial stress. A named structure and a named risk, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are two very simple questions to answer, and that is—as the Hon Kieran McAnulty has just referred to—why is clause 59 there and why is this repeal of section 58 needed?
focus.explanation: Purely about the measure: two named clauses of the bill and the rationale for a specific repeal. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Under the Local Government Act, there are only a few occasions when the special consultative procedure must be used. It is usually up to councils to decide how to consult, using the principles of consultation in section 82 of the Local Government Act 2002.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Local Government Act 2002 mandates the special consultative procedure in only a limited number of situations, and that outside those, councils choose their consultation method subject to the principles of consultation in s82.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Local Government Act 2002: true if s83 (special consultative procedure) is required only in a small number of enumerated instances and s82 sets out general 'principles of consultation' that otherwise govern council consultation; false if the SCP is a general requirement or if s82 contains something other than consultation principles.

veracity.statement: The answer to the member’s question around privatisation is that there are protections in place in several sections of the Local Government Act that will continue to apply unaffected. This part of the bill, though, that we are debating today here is about consultation and decision making.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Local Government Act 2002 contains provisions restricting the divestment/privatisation of water services assets, and that the bill under debate leaves those provisions unaffected.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Local Government Act 2002 (notably ss130-137 on water services, which bar local government organisations from divesting ownership or control of water services) read against the amendments in the bill before the committee: true if such restrictive sections exist and the bill does not repeal or weaken them; false if no such restriction exists or the bill amends it.

veracity.statement: We also know that, in England, many of their water services were privatised and it has been an absolute disaster for that country and the communities that it services.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that water services in England were privatised, and characterises the outcome for consumers and communities as a failure — the checkable element being privatisation plus documented underinvestment/unaffordable charges.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: UK records: true if the ten regional water and sewerage authorities in England and Wales were privatised (Water Act 1989) and regulator/parliamentary reporting (Ofwat, Environment Agency, NAO) documents widespread service and investment failures; false if English water remained publicly owned or if regulators record no material service failure.

civility.statement: Instead of actually allaying the fears that not just this side of the Chamber has but many New Zealanders have around what protections are in place to prevent the privatisation of water services assets, he decided to make a glib political comment.
civility.explanation: Criticises the Minister's answer, but 'glib' characterises the man's attitude rather than the content of the reply — a sneer at how he chose to conduct himself, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: He’s just sat down and stayed down and thought, “Oh well, eventually time will run out.” He proved to be correct and he hasn’t had to answer those questions.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith directly to the Minister by putting words in his mouth — that he deliberately ran down the clock to avoid answering. That is an attack on the person's motives, not on the answer given.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This part was part of the negotiation between Auckland Council and the Government in relation to the Local Water Done Well deal, announced in May, between the mayor and the Prime Minister.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Auckland water arrangement in this Part arose from a Local Water Done Well deal announced in May between the Auckland mayor and the Prime Minister.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government/Auckland Council announcements from May 2024 on the Auckland water services agreement under Local Water Done Well; true if such a deal was jointly announced by the Auckland mayor and the Prime Minister in May 2024, false if no such May announcement or if announced by different parties.

veracity.statement: But the issue here is that the powers belong to the secretary to prepare the Watercare charter, and not to Aucklanders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the clause as drafted the power to prepare the Watercare charter sits with the secretary rather than with Auckland Council or Aucklanders.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of clause 62A(1) of the bill as introduced/amended; true if it vests preparation of the Watercare charter in the secretary, false if it vests that power in Auckland Council or another Auckland body.

veracity.statement: Part 4 deals with services for Watercare in the Auckland region—it does not apply to Northland—but it does not prevent Auckland Council from entering into joint arrangements with other councils if they wish.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Part 4 applies only to Watercare in Auckland, not to Northland, and contains no bar on Auckland Council entering joint arrangements with other councils.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of Part 4 of the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill; true if its application provisions are confined to Watercare/Auckland and no clause prohibits joint arrangements with other councils, false if it extends to Northland or restricts such arrangements.

veracity.statement: And it’s a very significant part because it concerns the water services for a third of the population of the country and the biggest city in the country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Auckland, whose water services this Part governs, holds about a third of New Zealand's population and is the country's largest city.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates for the relevant year; true if Auckland's share of national population is approximately one-third and it is the largest urban area, false if materially below that share.

focus.statement: I’d really like some clarification from the Minister about the breadth of this part of the bill. Is it only supposed to be where there is little or no competition? Presumably, again, that would always be around stormwater.

focus.statement: My final question, for now, is: given the Minister’s statements about this as the deal for Auckland, what happens to Northland? Is there any ability for Northland to enter this arrangement or not? Of course, we all know that Northland has a number of councils with very small ratepayer bases that have had huge problems, historically, with water treatment in particular.
focus.explanation: A substantive question about which regions the legislated arrangement can extend to, with reasons drawn from Northland councils' ratepayer bases and water treatment history.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If he’s going to remind this committee of his commitment to localism, is it then a mistake in clause 62A(1) that it’s the secretary preparing the Watercare charter, and, at clause 62A(2), that it’s consultation with Auckland Council rather than development by Auckland Council?
focus.explanation: Entirely on the measure before the committee — two named subclauses and the allocation of a specific power.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The arrangement set out in Part 4 is mutually beneficial for both Auckland Council and Watercare, and, ultimately, consumers, because it enables them both to borrow independently of each other.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the financial-separation mechanism created by the Part and who it benefits.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think there are some particularly important issues around what is to be done with water in Northland. Northland has been left isolated by this treatment for Watercare.
focus.explanation: Directed at a real consequence of the measure — Northland's exclusion from the Watercare arrangement — but asserted in general terms rather than tied to a clause or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’d really like some clarification from the Minister about the breadth of this part of the bill. Is it only supposed to be where there is little or no competition? Presumably, again, that would always be around stormwater.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific test (little or no competition) and the service type at issue (stormwater), though the question itself is framed broadly rather than with figures or mechanisms.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My final question, for now, is: given the Minister’s statements about this as the deal for Auckland, what happens to Northland? Is there any ability for Northland to enter this arrangement or not? Of course, we all know that Northland has a number of councils with very small ratepayer bases that have had huge problems, historically, with water treatment in particular.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete gap (Northland's ability to enter the arrangement) and a reason, but supplies no figures, named councils, or mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If he’s going to remind this committee of his commitment to localism, is it then a mistake in clause 62A(1) that it’s the secretary preparing the Watercare charter, and, at clause 62A(2), that it’s consultation with Auckland Council rather than development by Auckland Council?
specificity.explanation: Names clause 62A(1) and 62A(2), the exact power at issue, and the alternative wording she wants (development by, not consultation with, Auckland Council).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Part 4 deals with services for Watercare in the Auckland region—it does not apply to Northland—but it does not prevent Auckland Council from entering into joint arrangements with other councils if they wish.
specificity.explanation: A direct, checkable statement of the Part's geographic scope and of what it does not preclude, though no mechanism or process for joint arrangements is described.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I think there are some particularly important issues around what is to be done with water in Northland. Northland has been left isolated by this treatment for Watercare.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a region and a concern but offers no clause, figure, mechanism or alternative; 'left isolated' is not operationalised.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If he’s going to remind this committee of his commitment to localism, is it then a mistake in clause 62A(1) that it’s the secretary preparing the Watercare charter, and, at clause 62A(2), that it’s consultation with Auckland Council rather than development by Auckland Council?
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: the Minister's stated commitment to localism is set against the drafting that gives the charter-preparation power to the secretary and reduces the council to a consultee, so the tension drawn is real; the small gap is treating consultation as necessarily incompatible with localism.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The arrangement set out in Part 4 is mutually beneficial for both Auckland Council and Watercare, and, ultimately, consumers, because it enables them both to borrow independently of each other.
rigor.explanation: Independent borrowing capacity plausibly supports the claim of benefit to the council and Watercare, but the extension to consumers is asserted rather than shown — a gap between the premise offered and part of the conclusion drawn.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If he’s going to remind this committee of his commitment to localism, is it then a mistake in clause 62A(1) that it’s the secretary preparing the Watercare charter, and, at clause 62A(2), that it’s consultation with Auckland Council rather than development by Auckland Council?
civility.explanation: Pointed challenge to the Minister's consistency but framed wholly around the drafting; no imputation of bad faith or attack on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: However, interestingly, in the advice that was given to the Minister around this bill and Auckland Council, there was a finding from Standard & Poor’s that, in fact, the debt-servicing costs for Watercare would go up under this arrangement and that, in fact, the cost to run Watercare would increase.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that ministerial advice on the Auckland Council/Watercare arrangement contained a Standard & Poor's finding that Watercare's debt-servicing costs and its operating costs would rise under the separation arrangement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published DIA/Treasury advice to the Minister of Local Government on the Auckland Council water services arrangement, and Standard & Poor's ratings commentary on Watercare/Auckland Council in 2024; true if that advice or S&P commentary records a finding that Watercare's debt-servicing costs and running costs increase under the financial separation, false if no such finding appears or S&P found the opposite.

veracity.statement: Auckland Council was proposing to increase water charges by 25.8 percent from 1 July.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that, prior to the financial separation deal, Auckland Council's proposal was a 25.8 percent water charge increase effective 1 July.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council's 2024–34 Long-term Plan consultation documents and Watercare pricing proposals; true if a proposed water charge increase of 25.8 percent from 1 July is recorded, false if the proposed figure was materially different.

specificity.statement: However, interestingly, in the advice that was given to the Minister around this bill and Auckland Council, there was a finding from Standard & Poor’s that, in fact, the debt-servicing costs for Watercare would go up under this arrangement and that, in fact, the cost to run Watercare would increase.
specificity.explanation: Names the source (Standard & Poor's), the document (advice to the Minister) and the specific effect claimed (debt-servicing and operating costs rising), though no figures are given.

specificity.statement: Auckland Council was proposing to increase water charges by 25.8 percent from 1 July.

specificity.statement: Going to the previous questions about “When a monitor is appointed, what are the criteria?”, the Crown monitor will require, as you would expect, a range of skills, expertise, and experience in, for example, the regulation of a monopoly business, and will have familiarity with the water industry and the economic and financial skills which you might expect of a monitor.

specificity.statement: In New Zealand, we tend to try and value the overall asset base and give a fair return on the overall asset base, with some incentive for new investment. In the United States, they tend to give a greater incentive to the next investment, because you need the next investment in the new piece of infrastructure.
specificity.explanation: Describes two identifiable regulatory pricing mechanisms (whole-asset-base return versus marginal-investment incentive with historic-cost valuation) and attributes the analysis to a named economist; no figures or clause references.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In clause 62A, it states that the secretary—which is the Secretary for the Department of Internal Affairs—must prepare a charter for Watercare. The question I have for the Minister is: we’ve heard a lot of rhetoric around this bill making sure that local services and local people are in control of local affairs, how does that work with this proposal for the Secretary of the Department of Internal Affairs to create this new charter for Watercare?

divination.statement: In actual fact, we know that water rates in Auckland will actually go up—I think the projection is by about 8 percent.

divination.falsification_criterion: Watercare's published price schedule / Auckland Council's adopted water charges for the year following this statement; true if the headline water price increase is approximately 8 percent (say 7–9 percent), false if materially outside that band.

divination.statement: With the financial separation, the price increase will be around about 7.2 percent, and future charges are also expected to be lower than they would have been.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that under the financial separation the water price increase will be about 7.2 percent, and that subsequent years' charges will be lower than they otherwise would have been.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Watercare's adopted price increase for the year following this statement, and its price path in subsequent years compared with the pre-separation Auckland Council proposal; true if the increase lands at approximately 7.2 percent and later increases run below the pre-deal projected path, false if the increase materially exceeds that or later charges track at or above the pre-deal path.

rigor.statement: Yet we know the costs associated with Watercare are going to go up. I don’t understand how the arrangements that the Minister is putting in place can possibly achieve this part of the purpose, and I would like the Minister to speak to the costs that are going to be incurred by Watercare.

The gap is that the clause concerns prices relative to a counterfactual and efficiency gains over time, not absolute cost levels — the conclusion overreaches the premise somewhat.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But you can still have the problem of under-investment by the monopoly, and we’ve seen that up and down the country in the water and sewage space for a long space, which is why we have the problem in New Zealand of poor water quality delivered by some of our councils and inadequate treatment of their sewage. So I accept that history in New Zealand shows we need a regulatory model around the monopoly services that councils provide for water and sewage.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of clause 1.3(5) of the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management 2020 (as amended); true if it sets the priority order as (a) health and well-being of water bodies and freshwater ecosystems, (b) health needs of people such as drinking water, (c) ability of people and communities to provide for their social, economic and cultural well-being; false if the order or content materially differs from Parker's description.

veracity.statement: It has been under-invested in for decades, and every single time we have any significant rain event, waste water flows into the creek, and anybody who gets into that creek gets sick.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Watercare/Auckland Council wastewater overflow records and Safeswim water-quality monitoring for Henderson Creek / Te Atatū over the years preceding August 2024; true if overflows are recorded for essentially all significant rainfall events and health warnings on contact are standing, false if overflows occur only in a minority of significant rain events or monitoring shows the creek is generally within contact-recreation guidelines.

veracity.statement: In their 2021 long-term plan, it was going to be $390 million, and it has escalated to over $650 million in 2024 due to that requirement to discharge to land.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Palmerston North City Council 2021 and 2024 long-term plan / Nature Calls project cost estimates; true if the figures are approximately $390m (2021) and above $650m (2024), false if either figure is materially different. veracity.statement: The hierarchy of obligations is something that we were very clear about in our campaigning.

rigor.statement: I don’t understand what the need is for that revocation of that principle, because my understanding, based on when I was the Minister, was that it wasn’t something that would prevent councils from getting resource consents for what they currently do or want to do in the future.

rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So it’s really the regulations that are going to be possible for the councils, and to achieve, over time, those improvements without causing the economic harm that would have been caused by leaving that hierarchy in place.

veracity.statement: Can I just reflect, I just did a document search on the entire legislation for the word “safe”. And the number of times the word “safe” appears in the entire document is zero.

specificity.statement: Can I just reflect, I just did a document search on the entire legislation for the word “safe”. And the number of times the word “safe” appears in the entire document is zero.

civility.statement: But then, given it is in here, the justification for using the “King Henry VIII” clause needs to be strong, and it just seems to be incredibly weak.

civility.subject: speaker

specificity.explanation: Names the specific instrument (NPS-FM), the specific mechanism (the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy of obligations) and the specific application (resource consents) — a precise, checkable question.

focus.explanation: Entirely on the drafting of the measure before the committee; no reference to the other party at all.

focus.statement: So I wondered: is there a simpler, better way—according to the Minister—to introduce this piece of legislation, rather than having four different time frames that people who are wanting to utilise this bill will have to look at in order to determine when things come into force?
focus.explanation: Engages the commencement provision of the bill in detail; no party content.

focus.statement: My question is whether or not the Minister considered, rather than amending section 138A, I think, of that Act, if it would have been much simpler to amend the section 14 to say that it applies to the functions, powers, or duty, and the hierarchy does not apply to whatever it is that the Government wants to do?

rigor.statement: If I’m right, you’re not just stripping this requirement out from Taumata Arowai, you’re actually, effectively, saying that the councils that are considering applications by water services entities don’t have to apply it either.

rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One of the examples of that is a section we were debating previously where the Secretary for the Department of Internal Affairs actually makes up, essentially, the charter for Watercare, meaning that there’s much more central government control over water services than there is in, actually, local government.

rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.explanation: The adequacy of the borrowing provisions is settled by a mayor's metaphor rather than by argument — an appeal to authority plus a loose analogy, which asserts rather than shows that extra borrowing headroom fails to help indebted councils.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: My first question to the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries relates to this rather unusual provision in this Draconian piece of legislation that says that on the rare occasions that a council might be so brave as to embark upon a review of a decades-old consent for use of a marine farm, they can’t recover the costs of doing so.
civility.explanation: Harsh language ('Draconian', sarcasm about councils being 'brave') aimed entirely at the provision and the legislation, not at any person. Under the re-anchored scale, fierce criticism of a policy is civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: My question of the Minister, who is so old that he was in the office of Geoffrey Palmer when the Resource Management Act (RMA) was originally passed and so has intimate knowledge of the Resource Management Act more generally—my question of the Minister, who will be aware that the Resource Management Act has always allowed for a charging regime to be imposed by regional councils for the use of marine space—for example, if a regional council wants to charge for a boatshed or for the occupation of marine space for marine farming, my understanding, under the RMA, is that a regional council would be able to embark upon a charging regime for the private use of the public space.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe about the Minister's age, but immediately turned into a point about his expertise rather than his competence or character. Pointed, edging toward the person without landing hard on him.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The council can conduct a review of the conditions, but no council is going to be allowed any longer to pursue their aberrant ways or, indeed, act on nimbyism, which has driven, sadly, an enormous amount of cost structure into this industry.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith — 'aberrant ways', 'nimbyism' — to councils rather than arguing about their decisions. It falls short of a personal insult of a named individual, but it is sneering about the motives of those on the other side of the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Ecologists must not be allowed to interfere any longer in any indiscriminate, unreasonable way with the march of economic growth to get some jobs in the regions.
civility.explanation: Characterises an entire professional group as indiscriminate and unreasonable interferers rather than engaging what the ecologists actually said. Dismissive of the people, not of an argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Aquaculture is an industry equally as important as the landscape and amenity values enjoyed by the small number of Marlborough bach owners who have had a very long and successful career at driving aquaculture out of the Marlborough Sounds, and I don’t like that council, because they actually created the seabed and foreshore debacle.
civility.explanation: Attributes a deliberate campaign ('a very long and successful career at driving aquaculture out') and blame for a national controversy to a group of identifiable local property owners and their council, imputing bad faith rather than engaging their submissions.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My first question to the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries relates to this rather unusual provision in this Draconian piece of legislation that says that on the rare occasions that a council might be so brave as to embark upon a review of a decades-old consent for use of a marine farm, they can’t recover the costs of doing so.
focus.explanation: Identifies a specific mechanism in the bill before the committee — the bar on councils recovering the cost of reviewing an existing marine farm consent — with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I would like to ask the Minister whether he is satisfied, given the passage of time since he has considered this matter, that there is a view out there that, actually, a more appropriate term could be that of a 10-year period of extension that is automatic—there’s an Amendment Paper in my name that does reflect that; that’s Amendment Paper 55—or what was offered up, which was actually widely supported by the public in terms of submissions, which was a five-year period.
focus.explanation: Entirely directed at the length of the consent extension in the clause before the committee; no party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s not they who are potentially causing pollution, it is not they who are causing any issues, and yet, unfairly, they will have to be the ones that will ultimately pay for any review, thereby making it difficult for their councils, I think, to undertake reviews, because ratepayers will be up in arms if they think councils are spending their money on things that they don’t think are fairly their cost.
focus.explanation: Engages the cost-allocation mechanism of the bill and who bears it; makes no reference to the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yes, it will require the council to meet the costs on the rare occasion that they may find that there is a strong need to review the conditions of farms that had existed for decades, and the next 25 years will give the confidence to the owners of these farms and their permits that they can dedicate their scarce resources to actually achieving economic outcomes, rather than playing a type of roller derby with the local councils.
focus.explanation: Directly answers on the mechanism at issue — who pays for reviews and why the consent term is set as it is.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: My question of the Minister, who is so old that he was in the office of Geoffrey Palmer when the Resource Management Act (RMA) was originally passed and so has intimate knowledge of the Resource Management Act more generally—my question of the Minister, who will be aware that the Resource Management Act has always allowed for a charging regime to be imposed by regional councils for the use of marine space—for example, if a regional council wants to charge for a boatshed or for the occupation of marine space for marine farming, my understanding, under the RMA, is that a regional council would be able to embark upon a charging regime for the private use of the public space.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the RMA has 'always' permitted regional councils to impose a charging regime for private occupation of marine space, such as boatsheds or marine farms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Resource Management Act 1991 and its amendments on coastal occupation charges (notably s 64A and the regional coastal plan provisions): true if regional councils have been empowered from the Act's original enactment to impose charges for occupation of coastal marine space; false if that power was absent from the 1991 Act and only introduced by later amendment, or if no such charging power exists.

veracity.statement: One of the issues that was raised by submitters—and I’d just note that even with the reduced number of days that were available for select committee submissions, actually 13, over 1,000 submissions were received.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee's report on the Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Bill and the Parliament website submission record: true if the submission period was 13 days and more than 1,000 submissions were received; false if the submission window or the submission count differ materially.

veracity.statement: In the select committee process, the majority of all councils that submitted on this piece of legislation were in opposition to this rollover of consents, regardless of environmental impacts or the ability for people to participate in the process and encourage a review.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that most councils that made submissions on the bill opposed the automatic rollover of marine farm consents.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The submissions register and select committee report for the bill: true if, among submitting local authorities, more opposed than supported the automatic extension of coastal permits; false if a majority of council submitters supported it or were neutral.

veracity.statement: Aquaculture is an industry equally as important as the landscape and amenity values enjoyed by the small number of Marlborough bach owners who have had a very long and successful career at driving aquaculture out of the Marlborough Sounds, and I don’t like that council, because they actually created the seabed and foreshore debacle.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Marlborough District Council caused the foreshore and seabed controversy.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The litigation history of Ngāti Apa v Attorney-General (2003) and contemporaneous accounts of the foreshore and seabed controversy: true if the proceedings that triggered the controversy arose out of Marlborough District Council's handling of marine farming permit applications in the Marlborough Sounds; false if the controversy originated from unrelated proceedings or a different consenting authority.

veracity.statement: There is a situation we have here where we did receive substantial submissions from the Marlborough District Council, which the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries is so disdainful of; a council, I might add, which, in its region, manages 80 percent of the entire value of aquaculture in New Zealand and has 600 of the 1,200 farms in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Two quantitative claims about Marlborough's share of New Zealand aquaculture: 80 percent of total value, and 600 of 1,200 farms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Aquaculture New Zealand / MPI aquaculture production and farm-count statistics for the relevant year: true if Marlborough accounts for approximately 80 percent of the national value of aquaculture and roughly 600 of about 1,200 consented marine farms; false if either share is materially different.

veracity.statement: One amendment that I propose to you is to make it a five-year extension. Now, that was the most commonly struck-upon number by submitters.
veracity.explanation: Claims that a five-year extension was the term most commonly proposed by submitters on the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The written submissions to the select committee on the bill and the committee's summary of them: true if five years was the extension period most frequently proposed by submitters who proposed an alternative term; false if another period (e.g. 10 years, or retention of the status quo) was proposed more often.

specificity.statement: I would like to ask the Minister whether he is satisfied, given the passage of time since he has considered this matter, that there is a view out there that, actually, a more appropriate term could be that of a 10-year period of extension that is automatic—there’s an Amendment Paper in my name that does reflect that; that’s Amendment Paper 55—or what was offered up, which was actually widely supported by the public in terms of submissions, which was a five-year period.
specificity.explanation: Names a numbered Amendment Paper and two concrete alternative extension terms (10 years, five years) against the bill's period. Anyone could check the paper and act on the proposal.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We can’t allow a minority range of concerns to overwhelm the need for regions to boost and create and enlarge the economic footprint in their own neighbourhood to keep people employed and to keep the confidence in the community so that we don’t see this onward drift of people away to Australia, or, indeed, the urban drift.
specificity.explanation: A string of general goods — economic footprint, employment, community confidence, stemming migration — with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named measure. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There is a situation we have here where we did receive substantial submissions from the Marlborough District Council, which the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries is so disdainful of; a council, I might add, which, in its region, manages 80 percent of the entire value of aquaculture in New Zealand and has 600 of the 1,200 farms in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Carries two precise, checkable figures tying a named consenting authority to a measurable share of the industry.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Also, the other amendment I’d like to speak to—that first one I spoke to was Amendment Paper 60; that’s changing it from 20 years to five years in new section 165ZFHC of new Subpart 1A, inserted by clause 4.
specificity.explanation: Names the Amendment Paper number, the exact new section and clause it amends, and the precise change of figure from 20 years to five. Fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s not they who are potentially causing pollution, it is not they who are causing any issues, and yet, unfairly, they will have to be the ones that will ultimately pay for any review, thereby making it difficult for their councils, I think, to undertake reviews, because ratepayers will be up in arms if they think councils are spending their money on things that they don’t think are fairly their cost.
rigor.explanation: A real chain of inference: review costs fall on ratepayers who are not the source of the effects, therefore councils face political resistance, therefore reviews become less likely. The chain is coherent but the crucial middle link — that ratepayers 'will be up in arms' — is asserted with no evidence, so there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yes, it will require the council to meet the costs on the rare occasion that they may find that there is a strong need to review the conditions of farms that had existed for decades, and the next 25 years will give the confidence to the owners of these farms and their permits that they can dedicate their scarce resources to actually achieving economic outcomes, rather than playing a type of roller derby with the local councils.
rigor.explanation: Concedes the premise put to him and offers a reason: long-duration certainty redirects operators' resources from litigation to production. The inference is intelligible but the link between a 25-year term and the claimed investment behaviour is asserted rather than supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s the overwhelming majority consenting authority for the wealth and value that is in marine farming, so it’s strange that we can’t pay some attention to their wisdom on it.
rigor.explanation: An appeal to authority, though a relevant one: the council's scale of consenting experience is offered as the reason its view should carry weight. Experience is evidence of expertise but does not establish that its position is correct, so there is a real gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We also propose that that is an amendment so that if the consenting authority does determine that they’re going to do a review, they don’t have to get the director-general’s approval—that would be less top-down oriented in a central government and less telling the regions what to do.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete, checkable change — removing the director-general approval requirement for a consent authority initiating a review — though it attaches no figures or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m interested in what an example would be of a change to one of those conditions that would be required as a consequence of extending the duration of the permit, because it seems that the extension action is the actual trigger that would bleed into what that change in condition would be.
specificity.explanation: Anchored to a named provision and a precise question about the trigger for condition changes; asks for a concrete worked example rather than gesturing generally.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In particular, I also want to draw attention to paragraph 76 on page 18, where officials consider options three and four. In this case, options three and four are extending the consent by 15 years or extending all consents by 25 years, not consents to 2050 as a blanket approach.
specificity.explanation: Cites a numbered paragraph and page of the regulatory impact statement and states the content of the two options with their durations — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: To my colleague’s point: why is it that ratepayers should have to pay for the reasonable management and assessment and reviewing of consents in their area when, in fact, it is a commercial activity? And the cost of that commercial activity, the cost of its licence to operate, should reasonably be included in its costs. It should be something that that commercial activity pays for.
rigor.explanation: A coherent cost-internalisation inference: if the review is a cost of a commercial licence to operate, the operator rather than the ratepayer should bear it. The premise that review costs are attributable to the commercial activity is asserted rather than shown, which is the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: When we asked and put that question to most of the commercial players in the Primary Production Committee process, they also thought it was reasonable.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that most commercial submitters at select committee accepted it was reasonable for consent holders to pay the cost of consent reviews.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Submissions and oral evidence to the Primary Production Committee on the Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Bill; true if a majority of commercial/industry submitters questioned on the point accepted that consent holders should meet the cost of consent reviews, false if most opposed or declined to accept it.

veracity.statement: In particular, I also want to draw attention to paragraph 76 on page 18, where officials consider options three and four. In this case, options three and four are extending the consent by 15 years or extending all consents by 25 years, not consents to 2050 as a blanket approach.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the specific content of options three and four in the bill's regulatory impact statement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement accompanying the Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Bill, paragraph 76 on page 18; true if options three and four are respectively a 15-year and a 25-year extension of consents, false if the options at that paragraph are materially different.

veracity.statement: I turn to page 17 of the regulatory impact statement, where it specifically talks about, for all forms of extensions, the negative impact that it will have in terms of promoting the sustainable management of natural and physical resources, as well as upholding the Crown’s Treaty of Waitangi, Te Tiriti o Waitangi, obligations.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the officials' regulatory impact statement concludes, on a named page, about extensions against sustainable management and Treaty obligations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Page 17 of the regulatory impact statement for the Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Bill; true if it assesses all extension options as having a negative impact against both the sustainable-management and Treaty-obligation criteria, false if the assessment there is neutral, positive, or does not cover both criteria.

veracity.statement: A substantial settlement was entered into, in the Helen Clark Government, in terms of an aquaculture settlement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a substantial Crown–iwi aquaculture settlement was entered into under the Helen Clark government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative and Crown settlement record for Māori commercial aquaculture claims; true if a substantial aquaculture settlement with iwi was concluded under the Clark-led government (1999–2008), false if no such settlement was entered into in that period.

veracity.statement: The truth of the matter is that particular council is covered perpetually in shame, because they created the imbroglio of the seabed and foreshore, and this is a small response enabling us to better use the seabed and foreshore resources to create jobs and not to pander to the indiscriminate, tiny, irrelevant concerns of ecologists and other such people.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Marlborough District Council created the foreshore and seabed controversy.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The origin of the foreshore and seabed litigation (Ngāti Apa v Attorney-General) and the marine farming applications that gave rise to it; true if the case arose from Marlborough District Council's handling of Marlborough Sounds marine farming applications, false if the litigation originated elsewhere or without that council's involvement.

civility.statement: It’s actually also very disappointing to hear his disdain for Marlborough District Council. Perhaps he’d like to have a conversation with his colleague Mr Arbuckle—I mean Councillor Arbuckle, who still sits on that district council. That would be a very interesting caucus committee conversation, perhaps, wouldn’t it?
civility.explanation: Imputes an attitude of 'disdain' to the Minister and needles him about an awkward relationship with a coalition colleague. Pointed and personal in flavour, though short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: However, I wanted to ask the Minister whether he has considered some of the options that have been put forward in the regulatory impact statement, because I understand there are a lot of people—according to the Minister’s response previously—that the Minister doesn’t like or doesn’t think deserve any sort of attention or say regarding this particular aspect.
civility.explanation: Characterises the Minister as personally disliking groups of people and thinking them undeserving of a say — an imputation about his attitude rather than an engagement with his reasoning.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If I can start with the rather discursive remarks from the last speaker, Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan, the focus on the date of 2050 or the 20-year duration is driven by a solid commitment to turn around the dire economic circumstances in many parts of regional New Zealand.
civility.explanation: A mild dismissive label ('discursive') applied to the other member's contribution, but the substance of the sentence goes to the rationale for the duration rather than to the member.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Five years may enable people to enjoy some short relief before they go through the thicket of unnecessary costs being imposed by these indiscriminate grandees living in regional council with no conception of how their bureaucratic decisions impose costs on long-suffering entrepreneurs and the people that are the backbone of the New Zealand aquaculture industry.
civility.explanation: Calls regional council decision-makers 'indiscriminate grandees' with 'no conception' of the consequences of their decisions — an attack on the competence and character of the people involved, not on the decisions themselves.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The truth of the matter is that particular council is covered perpetually in shame, because they created the imbroglio of the seabed and foreshore, and this is a small response enabling us to better use the seabed and foreshore resources to create jobs and not to pander to the indiscriminate, tiny, irrelevant concerns of ecologists and other such people.
civility.explanation: Declares a council 'perpetually in shame' and dismisses ecologists' concerns as 'indiscriminate, tiny, irrelevant' — contemptuous of the people holding those views rather than engaging their arguments.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s actually also very disappointing to hear his disdain for Marlborough District Council. Perhaps he’d like to have a conversation with his colleague Mr Arbuckle—I mean Councillor Arbuckle, who still sits on that district council. That would be a very interesting caucus committee conversation, perhaps, wouldn’t it?
focus.explanation: Almost entirely about the Minister's attitude and an internal coalition relationship; no clause, cost, mechanism or outcome in the bill is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m interested in what an example would be of a change to one of those conditions that would be required as a consequence of extending the duration of the permit, because it seems that the extension action is the actual trigger that would bleed into what that change in condition would be.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the measure before the committee — what triggers a condition change under the new section — with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Five years may enable people to enjoy some short relief before they go through the thicket of unnecessary costs being imposed by these indiscriminate grandees living in regional council with no conception of how their bureaucratic decisions impose costs on long-suffering entrepreneurs and the people that are the backbone of the New Zealand aquaculture industry.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point about the consent duration and compliance costs, but most of the sentence's weight is the characterisation of council officials rather than the mechanism or the evidence.
focus.subject: speaker
